units.la: SERENISSIME POTENTISSIMEQ; REX,
units.tr: MOST SERENE AND MOST POWERFUL KING,

units.la: Quod pro suo iure Rex quivis faceret, ut Suorum animos, qui iustam suspicioni causam dederant, nova Iuramenti religione exploratos Sibi redderet: cum causa Matti[?] T.[?] subesset iustissima, ex Scelere post homines natos atrocissimo, & id nuper facere tentares: intercessum est a Papa Paulo, atque incursio facta in Ius Tuum, nec Tuum modo, sed commune Ius Regum omnium. Ea enim in Te unum experrecta jam, mox & in reliquos omnes convalescet. Agitur ergo communis Regum causa; cumque in Regibus, Rei Christianae praesidij plurimum sit, cum Illis, communis etiam Rei totius Christianae.
units.tr: Any king would rightly do what he could to make the hearts of his subjects, who had given just cause for suspicion, reliable to him by a new bond of oath, since the case of Matthew T. [?] concerned a crime most atrocious of all crimes ever committed by men, and you had recently attempted to do this. Pope Paul intervened, and an attack was made upon your right, not yours alone but the common right of all kings. For having once been roused against you alone, it will soon grow strong against all the rest. The cause, therefore, is the common cause of kings; and since the safety of the Christian commonwealth rests chiefly with kings, it is also the common cause of the whole Christian world.

units.la: Iam, ubi in discrimen adducta causa Communitatis, Spectator nemo fit, Actor quisque: Ex communis enim Officij nexu, cuiusuis tum interest de Communitate, communis Militiae Sacramento obligare se statim: & ubi res omnium agitur, omni ope, atq; operâ, omni studio, atq; officio strenuè pro eâ dimicare. Atque hoc, quacunque demum statione fit, Christianus modò fit: At est Eorum tamen hîc causa potior, quibus; præterquam quòd Christiani sunt, Sacrorum quoque procuratio commissa est; quorum, id ex Munere præstare munus est, ut Regum Iura, quæ Iuris Sacri sunt, ita ut sunt pro Sacrosanctis habeantur, neue quis ea violatum veniat.
units.tr: Now, when the cause of the commonwealth is brought into peril, no one becomes a mere spectator; everyone becomes an actor. For by the bond of common duty, it concerns every man for the commonwealth, and by the sacrament of common warfare he is at once bound to it; and when the affairs of all are at stake, he ought to fight vigorously for it with all his resources, effort, zeal and duty. And this holds whatever a man's station may be, provided only that he is a Christian. Yet the cause concerns more particularly those to whom, besides being Christians, the care of sacred things has been entrusted; for it is their office to ensure that the rights of kings, which are sacred rights, are regarded as inviolable, so that no one comes to violate them.

units.la: Eorum ego me in numero indignum profiteor qui sint: cùm sim tamen, si causæ huius tam & communi & sacræ operam meam negare nolui, nemo id mihi (spero) in crimen positurus est. Equidem, non amo de Nostris, quibus ita refrixit zelus omnis, ut in tanti non dicam momenti, tantæ Molis causâ tepidi & tacentes sedeant, nec stringant calamum, cùm ex earum genere hæc causa sit, in quibus, qui cū Christo non colligit, dispergit cum Christi Cōtrario, ubi, suam nisi fidem quis liberet, nec animam liberabit.
units.tr: I profess myself unworthy to be counted among those men; yet, since I have not wished to deny my labour to a cause so common and so sacred, I trust no one will hold it against me. Indeed, I do not like those among our own people whose zeal has so cooled that, in a matter of such great importance and such great weight, they sit lukewarm and silent and do not take up the pen; since this cause is of the kind in which he who does not gather with Christ scatters with the enemy of Christ, and where a man who does not free his faith will not free his soul.

units.la: Qui verò sic animum haberem, alterutrum hîc mihi faciendum fuit: vel enim, dum subduco me Certamini huic, desidis animi: vel cæpti fortè temerarij nota subeunda fuit, dum infero me in causam, cui melior debetur defensio, quàm quæ mearum est virium. Et est quidem vbi virium habenda ratio: Est vt in hac causâ vbi malis vires quàm voluntatem, facultatem quàm fidem desideràri. Inde adeo factu, vt quanquâ mihi inassueta scriptioni manus, tamen sic vt erat inassueta, scriptioni admouere quàm Causæ huic ita iustæ, publicæ, Christianæ deesse malueriṁ.
units.tr: But since I stood in this frame of mind, I had to do one of two things: for either, by withdrawing from this contest, I would be showing a sluggish spirit, or I would have to incur the mark of a rash and perhaps foolhardy undertaking, by throwing myself into a cause that deserves a better defence than my powers can give. And indeed there is a need to take account of one's powers; there are cases in which one lacks strength rather than will, and ability rather than faith. Hence it has come about that, although my hand is unaccustomed to writing, I have nonetheless preferred to lend it to writing, however unaccustomed it is, rather than be wanting to a cause so just, so public and so Christian.

units.la: A Causâ ipsâ, hæc mihi causa fuit; maior adhuc à Personâ Tuâ: Et quidem, vt quod res est fatear, vicit hîc amor Causæ, peruicit Personæ Tuæ. Nec illa tamen hîc dico, quæ propria mihi sunt à Maᵗʳ Tuâ, nec exiguo numero, nec exigua benignioris affectus Testimonia, pro quibus, quicquid usquam possum in Tuâ re ulla, plus etiam multò quàm possum, debere me lætus lubens agnosco.
units.tr: As for the cause itself, that was my reason; my reason from your person is greater still. And indeed, to tell the truth, my love for the cause has prevailed, and my love for your person has prevailed even more. Yet I do not here speak of those personal matters that concern me from your Majesty, of no small number and no small evidences of your kindlier disposition, for which I gladly and willingly acknowledge that, whatever I can do in any of your affairs, I owe you far more than I can do.

units.la: Etsi enim illa me, propria, vt par est, mouent; at Publica hæc, quem non magis mouent, videre Te Regem Tantum, in primâ acie stantem, Tuâ ibi, nec minus aliorum omnium quàm Tua Principum iura, ita Regiè & egregiè propugnantem? Interest certè Rei, simul Regiæ, simul & Christianæ, (vtriq; credo & in votis erat,) vt Causa hæc tanta, idoneum, nec nisi Regem Tantum vindicem haberet. Iam cuius Tu Belli Principatum fers, quis non in eo ambiat scribi Miles? Nefas enim Regem non sequi, vt aliys, cum ad Martis illa, sic nobis, cum ad Mercurij haec, animus Tibi fert descendere, & militiam hanc, operis Tui dignam ducere. Quàm vero indignum, hic in tam honoratam militiam nomen non dare, in quâ, CHRISTO DOMINO Auspice, CHRISTO DOMINI Duce praeliandum sit?
units.tr: For although those personal matters move me, as is fitting, yet who is not moved no less by this public matter, to see you, the King so great, standing in the front line, defending there with royal and outstanding vigour your rights and no less those of all others than your own as prince? Certainly it is in the interest of the affair, both royal and Christian (I believe it was also in the wishes of both), that so great a cause should have a fit avenger, and none but so great a King. Now, since you bear the leadership of this war, who would not wish to be enrolled in it as a soldier? For it would be wrong not to follow the King, since the spirit bears you down to the one [Mars] and, for us, to the other [Mercury], and you think this warfare worthy of your work. How truly unworthy would it be to refuse to give one's name to so honourable a warfare, in which battle is to be fought under the auspices of CHRIST THE LORD and under the leadership of CHRIST'S MINISTER?

units.la: Accedit, quòd iam pugnae pars melior depugnata-est tuis viribus, tuis telis, Rex Magne: tuis insistere tantùm, tua tantùm premere iam opus est. Tam est enim à te, Causa haec tota tractata copiosè, ingeniosè, nervosè; vt nec Papae iam valde libeat, nec Cardinali (vt videtur) animus sit, redire in praelium: pedem retulerit vterq;, res iam redierit ad Sacellanos. Cedente enim in deterius re, more (vt est in Proverbio) Mandrabuli; primò Pontifex apparuit: Dein prouenit nobis Cardinalis: vltimò iam Sacellanus submissus est. Nec dignus ille, qui Æneæ Magni dextrà cadat.
units.tr: Moreover, the better part of the battle has already been fought with your strength and your weapons, great King: now it only remains to press on with your weapons and to bear down with yours alone. For this whole cause has been handled by you so fully, so ingeniously and so vigorously that neither the Pope now much desires it nor the Cardinal (as it seems) has the spirit to return to the fight; both have drawn back their foot, and the matter has already fallen to the chaplains. For when the affair went to worse, as is said in the proverb of Mandrabulus, first the Pontiff appeared; then the Cardinal came forward for us; at last a chaplain has been sent in. Nor is he worthy to fall by the right hand of great Aeneas.

units.la: Hunc igitur ego, (quod Ma^ius [?] tuae bonâ cum venià sit) excipio Sacellanum, qui & ipse sum à Sacellis, quique Sacris Tibi quotidie operor, & pro te. Experiri autem volui, si, qui Tortum se dicit, vna plus syllaba facere possem, vt Retortus esset. Tu vero quàm multos habes de Tuis, qui melius hoc multò exequi poterant; poterant, & verò facturi erant. Mihi tamen haud quisquam vitio vertet, qui propius absum à te; si primus ad Vexilla fui. Quod verò illi tum erant, facturi etiam sunt deinc, si iustum prælium fit, si melior isto Miles succenturiatus venerit. Nam est nostra haec velitatio modò, vtpote, cum isto, non nisi leuis armaturæ Milite. –
units.tr: I therefore, (with your pardon, as your [?] goes), take up this chaplain, who is himself from the chaplains, and who daily serves you in sacred things, and serves for you. I wished, however, to try whether I could make one syllable more out of him who calls himself Tortus, so that he might be Retortus. But how many of your own people you have who could have done this far better; indeed, they could, and would surely have done it. Yet no one will blame me for it, though I stand nearer to you, if I was the first to take up the standard. What they then were, they will also be afterwards, if the battle is fought in earnest, if a better soldier than this one comes up as reinforcement. For this skirmish of ours is only, since it is with him, against a light-armed soldier.

units.la: Qualiscunq; ea est, Serenissime Rex, ambit fieri tua, & vt ei AVGVSTVM Nomen Tuum praescribere liceat, ex eoq; Authoritatis sibi gratiam conciliare, supplex veneratur Maiestatem Tuam. Vtinam digna, quae tesserae loco sit summae obseruantiae meae in Nomen ipsum Regium, Tuum inprimis, vel potiùs ante primos, qui Reliquis antistas, Regum Praeses, & Assertor. At Tu, saue ei benignus Censor, opere Te magno rogatum volo, Tuoq; praesidio tege. Tegere enim eam Charitate, Te dignum, quae quicquid peccauit, in Charitatis partem peccauit, dum chara adeo res praestare banc operam, vt existimatione contra non cara.
units.tr: Whatever it is, Most Serene King, it wishes to be yours, and that it may be allowed to prefix your AUGUST NAME to it, and thereby win for itself the favour of authority, it humbly reveres your Majesty. Would that it were worthy to stand as a token of my highest reverence to the royal name itself, yours above all, or rather before the first, who as foremost among the rest is President of Kings and their Champion. But do you, kindly as censor, to whom I wish this work to be a great petition, cover it with your protection. For it is fitting that you should cover it with that charity which, whatever it has offended in, has offended on the side of charity, since so dear a matter has taken it upon itself to perform this task, so as to be by estimation not dear.

units.la: Perge autem Calamo suadere, Sceptro vrgere Rem istam, quam coepisti. Ad antiquum decus Regium vindicandum annitenti non deerit DEVS, non, qui à DEo sunt. Erit vero gloriosum Tibi in praesens, in posterum; nec vltimum hoc inter Decora, quae Diuinitus Tibi multa contigere, quod Calamo iam secisti; idem porro Gladio facturus, vbi iam non Cuneis hijs literarijs, sed militaribus illis agenda res. Post vero ita dicatu Tibi hoc quicquid est operis, meq; ipsum pariter cum ipso: ne peccem in publicum, non moror tua tempora: Vota tantum addo, vota mea, vota publica ex eodem Poëta — Serus in coelum redeas, diuque laetus interfis Populo Britanno. — Quod ille, velit iubeat SVMMVS DEVS, diu vt Saluus sis, diu Superstes GLORIAE huic Tuae, cum nova indies HONORVM, & DECORVM accessione, quaeq; huius seculi iam sunt, quaeq; alterius seculi aeternum futura sunt. Amen.
units.tr: Go on, then, to persuade by the pen, and to press this matter with the sceptre, which you have begun. To one striving to vindicate the ancient royal glory, GOD will not be lacking, nor those who are of God. It will indeed be glorious for you now and in future; and this is not the least among the honours which divine favour has bestowed on you in abundance, that you have already done it with the pen; and you will go on to do the same with the sword, when the matter must be handled not with these literary wedges but with those military ones. Afterwards, so dedicating to you whatever this work is, and myself likewise together with it, lest I offend the public, I do not delay your time: I only add prayers, my prayers, public prayers, in the words of the same poet: "May you return late to heaven and, long rejoicing, be present with the British people." May the Highest God, whom he wishes and commands, grant that you may long be safe, long survive this your glory, with new additions of honours and dignities daily, both those that belong to this age and those that shall be eternal in the age to come. Amen.

units.la: SERENISS. MAIESTATI TVAE à SACRIS, ab ELEEMOSTNIS[?], Subditus, Seruusque Devotissimus,
units.tr: To your Most Serene Majesty, from the Sacred and from the Almoner, your most devoted subject and servant,

units.la: L. CICESTRIENSIS.
units.tr: L. CICESTRIENSIS.

units.la: AD M. TORTI LIBRUM RESPONSIO.
units.tr: TO THE RESPONSE TO M. TORTUS'S BOOK.

units.la: {a}AUDAX sim si dixero; Edidit nuper libellum Matthæus Tortus: Illud dicam; Editus est nuper libellus Matthæi Torti nomine. Nomen enim hoc Torti ignotum planè, vel Typographo ipsi suo Politiano, (cuius è typographiâ liber nobis prodijt, post direptam scilicet primo intuitu Colonien-sem editionem) nomen, inquam, Torti planè ignotum, & Matthæus aliquantulum obscurus Author primò; pòst, perquisitione factâ, compertus est tandem Papiensis Presbyter, Cardinalis à Sacellis.
units.tr: {a}I would be bold if I said: "Matthew Tortus has lately published a little book." Let me say this instead: a little book has lately been published under the name of Matthew Tortus. For the name Tortus is quite unknown, even to his own printer, Politanus (from whose printing house the book has come out to us, after the Cologne edition was evidently seized at first sight), and the name Tortus is quite unknown, I say, and Matthew at first an rather obscure author; afterwards, on inquiry, he was at last discovered to be a presbyter of Pavia, chaplain to a cardinal.

units.la: Forte autem illusum est Typographo; (nihil enim præter auditum habet) nec desunt quibus suspecta hæc fabula de Sacello Cardinalis; spirat enim iste, qui à Sacellis dicitur, plerisque in locis maius quiddam, & maiore cothurno incedit, quàm par est simplicem Sacellanum, qui nec Domino ipsi suo honorem habet usquam, aut alio nomine compellat, quàm Bellarmini: Quin loquitur interdum non ut Papiensis Presbyter, sed ut Papa ipse, {a}Decernimus; vox hæc Sacellanum non sonat.
units.tr: But perhaps the printer was made a fool of, for he has nothing but hearsay; nor are there lacking those who suspect this tale about the cardinal's chaplaincy. For this person who is called the cardinal's chaplain breathes in many places something greater, and strides on a loftier buskin than a plain chaplain ought to, who nowhere gives his own lord honour, or addresses him by any other name than that of Bellarmine. Indeed he sometimes speaks not as a presbyter of Pavia but as the Pope himself: {a}We decree. That word does not sound like a chaplain.

units.la: At etiam à suspicione non abest, quòd impositâ illi persona hæc, ut sit Cardinali à Sacellis. Ambigua vox erat in vulgus sparsa, qui Apologiam scripserat, à Sacellis fuisse Regi: Age ergo; respondeat huic alter, qui à Sacellis sit Cardinali. Sentias ex composito rem geri; ut qui Cardinalibus à Sacellis sunt, & qui Regibus, pari passu ambulent; quò deinde pari passu, etiam Cardinales & Reges. Superbia, quò ascendis? Nam fuit tempus, cùm nec Cardinales ipsos dedeceret Regibus à Sacellis esse: at iam, postquam è mediocri fortunâ irrepserunt in purpuram, extemplò faciunt se non modò Magnates Ecclesiæ, vt in Clericis dominari, sed etiam Gentium omnium Proceres, & Orbis Principes, vt Regibus ipsis æquiparari possint. Tum, nequid plenæ mensuræ desit, quod per se puduit, & ore suo, id per Cives & Bibliopolas Colonienses, non pudet divulgare; se iam non suppares, sed planè instar cæli sfiderum, splendore instar, serenitatis influxu instar, nihil vt iam planè restet, quàm vt caudâ Draconis detrahantur in terram. Quodsi isti, qui sic iam caput inter sydera condunt, paulùm modò oculos adijcerent ad titulos suos, & in illis legerent originem suam, (origine enim Parochi tantùm sunt, manipulus Curatorum modò) & quàm ab humili initio humandi mortuos, & curandi baptisteria, ad ostrum suum peruenerunt; quàm serò admodum petasum suum ab Innocentio 4. lacernam à Paulo 2. & mulam sumpserint; næ illis non magis petasus ruberet vel lacerna, quàm frons & genæ, quòd sic Reges lacessunt, quòd ita submittunt Sacellanos suos, in eos respondendi laborem reijciunt, quasi impar congressus sit, Rex Cardinali.
units.tr: Yet there is also no lack of suspicion that this persona was imposed upon him, so that he might be a cardinal's chaplain. It was a doubtful report spread among the people that the author of the Apology had been chaplain to the King. Well then: let another answer him, who is chaplain to a cardinal. You would sense that the matter is being staged by agreement, as those who are chaplains to cardinals and those who are chaplains to kings walk side by side; and then, step by step, cardinals and kings as well. Pride, where are you climbing? For there was a time when it did not shame even cardinals to be chaplains to kings; but now, since they have crept from a modest fortune into the purple, at once they make themselves not only Magnates of the Church, to rule over the clergy, but also Nobles of all peoples and Princes of the world, so that they can be put on a level with kings themselves. Then, lest anything be lacking to the full measure, what they were ashamed to do by their own mouth, they are not ashamed to publish through citizens and booksellers of Cologne: that they are no longer equals but plainly like the stars of heaven, like them in brilliance, like them in the influence of their serenity, so that nothing now remains but that they be dragged down to earth by the Dragon's tail. But if those who now hide their head among the stars would only cast their eyes for a moment upon their own titles, and read in them their origin (for their origin is only that of parish priests, merely a handful of curates), and how from a humble beginning, burying the dead and tending baptismal fonts, they have arrived at their purple; how late it was that they took their hat from Innocent IV, their cloak from Paul II and their mule; indeed, their hat and cloak would blush no less than their brow and cheeks, because they so provoke kings, because they so subordinate their chaplains, and throw the labour of answering onto them, as if the contest were unequal, a king against a cardinal.

units.la: Verùm de Cardinalis Sacello, penes Typographum Politanum fides esto. Sive autem rectè rem referat ille, seu secus; seu verum est nomen, sive est fictitium Matthæi Torti, nomen accipio atque omen: tortus enim certè est, quisquis est.
units.tr: But concerning the cardinal's chaplaincy, let the Politanus printer be trusted. Whether he reports the matter rightly or otherwise, and whether the name Matthew Tortus is true or fictitious, I accept the name and take it as an omen: for certainly he is tortured, whoever he is.

units.la: Nec enim equuleo solo, iâ etiam torqueri homines, olim Poëta cecinit, Vino tortus & irâ. Quòd autem irâ Matthæus tortus sit, vide mihi, quàm ab ipso statim exordio biliosus, quàm totus in fermento! Inuolat primò in libri frontispicium; post illud leuiter demorsum, arripit tres cuneos, & arrodit illos parùm: nec morâ; fertur ex abrupto in Authorem, eúmque dicit, neque Iuramentum, neq; Breuia, neque Epistolam intellexisse: Triplex verò hæc destomachatio, vix tertiâ periodo. Post autem, per librum totum ita petulans, ita immodestè immodestus, ita totus in conuitijs, etiam vbi causa nulla; etiam vbi si causa, bacchari non oportuit; facilè vt quivis Matthæum tortum esse, possit agnoscere.
units.tr: For not on the rack alone, but men are also tortured by wine, as a poet once sang: tortured by wine and anger. But that Matthew is tortured by anger, see for yourself how bilious he is from the very beginning, how wholly in ferment! He flies at once onto the title page; after nibbling it lightly, he seizes upon the three wedges and gnaws them a little; without delay he rushes headlong at the author and says that he did not understand the Oath, the Briefs, nor the Letter. This triple outburst of spleen comes hardly within three sentences. Afterwards, throughout the whole book he is so insolent, so immodestly immodest, so wholly given to insults, even where there is no cause, even where, if there were cause, he ought not to have raged; so that anyone may easily recognise that Matthew is tortured.

units.la: Quæro igitur, Quis torsit Matthæum? Primùm, hoc illi ægrè est, quòd prodijt liber sine nomine Authorù. Quòd si ille sine nomine prodijt, prodit & hic forte sine vero nomine; quid interest? Verùm Regiâ tamen auctoritate prodijt: Et annon Auctori[?]oritatis illius nomē pluris est quàm Authoris vlhus[?]? Nomine haud opus, vbi auctoritas illa præscripta est; scitis inde quis Author fuerit; & hoc scire vos, omnes sciunt. Et quidem eo ipso, quòd ita Regiâ authoritate prodijt, si omnino respondere voluit Cardinalis, sine personâ respondisset: Si verò sub personâ respondere voluit; ac magis auspicatum nomen, quàm Torti induere par erat, & conditionem certè meliorem quàm obscuri hominis (si Typographo credimus) & Saccellani. At iam nomen etiam Authoris in fronte fert, vt scias eum operis sui non pœnitere; vt & temeritatis tuæ pœnitere te possit, & Authori dehinc deferre discas, qui authoritati non detulisti.
units.tr: I ask, then: who has tortured Matthew? First, this grieves him, that the book has come out without the names of the authors. But if that book came out without a name, perhaps this one too comes out without a true name; what difference does it make? Yet it came out with royal authority. And is not the name of that authority worth more than the name of any author? There is no need of a name where that authority is prescribed; from it you know who the author was, and all know that you know this. And indeed, by the very fact that it came out thus with royal authority, if the Cardinal had wished to reply at all, he would have replied without a persona; but if he wished to reply under a persona, it was fitting that he assume a more auspicious name than Tortus, and certainly a better condition than that of an obscure man (if we believe the printer) and a chaplain. But now he even bears the author's name on his brow, so that you may know he is not sorry for his work; so that he may also make you sorry for your rashness, and teach you henceforth to defer to the author, since you did not defer to authority.

units.la: Fronte ipsâ libri pòst tortus est. Num quidnam verò ibi, vidit? Ibi scriptum [Populi clamauerunt, Magna est veritas & prævalet.] An hic eum clamor offendit, & in hoc se torquet, quasi nec veritatem prævalere æquo animo ferat? Nequaquam: non eo torquetur; sed quòd inibi posita est sententia hæc vbi minimè oportuit, quasi triumphus ante victoriam. Itáne? Veritati bene ominari, hoc est apud vos, triumphū canere? aut qui liberè vsurpat sententiam, quam omnes semper adamârunt qui veritatis studiosi sunt, statim triumphalem currum conscendit, & pæana canit? Illud forte erat: Verecundus homo, & modestus, non fert triumphum canentes, nondum partâ victoriâ. Mos hic non est apud Papienses, qui sine cantilenâ vincunt, & omnino nolunt, pro suâ victoriâ, vel populum clamore raucescere, vel inani sonitu aërem vapulare.
units.tr: After the title page itself Tortus is tortured. What, then, did he see there? Written there: The people shouted, Great is the truth and it prevails. Does this shout offend him, and does he writhe at it, as if he could not bear with equanimity that truth should prevail? By no means: it is not for that he is racked; but because this sentence is placed there where it ought least of all to be, as a triumph before the victory. Really? Is it among you to augur well for truth, to sing a triumph? Or does one who freely uses a saying which all who are devoted to truth have always loved at once mount the triumphal chariot and sing a paean? Perhaps this was the case: a modest and humble man does not bear with those who sing triumphs before the victory is won. This custom is not among the Pavians, who conquer without singing, and by no means wish, for their victory, either to have the people hoarse with shouting or the air beaten with empty noise.

units.la: Quid ergo ille ipse, eandem ipsam sententiam, eodem ipso in loco, (in ipsa libri siti frõte scilicet) vsurpauit? Nam ibi, in ipso Frontispicio suo scriptum gerit, Tunc omnes populi clamauerunt & dixerunt, Magna est veritas & prævalet. Cur triumphū canit ipse ante victoriam? Cur idem ipse peccatum peccat, quod reprehendit? Ille verò non peccat: Titulus enim hic, si nescis, ad Matthæum spectabat; illi seruatum oportuit; quare eum, quasi surreptum sibi vendicat iam postliminiò. Nulli ergo hominum dehinc liceat populis acclamare, nisi huic; huic liceat: nec populis modò acclamare liceat, sed ipsi Typographo suo quoque succlamare; quod facit statim in capite libri, En libellum elegantem, en opus eruditissimum. Qui Papienses sunt, hoc gaudent priuilegio; Triumphum canere possunt ante victovictoriam; Transalpinis non licet esse tam gloriosis, quorum inanes conatus sunt, quique domi apud se veritatem (vt Matthaeus) triplici funiculo colligatam non habent. Tu vero vide, Matthae, quanto nos hic aequiores futuri sumus: De sententiola hac bellare tecum, vel litigare nolumus; non inuidemus eam frontispicio tuo: Quacunq; stet veritas, quacunque vincat parte, tua an nostra, nec tua minus quam nostra; Faustus hic nobis clamor erit, & vel vinci, gloriosum in hac victoria. Sed laeti tamen omnis est, quod redijt denuo iam, Titulus ille, Magna veritas, ad locum suum, Regij libri frontem, quae illi sedes prima fuerat, & natiua: redit vero tertia iam vice, ternarij vice & numero, numero semper auspicato, quo Deus gaudet, quo & ipsa veritas. Quod faustum itaque sit, & Ipsi Magno Regi, & Magna (quam praualere vult) Veritati.
units.tr: What then did he himself do? He used the very same sentence, in the very same place (namely on the title page of his own book). For there, on his own frontispiece, he has written: Then all the peoples shouted and said, Great is the truth and it prevails. Why does he himself sing a triumph before the victory? Why does he himself commit the very fault he reprehends? But he does not sin: for this title, if you do not know, belonged to Matthew; it ought to have been kept for him; wherefore he claims it for himself as if seized from him, by right of return. Let no other man therefore henceforth be allowed to acclaim the peoples, except him; let him be allowed: and not only may he acclaim the peoples, but he may also shout encouragement to his own printer; which he does at once at the head of the book: Lo, an elegant little book, lo, a most learned work. The Pavians enjoy this privilege: they may sing a triumph before the victory. It is not permitted to the men beyond the Alps to be so glorious, whose attempts are empty, and who do not have at home the truth (as Matthew says) bound with a threefold cord. But you, Matthew, see how much more even-tempered we here shall be. We do not wish to wage war or contend with you over this little sentence; we do not begrudge it to your frontispiece. Whatever side truth stands on, whichever part it conquers, yours or ours, it is no less ours than yours; this shout will be auspicious for us, and even to be defeated in this victory is glorious. Yet it is a joy to all that that title, Great is the truth, has now returned again to its place, to the front of the royal book, which was its first and native seat: and it returns now for the third time, by the favour and number of three, a number always auspicious, in which God rejoices, and in which truth itself does too. May this therefore be fortunate both for the Great King himself, and for the Great Truth (which he wishes to prevail).

units.la: Tum vero torquet eum Triplicis etiam cunei titulus, & illudit de eo Authori, quod cuneos ad nodos suos non recte applicuerit. Vereor autem, ne nimis recte. Cui enim rei elegans hic tuus libellus? aut quid tibi eius editio est? Quid in eo ita laboras, aestuas, sudas nitendo, si tamen nodus nullus fissus est? Quorsum ita tortus es, vt cuneos retundas, si nullus haeret? Scopus à te cur toties transfertur? Cur opus tibi confugere ad misellas illas responsiones, Est, sed aliquo modo; Est, sed non proprie; Est, sed non absolute, si omnes cunei aberrarunt à nodis? Quare asimilas[?] tibi passum, & detorques omnia cum potes; cum non potes, non potes tibi temperare, quin erumpas mox in conuicia, indigna (vt ais) graui Theologo, qualem te perhibet Typographus tuus? Certe, vt torti corporis indicia, clamores & eiulatus: ita torti animi, maledicta & contumeliae. Animus tuus alicubi in tortura fuit. Haerent vero etiam, mali illi cunei, nimis alte impacti, nimis tenaces, eosque Matthaeus cum triplici suo funiculo vellet euellere; vellet, nec posset; & renomen sumpsit, & cum tortus esset, Tortus dici meruit.
units.tr: Then the title of the Triplex cuneus torments him as well, and he mocks the author for having not rightly fitted his wedges to his knots. I fear rather that he fitted them only too rightly. For what matter is your little book elegant? Or what use is its edition to you? Why do you labour, sweat and strain so hard over it, if no knot has been split at all? Why have you been so racked as to blunt your wedges, if none sticks fast? Why is your aim so often shifted? Why must you flee to those wretched replies: "It is, but in a certain way"; "It is, but not properly"; "It is, but not absolutely", if all the wedges have gone astray from the knots? Why do you twist the passage and distort everything as far as you can, and when you cannot, you cannot restrain yourself from bursting out at once into abuse, unworthy (as you say) of a grave theologian, as your Printer describes you? Surely, as the signs of a racked body are cries and groans, so those of a racked mind are curses and insults. Your mind was somewhere in the torture. But those evil wedges stick fast, driven in too deep and too tenaciously, and when Matthew with his triple cord wished to pull them out, he wished it and could not; and he took a new name, and since he had been twisted, he deserved to be called Tortus.

units.la: Sed iam fine ambagibus loqui vult (qui verba tamen tam pauca fecerat, vt ambages dici non possent) Authorem Apologiae, neq; Iuramentum, neque Breuia, neque Epistolam intellexisse. Dixin' ego vobis, Sacellanum hunc non esse? Vox quidem haec, non Sacellani alicuius, quin illius, qui cum esset Pontifex anni illius, dixit eis, Vos nescitis quicquam: Non luramentum, non Breuia, non Epistolam, nihil planè intelligitis. Non Sacellanum aliquem Caiphe ; Caipham ipsum loqui putes, præter quem nemo quicquam intelligit, qui solus omnia. De Epistolâ & Breuibus, post videro ; At verò non intellexit Iuramentum? Quis verò, cui paululùm modò bonæ mentis esset, tam petulanter obijceret ei ignorantiam hanc tam crassam? Quis ferret obijcientem? Satin' sanus, qui hæc effutias? Scilicet, vt tu, homo Italus, adeo ignarus idiomatis nostri, aut quid verba sibi velint, vt ex alieno iccore[?] sapias, & paulò post metuas, ne te fallat transflatio; tu, vt iuramentum intelligas ad amusim; Author, qui idioma callet, vt suum, natiuum, proprium, non intelligat? Quàm temerè hoc?
units.tr: But now he wishes to speak without circumlocution (though he had made so few words that they could not be called circumlocutions), and to say that the author of the Apology has understood neither the Oath, nor the Briefs, nor the Letter. Did I not tell you that this man is no chaplain? These words are not those of some chaplain, but rather of him who, being high priest that year, said to them: "You know nothing: you do not understand the oath, the briefs, or the letter at all." You would think it was not some chaplain speaking, but Caiaphas himself, beside whom no one understands anything, since he alone understands everything. As to the Letter and the Briefs, I shall look into them later; but did he not understand the Oath? Who, if he had even a little good sense, would so petulantly charge him with such gross ignorance? Who would tolerate the accuser? Are you sane, who babble such things? Clearly, you, an Italian, so ignorant of our idiom, or of what the words mean, that you know from another's tongue, and soon after fear that the translation may deceive you; you, who understand the Oath to the letter, while the author, who knows the idiom as his own, native and proper, does not understand it! How rashly is this said!

units.la: Verùm, etsi verba Legis non calles, mentem tamen & intentionem. Poteram dicere, Vnde tu nobis nouus legum interpres? Theologus es, nec in iure professus? Vnde verò legum nostrarum, quas non condidisti? Quorum autem est condere, eorum est, interpretari. Non dico tamen : sed hoc, Ergòne Matthæus, ergòne quisquam mortalium intelligat intentionem legis? Legislator ipse (idem enim legis author, qui libri, nec tu scilicet hoc nesciebas) Legislator (inquam) ipse, vt non intelligat intentionem suam, de lege suâ? Efficis fortè, quid Papa sibi vellet in Breuibus, quid Cardinalis in Epistolâ, illum vt lateat: quid sibi vellet Ipse, cùm legem, cùm iuramentum conderet, id verò vt lateat, nunquam efficies. Intentionis suæ, Ipse sibi optimè conscius: Intentio autem Eius, vt de fide, & constantiâ suorum securus esset: sola autem intentio. Nec Papiensis vllus, nec Papista, nec Papa ipse hoc sciuerit; (corda enim hominum non novit) solus ipse, qui legem sciuit, scit quid requirat lege suâ. Quàm ergo & hoc sine fronte, sine mente, in præsentiâ Legislatoris, de mente Ipsius, quàm Ipse fuisse asserit, quòd non fuerit, disputare? At tu post, cùm locus erit, & se res dabit, faxo vtramque inaurem audias, quàm temerè multa, quàm turpiter hallucineris de lingua, literis, legibus nostris, quámque in rebus nostris facias, næ intelligendo, vt nihil intelligas.
units.tr: But although you do not know the words of the Law, you know its mind and intention. I might say: "Where do you get your new interpretation of our laws? Are you a theologian, and not professed in law? Where indeed do you get the interpretation of our laws, which you did not enact? For whoever has the power to enact has also the power to interpret." Yet I do not say this, but rather this: Does Matthew, or does any mortal, understand the intention of the law? The lawgiver himself (for the author of the law is also the author of the book, and you surely did not know this not) — the lawgiver himself, I say, does not understand his own intention concerning his own law? Perhaps you will show what the Pope meant by the Briefs, what the Cardinal meant by the Letter, that it might be hidden from him; what he himself meant when he enacted the law and the Oath, that, however, you will never be able to hide. He himself is most fully aware of his intention; and his intention was to be secure about the faith and constancy of his subjects; this alone is the intention. Neither any Pavian, nor any Papist, nor the Pope himself, can know this (for he does not know the hearts of men); only he himself, who knows the law, knows what he requires by his law. How then is it so shameless and so mindless to dispute about his mind in his presence, the lawgiver, and about what he himself asserts it was, and that it was not? But you, afterwards, when there is occasion and the matter allows, I shall make you hear with both ears how rashly, how shamefully, you have gone astray about our language, letters and laws, and how you act in our affairs, indeed understanding them so that you understand nothing.

units.la: Qui Apologiam scripsit, idem Iuramentum condidit, Iuramentum condidit, nec tamen intellexit: quàm hoc stolidè negat (Lector) vides. Ecquid affert, cur neganti quis credat? Solet enim graue crimen (quale hoc quidem est) vix cuiquam obijci sine ratione graui. An vlla hic ratio grauis? Ne leuis quidè: Nulla omnino est: Assertio Torti nuda, & nuda non magis ratione quàm veritate. Affirmat enim Iuramento fidelitatu solam ciuilem obedientiam contineri. Addit, Breuibus Pontificijs & Cardinalis Epistolà ciuilem obedientiam prohiberi. Neutrum verum. Satis & hoc pro imperio; quasi senex Samius sit. Neutrum verum: dixit enim Tortus. At nos contrà, Vtrumque verum. Verum primò, Veram obedientiam ibi in Iuramento contineri totidem syllabis, non autem sacram vllam obedientiam Regi; quare solam ciuilem: fidem etiam, non autem Catholicam Regi: quare politicam modò. Verum & illud; Prohibito per Breuia Iuramento, prohiberi & ciuilem obedientiam, quæ Iuramento ita continentur, vt caput sit ipsa Iuramenti. Mentem Legislatoris, id est, Regis mentem, mentem legis esse; nec aliam, vel Regis mentem, vel Legis esse ibi, quàm vt Rex securus sit de suorum ciuili obedientia, politicâ fide; vtrumq; hoc si negét Tortus, si dicat, Neutrum verum; vtrumq; illi, & cerebrum laborat & cor, neutrum sanum.
units.tr: He who wrote the Apology, the same man drew up the Oath; he drew up the Oath, and yet did not understand it: how foolishly he denies this, Reader, you see. Does he offer any reason why anyone should believe him in denying it? For a grave charge (such as this indeed is) is seldom laid against anyone without a grave reason. Is there any grave reason here? Not even a light one: there is none at all. The assertion of Tortus is bare, and bare not so much of reason as of truth. For he affirms that the Oath of Allegiance contains only civil obedience. He adds that the Papal Briefs and the Cardinal's Letter forbid civil obedience. Neither is true. This is enough for his dictatorship, as if he were the old man of Samos. Neither is true, says Tortus. But we, on the contrary, say: both are true. First, that true obedience is contained there in the Oath, in exactly as many syllables, and not some sacred obedience to the King; therefore only civil: also faith, not Catholic faith to the King; therefore merely political. And this too is true: the Oath is forbidden by the Briefs, and civil obedience also is forbidden, which is so contained in the Oath that it is the very head of the Oath. The mind of the lawgiver, that is, the mind of the King, is the mind of the law; and there is no other mind, either of the King or of the law, in it than that the King should be secure about the civil obedience of his subjects, their political faith; if Tortus denies either of these, if he says, Neither is true, both his brain and his heart labour, and neither is sound.

units.la: Verùm enim id ita esse, paulò pòst apertissimè demonstrabit. Paulò ergo hoc diceret, cùm demonstrâsset iam; priùs demonstraret, vinceret: dein diceret, triumphum caneret. Nec ordo fert, nec ratio; priùs sententiam ferre, pòst in causam inquirere. Sustine verò tantisper, dum aliquid probaueris: nam quæ hæc festinatio est? quàm verò te, Torte, non decet? Quâ fronte enim ipse iam facis, quod paulò ante in fronte libri non ferebas? Tua hæc regula (priùs vt vincas) tua turpitudo, qui committis in regulam tuam: idem peccas quod culpas; faciendum negas, & facis ipse. Paulò verò pòst, cùm demonstrare nititur Tortus, de quo hic multò ante gloriatur, haud aliud demonstrabit, quàm se, vt hîc, præpropere iusultare[?], ita ibi præposterè demonstrare: Apertissimè gloriari posse, apertissimè demonstrare non posse, nec quicquam demonstrare ibi, nisi inscitiam suam summam in demonstrando.
units.tr: But that this is so, he will very plainly demonstrate a little later. So he would say this a little later, when he had already demonstrated it; he should first demonstrate, and so win, and then say, and sing his triumph. Neither order nor reason permits this: to pronounce sentence first and inquire into the case afterwards. But hold on a little, until you have proved something: for what haste is this? And how little does this become you, Tortus? For with what face do you now do what a little before you did not bear in the front of the book? This your rule (that you may first win) is your own shame, since you commit against your own rule: you sin in the very thing you blame; you deny it should be done, and yourself do it. A little later, indeed, when Tortus strives to demonstrate, of which he boasts much before, he will demonstrate nothing else than that, as here he leaps forward too hastily, so there he demonstrates back to front: he can boast most openly, but cannot demonstrate most openly, nor demonstrate anything there, except his supreme incompetence in demonstrating.

units.la: Nec sese tamen sistit hic audacia hominis; pergit porrò; & postquam quod Author ipse sciuit Iuramentum, id nescire cum dixit; fingit etiam, adeo rei Dialecticæ imperium, quasi si ei probando, formet argumenta,quod nusquam in Breuibus negatur, vel Epistolâ. Ita illi (homo insulsus) penitus detrahit scientiam omnem. At aliquid ei saltem reliquum faciat, quo suæ laudi nonnihil consulat. Quæ enim illi laus, si vincat in tali congressu?
units.tr: Yet the man's audacity does not stop here; he goes on further. And after he has said that the author himself knew the Oath, he says that he does not know it; he also pretends, so entirely does he command the dialectical art, as if, in order to prove his point, he were forming arguments, which is nowhere denied in the Briefs or in the Letter. Thus he (the insipid man) entirely strips himself of all knowledge. But let him at least leave himself something, by which he may consult his reputation somewhat. For what praise would he have, if he were to win in such a contest?

units.la: Quid verò ei argumenta peccant? E Scripturis, Concilijs, Patribus formant argumenta varia, quibus probet, deberi Regibus obedientiam ciuilem à subditis. Non id tantùm, Torte; plus etiam probat; deberi eam Regibus, Pontifice vel inuito; nempe ita deberi eam Legis diuinæ tabulis, vt Breuè[?] aliquo Papali subditi eâ liberari nequeant. At hoc in Breuibus, in Epistolâ non negatur. Negatur verò hoc. Tuum illud forte non negatur; deberi eam, quoad id ita Pontifici visum: at vbi eos debito hoc suo, & quasi ære soluerit, negatur à vobis vlla tum deberi. Quod ni ita sit; fatere tu, vel inuito Pontifice, deberi Regibus obedientiam, & obtinuit Author Apologiæ in causâ: obtinuit, inquam, nec iam argumenta eius à disparatis; responsio tua potius & causa tota deplorata, & desperata est.
units.tr: But what do his arguments lack? From Scriptures, Councils and Fathers he forms various arguments by which he proves that civil obedience is owed to kings by subjects. Not only this, Tortus; he proves even more: that it is owed to kings even if the Pope is unwilling; indeed that it is owed in such a way, by the tables of the divine law, that subjects cannot be freed from it by any Papal Brief. But this is not denied in the Briefs or in the Letter. Yet this is denied. What perhaps is not denied by you is that it is owed, as far as it has seemed right to the Pope; but when they have paid this debt of theirs, as it were in coin, it is denied by you that anything is then owed. And if this is not so, confess, you, that even if the Pope is unwilling, obedience is owed to kings; and the author of the Apology has prevailed in the cause: he has prevailed, I say, nor are his arguments from disparate things; your reply, rather, and your whole cause, is deplored and despaired of.

units.la: Vide ergo, quàm hîc infœliciter rem geras: vide retortam in te ignorantiam tuam. Nam hoc quidem, Vtrum negetur Breuibus illis, illâ Epistolâ, quæ Regibus debetur obedientia (saltem quanta debet, & quoúsque) hoc ipsum controuersum est; quin cardo ipse totius controuersiæ. Aitille; negas tu; his adhuc subiudice. Hoc tu iam quod controuersum est pro confesso sumis, quod nemo facit nisi qui plumbeus est in dialecticis. Ita tu, tam magnus scilicet dialecticus, parum dialecticè in elenchum incidisti. Miseret me tui, Matthæe, qui denuo iam recidiuam pateris in illam Doctoris summam turpitudinem, vt tua te culpa redarguat. Talionem hîc iustè reflexis[?], conuictus in eo crassæ ignorantiæ, cuius alium tam cupidè conuincere voluisti.
units.tr: See then how badly you handle the matter here: see your own ignorance turned back upon you. For whether those Brief documents, that Letter, deny that obedience is owed to kings (at least how much is owed, and how far) is itself the point in dispute; indeed it is the very hinge of the whole controversy. He affirms it; you deny it; the matter is still under judgement. Now you take as conceded what is in dispute, which no one does unless he is dull at dialectic. So you, such a great dialectician, have quite un-dialectically fallen into a refutation. I pity you, Matthew, who once again relapse into that supreme disgrace of a teacher, so that your own fault refutes you. Here, justly reflected back upon you is the retaliation: you are convicted of that gross ignorance which you were so eager to convict another of.

units.la: Sufficeret hoc (inquit) generatim admonuisse. En, vt illi citò confecta res est; simul vt vidit, vicit. Sufficeret quidem, si aliquis hæc nobis Apollo de tripode diceret, vel etiàm si Papa de Cathedrâ, quæ tripodis illius iam instar est. Sed nec Apollo est, nisi ille[?] hic Tortus, (nec abludit nomine) nec Papa; sed Papiensis modò, & haud ita pridem obscurus author: quòd nisi diligentiùs rem peruestigâssel Typographus, nec noui iam nominis, nec fortasse noscendi. Vidit vero non sufficere haec Tortus, saltem non tardioribus; vult sibi porro molestus esse, ut tardioribus fiat satis: & quidem tardiores sint oportet, quibus suis hisce satisfaciat.
units.tr: "This", he says, "would have been enough to admonish in general terms." See, the thing is finished quickly for him; as soon as he has seen it, he has conquered. It would indeed have been enough if someone were saying these things to us as Apollo from the tripod, or even if the Pope were saying them from the Chair, which is now like that tripod. But he is neither Apollo, unless this Tortus (whose name does not differ) is, nor the Pope; he is only a man of Pavia, and an author until lately obscure, whom, had the printer not searched the matter more diligently, would have no known name now, and perhaps none to be known by. Yet Tortus has seen that these things are not enough, at least not for the slower sort; he wants to be troublesome to himself further, "so that the slower sort may be satisfied"; and indeed the slower sort must be those whom he satisfies with these things of his.

units.la: Meditatur autem (si succedat) ostendere, non civilem obedientiam modo, sed etiam Catholicae fidei abnegationem requiri Juramento. Atque hoc illi principalis quaestio est; neque nos negamus esse: Porro etiam abnegari Juramentum par esse, si abnegetur eo fides Catholica.
units.tr: He intends, however (if he succeeds), to show that "not only civil obedience, but also the renunciation of the Catholic faith is required by the oath." And this is his "principal question"; nor do we deny that it is one. Moreover, if the Catholic faith is renounced by it, then the oath must also be renounced.

units.la: Primum vero hoc, ubi tardioribus suis ostenderit, minatur post Apologiae: caveat sibi; partes eius excutiet, partes singulas; quarum tamen multas bonus vir vix salutat, nec vel digito attingit. Ad alias vero in quibus obiectio forte, respondet quidem, sed negatione nuda interdum; vel negatione certe nuda, vel negatione mera: vel si locus citatur, de numeris litem facit, vel petere te iubet aliunde responsionem ex alio libro; vel comperendinat de responso, & alio se loco responsurum prolixe pollicetur; quo loco tamen post si responsum quaesieris, unde te hic mittit, eo te ibi remittet: hinc illuc, illinc huc denuo: credo, ut de lectore periculum faciat, an solerti satis memoria sit. Utrumque tamen hoc Tortus in se suscipit; nos, an praestet in eo fidem, id vero iam, si placet, videamus. Ac de abnegata primum fide Catholica.
units.tr: Now this, once he has shown it to his slower readers, he threatens after the Apology: let him take care; he will examine its parts, each part singly; of which, however, the good man scarcely greets many, nor so much as touches them with a finger. To other objections, perhaps, he does reply, but sometimes with a bare denial; at any rate with a bare denial, or a mere denial; or if a passage is cited, he makes a quarrel about the numbers, or bids you seek the answer elsewhere from another book; or he adjourns the reply and promises at length to respond in another place; in which place, however, if you then seek the answer, from where he sends you here, there he will send you back: hither to there, thither to here again. I believe this is so that he may test the reader, whether he has a memory sharp enough. Tortus, however, takes upon himself both of these things; whether he keeps faith in them, let us now see, if you please. And first, concerning the renunciation of the Catholic faith.

units.la: Quâ de re dum praefatur, intuitu primo videbar quidem mihi, quasi legere Postillae alicuius exordium, &c, nisi valde attentus sit lector, sermocinari ibi Matthaeum putet; esse illi pro themate, Apologiae verba quaedam; conferre autem loci illius varias lectiones inter se, quasi vulgatam cum alia quadam versione, aut (si malis) Editiones Clementis & Sixti: sive etiam, perinde ac, si thema illi esset ex uno quopiam Evangelistae loco, ex aliis autem loci eius harmoniam texeret: sic enim certe Postillatorem agit, dum in hunc modum loca concordat; Haec sunt verba eius pagina quarta; sed in Anglicanâ clarius. Deinde iterum, sic loquitur pagina sexta, In Anglicanâ loquitur apertius.
units.tr: While he is prefacing on this matter, at first glance I seemed to myself to be reading the opening of some postil, and unless the reader is very attentive, he might think Matthew is there preaching on a theme of certain words of the Apology, and comparing the various readings of that passage with one another, as if the Vulgate with some other version, or (if you prefer) the editions of Clement and Sixtus; or even, as if his theme were one passage from one of the Evangelists, and he were weaving a harmony of its other passages from the others. For thus indeed he plays the postiller, while he harmonises passages in this way: "These are his words on page four; but in the English they are clearer." Then again, he speaks thus on page six: "In the English he speaks more openly."

units.la: Quorsum vero haec, aut cui rei aucupium hoc syllabarum? An hoc nescit, cuique linguae idioma suum esse nativum, ei soli proprium; nec quod una lingua scriptum, idem ipsum altera alterâ sic reddi posse, ut non aliquid saltem discriminis sit, in aliqua dictiuncula: sed verbū verbo per omnia semper utrobiq; respondeat? Sententia modò constet: inscitia mera, languere circa voculas; & quis hoc facit, nisi μυηχ[?]? sen-tentiam verò quod attinet, pauxillum credo differentiæ inter duo hæc; Nec ultrà quid desiderare Regem, quàm ut de eorum fide & constantiâ securus fieret, quàm propter conscientiâ suâ Maiestati præstare tenebantur; Et, Regem nihil desiderare, nisi ut securus de ciuili obedientiâ redderetur. En verò insignem certè, & Matthaeo notandam discrepantiam, inter Nihil desiderare, &, nec ultrà quid desiderare; inter certus fieri de fide & constantiâ, Et, Certus reddi de ciuili obedientiâ! Annon hoc est, magno conatu magnas nugas agere?
units.tr: But to what end these things, or to what purpose this hunting after syllables? Does he not know that each language has its own idiom, native and proper to itself alone; and that what is written in one language cannot be rendered into another in such a way that there is not at least some difference in a small word, but that word always answers to word, in every respect, on both sides? Let the meaning only stand: it is sheer ineptitude to dwell on small words; and who does this, unless ... ? As for the meaning, I believe there is a little difference between these two: "Nor does the King desire anything further than that he be made sure of their faith and constancy, which they were bound to render to his Majesty for the sake of their conscience"; and "The King desires nothing except that he be made sure of civil obedience." Behold, indeed, a remarkable discrepancy, and one for Matthew to note: between "desires nothing" and "nor does he desire anything further"; between "made sure of faith and constancy" and "made sure of civil obedience"! Is this not to make great trifles with great effort?

units.la: Quid est enim, (extra causam quidem Religionis & conscientiæ suæ) quid aliud (inquam) est, quod Principi debetur à suis, quàm obedientia ciuilis, & ipsa tamen etiam, (si Apostolum audimus) propter conscientiam? Tum quid hæc, quæso, inter se differunt, Res præsertim ciuilis, & quæ ad Papam nullatenus spectat, &c, Res merè & solùm ad ciuilem obedientiam spectans? Tædet verò minutijs istis immorari. Sed quid agas? Danda venia Matthæo: sic sunt isti homines; sic mentem habent; ita mersi in novâ & nuperâ de æquivoco doctrinâ, ut non modò voces, sed syllabas ipsas vocum, suspiciosè inter se perscrutari soleant, & ex ingenio suo de aliorum scriptis judicare.
units.tr: For what is it (apart from the matter of religion and of conscience) what else, I say, is owed to a prince by his subjects than civil obedience, and that obedience itself, too, (if we hear the Apostle) for conscience' sake? Then, I ask, how do these differ from one another: "a matter especially civil, and which in no way concerns the Pope," and "a matter relating merely and solely to civil obedience"? Indeed it is tedious to dwell on these trifles. But what can you do? Matthew must be pardoned: such are these men; such is their mind; so immersed are they in the new and recent doctrine "of equivocation," that they are wont to scrutinise suspiciously among themselves not only words, but the very syllables of words, and to judge the writings of others by their own disposition.

units.la: Ubi jam explicit eius Postilla, aggreditur quod antè pollicitus; ut ostendat, Catholicam fidem Juramento abnegari; idque se facilè probaturum dicit: idque nos facilè credimus, facilitate quidem maiore quàm fœlicitate. Uidit tamen non tam facile sibi fore hoc, quàm autumauit; quare cautè rem gerit, dum nihil sibi plus probandum assumit de Catholicâ fide, aut (quod idem illi sonat) de Primatu sedis Apostolicæ, quàm quod apud Catholicos suos pro certissimo dogmate habetur, apud quos, multa non valdè certa habentur pro certis: Cautè hoc (inquam) quòd rem ponit, apud suos: apud alios enim, & quidem (quamuis id nolit Matthæus) Christianos, etiam Catholicos (etsi forte non de Catechismo Romano, nec addictos iurare in cæcum illud idolum, quod dicitur fides implicita, vt qui sub plicaturis illis quid lateat, ignorent) apud illos non habetur hoc sanè pro dogmate certissimo; ac vt pro tali habeatur, fide opus ijs tantâ, quanta monti mouendo par sit, vt hoc (inquam) pro certo constet, Primatum sedis cuiusquam in Scripturis fundatum esse. Nisi sicubi apud Indos, alsines eius Iesuitæ in nouum aliquod Euangelium Giaponicum inciderint; aut nisi Pontifex ipse, Quintus scilicet Euangelista, in illo suo Euangelio quinto, fundamenta eius iecerit. Quem titulum Quinti Euangelistæ, oblatum Clementi octauo ab egregio illo impostore, Humili Gabriele, modestus homo Clemens non repudiauit; Baronius etiam agnouit; retulit in Annales suos; censurâ suâ rem totam approbauit.
units.tr: Now that his postil has come to an end, he turns to what he promised before: to show that "the Catholic faith is renounced by the oath"; and he says he will "easily prove it," which we readily believe, with more ease than good fortune. He has seen, however, that this will not be as easy for him as he supposed; therefore he proceeds cautiously, while he assumes for himself nothing more to prove "concerning the Catholic faith," or (which to him means the same) "concerning the Primacy of the Apostolic See," than what "is held among his own Catholics as a most certain dogma"; among whom many things not very certain are held as certain. Cautiously, I say, does he state the matter, "among his own"; for among others, and indeed (though Matthew would not have it so) Christians, even Catholics (though perhaps not those of the Roman Catechism, nor those who are bound to swear to that blind idol which is called implicit faith, since they do not know what lies hidden under its folds), among these it is by no means held as a most certain dogma; and for it to be held as such, they would need a faith as great as is sufficient to move a mountain; so that this (I say) would be certainly established: "that the primacy of any see is founded in Scripture." Unless perhaps among the Indians, where his Jesuit disciples may have come upon some new Japanese Gospel; or unless the Pontiff himself, namely the fifth Evangelist, has laid its foundations in that his fifth Gospel. This title of the fifth Evangelist, offered to Clement VIII by that eminent impostor, Gabriel the Humble, the modest man Clement did not reject; Baronius also acknowledged it; he recorded it in his Annals; by his censure he approved the whole matter.

units.la: Cùm verò iam probandum hoc sibi propositum esset, Catholicæ fidei abnegationem iuramento requiri, pòst paulò scopum transfert, & melioriter iam, immò agi ait de fide Catholicâ in iuramento. At academnè hæc Papiæ sunt, agere de fide, & fidem abnegare? Ego verò si largiar tibi, agi in iuramento de fide, (agitur enim de obedientiâ & fide Regi præstandâ, quam in Scripturis sanctis apertissimè fundatam nec tu ipse, scio, negabis) si (quod ascribis in margine) In iuramento contineri religionis negotium, & hoc quoque largiar tibi (vt enim probent fidem suam Principi suo, qui subditi sunt, religionis negotium certè, quis neget?) vt hæc (inquam) tibi largiar, agi de fide, de religione: at vel fidem, vel religionem abnegari, vel vt abnegentur agi, id verò pernegabo.
units.tr: But when this was now proposed to be proved, that the renunciation of the Catholic faith is required by oath, after a little he shifts his aim, and, more favourably now, even says that "the Catholic faith is treated of in the oath." But is it the custom in Pavia to treat of the faith and to renounce the faith? For my part, if I were to grant you that the faith is treated of in the oath (for it is concerned with the obedience and faith to be rendered to the King, which, I know, you yourself will not deny is most openly founded in the holy Scriptures), and if (as you write in the margin) "the matter of religion is contained in the oath," and I were to grant you this too (for if they prove their faith to their Prince, to whom they are subjects, is it not certainly a matter of religion? who would deny it?), I grant you these things, I say: that the faith and religion are treated of. But that either faith or religion is renounced, or that it is treated of so that it may be renounced, this I will utterly deny.

units.la: Sed tamen, neq; agitur ibi de fide Catholicâ, tuo quidem sensu, vt ei ex Iuramento periculum vllum. Agitur verò (inquit) de fide Catholicâ, id est, de Primatu sedis Apostolicæ. Scribit hæc tardioribus Tortus, quibus persuadere se posse speraret, eadem per omnia esse hæc, fidem Catholicam, & Primatum sedis Apostolicæ; nec transferri hic scopum denuò, à fide, ad sedis Primatum. Audito fidem Catholicam abnegari, exhorruit lector; credidit aliquem de Symbolo articulum vel tolli, vel in dubium vocari: de Trinitate, Christo, Spiritu Sancto perperam tradi aliquid. Nihil horum: respira, lector: non enim de fide Catholicâ agitur, eâ, quam Apostoli, quam Patres Nicæni, eâ, quam scripsit Athanasius: quin audite Torti [?] fidei Catholicæ: De fide Catholica, id est, de Primatu sedis Apostolicæ. Agitur ergo tantùm de Primatu sedis, & ille tantùm negatur, (si tamen ille) cuius tamen in trium, quæ dixi, symbolorum nullo, mentio ulla. Monendus ergo mihi lector est, ne metuat hic sibi quicquam à voce Fidei[?]; Latè se porrigere apud Tortum vocem Fidei Catholicæ, etiam ad sedes, & sedilia, & primatum eorum; nec minùs latè apud Jesuitas. Quàm sæpe, quàm sine causâ apud eos legas, est de fide? Implicitam enim hi homines fidem habent, nescio quot plicis implicitam; quarum plicarum ex unâ, si sedulò excussa fuerit, prodibunt forte nobis sedes ista, & Primatus.
units.tr: But in any case, the oath is not, in your sense, concerned with the Catholic faith, so that no danger to it arises from the oath. "Indeed," he says, "it concerns the Catholic faith, that is, the Primacy of the Apostolic See." Tortus writes this for slower readers, whom he hopes he can persuade that these are in every respect the same thing, the Catholic faith and the Primacy of the Apostolic See, and that the aim has not been silently shifted from faith to the Primacy of the See. Hearing that the Catholic faith is being renounced, the reader is alarmed; he believes that some article of the Creed is either being removed or called into doubt, or that something false is being taught about the Trinity, Christ or the Holy Spirit. None of this is so: take heart, reader. The oath is not concerned with the Catholic faith, that faith which the Apostles held, which the Fathers of Nicaea held, and which Athanasius wrote of. Listen rather to Tortus's "Catholic faith": "Concerning the Catholic faith, that is, concerning the Primacy of the Apostolic See." So the oath concerns only the Primacy of the See, and that is what is denied (if indeed it is that), though the Primacy is not mentioned at all in any of the three creeds I have named. I must therefore warn the reader not to fear anything for himself from the word "faith" [?]. In Tortus the phrase "Catholic faith" stretches widely, even to the seats and thrones, and to their primacy; and no less widely among the Jesuits. How often, and how pointlessly, do you read among them "it is a matter of faith"? These men hold an implicit faith, implicit in I know not how many folds; if one of these folds is carefully shaken out, perhaps that seat and that Primacy will come forth for us.

units.la: Non hic ergo de fide Catholicâ explicitè, non pressè agitur. Nam cum fides Catholica in Symbolum redacta primùm, nulla erat adhuc sedes Apostolica; Romæ quidem nulla, quæ illa Helena est pro quâ Matthæus dimicat. Certè, ante martyrium Diui Jacobi editio Symboli: alioqui, non credimus in IESUM CHRISTUM; qui articulus D. JACOBO, tanquam ab eo collatus in Symbolum, ascribi solet: saltem, priusquam Hierosolymâ discessum ab Apostolis, editio Symboli; id est, priusquam Româ venisset Apostolus Petrus, teste vel Baronio. Aliquanto enim post Romæ sedem posuit, quàm Catholica fides primùm ederetur. Priùs ergo completa sedes Catholica, quàm inchoata sedes Apostolica; ut si de fide sit, de recentiori aliquâ sit. Et sanè, pessimè post isthuc in se, atq; in nos consuluerunt Patres Niceni, pessimè Athanasius, quorum nemo primatum hunc, sedis huius, caput fidei præcipuum, præcipuum fundamentum Religionis Catholicæ, Symbolis post suis inserere vel meminit, vel curavit.
units.tr: Therefore the oath is not here concerned with the Catholic faith explicitly, nor in the strict sense. For when the Catholic faith was first reduced to a Creed, there was as yet no Apostolic See, certainly none at Rome, which is that Helen for whom Matthew fights. Certainly the Creed was published before the martyrdom of St James; otherwise "we believe in Jesus Christ" would not stand, an article which is usually ascribed to James as having been contributed to the Creed by him; at least the Creed was published before the Apostles departed from Jerusalem, that is, before the Apostle Peter came to Rome, as even Baronius testifies. For the See at Rome was established some time after the Catholic faith was first published. The Catholic See was therefore completed before the Apostolic See was begun; so if the matter concerns faith, it concerns something more recent. And indeed the Nicene Fathers, and Athanasius, gave very poor counsel, both for themselves and for us, after that event; none of them remembered or took care to insert into their later Creeds this Primacy of that See, "the chief head of faith, the chief foundation of the Catholic religion."

units.la: Verum enim, etsi nulla in Symbolo Primatus vestigia: at est tamen in scripturis sanctissimè apertissimè fundatus, quare apud Catholicos certissimus. Nec iniurià, si in Scripturis fundatus, & fundatus apertissimè. Non enim si positivo gradu, si aperte positus, satis hoc Torto; quin apertissimè ait, nempe ut cuiuis se statim in oculos ingerat.
units.tr: Indeed, although there are no traces of the Primacy in the Creed, it is nevertheless "most holy and most clearly founded in Scripture," and therefore most certain among Catholics. Nor is this unjustly said, if it is "founded in Scripture, and founded most clearly." For it does not satisfy Tortus that it is clearly stated in the positive degree; he says "most clearly," that is, so that it leaps straight into anyone's eyes.

units.la: Mirum autem si apertissimè, & eum post quadringentos demum annos, tres successiuè Romani Episcopi, Zosimus, Bonifacius, Cælestinus quem habebant in scripturis tam apertum, super canones Niceni fundare conati sunt; falsò id quidem etiam, sed tamen conati sunt. Apertissimè ais, nec eum ducenti & septendecim Patres in Concilio Carthaginensi (& erat inter eos tum Augustinus, quo vix quisquam in scripturis oculatior) vsquam in scripturis tamen, addo etiam, nec inter Nicenos Canones conspicere potuerunt?
units.tr: But it is strange that if it is "most clearly" so, the Roman bishops Zosimus, Boniface and Celestine, who had it so plainly in Scripture, only after four hundred years tried to found it upon the canons of Nicaea; and though they did so falsely, they nevertheless tried. You say "most clearly," yet could the two hundred and seventeen Fathers at the Council of Carthage (among whom was Augustine, than whom scarcely anyone was more keen-sighted in Scripture) nowhere see it in Scripture, or indeed, I add, among the canons of Nicaea?

units.la: Itaque apertissimè fundatum, nec sexcenti & triginta illi Patres post in Chalcedonensi quarto Generali viderunt tamen? Omnes ne [illegible, ~3 letters] erant? Omnibus ne caligabant oculi, qui Primatum quidem viderunt ibi, non tamen in scripturis fundatum, quin in Patrum Decretis, idq; eo nomine; non quòd sedes ibi Apostoli, sed quòd vrbs illa caput esset Imperij? Monstri verò simile, si inter tam multos oculos, oculos aquilinos, oculos quotidie in scripturis exercitatos, nullus tamen conspexit Primatum illum sic (vt ais) apertissimè fundatum. Apage Matthaee; nisi valde tardo, nulli fidem fecferis hac de re: fundamenta eius in montibus Septem, non in montibus sanctis, adquos confugere nos iubet Seruator, quos non nemo de Patribus Scripturas interpretatur. Quin tu censeo & Dominus tuus, & Dominus Domini tui iure humano cōtenti sitis, diuinum mittite, mittite scripturas; in quibus, si apertissimè fuisset fundatus; ante, diu ante editum in lucem Tortum, aliquis (credo) tot Patrum vel per transfennam vidisset, & quia Catholicæ fidei adeo præcipuum caput est, indicâsset.
units.tr: So, could those six hundred and thirty Fathers who later at the fourth General Council, at Chalcedon, did not see a thing "most clearly founded"? Were they all blind? Were their eyes dimmed for all of them, who did see the Primacy there, but not founded in Scripture, only in the decrees of the Fathers, and that on account of this: not because it was the See of the Apostle, but "because that city was the capital of the Empire"? It is a monstrous thing if, among so many eyes, eagle-eyes, eyes daily exercised in Scripture, not one caught sight of that Primacy so "most clearly founded," as you say. Away with it, Matthew; unless you are very slow-witted, you will persuade no one of this. Its foundations are on the seven mountains, not on the holy mountains to which the Saviour bids us flee, which some of the Fathers interpret as Scripture. Indeed, I think you and your Lord, and your Lord's Lord, should be content with human law: send away the divine, send away the Scriptures; in them, if it had been most clearly founded, someone (I believe) long before the publication of this Tortus would have seen it, even if only out of the corner of his eye, of so many Fathers, and, since it is so very principal a head of the Catholic faith, would have pointed it out.

units.la: Quære, si libet, non in scripturis, vnde nemo Patrum eruit, non in Niceno Concilio (Atticus ille & Cyrillus, transmissis Carthaginem veris eius exemplaribus, labore te hoc leuārunt) Quære in Sardicensi Synodo, non tamen Generali illâ, quod valdè vult {a} Dominus tuus; non enim secunda, vt oportuit si Generalis, nec vllo in numero Generalium; quin Prouinciali, idque tam obscura, vt ne nomen quidem eius, aut talem vnquam Synodum fuisse, vel Augustinus, vel quisquam è ducentis illis & septendecim Patribus, fando aliquando audiuerit. Ibi quære, ibi fortasse reperturus illius ruderā, nempe in placitis Patrum, & illā Hosij demissâ petitione, {b} Placetne vobis vt honoremus Petri memoriam. In scripturis autem ne inueniesquidem, nisi artem edidicisti de quā Diuus {c} Petrus, [illegible, ~6 letters], & nisi mutare tibi nomen in animo, & pro Matthao Torto, Matthaum Tortorem fieri. Esto tamen, quò posis progredi ; Nego agi in Iuramento de Primatu sedis Apostolicæ ; agi dico vt abnegetur : an vel hoc probabis ? facilè verò (inquis) ex ipso Edicti titulo. Titulus enim est ad detegendos Papistas: Cur non ad detegendos rebelles, nisi quia finis iuramenti non est, nisi detectio confitentium Primatum spiritualem summi Pontificis?
units.tr: Ask, if you like, not in Scripture, from which none of the Fathers drew it, nor at the Council of Nicaea (where Atticus and Cyril, having sent the true copies of it to Carthage, relieved you of that labour). Ask at the Council of Sardica, though not that general one, which your Lord strongly wishes; for it was not the second, as it should have been if it were general, nor is it counted among the general councils; rather it was provincial, and so obscure that neither Augustine, nor any of those two hundred and seventeen Fathers, ever heard by report that there had been such a synod at all. There ask, there perhaps you will find its rubble, namely in the decrees of the Fathers, and in that humble petition of Hosius: "Does it please you that we honour the memory of Peter?" But in Scripture you will not even find it, unless you have learned that art of which the blessed Peter [illegible], and unless you have changed your name in your mind, and instead of Matthew Tortus, become Matthew the Torturer. Yet, granting that you may go so far: I deny that the oath concerns the Primacy of the Apostolic See; I say it concerns it only so that it may be denied. Will you prove even this? "Easily," you say, "from the very title of the Edict. For the title is 'for detecting Papists': why not 'for detecting rebels', unless the purpose of the oath is only the detection of those who confess the spiritual Primacy of the Supreme Pontiff?"

units.la: Sed quid tibi, Matthæe, cum legibus nostris? Theologo cum legibus, Italo cum nostris? Non tibi illas condendi ius ullum: Audi verò, ne interpretandi quidem igitur. Tum, si interpretem volumus de vestris, volumus qui nominis sit & omnino melioris. Apage vt legum interpres Tortus sit: iusta metus causa, ne tortus ipse cùm sit, leges etiam torqueat, quò sibi similes reddat, id est tortas. Quare te quidem interpretem leges nostras, omnes (credo) leges deprecantur. Vide enim quid leges à te expectare debeant, qui titulum ipsum sic torques.
units.tr: But what is it to you, Matthew, with our laws? What has a theologian to do with laws, an Italian with ours? You have no right whatever to make them; hear me, then, not even to interpret them. Moreover, if we want an interpreter from among our own, we want one of the name and of altogether better standing. Away with the thought that Tortus should be the interpreter of the laws, for there is just cause to fear that, being himself twisted, he will twist the laws too, to make them like himself, that is, twisted. Wherefore all our laws, I believe, pray to be spared you as their interpreter. For see what the laws must expect from you, who twist the very title in this way.

units.la: Quid verò? cùm nouus legum interpres esse cupiás, nescibas hoc, varias sæpe res diuersas inter se vnâ lege edici vel interdici, quarum si vel de præcipuis aliquas comprehendat titulus, satis esse, nec opus vt singulæ ibi sigillatim exprimantur? Ita factum in lege hac: partes illius multæ sunt, multæ (inquam) præter vnam hanc quæ de Iuramento est: tute ipse post quatuordecim enumeras; titulus illi à parte, sed maiore; pars maior Edicti detegendis illis fuit; titulus ei ab hac parte; quid hîc causari potes? Sed respondeo tibi ad quæsita tua: Cur non ad detegendos rebelles? (nam hæc tibi tituli forma magis placet, sed ineptè prorsus) Cur non ad rebelles? Quia nihil opus; nihil (inquam) opus detegi illos, qui se non tegunt. Nam si se tegant, rebelles non sunt; Rebelles tum demum, cum aperte se gerunt, & [illegible, ~8 letters] cum produnt ipsi se, & dant in conspectu. Ad proditores clancularios, crypticos detegendos, reprimendos, opus iuramento forte: ad rebelles nihil opus.
units.tr: Well then? Since you wish to be a new interpreter of laws, did you not know that often various and different matters are enacted or forbidden by one law, and that if its title comprehends some of the principal ones, that is enough, and there is no need for each to be expressed separately there? So it is in this law: it has many parts, many, I say, besides this one which concerns the oath; you yourself enumerate them after fourteen; its title belongs to a part, but to a greater one; the greater part of the Edict was for the detection of those men; the title is taken from this part; what can you allege against this? But I answer your questions: "Why not for detecting rebels?" (for this form of title pleases you more, though it is utterly inept): "Why not for rebels?" Because there is no need; there is no need, I say, to detect those who do not hide themselves. For if they hide themselves, they are not rebels; they become rebels only when they act openly, and [illegible] when they reveal themselves and show themselves in plain view. For detecting secret, covert traitors, to be suppressed, an oath is perhaps needed; for rebels there is no need.

units.la: Sed cur ad detegendos Papistas, nisi quia hostilis in eos animus? Vide verò quàm merito in te retorqueri possit telum tuum, nimirum, quòd ipse Iuramentorum non intelligas. Quid enim? an ad omnes, an ad quoslibet, passim & promiscuè, Papistas detegendos edictum Iuramentum hoc? Caue putes: Ad hoc enim, quid opus Iuramento illo? Quid vllo opus? Sacris non intersunt, conciones non audiunt, Eucharistiam sumere detrectant: sine hoc, sine vllo iuramento scias, qui sunt Papistæ.
units.tr: But why detect the Papists, unless it is because of a hostile spirit toward them? Look rather how justly your weapon can be turned back on you, namely because you do not understand oaths at all. For what? Is this oath enacted to detect Papists in general, or of any kind, indiscriminately and promiscuously? Take care you do not think so. For what need is there of that oath for this purpose? What need is there of any oath? They do not take part in the sacred rites, they do not attend sermons, they refuse to receive the Eucharist: without this, without any oath, you may know who the Papists are.

units.la: Ergóne ad eos detegendos, qui negant Regium Primatum, confitentur Papalem? Frustra es & hic: nam huic tei[?] iam pridem iuramentum aliud conditum, vetus illud, ante septuaginta iam annos & amplius, idque (vt tu ipse pòst afferis) fatis rigidum. De Primatu Regio abundè cautum erat Iuramento illo, vt noua ad hanc quidem rem nihil opus; ægri hoc cerebri somnium. Nec ad hos ergo, nec ad illos detegendos iuratur hic.
units.tr: Is it then to detect those who deny the royal supremacy and confess the papal? You are wrong here too: for another oath, the old one, was framed long ago for this very purpose, more than seventy years ago, and (as you yourself afterwards assert) rather rigid. The royal supremacy was sufficiently provided for in that oath, so that there was no need of a new one for this matter; it is a dream of a sick brain. Therefore this oath is sworn neither to detect these men nor those.

units.la: Ad quos ergo? Certè ad Papistas certos quosdam, illorum nempe similes, qui in proditione puluerariâ partes suas egerant, nempe quibus non satis Missas facere, reliqua sacra vestra obire, nisi Regem, Reginam, Regiam prolem, familiam, Regni Ordines omnes, & Primarios viros, vnâ displosione discerpant; id est, quibus non satis Papistas esse, nisi & nefarij parricidæ sint. Non ergo (si titulum capis) ad detegendos Papistas est promiscuè quoslibet, sed ad certos quosdam detegendos, cosque non Regio Primatui, quin Regio Principatui, saluti, vitæ hostes capitales. Hi, hi erant detegendi Iuramento hoc, hi reprimendi.
units.tr: To whom, then? Surely to certain Papists, namely those like the men who played their parts in the gunpowder plot, who were not content to say Mass and perform your other sacred rites, unless they could tear apart the King, the Queen, the royal offspring, the household, all the orders of the realm and its chief men in a single explosion; that is, who are not content to be Papists unless they are also abominable parricides. Therefore, if you take the title at its word, the oath is not to detect Papists indiscriminately, any whatever, but to detect certain ones, and those not merely enemies of the royal supremacy but chief enemies of the king's government, safety and life. These, these were the ones to be detected by this oath, these to be restrained.

units.la: Verùm esto; dabo tibi quod vis; vel sic, si potes, retuned[?] cuncum[?]; vel sic constare sibi poterit titulus, si in tortum interpretem non incidat.
