Aptum enim iuramentum, & imprimis accommodum ad Papistas tum detegendos, tum reprimendos, Papistas (inquam) qui ex conscientiæ scrupulis quibusdam sic sunt homines alioqui non mali, nec ab officio erga Principem alieno animo; ad Papistas hos detegendos, non tamen reprimendos, sed distinguendos ab alijs illis (Papistis quoque & ipsis) quibus religio nulla, imò quibus religio tota machinari in Regem, suffodere muros, exinanire vsque ad fundamenta: ad hos verò cùm detegendos, tum reprimendos. Quid? annon tibi hoc est detegere? & aptè quidem, quò sic quémque eorum suo in genere nosse detur: nosse qui sedati sunt, & illos sinere: nosse qui turbulenti, & illos reprimere. Vide ergo vt titulus iam constet, Ad Papistas omnes, quo sint in Regem animo detegendos; Ad Papistas illos, qui maligno sunt in Regem animo, reprimendos.
units.tr: But grant it; I will give you what you want. Or in this way, if you can, retuned cuncum; or in this way the title can stand consistent with itself, provided the interpreter does not fall into twisting it. For the oath is fitting, and especially suitable both to detect and to restrain Papists: Papists, I say, who, from certain scruples of conscience, are otherwise men not evil, nor of a mind alienated from their duty toward the prince; these Papists are to be detected, though not restrained, and to be distinguished from those others (Papists too, even themselves) for whom there is no religion at all, indeed for whom the whole of religion is a means of plotting against the King, of undermining walls, of laying bare even to the foundations: these latter, however, are to be both detected and restrained. What? Is this not for you to detect? And rightly so, since in this way each of them is made known in his own class: to know who are quiet, and to let them be; to know who are turbulent, and to restrain them. See, then, how the title now holds together: To all Papists, that they may be detected as to their attitude toward the King; To those Papists who are of a malicious mind toward the King, that they may be restrained.

units.la: Atque hoc te uel ipsum tempus (magister optimus) docere potuit: nempe ex quo facto ortum ius istud, ex quibus moribus nata lex, quod genus hominum huic Iuramento condendo causam dederit. Statim enim à proditione illâ detectâ, prima cura statuendi Iuramenti huius: ante illam, nec mentio vlla, nec in mentem cuiquam venerat, aut huius, aut ullius de nouo excogitandi. Totum hoc Regiæ clementiæ tribuendum; nempe in superstitiosos illos æquior volebat esse: in istos, non homines, sed monstra hominum, iniquum erat æquum esse. Voluit ergo, vt par erat, hos ab illis internoscere, ne aut utrisque cum periculo sideret, aut utrósque sine discrimine plecteret. Nec alia occurrit commodior ratio RegniOrdinibus in Conuentu illo, quàm Iuramento hoc nouo, tanquam tesserâ quadam, hos ab illis distinguere. Etenim quos superstitio modò detineret, quibus alioqui non læua mens, libenter præstituros: at quibus præter superstitionem, vlcerosus animus, suppurata fides, quiduis potiùs admissuros. Ac superstitiosos quidem illos detegi, nec opus, nec scopus fuit: hos verò detegi, retegique, opus & scopus; ius & fas. Quod & potuit fieri, & factum est, fide Catholicâ illibatâ atque integrâ permanente, etiam (ut fors tulit[?]) Primatus spiritualis sedis Apostolicæ nulla ex parte violato. Uides verò in Paratitlis tuis superesse tibi spem nullam.
units.tr: And this very time (the best teacher) could have taught you this much: from what deed that right arose, from what customs that law was born, what kind of men gave cause for framing this oath. For immediately after that treason was discovered, the first care was to establish this oath; before that, there was no mention of it at all, and it had come into no one's mind to devise such a thing anew, either this or any other. All this must be attributed to the King's clemency: he wished to be more lenient toward the superstitious; toward those, who are not men but monsters of men, it was unjust to be fair. He therefore wished, as was fitting, to distinguish these from those, lest he either let both sit with danger, or punish both without discrimination. Nor did the Lords of the Realm in that assembly find any more convenient method than this new oath, as a sort of token, to distinguish these from those. For those whom superstition alone detained would gladly perform what was required, since otherwise their mind was not perverse; but those in whom, beyond superstition, there is an ulcerous spirit and a festering faith would admit anything rather. Now, to detect those superstitious ones was neither necessary nor the aim; but to detect and uncover these was both the necessity and the aim; it was right and lawful. And this could be done, and was done, with the Catholic faith remaining unimpaired and whole, and (as chance would have it) with the spiritual primacy of the Apostolic See violated in no part. You see, however, that in your Paratitla no hope remains for you.

units.la: Locum tandem hunc de titulo Edicti claudit titulo alio, unde illi oculi dolent, titulo Papistarum, quo scilicet Catholicos eius appellamus: & hoc illum male habet, non vultullos[?] dici Papistas. Qui verba hæc hoc loco legis, lege amabo & verba libri pene postrema; Torti[?] vicem, scio, dolebis, sic eum, in opere non longo, somno oppressum esse, vt tam parum sibi constet. Papistas hic dici, homo stomachatur; idem ipse, eosdem ipsos, extremo libro suo, dicit tertio quoq; verbo in Apologia Catholicos appellari. Ecqua gratia de titulo Catholici? non: sumit inde argumentum, vt Authorem Hæreticû vocet, vt qui, quos ipse Catholicos nominat, oppugnet tamen. Interim huic homini, tortuoso huic Proteo, quid faciás? quomodo placeas? Papistam dic, ægrè fert, obnurmurat: Indulge illi paululum, Catholicum appella, de sententiâ suâ; Itáne verò, inquit? ergo tu Hæreticus, qui aduersùs me scribis: neutro placere potes, quasi puer esset in foro sedens: cane tibijs, non saliet [?]: plora, non plangent [?]. Si verò nomine appelles Papistæ, non potest ferre nomen suum: sin ita appelles vt ipse se gestit appellari, ne sic quidem boni consulet: eo ipso, quòd cum vocâsti vt ipse vocari vult, nihilominùs vapulabis.
units.tr: Finally, this passage on the title of the Edict closes with another title, at which those eyes are sore: the title of Papists, by which of course we call its Catholics; and this irks him, that they are not willing to be called Papists. You who read these words in this place, please read also nearly the last words of the book; Torti's place, I know, you will grieve over, that he, in a work not long, was so overcome by sleep that he is so little consistent with himself. That they are called Papists here, the man frets; the same man, in the last part of his own book, says that they are called Catholics in the Apology every third word. Is there any favour regarding the title of Catholic? No: he takes from this an argument to call the author a heretic, so that he may attack those whom he himself calls Catholics. Meanwhile, what are you to do with this man, this tortuous Proteus? How will you please him? Call him a Papist: he takes it ill and mutters; indulge him a little, call him a Catholic, according to his own opinion: "Is it so, then?" he says. "So you are a heretic, who write against me": you can please neither way, like a boy sitting in the forum: sing to the flutes, he will not dance; weep, they will not mourn. But if you call them by name Papists, he cannot bear his name; if you call them as he himself wishes to be called, he will not be satisfied even so: by the very fact that you have called him as he wishes to be called, you will nonetheless be thrashed.

units.la: Vsurpaut quidem Apologiæ Author, etsi non tertio quoque verbo, ne tricesimo, ne trecentesimo quidem, sæpe tamen nomen Catholici: non quòd sic de illis sentiret, aut quòd ita debeant appellari; sed quòd verbo duriore noluit lædere, dedit hoc auribus illorum. Vides verò, quam illi gratiam referat Matthæus, vt in illum homo inhumanus inuolet, deinceps vt hac voce prorsus abstinendum sit. Sciat ergo dehinc Matthæus, vsurpari nobis terminos hosce duos, Papistæ & Catholici, pro ratione scholæ suæ, vbi nominales sunt, sunt & reales. Quodsi quando posthàc Papistam legat, terminum realem intelligat statim; sic enim reuera sunt: sin aliquando Catholicum, terminum nominalem; sic enim titulo tenus dicuntur, nec secus quàm Danus vir bonus in Comœdiâ, veri nominis Papistæ, titulares Catholici.
units.tr: The author of the Apology, indeed, though not every third word, nor every thirtieth, nor even every three hundredth, yet often uses the name Catholic: not because he thought so of them, or because they ought to be so called; but because he did not wish to wound them with a harsher word, he gave this to their ears. And you see what thanks Matthew returns for it, how the inhuman man pounces upon him, so that from then on this word must be avoided altogether. Let Matthew then know henceforth that these two terms, Papists and Catholics, are used by us according to the method of his own school, where they are nominal and are also real. If at any time hereafter he reads Papist, let him understand at once the real term; for so indeed they are. But if at some time Catholic, the nominal term; for so they are called in name only, and no differently than the good Dane in a comedy, a Papist in true name, is a Catholic in title only.

units.la: PErgis iam ad Edictum ipsum, & in Edicto, ad illa Iuramenti verba, quibus configis quidem cornicis oculos. Quòd Papa potestatem non habet Regem deponendi, vel Subditos eius ab eius obedientiâ & subiectione exonerandi. Hic iam manifestò, inquis, perspicitur non contineri solam ciuilem obedientiam. Imò, manifestò perspicitur non abnegari fidem Catholicam: potestas enim illa, quâ Reges deponit, de fide Catholicâ non est: etiam (quod tu negas) non minùs manifestò, solam ciuilem obedientiam contineri. Non enim sub vera ibi obedientiæ nomine, sacram vllam requiri, vel in sacris; nec aliam præter ciuilem illam, quam ciues Principi præstare debent, & ad quam Principi præstandam, iure omni, naturali, morali, ciuili, municipali obligantur. Eius verò vis sic inibi explicatur: nempe, vt in officio suo erga Principem constanter permanent; ab eo, nullius (nec vel Papæ suasu) monitis, minis deficiant; prompti sint & parati, si hostis vllus contrauenerit, qui deponere de regno Regem, qui de regno eius disponere, qui impressionem facere, motus concitare, vim afferre moliatur, vel si Papa is sit, ne haec Regi fiant, quacunque possunt ratione resistere: fortunis omnibus, viribus totis Regi fideliter assistere, pro eo fortiter dimicare, etiam si res ferat, viriliter occumbere. Et quid hic nisi civilis obedientia? Porro etiam cautur ibi, haec civium fides & civilis obedientia tam firma sit, tam adversus omnes inconcussa, ut nullus inde eos possit divellere, ne Pontifex quidem ipse, quin si ille Regem (quà potest) deponat, at hij fidem tamen in Regem ne deponant. Haec illa est merè civilis, sola civilis obedientia, quae Juramento continetur, nec mentio in eo Pontificis unquam fecerit, ut non sit merè civilis: Hanc oppugna tu; hic Rhodus, hic saltus.
units.tr: You now proceed to the Edict itself, and in the Edict to those words of the oath, on which you indeed fix the eyes of a crow. That the Pope has no power to depose the King, or to release his subjects from his obedience and subjection. Here, you say, it is plainly seen that not only civil obedience is contained. Rather, it is plainly seen that the Catholic faith is not denied: for that power, by which kings are deposed, is not of the Catholic faith; and (though you deny it) it is no less plainly the case that only civil obedience is contained. For under the name of true obedience no sacred obedience is required there, nor in sacred matters; nor any other than that civil obedience which citizens owe to the prince, and to which they are bound by every right, natural, moral, civil and municipal, to render it to the prince. But its force is explained there thus: that they remain constantly in their duty toward the prince; that they fail in it at no one's counsel (not even at the Pope's persuasion), nor at threats; that they be ready and prepared, if any enemy whatever should attempt to depose the King from the realm, to dispose of his kingdom, to make an assault, to stir up commotions, to use force, or, if he be the Pope, to resist by whatever means they can that these things be done to the King; with all their fortunes and all their strength to assist the King faithfully, to fight bravely for him, and, should the occasion require, to fall manfully. And what is this here but civil obedience? Moreover, it is also provided there that this fidelity and civil obedience of the citizens shall be so firm, so unshaken against all, that no one, not even the Pontiff himself, can tear them away from it: so that, even if he (so far as he can) deposes the King, they nevertheless do not abandon their faith in the King. This is that purely civil, the only civil obedience, which is contained in the oath, and the Pontiff is never mentioned in it, so that it is not merely civil. Attack this; here is the Rhodes, here the leap.

units.la: Et continere inquis verba hac abnegationem Pontificia potestatis. Qui paulò iam antè delapsus à fide Catholicâ ad sedis Primatū, iterum, & quidem bis; delaberis à primatu primùm ad potestatem tum à potestate Apostolicâ ad Pontificiam. A primatu ad potestatem non oportuit. Primatus ordinis est, qui etiam sine potestate consistit; potestas se porrigit ulterius. Sit sedes Apostoli, sedes prima; (saltem in occidente) fit sessor eius primae ibi sedis Episcopus; de potestate nova quaestio: quam tu tamen sic sumis, quasi nihil interesset. Primatum, etiam (si voles) Principatum inter Philosophos facilè daturi sumus Aristoteli, inter Rhetores Demosthenei: quibus tamen in reliquos, vel Philosophos vel Rhetores, inde haud ulla potestas è primatu suo. Quòd si de primatu ad potestatem sic transire voluit, scire perunlum[?], cùm Primatus illi sit Apostolicus; cur non & potestas itidem Apostolica, sed Primatus Apostolicus, potestas Pontificia? Non id de nihilo erat; Primatum utcunque probare se posse putat in Apostolo; Primatum potuit ergo Apostolicum: potestatem, quam Papae vindicatam vult, in Pontifice forte, in Apostolo vidit probari non posse. Noluit ergo Apostolicam dicere, ne potuit quidem, cum illam non posset, dixit Ponti-ficiam.
units.tr: And you say that these words contain a denial of papal power. You who a little earlier slipped from the Catholic faith to the primacy of the see, and again, and indeed twice: you slide from primacy to power, and then from apostolic power to papal power. There was no need to move from primacy to power. Primacy is a matter of rank, which can exist even without power; power extends further. Grant that the see is the Apostle's see, the first see (at least in the West), and that the bishop who sits there is its first occupant: the question of a new power remains, and you assume it as though it made no difference. We would readily grant primacy, even principate if you like, among philosophers to Aristotle, and among orators to Demosthenes; yet neither has any power over the other philosophers or orators by virtue of that primacy. But if you wished to pass from primacy to power in this way, you should know that the primacy in question is apostolic. Why, then, is the power not likewise apostolic, but papal? This was not without reason. He thinks he can somehow prove primacy in the Apostle; so he could name it apostolic primacy. The power which he wants claimed for the Pope, he saw perhaps could not be proved in the Pope, or in the Apostle. So he did not want to call it apostolic, and since he could not, when he could not do so, he called it papal.

units.la: Sed neque de Apostolicâ ad Pontificiam, transire debes sic desultorie: Non enim, si Apostolica est potestas ulla, statum erit & Pontificia. Climax prius conficiendus est tibi bene longus, & ducendus Sorites sesquipedalis, quàm vt ista tibi duo detur coniungere. De potestate primùm, vt transfire possit in Apostolum, atque inde in Pontificem deriuari. Fuerit ne vel in ipso Christo (quà homo Christus) temporale dominium, & potestas regna transferendi? Si fuerit, voluerit ne illam de se deriuare? Si voluit, in vnum ne, an plures? si in vnum, an vnus is Petrus? Post de Apostolica. Ecquid in Apostolo hæreditaria fuerit? Tum, quis eius hæres? Episcopusne aliquis sit dicendus hæres Apostoli? an ex asse hæres, vel quatenus? Postremò de Pontificia. An fuerit Petrus Episcopus, an Romanus fuerit? Tum de legitimo succedendi iure. Denique de illius canonica electione, qui nunc sedet Pontifex. In lite hac insunt omnia hæc, quæ tu tamen vnico saltu transcurris omnia, & pro Pontificio statim sumis quicquid est Apostolicum. Tum, de quo subinde mihi monendus es, hæc tibi si concedantur omnia, at omnia tamen hæc de fide non sunt; teipsum appello.
units.tr: But you ought not to leap so carelessly from the apostolic to the papal either. For even if there is some apostolic power, it does not follow that there is papal power too. You must first construct a climax, quite a long one, and lead up a sorites a foot and a half long, before you can join these two things together. First, the power must be shown capable of passing into the Apostle and thence being derived into the Pope. Was there even in Christ himself (as man) temporal lordship and power to transfer kingdoms? If there was, did he wish to derive it from himself? If he wished it, was it to one person or to several? If to one, was that one Peter? Then the question of apostolic power: was there any hereditary element in the Apostle? Then, who is his heir? Is some bishop to be called the Apostle's heir? Is he heir to the whole estate, or in what respect? Finally, the papal question: was Peter a bishop, or was he a Roman? Then the question of the lawful right of succession. Lastly, the canonical election of him who now sits as Pope. All these things are involved in this dispute, yet you run through them all in a single leap, and at once you take whatever is apostolic as papal. Then, since I must remind you of this from time to time: even if all these things were granted you, still none of them belongs to the faith. I appeal to yourself.

units.la: Interim vides, lector, vtcunque fides Catholica prætenditur, negotium hic agi Pontificis; caput esse in procuratione omni negotium eius: vtque scias rem ita se habere, non iam ait fidem Catholicam, puta de symbolo articulo aliquo, sed fidem Catholicam de primatu sedis Apostolicæ; ac nec illam etiam, sed fidem Catholicam de potestate Pontificis hic periclitari.
units.tr: Meanwhile you see, reader, that however much the Catholic faith is pretended, the business here is the Pope's; that the whole matter of his cause is the chief point. And so that you may know the matter stands thus, he does not say the Catholic faith, for instance concerning some article of the creed, but "the Catholic faith concerning the primacy of the apostolic see"; and not even that, but "the Catholic faith concerning the power of the Pope" is put in jeopardy here.

units.la: Quæ verò potestas illa tandem Pontificis, quam abnegari autumas? Potestas qua non est res merè temporalis. Vtinam dixisses, non omnino temporalis: vox illa, non merè, suspecta est mihi. Nam dic quæso, estne temporalis, quanquam non merè? Videtur certè. Quanquam quid trepidas hic, & esse non merè temporalem, quasi hæsitanter affirmas? Dominus tuus absque tuo hoc non merè, absque vlla trepidatione temporalem dicit, & temporalem summam, atque ita inscripsit librum suum quintum de Pontifice, De potestate Pontificis temporali. Nec Dominus tuus modò, quin ille alter personatus histrio, qui hoc idem tentauit Anglicè in Apologiam, quod tu hic Latinè, (pari successu vterque) vltro fatetur, quicquid hoc est potestatis, totum temporale esse, quam Pontifex in deponendis Regibus adhibere solet. Tuque adeo ipse paulò pòst potestatem excommunicandi intrinsecam esse dicis, primatui tuo & inseparabilem, & alio pòst loco propriè ad ipsum pertinere. Cúmque hoc dicis, id videri vis innuere, alteram potestatem hanc, eiusdem naturæ non esse, sed extrinsecam certè, & separabilem, & ad Pontificem minus propriè pertinere. Quodsi autem non merè temporalis potestas hæc Reges deponendis an ex aliquâ vobis parte spiritualis est? Sic enim non nemo de vobis scripsit.
units.tr: But what, pray, is that power of the Pope which you claim is denied? "A power which is not purely temporal." I wish you had said "not wholly temporal": the phrase "not purely" makes me suspicious. For tell me, please, is it temporal, though not purely? It certainly seems so. But why do you tremble here, and assert in a hesitant way that it is "not purely temporal"? Your lord, without this "not purely" of yours and without any hesitation, calls it temporal, and the highest temporal power, and so he entitled his fifth book on the Pope "On the Temporal Power of the Pope". Nor is it only your lord who does so; that other masked actor, who attempted the same thing in English in his Apology that you attempt here in Latin (with equal success on both sides), freely admits that whatever power this is, which the Pope is accustomed to employ in deposing kings, is wholly temporal. And you yourself a little later say that the power of excommunication is intrinsic to your primacy and inseparable from it, and in another place that it belongs properly to the same. When you say this, you wish to hint that this other power is not of the same nature, but is certainly extrinsic and separable, and belongs to the Pope less properly. But if this power of deposing kings is not purely temporal, is it then in some respect spiritual among you? For someone has written of you in this way.

units.la: At ridiculus homo ille, qui quia ad salutem animæ (rem nempe spiritualem) referetur potestas hæc, spiritualem ex eo vult dici posse. Quanquam hoc ipsum quod dicit, dici posse, timidè ab illo positum & diffidenter; Dixisset vero spiritualem esse, si sic esset, & nisi vidisset id propriè dici non posse: nunc cùm illud nec ausus nec potuit, loco eius posuit, posse quidem dici, veniá datâ fortasse, licèt siquis illam sumat in manus serio atque excutiat, non sit tamen. Hæc verò si regula datur, si sic loqui liceat, dic age; si spiritualis potestas ad temporale quid, aut terrenum referatur; si hunc sibi scopum habeat, potestne dici temporalis? Vide verò quid respondeas: sæpius enim spiritualis potestas Pontificis vestri, ad temporalem finem refertur, quàm temporalis ad spiritualem. Quin si fine metienda sit, vix alium ad finem referri iam diu solet, etiam spiritualis illa eius potestas, quàm ad dilatandas fimbrias eius in temporalibus. Ita si viam hanc pergas, breui, nisi temporalis solùm, nulla futura est potestas in Pontifice. Tace ergo de fine, si sapis. Addo verò etiam cautionem hic alteram: Nam hoc si semel constet, temporalem potestatem (quam & Principes habent) si ad spiritualem finem referatur, ex eo quòd ita referatur, transfire statim in spiritualem: næ & Principes vestri quoque Catholici, spirituali esse potestate præditos sentient, non minùs quàm Pontificem ipsum. Nam si potestatem hanc suam ad Ecclesiam in Regnis suis reformandam adhibeant, spiritualis iam erit, ad spiritualem nempe finem relata: verendum autem, ne sic turbas dent, & submolestì sint Pontifici, nouâ hac suâ spirituali potestate.
units.tr: But that ridiculous fellow, who because this power is referred to the salvation of the soul (a spiritual matter, of course) wishes it to be called spiritual on that account. Yet even this which he says, that it "can be called" spiritual, he puts forward timidly and diffidently. He would have said it was spiritual, if it were so, and unless he had seen that it cannot properly be so called. Now, since he neither dared nor was able to say that, he put in its place "can indeed be called", perhaps granting indulgence, although if anyone takes it up seriously and examines it, it is not so. But if this rule is given, if we may speak in this way, come now: if spiritual power is referred to something temporal or earthly, if it has that as its aim, can it be called temporal? Yet see what you will answer: for more often the spiritual power of your Pope is referred to a temporal end than the temporal to a spiritual one. Indeed, if it is to be measured by its end, that spiritual power of his has for a long time been referred to scarcely any other end than the extending of his fringes in temporal affairs. So if you continue along this road, soon there will be no power in the Pope except a temporal one. Therefore keep silent about the end, if you are wise. I add here yet another caution. For if this were once granted, that temporal power (which Princes also have), if it is referred to a spiritual end, then by that very fact of being so referred it passes at once into the spiritual: for your Catholic Princes too will find themselves endowed with spiritual power, no less than the Pope himself. For if they use this power of theirs to reform the Church in their kingdoms, it will then be spiritual, namely because it is referred to a spiritual end. But it is to be feared that in this way they will cause disturbances and be troublesome to the Pope with this new spiritual power of theirs.

units.la: Saltem de quâ nunc agis, concedes; etsi non merè, temporalem tamen esse. Vide verò, tua hæc quàm non cohærent. Ad potestatem hanc deveniisti à Primatu. At Primatus modò Spiritualis erat, cuius confessionem aiebas Catholicorum propriam. Quintò iam ergo Proteum agis, delapsus à Primatu Spirituali ad potestatem temporalem, & à fide Catholicâ de Primatu Spirituali ad fidem Catholicam de potestate temporali. Valdè autem impropriè hoc. Sed quid facias? Omnia quæ quidem ad potestatem hanc spectant, ipsaque adeo potestas, impropria est, & indirecta, vt nihil de eâ, aut directè, aut proprie dictum expectari possit.
units.tr: At least you will concede regarding the power of which you are now speaking, that even if not purely, it is nonetheless temporal. But see how little your statements cohere. You arrived at "this power" from "primacy". But primacy was just now spiritual, and you were saying that its confession is "proper to Catholics". So now in the fifth place you play Proteus, having slipped from spiritual primacy to temporal power, and from the Catholic faith concerning spiritual primacy to the Catholic faith concerning temporal power. And this is most improper. But what can you do? Everything which indeed pertains to this power, and power itself, is improper and indirect, so that nothing about it can be expected to be said either directly or properly.

units.la: Cùm iam temporalem esse constet potestatem istam, quæro porrò: Quænam temporalis sit? Quàne præest Pontifex, & ius dicit vbi & ditioni suæ subiurbicariæ, vt Princeps aliquis temporalis? Non: sed alia, longè alia potestas temporalis, longè scilicet, latéque diffusa, in vrbes, ditiones, subditos omnes Regum, imò in Reges ipsos: nec in Reges quouis, sed longè omnium maxima, nimirum ad ipsum vsque actum depositionis de Regnis (si actus dicendus sit, non priuatio, depositio de regno.) Ac Reges quidem, personæ omnium summæ; & corona, res Regum summa: priuatio itaque coronæ priuatio summa, summa dico, & summopere eis metuenda. Summa ergo hæc quidem potestas temporalis est, vtpote in summos, & ad summæ rei discrimen summum, quin apex ipse, atque summitas totius potestatis temporalis. Hæc illa est potestas temporalis in Reges, plusquam Regia, quam Tortus vindicatum it Pontifici, quâ scilicet coronas Regum capitibus detrahere, sceptra manibus excutere, trabeas humeris reuellere, ipsósque adeo Reges & Monarchas summos de solijs deturbare, & ad vsque scabellum Pontificum humiliare posit. Regnum res temporalis est: rei temporalis priuatio, pœna temporalis: Temporalis pœna temporali iure infligitur: temporale per eum ius dicitur, qui in temporalibus superior est. Id ergo agitur, vt Regum in temporalibus superior Papa sit, in Reges temporale ius habeat, temporalem ei in Reges, & regna Regum, potestatem exercere fas sit. Et hæc iam potestas Catholicæ fidei, procul dubio, pars magna est, & fundata in Scripturis; vah quàm aperte. Atqui nos vt demus tibi, fidem esse aliquam vestris hominibus de spirituali primatu: de potestate temporali, & præsertim priuatiuâ hac potestate, nunquam dabimus: imò, nec vestri vnquam hoc homines datum sunt.
units.tr: Since it is now agreed that this power is temporal, I ask further: what kind of temporal power is it? Is it the kind by which the Pope presides and gives judgment in his own dominions, and in his suburbicarian territories, as any temporal prince does? No: it is another power, a far different temporal power, far-reaching and widely spread, over the cities, dominions and all the subjects of kings, indeed over the kings themselves; and not over any kings whatever, but over the greatest of all, namely, up to the very act of deposition from kingdoms (if it is to be called an act, not a deprivation, a deposition from the kingdom). And kings are indeed the highest of persons, and the crown is the highest of royal possessions; the deprivation of the crown is therefore the highest deprivation, the highest I say, and to be feared above all by them. This, then, is indeed a supreme temporal power, since it is exercised over the highest persons, and to the supreme peril of the supreme thing; indeed, it is the very peak and summit of all temporal power. This is that temporal power over kings, more than royal, which Torti claims for the Pope: by it, of course, he may pull crowns from the heads of kings, shake sceptres from their hands, tear robes from their shoulders, and indeed hurl kings and the highest monarchs themselves from their thrones, and humble them down even to the footstool of the Popes. A kingdom is a temporal thing; the deprivation of a temporal thing is a temporal penalty; a temporal penalty is inflicted by temporal right; temporal law is pronounced by one who is superior in temporal matters. The aim, therefore, is that the Pope be superior to kings in temporal matters, that he have temporal right over kings, and that it be lawful for him to exercise temporal power over kings and the kingdoms of kings. And this power, without doubt, is now a great part of the Catholic faith, and is founded in the Scriptures; oh how plainly! Yet, although we grant you that your men have some faith concerning a spiritual primacy, we shall never grant concerning temporal power, and especially this deprivatory power; indeed, your men have never been given it either.

units.la: Potestas hæc est tamen Torto res sacra: at non merè sacra; licèt enim non merè temporalis: temporalis tamen est: at quâ parte temporalis, sacra non est. Sed esto sanè sacra, si voles: multa enim Romæ sacra, quæ nihil ad fidem sanctam & Catholicam, præsertim auri sacra fames, nec minùs sacra fa-mes dominandi; præ quibus, Romæ diu iam nihil sacrum: quo in genere, tua hæc potestas, esto sanè res, si voles, vel sacerrima.
units.tr: This power is nevertheless, as Torto says, a sacred thing; but not merely sacred. For although it is not merely temporal, it is nonetheless temporal, and in so far as it is temporal it is not sacred. But grant, if you like, that it is sacred: for there are many things at Rome that are sacred, which have nothing to do with the holy and Catholic faith, above all the "accursed hunger for gold," and no less the "accursed hunger for domination." In comparison with these, nothing at Rome has been sacred for a long time now; so in this class your power, if you like, is a thing most sacred indeed.

units.la: Etiam cælitus data. Cœlitus autem? Quando? Quandone audivit vocem de cœlo, Surge Petre, occide? Unum enim hoc, illi de cælo dictum: cætera quæ accepit, quæ audivit, de clanibus, de ovibus, super terram data, & dicta sunt omnia: illa una est, quæ cælitus data est; atque hoc nuper Baronium in septicipiti somniasse Parnasso memini. De quâ nihil opus est addas, quòd nullus tam mortalium vel tollere vel minuere possit. Nam Theologi illam Veneti, Galli, Germani, valdè minuerunt non ita pridem, addo etiam, penitus iam pœne sustulerunt.
units.tr: "Also given from heaven." From heaven? When? "Did he ever hear a voice from heaven, saying, Rise, Peter, and kill?" For that one saying alone was spoken to him from heaven; all the rest that he received and heard, concerning "the thieves and the sheep," were given and spoken upon the earth. That one alone was given from heaven; and I remember that Baronius lately dreamed this on the two-peaked Parnassus. Nothing need be added about it, since "no mortal could either remove or diminish it." For the theologians of Venice, France and Germany have greatly diminished it not long ago, and I add that they have now almost entirely abolished it.

units.la: Ac tu ipse quidem huic partui tuo malè videris ominari. Nam priusquam edis in lucem, vel eius nomen nominas, præfaris de eo parum honorificè; nempe, nec quomodo potestas hæc accipi debeat, nec qua de causa exerceri, convenire adhuc inter Theologos & Jurisconsultos. Ain'? non convenit de modo, de causis, cùm tamen de fide Catholica sit scilicet, & apertissimè fundata in Scripturis? Egregiam verò potestatem, & omnibus fide Catholicâ credendam; de cuius tamen modo, quo accipienda; causis, ob quas adhibenda, etiamnum post mille sexcentos annos adhuc disputatur. Sed quid ita tandem duo illa, de modo, de causis, sic leviter pede transilis? Nihilne in modo, nihil in causis momenti apud te? Tuâ scilicet, quo modo habeat Pontifex tuus, nihil refert, habeat modò potestatem hanc: nec justa sit causa, an injusta, propter quam exerceat, tantùm ut exerceat Pontifex ubi volet, potestatem. Atqui nobis momentum magnum in modo, in causis hijs. Quare moneo hic jam; conveniemus te post de utrisque: nec enim sic leviter transeunda sunt, quin necessarium hoc loco de iis disputare.
units.tr: You yourself seem to have given an ill omen for this offspring of yours. For before you bring it into the light, or even name it, you speak of it rather disparagingly: namely, that how this power ought to be received, and for what cause it should be exercised, are still matters of dispute among the theologians and jurists. Do you say so? Is there no agreement about the mode and the causes, though it is surely a matter of Catholic faith and most clearly founded in Scripture? A splendid power indeed, to be believed by all in the Catholic faith; yet about its mode, how it is to be received, and its causes, for which it is to be applied, it is still disputed even after sixteen hundred years. But why, pray, do you skip so lightly past those two things, the mode and the causes? Are the mode and the causes of no weight with you? Of course, you think it makes no difference in what way your Pontiff holds this power, so long as he holds it; nor whether the cause for which he exercises it is just or unjust, provided only that the Pontiff exercises his power wherever he wishes. But to us the mode and the causes are of great weight. Therefore I warn you now: we will meet you later on both points; for they must not be passed over so lightly, since it is necessary to dispute about them here.

units.la: Verùm enim ut de modo, de causis non conveniat, de re inter omnes conuenit; posse scilicet Pontificem Maximum haereticos Principes iure deponere. Quorsum hoc iam, conuenit inter omnes, si de fide Catholica est? Ecquid de fide Catholica interdum apud vos non conuenit? Vllane dissentio de rebus fidei? Quid ergo attinet ista dicere, conuenit inter omnes, cùm de fide Catholica esse contendas? Enimuerò, non si aliquà de re conuenit, statim de fide est: de multis conuenit, quae tamen de fide non sunt, in fidem non veniunt, infra fidem subsistunt, qualis haec de potestate temporali. Ea enim certè, recepta potiùs opinio dicenda, quàm caput fidei; & alicubi in Theologiâ vestrâ locum habere potest, quae habitus est conclusionum; in fide non potest, quae habitus est principiorum. Quae receptae apud vos opiniones sunt, de iis forte inter omnes conuenit: at ex tamen de fide non sunt. Atqui de Catholicâ fide dixti modò potestatem hanc esse: iamne sat putas, si de eâ conueniat modo? nec dum ergo fixus Torto scopus: modò fidem Catholicam crepuit, iam sat illi si de eâ conueniat, si inter receptas opiniones locum habeat. Quanquam, quod mox doceo, tantùm abest, ut sit de fide, ut etiam nec inter opiniones illas annumeranda sit.
units.tr: But even if there is no agreement about the mode and the causes, there is agreement among all about the thing itself: that the Supreme Pontiff can lawfully depose heretical princes. Why bring this up now, "there is agreement among all," if it is a matter of Catholic faith? Is there never disagreement among you about matters of Catholic faith? Is there any dissent about matters of faith? Why, then, do you say "there is agreement among all," when you contend that it is a matter of Catholic faith? Indeed, it does not follow that because there is agreement about something, it is at once a matter of faith: there is agreement about many things which are nonetheless not of faith, which do not come into the faith, but remain beneath the faith; such is this matter of "temporal power." For this is certainly to be called a received opinion rather than an article of faith; and it can have a place somewhere in your theology, since it is a habit of conclusions, but it cannot have a place in faith, which is a habit of principles. As for the opinions received among you, perhaps there is agreement about them among all; yet they are not therefore matters of faith. But you have just said that this power is a matter of the Catholic faith: do you think it is enough if there is agreement about it merely as such? So the aim of Torto is not yet fixed: he has just clamoured about the Catholic faith; now it is enough for him if there is agreement about it, if it has a place among the received opinions. Yet, as I shall presently show, it is so far from being a matter of faith that it is not even to be counted among those opinions.

units.la: Sed vbi tibi animus, cum sic instituisti thesin tuam hijs terminis, Posse Pontificem Principes haereticos iure deponere? Perinde enim hoc intelligi, perinde explicari potest, ut illud Delphicum, Aeacidem Romanos vincere posse, tam ut Aeacides Romanos, quàm ut Romani illum: Itidem hic, tam ut Principes Pontifice possint deponere, quàm ut Pontifex illos, atque itâ eludi tota res tam stera: quod fuit ergo à te malè prouisum, & positum terminus parum magistralibus. Verùm videtis tu quidem, ita diu aequiuocis tuis assuevisse, ut nec iam, cum tanti momenti res agitur, repentè vniuocus prodire possis.
units.tr: But where has your courage gone, when you have framed your thesis in these terms: "The Pontiff can lawfully depose heretical princes"? For this can be understood and explained just as well as that Delphic oracle, "The Aeacid can conquer the Romans": understood either as "the Aeacid can conquer the Romans" or as "the Romans can conquer the Aeacid." So too here: it can be explained either as "princes can depose the Pontiff" or as "the Pontiff can depose princes," and thus the whole matter is rendered ambiguous. This was therefore badly provided for by you, and you set down terms of little scholastic precision. But you yourselves see that you have grown so accustomed to your equivocations that, when a matter of such importance is in hand, you cannot suddenly come forward unambiguously.

units.la: Quid verò illud, de quo ita inter omnes conuenit? Posse Pontificem Maximum Principes iure deponere. Ain' verò? Conuenit de hoc inter omnes? Iam ne hoc nuper? non enim certè olim haec de re inter omnes conueniebat; non inter eos, quos, inter omnes haec causa tangit maximè, Principes, dico, vestros Catholicos, & Pontificem. Etiamne inter hos conuênit vnquam, ut si quando Papa deponere, illi deponi vellent, & loco cederent statim latâ sententiâ? Per tot secula merè Catholica, diu ante natos Reformatores istos, ecquis unquam Papa deposuit Regem ex hoc conuento, sine vi? Ecquis virtute clauium Petri, sine gladio Pauli? Ecquis Rex, audita Papæ sententia, statim coronam cum sceptro deposuit, statim potestatem hanc sacram, & cælitus datam, agnouit? Non est factum. Quare autem non, si inter omnes conuenit, Posse eum Reges iure deponere? Nostro hoc seculo, faciat, cùm volet, periculum inter Catholicos suos: non reperiet Regem tam Catholicum, non tam Christianum Regem, etsi vel maximè Christianum, qui morem gesturus sit. Sentiet me vera vaticinari, non conuenturos hac de re, præcipue autem non illos, inter quos de eâ omnium maximè conuentum oportuit.
units.tr: But what is that thing about which there is so much agreement among all: "that the Supreme Pontiff can lawfully depose princes"? Do you say so? "Is there agreement among all about this?" Has there been agreement about it only lately? For certainly it was not agreed of old "about this matter among all"; not among those whom this cause touches most of all, the princes, I mean your Catholic princes, and the Pontiff. Has there ever been agreement even among these, that if the Pope wished to depose someone, and they wished to be deposed, they would at once give up their place upon the sentence being pronounced? Through so many centuries, purely Catholic, long before those Reformers were born, did any Pope ever depose a king by this authority, without force? Did any by the power of the keys of Peter, without the sword of Paul? Did any king, on hearing the Pope's sentence, at once lay down his crown with the sceptre, and at once acknowledge this sacred power given from heaven? It has not been done. Why then, if there is agreement among all that he can lawfully depose kings, does he not let him make the attempt, whenever he wishes, among his own Catholics? He will not find a king so Catholic, not so Christian a king, though most Christian, who will be disposed to comply. He will feel that I prophesy truly: they will not agree about this matter, and especially not those among whom agreement above all was needed.

units.la: At cùm dixti Omnes, id voluisti, Theologos & Iurisconsultos omnes. Nec sic feres tamen? Nego, vel inter hos. Olim nullus in mundo Theologus, vel Iurisconsultus, Lutheranus, nec tamen unquam Pontifex potestate hac suâ sacrâ & cælitus datâ uti voluit Reges deponendi, quin aliquis semper Theologus exturerit, puta Canonici Leodienses, Conradus Traiectensis, Guliclmus Occham; aliquis Iurisconsultus semper, puta Venericus Vercellensis, Waltramus Naumburgensis, Petrus de Vineis, qui pendente lite opposuerit se huic tam sacræ potestati, eamque nec sacram, nec cœlestem esse, sacramento contenderit. Quare, ludis nos Matthæe, ludis certè; & cùm rem planam, rem confessam pollicitus es, reponis controuersam, quamque nullus mortalium, quando eos hæc causa tetigit, aut ferre unquam voluit, aut agnoscere.
units.tr: But when you said "all," you meant all theologians and jurists. Will you not even so give way? I deny it, even among these. Formerly there was no theologian or jurist in the world, Lutheran or otherwise, who did not reject this power, though the Pontiff never wished to use his sacred power given from heaven to depose kings; there was always some theologian who objected, for example the canons of Liège, Conrad of Utrecht, William of Ockham; there was always some jurist, for example Vinericus of Vercelli, Waltram of Naumburg, Peter de Vinea, who while the suit was pending opposed himself to this so sacred power, and contended on oath that it was neither sacred nor heavenly. Therefore, Matthew, you mock us, you certainly mock us; and when you promised a plain matter, a matter admitted, you put forward something disputed, which no mortal, whenever this cause has touched them, has ever wished either to bear or to acknowledge.

units.la: At enim hij, quos nominati, vel sapiunt hæresin, vel olent schisma. Vis ergo putè Catholicos? Quid tibi de Iohanne Parisiensi videtur, de Iacobo Almain, de Iohanne Maiore, Theologis? Quid de Cardinale Zabarella, Alberico de Rosate, Antonio à Rosellis, Iurisconsultis? An suspectæ unquam fidei? Annon puti puti Catholici? Notum tamen, de hac temporali Papæ potestate, non satis inter vos atq; illos conuenire.
units.tr: But surely those whom you named either smell of heresy or savour of schism. Do you therefore wish us to consider them Catholics? What do you think of John of Paris, of James Almain, of John Major, theologians? What of Cardinal Zabarella, Alberic of Rosate, Antonio of Rosellis, jurists? Were they ever suspect in faith? Are they not, I ask, considered Catholics? Yet it is well known that about this temporal power of the Pope, they did not sufficiently agree with you and with those others.

units.la: Etiamne (ô bone) Sorbona Parisiensis Catholica tibi non videtur? Numquid in illâ, aut odor ullus hæresis, aut sapor schismatis? Adi ergo illam, sodes, si placet, ibíque percontare, quid factum memoriâ nostrâ Iohanni Tanquerello, qui potestatem hanc, de quâ nimirum conuenit inter omnes, vindi-
units.tr: Is not even the Sorbonne of Paris (good heavens!) Catholic in your eyes? Is there in it any smell of heresy, or any savour of schism? Go to it then, I pray you, if you please, and there ask what was done in our own memory to John Tanquerel, who wished to defend against the Pontiff this very power about which "there is agreement among all," and openly to defend the thesis that the Pope can deprive princes who are rebellious to his commands of their kingdom and dignities. Ask whether he went unpunished; ask whether it did not return upon him through the throat...

units.la: [The word "exturerit" and the name "Guliclmus" are doubtful readings; see notes.] care Pontifici voluit, & palam defendere thesin hanc, Papa Principes suis praeceptu rebelles, regno & dignitatibus privare potesit. Quære an impune tulerit? Quære annon redierit ei per iugulum thesis illa? Annon haec illius palinodia? Hanc à se thesin temerè & inconsideratè disputatam: sententiam verò illi contrariam verissimam esse. Audin'? sententiam contrariam verissimam. Non est ergo tua haec de fide Catholicâ: vel Sorbonâ iudice. Vis quod recens adhuc magis sit exemplum? Et illud ergo scisscitare, quid Florentino Iacobo & Tho. Blanzio factum, cum id modò proponerent, Pontifex temporalem in omnes habet potestatem: annon in causâ consimili, consimilis illis poena cum Tanquerello? Vides abnegatam in Sorbonâ Catholicam fidem tuam, bis abnegatam; primò, anno 1561. iterum, anno 1595: relapsos ibi Theologos denuò in tuam fidei abnegationem: In Sorbona igitur friget fides haec. At tu Sorbonam cave irritatsis[?], cave verò habeas honorificè; magno semper in precio habiti Doctores illi, & vel ipsi Roma metuendi; inter quos tamen (uti vides) hac de re tecum non convenit. Quin alia est apud Papienses de hoc, alia apud Parisienses Catholica fides. At Catholica fides, nisi vnica, non solebat esse.
units.tr: [The word "exturerit" and the name "Guliclmus" are doubtful readings; see notes.] to defend this thesis openly, that the Pope can deprive rebellious princes of their kingdom and dignities for their disobedience. Ask whether he got away with it unpunished. Ask whether that thesis did not return to strangle him. Was this not his recantation? "That thesis, rashly and inconsiderately argued by me; the opposite opinion is most true." Do you hear? "The opposite opinion is most true." This, then, is not your doctrine of the Catholic faith, at least by the judgment of the Sorbonne. Would you like a more recent example still? Then ask also what happened to Florentinus Jacobus and Thomas Blanzius, when they put forward this proposition: "The Pope has temporal power over all." Was it not, in a similar case, a similar punishment as with Tanquerellus? You see that your Catholic faith has been disowned in the Sorbonne, disowned twice: first in the year 1561, and again in 1595, when the theologians there relapsed into the same disowning of your faith. In the Sorbonne, then, this faith grows cold. Yet beware of provoking the Sorbonne, and beware of not holding them in honour; those doctors have always been held in high regard, and even Rome itself fears them; and yet, as you see, on this matter they do not agree with you. Indeed, there is one Catholic faith among the Papists of Pavia and another among the Parisians. But the Catholic faith was not wont to be anything but one.

units.la: Addo etiam & de nostris specimen, ut videas, nec inter vos atque eos hac de re convenire. Sic enim Iesuita Iacobus Bolgrauius scripto suo, quod etiam apud nos extat manu ipsius consignatum. {a}Existimare se, idq; coram Deo, Pontifici, nec de facto, nec de iure, authoritatem vllam esse soluendi, vel Regine subditos, vel alterius cuiusquam Christiani Principis, à fidelitate suâ; pro quacunque demum causâ: idq; sibi ita intimè in conscientiâ persuasum esse. Reginam & esse Principem legitimam, & pro tali habendam esse, non obstante Bullâ seu sententiâ quanu[?], quam Papa tulit, feret, poteritue ferre in posterum: parutamq;[?] esse se, vt hoc (si ita opus) vel iureiurando testetur. Satin' diserte hoc? En ergo, nec Iesuitis vestris vobiscum in hac de re convenit. Possem & Eduardi Rishtoni, possem & Henrici Ortoni, in eandem sententiam scriptâ subijcere, & ipsâ, vbi se res dabit, proserenda. Hartum verò ipse pòst laudâs; audi ergo quem laudas Hartum, cuius excusa iamdudum hac de re prostat sententia. {b}Verè (inquit) affirmaui, usurpari praeter ius saque à Póntifice potestatem Principes deponendi; verè enim id sentio, nempe, tametsi dignior multò, & sublimior sit potestas spiritualis temporali: esse tamen utramque à Deo, nec alteram ab altera pendere. Conclusionem autem inde hanc elicio; eorum sententiam, qui Pontificem statuunt supra Reges & Principes Dominum temporalem esse, nihil prorsus vel rationi habere, vel etiam probabilitatis. Nihil enim Pontifici esse quod cum Regibus agat, vel ijs quae Regum sunt; civiliter quidem: tantum abest, ut deponere possit eos, vel de eorum Regnis statuere. Pars haec Pontificij muneris nulla est. Ac meo quidem judicio, paternum Ecclesia regimen habet, principatum mundi non habet. Nec enim talem sibi titulum Christus unquam vendicavit, nec vel Petro eum contulit, vel cuiquam discipulorum. Hunc verò tu testem, spero, non invitus admittes, laudatum à te, Torte, laudato viro. Nec alia Archipresbytero vestro mens, nec alia nonnullis hic illius compresbyteris. Nec minùs ergo hic tibi à tuis in Britannià, quàm in Galliâ contradicitur, ut parum quidem à te consideratè positum fuerit, de potestate hac inter omnes convenire.
units.tr: I will add also a specimen from our own side, so that you may see that you and they do not agree on this matter either. For the Jesuit James Bolgrau, in his writing, which is also extant among us, signed with his own hand, says: {a}"He judges, and this before God, that neither in fact nor in right has the Pope any authority to release the subjects of the Queen, or of any other Christian prince, from their allegiance, for whatever cause at all; and that he is so inwardly persuaded in his conscience. That the Queen is and ought to be held the lawful prince, notwithstanding any bull or sentence which the Pope has pronounced, or will pronounce, or may be able to pronounce in the future; and that he is prepared to attest this even by oath, if need be." Is that plain enough? Here, then, your Jesuits do not agree with you on this matter either. I could also set down in writing the opinions of Edward Rishton and Henry Orton to the same effect, and bring them forward when the occasion arises. But Hart you yourself praise; hear then what that Hart, whose writing on this matter has long been published, says: {b}"I have truly affirmed (he says) that the power of deposing princes is usurped by the Pope beyond and against right; for I truly think so, namely, that although spiritual power is far more worthy and more sublime than temporal, yet both are from God, and neither depends on the other. From this I draw the conclusion that the opinion of those who hold that the Pope, above kings and princes, is a temporal lord, has no basis at all either in reason or even in probability. For the Pope has nothing to do with kings, or with what belongs to kings, in civil matters; so far is it from being the case that he can depose them or decide concerning their kingdoms. This part of the papal office is nothing. And in my judgment, the Church has a paternal government; it does not have a principality of the world. For Christ never claimed such a title for himself, nor conferred it on Peter or on any of the disciples." This witness, I hope, you will not unwillingly admit, Torte, praised by you, and a man you praise. Nor is the mind of your Archpresbyter any different, nor that of some of his fellow presbyters here. Therefore it is contradicted here by your own people in Britain no less than in France; so that it was put forward by you with little careful consideration, when you say that this power is "agreed upon by all."

units.la: Age, convenio te domi iam iu Sacello tuo, idque de modo primùm, de quo ipse nobis initio scrupulum iniecisti: post etiam, de causis denuo conventuri. Quid? Tune non putas necessarium hoc loco disputare de modo? Credo equidem; nec iniuriâ. Nam si habeat eam Pontifex, si accipiat, id tibi satis est; quo modo autem accipiat, aut habeat, non laboras. Scis hoc; esse illi potestatem: quomodo fit; nec scis, nec curas. Atqui nos magnopere referre dicimus, non ut habeat tantùm, sed ut habeat quo oportet modo. Quare & de modo putamus pernecessarium hoc loco pauca interrogare. Nam si duplex tantùm est potestatem hanc habendi modus, rectus & obliquus; nec recto habeat, (ut quidam de vobis) nec obliquo (ut alij) si neutro habeat, ne habet quidem. Et quidem latet hic anguis aliquis, quòd tu ita deprecaris de modo; eò magis libet inquirere, quò tu minùs hoc vis, ut quae sint in fide hac vestrâ Catholicâ trepidationes vestrae, videat lector, & si volet, rideat. Volo ergo paulisper percontari, & primùm, ecquid inter Dominum & te hac de re conveniat. Certè is, nisi mutauit in causâ, sic lusit olim, nondum Cardinalis, de hac potestate, Non potest Papa, ut Papa, ordinariè temporales Principes deponendi; ut Papa, ordinariè temporales Principes deponere, etiam iusta de causa, tanquam Iudex ordinarius, nec ordinarie iudicare de rebus temporalibus.
units.tr: Come now, I meet you at home, already in your little chapel, and first about the manner, of which you yourself at the outset threw a doubt upon us; afterwards we shall come back to the causes. What? Do you not think it necessary to dispute about the manner at this point? I believe so, and not without reason. For if the Pope has this power, if he receives it, that is enough for you; but you do not trouble yourself about how he receives or has it. You know this: that he has the power; how it comes about, you neither know nor care. And yet we say it matters greatly, not only that he has it, but that he has it in the manner he ought. Therefore we think it most necessary at this point to ask a few questions about the manner as well. For if there is only this twofold manner of having this power, the direct and the indirect, then if he has it neither directly (as some of you say) nor indirectly (as others), if he has it in neither way, he does not have it at all. And indeed some snake lies hidden here, in that you so deprecate discussion of the manner; the more I am inclined to inquire, the less you wish it, so that the reader may see what the anxieties of your Catholic faith are, and, if he wishes, laugh at them. So I want to ask a little, and first whether there is agreement between your Lord and you on this matter. Certainly he, unless he has changed his mind on the question, once played thus, not yet a cardinal, about this power: "The Pope, as Pope, cannot ordinarily depose temporal princes; but as Pope he can ordinarily depose temporal princes, even for a just cause, as an ordinary judge, nor ordinarily judge in temporal matters."

units.la: Non ordinariè (dices) posse, at extraordinariè posse convenit. Neid quidem. Omnis enim Pontificis potestas, mediante Petro. Quæro igitur, in Petro potestas hæc ordinaria fuerit, an extraordinaria? Ordinaria? Atqui tum ordinaria est in Pontifice, si in Petro fuit; fas Petro, fas Pontifici ordinariè deponere: id quod negat Dominus tuus. Extraordinaria? At Extraordinaria potestas non transit in successorem. Ita nec ordinariè, nec extraordinariè.
units.tr: You will say that he cannot "ordinarily", but that he can "extraordinarily"; that too is agreed. No indeed. For all the power of the Pope is through Peter. I ask then: was this power in Peter ordinary or extraordinary? Ordinary? But then it is ordinary in the Pope, if it was in Peter; it was lawful for Peter, and lawful for the Pope, to depose ordinarily; which your Lord denies. Extraordinary? But extraordinary power does not pass to a successor. So neither ordinarily nor extraordinarily.

units.la: Dices forte illud, Si non potest ut Papa, at ut {a}Princeps spiritualis potest. Quo, tanquam sæpiè atramento, offucias fecit lectori Dominus tuus, atque elapsus est. Consule ergo Dominum de hoc, ubi tam diu subsitit Principatus iste spiritualis à Papatu distinctus. Quando, & per quæ verba institutus? Quis illum mortalium vidit vel per somnium, antequam venisset Domino tuo in mentem, Principatum hunc creare de novo? Etiam id, eò forte, ut cum opus est, illuderet & Papæ ipsi distinctionem hanc suâ. Eundem enim per omnia, cùm illi visum fuerit, tenebit esse Papatum & Principatum, ut nec Principi spiritualis liceat deinceps, quod Papa non licet.
units.tr: Perhaps you will say that, "If he cannot as Pope, yet as {a}spiritual prince he can." Here your Lord, as often with ink, has made a fog for the reader and has slipped away. Consult your Lord then about this: where has this spiritual principality, distinct from the papacy, stood so long? When and by what words was it instituted? Which of mortals has seen it, even in a dream, before it came into your Lord's mind to create this principality anew? He perhaps did it so that, when need arose, he might also deceive the Pope himself with his own distinction. For he will hold, in all respects, that when it seems good to him, the papacy and the principality are one and the same, so that the spiritual prince may not thereafter do what the Pope may not do.

units.la: Sed nouus iste spiritualis Princeps, habetne potestatem hanc, ut potestas haberi amat, directè? Caue autem dixeris directè; respicit te, sublato digito, Dominus tuus. Ille verò, etsi valdè vellet, tamen per rectas lineas perducere non potest ad Principem suum spiritualem potestatem hanc; attraxit saltem per obliquum ductum. Præiuit tibi viam, nec tu plus audebis sapere quàm ille, nempe {b}indirectè competere; ut verò indirectè dicas, rectè tibi convenit qui Tortus es, quasi dicas potestatem quandam, verùm non directam, sed obliquam & tortam; In ordine quidem ad bonum spirituale, quare extra ordinem spiritualium; Alioquin potestas ipsa spiritualis si esset, ad spiritualia illum ordinari nihil opus, quorum ipsa per se in serie esset, atque ordine directo.
units.tr: But this new {a}spiritual prince: does he have this power, as power loves to be had, "directly"? Beware, however, of saying "directly"; your Lord, lifting his finger, looks at you. He indeed, although he would very much wish it, still cannot bring this power by straight lines to his spiritual prince; he has at least drawn it by an oblique course. He has gone before you on the way, and you will not dare to be wiser than he, namely, that it belongs {b}"indirectly"; and to say "indirectly" is fitting for you, who are Tortus, as if you were to say some power, but not direct, rather oblique and twisted: "in relation indeed to spiritual good", and hence outside the order of spiritual things. Otherwise, if the power itself were spiritual, there would be no need for him to be ordered to spiritual things, whose order it would itself be, and which lies in a direct series and order.

units.la: Interim adverte quæso, quò sese adigant homines hij in suâ Catholicâ fide; Credis tu esse in Papâ potestatem deponendi Reges? In Papane? In Papa, credo, {c}non tamen ut Papa. Sed anne potestatem credis? Certè potestatem, {d}saltem quandam. Illamne quandam, an temporalem? Temporalem, sed non mere tamen. Sed vel illam absolute in eo putas esse? Non sed {e}aliquo modo, {f}quadamtenus. Quomodo autem? direcie ne & proprie? Non, sed {g}saltem indirecte {h}& improprie. Sed vel sic, an perpetuo? Non, sed casualiter, & incidenter. Tuam fidem Torte[?]: audi iam fidem tuam. Credo, quod Papa, non vt Papa, habet aliquo quidem modo, sed modo tamen indirecto, potestatem, saltem quandam; temporalem, sed non mere; nec absolutam, sed adaliquid relatam; nec perpetuam, sed casualem. Sed dicdum, obsecro, hoc rursum. Omniane haec de fide Catholica? Vah; quam vero dictas nobis fidem Catholicam, ita ex obliquis, tortis, indirectis, improprijs, casualibus, quadamtenus consistentem; de potestate [saltem quadam, temporali, non tamen mere, in Papa, non tamen vt Papa, idque non absolute, sed aliquo modo, nempe indirecto & improprio, nec perpetuo tamen, sed tantum casuali?] Praestaret omnino, fidem de potestate hac nullam habere, quamtalem; & prorsus dimittere potestatem illam, quam sic retinere. Sed retinere tamen animum Pontifici, quo sic excurrere possit interdum in Principes; minus tamen caute hoc: nam si indirecte habet potestatem temporalem Papa, quidni & Principes per eundem ductum habeant & ipsi indirecte quoque spiritualem, vt & illis incidenter agere cum Papa liceat? quale nescio quid tentatum in Synodo Constantiensi; praestaret forte hunc lapidem non moyere: Latam interim (vt initio dixi) largam, & laxam, ac plane [illegible, ~8 letters] id est, abusiuam fidem habetis, quae potestatem hanc habeat pro obiecto; sed aptam tamen, abusiuam nempe fidem, de abusiua potestate.
units.tr: In the meantime, I beg you to notice where these men drive themselves in their Catholic faith. Do you believe that the Pope has the power to depose kings? In the Pope, you say? In the Pope, I believe, but not as Pope. But do you believe it is a power? Certainly a power, at least some kind of power. Some such power, or a temporal one? A temporal one, but not purely so. But do you think he has it absolutely? No, but in some way, to some extent. But in what way? Directly and properly? No, but at least indirectly and improperly. But even so, is it perpetual? No, but casually and incidentally. Hear now your faith, Torte: "I believe that the Pope, not as Pope, has in some way, but in an indirect way, a power, at least some kind of power; a temporal power, but not purely so; neither absolute, but related to something; nor perpetual, but casual." But tell me again, I beg you: are all these things part of the Catholic faith? Alas, what a Catholic faith you tell us, made up of oblique, twisted, indirect, improper, casual and somewhat unstable elements, concerning a power [at least some kind of power, temporal, not purely so, in the Pope, not as Pope, and that not absolutely but in some way, namely indirectly and improperly, nor yet perpetually, but only casually?] It would be altogether better to have no such faith about this power at all, and to give up entirely the power which is retained in this way. Yet let the Pontiff keep the disposition by which he may now and then make sallies against princes, though he should do this with less caution: for if the Pope has temporal power indirectly, why should not princes also have spiritual power indirectly by the same reasoning, so that it may be lawful for them to act incidentally against the Pope? Something of this kind was attempted at the Council of Constance; perhaps it would be better not to move this stone. Meanwhile, as I said at the start, you have a faith that is broad, loose and plainly [illegible], that is, abusive, which holds this power as its object; yet it is a fitting faith, namely an abusive faith, concerning an abusive power.

units.la: Sed quid agimus? Etsi enim ad [illegible, ~8 letters] istas deuenimus, quibus nec aranearum telae magis subtiles sunt, indirecte, quodammodo, quadamtenus: tamen nec vel de hijs, vobis inter vos conuenit. Ecce enim, non desunt inter vos, quibus totum hoc displicet, quod dixit Dominus tuus, de obliquitate potestatis huius: inauspicatam hanc vocem indirecte: Christum nunquam quicquam indirecte dedisse: cum vident tam tepide ab eo, tam ieiune tractari negotium hoc tanti momenti, stomachantur plane, etiam publice protestantur, sibi cum Domino tuo non convenire: nec vnus ibi Baronius in acie stat, magna cum illo manus; Carerius, vterque Bofius, Mofconius, Mancinus, Pesantius (& quos dicere longum est) nec cauponantes bellum, aut frigidè rem gerentes, sed pedem pede prementes, librum libro (in quo discordia Cardinales) vt non modò non conueniat de illâ, sed nec spes sit posse vnquam conuenire.
units.tr: But what are we doing? For even if we have arrived at those distinctions, finer than spiders' webs, "indirectly, in some way, to some extent", yet you do not agree among yourselves even about these. For there are not lacking among you those who dislike the whole of what your Lord has said about the indirectness of this power: they dislike this ill-omened word "indirectly", and say that Christ never gave anything indirectly. When they see that this matter of such great importance is handled so tepidly and so meagrely by him, they are plainly indignant, and openly protest that they do not agree with your Lord. Nor does Baronius stand alone in the battle line, with a great band beside him: Carerius, both Bosius, Mosconius, Mancinus, Pesantius (and others too many to name), not hesitating in the war nor conducting it coldly, but pressing foot to foot, book against book (in which the Cardinals disagree), so that they not only do not agree about it, but there is no hope of ever being able to agree.

units.la: Dum sic vtrinque strenuè dimicatur, & hinc Bellarminus ait, illinc Baronius negat; venit mihi in mentem de Aeneâ Sylvio, Cardinale & ipso, & pòst, Pio Papa secundo: Is solitus dicere de donatione Constantini, cautè id prouisum à Pontificibus, vt acris esset vtrinque controuersia, Valerétne donatio illa de iure, annon valeret, quò sic, semper talis donatio facta praesupponi posset; sed tamen ridiculos interim esse Legistas, qui, quae nunquam fuissent facta, ea valeret necne, disputarent. Idem hîc penitùs locum habet; feruere enim scholas & subsellia quotidie de potestate hac Pontificis temporali, directéne illam an indirectè habeat, quò fit extra litem, habere eam Pontificem. Sed non minùs ridiculos hîc Theologos, quàm ibi Legistas, qui quam omninò non habeat, eam directéne habeat an indirectè, sudant nitendo vt se expediant, nec expediunt tamen; sed tot iam secula litigant, & æternùm, credo, litigabunt.
units.tr: While the fight rages so vigorously on both sides, and here Bellarmine says one thing, there Baronius denies it, there comes to my mind the case of Aeneas Silvius, a cardinal and afterwards Pope Pius II. He used to say that concerning the donation of Constantine the Pontiffs had cleverly arranged that the controversy on both sides should be sharp: whether that donation would be valid in law or not, so that such a donation, once made, could always be presupposed; yet meanwhile the lawyers were ridiculous, who argued whether things that had never been made would be valid or not. The same applies entirely here; for the schools and benches seethe daily over this temporal power of the Pontiff, whether he has it directly or indirectly, with the result that it is beyond dispute that the Pontiff has it. But the theologians here are no less ridiculous than the lawyers there, who sweat with struggling to extricate themselves, over whether he has it directly or indirectly, when he does not have it at all; and they still do not extricate themselves; but they have been quarrelling for so many centuries, and will, I believe, quarrel for ever.

units.la: Námque ita se rem habere per omnia, vel inde liquet, quòd non pauci, nec [?] de scholâ nostrâ, quin vestri homines, & qui inter vestros cordati sunt maximè, totum hoc de potestate Papæ temporali, quoúsque se porrigat, controuersum asserunt, etiam extra periculum hæresis controuerti tutò posse, {a}cum nihil dum, hac quidem de re ab Ecclesiâ definitum sit. Certè malâ fide res geritur; nam quod nondùm definiuit Ecclesia, de quo adhuc lis est sub iudice, id ipsum quasi fidei Catholicæ fundamentum, & caput praecipuum obtrudere, malæ fidei est; Torti est; eorum est, qui ludos faciunt humano generi, & dum Papali potestati consulatur, vt caput sit fidei, quæ nec cauda est, siue per rectas lineas, siue per obliquum ductum id fiat, sùsque déque habent
units.tr: For that the matter stands in every respect thus is clear from this: that not a few, and not from our school, but your own people, and those among yours who are most judicious, assert that this whole question concerning the temporal power of the Pope, however far it extends, may safely be disputed even outside the danger of heresy, since nothing has yet been defined by the Church on this matter. Certainly the thing is done in bad faith; for to press as the foundation of the Catholic faith and its chief head what the Church has not yet defined, and what is still a matter in dispute before the judge, is bad faith; it is Torte's way; it belongs to those who make a mockery of the human race, and who, while they consult for the papal power so that it may be the head of the faith, which is not even the tail, whether this is done by straight lines or by oblique course, make light of it and care nothing for it.

units.la: Sed audi etiam; Exortus est è vobis nuper Iesuita (& habet sectatores non paucos) qui cum videret nodosam hanc quæstionem nimis, & laboriosum negotium deponendi Reges, nec modò, multo clamore & rixis in scholâ, sed & multo sanguine & vulneribus in acie staturum; lepidum commentum commentus est, & nouum, sed tamen {a}certum & de fide (vt vestra sunt omnia) & {b}Apostolicæ doctrinæ conforme imprimis & consonum. Is homo deponi vult à vobis hac totâ de re controuersias; Nihil opus esse depositione vllâ, nihil potestate vllâ deponendi; {c}excidere enim Reges statim omni potestate suâ Regiâ (putà vt autumno folia) si à religione Catholicâ manifestè deflexerint, hocque ante sententiam summi Pastoris contra eos prolatam; proin superfluum esse hunc in Pontifice laborem deponendi, superfluam totam, câ de potestate, quæstionem. Vide verò vt expedierit rem Iesuita hic, vt nihil iam opus potestate hac, vt iuretur necne in eam, aut quid eâ fiat iam magnopere curandum non sit.
units.tr: But listen further: a Jesuit has recently risen up from among you (and he has not a few followers), who, seeing that this knotty question and laborious business of deposing kings would stand not only with great clamour and quarrels in the schools, but also with much blood and wounds in the field, has devised a pleasant and new contrivance, which is nonetheless "certain and of the faith" (as all your things are) and "especially agreeable and consonant with apostolic doctrine." This man wishes that the controversies on this whole matter be removed by you: there is no need of any deposition, no need of any power of deposing; for kings fall at once from all their royal power (just as leaves fall in autumn) if they have clearly departed from the Catholic religion, and this before any sentence of the supreme Pastor is pronounced against them; therefore the labour of deposing in the Pontiff is superfluous, and the whole question concerning that power is superfluous. But see how well this Jesuit has managed the matter, so that there is now no need for this power, and it need not greatly concern us whether one swears to it or not, or what becomes of it.

units.la: Sed esto; vt de modo conueneritinter omnes; tamen est & alter iniectus scrupulus à te, Matthæ, atque is quidem partim opportunè, de causis ob quas exerceri possit. Quid tibi autem mentio fuit de eis? Quare non silentio prætereiisti? Quare sic de causis intempestiuè monuisti? iam enim, siquando illam Pontifici in animo exercere, statim lis noua de causis, an iustâ de causâ exerceat; nam si causa minùs iusta, mox quasi brutum fulmen contemnent, vt nuper Nauarra, Galliæ iam & Nauarra Rex; vt nuperrimè Veneti, causati nec modum rectum, nec causam iustam; fiet hinc, vt potestas hæc frustra sit, in actum ne exeat vnquam. Perinde autem esse ne fiat in eo potestas, & ne vllì rei sit; eòdem redeunt defectus potentiæ & actus. Quod vtinam ne excidisset tibi mentio de disputatione istâ causarum: tota enim hæc de causis cognitio (vti tu pro tuâ prudentiâ nosti) longè difficillima est, vt si semel inquirant in eam, & quibus de causis exerceri possit, spes omnino sublata sit, fore, vt vnquam de eâ conueniat inter omnes: multò autem minùs, vt in Catholicam fidem transeat.
units.tr: But grant it; let it be agreed among all on the manner; yet there is also another doubt thrown in by you, Matthew, and indeed partly opportunely, concerning the causes for which it may be exercised. But why did you mention them? Why did you not pass over them in silence? Why did you so untimely warn us about causes? For now, whenever the Pontiff intends to exercise that power, there at once arises a new dispute about causes, whether he exercises it for a just cause; for if the cause is less just, they will soon despise it like an empty thunderbolt, as lately Navarre, both of France and of Navarre, did, and as most recently the Venetians did, alleging neither a right manner nor a just cause; the result will be that this power is in vain and never comes into act. Whether the power exists in him and whether it has any effect amount to the same thing: the defects of power and of act come to the same. Would that the mention of this disputation about causes had not slipped from you: for this whole inquiry into causes (as you know in your prudence) is by far the most difficult; so that if once they begin to inquire into it, and into the causes for which it may be exercised, all hope is utterly removed that there will ever be agreement among all about it; and much less that it will pass over into the Catholic faith.

units.la: Vis dicam quod res est, & quomodo inter vos de potestate ista conuenit? Dum alta pax, dum nihil turbatum est domi, fruuntur liberalitate temporis Principes vestri; non impediunt vos Papi:nsis[?] Theologos, qui estis à Sacellis Cardinalium, vel Bononienses Iurisconsultos, qui sunt in terra Ecclesiæ, quò minùs disserere vobis per otium liceat, de potestate hac in actum haud vnquam perducendâ, plateos cædere, pòst etiam magistralem aliquam conclusionem facere, & de eâ, si vultis, inter vos convenire; Cùm ad rem ventum est, cùm non proximus, sed suus cuique paries ardet, cùm deponi iubetur Princeps quis, Nauarrenus, Hispanus, Gallus, tum demum non ex iure manu confertum, sed magè ferro rem repetent, tum demum non conuênit vnquam, non conuenict[?]; me vide. Si Pontifices Regibus coronas suas, Reges Pontificibus mitras suas deponere iubebunt, & depositis mitras ad sobrietatem sapere; Quod nos iam sentimus, idipsum, cùm non nostra iam res agitur, sed sua, sentient & illi. Dum reliquis in rebus inter eos & Papam bene conuenit, nihil opus inouere hunc lapidem; vbi mota fis, de hac omnium minimè conuenient: Est enim inter opiniones illas vestras, quæ non probantur, nisi dum intra scholæ parietes se continent, vbi prodeunt ad praxim, explodunt[?] statim.
units.tr: Do you want me to say what the matter really is, and how you and your people have come to agree on this power? While peace is deep and nothing at home is disturbed, your princes enjoy the leisure of the times. The Papist theologians, who are in the service of the Cardinals, or the Bolognese jurists, who are in the land of the Church, do not stop you from arguing at your leisure about this power, which is never to be brought into action: you may beat the streets, and even make some learned conclusion about it, and, if you like, reach agreement among yourselves. But when it comes to the point, when it is not the neighbour's wall but each man's own that is on fire, when some prince is ordered to be deposed, a Navarrese, a Spaniard, a Frenchman, then at last they will seek the matter not by the law of the hand-to-hand contest but by the sword, and then at last there will be no agreement, "does not agree"; see for yourself. If the Pontiffs order kings to surrender their crowns, and the kings order the Pontiffs to surrender their mitres and come to their senses, then what we already feel, they too will feel, when the matter at issue is no longer ours but theirs. As long as they agree well with the Pope on other matters, there is no need to stir this stone; once you do stir it, they will agree least of all on this one. For among those opinions of yours, which are not approved except while they stay within the walls of the schools, once they come out into practice, they are immediately exploded.

units.la: Nec defuerunt vnquam Theologi, vel Iurisconsulti, qui secus sentirent: Non Henrico quarto olim, Synodus Wormatiensis 1077. & Brixinensis 1080; non Frederico primo, Synodus Papiensis, 1160: non secundo, Theologi aliqui Gibellini: non Ludouico Bauaro, Synodus Francfordiensis, 1338. qui irent in alia omnia. Neque etiam ætate demum nostrâ defuerunt, qui contra literas, processus in diem cœnæ Gregorij 13. 1580: contra brutum fulmen Sixti quinti 1585: contra bullas monitoriales Gregorij decimiquarti 1591: contra bullam Clementis octaui, pro Rege nouo in Gallia eligendo, 1592. strenuè se opposuerunt, tum Iurisconsulti, tum Theologi, etiam vestri, vt mira sit hominis huius frons, qui scripserit, de hoc inter omnes conuenire. Vel nuper in causâ Venetâ, quàm hac de re conueniat inter omnes, notum iam orbi terrarum, quàm vnanimes tum Theologi & Iurisconsulti fuerint; necdum tamen ventum erat ad deponendi potestatem; hærebant modò in illâ tuâ intrinsecâ potestate, & propriâ excommunicandi; extrinsecam hanc, & impropriam ne attingebant quidem. Quòd nisi cautè Paulus Pontifex rem totam silentio premi, nec ad vlteriora descendi procurâsset; si de depositione, verbum vllum fecisset: quid Patri Paulo, quid reliquis futurum fuisse sentis? Numquid qui sacris interdicenti non paruerunt; Subditis, neparêrent interdicenti unquam paruissent? Res ipsa loquitur,.
units.tr: Nor have there ever been lacking theologians or jurists who thought otherwise. Not under Henry IV of old, the Synod of Worms in 1077 and of Brixen in 1080; not under Frederick I, the Synod of Pavia in 1160; not under Frederick II, certain Ghibelline theologians; not under Louis of Bavaria, the Synod of Frankfurt in 1338, "who went against all the rest." Nor indeed have they been lacking in our own age: against the letters and processes on the day of the Lord's Supper of Gregory XIII in 1580; against the "brutum fulmen" of Sixtus V in 1585; against the monitory bulls of Gregory XIV in 1591; against the bull of Clement VIII on the election of a new king in France in 1592, both jurists and theologians, including your own, have strenuously opposed them. So that the man who wrote "that there is agreement among all on this" has a remarkable brazenness.
