Or lately, in the Venetian cause, how unanimous both theologians and jurists were, is now known to the whole world, yet it had not yet come to the question of deposing power; they were still stuck on that "intrinsic power" of yours and the "proper" power of excommunicating; they did not even touch this extrinsic and improper power. But if Pope Paul had not cautiously made sure the whole matter was buried in silence and that they did not go on to further points, had he made any mention of deposition at all, what do you think would have happened to Pope Paul and to the rest? Did they not obey the interdict of the sacred rites? Would they ever have obeyed an interdict laid on their subjects? The thing itself speaks.

units.la: Sed, deposuit tamen Papa Principes interdum; etiam Principes illum; Quid tum? Non autem hoc sine potestate; Imò aliud vis, aliud potestas. Sic, si bene memini, quodam in loco Dominus tuus. {a}Quòd olim non deposuerit Ecclesia Imperatores Ethnicos & haereticos, id fuit quia deerant vires. Nescio quàm verè illud, vel potiùs scio non verè; nec enim deerant Petro vires contra Neronem, quibus usus contra Ananiam; nec Tertulliani seculo vires deerant, nedum Basilij. Hoc scio verissimè. Quòd, exin deposuerint Papæ Imperatores Christianos, id fuit, quia aderant vires: tota enim in viribus fidei hæc fundata est, nec alia de articulo hoc, nisi quæ per vires fit, fides ulla. Etiam, vires forte si adfuissent Paulo quinto, Veneti hoc iam crederent; quia deerant, articulo huic hactenus credere supersederunt. Certè veri nominis fides cogi non potest: hæc fides, nisi coacta, nulla fuit antehac; nisi cogatur etiam denuo, neque posthæc ulla unquam sutura est.
units.tr: But, you will say, the Pope has nevertheless sometimes deposed princes, and princes have deposed him too. So what? But this was not done without power; rather, the one is one thing, the other is another thing entirely: power. Thus, if I remember rightly, your master says in a certain place: "That the Church did not depose the heathen and heretical emperors in former times was because it lacked the strength." I do not know how true that is, or rather I know it is not true; for Peter did not lack the strength against Nero, the strength he used against Ananias; nor did the strength fail in the age of Tertullian, much less in that of Basil. This I know most certainly. That afterwards the Popes deposed Christian emperors was because the strength was present: for this whole matter is founded on the strength of faith, and there is no other faith on this article except what comes by force. Indeed, had the strength been present for Paul V, the Venetians would now believe this already; because the strength was lacking, they have hitherto refrained from believing this article. Certainly faith of the true name cannot be compelled: this faith, unless it has been compelled, has never existed before; unless it is compelled again, and afterwards too, it will never be at all.

units.la: Collige iam ista si placet, Non conuenire inter omnes de hoc tuo problemate; Non inter Reges vestros Catholicos & Pontificem: Non inter Theologos eorum utrinque & Iurisconsultos, sive qui in lite illa fuerunt, sive qui extra litem: Non inter Papienses, & Parisienses; Non inter Cardinales Baronium & Bellarminum: Non Iesuitis cum illis, sed nec inter se: Nec domi hic apud nos, quibus hæc Tortus scribit: Denique nec opus esse ut conueniat; nihil enim de hac quidem indirectà potestate, directè adhuc definitum. Inter omnes saltem non conuenit. Abi nunc, & sæpe, ac dehinc cautius usurpa vocem istam, inter omnes: Periculosa enim vox omnes, & parciùs adhibenda; à te autem hic, non omninò quidem; præsertim, cùm videas iam de nullo prorsus hic conuenire inter omnes præterquam quod inter omnes non conuenit. De fide Catholicâ quid fiet interim? mutilari illam necesse iam est, & uno saltem articulo minorem esse: De quo enim haud in Symbolo quicquam vel in Scripturis, haud quicquam ab ecclesiâ definitum: illud sanè Catholicæ fidei caput præcipuum esse non posse, vel tu ipse dixeris. Atque ita nullam iam esse Catholicam fidem de potestate hac Pontificia.
units.tr: Gather up these things now, if you please: that there is no agreement among all on this problem of yours; not among your Catholic kings and the Pope; not among their theologians and jurists on either side, whether those who were in that dispute or those who were outside it; not among the Pavians and the Parisians; not among the Cardinals Baronius and Bellarmine; not with the Jesuits, and not even among themselves; nor here at home among us, to whom this Tortus writes. Finally, there is no need for it to be agreed; for nothing has yet been defined directly about this indirect power. At least there is no agreement among all. Go now, and use that phrase "among all" often, and from now on more cautiously: the word "all" is dangerous and must be applied more sparingly; but you, here, not altogether indeed; especially since you see that there is now no agreement at all about anything here, except that there is no agreement among all. What will become of the Catholic faith in the meantime? It must now necessarily be mutilated and made smaller by at least one article: for that article, about which there is nothing in the Creed or in the Scriptures, and which the Church has not defined, can certainly not be the chief head of the Catholic faith, as you yourself would say. And so there is now no Catholic faith concerning this Papal power.

units.la: {a}PArum successit in re tibi; ecquid in ratione magis meliúsuè? addis enim & rationem; Reges scilicet cum hac conditione admitti ad Ecclesiam; ut Christo sceptra subiiciant. Et cum eadem conditione, Pontifices ut Christo pedá sua subijciant, ut hæc ratio, non minùs contra Pontifices militet.
units.tr: You have been as successful in the matter as ever; but is your argument any better? For you also add an argument: "Kings, namely, are admitted to the Church on this condition: that they submit their sceptres to Christ." And on the same condition the Popes submit their feet to Christ, so that this argument militates no less against the Popes.

units.la: Sed excutiamus etiam; Reges, quinè iam sunt, an qui olim fuerunt? Reges enim qui iam sunt cum hac conditione non admitti quis nescit, cùm diu ante ad Ecclesiam admittantur quàm Reges sint? Non enim postquam Reges iam facti sunt, admittuntur ad Ecclesiam: sed postquam ad Ecclesiam admissi sunt, Reges fiunt. Quare ratio hæc tua nihili.
units.tr: But let us examine this too: are they kings who now are, or those who were once? For the kings who now are, who does not know they are not admitted on this condition, since they are admitted to the Church long before they are kings? For it is not after they have already become kings that they are admitted to the Church; rather, after they have been admitted to the Church, they become kings. Wherefore this argument of yours is worth nothing.

units.la: Quodsi de Regibus ijs, qui primi de Ethnicis Christiani facti, intelligi vis conditionem tuam, sic illos tum admissos ad Ecclesiam: dura tibi incumbet provincia probandi quod dicis; vix enim tabulas vllas reperias apud Protonotarios vestros, quibus expressè constet, quâ illi tum conditione admissi fuerint.
units.tr: But if you wish your condition to be understood of those kings who were the first to become Christians from among the heathen, admitted to the Church in that way at that time: a hard task will lie upon you to prove what you say; for you will hardly find any records among your registrars showing expressly on what condition they were then admitted.

units.la: Nisi si quæ in baptismo est, conditionem velis; sed nec sic quicquam efficies: Vnus enim baptismus est semperque fuit, idem prorsus quo illi tum, quo nostri nunc admittuntur in Ecclesiam, vtrobique conditiones eædem. Addo etiam, neque qui tum erant Reges, neque qui iam sunt, neque Regum filios, cùm hac quam dicis conditione baptizari, nec cum alia vlla, quàm quiuis de plebe, quàm cuiusuis de plebefilius: Eisdem abrenunciant, eadem credunt, idem petunt hij & illi; non alia, non plura spondent illi quàm hij, nec est ibi de sceptris verbum vllum. Per baptismum enim admittimur, vt in Christo simus, vbi non est liber vel servus, Rex aut subditus, imò nec mas vel fœmina, quod te Apostolus docere potuit. At nec plebeius ibi quis pacisci tur de fundo suo, si censurâ notatus sit, abdicando: Ne Rex quidem igitur de Regno; nec sub pœnâ fundi perdendi priuatus quicquam spondet: nec Rex {a}sub pœnâ regni perdendi.
units.tr: Unless perhaps you wish the condition to be found in baptism; but you will achieve nothing even so: for there is one baptism, and always has been, exactly the same then as now, by which men are admitted into the Church, and the conditions are the same on both occasions. I add also that neither those who were kings then, nor those who are kings now, nor the sons of kings, when baptised under this condition that you speak of, nor under any other, are different from any man of the common people, or from the son of any common man: they renounce the same things, believe the same things, ask the same things, both these and those; they promise no other things and no more than these, nor is there any word there about sceptres. For through baptism we are admitted that we may be in Christ, "where there is neither bond nor free, neither king nor subject, nor even male or female," as the Apostle could have taught you. But neither does a commoner there bargain about his land, if he has been marked by censure by renouncing it; so neither does a king bargain about his kingdom, nor does he promise anything under penalty of losing it, nor does the king {a} "under penalty of losing his kingdom."

units.la: Quod si in baptismo non fuit, haud vnquam, credo, fidem feceris, extra baptismum delatam illis conditionem hanc, aut Constantino dictum, & prisceis illis Regibus ad Christianismum transeuntibus à paganismo, Tu Constantine, vos Reges ad Ecclesiam admittendi; audite: non eadem sub Christo
units.tr: If you were not baptised, I doubt you will ever win belief by bringing forward that condition, which is not part of baptism, and which is said to have been said to Constantine and those early kings passing from paganism to Christianity: "You, Constantine, and you kings, are to be admitted to the Church; hear this: under Christ the condition of your reign is not the same..."

units.la: {a} Bellarm. de Pont. lib.5. c.7. Christo vobis regnandi conditio est, quæ sub Ioue fuit. Soli iam Ioui sceptra vestra submittitis; nec vllii mortalium ius, nec potestas vlla est, vel in sceptra vestra, vt iubeat deponere, vel in subditos, vt iubeat non parere. Cœlo soli iam debetis innocentiam vestram, nec vllus vobis Pontifex, vel Maximus, maior est. Si Christianis iam esse licebat, narrent vobis; apud Christianos non eodem iure regnatur; non soli Christo sceptra vobis subiicienda Regi immortali: alter est præterea quidam, mortalis homo, tuus nunc, Constantine, subditus, (subditi tui filius, forte stipendijs tuis & altus & educatus, nempe urbis tuæ Romanæ Episcopus;) huic etiam sceptra vestra subijci oportet. Cui nisi tu, nisi omnes situs ex sententia, statim euersa est religio, statim ius illi & potestas in sceptra vestra & solia, vt illa vobis tollere; etiam in subditos ius, vt fide sua erga vos exoluere possit. Nuper quidem sub Regno, Pontificatus; iam sub Pontificatu Regnum: nec soli, iam, Ioui cælesti, sed & Latiali cuidam Veiovi probare vos oportet obsequium vestrum: alioqui, mox sine sceptro, sine subditis, abituri; alioquin, admissio iam vestra ad Ecclesiam, amissione regni vestri constabit. Vllne hoc persuaseris, tam vecordes Reges illos fuisse, vt audita statim lege hac, acquieuerint primo quoque tempore, læti lubentes conditionem acceperint, & certatim; cum gaudio, Pontifici sceptra submiserint?
units.tr: Under Christ you kings have a condition of reigning that is not what you had under Jove. Now you submit your sceptres to Jove alone; no mortal has any right or power over your sceptres to order you to lay them down, or over your subjects to order them not to obey. To heaven alone you now owe your innocence, and no Pontiff, not even the Greatest, is greater than you. If it is permitted to Christians now, let them tell you: among Christians the law of ruling is not the same; your sceptres are not to be submitted to Christ the immortal King alone. There is also another, a mortal man, now your subject, Constantine (the son of your subject, perhaps nourished and reared at your expense, namely the Bishop of your city of Rome): to him also your sceptres must be submitted. If you and all of you do not agree with him, religion is at once overthrown; at once he has the right and power over your sceptres and thrones, to take them from you; and also the right over your subjects, so that he may discharge his faith toward you. Lately the Pontificate was under the kingdom; now the kingdom is under the Pontificate; and you must prove your obedience not only to the heavenly Jove alone, but also to a certain Latin Veiovis: otherwise, soon you will depart without sceptre, without subjects; otherwise, your admission now to the Church will cost you the loss of your kingdom. Can you persuade yourself that those kings were so senseless that, as soon as this law was heard, they immediately acquiesced at the first opportunity, joyfully and willingly accepted the condition, and eagerly, with delight, submitted their sceptres to the Pontiff?

units.la: Vide verò, quò res iam nobis peruenerit. Reges Gentium, ij demum Reges sunt; quorum nullius in manu sceptra, nisi sua; nullius ad nutum subditi, nisi suum: Miselli verò Christianorum Reges precarij sunt, Reges sunt, tantisper dum Pontifici se probent. Nec enim Reges qua Reges, nec subditi qui subditi iam, nisi ad placitum, nec nisi velit iubeat hoc summus Pontifex.
units.tr: Now see where matters have come to us. The kings of the Gentiles are kings indeed; no sceptre is in the hand of any of them except their own, and no subjects obey any nod except their own. But the poor kings of the Christians are tenants at will: they are kings only so long as they prove themselves to the Pontiff. For they are not kings as kings, nor subjects as subjects now, except at the pleasure of the Pontiff, and unless the supreme Pontiff wills and orders it so.

units.la: Quid illi verò in Iaponia Iesuitæ? siccine Regulos, qui inibi sunt, inuitant ad Christum? Hæcine conditione proposita blandiuntur illis, vt Christiani fiant? fungi quidem sunt, si Iesuitam vllum audiunt, vt sic fiant. Illi verò de conditione hac nihil audiunt; nec vel hiscere audet Iesuita quispiam de ea, cum admittendi sunt. Fateri tam omnes, (dicunt) per se esse satis certum, etiamsi Barbari conuertantur ad Christum, non tamen rerum suarum, (nec Regni proin) iure excidere. Prius in rete pertrahi oportet; quo vbi conclusi sunt, tuni demum forte, de conditione hac non nihil audituri: si semel religionem, euertant, id est, si Pontifici morigeri non sint; & vites adsint Iesuitis, vt praestare rem possint.
units.tr: What then of the Jesuits in Japan? Do they invite the petty kings who are there to Christ in this way? Do they flatter them with this condition proposed, so that they become Christians? They indeed are, if they hear any Jesuit, so made. But they hear nothing of this condition; nor does any Jesuit dare even to murmur about it when they are to be admitted. "All men concede," they say, "that it is certain enough in itself that, even if barbarians are converted to Christ, they nevertheless do not lose the right of their own property (and therefore not of their kingdom)." First they must be drawn into the net; and when they are enclosed in it, then perhaps at last they will hear something about this condition, if once they overthrow their religion, that is, if they are not obedient to the Pontiff; and the Jesuits are at hand, so that they can carry the matter through.

units.la: Interim iniuria Christo fit, summa iniuria, dum hoc credere docentur homines de Christo, minui cuiquam, aut deteriore loco ius suum esse, ex eo quòd ad Christum transeat. Quare enim, si Pater, si Dominus, qui fuit Ethnicus, & Christianus iam est, tam pater est, tam Dominus, iam Christianus, quàm ante fuit Ethnicus; Rex idem si faciat, non tam erit Rex sub Christo, quàm fuit sub Ioue? Quid Reges meruere, quid illi tantum committere, vt inter omnes Christianos conditio illorum pessima, soli vt Christum in se iniquiorem sentiant? Si apud Gentes, [illegible, ~6 letters] Si apud Iudæos, summus Sacerdos sub Rege; quid peccavit Caesar, quid Rex, cum Christianus esse voluit, vt quo iure ante vsus est, post vti non liceat: sed excidat statim antiquo iure suo, quod praeter eum Christiano nulli contigit? Omnes enim integro iure stant; solus Rex capite minutus, solus [illegible, ~3 letters].
units.tr: Meanwhile an injury is done to Christ, the greatest injury, while men are taught to believe about Christ that anyone's right is diminished, or is of a worse standing, because he passes over to Christ. For why, if a father, if a lord, who was a Gentile and is now a Christian, is as much father and lord as he was before a Gentile, should a king, if he does the same, not be as much king under Christ as he was under Jove? What have kings deserved, what crime have they committed, that among all Christians their condition alone should be the worst, so that they alone feel Christ to be more unjust to them? If among the Gentiles... If among the Jews the high priest was under the king; what sin did Caesar commit, what did the king commit, when he wished to be a Christian, that the law which he used before should not be lawful for him after, but he should at once lose his ancient right, which no one but a king has suffered as a Christian? For all others stand with their full right; the king alone is reduced in status, the king alone...

units.la: Tu vero veniam dabis, si fidem in hoc tibi Reges non habeant, Christum aequiorem sibi sperent, de illius benignitate prolixius sibi spondeant, de Christo credant quod Christo dignum est: eadem scilicet conditione Reges ab eo accipi, qua reliquos; eadem sakem[?]: potiore aequum erat, sed eadem certe. Nec enim illos vnquam eo adiges, vt credant de Christo, quod si credant, Christum minus diligant necesse est; cui tam vilis sit Regum conditio, vt meliore iure omnes: apud cum[?] sine quàm Reges: vt meliore iure Constantini multo, quàm Constantinus ipse.
units.tr: You, however, will pardon me if kings do not have faith in this, if they hope that Christ will be more fair to them, and promise themselves more liberally from his kindness, and believe about Christ what is worthy of Christ: that kings are received by him on the same condition as the rest; on the same condition... it was fair that they should have a better one, but certainly the same. For he will never drive them to believe what, if they believed it, they would necessarily love Christ less; to whom the condition of kings is so cheap that all have a better right; with whom, without... than kings: so that, by a much better right, Constantine, than Constantine himself.

units.la: Sed age, de conditione non contendam. Æqua enim: certè est, vt sceptra sua Christo subiciant, Regi nempe Regum, & Domino Dominantium. Subiciant ergo sceptra Christo. Quid tum? Nihil agis, nisi opportune tibi subueniat illa tua [id est,] cui multum debes; vt ante fides Catholica, id est, Primatus Pontificis: sic iam Christo sceptra subiicere, id est, Pontifici. Quare autem omissum hic tuum [id est] non oportuit factum. Nec enim si Christo sceptra submittant, satis hoc instituto tuo, nisi concinnâ illâ ὡς[?], Christo, idest, Pontifici, Pontificem stare facias pro Christo. Nam de Christo statum omnes fatebuntur, scio: de Papa censebunt porrò amplius deliberandum, nec statim, censeo, censebunt, eadem haec esse per omnia, Christo sceptra subjicere, & Papa iussu sceptra deponere; neque vero haec eadem, & Ecclesiam admissionem, & Regni amissionem.
units.tr: But come, I will not contend about the condition. For it is surely fair that they should submit their sceptres to Christ, the King of kings and the Lord of lords. Let them therefore submit their sceptres to Christ. What then? You accomplish nothing, unless that thing of yours comes to your aid at the right moment [that is], to which you owe much; namely, as before, the Catholic faith, that is, the primacy of the Pontiff: so now to submit sceptres to Christ, that is, to the Pontiff. Why was your own fact not stated here? For if they submit their sceptres to Christ, that will not satisfy your purpose unless, by that neat ... "Christ, that is, the Pontiff," you make the Pontiff stand for Christ. For all will confess the state of things concerning Christ, I know: they will think further deliberation is needed about the Pope, and not at once, I think, they will think that these things are the same in every respect, "to submit sceptres to Christ" and "by the Pope's order to lay down sceptres"; nor indeed are these the same, "admission to the Church" and "loss of the kingdom."

units.la: Quid si autem Reges, quoad hoc in sceptra ius, Christum abstrahant à Pontifice, Christo se, sceptra, subditos, subjiciunt, cuius de fide, optimè sibi spondeant; de Pontifice nihil audiant, cuius fluxam saepe fidem experti sunt? Audite iam fulminantem Matthaeum. Quodsi nolint, ius est illi, qui toti Ecclesiae vice Christi praeest, eos à communione fidelium segregare, subditosq; interdicere ne pareant. Disjunge vero haec, Matthaeu: primum, Ius est illi qui toti Ecclesiae vice Christi praeest, eos à communione fidelium segregandi; esto illi ius sanè, qui Ecclesiae praeest, ab Ecclesiâ segregandi.
units.tr: But what if kings, as regards this right over sceptres, withdraw Christ from the Pontiff, submit themselves, their sceptres and their subjects to Christ, whose faith they can well promise themselves, and hear nothing from the Pontiff, whose wavering faith they have often experienced? Now hear the thundering Matthew. "But if they are unwilling, he who presides over the whole Church in the place of Christ has the right to separate them from the communion of the faithful, and to forbid subjects to obey them." Now separate these things, Matthew: first, "He who presides over the whole Church in the place of Christ has the right to separate them from the communion of the faithful"; grant indeed to him who presides over the Church the right to separate from the Church.

units.la: Imò ius aliud est, interdicendi etiam subditu ne illi pareant. Imò non est. Nam unde illi ius hoc in subditos? Non enim ex eo quòd praeest Ecclesiæ: nec enim Regum subditi, quâ subditi, Ecclesiæ pars ulla sunt, sed regni. Antequam de Ecclesiâ essent, subditi erant; cùm extra Ecclesiam sunt, nihilominùs manent subditi. Quâ fideles sunt, pars Ecclesiæ sunt; & qui praeest Ecclesiæ, potest, ne in Ecclesiâ appareant, interdicere. Quâ subditi sunt; Regni, Reipublicæ pars sunt; non potest qui Ecclesiæ praeest, nisi & Regno praesit, Regi ne pareant interdicere. Pontifex autem, quanquam toti Ecclesiæ (ut ais) Christi vice praeest, non tamen est orbis Dominus, non toti terrarum orbi, non regnis omnibus Dei vice praeest. At sic oportet, totu terrarum orbi praesse, & subditis, qui usquam sunt, omnibus, & vice Dei praesse, si vult sic totius orbis subditos à Regibus suis segregare; Vicarij Christi titulus nimis angustus ad hoc: maturate quantum potestis, & procudite illum alterum titulum, quem Romæ diu iam habetis sub incude Vicedei: eo semel edito, per Papam Reges regnabunt, & deponet potentes de fede, & reliqua omnia facient, quae Deus ipse; quod erit in rem vestram valde commodum. Christus enim, cuius hîc vicem obtendis, non sic praefuit dum
units.tr: But there is another right, "to forbid even subjects to obey them." No, there is not. For whence does he have this right over subjects? Not from the fact that he presides over the Church: for kings' subjects, as subjects, are not any part of the Church, but of the kingdom. Before they were of the Church, they were subjects; when they are outside the Church, they nonetheless remain subjects. As faithful they are part of the Church; and he who presides over the Church can forbid them to appear in the Church. As subjects they are part of the kingdom, the commonwealth; he who presides over the Church cannot forbid them to obey the king, unless he also presides over the kingdom. The Pontiff, however, although he presides over the whole Church (as you say) in the place of Christ, is nevertheless not the Lord of the world, does not preside over the whole globe, nor over all kingdoms in the place of God. But thus it would be necessary to preside over the whole globe, and over all subjects who are anywhere, and to rule in God's place, if he wishes thus to separate the subjects of the whole world from their kings; the title "Vicar of Christ" is too narrow for this: hasten as much as you can, and forge that other title, which you have long had at Rome under the anvil, "Vice-God"; once that is published, through the Pope kings will reign, and he will depose the powerful from their seats, and will do all the other things that God himself does; which will be very profitable for your cause. For Christ, whose place you put forward here, did not preside in this way while

units.la: Matthaeum: the sign before the name is a printed mark, not a note. in tertis fuit; Regnum quod habuit de mundo non fuit; Regnum quod de mundo fuit, non habuit: Regni, quod non habuit, vices non commisit. Quodsi Pontifici animus est ad regna mundi; est in Evangelio (memini) mentio de quodam, qui regna mundi penes se esse, eáque disponendi ius habere se dixit, cum adeat [?], censeo, cum illo transfigat, illius vices obeat, Vicarius sit. De Christo nihil tale legisse memini; sceptrum illi Rex nemo in manum tradidit, quod vel redderet vel retineret; subditis nulli ne parerent interdixit: nec misit eum pater ad hoc, nec ille quenquam. Est ille quidem Rex Regum; sed qua Regum Rex est, immortalis est; mortalem nullum, proregem habet. Papa mortalis ipse, non alter Christi Vicarius, quàm quà mortalis Christus. Consule Dominum tuum; vera haec agnoscet, & sua.
units.tr: Matthaeum: the sign before the name is a printed mark, not a note. In tertis fuit; the kingdom he had was not of the world; the kingdom which was of the world, he did not have: he did not commit the functions of the kingdom which he did not have. But if the Pontiff's mind is set on the kingdoms of the world, there is (I remember) in the Gospel a mention of a certain man who said that the kingdoms of the world were in his power and that he had the right to dispose of them; let him, I suppose, make a bargain with that man, take over his functions, and be his Vicar. I remember reading nothing of the kind about Christ: no king ever handed him a sceptre to give back or to keep; he forbade subjects to obey no one; nor did the Father send him for this purpose, nor did he send anyone. He is indeed King of kings; but insofar as he is King of kings, he is immortal; he has no mortal viceroy. The Pope is himself mortal, and is no other Vicar of Christ than in so far as Christ was mortal. Consult your Lord; he will acknowledge these things as true, and as his own.

units.la: Cætera autem, ut potes, expedi; Illud scio; vna illa huius loci clausula, vna atque vnica, de sceptris sic (vt ais) Pontifici subijciendis, de interdicto subditis mittendo, ne pareant, procul hinc, procul abigat omnes qui adhuc foris sunt Reges, ne velint intrare in domum vestram Ecclesiae, vbi sic excipientur, vbi Regum sceptra tam nutantia, vbi subditorum fides tam profluuia-fit. Compellat eos intrare Pontisex, si potest: (quod fecit Occidentalis India Regulis) vltro enim haud quisquam iam introibit; si haec introitus conditio, vt de sceptri sui, de populi sui in officio retentione tam incerti pendeant. Subiectio sceptrorum haec Christo, si hoc secum trahat, vt ius accrescat inde Pontifici, quoties illius voluntati repugnatur (toties enim Religio oppugnatur) interdicendi subditis ne diutius pareant, Regibus ne diutiùs Reges sint: doctrinâ hac promulgatâ semel & propagatâ, non multa post sceptra, credo, Christo subijcientur. Quid enim? Rex Ethnicus deponi non potest à Papa, Christianus potest; meliore ergo iure regnatur apud Ethnicos. Quis non dehinc iam (sic vt est) manebit Ethnicus? Subditi, qui Ethnici sunt, officio suo in Reges laxari nequeunt: at Christiani queunt. Quis non subditos suos malit Ethnicos, quàm Christianos? Quis Christianus Rex esse velit, vbi paretur, non paretur, ad nutum Pontificis? Atqui magnos hosce hospites inuitari par erat ad religionem, non inuitos reddi; attrahi pro-popositis inuitamentis, non absterreri obiectis impedimentis; [?]illis, non [?]illicem, non obicem ponere. Quod an tuâ hac tam non æquâ regnandi conditione fiat, viderint ij,
units.tr: As for the rest, sort it out as you can; this I know: that single clause of this passage, one and only, that the sceptres are thus (as you say) to be submitted to the Pope, and an interdict sent to subjects that they should not obey, should drive far from here all those kings who are still outside, lest they wish to enter your house, the Church, where they would be received in such a way, where the sceptres of kings are so unsteady, where the faith of subjects is so fluid. The Pontiff summons them to enter, if he can (as he did with the kinglets of the Western Indies); for no one will now enter of his own accord, if the condition of entrance is that their sceptre and their people's retention in obedience hang so uncertainly. If this submission of sceptres to Christ carries with it that a right accrues thence to the Pontiff whenever his will is resisted (for then religion is attacked) to interdict subjects that they obey no longer, and to strip kings of kingship any longer: once this doctrine is promulgated and propagated, I believe, not many sceptres will afterwards be submitted to Christ. For what? A heathen king cannot be deposed by the Pope; a Christian king can; so kings are ruled among the heathen by a better right. Who will not then (as things stand) remain a heathen? Subjects who are heathen cannot be released from their duty toward their kings; but Christians can. Who would not prefer his subjects heathen rather than Christian? What Christian would wish to be king where obedience is given, or not given, at the nod of the Pontiff? Yet these great guests ought rather to be invited to religion, not made unwilling; they ought to be drawn in by the inducements offered, not scared off by obstacles set before them; they ought to be lured, not barred. Whether this comes about through your so unfair condition of ruling, let those see to it,

units.la: Quos penes arbitrium est & ius & norma regendi.
units.tr: In whose hands is the judgment, and the right and the rule of governing.

units.la: Vide verò, an locus ille in Euangelio non faciat pro vobis, ad rem vestram non sit, Reges Gentium dominantur eorum, & principes eorum potestatem habent ipsorum: Vos autem non sic. Poterit quidem Emanuel Sa vobis breui aliquâ glossâ rem conficere: (Salmeron faceret non inuitus, si in viuis iam esset) quasi diceret, Gentium Reges in subditos suos, merum dominium, absolutam potestatem habent; Illi quidem sic: Atqui vos (glossando vos) vos Reguli potius quàm Reges Christiani, vos non sic: Imperium quantum vel quale Gentium Regibus, frustra exp:ectatis; non decet, non datum est vobis sic regnare; noua religio, nouum regendi ius affert. Nouus quidem hic sensus elici posset è verbis, Vos autem non sic; non sic, vt illi Gentium Reges; dominantur illi suorum, potestatem habent in ipsos: vos autem sic, vt dominetur vestri, potestatem in vos habeat quidam de vestris; sic, vt nisi in illum officiosi sitis, exuendi sitis dominio vestro, & potestate omni. Atque hoc sanè, vt decet & par est Christianos Principes; Reges enim Gentium non gaudent hoc priuilegio; ex gratiâ speciali Christianis hoc Regibus reseruatum est. Expende, quaeso, locum hunc diligentius, qui vos forte praeterijt; paululum tortus valde iuuaret rem vestram, contra Reges istos, quibus tàm infensè infensi istis.
units.tr: But see whether that passage in the Gospel does not favour you, and is not relevant to your case: The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their princes have power over them: but it shall not be so among you. Emanuel Sa will be able to settle the matter for you in a short gloss (Salmeron would do it not unwillingly, if he were still alive), as if he were to say: the kings of the Gentiles have over their subjects mere lordship and absolute power; they indeed are so. But you (glossing "you") are petty princes rather than Christian kings; you are not so: the empire, whatever its size or kind, which the kings of the Gentiles have, you hope for in vain; it is not fitting, it has not been given to you to reign so; the new religion brings a new right of ruling. This new sense could indeed be drawn from the words, But it shall not be so among you: not as with those kings of the Gentiles, who lord it over their own people and have power over them; but among you it shall be such that someone of your own people has power over you, such that, unless you are obedient to him, you are stripped of your lordship and all power. And truly this is fitting and proper for Christian princes; for the kings of the Gentiles do not enjoy this privilege; by special grace this has been reserved for Christian kings. Please weigh this passage more carefully, which perhaps escaped you; a little twisting would greatly help your cause against those kings, with whom you are so hostilely at odds.

units.la: De Ecclesiâ verò viderit Pontifex, & de iure suo excommunicandi: De sceptris suis, de iure subditis suis interdicendi, videbunt, credo, Reges. Ius hoc nouum Pontificis vocabunt in ius; imò ne vocabunt quidem, sed qui hoc illis ius suum in suos ereptum venerit, næ illi facient vt persentiscat, non sine causâ se gladium portare.
units.tr: As for the Church, let the Pontiff look to it, and to his right of excommunicating; as for his sceptres, and his right of interdicting his subjects, the kings, I suppose, will see to it. They will summon this new right of the Pontiff to judgment; or rather they will not even summon it, but those who have come to seize this right from them over their own subjects will be made by them to perceive that it is not without cause that they carry the sword.

units.la: Interim quae haec proterua est, aut quis ferat, vt egressus Sacello Papiensis Presbyter, tam petulanter audeat, de ciuium fide, de sceptris Regum ludere, authoritatem Principum deprimere, subditorum officium eleuare, deponere illos ne regnent, interdicere hís ne pareant? ferret hoc Cardinalis, cui à Sacellis est; ferret hoc Pontifex, cuius sub ditione est: si Regibus ex animo consultum vellent, non ferrent, quin infolentiam hanc eius, tantam, tam procacem, seuerè compescerent.
units.tr: Meanwhile, what insolence is this, or who could bear it, that a presbyter who has left the chapel at Pavia should so impudently dare to make sport of the loyalty of citizens, of the sceptres of kings, to lower the authority of princes, to raise the duty of subjects, to depose them so that they may not reign, to forbid these people to obey? A cardinal, to whom the chapel belongs, would not bear it; the Pope, under whose authority he is, would not bear it: if they wished the kings to be consulted in good faith, they would not bear it, but would sharply check this arrogance of his, so great and so bold.

units.la: Scias verò vbi gentium sit, quà in republicâ viuat scriptorcste[?] tores te; vbi Rex scilicet non sit, quem hic homo tam leuiter & nullo negotio deponit, quàm peractâ missâ casulam suam. Scis vbi sis Matthæe; Romæ es, atque audi, Romæ fac sis vide. Intra septem montes tutus es, atque ibi te contine; ne si quando eò loci veneris cum næniis hijsce tuis, vbi sub Rege viuitur, scias forte quid sit de Regum depositione, de subditorum defectione tam laxè loqui. Tam enim certè seditionem sapiunt dogmata tua, tam sunt & Regum saluti, & regnorum paci perniciosa, vt si pro merito fiat, non illis verba reddere, sed furcam figere oporteret. Nec enim, credo, tam abiecto animo Rex vllus, qui intra ditiones suas dogmatizari hæc vestra ferat, quin compescat citò insolentiam hominis malè conciliati, nec vllum nodo huic cuneum quærat: Gordius est, cuneum non vult; gladium vult Alexandri, doctrinæ huius tam tetræ vltorem & vindicem.
units.tr: Yet you should know where in the world you are, in what commonwealth you are living, you writer (where, that is, there is no king, whom this man deposes so lightly and without any trouble, as he would lay aside his chasuble after Mass). You know where you are, Matthew: you are at Rome, and hear this: at Rome, do as those at Rome do. You are safe within the seven hills, and keep yourself there; lest if ever you come to a place where men live under a king, you should perhaps learn what it is to speak so loosely about the deposition of kings and the defection of subjects. For your doctrines certainly smack of sedition, and are so ruinous both to the safety of kings and to the peace of kingdoms, that if they were given their deserts, it would be right not to return words to them but to fix them to a gallows. For I do not believe any king is so spiritless as to bear these teachings of yours being propagated within his dominions without swiftly checking the insolence of a man so ill-disposed, nor does any king seek a wedge for this knot: it is a Gordian knot, and does not want a wedge; it wants the sword of Alexander, the avenger and punisher of this so foul doctrine.

units.la: Pergis pòst ad alium Editi locum; Ibi ex verbis hijs, Non obstante sententiâ excommunicationis, fidelitatem tamen & obedientiam præstabo Regi, sic concludis: Hic aperte negatur summo Pontifici potestas excommunicandi Reges, etiam hæreticos. Imò hic aperte negatur Matthæus, & prodit imperitiam (quanquam quæ potest esse in hoc imperitia?) malitiam potius suam, qui quod aperte affirmatur, aperte negari asserit.
units.tr: You go on next to another place of the edict; there, from these words, Notwithstanding the sentence of excommunication, I will nevertheless render faithfulness and obedience to the King, you conclude thus: Here it is plainly denied that the supreme Pontiff has the power to excommunicate kings, even heretics. Nay, here it is Matthew who is plainly denied, and reveals not his ignorance (though what ignorance could there be in this?) but rather his malice, since he asserts that what is plainly affirmed is plainly denied.

units.la: Quæro enim ex te, Annon ponit qui supponit? Qui dicit, Parebo Regi excommunicatione non obstante, nonne hoc dicit, etiamsi excommunicatus fuerit Rex, parebo tamen? Qui verò hoc dicit, etiamsi excommunicatus fuerit Rex, nonne præsupponit, excommunicatum esse, & proin pro confesso sumit, excommunicari posse? Perinde enim est, ac si diceret; Potest quidem Pontifex excommunicare; Age; quod potest, faciat, si volet; excommunicet Regem; ego tamen perfistam in fide; excommunicatio non obstabit, quò minus fidelis sim. Non obstabit excommunicatio; Potestne verò quod non est, obstare cuiquam? Quæ nulla sunt, quæ non entia dicuntur in scholis, aguntne quicquam, aut operantur apud Papienses? Imò eo ipso quod obstant, quòd operantur, sunt; sunt (inquam) nec etsi sunt, obsunt tamen. Hoc ergo ibi dicitur, stante excommunicatione, nec tamen obstante, fidelitatem præstabo. Audi verò tuæ huic similem alteram, & agnosce vel ex eâ, errorem tuum. Non obstante quod Cardinalis sis à sacellis, ridebunt omnes consequentiam hanc tuam; neque tamen aperte negabunt te esse à sacellis Cardinali, quin ut vel maximè sis à sacellis, ridebunt tamen.
units.tr: For I ask you: does not he who supposes, posit? He who says, I will obey the King notwithstanding excommunication, does he not say this: even if the King has been excommunicated, I will nevertheless obey? But he who says this, even if the King has been excommunicated, does he not presuppose that he has been excommunicated, and thus take it as granted that he can be excommunicated? For it is just the same as if he said: the Pontiff can indeed excommunicate; come, let him do what he can, if he wishes; let him excommunicate the King; I shall nonetheless persist in the faith; the excommunication will not hinder me from being faithful. The excommunication will not hinder; but can what is not, hinder anyone? Things that are nothing, which in the schools are called non-entities, do they accomplish anything, or do they work anything among the people of Pavia? Indeed, by the very fact that they hinder, that they work, they are; they are (I say) and, even if they are, they do not hinder. So what is said there is: with excommunication standing, yet not hindering, I will render fidelity. Now listen to another of your own similar statements, and recognise your error even from it: Notwithstanding that you are a cardinal of the chapel, everyone will laugh at this consequence of yours; yet they will not, for all that, plainly deny that you are a cardinal of the chapel; but even as much as you may be a cardinal of the chapel, they will laugh all the same.

units.la: At etiam delirium hoc suum probare vult, idque non minùs, quin, si fieri posset, magis etiam inepto argumento; Quomodo enim iurabit se non paritùrum Pontifici Regem excommunicanti, nisi credat à Pontifice Regem non posse excommunicari? At qui, ô bone, ne id quidem iurabit, se non paritùrum Pontifici excommunicanti: ille verò parebit, Pontificis censuram agnoscet, nec id quidem faciet quod nuper fecerunt Veneti, nullitates nullas allegabit, vel de ijs protestabitur; perinde Regem habebit, ac Ecclesiæ vestræ communione priuatum, nihil cùm eo sacri attinget; Annon hoc est excommunicanti parere? Vbi tamen hæc fecerit omnia, præstabit fidelitatem nihilo minùs ut Regi suo. Excommunicare Ecclesiâ,legitur; parebit igitur in rebus Ecclesiæ: Excommunicare Regno non legitur; in regni rebus non parebit. Aliud est enim priuare Regem bonis Ecclesiæ communibus, quod facit sententia, & potest forte Pontifex: aliud priuare bono proprio, id est, regno suo, Regi, non Ecclesiastico iure vllo, quin(ut tutò vis) Gentium iure competenti, quod non facit sententia, nec potest Pontifex. Priuabit censura Pontificis societate fidelium, quâ fideles sunt: bonum enim illud spirituale, & ab Ecclesiâ. Non priuabit obedientiâ subditorum, quâ subditi sunt: Bonum enim ciuile hoc, nec ab Ecclesiâ.
units.tr: But he also wants to prove this delusion of his, and no less so, indeed, if it were possible, even more so, with a most foolish argument: "For how will he swear that he will not obey the Pope excommunicating the King, unless he believes that the King cannot be excommunicated by the Pope?" But, my good man, he will not even swear that he will not obey the Pope excommunicating him. Rather he will obey; he will acknowledge the Pope's censure, and he will not even do what the Venetians recently did: he will not plead nullities, nor protest about them. He will regard the King as cut off from the communion of your Church, and will have nothing sacred to do with him. Is this not "to obey the excommunicator"? Yet when he has done all these things, he will nonetheless "render fidelity" to his King. The Church may excommunicate, we read; therefore he will obey in matters of the Church. The King may not be excommunicated in the kingdom; therefore in matters of the kingdom he will not obey. For it is one thing to deprive the King of the goods common to the Church, which the sentence does, and which the Pope perhaps can do; another thing to deprive him of his own good, that is, his kingdom, and his rule, by no ecclesiastical right at all, but (to speak plainly) by the competent right of nations, which the sentence does not do, nor can the Pope. The Pope's censure deprives him of the fellowship of the faithful, by which they are faithful, for that is a spiritual good and from the Church. It does not deprive him of the obedience of subjects, by which they are subjects, for that is a civil good and not from the Church.

units.la: Vel hinc videas errorem tuum, ex instituto ipso Excommunicationis, vi verborum, Si Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut Ethnicus. At an non Regi Ethnico præstare fidem fas? Imò nefas non præstare. In Ethnico enim est vera potestas temporalis, idque sine ordine ad potestatem Ecclesiasticam. Dominia non fundantur in fide; & vt fide non fundantur, sic infidelitate non euertuntur. Quin Rex quiuis, cùm de Ethnico Christianus fit, non perdit terrenum ius, sed acquirit ius nouum, putà, in bonis Ecclesiæ (spiritualibus. Omnia hæc {a}Dominus tuus totidem verbis. Idem, cùm de Christiano fit sicut Ethnicus, vigore sententiæ amittit nouum ius quod acquisierat in bonis Ecclesiæ (spiritualibus: sed retinet tamen terrenum ius, antiquum ius suum in temporalibus, quod fuerat illi proprium priusquam Christianus fieret. Omnino eo statu erit, nec deteriore quàm esset, si Christianam fidem amplexus nunquam fuisset.
units.tr: Even here you may see your error, from the very institution of excommunication, by the force of the words: "If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen." But is it not lawful to render fidelity to a heathen King? Indeed it is unlawful not to render it. For in a heathen there is true temporal power, and that without any relation to ecclesiastical power. Dominions are not founded on faith, and as they are not founded by faith, so they are not overthrown by unbelief. Indeed any King, when from a heathen he becomes a Christian, does not lose his earthly right but acquires a new right, for instance over the goods of the Church (spiritual ones). All these things your Lord says in so many words. Likewise, when a Christian becomes "as a heathen," by the force of the sentence he loses the new right he had acquired over the goods of the Church (spiritual ones), but he keeps nonetheless his earthly right, his old right in temporal things, which had been his own before he became a Christian. He will be in exactly that state, and no worse than he would have been had he never embraced the Christian faith.

units.la: Litem hanc totam dirimit exemplum Theodosij, cui per octo menses illos quibus sub censurâ fuit Ambrosij, fidelitas interim à nullo negata est. Vel Theodosij certè; vel sine dubio Iuliani. Christianus is fuit primò; post de Christiano Apostata, nec iam sicut, sed planè Ethnicus. Quid? an ex eo, Imperiali potestate exutus? An nefas illi parere, vt Cæsari, aut obediendum præstari à Christianis? Non dices, scio. Non tam madidâ memoriâ es, qui laudas post Augustinum, qui ipse laudat Christianos milites, etiam infideli huic Imperatori, etiam Idololatræ, etiam Apostatæ, subditos tamen & seruientes.
units.tr: The example of Theodosius settles this whole dispute: for those eight months in which he was under the censure of Ambrose, fidelity was in the meantime denied by no one. Certainly Theodosius, or undoubtedly Julian. He was first a Christian; afterwards, becoming an apostate from Christianity, he was no longer "as" a heathen, but plainly a heathen. What then? Was he stripped of imperial power on that account? Was it unlawful to obey him, as to Caesar, or was obedience to be rendered to him by Christians? You will not say so, I know. You are not so soft in memory as to praise Augustine, who himself praises Christian soldiers who were subject to and served even this unbelieving Emperor, even this idolater, even this apostate.

units.la: Quid remota confector? Henrico quarto Galliarum nunc Regi, Excommunicationis vinculis innodato, nec dum soluto, necdum legato eius Romæ virgâ sacerdotali percussò: corona impositâ est, Sacramentum fidelitatis præstitum. At à quibus præstitum? A vestræ partis hominibus; addo, & rectè præstitum: nec enim potest impetratam demum Romæ absolutionem, aut corona de nouo Regi impositâ, aut fidelitatis denuò Sacramenta præstita. Fuissent autem de nouo, nisi priora illa valuissent. Valuerunt ergo illa, ac proin Regi forte post, in sacris non communicârunt; (etsi etiam in hoc multi audaciores quàm par erat) at extra sacra, fidem omnem, studia atque officia prolixè detulerunt. Et hos tamen omnes negasse Pontifici authoritatem excommunicandi Reges, caue dixeris; Sorbona non feret, nec tu feres impunè, si dixeris. Citra ergo, vel fidei, vel clauium abnegationem, fidelitatem licet atque obsequium Regi præstare, vel Excommunicato. Priusquam vero ad reliqua descendam, pauca hic mihi dicenda de Censurâ ipsâ, quousq; scilicet sese vis eius extendat: Indè quàm tua haec consequentia nulla sit, liquidò liquebit. Censura duplex est; Publicani & Ethnici, minor & maior; nam de Maranatha illo mitto iam dicere. Minor à Sacramentis excludit modò, de eâ quæstio iam nobis non est.
units.tr: Why go far? To Henry IV, now King of France, bound in the chains of excommunication, not yet loosed, and not yet struck with the priestly rod by his legate at Rome, the crown was placed on him and the sacrament of fidelity rendered. But by whom was it rendered? By men of your party; and I add, rightly rendered. For it cannot be that after absolution obtained at Rome, either the crown was placed on the new King, or the oaths of fidelity were rendered again. But they would have been rendered anew, had not those former ones been valid. Those, then, were valid; and consequently, perhaps, after the King did not take communion in the sacred rites (although in this too many were bolder than was fitting), yet outside the sacred rites they lavishly gave him all faith, zeal and service. And do not say that all these men denied to the Pope the authority of excommunicating Kings; the Sorbonne will not bear it, nor will you bear it with impunity if you say so. So without denying either faith or the keys, it is lawful to render fidelity and obedience to the King, or even to one who is excommunicated. But before I descend to the rest, I must say a few things here about the censure itself, namely how far its force extends; from this it will become clear how null your consequence is. The censure is twofold: that of the publican and the heathen, the lesser and the greater; for I omit now to speak of that "Maranatha." The lesser excludes only from the sacraments, and about that there is no question for us now.

units.la: De maiore vero altera, quæ arcet Ecclesiâ ipsâ, quæ perinde reddit, ut Ethnicos; quibus nec fas Templum ingredi, quod tamen licuit Publicanus: de illâ (inquam) vix quisquam est quin fateatur, institutam eam à Christo, Matth. 18. per verba, Die Ecclesiæ; si Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut Ethnicus. De exteriore foro ibi agitur; exterioris fori iurisdictio, illo, nec alio loco fundata est. Quæremus ergo paucis; Potestas haec ibi cui data? Quæ illius ibi latitudo, qui limites? Cui etiam, ratihabitio eo loco facta, de iure competat?
units.tr: As for the greater, the other, which keeps one out of the Church itself, which makes one "as a heathen," to whom it is not lawful to enter the Temple, although it was lawful for the publican: of that I say there is scarcely anyone who does not admit that it was instituted by Christ, Matt. 18, by the words, "Tell it to the Church; if he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen." There it concerns the outward forum; the jurisdiction of the outward forum is founded in that place and in no other. We shall inquire therefore briefly: to whom was this power given there? What is its breadth there, what its limits? And to whom, too, does ratification made in that place belong by right?

units.la: 1. Cui data? Non Apostolo Petro; Petrus enim, si peccaverit in eum frater eius, iubetur, Ecclesiæ dicere; Petro dicitur, Die Ecclesiæ: Nimis autem violentum sic explicare, Ecclesiæ dicere, id est, sibi ipsi: quod attoniti legimus, apud {a}Dominum tuum. Quòd si autem & Petrus peccâsset in fratrem, (nam & hoc in Petrum cadit) an frater id Ecclesiæ diceret, id est, Petro ipsi peccanti? Ecclesiæ ergo hoc dicitur: Petrus ipse, &c., si Petrus, Papa subijcitur legi de correctione fraternâ: si peccaverit &c. die Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 1. To whom was it given? Not to the Apostle Peter; for Peter, "if his brother sins against him," is commanded, "Tell it to the Church." It is said to Peter, "Tell it to the Church." It is too violent to explain "tell it to the Church" as "tell it to himself," which we read with astonishment in your Lord. But if Peter too had sinned against a brother (for this also falls upon Peter), would the brother tell it to the Church, that is, to Peter himself, who was sinning? So this is said to the Church: "Peter himself," etc. If Peter, the Pope, is subject to the law of fraternal correction: "if he sins, etc., tell it to the Church."

units.la: 2. Latitudo autem ad quam se porrigit, (verbis hijs) Sit tibi sicut Ethnicus. Limites verò: Sit tibi sicut, ne sit tibi plus, aut peiore loco, quàm Ethnicus. Nefas autem Ethnicos bonis suis priuare, nedum exhæredare; nedum adhuc, omnium qui inter Ethnicos erant, optimos, atque maximos, hæreditate optimâ atque maximâ; coronâ suâ, hæreditario iure, suâ, exuere penitus atque expoliare. Agitur ergo illud tantùm hoc loco, ne communionem vllam cum ijs, quoad Ecclesiæ res vel Religionis, habeamus, nec ad Ecclesiam magis cosputemus pertinere, quàm quemuis alium de Ethnicis; De iactura Regni non agitur.
units.tr: 2. The breadth to which it extends is (in these words) "let him be to you as a heathen." The limits: "let him be to you as" a heathen, that he may not be to you more, or in a worse position, than a heathen. But it is unlawful to deprive heathens of their goods, let alone to disinherit them, let alone further to strip and wholly despoil the best and greatest of all who were among the heathens of the best and greatest inheritance, of their crown, of their hereditary right. So in this place only this is dealt with: that we should have no fellowship with them in respect of the things of the Church or of religion, nor should we be more concerned with them as belonging to the Church than with any other heathen. The loss of the kingdom is not at issue.

units.la: 3. Vt autem Petro potestas ibi non data, censuram hanc vsurpandi; ita nec Petro, si vsurparet, ratihabitio promissa. Dicitur enim, Quoscunque ligaveritis; non Petro igitur, vel Papa, sed Ecclesia. Scio recipies te statim ad Matth. 16. vbi singulari numero dicitur Petro, Tibi dabo claues, Quodcunq; ligaueris &c. Tibi, est ibi quidem singulari numero positum; sed etsi numerus est singularis, singularis ibi tamen persona Petri non est. Petro, ibi promissæ claues, non tamen vt Petro, huic homini, quin Petro vt in persona Eccle-fiæ, vt Ecclesiam referenti, vt Ecclesiæ personam gerenti. Personam in eo loco gesit Ecclesiæ, vbi potestas promittitur: Ecclesiæ autem ipsi potestas hoc loco datur, cuius gesit ibi personam, Petrus, non suam. Nouit Dominus tuus, nemo melius, quanta hoc nube testium eminci posit; quæ illum nubes pessimè habet; eique dum respondet, quasi si in nebula esset, excidit ipse sibi, & aberrat tota via.
units.tr: 3. But just as no power was given to Peter there to usurp this censure, so no ratification was promised to Peter if he should usurp it. For it is said, "Whatsoever you shall bind"; not to Peter, therefore, or to the Pope, but to the Church. I know you will at once retreat to Matt. 16, where in the singular number it is said to Peter, "To you I will give the keys, whatsoever you shall bind, etc." "To you" is indeed there put in the singular number; but even if the number is singular, the person there is not the singular person of Peter. To Peter the keys are promised there, but not as to Peter, this man; rather to Peter as bearing the person of the Church, as representing the Church, as sustaining the person of the Church. In that place he bore the person of the Church where the power is promised; but the power in that place is given to the Church itself, whose person Peter there bore, not his own. Your Lord knows, none better, how much this is hidden by a cloud of witnesses; a cloud which treats him very badly, and while he answers it, as if he were in a mist, he loses himself and goes astray all along the way.

units.la: Quæro jam de praxi Censuræ huius. Reperio 1.Cor.5. Inbeti ibi deduci in ptaxin, potentiam hanc Apostolus, in nomine CHRISTI cum spiritu suo. Forte autem minus ibi caute loquutus; illud credo dicere debuit, vel in nomine vel cum spiritu Petri saltem. Neutrum vero Paulus ibi dicit, quin congregatio illis potestatem censuræ denunciandæ facit. Ita non Petro datur vni; non in Petro vno habetur rata; non ab vno illo in praxin deducitur. Res ipsa, rei ipsius promissio, ratihabitio, vsus denique Ecclesiæ datur; ab Ecclesia, & habetur, & transfertur in siue vnūsiue plures, qui eius post vel exercendæ vel denunciandæ facultatem habeant. Notum est, in Concilio Constantiensi quæstionem hanc totam diu ventilatam; tandem etiam conclusam esse; notum, Cardinales Cameracensem & Cusanum, Gersoncm, & Sorbonā totam non secus sentire.
units.tr: I now inquire about the practice of this censure. I find in 1 Cor. 5 that the Apostle, "in the name of Christ with his spirit," bade this power be brought into practice. But perhaps he spoke less cautiously there; I think he ought to have said either "in the name" or at least "with the spirit of Peter." Yet Paul says neither there, but that the congregation gives them the power of pronouncing the censure. Thus it is not given to Peter alone; it is not held ratified in Peter alone; it is not brought into practice by that one alone. The thing itself, the promise of the thing, its ratification, and finally the use of the Church, is given; it is both held by the Church and transferred to one or to several, who afterwards have the faculty either of exercising or of pronouncing it. It is well known that at the Council of Constance this whole question was long debated, and at last concluded too; well known that the Cardinals of Cambrai and of Cusa, Gerson, and the Sorbonne all thought the same.

units.la: Quæro jam de exitu; & quid illo factum, qui Ecclesiâ sic eiectus est Corinthi. Ecquid ulterius processum, quàm ut à societate seclusus, ex eoque pudore suffusus, ad meliorem mentem ptimò[?], post & ad Ecclesiam redire posset? Urbe certè exactus non est, non domo pulsus; non fortunis exutus, bona eius in Corbonam redacta non sunt. Ignota hæc, inaudita apud Ecclesiam prisca. Etiam illa quæ tum Corinthi fuit Ecclesia, manipulus tantùm fuit hominum, qui malè multati essent ipsi, si sic quempiam mulctassent. Non multi inter eos potentes, non multi nobiles. Quibus, in bona tum hominum[?] potestas fuit, quibus in capita: omnes iurati hostes Ecclesiæ. Sin de Ananiâ mutire velit Matthæus, qui ad Petri vocem cecidit, & expirauit; inde ut Papæ potestatem asserat; habebit nos satis æquos. Age, surgat de Cathedrâ suâ Pontifex, transeat; transiens, umbrâ suâ faciat quod fecit Petrus, curet ægros, alia eiusdem generis signa edat, Petri per omnia instar sit; post de censurâ fatebimur, nec in morâ erimus, quin & eam exercere possit. Quantillum autem iam est Petri, in Pontifice Romano?
units.tr: I now ask about the outcome, and what happened to the man who was thus cast out of the Church at Corinth. Did anything further follow, beyond his being cut off from fellowship and, out of shame at that, being able to return to the Church once he came to a better mind? He was certainly not driven out of the city, nor thrown out of his house; he was not stripped of his property, and his goods were not confiscated into the treasury. These things were unknown and unheard of in the early Church. Even the Church at Corinth at that time was only a small band of people, who would themselves have been badly punished if they had fined anyone in that way. "Not many among them were powerful, not many were noble." They had no power over men's goods or their lives, and all of them were sworn enemies of the Church. But if Matthew wishes to mutter about Ananias, who fell dead at Peter's word and expired, and from that to claim the power of the Pope, he will find us reasonable enough. Come, let the Pontiff rise from his chair and walk across; as he walks, let his shadow do what Peter's did, let him heal the sick and perform other signs of the same kind, and let him be in every respect like Peter. Then we will admit the censure, and we will not delay in allowing him to exercise it. But how little of Peter is there left in the Roman Pontiff?

units.la: Quanquam, vel si ad Pontificem spectet potestas hæc tota, nihil ad iuramentum[?]. Dicat, decernat, declaret Regem fore Catholicis suis, sicut Ethnicum; Quid tum postea? non hoc Catholicos illius subditos officij nexu eximet. Sit Rex, si velit, Ethnicus; at Rex esse non definit: sit Julianus Apostata, peior Ethnico; at est Imperator, nec illi tributa soluere, nec ad tribunal eius stare, nec iussa capessere detrectabunt: si vel milites Christiani sint; dicat, Ite contra illam Gentem, ibunt illico. Rex est ergo etiam tum, cùm (non dico lapsus in hæresin, sed) merus Apostata; cùm (non dico sicut, sed) planè iam Ethnicus est; eo loco scilicet, quo Reges Ethnici, contra quos tamen, nefas arma sumere, imò ad quorum iussa, nefas arma non sumere. Reges enim ipsi tum fuerunt Ethnici, Cæsar ipse tum fuit Ethnicus, cùm hanc censuram Christus primò instituit, cùm hanc censuram Paulus post exercuit: Reddenda tamen Cæsari quæ Cæsaris dixit Christus; ἀπόδοτε[?] tamen, id est, obedire illis, & subijci monuit Paulus.
units.tr: Yet even if this whole power belonged to the Pontiff, it would have nothing to do with the oath of allegiance. Let him say, decree and declare that the King shall be to his Catholics as a heathen is: what then? This will not free the Catholic subjects of the King from the bond of their duty. Let the King be a heathen, if he likes; but he does not cease to be king. Let him be Julian the Apostate, worse than a heathen; yet he is Emperor, and they will not refuse to pay him tribute, to stand before his tribunal, or to carry out his orders, even if they are Christian soldiers. Let him say, "Go against that nation," and they will go at once. So the King is still king even when he has not merely fallen into heresy (I do not say that), but is a plain apostate; even when he is (I do not say like a heathen, but) now plainly a heathen; in that position, namely, in which heathen kings stand, against whom it is nevertheless wrong to take up arms, and indeed, at whose orders it is wrong not to take up arms. For the kings themselves were heathens then; Caesar himself was a heathen when Christ first instituted this censure, and when Paul afterwards exercised it. Christ did say, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's"; yet Paul warned that men should give (that is, "obey them") and "be subject" to them.

units.la: Quin (quod fatetur Tortus) post censuram demùm, cùm Ecclesiâ summoti Reges; extra potestatem sunt Pontificis. Torto enim ipsi (qui in eo inclementior paulò est) nec Christiani sunt. Quare nullum in illos ius tum, titulus nullus Pontifici. Ipsius hæc scilicet sententia est; Admissi ad Ecclesiam, Papæ sceptra subijciunt: extrusi ergo Ecclesiâ, sceptra iam erecta gerunt. In ordine sunt Ethnicorum Regum, & exemptionis eiusdem capaces, cuius Ethnici; ut nimirum immunes tum sint, à Papali omni, vel iure vel dictione iuris.
units.tr: Indeed (as Torto admits), only after the censure, when the kings are removed from the Church, are they under the power of the Pontiff. For to Torto himself (who is rather more merciless in this), they are not even Christians. Therefore the Pontiff has then no right over them and no title. This, of course, is his own opinion: "Those admitted to the Church place their sceptres under the Pope's rule." So those who have been thrust out of the Church bear their sceptres now upright. They are in the order of heathen kings, and are capable of the same exemption as heathens, so that, of course, they are then free from every Papal power, whether by right or by jurisdiction of right.

units.la: Certum hoc quidem in Theologiâ, & receptum ab omnibus; Non eò venisse Christum, ut, qui iam ante aduentum suum erat, ordo vel naturæ, vel politiæ, eum vel inuerteret, vel euerteret: sanciret potiùs, & sanctum magis redde-ret, rat. Naturæ vincula non soluit; à potestate mariti uxorem, à parentum obsequio filios non eximit. Tantum abest, ut nexum illum magnum dirumpat, & quasi catenam adamantinam, quâ subditos tanquam filios familiæ magnæ (quam rempublicam dicimus) Parenti suo magno certum est obligari. Rectè verò litem hanc totam dirimit Navarrus, cuius par est magna sit authoritas apud Iesuitas, quorum ille Patronus magnus est. Excommunicatione homo non definit esse verum homo, imo nec liber, nec perdit potestatem naturalem, & ita potest regulariter contrahere, ut quilibet alium, & facere omnia, quæ iure naturali, Gentium, civili, nituntur. Niti autem vel naturali, vel Gentium, vel civili, vel omnibus hujs potius, certum est, coniunctionem eam, quæ inter magnum hunc Patremfamilias est & familiam suam; ac proin censura nulla dissociari posse. Verissimum ergo verbum fuit, nec de eo Apologiæ Apologia ullà opus, quod dixerit, non alio tendere, non intromittere se Legis Authorem in quicquam aliud, quàm ciuium suorum fidelitatem & veram obedientiam. Parte vero ex al-tera, malè à Matthæo deduci, torqueri potius: vel, ex eo, quòd excommunicari contingat Reges, necessariò consequi, ut Regno priuari debeant: vel, ex eo quod negatur priuari eos regno debere, excommunicationem ipsam, vel aliquid ibi quod de Catholicâ fide sit, abnegari.
units.tr: This is certainly a point settled in theology and accepted by all: that Christ did not come to overturn or subvert the order of nature or of the state which already existed before His coming; rather, He came to sanction it and make it more holy. He does not loosen the bonds of nature; He does not free wives from the authority of their husbands, nor children from obedience to their parents. Far from breaking that great bond, or the adamantine chain by which subjects are bound, as sons of the great family (which we call the commonwealth), to their great Father, it is certain that they are so bound. Navarrus rightly settles this whole dispute, and his authority should be great among the Jesuits, for he is their great patron. A man does not cease to be a true man through excommunication; nor is he made unfree, nor does he lose his natural power, and so he may, as a rule, make contracts as anyone else does, and do all the things that rest on natural law, the law of nations, civil law, or rather on all of these together. It is certain that the bond between this great Father of the household and his family rests on natural, national or civil law, or on all of them; and therefore no censure can sever it. So the word was most true, and there is no need for any apology for it, that he [Christ] was aiming at nothing else, and did not interfere in anything else, than the "fidelity and true obedience of His citizens," the Author of the Law. On the other side, Matthew is wrongly deducing, or rather twisting, the argument: either, from the fact that it happens that kings are excommunicated, it must necessarily follow that they ought to be deprived of their kingdom; or, from the fact that it is denied that they ought to be deprived of their kingdom, the excommunication itself, or anything in it that belongs to the Catholic faith, is denied.

units.la: Tum quæ hæc consequentia est, Perfistam in fide Regi, nec ab eo deficiam, nec parebo vel Pontifici siquid in Regem moliatur; ergo non agnosco in Pontifice potestatem Excommunicandi? Peccâsti hic quidem in Logicam, peccâsti largiter. Non si funiculo illo triplici (de quo, unitio[?] gloriatus es) attraxeris, efficies ex eo, hoc ut consequatur. Nisi si error errori errorem affert; error nempe Logicus, errorem Theologicum; nisi (te iam Authore) qui excommunicatus est, eo ipso quòd fit excommunicatus, regnum amittat; nec secus depositionem, & excommunicationem, mutuò se consequi putes, quàm corpus umbra, aut ignem calor. At hoc hallucinari est. Qui excommunicatus est, tolerari ad tempus potest. Declaratio post accedat oportet, & Publicatio. Tum & Appellationi locus (si ita opus) à Papâ, ad Concilium. Scis à quibus id factum, & quando. Nec id in Philippo factum, nec in Theodofio[?]; vterque sepositus à communione, neuter depositus Imperio. Disparata hæc sunt prorsus, túque[?], qui sic odio habes argumenta inde ducta, ipse iam ducis à disparatis.
units.tr: Then what kind of inference is this: "I shall persist in faith towards the King, and shall not desert him, nor obey the Pontiff if he plots anything against the King; therefore I do not acknowledge in the Pontiff the power of excommunicating"? You have here indeed sinned against logic, and sinned greatly. Even if you draw out that triple cord (of which you boasted in your unity), you will not bring it about that this follows from that. Unless perhaps error brings error to error: a logical error, namely, bringing a theological error; unless (with you as its author) the man who is excommunicated loses his kingdom by the very fact that he is excommunicated; nor should you think that deposition and excommunication follow each other mutually, any more than the body casts a shadow or fire produces heat. But this is to wander in error. The man who is excommunicated can be tolerated for a time. A declaration must come afterwards, and a publication. Then there is also room for appeal (if need be) from the Pope to a Council. You know by whom this was done, and when. It was not done in the case of Philip, nor in the case of Theodosius; each was set apart from communion, and neither was deposed from empire. These cases are wholly unlike, and you, who so hate the arguments drawn from them, now yourself draw from unlike cases.

units.la: Accipe verò paucis,. quæ hinc absurda consequuntur, si statim ut excommunicati sunt Principes, regnis excidant.
units.tr: Hear briefly what absurdities follow from this, if princes lose their kingdoms as soon as they are excommunicated.

units.la: Dixit olim Pontifici Bernardus, {a}In criminibus, non possessionibus, potestas vestra: Regnum autem certè possessio, ad quam igitur potestas illa non transit. Sed neque peccati quidem causa sufficit, ad priuandum quem Regno, cuius non est maior ratio quàm priuationis feudi, ait {b}Doctor Marta. Fac verò priuatæ sortis hominem in censura vltimam incidisse; ecquid illi de opibus, de possessione suâ peribit? Ecquis ei vel partem adimet de fundo, vel teruncium de re suâ? Nunquam factum, ne tentatum quidem; Quid ergo? Aliane quoad Reges censuræ natura, quàm quoad reliquos? Mutatne naturam fulmen Pontificum, si vibretur in Regem, & tollit illi possessionem suam, quam nusquam alibi tollit? {c}Ita iudicabis magnum sicut parvum, ait lex; nec aliter {d}oues pascere, aliter agnos, Euangelium; vna enim vtrobique vox est.
units.tr: Bernard once said to the Pontiff: "Your power is over crimes, not over possessions." But a kingdom is certainly a possession, so that power does not pass to it. "But not even the cause of sin is enough to deprive anyone of a kingdom, whose penalty is no greater than the deprivation of a fief," says Doctor Marta. Suppose a man of private rank has incurred the last censure; will his wealth, his possessions, perish for him? Will anyone take from him even a part of his land, or a penny of his property? This has never been done, nor even attempted. What then? Is the nature of the censure different for kings from what it is for the rest? Does the thunderbolt of the Pontiffs change its nature if it is aimed at a king, and does it take away from him his possession, which it takes away nowhere else? "You shall judge the great as well as the small," says the law; nor does the Gospel say that one should feed sheep one way and lambs another, for there is one voice in both cases.

units.la: Vide porrò quod supra dixi annon hinc sequatur; Deterior erit quoad Ecclesiam, conditio Regis, quàm cuiusuis de plebe infimâ. Baro si sub censurâ est, Baroniam non amittit, nec de Barone fiet non Baro. Non eques equestrem ordinem, nec de vllo gradu suo excidit. Quin vel vllus hominum de vulgo, quicquid fit quod habet, ex censurâ quam incurrit nihilo minùs habiturus est: Rex autem si tactus est de Vaticano, Regno statim exuetur, & de Rege fiet plebeius, & quod subditorum nulli fit, illi fiet.
units.tr: Look further: what I said above, does it not follow from this? The condition of a king will be worse, as regards the Church, than that of any man of the lowest rank. If a baron is under the censure, he does not lose his barony, nor does a baron cease to be a baron. A knight does not fall out of the order of knights, nor does he drop from any of his ranks. Indeed, whatever any ordinary man of the people has, he will still have in spite of the censure he incurs. But if a king is touched by the Vatican, he will at once be stripped of his kingdom, and from being a king he will become a commoner, and what belongs to no one among the subjects will become his.

units.la: Hoc si sciffet, (iterum dico) haud puto Ethnicus Rex quisquam fuisset de Ethnico Christianus; nec si ita res se haberet, vllus etiam præterea fiet; si sapiunt, erunt quod sunt, nec in hanc se conditionem demittent, vbi cuiuis subditorum quàm ipsis melius futurum est. Siccine vero Nutricis suis vicem refert? Siccine [illegible, ~8 letters]? Siccine quæ pia mater est priuatis hominibus, solis Regibus nouerca est Ecclesia?
units.tr: Had he known this (I say it again), I doubt any Ethnic king would ever have become a Christian; and if things were so, no one else would either. If they have sense, they will remain what they are, and will not lower themselves into a condition where it will be better for anyone of their subjects than for themselves. Does the Church really repay her nurses in this way? Does she [illegible, ~8 letters]? Is the Church, which is a loving mother to private men, a stepmother to kings alone?

units.la: Tum id cautum imprimis, ne cuiquam fraudi sit anathematis sententia, præterquam ei qui crimen admisit; ad alios ne pertingat; alios ne inuoluat, qui nonpeccârunt. Reg
units.tr: Above all, let this be secured: that the sentence of anathema should be no harm to anyone except the one who has committed the crime; that it should not reach others, nor entangle those who have not sinned. Reg

units.la: {a} Lib.1.de confiderat. Cum autem hæreditas, quâ si pater multatus fuerit, nunquam adibit hæreditatem filius, nec si insons, nec si infans quidem fuerit: quin filius qui nihil quicquam peccauit, portabit tamen iniquitatem patris, & noxæ non suæ[?], pœnas luet Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: {a} Lib. 1 de confid. Yet when an inheritance is concerned, if a father has been fined, the son never enters the inheritance, whether he is innocent or even an infant. Indeed the son who has sinned in nothing shall bear nevertheless the iniquity of the father, and he will pay the penalties of another's offence [?] to the Church.

units.la: Absit ab Ecclesiâ Dei hoc, quod à Deo abfuit, {a}vt rem hanc faciat, & deponat iustum cum impio, fiatq; iustus sicut impius.
units.tr: Let this be far from the Church of God, which is far from God: {a} that it should make this thing, and should set the just with the wicked, and the just become as the wicked.

units.la: Quid, quòd pœnitentiæ locus relinquitur, in omni censurâ Ecclesiæ, idque ita, vt cùm ad bonam mentem redierit, in integrum restitui oporteat; nec è culpâ, cuius iam piget, detrimenti aliquid accipere? factum hoc Petro post trinam negationem, quò alijs id faceret, quod sibi factum voluit. Certè autem qui regno motus, cuius in alium translatum Regni ius, serò iam sapit, serò pœnitet: Non dimittet is qui semel inuasit ad ius suum, quod priùs ei cõpetebat, redire non poterit, nec si vel maximè serò pœniteat, nec si liquescat in lacrymas.
units.tr: What of the fact that a place for repentance is left in every censure of the Church, and that so, when he has returned to a good mind, he ought to be restored to his former state, and not to receive any loss from the fault he now regrets? This was done for Peter after his threefold denial, so that he might do for others what he wished done for himself. Certainly he who, moved by a kingdom whose right has been transferred to another, comes to his senses too late and repents too late: he who has once seized it will not let go; he who has been driven from it cannot return to his former right, not even if he repents most bitterly, not even if he melts into tears.

units.la: Ne lectorem morer longiùs; nec Paulo Apostolo, nec Paulo Pontifici, nec vlli mortalium, potestas vlla, nisi ad ædificationem, vsque adeo vt si ædificandi spes nulla, ne adhiberi quidem censura debeat. Tantum autem abest, vt priuatiua hæc potestas ædificet, vel peccantis saluti consulat, vt, historiâ teste, teste experientiâ, semper ad destructionem operata fuerit. Nec enim repertus vnquam Rex, credo nec repertum iri, qui æquo animo ferre posset, transferri coronam suam ad alium; vel qui exin fanior factus sit, quin potiùs ruerit ad arma præceps, & nescio quot clades dederit, quot — [illegible, ~20 letters], potiùs quàm vt iure suo cederet. Cùm deponuntur Reges, prædæ exponuntur Regna. colliduntur Reges & Regna: nec tentatis hoc vnquà sine tristi successu, nec vnquà hoc fulmen sine ingenti incendio. Absit autem, vt tantarum calamitatum Ecclesia causa sit: & propter vnius noxam, tam multos committat inter se, cum certâ non minus animarum pernicie, quàm corporum. Ausim verò dicere, plus hinc detrimenti, fidei professoribus, plus lucri fidei hostibus obuenisse, quàm vllâ aliâ ex re. Dum enim Henrici, Friderici, Ludouici pugnant, Sultani, Chani, Ottomani, miseriâ nostrâ magni sunt, ditiones suas perditione nostrâ dilatârunt.
units.tr: I will not detain the reader longer. Neither to the Apostle Paul, nor to the Pontiff Paul, nor to any mortal is any power given except for building up; so much so that if there is no hope of building up, the censure ought not even to be applied. Yet this private power is so far from building up, or caring for the salvation of the sinner, that, as history attests and experience attests, it has always worked for destruction. For never has a king been found, nor do I believe one will ever be found, who could bear calmly that his crown should be transferred to another; or who, having become wiser from this, did not rather rush headlong to arms and inflict I know not how many disasters, how many [illegible, ~20 letters], rather than yield his right. When kings are deposed, kingdoms are exposed as spoil; kings and kingdoms are dashed together: nor has this ever been attempted without a sad outcome, nor has this thunderbolt ever fallen without a great conflagration. Far be it that the Church should be the cause of such great calamities, and, on account of one man's offence, set so many against one another, with a certain destruction of souls no less than of bodies. I would venture to say that more loss has come to the professors of the faith from this, and more gain to the enemies of the faith, than from any other thing. For while Henry, Frederick, Lewis fight, the Sultans, the Khans, the Ottomans grow great by our misery, and by our ruin they have enlarged their dominions.

units.la: Viden' ad quot nos absurda abducat assertio tua? fiet Regi quod nulli praeterea fit. Peiore conditione Rex, quàm ullus de plebe. Peiore conditione Rex Christianus, quàm Ethnicus.
