Plectitur hæres, qui non peccauit. Pœnitens in integrum restitui non potest. Ad destructionem erit potestas illa, quæ ædificando solùm data est: Et harum omnium tum iniuriarum, tum miseriarum, fons Pontifex.
units.tr: Do you see to how many absurdities your assertion leads us? A king will suffer what no one else suffers. A king is in a worse condition than any commoner. A Christian king is in a worse condition than an Ethnic one. The heir who has not sinned is punished. A penitent cannot be restored to his former state. That power, which was given only for building up, will work for destruction. And the source of all these injuries and miseries, both the wrongs and the sufferings, is the Pontiff.

units.la: Quodsi iam, eò dixeris, Pontifici Regem excommunicanti non parituros, quòd Regem sic excommunicatum non vitabunt, (quicum conuersari tum non liceat:) gratis dixeris. Quid enim? an excommunicato per Apostolum Corinthio, statim abeo, coniugem, liberos, famulos profugisse omnes putas, atque desertum in vacuis ædibus reliquisse? Ille autem propter hæresin excommunicatus non fuit, inquis: alia verò hæreticorum causa est. Imò non alia; siue enim fornicarius, siue idolis seruiens fuerit, qui frater & Christianus est, pariter ab utroque, nec magis ab hoc, quàm illo abstinendum suadet Apostolus; Neutri commisceri[?] fas, cibum cum neutro sumere. Non est autem grauius in Christiano crimen hæresis, quàm seruitus idolorum; Eadem in utroque crimine censuræ vis: Nec magis ab idolorum seruo nos arcet Apostolus, quàm à fornicario: vestra igitur hæc, alterius, & noui iuris sunt.
units.tr: But if you should go on to say that they will not obey the Pontiff when he excommunicates a king, because they will not shun a king so excommunicated (with whom it would then not be lawful to associate), you will have said it to no purpose. For what? Do you think that everyone fled from the Corinthian excommunicated by the Apostle, at once leaving his wife, children and servants, and left him deserted in an empty house? But you say he was not excommunicated on account of heresy: the cause of the heretics is another. Nay, it is not another; for whether he be a fornicator, or one who serves idols, if he is a brother and a Christian, the Apostle urges that we abstain equally from both, and no more from this one than from that one: it is not lawful to mix with either, nor to eat with either. Yet in a Christian there is no greater crime than heresy than the service of idols; the force of the censure is the same in each crime: nor does the Apostle keep us more from the servant of idols than from the fornicator. These rules, therefore, are of another and a new law.

units.la: Sed tamen & Hildebrandus ipse, qui primus omnium bacchari ausus in Cæsarem, etiam in Cæsareos omnes, hæreseos nomine (hæresis autem erat, quòd ei non parérent) cùm nimis etiam strinxisset, laxare coactus est paululùm, capite * Quoniam multos: per cuius Interpretes, ij quibus religio non erit cum Principe conuersari, (censurâ non obstante:) co tamen se casu sperant à contumaciâ vindicari posse. Concinnarunt enim nobis Interpretes Distichon illud:
units.tr: But yet Hildebrand himself, who first dared to rage against Caesar, when he had also struck too hard at all the Caesareans, under the name of heresy (and it was heresy, because they did not obey him), was compelled to relax a little, in the chapter * Quoniam multos; through whose interpreters, those for whom religion will not be to associate with the Prince (the censure notwithstanding) hope they can nevertheless be defended from contumacy in that case. For the interpreters have framed for us that couplet:

units.la: Hæc anathema quidem faciunt, ne possit obesse: Utile, Lex, Humile, Ignorata, necesse[?].
units.tr: These make it an anathema indeed, lest it should harm: Useful, Law, Humble, Unknown, necessary [?].

units.la: Et affulget inde spes aliqua, quòd, si Regem non vitent, sicut eo conuersentur, excusabit eos tamen aliquod de quinque huius, puta, vel Lex; Lex enim Dei, quæ lege omne superat: vel Humile; nec est enim subiectio magis humilis, quàm subditorum.
units.tr: And from this some hope shines forth, that if they do not shun the king, but associate with him as before, one of these five will excuse them, namely either Law, for the law of God, which overcomes all by law; or Humble, for there is no subjection more humble than that of subjects.

units.la: Theologi certè æquiores videntur, qui seruos excipiunt: Sadoc verò Sacerdos, Propheta Nathan, militum magister Ioab ultrò seruos seducent[?], nec Regem ergò deserunt. Excipiunt & filios: Rex autem & esse vult, & haberi suorum Pater, & quicquid à filijs patre præstari debet, suo sibi iure impe-rito vendicat. Excipiunt & coniuges: Est autem Regi cum regno connubij ius, cuius tessera & testis, annulus coniugalis: nec si vi vocum illarum Regi adhæreant, magis in Politicis angi sinent conscientias suas, quàm in Oeconomicis; qui cordatè sint. Quin Cardinalis Toletus bene sperare nos iu-bet. {a} Cùm enim (ait) aliqua graui necessitas occurrit, videlicet, consilij vel refugij, vel alterius, (aduerte quaeso hoc, vel alterius) tum licet conuersari. Credo autem alterius alicuius necessitas non levis subdito incumbet conversandi cum Rege tum, nec ab eo recedendi.
units.tr: The theologians certainly seem more equitable, who except servants: but the priest Zadok, the prophet Nathan, and Joab the commander of the soldiers, will of their own accord lead astray servants, and therefore do not desert the king. They except sons also: but the king wishes to be and to be held a father of his people, and claims for himself by his own right whatever a father ought to be given by his sons. They except wives: but the king has a right of marriage with the kingdom, whose token and witness is the wedding ring; nor if they cling to the king in the force of those words, will they let their consciences be more troubled in political matters than in domestic ones, if they are sensible. Indeed Cardinal Toledo bids us hope well. {a} For when (he says) some grave necessity arises, namely of counsel or of refuge, or of another (please note this, or of another), then it is lawful to associate. I believe, however, that the necessity of some other person, no slight one, will lie upon the subject then to associate with the king, nor to withdraw from him.

units.la: Quòdsi autem ex Regis conversatione vitandà probabiliter timetur scandalum, (& timetur quidem) si turbae oritu-rae, (& oriuntur certè) fixes vergat ad graue periculum, (& verget procul dubio,) tum demum {d}Sylvester nos iubet securos esse, etsi non pareamus. Et ratio fauet; Censura enim quæ ex charitate est, non debet contra charitatem militare, nec potestas quæ ad structuram est, ad destructionem operari.
units.tr: But if, indeed, from the king's association a scandal is probably feared to be avoided (and indeed it is feared), if disturbances are about to arise (and certainly they do arise), if the matter tends toward grave danger (and undoubtedly it tends there), then at last {d} Sylvester bids us be safe, even if we do not obey. And reason favours this; for a censure which proceeds from charity ought not to fight against charity, nor a power which is for building up to work for destruction.

units.la: Quid Sylvestrum memoro? Idem hoc {e}Alexander ipse Papa tertius indulget; si non potest sine scandalo prouideri, aequanimiter sustinebimus, si mandatum nostrum non duxeris exequendum. Aequanimiter ergo sustineat hic; sine scandalo enim prouideri non poterit & ruina multorum. Regula autem est, prouidendo scandalo cessat rigor disciplinae. cuius ratio; Regem enim vitare iubet Papa, ac scandalum vitare iubet Christus; puto autem, cuius hic, Christo potiùs parendum, quàm Papae.
units.tr: Why do I mention Sylvester? The same thing is granted by {e} Alexander the Third, the Pope himself: if it cannot be provided for without scandal, we shall bear it calmly, if you do not think our command should be carried out. Let him therefore bear it calmly here; for it cannot be provided for without scandal and the ruin of many. The rule, moreover, is: when scandal is provided for, the rigour of discipline ceases. The reason for this: the Pope bids us avoid the king, and Christ bids us avoid scandal; but I think that here one must obey Christ rather than the Pope.

units.la: Atque hæc quidem; si legitima sit, & (ut loquuntur) rectè procedat censura, si denunciata uti debet & publicata: Sin ordo iuris non seruatus, modus non debitus, causa non iusta, ne pariturus quidem Catholicus tuus excommunicanti iure quoque (si opus) se non pariturum. Nam si qui excommunicatus est, prætendat & publicet excommunicationem suam, esse nullam; nemo illum cum præiudicio suo tenetur vitare, imò si vitet, iniuriam faciat, {f}Nauarrus ita nos docuit. Vidit verò ætas nostra Principem bis tèrue à Pontifice excommunicatum, quem sui tamen non vitarunt, quantumuis Catholici, cùm excommunicationem suam, nullam esse prætenderent. Quidni autem prætenderet? Monitoriales Pontificum Bullæ, interdum merè bullæ, merè nullæ sunt[?], si clauem potestatis non præcedat clauis discretionis. Sit enim vel maximè intrinseca ligandi potestas hæc Pontificis, at limites habet, ut si limites excedat; regulam habet, ut si à regula discedat; abusus iam potestatis sit, non potestas. In Cathedrâ docentis Papam errare non posse dicitis; in tribunali judicantis errare posse tenetis omnes; Erranti verò parere tenetur nullus. Ita igitur detonare potest Pontifex, ut fulmen eius brutum sit; talem ferre sententiam, ut considerari de eâ porrò possit, annon sit nulla. Quæ si nulla sit, nullus pareat.
units.tr: So much for this: if the censure is lawful, and (as they say) rightly proceeds, if it has been announced as it ought to be and published; but if the order of law has not been observed, the measure not due, the cause not just, then your Catholic will not obey an excommunicator, not even by law (if need be), that he will not obey. For if someone who is excommunicated should allege and publish that his excommunication is null, no one is bound to avoid him to his prejudice; indeed if he avoids him he does wrong, as Navarrus taught us. Yet our age has seen a prince excommunicated by the Pontiff twice or even thrice, whom his own people nevertheless did not avoid, though they were Catholics, since they alleged that his excommunication was null. And why should they not allege it? Monitory bulls of the Pontiffs, sometimes mere bulls, are mere nullities [?], if the key of power is not preceded by the key of discretion. For let this power of the Pontiff of binding be ever so intrinsic, yet it has limits, so that if he exceeds the limits; it has a rule, so that if he departs from the rule; it is already an abuse of power, not power. You say that the Pope cannot err in the chair of teacher; you all hold that he can err in the tribunal of judge; and no one is bound to obey one who errs. So the Pontiff can thunder in such a way that his thunderbolt is a dud; he can pass such a sentence that it may afterwards be considered whether it is not null. And if it is null, no one should obey it.

units.la: Casus quidem sunt apud ◡Angelum quindecim nec pauciores, in quibus excommunicatio est de iure nulla; De tot istis, aliquis unus occurret forte in sententiâ, quam laturus est Pontifex; unus aliquis. ◡Aliquis unus nuper occurrit in causâ Venetâ, quâ freti, Papæ excommunicanti, etiam interdicenti non paruerunt, nec eo minùs Catholici iam sunt. Aliquis alter; Aliquis verò? Omnes quindecim, etiam quindecim pæne plures, viginti enim & sex nullitates reperte sunt, atque{*} obiectæ Gregorio 14. non ita pridem in causâ Gallarum Regis; quibus freti multi tum, atque ij Catholici, parere renuerunt. Quid quærimus? Quæsitum hoc 1510. in Synodo Turonensi, cùm intonuisset tum Iulius secundus contra Ludovicum duodecimum: an sententiæ tùm eius parendum esset? Responsum autem ibi à Synodo totâ, Talem sententiam nullam esse, nec de iure, vel alio quocunque modo ligare. Non est ergo flagitium, in loco, Pontificis sententiæ non parere.
units.tr: There are indeed fifteen or more cases in Angelus in which excommunication is by law null. Of all these, some one will perhaps come up in the sentence which the Pope is about to pronounce: some one. Some one recently came up in the Venetian case, on the strength of which the Venetians disobeyed the Pope when he excommunicated them and even laid an interdict on them, and yet they are still Catholics. Another one, and then another? Why, all fifteen, even nearly fifteen more, for twenty-six nullities have been found, and were objected to Gregory XIV not long ago in the case of the King of the French; relying on them, many Catholics then, and those too, refused to obey. Why do we ask? This was asked in 1510 at the Synod of Tours, when Julius II thundered against Louis XII: whether his sentence was then to be obeyed? The answer given there by the whole Synod was: such a sentence is null, and binds neither by law nor in any other way. It is therefore no disgrace, in such a place, not to obey the Pope's sentence.

units.la: Vides rem totam lubrico in loco versari. Nihil quidem frequentius in historijs, quàm ex omni gente, ex omni genere Catholicorum, multos excommunicanti Pontifici, sæpe non paruisse. Credo autem, permotos Alexandri tertij Pontificis authoritate illâ, quàm minùs cautè retulit Innocentius in 8 Decretalia{§}, qui liberum fecit Archiepiscopo Rauennæ, vel quod mandaret Pontifex adimplere, vel quare adimplere non posset rationabilem causam pretendere. Quisq; sibi exin arripit libertatem illam, nempe indultam à Pontifice; aut enim parebunt excommunicanti, aut pratensâ causâ (& quidem ut sibi videtur rationabili) Pontificem rogabunt, ut habeat se excusatos. Immorari hijs nolo diutius. Parituri ergo sunt Catholici tui Ponti-
units.tr: You see that the whole matter turns on slippery ground. Nothing is more frequent in histories than that, from every nation and every kind of Catholic, many have often disobeyed a Pope who excommunicated them. I believe, moreover, that they were moved by the authority of Pope Alexander III, which Innocent reported less carefully in the eighth Decretal, who left the Archbishop of Ravenna free either to carry out what the Pope commanded, or, if he could not carry it out, to plead a reasonable cause. Everyone then seizes for himself that liberty granted by the Pope; for they will either obey the excommunicating Pope, or, with a pretended cause (and indeed, as it seems to them, a reasonable one), they will ask the Pope to hold them excused. I do not wish to dwell on these matters any longer. Your Catholics, then, will obey the excommunicating Pope...

units.la: {*} Desin. Princ. fici excommunicanti: quanquam etsi non pareant, erunt tamen Catholici. Reliqua non commemoro, ne tu quidem debebas commemorare; Sciamachia mera sunt. Id agunt omnia, ut probent, esse in Pontifice potestatem clauium. De quo etsi alibi fortasse aliter differendum esset, tamen hic pro posito (non tamen concesso) haberi volumus.
units.tr: Ending of the Principle. Nevertheless, even if they do not obey, they will still be Catholics. I do not mention the rest, nor should you have mentioned it; they are pure skirmishing. They all aim to prove that the power of the keys resides in the Pope. Although this might perhaps be discussed differently elsewhere, nevertheless here we want it taken as a proposition (not, however, as granted).

units.la: Nam quòd in medio argumento suo, parenthesin, quasi aliud agens, interijcit, eámque cornutam, quâ aut subjici se Papæ fateatur Rex, aut de Grege Dominico non sit; planè hoc [illegible, ~7 letters]. Alia res illi præ manu fuit, ut Catholicos suos erudiret in nouo hoc fidei suæ dogmate: inopinato Regem ipsum inuoluit quasi (parenthesi suâ) & necessitatem affert, vel ut Papam Pastorem agnoscat, vel ut Dominici Gregis pars nulla habeatur. Quot verò hic, quàm in scala hac Papæ, multi gradus, quàm hiantes atque inter se diffisiti, quàm verò putres & malè fidi; ut qui per eos scandere velit aut descendere, ei à præcipitio valdè metuendum sit?
units.tr: For what he inserts in the middle of his argument, as if doing something else, a parenthesis, and a horned one at that, by which the King must either confess that he is subject to the Pope, or else is not of the Lord's flock: this plainly [illegible]. He had another matter at hand, to instruct his Catholics in this new dogma of his faith: unexpectedly he entangles the King himself, as it were (in his parenthesis), and imposes a necessity: either that he acknowledge the Pope as Shepherd, or that he be regarded as no part of the Lord's flock. But how many steps are there here on this ladder of the Pope, how gaping and mutually discordant, and how rotten and ill-trusted; so that for anyone who wishes to climb or descend by them, there must be great fear of a fall?

units.la: Malè fida primùm in eâ statione; Totum mundum pro Grege suo, vni Petro commissum, aliter quàm cæteris; unum illum, universalem orbis totius pastorem institutum, secus quàm cæteri: Cæteros enim omnes simul Apostolos, Pastores ex æquo, magni illius Gregis institutos esse. Cauere nos iubet {a}Cyprianus à gradu hoc: nota illius sententia, Hoc erant utique & cateri Apostoli quod fuit & Petrus, pari consortio praditi, & honoris & potestatis. Cauere & Augustinus: {b}Ecclesia, Regni cœlorum claues datæ sunt, cùm Petro datæ sunt, & cùm ei dicitur, ad omnes dicitur, Amas me? pasce oues meas.
units.tr: First, a poorly trusted footing at this station: that the whole world was committed to Peter alone as his flock, otherwise than to the others; that he alone was appointed as universal shepherd of the whole world, otherwise than the rest: for all the others together were Apostles, appointed as shepherds on equal terms of that great flock. Cyprian bids us beware of this step: note his saying, "The other Apostles were indeed what Peter also was, endowed with an equal partnership both of honour and of power." Augustine also warns: "The keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to the Church, when they were given to Peter; and when it is said to him, it is said to all: 'Do you love me? Feed my sheep.'"

units.la: Mysterium enim illud trinæ interrogationis, triplicatæ pastionis, altum quidem, & plus in eo Petro dictum quàm cæteris. Sic est; Sed altitudo, huius mysterij; in eo, quòd solus ille, præter, supráque cæteros Apostolos, toties (id est) ter Dominum paulò ante negauerat, in eòque plus à Petro factum quàm cæteris. Plus ergo dicendum illi, plus ab illo faciendum quàm cæteris: ter ad tria interrogata respondendum, quò sic triplicem negationem triplici confessione deleret. Hoc nos mysterium docuit Cyrillus, docuit Augustinus, qui locum hunc non perstringunt leuiter, sed pertractant iusto commentario: Aliud hinc mysterium nullum: vestrum sanè, non eliciunt. elicrunt[?]. Sicc Cyrillus: Altius quiddam hæc oratio certè parturit. Nam quoniam cum alijs Apostolatus nomine Petrus ab ipso Christo decoratus, ter in tempore passionis negârat: iure nunc ab eo terna dilectionis confessio petitur, vt terna negatio æquali confessionis numero compensetur. Trinâ igitur confessione, trina negationis delictum euacuatum est; Dixit autem, Pasce, Apostolatus sibi renouans dignitatem, ne propter negationem, quæ humanâ infirmitate accidit, labefactâ videretur. Aduerte quòd, cum alijs dicit, non præ alijs: & renouans, non augens dignitatem. Sicd Augustinus: Redditur negationi trina, trina confessio; ne minùs amori lingua seruiat quàm timori, & plus vocis elicuisse videatur mors imminens, quàm vita præsens: sit amoris officium, pascere Dominicum Gregem, si fuit timoris indicium, negare pastorem. Hoc illi Patres mysterium viderunt, hoc nobis indicârunt; vestrum verò, de ordinariâ in Apostolos ipsos totámq; Ecclesiam potestate, nulli viderunt. Nam si vidissent, cùm pra cipuum sit fidei caput & fundamentum religionis, nobis non inuidissent; non celâssent eo loco nos, tantam, tam & nobis, & omnibus cognitu necessariam.
units.tr: For that mystery of the threefold question and the threefold feeding is indeed profound, and more was said to Peter in it than to the others. That is so; but the depth of this mystery lies in this: that he alone, besides and above the other Apostles, had shortly before denied the Lord so many times, that is, three times, and so more was done by Peter than by the others. More therefore was to be said to him, more was to be done by him than by the others: he had to answer three times to three questions, so that by a threefold confession he might thus wipe out his threefold denial. This mystery Cyril taught us, Augustine taught us, who do not touch lightly on this passage but handle it with a fitting commentary. There is no other mystery here; but your own, certainly, they do not draw out. Thus Cyril: "This saying certainly brings forth something rather deeper. For since Peter, honoured by Christ himself with the name of Apostle, had denied him three times at the time of the passion, he is now rightly asked for a threefold confession of love, so that the threefold denial may be balanced by an equal number of confessions. By a threefold confession, therefore, the offence of a threefold denial was undone. He said, however, 'Feed,' renewing for him the dignity of the Apostleship, lest it should seem to be weakened on account of the denial, which happened through human weakness. Note that he says 'more than the others,' not 'above the others'; and 'renewing,' not 'increasing' the dignity." Thus Augustine: "The threefold denial is repaid with a threefold confession; so that the tongue may serve love no less than fear, and so that the imminent death may not seem to have drawn more voice than the present life: let it be the office of love to feed the Lord's flock, since it was the sign of fear to deny the shepherd." Those Fathers saw this mystery, they pointed it out to us; but your claim, concerning the ordinary power over the Apostles themselves and the whole Church, nobody saw. For if they had seen it, since it is "the chief head of the faith and foundation of religion," they would not have begrudged it to us, nor would they have concealed from us in that place so great a thing, so necessary for us and for all to know.

units.la: Neque etiam in proximo huic gradu pedem audemus figere. Nam, si fuit tanti Gregis pastor Petrus, ( quantus hinc illinc colligi potuit, ad Neronis vsque tempora, aliquot ex hoc regno, ex illâ natione aliquot :) at numerosior longè Grex præerat tum fuit, immane quantum: Tota ex eo Regna, totæ nationes intrârunt, intrauit plenitudo Gentium, Noui etiam Orbis accessio facta est, vt vnus eis iam Petrus non sufficiat, nisi & illud respondere possis de Papâ vestro, Ecce plus quàm Petrus hic.
units.tr: Nor do we dare to set foot even on the next step. For if Peter was the shepherd of so great a flock (as much as could be gathered from here and there, down to the times of Nero: some from this kingdom, some from that nation), yet at that time a far more numerous flock was under his care, an immense number: whole kingdoms, whole nations entered from it, the fullness of the Gentiles entered, and an addition of the New World has been made, so that Peter alone no longer suffices for them, unless you can also answer about your Pope: "Behold, more than Peter is here."

units.la: Sed neque in illo tutum insistere, de successione. Quis enim nobis fidem faciet, aut ex quo Euangelistâ loco, munus hoc hæreditatium esse, Orbis pascendi? Petro vni, magis in eo successum, quàm vlli de reliquis vndecim? vnum modò fuisse Apostolum ordinarium, Petrum scilicet, cui successor sit? vndecim reliquos extraordinarios omnes, sine successore vllo orbos periisse?
units.tr: But neither is it safe to stand on that either, the matter of succession. For who will give us assurance, or from what evangelical passage, that this office is an inheritance to be passed on, the feeding of the whole world? Did more of a succession pass to Peter alone than to any of the remaining eleven? Was he the only ordinary Apostle, namely Peter, who had a successor? Were the remaining eleven all extraordinary, and did they perish without any successor, bereaved?

units.la: Tum & illud, si fuit hæreditarium munus hoc, vt posset adiri; quibus hæc tabulis sibi vendicabit Romanus vester? Nullum illi ius sanguinis, vt sic adeat: De conclauí autem Dominorum Cardinalium mentio in Euangelio, in Actis, nulla, sed nec in vetere historiâ. Tum electionis forma ipsa, nescio quot vicibus vatiata, proin à Christo non sancita. Sin ex doctrinæ sincerâ successione titulum adornet; titulum illum libenter accipimus; Sed ille, credo, hic potiùs cogitabit de non reddendâ ratione. Vides jam ut gradus hic lubrici, ut omnia hic incerta sint.
units.tr: Then too, if this office were hereditary, so that it could be claimed, by what documents will your Roman claim it for himself? He has no right of blood by which he may thus lay claim to it. But as for the conclave of the lord Cardinals, there is no mention of it in the Gospel or in the Acts, nor even in ancient history. Then the very form of election, varied I know not how many times, has therefore not been sanctioned by Christ. But if he adorns his title with a pure succession of doctrine, we gladly accept that title; but he, I believe, will rather think here of not having to render an account. You now see how slippery this step is, how uncertain everything here is.

units.la: Denique, ad illum vltimum gradum, non peruenitur nisi ex abrupto; nimirum, ut si vel maximè succedat Petro in munere pastoritio, liceat ei per hoc, regno Reges abdicare. Pasce oues meas, id est, ouium Duces mactá; (mactari enim certum potiùs, quàm abdicari.) Pasce oues meas, id est, oues meas arceto caulis suis; fides enim & officium erga omnes, omnium maximè Principes, caulæ sunt ouilis Christi. Pasce oues meas, id est, dissipa, dispergè oues meas: (hæc enim Rege abdicato effecta semper fere consequuta sunt.) Accipe claues regni cælorum, quibus excludas regno terrarum. Quodcunq; ligaueris, id est, quodcunq; sceleris[?] pactum vel proditionis magis astrinxeris: Quodque solueris, id est, quodcunq; legis, officij, fidei, juramenti vinculum laxaris. Chaos magnum inter hæc; Disparata hæc valde quidem, & tu hic[?] iam denuò ducis à disparatis.
units.tr: Finally, one does not reach that last step except by a sudden leap; namely, that even if he succeeds Peter in the pastoral office, it should be lawful for him, by this means, to depose kings from their kingdom. "Feed my sheep," that is, slaughter the leaders of the sheep (for it is more certain to be slaughtered than to be deposed). "Feed my sheep," that is, shut my sheep away from their folds; for faith and duty towards all, and especially towards princes, are the folds of Christ's fold. "Feed my sheep," that is, scatter and disperse my sheep (for these things have almost always followed when a king has been deposed). "Receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven," with which you may shut out from the kingdom of the earth. "Whatever you bind," that is, whatever pact of wickedness or treason you bind more tightly; "and whatever you loose," that is, whatever bond of law, duty, faith, or oath you loosen. A great chaos lies among these things; these are very much disparate things, and you here now again lead from disparate things.

units.la: Hoc quidem pascere oues non est. Ad verbi, ad doctrinæ pastionem referunt ferè Patres, quod Christus ibi in mandatis dedit; hoc illi inclamant, ingeminant, in hoc toti sunt. At vester ille pastoritium hoc munus non attingit. Quantum enim annorum est, ex quo ullus illorum hoc attigit? nec Torti vel atauus gustauit de pabulo hoc Pontificio. A seculo non est auditum, pauisse verbo vel doctrinâ Pontificem ullum. Totum gregem Dominicum volunt; totum munus pascendi defugiunt. Geminum ibi [illegible, ~6 letters] est, unicum [illegible, ~6 letters], [illegible, ~6 letters] illud ibi unicum arripiunt. Habet vox illa in se, (aliquo significato) regendi vim. Geminum [illegible, ~8 letters] (etsi verbum illud proprie designat pascere) fraterculis relinquunt. Factum igitur ab illis non imprudenter, quòd arcessunt à Petro pastoritium jussuum; nolunt verò à Paulo. Paulinum illud, ut qui benè præsunt, laborent verbo & doctrinâ; laboriosa nimis pastio est. Ad illum canonem fit Pastor qui volet: prædicari mauult Papa de Regibus, quàm prædicare illis.
units.tr: This certainly is not feeding the sheep. The Fathers almost always refer the command Christ gave there to the feeding of the word, to the feeding of doctrine; this is what they cry out, repeat, and devote themselves to entirely. But your man does not touch that pastoral office at all. For how many years has any of them touched it? Neither Tortus nor his grandfather has tasted from this Papist pasture. From age to age it has not been heard that any Pope fed anyone with the word or with doctrine. They want the whole Lord's flock; they flee the whole duty of feeding. There the word is twofold, and they seize the one word that is single. That word has in itself (in some sense) the power of ruling. They leave the twofold word (although that word properly signifies feeding) to the little brothers. So what they have done is not unwise, in that they summon the pastoral charge from Peter; but they will not take it from Paul. The Pauline text, that those who rule well should labour in word and doctrine, is too laborious a feeding. By that rule, whoever wishes becomes a pastor: the Pope would rather preach about kings than preach to them.

units.la: Sed protrita jamdudum obiectio hæc de Petri pastione;
units.tr: But this objection about Peter's feeding is long since worn out.

units.la: Quære vero alium, si placet, cui persuadeas; Rex illam non moratur. E cerebro vestro illa est, è decreto alato: Scripturæ eam nesciunt; Ecclesiæ priscæ nec audita, nec visa est. Erit per Dei gratiam de Grege Dominico Rex noster, nec agnoscet Romani Pastoris fistulam. Vnum ille quidem pastorem vniuersi Gregis agnoscit, non alium tamen, quàm Christum ipsum, cuius de Grege honorem sibi ducit quòd sit: Quo de Grege etiam, sic est; vt & Dux Gregis sit sub Christo Pastorum Principe. Sic ille quidem est, sic sunt & alij (certè sic esse debent) Reges Christiani ad vnum omnes, iura si sua nôssent, & vel vires eis, vel animus non deesset.
units.tr: Seek, if you please, another person whom you can persuade; our King does not dwell on that. It is from your own brain, a winged decree: the Scriptures do not know it; the ancient Church neither heard nor saw it. By the grace of God our King will be of the Lord's flock, and he will not acknowledge the pipe of the Roman Shepherd. He acknowledges one shepherd of the whole flock, yet not another than Christ himself, from whose flock he counts it an honour to be; and in this flock he is so placed that he is also leader of the flock under Christ, the Prince of Shepherds. So he indeed is, and so are the other Christian kings (certainly they ought to be), all of them alike, if they knew their rights, and if strength or spirit were not lacking to them.

units.la: Tantùm illud moneo; Cùm Papam toti Dominico Gregi hîc præficis, subiungisque, vel Regem nostrum ad Gregem Dominicum nullo modo pertinere; vel certè subditum esse B. Petro, eiusque successoribus, ab eisque tum ligari tum solui posse; vide quàm hoc à te positum præposterè, qui post homo futilis {b}Christianum negas, quem hîc cupis conijcere in vincula Pontificis tui. Nam qui foris sunt, nec iam Christiani, ad illius Tribunal non pertinent; nec enim iudex est Regum; nisi ut Christiani sunt, (vt pòst asseris) vbi ergo Christiani non sunt, nihil Regibus cum eo, nihil ei cum Regibus. Vides, per te iam, & per tuam stultitiam, non[?] licere nobis, si maximè vellemus, confiteri Regem à Pontifice ligari posse, quem ipse ligari posse negas, cùm negas Christianum, eoque nomine ad Dominicum vestrum Gregem non pertinere.
units.tr: I give only this warning. When you set the Pope over the whole Lord's flock here, and add that our King in no way belongs to the Lord's flock, or at least that he is subject to St Peter and his successors, and can be bound and loosed by them; see how absurdly this is put by you, who, being a trifling man, afterwards deny that he is a Christian, whom here you wish to cast into the chains of your Pontiff. For those who are outside, and no longer Christians, do not belong to his tribunal; nor indeed is he judge of kings, except insofar as they are Christians (as you assert afterwards). Where then they are not Christians, kings have nothing to do with him, nor he with kings. You see, through yourself and through your folly, that we are not permitted, even if we most wished, to confess that the King can be bound by the Pope, whom you yourself deny can be bound, when you deny that he is a Christian, and on that ground that he does not belong to your Lord's flock.

units.la: Quòdsi præsentis instituti foret, edoceri posses, Serenissimum Magnæ Britanniæ Regem, & qui cum eo sentiunt Reges Daniæ & Sueciæ, Germaniæ Principes, Respublicas Heluetiæ, & Rhetiæ; quique per Galliam, Belgium, Poloniam, Hungariam; Ordines, à nobis sunt, partem esse Dominici Gregis, & multò nobiliorem partem, quàm quæ est pars Pauli quinti: Christianos esse omnes hos: & vt scias Christianos esse, vt Christianos pareft, meliorem tibi mentem optare, dehinc vt quiescas porrò, & desinas maledicere.
units.tr: But if it were the purpose of the present undertaking, you could be taught that the Most Serene King of Great Britain, and those who agree with him, the Kings of Denmark and Sweden, the Princes of Germany, the commonwealths of Switzerland and Rhaetia; and those who through France, Belgium, Poland, Hungary, and the Estates are on our side, are part of the Lord's flock, and a much nobler part than that which is the part of Paul V: that all these are Christians; and that you may know they are Christians, as becomes Christians, I wish you a better mind, and then that you may rest from now on and cease to speak evil.

units.la: Quid verò? An ægrè tibi fuit à bile cum hæc scriberes? An vt catharticon illi quæreres, Scholam Salerni habuisti forte præ manibus, cuius è versu primo desumptus tibi titulus ille Anglorum Regi? Anglorum Regem, quis nisi Tortus, iam diceret? Non est in orbe Christiano Rex aut Princeps, qui non hoc titulo iam abstineret, qui non Magnæ Britanniæ Regem scriberet. Auctum illi iam Regnum novi alterius accessione; titulus etiam auctus: hocq; te scire (sed quis hoc nescit) etiam agnoscere, boni mores voluerunt. Inelegans ille titulus in tam eleganti libello scilicet; & bene fecerit ille tuus è Polità Typographo, si te paulò nobis reddat magis politum. Nimis enim impolitè hoc, & quasi Cardinalis à clientella[?] potiùs sis quàm Saecelli[?].
units.tr: But what? Was it with difficulty, from bile, that you wrote these things? Or did you perhaps have the School of Salerno in hand, in order to seek a purgative for it, and from its first verse was that title To the King of the English taken by you? Who but Tortus would now say King of the English? There is no king or prince in the Christian world who would not now refrain from this title, who would not write King of Great Britain. His kingdom has already been enlarged by the addition of another new one; the title too has been enlarged; and that you should know this (but who does not know it?) and even acknowledge it, good manners have required. That inelegant title is certainly out of place in so elegant a little book; and your printer from Polito would do well if he made you a little more polished for us. For you are too unpolished in this, and are more like a Cardinal's hanger-on than a Saecellus.

units.la: Porrò videamus iam, ecquid fælicior in soluendi potestate futurus sit, quàm fuerit in ligandi. Ex hijs verbis Quòd Papa potestatem non habet me ab hoc iuramento absoluendi; En potestas inquit soluendi negatur in Pontifice. Ad Pontificis authoritatem pertinere non solùm potestatem absoluendi à peccato, sed etiam à poenis, censuris, legibus, votis, atq; iuramentis. Hoc autem Catholicos omnes colligere ex verbo Dominicio, Quodcunque solueris super terram, &c. Quò vero hæc tam inanis ostentatio, tam superflua, tam nihil ad rem? De unico hic Iuramento quæstio nobis erat, an eo absoluí possint, qui iurati sunt? De Iuramento igitur hoc solo, ageret, cæteramitteret. Hic verò etiam pompam ducit, & non modò unicum hoc Iuramentum, sed & alia Iuramenta, sed & peccata, & censuras, & poenas, & leges, & vota agit ante currum Pontificis, quasi totidem captiuos. Quorsum hoc ad unius Iuramenti solutionem? aut quid opus quinque illis, nisi si explicare voluit hic pennas Pontificis sui, ut sciant omnes quantus vir sit, nec quicquam abscondi à potestate eius?
units.tr: Further, let us now see whether he will be any more fortunate in the power of loosing than he was in that of binding. From these words, That the Pope has no power to absolve me from this oath; Behold, he says, the power of loosing is denied in the Pope. It pertains to the authority of the Pope not only to absolve from sin, but also from penalties, censures, laws, vows, and oaths. But that all Catholics gather this from the Lord's word, Whatsoever you shall loose on earth, etc. Why then this so empty a display, so superfluous, so irrelevant? The question before us was about this single oath: whether those who have sworn can be absolved by it. He ought therefore to have treated of this oath alone, and left the rest aside. But here he even parades, and not only this single oath, but also other oaths, and also sins, and censures, and penalties, and laws, and vows, he drives before the chariot of the Pope, as so many captives. What has this to do with the loosing of one oath? Or what need is there of those five, unless he wished here to display the wings of his Pope, so that all may know how great a man he is, and that nothing is hidden from his power?

units.la: Ain' verò, à peccatis, poenâ, censuris, legibus, votis, Iuramentis? ut, hic homo leuiter decurrit per sex ista, quasi res non magni momenti? ut, leui brachio, quasi in transitu, soluit omnia? Nos hic homines obtusi, cuique nodo cuneum suum, tribus nodis totidem cuneos quærimus: Hic uno cuneo sex nodos soluit, nodos planè Gordios, si tamen soluit; soluit (inquam) & non secat.
units.tr: But do you say, from sins, penalty, censures, laws, vows, oaths? So this man runs lightly over those six, as if they were matters of no great moment? He looses all of them with a light arm, as it were in passing? We dull men here seek for each knot its own wedge, three knots, as many wedges: he, with one wedge, looses six knots, knots indeed Gordian, if indeed he looses them; he looses (I say) and does not cut.

units.la: Et, quod cuiquam mirum sit, ita se gerit in potestate hac Pontificia, ita res confundit; ut nescias planè quid ligandum iam, quid soluendum sit. Solebant enim soluì peccata, censuræ, poenæ; ligari autem leges, iuramenta, vota, & astringi magis: si & hæc iam soluit etiam, quid tandem ligat Pontifex? Ossicio solui homines opus non habent, nec officij vinculo: ossicio autem soluuntur dum lege: officij vinculo, dum iuramento. Quin quod adhuc mirêre magis, nec secus legem ipsam soluit, quàm peccata in legem: vtráque pari facilitate. Lex sit, peccatum sit contra legem, perinde illi est; tam facile Pontifici soluere leges quàm peccata. Vix tamen fiet vt vnâ clauè, vtráque hæc & præcepti, & peccati iamua[?] reserari possit. Binæ ergo fortè sunt claues, quarum vna, peccatis, panis, censuris: altera, legibus, votis, iuramentis, aperiendis sit. At hæ quidem ambæ cœlorum claues esse nequeunt. Quin si ad soluenda peccata, claues regni cœlorum; ad soluendas leges & legum præcepta, claues inferorum datas oportuit.
units.tr: And, which may seem strange to anyone, he so conducts himself in this Papal power, and so confuses matters, that you truly do not know what is now to be bound, and what to be loosed. For it used to be that sins, censures, and penalties are loosed; but laws, oaths, and vows are bound, and tied more tightly: if he now looses these too, what then does the Pope bind at all? Men have no need to be loosed from duty, nor from the bond of duty: yet they are loosed from duty while they are released from law, and from the bond of duty while released from oath. Moreover, what you should wonder at even more, he looses the law itself no differently than sins against the law: both with equal ease. Let there be a law, let there be a sin against the law; it is all the same to him; it is as easy for the Pope to loose laws as sins. Yet it will hardly come about that by one key both these gates, of precept and of sin, can be unlocked. There would therefore perhaps be two keys, one by which sins, penalties, and censures are to be opened, the other by which laws, vows, and oaths. But neither of these two can be the keys of heaven. Indeed, if for loosing sins the keys of the kingdom of heaven, then for loosing laws and the precepts of laws the keys of hell ought to have been given.

units.la: Certè, quæ paulò ante à nobis pertractata est potestas ligandi, ad excommunicationem modò, & censuras, sese extendit Ecclesiæ. Oportet autem, vt relatiui sint inter se mutuò actus hij duo, ligandi & soluendi, vt non latiùs patere debeat hîc soluendi potestas, quàm illic ligandi; reciproci sunt; hoc enim relatorum natura postulat. Ligatur quis? arcetur cœlo; soluitur? ad cœlum, vnde arcebatur prius, per peccati contumaciam, denuò admittitur: Ibi verò non ligauit leges vel iuramenta; nec hîc quidem soluat igitur.
units.tr: Certainly, the power of binding that we treated a little earlier extends in the Church only to excommunication and censures. But these two acts, binding and loosing, ought to be mutually relative, so that the power of loosing here should not extend more widely than the power of binding there; they are reciprocal, for the nature of correlatives requires this. Is someone bound? He is shut out from heaven; is he loosed? He is admitted again to heaven, whence he had been shut out before, through the obstinacy of sin. But there he did not bind laws or oaths; so neither should he loose them here.

units.la: Audiant verò Pontificis potestatem hanc, quorum interest. Deposuit Reges Pontifex: deposuit iam leges; subditos soluit ab obedientiâ Regum, iam & ab obedientiâ legum: Leges enim dissoluit, iuramenta eiurandi, vota deuouendi potestatem facit. Lege cautum est? Dispensabit cum lege. Iuramento firmata lex? Et cum iuramento. Votum etiam emissum est? Etiam cum voto. Nec tamen qui hæc omnia ruperit, futurus peccatireus, nec censuris obnoxius: Nam & illa & illa etiam soluendi potestatem habet. Non potest quisquam iam (vt videtur) cuiquam, Deo vel homini, quocunque nexu sic astringi, quin illum nullo negotio, statim exoluet Pontifex. Ita: quid fixum erit inter homines, vel firmum? Quò nobis cedent, conuenta, fœdera, vincula societatum omnia? Quid posthæc fiet, quò nobis certis esse detur de cuiusquam pacto vel fide?
units.tr: Let those whom it concerns hear this power of the Pontiff. The Pontiff has deposed kings; he has now deposed laws, and he releases subjects from obedience to kings, and now also from obedience to laws. For he dissolves laws, and he gives the power of renouncing oaths and annulling vows. Is something secured by law? He will dispense with the law. Is a law confirmed by oath? He will dispense with the oath as well. Has a vow also been made? He will dispense with the vow too. Nor will anyone who breaks all these things be guilty of sin or liable to censures, for he has the power of releasing from all of them. (As it seems,) no one can now be bound to anyone, whether to God or to man, by any bond whatsoever, without the Pontiff at once loosing him from it with no trouble at all. So what will be fixed or firm among men? What will become of agreements, compacts, covenants, and all the bonds of societies? What will happen after this, and how will we be able to be sure of anyone's promise or faith?

units.la: Haud itâ pridem, dum scholam aperirent Iesuitæ, & artem profiteprofiterentur aquinocandi, visi sunt pessimè isthuc consuluisse, in vitae societates omnes: nexus de rebus humanis, qui in promissis, qui in pactis, qui in juramentis sunt, sustulisse.
units.tr: Not long ago, when the Jesuits opened their school and professed the art of ... (they were seen to have advised very badly for all societies of life), they removed the bonds of human affairs, those that lie in promises, those in pacts, and those in oaths.

units.la: Quarè merito exosi omnibus, etiam compresbyteris suis secularibus. At jam, palam hic quasi praeconis voce edicit Matthaeus, id penes Pontificem esse, ut nullus sit legum, nullus iuramentorum nexus, ut nemo de iurato certior sit, quam iniurato. Licere enim Pontifici haec omnia ut soluat, Licere apud Ponuficem haec omnia ut solvantur. Licere (inquam) & venales haberi Romae, legis, voti, iuramenti solutiones, id est, peccatis, votifragij, & periurij immunitates. Legum enim solutio, peccati; Iuramenti solutio, periurij authoramentum est. Qui pars iam Pauli quinti sunt, ne parcant iniurijs: leges solvit: ne parcant periurijs: iuramenta soluit Pontifex.
units.tr: Therefore they have justly become hated by all, even by their own secular fellow-presbyters. But now Matthew openly proclaims, as if with the voice of a herald, that it rests with the Pontiff that there be no bond of laws, no bond of oaths, so that no one is more certain of a sworn man than of an unsworn one. For it is lawful for the Pontiff to release all these things, and it is lawful (I say) for them to be bought at Rome: releases from law, from vow, and from oath, that is, immunities from sin, from breaking a vow, and from perjury. For the release from law is the authorization of sin; the release from oath is the authorization of perjury. Since they are now the party of Paul V, let them not spare injuries: he releases laws; let them not spare perjuries: the Pontiff releases oaths.

units.la: Potestas haec quidem soluendi dicenda non erat, sed dissol-vendi omnia, etiam mundi credo machinam, si sic pergat. Quid est enim in rebus humanis firmum & stabile, quod trium horum vnum non nitatur? Quid habet Lege fortius Respublica, vel sacra vel civilis? Atqui lex vlla, si Pontifici stomachum mouit, fax jam est, non lex. Quid habet religio ipsa, juramento magis religiosum? Atqui jam religio non est, & illud violare. Arctissimum quidem habitum est semper voti vinculum: quasi stupa jam est. Omnia haec soluit Pontifex expknitudine[?] potestatis, vel tempestatis potius: ut in animis solutam potestatem (qualis haec) ludere solent Jurisconsulti.
units.tr: This power ought not indeed to be called a power of loosing, but of dissolving everything, even, I believe, the machinery of the world, if it goes on like this. For what in human affairs is firm and stable that does not rest on one of these three? What does the state, sacred or civil, have stronger than law? Yet any law, if it has stirred the Pontiff's bile, is now a torch, not a law. What does religion itself have more sacred than an oath? Yet now it is no longer religion, and violating it is ... The bond of a vow has always been the tightest; it is now like tow. The Pontiff releases all these things by the (?) power, or rather by the storm of power, so that, as lawyers are wont to play with an unrestrained power in souls, (so does he with this one).

units.la: Videbo paululum de Legibus & Juramentis, de Votis non attingam. Quorsum enim de ijs mentio nihil nobis hic cum votis negotij. Legis quidem mentio facta, quia Edictum forte ipsum exauctorare Pontifex; Juramenti etiam, quia & illud enucleare cogitat. At votum non video cur à Matthaeo nominari debuit, aut inferi, nisi si interposita voti mentione, Domino suo gratificari voluit, qui olim Jesuita factus, voti sui reum fecit, & hoc votum jam fregit, postquam ostrum induit. Quod nisi subveniat hic solutiva haec potestas Pontificis super vota, causam nullam potest dicere, quò minus votifragus habendus sit, & desertor ordinis. Certè voto hoc, nisi illum Papa bene soluerit, etiamnum tenetur Patri Ignatio, nec potest sic purpuratus incedere, nec sacellum habere à Papa, quod Matthao male cederet: Redeundum enim tum illi Exsacellano ad Papienses suos, vbi minùs pinguia sunt quàm Romæ Sacerdotia.
units.tr: I will say a little about laws and oaths; I will not touch on vows. For why should we mention them, since we have no business with vows here? Mention has indeed been made of law, because the Pontiff perhaps intends to discharge the edict itself; and of oath too, because he also intends to unravel that. But I do not see why Matthew ought to have named the vow or introduced it, unless, by inserting the mention of a vow, he wished to gratify his lord, who once became a Jesuit, became guilty of his vow, and, after he put on the purple, has now broken this vow. Unless this power of releasing vows, belonging to the Pontiff, comes to his aid, he can give no reason why he should not be held a vow-breaker and a deserter of his order. Certainly, unless the Pope absolves him well, he is still bound by this vow to Father Ignatius, nor can he walk about thus in purple, nor have a chapel from the Pope, which would turn out badly for Matthew: for then that former sacristan would have to return to his Pavian people, where the priesthoods are less fat than at Rome.

units.la: De legibus prin[illegible, ~3 letters] Etiamne porrigis ad leges potestatem hanc indefinitè, nec restringis? Crudius hoc à te positum. At puto excipies hic leges naturæ; nec illas soluerit Pontifex: {a}Naturale ius ab exordio rationalis creaturæ, immutabile permanet. Atqui subditorum ius, naturæ lege nititur. Nascimur, vt filij, sic subditi: filij eius cuius ex stirpe; subditi eius, cuius in ditione nascimur. Ecquis præstabit filium, vt filius huic Patri, subditus, vt subditus huic Regi ne fiet?
units.tr: Concerning laws ... Do you extend this power to laws indefinitely, without restriction? This is put down by you too crudely. But I think you will except here the laws of nature, and the Pontiff will not dissolve those either: "Natural right, from the beginning of rational creation, remains unchangeable." Yet the right of subjects rests on the law of nature. We are born, as sons, so also as subjects: sons of him from whose stock we are, and subjects of him under whose rule we are born. Who will ensure that a son does not cease to be a son to this father, or a subject does not cease to be a subject to this king?

units.la: Etiam puto, excipies & leges ipsas Dei, nec dabis Pontifici potestatem,{b}vt mutet ius, aut dissipet fœdus sempiternum. {c}Præcepta Decalogi apud vestros sunt omnino indispensabilia. Nullam humanam dispensationem admittunt, nec cuiquam homini ex ijs aliquo modo soluere aut licuit, aut licebit. Tantum autem abest Papam posse, vt (si in eo vestris fas credere) in quibusdam,{d}nec Deus ipse dispensare possit. Dei autem lex est, de obedientiâ, de fide Regibus præstandâ; lex mandato quinto comprehensa, filius vt patrem, subditus vt patriæ patrem debito obsequij, fidei, subiectionis honore afficiat. Ecquis verò mortalium hac lege liberabit? Legù autem nostræ æquitas, diuinâ hac nititur. Quasi enim familia quædam magna, Regnum est; quam Rex sic ducit, vt Paterfamilias. Quare quæcunque Patri iura, quintæ legis vi, debentur, suo sibi iure vendicabit omnia.
units.tr: I also think you will except God's own laws too, and will not give the Pontiff power "to change right, or to dissolve an everlasting covenant." The precepts of the Decalogue, among your people, "are altogether indispensable." They admit no human dispensation, nor has it been, or will it be, lawful for anyone to release anyone from them in any way. Indeed, so far is it from the case that the Pope can do this (if it is permitted among you to believe it of him), that God himself cannot dispense with some of them. But God's law is that obedience and faith are to be rendered to kings; a law contained in the fifth commandment, that the son should honour his father, and the subject his country's father, with the due honour of obedience, faith and submission. But which of mortals will free anyone from this law? The equity of our laws, moreover, rests on this divine law. For a kingdom is, as it were, a certain great family, which the king leads as a father of a household. Therefore whatever rights are owed to a father by virtue of the fifth law, he will claim for himself, by his own right, all of them.

units.la: Pari autem ratione, excipies, puto, & leges Euangelicas: Euangelica autem est, & à Petro lex ista, Estote subditi Regi tanquam præcellenti. Hæc est enim voluntas Dei. Quid hic, verè? Soluitne legem hanc Petri, & dicit, Regi quamuis præcellenti ne estote subditi; hæc est enim voluntas Papæ? non puto: non committet Paulum quintum cum Petro.
units.tr: By the same reasoning, you will except, I think, the Evangelical laws as well: and that law of Peter is evangelical: "Be subject to the king as to the one who excels. For this is the will of God." What here, truly? Does he dissolve this law of Peter, and say, "Do not be subject to the king, however excellent he may be; for this is the will of the Pope"? I do not think so: Paul V will not set himself against Peter.

units.la: Quin & ciuiles porrò excipies etiam: hoc argumento; Quòd ad idem spectent, potestas ligandi & soluendi, eòdem referantur, vt quod ligare non possit Papa, nec possit soluere. Leges autem ciuiles Regno vlli, vlli Reipublicæ condere non potest; nullus hoc Papa dixerit, nullus Rex tulerit. Faciat, si volet, in Galliâ periculum, faciat vel in Hispaniâ, legem ferat illis; non ferent ferentem. Legem ergo ponere non potest, nec rogare: ne soluere quidem igitur, aut abrogare. At noftra quoque civilis lex est, legitimè [illegible, ~4 letters]a, plenis Comitijs lata, omnium Ordinum consensu comp[illegible, ~1 letter]bata.
units.tr: Moreover, you will also except civil laws, by this argument: since the power of binding and loosing concerns the same things, and is referred to the same, the Pope cannot bind what he cannot loose. But no Pope can enact civil laws for any kingdom or any commonwealth; no Pope would say it, no king would endure it. Let him try, if he wishes, a test in France, or indeed in Spain; let him pass a law for them; they will not accept the one who passes it. Therefore he cannot lay down a law, nor propose one: neither, then, can he loose or abrogate one. But our civil law too is legitimately ... enacted in full assemblies, passed with the consent of all the orders.

units.la: Nullàne ergò soluendi potestas in Ecclesiâ ad leges, nec vllus dispensationi locus? Est verò: quis negat? Laxet nodos Ecclesia, quos ipsa nexuit; leges quas fixit, refigat; quas posuit, tollat denuò; positiuo iuri derogét. Parcè tamen hoc quoque: Rectè enim dixit quispiam, Dispensationes nihil aliud esse, quàm legum vulnera. Nec ergo hoc laudi sibi ducat Pontifex, si multis vulneribus sauciæ sint apud eum leges vel positiua. Et parcè (inquam) & moderatè. Nota satis in Decretû glossa Canonis, fuit tamen hic nimium papaliter dispensatum. Semel ibi notatum; sæpe factum à Pontifice, sæpe dispensauit, nimis papaliter. Potestas autem si longiùs se quàm par est extendat, abusum patitur, nec iam actus eius dispensatio est, sed dissipatio. Vtcunque autem se res habet; contraria Papæ vox, atque Christi, de lege. Christus; Non veni soluere, sed implere: Papa; Non veni implere, sed soluere.
units.tr: Then is there no power of loosing in the Church with regard to laws, and no place for dispensation? There is indeed; who denies it? Let the Church loosen the knots that it has tied itself; let it unfasten the laws that it has fixed, and take away again those it has laid down; let it derogate from positive right. Yet let it do this sparingly too: for someone has rightly said, "Dispensations are nothing other than wounds of laws." Therefore let the Pontiff not count it to his praise if positive laws and statutes are, in his hands, wounded in many places. And sparingly (I say), and moderately. There is a well-known gloss in the Decretum of the canon: "Yet this was dispensed in too papal a manner here." It was noted once there; it was often done by the Pontiff, he often dispensed "too papally." But if a power extends itself further than is fitting, it suffers abuse, and its act is no longer dispensation but dissipation. However the matter stands, the voice of the Pope is opposed to that of Christ concerning the law. Christ: "I came not to loose, but to fulfil." The Pope: "I came not to fulfil, but to loose."

units.la: Pergo iam ad iuramenta. Etiamne & illa in vniuersum soluendi potestas illi? At si leges non potest, nec iuramenta potest, quibus iuratur in leges. Quid si enim legi alicui diuinæ, obligare me volo iuramento, ecquis me impedit? Olim ita Dauid; Iurani, & certò apud me statui, custodire iudicia iustitiæ tuæ. Petrus ipse si tum vixisset, an potuisset efficere, ne Dauid iuramenti reus esset? aut an soluisset eum hoc iuramento? Dauidis exemplo, iuramento se obstringet, quis putà de non mœchando; hoccine illum iuramento vllus soluet Pontifex? Par faciet de mandato quinto iuramentum, nec magis illum soluet Pontifex; non magis (inquam) de quinto, subiectionis, quàm de septimo, castitatis; nec magis præstabit vt rebellis, quàm vt mœchus sit.
units.tr: I now proceed to oaths. Does he also have a general power of loosing those too? But if he cannot (dispense with) laws, neither can he (dispense with) oaths by which one swears to laws. For what if I wish to bind myself by oath to some divine law: who hinders me? Thus once David: "I have sworn, and firmly resolved, to keep the judgments of your righteousness." If Peter himself had lived then, could he have brought it about that David was not guilty of the oath? Or would he have released him from this oath? Following David's example, someone binds himself by oath, for instance not to commit adultery: will any Pope release him from this oath? Likewise he will make an oath about the fifth commandment, and the Pope will not release him from it any more; not any more (I say) from the fifth, of submission, than from the seventh, of chastity; nor will he allow him to be a rebel any more than to be an adulterer.

units.la: Sed & iuramenta quædam interdum solui possunt; & habet in illis dispensatio locum suum: quæ tamen, dispensatio vix proprie dicitur. Si quis se temerè irretiuit iuramento, vt Herodes; etsi debet esse de eo scrupulus nullus; si quis tamen est, illum eximat. Iuramentum de malo vel bono impeditiuo, dispensatione non indiget; tenetur enim iurans non seruare. In iurando si fuit stultus, in reddendo ne sit impius. Addo etiam, si non cuentu, ut Herodu[?] illud: sed si ab initio statim sacrilegum est iuramentum, si proditorium (quale hic nuper apud nos inter Coniuratos) etii[?] nihil opus, quia iurati in malum; si videtur tamen opus, & si volet, soluat & illud; in quo tamen non soluendo, quin astringendo magis, operam omnem suam posuerunt, quibus tum apud nos potestatis suae copiam Pontifex fecerat. Soluerent vero hic: hic vero recondunt in vaginâ, ubi exertam oportuit, aciem atque aculeos authoritatis suae: ubi minimè oportet, ibi demum exerunt. Soluunt fidelitatis Sacramenta, non soluunt perfidiae: soluunt scilicet liganda, ligant soluenda.
units.tr: But some oaths can also be loosed at times, and dispensation has its place in them, though this can hardly be called dispensation in the proper sense. If someone has rashly bound himself by an oath, as Herod did, then, although there ought to be no scruple about it, if there is one, let him free himself from it. An oath concerning something evil or something good that hinders is not in need of dispensation; for the one swearing is bound not to keep it. If he was foolish in swearing, let him not be impious in performing. I add also: if it is not as with Herod, but the oath was sacrilegious from the start, or treasonous (such as the one recently sworn here among us by the conspirators), then there is no need even to loose it, since they swore to do evil; yet if it seems necessary, and if he wishes, let him loose that too. In this matter, however, they have not loosed but rather tightened the bonds, and they have put all their effort into it, since the Pontiff had then given them a display of his power among us. Here they ought to loose, but here they keep sheathed the edge and the goads of their authority that ought to have been drawn out; where it is least fitting, there they finally draw them out. They loose the sacraments of fidelity, they do not loose perfidy: they loose, of course, what should be bound, and bind what should be loosed.

units.la: Nec tamen hoc miretur lector: Ita enim se habent Pontifices in hoc negotio ligandi & soluendi, ut solent agyrtae. Ligare ad tempus suiunt, tum non ligare; ligare dum desunt vires, non ligare cum iam adsunt; Ita ligatus solutus est, solutus ligatus, nec ligatus nec solutus, prout Pontifici visum fuerit. Sic lusit nuper Gregorius 13. de Bulla Pij quinti, * ut ligaret illa Reginam, & subditos haereticos; subditos autem Catholicos non ligaret: non ligaret quidem Catholicos rebus sic stantibus; ligaret tamen, quando publica eius Bullae executio fieri poterat. Mirus artifex: unâ eademque Bullâ ligat, non ligat; ligat haereticos, non ligat Catholicos; & Catholicos non ligat, ligat tamen. Profecto non redemit animos hominum Pontifex, qui sic ludit periurio.
units.tr: Nor should the reader be surprised at this: for the Pontiffs in this business of binding and loosing behave like quacks. They bind for a time and then do not bind; they bind while the strength is lacking, and do not bind when it is now present. Thus the bound is loosed, the loosed is bound, neither bound nor loosed, as seems good to the Pontiff. So recently Gregory XIII played with the Bull of Pius V, so that it bound the Queen and her heretical subjects, but it did not bind Catholic subjects: indeed it did not bind Catholics with things standing as they are; yet it would bind them when the public execution of his Bull could be carried out. A wonderful craftsman: by one and the same Bull he binds and does not bind; he binds heretics, does not bind Catholics; and he does not bind Catholics, yet binds them. Certainly the Pontiff has not won over men's minds, when he plays thus with perjury.

units.la: Enimuerò, si haec sit in Pontifice soluendi potestas, dic quaeso, quid opus Breui, vel primo vel secundo, quae interdicunt, ne iuretur iuramentum? Quid opus Epistolâ Cardinalis, ut abiuretur? Nihil certè. Iurate Catholici omnes; iurate liberè iuramentum Regium, duplici Breui non obstante. Nam quid ni iuretis? Annon Roma est, qui iuramenta vestra sic soluit, ut corrigiam calceamenti sui, qui vno verbo facet[?], iurati ut iniurati estis? Cùm tam leue hoc illi, cur arcet à iuramento; nec sinit iurare, tamcitò, tam leuiter soluendos? Iurate verò. Quid enim inani metu se cruciet quisquam, cur multam subeat, cur in carcerem se duci sinat propter ista, vel iura, vel iuramenta? pareat iuri, nec parcat iuramento; Roma est, qui haec dissi-pabit omnia; perinde est, iurent[?], non iurent Catholici, praestabit Papa, ne qui rei sunt iuramenti, rei sint periurij; & quâ est potestate. solvet illos primùm, deinde & inuoluet illos plenariis suis indulgentijs, tam densis, tam confertis, vt nec ipsa perditio illos possit perdere.
units.tr: Indeed, if this power of loosing exists in the Pontiff, tell me, I ask, what need is there of the Briefs, either the first or the second, which forbid that an oath be sworn? What need is there of the Cardinal's letter, to make you abjure? None at all. Swear, all you Catholics; swear freely the royal oath, notwithstanding the two Briefs. For why should you not swear? Is it not Rome that loosens your oaths as easily as the thong of his shoe, that makes a jest of it with a single word, so that you are sworn as if unsworn? Since this is so light a matter to him, why does he keep you from the oath; why does he not allow you to swear, to be loosed so quickly and so lightly? Swear, then. For why should anyone torment himself with vain fear, why undergo a fine, why allow himself to be led into prison on account of these things, whether rights or oaths? Let him obey the law and not spare the oath; it is Rome that will dissipate all these things. It makes no difference whether Catholics swear or do not swear: the Pope will ensure that those who are bound by the oath are not guilty of perjury; and by what power? He will first loose them, and then he will wrap them up in his plenary indulgences, so dense and so compact that not even perdition itself can destroy them.

units.la: Sed bene; quòd tempore saltem circumscripsit potestatem hanc, vt non semper vti detur, sed tum demum quando ad Dei gloriam expedit, aut salutem animarum. Hoc ipso jam nobis per te aditus est, januaque patefacta, vt potestas hæc in nos, nihil possit, aut juramentum nostrum. Nam vtcunque de soluendi potestate fateamur: hic tamen negamus adhibendam in juramento, quòd certè nec expedit ad gloriam Dei, nec animarum salutem, vt soluantur eo subditi. Non est enim adhibenda, ais, nisi quando expedit ad Dei gloriam & animarum salutem. Illud autem Quando, quando est? An iam est in juramento hoc nostro? Ecquid Deo de gloriâ deperit? ecquid animabus de salute, si nihil horum Regi fiat, quorum in juramento mentio, si nemo Regem deponat, inuadat, vim afferat? Nihil horum.
units.tr: But well; at least he has limited this power by time, so that it is not always to be used, but only then, when it is expedient for the glory of God or the salvation of souls. By this very thing an entry has already been opened for us through you, and the door has been thrown open, so that this power can do nothing against us, nor against our oath. For however much we may concede the power of loosing, here we deny that it is to be applied to the oath, since it is certainly not expedient for the glory of God, nor for the salvation of souls, that subjects be loosed by it. For, you say, it is only to be applied when it is expedient for the glory of God and the salvation of souls. But that word when: when is it? Is it now, in this oath of ours? Does anything fall away from God's glory? Does anything fall away from souls' salvation, if none of those things which are mentioned in the oath are done to the King, if no one deposes the King, attacks him, or does him violence? None of these.

units.la: Sed scire vis, lector, quid sibi velit Quando hoc? Lege Historias; videbis haud vnquam fere reduci in actum hanc Papæ potentiam, quando aut diuina gloria quid, aut humana saluti impendet periculi, sed quando Pontifici mota bilis est: mota autem fere est, quando negatæ decimæ, quando prouisum contra promissiones, quando Indulgentiarum nundinationes interdictæ. Nec enim hæc, si nescis, in rem pietatis & fidei potestas astruitur, nec illorum hic incrementum quæritur: quæritur, vt Taxa Cancellariæ bene fit, id est, vt culinæ Pontificis, dum pro tali voto soluto tot grosi; pro tali iuramento rupto tot florenì; pro tali lege violatâ tot aurei numerantur: in quo non Dei gloria, sed Principum ignominia; nec salus animæ, sed pernicies crumenæ quæritur: Huic dum consulatur, eat gloria Dei, eat animarum salus, quâ potest.
units.tr: But you wish to know, reader, what this when means? Read the histories; you will see that this papal power is almost never brought into action when either something threatens the divine glory or danger hangs over human salvation, but when the Pontiff's bile is stirred; and it is almost always stirred when tithes are refused, when provision is made against promises, when the trading in indulgences is forbidden. For this power, if you do not know, is claimed not for the sake of piety and faith, nor is its increase sought here: it is sought that the Taxa Cancellariae may be well provided for, that is, that the Pontiff's kitchen may be supplied, since for such a vow broken so many groats, for such an oath violated so many florins, for such a law violated so many gold pieces are counted out: in which case it is not the glory of God that is sought, but the dishonour of princes; nor the salvation of the soul, but the ruin of the purse. While this is looked after, let the glory of God and the salvation of souls go wherever they can.

units.la: Sed dic tandem, ubi data, ubi fundata potestas hæc. Certè, in verbis Dominicis, nimirum hiis; Quodcunque soluerís super terram &c. At hiis verbis Dominus clauem promittit, clauem, dico, ad aperiendum, non vectem ad perrumpendum omnia; & soluere dicit, quod summis digitis fit; non diffecueris, quod gladio fit, aut bipenni; denique facultatem pollicetur dispen[?]nadi, non dissipandi [?]omnia.
units.tr: But tell me at last, where is this power given, where is it founded? Certainly, in the words of the Lord, namely these: Whatsoever thou shalt loose upon earth, etc. But in these words the Lord promises a key, a key, I say, for opening, not a crowbar for breaking through everything; and he says loose, which is done with the fingertips, not shatter, which is done with a sword or an axe; in short, he promises the faculty of dispensing, not of dissipating everything.

units.la: Verùm ( quod [illegible, ~3 letters]ertit Hieronymus, & nos monuit) loco quem affers, promisit modò Christus, non etiam dedit: de futuro hoc verbum est, Dabo tibi. Quæro vbi dederit? Scio te de nouâ scholâ esse, dicturum, cùm dixit, Pasce oues meas. Quid hoc verbi est? Quid sibi vult, pasce? An hoc? Doce illas, potestatem hanc quâ tibi nunc trado, eò se porrigere, vt si tuæ sint oues, eis, votifragis, periuris, exlegibus esse liceat, nec vllis aut officij caulis, aut legum repagulis contineri? Venenum hoc quidem, non pabulum est. Malus pastor, qui has de grege suo caulas; malus Pontifex, qui has de ponte suo sublicas summotas vult. Nec ergo, vel hoc loco quicquam euiceris.
units.tr: But (as Jerome translated and reminded us) in the passage you cite, Christ only promised, he did not yet give: this is a verb in the future, I will give to you. I ask where he gave it. I know you will say, being of the new school, when he said, Feed my sheep. What is this word? What does feed mean? Does it mean this? Teach them that the power which I now hand over to you extends so far that, if they are your sheep, it is lawful for them, the breakers of vows, the perjured, the outlaws, not to be held by any folds of duty or barriers of laws? This is poison, not pasture. A bad shepherd is he who removes these folds from his flock; a bad Pontiff is he who wishes these stakes removed from his bridge. Therefore you have won nothing even at this point.

units.la: Sed tamen nec hoc loco dedit, quod illo tuo promisit. Quin si veteres illos audimus, illo potius, Ioh. 20. Quorum peccata, &c. Atque ita ad peccata modò reuocanda est, & censuras, poenasque peccati, contrà quàm tu, non modò ad peccata, poenas, censuras. Noua enim hæc tua glossa est, & Catholicorum (quos tu vocas) quorundam modò, non omnium; non omnes verba illa ad Leges & Iuramenta protendi volunt. Caietanus fortè sic voluit; & cum eo nouitij aliquot Pontificiæ potestatis amplificandæ cupidi; multum abest ut Catholici omnes hoc senserint.
units.tr: But even at this point he did not give what you say he promised. Indeed, if we listen to the ancients, it is rather that passage, John 20. Whose sins, etc. And so it is only sins that are to be called back, and censures and penalties for sin, contrary to what you say, not only sins, penalties, and censures. For this gloss of yours is new, and is held only by some Catholics (whom you call so), not by all; not all want those words to be extended to laws and oaths. Cajetan perhaps wished so; and with him a few novices eager to enlarge papal power; but it is far from the case that all Catholics have thought this.

units.la: Ignota quidem hæc Augustino glossa. Sic olim ille. Ecclesia quæ fundatur in Christo, claues ab illo regni cælorum accepit, idest, potestatem soluendi, ligandi, peccata. Ignota Theophylacto, ac proin Chrysostomo (cuius ille abbreuiator tantùm est) Sic enim ille. Claues autem intelligas, quæ ligant & soluunt, hoc est, delictorum vel indulgentiæ vel pœnas. Audis Augustini [id est] Thophylacti [hoc est] satis ut credo dilucidè: ad peccata modò & delicta potestatem accommodant, nec porriguntur ulterius. At hij certè pro Catholicis habentur.
units.tr: This gloss, indeed, was unknown to Augustine. Thus he said long ago: The Church, which is founded on Christ, received the keys of the kingdom of heaven from him, that is, the power of loosing and binding sins. It was unknown to Theophylact, and therefore to Chrysostom (of whom he is merely an abridger). For thus he said: Understand the keys as those which bind and loose, that is, the penalties or the remissions of offences. You hear Augustine [that is] Theophylact [that is] clearly enough, I believe: they apply the power only to sins and offences, and do not extend it further. Yet these are certainly regarded as Catholics.

units.la: Sed enim libero iam tibi fidem meam de Catholicis, qui quod Matt. 16. promissum est, id exhiberi non Ioh. 21. verbo pascendi, sed ante illud, Ioh. 20. verbis peccata remittendi, uno ore fatentur omnes; ut Christus ipse fuerit interpres suus, interpres optimus, qui quod Matt. 16. Quodcunque solueris dixit, id ipsum Ioh. 20. Quorumcunque peccata &c. interpretatus ipse fuerit; nec vel de lege, vel iuramento verbum addiderit. Simul & potestatem hanc in criminibus esse, & peccatis unde patebit, & Catholicos tuos qui hoc [?]colligunt, colligere quæ Christus ibi non sparsit.
units.tr: But now that I have given you my word about the Catholics, let me show what they all confess: the promise made in Matthew 16 was not fulfilled by the word "feed" (John 21), but before that, by the words "remit sins" (John 20). Christ himself was his own interpreter, the best of interpreters: when he said in Matthew 16, "Whatever you shall loose," he himself interpreted that same thing in John 20, "Whose sins you remit, etc." He added no word about law or oath. At the same time it will be clear that this power concerns crimes and sins, and that your Catholics, who gather otherwise, gather what Christ did not scatter there.

units.la: Ordior autem à Papa {a}Hadriano 6. Catholicum hunc nullus negabis. Videndum est (inquit) quæ sint ista claves. Has duas claves notat Augustinus, & post eum Glossa interlinearis, Ioh. 20. Quorum remiseritis peccata, &c. Vnum pollicitus sum, tres in vno dedi. Habet enim Hadrianus, Augustinum, & Glossam secum sentientes: En claves promissæ, Mat. 16. dantur Ioh. 20. per verba, Quorum remiseritis, non autem, per verba, Pasce oues. Atque idem illud post iterat. De clave ministerij dictum est Petro, tibi dabo claves, & in Petro omnibus Sacerdotibus, quibus in ordinatione datur Spiritus Sanctus, ut quorum remiserint, &c.
units.tr: I begin with Pope Hadrian VI, whom you will deny is a Catholic. "It must be seen (he says) what those keys are. Augustine marks these two keys, and after him the interlinear Gloss, John 20, 'Whose sins you remit, etc.' I promised one, and I have given three in one." For Hadrian has Augustine and the Gloss agreeing with him: behold the promised keys of Matthew 16 are given in John 20 through the words "Whose sins you remit," not through the words "Feed my sheep." And again he repeats the same thing afterwards: "The key of the ministry was spoken of to Peter, 'I will give you the keys,' and in Peter to all priests, to whom the Holy Spirit is given at ordination, so that whose sins they remit, etc."

units.la: Proximus à Papa Cardinalis {b}Hugo, & hic quoque Catholicus. Sic verò ille: Et tibi dabo claves; Claves sunt potentia & scientia discernendi, quid dignos recipere, & indignos excludere debet à regno, & idem habetur Ioh. 20. Quorum remiseritis, &c. Pro clauium intelligentia, refert nos ad Ioh. 20. vbi, idem inquit, habetur. Cardinali succedit Archiepiscopus {c}Theophylactus. Quamuis autem Petro soli dictum sit, Tibi dabo claves; omnibus tamen Apostolis concessa sunt. Quando? cum dixit, Quorumcunque remiseritis, &c. Etenim cum dixit, Dabo, futurum tempus signat, hoc est, post resurrectionem. Audi & alterum è Latinis, & quidem Archiepiscopum nostrum. Is {d}Anselmus est. Notandum est, quòd hæc potestas clauium non solum Petro data est: sed sicut Petrus, vnus pro omnibus respondit, sic in Petro, omnibus hanc potestatem dedit: unde post passionem dictum est, Quorum remiseritis. Etiam, si placet, è Germania {e}Druchmarum[?]. Hoc tam Petro, quàm omnibus Apostolis & successoribus eorum, qui in Ecclesiâ eundem locum tenent, rectè credimus concessum, quia ipse post passionem apparens iis dixit, Quorum remiseritis, &c.
units.tr: Next after the Pope comes the Cardinal Hugo, also a Catholic. Thus he writes: "And I will give you the keys. The keys are the power and knowledge of discerning who ought to be received and who excluded from the kingdom, and the same is found in John 20, 'Whose sins you remit, etc.'" For the understanding of the keys he refers us to John 20, where, he says, the same is found. The Cardinal is succeeded by the Archbishop Theophylact. Although it was said to Peter alone, "I will give you the keys," they were nevertheless granted to all the Apostles. When? When he said, "Whose sins you remit, etc." For when he said "I will give," he signifies a future time, that is, after the resurrection. Hear also one of the Latins, and indeed our own Archbishop. He is Anselm. It must be noted that this power of the keys was not given to Peter alone; but as Peter, one for all, answered, so in Peter he gave this power to all: whence after the passion it was said, "Whose sins you remit." Also, if you like, from Germany, Druchmar[?]. We rightly believe this was granted as much to Peter as to all the Apostles and their successors, who hold the same place in the Church, because after the passion he himself, appearing to them, said, "Whose sins you remit, etc."

units.la: Quòd si malis è schola, Scotum inde tibi sistam[?]. Sic ille: Sed contrà, Matt. 16. promittitur Petro & sacerdotibus, Tibi dabo claves, Ioh. 20. impletur illud promissum, dicente Christo, Quorum remiseritis, &c. Poteram & plures; sed hoc testium satis erit. Hij vero Catholici omnes. Non[?] omnes ergo Catho-lici,
units.tr: But if you prefer the schools, I will bring Scotus forward for you. Thus he: "But on the contrary, Matthew 16 promises to Peter and the priests, 'I will give you the keys'; John 20 fulfils that promise, Christ saying, 'Whose sins you remit, etc.'" I could bring more; but this will be enough of witnesses. These, however, are all Catholics. Not all, therefore, Catholics...

units.la: {a} Hadriano 6.: Papa Hadrianus VI, cited as the authority for the keys. licl[?], sic vt dicis, colliguntur; Et tu iam denuò tamen dicis omnes? & ad eundem scopulum bis allidis; nec vocem hanc tam laxam, omnes, iterum hic vsurpare pertimescis?
units.tr: {a} Hadrian VI: Pope Hadrian VI, cited as the authority for the keys. Are all Catholics gathered, as you say, in this way? And do you again, after all, say "all"? And do you dash yourself twice against the same rock; and do you not fear to use again here this word "all", so loose?

units.la: Sed & in hoc mysterium est, cùm se Matthaeus recipiat ad locum Matthaei, vbi promissae tantùm sunt, non datae; cur ad Ioh. 21. Pasce oues meas, vbi quae promissae illinc sunt, non sunt datae. Vulgabo sacrum hoc. Tibi dabo libenter audit; placet illi hoc Quodcunq; ligaueris; Pasce oues mirum in modum arridet.
