Quid ita? singulari enim numero prolata, vnimodò proin (vt putat) dicta, vnde illi spes, vt quae Petro vni potestas data est, & vni Pontifici tota propria sit, eique soli peculiaris. Pontifex enim Petro ex asse haeres, Verùm hîc etiam vanâ spe se lactat, & illudit sibi suauiter; Nec enim hoc ex verbis illis Catholici omnes colliguntur; multi magnique contrà sentiunt. Non Petro haec dicta soli vel data; dicta & data etiam caeteris omnibus. Et vtcunque verba sint singularia, Tibi, ligaueris, soluueris, & pasce: non tamen Petro dicta in personâ suâ, sed Petro representanti Ecclesiam, eamque mysticè significantes.
units.tr: But there is also a mystery here: when Matthew withdraws to the place of Matthew, where the things were only promised, not given, why to John 21, "Feed my sheep," where what was promised is not given at all? I will publish this sacred matter. He gladly hears "I will give you"; this pleases him, "Whatsoever you shall bind"; "Feed my sheep" smiles upon him in a wonderful way. Why so? For these words, spoken in the singular number, and therefore (as he thinks) said for him alone, give him hope that the power given to Peter alone is wholly his own, belonging to the one Pontiff and peculiar to him alone. For the Pontiff is Peter's heir in full. But here too he delights himself with empty hope and sweetly deceives himself; for it is not from those words that "all Catholics are gathered"; many great men think otherwise. These things were not said or given to Peter alone; they were said and given also to all the others. And however singular the words may be, "to you, bind, loose, and feed," they were nevertheless not said to Peter in his own person, but to Peter representing the Church, mystically signifying it.

units.la: Audi, si placet, de aceruo manipulum. {a}Origenem primò. An verò soli Petro dantur à Christo claues regni coelorum, nec eas beatorum quisquam accepturus est? Quodsi dictum hoc, Tibi dabo claues, caeterisque quoque commune est; cur non simul omnia, & quae prius dicta sunt, & quae sequuntur, velut ad Petrum dicta, sunt omnium communia? Nihil ergo hic, nec tuum illud, Quodcunq; ligaueris, Petro peculiare; commune & reliquis. {b}Hieronymum: At dicis, super Petrum fundatur Ecclesia, licet id ipsum in alio loco super omnes Apostolos fiat, & cunctis claues regni coelorum accipiant, & ex aequo super eos Ecclesiae fortitudo solidetur.
units.tr: Hear, if you please, a handful from the heap. First Origen. Are the keys of the kingdom of heaven given by Christ to Peter alone, and will no one of the blessed receive them? But if this saying, "I will give you the keys," is common also to the others, why are not all things common, both those said before and those that follow, as if said to Peter? Nothing here, then, is peculiar to Peter, not even that saying of yours, "Whatever you bind"; it is common to the rest as well. Jerome: But you say that the Church is founded upon Peter, although in another place the same thing is done upon all the Apostles, and all receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and the strength of the Church is equally made firm upon them.

units.la: Augustinum verò non modò locupletem testem, sed & multis testimonijs locupletem. {c}Quaedam dicuntur, quae ad Apostolum Petrum propriè pertinere videntur, nec tamen habent illustrem intellectum, nisi cùm referuntur ad Ecclesiam, cuius ille agnoscitur in figurâ gestâsse personam, propter primatum quem in Discipulis habuit: sicuti est, Tibi dabo claues regni coelorum, & siqua huiusmodi. Et alio {d}loco: Nam si in Petro non esset Ecclesiae Sacramentum, non ei diceret Dominus, Tibi dabo claues regni coelorum, & Quodcunque &c. Si hoc Petro tantum dictum est, non facit hoc Ecclesia; si autem & in Ecclesia fit, ut quæ in terra ligantur in cælo ligetur, & quæ solvuntur in terra solvantur & in cælo, quia cum excommunicat Ecclesia, in cælo ligatur excommunicatus; si hoc ergo in Ecclesia fit, Petrus quando claves accepit, Ecclesiam sanctam significavit. Et {a}alio. Quod ad Petrum proprie pertinet, natura unus homo erat, gratia unus Christianus, abundantiore gratia unus idemque primus Apostolus: sed quando ci dictum est, Tibi dabo claves regni cælorum, & quodcunque ligaveris &c. universam significabat Ecclesiam. Audi vero & quæ Augustini mens de vestro illo Pasce oves. Sic ait, {b}Non sine causa inter Apostolos, huius Ecclesiæ Catholicæ personam sustinet Petrus. Huic enim Ecclesiæ, claves Regni cælorum datæ sunt, cum Petro datæ sunt, & cum ei dicitur, ad omnes dicitur, Pasce oves meas. Audi & quæ mens {c}Ambrosij; Quæ oves, & quem Gregem non solum tum B. suscepit Petrus, sed & nobiscum eas accepit, & cum illo eas nos accepimus omnes. Audi quæso, pasce oves ad omnes dicitur, Oves Petrus non solus suscepit, sed nobiscum ille, & nos cum illo.
units.tr: Augustine, however, is a witness not only rich but rich in many testimonies. "Some things are said which seem properly to pertain to the Apostle Peter, and yet they do not have a clear meaning unless they are referred to the Church, of which he is acknowledged to have borne the person in a figure, on account of the primacy he had among the disciples; such as, 'I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,' and whatever else is of this kind." And in another place: "For if the sacrament of the Church were not in Peter, the Lord would not say to him, 'I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,' and 'Whatsoever, etc.' If this was said to Peter only, the Church does not do it; but if it is also done in the Church, that what is bound on earth is bound in heaven and what is loosed on earth is loosed also in heaven, because when the Church excommunicates, the excommunicated is bound in heaven; if this therefore is done in the Church, Peter when he received the keys signified the holy Church." And again: "What pertains properly to Peter, he was by nature one man, by grace one Christian, and by more abundant grace one and the same first Apostle; but when it was said to him, 'I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatsoever you shall bind, etc.,' he signified the whole Church." Hear also what Augustine's mind is about your "Feed my sheep." He says: "Not without cause does Peter, among the Apostles, bear the person of this Catholic Church. For the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to this Church together with Peter; and when it is said to him, it is said to all, 'Feed my sheep.'" Hear also what the mind of Ambrose is: "What sheep, and what flock, the blessed Peter did not take alone, but received them with us, and with him we all received them." Hear, I beg you: "Feed my sheep" is said to all; Peter did not take the sheep alone, but with us, and he with us, and we with him.

units.la: Etiam {d}Leonem. Propter quod dicit B. Petro, Tibi dabo claves, &c, transfivit quidem in alios Apostolos vis potestatis istius, & ad omnes Ecclesiæ Principes Decreti huius constitutio commeavit, & non frustra uni commendatur, quod omnibus intimatur. Theophylactum audivisti iam ante & Anselmum. Quamvis soli Petro dictum, Dabo: datum tamen pòst omnibus à Christo. Satis hoc diserte credo. Audi & {e}Euthymum; Tibi dabo claves, &c. Atqui donum hoc cæterorum fuit Apostolorum. {f}Rabanum etiam. Hæc autem ligandi atque solvendi potestas, quamvis soli Petro data videatur, à Domino tamen & cæteris Apostolis datur, nec non etiam nunc, in Episcopis & Presbyteris, omni Ecclesiæ. Claudet vero agmen {g}Hugo à sancto Victore. Ille autem, sic. Vide quando dictum est Petro in typo Ecclesiæ, Quodcunque ligaveris, invenies hoc dictum esse in donatione clavium Regni cælorum.
units.tr: Also Leo. "Because of this he says to the blessed Peter, 'I will give you the keys, etc.' The force of this power has indeed passed over to the other Apostles, and the constitution of this decree has passed to all the princes of the Church, and it is not in vain that what is made known to all is committed to one." You have heard Theophylact already before, and Anselm. Although it was said to Peter alone, "I will give," it was nevertheless given afterwards to all by Christ. I believe this is said plainly enough. Hear also Euthymius: "I will give you the keys, etc. Yet this gift belonged to the other Apostles." Also Rabanus: "This power of binding and loosing, although it seems given to Peter alone, was nevertheless given by the Lord also to the other Apostles, and even now is given, in bishops and presbyters, to the whole Church." Hugo of St Victor will close the line: "Look: when it was said to Peter, as a type of the Church, 'Whatever you shall bind,' you will find that this was said in the gift of the keys of the kingdom of heaven."

units.la: Quod si recentiores mavis (& mavis opinor) accipe & illos. Primùm autem Papam {h}Pium 2. Inter Discipulos, pænè unus Petrus solus totius Ecclesiæ gestabat personam, & propterea audire meruit, Tibi dabo claves. Has enim claves, non ille ut homo unus, sed unitas accepit Ecclesiæ. Et cum Papa, Cardinales duos: {i}Lyranum, [Et tibi dabo claves] non solum pro te, sed etiam pro alijs. Sicut enim confesio Petri erat confesio aliorum; ita po-testas haec data Petro, intelligitur dari alijs. {a} Cusanum. Etsi Petrus, per petram, tanquam lapis fundamenti Ecclesiae intelligi deberet: tamen secundum Hieronymum, similiter alij Apostoli fuerunt lapides fundamenti Ecclesiae, de quibus habetur Apocal. penult. ubi per duodecim lapides fundamenti ciuitatis Ierusalem, nemo dubitat, duodecim Apostolos intelligi debere. Ideo recte dicimus, omnes Apostolos in potestate cum Petro aequales. {b}Gerson vero succinctè. Claues datae sunt Ecclesiae, vt in actu primo; & Petro, vt in actu secundo. Et cùm vnum hunc nomino, cum illo intellige omnes, qui Constantiae fuerunt in Concilio. Omnes enim idem sentiunt. Ne longius lectorem habeam; Glossa denique ipsa ordinaria. Tibi dabo claues &c. Habent quidem eandem iudiciariam potestatem alij Apostoli, quibus post resurrectionem ait, Accipite spiritum sanctum, Quorum remiseritis &c.
units.tr: But if you prefer more recent authorities (and I think you do), take these as well. First, Pope Pius II. Among the disciples, almost Peter alone bore the person of the whole Church, and for that reason he deserved to hear, "I will give you the keys." For he received these keys not as a single man, but as the unity of the Church. And after the Pope, two Cardinals: Lyranus, "[And I will give you the keys] not only for you, but also" for others. For just as Peter's confession was the confession of the others, so this power given to Peter is understood to be given to the others. Cusanus: Although Peter, through the rock, ought to be understood as the stone of the foundation of the Church, nevertheless, according to Jerome, the other Apostles likewise were stones of the foundation of the Church, of whom we read in the penultimate chapter of the Apocalypse, where by the twelve stones of the foundation of the city of Jerusalem no one doubts that the twelve Apostles must be understood. Therefore we rightly say that all the Apostles were equal to Peter in power. Gerson, however, briefly: "The keys were given to the Church, as in the first act; and to Peter, as in the second act." And when I name this one, understand with him all who were at the Council of Constance, for they all think the same. To avoid keeping the reader longer, lastly the Ordinary Gloss itself: "I will give you the keys, etc. The other Apostles indeed have the same judicial power, to whom after the resurrection he says, 'Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, etc.'"

units.la: Frustra ergò pertendis hîc de singulari illâ & solitariâ Pontificis authoritate. Non huic foli, sed neque foli Petro concessa; vt si per verba illa, soluendi potestas facta sit in leges & iuramenta, pluribus iam communicanda sit potestas haec, quàm aut tu vis, aut fortasse etiam expedit; Pontifex verò hoc runquàm tulerit. Vides verò iam, opinor, hîc, vbi tu colligis, Catholicos alios dispergere; quae tu dilatas, ad iuramenta, coarctare eos ad peccata; quae tu coarctas ad Petrum, eos, ad reliquos etiam Apostolos omnes dilatare. Ita, nec de hâc quidem potestate, magis quàm de primâ, vobis inter vos conuenit. Verbo dicam; non negatur à nobis potestas soluendi, negatur collectio tua, & ea Catholicorum omnium negatur esse.
units.tr: Therefore you labour in vain here about that singular and solitary authority of the Pontiff. It was granted not to him alone, nor even to Peter alone; so that if by those words the power of loosing was given over laws and oaths, this power would have to be shared with more people than you wish, or perhaps even than is expedient; and the Pontiff would never have tolerated this. But you now see, I think, here, where you gather that other Catholics scatter, what you expand to oaths, you restrict to sins; what you restrict to Peter, they expand to all the other Apostles as well. Thus you do not agree among yourselves about this power any more than about the first. In a word, the power of loosing is not denied by us; your collection is denied, and it is denied to be that of all Catholics.

units.la: Confero iam manum. Nego negari, potestatem soluendi in Pontifice, ex eo quòd potestas negatur soluendi iuramenta. Etsi enim iuramenta non soluat; praeter iuramenta, multa illi restant, in quibus soluendi potestas illa, se exerceat. Latus admodum campus, ampla materia soluendi. Extra haec, peccata sunt, sunt poena & censura peccatorum. Annon satis illi, haec soluere? Vtinam verò adhibeat ad haec potentiam suam; bene soluat haec. Haec enim multò magis merentur, multò magis opus est soluí. Peccas igitur hîc primùm.
units.tr: Now I join battle. I deny that the power of loosing is denied to the Pontiff because the power of loosing oaths is denied. For although he does not loose oaths, apart from oaths many things remain to him in which he may exercise that power of loosing. The field is very wide, the matter of loosing ample. Beyond these, there are sins, and there are the penalty and censure of sins. Is it not enough for him to loose these? Would that he would apply his power to these; let him loose these well. For these deserve much more, and there is much more need that they be loosed. You err therefore here first.

units.la: Nego negari potestatem soluendi iuramenta. Et hîc peccas iterum, dum concludis, Potestatem soluendi negat, à Iuramento, hoc; negat ergò à iuramentus. Æthiops albus dentes; ergo albus; elenchus manifestus, à dicto secundùm quid, ad dictum simpliciter. Non negat potestatem soluendi juramenta simpliciter, qui de uno aliquo negat. Qui dictum sic limitat, non habet potestatem absoluendi me ab hoc juramento; Ab hoc, de uno hoc negat: in universum non detrahit potestatem Pontificî, absoluendi à juramentis. De uno cauet; cæteris quid possit, non possit, ne attingit quidem. Utrobique malè conclusum. Negat potestatem soluendi juramenta; negat ergò potestatem soluendi: Negat potestatem soluendi juramentum hoc; negat ergo potestatem soluendi juramenta.
units.tr: I deny that the power of loosing oaths is denied. And here you err again, when you conclude: "He denies the power of loosing from this oath, therefore he denies it from oaths." An Ethiopian is white in his teeth; therefore he is white: a manifest fallacy, from a statement secundum quid to a statement simpliciter. He who denies one thing does not deny simply the power of loosing oaths. He who limits the statement thus, "he does not have the power to absolve me from this oath," denies that about this one oath; in general he does not detract from the Pontiff's power of absolving from oaths. He is cautious about one matter; as to what he can or cannot do in others, he does not even touch it. The conclusion is badly drawn in both directions: "He denies the power of loosing oaths; therefore he denies the power of loosing" and "He denies the power of loosing this oath; therefore he denies the power of loosing oaths."

units.la: Non enim, credo, proijcies à te pudorem omnem, & dices, esse illi potestatem omnia juramenta soluendi. At sic oportet, ut concludas quod conclusum vis. Quodsi omnia potest, certè & hoc nostrum poterit, quo de agitur. Sed non dices omnia; non enim legitima. Aliqua ergo tantùm potest. At potest aliqua, nec tamen hoc nostrum; nec tu unquam concluseris, Potest aliqua soluere; potest ergo & hoc; quia ludibrium ita debebis pueris in schola, qui cantillant ibi versiculum, Syllogizari, non est ex particulari.
units.tr: For I do not think you will cast off all shame and say that the Pontiff has "the power of loosing all oaths." But that is what you must claim if you want to conclude what you want. If he can loose all, then certainly he will be able to loose this one of ours, which is in question. But you will not say "all," for that is not a lawful premise. He can therefore loose only "some." But he can loose "some," and yet not this one of ours; nor would you ever conclude, "He can loose some; therefore he can loose this." You would deserve the mockery of schoolboys, who chant there the little verse: "one cannot syllogize from the particular."

units.la: At inter illa quæ soluit, est & nostrum: De hoc quæritur. Probandum tibi hoc, non præsumendum fuit. Videtis interim, ut abeat jam à potestate soluendi, ad rem solubilem. Res enim hic negatur solubilis, quam Papa vult soluere[?]: Potestas soluendi non negatur. Potestate[?] stante, incongrua hæc materia dicitur, super quam potestas cadat. Et verus hic quæstionis status; non an possit juramenta soluere; sed, an possit hoc. De hoc qui negat, de re soluenda negat, non de soluendi potestate. Potestas sit sanè, habeat in multis locum suum; in hoc non habet: Ab alijs potest, alijs non paucis, ab hoc non potest soluere.
units.tr: But among those things which he can loose is also ours: this is the question. It was for you to prove this, not to presume it. You see meanwhile how he moves away from the "power of loosing" to the "matter that can be loosed." For here the matter is denied to be loosable, which the Pope wishes to loose: the power of loosing is not denied. The power standing, this matter is said to be unsuitable, upon which the power would fall. And the true state of the question is not whether he can loose oaths, but whether he can loose this one. Whoever denies this denies it about the matter to be loosed, not about the power of loosing. Let the power certainly exist; let it have its place in many things; in this it has no place: he can loose from others, and from not a few others, but from this one he cannot loose.

units.la: Dicam verò etiam, cur non possit ab hoc: Quia magna ex parte assertorium est. Siquidem ex toto promissorium esset, {a}materia eius, cùm sit aliquid futurum, variari posset, & in eventu reddi illicita. Atqui hoc jam maiori ex parte assertorium est: Quatuor habet partes; quarum tres assertoria sunt, quarta modò promissoria. De præsentieft: Juro quòd Papa, nec per se, nec per alium, & potestatem vel authoritatem habeat Regem deponendi.
units.tr: But I will also say why he cannot loose from this one: because it is for the most part assertory. For if it were entirely promissory, its matter, since it is something future, could vary and, in the event, become unlawful. But this oath is already for the most part assertory: it has four parts, three of which are assertory and only the fourth promissory. In the present: "I swear that the Pope, neither in himself nor through another, has the power or authority to depose a King."

units.la: {a} nendi. Item: Iuro quòd in corde abhorreo, tanquam impiam, hanc doctrinam. Item: Credo quòd nec Papa, nec alius quicunq; potestatem habet, me ab hoc iuramento absoluendi. Assensit [?] (vt audis) per omnia. De praesenti est. {a}Assertorij autem materia in necessitatem transijt, & est immutabilis. Dispensatio in eo referretur, non ad materiam, sed ad actum ipsum iuramenti. Talis autem dispensatio est directe contra praeceptum diuinum.
units.tr: ...ning. Likewise: "I swear that in my heart I abhor this doctrine as impious." Likewise: "I believe that neither the Pope nor anyone else has the power to absolve me from this oath." He has assented (as you hear) in all things. It is in the present. The matter of an assertory oath has passed into necessity and is immutable. A dispensation in this would refer not to the matter but to the act of the oath itself. Such a dispensation is directly against the divine precept.

units.la: Scis enim (quod te schola vestra docuit) si proprie loqui detur, haud vnquam solui nexum iuramenti. {b}Non dispensatur vnquam, vt aliquid fiat contra iuramentum; impossibile hoc. Obseruatio iuramenti cadit sub praecepto diuino, quod est indispensabile. Id tantum à Pontifice fit; Materia qua fuit iuramenti, debetur indebita, vt sub iuramento cadat. At hoc iam non est ligaturam soluere, sed rem ligatam subtrahere. Nodus manet, nexus manet, tollitur id cui nectendo fuit [?]. Ac materia quidem haec, si de futuro est, (vt in promissorio) quia nondum est, mutari potest, & reddi indebita ex euentu, atque ita pro indebita declarari: sin de praeterito est, vel praesenti, mutari nequit, in necessitatem transijt; solutionis iam capax non est. Locus ergo (vt vides) hic solutioni nullus; & otiosa hic omnis soluendi potestas.
units.tr: For you know (as your school taught you) that, if one speaks properly, the bond of an oath is never loosed. "A dispensation is never given that something be done against an oath; this is impossible. The observance of an oath falls under a divine precept, which is indispensable." This alone is what the Pontiff does: "The matter which was of the oath is owed as not owed, so that it falls under the oath." But this is now not "to loose the bond, but to withdraw the bound thing." The knot remains, the tie remains; what the tie was made for is removed. And this matter, if it is about the future (as in a promissory oath), because it does not yet exist, can be changed and, from the event, be made not owed, and so declared not owed; but if it is about the past or the present, it cannot be changed, it has passed into necessity, and is no longer capable of loosing. There is therefore, as you see, no place here for loosing, and all this "power of loosing" is idle.

units.la: Praeterquam verò quòd otiosa sic est; & aliae multae causae sunt, cur esse possit in Pontifice potestas haec, nec tamen operari. Nam si (quod ante docuimus) casus multi, in quibus Excommunicatio de iure nulla: nonnulli itidem erunt, in quibus, absolutio quoque ipsa reddetur nulla. Quippini? errante claue nemo aperit, errante digito nemo soluit. Quid autem? Digitus nunquam, Pontifici, nunquam clauis errat? Quid ergo opus sic distinguere in scholis, Claue non errante, nisi erret ei interdum clauis? Hic verò nos, errare clauem ei dicimus, & digitos, si ad ea soluit homines, quae cauentur iuramento: {c}Nimiam remissionem esse; non ex Petri aequitate iudicium ferri; Petri ergo priuilegium non manere. Non ex æquitate Petri: Æquum enim Petro, & voluntati diuinae consentaneum, vt Regi tanquam praecellenti, subijciant se omnes; Regi etiam Ethnico, etiam dyscolo. Hoc Petrus non soluueret [?]. Nihil ergo hic solutum. Potestas soluendi, quae à Christo, manebit integra; integrum etiam iuramentum, & insolubile.
units.tr: Besides being idle in this way, there are also many other causes why this power may exist in the Pontiff and yet not operate. For if (as we taught before) there are many cases in which excommunication is null by law, there will likewise be some in which the absolution itself will be null. Why not? "If the key errs, no one opens; if the finger errs, no one loosens." But what then? Does the finger of the Pontiff never err, does his key never err? Why then is it necessary to distinguish in the schools, "The key not erring, unless the key sometimes errs"? But here we say that the key errs for him, and his fingers as well, if he looses men from those things which are secured by oath: that this is too great a remission; that judgment is not given with the equity of Peter; therefore the privilege of Peter does not remain. Not with Peter's equity: for it is right for Peter, and consonant with the divine will, that all should submit themselves to the King as to one who excels, even to a heathen King, even to a perverse one. Peter would not have loosed this. Nothing therefore is loosed here. The power of loosing, which is from Christ, will remain whole; the oath also whole, and unloosable.

units.la: Sequitur verò nouum crimen, & graue, & quo necesse est Catholicam fidem abnegari. Qui iuramentum agnoscit authoritate sibi plenâ à latum, eo ipso affirmare, Regu supremam in spiritualibus potestatem. Quid audio? Primatus spiritualis infertur ex iuramento plenâ authoritate delato? Quis non risu excipit? Quis enim vel sacrosancta tangit, nisi de eo primùm constet, rite sibi & legitimè deferri iusiurandum? Quot verò quotidie passim in Praetorijs, in Consistorijs iuramenta subeuntur, vbi de luminibus, de stillicidijs agitur, plenâ authoritate omnia; & tu horum iuramenta omnia, eum sensum habere vis, vt ex eo quòd legitima sunt, Regum per ea in spiritualibus primatus stabiliatur? Apage verò! At sic oportet, si ad Primatum stabiliendum sit satis agnitio plenae authoritatis in deferente. Quàm multa verò iudicia sunt, quàm multa iuramenta deferuntur, vbi nec Iudici, nec vel Actori, vel Reo, vel Testibus, nec ei qui defert, nec ei cui defertur iuramentum, nulli (inquam) horum, quicquam de Primatu, vbi sit, penes Papam an Regem; imò an sit Primatus vllus, semel in mentem veniat?
units.tr: There follows, however, a new and grave charge, one which necessarily amounts to denying the Catholic faith: "Whoever acknowledges an oath administered by full authority thereby affirms the King's supreme power in spiritual matters." What do I hear? Is spiritual primacy inferred from an oath administered "by full authority"? Who would not laugh at this? For who even touches sacred matters unless it is first established that an oath has been rightly and lawfully administered to him? How many oaths, however, are daily taken everywhere in the courts and consistories, where the matters at issue are lights and gutters, all "by full authority"; and do you want all these oaths to carry the sense that, because they are lawful, the King's primacy in spiritual matters is thereby established? Far be it! Yet this would have to follow, if acknowledgement of "full authority" in the one administering were enough to establish primacy. How many judgments there are, how many oaths are administered, where neither the judge, nor the plaintiff, nor the defendant, nor the witnesses, nor he who administers the oath, nor he to whom it is administered, not one of them (I say) ever so much as thinks for a moment about primacy: where it lies, with the Pope or the King; or indeed whether there is any primacy at all.

units.la: Nisi illud dicere vis, Nullum legitimè deferri iuramentum, nisi vbi Pontificis authoritas interuenit, nec à quoquam, nisi cui illè facultatem dederit deferendi. At illud, quicquid senseris, rauciscès[?] credo, & non dices. Quid enim Pontifici, quid Primatui cum iuramentis? Annon etiā[?] apud Ethnicos iuratur, fdque[?] legitimè, vbi nec spiritualia, nec Primatus, nec Primas vllus? An offendit te forte vox, plena? Atqui, exigendi iuramenti semiplena authoritas, nulla. Aut ergo plena, aut nulla; si nulla exigendi, nec subeundi vlla; si non subeundi, nec iurandi; si non iurandi, nulla sunt iuramenta; si non iuramenta, non Testes, non iudicia, non Iudices vlli. Dixin' ego vobis, soluendæ potestas hæc quò cuaderet? Reges deposuit, leges dissoluit; iudicia, & iudices iam exauctorat. Itâ nec leges, nec Reges, nec iudicia, nec iudices vllos habituri iam sumus. Soluit iuramenta, iura, iudicia, iudices, leges, Reges. Quod initio dixi, mundi (credo) machinam solvet, nisi citiùs solvatur ipsa.
units.tr: Unless you mean to say that no oath is lawfully administered except where the Pontiff's authority intervenes, or by anyone to whom he has given the power to administer it. But that, whatever you may think, I believe you will hoarsely hesitate to say. For what has the Pontiff, what has primacy, to do with oaths? Are not oaths taken among the heathen too, and lawfully, where there is neither spiritual power, nor primacy, nor any primate? Or perhaps the word "full" offends you? Yet the authority to require an oath is never half-full: it is either full or nothing. If it is nothing, then there is no authority to require one, nor to undergo one; if no one undergoes one, no one swears; if no one swears, there are no oaths; if no oaths, no witnesses, no judgments, no judges at all. Did I not tell you where this power of loosing would lead? It deposes kings, dissolves laws, and now strips judgments and judges of their office. So we shall have neither laws, nor kings, nor judgments, nor judges any more. It dissolves oaths, rights, judgments, judges, laws, kings. What I said at the start, I believe, is that it will dissolve the whole machinery of the world, unless the machinery itself is dissolved more quickly.

units.la: Sed & rationem reddit, se dignam. Agnoscit enim in illo plenam authoritatem iubendi, vt contemnatur excommunicatio.
units.tr: But he also gives a reason, and one worthy of himself: "For he acknowledges in him full authority to command, so that excommunication may be despised."

units.la: Ille vero non agnoscit authoritatem iubendi vllam, aut hoc aut aliud quicquam, quin solius iuramenti ministrandi authoritatem agnoscit. Nec tu hic repone mihi quicquam de contemptu excommunicationis; nihil agis. Frustra prius tentasti, frustra hic iam iteras. Non iubetur contemni excommunicatio, sed neque contemnet illam, nisi si nulla est (ut eam nuper spreuere Veneti:) deferet censurae iustae Catholicus tuus, sic tamen, ut & officio suo ciuili simul deferat.
units.tr: He, however, acknowledges no authority to command at all, either this or anything else, but only the authority to administer an oath. Nor should you bring up here anything about the contempt of excommunication; you achieve nothing. You tried this earlier in vain, and now you repeat it in vain. Excommunication is not commanded to be despised; yet your Catholic will not despise it either, unless it is (as the Venetians recently scorned it) nothing. He will yield to the just censure, but in such a way that he also yields to his civil duty at the same time.

units.la: Habes ad Edicti loca tria; quorum primo, negatur Pontifici potestas deponendi Reges. Certè; sed, & negatur simul potestas illa, ad fidem Catholicam spectare. Quae ad fidem spectare videri potest, potestas excommunicandi, ea caste integreq; adhibita, non negatur; negatur tamen, excommunicato fides non seruanda. Sed neque negatur etiam potestas soluendi: Nostrum modo iuramentum, ex eorum numero negatur, super quo currat potestas illa. Horum, nihil contra Catholicam fidem, nihil contra Primatum, vel Apostolicum, vel sedis Apostolicae, nec vel ipsius Pontificis spiritualem, nihil etiam contra potestatem vel Apostolicam, vel Pontificiam in spiritualibus. Quicquid id est quod negatur, de temporali quadam est, nescio qua, (sed nec ipsi sciunt) indirecte ad Pontificem spectante. Quae, sit, non sit, nihil ad fidem Catholicam, nihil ad fundamenta religionis: fide integra, illaesa, illibata, quaeri de ea etiam porro, & disputari potest. Utcunque est, res fidei non est; cum non sit de indirecta hac potestate, quicquam adhuc directe definitum.
units.tr: You have three passages in the Edict. In the first, the Pope is denied the power to depose kings. Certainly; but that power is at the same time denied to pertain to the Catholic faith. The power of excommunication, which may seem to pertain to the faith, is not denied when used chastely and with integrity; yet it is denied that faith is to be kept with an excommunicated person. Nor is the power of loosing denied; only our present oath, which is among those things over which that power would run, is denied. None of these things is against the Catholic faith, nor against the primacy, whether apostolic, or of the apostolic see, nor against the spiritual authority of the Pope himself; nor even against the power, whether apostolic or papal, in spiritual matters. Whatever it is that is denied is of some temporal kind, I know not what (and they themselves do not know either), pertaining to the Pope only indirectly. Whether it is so or not, it has nothing to do with the Catholic faith, nothing to do with the foundations of religion: with faith whole, unharmed and unimpaired, it can be investigated and disputed further. However it is, it is not a matter of faith; since there is nothing yet defined directly about this indirect power.

units.la: Pontifex autem multa dixit contineri iuramento, quae fidei & saluti aperte aduersantur. An haec illa multa sunt? Etiam tu aiebas, de quatuordecim, propositiones undecim, Pontificis primatum in spiritualibus attingere. Cur tres tantum apponis? Quid octo reliquis factum? An tria haec sunt omnia? sic videtur: De quibus tamen tribus, duae non negantur, una modo est quae negatur, eaque nihil ad fidem.
units.tr: The Pope, however, has said that "many things are contained in the oath which openly oppose faith and salvation." Are these the many things? You too were saying that of fourteen propositions, eleven touch the Pope's primacy in spiritual matters. Why do you set out only three? What has become of the other eight? Or are these three all of them? So it seems. Yet of these three, two are not denied at all, and only one is denied, and that has nothing to do with faith.

units.la: Ubi ergo illa iam evidentissima, gravissimaque divini honoris iniuria est? Ubi Dei in eo Maiestas laeditur? Ubi periculum conscientiae, iactura fidei, detrimentum salutis, ex verbis ipsis iuramenti tam perspicua, de quibus sic in Breui [?]pararagraedia Pontifex? Si vera narrare voluit, nec Catholicis suis Iaruatus illudere, loco illius quod dixit, Euidentissima grauissimáq, diuini honoris iniuria, & Maiestas Dei læsa, & reliqua illa dictu grauia, auditu aspera; illud quod res est, dicere debuit: Suscepto per vos Iuramento hoc, peribit mihi nonnihil de sumoso sæculi typho, & fastu meo Pontificali: si res sic pergat, non potero iam, quoties animus mihi est, Reges vestros, Reges alios deponere, non subditos ipsorum armare in ipsos. Hæc illa sunt verè in me, & ambitionem meam: (& hic Breuium tenor verus esse debuit.) Etsi autem mea sunt sola, etsi nihil ad Deum: tamen ex veteri arte mea, & diu iam vsurpato dicendi genere, cùm quis mea vel leuiter attigerit, confugiendum mihi statim ad illa tragica, Euidentissima grauissimáque diuini honoris iniuria &c. Hæc illa spectra sunt & [illegible, ~3 letters] quæ soleo obijcere; hæc, quæ horrere pilos facient pauperibus Anglis, & misellis ibi Catholicis, pauorem incutient, seu verù, seu vanum terrore, parum refert, dum terrorem: dum detrectent modò suscipere, dum, quanquam nihil in Iuramento timendum videant, timeant tamen: & quanquam nihil tale perspiciant, quia tamen in Breue, ex ipsis verbis perspicuum dicitur; auribus, non oculis credant, perspicuum esse scilicet, quod tamen non perspiciant. Etsi locus ibi sit nullus, vbi iniuria hæc fiat, credant tamen fieri: & quanquam ab initio non crediderint, credant iam tamen: Argumento est, quod initio plurimi iurarint non inuiti, at velut auiculæ hoc sonitu abterritæ, non audent iam accedere. Quibus, quid faciat quis, quàm quod iam factum est, larvam detrahat, & ostendat terriculamenta esse hæc puerorum? De honore enim Diuini iniuria non agitur, nec de læsa Dei maiestate; nihil Deo hic de honore suo perit; perit Regibus de honore, si quid perit. Maiestas, non Dei, Regum læditur, si qua læditur; quorum tamen cum diuino honore & maiestate, maiestas & honor coniuncta sunt. Fidelitas verò in Reges, cum fide Catholica consistit, & salus Regia, cum animarum salute. Denique, tuta conscientia præstari possunt, quæ propter conscientiam præstanda sunt. Potest verò sine Maiestate Dei læsa, tuta conscientia, salua fide, & integra salute animarum, potest negari esse in Pontifice, indirectam illam potestatem ad Reges solio deturbandos: Vbi autem iusta vel ligandi causa subest, vel soluendi; potestas vel ligandi vel sol-uendi in Pontifice, non negatur.
units.tr: Where, then, is that injury to the divine honour, "most evident and most grave," which you now have? Where is the majesty of God wounded in it? Where is the "danger to conscience, loss of faith, detriment to salvation, so plain from the very words of the oath," about which the Pope speaks thus in the Brief? If he had wished to tell the truth, and not to mock his Catholics with a ruse, he ought, instead of what he said, "a most evident and most grave injury to the divine honour, and the majesty of God is wounded," and all those other things "grave to say, harsh to hear," to have said what is the case: "Since you have taken this oath, I shall lose somewhat of the lofty pride of the age and of my pontifical haughtiness; if things go on like this, I shall no longer be able, whenever I wish, to depose your kings or other kings, nor to arm their subjects against them. These are the things that truly concern me and my ambition." (And this should have been the true substance of the Brief.) Yet although these things are mine alone, and nothing to do with God, nevertheless, from my old art and the manner of speaking I have long practised, whenever anyone touches my affairs even lightly, I must at once take refuge in those tragic phrases, "most evident and most grave injury to the divine honour," and so on. These are the phantoms which I am accustomed to throw in; these are what will make the hair stand on end for poor English people and the wretched Catholics there, and strike terror into them, whether the terror is real or empty, it matters little, provided they terrify, provided they refuse to take the oath; and although they see nothing to fear in the oath, yet they fear, and although they perceive nothing of the kind, yet because it is said in the Brief that it is "plain from the very words," they believe with their ears, not their eyes, that it is plainly so, which they do not in fact perceive. Even though there is no place where this injury occurs, they believe it occurs; and although at first they did not believe it, they now believe it: the proof is that at first very many swore not unwillingly, but now, frightened as little birds by that sound, they dare no longer approach. What is there to do with such people but what has already been done: tear off the mask and show that these are the bugbears of children? For there is no question of an injury to the divine honour, nor of a wound to the majesty of God; nothing of God's honour perishes here; if anything perishes, it is the honour of kings. The majesty wounded, if it is wounded, is the majesty of kings, not of God; yet majesty and honour are joined with the divine honour and majesty. Fidelity to kings, however, stands with the Catholic faith, and the safety of kings with the salvation of souls. Finally, what ought to be given for conscience's sake can be given with a secure conscience. Indeed, without a wound to the majesty of God, with a secure conscience, with faith intact and the salvation of souls unimpaired, it can be denied that the Pope has that indirect power to cast kings from their thrones; but where a just cause of either binding or loosing lies, the power of binding or of loosing in the Pope is not denied.

units.la: Audi iam aliud. Est aliud iuramentum vetus, iam usque ab Henrico octauo, quo asseritur suprema Regis gubernatio ad causas Ecclesiasticas. Ex vetere illo, tertium argumentum ducit, vel trahit, vel torquet potius, ut faciat fidem scilicet, noua hoc Iuramento, abnegari fidem Catholicam. Probatur (inquit) ex alio simili iuramento. Quid? Abnegari iuramento hoc fidem Catholicam? Quomodo probatur? Sic pote. Rex Henricus octauus, ante annos iam septuaginta, iuramentum edidit, quo voluit agnosci summum in Regno suo gubernatorem, etiam quoad res religionis: Quocirca necesse est, ut fides Catholica abnegetur Iuramento isto, quod nuper instituit Rex Iacobus, quo incolumitati suae prospiceret. Ecquis unquam argumentum vidit, magis obtorto collo? Quid? Istánc apud vos æquipollent? Rex vult esse incolumis, &c, Rex vult esse gubernator Ecclesiae? utrobique quidem Rex; sed quid Regis incolumitas, ad caput Ecclesiae? Auersa sunt penitus, nec tu, nisi obstrictâ ceruice, unquam efficies, ut se mutuò respiciant.
units.tr: Listen now to another matter. There is another oath, old already, dating from Henry VIII, by which the supreme government of the king over ecclesiastical causes is asserted. From that old oath he draws, or rather twists, a third argument, namely that the new oath abjures the Catholic faith. It is proved (he says) from a similar oath. What? That this oath abjures the Catholic faith? How is it proved? Like this, he says. King Henry VIII, more than seventy years ago, issued an oath by which he wished the supreme governor of his realm to be acknowledged, even in matters of religion. Therefore it is necessary that the Catholic faith be abjured by that oath which King James lately established, by which he provided for his own safety. Has anyone ever seen an argument twisted more violently? What? Do you consider these equivalent? The king wishes to be safe, etc.; the king wishes to be governor of the Church? In both cases it is indeed the king; but what has the king's safety to do with the headship of the Church? They are wholly unrelated, and you will never make them look at each other unless you bend your neck to the yoke.

units.la: Ad repetitam vero, nec bis iam, sed ter repetitam assertionem tuam, de abnegari ibi iussa excommunicandi potestate, accipe iam tertiò repetitam negationem nostram. Nihil iuramento negotij cum potestate illa, cum potestate ullâ spirituali. Fidem ibi requiri temporalem, censuram non tolli spirituali.
units.tr: As for your assertion, repeated not twice but three times, that the power of excommunication is renounced there, take now our denial, repeated for the third time. There is nothing in the oath to do with that power, with any spiritual power at all. There, a temporal fidelity is required; the spiritual censure is not taken away.

units.la: Sed etsi consequentia hic nulla; incidit tamen in phantasma Matthaeus (Domini in hoc similis) &c malè metuit, ne quid huic Iuramento fraudis subsit, ne ad nullam aliam rem compositum sit, quàm ut ad alterum illud Henrici aditus patefiat. Certè enim affinitas magna inter hæc duo, Ambæ[?] eodem formulæ tendunt: Hoc solo distant, quòd in eo, verbis expressis & propriis abnegetur Primatus Apostolicus: in hoc, obscuritoribus verbis, & per ambages circumlocutionum. Sed ex hac formulâ facilè possunt viri prudentes intelligere, quò tendat altera: facilè verò possunt viri prudentes intelligere, si utrâmq; modò formulam legant, te, nec quid velint illæ, nec quid velis ipsè, satis intelligere. Hoc solo distant? Hoc solo non distant: imò & fine distant. Illo enim, prærogatiua Regi & potestas aliqua ascribitur; Hoc, plane nulla: vt tantùm ab illo, &c, vt nocentior fraus submouetur. In illo, de Ecclesiâ agitur, nec nisi de Ecclesiâ: In hoc ne mentio quidem vlla Ecclesiæ. Illud à clero primùm editum in Synodo suâ, pòst relatum ad Regni Ordines: De hoc, ne consultus quidem clerus (præter forte Episcopos Procerum assessores) nec vllum ad hoc Synodi aliud vel consilium, vel suffragium interuenit. Conditum prius illud, vt distingueret Pontificios à nobis: conditum hoc, vt Pontificios ipsos distingueret à Pontificijs; Pontificios scilicet moderatos, quietos, sobrios, à Pontificijs sulphureis, nitratis, igneis. Prius illud, vt mentem habet Archipresbyter, credo, detrectaret: Atqui hoc, vltrò, primo quoque tempore, iurare voluit; nec vult, rogatu Domini tui, sanguinis sui pro eo vel guttam effundere. Neque verò ad subeundum hoc, captus ille, vel deceptus; diu enim antè in quæstionem hanc incubuerat, etiam pòst incubuit; ac ne nunc quidem subijsse pœnitet. Habetis iam librum ab illo; excusus est; prostat; quo, quod à se factum, iure factum defendit. Lege sodès. Docebit te, & potuisse à se suscipi iusiurandum illud, & à quoquam Catholico posse, & quidem illæsâ Pontificis potestate spirituali posse, seque, in eo non deceptum, vos qui secus sentitis, potiùs decipi.
units.tr: But even if the inference here is null, Matthew has nevertheless fallen into a fantasy (in this he is like his Lord), and he fears badly that some fraud lies under this oath, that it was composed for no other purpose than to open the way for that other oath of Henry. For there is indeed a great affinity between these two; both tend to the same formula. They differ only in this: that in the one, the Apostolic primacy is renounced in express and proper words; in the other, in more obscure words and through the ambages of circumlocution. But from this formula prudent men can easily understand where the other tends; and prudent men can easily understand, if they read both formulas, that you understand neither what those want nor what you yourself want. They differ only in this? They do not differ only in this; indeed they differ also in purpose. For in the one, a prerogative and some power is ascribed to the king; in this one, none at all: it is only so that the more harmful fraud may be removed. In the one, the matter concerns the Church, and only the Church; in this there is not even any mention of the Church. The one was first issued by the clergy in its own synod, afterwards referred to the orders of the realm; for this one, not even the clergy was consulted (except perhaps the bishops, assessors of the nobles), and no other counsel or vote of the synod intervened. The former was framed to distinguish Papists from us; this was framed to distinguish the Papists themselves from Papists, namely the moderate, quiet, sober Papists from the sulphurous, saltpetre-laden, fiery Papists. The former, as the Archpriest (I believe) has in mind, he would refuse to do; but this he has willingly wished to swear at the first opportunity, and he does not wish, at your Lord's request, to shed a drop of his blood for it. Nor was he captured or deceived into undertaking this; for he had long brooded over this question before, and afterwards brooded over it again, and even now he does not regret having undertaken it. You have now the book from him; it has been printed and is on sale, in which he defends as lawful what he has done himself. Read it, please. It will teach you both that that oath could be taken by him, and could be taken by any Catholic, and indeed could be taken while the Pope's spiritual power remains intact; and that he himself was not deceived in it, but rather you, who think otherwise, are deceived.

units.la: Denique quo solo distare ais, eo omnium minimè distant. Nam si in priore verba expressa & propria, & hic quoque non minùs. Quodsi etiam ambages aliquæ essent, aut circumlo-cutio; non in hoc culpanda foret. Agitur enim de re, quâ nulla nobis in terris pretiòsior; hic si paulò verbosior lex esset, ferri posset; sed enim ambages nullæ ibi, nulla circumlocutio, nihil obscurum, tortum; explicata sunt omnia. Vides iam, nec illo solo, aliis distare pluribus, nec illuc, quò tu prætendis, tendere.
units.tr: Finally, the thing by which you say they differ, by that very thing they least of all differ. For if in the former the words are express and proper, so here too they are no less so. And if there were any ambages or circumlocution, it would not be blamed in this case. For the matter concerns something than which nothing is more precious to us on earth; if this law were a little wordier, it could be borne. But there are no ambages here, no circumlocution, nothing obscure or twisted; everything is explained. You see now that they do not differ in that alone, but in many other respects, and that this one does not tend to where you aim.

units.la: Vanus enim ille metus tuus, vanus Domini tui, de hoc quasi præludio ad Iuramentum Primatus. Annus iam tertius agitur, & qui Fidelitatis hoc iurárunt, ad Primatus illud non vrgentur, nec vocantur quidem. Et tamen lex illa prior de Primatu, etiamnum antiquam vim obtinet, & in vsu est, & quotidie deferri solet Primatus iuramentum, sæpiùs tamen subditis Regijs, qui in officio sunt, quàm vestris: sed & vestris deferri potest interdum, qui peruicaces sunt & protervi, rarissimè id tamen. Hoc vero fidelitatis vt deseratur, nupera occasio fecit; subeant hoc: de altero ne metuant. Quod hic piger Propheta Matthæus vaticinatur, nusquam cueniet. Quid porrò huic homini facias, qui quod nusquam fuit, nec futurum fortasse est, id sibi meridiani somniat: pòst, experrectus, suspiciones suas pro argumentis, somnia pro oraculis haberi vult?
units.tr: For that fear of yours is vain, and vain is your Lord's fear, about this as a kind of prelude to the oath of Primacy. The third year is now running, and those who have sworn this oath of Fidelity are not urged to that oath of Primacy, nor are they even summoned. And yet that earlier law on Primacy still keeps its old force and is in use, and the oath of Primacy is still offered every day, though more often to the royal subjects who are in office than to yours; but it may sometimes be offered also to yours, those who are obstinate and wilful, though very rarely. That this oath of Fidelity should be abandoned, a recent occasion has brought about; let them take it, and let them not fear about the other. What this lazy Prophet Matthew prophesies will nowhere come to pass. Moreover, what can one do with this man, who dreams in broad daylight of what has never been and perhaps never will be; and then, awakened, wishes his suspicions to be held as arguments and his dreams as oracles?

units.la: POstremò vide, quàm cautus hic homo & peruigil, subsecutus Apologiæ Authorem, ad singula vestigia: aduertit etiam excidisse ei nescio quid, quodam in loco, quod excipit statim, & iam torquet in Authorem. Et quid illud tandem quod excidit? Dixit, scilicet, aliquo in loco minùs cautè, institutum iuramentum hoc, quo populus arceretur, ne tam alte ebiberet poculum Antichristianarum fortationum: Et quid esset (inquit) apud Aduersarios Antichristiana fortatio, nisi Pontificiæ potestatis veneratio? Atque ita conclusum in causâ.
units.tr: Lastly, see how cautious and vigilant this man is, who followed the Author of the Apology step by step: he has noticed that something or other slipped from him in a certain passage, which he immediately seizes and now turns against the Author. And what, pray, is that which slipped? He said, namely, that in one place rather carelessly, this oath was instituted "so that the people might be kept from drinking so deeply of the cup of Antichristian fornications"; and "what (he says) among the Adversaries would be an Antichristian fornication, except the veneration of papal power?" And thus the case is concluded.

units.la: Hoc ille tam auidè arripuit, vt non aduerterit duas illas vocu-las, Tam alte. Dixisset aliquid, si vt ne omnino biberent de poculo, institutum fuisset iuramentum. Non id dicit iuramentum, sed ne tam alte ebiberent. Biberent sanè, quando ita stat sententia, quando inde arceri nolunt; atque ebiberent, idque alte etiam: id est, (te interprete) venerentur, si placet, Pontificem, pèdem eius, sedem eius osculentur, venerentur & potestatem eius, sanctos canonizandi, Purgatorium evacuandi, Iubilæum celebrandi, Indulgentias depluendi. Satis hoc, imò nimis hoc, alte: bibant tamen eòisque si sapere nolunt. At ne tam alte tamen, vt & Regem deponenti adhaereant; vt licentiam abeo sumant, arma contra Regem gerendi, tumultus seminandi, vim inferendi. Alte, si videtur, sed non tam alte: vt enim tam alte, Edictum non fert; quin aliud poculum temperabit illis ebibendum, si hoc tam alte ebibant. Etiam à degustando poculo illo, si saperent, abstinerent; Quis negat? Sed id tamen vt faciant, Iuramento non cauetur: nec enim de bibendo ibi cautum, sed nec de alte bibendo: sed de tam alte bibendo; tam alte, vt ebrij sint plane, vt neque manus, neque pedes erga Principem quidem officium faciant; tam alte, vt in illum cornua sumant[?]; tam alte, vt titubent, atque impingant ad petram proditionis. Alioqui (vt par est) sobrij luant, quod ebrij peccârunt.
units.tr: This he seized so eagerly that he did not notice the two little words, "so deeply." He would have said something if the oath had been instituted so that they might not drink at all from the cup. The oath does not say that, but "so that they might not drink so deeply." They would indeed drink, since that is the sense of the sentence, since they are not willing to be kept from it; and they would drink, and that deeply too: that is (on your interpretation) they would venerate, if you please, the Pope, kiss his foot and his seat, venerate also his power of canonizing saints, emptying Purgatory, celebrating Jubilees, showering down Indulgences. That is enough, indeed too much, to drink deeply; yet let them drink, if they are unwilling to be wise. But not so deeply as to cling also to one who deposes a king; so as to take from it a license to bear arms against the King, to sow tumults, to use violence. Deeply, if you like, but not so deeply: for the Edict does not prescribe "so deeply"; indeed it will temper for them another cup to be drunk, if they drink so deeply as that. Even from tasting that cup, if they were wise, they would abstain; who denies it? But that they should do so is not secured by the oath: for it provides nothing about drinking, nor even about drinking deeply, but about drinking so deeply; so deeply that they are plainly drunk, so that neither hands nor feet perform their duty toward the Prince; so deeply that they take up horns against him; so deeply that they stagger and stumble against the rock of treason. Otherwise (as is fitting) the sober may pay for what the drunk have sinned.

units.la: Rectè ergo illud in Apologia positum, & ad rem, ne tam alte; nec eò spectat vt detestentur spiritualem obedientiam, sed vt testentur modò temporalem; temporalem (dico) saltem, nec adeò Cyclôpes sint, & exoculati implicitâ suâ fide, vt (quod nuper apud nos Puluerarij) inducant in animum, Regis, Regnique excidium, id verò Romanæ Ecclesiæ suæ, obsequium ratum & gratum, hostiam acceptam esse, & in odorem suavitatis. Hæ namque fæces in fundo amari illius poculi, dum non satis illis, profiteri fidem in Ecclesiam, nisi cum perfidiâ in Rempublicam: nec traditiones fidei suæ addere, nisi & proditiones simul addant perfidiæ suæ, & suam testatam faciant, dum se scilicet obiiciunt morti, (quod martyrium dici volunt) pro immani aliquo & horrendo parricidio perpetrato. Fæces has hij quidem homines biberunt de fundo venenati calicis: ne verò & alijs venenum simile propinent, maturè arcendi. Cui rei Iuramentum fuit.
units.tr: Rightly, then, that was put in the Apology, and to the point: "not so deeply"; nor does it look to their renouncing spiritual obedience, but only to their bearing witness to temporal obedience; temporal (I say) at least, and they are not so much Cyclopes, blinded and dazzled by their implicit faith, as to persuade themselves, as the Gunpowder men lately did among us, that the destruction of the King and the realm is a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to their Roman Church, a sweet-smelling savour. For these dregs at the bottom of that bitter cup, while it is not enough for them to profess faith in the Church unless they do so with treachery toward the Commonwealth, and not enough to add traditions to their faith unless they also add treasons to their treachery, and make their own witness by exposing themselves to death (which they wish to be called martyrdom) on account of some monstrous and horrible parricide committed: these men have indeed drunk the dregs of the poisoned chalice; but lest they offer a similar poison to others as well, it must be restrained as early as possible. To this end the oath was made.

units.la: Attu, lector, jam cernis, quò hæc redeant omnia, quid dignum tulerit hiatu tanto, promissor hic, quàm principalem suam causam nullus probarit. Torsisse[?] temporalem Pontificis potestatem, vt ad fidem Catholicam spectet, ad quam illa nullo modo spectare potest. Tum torsisse fidiculis suis Iuramentum, vt excommunicandi potestatem negaret, quam tamen affirmat. Tum, vt & neget potestatem soluendi, quam non negat; locum tantùm negat habere in uno hoc & unico Iuramento. Tum, vt de Primatu spirituali Regis diceretur, quæ de incolumitate eius corporali dicuntur. Postremò, vt intiio[?] Ticulum[?] torserat, vt esset de Papistis promisuè, qui erat de cetis quibusdam detegendis: ita torquere clausulam, vt quod dictum est, ne tam alte: id perinde fit, ac si dixisset, ne omnino bibant. Hominem denique cernis respondere nomini: Scias argumenta hæc, cuius hominis, homo cuius nominis sit; agnoscas Torti esse omnia; torta enim omnia.
units.tr: Look, reader, you can now see where all this ends up, and what "worthy of so great a gaping" this promiser has brought forth: how little he has proved of his principal case. He has tortured the Pope's temporal power so that it may pertain to the Catholic faith, to which it can in no way pertain. Then he has tortured his oath with his racks, so as to deny the power of excommunication, which nevertheless he affirms. Then, so as to deny the power of absolution, which he does not deny; he denies only that it has place in this one and single oath. Then he has made it say of the King's spiritual primacy what is said of his bodily safety. Finally, just as he tortured the passage about the rest of the ... [unclear], so as to make it be "of the Papists in general," though it concerned certain factions to be exposed; he twists the clause "not so deeply" so that what was said is taken as if he had said "not at all drink." In short, you see the man answering to his name: learn what kind of man this is, whose arguments these are, and acknowledge that they all belong to Torti, for everything is tortured.

units.la: Ecce autem relegendum hic ubi (Lector) iam denuò, totum Pontificis Breve primum, deinde suo loco totum etiam secundum; tum Cardinalis Epistola integra, à capite ad calces, tanquam Theseis Codri. Quorsum autem hæc inanis chartæ carnificina, vt ista sic de nouo iterari oporteat, eisque tanquam Crambe bis posita, lectorem enecari? Sat erat, semel hæc legisse apud Apologiam; vbi necessitas fuit inserendi. Ignota enim tum; Iam lippis nota & tonsoribus. Eadem hic iam iterum infercire; quid opus, nisi pagellæ forte aliquot, alioqui vacuæ, Pontificijs erant Breuibus linendæ? vel certè nisi tam hæc illi Breuia mellita visa sint, vt nec iterum appositæ atque iterum, nauseam paritura essent; quæ tamen hic nec coæta sunt, nec condita de nouo. Reponit tantùm & transit: nos quoque transeamus, tanquam tot pagellas, si non vacuas, certè superuacuas.
units.tr: But here, reader, one must read again, now a second time, the whole of the Pope's first Brief, and then, in its place, the whole of the second as well; then the Cardinal's letter entire, from head to foot, like the Theses of Codrus. Why, however, this futile butchery of paper, that these things must be repeated thus anew, and that the reader should be killed off by them, as by a Crambe served twice? It was enough to have read them once, in the Apology, where there was need to insert them. For they were then unknown; now they are known to the bleary-eyed and the barbers. To cram them in again here: what is the point, unless perhaps some pages, otherwise blank, had to be smeared with the Papists' Briefs? Or certainly unless those Briefs seemed so honeyed to him that, placed again and again, they would breed nausea; yet they are neither gathered together nor newly compiled here. He merely replies and passes on: let us too pass on, as over so many pages, if not blank, certainly superfluous.

units.la: Ordiri Apologiam dicis, à deplorationis conspirationis in Regem. Quam ipsam, & vos, nobiscum pariter deplorare, post asseris. Mallem autem dixisses, detestari. Nam ambigua quidem hæc vox est deplorandi. Potest enim deplorare quis, exitisse [?] aliquos humanâ specie, qui hanc mentem habuerint, tam inhumanam. Potest & ex alio capite, quòd successu caruerint, quodque in illo conatu suo fœlices, fortunatiqúe non fuerint. Nec id ergo ad rem, deplorare vos; nobiscum pariter, nisi (quod valdè vereor) idem vtrumque deploremus. Atqui pòst dicis, odisse te parricidia, execrari conspirationes. Esto. At vos, nescio quomodo à Sixto Papa vestro, didicistis, in eo quod odiosum est & execratione dignum; id si accidat in rem vestram, prouidentiam Dei admirari, & laudibus in cœlum tollere, quòd ita scilicet res acciderit, idque non sine manifesto miraculo: & opus in eo Dei abstrahere à scelere, atque ita abstractum mirificè prædicare: quæ quid sibi velint, quis nescit? Verùm si ita, vt dicis, odistis, execramini conspirationes, qui fit (nam legistis iam, scio, Actionem illam in Garnettum, ante annum & amplius latinam factam) qui fit (inquam) vt odium, & execratio vestra non redundet in G. & G. conscios, participesque criminis, quos & excepiistis[?] recentes à scelere, & etiamnum in sinu fouetis? An illud didicistis forsan (contrà quàm ille in historiâ) proditiones odisse & execrari; proditores tamen vnicè amare, addo, & viros fouere, & mortuos consecrare? Qui námque factum, vt si vobis execranda res conspiratio illa: qui caput erat conspirationis, Garnettus, relatus sit in Martyrologium Iesuitarum? Qui factum, vt impostura illa straminea, tanti apud vos facta, ita sedulò apud vos impressa, ita passim diuendita? An & illud didicistis, qui facta habent latronum; Martyrum cis cultum decernere, & (dum piæ sint) vel stramineas fraudes vestris, & fumos vendere? Sed hæc suo loco pòst.
units.tr: You say the Apology begins "from the lamentation of the conspiracy against the King." And afterwards you claim that you and we alike lament this same thing. But I would have preferred you to say "detest." For this word "to lament" is ambiguous. One may lament that certain men of human form existed who held so inhuman a purpose. One may also lament from another standpoint, that they lacked success, and were not fortunate or prosperous in that attempt of theirs. So "you lament, together with us" has nothing to do with the matter, unless (as I greatly fear) we both lament the same thing. Yet afterwards you say, "We hate parricides, we execrate conspiracies." Very well. But you, I know not how, have learned from your Pope Sixtus that in the case of what is hateful and worthy of execration, if it happens to be to your advantage, you should admire the providence of God and raise it to heaven with praises, because the thing so turned out, and not without a manifest miracle; and that you should draw from it a work of God freeing [the perpetrator] from the crime, and so, once freed, proclaim him wondrously. What these things mean, who does not know? But if, as you say, you "hate and execrate conspiracies," how does it come about (for you have now read, I know, that Action against Garnet, made in Latin more than a year ago) how, I say, does it come about that your hatred and execration do not spill over onto Garnet and his accomplices and sharers in the crime, whom you have received fresh from the deed and still foster in your bosom? Or perhaps you have learned this (contrary to what that man did in history): to hate and execrate betrayals, yet to love the traitors alone, I add, and to cherish them, and to consecrate them when dead? For how is it that, if that conspiracy is for you a "thing to be execrated," the one who was the head of the conspiracy, Garnet, has been entered in the Martyrology of the Jesuits? How is it that that flimsy imposture, made of such importance among you, has been so diligently printed among you and so widely hawked? Or have you also learned this, that those who have "the deeds of robbers" should decree worship for them as martyrs, and sell straw frauds and smoke to your own people, as long as they are pious? But these matters belong later, in their place.

units.la: Postquàm autem quasi vnâ lacrymulâ, vno verbo, de proditione expedisses, subiungis & consilium ad similes auertendas, idque ipsi Regi Serenissimo referri vis. Satis hoc quidem comiter: eò dixi, quia lego hîc titulum Serenissimi. Hîc lego, & hîc tantùm; nec ante per totum, nec per totum pòst librum honor habetur Regi, huius tituli. Id eò magis notandum, in tè homine Italo, cùm non sit in minimis laudem nationis vestræ, quòd non tantùm curiosi, penè etiam superstitiosi, in eo estis, ne cuiquam (aliquo loco qui sit) titulus vllus pereat; qui illi vel à statu, vel à merito suo debitus videri potest; vt sæpe hîc subeat mirari, & quasi Italum in Italo quærere, cùm tam immemorem video te eius, quod Gentile vobis est. Flagitiosa hæc quidem fuit obliuio.
units.tr: After you had, as it were with a single little tear and a single word, dispatched the matter of treason, you add also a counsel for averting similar things, and you want this referred to the most Serene King himself. That is certainly courteously put; I say so because I read here the title "Most Serene." I read it here, and only here; neither before nor after throughout the book is this title of honour given to the King. All the more is this to be noted in you, an Italian, since it is no small praise of your nation that you are not merely careful but almost superstitious that no title at all should be lost to anyone (in whatever place he may be) which seems due to him either from his station or from his merit; so that I often here wonder, and seek, as it were, an Italian in an Italian, when I see you so forgetful of what is native to you. This indeed was a shameful oblivion.

units.la: Quid verò referri vis? Quid monest? Quomodo securè Rex regnare possit. Non malè hoc, nisi quòd frustrà, nisi quòd Regem mones, si de quoquam alio, de hoc certè non monendum. Rex enim Dominus noster (si quis mortalium alius) compositus non est vel à naturâ factus ad diffidentiam: Tantùm autem abest, vt paulò minùs; vt nimio plus fidat quàm par est; & in eam partem peccet potiùs. Dum enim, optimè sibi conscius, & ex suo ingenio metitur alios, adeo securus sæpe est, & sui negligens; vt etiam, vbi causa data, etiam vbi prædictum illi vt cauerent; tàm lentus tamen fuerit & tardus in fide non habenda; vt vita hoc illi pènè steterit, vt in vltimum discrimen adductus sit; nisi fidelis illi Deus eripuisset cùm, qui alios tam fideles credebat. Nòrunt omnes, quotquot illum nôsse contigit, non hæc illi narrari oportere. Certè cui paululùm notus, cui ratio vitæ explorata, & egressus & ingressus eius, fidenter affirmare poterit, haud unquam Regem quenquam extitisse, qui subditis magis sideret, quàm Nostrum: & (est Deo gratia) habet, quibus tutò possit fidere:. Quâ de re, vel integer scribi posset liber, si opus libro; sed libro nihil opus: pari operâ scribendus liber, ut lucere solem, vel ignem ardere doceatur: ac ut Serenissimum Regem IACOBUM suorum in fide acquiescere, & securè regnare. Utinam vero consilium dare posses, ne tam velit esse securus.
units.tr: But what do you want referred? What does it advise? "How the King may reign securely." This is not badly put, except that it is in vain, except that you are advising the King, when if it concerned anyone else, yet certainly not here is advice to be given. For the King, our Lord (if any mortal at all), is not disposed or made by nature to distrust: so far is he from being a little less, that he trusts far more than is right, and sins rather in that direction. For while, most conscious of himself, and measuring others by his own disposition, he is so often secure and careless of himself; so that even when cause was given, even when it was foretold to him that he should take care, he was nevertheless so slow and tardy in not giving faith that his life nearly paid the price, so that he was brought to the utmost peril; unless God, faithful to him, had snatched him away, when he believed others so faithful. All who have had the chance to know him know that these things should not be told to him. Certainly anyone who knows him even a little, whose manner of life is examined, and his coming in and going out, can confidently affirm that never has there been a king who trusted his subjects more than ours; and (thanks be to God) he has those in whom he may safely trust. On this matter a whole book could be written, if there were need of a book; but there is no need of a book: a book is to be written with as much effort as one would teach that the sun shines or fire burns; and so that King James, most Serene, may rest in the faith of his people and reign securely. Would that you could give counsel that he might not wish to be so secure.

units.la: Quò verò sic securè regnet, quid mones? Parum in iuramentis, multum in benevolentiâ populi praesidij esse, ad conspirationes huiusmodi praecavendas. Quòd nimirum qui parricidium non timent, periurium non timebunt. Apponis pòst, Subrij exemplum è Tacito. Quid tu? An Iuramentum hoc ideo putas editum, quasi non satis certa sit illi benevolentia subditorum? Toto coelo erras. Quanquam ne sic quidem mones rectè. Nam etsi sint ista, ut dicis, & sit in amore multum, in iuramento parum praesidij: tamen quod te ratio docebit, Parum & multum, plus sunt multo; & hoc & illud simul, melius quàm illud solum, nec incommodum ullum, ad cautelam, utrumque hic coniunctim adhiberi. Nam, quod aduerfusti [?], credo, populus ex hominibus est; homines sunt, & ut homines sunt, ita animum mutant: & benè velle illud tuum, affectio tenella est, citò de subiecto mobilis, multo plus praesidij habitura, multo futura constantior, si nexu etiam iuramenti stringatur, & firmetur arctius. Antiquus hic mos est iam usque à Iacobo Patriarchà (teste vel Gilead, cumulo testimonij) initam alijs ex causis benevolentiam, iuramenti interventu & foedere sanciendi.
units.tr: But as to what you advise, that he may thus reign securely: you say that oaths are of little protection, and the goodwill of the people of great protection, against conspiracies of this kind; namely, that those who do not fear parricide will not fear perjury. You add the example of Subrius from Tacitus. What of you? Do you think this oath was issued as if the goodwill of the subjects were not sufficiently certain? You are wrong by the whole heaven. Yet not even so do you advise rightly. For although these things are as you say, and there is "much protection in love, little in oath": nevertheless, as reason will teach you, "little and much are far more," and this and that together is better than that alone; nor is there any inconvenience at all, for caution, in both being used here jointly. For what the people, I suppose, has thought against you, is composed of men; they are men, and as men they change their minds; and that goodwill of yours is a tender affection, quickly moved from its object, which would have much more protection, and would be much more constant, if it were also bound by the bond of an oath and confirmed more tightly. This is an ancient custom, now used since the Patriarch Jacob (witness even Gilead, a heap of testimony), that goodwill, won by other causes, should be sanctioned by the intervention of an oath and a covenant.

units.la: Neque verò benevolentia, utcunque omni modo conciliari debet, præstabit tamen per se, ut tuti sint Reges, quando & frater in fratrem, & filius in patrem legūtur conspirâsse, inter quos tamen fuit, & [illegible, ~8 letters] id est, benevolentia, quam natura quoque ipsa conciliârat. Neque verò quòs tu nominas, quantumuis magni conciliatores benevolentia, usquequaque tuti erant omnes, vel immunes à conspiratoribus. Augustum si immunem dicas, rudis es certè in historiâuide capitulum Suetonij 19. mutabis mentem; decies ibi periclitatum scribit, lineis vix decem. Ad Vespasianum uero cum veneris, uide capitulum ibi 25. narrabit tibi, assiduas in eum coniurationes extitisse. Habuit & Titum Cecinam: & Antoninum Cassium, Titianum, & Priscianum. Constantinum quis nescit, veneno periisse? Tute ipse non dices tutos fuisse hos, cum historiam melius inspexeris. Neque etiam ijdem illi, iuramenti religionem inanem rem esse rati sunt, quin & ipsi, ubi res se dedit, usi sunt & eo, nec leue sibi in eo praesidium arbitrati sunt; Vt in hoc audiendus non sis, novus Regum monitor; nec, quod in sacramenti fide adminiculum, negligendum: quin obedientia Principum, &c hoc, & quocunque alio potest, statumine fulcienda.
units.tr: Nor, however benevolence may be won over, will it by itself make kings safe, since brother has been read conspiring against brother and son against father, and among these there was [illegible, ~8 letters], that is, benevolence, which nature herself had also secured. Nor were all those whom you name, however great the winners of benevolence, altogether safe or free from conspirators. If you say Augustus was free of them, you are certainly ignorant of history; you will change your mind when you read the nineteenth chapter of Suetonius, where he writes that he was endangered ten times, in scarcely ten lines. As for Vespasian, when you come to him, see the twenty-fifth chapter there; it will tell you that conspiracies against him were constant. He had Titus, Cecina, Antoninus, Cassius, Titianus and Priscianus. Who does not know that Constantine perished by poison? You yourself will not say these men were safe, once you have examined the history more carefully. Nor did those same men think the religion of an oath an empty thing; rather, when the occasion arose, they used it themselves and did not regard it as a slight support to them. So in this you should not be heard, you new adviser of kings; nor should what serves as a support in the faith of an oath be neglected. Indeed the obedience of princes is to be upheld by this, and by whatever other means it can be.

units.la: Et tamen, ut quod res est loquar, si causam scire vis, si veram, cur in Comitijs illis de iuramento illo tractatum sit; non eo factum, quo sibi suorum corda, magis etiam vel arctius astringeret (nam quibus maximè fidit, ij iniurati) sed quo illos nosse detur, quorum in cordibus erga Regem nil tale meritum, vomica pessimae perfidiae delitesceret. Effosis enim paulò ante cadis illis pyrio puluere oppletis, qui defosi inibi erant, ad ruinam, non Regis modò, sed floris totius Regni; visum est, idque ratione summâ visum, tum Regi, tum qui illi aderant Primarijs Regni viris, quacunque demum possent ratione, eruere, ecquis praeterea essent, nondum comprehensi, quorum in pectora, vestri homines, virus illud tam tetrum instillassent. Inde autem extitit Iuramentum, quo sic illud (tanquam Galaaditis Shibboleth suum) tesserae loco esset, quo Ephratai vestri à veris subditis internosci possent. Eo magis hoc, quòd vnus & alter ex illis qui comprehensi, cùm propter facinus illud tam atrox ad supplicium ducerentur, & iam iamque morte multandi essent; visi sunt ne tum quidem ad furcas poenitere, nec veniam petere sceleris tam nefandi.
units.tr: And yet, to speak as the matter stands, if you want to know the true cause why that oath was discussed in those assemblies, it was not done so that they might bind their people's hearts more closely to themselves (for those in whom they trust most are the ones who are unsworn), but so that they might discover who, among those whose hearts held no such merit toward the King, harboured the poisonous canker of the worst treachery. For shortly before, the casks filled with gunpowder, which had been buried there for the ruin not only of the King but of the whole flower of the realm, had been dug out; and it was judged, and judged with the greatest reason, both by the King and by the chief men of the realm who were with him, that by whatever means they could, they should root out whether any others, not yet apprehended, had had that foul poison instilled into their breasts by your men. From this the oath arose, so that it might serve, like the Shibboleth of the Gileadites, as a password by which your Ephraimites could be distinguished from the true subjects. All the more so because one or two of those who had been seized, when they were being led to execution for so atrocious a crime and were on the point of being punished with death, were seen not even then to repent at the gallows, nor to ask pardon for so wicked a crime.

units.la: Non certè: nisi lege hâc, si Papae & Ecclesiae suae visum, illorum hoc factum male factum, decernere & declarare. Adeò illi de scelere illo tam horrendo pendebant animi, bene, an male factum esset, & tanquam in re dubiâ, Papae sententiam expectabant. Etiam (quod mireris) mirati, vestrorum hic hominum tarditatem, quòd illorum nemo Apologiam festinârit factí huius tam Catholici scilicet, tam apud Catholicos magni & memorabilis.
units.tr: Certainly not: unless by this law, if it seemed good to the Pope and to his Church, they might decree and declare that deed of theirs to have been ill done. So anxious were they about that so horrible a crime, whether it had been done well or ill, that they waited for the Pope's judgment as if the matter were doubtful. Indeed (which you may wonder at) we also marvel at the slowness of your men here, that none of them has hastened to publish an Apology for this deed, so truly Catholic, and so great and memorable among Catholics.

units.la: Vbi iam de praesidio dixisti quod in beneuolentiâ est; vis & de beneuolentiâ captandâ monere etiam. Nihilo tamen hic fœlicior; Nec magis compendio fieri posse autumas, quàm si sinat Rex vestros homines frui religione suâ à proauis culta, à Gregorio magno acceptâ. Tum demum iubes securum esse iubes: continuo (quasi in tuâ manu esset) iubes pericula omnia timoresque cessare: Et hanc tu viam ei statuis, si sibi consultum velit. Nec est tamen. Sciut enim omnes suos Catholicâ religione frui, non ita pridem in Galliâ Henricus 3. parum tamen tutus. Hic ipse qui rerum nunc potitur Rex, postquam etiam hoc idem siuit; at eum tamen non siuerunt: quin ei (quod Iesuitæ adhuc meminisse possunt) et sciëntem[?] tantùm excusserunt, at iugulum tamen petierunt. Sed tamen, qui consilium hoc Regi nostro datis, didicistis alijs alibi Regibus, aliud dare, huic quidem plane contrarium: Etiam datis. Vnde enim illæ in Galliâ, in Belgio, clades tot, unde nuper in Hungariâ, in Poloniâ turbæ, nisi quòd illis ibi Regibus persuasum vultis, tutos se esse non posse, nec suæ vel salutì, vel dignitati satis consulere, si sinant intra ditiones suas, nostros homines, religionis suæ sacra retinere? Quod hic vrgetis apud Nostrum, id, vbi rerum summa penes vos est, audire non sustinetis.
units.tr: Now that you have spoken of the security that lies in benevolence, you also wish to advise us on winning benevolence. You are no more fortunate here; nor do you claim that it can be done more quickly than by this: "if the King allows your men to enjoy their religion, cultivated by their forefathers and received from Gregory the Great." Then at last you bid him be secure; you bid him, as though it were in your hand, at once to let all dangers and fears cease; and you set this as the way for him, if he wishes to consult his own good. But it is not so. For they know that all their people enjoy the Catholic religion, and not long ago Henry III in France, though he did, was not very safe. The present King himself, who now holds the reins of the realm, after he too allowed this same thing, yet they did not allow him to live: indeed (as the Jesuits can still recall) they shook him loose as he knew it, yet they sought his throat nonetheless.
