But you who give this counsel to our King have learned to give another, quite the opposite, to other kings elsewhere: you give it even so. For whence came those many disasters in France and in the Netherlands, whence lately the tumults in Hungary and in Poland, except that you want those kings there persuaded that they cannot be safe, nor sufficiently look to their own health or dignity, if they allow our men, within their dominions, to keep the rites of their religion? What you press upon our King, you cannot bear to hear when the supreme power of affairs is in your own hands.

units.la: Postremò, consilij tui clausula; consilij expers; vt vix (credo) tui hic stipem aliquam tibi nummetaturi, sed neque gratiam de illo vllam habituri sunt. Sic enim dicis, idque non tam consultò: si securum regnare velit Rex, si vitæ suæ & suorum consulere cupiat, sinat frui Catholicos religione suâ. Quid si autem non sinat? actum igitur de securitate, de vitâ, & suorum & suâ. Perinde enim hoc, ac si saltem innuendo diceres: Ni sic frui sinat, non impunè hoc illi fore. Minari hoc quidem, non monere est; Tuque ipse, quantum in te est, occasionem non leuem submini-stras (nisi Rex clementior) quâ ab illâ religione sunt, vt arctius habeantur. Ni sinat enim Rex, maleficium meditari.
units.tr: Lastly, the conclusion of your counsel: it is empty of counsel, so that (I think) scarcely anyone would pay you a coin for it, yet they will have no thanks for it at all. For you say this, and not very deliberately: "if the King wishes to reign securely, if he desires to consult the safety of his own life and that of his people, let him allow the Catholics to enjoy their religion." What if he does not allow it? Then there is an end to security, to life, both of his own and of his people. For this is just the same as if you had said, even by hinting, that unless he allows such enjoyment, it will not go unpunished for him. To threaten this is not to advise. And you yourself, as far as lies in you, supply no slight occasion (unless the King is more merciful) by which those men are held more tightly under that religion. For if the King does not allow it, you contrive mischief.

units.la: Quod tu autem hic pro concesso ponis & confesso, religionem à patribus, auis, & proauis hic cultam; id verò fecisti se habere Regiæ Maiestatis constat. Quam enim nostri homines religionem profesi sunt, ineunte illo hic Regnum suum auspicatisimum, eandem esse nec aliam, quam & Patres eorum profesi erant, quaeque illis à Patribus transmissa fuerat. Etiam permultos ex ijs, ad anos vsque & proanos seriem dicere; ut necesse iam habeas, quod de anus & proanus dixisti, retractare. Quodsi vltra anos iam & proanos, ad multa saecula retrospicias: at maiores & illorum, & vestros per multa saecula constat Ethnicos fuisse, quorum tamen (scio) author non eris, vt vestigijs vestri insistant. Quam ergo de sequendis maioribus regulam figis, parum fida est, fallet sequentem. Nec enim apud Deum excusatio erit vlla, fecisse se quod à maioribus factum, nisi id ab illis factum quod faciendum fuit. Neque verò quod fecerunt illi, id & nos facere oportet: id oportet in cultu Dei, non quod illi fecerunt, sed quod ex voluntate Dei, verbo tuo reuelatâ, facere debuerunt.
units.tr: But as for what you here take for granted and as admitted, that the religion here practised was handed down by fathers, grandfathers and great-grandfathers, that is clearly not true of the King's Majesty. For the religion which our men professed at the beginning of this king's most auspicious reign here was the same and no other than that which their fathers had professed, and which had been handed down to them by their fathers. Even if you were to count many of them back to grandfathers and great-grandfathers, you would now have to retract what you said about grandfathers and great-grandfathers. But if you look back beyond grandfathers and great-grandfathers, to many centuries, it is clear that your ancestors and theirs were pagans for many centuries; yet (I know) you will not be the author of following their footsteps. So the rule you set up for following our ancestors is not trustworthy; it will deceive whoever follows it. For there will be no excuse before God that one did what had been done by one's ancestors, unless what was done by them was what ought to have been done. Nor must we do what they did; in the worship of God we ought to do not what they did, but what they ought to have done according to the will of God, revealed in your Word.

units.la: Haec námque si primis illis Ecclesiæ temporibus Régula valuisset, de sequendâ Maiorum religione; starent adhuc idôla, essemus adhuc Pagani omnes, nec in Ecclesiam vnquam intrâsset plenitudo Gentium. Etiam hodie iam, dicat hoc Indus quispiam Iesuitis ibi, (siqui ibi sunt) fine fruar antiquâ religione, à patribus, auis, proauis cultâ, per multa iam secula; haud credo vocem hanc libenter audient. Si audiant, impugnabunt vt falsam & fallacem, & quâ, nulla magis saluti perniciosa. Valeat ergo Regula haec vestra; quæ si obtineret, cui parentes, auî, proauî Pagani; non vllus olim fieret; si obtineat, non vllus hodie fiat Christianus.
units.tr: For if this rule about following the religion of our ancestors had prevailed in the first times of the Church, the idols would still stand, we would all still be pagans, and the fullness of the Gentiles would never have entered the Church. Even today, if some Indian were to say this to the Jesuits there (if any are there), "I will enjoy the ancient religion, cultivated by fathers, grandfathers and great-grandfathers, through many centuries now," I do not think they would gladly hear this voice. If they heard it, they would attack it as false and deceptive, and as a thing more hurtful to salvation than any other. Let this rule of yours, then, be of no value; if it were to hold, no one would once have become a Christian, whose parents, grandfathers and great-grandfathers were pagans; if it holds now, no one would become a Christian today.

units.la: Nihil verò in eo nouum facis, quòd nobis nouas sectariorum opiniones obijcis. Antiquum obtines. Nobis verò opiniones nouas? Imò narro tibi, si noua sunt, nostrae non sunt. Prouocamus ad antiquos, ad antiquitatem vsque vltimam. Quo nouum quidque magis, eo minùs gratum nobis; quò minùs nouum, eo magis; nec vlla auribus nostris gratior vox accidit, quàm illa seruatoris, Ab initio fuit sic. Neque verò haeresin alia magis ratione definimus, quàm si veterum trium Symbolorum, vel si veterum quatuor Generalium Conciliorum vlli contraueniat. Annon hoc est, odisse opiniones nouas? Nec innouamus quicquam; renouamus forte, quae apud veteres illos fuerunt, & apud vos iam in nouitates abierunt.
units.tr: Nothing new in that, when you throw at us the "new opinions of the sectaries." You hold to the old. But "new opinions" against us? I tell you, if they are new, they are not ours. We appeal to the ancients, to the most ancient antiquity. The newer a thing is, the less it pleases us; the less new, the more; and no voice is more welcome to our ears than that of the Saviour: "From the beginning it was so." Indeed, we define heresy in no other way than by its contradicting the three ancient Creeds or the four ancient General Councils. Is this not to "hate new opinions"? Nor do we introduce anything; perhaps we revive what existed among those ancients, and what among you has already passed into "novelties."

units.la: At vos quis ferat de nouitate verba facere, qui nouas indies sectas, nouas glossas, nouas opiniones commenta procuditis? Audi sodes, si tibi ad nouas opiniones aures pruriant, nouitates Domini tui iam noui facti calentes adhuc, postquam veteres de iis errores suos nuperrimè, vix ante annum, recognouit. {a}Paulus de iure Cæsari subiectus non fuit, nec ad eum appellauit tanquam superiorem suum. {b}Canones [Adrianus] & [In Synodo] reprobi sunt. {c}Infideles, hoc ipso quòd infideles, etiam innoxij, priuari possunt dominio suo. {d}Pontifex olim Imperatori de iure subiectus non erat. {e}Cùm dixit Christus Petro, Pasce, id voluit, Regio more impera. {f}Pontifices nunquam eligi solitt ab Imperatoribus. {g}Principes à Deo immediate electi, opus habebant consensu populi. {h}Christum in Eucharistiâ sub specie panis delitescere. Nec {i}conuersionem ibi productiuam esse, sed adductiuam. Quare nouatù & vos vobis nouālia, atque is quæstus vobis multò vberrimus. Quodsi quid antiquum retinetis, id ita interpolatum est, apud vos, vt nemo veterum rediuiuus agnoscat: vt qui Ecclesiam Romanam veterem in vestrâ hodiè Romanâ quærat, is operam luserit.
units.tr: But who could bear you speaking about novelty, you who churn out new sects, new glosses and new opinion-inventions every day? Listen, please: if your ears itch for new opinions, your Lord's novelties, only just made new and still warm, are at hand, since he has very recently, scarcely a year ago, retracted the old errors he held about them. {a} "Paul was not subject to Caesar by right, nor did he appeal to him as his superior." {b} "The canons [of Adrian] and [of the Synod] are rejected." {c} "Infidels, simply because they are infidels, even if innocent, can be deprived of their lordship." {d} "The Pontiff was formerly not subject by right to the Emperor." {e} "When Christ said to Peter, Feed, he meant it in the manner of a king: rule." {f} "Pontiffs were never accustomed to be elected by Emperors." {g} "Princes, chosen immediately by God, needed the consent of the people." {h} "That Christ lies hidden under the species of bread in the Eucharist." Nor is the conversion there productive but only attractive. So you too are making new things for yourselves, and that is a far richer profit for you. But if you retain anything old, it has been so interpolated among you that no one of the ancients, returned to life, would recognise it; so that whoever seeks the old Roman Church in your present-day "Roman" Church will have wasted his labour.

units.la: Nec etiam Gregorium nobis exprobrare potuit, quasi nos illum, quâ par est reuerentiâ, non prosequamur; quasi quæ in scriptis eius ex veterum Conciliorum & Patrum, qui ante illum sensu & sententiâ, sunt, ea nos libenter non amplectamur. Etiam & multa, quæ apud illum neruosè contra nomen vniuersalis: multa quæ apud illum officiosè dicta de Cæsare, vobis obijcimus. Gregorius certè magnus, in hijs quidem, apud vos parum est, & parui: plus ad rem vestram septimus quàm primus Gregorius. Neque tamen verum est quod venditas, fidem nostram Britanniæ à Gregorio acceptam. Habuit enim hæc insula, Archiepiscopum, septem Episcopos habuit, veteris fidei cultores, & prædicatores, eo ipso tempore, quo illi monachos suos huc immittere libuit; eósque noui illi aduenæ opprimendos omnino curârunt, non quòd perperam quid vel crederent vel docerent, sed quòd sese illis per omnia nollent submittere. Roma enim subijci, inde pendere, hæc vestræ religionis summa est.
units.tr: Nor could he reproach us with Gregory, as though we did not honour him with the reverence that is his due, as though we did not gladly embrace whatever in his writings agrees in sense and opinion with the Councils and Fathers who came before him. You also object to us the many things said vigorously by him against the name "universal," the many things said dutifully by him about the Emperor. Certainly Gregory the Great, in these matters, is of little account among you and of little weight: the seventh Gregory is more to your purpose than the first Gregory. Nor is it true, as you claim, that Britain received the faith from Gregory. For this island had an Archbishop and seven Bishops, cultivators and preachers of the old faith, at the very time when he chose to send his monks hither; and those new strangers took great care to have them oppressed, not because they believed or taught anything wrongly, but because they would not submit to them in all things. For to be subject to Rome, to depend on it, is the sum of your religion.

units.la: Nec in eo Regi audiendus, quòd consilium dei de religione liberè habendâ: integrum hoc iam illi non est. Nam, (quod cum eâ, quâ decet, reuerentiâ dictum volo) non semel periurus sit, quin bis, si te audiat. Quâ enim (fiqua est fidei bis datæ conscientia) vel conscientiâ, vel fide ferret in Regnis suis ritus vestros, vel vsum eorum publicum, qui suscepta primum Scotiæ; suscepta dein Angliæ, coronâ Regiâ, vtrobique que solenni ritu, Deo iusiurandum præstitit, de conseruandâ in statu suo, illâ colendi Dei formulâ, nec aliâ quàm quæ in Regnis suis tum publicè recepta, & vtriusque gentis legibus stabilita esset: Quarum etiam se tum legum quoque, non minùs quàm religionis, sanctissimè in se suscepit defensorem fore? Eò autem consilium hoc tuum tendit, vt nouatorum, vt periurus, vt vtrumque sit: esset enim vtrumque, si vtrumque hoc tam graui crimine, vel coronæ suæ, vel etiam vitæ, securitatem redimeret. Hoc verò quàm à ratione prorsus alienum, tu, Lector, iudica, Regi nostro præsertim, cui nulla hîc apud nos periurii dispensatio speranda, cui nulla de Pontificis opinio, quòd tam sit omnipotens, vt suscepti eum bis iuramenti religione possit exoluere.
units.tr: Nor is the King to be heard on this point, that he has given counsel about holding religion freely: that is no longer open to him. For (I wish this said with the reverence that is fitting) he would not be perjured once, but twice, if he listened to you. For by what conscience of a pledged faith (if there is any such) or by what faith would he tolerate in his kingdoms your rites, or their public practice, he who, first on his accession to Scotland and then to England, with a solemn rite in each place, swore before God to preserve, in its state, that form of worshipping God which was then publicly received in his kingdoms and established by the laws of each people, and no other; and whose laws, no less than the religion, he took upon himself in the most holy manner to defend? But your counsel tends toward this: that he should be both a innovator and a perjurer, for he would be both if he bought the safety of his crown or even of his life with so grave a crime. Judge for yourself, reader, how utterly foreign this is to reason, especially with regard to our King, for whom no dispensation from perjury is to be hoped for here among us, and who holds no opinion of the Pontiff such as that he is so omnipotent that he could release him from the obligation of an oath twice sworn.

units.la: Cùm verò videres fruitionem illam, pro quâ interpellas, vestros homines illo suo tam tetro facinore parum ex congruo meruisse, descendis ad facinus ipsum; atque (ais) non excusare te (nam vt excusare te diceres; grauior tibi vox fortasse videbatur) sed non excusare te ais, & excusui tamen eodem spiritu: nam subnectis illud tuum, sed: Sed occasionem desperationis datam, nemo inficiari poterit. Hoc, quo animo à te dictum, si non excusandi? Sed quid tum si occasio data? Nosti quid Dominus tuus, Occasio neque physicè neque moraliter quicquam operatur: Etiam peccandi, Deus apud illum occasionem dat, neque tamen ex eo excusandi peccantes. Nihil ergo hoc ad excusationem, si nemo occasionem datam inficiari posset. Sed nec hoc verum, nemo potest inficiari. Omnes enim possunt, túque ipse, re cognitâ faxo vt inficiari, & possis, & necesse habeas. Quæ enim tandem illa desperandi occasio? sperasse (ais) respirationem aliquam, sub nouo Principe; post, suâ hac spe excidisse. Quæro primùm, si quis sine ratione, inanem spem, atque stultam animo concipiat, post verò spei exitus non respondeat, an huic datam putes occasionem desperandi? nam desperare id quidem est, vbi vera spes ptæcisa, non siquis falsam fouear, eaque non succedat. Falsam autem fo-uerunt tum vestri: tum, promissa nescio quæ commenti sunt, quæ nulla tamen fuerunt: & quod factum nunquam est, id fuisse tamen factum, in vulgus spargebant: in eóque sibi iniuriam factam, quòd non auaris votis suis per omnia satisfieret, quòd non frui daretur, quicquid illis sperare in animum venisset.
units.tr: But when you saw that the "enjoyment" for which you plead had been little deserved by your people through that foul deed of theirs, you descend to the deed itself; and you say (for you might have said "excuse"—perhaps that word seemed too heavy for you) that you "do not excuse them," yet you say it and "excuse" them with the same spirit; for you add that clause of yours: "But the opportunity for despair given, no one can deny." With what intention did you say this, if not to excuse them? But what then if an opportunity was given? You know what your Lord says: "Opportunity works neither physically nor morally anything." Even of sinning, God, in his view, gives an opportunity, and yet from that one does not excuse the sinners. So this has nothing to do with excuse, even if no one could deny the opportunity given. But neither is this true, that no one can deny it. For all can, and you yourself, the thing being known, I will make deny it, and you are able to and must. For what, after all, is that "opportunity for despair"? They "hoped" (you say) for some respite under a new Prince; afterwards they fell from that hope. I ask first: if someone without reason conceives an empty and foolish hope in his mind, and afterwards the outcome of the hope does not answer, do you think an opportunity of despairing has been given to him? For to despair is indeed when a true hope has been cut off, not when someone cherishes a false one and it does not succeed. But your people, indeed, cherished a false hope; they invented certain promises, which in fact were nothing; and what never happened they spread among the common people as having happened; and in this they claimed a wrong was done to them, because their greedy wishes were not satisfied in every respect, because the enjoyment they desired was not granted, whatever had come into their minds to hope for.

units.la: Quæro deinde, unde illis sperandi occasio? à Regis clementiâ. Vbi, si spem dicis religionis liberæ, responsum iam habes; Educatione ipsâ primùm in religione nostrâ, pòst constanti semper eius professione, gemino deinde iuramento eius, sublatam vobis spem omnem, fieri posse, ut in religione mutaret. Neque verò eâ clementiâ fuit apud Scotos suos, ut Catholicis vestris religionem suam liberam retinere, permiserit, (quod apud te respirare est) & tamen respirare eis permisit. At hic maior speranda fuit, Quia vestri scilicet, illum magnâ alacritate suscepe-runt. Nescio quàm magnâ alacritate: sed suscepe-runt certè: Verum post Breuia duo Clementis igni tradita, quibus cautum erat, ut acriter resisterent potiùs quàm alacriter reciperent: Et postquàm non aliqua iam superesset spes de personâ aliâ, quæ vobis magis in votis. Cùm enim certatim ab omnibus suscepтum videretis, & aut hunc iam, aut nullum præter hunc vobis suscipiendum: tùm demum, quod necessariò faciendum fuit, fecistis; & quem omnino suscipi oportuit, eum an alacriter nescio, clementer certè suscepistis. Sin spem dicis clementiâ, in legum severitate temperandâ magis atque leniendâ: quantum quidem Principi fas, qui cum laude clementiâ, iustitiâ quoque laudem retinere vellet, satis in eo superque vestræ omnium spei satisfactum est. Apologia te hoc, abundè docere potuit.
units.tr: I ask next: whence the opportunity for their hoping? From the King's clemency. Here, if you mean by "hope" the hope of free religion, you already have the answer: first by the very upbringing in our religion, then by his constant profession of it ever after, and then by his twofold oath, every hope of yours was taken away, namely that he might change in religion. Nor was he so merciful toward his Scots that he permitted your Catholics to retain their religion freely (which, in your view, is "to breathe"), and yet he permitted them to breathe. But here a greater hope was to be expected, "because your people, of course, received him with great eagerness." I do not know with how great eagerness; but certainly they received him. But after two Briefs of Clement were burned, by which it was provided that they should resist sharply rather than receive eagerly; and after there no longer remained any hope of another person, whom you would have preferred. For when you saw him received by all with eager rivalry, and that either him now or no one other than him was for you to receive: then at last you did what had to be done; and whom it was absolutely necessary to receive, him you received, if not eagerly (I do not know), at any rate graciously. But if you call "hope" the hope from clemency, in tempering and softening the severity of the laws: as far as it is right for a Prince, who wished to retain praise for justice together with praise for clemency, enough and more than enough has been done in this for the hope of you all. The Apology could have taught you this amply.

units.la: Obiter hæc. Exoluo iam quod pollicitus sum; Non esse datam desperandi occasionem ullam. Tu forte, eo quòd erupit demum proditio hæc Novemb. 1605. vel eo tempore, vel non ita multò ante, initam existimas. Audi ergo rem veram, & quam nec ipsi negabant. Primo Regis anno, inita est proditio pulueraria, tractatus de eâ habitus, idque tum scilicet, cùm neque Edicta ulla crudelia renouata, nec Ducenti Floreni exacti, nec, (quod tu odioso nomine vocas) quisquam opibus spoliatus. Nam, quod tu forte nescis, anno primo Regis Floreni illi cui ( de quibus tam frequens tibi mention) à nemine exacti, addo etiam nec secundo, ante quintum mensem. Nemo autem vitae discrimen, nemo fortunarum omnium iacturam adijt. Quare inficiamur omnino (quod tu posse putabas neminem) tum cùm designabant ista primùm, ullam esse desperandi occasionem datam. Noli ergo dehinc excusare, noli extenuare hoc tam immane facinus. Praecesserat quidem pulueriariam proditio alia, ipso Regis initio, necdum coronato Rege, quae mense Iunio erupit, procurantibus rem totam duobus sacerdotibus vestris, Watsono & Clerco, quod quidem hominum non erat, Regem sic (ut dicis) alacriter suscipientium. Poterat hic iam Rex, commoueri[?] esse, & leges renouare, & Florenos menstruos exigere: non est factum; proditione illa vestrorum hominum non obstante, nec Ducenti illi floreni, nec vel eorum assis ullus, multae nomine à vestrorum quoquam exactus, quod sacris interesse recusaret.
units.tr: By the way, here I pay the debt I promised: that no occasion for despair was given at all. Perhaps you think this plot, which broke out only in November 1605, was hatched at that time or not much before. Hear then the true account, which even they did not deny. In the first year of the King, the gunpowder plot was undertaken and discussed, and that at a time when no cruel edicts had been renewed, no two hundred florins had been exacted, and (to use your hateful word) no one had been stripped of his goods. For, as perhaps you do not know, in the first year of the King those florins of which you speak so often were exacted from no one, and I add, not even in the second, before the fifth month. Nobody faced peril of life, nobody incurred the loss of all his fortunes. Therefore we flatly deny (though you thought no one could) that when these men first planned it, any occasion for despair had been given. Do not, then, go on to excuse, do not to minimise, this so monstrous crime. Indeed, an earlier plot to the gunpowder plot had gone before, at the very beginning of the King's reign, before the King was crowned, which broke out in June, the whole business being carried on by two of your priests, Watson and Clerk, who were certainly not men of the sort who, as you say, received the King willingly. The King could then have been moved, and renewed the laws and exacted the monthly florins; he did not do so. Despite that plot of your men, neither those two hundred florins nor even a single penny of them, no fine in the name of many was exacted from any of your people for refusing to attend the sacred rites.

units.la: Mentio mihi facta modò de Watsono, qui ante coronam impositam capiti Regis, capiti eius perniciem machinatus est. Ille ipse, cùm de illo habita quaestio, ultrò fassus est, conatum se in illam conspirationem suam, Iesuitas etiam pertrahere; nec obtinuisse quicquam, tantùm ab illis hoc responsum accepisse; Pergeret in suo illo instituto, rem suam ageret strenuè: se quidem illi iam cooperari non posse, aut operam suam impendere: Suam enim sibi technam esse alteram, ac peculiarem, satis operosam, cui intenti sint toti; eam conaturos se, suo quoque tempore effectam dare: Interim nolle misceri[?] illius, & suam, ne alter alteri impedimento sint. Watsoni dictum hoc, rei exitus comprobauit. Credo ergo, & oculis tuo nonnihil pulueris iniectum; nam nihil hîc verè affirmas. Non enim, quod tu ais, viderunt Edicta confirmari, non multam ullam novum imponi, non quenquam florenis suis ducentis (in quibus tam multus es) spoliari, nec vel leuissimâ iniuriâ, laesa illis patientia est, cùm in hoc nefas ruerent.
units.tr: A moment ago I mentioned Watson, who, before the crown was placed on the King's head, plotted ruin for that same head. When he himself was questioned about him, he freely confessed that he had tried to draw the Jesuits too into that conspiracy of his, but had obtained nothing; he had received only this answer from them: let him press on with his project and carry out his business vigorously; they for their part could no longer cooperate with him or devote their effort to it, for they had another art of their own, a separate one, quite laborious, to which they were all wholly intent; they would strive to bring it to completion at its own time; meanwhile they were unwilling for his plan and theirs to be mixed, lest the one should hinder the other. The outcome of the affair confirmed Watson's statement. I believe, then, that some dust has been thrown into your eyes too, for you assert nothing true here. For, as you say, they did not see the edicts confirmed, no new fine imposed, no one stripped of his two hundred florins (about which you are so voluble), and not even by the slightest wrong was their patience harmed, while they were rushing into this crime.

units.la: Vis paucis tibi expediam, quo pacto habuit res tota ex serie temporum? paucis accipe. Auspicatus est hic Regnum in nos suum Serenissimus Rex Iacobus, executione Martio 1603. (quod velit iubeat Deus Opt. Max, esse diuturnum)
units.tr: Do you want me to explain to you briefly how the whole matter stood in the order of the times? Take it in brief. His Most Serene Majesty King James began his reign over us in March 1603 (may God, the Best and Greatest, will it to be long-lasting).

units.la: Ille verò, primo quoque tempore post adventum huc ad nos suum, ferìò vetuit, ne quicquam, vel quod iam fisco debitum esset, vel quod post debceretur[?], de ducentis illis florenis multæ nomine exigi posset à quoquam, ex eo quòd sacris non interesset. En,[?] temperata ab eo Lex, & exarmata penitus; nónne aliquantulum tum respirare poterant? Quam verò illi de hoc facto gratiam retulerunt, ut novam invitare[?] possent? Mensis vix tertius agebatur, cùm detecta proditio prima, cui facem praetulerunt duo de vestris Sacerdotibus, antè mihi nominati, Watsonus & Clerus. Ineunte hoc Junio contigit 1603. Alius iam Rex, cui non tam constans clementia, fieret alienior hoc facto, mentem mutaret. Non est factum; nulla spolia, multa nulla de novo dicta: ducenti illi floreni, à nemine persoluti; liberè etiam tum respirare licuit. Nec dum igitur desperandi occasio.
units.tr: Indeed, at the first opportunity after his arrival here among us, he forbade at once that anything be exacted from anyone in the name of a fine, for not attending the sacred rites, whether it were the sum already owed to the exchequer or what would later be owed, of those two hundred florins. Behold, the law was tempered by him and wholly disarmed; could they not then breathe a little? But what thanks did they render him for this act, so that they could invite a new one? Scarcely three months had passed when the first plot was discovered, to which the two priests I named before, Watson and Clerk, applied the torch. This happened at the beginning of June 1603. Another king, to whom such constant clemency would not have seemed a reason to become more hostile, might have changed his mind by this act. He did not; no spoils were taken, no fine was newly announced; those two hundred florins were paid by no one; and they were still free to breathe. Not yet, then, was there an occasion for despair.

units.la: Sic tamen constante sibi Regis clementiâ, nec uno hoc, sed multis praeterea in eos beneficijs testatâ, redeunte Martio, rebus eodem quo erant statu etiamnum permanentibus, nihil immutatis, nec ullâ de florenis mentione factâ, Martio illo, ovum[?] exclusum est, tela ordita, immanissimæ illius pulveraria proditionis. Perstitit tamen etiam Rex in lenitate suâ, nec ad Julium sequentem, ann. 1604. ulla prorsus pecuniariæ, de florenis, legis factæ executio. Post annum demum integrum & quadrimestre, cùm jam immodestè se gererent, impunitate nimirâ deteriores facti, coeptum est exigi ab ijs, quod lege debitum, & fisco applicari.
units.tr: Yet, the King remaining constant in his clemency, attested not by this single act but by many other benefits toward them, when March returned and affairs were still in the same state as before, nothing changed, and no mention made of florins, in that March the egg was hatched, the web was woven, of that most monstrous gunpowder treason. Nevertheless the King persisted in his mildness, and until the following July, in the year 1604, no execution whatever of the monetary law concerning the florins was carried out. Only after a full year and four months had passed, when they were already behaving insolently, made worse by impunity, did they begin to be required to pay what was owed by law and assigned to the exchequer.

units.la: Novembri autem subsequente 1604. cùm nonnulli de vestris Regem supplices adijssent, quæsti, quòd præter mentem eius, solutione granarentur[?] cuiusdam summæ, quæ debita quidem Reginæ, & novissimè debita, fisco tamen, sub initio ipso Regni Regis persoluta fuisset, priusquam de mente Regis constaret: exaudijt Rex clemens, & solutiones illas in fiscum factas, refundi iussit, & (quod ex aerarij tabulis constat) à quibus collectæ fuerant, ijsdem ad assem sunt redditæ; atq; ut summam ipsam scias quàm hac ratione ab auspicato hic Regno ad tricesimum Julij 1604. condonauit illis munificentissimus Rex, fuit ea quidem ad 5 2000[?] florenorum. Nulla dum (ut tu ipse vides) ex florenis illâ occasio desperandi data, imò[?] sperandi potiùs potiús. Et illo pòst tamen, qui tum instabat, Decembri, cum hæc agerentur, tam in illorum rem & spem bonam, illi tum toti erant in muro suffodiendo, & de quo præcedente Martio tractatu inter eos, id ipsum per totos decem menses strenuè tum peragebant. Non, eò desperatione acti (quid enim tum desperarent tàm clementer exauditi) sed alia re, quam dicere nolo.
units.tr: In November of the following year, 1604, when some of your people came as suppliants to the King, complaining that, contrary to his intention, a certain sum was extracted from them, which, though indeed owed to the Queen, and most recently owed to the exchequer, had been paid at the very beginning of the King's reign, before the King's intention was known: the merciful King listened, and ordered those payments made to the exchequer to be refunded, and (as the records of the treasury show) they were returned to the very persons from whom they had been collected, to the last penny. And so that you may know the sum itself which, by this method, the most generous King remitted to them from the auspicious beginning of his reign up to 30 July 1604, it amounted to about 2,000 florins. As you yourself see, no occasion for despair was then given from the florins; rather, if anything, an occasion for hope. And yet, at that time, when these things were happening, in the following December, they were wholly absorbed, with their hopes and their affairs in good state, in digging under the wall, and for the whole ten months they had vigorously carried on that very business, which had been discussed among them the previous March. They did this not driven by despair (for what could they despair of, having been heard so mercifully?) but by another motive, which I am unwilling to name.

units.la: Bienuium autem penè, hoc monstro grauidi, Nouembri demum 1605. parturiebant illud. Sed etsi articulatum tum plenè: tamen (ita miseratus nostri Deus voluit) abortiuum; vt cum iam filij venissent ad partum, vires non essent pariendi. Habes breui rem, vt gesta est; habes & tempus. Miraberis, scio, fucum tibi sic factum de occasione, quam ipse iam vides nullam fuisse. Nullam certè publicam: sin priuatum dicas, occasio inde illis desperandi qui esse potuit, quorum de primarijs qui fuit, fuit ex Cohorte Prætoriâ (loco apud nos inprimis illustri) quíque Regi etiam, tum, cum nondum hoc regnum adeptus esset, munificentiam nunquam sibi clausam senserat? Incendiarius vero ipse, militabat tum in Belgio, stipendijs Archiducis, nec illi vel domus apud nos, vel res. Ille vero, fassus est vltro, nec vindictâ irritatum se, nec actum desperationè, inde de castris huc in Angliam appulisse: quin zelo solo, nec vllâ præterea re, adductum Romanæ hic religionis instaurandæ. Eo autem magis adductum, quòd propositum hoc suum, nonnulli de transmarinis viri docti, ei persuasisset, non licitum modò, sed & pium esse, & (vt vos loqui soletis) meritorium. Hæc illi. Alij etiam liberè confessi sunt & ipsi, à notis quibusdam suis & amicis, illectos se in sceleris societatem, nulla vel iniuidiâ cuiusquam vel iniuriâ prouocatos, vt nec exasperatio aliqua publica, nec priuatum odium præcesserit, quæ ansam præberent ista machinandi: tantùm in transfuersum acti sunt, & accensi zelo quodam prapostero; cui arida subijcicbant, nescio qui de vobis, quorum de doctrinâ opinio illis aliqua. Et, iam in profcenio erat Tragœdia, tam sanguinolenta, tam feralis, vt Deus agi illam noluerit; scenam sustulerit, theatrum aliud eodem loco erigi, in quo eosdem histriones, fabulam aliam sibi suneslam agere, magnus ille Choragus mandauerit; nec illam sane spectatu iucundam, nisi quòd, per illam, alia longè magis Tragica, à Rege, regnóque universo, interversa atque aversa est.
units.tr: For almost two years, pregnant with this monster, they were in labour, and only in November 1605 did they bring it forth. But although it was then fully formed, yet (as our merciful God willed) it was stillborn, so that when the sons had come to the birth, there was no strength to bring forth. You have here the matter briefly as it was done, and you have the time too. You will be astonished, I know, that you have so fabricated a pretext about an occasion which you yourself now see was none. None, certainly, in public; but if you call it private, what occasion for despair could there be for those of whom one of the chief men was from the Praetorian Cohort (a position especially distinguished among us), and who had felt that the King's generosity was never closed to him, even when he had not yet obtained this kingdom? The incendiary himself, moreover, was then serving in the Netherlands, on the pay of the Archduke, and had neither house nor property among us. Yet he freely confessed, that he was neither provoked by revenge nor driven by despair to come from the camp here to England; indeed, that he was moved by zeal alone, and by nothing else, to restore the Roman religion here. He was all the more moved, because some learned men from overseas had persuaded him that his purpose was not only lawful but also pious, and (as you are wont to say) meritorious. Such were his words. Others too freely confessed, as well, that they had been lured into the society of this crime by certain acquaintances and friends of theirs, and were provoked by no hatred or injury from anyone, so that no public exasperation nor private hatred had gone before, to furnish a pretext for devising such things; they were merely driven sideways and inflamed by a certain perverse zeal, to which, I know not who among you, whose teaching they had some opinion of, added dry fuel. And now the tragedy was already on the stage, so bloody and so deadly that God would not allow it to be played out; he removed the stage, and ordered another theatre to be erected in the same place, in which that great Chorus-master commanded the same actors to play another drama, baneful to themselves; nor was that one at all pleasant to watch, except that through it another far more tragic one was overturned and reversed, by the King and the whole kingdom.

units.la: Nam, quod etiam quasi partem occasionis commemoras, Confirmata Regina Elizab. Edicta. Id verò ita factum oportuit, nec secus omninò tum habere se res potuit. Pars enim Regij Iuramenti fuit, tum, cùm publicis ceremonijs inauguratus est, de patria religione, de legibus (quo erant tum statu) conseruandis, tum à populo suo obseruari faciendis. Verum nec de nouo, acrior vlla lex, nec grauior vlla multa prius decreta est, quàm trium Ordinum, suâ hac (vtinam non tam sæpe mihi nominanda, sed quoties nominanda, toties detestanda semper) proditione, languenti iam senectuti calcar, & quasi sopito iam igni oleum addidissent? Vides ergò non minui flagitium hoc, augeri potiùs, cùm citra vllam occasionem vel leuissimam, inita tamen est ratio tam barbarae proditionis, vt tu iam, qui, quòd actos putares in desperationem, ideo fortasse deplorasti, posses iam oculos abstergere, & minus plorare posthac, & dolorem tuum in odium potius, lacrymas in diras commutare. Nec enim, desperatio illa misera fuit, vt miseranda; sed præsumptio dira potius, vt diris proin omnibus fuerit denouenda.
units.tr: For as for the point you bring up as if it were part of the cause, namely "the edicts issued once the Queen Elizabeth was confirmed": that had to be so, and in those circumstances matters could not have stood otherwise. For it formed part of the King's oath, when he was inaugurated with public ceremonies, that he would maintain the native religion and the laws (as they then stood), and cause them to be observed by his people. But was any law ever newly enacted more severe, or any penalty more grave, than what the three Orders had decreed beforehand, by their own treachery (I wish I did not have to name it so often, but whenever I name it, I should always detest it), when they had added a spur to an already failing old age, and oil to a fire already smouldering? You see, then, that this crime is not diminished but rather aggravated, since the plan of so barbarous a treachery was formed without any occasion, however slight, so that you, who perhaps lamented because you thought they had been driven to despair, may now dry your eyes, weep less from now on, and turn your grief into hatred and your tears into curses. For that despair was not a wretched thing deserving pity; it was rather a dreadful presumption, and so ought to be condemned by all the dreadful.

units.la: ACtum dein agis. Ubi dictis tu quidem, non egere te argumentis, & tamen eges, & cum aliud tibi argumentum, nullam suppetat (miser homo) cogit te durum telum necessitas, vt recurras ad ea quæ de titulo Edicti paulò prius dixeras. Nihil habuit hic egestas tua, præter titulum illum: Ille autem quantum valeat, sat iam liquet lectori; vt verò magis adhuc liqueat, visum est subijcere hic Edicti seu legis ipsius proœmium; quo fere apud nos, & legis ratio, & latoris intentio contineri solent. Ex eo tibi (lector) perspicuum erit, quàm vtriusque mentem, & legis & latoris, sciens, prudens Tertius detorqueat. Sic autem habet:
units.tr: Next you take up the matter in hand. Here you say, indeed, that you need no arguments; yet you do need them, and since no other argument is at hand, poor man, necessity forces you to a hard weapon: to return to what you said a little earlier about the title of the Edict. Your want here had nothing but that title. How much that is worth is already clear enough to the reader; but so that it may become clearer still, I have thought fit to append here the preamble of the Edict or statute itself, in which, among us, both the reason of the law and the intention of the lawgiver are usually contained. From it, reader, it will be plain to you how the Tertius, knowingly and deliberately, twists the mind of both the law and the lawgiver. It runs as follows:

units.la: Cùm iam experientiâ quotidianâ compertum sit, multos Regiæ Maiestatis subditos, ex animo Pontificiæ religioni adhærentes; partim eâ quam inde hauriunt consuetudine, partim sceleratò & Satanico consilio (quod illis à Iesuitis fugere solet, & è seminariorum alumnis, aliisque id genus hominibus, qui omnes Ecclesiæ, Regnoq; huic perniciosi semper sunt habiti) vsque adeo peruerti. perdu[?]elli indicet, quod ad officium attinet, & fidelitatem suam Regiæ Maiestati & Coronæ suæ debitam, vt promptos se præbeant, quò conspirationem vllam, seu machinationem proditoriam aggrediantur, seu exequantur: Id quod manifesto liquet ex illo plusquam barbaro & planè horrendo facinore, quo nuper conati sunt, Regem, Reginam, Principem, Senatum, atq; Populum, cùm in domo Parliamenti convenissent, pulveris pyrij vnicâ displosione, simul omnes ad internecionem dare, quod eorum facinus certam toti Reipub. ruinam attulisset: Cumq; compertum sit, scelus hoc fuscepsum esse; Iesuitis, & qui de seminarijs sunt, eorumque Discipulis in eum finem institutis, rem totam procurantibus, quò scilicet inde religio eorum revocari posset: (Quod eorum consilium solâ Dei omnipotentis benignitate detectum atque oppressum est:) Cumque nonnulli, qui sic animo affecti sunt, quo tamen melius possint virum[?] internum tegere, & quò tutius opportunitatem[?] articulos consectari, vt simile illi alterum scelus, si res feret, exequantur, templa nobiscum adeant, & cætibus nostris intersint, quò sic multiam euadentes lege impositam, magis adhuc latent: Ad hos igitur tales detegendos, & eorum animos in Maiestatem Regiam, inq; ipsam Rempublicam pessimè afsectos, quò sic detectû, nefarios eorum conatus præuenire detur[?];
units.tr: Since it is already established by daily experience that many subjects of His Royal Majesty, adhering heartily to the Papist religion, are perverted, partly by the custom they absorb from it, partly by a wicked and Satanic counsel (which is wont to be drawn from the Jesuits, and from the seminary students and other men of that kind, who have always been held pernicious to the Church and to this realm), so far that they should be shown to have lost their duty and their fidelity owed to His Royal Majesty and his Crown, so that they are ready to undertake or carry out any conspiracy or treacherous machination: this is clearly evident from that more than barbarous and plainly horrible deed, by which they recently tried, when they had gathered in the House of Parliament, by a single explosion of gunpowder to destroy at once the King, the Queen, the Prince, the Senate and the People all together, which deed would have brought certain ruin on the whole commonwealth. And since it is established that this crime was undertaken by the Jesuits and those from the seminaries, and by their disciples instituted for that end, who arranged the whole business, so that by it their religion might be restored (which counsel of theirs was discovered and crushed by the sole goodness of Almighty God); and since some who are so disposed, in order to conceal the inward man better, and to pursue opportunities and occasions more safely, so that they may carry out another such crime if circumstances allow, approach our churches and attend our assemblies, so that by thus escaping the fine imposed by law they hide themselves all the more: To detect these people, therefore, and to prevent their wicked attempts, once detected, against the mind of His Majesty and against the Commonwealth itself, which are so ill-disposed (...);

units.la: LEGE SANCITVM ESTO, &c.
units.tr: BE IT ENACTED BY THIS LAW, etc.

units.la: Hoc totius Legis proœmium est. At verò paragrapho demum vndecimo, vbi pars ipsa Edicti orditur quæ est de Iuramento hoc, audi & eo loco si placet iteratam Legislatoris intentionem. Verba ibi sunt.
units.tr: This is the whole preamble of the law. But at the eleventh paragraph, where the part of the Edict itself begins which concerns this oath, listen, if you please, to the lawgiver's intention repeated in that place. The words there are:

units.la: Quò verò melius constet, magisq; exploratum sit, quomodo subditi Maiestatis suæ animo affecti sint in officio fidelitatis suæ, & debita obedientia, LEGE ETIAM SANCITVM ESTO. Aduertis hic, scio, Lector, legis Occasionem, Cautionem, Æquitatem, Intentionem. Occasionem. Odiosum enim illud, &c. post hominum memoriam atrocissimum scelus pulveris nitrati, occasionem legi dedit, eo ipso die deprehensum, quo inchoata Ordinum Sessio. Lex absque eo certè futura tum nulla. Cautionem. Quò ne quid tale in posterum tentari posset, rationem iniri, de iis per quos simile quid tentari posset, maturè detegendum. Æquitatem. Etsi enim erant omnes Papistæ, qui in scelere illo; alios tamen qui sic essent ad religionem, non ad tam immane nefas pariter affectos statuebant. Quosdam modo, quos Jesuita usque adeo pernerterant, ut si res ferret, ad simile scelus perpetrandum, non inuiti accederent, quique etiam sacris nostris non detrectarent interesse, quo malam mentem tegere, & tale quid sine suspicione machinari possent, quale illud de puluere. Intentionem. Verba ipsa sunt legis, Ad hos igitur tales detegendos. Quid? an hos tales detegendos ægrè fert Pontifex, & reprimendos? An tectos vellet & protectos? Alioqui quid hic culpat? Annon Occasio legem expresit? Annon Cautio plusquàm necessaria? Annon distincta ibi satis fides officij, à fide religionis? Annon ex hijs verbis, Ad hos igitur tales detegendos, Intentio manifesta? Quis hæc, nisi sinister interpres fit, ad Catholicam fidem detorqueat? Quis fidei rem dicat hic agi? Imò fidem ne negent, negent perfidiam: fidem religionis profiteantur, dum fidem officij simul; & legi satisfactum est, quæ nulla est ad fideles, tota ad perfidas detegendos. Tu tamen recte dixisti de titulo, quòd fraudes detegat: vestras enim profecto detegit.
units.tr: But so that it may be better established and more fully ascertained how the subjects of His Majesty stand affected in the discharge of their duty of fidelity and due obedience, BE IT ALSO ENACTED BY THIS LAW. You notice here, I know, reader, the occasion of the law, its caution, its equity, its intention. The occasion. For that hateful deed of gunpowder, the most atrocious in human memory, gave occasion to the law, having been detected on the very day on which the session of the Orders began; without that, the law would certainly then have been nothing. The caution. That, so that nothing of the kind could be attempted in future, a plan was devised, to detect early those through whom something similar might be attempted. The equity. For although all the Papists were in that crime, yet they judged that others who were so attached to the religion, but not equally to so monstrous a wickedness, were not to be treated alike: only those whom the Jesuit had so perverted that, if circumstances allowed, they would not be unwilling to commit a similar crime, and who would also not refuse to attend our services, so that they could hide an evil mind and plot such a thing without suspicion, like that business with the powder. The intention. The very words of the law are: To detect these people, therefore. Well? Does the Pope take it ill that these people should be detected and restrained? Or would he wish them concealed and protected? Otherwise, what does he blame here? Has not the occasion been expressed by the law? Is not the caution more than necessary? Is not the fidelity of duty clearly distinguished here from the faith of religion? Is not the intention plain from these words, To detect these people, therefore? Who would twist this to the Catholic faith, unless he were a sinister interpreter? Who says that the question here is one of faith? Rather, let them not deny faith; let them deny perfidy: let them profess the faith of religion, while also professing the faith of duty; and the law is satisfied, which is not aimed at the faithful at all, but wholly at detecting the faithless. Yet you rightly said of the title that it detects frauds: for it certainly detects yours.

units.la: Etiam de nomine Juramenti fidelitatis nugatur, quòd sic in lege ne nominetur quidem. Quid tum, si aliud illi in Edicto nomen? An illud apud vos nouum: rem unam variis nominibus notare, dum ne contrarijs; & diuersis, dum ne aduersa sint, & inter se pugnent? Atqui nec nomen illud, nec aliud, nec ullum ibi omnino nomen inditum. Haud aliter ibi designatur, quàm ita, Juramentum hic subjiciendum. Author verò Apologiæ sic nominauit, Juramentum fidelitatis: primùm, quia ex substantiâ, fine, scopo, ita nominari debet: deinde, quia communi loquendi more, tàm à vestris quàm nostris hominibus, ita nominari solet, meritóque fidelitatis Juramentum ex eo dicitur, quòd in eo verba hæc posita, quæ ibi verba operatiua sunt, fidelitatem tamen & veram obedientiam Regiæ Majestati, & successoribus eius præstabo. Audis hic jam, non colorem fidelitatis, (vt tu sinistrè) sed fidelitatem ipsam: habes fidelitatem, in terminis quod aiunt terminantibus. Quid quæris ampliùs? Proinde fidelitas, non (vt tu dicis) color ullus, sed substantia est ipsa Juramenti.
units.tr: You also trifle about the name Oath of Fidelity, saying that it is not even named so in the law. What of it, if the Edict gives it another name? Is it new among you, that one thing should be marked by various names, so long as they are not contrary and different, or hostile and at war with one another? But neither that name, nor any other, is given there at all. It is designated there in no other way than thus: The oath to be imposed here. The author of the Apology, however, named it Oath of Fidelity: first, because by its substance, end and aim it ought to be so named; second, because by common usage of speech, both among your people and ours, it is customarily so named, and rightly the oath is called an oath of fidelity from this, that in it are set these words, which there are the operative words: I will perform true fidelity and obedience to His Royal Majesty and his successors. You hear here now, not the colour of fidelity (as you maliciously put it), but fidelity itself: you have fidelity in the terms, as they say, which terminate. What more do you seek? Therefore fidelity is not, as you say, some colour, but the very substance of the oath.

units.la: At etiam, post reperit quòd pueri in sabâ[?], mentionem in Edicto de juramento, contra potestatem Pontificis in Principes
units.tr: But then also, after he found that children in a sabbath [?] ... mention in the Edict of the oath, against the power of the Pope over princes

units.la: [?] Christianos, quæ quidem ibi nulla est. Tu qui iuramentum initio ita intelligebas, vt præter te nemo, en iam quàm nihil intelligis, fefellit te translatio tua. Nihil ibi de potestate Papæ in Principes Christianos. Propè finem dicis esse; propè certè, fortè enim, paulò post finem est. Hoc vbi reperit quod nusquam est: copiam tum nobis facit eligendi de duobus, vtrùm malimus appellari, an Iuramentum de Primatu Regis in spiritualibus, an Iuramentum contra potestatem Pontificis in Christianos Principes. Nugatur homo ineptus, vtrumque reiicimus. Prius. Iuramentum enim de Primatu in spiritualibus appellari non poterit, nisi, non dico falsò, sed, nisi absurdè loqui volumus. Nam nulla ibi, vel de primatu, vel de spiritualibus, syllaba, nulla prorsus. Posterius. Quia ab illo fictum, nec tale quid in Edicto. Illud tamen, si contra potestatem velit temporalem, accipimus libenter; sed eam tum ad fidem Catholicam haud vnquam, ne tortam quidem pertraxerit: sin spiritualem, (ad quam pòst trahit) reiicimus. Spiritualis ibi nulla, vel Regi ascribitur, vel Pontifici tollitur; Etiam nec temporalis tollitur, quam scilicet nunquam habuit, vt tolli posset, non magis quàm cornua. Neque verò quoad spiritualia, alium nos Regi Primatum tribuimus; neque quoad temporalia, alium Pontifici detrahimus, quàm debemus. Prior illi Regibus omni iure; posterior hic Pontifici, nullo iure debetur.
units.tr: [?] Christian, which indeed is not there at all. You who at the outset understood the oath in such a way that no one but you did, behold how little you now understand: your translation has deceived you. There is nothing there about the power of the Pope over Christian princes. Near the end, you say it is; near, certainly, for perhaps it is a little after the end. Having found here what is nowhere, he then gives us a choice between two things, whether we would rather be called the oath about the King's primacy in spiritual matters or the oath against the power of the Pope over Christian princes. The foolish man trifles; we reject both. The first: an oath about primacy in spiritual matters cannot be called such, unless we want to speak, I will not say falsely, but absurdly. For there is not a syllable there, of primacy or of spiritual matters, none at all. The second: because it is invented by him, and nothing of the kind is in the Edict. Yet if he means against the temporal power, we gladly accept it; but he never dragged such a thing, not even twisted, to the Catholic faith; but if spiritual (to which he afterwards drags it), we reject it. Nothing spiritual is there, either ascribed to the King or taken away from the Pope; nor is even the temporal taken away, which he of course never had, so that it could be taken away, no more than horns. Nor indeed, as regards spiritual things, do we grant the King any other primacy than we owe; nor, as regards temporal things, do we take from the Pope any other than we ought. The former is owed to kings by every right; the latter is owed to the Pope by no right at all.

units.la: Quod enim parùm interesse putas, iuramentum de primatu Regum in spiritualibus, an iuramentum de potestate Pontificis in Principes habeatur, vtrumque enim fidei Christianæ repugnare: parùm & ego interesse puto, sed eius hominis, cuius quid dicat parùm interest; alioqui interest non parum. Nam inter spiritualem Primatum, & temporalem potestatem, non parùm interest: & vt priori illi fides vestra parùm faueat; tamen posterior hæc nihil ad fidem. Proin illa quæ sequuntur: Prius illud Henrici octaui iuramentum, negare Primatum Pontificis spiritualem: Verè id quidem: Posterius hoc, tribuere eundem Regi primatum, temerè à te dictum. Nec enim verum est, nec veri vel vmbram habet. Nihil in eo tribuitur Regi præter Dominium suum, articulo primo: reliqui omnes articuli negatiui sunt; nec tribunt quicquam Regi, imò nec Regis sunt, sed subditorum. Non est autem de Papæ spirituali potestate, vlla nobis hic quæstio, ne mentio quidem: Ponimus eam, non concedimus: Ideo autem ponimus, quia non negatur in Iuramento: Ideo autem non negatur in Iuramento; quia sit, ne sit in Pontifice potestas illa, nihil ad rem nostram, nihil ad fi-delitatem subditorum.
units.tr: For you think it matters little whether the oath concerns the primacy of kings in spiritual matters or the oath concerns the power of the Pontiff over princes, since both are repugnant to the Christian faith. I too think it matters little, but to a man of whom you say something matters little; otherwise it matters not a little. For between the spiritual primacy and the temporal power there is not a little difference. And although your faith favours the former less, the latter has nothing to do with faith. Therefore what follows: "That first oath of Henry VIII, denying the spiritual primacy of the Pope": "Truly so." "The second, attributing the same primacy to the king," you say rashly. For it is neither true nor has even a shadow of truth. In it nothing is attributed to the king except his own dominion, in the first article; all the remaining articles are negative, and they attribute nothing to the king; indeed they are not the king's, but the subjects'. But there is no question here at all, not even a mention, of the Pope's spiritual power: "We posit it, we do not concede it." And we posit it because it is not denied in the oath; and it is not denied in the oath because whether that power exists in the Pope is nothing to our business, nothing to the allegiance of the subjects.

units.la: Neque quicquam ad rem, quod de Christo addis, non Regem aliquem, sed Apostolum Gregis sui Pastorem designante. Certè, vt nec Regem sub Lege, quia nondum ibi Rex vllus; at vbi iam Rex, tum nec ei Pastoris nomen negatum: ita sub Euangelio, cùm non essent Reges adhuc, qui tum nulli erant, Pastores esse non poterant. At vbi Reges Christo nomen dederant, tum demum, non minùs Pastores hij, quàm olim Reges Israelis. Quodsi autem ab initio statim nomen Christo dedissent, nulla ratio, quo minùs vt olim {a}Iosua Gregis Israelitici designatus est Pastor; itidem & hij Gregis Christiani Pastores, qualis Iosua, qualis {b}David designari potuissent. Sed & antè iam huic responsum est. Nec enim succedere Petro Pontificem, Scriptura vlla consignatum est: sed neque Petro vni (quantum vos vultis) authoritas à Christo delegata est. Et vtcunque Pastoralis delegata est quàm amplissima: tamen potestas, quà Reges simul de solio, simul de vitâ deiicitis, nihil ad Pastoralem. Lanionum illa potestas, non Pastorum est. Bonus senex Baronius hoc vidit: surgere iubet in causâ Venetâ Petrum, & non pascere quin occidere tum, gladio scilicet, non pedo rem getere.
units.tr: Nor is anything to the point in what you add about Christ, that he designated not some king but the Apostle as shepherd of his flock. Certainly, just as there was no king under the Law, because there was no king yet, but where there already was a king, the name of shepherd was not denied him either; so under the Gospel, when there were not yet kings, who then did not exist, there could not be shepherds. But when kings had given themselves the name of Christ, then at last these men were shepherds no less than the kings of Israel once were. But if they had given the name to Christ from the beginning, there would be no reason why, as Joshua was once designated shepherd of the Israelite flock, these men too could not have been designated shepherds of the Christian flock, like Joshua, like David. But this has already been answered before. For no Scripture records that the Pontiff succeeds Peter; nor was authority delegated by Christ to Peter alone (as far as you wish). And however ample the pastoral authority delegated was, that power by which you cast kings both from the throne and from life belongs nothing to the pastoral. That power belongs to butchers, not to shepherds. The good old man Baronius saw this: he bids Peter rise in the Venetian cause, and not feed but, of course, kill, with the sword, not with the staff.

units.la: Tu verò qui semel antè falsus, cùm Iuramenti nomen inesse Edicto diceres, quod ibi nullum; bis iam falleris, quòd Iuramentum idem detrectari hic dicis; cum vitæ discrimine. Ibi te translatio fefellit, hic relatio. Fortunatum quidem iactura est, vitæ discrimen haud vllum, neque causa mortis temporalis. De sempiternâ morte pacisceantur vt possunt cum Pontifice: de temporali nullum à lege periculum. Nec quod de Iuramento dicis, ad decipiendum compositió, verum est. Qui potest? Ad decipiendum non potuit; quòd contra fraudes vestras compositum est, vt ne eis deciperemur. Nisi in eo forte vos decipit, quòd deceptioni vestræ locum non relinquit; & tu ideo fraudem vobis factam dicis, quòd per illud, vestra fraus omnis exclusa sit.
units.tr: You, who before were mistaken once, when you said that the name of oath was in the Edict, though there was none, are now mistaken a second time, because you say the same oath is refused here "at risk of life." There the translation misled you, here the report. Fortunately there is no risk of life, nor is it a cause of temporal death. Let them bargain over eternal death with the Pontiff as they can: there is no danger from the law regarding temporal death. Nor is what you say about the oath, that it was composed "to deceive," true. How could it be? It could not be composed to deceive, since it was composed against your frauds, so that we should not be deceived by them. Unless perhaps it deceives you in this, that it leaves no room for your deception; and you therefore say that a fraud has been practised upon you, because by it all your fraud is shut out.

units.la: Neque dexter, sed sinister interpres Pontifex, qui quod pro salute Regiâ tactum est, & regni: id contra titulos suos fieri interpretatus est: potiùs autem quàm de titulo suis, titulus vllus deperiret, nihil pensi habuit, Catholicos suos coijcere in difficultates non necessarias. Certè enim, si Breuia illa illius breuiora, si breuissima, imò si nulla penitus fuissent, vestri hic (quorum sic vicem dolet) omnino non laborarent. Sed interea tamen dextrà datum, dextrà positum, quicquid in iuramento positum: Quod dextrà datum est, vos sinistrà accepistis, & de Malchi prosapiâ estis, cui præcisa auris dextra, nec vlla vobis auris reliqua nisi sinistra, quâ audi tis omnia, omnium quæ à nobis dicuntur sinistri auditores, & interpretes.
units.tr: Nor is the Pontiff a right but a left interpreter, who has construed what was done for the safety of the king and the kingdom as done against his own titles; and rather than any title of his should perish, he took no account of throwing his Catholics into unnecessary difficulties. For certainly, if those briefs of his were shorter, or very shortest, or indeed not at all, your men here (whose plight he so laments) would not be labouring at all. But in the meantime, whatever is contained in the oath was given with the right hand and placed with the right hand: what was given with the right hand you have received with the left, and you are of the stock of Malchus, whose right ear was cut off, so that you have no ear left but the left, with which you hear all things, being left-handed hearers and interpreters of everything that is said by us.

units.la: Dixit Apologia; Peccâsse Pontificem, in bonos mores peccâsse. Quid ni diceret? Peccare posse Pontificem etiam vos dicitis, (etsi errare non posse) & quidni in mores? Pontifex enim, etsi apud vos legum Dominus, morum tamen Dominus non est. Quod dixit, id ita conclusit, dilemmate. [Factum Regis; vel aliquod erat ab illius facto [?], & cur falcem immisit; vel non aliquod, & cur Regem non monuit, sed citra monitionem damnauit?] Damnásse negas, vel iudicásse Pontificem de Regis ne quid tamen illi de potestate pereat, ais potuisse. Atque hic primò aperis nobis forum, & tribunal ponis Pontifici, ac prætoris de iudice competenti; Esse Pontificem omnium Christianorum iudicem, ac per hoc etiam Regum, vt Christiani sunt. Bene habet, quòd tantùm vt Christiani, non etiam vt Reges sunt. Illi verò, non vt Christiani, fidelitatem exigunt à suis, aut iuramentum postulant, sed vt Reges; possent hoc etiam non Christiani, quà Reges tantùm. Vt Reges ergo, nihil ad forum eius pertinent. Quare claudenda tibi iam denuò Curia, & tollendum tribunal est: exceptionem enim habent, vt vides, de foro incompetenti.
units.tr: The Apology said: the Pontiff has sinned, has sinned against good morals. Why should it not say so? You too say that the Pontiff can sin (though you say he cannot err), and why not against morals? For the Pontiff, though among you the Lord of laws, is not the Lord of morals. What he said, he concluded by a dilemma: [Either the king's deed was something, or it was of something from his deed [?], and why did he put in the sickle; or it was not something, and why did he not warn the king but condemned him without warning?] You deny that he condemned, or that the Pontiff judged of the king; yet you say he could judge, lest anything of power perish for him. And here first you open a court for us, and set up a tribunal for the Pontiff, and a competent judge: that the Pontiff is judge of all Christians, and therefore also of kings, insofar as they are Christians. Well and good, that only insofar as they are Christians, not also insofar as they are kings. But these men, not as Christians, exact fidelity from their subjects, or demand an oath, but as kings; and even non-Christians could do this, insofar as they are merely kings. Therefore, insofar as they are kings, these things do not pertain to his court. Wherefore the court must again be closed for you, and the tribunal removed: for you have, as you see, an objection of an incompetent forum.

units.la: De persona non successit; melius forè succedet de re. Saltem in quæstione de iuramento index est, atque ita, vt nec fingi possit iudex magis competens. Quippe res sacra iuramentum, res spiritualis, res quæ ad salutem animæ pertinet. Itane? Quæ modò dicebas soluit iuramenta, nec secus quàm peccata, ne tenerent quenquam: ea iam, res sacras, spirituales, ad salutem pertinentes agnoscis? Prorsus res ita sacra, Pontifici tuo plus magis alligande, nodum tam leuiter soluende? nec si res soluat ita sacras, ita ad salutem animae pertinentes, causa sit ijs ipse, quos ita soluit, mortis sempiternae. Fuerit tamen Iudex (vt tu vis) de persona; de re etiam; An hae Iudicis partes, nec vocato in ius reo, nec dictâ causâ, nec defensione audita eius quod fecit, prosilire statim ad damnandum? Perperam id omnino à te dictum, non opus vt causam diceret, qui in ius vocatus non fuerat. Opus enim fuit, in ius illum vocari, vt causam diceret; nec sic, causa non dicta, personam damnari contra ius; in eoque Pontifex, si Iudex, Iudex sanè iniquissimus. Non potuit ipse sibi Tortus solutione hac suâ satisfacere; vidit mirum rem esse penitus. Aliud ergo effugium quærit, & negat iudicâsse Pontificem, &, quod planè ridiculum, non de persona faciente, sed de facto iudicâsse. Et quidem, si ignota prorsus persona facientis, aliquid diceret: ibi enim de facto solo ferri posset sententia, cùm de faciente non posset. At hîc qui poterat, vbi notus satis author Iuramenti? vbi autem de persona constat, quis vnquam audiuit, in iudicio abstrahi personam à causâ, in factum ferri sententiam, persona dimissa? Præterea, in ipso quidem Breui, priùs de Rege mentio fit Authore Iuramenti, quàm de Iuramento ipso: Præfatur enim de atrocissimis eius persecutionibus, priusquam ad Iuramenti mentionem descendat. Quorsum autem ei de persona mentio prima, si personam eius attingere noluit? Perinde verò illud erat, quasi si dixisset, Regem habetis Persecutorem atrocissimum (coniugata enim, persecutio & persecutor) ille iam vobis, contra ius omne atque fas, edixit Iuramentum omni modo illicitum: potiùs autem quàm hoc Iuramentum, tam iniustum, ab eo Persecutore tanto, suscipiatis, atrociora vobis tormenta adhuc subeunda, etiam mors ipsa oppetenda est.
units.tr: You have not succeeded regarding the person; you will perhaps succeed better regarding the matter. At least in the question about the oath, he is the judge, and so that no more competent judge could be imagined. For an oath is a sacred thing, a spiritual thing, a thing that pertains to the salvation of the soul. Really? You who just now said he dissolves oaths, and no differently than sins, so that they bind no one: do you now acknowledge these as sacred things, spiritual, pertaining to the salvation of the soul? Surely a thing so sacred should bind your Pontiff more and not be dissolved so lightly; and if he dissolves things so sacred, so pertaining to the salvation of the soul, the cause of eternal death is for those very persons whom he so dissolves. Yet let him be judge (as you wish) of the person; of the matter too? Are these the functions of a judge: to leap at once to condemnation, without the accused being summoned to court, without the case being stated, without a hearing of the defence of what he did? That is entirely wrongly said by you: that there was no need for him to plead the case who had not been summoned to court. For there was need for him to be summoned to court so that he might plead the case; nor is it so, that the person is condemned against law when the case has not been pleaded; and in that case the Pontiff, if he is judge, is certainly a most unjust judge. Tortus himself could not satisfy himself by this solution of his; he saw that the matter was altogether strange. So he seeks another escape, and denies that the Pontiff judged of the person, and (what is plainly ridiculous) says he judged "not of the person doing, but of the deed." And indeed, if he said something when the person doing it was wholly unknown: then sentence could be passed on the deed alone, since it could not be passed on the doer. But here, where could that be, when the author of the oath is well known enough? And where it is established about the person, who has ever heard that in judgement the person is separated from the cause, and sentence is passed on the deed, the person being dismissed? Moreover, in the Brief itself, mention is made of the king as author of the oath before mention of the oath itself: for he speaks first of his most atrocious persecutions, before he descends to mention of the oath. But why should he have first mentioned the person, if he did not wish to touch his person? It would be just as if he had said: "You have a most atrocious persecutor as king" (for persecution and persecutor are cognates); he has now, against all law and right, decreed an oath altogether unlawful: rather than that you should take up this oath, so unjust, from so great a persecutor, you must undergo still more atrocious torments, and even death itself must be faced.

units.la: Aptum ergo dilemma illud, sed inepta tua responsio: nec enim damnari potuit Iuramentum, Authore Iuramenti cognito, & non damnato. Vidit ipse incommodè dictum hoc à se, & pœnituit. Quare non proprie dicit damnâsse Regem. Non proprie damnâsse? Damnâsse igitur. Vera ergo accusatio, & peccasse Pontificem fatetur. Et eo ipso loco tamen, quo fatetur, quasi correptus vertigine, [?]solo dicit Apologiam clamare, Regem indictâ causâ condemnatum, quo Regem, etsi non proprie, at condemnatum tamen dixerat.
units.tr: Apt, then, is that dilemma of yours, but your reply is inept: for the Covenant could not be condemned while its Author was known and not condemned. He himself saw that he had said this awkwardly, and regretted it. Therefore he does not say that the King was condemned "strictly speaking." Not condemned strictly speaking? So condemned, then. He therefore confesses the accusation is true, and that the Pontiff has sinned. And yet in the very place where he confesses it, as if seized by dizziness, he says only that the Apology proclaims that the King was condemned without a hearing, although he had said that the King was condemned, even if not strictly speaking.

units.la: Vide autem commentum aliud non illepidum. Cùm hoc, (quod dixi) à Pontifice, tanquam iudice, fieri minùs iustè cerneret, forum relinquit; & rus in agrum se recipit, ac Pontificem subitò, de Iudice transmutat in Pastorem; ut quod facere non potuit ut Iudex, saltè faciat ut Pastor, qui à pabulo quod noxium est abstterret oues, terram tamen, nec vocare in ius, nec iudicare, nec punire solet, pabulum illud proferentem. Quis ferat primò, quoad peccatum & peccati poenam, cum homine reo terram, rem mutam, sine omni vel reatu, vel sensu, conferri? Et quis nescit tamen, quàm saepe terra haec Pontificei poenas dederit; quàm saepe illi male tum dixerit, tum fecerit? Hoc tamen interest: quando hoc facere, quando punire vult Pontisex, homines tum erunt, quos aequum est luere; quando non libet facere, erunt terra tum & agri, quae non est aequum vapulare. Ita & rei, nunc agri sunt, nunc homines: & Pontifex ipse, de Pastore, iudex, de iudice pastor, cùm ei visum fuerit.
units.tr: But look at another not unclever device. Seeing that this (which I mentioned) is done unjustly by the Pontiff as judge, he leaves the court and retires to the country, and suddenly changes the Pontiff from judge into shepherd; so that what he could not do as judge, he may at least do as shepherd, who keeps the sheep away from harmful pasture, yet is accustomed neither to summon to court, nor to judge, nor to punish the one who offers that pasture. First, who could bear that a guilty man should be compared with the earth, a dumb thing, lacking any guilt or sense, as regards sin and the penalty for sin? And yet who does not know how often this earth has paid the Papists' penalties, how often they have cursed it and done it harm? There is this difference, however: when the Pontiff wishes to do this, or to punish, then it will be men who ought rightly to pay; when he does not wish to act, then it will be the land and the fields, which ought not to be beaten. So also the accused are now fields, now men; and the Pontiff himself, from shepherd becomes judge, and from judge shepherd, whenever it pleases him.

units.la: Sed & illud dicendum fuit; Si sic voluit personam Iudicis exuere, cur non induit personam viri boni & benevoli? Cur non, quod boni mores postulabant, & consuetudo Principum, prius ipso cum Rege egit, quàm cum Regis subditis, Regu dico subditis, non suis? Insolens id verbum, ut ullos hic dicat subditos suos. Cur illum non prius monuit, quàm hos abstterruit? Cur [illegible, ~5 letters], pastore populi praeterito, populum primò adijt?
units.tr: But this also needed to be said: if he wished to put off the person of judge in this way, why did he not put on the person of a good and kindly man? Why did he not, as good morals demanded and the custom of princes required, first deal with the King himself before dealing with the King's subjects (I say subjects, not "his own")? That word is unusual, as if he had any subjects of his own here. Why did he not first warn the King before he frightened these people? Why, with the shepherd of the people passed over, did he first approach the people?

units.la: Porrò autem & hîc, mali responsi malè sibi conscius, rem tentat iterum, iterúmque in eodem luto haeret. Sic enim ipse sibi obijcit. Qui iuramentum reprehendit, sanè reprehendit & illum qui illud iubet suscipi. Quid verò respondet? Negari non potest, quin aliquo modo reprehensio ad Regem pertineat; id est nimirum, negari non potest quin reprehendat. Et tamen ecce alterum scotoma; qui hoc fassus verbis hijs, verbis proximis putidam illam suam, & ante damnatam à seipso distinctionem, tanquam non propriam, rei & personae, reponit hic denuo, sub terminis tantùm alijs, operu & hominis; operis, quod reprehenditur: hominis, qui in iudicium non vocatur: operis, quod non placet: hominis, qui iuridicè non damnatur. Ubi si urgeas, Regem aliquo modo reprehensum (ut hîc iam dicit) negare non poterit. Sic igitur, quod negare non potest, fateri non audet, & ubi sit, nescit, quasi non curet, si interim illum Lector sensu carere putet, dum Pontifex modò culpâ carere possit.
units.tr: Furthermore, here too, conscious of his bad answer, he tries the matter again and sticks fast in the same mud. For he objects to himself thus: "He who finds fault with the oath certainly finds fault also with the one who commands it to be taken." And what does he answer? "It cannot be denied that the blame in some way pertains to the King; that is to say, it cannot be denied that he finds fault." And yet look, another stumble: having admitted this in these words, he brings back in the next words that foul distinction of his, already condemned by himself, between the thing and the person, as if it were not a proper one, now under other terms only, "of the work and of the man": of the work, which is found fault with; of the man, who is not summoned to judgment: of the work, which does not please; of the man, who is not condemned by law. Here, if you press him, that the King has in some way been blamed (as he now says), he will not be able to deny it. So he does not dare to admit what he cannot deny, and does not know where it stands, as if he did not care whether the reader meanwhile thinks him devoid of sense, so long as the Pontiff can be free of fault.

units.la: Nec fœlici magis successu, accusationem geminam declinat. Priorem, de Rege inter persecutores numerato ; non (inquit) absolutè hoc fecit Pontifex : fecit ergo. Ita iam, quod tu initio ludens dixisti insolubile ; per te quidem, sic est. Ter enim conatus es soluere : ter in eo lusisti operam. Recognosce enim hic paululùm nugamenta tua. Damnauit, sed non proprie: reprehendit aliquo modo: numerauit, sed non absolutè. Benè sit tribus hijsce particulis; aliquo modo,non proprie, non absolute; absque hijs foret, nullus fuisses. Tria verò haec, si dentur cuiquam anniculo Sophistæ in Papiensi Scholà, non dubium quin contemnet omnia statim argumenta, tutus sub hijs tanquam sub Aiacis clypeo. Nunquam vrgebis, quin statim dicturus sit, Concedo, sed non proprie, sed quodammodo, sed non absolutè. Ita quicquid attuleris, eludet. Macte verò Dialectica (Matthæ) tria hæc in promptu habe; cum tribus hijs, nec te Chryssippus vicerit.
units.tr: Nor does he avoid the twofold accusation with any greater success. He deals with the first, that the King was numbered among the persecutors: "The Pontiff did not say this absolutely," he says; "therefore he did it." So now what you said at the beginning in jest, an insoluble matter, is so, at least by your own account. For you have tried three times to solve it, and three times you have wasted your effort in trifling. Consider here for a little while your trifles: "He condemned, but not strictly; he found fault in some way; he numbered, but not absolutely." Well done with these three particles, "in some way," "not strictly," "not absolutely"; without them you would be nothing. And if these three were given to any first-year sophist in the school of Pavia, there is no doubt he would at once despise all arguments, safe under them as under the shield of Ajax. You will never press him but he will at once say: "I grant it, but not strictly, but in a way, but not absolutely." So whatever you bring, he will evade. Well done, indeed, Dialectic (Matthew): keep these three at hand; with these three, not even Chrysippus would have defeated you.

units.la: Repeto iam responsum tuum; Numerauit (ais) quanquam non absolutè ; Non absolutè verò, quia in Regis arbitrio, vellet necessare à iuramento obtrudendo, & Rex pacificus haberi, an seuire vellet in innocentes, & persecutor sanctorum martyrum nominari. Itáne? reliquit hoc in Regis arbitrio? Scin' quomodo reliquerit? Audi ergo, &c, si vlla tibi frons est, erubesce. Annon disertis verbis dicit in Breui; cùm sustinuissent antea, tribulationes & calamitates (nimirum sub Reginâ Elizabethâ) omnia hoc tempore (sub Rege scilicet) exaterbari magù[?]? Annon grauissimè iam (sub Rege scilicet) pœnis propositis compelli? Annon resplendere hijs temporibus (sub Rege scilicet) egregiam virtutem & fortitudinem in martyribus vestris? Quid verò? Annon apud te relata sunt, Martyr & Persecutor? Sine persecutore non fiunt Martyres, nihilo magis sanè, quàm filij sine patre : túque adeo ipse priùs duo hæc coniunxisti, Persecutor martyrum. Dic nunc igitur, si vestri Martyres sunt, annon Rex persecutor? An hoc in arbitrio iam positum Regis, velit ne sic haberi, annon? Nonnè, habeatur necesse est pro persecutore, si vestri illi pro martyribus habeantur? Numquid non ille est, qui omnia hoc tempore exacerbat? Numquid non ille est, qui gravissimis poenis propositis iam compellit? Quis non miretur iam os illud, à quo, tam sine veritate, fide, fronte, affirmatur, in Regis arbitrio positum, an velit Perfecuter nominari?
