Imò possit rem totam Pontifex arbiter tuus, extra Regis arbitrium, Breui suo; túque infelix, Breue illud praefigi hic curasti, ut tanquam sorex tuo iudicio petires. Nihil ibi in dubio: asseruntur, asfertiuè ponuntur omnia, nec magis, in Regis arbitrio reliquit, velitne persecuter, quàm tu iam in lectoris arbitrio reliquisti, debeasne Calumniator appellari.
units.tr: I now repeat your answer: "He numbered (you say), though not absolutely; but not absolutely, because it lay in the King's will whether he wished to force the oath, and to be held a peaceful king, or to wish to rage against the innocent, and be named a persecutor of the holy martyrs. Really? He left this to the King's will? Do you know how he left it?" Listen, then, and if you have any face left, blush. Does he not say in plain words in the Brief that, whereas before (under Queen Elizabeth, no doubt) they had endured troubles and calamities, now at this time (under the King, that is) all things have been made worse? Has he not now, most gravely (under the King, that is), compelled men by penalties set before them? Does not an outstanding virtue and fortitude shine forth in your martyrs in these times (under the King, that is)? Well? Are not "Martyr" and "Persecutor" set down together in your writings? Without a persecutor there are no martyrs, no more than there are sons without a father; and you yourself earlier joined these two together: "the persecutor of the martyrs." Tell me now, then: if your men are martyrs, is not the King a persecutor? Or is it now left to the King's will whether he wishes to be so regarded or not? Must he not be regarded as a persecutor, if your men are regarded as martyrs? Is he not the one who now makes everything worse at this time? Is he not the one who now compels with the most severe penalties set before him? Who would not marvel at that mouth, by which it is asserted, with such lack of truth, faith and face, that it lies in the King's will whether he wishes to be named a persecutor? Indeed, the Pontiff may be your arbiter of the whole matter, apart from the King's will, by his Brief; and you, unhappy man, took care to have that Brief prefixed here, so that you might seek your judgment like a mole. Nothing is in doubt there: everything is asserted, and stated positively; and he did not leave it more to the King's will whether he wishes to be a persecutor, than you have now left it to the reader's will whether you ought to be called a slanderer.

units.la: De accusatione vero posteriore, quod prohibuit Iuramentum Pontifex, & prohibendo fecit ut subditi obedientiam Regi debitam non haberent; cùm nimis in aperto res esset, fatetur prohibuisse, sed protestando tamen; non id facturum fuisse, neque Breuibus Apostolicis opus futurum, si solus fidelitatis esset, si nihil requireret aliud, nisi ut subiecti essent in iis omnibus, quae contra fidem Catholicam non essent, aut obedientiam Deo & Pontifici debitam. Fides enim Catholica non sufficit iam, & obedientia Deo debita; nisi Deo Pontifex accedat: nam sine Pontifice, non satis si Deo. Incurreret certè in reprehensionem Pontificis, soli Deo obedientia, & opus erit Breuibus, ut populus de eâ (ne praestet) admoneatur, si Deo tantùm, & non Pontifici. *Quodsi autem Deo & Pontifici, tum demum plena est; alioqui, inventa est minus habens.
units.tr: As to the later accusation, that the Pontiff forbade the oath, and by forbidding caused the subjects not to have the obedience due to the King: since the matter was too plainly open, he confesses that he forbade it, but by protesting; that he would not have done it otherwise, nor would apostolic Briefs have been needed if fidelity alone were required, if it asked nothing more than that the subjects should be obedient in all those things which were not against the Catholic faith or the obedience due to God and the Pontiff. For the Catholic faith is no longer sufficient, nor obedience due to God; unless the Pontiff be added to God: for without the Pontiff, God alone is not enough. Certainly he would fall under reproach from the Pontiff if obedience were given to God alone; and there will be need of Briefs, so that the people may be warned about it (lest they render it), if it is rendered to God only and not to the Pontiff. But if it is rendered to God and to the Pontiff, then at last it is complete; otherwise it is found wanting.

units.la: Breuibus autem Apostolicus? Quid hoc verbi est? Nam de sede Apostolica, quia forte in eâ aliquando sedit qui Apostolus fuit, etsi eadem iam non sit, (ut de Thesis naue) ferre possumus. At Breuia Apostolica quis ferat, quae nullo sensu sano quidem Apostolica dici possunt? Non enim, ut sedes olim illi fuit dum viveret: ita haec olim illi dictata, dum in terris esset, & in scrinio aliquo asseruata, eximenda cum opus esset, & (quasi Canonicae Epistolae) per orbem transmittenda. Breuibus dic Papalibus, dic Pontificijs, si voles; Apostolicis non damus, nisi Apostolus sit vnus aliquis de duodecim qui scripsit, nisi Paulus 5. Apostolus iam sit supernumerarius. Quodsi Paulus 5. quid ni & Paulus secundus, qui fuit tamen si Genebrardo vestro credimus) efor virtutis & Literarum? Nos Paulum vnum agnoscimus, sed sine numero ordinali, qui secundum non habuit, & de Saulo Paulus fuit,non deCamillo ; cui Tertius amanuensis, non Petrus Strozza ; quisè[?], Paulum Apostolum nominare ausus, vt Epistolæ eius merito Apostolicæ dicantur, non (quod facit vester) qui se Paulum Episcopum scribit, vt illius Breuia Episcopalia dici debeant, non Apostolica. Paulum nouimus : ab illo si Breue habetis vllum, erit sanè Apostolicum. Paulos vero secundos & quintos nescimus, nec Breuia illorum, nec Bullas magis Apostolicas censemus, quàm atramentum Apostolicum, quo scribuntur, vel plumbum Apostolicum, quo obsignantur.
units.tr: "Apostolic Briefs?" What sort of word is this? For as to the Apostolic See, since perhaps at some time one who was an Apostle sat in it, even though it is no longer the same (as in the case of Thessalonica), we may endure it. But who could endure "Apostolic Briefs," which in no sound sense can be called apostolic? For it is not as the See once was to him while he lived: so these, once dictated by him while he was on earth and kept in some chest, were to be taken out when needed and sent throughout the world like the canonical Epistles. Call them papal Briefs, call them Pontifical, if you will; we do not grant them the name Apostolic, unless the Apostle is one of the twelve who wrote them, unless Paul the Fifth is now a supernumerary Apostle. And if Paul the Fifth, why not Paul the Second, who was nevertheless (if we believe your Genebrardus) a man of virtue and letters? We acknowledge one Paul, but without an ordinal number, who had no second, and who was Paul from Saul, not from Camillus; whose amanuensis was Tertius, not Pietro Strozzi; who dared to call himself Paul the Apostle, so that his Epistles may rightly be called apostolic; not (as yours does) one who writes himself Paul the Bishop, so that his Briefs ought to be called episcopal, not apostolic. We know Paul: if you have any Brief from him, it will certainly be apostolic. But Pauls the second and the fifth we do not know, nor do we judge their Briefs or Bulls more apostolic than the apostolic ink with which they are written, or the apostolic lead with which they are sealed.

units.la: Redeo vnde digressus sum. Nisi aliud quid, quàm fides & obedientia requisitum esset iuramento, Pontifex haud vnquam reprehendisset. Fauere enim Pontifices certum est ijs omnibus, quæ contra fidem Catholicam, & obedientiam Deo & Pontifici debitam non sunt. Fauisse[?] Clementem 8. & de obedientiâ Regi diligentissimè exhibendâ, non semel monuisse. Quàm fauerit Clemens Regi nostro, quàm clementer cauerit de præstandâ illi obedientiâ, qui cum Catholicis egit, ne eo loco esset, quo obedientia illi præstari posset; appello Breuia illa in cineres versa, sed quæ tamen adhuc in exemplis suis supersunt. Vidit inuitus Clemens, quod noluit videre, Breuia illa sua non successere: Aliâ rem aggressus est viâ; Ad faciendum populo fucum, quem Regem esse noluit, Regi iam (vellet nollet) facto, obsequi omnes voluit, & huic rei Breuia alia transmisisset. O bona fidei Pontificem! Breuia ad excludendum habet, Breuia habet ad obsequendum, & Apostolica vtrâque. Sed monuit Clemens de obedientiâ exhibendâ. Quali autem obedientiâ. Nemo hoc melius nobis dixerit {a}Domino tuo, qui alicubi sic interpretatus est obedientiam, quam Gregorius Asauritio exhibuit, nempe ex necessitate, ferreâ illâ necessitate, & non debitâ, sed coactâ. Proin; coactam, & non aliam fuisse obedientiam, quàm Tyrannis præstitit Ecclesia tota Primitiua. Ita scilicet Clemens vestros homines obsequi voluit. Quoúsque vero hoc? Quoúsque nimirum adesseni vires, Illius eiiciendi, cuius admittendi, aditum omnem interclusum voluit. Nec enim tam stolidi Pontifices sunt, vt consultum putent, nouo tumultu quotidie permiscere omnia, vnde ad Authores cœrta crux, vnde ad sectam totam perennis infamia redundare possit. Nolunt etiam Reges ipsos, ita ut se suspicio[?] sos reddere & vigiles. Aliquando Brevibus obsequio placus[?] demulcendi sunt, ut remittant de diligentia, atque eo facilius opprimantur. Interim Pontificis mentem, veltri[?] tenent, & voluntatem (ut loquuntur) interpretatium. Sic enim, cum de toto consilio suo, tollendi de medio Regis, referri vellent ad Clementem & alij quidam de Coniuratis, in novissimâ hac pessimâque prodicione, Caput Coniuratorum Catisbeius respondisse fertur, Quorsum hoc? nihil opus certè: Ego verò (inquit) de Pontificis mente nullum dubito; quin, qui admissum noluit, ejectum velit; nec sublatum è medio ægrè ferret, quem exclusum invito cupiebat. Et obtinuit, nec tum referrent; usque adeo conscii hujus hominis, quid Pontifici in votis. Atque hæc fuit Clementis in Regem clementia.
units.tr: I return to where I left off. Unless something other than faith and obedience were required by the oath, the Pope would never have censured it. For it is certain that the Popes favour all those things which are not contrary to the Catholic faith and the obedience owed to God and the Pope. Clement the Eighth favoured it, and more than once admonished that obedience to the King be most diligently rendered. How much Clement favoured our King, and how kindly he provided for the obedience owed to him, is shown by the fact that he dealt with the Catholics so that they would not be in a place where obedience could be rendered to him; I appeal to those briefs, reduced to ashes, yet which nonetheless survive in their copies. Clement saw, against his will, what he did not wish to see: those briefs of his did not succeed. He undertook the matter by another way. To deceive the people, he wished all to obey the King, whom (willy-nilly) he had already made a King, and he would have sent other briefs for this purpose. O Pope of good faith! He has briefs for excluding, and briefs for obeying, and both are apostolic. "But Clement admonished that obedience be rendered." Yet what kind of obedience? No one could have told us this better than your Lord, who somewhere interpreted obedience in the manner that Gregory of Asaurita displayed it, namely from necessity, that iron necessity, and not owed but coerced. Therefore the obedience of the whole primitive Church, which it rendered to tyrants, was coerced and was no other. So, clearly, Clement wished your people to obey in this way. But how far did he wish this to go? Clearly as far as his strength allowed, for he wished every access to be closed off, to eject the one whom he did not want admitted. For the Popes are not so foolish as to think it expedient to throw everything into confusion daily with fresh tumult, from which a certain cross might come back upon the authors and a perpetual infamy upon the whole sect. Nor do they wish kings themselves to be suspicious and watchful. At times they must be soothed and placated by briefs of obedience, so that they relax their diligence, and are the more easily overpowered. Meanwhile they hold the mind of the Pope, as they say, and interpret his will. For when the conspirators, in this last and most wicked treachery, wished to refer their whole plan of removing the King to Clement, and certain others of the conspirators, the head of the conspirators, Catesby, is said to have replied: "What is the point of this? There is certainly no need. But I (he said) have no doubt about the Pope's mind: he who did not want him admitted wants him ejected; nor would he bear it with difficulty if he were removed from the midst, whom he desired to be shut out against his will." And he prevailed, nor did they then refer it; so thoroughly were they aware of what the Pope wished. And this was Clement's clemency towards the King.

units.la: Ut verò fuisse Clementem ante, ita non minùs nunc fuisse hunc ipsum Paulum quintum, virtutum reliquarum in Clemente, atque inter reliquas favoris huius successorem. De quo mirum inprimis, quòd qui obedientiam Regi diligenter exhiberi non semel monuit, is obedientiam Regi diligenter exhiberi non semel vetuit. De priore illo, tibi credimus: De posteriore hoc, duo ipsa Brevia loquuntur. Idemne, obsecro, Paulus quintus? Idemne, qui à seditionibus omnino cavere monuit; Et qui omnino cavere monet ne iurent, tamen se cauturos? Aut numquid divisus est Paulus quintus? Non: sed eodem spiritu aguntur utrique, Clemens & ille. Clementina fuerunt litera binæ: Binæ unæ, ut Regem non agnoscerent; binæ alteræ, ut Regi obsequerentur. Pauliana iam Brevia nihilo meliora. Duo Brevia, ut velint præstare: Duo alia, ne velint iurare obedientiam. Annon hij Satyri Satiram merentur?
units.tr: But just as Clement was before, so no less now is this very Paul the Fifth, the successor in the favour of the rest of the virtues in Clement, and among the rest of his favour. Concerning him this is especially remarkable: that he who more than once admonished that obedience be diligently rendered to the King, has more than once forbidden that obedience be diligently rendered to the King. We believe you concerning the former; the two briefs themselves speak concerning the latter. Is it the same Paul the Fifth, I beg you? Is it the same who admonished to beware altogether of seditions; and who altogether admonishes not to swear, yet that they will be on their guard? Or is Paul the Fifth divided? No: both Clement and he are driven by the same spirit. The Clementine letters were of two kinds: two to not acknowledge the King, two others that they should obey the King. The Pauline briefs are now no better. Two briefs, so that they may be willing to render; two others, so that they may not be willing to swear obedience. Do not these satyrs deserve a satire?

units.la: De Paulo verò quinto, operæ pretium puto advertere, quòd Regi exhiberi monet obedientiam quæ Regibus, secundum scrip-turas Sanctas debetur. Ubi, si vera narrat Matthæus, bona spes est. Novum enim hoc in Pontifice, ut Scripturas Sanctas, regulam figat obedientiæ. Nos verò regulam hanc agnoscimus, atque ad eandem, eam quoque non minùs quàm sibi Pontisex quæri, obedientiam expendi volumus. Denique omnia, quæ inter nos [?]litò, sitíque controversa sunt, ad hoc examen reuocari, secundùm Scripturas Sanctas: secundùm eas quæ de-bentur, dentur; quæ non debentur, ne nominentur quidem. Sed ô illas Scripturas Sanctas: ut semel eas videre contingat, secundùm quas hæ Regum depositiones, regnorum dispositiones, in-uasiones, machinationes sint licitæ: Valde vereor, ut contingat. Interim dabit mihi veniam Matthæus, si reuocem illi subinde in memoriam, Pontificium hoc de exhibendâ obedientiâ, non alia, quàm quæ secundùm Scripturas Sanctas debetur. Iam verò cùm secundùm Scripturas Sanctas certè Regi debeatur, illum non deponere, non consentire deponenti, non de regno disponenti[?], non inuadenti, non tumultus seminanti[?]: Cur non sint sic prositeri? Quia Catholicæ fidei abnegatio petitur, id est, quia principium petitur; vides enim quò reuoluimur. Nos verò contrà, non abnegari. Potestatem enim illam priuatiuam in Principes, quæ negatur sola, non esse de fide Catholicâ: Potestatem ligandi, vel soluendi, quod B. Petrus, vel ligaret vel solueret, esse de fide, sed non negari.
units.tr: Concerning Paul the Fifth, I think it worth noting that he admonishes that obedience be rendered to the King which is owed to kings according to the Holy Scriptures. Here, if Matthew tells the truth, there is good hope. For it is new in a Pope to fix the Holy Scriptures as the rule of obedience. We, indeed, acknowledge this rule, and we wish that obedience be weighed by it no less than the Pope himself seeks it. Finally, let all those things which are disputed between us, both in our public discussion and in writing, be referred to this test, namely according to the Holy Scriptures: according to them, what is owed should be given, and what is not owed should not even be named. But, O those Holy Scriptures: may it once happen that we see them, according to which these depositions of kings, dispositions of kingdoms, invasions and machinations are lawful. I greatly fear that this will happen. Meanwhile Matthew will pardon me if I now and then recall to him this Papal statement, "obedience to be rendered, and no other than what is owed according to the Holy Scriptures." Now, since according to the Holy Scriptures the King is certainly owed that he not depose, not consent to one deposing him, not dispose of the kingdom, not invade, not sow tumult: why not profess this? Because a denial of the Catholic faith is demanded, that is, because the principle is begged; for you see where we are carried back. We, on the contrary, do not deny. For that negative power over princes, which alone is denied, is not "of the Catholic faith": the power of binding or loosing, which blessed Peter either bound or loosed, is "of the faith," but it is not denied.

units.la: Hic Tortus de suo addit, monuisse Pontificem ut caverent insidias Catholici sui, & Apostolici dicti memores essent, Obedire oportet Deo, magis quàm hominibus: & hoc tamen in Breui non legitur. Credo ut aliquid diceret, secundùm Scripturas Sanctas. Quorsum enim hæc; nisi Torto detur, fidiculas suas hic adhibere, magis Deo, id est, Pontifici, quàm hominibus, id est, Regibus.
units.tr: Here Torto adds of his own that the Pope admonished that they beware the snares of his Catholic one, and that they remember the apostolic saying, "We ought to obey God rather than men"; yet this is not read in the brief. I believe he said it so that he might say something "according to the Holy Scriptures." For why these things, unless it is granted to Torto to apply here his little strings: "rather to God, that is, to the Pope, than to men, that is, to Kings."

units.la: Accidit tamen hic sanè incommodè. Nos enim verba hæc, ex Apostoli ipsius, tum vsu, tum sensu, contra vos atque Pon-tificem ipsum militare dicimus. Nam verba hæc Pontificibus ipsis in os dicta sunt ab Apostolo, non Regibus. Hij homines, de quibus sic Apostolus, magis quàm hominibus, Pontifices erant ipsi: ut Apostolicus sensus sit genuinus & natiuus, Oportet Deo magis obedire quàm Pontificibus: ut non fuerit in sacris literis sententia vlla, quæ proposito hic tuo, minùs quadrare, quæ in te, tuíque similes Pontificios, fortius retorqueri posset, quàm eadem hæc quam attulisti. Petri est, & contra vos est.
units.tr: Yet this turns out very inconveniently for him. For we say that these words, taken from the Apostle himself both in use and in sense, fight against you and against the Pope himself. For these words were spoken by the Apostle to the Popes themselves, not to Kings. Those men of whom the Apostle thus speaks, "rather than men," were themselves the Popes; so that the apostolic sense is genuine and native: "We ought to obey God rather than the Popes." Therefore there is no sentence in the sacred letters which fits less with your purpose here, and which could be retorted more strongly against you and your like, the Papists, than this very one you have brought forward. It is Peter's, and it is against you.

units.la: Nec enim vllum est sub coelo genus hominum, qui hominibus plus tribuant, prius auscultent, magis obediant, quàm Ponti-ficij & Papistæ: Pontificij ideò dicti, quia Pontificij, Papistæ, ideò, quia Papæ tantùm tribuunt, ut toti ab eo pendeant; illius Breuia, pro oraculis, sanctiones quasi Scripturas Sanctas, imò illius dispensationes, contra Dei leges, contra Scripturas Sanctas sufcipiant. Noli vero dehinc loco huic manum admoliri, vita quantum potes, quem nescio quis hic tibi malus Genius fuggesit. Qui homines quos Papas dicitis (homines enim sunt) ad Dei locum usque, si non supra Deum, extulistis, vobis nihil posthac si sapitis, cum hac sententia, Obedire oportet Deo magis quam hominibus.
units.tr: For there is no race of men under the sky who attribute more to men, listen more readily, and obey more, than the Pontifics and Papists: they are called Pontifics because they attribute so much to the Pope that they wholly depend on him; they receive his briefs as oracles, his decrees as if they were the Holy Scriptures, and indeed his dispensations even against the laws of God and against the Holy Scriptures. Do not, then, henceforth undertake to handle this passage, which some evil genius, I know not who, has suggested to you. You who call men "Popes" (for they are men) have raised them up to the place of God, if not above God; if you have any wisdom, henceforth take to yourselves this saying, "We ought to obey God rather than men."

units.la: Agedum iam de Bulla Pij quinti, & Breuibus Pauli quinti videamus, quam conueniant inter se [?] Vel quantum etiam interfit, Pij quinti, ab obedientia Reginæ, absoluentis; Pauli quinti, ne obedientiam Regi præstent, prohibentis. Rhetorem hic agit Matthaeus (est enim Rhetor non malus.) Cum enim in more positum sit, instituto{que} Rhetorum, vt reticere se multa dicant, quæ tamen si subeas dicere, dicenda non habent: hoc te Rhetoricæ suæ flosculo (Lector) hic beare vult Matthaeus. Omittere enim se dicit, quod si permittas eloqui, mutus sit illico, & tamen ex eo laudem captat, quasi pij inimici, quòd ad illa non respondeat, quæ nunquam dicta, quæ nulla ibi erant, ad quæ posset respondere. Quæ enim conuitia illa sunt, vel blasphemiæ in Pium quintum? Dixit Apologia, Pium, etsi minas spirasset, & ruinam Regina meditatus esset, etsi atrociter in eam sæuisset, & anathemate fulminasset; nihil tamen in eam statuisse grauius, quam in Regem iam nostrum Paulus Pontisex. Quis hoc negat? Ex ipsa Bulla ebulliunt omnia hæc. Lege vero Bullam, leges, minantem, ruinam meditantem, atrociter sæuientem, anathemate fulminantem. Quid tu? Negas minari interdum Pontifices & sæuire; & cum fulmina sua vibrant, ruinam meditari? Seuera tu hæc paulò post vocas (& in hoc facta fateris) nos vero qui sensimus, fana etiam, citra tamen blasphemiam: quando & sæuisse leguntur Pontifices, & leui de causa; nec tam placidæ naturæ fertur fuisse Pius, vt in eum sanitia non caderet.
units.tr: Come now, let us see concerning the Bull of Pius the Fifth and the Briefs of Paul the Fifth, how they agree with one another, or how much the difference is, between Pius the Fifth, who absolved from obedience to the Queen, and Paul the Fifth, who forbids that obedience be rendered to the King. Matthew here plays the rhetorician (for he is not a bad rhetorician). For since it is the custom and practice of rhetoricians to say that they pass over many things, which yet, if you undertake to say them, they do not have to be said: Matthew here wishes to enrich you, reader, with this little flower of his rhetoric. For he says he omits things which, if you allow him to speak, he would at once be mute; and yet from this he seeks praise, as if he were answering the pious enemies, because he does not reply to those things which were never said, which were not there at all, to which he could reply. For what insults, or blasphemies, are these against Pius the Fifth? The Apology said that Pius, although he breathed threats and meditated the ruin of the Queen, although he raged against her atrociously and thundered with anathema, nevertheless decreed nothing against her more grievous than what Paul the Pope now (decrees) against our King. Who denies this? All these things well up from the Bull itself. Read the Bull: you will read "threatening," "meditating ruin," "raging atrociously," "thundering with anathema." What do you say? Do you deny that Popes sometimes threaten and rage, and when they brandish their thunderbolts, meditate ruin? You call these things "severe" a little later (and in this you confess the facts); but we who perceived them call them mad, yet not blasphemous: since both Popes are read to have raged, and for a slight cause; nor is Pius said to have been of so placid a nature that madness did not fall upon him.

units.la: Vis Gabutium audire? vis Catenam, homines vestros? Cogitabat (inquit {a}Gabutius) Pium Reginam, illam malorum sententiam, seu, vt appellabat ipse, flagitiorum seruam, de medio tollere. De medio tollere, annon sæuum apud te? Vis etiam aliud? Pius omni studio faciendum curauit, vt per Rodolphum suum, incolarum animos ad Elizabethæ perditionem, (destructionem, ait {b}Catena) rebellione factâ commoueret. Perditio, destructio, & rebellio, nec haec tibi saeua videntur? Adhanc conspirationem augendam & confirmandam, extrema remedia Pius adhibere constituit. Extrema remedia, annon atrox verbum? Pius non modò quicquid posset collaturum auxilij, sed etiam si opus fuisset, vt optimè de Christiana Repub. mereretur, {c}præsentem se affuturum, cunctaq; sedis Apostolicæ vestigalia[?], item sacros calices, cruces, atque adeo vestimenta sua ad id oppignoraturum pollicebatur.
units.tr: Do you want to hear Gabutius? Do you want Catena, your men? Gabutius says: Pius was thinking of removing the Queen, that judgment of evils, or, as he himself called her, the slave of crimes, from the midst. To remove from the midst: is that not savage in your eyes? Do you want something else? Pius took care, with all zeal, that by his Rodolph he should stir the minds of the inhabitants to the destruction of Elizabeth (the word Catena uses is destruction) by bringing about rebellion. Destruction, ruin and rebellion: do these not seem savage to you? To increase and strengthen this conspiracy, Pius resolved to apply extreme remedies. Extreme remedies: is that not a harsh phrase? Pius promised not only whatever help he could contribute, but even, if it were needed, that he would come in person, as one who deserved best of the Christian commonwealth, and that he would pledge the revenues of the Apostolic See, likewise the sacred chalices and crosses, and even his own vestments, for this purpose.

units.la: Annon saeuum hic homo, qui ipse præsens rebellioni, & perditioni interesse vult, qui ad eam rem calices & cruces, qui suas ipsius vestes oppignorat, vt Regina male sit? Nam de anathemate scio non dubitas: Omni Regni iure & titulo spoliatam decernit, & declarat. Subditos à Sacramento solutos; etiam anathemate ijs proposito, qui ei deinceps paruissent, {d}etiam concessione factâ, vt quiuis contra eam possit insurgere. Et vbi iam conuitia illa? quae, pergratam rem nobis facere, si promeres potiùs quàm salares, Moneo verò Lectorem hîc, de inhonesto hoc Matthaei, & pessimo istorum hominum more insinuandi; per quem, siquis parum attentus sit, fraus illi fiat, vt inaudita nescio quae conuitia ibi congesta putet, vbi nihil conuitij, nedum blasphemiae, vbi minus etiam dicitur, quàm res postulat.
units.tr: Is this man not savage, who himself wishes to be present at the rebellion and destruction, who pledges chalices and crosses for this matter, who pledges his very own vestments, so that the Queen may come to harm? For you do not doubt his anathema: he decrees and declares her stripped of all right and title to the kingdom. He releases the subjects from their oath, and even, with anathema proposed to those who henceforth obey her, grants leave that anyone may rise up against her. And where now are those reproaches? Which would be a very welcome thing for us to do, if you deserved them rather than cured them. I warn the reader here about this dishonourable habit of Matthew's, and about the worst custom of these men, of insinuating; by which, if anyone is not very attentive, he is cheated into thinking that some undefined abuse has been heaped up there, where there is no abuse at all, much less blasphemy, where even less is said than the matter demands.

units.la: Rem verò hîc astutè gerit, vt quae sibi ipsi merito obijcienda videat, prior ipse obijciat. Vtinam verò, si animus est illi conuitia omittere, non haec Apologiae, quae nusquam ibi sunt, sed sua omittat. Cùm enim per Apologiam integram, duo tantùm loca sint, quae ad falsi vel umbram pertrahi possint, quae tamen ipsa, asperius multo Latinè sonant quàm Anglicè (nec enim aegrè feret, si iam inter Editiones has duas distinguimus, quod ipse nos facere docuit) cùm duo (inquam) sint tantùm pro duobus his modò, nec tamen tam vel asperis vel directis; vix vllum concludit locum, in quo non falsum sub ipsis terminis: etiam mendacij sæpe vox ipsa, tam odiosa. Cuius liber ipse, farrago tota conuitiorum & scommatum, qualia nimirum haec: Nolo in vanis tempus consumere: Post varias nugas atque calumnias: Mitto lutulentam orationem: More suo calumniatorem se prodere: Aduersarium satis feliciter progredi: Atrum est quâ fronte Author Apologiae. Quid quòd homo procax & contumeliosus, non Regiâ Maiestate, non ipsâ ipsius personâ abstineat[?] Quem autem sine omni circumlocutione, ore spurco, conferre cum Iuliano Apostata: Quem Christianum disertus verbis pernegare, Iacobus non est Christianus: Quem petulanter affirmare, Puritanum in Scotia fuisse, & Protestantes persecutum; hic iam in Anglia, vice versa; Protestantem factum, & Puritanos persequi. Tum nec titulos illi adhibere, de more, de iure debitos, sed interdum Iacobum modo (quasi quidam de plebe esset) interdum Regem Anglorum, de quo ante mihi monitus. Denique quod Apologiae vitio vertit, id ipse praestat strenuè, magnus scilicet conuitiorum artifex, & quasi ex Scioppij schola formatus: qui proin bene faciat, si ipse sibi suum illud accommodet, quod conuitia solis conuitiantibus nocent. Nocent certè soli; proin tu posthac illa omitte, non Apologiam quidem, sed tua.
units.tr: Here, however, he cunningly manages the business, so that he himself first brings up the charges that he sees rightly ought to be brought against himself. Would that, if he has any intention of dropping reproaches, he would drop his own, not the Apology's, which are nowhere to be found in it. For in the whole Apology there are only two passages that can be dragged even to the shadow of a falsehood, and these sound far harsher in Latin than in English (for he will not be aggrieved if we now distinguish between these two editions, as he himself taught us to do). Since there are only two (I say) for these two alone, and not so harsh or direct, he hardly concludes any passage in which he does not state a falsehood in so many words, even the word "lie" itself, so hateful, is often used. His book itself is a whole hash of insults and jests, such as these, of course: "I do not want to waste time on trifles"; "After various trifles and calumnies"; "I pass over his muddy oration"; "to betray himself as a calumniator in his usual way"; "the adversary advances quite successfully"; "how dark is the brow of the author of the Apology!" Why, a shameless and abusive fellow does not even refrain from His Royal Majesty, nor from His Majesty's person itself. Whom, without any circumlocution, with a foul mouth, he compares with Julian the Apostate; whom, with eloquent words, he flatly denies to be a Christian: "James is not a Christian"; whom he wantonly affirms to have been a Puritan in Scotland and to have persecuted Protestants, "here now in England, conversely, made a Protestant and persecuting Puritans". Then he does not give him the titles customarily and rightly due, but sometimes "James" alone (as if he were some man of the common people), sometimes "King of the English", which I was previously warned about. Finally, what he finds fault with in the Apology, he himself performs vigorously, a great craftsman of insults, and as if trained in the school of Scioppius: so he would do well to apply to himself that saying, "insults harm only those who insult". "Only they harm": therefore you, Matthew, drop those things from now on, not the Apology, but your own.

units.la: Post autem prolixè rem repetit, ut doceat, multùm inter duos hos Quintos interesse, Pium, & Paulum: Seuerus nempe Pius, sed non sine iustâ causâ, (& causam tamen reticet) & pro illâ suâ seuerâ pietate, Reginam ante à iure & generatim excommunicatam, iterum nominatim excommunicauit, & excommunicatam declarauit. Subditos post ab eius obedientiâ iustissimè absoluit & liberauit. Haec Seuerus ille Pius. Lenis autem Paulus (medicus iam factus, & medicinam profiteri volens) prius mitia quaedam medicamenta experiri voluit, an laborantem graui morbo Regem curarent: nec iudicauit hoc tempore expedire, (quid alio post iudicaturus, incertum) ut Rex (quamuis & ipse forsan à iure, & generatim quoque excommunicatus) nominatim excommunicari, & pro excommunicato publicè declarari debeat: Nec soluit obedientia subditos (sed nec ligari finit iureiurando) nec vetuit, ut Regi praestent tam in temporalibus, sed vetuit tamen iurare se eam praestituros. En Paulus Pio quid praestet; En quantum interest, inter lenitatem Pauli, & seueritatem Pij. Sed noster[?] tamen adhuc scrupulus manet. Discrimen enim quaerimus, inter soluentem ab obedientia subditos, (quod fecit durus ille Demea) & (quod fecit nouus iste Mitio) subditos, ut eâ se afstringant non ferentem: inter solutum ab obedientia subditum, & ea se obligare recusantem; hoc est, inter eum qui solutus sit, & eum qui ligari noluit. Soluebat Pius; ô cauterium, ô cruenta incisio! non finit ligari Paulus; Paulus; ô dulce pharmacum, ô lenis olei infusio !
units.tr: Afterwards, however, he repeats the matter at length, to teach that there is a great difference between these two Fifths, Pius and Paul: Pius, indeed, was severe, but not without a just cause (and yet he keeps the cause silent), and, in keeping with that severe piety of his, he again excommunicated the Queen by name, already excommunicated before by law and in general, and declared her excommunicated. He most justly absolved and freed the subjects from obedience to her. These things Pius the severe did. But gentle Paul (already made a physician, and wishing to profess medicine) wanted first to try some mild medicines, to see whether they would cure the King, who was suffering from a grave disease; and he did not judge it expedient at this time (what he will judge at another time is uncertain) that the King (although perhaps himself excommunicated by law and in general as well) should be excommunicated by name and publicly declared excommunicate. He did not release the subjects from obedience (but nor does he allow them to be bound by an oath), nor did he forbid them to render obedience to the King in temporal matters, but he did forbid them to swear that they would render it. Behold what Paul grants to Pius; behold how much difference there is between the gentleness of Paul and the severity of Pius. But our scruple still remains. For we are seeking the distinction between releasing subjects from obedience (which that harsh Demea did), and (which that new Micio did) subjects being bound to it by not allowing them to be bound: between a subject who has been released from obedience and one who has refused to bind himself to it; that is, between one who is released and one who did not want to be bound. "Pius released; O cautery, O bloody incision! Paul does not allow binding; Paul; O sweet remedy, O gentle infusion of oil!"

units.la: Sed tamen audi (Matthae) si hoc illud tuum sit tam lene medicamentum, vt interdicat subditis, ne sub interuentu sacramenti Regi parere velint, unde necesse est sequatur, vel, vt sinat se contemni Rex, & leges suas; vel, cum distinguere nequeat inter eos de subditis qui religionem vestram prositentur, & animo non malo sunt; & eos qui sub eius praetextu, animo maligno sunt & perfido, vt sic inceßo addat integrum: atque ita rigoris nomine, male apud exteras gentes audiat, quae quidem religioni Romana fauent: tum vt seueritate illa promiscua (quia iuramento locus non est) suorum quoque, alioqui non male affectos animos in se concitet: si hoc (inquam) illud est medicamentum lene quod laudas; non aliam equidem lenitatem video, quam qualis olim erat cicuta, quae damnatis porrigi solebat ebibenda: noxia enim certe, & perniciosa, tum Regi, tum Reipublicae. Quamobrem si medicus esse vult, & vult lenis esse, (vt dicis) petimus ab eo porro medicinam adhuc paulo magis temperatam, vt vnguentum etiam mollius illinat, pharmacum adhuc dulcius propinet. Nam hoc quod dat, nescio quam tibi dulce; hoc scio, vt aeger est, parum salubre est.
units.tr: But listen, Matthew: if this is that "gentle medicine" of yours, which forbids subjects to be willing to obey the King under the pretext of the sacrament, from which it necessarily follows either that the King must allow himself and his laws to be despised, or, since he cannot distinguish between those subjects who profess your religion and are of good disposition, and those who under its pretext are of malicious and treacherous disposition, so that he would add an entire injury to this insult, and thus, under the name of harshness, he would be ill spoken of among foreign nations which favour the Roman religion; and then that by that indiscriminate severity (since there is no room for an oath) he would stir up against himself the minds even of his own people, who are otherwise not ill disposed: if this (I say) is that "gentle medicine" which you praise, I see no other gentleness than that which once was the hemlock, which was usually offered to condemned men to drink: for it is certainly harmful and pernicious, both to the King and to the commonwealth. Wherefore, if he wishes to be a physician, and wishes to be gentle (as you say), we ask him further for a medicine still somewhat more tempered, so that he may apply a softer ointment and offer a sweeter drug. For what he gives, I know not what sweetness it has for you; this I know, that for a sick man it is not very wholesome.

units.la: Etiamne, putas, haberi sibi gratias expectat Pontifex, quod non iudicauit hoc tempore expedire, vt Rex nominatim excommunicetur, vel excommunicatus publicè declaretur? Expectet verò; nam quod hoc tempore non iudicauit, poterit alio iudicare; Experiri vult paululum, vt dicis; quare, ni filium se praebeat dicto audientem, & morigerum, lubrico in loco versatur, à Papâ, si non hoc tempore, at alio corrigendus. Tum forte, lenis Paulus fiet securus Pius. En, quo loco sit Nostersen[?], quo Reges reliqui per orbem Christianum; quàm non certi de fide suorum. Ex hypothesi tantùm subditos habent fideles, atque eâ lege, dum ne eos Papa in ius vocet. Soluendos enim habent ab omni obedientia subditos, si non hoc iam, at alio vllo tempore, quocunque Papa iudex eorum competens, id iudicet expedire. Non iudicauit hoc tempore expedire. Verba sanè sunt attentione dig-na; Regum autem praecipuè, Regis cuiusque pro se, eorum verò praecipuè, quorum propitium fiunc[?] sibi iudicem habere praecipuè interest; Nostèr enim exceptionem fori habet, & vt habet, ita semper habituru est: Papam scilicet pro non indice, vt frustra hic ponatur terretrum illud, non hoc tempore: Nam quocunque tempore hoc expedire iudicet, fortasse illi expediet non indicasse.
units.tr: Do you think that the Pontiff expects even to be thanked, "because he did not judge it expedient at this time that the King should be excommunicated by name, or publicly declared excommunicate"? Let him expect it indeed; for what he did not judge at this time, he will be able to judge at another time. He wishes to try a little, as you say; therefore, unless he shows himself a dutiful and obedient son, he is treading on slippery ground, to be corrected by the Pope, if not at this time, then at another. Then perhaps "gentle Paul" will become "secure Pius". Behold where our Nostersen stands, and where the other Kings throughout the Christian world stand; how uncertain they are of the faith of their subjects. They have faithful subjects only on a condition, and under that law, provided that the Pope does not summon them to judgment. For they must release their subjects from all obedience, if not now, then at any other time, whenever the Pope, their competent judge, judges it expedient. "He did not judge it expedient at this time." These words are certainly worthy of attention; especially for Kings, each for himself, and especially for those whose interest it most is to have a favourable judge. For Nostèr has the exemption of the forum, and as he has it, so he always will have it: namely, the Pope as a non-judge; so that the bugbear "not at this time" is set up here in vain: for whatever time he judges it expedient, perhaps it will be expedient for him not to have judged.

units.la: Sed tamen & illud percontari iuuat a Matthaeo, quorsum tam longos logos habeat de excommunicato a iure & generatim, & de excommunicato nominatim: de excommunicato tantum, & de excommunicato, & sic publicè declarato? An hoc ad rem? An totus hic processus necessarius? At rident haec, & irridènt Roffeus, Philopater, Didymus, & alij, quorum nota vobis vera nomina. Illis verò quae a iure est generatim sufficit, nec expectandam tuam hanc, quam dicis nominatim, & a Pontifice. Citra & illam, & Pontificem, posse Reges excuti, palam scripserunt. Excommunicatio sola sat est, quae a iure est, vt nec Pio nec Paulo opus sit. Et quidem mirum, si sic (vt ais) iuridicè affectus est Papa Paulus; quòd hos homines non compescat, quòd coram Collegio Inquisitorum sisti non iubeat: si sic pergant vtique, & Reges abdicent, Pontifice non vocato, superuacuum reddent totum Curiae processum; pòst forte & Curiam; & Pontificem quoque ipsum superuacuum denique; videat verò, an quaestionem haberi de illis, non indicet hoc tempore expedire.
units.tr: But it is worth asking Matthew also why he has such long discourses on the excommunicated man in general by law, and on the excommunicated man by name, on the excommunicated man only, and on the excommunicated man who has been so publicly declared. Is this to the point? Is this whole procedure necessary? But these things are laughed at, and Roffeus, Philopater, Didymus and others laugh at them too, whose true names are known to you. For them, what is excommunicated in general by law is enough, and your so-called "by name, and by the Pope" need not be awaited. They have written openly that kings can be shaken off without that, and without the Pope. Excommunication alone is enough, the excommunication which is by law, so that there is no need for Pius or Paul. And indeed it is a wonder, if Pope Paul has been so legally disposed (as you say), that he does not restrain these men, and does not order them to be summoned before the College of Inquisitors. If they continue in this way, and renounce their kings with the Pope not summoned, they will make the whole process of the Curia superfluous; afterwards perhaps the Curia too, and finally the Pope himself as well. Let him see whether the question about them should be raised at all, since he does not judge it expedient at this time.

units.la: Quod verò dicis, non vetuisse Papam, vt Regi obedientia in temporalibus praestaretur: cùm nihil ibi in iuramento insit, nisi de temporalibus; cur illud vetat? cur illud non finis suscipi? Recipis ergo te tandem ad murum illum tuum ahaeneum, & dicis, non prohiberi iuramentum fidelitatis cuiuscunque. En iam, vt insenuit, cuiuscunque. Non cuiuscunque? Cuius igitur? Solius fidelitatis, quae cum infidelitate coniuncta est. Mira verò rerum oppositarum coniunctio: quasi si pietatem coniungas cum impietate, cum luce tenebras; sed quae haec fidelitas infidelitas? Hic tu missam facis fidem Catholicam in Deum, quae te hactenus detinuit, & fidelitati iam inhaeres in Principem nescio quem, certum autem est, non Deum. Commiscceris autem nobis principatus duos; terrenum, & spiritualem: terrenum sub Principe terreno, id est, Rege; Spiritualem, sub Principe spirituali, id est, Papa. Fidelitatem vtrique huic Principi deberi vis, Iuramentum fidelitatis vtrique praestandum; Cauendum ne iuramentum iuramento elidatur, id fieri in Regio, rectè ergo interdici.
units.tr: As for what you say, that the Pope did not forbid that obedience be rendered to the King in temporal matters: since there is nothing in the oath but what concerns temporal matters, why does he forbid it? Why does he not forbid it to be undertaken? So you retreat at last to your brazen wall, and say that the oath of fidelity of whatever kind is not forbidden. Behold now, as it has grown old, "of whatever kind." Not of whatever kind? Of which kind then? Of fidelity alone, which is joined with unfaithfulness. A strange conjunction of opposites indeed, as if you were to join piety with impiety, or darkness with light. But what is this "faithful unfaithfulness"? Here you set aside the "Catholic faith in God", which has held you until now, and you now cling to "fidelity" toward some prince I know not who, though it is certain he is not God. You mix up for us two principates: the earthly and the spiritual. The earthly under an earthly prince, that is, the King; the spiritual under a spiritual prince, that is, the Pope. You want fidelity owed to each of these princes, and an oath of fidelity to be sworn to each. Take care lest oath be cancelled by oath; this would happen in the King's case, and therefore it was rightly forbidden.

units.la: Expedi primùm, cur terreno, spiritualem opponas? Caelestem oportuit. Videbas caelestem Principem tuum non esse, sed sublunarem: maluisti incidere in τὸ ἄνω [?], quàm in τὸ κάτω [?], & spirituale potiùs dicere, quàuis impropriè; quàm caelestem, absurdè. Laudo verecundiam; nam {a}Salmeron non est veritus Proregem caelestem nuncupare: Frons enim durior solet esse Iesuitis. Vbi de caelesti dixisti, dic etiam de Principatu hoc nouo. Nouus enim est, necdum nobis satis intellectus, credo autem nec vobis ipsis. Papatus certè non est. Papa enim non facit multa, quae tamen Princeps spiritualis facit. Papa, vt Papa, Reges non deponit; id scilicet spirituali huic Principi reseruatum, qui nuper emersit: calet enim adhuc ab incude Domini tui, & est certè Eleusinium sacrum hoc de Principe isto nouo, illi cum paucis cognitum. Tum dicendum tibi, vbi loci, aut in quibus scripturae Sanctae verbis fundatus sit Principatus hic. Meministi enim obedientiam praestandam nobis, secundùm scripturas sanctas. Vetera autem verba ad eam non satis: in illis Papatus, vt Papatus creatur; Sublimiora aliqua, alicunde vobis quaerenda sunt, vt Principatus hic subster[?].
units.tr: First explain why you set "spiritual" against "earthly". You ought to have said "heavenly". You saw that your prince is not heavenly but sublunary; you preferred to fall into the upper rather than the lower [?], and to say "spiritual" rather, though improperly, than "heavenly", which would be absurd. I commend your modesty; for Salmeron did not hesitate to call his viceroy "heavenly". The Jesuits are wont to have a harder brow. Where you have spoken of the heavenly, speak also of this new principate. For it is new, not yet sufficiently understood by us, and I believe not even by yourselves. It is certainly not a papacy. For the Pope does not do many things which nevertheless the spiritual prince does. The Pope, as Pope, does not depose kings; this is reserved, of course, to this spiritual prince who has lately emerged. For he is still warm from the anvil of your Lord, and this sacred Eleusinian mystery concerning this new prince is certainly known to a few. Then you must tell us where, or in what words of Holy Scripture, this principate is founded. For you remember that we must render obedience "according to the holy Scriptures". But the old words are not sufficient for it: in them the papacy is created as a papacy; some loftier ones must be sought for you from somewhere, so that this principate may be supported.

units.la: Sed & explica nobis adhuc aliud. Cùm dicas Vicarium esse Christi hunc Principem, quomodo id sibi constet: cùm vicarius Principi non soleat dici Princeps, non magis quàm Prorex Salmeronis Rex dicendus? Christus autem Rex ille sit, & Princeps noster spiritualis, cui iam in baptismo fidem sacramento astrinximus, vt iam vicario eius non oporteat. Regi enim ipsi solet fides iurari, non Proregi vel Vicario; Gentium hoc iura non sinunt. Quare male omnino mentio tibi facta de Vicario, cùm volebas Principem creare. At etiam ei (quem tu vis) Principi vt praestetur[?] iuramentum à populis, inauditum antehac; Terreno quidem praestatur, vbi non Gentium? At tuo illi haetenus haud quisquam praestitit, nisi forte qui de Clero, & promoti. Qui ergo abiuret quis, quod illi nusquam iuratum est? Postremò, quod tu speras, propulsabo facilè. Non enim iurabit quisquam se illi non pariturum in iis, quae proprie ad ipsius pertinent potestatem. Nam spiritualia proprie ad ipsius potestatem spectant qui vult eluere[?] Princeps spiritualis. At hic nulla de spiritualibus mentio. Spirituale ius illi non lædítur, securus sit; salutì tantùm terreni Principis, Iuramento prospectum est.
units.tr: But explain to us also one further thing. When you say that this Prince is the Vicar of Christ, how is that consistent? Since a vicar is not usually called a prince, any more than Salmeron's viceroy should be called a king. Christ, however, is that King and our spiritual Prince, to whom we have already bound our faith in baptism by a sacrament, so that there is no need for his vicar. For the oath of faith is customarily sworn to the King himself, not to the viceroy or the vicar; the laws of the nations do not allow this. So it was altogether wrong to make mention of a Vicar, when you wished to create a Prince. Moreover, an oath to be rendered by the peoples to that Prince (whom you want), hitherto unheard of: it is indeed rendered to the earthly prince, where is it not so among the nations? But to your prince no one has hitherto rendered it, except perhaps those of the clergy, and the promoted. Who then would abjure what has never been sworn to him? Finally, what you hope for I will easily repel. For no one will swear that he will not obey that prince in those things which pertain properly to his power. For spiritual things properly pertain to his power, as the spiritual Prince wishes to wash clean. But here there is no mention of spiritual things. The spiritual right is not injured for him; let him be at ease. Provision has been made by the oath only for the safety of the earthly prince.

units.la: Sic habet Breue. Vobis ex verbis ipsis perspicuum esse debet, quòd huiusmodi iuramentum salutì fide Catholicâ, & salute animarum vestrarum, præstari non poterit. Perspicuum esse dicit ex verbis, nec verba tamen illa indicat: multa continere affirmat, nec unum tamen no at[?] de multis. Quæritur, annon parum prudenter hoc factum à Papâ Paulo, annon minùs iustè? Non vult desiderari vel prudentiam in Pontifice suo Matthæus vel iustitiam; non cadunt in illum incuria, vel iniuria. Defensionem ergo meditatur. Nec ita tamen festinat Matthæus, aut zelo rapitur, ad Pontificis defensionem, vt non impingat ad nugas, ad verba impropria adhærescat, & lutum hic interpretis transfire non posset. Mitte verò interpretem; de Libro dic, si quid habes. Fuit ibi culpa leuis interpretis: Quid interpres ad librum? Eóne peccauit liber, quòd interpretem nactus fortè minùs commodum? Fortè & satis, si & tu commodus interpres. Et tamen, vt quod verum est eloquar, (nam de vero, scuere[?] edixit nobis Rex ipse, ne quid de eo quis celare andeat) tantillum temporis interfuit inter Editionem hanc & illam, Anglicam & Latinam, vt non posset, qui interpres fuit, per otium omnia ad normam exigere, & enixè voculas omnes perscrutari, quò vel lectori Torto placere posset. Id modò pensi habuit, vt sensum verè redderet, fidelis magis quàm curiosus interpres. Nec erat id initio consilium, vt Latinè quicquam ederetur. Quare enim? Cùm iusiurandum ipsum, cùm Edictum de iureiurando, Anglicè conceptum, vtpote Anglis hominibus, & solis illis promulgatum: Etiam Breuia ipsa Pontificis vtcunque Latinè missa, ad Anglos tamen missa, quos etiam illa solos spectabant: Quid hic vllâ opus Apologiâ Latinâ? Nescio tamen quomodo factum, cùm hoc ab initio propositum non esset, visum post quibusdam factu opus; quò totius causæ processus, quò Regis iustitia Orbi Christiano innotesceret; ex eo festinatum est, vt Editionem Anglicam, Latina quamprimùm subsequeretur. Inde adeo factum, vt properaret interpres; quì si tempus sit, & si eò velit incumbere, polire potest quæ scribit, vt nemo Papiâ magis luculentè. Et vbi tamen lutum illud sit, quod te tam male habet, non facilè conijciat quis; aut quæ illa vocum improprietas, quam non libet discutere. Lector verò, qui nimis tibi familiarem iam nouit, reticentiam, nec vllam ibi improprietatem vocum esse, quam discutere possis, nec lutum vllum, quod excutere, facilè suspicetur, sed quòd more tuo, vbi luti nihil est, lutum tamen te dicis transilire.
units.tr: So the Brief says: "It must be clear to you from the words themselves that an oath of this kind cannot be rendered without danger to the Catholic faith and to the salvation of your souls." It says that it is clear from the words, yet it does not point out those words: it affirms that they contain many things, yet does not name even one of the many. The question is raised: was this not done imprudently by Pope Paul, was it not less just? Matthew does not want prudence in his Pope, or justice, to be found lacking; neither carelessness nor injustice falls upon him. He therefore takes up a defence. Yet Matthew does not hurry, nor is he carried away by zeal, to the defence of the Pope, without stumbling over trifles, clinging to improper words, and failing to pass over the mud of the translator here. Set aside the translator; speak about the book, if you have anything. There was a slight fault in the translator: but what has the translator to do with the book? Did the book sin because it chanced upon a less suitable translator? Perhaps it is enough, if you too are a suitable translator. And yet, to say what is true (for the King himself has ordered us to speak of the truth, lest anyone dare to conceal anything about it), so little time lay between this edition and that one, the English and the Latin, that the one who was the translator could not, at leisure, bring everything to a standard and diligently scrutinise every little word, so that he might please even Torto the reader. He had this one concern, to render the sense truly, a translator more faithful than curious. Nor was it at first the plan that anything should be published in Latin. Why would it be? When the oath itself, and the Edict concerning the oath, were drawn up in English, as being addressed to English people and to them alone; and even the Pope's Briefs, though sent somehow in Latin, were sent to the English, whom they alone also concerned: what need is there here of any Latin Apology? Yet somehow it happened that, although this had not been proposed from the beginning, it seemed afterwards that some such work was needed, so that the whole course of the cause, and the King's justice, might become known to the Christian world; from that it was hastened that the Latin should follow as soon as possible after the English edition. Hence it came about that the translator hurried; who, if he has time and is willing to devote himself to it, can polish what he writes, so that no one could do so more elegantly than Papias. And where that "mud" is which troubles you so badly, one would not easily guess; nor what that "impropriety of words" is, which it does not please to discuss. But the reader, who already knows you too well as one given to reticence, will not suspect easily that there is any impropriety of words here that you could discuss, nor any mud that you could easily shake off, but that, in your usual way, where there is no mud at all, you nevertheless say you are passing over mud.

units.la: Videamus iam de Pontificis prudentiâ. Ad æquissimum Apologiæ postulatum, si refutare nollet, saltem indicaret, quid illud esset in Iuramento quòd sibi tantopere displiceret; vide tu hîc quàm lutulentè respondeas; Non fuisse Pontificis propositum, non necesse illi fuisse, vt librum refutationis conscriberet, Philosophorum more, argumentis, variis ex locis petitis. Et quis hoc postulauit, de libro Philosophorum more, aut tanta argumentorum varietate, quantam tu prædicas? Quasi vel in Epistolâ ipsâ adeo hoc illi operosum fuisset, indicare paucis, & digitum ad locos intendere, quibus peccabat illi Iuramentum. Poterat verò, si ita illi visum, præstare hoc, nec epistolæ tamen modum excedere. Esset enim imprudentiæ summæ, quam tu tamen omni conatu remouere hîc conaris à Pontifice, si vel existimaret non posse se indicare, quid minùs sibi placeat, nisi scripto libro integro. De actione quidem, (inquam) si constet iniquam esse, nihil opus eam notare: sed vbi agenti videtur æqua, ne id quidem iniquum videri solet, quâ parte iniquum sit, quáue ratione, indicare paucis. Et hoc quotidie fit in Regum Edictis, nec ex eo tamen Philosophi fiunt, aut Philosophorum more libros conscribunt. At in Pontificis hoc non fit; alius Curiæ Romanæ stylus est; id querimur, quòd se ad tantæ magnitudinis instar emicuisse, vel extumuisse potiùs censeat Pontifex, vt nec charitatis lege, nec vel æquo & bono teneri se putet. Æquum enim certè ;& eò vsque condescendere, à charitatis regulâ non alienum, aliquam saltem vt rationem redderet, cur vnâ litura ita simul totum obduxerit. Eo magis, quòd Regi in animo ( quod & ego ex ore audiui ipsius sanctissimè id asserentis) vel delere ex eo, vel certè mollire in eo, si coniecturâ modò posset assequi, phrasin ibi vllam esse, vllam clausulam, vnde iusta metus causa vestris hominibus; dum id tamen capiti ipsi Iuramenti de fidelitate fraudi ne foret.
units.tr: Let us now look at the Pontiff's prudence. To the most reasonable demand of the Apology, that if he would not refute it, he should at least indicate what it was in the Oath that so greatly displeased him, see here how muddily you answer: It was not the Pontiff's purpose, nor was it necessary for him, to write a book of refutation in the manner of the philosophers, with arguments drawn from various places. And who has demanded a book in the manner of the philosophers, or such a variety of arguments as you make out? As if it would have been so laborious for him, even in a letter itself, to indicate briefly and point a finger at the places where the Oath went wrong. He could, if it seemed good to him, have done this without exceeding the limits of a letter. For it would be the height of imprudence, which you nevertheless try with all your might to remove here from the Pontiff, if he thought he could not indicate what displeased him less, unless in a whole written book. As for the action itself (I say), if it is clear that it is unjust, there is no need to note it; but where it seems fair to the one acting, it is not usually even seen as unjust in what part or for what reason it is unjust, to indicate briefly. And this is done daily in the edicts of kings, yet men do not thereby become philosophers, or write books in the manner of the philosophers. But this is not done in the Pontiff's case; it is another style of the Roman Court; this is what we complain of: that the Pontiff thinks himself to have risen up, or rather swollen, to such a height of greatness that he believes himself bound neither by the law of charity nor even by what is fair and good. For it is certainly fair, and not foreign to the rule of charity, to condescend so far as to give at least some reason why he drew such a blanket line through the whole thing at once. All the more so because the King had it in mind (as I also heard from his own mouth, when he most solemnly asserted it) to delete from it, or at least soften in it, if he could by conjecture discover, any phrase or clause there that gave your men just cause for fear; provided, however, that this would not be a fraud against the very heading of the Oath of Allegiance.

units.la: Sed dic etiam hoc, Epistolæ ne Pontificis, vicem Edicti repræsentant, & vestrósne[?] semper obligant? Scis ipse, non obligare; Edicti vim non habere; Breuia tantum esse, & vada; à ipedite tuto transmeari posse: ut si quantum possint, velint Catholici tui, possint si velint, iusiurandum etiam iurare, ni maior quàm Epistolæ authoritas superuenerit. Quodsi recusent, ex alia id causa fieri quàm Epistolâ, aut certè Epistolæ ab ijs vim ignorari, quæ, ut de astris dicitur, inclinat, non necessitat. Etiam, si vel Bulla foret; at & peti potest, & concedi solet facultas eius explicanda, sic ut non obliget, nisi cùm Pontifici visum facultatem reuocare. Sed clandestinum hoc mysterium, nec temerè vulgandum: Non enim omnibus hoc datum, at quibusdam certè.
units.tr: But tell me also this: do the Pontiff's letters represent the force of an edict, and always bind your people? You yourself know they do not bind; they do not have the force of an edict; they are only brief notes and shallows, which can be crossed safely on foot: so that if your Catholics wished, as far as they are able, they could, if they wished, even swear the oath, unless the greater authority of the letter should intervene. But if they refuse, this happens for some cause other than the letter, or at least the power of the letter is unknown to them, which, as is said of the stars, inclines, does not necessitate. Even if it were a Bull; yet a faculty to explain it can be sought, and it is customarily granted, so that it does not bind, except when it seems good to the Pontiff to revoke the faculty. But this is a secret mystery, not to be rashly spread abroad: for this is not given to all, but certainly to some.

units.la: Quòd enim benignitatem hic Regis respuis, nec partem vllam iuramenti circumducti vis, sed quasi ex tripode (consulto primùm, vt puto, Pontifice) totum deleri iubes, (non enim particulam eius aliquam, quin substantiam ipsam iuramenti, scopumq; adeo ipsum & finem penitus displicere: in eo biliosè nimis & proterue; at alicubi vrbanior aliquanto es. Ibi enim maximâ tantùm ex parte, non vt hic, ex totâ substantiâ; & vndecim modò ibi, non omnes quatuordecim reiicis; ibi, præterquam quòd mentio facta de Excommunicatione, & aliquo modo tacta in eo potestas Pontificis; cætera non malum Iuramentum aiebas: hic tanta peccati vis, vt deleat substantiam etiam ipsam Iuramenti, quod tamè in Schòlis peccatum non facit. At substantia quidem eius, detestatio proditionis in deponendo Rege, disponendo de regnis, inuadenda, armis gerenda, tumultus concitando, vim asserendo. Caue enim putes Papam, aut potestatem eius, substantiam esse hic: Nam si sit, inhærent illi accidentia pessima. Accidens illud quidem est iuramento; substantia autem, proditionis ciuratio. Quod nisi Papa se interdum negotijs hisce immisceret, nec nomen ibi Papæ, nec mentio vlla fuisset. Indirectè hic potestas eius interuenit, quemadmodum & potestas ipsa illi conuenit indirectè: Scopus autem & finis eius, Regis salus, Regni pax. Illa (quæ modò dixi) media sunt, hic autem finis. Et hæccine media, hic finis Pontifici displicet? Nam de scopo nunquam dabimus, vt Papicolis[?], vt Papistæ, vt Papæ ipsi notior fit, quàm legislatori ipsi, qui Dei virtute in viuis est, & delegis suæ scopo, atque intentione optimè testari potest. Ei, par est, credamus de intentione suâ, & hoc leges ipsæ, æquissimum semper censuerunt. Quanquam quæ ex proditione nata lex est, res ipsa loquitur, quòd contra proditionem destinata fuerit. Verùm etsi proteruè tu in hoc, directè tamen cùm ipsam dicis Iuramenti substantiam Pontifici non probari, scepúmque adeo, quò verba omnia diriguntur; Diriguntur autem eò, vt simplex sit subditorum, & per se constans obedientia. Id Papæ non probatur, (vt dicis) qui scilicet absolutam non vult obedientiam, quæ ad Reges est; sed ex Hypothesi, & conditionalem, nec simplicem, sed relatam ad aliquid, ad aliquem, vt conditio sit illis regnandi, si probent se; vt persona cui probent, sit ipse ille Pontifex. Ita enim paulò suprà, Principem spiritualem fecisti & terrenum: Spiritualem autem, Categoricum, terrenum, ex hypothesi, cui nulla obedientia deberi, nullum iuramentum præstari debeat, nisi annexa illi conditio hæc, tantisper dum probatur Categorico illi, spirituali, nuper erecto Principi; nec sine conditione hac, subsistet iusiurandum vllum, sed sine eâ semper vobis aberret à scopo.
units.tr: For since you here reject the King's kindness, and will not have any part of the oath as it has been altered, but, as from a tripod (first consulting the Pontiff, I suppose), you order the whole to be deleted (for not merely some small particle of it, but the very substance of the oath, its scope and very end, you say displeases entirely): in this you are rather too bilious and insolent; yet elsewhere you are somewhat more courteous. For there you say only in the greater part, not, as here, in its whole substance; and there you reject only eleven, not all fourteen; there, apart from the fact that mention is made of Excommunication, and the power of the Pontiff is in some way touched upon in it, you said the other parts were not a bad oath; here the force of sin is so great that it destroys the very substance of the Oath, which nevertheless does not make a sin in the schools. But its substance is indeed the detestation of treason: in deposing the King, disposing of kingdoms, invading, bearing arms, stirring up tumults, asserting violence. Take care that you do not think the Pope, or his power, is the substance here: for if it were, the worst accidents would cling to it. That thing is an accident of the oath; but the substance is the swearing against treason. And unless the Pope sometimes meddled in these affairs, neither the name of the Pope nor any mention of him would be there. His power enters here indirectly, just as the power itself belongs to him indirectly: but its scope and end is the King's safety, the peace of the realm. Those things (which I have just mentioned) are the means, but this is the end. And do these means and this end displease the Pontiff? For we will never give an account of the scope as it becomes better known to the Papists, to the Pope himself, than to the lawgiver himself, who lives by the power of God and can best bear witness to the scope and intention of his own law. It is fitting that we believe him about his own intention, and this the laws themselves have always judged most fair. Although the thing itself speaks, a law that arose from treason was intended against treason. But although you are rude in this, yet when you say directly that the very substance of the Oath is not approved by the Pontiff, and indeed its scope toward which all the words are directed; they are directed there so that the obedience of subjects may be simple and constant in itself. This, as you say, does not please the Pope, who evidently does not want absolute obedience, which is due to kings; but a conditional one, depending on a hypothesis, and not simple, but related to something, to someone, so that the condition of their reigning is if they prove themselves; and the person to whom they should prove themselves is that very Pontiff. For a little earlier you made him a spiritual prince and also an earthly one: the spiritual one indeed is categorical, the earthly one hypothetical, to whom no obedience ought to be owed, nor any oath given, unless this condition is attached to it: for as long as it is proved to that categorical, spiritual, recently erected prince; and without this condition no oath whatever will stand, but without it, it will always wander from its aim for you.

units.la: Sed tu tamen in hoc magis probandus, quàm ille alter Tortus Anglicanus: spem nobis facit homo ille ineptus, satis Pontifici fore, si id modò constaret ei, Regem ita animum habere, vt si quam ibi particulam Pontifex culpare posset, mutare vellet. Ille autem est homo, nescio quis, nihili: tibi, qui Cardinali tanto à sacellis es, magis credendum est, qui nisi transubstantietur Iuramentum, apertè dicis Pontifici non placiturum. Sed etsi nota magis Domino tuo mens Pontificis, & per eum tibi: tamen quid tibi in mentem venit, vt cùm sperare iubeat Apologia de mutandis etiam in Iuramento (si cui bono foret) particulis quibusdam; tu contrà, de eo prorsus desperare iubeas? Non hoc tibi reuelare potuit vel Pontifex ipse, qui corda hominum non nouit, qui corda Regum in manu non habet. Nimis ergo hoc temerè abs te dictum, nunquam hanc Regi mentem fuisse, nunquam facturum fuisse quod diceret: Vide autem quàm fragili[?] ratione, quia nihil mutauit in Iuramento Henrici octaui, fragili[?] sanè, ab alieno facto, ad suum. Forte enim in alieno, à se non edito, nec authoritate suâ, edito ante tot annos, per tot iam annos recepto, hoc non faceret. At in suo faceret, quod ipse nuper curâsset edendum, & in quo solo, ipsius authoritas interuenisset; faceret certè si diceret, cui tam facile hoc facere, quàm dicere. Quare & tu hic nimis importunus interuenis, qui vbi nihil opus, adigis ad desperationem homines tuos, & quod in procliui erat vt fieret, vt aspera mutarentur in plana, dura in mollia, id tu impedis, cumque dicas ferri ab illis tuis onus importabile, Pharisaum te præbes, nec vis illud vel vno digito leuare.
units.tr: But you are to be tested more in this than that other English Tortus: that foolish man gives us hope that it would be enough for the Pontiff, if it were only clear to him that the King has such a mind that, if the Pontiff could blame any particle there, he would wish to change it. But he is a man, I know not who, of no account: you, who are so great a chaplain to the Cardinal, are to be believed more, since you plainly say that unless the Oath is transubstantiated, the Pontiff will not be pleased. But although the Pontiff's mind is better known to your Lord and through him to you, what came into your head, that when the Apology bids us hope for changes of certain particles even in the Oath (if it would be to anyone's good), you on the contrary bid us despair of it altogether? Not even the Pontiff himself, who does not know the hearts of men, who does not hold the hearts of kings in his hand, could have revealed this to you. Therefore it was too rashly said by you, that this mind was never in the King, that he never would have done what he said: see, however, on how fragile a ground, because he changed nothing in the Oath of Henry VIII, surely a fragile argument, from another's act to his own. For perhaps he would not do this in another's work, one not published by himself nor by his authority, published so many years ago and so long received; but he would do it in his own, which he himself had lately seen to be published, and in which alone his authority had intervened; he would certainly do it, if he said it: for it is as easy for him to do this as to say it. Wherefore you too intervene here too importunately, who, where there is no need, drive your people to despair, and when it was on the slope to happen that rough things should be changed into smooth, hard into soft, you hinder this; and while you say that a burden not to be borne is laid on them by your men, you show yourself a Pharisee, and will not lift it even with one finger.

units.la: Nec hoc tibi visum satis, nisi & admisceres etiam de Puritanis, etiam illos abhorrere à Iuramento Primatus. Quid? numquid & Tortus inter Puritanos? An & vos iam amicis illis, illi vobis, inter quos idem velle & nolle? Atque idem iungat vulpes? Quis non Torto de illis, iam suis; Quis non illis de Torto, iam suo gratuletur? Sed in hoc tamen, aut te certè falleris, aut illi nos fallunt; cùm & suscipiant vtrò Iuramentum hoc, & professi sint sæpe, idque editis à se libris, calumniam esse hanc meram, nec se Iuramentum illud vnquâ detrectâsse. Quodsi illis scrupulus fuit vnquam, de voce fuit, de re non fuit. Caput Ecclesiæ cùm de Christo dicatur, titulus ille magis augustus videbatur, quam vt mortali cuiquam tribui posset. Ita de titulo hærere aliquandiu, iam non hærent: De re autem ipsâ, de authoritate Regiâ prolixè semper professi sunt. Sin intus apud se secus sentiant, & æquiuocè vobiscum respondeant; non certè tanti apud nos sunt, vt valdè referre putemus, si quomodo olim Herodes & Pilatus ad interimum Christi Domini: ita vos inter vos, in præiudicium Regis (qui Christus est Domini) conspiretis; tu vt Pontifici tuo, illi vt Presbyterio suo, primam atque summam authoritatem diripiatis: Vtérque in Reges iniuriosi ex æquo, qui authoritatem illis suam, quam vos sub lege habuisse non negatis, nec sub Euangelio exuere iussos, detractam vultis.
units.tr: Nor did this seem enough to you, unless you also mixed in that the Puritans too shrink from the Oath of the Primacy. What then? Is Tortus among the Puritans as well? Or are you now friends with them, and they with you, among whom to wish and not to wish are the same thing? And does the same fox join with them? Who would not congratulate Tortus on them, now his own; who would not congratulate them on Tortus, now theirs? Yet in this one thing either you are certainly mistaken, or they are deceiving us; since they both accept this Oath of their own accord, and have often professed, and that in books published by them, that this is mere calumny, and that they never refused that Oath. If ever there was a scruple for them, it was about the word, not the thing. When Head of the Church is said of Christ, that title seemed too lofty to be given to any mortal. So they hesitated for a while over the title, but now they no longer hesitate. As for the matter itself, the royal authority, they have always professed it at length. But if inwardly they think otherwise and answer you with equivocation, they are certainly not so important to us that we think it matters much whether, as once Herod and Pilate conspired against the life of Christ the Lord, so you now conspire among yourselves, to the prejudice of the King (who is the Christ of the Lord): you, that your Pontiff, and they, that their Presbytery, may tear away the first and highest authority. Both are equally injurious to kings, since you wish to strip away the authority that they had, which you do not deny they held under the law, and which they were not commanded to lay aside under the Gospel.

units.la: Sed & illud etiam quod ais, Iuramentum Primatus, Regem sub pœnâ capitis suscipi iussisse à quoquam, aperte falsum est. Nostri homines illud indies suscipiunt, illis defertur: At vestrûm adhuc nemo suscipere iussus, sub pœnâ capitali; imò nec omninò iussus suscipere, nisi quis mutâsse se in opinione professus, vltrò illud sibi deferri postulârit.
units.tr: But also what you say, that the Oath of the Primacy was enjoined by someone on the King under pain of death, is plainly false. Our men take it every day; it is offered to them. But none of yours has yet been commanded to take it under pain of capital punishment; indeed none is commanded to take it at all, unless someone who has professed a change of opinion asks of his own accord that it be offered to him.

units.la: Tum denique, cùm vindicare vis Pontificem iterum à secunda notâ iniustitiæ in Catholicos suos, secundò jam desperare te dicis factuurum Regem, quod diceret: atque hîc tibi responsio vere ducitur à desperatiù, ubi nulla tamen desperandi occasio data. Quanquam enim de reliquâ tuorum anxietate, nihil ad hanc rem de quâ agitur: siquà tamen ex Iuramento isto suo, animi anxietas incidisset, eam Rex illis eximere voluit. Cúmque vellet, næ tu parum anxius videris de tuorum hominum anxietate, qui malis torqueri illos, quàm animi hac sui anxietate releuari; nec cessare vis persecutionem hanc tam apud te gravem, quæ, si vllam partem æqui boniquè dixisset Papa, tam facilè cessare potuisset. Totum hoc illi [illegible, ~10 letters]; posset leuare si vellet; si cùm possit, nolit, iniquus esto.
units.tr: Then finally, when you want to clear the Pontiff a second time of the second charge of injustice against his Catholics, you say that a second time you are in despair that the King will do what he said; and here your answer is truly drawn from despair, where yet no occasion for despair has been given. For although the rest of your anxiety has nothing to do with the matter in question, yet if any anxiety of mind had arisen from this Oath of theirs, the King wished to free them from it. And since he wished it, indeed you seem little anxious about the anxiety of your men, since you would rather have them tormented by evils than relieved of this anxiety of their mind; nor do you cease to call this persecution so grievous to you, which could have been ceased just as easily if the Pope had said any part of it fairly and well. All this he [illegible] could relieve if he wished; if, while he is able, he does not wish, then be unjust.

units.la: Tui verò illi, si (ut ais) semel jam in coronatione Regis obedientiam illi exhibuerunt, quid obstat quò minùs exhibeant eam jam denuò? Et si non abhorrent à Iuramento fidelitatis, ubi fides Catholica non periclitatur; fatere tu illis, quod res est, fidem ibi Catholicâ non periclitari; & suscipient Iuramentum: quo suscepto, continuò cessabit hæc tam gravis scilicet persecutio.
units.tr: Yet if, as you say, they have already once at the coronation of the King shown obedience to him, what stands in the way of their showing it again now? And if they do not shrink from the Oath of allegiance, where the Catholic faith is not endangered, then tell them what is the case, that the Catholic faith is not endangered there; and they will take the Oath. Once it is taken, this so grievous persecution will at once cease.

units.la: EXordium Brevis à falso, negari non potest, túmq; adeò dum negare vis, fortiùs etiam impingis, in Pontificem tuum. Negas autem crimen falsi, & negas subiratus: Ut verò placatior fis, nolim hîc crimen falsi sic accipi, ut in Iure Civili, quasi syngraphan, aut scriptum aliquod falsâsset Papa; tum enim dextra illi amputanda, ut Apostolicam pòst benedictionem non possit vobis clementer impertiri. Falsum ibi dixisse volumus, (atque id tantùm vult Anglicana vox) non falsarium fuisse, ut Latina paulò durior: falsum certè, si in Regis contumeliam, tribulationes vel calamitates commemoret ab illo illatas, propter quas magno animi mœrore affici debuerit. Fallum ergo Pontificem dicimus, si hæc asserat: te verò, Malthæ[?], qui negas asserere, salsissimum. Tam enim hîc cupidus es[?] reperendi in Apologiam mendacium aliquod, ut depositâ omni verecundiâ, mentiri te non pudeat; de præteritis calamitatibus, quas Reginæ Elizabethae, vel etiam Regis temporibus, passi sunt Catholici, nullam etiam in Brevi mentionem: onem fieri, quin tantùm de ijs, quas illi hoc tempore patiuntur. Verba enim haec tua sunt. Principio, non scripsit Pontifex, se mærore affici ob calamitates, quas tempore Regina Elizabethae, aut initio Regni Iacobi in Angliâ pro retinendâ orthodoxâ fide Catholici patiebantur, sed ob calamitates quas hoc tempore patiuntur. Vide verò tu, quâ attentione legas, quo acumine intelligas. Breue illud, quod initio praeter te intelligebat nemo. Non scripsit (ais) Pontifex, mærore affici se ob eas calamitates, quas patiebantur, sed ob eas, quas iam patiuntur. Audi iam ipsum Pontificem.
