Magno animi mærore, nos semper affecerunt, tribulationes & calamitates, quas pro retinendâ Catholicâ fide iugiter sustinuistis. Sed cùm intelligamus, omnia hoc tempore magis exacerbari, afflictio nostra mirum in modum aucta est. Bis mœstus hic Pontifex, duplici mærore affectus: semel, vno, propter calamitates quas iugiter sustinuerunt, periodo priore: iterum, altero, quòd omnia hoc tempore magis exacerbentur, periodo posteriore. Magnus illi mæror ex ijs quas sustinuerunt: Aucta [?] autem afflictio, & mirum in modum aucta ex ijs, quas iam sustinent. Dic iam, potestne augeri quod prius non fuit? Sed quid ego de priore aucto? Dic potiùs ad illa, semper affecerunt, iugiter sustinuistis: Affecerunt & sustinuistis, cuius temporis? annon praeteriti? Hoc tempore exacerbari, nonne praesentis? Quid ego te, nunc Presbyterum & Theologum, Grammatica haec doceam? Sustinuistis, referri non posse nisi ad calamitates quas patiebantur; exacerbari autem hoc tempore, referri solùm ad illas quas iam patiuntur. Pontifex diserte dicit assecisse se mærore calamitates, quas sustinuerunt: at tu incurris in ipsum Pontificem, & ex opposito dicis, non affectum mærore vllo ob calamitates quas patiebantur: id est, dicis Pontificem teneri falsi.
units.tr: That the Exordium of the Brief is false cannot be denied; and indeed, while you want to deny it, you strike even more hard against your Pontiff. You deny the charge of falsehood, and you deny it in anger. But that you may be calmer, I would not have the charge of falsehood taken here as in Civil Law, as if the Pope had forged some bond or writing; for then his right hand would have to be cut off, so that he could never be graciously granted the Apostolic blessing by you. We mean that he said something false there (and this is all the English word wants), not that he was a forger, as the Latin is rather harsher: certainly he spoke falsely, if, to the King's reproach, he recalled tribulations or calamities inflicted by him, on account of which he ought to have been greatly grieved in mind. So we say the Pontiff is false if he asserts this; but you, Matthew, who deny that he asserts it, are most false. For you are so eager here to find some lie for your Apology that, having put aside all shame, you are not ashamed to lie: about the past calamities which Catholics suffered in the times of Queen Elizabeth, or even of the King, there is not even a mention in the Brief, except only of those which they now suffer. For these are your own words: In the first place, the Pontiff did not write that he was affected with grief because of the calamities which the Catholics suffered in England in the time of Queen Elizabeth, or at the beginning of the reign of James, for retaining the orthodox Catholic faith, but because of the calamities which they now suffer. But see with what attention you read, with what keenness you understand. The Brief, which at first nobody but you understood! The Pontiff did not write (you say) that he was grieved at those calamities which they suffered, but at those which they now suffer. Now hear the Pontiff himself. With great grief of mind, the tribulations and calamities which you have constantly endured for retaining the Catholic faith have always afflicted us. But since we understand that all things are now made more bitter, our affliction has increased in a wonderful way. Here the Pontiff is twice sad, affected by a double grief: once, by one, on account of the calamities which they have constantly endured, in the first period; again, by another, because all things are now made more bitter, in the later period. He has great grief from those which they endured; but his affliction is increased, and increased in a wonderful way, from those which they now endure. Tell me now, can what was not there before be increased? But why do I speak of the first increase? Rather tell me about those words, have always afflicted, have constantly endured: they afflicted and they endured; of what time? Is it not of the past? Be made more bitter now: is that not of the present? Why should I, now a Presbyter and Theologian, teach you this grammar? Have endured can only refer to the calamities which they were suffering; but be made more bitter now refers only to those which they now suffer. The Pontiff plainly says that he was affected with grief by the calamities which they have endured; but you run against the Pontiff himself, and on the contrary you say that he was affected by no grief at all because of the calamities which they were suffering: that is, you say the Pontiff is guilty of falsehood.

units.la: Nihil autem te iuuabit, quòd nulla ibi de Reginâ mentio, quòd nomen ibi Regis praetermissum. Dic enim bonâ fide, quaenam tandem calamitates illae prioris periodi, quas antea iugiter sustinuerunt, magni illius mæroris causa Pontifici? Quando inflictae, vel à quibus? Non enim sustinuerunt iugiter, quas nemo imposuit; Certè autem nemo, si neque Regina neq; Rex. Ita vel calamitates illae nullae, & sine causa mæstus, atq; ita mendax Pontifex: vel si verè mæstus, horum alter necesse est imposuerit quas illi sic sustinuerunt, atque ita mendax Mat-thaus; & quod grauius est, mendax in Pontificem ipsum, fan&tiffimum Dominum suum, & Beatissimum Patrem, cui crimen falsi ascribit, in quem fi non regerit, egerit mendacium; quod non modò conuitium, sed & blasphemia est. Blasphemia enim capax, non minus Paulus quàm Pius, vtrque quintus. Ecce tibi iam non colorem, sed veritatem ipsam, per quam liceat accusare falsi Pontificem, quem tu, dum ne leue quidem ei vestigium adhaerere sinis, totum volutas in mendacio, dum prima ipsa Breuis verba mendacii arguis, vbi etsi mendacium reuera est, non id tamen quod tu affingis. Et ob calamitates pristinas, & ob recentiores has, maerebat Pontifex, & Matthaus qui sic bis maerere negat, ipse maerendus, bis maerendus; propter intelligentiae defectum primo, post etiam propter excessum arrogantiae, qui alios contemnit prae se, quasi solus omnia sciat, qui solus nihil.
units.tr: Nor will it help you that there is no mention there of the Queen, that the name of the King is omitted there. For tell me in good faith, what then were those calamities of the earlier period, which they had constantly endured before, the cause of that great grief for the Pontiff? When were they inflicted, and by whom? For they did not constantly endure those which no one imposed; and certainly no one imposed them, if neither the Queen nor the King did. So either those calamities did not exist, and the Pontiff is sad without cause, and thus the Pontiff is a liar; or if he is truly sad, one of these two must have imposed the calamities which they so endured, and thus Matthew is a liar; and what is more serious, a liar against the Pontiff himself, his most holy Lord and Most Blessed Father, to whom he ascribes the charge of falsehood; and if he does not return it to him, he has done a lie, which is not only abuse but blasphemy. For Paul is capable of blasphemy no less than Pius, both the fifth. Here you have now not a colour but the very truth, by which it is lawful to accuse the Pontiff of falsehood; you, while you do not allow even the slightest trace to cling to him, roll him altogether in a lie, while you accuse the very first words of the Brief of lying, where, although it is indeed a lie, it is not the one you invent. And the Pontiff grieved both for the former calamities and for these more recent ones; and Matthew, who denies that he grieved twice, is himself to be grieved over, twice to be grieved over: first because of his lack of understanding, and afterwards also because of the excess of his arrogance, which despises others in comparison with himself, as if he alone knows all things, when he alone knows nothing.

units.la: Opportunè hic videor Lectorem monere posse, quàm iusta illa dehinc causa sit, vt suspectam habeat fidem istorum hominum, siquando de Patrum scriptis, si de historia veteri quicquam proferentes legat (quorum etiam vix iam breui vetera vlla & incorrupta suppetent exemplaria, non vlla sanè, nisi expurgata ad eorum Indices, Priscis illis verò purgatorios) cùm hic illustre specimen videat in Torto tam ferreae frontis homine, vt in Breui ipso Pontificis sui, re ita publicâ, ita præ manu, præ oculis lectoris ipsius, quod ante quintum vix solum, ille ipse descripsit integrum, & praefixit, clausulam tamen eius, atque omnium primam clausulam, homo impudens impudenter inficiari audeat.
units.tr: It is opportune here, I think, to remind the reader how well-grounded is the suspicion he should have of these men's good faith, whenever he reads them putting forward anything from the writings of the Fathers or from ancient history. Hardly any ancient and uncorrupted copies of these survive now, and none at all except those purged to suit their Indexes, whereas in former times they were purged for the purpose of cleansing. And here he sees a notable example in Torto, a man of such brazen face that, in the very Brief of his Pontiff, which is publicly before his eyes and in the hands of the reader himself, he dares shamelessly to deny the first clause of it, though he himself copied out the whole Brief, and prefixed it, and it is before the reader's eyes, in which he had hardly reached the fifth clause.

units.la: Parentasse se dixit Regina defuncta manibus Apologie Author. Id tu leuiter modo perstringis, & praeteris. In eo humanior multo, altero illo tenebrione Anglo, qui petulanter nimis desaeuit in phrasin illam, nec impropriam ei rei, nec ineruditam. Vbi quicunque tibi in Illam animum, etsi nihilo forte aequior, at plus tamen eruditionis ostendis, quàm ille homo non modò politioris literaturae, sed & humanitatis expers, qui & inde occasionem arripuit non valde idoneam, manes eius mordendi. Nec dubito quin lectori haud vlla videatur melior parentandi ratio, quàm siquis honoris eius quae diem obijt, atque existimationis justam defensionem suscipiat. Parentandi autem verbo, quod quidem Anglicè respondeat, habemus nullum, sacrificandi pro eo vsurpamus, transumptâ voce à ritibus Ethnicorum; quis negat? sed ad pium, Christianúmque erga defunctos officium accommodatâ; quis vetat? vobis enim & qui vestrae sunt professionis, non potest hoc incongruum videri, quorum tota religio conspersa est illiusmodi flosculis, quâ ex Poëtarum hortulo, quâ ex Rhetorum officinâ petitis. Nec excusari potestis aliter, cùm B. Virginem stellam maris compellatis; Propria enim illa Veneris Cypria nomenclatura, quæ maris orta, & de spumâ maris, mare præstat eunti. Nec verò de rythmis vestris & versibus Leoninis, quibus B. eiusdem Virginis interulam, vittam, zonam, quibus Christi fascias, & ascias salutatis, aliter soletis respondere, quàm plerasq; in illis voculas, ex Poëtis desumptas, & ad eorum imitationem expressas esse.
units.tr: The Author of the Apology said that the dead Queen had been "given funeral rites" (parentasse). You touch on this lightly and pass it by. In this respect the other Englishman, that obscurer, was much more humane, though he raged too wantonly against that phrase, which is neither improper for the matter nor unlearned. Whoever you are, you show, if not a fairer mind towards her, at least more learning, than that man, who was not only lacking in polished literature but also in common humanity, and who seized on that not very fitting occasion to bite at her shade. Nor do I doubt that to the reader no better way of giving funeral rites can seem to exist than for someone to take up the just defence of the honour and reputation of her who has died. We have no single word in English that exactly answers to the word parentare; we use "sacrificing" in its place, a word taken over from the rites of the heathen. Who denies it? But it has been adapted to the pious and Christian duty towards the dead. Who forbids it? For this cannot seem out of place to you and to those of your profession, whose whole religion is sprinkled with such little flowers, some picked from the poets' garden, some from the rhetoricians' workshop. Nor can you excuse yourselves otherwise, since you address the Blessed Virgin as "Star of the Sea"; for that is the proper name of "Venus of Cyprus," which "was born of the sea, and from the foam of the sea, surpasses the sea to the one who sails." Nor, indeed, in your rhythms and Leonine verses, in which you greet the Blessed Virgin's shift, headband and girdle, and the swaddling-clothes and the axe of Christ, do you answer otherwise than by saying that most of those little words are taken from the poets and expressed in imitation of them.

units.la: Domino quidem tuo parentandi vel litandi phrasis non displicebit scio: Debet ille multum Virgilio, nec id modò de verbis interdum, quin de rebus ipsis etiam. Nec enim illum poenituit, cum de Purgatorio vestro ageret, non infimo apud vos, certè non infimi precij dogmate, inter Authores quos corrasit ad fidem de eo faciendam, Virgilium etiam, classicum sanè Authorem nominare. Vocem verò vos parentandi repudiare non potestis, quibus res ipsa tam est fructuosa.
units.tr: I know that the phrase "give funeral rites or sacrifice" will not displease your master: he owes much to Virgil, and not only in words at times, but also in the very matters. Nor was he ashamed, when he was dealing with your Purgatory, a doctrine of no small standing among you, and certainly of no small worth, to name among the authors whom he gathered to establish belief in it, even Virgil, a classical author indeed. But you cannot reject the word "give funeral rites," since the thing itself is so profitable to you.

units.la: Mihi vero multò magis improprium videtur & [illegible, ~7 letters] vicinum, de quo commonendus mihi iam es, quòd Pontificem nouo nomine, nec ei in scripturis Sanctis usquam attributo, Christum Domini indigitâsti. Nec id à te figuratè dictum (ut illud parentandi modò nobis) sed serò ut videtur, quasi cum stomacho. At non sic feres. Reges quidem reperio sic in sacris literis, sæpe saepiùs nominatos, tum ab hoc illorum nomine argumenta peti, ne quis manum contra illos levare audeat, ne quis ut levet dispensare audeat, quia nimirum Rex Christus Domini est: Pontifici nomen hoc tributum ibi non memini. Juvet nos Matthaeus, & vel unum locum designet, in toto volumine Bibliorum, ubi nomen hoc ulli Pontifici, sacri illi scriptores attribuerint. Non faciès. Tuque adeò ipse, quasi malæ fidei tibi conscius, & sermonis noui quem nemo intelligat, apponis hic tuum [id est] & Christum Domini, ais, id est Pontificem maximum: veritus scilicet, quod res erat, hoc nomine, Regem à Lectore aliquem intelligendum fore, (quos sic fere scriptura vocat) nisi hic tu nouam illam Glossam addidisses [id est Pontificem maximum] quam nisi addidisses, Pontificem ibi dici à te, haud quisquam, credo, somniasset.
units.tr: To me the phrase seems far more improper, and something near it, of which you ought now to be warned: you have called the Pontiff "Christ of the Lord" by a new name, one nowhere attributed to him in the Holy Scriptures. And you did not say this figuratively (as with that "give funeral rites" just now), but, as it seems, too late, as if with bile. But you will not get away with it so easily. I find that kings are indeed so named in the sacred letters, very often and more often still, and that arguments are drawn from this title of theirs, so that no one should dare to raise a hand against them, and no one should dare to dispense with their laws, because Christ the King is "of the Lord." I do not remember this name being given to the Pontiff there. Let Matthew help us, and point out just one passage in the whole volume of the Bible where those holy writers have attributed this name to any Pontiff. You will not do it. And you yourself, as if conscious of bad faith, and of a new way of speaking that no one understands, add here your "[that is]" and "Christ of the Lord," you say, "that is, the Supreme Pontiff." Evidently you feared that, as was the case, by this name the reader would understand a "King" (as Scripture usually calls them), unless you had added this new gloss [that is, "Supreme Pontiff"]. Had you not added it, I believe no one at all would have dreamed that "Pontiff" was meant there by you.

units.la: At tu, cùm titulus hic illius non sit, quid hic alienum titulum inuadis, & qui ad eum nihil attinet? Quorsum Pontifici titulum afferis, quasi suum, qui suus non est? An nihil ab illo intactum oportet, nihil immune? An omnia ille quasi gurges absorbet, haud quicquam cuiquam relicturus? An ius illi in titulos quosuis, quorumuis? nec liceat ei dicere, Mitte verò hunc; titulus hic Regum est, non tuus? Et quidem si amicus Regum, si illis, si illorum authoritati bene velet, litem forte illi non facerent, non inuiti illum fortasse, in huius sui nominis societatem admitterent. Sed quorsum ei gratificentur, vt Christum Domini appellari sinant, qui Christos Domini sic insectatur: nec illis regna sua, nec subditorum suorum fidem saluam vult? An quò Christos illos Domini Reges meliori iure deponat, Christus & ipse indigitari vult? Antichristum magis oportuit. Nam vt taceam de Christo Domini, certè Christus Domini nemo illo magis [illegible, ~6 letters] vel [illegible, ~4 letters] est. Quare quicquid id est criminis, siue falsum est, siue est mendacium, quod hic intentari vis: non rectè id in Christum Domini abs te dictum est intentari. Si verum vis Christum Domini, si est titulus ille (vt est) maximè honorarius, tua sunt (Matthaei) in Christum Domini mendacia; tu in illum committis; tu cum Shemei, maledicis Christo Domini. Illi, si peccatum est crimen inferre, magnum est peccatum tuum; & quod redundet in Dominum ipsum, cuius Christus est; de quo non parentandum quidem tibi, sed litandum, censeo.
units.tr: But you, since this is not his title, why do you lay hands on a title that is foreign here and has nothing to do with him? Why do you bring to the Pontiff a title as if it were his own, when it is not his own? Ought nothing to remain untouched by him, nothing exempt? Does he swallow up everything like a whirlpool, leaving nothing to anyone? Does he have a right to any titles whatever, of whomever? And may no one be allowed to say to him, "Let this title go; this title belongs to Kings," and not to you? And indeed, if he were a friend of Kings, if he wished well to them, to their authority, they would perhaps not bring a suit against him; they might not unwillingly admit him into the fellowship of this their name. But why should they favour him by allowing him to be called "Christ of the Lord," when he persecutes "the Christs of the Lord" in this way, and does not wish their kingdoms or the faith of their subjects to be safe? Or does he wish to be called "Christ" himself, so that he may depose those "Christs of the Lord, the Kings," with better right? He ought rather to be called "Antichrist." For, to say nothing of "Christ of the Lord," certainly no one is more "Christ of the Lord" than [he] ... Therefore whatever crime this is, whether it is a falsehood or a lie, which you wish to charge here: it has not been rightly charged by you against "Christ of the Lord." If you want "Christ of the Lord" to be true, and if that title (as it is) is most honorary, then the lies in this matter are yours (Matthew), against "Christ of the Lord"; you commit them against him; you, like Shimei, curse "Christ of the Lord." If it is a sin to bring a charge, the sin is great in your case; and it redounds upon the Lord himself, whose Christ he is. For him, I think, you should offer not funeral rites, but sacrifice.

units.la: Praestituis pòst, & praescribis ipse tibi, quid & quantum probare velis, quid satis sit si probes; vt verax sit, nec mendacij teneatur Pontifex, nempe si anno 1606. quo tempore Breue scriptum est, Catholici tui ingentes arumnas tulerint. In quo, prudenter tu quidem: nec enim legem à quoquam sumis probandi, nisi à teipso. Illud autem etsi satis non sit, (quod nos, satis iam, credo, docuimus) tamen quia tibi plus probare non libet, vel non suppetit, videamus sanè iam, videamus arummas[?] illas quas dicis ingentes. Hic tu Edicta duo nominas, quæ duo vel sola sufficere, ais, ad omnia Apologia mendacia coarguenda. Tu verò hic deficis, qui duo dicis sufficere: Etsi enim duo nominas, vnum modò recitas, cuius in titulo ante vellicando infoelix satis fuisti, in lege ipsa iam longè infoelicior. Eam verò in quatuordecim articulos diuidis; Credo autem ut numerus numero responderet, ut quatuordecim istis tuis Edicti, quatuordecim illis Iuramenti vicem referres, (sic simiæ hominès imitari solent) vel potiùs in articulos non diuidis, sed in tot frusta comminuis, retènè an secus, nihil pensi habes: nec enim ordo ibi nec methodus, sed nec veritas vlla in numerando.
units.tr: Afterwards you lay down and prescribe for yourself what and how much you wish to prove, what "it is enough to prove": that the Pontiff may be truthful and not held guilty of a lie, namely "if, in the year 1606, when the Brief was written, your Catholics suffered huge calamities." In this you are prudent indeed: for you take the law of proof from no one but yourself. But that, though it is not enough (as we have already shown, I think, sufficiently), since you do not wish, or are not able, to prove more, let us see now, let us see those "calamities" which you call "huge." Here you name "two Edicts," which you say "alone suffice to refute all the lies of the Apology." But you fail here, you who say that two suffice: for although you name two, you recite only one, in whose title you were unlucky enough to pluck at before, and in the law itself you are far more unlucky now. And this one you divide into fourteen articles. I believe, however, that you did this so that the number should match the number, so that your fourteen articles of the Edict should answer to the fourteen of the Oath (apes of men are wont to imitate in this way); or rather, you do not divide it into articles but grind it into so many scraps. Whether you keep them or not, you care nothing; for there is neither order nor method in it, nor any truth at all in the counting.

units.la: At quatuordecim illi articuli in Iuramento, ita omnes, & verè inde collecti, & bonâ fide, ita omnes manifestò veri, ut ille alter vernaculus, ut tu, ut neuter ausi filis attingere, urerent certè tangentem; quare, laudo ingenium vestrum, salutâstis à longè & transijstis; nec enim locus in ijs reliquus vobis, non vel dentem imprimendi. At quatuordecim illi tui, quàm fraudulenter auulsi, quàm verò malè conciliati? Plures possem; nolo Lectori molestus esse, quatuor tantùm tuas ibi malas artes indicabo.
units.tr: Those fourteen articles in the Oath, all of them rightly and truly gathered together, and all of them manifestly true and in good faith, were such that that other native, and you, and neither of them dared to touch them, would surely burn the one who touched them. Hence I praise your cleverness: you greeted them from afar and passed by; for there was no room left for you in them, not even to bite. But your fourteen, how fraudulently torn away, how badly put together! I could name more; I do not wish to be a nuisance to the reader, so I will point out only four of your bad tricks there.

units.la: 1. Dolus primùm in eo malus, quòd articulos quosdam de tuo capite comminisceris[?], pòst inferis quasi Edicto: quorum in eo vestigium nullum. 2. Tum fraudem olet, quòd ordinem interturbas eorum, nec sinis loco suo stare quemque, sed planè peruertis. 3. Tertiò, & in eo veteratorem agis, quòd & stilum immutas, & loquendi morem, & dialecto tuâ loqui facis non suâ, tuâ (inquam) sæpe non bonâ, sed planè Bœoticâ. 4. Postremò pessimâ fide & illud, quòd cum multa in eo sint ad mitigandam legis seueritatem, & in fauorem vestrorum hominum, ea tamen, quasi nihil tale sit, supprimis, & celas omnia.
units.tr: 1. First, the deceit is wicked in this: you invent certain articles out of your own head and then set them before the reader as if they were the Edict, and there is no trace of them in it. 2. Next, it smacks of fraud that you throw their order into confusion and do not let each one stand in its own place, but turn everything completely upside down. 3. Thirdly, you also act the cheat in this: you change both the style and the manner of speaking, and you make it speak in your dialect, not its own, your own (I say) and often not a good one, but plainly Boeotian. 4. Lastly, it is also in the worst faith that, although there are many things in it to soften the severity of the law and in favour of your people, you suppress them as if nothing of the kind existed, and conceal everything.

units.la: 1. In eo dixi primùm dolo malo agier, quòd affingis ei articulos, qui nulli ibi sunt, nec vsquam nisi in mendacis cerebri tui cellis, articulati; Ille scilicet omnium primus (fortunæ enim tibi auspicari tua semper à mendacio) Inprimis, confir-
units.tr: 1. In this I said, first, that you act with malice, in that you attach to it articles which are not there at all, and which are articulated nowhere except in the cells of your lying brain. That first one, of course (for your beginnings have always been made from lying), "First of all," confirm...

units.la: [Ed. note: the scan shows a small bullet before paragraph 1 in the body; not transcribed as text.] confirmari ibi in primo articulo leges ELIZABETHAE aduersus Catholicos iam olim stabilitas. At ibi nihil quicquam eâ de re. Non est articulo primo, vel legum, vel legis vllius, vlla renouatio, non vel Reginæ ELIZABETHAE ad eam rem mentio. Bonis auspicijs; primum ergo hoc crassum mendacium. Illud verò multò adhuc crasius à te positum, articulo decimo, decimum, & pessimum mendacium. Si tertiâ vice quis positum sibi iuramentum recusauerit, capitis vitaeque dispendium patiatur. Hîc lata nimis tua culpa est, & tu nimis insignitè mendax. Nec enim cuiquam tertiâ vice iuramentum proponitur, nec proponi lege iubetur, neque vitae dispendium possus quisquam est, neque verò pati debet, neque est capitalis lex ista cuiquam, quacunque vice, quocunque casu, neque est de tota hac re syllaba vlla in Edicto. En vt tu res nostras hic intelligas ad vnguem; En vt os vobis sublinant[?] nostri homines, vestri interpretes; En vt iam transferatur in nos labor tuus. Coarguere dixti velle te mendacia nostra: nobis iam tua, vt video, coarguenda. Sic iam habet lector primitias, & decimas mendacitatis tuae.
units.tr: [Ed. note: the scan shows a small bullet before paragraph 1 in the body; not transcribed as text.] ...confirmed there, in the first article, are the laws of Elizabeth against the Catholics, already established long ago. But there is nothing whatever about that there. There is no renewal, in the first article, of either the laws or any law, nor even a mention of Queen Elizabeth on that matter. A good beginning! So this is your first gross lie. But that one, placed by you in the tenth article, is far grosser still: the tenth and worst lie. "If anyone refuses the oath offered to him a third time, let him suffer loss of head and life." Here your fault is too great, and you are exceedingly and conspicuously lying. For no one is offered the oath a third time, nor is it commanded by law to be offered; nor is there any risk to life; nor should anyone suffer it; nor is that law a capital one for anyone, on whatever occasion or for whatever cause; and there is not a syllable of this whole matter in the Edict. See how exactly you understand our affairs here! See how our men, your interpreters, smear your faces with mud! See how your labour is now turned back upon us. You said you wished to refute our lies: now, as I see, your own lies are to be refuted. So the reader has already the first fruits and tithes of your mendacity.

units.la: 1. Posui loco secundo, peruersum à te Edicti ordinem totum. Multùm autem refert, quo quidque ordine, quo loco dicatur; & tu quasi si loco suo quidque referres, cautus homo, posuisti illos tuos ordinales primo, secundo, tertio, &c. quasi bonâ fide rem gerere velles. Posuisti primum quod nullum est, quasi si ciphram primo loco poneres. Qui verò primus est in Edicto, de ijs est: qui, cùm cætera conformes sint, concionibus, precibus, sacris intersint; ad Eucharistiam sumendam tergiuersantur. Is inter tuos nusquam comparet, nusquam certè vt in Edicto est; non vel primo tuo, vel secundo. Qui verò tibi est tertius, is perinde rem refert, quasi si ex eo solo mulctentur homines vestri, quòd recusent sacram communionem sumere; atque ita, mulcta sit vna, preces ipsas; altera, communionem detrectanti. Quod ipsum egregiè falsum est; cùm is totus articulus de ijs sit, qui sacrorum omnium participes esse volunt, Communionis nolunt; quos constat, vel apud vos Catholicos iam non esse, nec pro Catholicis reputari, quippe non immaculatè ambulantes in lege Domini. Pari modo in reliquis, mira crypsis methodi, & quasi fraus sola subfit, suo loco moti pene singuli & disiecti, quasi si fuisset ibi Dauus aliquis, qui interturbassèt omnia.
units.tr: 1. In the second place, I said you have turned the whole order of the Edict upside down. But it matters much in what order and in what place each thing is said; and you, as if you were a cautious man reporting each thing in its own place, have set down those numbered items of yours, first, second, third, and so on, as if you wished to deal in good faith. You have put first something that is not there at all, as if you were placing a cipher in the first place. The one who is first in the Edict is the one who, while otherwise conforming, is present at sermons, prayers and sacred rites, but shirks taking the Eucharist. He does not appear among yours anywhere, certainly not as he is in the Edict; not in your first place, nor your second. The one who is third in your list treats the matter as if your people were fined for this alone, that they refuse to take sacred communion; and thus there would be one fine for the prayers themselves, and another for the one who declines communion. This is grossly false, since that whole article concerns those who wish to share in all the sacred rites but are unwilling to take communion, who are known, among you Catholics, to be no longer such, nor to be regarded as Catholics, since they do not walk blamelessly in the law of the Lord. In the same way with the rest, there is a strange concealment of method, and fraud alone seems to lie beneath; almost each item is moved from its place and scattered, as if some Davus had been there who threw everything into confusion.

units.la: 3 Tertia tua fuit ars mala, mutati filii, dum effers more tuo maledicto, quæ in Edicto secus posita. Quis enim ferat, citari legem, verbis non suis? non suis dixi? imò penitus alienis, & à viperinâ glossâ detortis, in sensum planè contrarium, quale illud est Aduersus Catholicos, De perquirendis Catholicis, vt puniantur Catholici, leges stabiliri? Quasi vllæ apud nos leges ferantur in nomen illud; Imò in Papistas ibi dicitur: ita titulus, ita tenor, is stilus est legis totius. Sic enim estis; sic vt estis, audire debetis, vni homini, vnius hominis parti addicti, vt olim Donatistæ, & ex eo quòd sic vni addicti, Catholici esse non poteritis, nec de eo quod vniuersum est, (idem enim ἀπὸ [?] & vniuersum) nisi falsò nominari. Quale & illud, vbi lex Ecclesiam audire iubet, ad rem diuinam audiendam, tu iuberi dicis, (bonus legum citator) vt templa hæreticorum adeant, quò ibi hæreticorum sacrú intersint; quasi hæresis in ipsis terminis, eiusque tum templa, tum sacra Edicto stabiliantur.
units.tr: 3. Your third bad art was the changing of the words: when, in your usual manner, you carry off with curses what in the Edict is posited otherwise. For who could bear that a law be cited in words not its own? Not its own, I say? Nay, entirely alien, and twisted by your viperous gloss into a sense plainly contrary: such as that which the laws establish, "Against Catholics, on seeking out Catholics, that Catholics may be punished"? As if any laws were enacted among us under that title! Nay, the text says "against Papists": so is the title, so is the tenor, so is the style of the whole law. For that is what you are; and as you are, so you ought to be heard: bound to one man, to a part of one man, like the Donatists of old; and because you are thus bound to one man, you cannot be Catholics, nor can you be rightly so named in respect of what is universal (for the two words come from the same root). Similar is that place where the law commands that the Church be attended, that one may attend divine service, and you say (good citer of laws!) that they are ordered to go to the temples of heretics, there to attend the sacred rites of heretics; as if heresy were established by the Edict in these very terms, together with its temples and its sacred rites.

units.la: Præcipit lex de benedictio Sacramento cœnæ Dominicæ participando: tu statuere eam dicis, vt cœnam Hereticorum more sumant. Hoccine est referre legem? Quænam hanc tam barbara morem, permittat tellus? Non hæc summa Edicti est nostri, sed maledicti vestri. Nemo autem nostrûm Papa studuit vnquam, vt legerit ibi de cœnâ aliquâ à Caluino institutâ. Profundâ hæc Satanæ sunt, & vestra. Cœnam nostram Dominus ipse instituit, Paulus recensuit, & præiuit nobis nomine cœnæ Dominicæ: ita, vt recensuit; nos, nec aliter celebramus. Vos videritis, & Papa vester, de Missâ vestrâ, & crudâ victimâ, vnde nomen illud vobis, vnde res ipsa, annon prodierit vobis è gurgustio aliquo; annon Papæ alicuius constitutio sit, postquam mutulâssèt [?] institutum Domini, & parte eius alterâ, populum Domini fraudassèt. Simile verò tribus hiis & quartum, vt Rex inuadat duas tertias bonorum (quâ voce inuasit te Satanas, & oppleuit malitiâ cor tuum) quasi invasor dici possit odioso nomine, qui id adeat, quod ei Cutiatá lege legitimè rogatâ, adiudicatum sit. Simile & quintum, de carcere sicariorum & latronum; cùm ibi nec de sicariis vel latronibus vllâ mentio; & in carceribus ad quos vestri amandantur, ex genere hominum promiscuo sint, qui in ære alieno, qui Prætoris Edicto non parent, tam qui leuiter, quàm qui atrociter peccarunt; Nec opus fuit sicariorum adiunctum addere, nisi quia inuidiam inde vtcunque conflare voluisti.
units.tr: The law prescribes that the blessed Sacrament of the Lord's Supper be partaken of; you say it establishes that they take it "after the manner of the heretics." Is this what it means to report a law? "What land would permit such a barbarous custom?" This is not the substance of our Edict, but of your slander. Yet none of us Papists has ever taken care to read there anything about some supper instituted by Calvin. "These are the deep things of Satan," and yours. Our Supper the Lord himself instituted, Paul recounted, and he went before us with the name "the Lord's Supper"; as he recounted it, so we also celebrate it, and no otherwise. As to your Mass and your raw sacrifice, whence that name came to you, whence the thing itself, you and your Pope must see: whether it did not come forth to you from some hovel; whether it is not the decree of some Pope, after he had patched up (?) the institution of the Lord and defrauded the Lord's people of one half of it. Similar, however, is the third ground and the fourth: that "the king invades two thirds of the goods" (a word by which "Satan has entered into you, and filled your heart with malice") as if one could be called an "invader" in an odious sense, who approaches what has been adjudged to him by a law legitimately proposed in the assembly. Similar too is the fifth, "on the prison of assassins and robbers": whereas there is no mention there of assassins or robbers at all; and the prisons to which your people are sent are of a mixed sort of men, who are in debt, who do not obey the Praetor's Edict, both those who have sinned lightly and those who have sinned atrociously. Nor was there any need to add the word "assassins," unless you wished to stir up odium from it in some way.

units.la: 4 Postremò, vide ingenium hominis, quasi ex omni aștus dolíque genere contextum. Nam, vt principio superaddidit de suo, ac de novo conflauit, & percusit articulos qui nulli ibi sunt, per fraudem, nescio dicam, an malitiam, an vtramque: ita per vtramq; non imparem, tum malitiam, tum fraudem, subduxit alios data operâ, & de industriâ praeterijt, quos tamen praeterire minimè oportuit, si summam Edicti tibi (Lector) vt erat, repraesentare voluit. Eo autem solo nomine praeterijt, quòd per eos, duriora quædam quæ videri possunt inesse in lege, in Papistarum ipsorum commodum & fauorem, minuantur saltem, atque molliantur. 1. Prouisum ibi est & cautum, ne in duabus illis tertijs terrarum Regi (vt dictum est) adiudicatis comprehendi debeat, sed excipi plane, domus ipsa, & fundi, in quibus illis habitandi locus.
units.tr: 4. Lastly, see the man's character, as if woven from every kind of cunning and deceit. For just as at the beginning he added things of his own, and newly forged and struck articles which are not there at all, by fraud, I know not whether I should say by malice, or by both: so, by both, not unequally, both malice and fraud, he has deliberately and with purpose left out others, which nevertheless ought not to have been left out at all, if he had wished to set before you (reader) the substance of the Edict as it was. And he left them out for this reason alone: that through them, certain harsher things which might seem to be contained in the law are at least lessened and softened, to the advantage and favour of the Papists themselves. 1. Provision and caution is made there that, in those two thirds of the lands adjudged to the King (as has been said), the house itself and the estates in which their dwelling-place is shall not be included, but shall be plainly excepted.

units.la: 2. Tum si clocentur reliquæ dua cuiquam, id ita fiat, ne quid vel ædes, vel fundi detrimenti capiant. 3 Praeterea, etsi in famulatu suo, vel familiâ refractarium vllum Papistam retinere, sub certâ ibi poenâ interdictum fit: at id simul prouisum, ne hoc ad parentes se extendat, aut pupillos, quibus ex lege tutores, vel curatores sunt. 4 Tum ne de muliere vllâ coniugatâ exigatur multa, neque de marito eius, quantumuis illa ad Eucharistiam non accedat, siue, quoad marito conuixerit, siue postquam marito superstes fuerit.
units.tr: 2. Then, if the remaining two-thirds are let to anyone, this is to be done so that neither the houses nor the lands suffer any loss. 3. Moreover, although it is forbidden under a set penalty to keep any obstinate Papist in one's service or household, it is also provided that this does not extend to parents, or to wards who have guardians or curators under the law. 4. Likewise, no fine is to be exacted from any married woman, nor from her husband, however far she keeps away from the Eucharist, whether while she lives with her husband or after she has survived him.

units.la: Vbi, perspiciat facilè lector, abundare charitatem nostram, supra Papistarum illam & Romanam. Nec enim illi, totius Patriæ Patrem ipsum censuris eximunt, aut (quæ illas sequitur) subditorum à fide absolutione, in eoque (quantum quidem in ipsis est) gentem totam, & in eâ multa millena milia, quasi orphanos relinquunt cuius iam genti diripiendos; & tanquam ἁρπαγμα[?] abrepto per vim Palinuro. Atqui nos contrà, nec vel vni vllr familiæ ita grauiter incubamus, vt velimus, vel parente liberos priuari, vel pupillos Curatore. Ita, quod Pontifici videtur leue[?], in Dei ipsius Locum Tenentes exequi, quique superiorem in terrâ non agnoscunt, (vtcumque, cunque, totum ex eo politiæ corpus ruat in perniciem certam, & orbitatem:) id Regi nostro grauius videtur, quàm vt vel infimo cuiquam de subditis suis, velit infligi. Tanta est enim misericordia eius, in vel tenuissimum quemque, in vel familiæ etiam minimæ œconomiam, vt, quæ intra eam sunt naturæ vel fidei vincula, ea, legum suarum seueritate vel euerti, vel dissolui nullo modo patiatur.
units.tr: Here the reader will easily perceive that our charity abounds beyond that of the Papists and the Roman church. For they do not exempt even the Father of the whole country from censures, and (what follows from them) they absolve subjects from their allegiance to the faith; and so, as far as in them lies, they leave the whole nation, and in it many thousands of thousands, like orphans, to be torn apart, as if Palinurus had been seized and carried off by force. But we, on the contrary, do not press so heavily on any single family as to wish either parents deprived of their children or wards of their guardian. Thus, what seems a light matter to the Pontiff, to be carried out against the Vicars of God himself, who acknowledge no superior on earth (however and whatever this may be, the whole body of the state will collapse into certain ruin and bereavement), this seems to our King too grievous to be inflicted on even the humblest of his subjects. Such is his mercy towards the very least, even towards the management of the smallest household, that he will in no way allow the bonds of nature or of faith that lie within it to be overturned or dissolved by the severity of his laws.

units.la: Addo tribus hijs & quartum: vbi enim ad extrema dementum est, & mortis quis reus fit: hic tamen (quod in cæteris solenne semper est capite multatis, vt fiat) prouisum est ne fiat: ne vel dos vxori pereat, vel facultas liberū hæreditatis adeundæ, vel infamia iuris redundet in stirpem, vt vltra peccantem ipsum pœna non progrediatur, vt nulli suorum, præterquam ipsi soli, præiudicio sit. Prouisum etiam, vt quocunque demum tempore Papistæ cuiquam mens animúsque fuerit, conformem se reddendi, & iurandi iusiurandum: ex eo, fas vt ei sit, actionem vllam priorem, totúmque adeo iuris processum irritum facere, & possessionem adire suorum omnium. Vt verò, in extremo etiam actu sui similis sit, Primo ne medium, medio ne discrepet imum, vt vnde exorsa est summa eius, in eodem & terminetur (in mendacio (scilicet) verba ipsius sunt nouissima, Iuramentum in Edicto deferri contra potestatem Papæ in Principes Christianos. Nouissimum hoc eius mendacium, in verbis ipsis nouissimis, iam antè mihi nominatum, atque idem ipsum Omega mendaciociorum [?]. Hæc illa est Matthæi summa, ex tot mendacijs consummata.
units.tr: I add a fourth to these three: where someone is guilty of the utmost offence and becomes liable to death, yet (which is always customary in the case of those condemned to capital punishment) it is provided that this does not happen: so that the wife's dowry is not lost, nor the right of the children to inherit, nor does the infamy of the law spread to the stock, so that the punishment does not go beyond the offender himself, and so that it harms no one of his kin except himself alone. It is also provided that, at whatever time a Papist should have the mind and will to conform himself, and to swear the oath, it is lawful for him to make void any earlier action and the whole course of the law, and to take possession of all his kin's property. And indeed, so that in his final act too he may be like himself, "let the beginning not differ from the middle, nor the middle from the end": so that the sum of his argument may end where it began, namely in a lie. For his last words are: "An oath is imposed in the Edict against the power of the Pope over Christian princes." This final lie of his, in these very last words, I have already named before, and it is the very Omega of his lies. This is Matthew's summary, completed out of so many lies.

units.la: Proximum iam nobis est, vt de eo quæramus, eccqua illi causa fuerit iusta, in seueritatem eam, quæ verè ibi est in Edicto, tam acriter inuehendi, quasi in eo vno satis sit, ad Apologiam de mendacijs quæ dicit coarguendam. Vbi vim hanc videtur complecti argumentum eius, vt cùm iam omnium in oculis tot sint Edicti illius clausulæ, tam rigidæ, vt videri vult illas, exinde Lectori liquidò constet, Catholicos eius, erumnas hic ingentes sustinere, quò sic Authorem Apologiæ falsi teneat, qui dixerat nullam hîc conscientiæ causam grauiorem persecutionem sub Rege extitisse. Quò ergo, quod Regi semper in votis, quòque nihil illi vnquam antiquius, magna illa veritas hic semper præualeat, vincat semper, & triumphet (quod, vt in fronte libri fuit, ita in corde scriptoris) en, tibi jam (Lector) vera illius membra pandentur & scopus; perspectis ijs sedeto iudex, & sententiam ferto; illa Apologiæ affirmatio, & hæc Tarti negatio, vtra vtri præponderare debeat, ab vtrâ veritas sit; & quæ veritatem semper comitatur, pars potior, certa victoria.
units.tr: It is now next for us to inquire whether he had any just cause for so vehemently inveighing against the severity which truly is in the Edict, as if in that one point alone it were enough to refute the Apology concerning lies, which he says he is exposing. Here his argument seems to comprise this force: that, since so many clauses of that Edict are in everyone's eyes, and so harsh as he wishes them to appear, it should thence be plainly clear to the reader that his Catholics here endure enormous hardships; and so he might hold the author of the Apology to be false, who had said that no more serious persecution of conscience had arisen under the King. Therefore, so that what the King always desires, and nothing is ever dearer to him, that great truth may always prevail here, always conquer and triumph (which, as it was on the title-page of the book, so it is in the heart of the writer), behold, now, reader, its true limbs and aim will be laid open to you; having surveyed them, sit as judge and pronounce sentence: which of the two, the affirmation of the Apology or the negation of Tortus, ought to outweigh the other, on which side the truth lies; and the side which always accompanies the truth, the stronger part, has certain victory.

units.la: Verumtamen etiam illud priusquam aggredior, fac primum quæso cogites de tempore ipso, quo lata lex est. Tempus semper vim magnam habet; plus in illâ circumstantiâ, quàm in ipsâ sæpe substantiâ, ad res gerendas, momenti. Lata autem lex est, illi (vt hic loquimur) Parlamenti sessione illâ ipsâ sessione, quæ prima fuit & proxima, postquam horrendum illud, & iam iamque admittendum scelus, detectum est. Fac, quæso, vt & illud cogites, annon iusta Senatui populóque doloris causa, annon læsi animi, cùm considerent illis ipsis in ædibus, & subselliis, intra illos ipsos parietes, quorum abesse non potuit quin conspectus quotidianus eos admoneret, eisque in mentem subinde revocaret, quæ ibi in locum illum, inque ipsos immanis, & post homines natos, inaudita cædes, strages, clades designata tum esset, idque (quod apertè fassi sunt criminis conscij) zelo tantùm, vt obtinere posset hic religio Romana; idque intercedentibus ad consilium hoc, & rem totam procurantibus Presbyteris & Jesuitis, qui sæpe scelceratis illis Eucharistiam porrexerant, quíque ipsi cum scelceratis, ipsi magis scelerati, sumpserant sacramentum illud (Deum, vt appellant, suum) idque ad ipsorum animos atque fidem, ad hanc scilicet actionem tam piam confirmandam, & magis indies atque magis obligandam? Satis hæc, vt credo, valere potuerunt, ad Senatorum animos irritandos, cùm in flagrantia criminis hoc fieret, vt si etiam asperius aliquid tum statuissent: non id, credo, cuiquam, qui æquior modò esset, vel iniquum, vel mirum videretur.
units.tr: Nevertheless, before I proceed, I beg you first to consider the time itself at which the law was passed. Time always has great force; in conducting affairs, the circumstance often carries more weight than the substance itself. The law was passed (as we speak here) in that very session of Parliament which was the first and nearest after that horrible crime, now at hand and about to be admitted, was discovered. I ask you also to consider whether the Senate and the people did not have a just cause for grief, whether their minds were not wounded, when they considered that within those very buildings and benches, within those very walls, whose presence could not fail to remind them daily and to bring back to their minds, the monstrous slaughter, massacre and destruction, unheard of since men were born, was then being plotted against that place and against the men themselves; and this (as the guilty conspirators openly confessed) out of zeal alone, that the Roman religion might prevail here; and this with the Priests and Jesuits lending their counsel to the plan and managing the whole affair, who had often given the Eucharist to those wicked men, and who themselves, being more wicked than the wicked, had received that sacrament (which they call their God) together with them; and this, no doubt, in order to strengthen and bind more and more daily the minds and faith of these men to that so pious undertaking? These things, I believe, could well have been enough to stir the Senators' minds, since this was being done in the heat of the crime, so that if they had decided on something even harsher at that time, this, I believe, would not seem unjust or strange to anyone who was at all fair.

units.la: Ausim vero affirmare, vbi multitudo hominum tanta, hominum talium tanta, iusto dolore percitorum, iustâ etiam irâ (nam dolor addidit iram) contra illos, qui Regem, qui se qui quàm late patet Regnum totum, conati sic perfundere, vt nec parietibus, nec tectis parcere, si non seueram, sed sæuam aliquam Draconis legem, & sanguine[?] scriptam promulgassent, contra haeresin illam, quíque eam sectantur (ex qua quotannis pene pullulant fructus tam amari) Regem, qui quidem saperet, ex ipso rationis dictamine, & politica prudentia, cedere aliquantum turbae tantae, ita tum incensae, & graui, iustáque de causa ita incensa, debuisse. Certè, tempus non fuit refragandi. Parcius vero hic ista commemoro: legas enim haec apud Regem ipsum, multò & fusius, & ad vivum magis expressa.
units.tr: I would indeed venture to affirm that, where such a great multitude of men, of such men, was stirred by just grief and also by just anger (for grief had added anger) against those who had tried thus to drench the King, and as far as the whole kingdom extends, not sparing walls or roofs, against that heresy, and those who follow it (from which almost every year such bitter fruits sprout), it was fitting that the King, if he were wise, should yield somewhat to so great a tumult, so inflamed at that time, and inflamed for a grave and just cause. Certainly it was not a time for opposing. I mention these things more sparingly here; for you may read them in the King himself, much more fully and expressed more vividly.

units.la: Quae modò pollicitus sum, Edicti membra, nec qualia nuper Tortus, Absyrti diuulsa, sed suo loco posita, quaeque ipse sic agnoscat, de illis iam, Lector, sic habeto. Pro rerum quae ibi sanciuntur natura atque ratione, quatuor illius propagines videntur esse. Vna, de Refractariis in genere. Eos nos peculiari nomine, nec vsquam alibi noto quàm apud nos, Recusantes dicimus. Alia est de Apostatis, siue recidiuam passis. Tertia, de praestando Iuramento; cuius nos iam quaestio exercet. Vltima de iis, quae ad commodum Papistarum sancita sunt. De hac vero vltimâ, nisi pessimâ indole sit Tortus, & media nocte natus, etsi (vt video) gratias non meditatur, qui silentio premit quantum potest: at actionem, spero, haud vllam intentabit. Quo verior autem haec tibi herciscendi ratio constet esse, visum hic totius Edicti vim ob oculos ponere; non vt ille, quatuordecim, sed viginti duobus articulis comprehensam.
units.tr: Regarding the clauses of the Edict which I have just promised, not as Tortus recently tore them apart like Absyrtus, but placed in their proper order, and which he himself thus acknowledges, reader, you may now take the following as settled. In accordance with the nature and reason of the matters enacted there, they seem to be four branches of it. One concerns the Refractories in general. We call them by a special name, Recusants, a name not known anywhere else except among us. Another concerns Apostates, or those who have suffered relapse. The third concerns taking the Oath, which is now our question. The last concerns those things which have been sanctioned for the advantage of the Papists. Concerning this last one, unless Tortus is of the worst disposition and was born at midnight, although (as I see) he does not practise gratitude, he keeps silent as far as he can about it; yet I hope he will bring no lawsuit whatsoever. But so that this way of settling accounts with you may be shown to be more truthful, I have thought fit to set before your eyes the whole force of the Edict here, not as he did, comprised in fourteen articles, but in twenty-two.

units.la: 1. Sancitur, vt quicunque conuictus fuerit, quòd rei sacrae interesse pertinaciter recusârit; post autem conformem se reddiderit: ei vt non satis sit, si templa adeat, nisi & intra annum sacrae etiam Eucharistiae communicet, atque ita deinceps; semel saltem quotannis. Qui secus faxit, pecuniariâ multâ luat, anno primo viginti; secundo, quadraginta; tertio sexaginta librarum noftratium: sin vlli semel communicauerit, post detrectet iterum, quotannis sexaginta.
units.tr: 1. It is enacted that whoever has been convicted of stubbornly refusing to attend the sacred rite, and afterwards has conformed himself, shall not be satisfied merely by going to the churches, unless within the year he also receives the sacred Eucharist, and so on thereafter, at least once each year. Whoever acts otherwise shall pay a pecuniary fine: twenty pounds of our money in the first year, forty in the second, sixty in the third. But if he has once communicated and afterwards again refuses, sixty pounds each year.

units.la: Primum hoc est, in quo (vt vides) nihil vsquam de confirmatis confirmandisue Regina ELIZABETHAE legibus, sed neque vel nomen ipsum, vel legum, vel Regina Temerè ergò hoc, & falsò. Vnicum vero hoc nescio quo consilio (fide quidem non bonâ) diduxisse videtur Tortus in tertium & sextum; atque ita, de vno duo fecisse; fecisse dico; de duobus enim neutrum verè ponitur; utrique eorum attingit de suo.
units.tr: This first clause is, as you see, nowhere concerned with the laws of Queen Elizabeth on confirmed or to-be-confirmed (persons), but neither the name itself nor the laws, nor the Queen. Tortus has seemingly divided this single clause, with what intent I know not (certainly not in good faith), into a third and a sixth, and so has made two out of one; I say he has made two, for neither of the two is truly stated: he has attached to each of them something of his own. This is rashly and falsely done.

units.la: 2 Quotannis semel deferantur ad iudices, eorum nomina, qui de menstrua absentia notati sunt: etiam si quos habeant liberos nonennes[?], vel supra, qui apud parentes agant: tum seruorum etiam nomina. Ni deferantur, decem florenis multantur, quorum id ex lege munus est.
units.tr: 2. Once a year the names of those who have been noted for monthly absence shall be reported to the judges, even if they have children, not a few (?), or more, who live with their parents; also the names of their servants. If they are not reported, they are fined ten florins, and it is by law the duty of (a certain person) to do so.

units.la: Secundum hoc, Torti quoque; & in eo bis mendax; Duplicauit enim multam, & pro decem florenorum multa, viginti posuit. At illud vbi iuberi dicit, vt inquirant Catholicos omnis aetatis, mendacium est hyperbolicum. Inquirunt enim non nisi nouennes, nec eos vt rei sint; forte vt de familiae numero constet. Nec enim lege apud nos vlla inquiri potest in quenquam vt reus sit, qui annum aetatis decimum sextum non attigerit.
units.tr: In accordance with this clause, Tortus too; and in it he lies twice. For he doubled the fine, and in place of a fine of ten florins, he has put twenty. But where he says it orders them "to inquire after Catholics of every age," that is a hyperbolic lie. For they inquire only of those under nine years, and not so that they may be liable; perhaps so that the number of the household may be established. For under our law no one can be inquired after as liable who has not reached the age of sixteen years.

units.la: 3 Potestas iudicibus fit, vt statis temporibus, quibus ius dici solet, bis, quaterue in anno, audiant offensas cuiusmodi, atque statuant in reos ex legis sententia. Quodsi tum subducant se qui rei sunt; praeconio publico sistendi sunt, in terminum proximum iuridicum: quo tempore, ni se steterint, pro confessis habeantur.
units.tr: 3. Power is given to the judges that, at the set times when justice is customarily dispensed, twice or four times in the year, they hear the offences of every kind, and decide upon the guilty according to the sentence of the law. But if those who are liable then keep themselves away, they shall be summoned by public proclamation to the next court day; and if they do not appear at that time, they shall be held as having confessed.

units.la: Hic Tortus statui dicit, de Catholicis acriter puniendis qui Communionem sumere recusant. Falsò autem. Nihil enim habetur in tertio de poena eorum. Vbi vero habetur (in primo scilicet) non Catholicos passim, qui Communionem sumere recusant, ea multa attingit; nec alios, quam qui, cum templa prius adirent nobiscum, ac caeteris sacris interessent, post iterum defecisunt, non quidem à caeteris sacris, sed à cœnâ Domini sumendâ. At hij vobis, puto, Schismatici sunt, Catholici non sunt, saltem non immaculati, sed maculosi Catholici.
units.tr: Here Tortus says that it is decreed to punish Catholics severely who refuse to receive Communion. But that is false. For nothing is contained in the third clause about their penalty. Where it is contained (namely in the first clause), it does not touch on Catholics in general who refuse to receive Communion, nor on any others than those who, having first gone to the churches with us and taken part in the other sacred rites, afterwards fell away again, not indeed from the other sacred rites, but from receiving the Lord's Supper. But these, I suppose, are "schismatics" to you, not Catholics; at least not "unspotted" Catholics, but "spotted Catholics."

units.la: 4 Ediciur, vt qui pertinacis absentia à sacris legitimè conuictus fuerit, (vt legis quae iamdudum eâ de re rogata fuerat) Paschae termino vel Michaelis, qui proximè tum subsequetur postquam ita conuictus fuerit, soluat fisco Regio, multa nomine, libras nostrates viginti pro ratione mensium qui tabulis accusatorijs comprehensi sunt: atque vt eiusdem deinceps multa in menses post singulos teneatur, citra novam ullam in iudicio postulationem, praterquam, si dua tertia terrarum in manu Regia sint. Hoc autem, quoadusq; reus legi pareat, de sacris adeundis.
units.tr: 4. It is enacted that whoever has been lawfully convicted of obstinate absence from the sacred rites (as by a law long since passed on that matter) shall pay to the royal exchequer, by way of a fine, twenty of our pounds for each month that is comprehended in the accusing tables, at the term of Easter or Michaelmas that next follows after he has been so convicted; and that he be bound to pay the same fine for each following month, without any new suit in court, except if two thirds of his lands are in the Crown's hand. This, moreover, is so long as the offender obeys the law regarding attendance at the sacred rites.

units.la: Nihil vero hoc articulo vel accedit vel decedit legi diu iam latæ. Id tantùm cautur, ut vbi (alio post huius Edicti articulo) fisco datur optio, malitne duas terrarum tertias, an viginti libras in mensem: ibi si duas tertias terrarum optauit fiscus, ne & viginti quoque libras illas possit exigere, id est, ne utrique pœnæ reus obnoxius sit. Hæc huius articuli mens est. At Tortus ita rem refert, ac si nona articulo hoc pœna in absentes à sacris, & de nouo rogata esset, quæque priore aliquâ lege pridem sancita non fuisset: viciose vero illud, & malitiose.
units.tr: Nothing in this article either adds to or takes away from the law that was passed long ago. This only is provided: that where (by another article of this Edict) the exchequer is given a choice, whether it prefers two thirds of the lands or twenty pounds a month, then if the exchequer has chosen two thirds of the lands, it may not also exact those twenty pounds, that is, the offender is not liable to both penalties. This is the purpose of this article. But Tortus reports the matter as though a ninth penalty against absentees from the sacred rites were laid down by this article, and newly enacted, and one that had not been previously sanctioned by any earlier law: which is faulty and malicious.

units.la: 5 De ratione cavetur, quâ certiores reddantur qui fisco præsunt, quid à quoque, & quo tempore persolui debeat: tum, si cessatum sit à quoquam in persoluendo, quâ ratione multa leuari possit.
units.tr: 5. Provision is made for informing those who preside over the exchequer as to what must be paid, by whom, and at what time; then, if anyone has been remiss in paying, by what means the fine may be lightened.

units.la: Huic vero quod respondeat, nihil apud Tortum.
units.tr: As to what he might answer to this, Tortus has nothing.

units.la: 6. Cùm de multâ illâ viginti librarum compertum sit, magis onerosam esse eam, iis qui tenuiore fortunâ sunt, quàm qui ampla: quodq; ditiores hi, dum terris suis sibi frui datur, viginti libras malunt pendere, unde illis, etiam multâ solutâ copiosè superesset; quod verò ita superesset, in Iesuitas insumunt, aliosq;, qui regno huic Reipublicæque infesti sunt, edicitur, ut fisco Regio optio fiat, utrùm viginti libras menstruatim accipere, an verò illarum nomine malit duas tertias adire terrarum, relictâ Refractarijs tertiâ suâ. Itatamen, r.[?] ut cuiq; bonæ fidei creditori saluum maneat ius suum debiti sui exigendi: 2. ut in duabus illis tertijs (quas Fiscus adeat) fundus ipse primarius, vel ædes, comprehendi non debeat, in quibus commorari solent: 3. ut alteri, qui & Refractarius ipse sit, duas illas tertias dimittere ne liceat: 4. ut si cuiquam locentur duæ illæ tertiæ, de sartis tectis præstandis idonea sit cautio.
units.tr: 6. Since it has been ascertained that this fine of twenty pounds is more burdensome to those of slender means than to the wealthy; and since these richer men, while they are allowed to enjoy their own estates, prefer to pay the twenty pounds, from which they would still have a plentiful surplus even after paying the fine; and since they spend what is left over on the Jesuits and others who are hostile to this kingdom and commonwealth, it is ordered that the royal exchequer have the option of receiving twenty pounds monthly, or of choosing rather in place of those sums to take possession of two thirds of the lands, the recusants keeping their third. Provided, however: (1) that each creditor in good faith keep his lawful right to exact his debt; (2) that in those two thirds (which the exchequer takes) the principal estate itself, or the house, in which they are accustomed to dwell, shall not be included; (3) that it be not lawful for the one who is himself a recusant to transfer those two thirds to another recusant; (4) that if those two thirds are let to anyone, there shall be sufficient security for the upkeep of the buildings and roofs.

units.la: At quod in Edicto hoc sextum ⁊ Torto quintum est. In sexto autem suo, denuo iam inculcat, de pœnâ non communicantium Eucharistiâ, quâ de re nihil quicquam articulo hoc, nec nisi semel cauetur in Edicto, idque membro primo. Sed neque in illo, alia legis mens, quàm quæ explicata nobis, responso ad tertium. Æquè verò in hoc atque in illo mendax, & malâ fide. Peccat itidem in eo non leviter, dum statui dicit multam viginti librarum, leue onus esse copiosis hominibus. Non enim id dicitur sed compertum esse, quòd ditiores illi, abusi hac moderatione legis, cùm etiam post solutionem menstruam copiosè satis haberent; alerent ex residuo Iesuitas, & eius generis alios, ciues perditos, & perniciosos. Quò ergo ratio par seruetur in poenâ partiendâ in copiosos hosce; potestas Fisco fit, viginti libras illas repudiandi, atque eius loco duas tertias terrarum sublegendi.
units.tr: But as for what in this Edict is the sixth article and in Tortus the fifth: in his sixth he again urges, concerning the penalty for not receiving the Eucharist, a matter about which nothing is provided in this article, nor is anything provided in the Edict except in the first clause. But neither is the intent of the law in that clause other than what we have explained in our answer to the third; equally, then, he lies and acts in bad faith here as well. He errs in this not lightly, when he says that a fine of twenty pounds is a light burden for wealthy men. For this is not said, but it has been ascertained that those richer men, abusing this moderation of the law, since even after the monthly payment they had plenty left over, would feed from the remainder Jesuits, and other citizens of that sort, ruined and pernicious. So that, in order that a proportion be preserved in dividing the penalty among these wealthy men, power is given to the exchequer to refuse those twenty pounds and to take in their place two thirds of the lands.

units.la: 7 Quò exploratum sit quoad fidem in Regem, quo animo sint subditi, potestas sit Episcopo cuiuis in Diæcesi suâ, vel Eirenarchis duobus (quorum tamen, de Præsidentibus vnus sit) cuicunq;, qui de Nobilium numero non sit, quique decimum octauum annum agat, maiorue natu sit; qui quidem postulatum iam ante in iudicio pertinacis à sacris absentiæ; siue qui intra annum tum elapsum Sacramento bis non communicauerit; siue etiam qui ignotus eberrauerit, dum, vt fit, aliquâ se iter habere fingit, (cùm se tamen, de eo rogatus, non diffiteatur, sacris interesse nolle, vel superiore anno bis Sacramento non communicasse :) Iuramentum, quod nemo post articulo sequitur, deferendi..
units.tr: 7. In order that it may be ascertained, as far as concerns faith toward the King, what disposition the subjects have, the bishop in each diocese, or two justices of the peace (of whom one shall be among the presiding justices), shall have power to examine anyone who is not of the number of the nobles, who is eighteen years of age or older: whether he has been already convicted in court of obstinate absence from the sacred rites; or whether within the year then past he has not twice received the Sacrament; or even whether he has wandered about unknown, while, as is usual, he pretends that he is on some journey (when nevertheless, being asked about it, he does not deny that he is unwilling to attend the sacred rites, or that in the previous year he did not twice receive the Sacrament): the oath, which the following article describes as the one to be administered to anyone, is to be tendered.

units.la: Torto[?] hoc septimum non est; Quod illi est, de ijs est, quæ relabuntur in crimen templa non frequentandi. Mendacium verò & illud. Nihil enim ibi tale, sed nec in Edicto toto. Si cubi autem de Relapsis mentio fit in Edicto, in primo membro est, nec inde tamen relatum, nisi fide pessimâ. Nam quæ ibi recidiua taxantur, eorum modò est, quiurbi[?] communicauerunt mensâ sacrâ, relabuntur pòst, nec per annum integrum communicant. At, quoad recidiuam vllam de templis frequentandis, vel non frequentandis, figmentum merum.
units.tr: This seventh is not Tortus's; what he has is about those who relapse into the crime of not frequenting the churches. That too is a lie. For there is nothing of that kind there, nor in the whole Edict. If anywhere mention is made of "relapsed" persons in the Edict, it is in the first clause, and not even from there is it reported, except in the worst faith. For those who are censured there as "relapsed" are only those who have received the sacred table, and afterwards fall away and do not communicate for a whole year. But as for any "relapse" concerning the frequenting or non-frequenting of churches, it is pure invention.

units.la: 8 Statuitur, si quis iuramentum delatum repudiat, nec de numero Nobilium sit, vt in carcerem communem amandetur, ad proximum usque conventum iuridicum. Quodsi conuentum tum illo, publicè in ipso Iudicium consessu delatum ei denuò, denuò respuat, pœnam eam incurrat, quæ est amissionis bonorum, & carceris perpetui: mulieres tamen coniuges ibi excipiuntur, quibus nulla pœna est nisi solius carceris, nec eius, nisi tantisper dum iuramentum ita delatum iubeant.
units.tr: 8 It is laid down that if anyone refuses an oath that has been tendered to him, and is not of the rank of the Nobles, he shall be sent to the common prison until the next court sitting. But if, when the oath has been tendered to him again and again in the very court of justice, in public, he still refuses it, he incurs the penalty of forfeiture of goods and perpetual imprisonment. Married women, however, are excepted: for them the only penalty is imprisonment alone, and not even that for longer than while they are ordered to take the oath so tendered.

units.la: Octauum hoc quoque Torti est; sed & nonum eius octaui huius pars est. Verum carcer ibi in Edicto communis est, is scilicet, quò mandari solent homines qui laborant ære alieno, atque adeo plerique alij, qui Prætoris decreto non parent: Carcerem hunc Torti, vt horrorem incutiat, sed vanum & falsum, Sicariorum carcerem & latronum dicit; sed de suo dicit, extra Edictum scilicet, nec latronis enim ibi vsquam, nec sicarij nomen est. Tum quod generatim ponit, si quis recusset, vt amittat bona, & perpetuo in carcere sit, non oportuit ita positum. Non enim qui minor sit quàm annorum octodecem, quenquam attingit octaui hic articulus.
units.tr: The eighth is also Tortus's own invention; but his ninth is part of this eighth. Now the common prison in the Edict is that to which men are usually sent who are in debt, and indeed many others who do not obey the decree of the Praetor. This prison Tortus, to stir up horror (but an empty and false horror), calls the prison of assassins and robbers; but he says this on his own authority, outside the Edict, for there is nowhere in it any word for robber or assassin. Again, where he states in general terms if anyone refuses, so that he loses his goods and is kept in prison for life, he ought not to have put it so. For this article of the eighth does not touch anyone who is younger than eighteen years.

units.la: 9 Formula ipsa iuramenti, conceptis verbis, hoc Edicti membro ponitur.
units.tr: 9 The form of the oath itself, in set words, is given in this clause of the Edict.

units.la: Pars & hæc octaui est, in eaque peccat antiquum Tortus. Mulieres enim nuptæ excipiendæ erant, quibus solius carceris pœna est, si præfractè respuant iuramentum, nec nisi quoad ita præfractè respuant.
units.tr: This too is part of the eighth, and in it the old Tortus errs. For married women were to be excepted, for whom the penalty is only imprisonment, if they stubbornly refuse the oath; and only so long as they refuse it stubbornly.

units.la: 10 Cautetur, ne ad actionem intentatam, siue de re diuinâ neglectâ, siue de non sumptâ Eucharistiâ, vtli liceat diuerticula iuris quærere, ex, siue apicum defectu, siue alio quouis formulario, sed vt rectâ rem petat, & de facto suo vel affirmet, vel neget; interfuisse nimirum rei diuinæ; Sacramenti participem fuisse. Quodsi tamen quispiam in iudicio postulatus, de obedientiâ suâ in futurum respondeat, quocunque id tempore faciat, statim vt actionem institutam, ac processum iuris omnem, irritum facere liceat, nec Edicto obnoxius sit.
units.tr: 10 Care is taken that, in an action brought either for neglecting divine service or for not receiving the Eucharist, it shall not be lawful to seek legal loopholes, whether from a defect in the writs or from any other form of pleading; but that the party should claim the matter directly, and either affirm or deny his own act: namely, whether he was present at divine service, whether he was a partaker of the sacrament. But if anyone, when summoned in court, answers concerning his future obedience, at whatever time he does so, it shall be lawful at once to make the action brought, and the whole course of the law, void, and he shall not be liable to the Edict.

units.la: At quod Torto decimum est, adeo est enorme mendacium, vt nec pater ipse mendacij par ei possit fingere: totum, quantum quantum, ex Torti cerebro. Nam nec tertiâ vice Iuramentum proponi fas, nec de eo quenquam in capitis discrimen vocari, nec de totâ hac re verbum in Edicto. Tum verò in vndecimo Torti, quod videtur decimo huic respondere; vide frontem hominis, vim suam obtinere (ait) tabulas accusatorias, non obstante quocunque errore, qui in accusatione formandâ literæ contigerit. Partem legis allegat, quod reliquum est omittit : nam quod mox sequitur praecidit, praeterquam si inficietur factum, Templum, scilicet, adÿsse se, Eucharistiam accepisse. Hac enim parte si tabulae verae non sint, licet vim earum totam euertere. Id tantum agitur, ne delusorio, vel dilatorio responso locus hîc fit ex causidicorum formulis. At quae est, de accusatione totâ depellendâ, clausula benigna, eam perfidè dissimulat.
units.tr: But the tenth point in Tortus is such an enormous falsehood that the father of lies himself could hardly invent its equal: the whole of it, however much there is, comes from Tortus's brain. For it is not permitted to tender the oath a third time, nor to summon anyone to peril of life over it, and there is not a word about the whole matter in the Edict. Then, in Tortus's eleventh, which seems to answer to this tenth, he says: Look at the face of the man: the accusing tables (he says) have their force, notwithstanding any error that may occur in framing the accusation in writing. He cites part of the law and omits what remains; for he cuts off what immediately follows, unless he denies the fact, namely, that he went to the church and received the Eucharist. For if the tables are not true in this part, it is permitted to overturn all their force. The point is only to prevent a place being made here for an evasive or dilatory answer drawn from the formulas of the lawyers. But the kindly clause which exists for clearing the whole accusation, he treacherously passes over.

units.la: XI. Cùm & illud habeatur pro explorato, qui ultrò peregrè in militiam profecti sunt exterorum Principum, plerumque ab officio suo, quà in Deum, quà in Regem, abduci per transfugas quosdam nostros, & Iesuitas: cavetur, ne quis Regno exeat militaturus vspiam, neue ex aliâ causâ egressus, militet Principi cuiquam extero seu Potestati, nisi suscepto priùs iuramento hoc in Lege posito: qui secus fecit, vt pro felone habeatur. Pariter & ÿ, qui Equestris ordinis sunt, vel superioris villius, aut qui functi aliquo castrensi munere, vt ne exeant regno in militiam, neue cuiquam militent, nisi syngraphum priùs dent, & cum fideiussore geminose obstringant, (summa autem sit, viginti librarum, cautionis nomine) ne Papae reconcilientur, vel in coniuratione vllâ sint contra Regem, actu vel consensu, aut celent vllam, quacunque tandem ratione sibi cognitam.
units.tr: XI. Since it is also held as certain that those who of their own accord have gone abroad to the wars of foreign princes are for the most part drawn away from their duty, both to God and to the King, by certain of our own deserters and by the Jesuits, it is provided that no one shall leave the realm to serve as a soldier anywhere, nor, leaving for some other cause, serve any foreign prince or power, unless he has first taken the oath laid down in this Law: whoever does otherwise shall be held a felon. Likewise also, those who are of the equestrian order, or of a higher rank, or who have discharged any military office, shall not leave the realm to serve as soldiers, nor serve anyone, unless first they give a written bond and bind themselves doubly with a surety (the sum being twenty pounds, by way of security), that they will not be reconciled to the Pope, nor be in any conspiracy against the King, either in act or in consent, nor conceal any such, by whatever means it may come to their knowledge.

units.la: Vndecimum hoc discerpsit Tortus, atque ex eo duodecimum, & decimumtertium concinnauit: in quibus & omissa illi legis ratio, malus mos (nempe quòd fraude Iesuitarum, animum mutant, qui trans mare currunt) unde bona lex orta est. Et perduelles (in duodecimo) dicit habendos; falsò; cùm felones tantùm dicat lex. Aliud autem longè apud nos crimen, alia quoque poena, perduellis, & felonis. Tum, vbi de coniuratione non faciendâ, non reticendâ conditio etiam est; eam silentio praeterit.
units.tr: Tortus has torn this eleventh to pieces, and from it has patched together his twelfth and thirteenth; in which he has omitted the reason of that law, the evil custom (namely, that by the trickery of the Jesuits men change their minds when they run across the sea), from which the good law arose. And he says that traitors (in the twelfth) are to be held as such; falsely, since the law says only felons. Moreover, among us the crime is quite different, and the punishment also different, for traitor and felon. Then, where there is also a condition about not conspiring and not concealing, he passes over it in silence.

units.la: 12. Siquis de subditis Regijs quenquam, trans mare, vel in ipso maris transitu, seu alio quocunque loco, intra ditiones Regias vel absoluere tentet, vel abducere à naturali suâ obedientiâ Regi debitâ, aut Papae reconciliet Sedive Romanae; vel eò adducat, vt obedientiam suam spondeat, cuicunque authoritati praetensae, seu Sedis Romanae, seu exteri vel Principi vel Potestatis cuiuscunque: Qui fecerit, quiue instigator, consultor, aut patrocinator, conscius fuerit, lasæ Maiestatis crimine teneatur. Eadémque ut pœnâ plectatur, cui persuasum est, quiue abductus à fidelitate, vel reconciliatus, vel eiusmodi pratensa authoritati fidem spoponderit. Qui tamen ita reconciliati, si intra sextum à reditu suo diem, Regiæ Maiestati illiusque legibus parituros fidem dederint, suscepto eo quod hac lege propositum est, atque altero illo (quod Elizabethae primo conceptum olim) Primatus Iuramento, eiu[?] ut hoc nomine lex ista capitalis ne fiet. Qui inferioris ordinis sunt: ut peragantur rei, coram rerum capitalium Quæsitoribus, aut qui de subsellio Regio Iudices sunt, ex lege Maiestatis lata; idque quasi eâ ipsâ in provincia peccâssent, quâ primum eis manus iniecta est. Qui vero de ordine sunt Procerum: ut in eos statuatur, per Pares suos, Iudices Honorarios.
units.tr: 12. If anyone attempts to absolve any of the King's subjects, or to draw them away from their natural obedience owed to the King, or to reconcile them to the Pope and the See of Rome, whether beyond the sea, or in the very passage over the sea, or in any other place within the King's dominions; or to bring them to this, that they pledge their obedience to any pretended authority, whether of the See of Rome, or of any foreign prince or power whatsoever: whoever does this, or whoever is an instigator, adviser, or patron, or is privy to it, shall be held guilty of the crime of treason. And the same penalty shall be inflicted on the one who has been persuaded, or who has been drawn away from allegiance, or reconciled, or has pledged faith to such pretended authority. Yet those who have been so reconciled, if within six days from their return they give their pledge to obey the Royal Majesty and its laws, having taken the oath proposed in this law, and that other oath of Supremacy conceived in the first year of Elizabeth, this capital law shall not be made on that account. Those who are of the inferior rank are to be tried, before the judges of capital crimes, or those who are judges on the royal bench, under the law of majesty passed; and this as if they had sinned in that very province in which they were first laid hands on.
