But those who are of the order of the nobles: that sentence be pronounced against them by their peers, as Honorary Judges.

units.la: Hoc Torto ultimum est, in quo bis falsi tenetur: verba ponit Edicti, quasi fide Ecclesia loqueretur. Totum vero hoc commentitium est. Nec enim ea res agitur; tantùm ne à Reipublica, & nativâ in Regem fide discedant: tantùm ne Papæ reconcilientur, & vel ipsius authoritati prætensæ, vel extero cuiquam Principi seu Potestati fidem obstringant. Tum quod secundò iam iterat de Iuramento Regio, nusquâ id ibi dicitur, Iuramentum contra potestatem Papæ in Principes Christianos, id tantùm; Iuramentum Edicto hoc propositum. Atque ita unde exorsus est, à mendacio, in eodem illi summa terminatur. Sunt verò & alia Edicti membra à Torto prætermissa: Nam cautetur,
units.tr: This is the last point in Tortus, in which he is caught in falsehood twice: he sets out the words of the Edict as if the Church spoke by its faith. But this whole thing is made up. For that matter is not the subject; it is only that they should not depart from the Commonwealth and from natural allegiance to the King; only that they should not be reconciled to the Pope, nor bind themselves by faith either to his pretended authority or to any foreign prince or power. Then, because he now repeats a second time about the Royal Oath, nowhere is it said in it an oath against the power of the Pope over Christian princes; that is all; the oath set forth in this Edict. And so the matter with which he began, a falsehood, is in the same way the sum with which he ends. There are, however, other clauses of the Edict which Tortus has passed over. For it is provided:

units.la: 13. Siquis à re diuinâ abest diebus Dominicis (ex lege primo Elizabethae lata) multa ei sit femisfloreni, in stipem & eleemosynam eroganda eâ, qui in parœciâ illâ sunt pauperes. Qui vero huius Edicti multam soluerit, ut alteri illi, in Edicto priore, obnoxius non erit.
units.tr: 13. If anyone is absent from divine service on the Lord's days (under the law passed in the first year of Elizabeth), he shall be fined half a florin, to be given in alms and charity to those who are poor in that parish. But whoever has paid the fine of this Edict shall not be liable to the earlier one in the Edict.

units.la: 14. Siquis seruum alat, aut aduenam contubernio excipiat, qui rei sacræ recusset interesse, nisi legitimâ causâ impeditus, id si sciens prudens fecerit, multa ei in mensem dicitur (quamdiu ita penes se in familiâ retinuerit) decem librarum. At id simul sancitur, ut si Parentum alter, cui res vel ædes de suis non sunt: ut si pupillus; si custodia alicuius, ex authoritate vllâ publica mandatus; liceat apud se habere, atque [illegible, ~2 letters], quantumuis sacra adire recusantem.
units.tr: 14. If anyone maintains a servant, or receives a stranger into his household, who refuses to be present at sacred worship, unless hindered by a lawful cause, and he does this knowingly and wittingly, he is fined ten pounds for a month (for as long as he keeps such a person in his household). But at the same time it is enacted that if one of the parents, to whom the goods or house do not belong, as a ward, or one under guardianship by any public authority, may keep such a person with him, and [illegible, ~2 letters], even though he refuses to attend the sacred services.

units.la: 15 Si, Decreto Iudicis ad Provincia Prefectum transmisso, aut alium quenquam cui id exequendi ius est, de refractarij alicuius Papistæ prehensione, qui, ex eo quod refractarius sit, sub excommunicationis censura manent; sancitur, ut fas sit Præfecto (si aliter nequit) ædes eius intrare per vim; quodsi resistat, etiam vicinia opem advocare, ut educat inde, & incu-stodiam det.
units.tr: 15 If, the judge's decree having been sent to the Prefect of the province, or to any other person who has the right to carry it out, for the apprehension of some recusant Papist who, because he is a recusant, remains under the censure of excommunication, it is enacted that the Prefect may (if he cannot otherwise manage it) enter his house by force; and if he resists, that he may also call upon the neighbourhood for help, to bring him out and place him in custody.

units.la: 16 In admissa omnia contra Edictum hoc inquiri poterit, atque animaduerti per Regij subsellij[?] Iudices; vel eos qui in Provincias peragrant ut ius dicant: seu Quæsitores rerum capitalium. Quæ vero citra læsam Maiestatem consistunt[?], ab Eirenarchis Provinciarum, quo tempore Trimestres Conuentus agunt.
units.tr: 16 All offences committed against this Edict may be inquired into and punished by the judges of the Royal bench, or by those who travel through the provinces to administer justice, or by the commissioners for capital crimes. Those which do not touch on treason are to be dealt with by the Justices of the Peace of the counties at the time when they hold their quarterly sessions.

units.la: 17 Statuitur, quicunque demum felonie reus peractus fuerit, ex Edicto hoc violato; ut (quod in reatu illo apud nos fere fit) dos uxori ne pereat, neue heredes infamiæ iuris obnoxij sint, aut hereditate exclusi: sed ut prærogatiua sanguinis fruantur, & liberè hereditatem adeant.
units.tr: 17 It is enacted that whoever is convicted of felony for violating this Edict (as commonly happens among us in such a charge) shall not thereby lose his wife's dowry, nor his heirs be subject to the penalties of infamy or be excluded from inheritance; but that they shall enjoy the privilege of blood and take up the inheritance freely.

units.la: 18 Siquis ex eo capite, actionem in quenquam instituat, quod fecerit inseritne[?] quæ ad Edicti huius executionem spectent: reo fas sit in Genere, hunc sibi Causæ Statum constituendi, & per idoneas rationes probandi. Quæ ita fecit, ea se ex mente legis fecisse.
units.tr: 18 If anyone brings an action against someone on that ground, for having done something which pertains to the execution of this Edict, the defendant is permitted, in general terms, to establish his own state of the case and to prove it by suitable reasons. Whatever he has done in this way, he is taken to have done in accordance with the intention of the law.

units.la: 19 Cauetur, ne per Edictum hoc fraus ulla fiat Iurisdictioni Ecclesiasticæ; sed ut liberæ etiam maneant Censuræ eius omnes, in Refractarios, quibus uti fas fuit, ante legem hanc rogatam.
units.tr: 19 Care is taken that no fraud is practised through this Edict upon the ecclesiastical jurisdiction; but that all its censures remain free against the recusants, which it was lawful to use before this law was enacted.

units.la: 20 Sancitur, ne uxoris non communicantis pertinacia, redundet in maritum, aut is multa cuiusquam rei sit propter uxoris delictum: neue mulier ipsa, iam vidua, & sui Iuris facta, multam eius luat, quod nupta peccauit.
units.tr: 20 It is enacted that the obstinacy of a wife who does not conform shall not fall back upon her husband, or make him liable to a fine for another's fault; nor shall a woman who is now a widow, and has become her own mistress, pay a fine for what she did while married.

units.la: 21 Quibus in causis Episcopo ius est, vel duobus Eirenarchis, Iuramentum (de quo iam ante mentio) cuiuis, qui de inferiore ordine sit, deferendi: in ijsdem ipsis, idem ius sit quibusdam de sanctiore Regis Consilio Dominis, ab ijs, qui de Nobilium numero apud nos sunt, & decimum octauum annum excesserint, illud ipsum Iuramentum exigendi. Quodsi præstare renuant, (dum ne mulieres sint nuptæ) una est eademque pœna, bonorum publicationis, & carceris perpetui.
units.tr: 21 In those cases in which the bishop, or two justices of the peace, have the right to tender the oath (of which mention has been made above) to anyone of inferior rank, the same right shall belong, in the same cases, to certain lords of the more honourable Privy Council, of those who are among our nobility and have passed their eighteenth year, to exact that same oath. If they refuse to take it (provided they are not married women), the penalty is one and the same: forfeiture of goods and perpetual imprisonment.

units.la: 22 Quodsi quis peregrè in militiam profecturus nauem soluat, ex vllo quinque Portuum Nobiliorum, vlloue qui eis subsunt alio, Illustri Portuum illorum Limenarchæ, potestas datur, eiusque qui vices illius obtinet, Sacramenti huius illis deferendi.
units.tr: 22 If anyone about to set out abroad on military service puts to sea from any of the five chief Cinque Ports, or from any other port subordinate to them, the power is given to the Lord Warden of those ports, or to his deputy, to tender this Oath to them.

units.la: Propago, vti vides, Lector, prima de Refractarijs est in genere, multi autem eius ramusculi sunt. Vt verò iustam subesse causam videas, non communi illa ratione, quæ apud omnes valet, sed peculiari etiam quadam, quæ ad nos spectat, cur homines hij præfracti & contumaces, qui sacris se subducunt, legibus hic magis quàm alibi obnoxij esse debeant; operæ precium facturus videor, si rem repetam ab origine, quando scilicet, quaque occasione, genus hoc hominum primùm hic apud nos emerserit.
units.tr: As you see, reader, the first line of descent, concerning recusants in general, has many small branches. But so that you may see that there is a just cause, not only on the common ground which holds good for everyone, but also on a particular ground which concerns us, why these stubborn and contumacious men, who withdraw from our services, ought to be more liable to the laws here than elsewhere, I think it worth while to go back to the source: namely, when, on what occasion, this kind of men first emerged here among us.

units.la: Ineunte hic regnum Reginâ (exceptis aliquot de Clero Mariano) non multi præterea fuerunt, qui sacris tum nostris & ritibus abstinerent. Satis hoc superque notum ijs, qui per ætatem possunt adhuc prima illa Reginæ tempora recordari. Tanta quidem tum eorum paucitas, vt per aliquot lustra, Recusantem esse, quid sibi vellet, ignotum penitus; necdum enim nata hic apud nos vox ipsa, vel titulus Recusantis. Vel ex vno etiam hoc facilè id sciat Lector, numero fuisse non magno: quòd silerent Leges, quòd nihil actum in Senatu de ijs, toto decennio. Fuisset autem actum lege aliquâ vel Senatusconsulto, nisi numero fuissent contemnendo. Intererat enim Reipub. eos non negligere, si ad numerum tum aliquem excreuissent. Tam verò exploratum hoc, vt cùm sisteretur pro tribunali reus Garnettus, hócque illi, quod modò dixi, de numero tum exiguo obiectum esset, diffiteri non posset; id tandem diceret, nonnullos quidem, quos ipse vel nôssel, vel sic inaudissem [?], à sacris nostris per id tempus abfuisse. Nec si in hac tantâ Regni amplitudine, abfuerunt tum nonnulli, momentum in eo magnum: nobis enim ad causæ caput satis, si proluuies illa, quæ pòst fuit, Recusantium, ex Pij censurâ, (quasi ex pluuiâ ranæ,) prognata primùm atque propagata est.
units.tr: At the beginning of this queen's reign (apart from a few of the Marian clergy) there were not many others who abstained from our services and rites at that time. This is well enough known, and more than enough, to those who by their age can still recall those first days of the Queen. So small was their number then that for some years the meaning of "to be a recusant" was entirely unknown; the very word or title of "recusant" had not yet been born here among us. From this alone the reader may easily know that their number was not great: the laws were silent, and nothing was done in Parliament about them for a whole decade. Yet something would have been done by some statute or Senate decree, had they not been a number to be despised. For it was in the interest of the commonwealth not to neglect them if they had by then grown to any considerable number. Indeed this was so well established that when Garnet was brought before the tribunal as a defendant, and this was objected to him, namely the small number at that time as I have just said, he could not deny it; he said at last that certain persons indeed, whom he either knew or had heard of, had kept away from our services during that time. Nor, if some were absent at that time in so great an extent of the kingdom, is there great weight in that: for it is enough for our purpose, as regards the main point of the case, that the flood which afterwards came of recusants was first begotten and spread out of the censure of Pius (as frogs out of a shower of rain).

units.la: Atque, hoc quidem loco, res hic religionis, decennio primo, cùm nondum Pius 5. in Reginam anathema suum fulminâsset. Vndecimo demum anno, cùm prodijsset Bulla fulminūtiis[?], non eadem in multis meis[?]. Illipo[?]; quibus autem, religio nulla, sacris nostris interesse, Recusantes fieri, ut quid autem Recusantes? non culpâ religionis aliquâ (erat enim non alia tum quàm antè fuerat) sed, quòd intermisisset tum Pontifex; quasi non in rebus ipsis, vel conscientiis hominum, sed in plumbo Pontificio religio lateret.
units.tr: And indeed, in this place, the matter of religion stood thus during the first decade, when Pius V had not yet hurled his anathema against the Queen. Only in the eleventh year, when the bull of excommunication had come out, did the same persons, to whom no religion stood in the way of attending our services, become recusants. But why recusants? Not because of any fault in religion (for it was then no different from what it had been before), but because the Pontiff had then issued it; as if religion lay not in the things themselves, or in men's consciences, but in the Pontifical lead seal.

units.la: Non ergo Conscientiæ causa dicenda, vel Religionis, Recusantium hic causa apud nos. Nam si Religionis, quinquennio primo Reginæ Elizabethæ, cùm eadem per omnia fuit quæ nunc est Religio; cur non eadem tum illis Conscientiæ cur Sacra tum nostra execrati non sunt? cur Templa tum adierunt? Adierunt enim tum, si non omnes, at (quod fassus vel Garnettus) plurimi. Etiam de vetustis quibusdam, (addo, & primariis quibusdam) rationes scriptô divulgârunt, cur id liceret facere; etiam id ut facerent, quibusdam tum de suis, authores insuper fuerunt: ut consulenda fuerit eâ de re Synodus Tridentina. Quinquennio proximo, cùm iam Duodecim viri illi Tridentinæ sententiam eâ de re suam interposuissent, [de non adeundo nobiscum templa] cur neque tum Sacris abstinuerunt omnes? Discessio quidem ex eo factâ à nonnullis: pars tamen multò maxima, (sententiâ illâ non obstante) etiam tum, nobiscum assiduè tem divinam audiebant. Quæro iam, cùm nihil de novo mutatum tum fuerit in religione, quod ita licuit per decennium, cur anno post undecimo cœpit non licere? Adduco & aliud argumentum huic rei: Nam si religio ipsa Romana causa sit sola, cur hij sese sacris subducant, cùm & alibi etiam religio Romana sit, & ubique (ut præ se ferunt) eadem; quî fit, ut alibi; pérque alias passim gentes, illud quoque hominum genus non existat? Non enim existere, Scotia testis sit, in quâ, etsi plerique sint utriusque sexus Papistæ, noti satis: haud quisquam tamen ex illis fuit, quamdiu inter eos Rex, nec Sedem hic habuit in toto Scotiæ regno, qui se templo subduxerit, sed neque nomen ibi Recusantis, neque res cuiquam cognita. At illud, credo, Matthæus dabit, Catholicos suos, ubi ubi sunt gentium, quoad conscientiam pariter affectos esse, pariter quoad obedientiam erga Pontificem, quem quasi Ecclesiæ sux & fidei caput omnes venerentur.
units.tr: Therefore the cause of the recusants here among us is not to be called a matter of conscience, or of religion. For if it was of religion, in the first five years of Queen Elizabeth, when the religion was in every respect what it is now, why did they not then, in the same way as now, shun our services as a matter of conscience? Why did they then attend our churches? For they did attend then, if not all, at least (as even Garnet confessed) very many. Some of the old and even leading men also published written reasons why it was lawful to do so, and some of their own leaders then even urged them to do it: so that the Council of Trent ought to have been consulted on the matter. In the next five years, when those twelve men had already given their opinion of Trent on the matter [concerning not attending our churches], why did not all abstain from our services even then? Some indeed withdrew from them as a result of that opinion, but by far the greater part, notwithstanding that opinion, still continually heard divine service with us. I ask now: when nothing new was changed then in religion, and what had been lawful for the space of a decade, why did it begin to be unlawful a year after the eleventh? I add another argument to this matter: for if the Roman religion alone were the cause, why do these men withdraw from our services, when the Roman religion is also elsewhere, and everywhere (as they profess) the same; how does it come about that this class of men does not exist elsewhere, and among other nations throughout the world? For that it does not exist, Scotland is a witness, in which, although most of both sexes are well-known Papists, yet none of them, so long as the King was among them and the See had not been here in the whole kingdom of Scotland, withdrew from the church, nor was the name of "recusant" known there, nor the thing known to anyone. But Matthew will grant, I believe, that his Catholics, wherever they are among the nations, are alike in conscience, and alike in obedience towards the Pontiff, whom all venerate as the head of their Church and faith.

units.la: Extiterunt itaque hic apud nos Recusantes ex Bulla primùm, cuius ea tum vis, ut simul res sacras, simul ciuiles, eodem anathemate inuolueret, ut non modò sacra tum hic non sacra, sed neque Regina tum Regina, vel subditi dein subditi. Duo enim haec quasi connexa essent inter se atque implicita, nec separari possent, ita unam in Bullam compingebantur, ut non liceret iam Catholico esse, nisi et qui clandestinus hostis esset Regina, nec cuiquam caste Deo seruire, nisi Perduelli. Prouenerunt inde nobis, una eademque operâ Recusantes simul & prodítores Bullati: & olim quidem dici solebat, Homines Bullae: iam verò, Homines Catholici Bullae, quasi ex stillicidiis Romanae pluuiae, postquam detonuit. Simul ergo mutare tum in religione caeperunt, simul nutare in officio erga Principem, quasi iam non Principem, quàm sanctissimus eorum Pater, pariter Ecclesiae communione, patiter regnandi iure priuasset. Ita religioni permista seditionis, femina, nec quisquam iam in Deum pius, nisi qui in Principem, patriamque simul impius, nec bonus Catholicus, nisi malus subditus. Neque verò diu res ex emplo caruit: ebullit enim conscissim atque effervuit ex hac Bulla; quae subsecuta statim est, Rebellio Borealis. Inde quidem prima lex in vestros, ex Seditione Boreali, ut ex eodem fonte lex ultima, ex Proditione Fulminali.
units.tr: Thus recusants first came into being here among us from the Bull; its force was then such that it bound up sacred and civil things together under the same anathema, so that not only were our services then not sacred here, but neither was the Queen then a Queen, nor her subjects then subjects. For these two things were, as it were, connected and entangled with each other, and could not be separated, so that they were pressed together into one Bull; so that it was no longer lawful to be a Catholic unless one was a secret enemy of the Queen, nor to serve God purely unless one was a traitor. From this there arose among us, by one and the same work, recusants and at once traitors bullish: and formerly they used to be called "men of the Bull", but now "Catholic men of the Bull", as if from the drippings of the Roman rain, after it had thundered. At the same time, therefore, they began to change in religion, and at the same time to waver in their duty towards the Prince, as if the Pope, their most holy father, had deprived them no less of the right to reign than of communion with the Church. Thus sedition was mingled with religion, and no one was any longer pious towards God unless he was also impious towards the Prince and country at the same time; nor a good Catholic unless he was a bad subject. Nor indeed has the matter lacked its effect for long: for from this Bull there boiled up and frothed over, as soon as it followed, the Northern Rebellion. From that came the first law against you, arising out of the Northern Sedition, just as from the same source came the last law, arising out of the Thunderbolt Treason.

units.la: Cùm ergo fide Romanâ fidelitatem Anglicam labefactari, miscerì cum fide perfidiam, Maiestatem cum pietate laedi cernerent: fecit ea res, ut & Reginae ipsi, & Regni tum Ordinibus consultum videretur, maturè hijs, qui sic affecti erant (seu malis, infectiu) notam aliquam inurere lege aliquâ poenali: quae tum nota, quasi discriminaret à bonis ciuibus, quos ita non potuit recusare, quominus simul, & Sacris praesentiam, & Reginae officium praestarent, vsqueadeo ut non modò Religionem, sed nec authoritatem vllam Regiam agnoscerent in Reginâ[?], quàm Piissimus eorum Dominus non minùs Regno quàm Ecclesiâ mulctâsset[?]. Lege aliquâ dixi poenali, non erumnosâ tamen, vel atroci, nec quales scribuntur apud vos: florenorum enim ea, non flammarum fuit; pecuniae modò multa in mensem, non iactura semel & simul fama, capitis, fortunarum omnium. Atque haec vera origo fuit, vera conditio est Recusantium apud nos. Nec ex alio capite recusabant initio, nec ex alio iam recusant: ut aliter, apud nos habendi, aliter accipiendi sint Papistæ, quàm qui uspiam alibi gentium vel terrarum sint. Ex ijs quæ mihi dicta iam sunt, nemini potest esse obscurum, leges quæ feruntur, multas quæ dicuntur hic apud nos in Recusantes, ferri & dici non religionis causâ meræ, sed mixtæ; mixtæ cum malâ mente & fide in Principem: nec nisi in Recusantes Bullatos, quibus fides non solùm sacra, sed civilis etiam, ex Pontificis nutu pendet, nempe post missam ab eo Bullam vel Breve aliquod, nec præstanda iam Principi, nec profitenda: Qui vero sic Sacram confundunt cum Civili, ut sub Sacra obtentu civilem profiteri recusent, in eos tam injustè Recusantes, justè animaduerti, justum omnibus videatur necesse est, apud quos professionis illius recusatio, justam excusationem non habet.
units.tr: Since the Papists saw English loyalty being weakened by Roman faith, and faith mixed with treachery, and majesty harmed along with piety, that situation led the Queen herself and the orders of the realm of that time to think it right to brand those so disposed (or rather, infected) early on with some mark, by some penal law. This mark was meant to distinguish them from good citizens, whom it could not prevent from attending the sacred services and at the same time performing their duty to the Queen. Indeed, they came to acknowledge no religious authority and no royal authority at all in the Queen, since their most pious lord would have punished them no less in the realm than in the Church. I say a penal law, but not a harsh or savage one, nor such as are written about among you: for that law involved florins, not flames; only a fine of money each month, not the loss at once of reputation, life, and all fortunes. And this was the true origin, and this is the true condition of the Recusants among us. Nor did they refuse at first for any other reason, nor do they now refuse for any other reason: so that Papists must be regarded and treated differently among us than those who are anywhere else in the world. From what has already been said to me, it cannot be unclear to anyone that the laws which are passed, and the many which are said to be enacted here among us against Recusants, are not purely for religion but mixed; mixed with a wicked mind and faith toward the Prince. And they apply only to Recusants bound by Bulls, whose faith depends not only on sacred matters but also on civil matters, on the nod of the Pontiff: namely, after some Bull or Brief has been sent by him, which may no longer be granted to the Prince nor professed. But those who so confuse the Sacred with the Civil that, under the pretext of the Sacred, they refuse to profess the Civil, it must seem just to all, among whom refusal of that profession has no just excuse, that such people, who are unjustly called Recusants, are justly punished.

units.la: Venio jam ad eos, qui secundo loco sunt Edicti, Relapsi scilicet, seu recidivantes, quâ parte articulos illos complectoi[?] omnes, qui de ijs sunt, qui postquam omnem à se contumaciam abdicârunt, cætera quidem conformes satis sunt, ad Eucharistiam tamen nondum accedunt. Hos autem duplici in differentiâ sitos video. Nam vel nunquam illius participes fuerunt priùs: vel fuerunt sanè priùs, post verò esse desierunt. De duobus his, sunt in Edicto articuli nonnulli, sed de illis haud credo nos jubet causam dicere Matthæus, haud alius quispiam veri nominis Papista. Nam hi quidem cum sacris sæpe intersint (frustra toties reclamante Pontifice) schismaticorum in numero sint necesse est, nec pro vestris dehinc iam habendi, ut quicquid in illos statuantur durius, id totum redundet, vel in Hypocritas, vel in PseudoCatholicos, vel quocunque alio nomine appellare libeat, nec ullo modo in illos immaculatos fidei vestræ Romana professores. Et quæ tamen vel in istos multæ irrogantur, ita non graves sunt, præsertim vestræ illæ, quibus nos multatis, ut puderet, credo, quenquam, qui prudens videri velit; cùm de illis mentio fit, ingentes ærumnas vel nominare.
units.tr: I come now to those who are in the second place of the Edict, namely the Relapsed, or backsliders, who, in respect of those articles which concern all who, after they have renounced all their obstinacy, are indeed conformed in other respects, yet do not yet approach the Eucharist. I see that these are of a twofold difference. For either they never before took part in it, or they indeed did before, but afterward have ceased. Concerning these two kinds, there are some articles in the Edict, but Matthew does not, I believe, command us to plead the case on their behalf, nor does any other person who is truly a Papist. For these, since they often attend the sacred services (though the Pontiff often protests in vain), must necessarily be counted among the schismatics, and are not to be regarded henceforth as yours. So whatever harsher things are decreed against them, all of it rebounds either upon Hypocrites, or upon Pseudo-Catholics, or by whatever other name one pleases to call them, and in no way upon those unspotted professors of your Roman faith. And the fines which are imposed on these people are not so severe, especially yours, by which you fine us, so that I believe anyone who wishes to appear prudent would be ashamed to even mention great hardships when those are spoken of.

units.la: Nam de tertiâ Edicti parte, quæ ad illos spectat qui jurare nolunt, conceptum in eâ jusjurandum, mitto hic dicere. Arx ipsa quæstionis est: Nam si de religionis in eo rebus non agatur, sed de obsequio tantum, & fide ciuili (quod & Apologia docere vult, & haec Apologiae defensio) quaecunque tandem in eos poena fertur, qui iuramentum abiurarint, aerumna dici non potest, propter causam conscientiae vllam. Sed enim, vt ciuile delictum est, ita ciuilis & ipsa poena dicenda erit. Nam de fide quidem Catholica si sit: & haec iam ratio hic, & quaestio statim omnis nobis cessaret.
units.tr: Now as for the third part of the Edict, which concerns those who are unwilling to swear, and the oath framed in it, I pass over saying anything here. The very citadel of the question lies here: for if the matter at issue is not religion but only obedience and civil faith (which both the Apology wishes to teach, and this defence of the Apology), then whatever punishment is brought against those who refuse the oath cannot be called a hardship on account of any matter of conscience. For just as the offence is civil, so the punishment too must be called civil. For if it were a matter of Catholic faith, then this reasoning and the whole question would at once cease for us here.

units.la: De postremo vero eius membro, quo grauia multa mitigantur, idque in Papistarum commodum: dixi iam, gratias referre debent; si illas nolunt, at litem[?], credo non mouebunt. Vides[?] iam, Lector, quid montes Matthaei parturiant; quo ingentes illae aerumnae iam recidant, quas ille tanti putauit, tanti venditauit esse, vt solae sufficerent, ad Apologiam vel totam, vno impetu refutandam.
units.tr: As for the last part of that clause, by which many severe things are softened, and that to the advantage of the Papists: I have already said that they ought to give thanks for it; if they do not want those benefits, but a lawsuit, I believe they will not stir up strife. You now see, Reader, what Matthew's mountains bring forth; so that those huge hardships which he thought so valuable, so highly prized, and so sold as to be enough by themselves to refute the whole Apology in one assault, now fall back again.

units.la: At etiam vnum me praeterijt in Edicto, cum cetera recenserem, nec tamen iam praetereundum. Clausula autem est, in qua de poena agitur iis imponenda, qui ipsi cum sint Romanae sedis obsequio (vt loquuntur) iam reconciliati, id agunt, vt & alios auocent ab obedientia Regi debita. Ipsa vero ibi verba sic posita; Ab obedientia Regi debita, satis per se valere debent, quiuis vt ex illis, certo sciat ibi de poenis agi perditorum ciuium, & qui proiecti iam sunt ad seditionem aliquam: ad res autem fidei, religionis, conscientiae, a nemine cui quidem mens laesa non sit, traduci potuisse.
units.tr: But there is one thing in the Edict which I passed over while listing the rest, and yet it must not be passed over now. It is the clause in which the punishment is spoken of, to be imposed on those who, though they are now reconciled again to obedience to the Roman see (as they put it), are working to draw others also away from the obedience owed to the King. The words themselves, placed there as they are, away from the obedience owed to the King, ought to be sufficient in themselves, so that anyone at all may know for certain that the punishments there concern corrupt citizens, and those already thrown into some sedition; and that they could not be applied to matters of faith, religion, or conscience by anyone whose mind is not impaired.

units.la: Post quatuordecim demum articulos suos, (vere dixi suos, non enim sic in Edicto positos, sed mera figmenta sua) totus ad ironiam fertur clementia Regia, magis ipse dignus ironia, qui cum in crimen falsi incurrisset Pontifex, propellit etiam magis. Nam quod de Regis clementia in Pontificios dictum ibi in Apologia, locum habet in Pontificis maerore magno & primo, non in auctore iam & secundo, post Edictum scilicet. Neque satis commode diuisa tibi Matthaei temporibus haec. Priusquam inhumanum illo inceptu, ad iustam iram irritati Ordines: tum certe clementia summa fuit, nec vlla tum Pontifici causa magna maeroris. Fortasse causa iam aliqua ex Edicto, maerendi; nec tanta tamen, quantam videri vis; sed meminerit, ei faciendo homines suos execrando scelere suo, causam dedisse. Vide vero quid à nobis negetur hic: Pontificem adeo valde moestum esse debuisse, priusquam exiret Edictum hoc: vide autem quid à te probetur, Pontifici causam fuisse maerendi, postquam exijt Edictum hoc. Haec illa sunt quae in Dialecticis dicuntur disparata; nosti caetera.
units.tr: After his fourteen articles at last (I rightly say his, for they are not so set out in the Edict, but are his own mere fictions), the whole clemency of the King is turned into irony, and the Pontiff himself, who, having fallen into the crime of falsehood, is more deserving of irony, is driven even further. For what was said in the Apology about the King's clemency toward the Papists applies to the Pontiff's great and first grief, not to the author's now and second, namely after the Edict. Nor is this well divided for you by the times of Matthew. Before the inhuman undertaking, the orders were stirred to just anger: then certainly there was the greatest clemency, and at that time there was no great cause of grief for the Pontiff. Perhaps there is now some cause for grief from the Edict; yet not so great as you wish to appear; but let him remember that by doing this, he gave cause by his own execrable crime to his men. See now what is denied by us here: that the Pontiff ought to have been very sorrowful before this Edict came out: and see what is approved by you, that the Pontiff had cause to grieve after this Edict came out. These are the things which in the Dialectics are called disparate; you know the rest.

units.la: Sed neque tantum in Edicta arumnarum, quantum autumas; neque tantum, quantum meriti sunt illi, aut qui illorum similes, in quos ferebatur; saltem non tantum, ut mereatur tuum illud tragicum, Quae maior excogitari potest? Multari in menses singulos viginti librarum multa, non ita magna arumna est, quin maior excogitari possit, nempe quam nostros homines subire hic coegistis regnante Maria, ut bona eorum simul & semel, primo momento, omnia abirent in fiscum. Carceri perpetuo mancipari, calamitas quidem est; non tam magna tamen, ut non excogitari possit maior. Illa enim certe maior, quam vos nostris infligitis, damnari ad triremes, vel ad metalla. Tum morte multari, etiam magna & illa; sed maior adhuc excogitari potest, quod nobis scilicet facitis; lento igne torreri. Quare satis erat, si magnas arumnas dixisses, nec nisi quia Gnathonem volebas imitari, opus ullum ut ingentes diceres: Maiores autem excogitari non posse, id vero Gnathonem superrat. Quod si ingentes vere arumnas videre vis; & calamitatem qua maior excogitari non potest, abi ad Inquisitionem vestram; illam spectata; ibi visurus ea, prae quibus ludus iocusque sunt, quae vestri hic patiuntur apud nos.
units.tr: But the Edict does not bring hardships as great as you claim; nor are they as great as those deserve, or those like them, against whom it was directed; at least not so great as to earn your tragic phrase, What greater can be devised? To be fined twenty pounds every month. A hardship which can be devised greater is not so great as this; namely the one which you forced our people here to undergo under the reign of Mary, so that their goods all went at once, in a single moment, entirely into the treasury. To be condemned to perpetual imprisonment is indeed a calamity; yet not so great that a greater cannot be devised. For that is surely greater, which you inflict on ours: to be condemned to the galleys, or to the mines. Then to be punished with death, which is also great; yet a greater can still be devised, which you do to us, namely to be roasted over a slow fire. Therefore it would have been enough if you had said great hardships, and only because you wished to imitate Gnatho was there any need to say huge: but to say that greater cannot be devised, that indeed surpassed Gnatho. But if you really wish to see huge hardships, and a calamity than which a greater cannot be devised, go to your Inquisition; behold it there; there you will see those things before which our sport and jest are nothing, which your people suffer here among us.

units.la: Sacra vero nostra Sacrilega, qua fronte dixisti? Nihil ibi sacri tollitur; vide, ne vestra potius dicenda sint, in quibus sacra-rum orationum pars melior, mens otiantis scilicet & intellectus; in quibus sacer calix, altera nempe Eucharistiae pars, ausu sacrilego tollitur: in quibus diuini & Deo sacri honoris pars similitudini ligneae defertur, & cruftaceus panis pro Deo, non sine sacrilegio summo adoratur. En tibi, si quaeris, sacrilegium. Porro si fuisset in nostris tale quicquam, designasses scio.
units.tr: But our "sacred" rites you call "sacrilegious": with what face did you say that? Nothing sacred is taken away there. See rather whether it is your own rites that should be called that, in which the better part of the sacred prayers, namely the attention and understanding of the mind, is taken away; in which the sacred chalice, the other part of the Eucharist, is removed by sacrilegious daring; in which part of the divine honour, due to God as something sacred, is transferred to a wooden likeness, and a crusted bread is adored in place of God, not without the highest sacrilege. There you have sacrilege, if you are looking for it. Indeed, had there been anything of the kind among ours, I know you would have pointed it out.

units.la: Æque & illud absurde, cum id perfidiae Iuramentum dicis, quod perfidia qua in praeteritum notandae, qua in posterum cavendae, conditum est: quod iam contra perfidiam fertur, quodque erit in libris & legibus nostris aeternum perfidiae monumentum, & quidem vestrorum hominum perfidiae; qui gemino se sacramento ad perfidiam in Patriam ipsam, in Patriae Patrem obligârunt. Vos autem qui fidem, qui fidei vincula, iuramenta soluitis, quò perfidi esse liceat: vos qui fidem non feruandam, id est, perfidiam licitam, legitimamque dicitis, etiamne vos quisquam de perfidia audetus hiscere? & in turpitudinem vestram eius vel nomen nominare?
units.tr: Equally absurd is that other charge, when you call it the oath of perfidy, which has been devised with perfidy to be censured in the past and guarded against in the future. It is already brought against perfidy, and it will be an eternal monument of perfidy in our books and laws; and indeed of the perfidy of your own people, who bound themselves by a double oath to perfidy against the country itself and against the Father of the country. But you who loosen faith, the bonds of faith and oaths, so that it may be lawful to be faithless; you who say that faith is not to be kept, that is, that perfidy is lawful and legitimate: does anyone dare to accuse you of perfidy, or to utter its name against your own shame?

units.la: Ad cumulum denique accedit falsitatum & illud, quòd tu, tam magnus scilicet mendaciorum hostis, cui crimen falsi ita odiosum, tertio ibi loco falsò dicis & mendaciter, quòd scilicet, exhortatio ad fidem Catholicam cuiquam hic sit capitalis. Verius ibi dictum oportuit, Exhortatio ad perfidiam vel (si fidem vocari vis) ad fidem falsò nominatam, nempe perfidiae matrem, atq; nutricem. Ideo enim quia abstrahuntur per vos à nexu naturali fidei suae in Regem, ideo quia Pontificis nutui, contra Principem, patriam, ius fasque omne, quasi mancipia adiudicantur, & nexui dantur, (quod vos reconciliari dicitis) ideo plectuntur; non quòd Catholicam (quàm falsò sic putant) fidem profitentur. Alioquin extra perfidiae illius notam profitentur illam (quam dixi) fidem, & (quam tu ipse tertiâ post lineâ vocas) civilem obedientiam: sentient alteram illam (quam dicis) fidem eis non fore capitalem.
units.tr: Finally, to crown these falsehoods, there is also this: you, so great an enemy of lies, for whom the charge of falsehood is so hateful, falsely and mendaciously say in the third place there that the exhortation to the Catholic faith is here a capital offence. It should rather have been said: the exhortation to perfidy, or (if you wish it to be called faith) to a faith falsely so named, namely the mother and nurse of perfidy. For they are punished not because they profess the Catholic faith (which they falsely think it to be), but because, through you, they are drawn away from the natural bond of their faith to the King; because, at the nod of the Pope, they are handed over as slaves against the Prince, the country, and all law and right, and are given over to a bond (which you call reconciliation). Otherwise, apart from the mark of that perfidy, they profess that faith (which I mentioned) and what you yourself, a line later, call civil obedience; they will find that the other faith (which you speak of) will not be capital for them.

units.la: At etiam ærumnas has suas claudit ærumnis Archipresbyteri, vel post susceptum Iuramentum, in carceribus detenti. Quanquam ille iam Archipresbyter non est, Presbyter modò; excidit gradu suo; vos illum exauctorâstis, vt mirum videri possit quòd tu ita iam sis de illo sollicitus. Non vna modò Iuramenti, verùm aliæ sunt causæ Archipresbyteri: atque audi etiam, iustæ causæ inprimis, quòd sic multetur carcere, imò & gratia magna, quòd non nisi carcere. Qui enim contra leges publicas capitali poenâ sancitas, ausus iurisdictionem in regno hoc vllam sumere, & de Româ sumere, eâmque tot iam annos hîc exequi, censuras & facultates, & reliqua peregrina potestatis munia obiere; is si in carcere modò est, (quæ tamen libera potiùs cu Stodia dici debet, quàm carcer) secum non malè actum putet. Quod si simile quid nostrùm quis ausus esset in ditione vllâ, vbi Papa quid habet potestatis, vbi Inquisitio vim obtinet; quid illi futurum censes? an ei poena carcerè satis foret? annon acerbissimâ morte moriendum? vel Papam ipsum iudicem appellare ausim, ita res est in manifesto. Id vero etiam de eo affirmare ausim, detentionem illi suam beneficij loco esse, nec illi ipsi secus videri. Nam id illi, credo, satis exploratum est, si quo vellet, liber abire posset, atque ita liber in Papae manus veniret, ubi reddenda illi ratio de suscepto à se iuramento; peius etiam multò Romae, quàm nunc Londini est, acceptum iri. Verè tum quidem foret erumnosus senex.
units.tr: But he also closes these his miseries with the miseries of the Archpriest, or after taking the oath, detained in prisons. Although he is no longer Archpriest, only a priest; he has lost his rank; you have deprived him of it, so that it may seem strange that you should now be so anxious about him. Not only is there the one cause of the oath, but there are other causes of the Archpriest: and hear also, first of all just causes, that he is punished in this way with imprisonment, and indeed with great favour, that he is not held in anything but a prison. For whoever, against public laws sanctioned by capital punishment, has dared to exercise any jurisdiction in this realm, and to take it from Rome, and to carry it out here for so many years, and has performed censures and faculties and the other foreign functions of power: if he is now only in prison (which ought rather to be called a free custody than a prison), let him think he has not been badly treated. But if any of ours had dared such a thing in any territory where the Pope has some power, where the Inquisition holds force, what do you think would become of him? Would imprisonment be enough punishment for him? Must he not die by the most bitter death? I would even dare to call the Pope himself as judge, so plainly is the matter established. Indeed, I would also dare to affirm of him that his detention is for him in the place of a benefice, and that it does not appear otherwise to him either. For this, I believe, is well enough known to him: that if he wished, he could go away free, and so would come free into the hands of the Pope, where he would have to render account for the oath he had taken; and it would be received much worse at Rome than it now is at London. Truly then he would be a wretched old man indeed.

units.la: Sed quoniam incidit de eo mentio nobis, volo etiam à te scisciitari quidpiam, unde hoc (nos enim certè satis mirari non possumus) cùm scripta sit atque edita Apologia; (Cuius authoritate edita, scitis, scitis etiam à Quo) cùm etiam Qui scripsit eam, de Religione Suâ fateatur, ut mirum iam non sit, liberiùs ab Illo dictum quid, vel in Pontificem vel Cardinales; cùm haec (inquam) ita se habeant, eâ ut celeritate, & verò etiam vi, à duobus iam duplex, duabus linguis factus sit in Eam impetus, tam breui: & tamen Archipresbytero, à quo iamdiu Liber extat, in quo libro ingenuè respondet ad interrogata singula, ciúsque paginis singulis subscripsit se, nec mutauit ex eo mentem; qui Liber aequitatem Iuramenti illius de fidelitate non minùs asserit quàm Apologia: cui subiecta quoque per eum Epistola, quâ Catholicos suos, etiam atque etiam hortatur ut Iuramentum illud intrepidè, utroque Breui non obstante, suscipiant: ubi etiam & suprema Regis in temporalibus potestas propugnata ab eo, & Pontificis ad deponendos Reges potestas acriter oppugnata est: fusiùs autem utrumque & prolixiùs multò quàm in Apologia: nec dum vestrum ullus vel verbo responderit, nec (quod cuiquam hic constet) responsum ullum meditetur. At aequum erat vos in illum magis excandescere, qui vester fit, qui vos inter vos, tanquam Cadmaeos fratres, committit, & eos, qui inter vos, maximi momenti, Authores sunt, vestra in vulnera convertit.
units.tr: But since mention of him has arisen, I also want to ask you something, from which this comes (for we certainly cannot cease to wonder): since the Apology has been written and published (by whose authority it was published, you know, and you know also by whom), and since he who wrote it also confesses about his own religion, so that it is no longer strange that something was said more freely by him, either against the Pontiff or against the Cardinals; since these things (I say) stand thus, the attack has been made on it so quickly, and indeed with force, by two men already, and in two languages, and in so short a time: and yet no answer has been given by you to the Archpriest, from whom a book has long been extant, in which he frankly answers each question put to him, and at each page of which he has subscribed his name, and has not changed his mind since then; which book asserts the equity of that oath of fidelity no less than the Apology does; to which he has also appended an Epistle, in which he urges his Catholics again and again to take up that oath fearlessly, notwithstanding either Brief; where also both the supreme power of the King in temporal matters is defended by him, and the power of the Pontiff to depose kings is sharply attacked: and both are treated more fully and at much greater length than in the Apology. Yet none of you has answered even a word, nor (as is known to anyone here) does any of you intend an answer. But it would have been fair for you to be more inflamed against him who is one of yours, who sets you against one another like the Cadmean brothers, and who turns against your wounds those who are among you of the greatest importance as authors.

units.la: NOndum tamen debellatum est. Quò enim rem totam hic conficiat de persecutione Regiâ; En, ut homo Stratioticus (iures sacellum iam suum abiurasse) volo (inquit) ipsum adigere, velit nolit. Audire vocem visus sum modò militis; atque eccum; salve mi Thrase; Quis te enim aliter alloquatur, qui vim affers, atque adigis homines, velint nolint, ut in se, pro te testimonium dicant? En verò, ut adigat. Quicunque intra Regni fines sacrificuli consistunt, mortis rei sunt omnes; Lata ea lex est à Regina Elizabetha 27o. demum anno Regni sui; lata autem necessariò, cùm constaret id genus hominum confluere huc indies, vt flabella essent seditionum, & ad res nouas moliendas suorum hic hominum animos, quasi solum subactum redderent: cùm constaret, missis ad Patrem Generalem literis, subinde sic scripsitare, Ego intra proximum (trimestre vel semestre) tot (puta quinque vel sex) reconciliaui, pro quibus spondere ausim, quòd quaecunque occasio inciderit, à parte nostrâ futuri sint omnes. Moriendum ergo erat sacrificis, qui comprehensi erant: moriendum & reliquis, si quando comprehensi essent. Hic tu, falsi vbique prodigus, parcus veri relator, ex semisse rem decurtas. Gratiam vtrisque facere rex voluit; fecit: Liberi dimissi sunt quotquot tum erant vllo in carcere. Aude verò etiam hanc gratiam negare. Ad reliquos autem qui in latibulis tum erant, necdum comprehensi, parem gratiam suam Rex permanare voluit, ne vel eorum cuiquam ea lex capitalis foret, eúm vel si se profiterentur tales, dum intra certum diem Regni fines excederent. Tibi verò haec nulla gratia videtur, mortem exilio commutare? & illudis ei? Certè sub æstu Mariano, & diebus illis caniculaaribus[?], de nostris hic multi parem gratiam, vt flammas effugerent, summo beneficij loco erant habituri. Habe tu vt voles; gratia illa quidem fuit, etsi ij non grati, quibus facta est.
units.tr: Yet the matter is not yet finished. For to finish the whole business here concerning the royal persecution, see, like a soldier (you may swear that he has already renounced his shrine), he says: "I want to compel him, whether he will or no. I seemed just now to hear the voice of a soldier; and look, here he is: hail, my Thrasō!" For who would address you otherwise, you who bring force and compel men, whether they wish it or not, to bear witness against themselves on your behalf? Indeed, see how he compels! All the priests who remain within the bounds of the kingdom are guilty of death. That law was passed by Queen Elizabeth in the twenty-seventh year of her reign; it was passed necessarily, since it was established that this kind of men flocked here daily, so that they might be the bellows of sedition and, as it were, subdue the spirits of the people here to undertake revolutions; since it was established that they wrote to the Father General, and from time to time wrote in this way: "Within the next three months or six months I have reconciled so many (say five or six), for whom I dare to promise that, whatever occasion arises, they will all be on our side." The priests who were seized had to die; the rest too would have to die, if ever they were seized. Here you, lavish in falsehood everywhere, sparing in reporting the truth, cut the matter short by half. The King chose to grant favour to both, and did so: all who were then in any prison were released freed. Dare then to deny even this favour. But to the rest, who were then in hiding and not yet seized, the King wished to extend the same favour, so that no law of capital punishment would apply to any of them, even if they professed themselves such, provided they left the bounds of the kingdom within a set day. Does this seem to you no favour, to change death into exile? And do you mock him for it? Surely in the heat of the Marian persecution, and in those dog-days, many of ours here would have counted an equal favour, to escape the flames, as the highest benefit. Take it as you will; it was indeed a favour, though those to whom it was granted were not thankful.

units.la: Quaeris autem, si exilium gratia fit, quo nomine supplicia appellanda sint. Dicam; vita, vel membri iactura, supplicia sunt & appellantur, præ quibus exilium supplicium non est. Id tu Matthae, si hic fis, sentias, & quasi de gratia facta, gratias ageres, cùm capitis damnatus esses, si solum tibi tum daretur vertere. Non tum diceres, opinor, imò nolo exulare, supplicium verum est, calamitas magna est, exulem esse; gratia nulla est; nusquam cogar poenas graviores exilio praevenire. Non hoc certè tum diceres: vel si diceres, omnes te insanum Italum dicerent, qui malles trans Acheronta, quàm trans mare navigare. Mitte verò aliquem de nostris coram Inquisitione vestra ad flammas damnatum; iube illum intra certum tempus vltra Apenninum esse: vide, annon insignem sibi gratiam factam agniturus sit: Agniturus certè, sat scio. Quanquam
units.tr: You ask, however, "if exile is a grace, by what name are punishments to be called?" I will say: loss of life or of a limb are punishments and are called so; exile is not a punishment in comparison with them. If you were here, Matthew, and you were condemned to death, you would feel this, and you would give thanks as if for a favour, if you were then only given the chance to leave. You would not then say, I think, "No, I do not want to go into exile; it is a true punishment, a great calamity, to be an exile; it is no grace; I shall never be forced to anticipate punishments more severe than exile." Certainly you would not say this then; or if you did, every Italian would call you mad, for preferring to sail across the Acheron rather than across the sea. Now send one of our people condemned to the flames before your Inquisition, and order him to be beyond the Apennines within a set time: see whether he will not acknowledge that a remarkable grace has been done to him. He will acknowledge it, I am quite sure. Although

units.la: quid ego ista disputo? Quis nescit, grauiorem poenam leuiore praevenire, semper beneficij loco habitum esse, & minùs malum, boni, tum locum, tum nomen sortiri, si cum maiore conferatur? Id vel ipsa nos natura docet, quae brachium capiti nos obtendere docuit, & illius noxam, huius, vel liuore, vel vulnere praevenire: tum pedis vel manus praecisione, universi corporis excisionem redimere. Ad testimonium quidem nullum adigunt haec tua, praeterquam ut testlentur[?] omnes insulsum esse te, si neges, morte mitius supplicium, esse exilium: & quod mitius id, prae asperiore semper eligendum.
units.tr: why do I argue these things? Who does not know that to anticipate a heavier punishment by a lighter one has always been counted a benefit, and that the lesser evil takes on the place and name of a good when it is compared with the greater? Nature herself teaches us this, which taught us to hold an arm before the head, and to forestall the injury to the one by the injury to the other, whether by a bruise or a wound: and to buy off the loss of the whole body by cutting off a foot or a hand. Indeed, these arguments of yours compel no testimony at all, except that everyone should testify that you are foolish if you deny that exile is a milder punishment than death, and that the milder is always to be chosen before the harsher.

units.la: At comprehendi non poterant. Qui scis? An Gygû forte annulum acceperant à Papâ, cùm huc missionem haberent? Poterant verò. Quidni enim sic asseram, cum vix septimana ulla abeat, quo non contingat ex illo numero, aliquem comprehendi? Etiam ex illis, qui legis illius gratiâ tum euaserunt, erant, qui, (octiduum[?] modò hæsissent hîc) sensissent se posse comprehendi. Etiam & illud constat, ex ijs qui hinc tum abierunt, & ex eo reuersi denuò sunt, comprehensos aliquot, ac proin, ut nunc poterant, ita tum potuisse comprehendi. Quicquid ergo hîc garrit Tortus; & gratiosum illud Edictum, & Rex clemens. Nec enim iustior clementiae laus ulla in Principe, quàm si legum suarum seueritatem temperet, & mitiore poenâ contentus sit, praeut illa est, quam ipsa lex irrogat. Mitior autem illa, & in se, si ad mortem conferatur, quam auertit; & illis ipsis, in quos irrogata mitior, quibus nec exulare molestum: cùm, praeterquam quod semper incedant in vitae discrimine, nihil hîc habeant apud nos, nihil possideant eorum, quae ad victum faciunt. Exilio autem; unde proierunt è Seminarijs, cò redeunt, ubi commorari tutò possunt, ubi religio illis ex sententiâ, ubi persecutio nulla, nec ingentes arumnae, quae magno animi moerore afficiunt, adeoque poenè conficiunt Pontificem ipsum. Linguae autem Latinae beneficio, quo fere valent cùm educati in scholis sint, simul & victum sibi quaeritare, & defungi suo munere possint, quod in Missis, Horis, Officijs è Breuiario demurmurandis, maximâ ex parte versari solet.
units.tr: "But they could not be arrested." How do you know? Had they perhaps received a ring from the Pope, since they had permission to come here? But they could. For why should I not assert this, since scarcely a week passes in which someone from that number is not arrested? Even among those who then escaped by that law's grace, there were some who, having been here only eight days, perceived that they could be arrested. It is also established that some of those who then left from here and returned again were arrested, and therefore they could then be arrested just as they can now. Whatever Tortus chatters here, then, and that gracious edict, and the merciful King: there is no more just praise of clemency in a prince than when he tempers the severity of his own laws and is content with a milder penalty than the law itself imposes. That penalty is milder both in itself, if it is compared with death, which it averts, and for those very people on whom the milder penalty is imposed, for whom exile is not troublesome, since, apart from the fact that they always walk in danger of their lives, they have nothing here with us and possess nothing of what serves for living. But by exile they are sent back from the seminaries, where they may stay safely, where their religion is to their liking, where there is no persecution and no great hardships which afflict the mind with deep grief and almost wear out the Pope himself. And by the benefit of the Latin tongue, which they mostly have since they were educated in schools, they can both seek a living for themselves and discharge their office, which for the most part consists in muttering through the Masses, Hours and Offices from the Breviary.

units.la: Tum verò ut sciat Lector, non modò adigere homines obiectione suâ, sed & ab alijs obiecta non minùs eleganter abigere; sic ipse primò objicit sibi tacitè: liquid in Edicto durius, id eò fuisse, quòd praesserat dira illa conjuratio; nec enim nisi detectâ demum illâ, quicquam in illos asperius esse statutum; sic verò sibi subjicit. Non ad proditores puniendos pertinere Edictum, sed ad Catholicos vexandos. Non ad puniendos proditores? Non certè; Lege nouâ ad hoc nihil opus: ex vetustâ & fieri potuit, & factum est: Ad detegendos verò, nouâ opus. Malè autem distinguis hic Catholicos & Proditores, non Catholicos, sed Proditores, quasi hij alij essent ab illis. Conjunge verò, Matthae, & dic veriùs, ad Catholicos proditores pertinere; nec enim ulli erant proditores tum, nisi Catholici. Ad illorum similes Catholicos detegendos lex; detectos autem reprimendos: ad reliquos verò Catholicos, qui proditores esse oderunt, detegendos, quò ne simili ut illi poenâ involuantur. Causa autem justissima certè, ut in Papistas omnes tùm inquireretur. Papismus enim, & eiusque reuocandi zelus, proditionis causa unica. Ipsi fassi sunt. Jesuitae (qui Papismi jam Atlantes videri volunt) proditores ipsos, porrectâ eis Eucharistiâ, in scelere sæpe obfirmârant: ex ipsis etiam Patribus, non nulli participes criminis. Intererat tum Regis, tum Reipub. scire quo loco res esset. Poterant enim in aliorum nescio quot discipulorum animos, idem quod in hos venenum instillasse; cujus poterant, quod cuiquam poterant. Ita fere evenit, scelus ad paucos pervenit, suspicio ad multos: & zelotypia nulla inanis est, ubi Regis, ubi Regni totius salus agitur. Detegantur sanè omnes, de quibus suspicio est: ubi detecti omnes, reprimantur illi quos opus est.
units.tr: Now, so that the reader may know that they not only compel men by their objection, but also drive away objections raised by others no less elegantly, he first objects to himself silently: that something in the Edict was harsher, and that this was because that dreadful conspiracy had gone before; for nothing harsher was enacted against them except once that had been discovered. Then he adds to himself: "The Edict does not pertain to punishing traitors, but to harassing Catholics." Not to punish traitors? Certainly not; no new law is needed for that: it could and did happen under the old one. But to uncover them a new law is needed. You wrongly distinguish here "Catholics and traitors," not "Catholics," but "traitors," as if these were other than those. Rather join them, Matthew, and say more truly that it pertains to Catholic traitors; for there were no traitors at that time except Catholics. The law is to uncover Catholics like those, but to suppress those who have been uncovered: while for the remaining Catholics, who hate to be traitors, it is to uncover them, so that they may not be caught up in the same punishment as those. Certainly the cause was most just, that at that time inquiry should be made into all Papists. For Popery, and the zeal to restore it, is the sole cause of treason. They have confessed it themselves. The Jesuits (who want to seem Atlases of Popery now) have often hardened the traitors themselves in their crime by offering them the Eucharist; and some of the Fathers themselves were partners in the crime. It was of concern then, both to the King and to the Commonwealth, to know how matters stood. For they could have instilled the same poison into the minds of I know not how many other disciples, as they had into these; whatever they could do to anyone, they could do. So it generally happened: the crime reached a few, suspicion reached many; and no jealousy is vain where the safety of the King and of the whole realm is at stake. Let all be uncovered, certainly, against whom there is suspicion: and when all have been uncovered, let those be suppressed whom it is necessary to suppress.

units.la: Diffisus huic scopæ tàm dissolutæ, subjungit ei aliam: Ante conjurationem illam conceptam, primo anno primo Parlamento, confirmasse Regem omnia Regina Edicta; eáque non parum auxisse. Vide quàm multa peccet hic. Quorsum enim ante illam, si post aliam? Ante illam dixit; non satis dixit: ante ullam debuit dicere; debuit, sed non potuit. Nam ipso statim anni primi initio, & vel ante coronatum Regem, conjuratio alia praegressa est Sacerdotum; quæ an dederit forte, haud scio, certè causam dare potuit, ei, quæ subsecuta est, legum severitati. Tum anno primo dicit, ante illam conceptam. At etiam (quod ante docui) anno primo illa ipsa conjuratio concepta est, etiam articulata. Tum de primo Parlamento quod dicit, prodit in scitiam rerum nostrarum. Nondum enim absolutum est; etiamnum durat Parlamentum primum. Sessione prima credo dicere voluit, in qua tum confirmata sunt Edicta[?] priùs edita: sic est. Ad illa enim pariter, reliquasque Regni leges, legisme sancitas; pariter etiam ad receptam tum in regno religionem retinendam; cùm corona illi impositæ est, fidei suæ sponsione sanctè interposità, sese Rex de more deuinxerat. At verò quòd de additione adella addis, addilio verè est, sed tua, ficta scilicet à te, ab illo facta nunquam. Non illè tum Edicta auxit, cu augens maledicta tua & mendacia, ad periodos pene singulas. De confirmatione factum tum, quòd facto opus fuit: de cætero nihilo illa tum fuerunt auctores.
units.tr: Trusting in this aim so loose, he adds another: "Before that conspiracy was conceived, in the first year, in the first Parliament, the King confirmed all the Queen's Edicts, and greatly increased them." See how many errors he makes here. For why "before that," if after another? He said "before that"; he did not say enough: he ought to have said "before any"; he ought to, but could not. For at the very beginning of the first year, and even before the King was crowned, another conspiracy of priests had preceded; whether it gave occasion to the one that followed, I do not know, but certainly it could give cause to the severity of the laws which came after. Then he says "in the first year, before that was conceived." But also (as I showed before) in the first year that very conspiracy was conceived, and even articulated. Then as to what he says about the "first Parliament," it betrays ignorance of our affairs. For it is not yet ended; the first Parliament still continues. I think he meant the first session, in which the Edicts previously issued were then confirmed: so it is. For to those, and likewise to the other laws of the realm, the laws enacted, and likewise to retaining the religion received in the realm at that time, when the crown was placed upon him, the King had bound himself, solemnly pledging his faith, as is customary. But as for what you add about an "addition" to these, you are right that it is an addition, but it is yours, feigned no doubt by you, and never made by him. He did not then "increase" the Edicts, but you, increasing your curses and lies almost in every sentence. As to the "confirmation," this was done then, because it was needed; for the rest those laws were in no way then the authors of anything.

units.la: Verum semel hoc habeas pro responso, iniquum postulare te, ut abrogentur hæc ulla Lex, ulla legis particula, quæ vestris ho-minibus melius sit apud nos: nisi prius refigat ipse Pontifex, quæ vel ille, vel qui ab illius nutu pendent, in Regum omnium perniciem cum volent, & interea dum volent, [illegible, ~12 letters] ditionem, fixerunt diu iam: & libris in lucem editis defenderunt. Faciat exuri libros illos, scriptores eorum adigat ad palinodiam: tum demum verba faciat de restitutio, postquam ipse cavit de suis. Ni fecerit, frustra hic quicquam mutari speret. Quid enim, ut nostra iam sublata sint, stent illa illius, quibus stabi-bus, stare non potest incolumitas sua ulli Principi Christianoe? Qui & sciunt hæc iamdudum, & cùm simile quid in illos tentatum fuerit, simile & ipsi facturi sunt.
units.tr: Yet once and for all take this as an answer: it is unfair of you to demand that any such law, any part of a law, which is more favourable to your people among us, be repealed, unless first the Pope himself retracts what he, or those who depend on his nod, have long since set forth to the ruin of all kings, whenever they wish and for as long as they wish, and have defended in books published to the light. Let him have those books burned, and let him compel their writers to recant: then at last let him speak of restitution, after he has taken care of his own people. If he does not do so, let him in vain hope that anything here will be changed. For why, even if our own measures were removed, should his stand, on which the safety of no Christian prince can stand? They already know this long since, and when something similar has been attempted against them, they will do the same themselves.

units.la: Hic oblitus iam sin Matthæus, cuiusque quod ipse sibi safore dixerat, si probaret (de erumnis ingentibus anni 1606) postquam bene & graviter impudens, nusquam melius dixerat affectum Pontificem ob calamitates, quas tempore Reginæ ELIZABETHÆ passi sunt Catholici; recurrit tamen non ut de mendacio præcedente satisfaciat, sed ut Reginam etiam paululùm exagitare possit, & illius manes moveret. Quid autem commisit Regina? Non enim vitio vertendum fuit, filiges seueriores sciverint, quæ & sententiis excommunicationibus ... cessa fuerat, & eâ etiam, quæ sententiam illam subsecuta est, Rebellione. Res adeo vera, adeoque intra rei causâ ut & Presbyteri vestri, ediis à se libris fateantur, nullam in orbe Christiano Principem quantumuis Catholicum, ita à Pio Pontifice acceptum, secus fuisse facturum; nec Matthaeus ipse videtur abnuere ex eo tempore, iure illam exacerbatam esse.
units.tr: Here Matthew, having forgotten what he himself had said he would prove (the great calamities of the year 1606), after saying very well and very gravely, and nowhere better, that the Pope was moved by the calamities which the Catholics suffered in the time of Queen Elizabeth, nevertheless returns to the subject, not to make amends for the preceding lie, but so that he may also rebuke the Queen a little and stir up her shade. But what did the Queen commit? For it must not be counted against her that she enacted rather severe laws, both against the sentences and excommunications ... which had been brought forth, and also against the rebellion which followed that sentence. The matter is so true, and so deeply grounded in the cause, that your own presbyters confess in their published books that no Christian prince in the world, however Catholic, having received such a thing from Pope Pius, would have acted otherwise; nor does Matthew himself seem to deny that from that time the Queen was rightly provoked.

units.la: Subjicit ergo, ante latam illam à Pio sententiam, ante vel Pontificem, Pium: initio statim Regni iuramentum de Primatu revocâsse. Certè revocauit. Nam quid faceret, postquam vobiscum in Religione non sentiret; postquam ritu reformato, & sacris literis magis conformi Deum colere, fixum iam in animo haberet, ritu illo, quo fratre regnante imbuta fuerat; sineretne, quas Maria soror paulò antè leges rogauerat contra reformatam Religionem, suo loco stare, nec abrogaret illas? Aut cùm decretum ei esset, morem atque ritum meliorem Dei colendi reducere, à Sorore antiquatum; nonne & vnà, quâ sese Soror exuerat, potestatem reuocare ad se debuit? Quid ergo? eam, quæ iam est, religionem stabiliret, Papa tamen Primatum agnosceret? Certè illud tentatum constat; & à Paulo quarto conditionem impetratam, porrò & Reginæ ipsi delatam esse, dum in Primatum ipsius consentire modò vellet, de cæteris, si à se fieri peteret, si authoritate suâ factam agnosceret, gratiam factum Pontificem, vt sacra hîc omnia, hoc ipso quo nunc sunt apud nos modò procurari fas esset. Vt verò, Primatus sit illud ....., nec quicquam pensi sit Pontifici, quid reliquis illis fiat, si hoc vnum modò exorari posset.
units.tr: He therefore adds that, before that sentence was pronounced by Pius, before even the Pope, Pius had at the very beginning of the reign revoked the oath concerning the Primacy. Certainly he did revoke it. For what was she to do, since she did not agree with you in religion; since she had already fixed in her mind to worship God by the reformed rite and in a manner more conformed to the Holy Scriptures, rather than by that rite in which she had been instructed under her brother's reign? Would she allow the laws which her sister Mary had lately enacted against the reformed religion to stand in their place, and not repeal them? Or, since it was decided that she should restore the better custom and rite of worshipping God, which her sister had abolished, ought she not also to recall to herself, along with it, the authority which her sister had surrendered? What then? Would she establish the religion which now exists, and yet the Pope acknowledge her Primacy? Certainly that was attempted, and it is established that under Paul the Fourth the condition was sought, and further offered to the Queen herself: that if she would only consent to his Primacy, then, as to the rest, if she asked it of him, and acknowledged that it was done by his authority, the Pope would grant the favour that all these sacred matters might be lawfully carried on among us in the very same way as they are now carried on. But as for the Primacy, let that be ..... and the Pope cares nothing what becomes of the rest, if only this one thing could be obtained from him.

units.la: At hæc de Primatu noua Hæresi. At hîc iam Matthaeo vetus mos, petere principium, & quod probare debet, miserè illud & turpiter emendicare. Damus hoc tibi; si illa Hæresis est, mala materia est iuramenti, malè vrgetur iuramentum quod de Hæresi. Sin, quod rei veritas est, quod nos, cùm res feret, probando erimus, Hæresis in eo nulla, nec vlla iuramento eo obedientia requiritur, nisi quæ secundum Scripturas sanctas Regibus debetur; nihil à suis postulauit, nisi quod iure postulare potuit, & iniuriam in eo non fecit, cùm non nisi iure suo vteretur. Sed neque tu impugnas illud ratione vllâ; & nobis de Primatu hîc nulla, de fidelitatis iuramento tota lis est.
units.tr: "But these things concerning the Primacy are a new heresy." Here again Matthew falls into his old habit of begging the question, and wretchedly and shamefully begs for that which he ought to prove. We grant you this: if that is a heresy, the matter of the oath is ill-founded, and the oath which concerns heresy is ill-pressed. But if, as is the truth of the matter, which we shall prove when the occasion requires, there is no heresy in it, and no obedience is required by that oath except that which is owed to kings according to the Holy Scriptures; she demanded nothing from her subjects except what she could rightfully demand, and she did them no wrong in this, since she used only her own right. But you do not impugn it on any ground at all; and with us there is no dispute here about the Primacy, but the whole dispute is about the oath of fidelity.

units.la: Non demittimus ergo nos in quæstionem illâ, quin te potiùs remittimus ad Gardineri Wintoniensis Librum De vera obedientia, ad Boneri Londinensis ibi præfationem, ad Tonstalli Dunelmensis ad Polum Epistolam, ad Longlandi Lincolniensis concionem, ad alios multos libros & tractatus (atque audi) vestrorum hominum omnes, qui rem totam hanc accurate scriptis suis complexi sunt.
units.tr: We therefore do not let ourselves be drawn into that question; rather we refer you back to Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, his book On True Obedience; to the preface of Bonner, Bishop of London, there; to Tunstall, Bishop of Durham, and his Letter to Pole; to the sermon of Longland, Bishop of Lincoln; and to many other books and treatises (and listen) of all your men, who have set out this whole matter accurately in their writings.

units.la: Illos, si cuiquam alij de vestris, si tibi Matthae libido est refellere, nos statim responsum adornamus, quod te torqueat. Satis interim hoc proposito nostro, quòd ineunte Regnum Reginâ, cùm plerosque de vobis iniquiores reperisset in ius ipsum, & successionem suam; quò subsisteret ipsa per se, ac regno securiore frueretur; iure suo usa sit, eámque à subditis observantiam exegerit, quam exigi per ius posse. Deinque verbum, ex tot suorum eruditis scriptis, diu iam ante didicisset.
units.tr: If you, Matthew, have a desire to refute those, or any other of your side, we shall at once prepare an answer which will trouble you. For the present it is enough for our purpose that at the beginning of the reign the Queen, finding most of you more hostile to her right and to her succession, so that she might herself stand more securely and enjoy a safer kingdom, used her right and exacted from her subjects that obedience which can be rightfully exacted. And she had learned this word long before, from the many learned writings of her own people.

units.la: Nam quod grauem Authorem imprimis Sanderum referre, refers, illa: non poteras ipse tibi magis incommodare, magis fidem omnem detrahere, vel tibi, vel argumento tuo, quàm si illo referente, quicquam nobis referas. Sanderum quis nescit?
units.tr: For as to your citing Sanders above all, a serious author, here is what you say: "You could not have done yourself greater harm, nor have stripped yourself of all credit more, either with yourself or with your argument, than if, by citing him, you cite anything for us." Who does not know Sanders?

units.la: Tune ut illum perditum transfugam, virulentum calumniatorem, nefarium patriæ proditorem, inque ipso proditionis suæ actu cæsum, prius tamen (diuina manu) rabie percussum, tune ut illum hic testem citare audeas? Notum vero iam orbi satis, quòd in libello illo famoso, de schismate congesserit prodigiosa mendacia, quot in reliquis etiam scriptis, quæ reliqui fere omnes hauriunt ex isto mendaciorum Patre Sandero.
units.tr: Would you dare to cite as a witness that lost deserter, that poisonous slanderer, that wicked traitor to his country, who was cut down in the very act of his treachery, yet first struck down by madness through the divine hand? That man, who in that famous little book on the schism has heaped up prodigious lies, as he did in his other writings too, which almost all the rest draw from that father of lies, Sanders.

units.la: Audiat illa tantum quis, rem nesciat; si non suffusus illi malevolentia animus, (ut tibi) statim conspuat ad singula: Produnt enim ipsa se, tam sunt, & turpia, & tamen stulta; mirabitur illi ita non frontem modo, sed & mentem omnem perijsse, ut talia referre non pigeat, quæ sic pigeat audire: silicem illi certè pro fronte, nouaculam pro lingua fuisse.. Quòd si nihil etiam esset præterquam hoc, quòd capitalis hostis, quòd perfidus perduellis fuerit, ecquem non pudeat hunc sibi testem producere? Illene, ut hic testimonium ferat, cui, quæ duæ res in omni teste requiri solent, & quarum neutra abesse potest, honesta fama, æquus, & in neutram partem propendens animus: ex in hoc, amba, ex toto prorsus deficiunt. Nisi fiquis putet, hærere posse honestam famam infami proditori, vel æquam mentem in furato hoste reperiri; qualem illum fuisse facta clamant, (nempe turpem proditorem?) qualem illum
units.tr: Let anyone hear those things who does not know the matter; if his mind is not suffused with malice (as yours is), he will at once spit at each point. For they reveal themselves, being so both shameful and yet foolish; one would wonder that he had lost not only his face but his whole mind, so that he was not ashamed to relate such things which are shameful even to hear: surely he had flint for a forehead and a razor for a tongue. But even if there were nothing more than this, that he was a capital enemy, a treacherous rebel, who would not be ashamed to produce this man as a witness for himself? One who is to give testimony here, in whom the two things which are usually required in every witness, and neither of which can be absent, an honourable reputation and an impartial mind inclining to neither side, are wholly lacking in him, both of them. Unless someone thinks that an honourable reputation can cling to an infamous traitor, or that an impartial mind can be found in a hostile enemy; such as the deeds cry out that he was (namely, a shameful traitor),

units.la: Hebrew, Greek and smaller-type notes: none printed on this page. fuisse scripta clamant (nempe hostem capitalem) non Principis modò suæ, sed & Principum qui uspiam sint omnium, illiúsque adeo, quæ omnibus inesse debet Principibus, authoritatis; quæ omnibus præstari debet à subditis, fidelitatis. Apage verò Sanderum; quid ille referat, parum certè, imò (parum hic nimium est) nihil omnino refert.
units.tr: Hebrew, Greek and smaller-type notes: none printed on this page. such as the writings cry out that he was (namely, a capital enemy) not only of his own prince but of all the princes who are anywhere, and so of that authority which ought to be in all princes, and of that fidelity which ought to be shown by all subjects. Away with Sanders! What he relates is of little account, indeed (little is too much here) it relates absolutely nothing.

units.la: Pòst verò de multi[?], multus sermo, quam irrogauit lex illis tum, qui ritu, veteri, dixit, (ritu enim vero dicere non potuit) & Romano (qui forte quàm Christi vel Apostolorum melior mos est) more officium missa procurabant. Ubi Lector aduerte scio, qui Edictum nostrum ante calumniatus est, eique mendaciter affinxit quòd cœnam Caluinisticam sumi juberet: is ipse jam Sacramentum sumi vult Romano more. Monendus mihi hic de more illo Romano. Nos enim non ex more Gentis ullius sumimus; is nobis sumendi modus solus placet, eo solo sumimus, quem Apostolus Corinthijs tradidit acceptum à Christo: Non illum quidem Romanum, quippe tum (cùm Roma nihil etiam audisset de fide) à Seruatore ipso more suo institutum. Eo & nos sumimus, & Roma ipsa sumeret, nisi Christo se & Paulo plus sapere putaret.
units.tr: Afterwards, concerning the many ... much talk about the fine which the law then imposed on those who, as it says, "by the old rite" (for he could not say "by the rite") and "by the Roman" (which perhaps is a better custom than that of Christ or the Apostles) procured the office of the Mass in the manner of the Romans. Here, reader, mark the man who earlier slandered our edict, and falsely attributed to it that the Calvinist supper be taken: he himself now wishes the sacrament to be taken in the Roman manner. I must be reminded here of that Roman manner. For we do not take it after the custom of any nation; that mode of taking alone pleases us, and by that alone do we take it, which the Apostle handed down to the Corinthians as received from Christ: not indeed the Roman mode, since it was instituted by the Saviour himself in his own manner, at a time when Rome had not yet even heard anything of the faith. By this we take it, and Rome herself would take it likewise, were she not to think herself wiser than Christ and Paul.

units.la: De multâ quid attinet dicere? Quasi verò quid in eâ nouum? Quis enim Princeps, nisi illi jam juxta[?] regum non sit, liberum & sine multâ saltem finitæ esse apud se exercitium cultus peregrini?
