Hospes es in historiâ si nescis, sub bono, pióque Principe Theodosio, & qui illum secuti sunt, Donatistis (qui perijsse de orbe toto Ecclesiam Catholicam, nusquam esse, nisi apud partem suam, ut vos jam apud vestram). Donatistis (inquam) refractarijs, libram auri multam dictam esse, fisco tum applicandam. Quam multam Augustinus sæpe, semper autem cum laude, commemorat. Quid ? vestrum quis aliter facit? Numquid cuique (quæ vult) sacra cudendi, liberum apud vos, aut cuique quæ vult sacra adeundi, copiam facitis? Non facitis. Alius verò generis multa vobis est. Quod si persecutionem addiscere voluisset Regina ELIZABETHA, poterat certè à MARIA sorore; quæ nostræ professionis homines sub se, qui Missam, lege tum (ut jam Liturgia nostra) sancitam audire nollent, non pecunia aut carcere multauit, multam infixit capitibus non aliam, quàm ut capita simul, & corpora eorum, in bonum & liculentum focum conijcerentur, ibi ad cineres vsque concremanda. Ea vestra tum mitis mulcta fuit, ita mulctatis nos, non lana, sed pelle ipsa, & (pro qua, cuncta quae habet, dabit homo) vitā & spiritu; Et vos, qui flammā rem geritis, de florenis hiscere audetis? Atqui nos tum, si pecuniā, & re tota transfigere, si carcere, si exilio licuisset; gratiosum illud Edictum ex animo omnes diceremus. Noli ergo rem istam nummariam magis premere; elicuistis sanguinem de nobis; sanguinem enim bibit meretrix vestra. Æquus autem Lector agnoscet ipse per se, constare pacem; non posse vlli Reipublicæ, si patria sacra aspernari liceat, si sacrum peregrinum operari, impunitate datâ. Indignum etiam esse in eâ Repub. quæ legibus tenetur, discedi à legibus. Quod autem fecit Regina, hoc tantùm fuit; quam Ipsa Sibi, vt veram maximè, ita animæ suæ maximè salutarem, in animum induxerat; quam lege sanciendam curauerat; eandem vt omnes religionem amplecterentur; qui secus facerent, eis vt vel pecuniario aliquo damno, vel libertatis (minùs autem id multo quàm Soror) impunè ne foret.
units.tr: Why is there need to speak about the fine? As if there were anything new in it! For what prince, unless he is not yet among the kings, does not allow the exercise of a foreign worship to be free among himself, or at least without a fine? You are a stranger in history if you do not know that under the good and pious prince Theodosius, and those who followed him, a pound of gold was imposed as a fine on the Donatists (who claimed that the Catholic Church had perished from the whole world, and was nowhere except among their own party, just as you now claim among yours), on the Donatists, I say, who were refractory, and the fine was then to be applied to the treasury. Augustine often mentions this fine, always with praise. What? Which of you does otherwise? Do you grant anyone the freedom to set up whatever worship he wishes among you, or access to whatever worship he wishes? You do not. Your fines are of another kind. But if Queen Elizabeth had wished to learn persecution, she could certainly have learned it from her sister Mary, who, among those of our profession under her, who would not hear the Mass, which was then enacted by law (as our Liturgy is now), did not punish them with money or prison; she imposed on their heads no other fine than that their heads and bodies together should be cast into a good and blazing hearth, there to be burned to ashes. That was your mild penalty then: those so fined by you were stripped not of wool but of the skin itself, and (for which a man will give all that he has) of life and breath. And you, who carry on the business with fire, dare to gape at florins? Yet we, if it had been permitted to them to punish us with money and the whole matter, with prison, with exile, would all have said that gracious edict from the heart. Do not, therefore, press this monetary matter so hard: you have drawn blood from us; for your harlot drinks blood. The fair reader will recognise for himself that peace cannot stand, nor can any commonwealth, if it is allowed to despise the sacred rites of its country and to perform a foreign rite with impunity. It is also unworthy that in a commonwealth which is bound by laws, one should depart from the laws. What the Queen did was only this: she resolved in her own mind that religion which she herself judged most true and most salutary for her soul; she took care that it should be established by law, so that all should embrace that same religion; and that those who acted otherwise should not go unpunished, with some monetary loss, or with loss of liberty (though much less of this than her sister inflicted).

units.la: Tum quod dicis ex Sandero, de plurimis Episcopis secundum eam legem, mox in carcerem coniectis; quàm falsum sit; vide, & crimine ab vno, discere reliqua. Nec enim plurimi, cùm & omnes illi quos memorat, non plurimi, nec tamen omnes illi coniecti; vix mediam omnes illi hîc partem superant Episcoporum apud nos; Nec mox coniecti, Actis enim publicis consignatum extat, cuius eorum quisque vel fratris, vel affinis, vel amici sui, priuatæ & libera custodiæ commissus fuerit: Nec secundum eam legem coniecti, sed quòd, forte quidam ex ijs insolenter se & protervè gererent. Falsi ergo tenetur de omnibus: nec pigebit tamen decurrere per singulos ab eo notatos, si tamen pauca præfatus fuero. Enimuerò, Regina si in omnes fuisset indelementior, plurimùm id eorum merito fecisset, cùm conspirâsset inter se maior eorum pars; ne quisquam ei coronam imponeret, vt redierit res ad Carliolensem[?] in illo ordine penè infimum, qui rem non inuitus præstitit. Tum, vbi capita religionis quædam tractari vellet, inter Episcopos, atque eos qui illis ex aduersâ parte; primò tergiuersari omninò, nec inicreisse[?] velle: pòst, vbi venissent tandem, atque audissent quid vrgerent Aduersarij, vt responsum eis vllum darent, omnino recusare. Meritas certè debitásque poenas luissent, si de contumaciâ hac suâ tam peruicaci, ijsdem omnes in carcerem. At Illa, cui mitior multo quàm Sorori indoles, durius in eos nihil statuit; Sororem quidem imitata non est, quæ ad ardentem pyram omnes, non custodiam amandâsset: quemadmodum & quinque de Episcopis suis, viuos exuri iussit, non quòd in eam, patriámue quicquam admisissent, sed quòd fidei suæ renunciare & Euangelio; & quod omnia quæ sic Pontifici visa sunt, vera itidem esse deierare, nollent.
units.tr: Then, as for what you say from Sanders, that many bishops were thrown into prison at once under that law: see how false this is, and learn the rest from this one instance. For not many, since all those he names are not many, nor were all of them thrown in prison; scarcely half of our bishops are all of them above that number. Nor were they thrown in at once, for it is recorded in the public acts that each of them was committed to the private and free custody of a brother, a relative, or a friend of his. Nor were they imprisoned under that law, but because some of them, by chance, behaved insolently and defiantly. So you are wrong about all of them. Still, I will not hesitate to go through them one by one, as noted by him, if I first say a few things. Indeed, if the Queen had been more merciless towards all of them, she would have done so with much justification, since most of them had conspired among themselves, so that none of them would place the crown on her head, and the matter came down to the Carlisle man, in that rank almost the lowest, who carried out the business not unwillingly. Then, when certain heads of religion were to be discussed between the bishops and those on the opposing side, at first they refused altogether to take part and would not come forward; afterwards, when they finally came and heard what the opponents urged, they utterly refused to give any answer. They would surely have deserved and paid the penalties due, if all of them had been thrown into prison for this so stubborn obstinacy. But she, whose disposition was far milder than her sister's, decided nothing more harsh against them; she did not imitate her sister, who would have sent all of them to the burning pyre rather than to custody. Likewise she ordered five of her bishops to be burned alive, not because they had committed anything against her or the country, but because they would not renounce their faith and the Gospel, and would not swear that everything which seemed right to the Pope was equally true.

units.la: Præfatus hæc, vt, quid optimo iure posset Regina si vellet, Lectori constet: redeo iam ad illud, quid fecerit, Plurimi illis Episcopi secundùm eam legem, mox in carceres coniecti, nec tamen plurimi, nec mox, nec secundùm eam legem coniecti. Nam vel ex illis quatuordecim, nouem extra carceres diem obierunt, tres vltrò excesserunt Regno, duo tantùm in carcere mortui.
units.tr: Having said these things, so that it may be clear to the reader what the Queen could rightly do if she wished, I now return to what she actually did: that many of those bishops were thrown into prison at once under that law, when in fact not many, nor at once, nor under that law, were imprisoned. For of those fourteen, nine died outside the prisons, three voluntarily left the kingdom, and only two died in prison.

units.la: E primis nouem, primus mihi sit N. Hethus solus Archiepiscopus, Eboracensis, qui honorificè semper à Reginâ habitus est, nec vnquam vllâ custodiâ detentus, non solùm vllâ parte exutus, permissus semper rure suo viuere, & cùm ad multam ætatem in otio vixisset, testamento etiam hæredes scribere. C. Tonstallus Dunelmensis qui ei proximus, consenuit in contubernio Archiepiscopi Cantuariensis, vbi summâ ætate octogenario iam maior, defunctus, nec fine pompâ funebri sepultus est. Idem hoc Thirlbeio Eliensi factum, qui ijsdem in ædibus Archiepiscopi laute exceptus, decennio post Tonstallū fatis concessit. Nam Whitus Wintoniensis in carcere quidem fuit ad tempus, non eam tamen ob causam, sed quòd quædam minùs pro officio dixisset in concione; verùm dimissus tamen inde post, atque extra carcerem, fato functus est. Bournus Bathoniensis, in Carewi ædibus, illustris viri, Decani Exoniensis, veteris amici sui, post undecim annos diem suum obiit. Turberuillus Exoniensis, cùm per multos annos priuatus vixisset, in summâ libertate & ipse defunctus est. Polus Petriburgensis, summâ comitate habitus, liber semper, Principis beneficio, & in agro suo, maturâ ætate decessit. De Oglethorpio Carliolensi, qui in Reginam officiosior quàm cæteri, dubium esse non potest, qui tamen non ita multò post apoplexiâ extinctus est. De Bayno itidem Lichfieldenfi, qui breui post tempore, ex calculi morbo vitâ cum morte mutauit. Salutârunt forte carcerem nonnulli ex hijs, dum non satis pro officij ratione responderent; sed dimissi tamen post, maxima ex parte, atq; amicorum fidei commissi sunt. Proximi mihi tres illi, qui ad exteras se partes receperunt. De Scoto enim Ceftrenfi, proteruo homine, & id constat, elapsum custodia, vltro post exulasse. De Pato Wigornenfi, de Goldwello itidem Asaphenfi, & illos excesisse Regno fatemur; neutrum tamen ex legis sententia aliquâ, tantum, quia sic ipsi voluerunt. Supersunt duo iam; Watsonus Lincolnienfis morosus homo, qui & ipse tamen laxius aliquandiu habitus in aedibus Episcopi Elienfis, post Roffenfis, tandem cum hic per Emissarios vestros turbatae res, in arcem insulae Elienfis ablegatus est. Bonerus autem Londinenfis, qui regnante Maria cum lanienae praesset, in odium venerat omni populo (vt nec tutum esset ei prodire in publicum, ne saxis obrueretur) ille quidem in carcere consenuit; sed vbi, si vidisses, inedia confectum non diceres; viuebat opiparè; horti erant & pomaria, si volebat spatiari; denique, nisi quòd certo spatio circumscriptus, haud quicquam instar carceris.
units.tr: Of the first nine, let the first be N. Hethus alone, the Archbishop of York, who was always treated with honour by the Queen, never held in any custody, not stripped of any part of his property, always allowed to live on his estate, and, having lived in leisure to a great age, even to make heirs by will. C. Tonstall of Durham, who came next, grew old in the house of the Archbishop of Canterbury, where he died at a great age, more than eighty, and was buried with no lack of funeral pomp. The same happened to Thirlby of Ely, who, lavishly entertained in the same house of the Archbishop, departed this life ten years after Tonstall. For Whyte of Winchester was indeed in prison for a time, but not for that reason; it was because he had said certain things in a sermon less dutifully; yet he was afterwards released from there, and, outside the prison, died a natural death. Bourne of Bath, in the house of Carew, a distinguished man, and of the Dean of Exeter, his old friend, died his day after eleven years. Turberville of Exeter, who had lived in private for many years, died himself in the greatest liberty. Pole of Peterborough, treated with the greatest courtesy, always free by the Prince's favour and on his own estate, died at a ripe age. Concerning Oglethorpe of Carlisle, who was more dutiful towards the Queen than the others, there can be no doubt; yet he died not long afterwards of apoplexy. Likewise Bayne of Lichfield, who shortly afterwards exchanged life for death from the disease of the stone. Some of these perhaps tasted the prison, since they did not answer with sufficient regard for their office; but they were nevertheless, for the most part, released afterwards and committed to the trust of friends. Next to me are those three who withdrew to foreign parts. For as to Scot of Chester, a headstrong man, it is established that, having escaped from custody, he afterwards went into voluntary exile. As for Pate of Worcester and likewise Goldwell of St Asaph, we admit that they left the kingdom, yet neither of them by any sentence of the law, only because they themselves wished it. Two remain now: Watson of Lincoln, a peevish man, who was himself also held rather loosely for some time in the house of the Bishop of Ely, and afterwards of Rochester, until at last, when through your emissaries affairs were disturbed, he was sent away to the castle of the Isle of Ely. But Bonner of London, who, while Mary reigned, presided over the butchery, had come into hatred with all the people, so that it was not even safe for him to go out in public, lest he be stoned; he indeed grew old in prison; yet if you had seen him, you would not say he was worn out by hunger; he lived sumptuously; there were gardens and orchards, if he wished to walk; in short, except that he was confined within a certain space, he was in no way like a prisoner.

units.la: Habes de quatuordecim illis quos coniectos aiebat in carcerem. At nec hij plurimi erant, & de hijs quos nominauit non plurimis, plurimi mancipati non sunt carceribus, nonnulli ne viderunt quidem; libera tantùm & priuata fuit (fiqua fuit omninò) custodia; recepti sunt in familias vel eorum, qui successerunt eis Episcopi, vel amicorum; quorum ipsi potiùs conuictum expetebant, gratis sine sumptu, copiosè sine defectu, in otio sine molestia omni, ad vltimas quas illis natura descripserat annorum metas, peruenerunt. Nulli intentata vis; nulli quæstio criminis vel Primatus, obiecta; quibusdam neque priuatis de rebus quicquam imminutum. Plurimi tui iam, tot tui Episcopi, vides quò reciderint. Tum, permulti illi Nobiles, de quibus proximâ periodo idem asseris, vnus aut alter forte fuerunt, nec plures. Ridént enim nostri homines, cùm Nobiles illos Sanderi audiunt; illusit vobis Nobilium titulo, quem bonus ille vir angustiorem esse nouit apud nos multò, nec posse ex toto illo numero quem nobilitat, præterquam vni forte aut alteri conuenire. Ita plurimi illi Episcopi tui, &c permulti Nobiles, tot Episcopi, tot Nobiles, summis coniunctis vix senarium efficiunt; & illi ipsi non solius (quod tu ais) religionis causa; non, sed procacitatis & insolentiae suae causa eo amandati.
units.tr: You have the account of those fourteen whom he said were thrown into prison. But neither were these many, and of those he named, not many were put in prison; many were not handed over to prisons at all, and some did not even see one; their custody was free and private (if indeed there was any custody at all); they were received into the households either of those who succeeded them as bishops or of friends; and they themselves rather sought that living together, free without expense, abundant without lack, in leisure without any trouble, and reached the final limits of years which nature had set for them. No violence was threatened against any of them; no charge of crime or of the Primacy was brought against them; some of them lost nothing even in their private affairs. Your "many" bishops, so many of yours, you see where they have ended. Then, as for "very many nobles", of whom you say the same in the next sentence, there were perhaps one or two, and no more. For our people laugh when they hear of those "nobles" of Sanders; he has mocked you with the title of nobles, which that good man knows is much narrower among us, and that out of that whole number which he calls "nobled" only perhaps one or two could apply. So your "very many bishops" and "very many nobles", so many bishops, so many nobles, taken together scarcely make up six; and those very men were sent away not on account of religion alone, as you say, but on account of their own impudence and insolence.

units.la: Omnino qui undecennium primum meminerunt Reginae ELIZABETHAE, haud quicquam eo mitius vel remissius fuisse praedicabunt. Decimo tertio demum anno, biennio scilicet postquam Pius quintus Bullam huc suam parum piam misisset, atque ex eâ Boreales illae turbae extitissent, paulò tum facta commotior, ut par erat, statuere coepit contra Bullas & earum tabellarios; sed praeterquàm in eos, nihil superstitionis tum vestrae causâ, sancitum est durius.
units.tr: Certainly those who remember the first eleven years of Queen Elizabeth will declare that nothing was milder or more lenient than that. Only in the thirteenth year, that is, two years after Pius V had sent his impious Bull hither, and those Northern disturbances had arisen from it, did she, somewhat more stirred, as was fitting, begin to decree against the Bulls and their bearers; yet, apart from those people, nothing harsher was enacted at that time on account of your superstition.

units.la: Decimo post, id est, anno 23. ut videas quàm illa Princeps pigra fuerit ad poenas; cùm Emissarij illi vestri sacrificij, ferè vel ante Missas vel post, venenum suum comperti sunt spargere, nec admittere ad eas, nisi qui[?] & ipsi missam facerent fidem omnem atque ossicium in Principem: coeptum est acriùs in eos animadverti, qui ita Missis interessent; multa tum illa (quam dicis) impositâ, remittenda tamen statim, cùm redirent ad mentem meliorem.
units.tr: Ten years later, that is, in the twenty-third year, so that you may see how sluggish that Princess was in punishing; when those emissaries of your sacrifice were found scattering their poison, almost either before or after the Masses, and not admitting anyone to them unless they themselves also made profession of full faith and obedience to the Prince: it began to be punished more sharply those who attended such Masses; a heavy fine was then imposed, as you say, but to be remitted at once, when they returned to a better mind.

units.la: Quinquennio post, cùm serperent indies longiùs, & quasi examen quoddam è novis Seminarijs sacrifici sese per regnum effunderent; cautum est lege capitali, ne Novitij isti, qui cum religione depravatâ in Seminarijs illis, animum etiam ab officio alienum imbiberant, & qualem ipsi imbiberant, talem aliis propinarent, ne illi (inquam) traijcerent huc in Angliam.
units.tr: Five years later, when they were creeping further each day and a swarm of new sacrificing priests was pouring out across the kingdom from the new seminaries, it was provided by capital law that these novices, who had soaked up from those seminaries a corrupted religion and also an attitude alien to their duty, and who would pass on to others the same thing they had absorbed, should not (I say) cross over here into England.

units.la: Notum enim satis quid hic, cùm venissent, agerent ad unum omnes, quàm neminem Ecclesiae suae Romanae reconciliarent, nisi, qui se sponderet, cùm res poscerret, ad omnia Pontificis mandata, praestò & paratum fore. Atque, huc Illam tandem, post annos 27. invitam & quasi reluctantem, nec ab indole suâ seuerâ Principem pertraxit, atque has Illi[?] leges extorsit, hominum vestrorum importunitas.
units.tr: For it is well enough known what they did here, once they had arrived, all of them alike: they reconciled no one to their Roman Church unless the person promised that, when the situation required, he would be ready and prepared for every command of the Pontiff. And so, after twenty-seven years, the importunity of your people finally drew that Queen, reluctant and as it were unwilling, and not by nature severe, into these laws and extorted them from her.

units.la: Quam proinde etiamnum audet Apologiae Author afferere, Neminem vestrum religionis causâ in iudicium vocâsse, neminem ad supplicium condemnasse, quamdiu scilicet rem religionis agerent, nec cum religione, rebellionis semina permiscerent, neque priusquam Pius Papa per Bullas suas hic in Angliam, per copias verò & cohortes suas ibi etiam in Hi-berniam, berniam, impetum, & impresionem fecisset: hic plumbo, ibi ferro ; in Anglia clauibus, in Hiberniâ gladijs rem gesisset.
units.tr: Therefore the author of the Apology still dares to assert that none of you was summoned to judgment for religion's sake, and none condemned to punishment, so long as you were engaged in "the business of religion" and did not mix the seeds of rebellion with religion, and not before the Pope by his Bulls had made an attack and an assault here in England, and by his troops and cohorts there also in Ireland: here he had done business with lead, there with iron; in England with keys, in Ireland with swords.

units.la: Nec enim tu satis videris intelligere illud in iudicium vocare, aut ad supplicium condemnare, quid sibi velit. Nemo vita, nemo membri, nemo fortunarum omnium vel perpetui carceris discrimen adijt. Hic, denarijs forte duodecim multatus, quòd die dominico templum non adijsset: alius, quòd ad Eucharistiam non accessisset: tertius, cum in missificandi actu deprehensus, per plateas in apparatu illo suo missatico traductus. Quid haec ad seria? Hoccine tu vocari in iudicium, vel, ad supplicium condemnari vocas? Nemini puella adulta manus, (ut Scaevola) nondum rea factae vel vocatae in ius: nemini gravide[?],.. cum aperta alvo Embryo vivus erumperet, transfixus cuspide infans primò, post etiam in flammam reiectus, & cum matre (barbaro & execrabili exemplo) ibi exustus est. Nemo fame enectus, nemo in carcere trucidatus; non quadriennio quadringenti & amplius flammis absumpti sunt. Duodecim toti anni erant, cum in Feltonum qui Bullam impiam hic ausus affigere, animaduersum est: is primus hic è veteris vocatus in iudicium, atque capite multatus est; ante illum nemo. Multa forte aliqua, sed non gravis: Lex etiam, sed non saevera. Exilio damnatus nemo; pauci carceribus mancipati; ubi causa fuit religionis nihil asperum; ubi quid asperum, causa religionis non fuit. Vis veritatem audire? vis quae te non fallat, ex ore hominis inimici? Audi Philopatrum ipsum Iesuitam, insignem alioqui conuiciatorem, sed veritatis vi victum, Reginam de Regni sui initijs sic alloquentem: {a}Dum initio Regni tui mitius aliquanto cum Catholicis ageres, dum nullum adhuc vehementissime vrgeres, nullum admodum premeres, vel adfecta tua participationem, vel fidei antiquae abnegationem, omnia sane tranquilliore cursu incedere videbantur, nec audiebantur magnae querelae, nec insignis aliqua dissensio aut repugnantia cernebatur, nec deerant (quanquam male) qui Ecclesias vestras, ut vobis placerent ac gratificarentur, corpore saltem, etsi non animo frequentabant. Legis hic, Iesuitico atramento depicta, quae tu tum fatua calumniaris Regni Principia. At tu, audire te hic existima loquentem invidiam ipsam; puta autem minus hic dici, plus intelligi.
units.tr: For you do not seem to understand what "to summon to judgment" or "to condemn to punishment" means. No one lost life, no one a limb, no one all his goods, or faced the danger of perpetual imprisonment. Here one man, fined perhaps twelve pence because he had not gone to church on the Lord's day; another, because he had not come to the Eucharist; a third, caught in the very act of saying Mass, was led through the streets in that Mass-vestment of his. What has this to do with serious matters? Do you call this "being summoned to judgment" or "being condemned to punishment"? No one had his hand cut off, like Scaevola, a grown girl who had not yet been made a defendant or summoned to court; no one was pregnant, when a living embryo burst out of her opened womb, and an infant pierced first with a spear and afterwards thrown into the flames, and burned there together with its mother by a barbarous and abominable example. No one was starved to death, no one butchered in prison; four hundred and more were not consumed by fire in four years. There were twelve whole years when the one called Felton, who had dared to post the impious Bull here, was punished: he was the first of the old faith to be summoned to judgment and punished with death here; before him, no one. A fine perhaps, but not a heavy one; a law indeed, but not a harsh one. No one was condemned to exile; a few were consigned to prisons; where the cause was religion, nothing harsh was done; where something harsh was done, religion was not the cause. Do you want to hear the truth? Do you want something that will not deceive you, from the mouth of an enemy? Hear the Jesuit Philopater himself, otherwise a notorious reviler, but overcome by the force of truth, addressing the Queen about the beginnings of her reign in this way: While at the start of your reign you dealt somewhat more mildly with the Catholics, while you did not yet press anyone very hard or oppress anyone at all, whether for participation in your rites or for the abjuration of the ancient faith, all things seemed to proceed in a very calm course, no great complaints were heard, no notable dissension or opposition was seen, and there were those (though wrongly) who, to please and gratify you, attended your churches, at least in body, even if not in mind. You read here laws painted in Jesuit ink, which you then foolishly slander as the principles of the kingdom. But you, think that the very envy itself is speaking here; and consider that less is said here than is understood.

units.la: Audis tamen, vel ab eo, neminem admodum tum pressum, non magnas tum querelas, non insignem aliquam dissensionem extitusse[?]: Non ergo ita tum refertos carceres, non tot Episcopos, tot Nobiles, fortunis omnibus exutos, actos in exilium, carcerisperpetuo mancipatos. Crede saltem huic Testi: inimicus homo est, nihil in gratiam dicit: crede (inquam) vel inimico huic homini, & de Reginâ posthæc obmutesce.
units.tr: Yet you hear, even from him, that at that time no one was greatly oppressed, there were no great complaints, and no notable dissension had arisen: therefore the prisons were not then crowded, not so many Bishops, so many Nobles, stripped of all their goods, driven into exile, consigned to perpetual imprisonment. At least believe this witness: he is an enemy, he says nothing in favour of you; believe (I say) even this enemy, and from now on be silent about the Queen.

units.la: Quid verò in animo tibi, quòd quæ paulò ante eâdem hâc vndecimâ sectione dixeras; eadem ipsa denuo, totidem penè verbis repetas? Adeone profluuiâ memoriâ Lectorem putabas esse, vt excideret ei Primatus iuramentum, nisi vnicâ sectione idem illi bis inculcâsses? Sine perfungar eo semel. Quòd delatum illud iuramentum Episcopis, non ita fuit, vt tu videri vis, facinus indignum. Nihil aliud ab ijs quæsitum, vt facerent, quàm quod bis iam ante fecerant, sub Henrico scilicet 8. & Eduardo 6. Heathus, Bonerus, Tonstallus, Thirlbeus tum Episcopi: Baynus, Bournus, reliqui, nondum Episcopi; præstiterant iam ante idem iuramentum omnes, aliis quoque vt præstarent, authores fuerant: etiam illorum quidam, libris scriptis defenderant. Quid hîc iniqui, si de eodem iterum compellentur?
units.tr: But what is in your mind, that you should now repeat, almost word for word, the very things you said a little earlier in this same eleventh section? Did you think the reader so forgetful that the oath of Supremacy would slip from his memory unless you had driven the same point into him twice in a single section? Let me indulge in it once. That the oath was offered to the Bishops was not, as you wish to appear, an unworthy deed. Nothing else was asked of them than that they should do what they had already done twice before, namely under Henry the Eighth and Edward the Sixth. Heath, Bonner, Tunstall, Thirlby, being Bishops at the time; Bayne, Bourne, and the rest, not yet Bishops, had all previously taken the same oath, and had been the authors of urging others to take it too; some of them had even defended it in written books. What is unjust here, if they are required again about the same thing?

units.la: Non enim credo tam eris vecors, vt litem moueas de sexu; fœmina fuit: fuit: at tu spero, cum Knoxo non sentis, & qui illius sectatores sunt, vt fœminam regnantem non feras. Regina fuit, æqualis per omnia iure cum regibus, nec quicquam illi negandum, quod Regi conueniat. Debora, cùm Israeli Iudex, ius illi pari authoritate dixit, nec deteriore, quàm vel Othoniel vel Gedeon vel mas quispiam. Vel ergo, Salica vobis religio fingenda est, quâ excludi regni iure fœminas oportet, atque ita Sororem quoque eius Mariam exhæredari; vel si regnare vultis fœminas; & iura illis omnia, quæ Regalia sunt, cum regno pariter, sunt deferenda. At Tortus æquior esse debet in Reginarum iura, cui totes[?] honorifica mentio fit de Regina Mariâ Serenissimi Regis nostri Matre, quæ ipsa, Regni hæreditarij Regina cùm esset, par vlli Regi fuit de tot proauis suis, atque pars cum illis & imperio & imperandi authoritate prædita.
units.tr: For I do not believe you are so foolish as to raise a dispute about sex; she was a woman: yes, she was; but I hope that, along with Knox and those who follow him, you cannot endure a woman reigning. She was Queen, equal in every right with kings, and nothing that belongs to a King ought to be denied her. Deborah, when she was judge over Israel, exercised the right with equal authority, and no less than Othniel or Gideon or any male whatever. Therefore either you must invent for yourselves a Salic religion, by which women ought to be excluded from the right of the kingdom, and so her sister Mary also be disinherited; or, if you wish women to reign, all the rights that are royal must be granted to them equally along with the kingdom. But Turton ought to be more just toward the rights of Queens, since an honourable mention is made of Queen Mary, the mother of our most Serene King, who, being herself Queen by hereditary right of the kingdom, was the equal of any King of all her forebears, and shared with them both the empire and the authority of ruling.

units.la: Velim autem ex Torto scire, cur licere non possit Reginæ, quod licet apud eos, Abbatissæ. Abbatissa enim capax est iurisdictionis spiritualis, eámque iurisdictionem in sibi subditos exercere potest. Delegatam dices à Papâ; Ergo si& Reginæ eam sibi à Papa delegatam, nec aliter quàm ab eo, sumere vellent, salua res esset. Sed nihil opus; delegari enim potest à iure positiuo, quod ad institutum nostrum satis. Verùm nec hoc etiam premo. Nam & hoc quoque contendo, ordinariam esse, quam Abbatissæ apud vos habent iurisdictionem. Abbas enim ordinariam habet, & in administratione suâ Abbati æquiparatur Abbatissa: eandem ergo, & eodem iure ordinariam obtinebit. Quid vero obstat? Quianè censuras exercere, excommunicare nequeunt? At Excommunicatio directè ad clauem ordinis non pertinet. {a}Aquinas hoc asserit. Excommunicatio non est actus clauis directè, sed magis exterioris fori. Et communis hæc apud vos sententia est: Omnis habens iurisdictionem spiritualem, etsi non habet clauem Ordinis, potest excommunicare. Negantur fœminis quæ Ordinis sunt, vel interioris fori: quæ verò ad forum exterius spectant, & Laicis communicantur, eorum, quin & fœminæ capaces sint, ratio nulla repugnat, vt pro Abbatissis suis acriter contendit, in eoque rem nostram agit Stephanus D'Alain {*}Sorbonâ sententiam eius approbante. Quanquam nos, Principi, censurae potestatem non facimus; in eoque, plus multo Abbatissæ vos, quàm nos Reginæ tribuimus.
units.tr: I would, however, like to learn from Turton why the Queen may not do what is lawful for them, namely for Abbesses. For an Abbess is capable of spiritual jurisdiction, and can exercise that jurisdiction over those subject to her. You will say it is delegated by the Pope; then if the Queen also wished to take it for herself as delegated by the Pope, and in no other way than from him, the matter would be safe. But there is no need: for it can be delegated by positive law, which is enough for our purpose. Indeed I do not press even this. For I also contend that the jurisdiction which Abbesses have among you is ordinary. For an Abbot has ordinary jurisdiction, and in his administration an Abbess is equal to an Abbot: she will therefore hold ordinary jurisdiction too, and by the same right. What, then, stands in the way? Is it that they cannot exercise censures, excommunicate? But excommunication does not pertain directly to the key of order. Aquinas asserts this: Excommunication is not an act of the key directly, but rather belongs to the outward forum. And this is the common opinion among you: everyone having spiritual jurisdiction, even if he does not have the key of order, can excommunicate. What belongs to order, or to the inward forum, is denied to women; but what belongs to the outward forum and is communicated to laymen, there is no reason against women being capable of it too, as Stephen d'Alain strongly contends for your Abbesses, and in this he argues our case, the Sorbonne approving his opinion. Although we do not grant the power of censure to the Prince; in this we attribute far more to your Abbesses than you attribute to our Queen.

units.la: Non est hæc (inquis) fortasse causa religionis. Vbi tuum illud fortasse, quod ludens ibi posuisti, nos quoque ludimus. Nec enim dubium hîc cuiquam est, quin quod Regi, idem & Reginæ conueniat, summùm scilicet regimen in suos, siue de Ecclesiâ, siue de republicâ sint, seu spirituales (vt loquimur) personæ, seu temporales. Præcipere etiam posse & prospicere de rebus religionis; nihilo autem minùs id quàm Regem quemcúnque Christianum. Nam prædicandi munus, vel sacra mysteria contrectandi, vel quæ reliqua sunt munueris Ecclesiastici, nec illa attigit vnquam, nec nos vel Reginæ, vel Regi putamus fas attingere; Nec hoc sibi ius ex illis quisquam vendicauit vnquam, quicquid hîc garriat illustris scilicet ille testis tuus Sanderus, mortalium mendacissimus, qui Reginam, quasi quid tale tentâsset, ausus est calumniari. At tu, cuitoties illud in ore est, repetit atque inculcat: hic iam, vbi nihil opus, otiosè penitus atque odiosè repetit ipse atque inculcat iterum atque iterum, ad tædium, nauseam, necem Lectoris: Et de Iuramento propositio 1558. & de multâ impositâ 1559. Sectione vnâ & eâdem, post lineas non multas, cùm semel dixisses; ingeminas rursus, idem ipsum, repetit, inculcas, nec repetendi finem vllum facis, vel inculcandi. Legem fuisse latam dicis: post, quomodo lata non fuerit, interrogas; Multam asseris impositam: post, quomodo non fuerit impósita, quæris. Id, credo, voluisti dicere, non modò coniectos in carcerem, sed & in carcerem coniectos; nec multatos tantùm qui audiebant Missam, verùm etiam qui Missam audiebant, multatos fuisse. Coccyfmus merus, Tortifmus merus.
units.tr: "This cause," you say, "is perhaps not a matter of religion." Here your "perhaps," which you put in there playfully, we also play with. For no one doubts that what belongs to the King belongs equally to the Queen: the supreme governance over her subjects, whether they belong to the Church or to the commonwealth, whether they are spiritual persons (as we say) or temporal. She can also give orders and take care of matters of religion, and no less so than any Christian King whatever. For the office of preaching, or of handling the sacred mysteries, or whatever else belongs to the ecclesiastical office, neither has she ever touched, nor do we think it right for the Queen or the King to touch them. Nor has anyone ever claimed this right from them, whatever your illustrious witness Sanders, the most lying of mortals, may babble here, who dared to slander the Queen as if she had attempted something of the kind. But you, in whose mouth that word is so often, "he repeats and inculcates," here again, where there is no need, you yourself idly and altogether odiously repeat and inculcate again and again, to the boredom, nausea and death of the reader. And about the "Proposition concerning the Oath" of 1558 and the "fine imposed" of 1559, in one and the same section, a few lines later, after you had said it once, you pile it on again: you repeat the same thing, you inculcate it, and you make no end to repeating or inculcating. You say a law was "enacted"; afterwards you ask how it was not enacted. You assert a fine was "imposed"; afterwards you ask how it was not imposed. I suppose you wanted to say that not only were men "thrown into prison," but also that men "thrown into prison" were fined; and that not only those who "heard Mass" were fined, but also those who "heard Mass" were fined. Pure coccyx-talk, pure Tortism.

units.la: Nam de lectione tuâ rerum nostrarum quòd ita valdè gloriaris: noste, Matthæe, nescimus qui vir sies, de Torto quàm multæ lectionis fit, nihil dum accepimus. De Domino tuo facilè credimus, quòd & legerit legendas nostras, & ex dono Authorum legerit. Nec nos in dubium vocamus an legitis illa quæ scripta sunt multa, de nostris rebus; sed quâ fide scripta sint, quæ sic legitis. A fugitiuis enim nostris falsò & perperam conscripta dicimus; superant ibi mendacia paginas, longè superant; certant etiam cum clausulis, vix enim vera in illis clausula. Sed neque potest esse vllo in libro acervus mendaciorum maior, quàm est in Legendâ illa plumbeâ, quæ de persecutione Anglicana apud vos circumfertur. Ibi legas, Catholicos infutos ferarum pellibus à rabidis canibus dilaniari; ibi Glires pelulibus inclusos Catholicorum viscera exedentes; ibi Catholicos ad equorum præsepia religatos, fœno ibi pascendos, nec legas solum, imò & videas; æræ enim ibi sculptæ imagines. Falsa, ficta, fucata omnia. Quod si vacet iam, & nisi peccem in Lectoris patientiam, subijcerem hic mendaciorum fastos, quæ in illis sunt; subijciendo facerem, vt vos lectionis vestræ, & memoriæ poeniteret; dehinc iam vt puderet, atque pigeret gloriari, quàm sæpe illa legeritis, vel quàm bene meminentis, quæ haud vlli rei sunt, præterquàm vt ignominiæ maculam inurant Authoribus ipsis, ad memoriam posteritatis sempiternam: in quibus malitia cum mendacio certat, perfidia cum impudentiâ, summa stultitia cum summo scelere. Et hæc tamen vos legendo bonas horas perditis, & ea lecta vobis & memoriæ mente recondita in laude vestrâ ponitis. Miseret me vestri: misit vobis Deus operationem erroris, vt crederetis mendacijs. At Lectori etiam sat tam notæ omissiones tuæ, ex ijs quæ prænotata mihi sunt, agnoscit statim, omittere te, quæ dicere non potes, quòd nulla ibi sint vt possis dicere; vt hic iam omittis quæ Rex ad Edicta Regine non pauca addidit. Non pauca certè; non enim vlla penitus. Quæ autem nullâ tuâ industriâ proferre posses: sine te exorem, vt omittas semper de industria.
units.tr: As for your "reading of our affairs," of which you boast so greatly: Matthew, we do not know what sort of man you are, and we have not yet received any account of how much reading Tortus has done. We readily believe of your master that he has read our writings, and that he has read them from the gift of their authors. Nor do we call into doubt whether you read the many things written about our affairs; but we ask with what good faith those things are written which you read in this way. For we say that they are falsely and perversely composed by our fugitives. Lies there outnumber the pages, far outnumber them; they even vie with the closing clauses, for hardly any clause in them is true. But no book can contain a heap of lies greater than that leaden Legend which circulates among you "concerning the Anglican persecution." There you may read that Catholics, sewn into bearskins, were torn apart by ravenous dogs; there, that dormice enclosed in fur-lined bags were eating out the vitals of Catholics; there, that Catholics were tied to horse-stalls and fed with hay there. And you may not only read this but also see it, for there are images engraved in bronze there. All false, feigned, painted over. But if I had the leisure now, and if I did not offend the patience of the reader, I would set out here the calendar of lies that are in those pages. By setting them out I would make you regret your reading and your memory, and then make you ashamed and sorry to boast of how often you have read those things, or how well you remember them, which serve no purpose at all except to brand the authors themselves with the stain of disgrace, for everlasting remembrance by posterity: in them malice vies with lying, treachery with shamelessness, the highest folly with the highest wickedness. And yet by reading these things you lose good hours, and by holding them read and stored in your mind and memory you put them to your credit. I pity you: "God sent you a working of error, that you should believe lies." But the reader already recognises at once, from what has been noted to me, that your omissions are quite plain as well: you omit what you cannot state, because there is nothing there that you could state. So here again you omit what the King added to the Queen's edicts, "not a few." Not a few, certainly; for in fact not a single thing. But as for what you could never bring forward by any diligence of your own, I beg you, as always, to omit it deliberately.

units.la: DIxerat Apologia, minus iustè Pontificem in Breui suo prohibuisse subditis, quò minus de obedientia sua erga Regem profiterentur. Quæris, vbi hæc prohibitio in Breui habeatur; nec dictum esse hoc, nec dici potuisse; haud vllam talem prohibitionem in Breui legi: hoc ergo inter falsa, quibus Apologia plenissima est, referendum. Ita tu. Audi ergo vbi: Hæc Iuramenti verba sunt. Ego fidelitatem & veram obedientiam Maiestati Regiæ, hæredibus, & successoribus eius præstabo. Annon hijs verbis de obedientia sua diserte profitentur? Quid potest esse clarius? Quid Pontifex? Annon & ille sic in Breui suo primo; Admonemus vos, vt ab hoc Iuramento præstando omnino caveatis, idque acriùs exigimus à vobis? Annon sic in Breui secundo; Strictè præcepimus, ne vllo modo Iuramentum illud præstaretis? Iam verò, quæ propria magis profesio, quàm Iuramento dato? Quarè, profitentur. Quid autem? Ego obedientiam Regi præstabo; Quarè, de obedientia profitentur. Quid Pontifex? Admoneo, acriter exigo, strictè præcipio ne præstetur Iuramentum illud. Qui iuramentum prohibet, quo profesio fit, is annon prohibet quò minùs profesio fiat? Iuramentum, in quo profesio diserta est obedientia præstanda; qui admonet, qui exigit, qui acriter exigit, qui præcipit, qui strictè præcipit, vt ne præstetur; is annon prohibet obedientiam prositeri? Quæ hæc vecordia est? An tu prohibitionem nullam putas de obedientia præstanda, nisi totidem syllabis sic legatur in Breui; Ego prohibeo vobis quò minùs obedientiam profiteamini? Quòdsi Subdito Sacrosancta tangenti, & dicenti, Iuro (est autem illa profitendi ratio vel certissima) Iuro me præstiturum; dixerit tum Papa; Admoneo verò, exigo, præcipio, ne iures Iuramentum; in quo profesio talis, annon prohibet profiteri?
units.tr: The Apology had said that the Pontiff had less justly forbidden his subjects, in his Brief, to profess their obedience to the King. You ask where this prohibition is found in the Brief, and you claim that this was never said, nor could it have been said, that no such prohibition is read anywhere in the Brief; therefore this must be counted among the falsehoods with which the Apology is very full. So you say. Hear, then, where it is: these are the words of the Oath. "I will give faithful and true obedience to Her Majesty, her heirs and successors." Do they not in these words plainly profess their obedience? What could be clearer? And what of the Pontiff? Does he not also say, in his first Brief: "We warn you to take the utmost care to avoid making this Oath, and we demand this from you more sharply"? Does he not say, in his second Brief: "We have strictly commanded that you by no means take that Oath"? Now, what profession is more proper than an oath given? Therefore they profess. And what then? "I will give obedience to the King." Therefore they profess obedience. And what of the Pontiff? "I warn, I demand sharply, I strictly command that that Oath not be given." Does not he who forbids the oath, by which the profession is made, also forbid the profession to be made? An oath in which obedience to be rendered is plainly professed; he who warns, who demands, who demands sharply, who commands, who strictly commands that it not be given: does he not forbid the professing of obedience? What madness is this? Or do you think there is no prohibition of rendering obedience unless it is read in the Brief in exactly these syllables: "I forbid you to profess obedience"? And if, when a subject touches the holy things and says, "I swear" (and that form of professing is most certain), "I swear that I will render it," and the Pope then says, "But I warn, I demand, I command that you not swear the Oath" (in which profession of this kind is made), does he not forbid professing?

units.la: Multò sanè illustrior hæc consequentia: Prohibet iuramentum, in quo profeßio; prohibet ergo profeßionem; quàm illa tua, Ex eo quòd iuret subditus hoc facturum se, non obstante excommunicatione Papæ, negari ab eo in Papâ potestatem excommunicandi Reges. Vides iam, hæc prohibitio vbi habetur, vbi legitur, dici potuisse, dictum esse: mendacio tuo locum hic nullum esse, referendum proin ad te, reponendum à te inter tua; ad complendam mensuram falsitatum tuarum, confertam iam sanè & superessluentem.
units.tr: Far more illustrious is this inference: he forbids the oath in which there is a profession; therefore he forbids the profession. It is far more illustrious than your own, that because a subject swears he will do this, "notwithstanding the excommunication" of the Pope, it is denied by him that the Pope has power to excommunicate Kings. You now see where this prohibition is found, where it is read, where it could have been said, where it was said: there is no room here for your lie, it must be referred back to you, and laid down by you among your own; to complete the measure of your falsehoods, which is now indeed full and overflowing.

units.la: Proximus est tibi locus Apologiæ, vbi de Breui dicitur, multa in eo dici, haud quicquam probari. Verissimum id verbum fuit, nec tu illud ausus es negare, quin fateris ipse, nihil probatum esse, dum contendis nihil probari debuisse. Breue enim, breuem fuisse & paternam admonitionem, Theologicam disputationem non fuisse. Cui, respònsum à nobis supra, semper vbi ratio quæritur, statim clamare Tortum requiri à Pontifice, vt disputet in scholis Theologicis, vt Librum integrum conscribat. Clamare autem stultè & pueriliter. Aduertit enim scio etiam extra disputationem Theologicam, etiam in paternâ admonitione, locum habere rationes, misceri monitis argumenta: & posse & solere etiam, quasi aculeos adhiberi à parentibus; vbi sic adhibentur, vbi miscentur monitis rationum momenta, citiùs multò & libentiùs monitis obtemperari. Tum, paucis hoc fieri potuisse, nec exire tamen res tota in disputationem, sed Breue etiam satis breue futurum. Quid, quòd non monet ibi solùm, asserit etiam: perspicuum esse dicit ex verbis ipsis? At illi, infirmis fortè oculis sunt, tale quid ibi non perspiciunt; iuuaret saltem caligantes eorum oculos, conspicillis rationum suarum. Verùm illud fortè erat: non decet Pontificem filius vllus, nisi Volumus & Iubemus: vel illud etiam, quò filiorum suorum obedientia merito maioris esset, cæcam esse voluit: vel quod magis credibile, commodum imprimis videri Pontificibus illud dicendi genus, vbi nihil necesse sit probationes adiungi. Ita semper, vbi quid probare debet Pontifex, nec potest, Pater est statim; monitiones pias scribit, in quibus deprecari potest, (quod fit in formulis) ne arctet se ad onus probationis.
units.tr: The next passage of the Apology concerns the Brief, where it is said that "many things are said in it, and nothing is proved." That word was most true, and you have not dared to deny it, except that you yourself admit nothing was proved, while you contend that nothing needed to be proved. For "the Brief was a brief and paternal admonition, not a theological disputation." To this we have answered above, whenever the reason is sought: you immediately cry out that Tortus should be required of the Pope, "to dispute in the theological schools, to write a whole book." But this cry is foolish and childish. For I know that reasons have a place even outside a theological disputation, even in a paternal admonition, and that arguments can be mixed into admonitions; and that they can and do also serve, as it were as goads, applied by parents; and where they are applied in this way, where the weight of reasons is mixed into the admonition, the admonition is obeyed much more quickly and more willingly. Moreover, this could have been done in a few words, and the whole matter would not have turned into a disputation, but the Brief would still have been brief enough. What is more, he not only admonishes there but also asserts, and says that it is "clear from the words themselves." But perhaps they have weak eyes and do not perceive any such thing there; it would at least help their dim eyes to have the spectacles of his reasons. But perhaps this was the case: no son ought to address a Pontiff except with "We will and We command"; or he also wished their obedience, as sons, to be deserving of greater merit, that it be blind; or, what is more credible, that this kind of speech seemed especially convenient to Pontiffs, where there is no need to add proofs. So it is always: where the Pontiff ought to prove something and cannot, he at once writes "Father that he is," and writes pious admonitions, in which he may beg (as is done in formulas) not to be bound to the burden of proof.

units.la: Etsi autem rem non neget [Dixisse ibi multa Pontificem, probâsse nihil] tamen, cùm nihil probârit, vt nihil probâsse dicatur, non sustinet; saltem non ijs verbis, quae fuerint Galeni, quae Auerrois, de Christo. Fauere linguis oportet, & abstinere illis, nec Christi Vicario scilicet tam inclementer applicare. Et quidni Galeni? Cardinali, flagitium nullum fuit, in re Capitali Galenum authorem citâsse: Rem magnam latè deducit ex eo; beneficij loco scilicet esse haereticis, vt de hac vitâ tollantur; quasi faueret Galenus Inquisitioni. Quàm verò iniquè comparatum est, illi vt liceat rem vitæ atque necis, ex Galeno confirmare: Apologia, tritam omnium sermone sententiam citare non liceat? De Auerroe autem vt video, tota res in incerto est: locum nullum citat, ferunt, modò dicit. Verùm non vult nescire nos, quàm bonus sit Galenista, legisse libros eius de pulsuum differentijs; ibi autem tale quid reperit. Sed neque Philosophi nomine Galenus intelligendus venit, Medici potiùs: & libro, quem apponit, verbum ibi nullum de Christo, libro tertio scilicet: secundo autem, quem volebat (credo) apponere, non illa dicit quae Tortus, dixisse multa Christum; Leges quasdam memorat modò, Mosis & Christi [illegible, ~5 letters]. Quid faceret? Nesciebat Christum Dei filium, nesciebat veritatem ipsam esse. Quodsi medicus ille, de eo credidisset, quod nos Dei virtute, iam credimus; non quaesisset ab eo demonstrationem vllam: quaesisset tamen à Vicario fortè, quippe qui homo sit, non Deus: nec haeresis sit dicere quod scripsit ille, qui contra haereses scripsit, {b}Omnis homo errare potest in fide, etsi {b}Papa sit.
units.tr: Although he does not deny the matter (that the Pontiff said many things there, but proved nothing), still, since he has proved nothing, I do not allow that he may be said to have proved nothing; at least not with those words which were Galen's, or Averroes's, about Christ. We ought to be sparing of our tongues and abstain from them, and not apply them so harshly to the Vicar of Christ. And why not Galen? For the Cardinal, it was no disgrace to cite Galen as an author in a capital matter: he argues the point at length from him, namely that it is a benefit to heretics to be removed from this life, as if Galen favoured the Inquisition. But how unfairly it is arranged that he may be allowed to confirm a matter of life and death from Galen, yet may not cite in his Apology a sentence worn smooth by everyone's talk! As for Averroes, so far as I can see, the whole matter is uncertain: he cites no passage; they say he merely speaks. Yet he does not want us to be ignorant of how good a Galenist he is, having read Galen's books on the differences of pulses; and there he finds something of the sort. But Galen is not to be understood as coming under the name of Philosopher, but rather of Physician; and in the book which he cites, there is no word about Christ, namely in the third book; but in the second, which he wished to cite (I suppose), he does not say what Tortus says, that Christ said many things; he merely recalls certain laws of Moses and of Christ [illegible, about 5 letters]. What would he do? He did not know that Christ is the Son of God, he did not know that he is the truth itself. But if that physician had believed concerning him what we now, by the power of God, believe, he would not have asked him for any demonstration; he would perhaps have asked it of the Vicar, since he is a man, not God. Nor is it heresy to say what he wrote who wrote against heresies: "Every man can err in faith, even if he be the Pope."

units.la: Vtut autem fuerit: quicquid de Auerroe sit vel Galeno: dictum hoc, multa dicis, nihil probas, tam frequens in Scholis, tam familiare, vt nullum magis. Vnde autem in Scholas venerit, difficile dictu; nec tu, credo, vnquam probâris ab Auerroe desumptum hoc, aut de libris pulsuum, vel inde in scholas profluxisse: aut illis omnibus Auerroen in mentem venire, qui ea verba proferunt: immò multos subinde proferre, qui an tale quid in libris de pulsuum differentiâ, imò an vlli libri de pulsuum differentiâ, haud sanè sciant, si interrogentur.
units.tr: However that may be, whatever is the case with Averroes or Galen, this saying, "you say many things, prove nothing," is so frequent in the Schools, so familiar, that nothing is more so. Whence it came into the Schools is hard to say; nor, I believe, will you ever prove that this was taken from Averroes, or that it flowed into the schools from his books on the differences of pulses, or that all those who utter these words think of Averroes: rather, many repeat it from time to time who, if questioned, would certainly not know whether any such thing is in the books on the differences of pulses, or whether there are any books on the differences of pulses at all.

units.la: Licet verò etiam, quae Ethnici de Christo falsò dicunt, interdum de Pontifice verè vel affirmare vel negare. Quidsi enim de Christo impiè diceret Paganus quis, Deum non esse, hominem merum esse ; alter autem hoc idem de Papa diceret ; tunc subiiceres, Bene habet quod Haereticus de vicario Christi dicit, quod de ipso Christo Paganum dixisse constat, aut quasi rē bene gestā apponeres in margine, En Haereticus loquitur de Pontifice maximo, sicut olim Ethnici de Christo? Tum vero ; quid? Pontifici tantùmne hic licere vis quantum Christo? Etiamne hoc ipsum inter cætera, vt ei satius sit dicere, nihil opus probare quicquam, non magis, quàm Seruatori ipsi. Permitte vero, vt plus hic aliquid Christo tribuere liceat quàm Vicario; Vicarius ille vester non potest dicere, Ego sum veritas: Christus potuit, & dixit. Multum ergo hic interest, magna li[?]: pulchrum differentia; Pontifici non licet esse tam[?]. Et hoc, vt non sumit sibi nisi turpis arrogantia: ita non tribuit illi, nisi turpis adulatio.
units.tr: Indeed it is also permitted, at times, to affirm or deny truly of the Pontiff things which heathens falsely say about Christ. For if some pagan were to say impiously of Christ that he is not God but mere man, and another were to say the same of the Pope, then you would subjoin: "It is well that the heretic says of the Vicar of Christ what it is established that a pagan said of Christ himself"; or you would put in the margin, as if it were a well-done deed: "Lo, the heretic speaks of the Supreme Pontiff just as the heathens once spoke of Christ." Then indeed: what? Do you want the Pontiff to be allowed here as much as Christ? Even this too among the rest, that it is better for him to say that he need prove nothing whatever, no more than the Saviour himself. But grant that something here may be allowed to be ascribed to Christ more than to the Vicar; that Vicar of yours cannot say, "I am the truth": Christ could, and did say it. There is therefore a great difference here: a fine distinction; it is not lawful for the Pontiff to be so [...]. And as he claims this for himself only by base arrogance, so it is attributed to him only by base flattery.

units.la: De quâ, Theologi vestri noudum Parasiti, sugillare olim soliti Canonistas: iam verò supparasitari & ipsi discunt, & tibi Theologo Papiensi, haeresis est haec & noua sectariorum opinio, & siquis dicat, quadrare Christo multa, quae Vicario vestro non quadrant, Haereticus audit. Non moror hic lectorem; audi paucis tu: Non est ille haereticus, qui hoc dicit: sed ille blasphemus qui contradicit.
units.tr: Concerning this, your theologians, not yet parasites, who once used to rail at the Canonists, now themselves learn to play the sycophant; and to you, Theologian of Pavia, this is heresy and a new opinion of sectaries; and if anyone says that many things fit Christ which do not fit your Vicar, he is heard as a heretic. I will not detain the reader here; hear it briefly from yourself: he who says this is not a heretic, but he who contradicts is a blasphemer.

units.la: Fingis autem ipse post, fingere Apologiam sibi propositiones, quae nullo modo in Breui continentur, eas oppugnare, in eo autem Dialectica terminos, & leges excedere: assumere enim Breui Pontificio prohiberi fidelitatem erga Principes, quasi eam cum religione & animarum salute pugnet, cum nihil eiusmodi habeatur in Breui Apostolico. Non certè in Breui Apostolico; Apostolorum nullus vnquam Breuia vlla conscripsit; si scripsisset autem vlla, haud vnquam quale hoc vestrum: omnium verò minimè Petrus, cuius expressa verba sunt, de subiectione Regi tanquam praecellenti; idque, quod Dei Voluntas illa sit. Sed neque Paulus Tarsensis ille (Senensem enim nullum nouimus Apostolum) cuius est illud Breue breuissimum, Oportet subditos esse, etiam propter conscientiam; cuius est illa paterna monitio, Admone illos, Principibus subditos esse, dicto obedire. Repetenti autem hic tibi negationem veterem, non contineri in Breui hoc, repetenda mihi quoque aequaxua responsio, Contineri. Profiteri enim, qui iurat; prohiberi autem ibi ne iuret: prohiberi ergo ne profiteatur. Prohibere fidelitatem erga Principes, quasi cum animarum sa-lute lute pugnet : qui prohibet Iuramentum, quo spondetur fidelitas, quasi cum animarum salute præstari nequeat.
units.tr: You yourself then add, pretending that the Apology sets up for itself propositions which are in no way contained in the Brief, and that it attacks them, in doing so exceeding the terms and laws of Dialectic: for it assumes that the Pontifical Brief forbids fidelity to princes, as if that were at odds with religion and the salvation of souls, whereas nothing of the kind is contained in the Apostolic Brief. Certainly not in the Apostolic Brief; none of the Apostles ever wrote any briefs at all; and if any had written them, never one like this of yours; least of all Peter, whose express words are: "concerning subjection to the King as supreme; and that this is the will of God." But neither is it Paul of Tarsus, that one (for we know of no Apostle of Siena), whose is that very brief brief, "It is necessary that subjects be subject, even for conscience' sake"; whose is that paternal admonition, "Remind them to be subject to princes and obey." But to you, who here repeat the old denial, "that this Brief does not contain it," I must in turn repeat the same old answer: "It does contain it." For he who swears professes; but it is forbidden there that one swear: it is forbidden, therefore, that one profess. He who forbids fidelity to princes, as if it were at odds with the salvation of souls, is one who forbids the oath by which fidelity is pledged, as if it could not be rendered together with the salvation of souls.

units.la: Tum demonstratum dicit à se, quid illud sit in iuramento, cum religione pugnans, propter quod ab eo abstineri debeat; quòd scilicet abnegetur eo potestas Apostolica ligandi, & soluendi; tum abiurari eo fidelitatem ad Christi Vicarium. Nihil vero horum demonstratum illi, nec vlla vsquam Torti demonstratio, nisi quæ posteriorum Analyticorum terminos, & leges excedat. At hic iam de potestate Reges deponendi, nihil mutare audet: conscius de illa sibi, quàm non sit Apostolica: potestas autem ligandi non negatur omnino, omnino etiam nec soluendi, nisi si quem soluerint Apostoli ab officio suo. Tum nullam vnquam fidelitatem iuratam esse; proin, nec abiurari posse, ei, quem tu Christi Vicarium dicis, quem sic esse tamen, nulla nos cogit fides Catholica vt credamus, præsertim cùm videamus, in hac prohibitione sua, Antichristi potiùs vices agere, quàm Christi. Christus enim Domini, Rex est; qui verò quam Christo Domini Christiani fidem debent, eam vetat exoluere, is Antichristi vicarius est; nisi sit Antichristus ipse. Hildebrandus certè qui primus hoc fieri; Bonifacius 8. qui primus hoc credi voluit, neuter Apostolus fuit: & quâ id potestate fecerunt, Apostatica fuit, non Apostolica; vel Apostatica certè, vel Apostaticta, quæ ordinem à Deo positum, aperte violabat. Cadit enim in Pontificem, Apostaticum, vel Apostaticum potiùs esse, quàm Apostolicum: quo elogio 50. plus minus Pontifices {a}Genebrardus vester insigniuit, per annos 150. sibi inuicem succedentes.
units.tr: Then he says he has "demonstrated" what that is in the oath, at odds with religion, on account of which one must abstain from it: namely that by it the Apostolic power of binding and loosing is denied; and then that by it fidelity to the Vicar of Christ is abjured. But none of these has been "demonstrated" by him, nor is there any "demonstration of Tortus" anywhere, except one which exceeds the terms and laws of the Posterior Analytics. But here he now dares change nothing concerning the power of deposing kings: aware of how little that power is Apostolic. Yet the power of binding is not denied altogether, nor even altogether that of loosing, unless perhaps some whom the Apostles loosed from their office. Then, that no fidelity has ever been sworn, and therefore it cannot be abjured, to him whom you call the Vicar of Christ; and that he is so, no Catholic faith compels us to believe, especially since we see that in this his prohibition he acts rather the part of Antichrist than of Christ. For Christ is the Lord's Anointed, King; and whoever forbids Christians to pay that fidelity which they owe to Christ the Lord, he is the vicar of Antichrist; unless he is Antichrist himself. Hildebrand certainly, who first wished this to be done, and Boniface the Eighth, who first wished this to be believed, were neither of them Apostles; and by what power they did it, it was apostate, not apostolic; or certainly apostate, or... which openly violated the order established by God. For it falls to the Pontiff to be apostolic rather than apostate, or apostate rather than apostolic: by which epithet your Genebrardus has marked some fifty Pontiffs, more or less, succeeding one another over 150 years.

units.la: Quæ verò subiunxit ibi Apologia de sacris scripturis testimonia, idfalsum probant, non quod finxit ipse, (fictio hæc tua est) sed quod scripsit Pontifex, salua fide iurari non posse in verba hæc, Ego obedientiam præstabo Regi. Dixit olim Iosuæ populus, (etiam, si iussus, iurasset) in omnibus parituros se ei, sicut & Mosi paruerunt: paruerunt autem & Mosi in Ecclesiasticis. Non intercessit tum Pontifex Eleazarus, ne in omnibus, sed temporalibus: ne in omnibus, sed ijs solùm (vt vester nunc Pontifex) quæ sibi tum recta viderentur. Quodsi quicquam hic interesse putet, quòd Iosua verus Dei cultor fuit, ne in Orthodoxis solis, locum habere videatur; Rex Babel certè hæretico par, nempe Idololatra; cui tamen Prophera non modò non dissuasit populo, sed author etiam fuit submittendi colla sub iugo eius, eique seruiendi. Idem Pharaoni factum, cuius absq; venia, nec pedem mouere voluerunt de Aegypto, ut Deo sacrificarent. Idem Cyro, cuius itidem absque venia, nec excedere Chaldaeā, ut templum aedificarent. Quid ad haec tu? Probari hinc obedientiam Regibus deberi, etiam Paganis, & vos hoc confiteri. Confiteri sanè, nec sinere tamen ut eandem iurent Principibus, etiam Christianis. Verum hoc quidem confiteri est, factis negare. Verum non probari dicis à nobis, obediendum Regibus vel Christianis, cum fieri iubent quod non licet Christianis. Absit verò ut probetur à nobis, quod nobis nullo modo probatur. Sed quid? Cùm iubet iurari sibi obedientiam Rex, idne fieri iubet, quo facto Christianis non licet esse? Prorsus ergo reijcienda responsio ibi tua. Nec enim in Iuramento, Rex idola coli, vel thurificari, vel praeponi Deo iubet, sed ire solum contra gentem perfidam, salutis suae hostem capitalem, etsi immissam à Pontifice, cum opus erit, & interea dum erit, ad tale seiter paratos fore profiteri.
units.tr: But what the Apology there subjoined about the testimonies of Holy Scripture, that "these prove it false," not because he himself invented it (this fiction is yours), but because the Pontiff wrote that one may not swear, with a safe conscience, these words, "I will render obedience to the King." Long ago the people of Joshua said (even though, if commanded, they had sworn) that they would obey him in all things, as they had obeyed Moses; and they did obey Moses also in ecclesiastical matters. The Pontiff Eleazar did not then intervene, to forbid obedience in all things, but only in temporal matters: not in all things, but only in those which (like your present Pontiff) seemed right to him. But if anyone thinks there is some difference here, in that Joshua was a true worshipper of God, so that it seems the case holds only among the orthodox; the King of Babylon, certainly a match for a heretic, namely an idolater: to him the Prophet not only did not dissuade the people, but was even the author of their submitting their necks under his yoke and serving him. The same was done to Pharaoh, without whose pardon they would not move a foot out of Egypt, that they might sacrifice to God. The same to Cyrus, without whose pardon likewise they would not leave Chaldea, that they might build the temple. What do you say to these things? That from this it follows that obedience is due to kings, even pagan ones, and that you yourselves confess this. Indeed you confess it, yet you do not allow that the same be sworn to princes, even Christian ones. But truly to confess this is to deny it by deeds. Yet you say that we do not prove that kings must be obeyed, even Christian ones, when they command what is not lawful for Christians. Far be it that we should prove what is in no way proved to us. But what then? When a King bids obedience be sworn to him, does he command that which, if done, is not lawful for Christians? Your answer there is therefore utterly to be rejected. For in the oath the King does not command that idols be worshipped, or incense burnt to them, or that they be placed before God; but only that they go out against a faithless nation, the capital enemy of his safety, even if sent in by the Pontiff, "when there shall be need," and meanwhile, "while there shall be," that they profess themselves ready for such service.

units.la: Denique obedire vis Regi terreno, dum ne iubeat quod Regi cœlesti displiceat: hoc autem in primis displicere, ut vicarij sui potestas negetur, vel ut ad alium transferatur. Sed quid tu de Rege cœlesti verba facis, quasi vnum modò vicarium habeat? Multos habet. Nam & Reges ipsi in regnis suis, Regis cœlestis vicarij sunt, aut nos fallit Eleutherius vester: Sic enim ille Lucio olim Regi nostro, Regum Christianorum primo, {a} Vicarium Dei illum in Regno suo. Aut nos fallit Anastasius Papa: Sic enim ille, ad Anastasium Cæsarem. {b} Præstantia vestra, quam velut Vicarium præsidere Deus insit in terris. Duo Papæ, duos Reges, Vicarios dixerunt. Nec minùs ergo Deo displicet, si Regi Vicario suo potestas detrahatur, si quæ debetur illi (quod vos fere facitis) in Papam vestrum transferatur, nec minùs illi displicent; vestræ, Pontificis vestri, in Reges contumeliæ. Alter iam error est, quòd ita videris de Papâ sentire, quasi de eo solo sollicitus sit Deus, & quid reliquis illis fiat, non magnopere curet; tantùm vt suus Papæ honor constet, cætera, vtcunque feret, non iniquo animo: Vnum hoc, si Papalis potestas vllà ex parte minuatur, excandescet ilico. Attrahi enim vult ad Papam, quoad fieri potest, detrahi nihil ab illo : Aliena transferri in illum, id non grauatè feret: Illius nihil in alium quenquam transferri; id enim mirificè displicebit.
units.tr: Finally, you want us to obey the earthly king, provided he does not command what displeases the heavenly King; and what displeases him most of all is that his vicar's power be denied, or transferred to another. But why do you speak of the heavenly King, as if he had only one vicar? He has many. For the kings themselves in their kingdoms are vicars of the heavenly King, unless your Eleutherius deceives us: for he once wrote thus to Lucius, our king, the first of Christian kings, calling him "God's vicar in his kingdom." Or unless Pope Anastasius deceives us: for he wrote thus to the Emperor Anastasius, "Your excellence, whom God has set over the earth as his vicar." Two popes called two kings vicars. Therefore it is no less displeasing to God if the power due to his vicar, the king, is taken away, and if what is owed to him (which you very nearly do) is transferred to your Pope; and no less displeasing to them is the insult to kings offered by your Pope and his followers. There is another error too, in that you seem to think so highly of the Pope as if God were concerned only about him and did not much care what happens to the rest, so long as the Pope's honour is secure, and bore the rest with some equanimity: "This one thing alone: if any part of papal power is diminished, he will flare up at once." For he wants things drawn to the Pope, as far as possible, and nothing taken away from him; he will not mind if things belonging to others are transferred to him; but if anything of his is transferred to anyone else, that will greatly displease him.

units.la: Sed cùm ita de Papâ loqueris, quasi solus is sit Dei Vicarius, an nescis existere; qui nec omninò Vicarium (nedum ut solum) agnoscant, nisi lectum à se, à seipso sic baptizatum, quémque haud vllus Patrum illo nomine aut nominet, aut agnoscat ab vllo sic nominatum? Neque verò dabunt, quòd constituit eum Christus super familiam suam. Ad quid enim? Nónne ut eam daret? At certè diu iam est, cùm eam nullam dedit familiæ; necpauit verbo: Quin neque vel verbum ijs permisit, quo ipsi se pascerent. Tùm, si Vicarius sit etiam, at id tamen usiuenire, ut crebrò Vicarius non sit tanta authoritatis, quanta{a} est superior, cuius est Vicarius. Sed neque de hoc, erit nobis lis{} vlla tecum, nihilopus; verè enim hîc de potestate agitur regna transferendi: Vicarý autem hæc non est; non enim fuit Christi ipsius: si & ille Vicarius esset Christi, quem tu maximè vis; Non est (inquam) Vicarý; non eius est, qui relictus in terris; non enim Christi fuit dum fuit in terris: Non eius quem super familiam constituit; non enim illam ipse Paterfamilias vnquam habuit. Paucis rem accipe. Quæ negatur illi potestas, ea Vicarý non est; quæ verò Vicarý est, ea non negatur.
units.tr: But when you speak of the Pope as if he alone were God's vicar, do you not know that there are those who do not acknowledge a vicar at all, let alone a sole one, unless he has been chosen by themselves and baptised in this way by themselves; and whom no Father has ever named by that title, or acknowledged as named so by anyone? Nor will they grant that "Christ set him over his household." For what for? Surely in order to give it to him? But it is long now since he gave him no household, and fed it not with the word; indeed he did not even permit them a word with which to feed themselves. Then, even if he is a vicar, it happens often that a vicar does not have the same authority as the superior whose vicar he is. But on this point there will be no dispute between us at all, for the question here truly concerns the power of transferring kingdoms; and this power does not belong to a vicar, for it was not Christ's own. Even if that vicar were a vicar of Christ, whom you most wish for, it is not (I say) a vicar's power; it is not the power of one left on earth; for it was not Christ's while he was on earth; it is not the power of him whom he set over his household, for the Householder himself never possessed that household. Hear the matter in few words. The power that is denied to him is not a vicar's power; and the power that is a vicar's is not denied.

units.la: AD Patrum testimonia sex, semel respondet & simul: nec vacat ei excutere singula: Pungebant, credo, hominem, quare quàm potuit leviter, attigit; quàm potuit celeriter, transsijt. Concedere se dicit, quod ex ijs probatur, deberi Principibus infidelibus, à subditis etiam fidelibus obedientiam. Concedere quidem, at si Papa eos soluerit, expungi statim debitum hoc ex tabula, nec post Principibus deberi quicquam, quantumlibet etiam fideles sint. Verum & in illis, quæ dicit concedere se, vide quàm per omnia, egregiè tergiuersetur. Non enim vestri homines, si diceretur illis, Producite aciem, ite contra aciem Pontificis fulminantis, obtemperarent, scio, omnes, quin terga darent multi, quasi Augustinum non audirent.
units.tr: You respond to six testimonies of the Fathers at once, once for all; and there is no time for him to examine each one. They were stinging the man, I suppose, so he touched them as lightly as he could and passed over them as quickly as he could. He says he concedes what is proved from them, that obedience is owed to unbelieving princes even from subjects who are believers. He concedes indeed; but if the Pope should absolve them, this debt would at once be struck from the ledger, and nothing would be owed to princes afterwards, however faithful they may be. But in those points which he says he concedes, see how thoroughly and in every respect he evades them. For I know that if it were said to your people, "Advance into battle, go against the army of the thundering Pontiff," not all would obey; many would turn their backs, as if they had not heard Augustine.

units.la: 2. Nec vos cum Tertulliano Regem à Deo secundum, quin tertium modò, nec Solo Deo minorem, quin & Deo & Papâ etiam, Domino Deo vestro.
units.tr: 2. Nor do you agree with Tertullian that the king is second to God, or rather third, and not less than the Only God; nay, "to your Lord God," that is, to both God and the Pope.

units.la: 3. Nec cum Iustino laeti inseruitis Principibus, sed (quod de Gregorio pòst asseris) volentes nolentes; vires sq. vobis, non animus deest à seruitute vos istâ vindicandi.
units.tr: 3. Nor do you cheerfully serve princes with Justin; but (as you say later about Gregory) willingly or unwillingly; you lack not the strength but the spirit to free yourselves from that servitude.

units.la: 4. Tum & alia vobis arma sunt, quàm Ambrosiani lacrymæ. Aquæ verò illæ : ignis autem & sulphur vobis sunt, eisque aliter, quàm Ambrosius, vestri homines debere se putant & posse resistere. §. Nec cum Optato, super Imperatorem dicitis non esse nisi solum Deum qui fecit Imperatorem; sed & alium, vel hominem, vel nec Deum nec hominem, sed inter utrumque, semiutrumque Deum, semideumq; virum. 6 Nec Serenissimum vel Pijssimum Dominum suum dicere sustineret Imperatorem Pontifex vester, nec accipere vel transmittere alijs, leges vllas illius, nec prabere illi obedientiam. Imò & Leges & Reges, vestri sublatos pariter voluerunt, etiam fundamenta quoque, parietes & tecta, vbi leges feruntur. Omnia hæc vestri illi. I nunc & dic, à vobis concedi, à vobis minimè negari, quæ Patres isti asserunt, cùm sententijs eorum singulis, praxis vestra in singulis contrauenit[?]
units.tr: 4. You also have other weapons than the tears of Ambrose. But those tears are water; fire and sulphur are yours, and with them your people think they ought, and are able, to resist differently from Ambrose. §. Nor, with Optatus, do you say that over the emperor there is no one but God who made the emperor; but also another, either a man, or neither God nor man, but between the two, a half-and-half God, a half-god and a man. Nor would your Pope be willing to call the emperor "Most Serene" or "Most Pious Lord," nor to receive or transmit to others any of his laws, nor to render him obedience. Indeed both laws and kings, you have wished alike to be removed, even the foundations too, the walls and roofs, where laws are carried out. All these are yours. Go now and say that you concede, and do not in any way deny, what those Fathers assert, when your practice contravenes each of their individual opinions?

units.la: At etiam ad Gregorij verba respondere voluisti. Quanto melius ibi tacuisses? fassus ille, subiectum se Mauritio Imperatori & obsequentem: tu, non sponte fassum, non id ab eo sponte factum videri vis; sed vt faceret vellet nollet, coactum esse. Præclaram verò narras Gregorij subiectionem, si non alia fuit quàm volenti nolenti expressa per vim. Hæccine Gregoriana illa obedientia, quam tuis, credo, proponis imitandam Apostolis fuisse? Parum verò Apostolica: aliam enim longè Apostolus obediendi vel Paganis Dominis præstari iubet, {a}ex animo, sicut Domino, & non hominibus, &{b} in simplicitate cordis, sicut Christo. At Tyrannus fuit Mauritius etiam, vt Nero. Primùm nec hoc dignum Gregorio, quem in Epistolis Serenissimum, cum in Commentarijs Nerenem appellare. Sed fuerit sanè; At si debita vel infidelibus obedientia, (& tu debitam dicis) sponte illa quidem exhibenda erat. Quid ego tibi verba redigam in memoriam P.tri ipsius, non tantum boni & benigni, J'd etiam Dyscolis; Pauli, non solum propter iram, sed propter conscientiam, vt se dixit Iustinus, vt suos, lætos inseruire Cæsari, non vt vos Gregorium dicitis, inuitum & gementem? Quin Gregorij ipsius mens alia longè, cuius hæc sententia est: {c}Patientia vera amat quem portat. Nam tolerasse, sed odisse, non est virtus manstuetudinis, sed velamentum furoris.
