Hæc quoque non minus ad rem. {d}Plerumq; idcirco paciuntes videmur, quia retribuere mala non possumus; sed qui idcirco
units.tr: But you also wanted to answer the words of Gregory. How much better you would have kept silent there! He confessed that he was subject to the Emperor Maurice and obedient; you wish it to appear that he did not confess this of his own accord, and that it was not done by him of his own will, but that he was compelled to do it, whether he wished or not. Indeed you describe a remarkable subjection of Gregory's, if it was nothing other than "willing or unwilling," extorted by force. Is this the "Gregorian obedience," which you propose, I suppose, to be imitated by your people, as if it had been the Apostles'? Hardly Apostolic; for the Apostle commands a quite different obedience, even to pagan masters, to be rendered "from the heart, as to the Lord, and not to men," and "in simplicity of heart, as to Christ." But Maurice was also a tyrant, like Nero. First, this is not worthy of Gregory, whom you call "Most Serene" in his Epistles, but "Nero" in his Commentaries. But let it be so; yet if obedience is owed even to unbelievers (and you call it "owed"), it had to be given willingly. Why should I call to your mind the words of Peter himself, "not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward," and of Paul, "not only because of wrath but because of conscience," as Justin said, that his people serve Caesar "gladly," not, as you say of Gregory, "unwillingly and groaning"? Indeed Gregory's own mind is quite different, and this is his opinion: "True patience loves what it bears. For to endure while hating is not the virtue of meekness, but the veil of fury." This too is no less to the point: "We often seem to be patient because we cannot repay evils; but whoever does not repay evil for this reason, since he by no means has the power, is certainly not patient."

units.la: a Coloss.3 23.
units.tr: a Col. 3.23.

units.la: b Ephes.6.5.
units.tr: b Eph. 6.5.

units.la: c Homil.7. in Ezech.
units.tr: c Homil. 7 in Ezech.

units.la: d Homil.35. in Euangel. idcirco malum non retribuit, quia nequaquam valet, proculdubio patiens non est.
units.tr: d Homil. 35 in Evang. Whoever does not repay evil for this reason, since he by no means has the power, is certainly not patient.

units.la: Multum vero tibi debet Gregorius, qui illum ita vel metieulosum facis, vel iniuriosum: si vel nolens paruit Tyranno in eo quod illicitum sciret, meticulosum: vel si licitum fuit, iniuriosum, quòd volens non paruit. Sed & mandatum illud non illicitum, & ille volens paruit; & tu insignis calumniator, ac in Gregorium iniuriosum certè, cùm impingis ei hanc culpam. Purus enim ille in omni quod locutus, in omni quod egerat. Quod si iam, ita subiectus fuit, vt tu vis, volens nolens, purus certè non fuit: purum enim, quod nihil alieni habet; nec pura esse potuit voluntas eius, si sic (vt ais) admixtam habuit noluntatem, nec quod debuit, vt debuit, exoluit, si ita malo animo exoluit.
units.tr: Gregory owes you a great deal, since you make him either timid or wronged: timid if he obeyed the tyrant unwillingly in what he knew to be unlawful; or wronged if it was lawful, because he did not obey willingly. But that command was not unlawful, and he obeyed it willingly; and you are a notorious calumniator, and certainly do Gregory an injustice when you lay this fault upon him. For he was "pure in all that he said, in all that he did." But if he was subject in the way you wish, "willingly or unwillingly," he certainly was not pure: for purity is that which has nothing foreign in it; nor could his will have been pure if, as you say, it was mixed with unwillingness, nor did he discharge what he owed as he ought, if he discharged it with an evil mind.

units.la: Magnam vero etiam inibis à Pontifice gratiam, si sic Prædecessores illius Summi Pontifices tractentur à te, vt eos subiectos neges vnquam, nisi velint nolint. Nolle enim, quod ad se attinet, cogi tamen interdum vt velint, cùm vires desunt eu, adsunt Cæsari; nec vllam ab ijs subiectionem expectandam fuisse, nisi vellent nollent, eam præstare cogerentur. Nec sese contumelia hæc sistit in Gregorio; ad reliquos etiam redundat Christianos omnes, quos ex illius ingenio iam omnes metientur, nempe, {a}Vt sacerdos,ita populus. Quanta vero infamiae macula, omnibus inuritur, si hoc ita detur, si itidem vt hic, illi, palpabant Epistolis, sugillabant Commentarijs, si obedientiam nullam exhibebant, nisi vi adhibita? Dæmonum illa quidem potiùs est, quàm Christianorum: nam & Dæmones sic obsequuntur, frementes & frendentes, velint nolint. Vbi verò laus illa Christianorum propria, in nascente Ecclesiâ, obedientiæ tam sincerae, vt nec hostes calumniari possent; patientiæ tam spontaneæ, vt & hostes admirari cogerentur?
units.tr: You will gain great favour with the Pontiff too, if you treat his predecessors, the Supreme Pontiffs, in such a way that you deny they were ever subject unless they were "willing though unwilling." For they were unwilling in their own view, yet at times were "forced to be willing" when their powers failed them, while Caesar's were present; and no submission was to be expected from them, unless they were "unwilling though willing" and were compelled to render it. Nor does this insult stop at Gregory; it spreads to all the other Christians too, whom everyone will measure by his character, namely: "As the priest, so the people." What a stain of infamy, moreover, is then branded on all of them, if it is granted in this way, if, just as these men, they flattered with their letters, belittled in their commentaries, and showed no obedience unless "force was applied"? That kind of obedience belongs rather to demons than to Christians, for demons also submit in this way, "raging and gnashing their teeth, willing though unwilling." Where, then, is that praise peculiar to Christians in the infant Church: obedience so sincere that even enemies could not slander it, and patience so voluntary that even enemies were forced to admire it?

units.la: Mihi autem pro certo id constat, si hanc, quam Gregorio infuisse ais indolem, in Martyribus illis prisci deprehendissent Imperatores Ethnici qui tum rerum potiebantur, si Tortus tum extitisset interpres, quo Christiani illis animo obedirent; explosa olim fides nostra, extinctum fuisset nomen Christianum, nec de tot millibus Christianis, Christianus vel vnus superesset: plurimùm autem id merito suo. Quem enim illorum misereat? Nempe qui genus hominum sint, qui nec agere quid velint, nec pati, nisi cum aliter non possint, qui nihil agant ingenuè, qui eo animo sint, ut quicquid faciunt, per vim faciant, non facturi si abesset modò vis; quicquid patiuntur, velint nolint patiuntur, non passuri, si adessent illis vires resistendi.
units.tr: Yet I am certain of this: if the Gentile emperors who then held power had detected in those early martyrs the disposition you say was in Gregory, and if Tortrain interpreter had then existed to explain the spirit in which Christians obeyed them, our faith would long ago have been driven out, the Christian name would have been extinguished, and of so many thousands of Christians not even one would have remained. And this would have been deservedly so. For whom would anyone pity? Namely, men of a kind who wish neither to act nor to suffer unless they cannot do otherwise, who do nothing honourably, who are so minded that whatever they do, they do by force, and would not do it if force were merely absent; and whatever they suffer, they suffer willing though unwilling, and would not suffer if they had the strength to resist.

units.la: At nec hoc, vel exemplo Christus docuit, vel praecepto. Non exemplo, qui ipse volens etiam oblatus est; non praecepto, qui cum angariante nos mille passus, ultrò, duo millia iusserit vadere. Non hoc à Petro habuit Gregorius, cuius illud, {a}Non co-actè, sed spontanè: Non à Paulo, cuius illud, {b}[?]ἐκ ψυχῆς[?] ex animo cum bona voluntate feruentes. Tota denique praxis repugnat Christianorum veterum, quorum in cruce gloria, in martyrio triumphus, qui laeti lubentes vitae munia obibant, quamdiu poterant; quando autem iam non poterant, mortem etiam non minus, vel laeti vel lubentes. Odiosus ergo homo es, Matthae, velis nolis, cum tuo hoc odioso theoremate, quomodo Pontifices paruerint Tyrannis, volentes scilicet nolentes, ut Discipuli Daemonis, non Christi. Et iusiùor quidem multo causa est, ut Tortus, vel qui sub Torto latet, Christianus nec sit, nec habeatur à quoquam: quàm, quem ille post Christianum negat: Ille (inquam) ut sit, Tortus ne sit Christianus, qui haec ita scribit de Christiano, tam vel homine indigna, vel nomine Christiano.
units.tr: But Christ taught neither this by his example nor by his precept. Not by his example, for he himself was offered up willingly; not by his precept, for when someone compelled us to go a mile, he bade us go two thousand willingly. Gregory did not have this from Peter, whose words were "not under compulsion, but willingly"; nor from Paul, whose words were "[?] out of the soul, with good will, fervently." Finally, the whole practice of the ancient Christians is opposed to this, whose glory was in the cross and whose triumph was in martyrdom, who gladly and willingly performed the duties of life as long as they could, and when they could no longer, submitted to death no less gladly and willingly. You are therefore a hateful man, Matthew, whether you wish it or not, with this hateful theorem of yours, that the Pontiffs obeyed tyrants "willing though unwilling," like disciples of the demon and not of Christ. And indeed, the cause of Torte, or of whoever lurks behind Torte, is far more unjust: that he is not a Christian and is not held to be one by anyone, than that of the one whom he denies to be a Christian after the Christian. He, I say, that Torte may be, and that Torte may not be a Christian, who writes these things about a Christian so unworthy either of a man or of the Christian name.

units.la: Auertit verò subditos Pontifex ab obedientiâ, & hoc in Breui eius legitur. Legitur enim in Breui, Iuramentum de praestandâ obedientiâ; in eodem Breui legitur, acris exactio, stricta praeceptio, de Iuramento illo non praestando. A praestando autem Iuramento, de praestandâ obedientiâ, qui auertit, annon is auertit ab obedientiâ? Nec ea summa Breui est, quam dicis, in quâ nec de potestate Vicarij Christi verbum vllum: potestas autem de fide Catholicâ non est, nec licita est, nec civilis, quae ibi abiuratur.
units.tr: But the Pontiff turns subjects away from obedience, and this is read in his Brief. For in the Brief there is read an oath to render obedience; in the same Brief there is read a harsh exaction and strict command concerning not rendering that oath. And he who turns men away from taking the oath of obedience, does he not turn them away from obedience? Nor is that the sum of the Brief, as you say, in which there is not a single word about the power of Christ's Vicar; but the power which is renounced there is not concerning the Catholic faith, nor is it lawful, nor is it civil.

units.la: AD Concilia te sequor, vbi illud te malè habet quod dicitur, Concilia etiam tota Episcoporum, Regibus fuisse subiecta. Dicitur certè, & probatur. Nam praesentare ea Principi supplenda, emendanda, perficienda; id demum, cuius sano, subijcere est. Quid ergo hîc nobis refers, egisse ibi multa Patres de negotijs politicis, statuisse multa, de Clericis, Laicisque, quae sine Imperatoris providentiâ executioni mandari non poterant? Dic pri-mùm, mùm,quare, sine Imperatoris authoritate, non dicas: authoritate enim, non prouidentiâ mandari solent leges executioni. Tum & illud dic etiam; annon aliud longè, supplere, emendare, perficere, quod illi petunt; aliud executioni mandare, quod tu somnias? Adiutorio perficere id fortè est, mandare executioni: at prudentiâ supplere, iudicio emendare, id quidem non est exequi, nec executioni mandare, nisi Tortus aliquis interpres hic sit.
units.tr: I follow you to the Councils, where what troubles you is the statement that even whole councils of bishops were subject to kings. It is certainly said, and it is proven. For to present these to the prince to be supplemented, amended, and completed, that is precisely to submit to his judgment. Why, then, do you bring us here the report that the Fathers there did many things concerning political matters, and decreed many things concerning clergy and laity, which could not be carried into execution without the emperor's providence? First tell me why you do not say "without the emperor's authority," for laws are usually committed to execution by authority, not by providence. Then tell me this too: is it not a very different thing to "supplement, amend, and complete," which they ask for, and to "commit to execution," which you dream of? To complete a thing with assistance may perhaps be "to commit it to execution," but to supplement with prudence and amend with judgment is not to execute, nor to commit to execution, unless some Torte interpreter is here.

units.la: Quæ verò politica illa quæ dicis? De sex enim illis, quæ enumeras, quatuor, quæ de Presbyteris & Episcopis sunt, ad politica referri nō possunt: illa tantum possunt, quæ de mensuris, & de rebus pauperum, id est, duo tantum de sex. Subiungis tandem satis pro authoritate; De hijs & similibus loqui Patres, cùm Imperatore rogant, vt velit Decreta Cœcilij supplere, corrigere, perficere. Qui scis de hijs & horū similibus loqui tantum? Vnde habes? Vbi legisti? Quis tibi suggessit? Quàm est hoc maius quiddam, quàm Sacchiano fas, sic authoritate suâ nudâ & solâ res transfigere tanti momenti? Ergone sex ista solùm Imperatori præsentata? Ergone sine cæteris? annon & reliqua cum hijs omnia? Negari nequit, aperta verba sunt; omnia mittunt, omnia præsentant, omnia subijciunt. Quòdsi autem in alijs præter sex istos, aliquid minùs, aliquid secus se quàm ratio haberet, illa non attingeret, nefas illi supplere quicquam, nefas corrigere, nihil in illis prudentiæ etus, nihil iudicio, nihil adiutorio, permissum? Et cui fidem feceris hæc ita esse? Habesne forte Concilij illius, vbi appositi vel asterisci, vel obelisci, ad vel duos vel sex istos Canones: qui, quot ex illis subiecti Imperatori fuerint, quot verò exempti, indicarent, qui significarent ei, Illos, si voles, sex Canones, supple, corrige, perfice: cum reliquos, nihil tibi negotij sit? Vnde ergo fides ei, quod dicis? non alia, quàm hæc; Tortus dixit. Concilium dicit; {b}De rebus spiritualibus se ora diffundere: Tortus, De politicis. Concilium{c} Capitula sua dicit esse de Ecclesiastica Disciplinâ; Tortus de negotijs ciuilibus. Concilium dicit, {d}Hæc quæ emendatione digna perspexerat, Imperatori præsentanda decernere: Tortus dicit, non hæc, sed sex de hijs, sex de viginti sex, cætera non decernere. Vtri credimus?
units.tr: But what are these "political" matters you speak of? For of those six matters you enumerate, the four which concern presbyters and bishops cannot be referred to politics; only those which concern "measures and the goods of the poor," that is, just two of the six, can be. Finally you add, enough by way of authority: "The Fathers spoke of these and similar matters when they asked the emperor to be willing to supplement, correct, and complete the decrees of Chalcedon." How do you know they spoke only of "these and similar matters"? Where do you have it? Where did you read it? Who suggested it to you? How is this something greater than what the Sacchian law allows, to dispose of such a weighty matter by his bare and sole authority? Are those six matters alone, then, presented to the emperor? Are they alone, without the rest? Are not all the rest with these as well? It cannot be denied; the words are plain: they send all, they present all, they submit all. But if in others, besides those six, something was less or otherwise than reason required, that would not touch them; would it be unlawful for him to supplement anything, unlawful to correct, nothing in them permitted to his prudence, nothing to his judgment, nothing to his assistance? And by what evidence will you make it believed that these things are so? Do you perhaps have a copy of that Council in which asterisks or obelisks are placed against these two or six canons, which might indicate how many of them were subject to the emperor and how many exempt, and signify to him: "Supplement, correct, and complete those six canons if you wish, while the rest are no concern of yours"? Where, then, is the trust in what you say? Not in anything but this: "Torte said so." The Council says: "to pour forth their prayers concerning spiritual matters"; Torte says: "concerning political matters." The Council says that its chapters are "concerning ecclesiastical discipline"; Torte says "concerning civil affairs." The Council says: "to decree that these things which it had perceived to be worthy of amendment should be presented to the emperor"; Torte says that it decreed not "these," but "six of these, six of twenty-six," and did not decree the rest. Which of them do we believe?

units.la: TUm, quod de aliis illis Carolinâ[?] quinque, quod de primis quatuor Generalibus dixit Apologia, Imperatorum authoritate conuenisse; illius sç[?] prudentiæ, & pietati submisse: id vitio vertis, quòd verba relata, loca notata non sint. Breuis esse voluit; ni vellet, procliue illi notare loca, referre verba, quod me nunc non pigebit facere: perfacile enim factu est. De Carolinis quinque, mandato illius congregata esse. Cabilonensi; {a}Auxiliante Domino nostro Iesu Christo, & imperante Carolo Serenissimo & inclyto Augusto, conuenimus in urbem Cabilonensem. Moguntinum; {b}Venimus, secundùm iussionem vestram in Ciuitatem Moguntiam. Rhemensi; {c}In conuentu à Domino Carolo piissimo Cæsare more priscorum Imperatorum congregato. Turonensi; {d}Quod à tanto Principe nobis iniunctum est, ad statuta loca convenimus. Francfordiensi; {e}Imperij eius (nempe Caroli) decreto, per diuersas prouincias Regni eius ditionis subiectas, summâ celeritate præcurrente, multitudo Antistitum sacris obtemperando præceptis, in uno collegio aggregata conuenient.
units.tr: Then, as for the other matters, the five Carolingian councils, and the first four general councils, which the Apology says were convened by the authority of the emperors, and were submitted to his prudence and piety, you find fault that the words quoted and the passages cited are not given. He wished it to be brief; had he wished otherwise, it would have been easy for him to note the passages and quote the words, which I too will not hesitate to do now, for it is very easy to do. Of the five Carolingian councils, they were gathered by his command. At Chalon: "With our Lord Jesus Christ helping, and with the most serene and renowned Augustus Charles reigning, we have assembled in the city of Chalon." At Mainz: "We have come, according to your command, into the city of Mainz." At Rheims: "In an assembly gathered by the most pious Lord Charles, Caesar, after the manner of the ancient emperors." At Tours: "What has been enjoined upon us by so great a prince, we have assembled in the appointed places." At Frankfurt: "By the decree of his empire (namely, Charles's), with the greatest speed running ahead through the various provinces subject to the dominion of his kingdom, a multitude of bishops, obeying the sacred commands, has been gathered and assembled in one college." [Submissively, indeed.] At Chalon: "The chapters which are inserted below are to be presented to the lord emperor and referred to his most sacred judgment, that they may be confirmed by his prudent examination, those things which we have reasonably decreed; and if we have accomplished anything less than fully, let it be supplemented by his wisdom." At Mainz: "Concerning these, however..."

units.la: Submisse autem sç[?]. Cabilonensi; {f}Capitula quæ subter inserta sunt Domino Imperatori præsentanda, & ad eius sacratissimum iudicium referenda, adnotauimus, quatenus eius prudenti examine, ea quæ rationabiliter decreuimus, confirmentur; si cubi minùs aliquid egimus, illius sapientiâ suppleatur. Moguntinum; {g}De hys tamen omnibus (Imperatorem alloquuntur, quem ibi Rectorem religionis, & Sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ defensorem nominant) valde indigemus vestro adiutorio, atque sanâ doctrinâ, quâ & nos iugiter admoneat, atque clementer erudiat, quatenus ea quæ paucis subter perstrinximus Capitulis, à vestrâ authoritate firmetur, si tamen vestra pietas dignum esse iudicauerit; & quicquid in eis emendatione dignum reperitur, vestra magnifica Imperialis dignitas iubeat emendari, vt ita emendata, nobis omnibus, & Sanctæ Christianæ plebi, & posteris nostris proficiant ad vitam & salutem.
units.tr: Submissively, however, [the Council of Arles? passage] at Chalon. {f} The chapters which are inserted below are to be presented to the lord Emperor and referred to his most sacred judgment; we have noted them so that, by his prudent examination, those things which we have decided reasonably may be confirmed; and if we have done anything less than fully, let it be supplied by his wisdom. At Mainz. {g} Concerning all these things (they address the Emperor, whom they call there the ruler of religion and the defender of the holy Church of God) we stand in great need of your help and of sound teaching, by which he may both constantly admonish us and kindly instruct us; so that those things which we have briefly set out in the chapters below may be confirmed by your authority, if your piety judges them worthy; and whatever is found in them that deserves correction, may your magnificent imperial dignity command it to be corrected, so that, thus corrected, they may profit all of us, the holy Christian people, and our posterity, unto life and salvation.

units.la: Ex hys autem, quæ mens fuerit Arelatensis supra citati, cuiuis facilè constabit. Turonensi; {h}Hæc nos in conuentu nostro ita ventilauimus, sed quomodo deinceps piissimo Principi nostro de hys agendum placebit, nos fideles eius famuli libenti animo ad nutum & voluntatem eius parati sumus. Francfordiensi; Quòd ibi disertis verbis dicitur, praesidente & praecipiente Carolo congregatum: Carolum congregationi ibi Sacerdotum, auditorem & arbitrum assedisse: locutum de causa fidei, prolixo sermone; etiam post Romanum Pontificem loco primo, Episcopos Italiae secundo, Germaniae, Galliae, Britanniae tertio, quarto loco consensum suum scripto subnexuisse: denique cuius & illa verba sunt, Decernimus & Deo donante decreuimus, quid esset de hac inquisitione firmiter tenendum. Erat autem causa fidei contra Eliphandum Toletanum, qui Christum filium Dei adoptiuum asseruerat.
units.tr: From these things, what the mind of the aforesaid Arles was will easily be clear to anyone. At Tours. {h} We discussed these matters thus in our assembly; but how it shall please us to deal with them hereafter with our most pious Prince, we, his faithful servants, are ready with willing mind at his nod and will. At Frankfurt. That it is said there in plain words that the assembly was gathered with Charles presiding and commanding: that Charles sat there at the assembly of priests as hearer and arbiter; that he spoke about the cause of the faith in a long speech; that, even after the Roman Pontiff in first place, the bishops of Italy in second, of Germany, Gaul and Britain in third, he subscribed his consent in writing in fourth place; and finally, whose words these also are: We decree, and by God's gift have decided, what should be firmly held concerning this inquiry. The cause of the faith, however, was against Elipandus of Toledo, who had asserted that Christ was the adoptive Son of God.

units.la: Refero iam verba, loca etiam cito, Conciliorum quatuor Generalium, e quibus, illa constet Imperatorum authoritate convocata. Nicaenum. 1. Constantini authoritate ex Concilij ipsius Synodica Epistola. {a}Convocata est, Dei amantissimo Rege Constantino congregante nos ex variis urbibus, & provincijs. Constantinopolitanum primum, Theodosij Senioris, ex Concilij ipsius Epistola. {b}Convenientes secundum rescriptum pietatis tuae; & ibidem, literis vocationis tuae Ecclesiam honorasti. Ephesinum, Theodosij iunioris & Valentiniani. Et quia pauca quaedam ex eo verba causatur adiecta, sciat extare ibi plurima, nec in ullo Concilio plura. Nam & Imperatores iubent, suo {c}Oraculo cogi; & Concilium septem Epistolas, septies fatetur se, {d}nutu authoritatu vestra coactam, & aliis multis, {c}secundum oraculum, mandatum, rescriptum, toties, verbis tam disertis, ut nihil Ephesino clarius, nihil planius. Chalcedonense, Valentiniani & Martiani; Quod, praeterquam frons ipsa loquitur, {f}facta est Synodus ex decreto piissimorum & fidelissimorum Imperatorum Valentiniani & Martiani. Concilium quoque, ipsum Epistolâ suâ fatetur; {g}Sancta & magna Synodus, secundum Dei gratiam, & sanctionem vestra pietatis congregata. Tum & in definitione ipsâ expresse idem habetur, & ab Illis denique {h}missione petunt, ut & Ephesini.
units.tr: I now report the words and places, quickly too, of the four General Councils, from which it is evident that they were convoked by the authority of the Emperors. Nicaea, 1. By the authority of Constantine, from the Synodal Letter of that same Council. {a} It was convoked, the most beloved of God, King Constantine gathering us from various cities and provinces. The First Council of Constantinople, of Theodosius the Elder, from the Letter of that same Council. {b} Meeting according to your pious rescript; and in the same place, by the letters of your summons you have honoured the Church. Ephesus, of Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian. And since a few words are alleged to have been added from it, let him know that very many are there, and in no Council more. For both the Emperors order it to be gathered by their {c} oracle; and the Council confesses seven times in its seven letters that it was gathered by {d} the nod of your authority, and in many others by {c} the oracle, command, rescript, so often, in words so plain that nothing is clearer or plainer than Ephesus. Chalcedon, of Valentinian and Martian: which, apart from what the title itself says, {f} the Synod was made by the decree of the most pious and most faithful Emperors Valentinian and Martian. The Council also confesses this in its own letter: {g} the holy and great Synod, gathered according to the grace of God and the sanction of your piety. Then too the same is expressly stated in the definition itself, and finally they themselves seek {h} dismissal, as also those of Ephesus did.

units.la: Possent & quatuor alia hic Generalia, subiungi, nisi tu hoc non postulasses: post, vbi postulas, faxo vt & illa habeas.
units.tr: These four other General Councils could also be added here, unless you had not asked for them: afterwards, when you ask, I shall see to it that you have those too.

units.la: Submisisse autem sese Imperatori, ab eoque confirmationem suam habuisse, profero tibi verba, cito loca. Nicaenum à Constantino; {i}Et Synodi Decreta confirmans consignauit. Constantinopolitanum, à Theodosio; Ex ipsâ Concilij ad Eum Epistolâ.
units.tr: That they submitted themselves to the Emperor and received his confirmation, I bring you the words and places, quickly. Nicaea, by Constantine: {i} And confirming the decrees of the Synod, he sealed them. Constantinople, by Theodosius: from the Council's own letter to him.

units.la: {f} Tom.2. pag. 129.
{g} ibid. pag. 183.
units.tr: {g} ibid., p. 183.

units.la: {h} ibid. pa. 288.
units.tr: {h} ibid., p. 288.

units.la: {i} Eusēb. lib.3. de vita Constant. pistolâ. {a}Necessario quae facta sunt in Sacra Synodo, ad Pietatem referimus. Petimus autem ut Clementiae tuae Scripta confirmentur Synodi sententia, & quemadmodum honorasti nos literis tuis cum hac convocares: ita & eorum quae decreta sunt clausulam velut etiam obsignare. Ephesinum, à Theodosio & Valentiniano, ex Concilij ipsius Epistolâ. {b}Vnde confugimus omnes ad Authoritatem Pietatis vestrae, petentes, vt quae contra Nestorium acta sunt, eosque qui cum eo desipiunt, habeant vim suam atque robur; quae vero ab illis qui Nestorium vindicant, vacua fiant atque irrita. Chalcedonense à Martiano. {c}Sacro nostro Serenitatis Edicto venerandam Synodum confirmantes. Entibi loca, en verba.
units.tr: {i} Eusebius, book 3, On the Life of Constantine, letter. {a} We refer what has been done in the holy Synod necessarily to your Piety. We ask, moreover, that the writings of your Clemency be confirmed by the sentence of the Synod, and just as you honoured us with your letters when you summoned us to this, so also, as it were, to set the seal to the close of those things which have been decreed. Ephesus, by Theodosius and Valentinian, from the Council's own letter. {b} Whence we all have fled to the authority of your Piety, asking that what has been done against Nestorius, and against those who go mad with him, may have their force and strength; but those things which are done by those who defend Nestorius may be made void and of no effect. Chalcedon, by Martian. {c} Confirming the venerable Synod by our holy Edict of Serenity. Here are the places, here are the words.

units.la: Fateris autem iussu Imperatoris congregata Concilia, sed addis, interdum. Dele vero interdum, vel designa nobis Generale unum aliquod, de primis illis octo, & doce, absque Illius iussu convocatum. Sed nec interdum etiam vis factum hoc fuisse ab Imperatore, nisi in executionem mandati summi Pontificis. Vbi, quid tu summum Pontificem crepas, vel mandatum eius, vel Executorem mandati Pontificij Caesarem? Nullum tum quidem Pontificis mandatum, quin submissa supplicatio; nec Pontifex tum mandavit, sed Caesar; nec Caesar executus est, sed Pontifex. Quin nullus tum Pontifex summus; Episcopus tantum Romanus; parvus ad Romanum tum habebatur reverentiae: Alij Episcopi illum tum, fratrem, & coepiscopum nominabant. Ita tum Cyprianus Episcopo Romano scribit; {d}Cyprianus fratri Cornelio. Ita Dionysius Corinthius Stephano & Sixto, {e}frater mi. Ita Marcellus Iulio, {f}Comministro. Ita Iohannes Constantinopolitanus, Hormisdae & fratri. Carthaginenses, {h}Innocentio, {i}Bonifacio; Ephesini {k}Caelestino fratribus suis, Comministris suis. Frater autem, Consacerdos, Comministerin, Coepiscopus, societatis sunt, & aequalitatis nomina; Summitas ibi nulla. Quid autem narras nobis Mandati Pontificij executionem? Etiamne Imperator tum accensus Pontificis, vel mandatarius? imò, Caesari tum mandati executor Pontifex, Imperatoris Domini sui servus humillimus; (vt Gregorius saepe de se) non Caesar Pontificij? Nam Gregorium Mauritij leges transmitti curasse, & mandasse executioni, tu ipse paulò ante non negabas. At, credo à Mauritio, vt sua mandaret executioni haud unquam postulasse, certè nunquam Illi eâ de re mandatum a-
units.tr: You admit that the Councils were gathered by the command of the Emperor, but you add, sometimes. Delete, however, "sometimes," or show us one General Council from those first eight that was convoked without his command. But not even sometimes was this done by the Emperor, unless in execution of the mandate of the supreme Pontiff. Where, then, do you so loudly cry up the supreme Pontiff, or his mandate, or the Caesar as executor of a Pontifical mandate? There was then no mandate of the Pontiff, but a humble supplication; nor did the Pontiff then command, but the Caesar; nor did the Caesar execute, but the Pontiff. Indeed there was then no supreme Pontiff; the Bishop of Rome only; and little reverence was then given to the Roman. The other bishops then called him brother and fellow-bishop. Thus Cyprian then writes to the Roman bishop: {d} Cyprian to brother Cornelius. Thus Dionysius of Corinth to Stephen and Sixtus, {e} my brother. Thus Marcellus to Julius, {f} fellow-minister. Thus John of Constantinople, to Hormisdas and brother. The Carthaginians, {h} to Innocent, {i} to Boniface; the Ephesians {k} to Celestine, their brothers, their fellow-ministers. "Brother," "fellow-priest," "fellow-minister," "fellow-bishop," are names of fellowship and equality; there is no supremacy there. But why do you tell us of the execution of a Pontifical mandate? Was the Emperor then kindled to the Pontiff's will, or his mandatary? Rather, the Pontiff then was the executor of a mandate to the Caesar, the most humble servant of his Lord the Emperor (as Gregory often said of himself), not the Caesar of the Pontiff's. For you yourself did not deny a little while ago that Gregory had taken care that the laws of Maurice be sent and carried into execution. But, I suppose, he never asked Maurice to carry out his own, and certainly never sent him a mandate on that matter a-

units.la: {k} Tom.1.1087. liquod deasse[?]. Iubeat verò vel iam, Cæsari, mandatum suum perferre vel exequi; frustra, opinor, faciet. At quantus tum Cæsar, præut nunc est, quot regnorum Dominus, quàm potens? Imperator verò, ut tum mandata Pontificis exequeretur? Pontifex, ut tum mandaret ei de Concilio convocando? Audi qualia mandata: audi autem de Leone ipso Pontifice, non, credo, inter Pontifices animi abiectissimi. Sic ille, tribus Imperatoribus, Theodosio, Valentiniano, Martiano, Mandatarijs scilicet suis.
units.tr: {k} Tom. 1, 1087. Let him either now order it to be carried out or executed by Caesar; he will do so in vain, I think. But how great was Caesar then, as he is now, lord of so many kingdoms, how powerful? Or the Emperor, to then execute the mandates of the Pontiff? The Pontiff, to then command him concerning convoking a Council? Hear what sort of mandates: hear, moreover, of Leo himself, the Pontiff, not, I think, among Pontiffs of the most abject spirit. Thus he, to the three Emperors, Theodosius, Valentinian, Martian, his mandataries, of course.

units.la: Theodosio. {a}Ecce ego (Christianissime & venerabilis Imperator) cum consacerdotibus meis, implens erga Reverentiam Clementiæ tuæ sinceri amoris officium, obsecramus, coram unius Deitatis inseparabili Trinitate, & coram Sanctis Angelis Christi, ut omnia in eo statu esse iubeatis in quo fuerunt, donec maior ex toto orbe sacerdotum numerus congregetur. Et paulò post. Omnes partium nostrarum Ecclesiæ; omnes mansuetudini vestræ cum gemitibus & lacrymis supplicant Sacerdotes, ut Generalem Synodum iubeatis intra Italiam celebrari. Qui & ita scribit, Augusta. {b}Quod ut obtinere mereamur, pietas vestra supplicationem nostram, apud clementissimum Principem dignetur asserre. Etiam Clero Constantinopolitano. {c}Et quoniam oportet vos, post diuinum auxilium, et iam Catholicorum Principum gratiam promereri, humiliter & sapienter exposcite ut petitioni nostræ quâ plenariam indici Synodum postulamus, Clementissimus Imperator dignetur annuere. Nec hoc modò, sed & {d}Valentinianum Imperatorem, & Eudoxiam uxoremeius, admemoriam B. Petri, cum multis Episcoporum, genibus provolutus Romanus Pontisex deprecatus est, ut Imperatorem Theodosium hortarentur, aliam fieri Synodum. Audis iam hic mandatum nullum, sed petitionem, deprecationem, supplicationem, ut iubeat Imperator. Ostendo ibi obsecrantem, cum gemitibus & lacrymis supplicantem, idque genibus provolutis deprecantem: Quæ voces, quíque habitus parum illi congruunt, qui Mandatario suo, mandatum suum tradit exequendum. Sed neque sic tamen, obtinuit Leo. Nec enim intra Italiam indictum est tamen, sed Ephesi à Theodosio: Niceæ primùm, post autem Chalcedone, à Martiano. Disiunge ergo quæ de Imperatore ibi scribis, in executionem mandati summi Pontificis. Nimis enim certè inepta sunt.
units.tr: To Theodosius. {a} Behold, I with my fellow-priests (most Christian and venerable Emperor), fulfilling toward the Reverence of your Clemency the office of sincere love, beseech, before the inseparable Trinity of the one Deity, and before the holy Angels of Christ, that you order all things to be in the state in which they were, until a greater number of priests from the whole world be gathered. And a little after. All the Churches of our parts; all the priests supplicate your gentleness with groans and tears, that you order a General Synod to be celebrated within Italy. He also writes thus, to Augusta. {b} That we may deserve to obtain this, may your piety deign to present our supplication before the most merciful Prince. Also to the clergy of Constantinople. {c} And since you ought, after divine help, to deserve also the favour of the Catholic Princes, humbly and wisely beg that the most merciful Emperor deign to grant our petition, by which we ask that a full Synod be proclaimed. And not only this, but also {d} the Roman Pontiff, kneeling before the Emperor Valentinian and Eudoxia his wife, and before the memory of blessed Peter, with many bishops, begged that they would urge the Emperor Theodosius that another Synod be held. You hear now that there is no mandate here, but petition, entreaty, supplication, that the Emperor may order. I show there one beseeching, supplicating with groans and tears, and entreating with prostrate knees: which words and which posture agree but little with one who hands his own mandate to his mandatary to be executed. But Leo did not obtain it even so. For it was not indicted within Italy, but at Ephesus by Theodosius: first at Nicaea, afterwards at Chalcedon, by Martian. Therefore disjoin what you write there about the Emperor, in execution of the mandate of the supreme Pontiff. For they are certainly most absurd.

units.la: Citas deinde nescio quid, de Epistolâ (ut ais) scriptâ ad Damasum à Concilio 2o. Generalis: id autem, vt doceas, ad Pontificem proprie pertinere ius Concilia conuocandi. Sed primùm, (vt supra citaui) illud ipsum Concilium suâ ad Theodosium Epistola vera & genuina, contrarium eius, quod tu hic ponis, testatur. Tum, quod vnum est in sententiâ quam citas, i.e. rem tuam, verbum operatiuum, ex mandato literarum, nullum ibi est in Epistolâ: [illegible, ~10 letters] ibi dicitur, de mandato, non apex ibi vllus. Tum denique, agnouit errorem suum Dominus tuus, in {a}Recognitione nupera librorum suorum, illam scilicet (vnde hoc, quicquid id est, citâsti) Epistolam non esse secunda Synodi Generalis; nec ex eâ igitur probari secundam Synodam indictam fuisse, iussu Damasi. Tu etiam, quem ex eo hausisti, cum illo itidem errorem tuum recognosce, & depone: nec proba, con-uocatum esse Concilium mandato Damasi, ex epistolâ Concilij; cùm nec illa iam Epistola Concilij sit, nec si esset, ibi de mandato verbum vllum.
units.tr: You then cite something or other from the letter (as you say) written to Damasus by the Second General Council, in order to show that the right of convening councils belongs properly to the Pope. But first, as I cited above, that very Council, in its true and genuine letter to Theodosius, testifies to the contrary of what you put forward here. Next, the one word that is the key to your claim, i.e. the operative verb of commanding, does not occur anywhere in the letter you cite: [illegible, ~10 letters] it is said there that the council was held by command, but there is no trace of any such word. Finally, your own Lord has acknowledged his error in the recent Recognition of his books, namely that the letter from which you took this (whatever it is) is not the letter of the Second General Council; so it cannot be proved from it that the Second Synod was convened by Damasus' command. You too, who drew this from him, should acknowledge and abandon your error along with his: do not prove that the Council was convened by Damasus' command from the letter of the Council, since that is no longer the Council's letter, and even if it were, there is no word of command in it.

units.la: Sed si ita est, vt dicis, cur non ante annum demum millesimum & penè centesimum intra Italiam, inque ipso Laterano, Concilium vllum Generale habitum est, si solus Pontifex proprie potestatem habet Concilia indicendi? Cur Constantinopoli quatuor, Nicea duo, Epheso & Chalcedone singula; Roma nullum? Trahere, dicunt, id quod magis dignum est, ad se, id quod minùs dignum. Dignior tum Imperator ad se traxit Pontificem, ad Sedem suam, ad loca sibi propinquiora; idemque hoc Pontifex pòst[?], excusso demum Cæsare Pontificalior iam factus, sed non ante, factitauit. De altero verò quod petijsse dicis Concilia ab Imperatore, vt decreta sua protegeret, & mandari executioni curaret: tute ergo authoritatem protegendi & exequendi non negas ab Imperatore, accipis; nec sine Illo executioni mandari posse, id est, perinde esse, ac si non essent. Sed serò hoc iam nimis; vides enim petijsse non protectionem, aut executionem, sed ratihabitionem, confirmationem, [illegible, ~12 letters] quasi, sine Illa, non nuda, sed irrita futura, nec executionem seram, sed vim plane nullam habitura.
units.tr: But if it is as you say, why was no General Council held in Italy, and indeed in the Lateran itself, until nearly a thousand one hundred years later, if the Pope alone properly has the power of convening councils? Why four at Constantinople, two at Nicaea, one each at Ephesus and Chalcedon, and none at Rome? "They say that what is less worthy is drawn to what is more worthy." Then the more worthy Emperor drew the Pope to himself, to his own see, to places nearer to himself; and the Pope himself later, when Caesar had at last been shaken off and he had become more Pontifical, did the same, but not before. As for your claim that the Councils asked the Emperor to protect their decrees and to see to their execution: you yourself therefore accept that the authority to protect and execute comes from the Emperor, and you do not deny it; and that without him they cannot be put into execution, that is, that they would be as if they did not exist. But this is too late: for you see they asked not for protection or execution, but for ratification and confirmation, [illegible, ~12 letters] as if without him they would be not bare but void, and their execution would not be late but would have no force at all.

units.la: Hic verò, vbi de Conciliis modò conuocandis & confirmandis agitur, etsi nobis lis nulla de Regiâ in Ecclesiasticis potestate, idque initio statim professi sumus, etiam iam quoq; contendimus, Primatu illo intacto, Iuramentum constare posse : tamen exorari non potest Mattheus, quin in campum exeat illius controuersiæ : & vbi quæstio nulla nobis eâ de re, obtrudat tamen nobis testes minimè necessarios. Explicare scilicet voluit opes suas, & ostendere quæ habebat in Aduersarijs suis : habebat autem ibi ad hanc rem nonnulla, si incidisset alicubi : iam quia non incidit, occasionem arripit non valde idoneam, ea, quoquo modo proferendi. Vult enim Lectorem videre, quàm Cupressum pingat eleganter. Ne tamen sibi dicat non responsum ad singula, audiamus sanè, atque execuiamus illa, quantumuis iam putida.
units.tr: Here, where we are discussing only the convening and confirming of councils, although we have no dispute with him about royal power in ecclesiastical matters, and we professed this from the very beginning, we also now contend that the oath can stand with the primacy left intact. Yet Matthew cannot be persuaded to refrain from coming out into the field of that controversy; and although we have no question with him about that matter, he thrusts upon us witnesses who are by no means necessary. He wished, of course, to display his resources and to show what he had against his opponents: he had some material for this matter there, in case it had come up somewhere; now, since it did not come up, he seizes on an occasion that is not very suitable for producing those things in whatever way he can. For he wants the reader to see how elegantly he paints the cypress. Lest he nevertheless say to himself "not a reply to each point", let us hear them indeed, and go through those points, however stale they already are.

units.la: 1 Quærit Athanasius grauis Author inprimis, Quando à condito euo auditum, quòd iudicium Ecclesiæ authoritatem suam ab Imperatore accepit? Quando? Nunquam certè; Iudicium Ecclesiæ à verbo Dei, à veritate ipsâ, authoritatem suam semper accepit; non ab Imperatore, non à Pontifice, non à mortali quoquam : nec secus, Rex quisquam pius vel Imperator dixerit. Sed hoc, tum demum locum habet, si de authoritate intrinsecâ dicas: De externâ enim si sensus sit, [ut nempe Canon Ecclesiæ vim Legis habeat,] haud quisquam sanæ mentis negabit, ab Imperatore authoritatem accepisse Ecclesiæ iudicia. Ei rei, abundè fidem faciunt, quæ de Conciliorum Decretis, suprà iam à nobis, etiam à Torto ipso, allata sunt.
units.tr: 1. The grave author Athanasius, above all, asks: "Since the world began, when has it been heard that the judgment of the Church received its authority from the Emperor?" When? Never, certainly; the judgment of the Church has always received its authority from the Word of God, from the truth itself; not from the Emperor, not from the Pope, not from any mortal whatsoever; nor would any pious king or emperor say otherwise. But this holds good only if you speak of intrinsic authority. For if the sense is external (namely that a canon of the Church has the force of law), no one of sound mind will deny that the judgments of the Church received their authority from the Emperor. The things that have already been brought forward by us, and even by Torto himself, above concerning the decrees of Councils, are ample proof of this.

units.la: 2 Intercedit Osius, & dicit, Ne præcipe nobis in hoc genere, sed ea potius à nobis disce. Multùm autem interest, Quis, Cui loquatur. Cui hic loquitur Osius? Constantio, scilicet Imperatori. Constantius autem qualis? totus, quantus quantus, Arrianus & pro Arrianis; tam verò, sine iudicio, ut nomies mutárit fidem, nouem fidei diuersas confessiones ediderit; tam arrogans, ut hæc illius vox fuerit; Quod ego volo, pro Canone sit; tam prophanus, ut si quem Episcopum esse vellet, hoc illi dictum sit, Sententias contra Christum, nec de moribus tuis sis anxius. Hoc enim sufficit tibi ad commendationem, & Principis amicitiam. Huic tali, ab Osio dictum, Ne præcipe. At in Quo genere, Qua causâ? Illud enim, etiam inteteft [?]; Intelligentia dictorum ex causis sumenda dicendi. Quid illud erat quod voluit Constantius, ut sic illum affari opus esset? nimirum ut Osius, qui Athanasium in Synodo, perspectâ ibi causâ eius & cognitâ, absoluerat, eundem in Palatio nec dictâ causâ, nec vocatum, quin absentem, subscriptione suâ condemnaret. In hoc sanè genere, tam contra ius omne & fas, Constantius Osio ne praecipiat; Osius, Constantio ne pareat: disceat potiùs ab Osio, quo modo, quo iudicij ordine depone debeant, qui deponi merentur Episcopi. Non Osius hoc illi modò, etiam Iudex Secularis, Papinianus diceret, Ne praecipe nobis in hoc genere. Quid hoc ad Primatum? Haecine tua illa potestas summa, ad damnandum indictâ causâ, Athanasium, legitimè ante in Synodo absolutum?
units.tr: 2. Osius intervenes and says: "Do not give orders to us in this kind of matter, but rather learn from us." But it matters greatly who speaks and to whom. To whom does Osius speak here? To Constantius, of course, the Emperor. And what sort of man was Constantius? Wholly, in every respect, an Arian and a partisan of the Arians; and so without judgment that he changed his faith nine times and published nine different confessions of faith; so arrogant that his word was: "What I want shall be the rule"; so profane that, if he wished someone to be a bishop, this was said to him: "Pass sentences against Christ, and do not be anxious about your conduct." For this is enough for you as a recommendation and friendship with the prince. To such a man Osius said: "Do not give orders." But in "What kind of matter, for what cause?" For this too must be considered; "The understanding of sayings must be taken from the causes of speaking." What was it that Constantius wanted, so that it was necessary to address him in that way? Namely, that Osius, who had acquitted Athanasius in the Synod, the case having been examined and known there, should condemn the same man in the palace by his own signature, without the case being heard and without his being summoned, indeed in his absence. In this kind of matter, so contrary to all law and right, Constantius should not give orders to Osius, and Osius should not obey Constantius: let him rather learn from Osius how, and by what order of judgment, the bishops who deserve to be deposed ought to be deposed. Osius would not say this only to him; even a secular judge, Papinian, would say: "Do not give orders to us in this kind of matter." What has this to do with the primacy? Is this your great power of condemning Athanasius, without a hearing of the case, although he had been lawfully acquitted before in the Synod?

units.la: 3. Ambrosium bis producit. Is Valentiniano primùm dixit; Noli te gravare, Imperator, ut putes te in ijs quae Domini sunt, aliquod imperiale ius habere. Certè ne hoc putet quisquam. Non est in ea, quae divina sunt, Imperiale, sed neque Pontificale ius vllum. At illa divina hic, quae tandem? Aedes, Templa, Basilicae. Neque verò in ea quae ita divina sunt, Rex noster vllum sibi ius vendicat. Neq; sibi Sacrarum Aedium ius commissum existimat; utque non domum priuatam vllius, iure: sic neque domum Dei auferre fas putat, neque qui abstulerunt, vnquam probauit. Quam eius Mentem Heroicam, Legibus iam suis testatam, de non alienandis, non elocandis, in longum tempus Ecclesiae rebus, vtinam qui per orbem Christianum Principes sunt, sciant omnes, vtinam & imitentur. Sed tu hic inepte prorsus, qui quae ad possessiones referuntur, ad alia deorsum, vt si Regi Sacrilego esse non liceat, neque liceat ei Ecclesiae aliam rem vllam moderari. Quo & illa referri possunt, non esse cum supra Ecclesiam, vt eam tollendam Orthodoxu[?], Arrianu tradendam, vel debeat vel possit decernere. Nam quod subijcis, alterum Ambrosij dictum de iudicijs fuit. Prouocatus ad disputandum de fide Christi cum Auxentio, sub iudicibus Ethnicis, Iudaeis, Arrianis, renuit. Iustam certè causam habuit, si noluit in Palatio coram Ethnicis & Iudaeis, de Christi diuinitate tractare cum Auxentio. Ad causas fidei aperte spectabat hoc: ne quis autem de sententia eius error fit, ingeminat ibi, in causa fidei, in causa (inquam) fidei. Atqui nos, vel Deus ipse potiùs non nos; gubernacula Regi mandauit externae disciplinae: ea autem ad causas fidei torquere, nimis violentum est. In quibus tamen, permitteret id, scio, Ambrosius Imperatori, quod cuiuis de populo permisit: permisit autem populo, vt audita disputatione, vnusquisq; eligat quod sequatur. tur. Et hic etiam operæ pretium scire, Quis, Cuis loquatur: loquitur autem Valentiniano iuniori, imberbi adhuc, & imperito adolescenti, necdum baptizato, omnia ex Matris suæ Arrianæ arbitrio, per fas atque nefas gerenti ; dum illud à Parafitis suis subinde audiret, Imperatori licere omnia. Certè ad hunc talem, quis putet iudicia, quæ dicis, pertinere? At ad Constantinum, Theodosium, Patrem eius eiusdem nominis alterum, & pertinuisse, & delata esse, mox doceo.
units.tr: 3. He brings forward Ambrose twice. First he said to Valentinian: "Do not trouble yourself, Emperor, to think that you have any imperial right in the things that belong to the Lord." Certainly let no one think this. In those things which are divine there is no imperial right, but neither is there any papal right. But what things are "divine" here, pray? Buildings, temples, basilicas. Nor does our King claim for himself any right in those things which are thus divine. Nor does he think that the right over sacred buildings has been committed to him; and just as he does not, by right, take a private house from anyone, so he does not think it lawful to take away the house of God, nor has he ever approved of those who have taken it away. Would that all the princes throughout the Christian world knew, and would that they also imitated, that heroic mind of his, already attested by his laws, concerning not alienating or letting out the property of the Church for a long time. But you here are utterly foolish, since you refer what concerns "possessions" to other matters, below, so that it would not be lawful for a sacrilegious king, and it would not be lawful for him to govern any other matter of the Church. To this may also be referred those words, that "he is not above the Church," so that he ought or may decree that the Church should be destroyed, handed over to Arians, or whatever. For what you add, the other saying of Ambrose was about judgments. Challenged to debate "concerning the faith of Christ with Auxentius," under judges who were pagans, Jews and Arians, he refused. He certainly had a just cause, if he did not wish to discuss the divinity of Christ with Auxentius in the palace before pagans and Jews. This plainly pertained to "causes of faith"; and lest any error arise about his meaning, he repeats there: "in a cause of faith, in a cause (I say) of faith." But we, or God himself rather than we, have committed the helm of external discipline to the King; and to turn that to "causes of faith" is far too violent. In these matters, however, I know Ambrose would have allowed the Emperor what he allowed to any "man of the people": he allowed the people, after the disputation was heard, that each one should choose what he would follow. And here it is also worth knowing who speaks and to whom: he speaks to Valentinian the younger, still beardless and an inexperienced youth, not yet baptised, who managed everything at the will of his Arian mother, by right and by wrong, while he kept hearing from his parasites from time to time that "the Emperor may do everything." Surely who would think that the judgments you speak of pertain to such a man? But that they pertained to Constantine, to Theodosius, and to his father, another of the same name, and were handed down, I shall soon show.

units.la: 4. Maximum verò tuum, Imperatorem negamus. Non enim legitimè, sed ritu tyrannico, & tumultuante militè initiatum. Neque ergo in Cæsarum albo numeratur, legitimi Imperatoris Parricida, inuasor Imperij, vir sanguinis, tanquam perduellionis reus capite tandem cæsus Aquileiæ: ita verò prophanus, vt sacrificia sua Gentilibus, aram quoque Victoriæ restituerit, fautor etiam fuerit Iudæorum. Notaui ; vt sciret Lector, quales tu tibi hic Imperatores selegeris. Tum, quæ hæc causa? De Gnosticorum hæresi, à Priscilliano renouatâ ; quam à seculi Iudice dijudicandam, nemo dixerit. Est tamen Maximi iussu cognitum ab Eusodio[?] Præfecto, non de causâ hæreseos, sed de obscoenis Priscilliani maleficijs, próque ijs, morteab eo mulctatus est. Denique, institutum hoc Maximi, vtcunque Martino Turonensi displicuit, at Leoni Romano (qui vobis Martino maior est) placuisse testatur Epistola eius ad Turbium 93. Tum Ithacius, qui Maximo, consilij eius author, in Synodo Treuirensi absolutus.
units.tr: 4. We deny that your Maximus was an Emperor at all. For he was not installed lawfully, but in the tyrannical manner, by a rioting soldiery. He is therefore not counted among the Caesars, being the murderer of a lawful Emperor, an usurper of the empire, a man of blood, who was at last beheaded at Aquileia as a traitor guilty of treason. Indeed he was so profane that he restored sacrifices to the Gentiles and even the altar of Victory, and he was also a patron of the Jews. I have noted this so that the reader may know what sort of emperors you have chosen for yourself here. Then, what was the cause? The heresy of the Gnostics, revived by Priscillian; and no one would say that this was a matter to be judged by a secular judge. Nevertheless, at Maximus' command, Eusodius[?], the Prefect, examined the matter, not on the cause of the heresy but on the obscene crimes of Priscillian, and for these he was punished with death by him. Finally, this action of Maximus, however much it displeased Martin of Tours, is attested to have pleased Leo of Rome (who is greater than Martin, as far as you are concerned), by his letter to Turbius, 93. Then Ithacius, the author of this counsel to Maximus, was acquitted at the Synod of Trier.

units.la: 5. De Augustino quod affers, nihil ad rem : deferri voluit causam Caeciliani ad Episcopos, non autem ad Cæsarem : æquum postulauit. Id voluit, quod Conciliorum Canones, Constantinopolitani 6°. Antiocheni 11°. & 12°. Carthaginensis 107°. voluerunt. Non oportere de causis Episcoporum [illegible, ~12 letters]. Regijs auribus molestum esse : sed referri primùm ad Episcopos, & ab ijs, si fieri posset, terminari. Sed & Augustinus ipse, & qui cum eo erant Patres in Synodo Carthaginensi, & [illegible, ~10 letters] in causa Primosi agnouerunt ; & vero de rebus Ecclesiasticis, leges ab Imperatore ferri, ab Ipso petendum esse, missâ ad hoc ipsum legatione statuerunt. Can. 100. 105. Malè id quidem à Donato factum, quod inter Episcopos placidè transigi potuit, de eo Imperatori molestiam exhibere. Sed tamen, cùm præter ordinem, Donatus rem retulit ad Constantinum, is Romano primùm Episcopo, cum alijs tamen Collegis; pòst Arelatensi Synodo delegauit; postremò ipse tota de re cognouit, & sententiam tulit. Donatistas Augustinus reprehendit, vt importunos: Constantinum, vt ius Ecclesiæ inuadentem, non reprehendit. Secus fecit Donatus quàm debuit, quòd rem itâ molestè detulit: Constantinus nihilo plus sibi sumpsit, quàm iure suo potuit, quod delatam, iustè iudicauit. Diuinitus enim præcipi Regibus, vt in suo Regno, bona iubeant, mala prohibeant, non solùm quæ pertinent ad humanam societatem, verùm etiam quæ ad diuinam religionem; Augustinus ipse Author est.
units.tr: 5. As to what you bring up about Augustine, it has nothing to do with the matter. He wished the cause of Caecilian to be referred to the bishops, not to the Emperor; he demanded what was fair. He wished what the canons of the councils wished: the Constantinopolitan 6th, the Antiochene 11th and 12th, and the Carthaginian 107th. That it was not fitting for matters concerning bishops to be [illegible, about twelve letters]. It was troublesome to royal ears; rather, the matter should first be referred to the bishops, and be settled by them, if it could be. But Augustine himself, and the Fathers who were with him in the Synod of Carthage, also acknowledged, in the cause of Primosus [illegible, about ten letters]; and indeed they decided that concerning ecclesiastical affairs, laws were to be enacted by the Emperor, but that this should be sought from him by sending an embassy for this very purpose. Canons 100 and 105. Donatus did wrongly in troubling the Emperor about a matter which could have been settled peacefully among the bishops. But nevertheless, since Donatus referred the matter to Constantine contrary to the proper order, the Emperor first delegated it to the Roman bishop, but with other colleagues; afterwards he delegated it to the Synod of Arles; lastly he himself examined the whole matter and pronounced sentence. Augustine rebukes the Donatists as troublesome; he does not rebuke Constantine as one who was invading the right of the Church. Donatus acted otherwise than he should have, in that he referred the matter so troublesomely; Constantine took no more upon himself than he could by his own right, since, having been referred to him, he judged it justly. For it is commanded by God to kings that in their kingdom they should order good things and prohibit evil ones, not only those which pertain to human society, but also those which pertain to the divine religion; Augustine himself is the author of this.

units.la: 6. De Gelasio fecisti factum Torto dignum; tortam enim rem refers, & mutilam, & malâ fide. De Sacramentis ibi agitur, in quibus non summam, quin nullam omnino potestatem Reges sibi vindicant. Apponam verba integra. Nosti, fili Clementissime, quòd licet præsideat humano generi, dignitate rerum, tamen præsulibus diuinarum denotus[?] colla submittis, atq; ab eis causas salutis tuæ expetis, inque sumendis cælestibus Sacramentis eisque vt competit, disponendis, subdi te debere cognoscis religionis ordine, potiùs quàm præsse. Itaque inter hæc, ex illorum te pendere iudicio, non illos ad tuam velle redigi voluntatem. Audin' in sumendis, in disponendis Sacramentis? Audin', inter hæc? quæ verba tu, ne quasi Sorex tuis indicijs perires, quasi mus Ponticus, prærosa posuisti.
units.tr: 6. Concerning Gelasius you have done a deed worthy of Torto; for you cite the matter in a twisted and mutilated way, and in bad faith. There it is treated of sacraments, in which kings claim for themselves not the highest power, but no power at all. I will set out the words in full. "You know, most merciful son, that although you preside over the human race in dignity, nevertheless you bow your neck to the prelates of divine things, and you seek from them the causes of your salvation, and you know that in receiving the heavenly sacraments, and in arranging them as is fitting, you ought to be subject to the order of religion rather than to be in charge. Therefore, in these matters, you depend on their judgment, and do not wish them to be brought under your will. Do you hear this, in receiving and arranging the sacraments? Do you hear this, in these matters?" These words you, lest you perish like a shrew by your own indications, like a Pontic mouse, have gnawed beforehand and set forth.

units.la: 7. Gregorÿ locus 25ª Epistolâ, non autem vt tu posuisti 21ª, est. In eo, nihilo melior fide rem geris. Quicquid enim scribat Gregorius de Pŷssimis Dominis, scis ipse, si locum inspexisti, sciat & Lector si vacat inspicere, iussiones Imperatoris in causis Ecclesiasticis (contrà quàm tu hîc ponis) ter in eâ ipsâ Epistolâ Gregorium agnouisse. Audienda erat causa Maximi Salonarum Episcopi, quicum Gregorio lis erat. Scribit Maximus, præcepisse Serenissimos Dominos, vt Salonis cognitio esse deberet. Quid Gregorius respondet? Nullas se, eâ de re iussiones accepisse; quòd siqua sit iussio, eam per obreptionem elicitam, se credere. At non respondet ibi; nullam de his iubendi authoritatem penes Imperatorem esse, quippe in causâ Ecclesiasticâ; sic autem respondere debuit, si causam tuam agere voluit. 2o. Incurrerat in Censuras Maximus; laxare eas se scribit Gregorius: laxare, quomodo? secundùm iussiones serenissimi Domini Imperatoris. 3o. Suspendit tamen interim Gregorius Maximum à missarum solennibus celebrandis; sed quousque? Quoadusq; voluntatem eiusdem Serenissimi Domini cognosceret. Ita, causam eo loco cognoscit, censuram relaxat, suspensionem suspendit, omnia haec ex voluntate, & pro iussione Imperatoris: ter in Ecclesiastica causa iubet Imperator, ter Pontifex paret iubenti. Potuitne à te locus adduci, vel testis, qui magis pro Aduersario tuo, magis contra te facerent? Et haec iam illa sunt, propter quae moratus es Lectorem; veteramenta omnia, detrita iam, & repetita millies. Scimus verò hinc interim, Pijssimos Dominos in rebus Ecclesiae: iussiones suas interposuisse.
units.tr: 7. The passage of Gregory is in his 25th Epistle, not, as you have set it, in the 21st. In it you deal no better in good faith. For whatever Gregory writes about the "most wicked lords," you yourself know, if you have looked at the passage; and the reader too, if he has leisure to look, will know that Gregory acknowledged, three times in that very letter, the commands of the Emperor in ecclesiastical causes (contrary to what you here set forth). The cause of Maximus, Bishop of Salona, with whom Gregory had a dispute, was to be heard. Maximus writes that the most serene lords had ordered that the examination should be held at Salona. What does Gregory reply? That he had received no commands in this matter; and that if there is any command, he believes it was extorted by misrepresentation. But he does not there reply that the Emperor has no authority to command in such matters, since they are ecclesiastical; yet he ought to have replied so, if he had wished to plead your cause. Second: Maximus had incurred censures; Gregory writes that he relaxes them: relaxes them how? According to the commands of the most serene lord the Emperor. Third: nevertheless Gregory meanwhile suspended Maximus from celebrating the solemnities of the Mass; but until when? Until he should learn the will of the same most serene lord. Thus he examines the cause in that place, relaxes the censure, lifts the suspension, all these things by the will and at the command of the Emperor: three times the Emperor commands in an ecclesiastical cause, three times the Pontiff obeys the one commanding. Could any passage or witness have been brought forward by you that would argue more for your adversary and more against you? And these are now those things on account of which you have detained the reader: all those old arguments, already worn out and repeated a thousand times. Meanwhile we know from this that the most pious lords interposed their commands in the affairs of the Church.

units.la: Nec meliora sunt, nec magis ad remilla, quae iam sequuntur, Principum. Constantinus ita dixit, cum appellarent ad eum Donatistae, ô rabidam furoris audaciam &c. Credimus. Optato, Constantinus sic dixit; sed Constantinus quid fecit? Delegavit primò, secundo, qui audirent; post audiuit ipse, & sententiam tulit. Quid verba audiam, cum facta videam? Culpa quae fuit, in Donato fuit, qui odiosè interpellauit, non in Constantino, credo, qui iustè rem iudicauit; Alioquin & tu exclama, ô rabidam Constantini audaciam, qui admisit sic appellantes, ut nos exclamemus, ô rabidam Torti audaciam, qui Constantinum damnat audaciae, quem Optatus Author suus non ausus damnare. Tum & Augustino credimus, non ausum initio. Sed enim, qui non ausus initio de causis hijs cognoscere, (quippe qui necdum assuetus ad illas, nescire forte quid illarum cognitio postularet) prouectior iam factus, & ausus, & fecit. Scis quid scripserit ad {a}Nicomedienses in causa Eusebij & Theogonij, quos deportari fecerat. Siquis faueret illorum audaciae; Ministri Dei, hoc est, meâ authoritate coercebitur. Scis quid ad {b}Synodum Episcoporum Tyri. Cunčti, quotquot Synodum Tyri complessi us, sine morâ ad Pietatis nostra Castra properetu, ac reipsa quàm sincerè ac rectè iudicaueritis, ostendatis, idque coram Me, quem sincerum esse Dei ministrum, neq; vos sanè negabitis: Imò & in hoc quoque ipso, quod initio non est ausus facere, paulò post, animus ei non defuit faciendi; fecit enim.
units.tr: Nor are those things which follow, of the princes, any better or more to the point. Constantine spoke thus, when the Donatists appealed to him: "O the raging audacity of fury, etc." We believe it. Optatus reports that Constantine spoke thus; but what did Constantine do? He first delegated the matter to others to hear it; afterwards he heard it himself and pronounced sentence. Why should I listen to words when I see deeds? The fault was in Donatus, who troublesomely interrupted, not in Constantine, I believe, who judged the matter justly. Otherwise, you too should exclaim, "O the raging audacity of Constantine, who admitted appellants of this sort!" so that we might exclaim, "O the raging audacity of Torto, who condemns Constantine for audacity, whom Optatus, his own author, did not dare to condemn!" Then, we also believe that Augustine did not dare at the beginning. But indeed he who did not dare at the beginning to take cognizance of these causes (since he was not yet accustomed to them, and perhaps did not know what the examination of them required), once advanced, both dared and did it. You know what he wrote to the Nicomedians in the cause of Eusebius and Theogonius, whom he had caused to be deported. If anyone favoured their audacity, the ministers of God, that is, by my authority, would restrain him. You know what he wrote to the Synod of Bishops of Tyre: "All of you, as many as composed the Synod of Tyre, hasten without delay to the camp of our Piety, and show in fact how sincerely and rightly you have judged, and do so before me, whom you will certainly not deny to be a sincere minister of God." Indeed, even in this very thing, which he did not dare to do at the beginning, a short time afterwards the spirit did not fail him to do it; for he did it.

units.la: 2 Quod autem de Valentiniano Seniore refert Sozomenus, & tu ex illo, non sanè cohæret. Quid enim petebant ab eo Episcopi? vt ipsis ad corrigendum dogma conuenire permitteret. Quid autem respondit ille? Fas sibi non esse talia curiosius perscrutari. Quàm malè cohærent hæc? Quid opus negare quod nemo rogabat? Nam hoc illi non petebant, neque eâ de re verbum in legatione vllum; tantùm, vt conuenire permitteret; quod ab eo permissum illis quocunque loco vellent. Locus sanè illustris, pro Synodi non sine authoritate Regiâ conuocandis: ad rem tuam nihil. Secundò, Voluisti forte de Historiâ tripartitâ rem referre; nam in eâ petunt quidem {a}vt dignetur interesse: Vnde autem id referat Cassiodorus vix dicas, cùm in nullâ sit trium partium, è quibus suum illud confecit Opus tripartitum. Sed neque sic cohæret. Illi enim de præsentiâ interpellant; ille respondet de scrutinio: Poterat autem interesse scrutinio, nec ipse tamen perscrutari. Tertiò, Nicephorus verò idem hoc sic expedit in historiâ suâ Quod hic Sozomenus: Mihi fas non est; id ille, {b}Mihi facilè non est, qui negotijs occupatus, & Reipublicæ curis distentus sum; vt cui vacare totus non posset, ei nec fas, manum admouere. Vt ita, quod Græci ἐξεῖναι[?] idem sit quod Latinis, Non licet per negotia. Quartò, esto tamen; petierint id Episcopi, negârit Imperator quod ipse vis; sensu; vel hoc nobis dicendum, totius Hellespontis & Bithyniæ Episcopos Orthodoxos, nescijsse quid fas imperatori facere, qui Hypatianum Heracleæ Episcopum legatum suum miserant, vt vellet interesse; vel hoc (inquam) dicendum, vel certè nescijsse Valentinianum, hominem militarem, in castris enutritum, quid sibi fas: vel si sciuit, ex pietate, non {c}debito (vt de Theodosio simili in re Dominus tuus) id responsum dedisse, modestè scilicet, non, quòd pro iure suo id ei non liceret. At si quæstio iam sit, liceátne in eum finem Imperatori Synodo interesse: quis non plus credat, tot Episcopis Orthodoxis, hoc ab eo petentibus, &c. per hoc, ius illud ei, &c. fas esse profitentibus: quàm in Castris semper versato Imperatori, modestè hoc, quasi fas non sit, deprecanti? Cuinam verisimile circa Synodos quid Imperatori fas, scisse illum: omnes autem hos nescijsse? Sed quicquid Valentiniano hic visum respondere, caue putes, nefas existimâsse eum, rebus hijs vacare; Lege sis Theodor.4.10. videbis ibi de dogmatibus Ecclesiasticis reformandis etsi non ꝛꝑ, (quod Constantio vidit cesssisse non foeliciter) at ꝓ etsi non curiosum fuisse; at, tantum accurâsse negotium hoc, quantum instituto nostro conuenit.
units.tr: 2. But what Sozomen reports about the elder Valentinian, and you from him, does not hold together at all. For what did the bishops ask of him? "That he would allow them to meet to correct the doctrine." And what did he answer? "That it was not lawful for him to inquire more curiously into such things." How badly do these things cohere! Why need he deny what no one was asking? For they did not ask this of him, nor any word about it in the embassy at all; only that he would allow them to meet, which was "granted to them by him, in whatever place they wished." It is certainly a notable place for the convening of synods not without royal authority, but nothing to your purpose. Second, perhaps you wished to refer to the Tripartite History; for in it they indeed ask "that he would deign to be present." But you could hardly say whence Cassiodorus reports this, since it is not in any of the three parts from which he compiled his own Tripartite Work. But it does not cohere even so. For they request his presence; he replies about the examination. He could indeed be present at the examination without himself examining. Third, Nicephorus expresses the same thing in his history in the same way as Sozomen here: "It is not lawful for me"; he says, "It is not easy for me, who am occupied with business and distracted by the cares of the commonwealth"; so that, since he could not be wholly at leisure for it, it was not lawful for him to put his hand to it. So that the Greek word for "it is permitted" [ἐξεῖναι] is the same as the Latin "it is not allowed because of business." Fourth, be it so; let the bishops have asked it, and let the Emperor have refused what you wish, in that sense. Even so we must say this: either that the orthodox bishops of the whole of Hellespont and Bithynia did not know what was lawful for an emperor to do, who sent their legate Hypatian, bishop of Heraclea, that he might wish to be present; or we must say this, I say, or at least that Valentinian, a military man, reared in camps, did not know "what was lawful for him"; or, if he knew, that he gave that answer out of piety, not out of obligation (as your Lord did in a similar matter concerning Theodosius), modestly, of course, and not because it was not permitted to him by his own right. But if the question now is whether it was lawful for an emperor to be present at a synod for that end: who would not rather believe that so many orthodox bishops, asking this of him, etc., professing that by this right it is lawful for him, etc.; than the emperor, always versed in camps, modestly begging off this as if it were not lawful? What is likely: that the emperor knew what was lawful for him concerning synods, but all these men did not know it? But whatever Valentinian thought fit to answer here, beware of supposing that he judged it unlawful for himself to be occupied with these matters. Read, if you please, Theodoret 4.10; you will see there that concerning the reform of ecclesiastical dogmas, even if not "by the authority" (which was seen to have turned out unhappily for Constantius), yet not without interest; but that he took care of this business as much as was fitting for our purpose.

units.la: 3. Magis autem insulsum multò, quod proximum ponis, de Theodosio iuniore, qui Comitem Candidianum ad Concilium Ephesi, in eum finem miserat, vt turbas ibi & tumultus compescerent; at Episcoporum constitutionibus, quæ circa fidei dogmata inciderent, sese non immiscerent. At de Imperatore instituisti, quomodo iam delapsus ad Comitem — amphora cœpit Institui, currente rotâ cur vrceus exit? Annon hoc est, à disparatis argumentum ducere? Recognosce enim, hic quid dixeris. Prohibetur à Rege Comiti, ne rebus se fidei immiscerat: Regi ergo in sacris potestas nulla. At tu, credo, Regi plus quam Comiti deferendum putas; & extra res fidei multa sunt, in quibus potestas eius se exerceat. Fidei enim nec Rex, sed nec Apostoli ipsi dominantur. Locus ergo hic totus, extra oleas.
units.tr: 3. Far more foolish, however, is what you put next, about the younger Theodosius, who had sent Count Candidianus to the Council of Ephesus for this purpose: to restrain the disturbances and tumults there, but not to meddle with the decrees of the bishops concerning matters of faith. But you have set out what the Emperor did, how you have slipped down to the Count: "When the jar began to be formed, why does the pot come out while the wheel is still turning?" Is this not to draw an argument from things that have nothing to do with each other? For consider again what you have said here. The king forbids the Count to meddle in matters of faith: therefore the king has no power in sacred things. But you, I suppose, think the king should be given more deference than the count, and that outside matters of faith there are many things in which his power may be exercised. For neither king nor even the apostles themselves have dominion over faith. This whole place, therefore, is "outside the olive groves."

units.la: 4. Nec enim de Basilio illo tuo est quod valdè laboremus, non magni momenti Imperatore, qui & Dominũ suum Michaëlem occidit, & Imperium inuasit; qui infimæ sortis homo, vt nec patriam nôsset, nec parentes; inter captiuos venundatus Constantinopoli, nec liberè educatus, nec excultus vllo doctrinæ genere, bono iure, prouinciam hanc poterat deprecari. Sed quid tamen dicit? Inuestigare illa & quærere, sacerdotum esse, non Laicorum. Nec nos hoc negamus. At erat tibi periodo eâdem, aliud magis in rem tuam; tam enim erat ex parte tuâ testis ibi prodigus Basilius, vt præcideris periodi huius partem priorem, in qua Laico nulli licere vult, vt vllo modo sermonem moveat de rebus Ecclesiasticis. Non sermonem movere de illis, non vllo modo movere sermonem? Nimium hoc quidem visum Matthæo, puduit inserere; laudo. Sic enim non modò partes præcipuæ, sed nec partes vllæ penes Principem forent: Gallionem, credo, imitari vult Principes, cui nihil horum cura. Parum verò basilicum Basilij hoc tesi monium.
units.tr: 4. Nor is it of great concern to us that your Basil, an emperor of no great importance, who also killed his lord Michael and seized the empire, a man of the lowest rank, who knew neither his country nor his parents, sold among captives at Constantinople, not reared freely nor trained in any kind of learning, could rightly have been allowed to claim this province. But what does he say? "To investigate and inquire into those things belongs to priests, not to laymen." Nor do we deny this. But in the same sentence there was something more to your purpose, for Basil was so lavish a witness on your side that you cut off the first part of this sentence, in which he wills that no layman may be allowed "in any way to move discussion about ecclesiastical matters." Not "to move discussion about them," but "in no way to move discussion"? Matthew thought this went too far and was ashamed to insert it; I commend him. For in this way the principal parts, indeed not even any part at all, would remain with the prince. I suppose you want princes to imitate Gallio, "to whom none of these things was a concern." This testimony is hardly kingly, as Basil's would be.

units.la: 5. Nec Caroli melius. Si tamen Caroli, & non Treburiensis Concilij potiùs, diù post Carolum: Quid tamen Ille? Nihil de rebus religionis, aut de potestate circa illas vel summâ vel infrâ[?]. De iugo nescio quo ferendo loquitur: non sanè Christi iugo; nam iugum illius leue. Puto igitur Antichristi, quia tam grave, vt ei ferendo vix Carolus ille Magnus par esset. Quid haec ad potestatem Principum? Nihil; ad patientiam certè aliquid. Et quidem id quaerit Pontifex, Principes parum potentes, valdè patientes, quos posset sub Sanctae Sedis iugo vix ferendo mittere.
units.tr: 5. Nor is it better with Charles. If it is Charles, and not rather the Council of Trier, long after Charles: what then does he say? Nothing about matters of religion, or about power over them, whether supreme or inferior. He speaks of some yoke to be borne: certainly not the yoke of Christ, for his yoke is light. I think, then, it is the yoke of Antichrist, since it is so heavy that Charles the Great himself would hardly be equal to bearing it. What has this to do with the power of princes? Nothing; to their patience, certainly, it has something to do. And indeed this is what the Pontiff seeks: princes who are not very powerful but very patient, whom he could send under the yoke of the Holy See, which they could hardly bear.

units.la: 6. At etiam hauris ad faeces? Ex loco obscuro, & corrupto? (sic enim in margine habetur Synodi illius tertia) Etiâ Haereticis, etiam Arrianis supplicas, vt opem ferant laboranti Pontifici; nec vereris si Arriani sint de potestate illâ cedere, ne Orthodoxum fit, eam tanto magis tueri? Quid verò, iste, qui hic est, post principia, simul Barbarus, simul haereticus? Quanquâ haeresis, credo, non erat: Nam & Constantius & Valens, qui eâdem haeresi infecti, Synodis & interesse & praesse soliti. Quare mera Barbaries erat. Sed quid aut tamen?
