Vocabant illum ad Concilii, Episcopi, vt interessent saltem: sciebant ergo ius illi esse, vt posset interesse; & aliquid ad eum de Synodo, praeter reverentiam pertinere. Ille contrà, nihil. Nihil enim forte apud Barbaros. Quid agimus? Vtrû credimus Episcopis qui petunt, & putant rem licitâ sic interesse, an homini Gotthô non putanti? Ego Episcopis: tu, si vis, crede Barbaro. Nec leuia tamen ibi sunt per Synodum illam impressa vestigia, ex quibus manifestò rem teneas, nempe, aliquid ad eum de rebus Ecclesiae praeter reverentiam Episcopos ibi putâsse pertinere. Nam ex praecepto Theodorici congregata est Synodus, Et, decernere Synodus sine Regiâ notitiâ non praesumit Et, procedunt, secundum principalia praecepta, quae illorum hoc tribuunt potestati. Et, quae proximè ibi sequuntur verba, haec sunt, Committere Regem, Potestati Pontificum, vt quid magis putarent vtile, deliberarent. Habuit ergo aliquid quod committeret praeter reverentiam: reverentiam enim suam, credo, non commisit. Collige iam: Synodum ibi Rex congregat: illa, sine Regis notitiâ nihil praesumit: Rex illorum potestati rem committit: illi secundum principalia praecepta, quae hoc illorum tribuunt potestati, faciunt quod facto opus est. Pro Primatu, haec quidem argumenta sunt, non contra Primatum. Nec dum igitur habetis, quae habere vos dicitis testimonia; abierunt enim omnia in fumos, vt consistat adhuc potestas sua Regibus, quâ & Synodos conuocare, & confirmare posint, & obire reliqua omnia, quæ & olim qui Imperatores, diligenter obierunt, & qui tum Episcopi libenter agnouerunt.
units.tr: 6. But do you also draw from the dregs? From an obscure and corrupt passage? (For so the margin has it for that third Synod.) You even appeal to heretics, even to Arians, to bring help to the Pontiff in distress; and you do not fear that if the Arians should yield that power, it would be the more firmly upheld by the Orthodox? What then is this man, who is here "after the first principles," at once a barbarian and a heretic? Yet he was not a heretic, I suppose: for both Constantius and Valens, who were tainted with the same heresy, were accustomed both to attend and to preside at synods. Therefore it was mere barbarism. But what then? Bishops summoned him to the Council, so that he might at least be present: they knew, therefore, that he had a right to be present, and that something concerning the Synod pertained to him beyond mere reverence. He, on the contrary, [says] nothing. Perhaps nothing among barbarians. What are we to do? Whom shall we believe: the bishops who petition, and think it lawful for him to be present in this way, or the Gothic man who does not think so? I believe the bishops; you, if you wish, believe the barbarian. Nor are there slight traces impressed in that Synod, from which you may clearly grasp the matter, namely that the bishops there thought something concerning the affairs of the Church pertained to him beyond mere reverence. For "the Synod was gathered by the command of Theodoric," and "the Synod does not presume to decide without the king's knowledge," and "they proceed according to the principal commands, which grant this power to them." And the words that immediately follow there are these: "The king committed the matter to the power of the bishops, that they might deliberate on whatever they thought most useful." He therefore had something he could commit beyond mere reverence: for his reverence, I suppose, he did not commit. Gather now: there the king convenes the Synod; the Synod "does not presume anything without the king's knowledge"; the king commits the matter to their power; they, according to the principal commands which grant this power to them, do what the business requires. These are arguments for the Primacy, not against the Primacy. Nor, then, have you yet the testimonies you say you have; for all of them have gone up in smoke, so that the power of kings still stands, by which they may both convene and confirm synods, and perform all the other things which the emperors of old diligently performed, and which the bishops of that time gladly acknowledged.

units.la: TVm, gratiæ tibi iam, vt video, à nobis habendæ sunt, qui nos aptam illam sanè distinctionem docuisti, ex hoc mundo, in hoc mundo. Sed audi tamen, quid nos hîc obtusi homines trans Alpes de eâ dicamus: Quod in hoc mundo est, si de hoc mundo sit etiam, id ad tuum (quod ibi vis) Regnum Christi non pertinet: cuius etsi in hoc mundo, tamen de hoc mundo Regnum non est. Regna autem mundi, non solùm in, sed de hoc mundo etiam sunt. Quare nihil illa ad Pontificem vestrum. Nihil ei in illa iuris, quippe cui (vt tu quidem vis) Regnum Christi, quod de hoc mundo non est, solùmodo sit creditum. Nisi id agas (& id certè agis) non solùm vt quæ in mundo, sed quæ extra mundum sunt, omnia sub pedibus eius subijcias: sic enim memini de vestris quispiam, eò torsit Psalmi versum illum, Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius, ad Pontificem vestrum: deinde sic explicuit, vt per pecora campi, homines, per volatilia cæli, Angelos, per pisces marinos, animas, quæ in Purgatorio, intelligeret. Pontifici pedibus subiectos omnes. Sic nuper D.Marta vt Pontifici subijceret non Christianos modò, sed & Sarracenos, serió nobis id narrat eodem Psalmo contineri, Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius, oues, & boues, & pecora campi. Oues, id est, Christianos; boues, id est, Sarracenos; qui iam etsi de Ouili Pontificis non sunt, at de Bovili sunt, nec Christus solùm Pasce oues meas, sed etiam Pasce boues meos dixit; & Pontifex iam non Pastor modò, sed & Bubulcus. Regna quidem mundi à Christo etiam sunt, & Christi sunt, si non quâ homo, at quâ Deus tamen; Regnum etiam Illi, quâ & homo peculiare & suum, Ecclesiæ scilicet. Quodsi autem & Regna Principum (quæ & in & ex hoc mundo sunt) Christi sint, & qui eis præsunt, Vicarij in terris Christi Regis: sua Vicarijs hijs Christi, Regibus, obedientia debetur, ab omnibus, non minùs quàm tuo Christi Vicario, in illo eius Regno, quod vtcunque in mundo sit, de mundo tamen non est. Sed vt semel expediam. Duo hæc Regna, Reipublicæ & Ecclesiæ, quamdiu duo manent, hoc ab illo diuisum, duos habent Primos: postquam in vnum
units.tr: Then, you have now, as I see, earned thanks from us, you who have taught us that neat distinction, "out of this world, in this world." But listen, nonetheless, to what we dull men beyond the Alps say about it: What is in this world, even if it is also of this world, does not pertain to that kingdom of Christ (which you mean), whose kingdom, though it is in this world, is not of this world. Yet the kingdoms of the world are not only in this world but also of this world. Therefore those kingdoms have nothing to do with your Pontiff. He has no right in them, since to him (as you indeed want) only the kingdom of Christ, which is not of this world, has been entrusted. Unless you intend this (and certainly you do intend it), not only to subject to his feet those things which are in the world, but also those which are outside the world. For I remember that one of your men twisted that verse of the Psalm, "You have put all things under his feet," to apply to your Pontiff, and then explained it so that by "the beasts of the field" he understood men, by "the birds of the air" angels, and by "the fishes of the sea" the souls in Purgatory: "all things subjected to the Pontiff's feet." So lately Doctor Marta, to subject to the Pontiff not only Christians but also Saracens, tells us in earnest that the same Psalm contains, "You have put all things under his feet, sheep and oxen, and the beasts of the field." Sheep, that is, Christians; oxen, that is, Saracens; who, though they are not of the Pontiff's sheepfold, are of his cattle-stall. And Christ said not only "Feed my sheep," but also "Feed my oxen," and the Pontiff is now not only a shepherd but also a herdsman. Indeed the kingdoms of the world are also from Christ and belong to Christ, if not as man, yet as God; and the kingdom also belongs to Him as man, peculiarly and as His own, namely the Church. But if the kingdoms of princes (which are both in and of this world) are Christ's, and those who preside over them are vicars of Christ the King on earth, then to these vicars, the kings, obedience is owed by Christ's people, by all, no less than to your Vicar of Christ, in that kingdom of his which, however much it is in the world, is nevertheless not of the world. But to dispatch the matter at once: these two kingdoms, of the commonwealth and of the Church, as long as they remain two, separated from each other in this way, have two first ones; once they coalesce into one,

units.la: a Antonin. [?] vnum coalescunt, non vt in duobus, duo, sed vt in vno, vnus Primus est; Rex scilicet, cui Pontifex semper subiectus in populo Dei Israele, Exemplari nostro. Nunquam ibi Rex subiectus Pontifici, semper Pontifex Regi: itidem hic, cùm Ecclesia & Respublica vnum in regnum aggregantur.
units.tr: a Antonin. [?] They coalesce into one, not as two in two, two, but as one in one, one, the First is the King; to him the Pontiff is always subject among the people of God, Israel, our exemplar. Never there was the King subject to the Pontiff; always the Pontiff to the King. Likewise here, when the Church and the Commonwealth are joined together into one kingdom.

units.la: Pòst, herciscis inter Deum & Cæsarem. Cæsari tributa, honorem, & obedientiam tribuis; sed obedientiam, circumscriptam, rebus & negotijs seculi. Quid ergo si bona iubeant Reges, mala prohibeant, non solùm quæ pertinent ad humanam societatem, verùm etiam quæ ad diuinam religionem? Quid si contra errorem pro ipsâ veritate decernant? Annon eis æquum obedire? Censet Augustinus, & nos cum illo: tu si voles, alia omnia. Nam & cùm Ioas æratium sacrum componeret, & cum Ezekias æneum serpentem comminueret, & cùm Ioas excelsa dimeret; extra vtraque res seculi iubebant, sacra iubebant, & populus tamen parendo nihil peccauit. Illis ergo, etiam cùm in re religiosa iusta iubent, debetur obedientia.
units.tr: Afterwards, you divide the inheritance between God and Caesar. To Caesar you give tributes, honour and obedience; but obedience, limited to the things and affairs of the world. What then if kings command good things and forbid bad things, not only those which pertain to human society but also those which pertain to divine religion? What if they decree against error on behalf of the truth itself? Is it not right to obey them? Augustine thinks so, and we with him: you, if you wish, think otherwise. For when Joash was arranging the sacred bronze, and when Hezekiah was crushing the bronze serpent, and when Joash was measuring the high places; they were commanding things outside the affairs of the world, they were commanding sacred things, and yet the people in obeying sinned in nothing. To such men, therefore, even when they command in a religious matter things that are just, obedience is owed.

units.la: Vbi verò de Deo dicis, adiungis ei & Vicarium; sed ille ibi, quem adiungis, nec solus est. Nam & vicem Christi Rex obit quoque, & Christus ipse dicitur: Nec in sacris solus. Plures enim Christus instituit, non vnicum modò; sicut misit me Pater, & ego mitto vos. Qui vos audit, me audit: vt rectè {a}Eusebius veter de illis, Christi autem Vicarij Sacerdotes sunt. Nam quem tu hic nominas, is nec vllus erat, nec vsquam, cùm Christus verba illa proferret: Christi enim tum, in terris præsentia, Vicarium non admisit. Nusquam existenti nihil reddi potuit. Erant verò etiam Reges in terra tum Christi Vicarij, cùm præter eos vicarius alius non esset. Sed nec illud satis æquè. Cùm vtrisque obedientiam deberi vis, Cæsari nudam vis: tuo huic vestitam duplicibus, fidelem, & puram. Quidni autem eandem & Cæsari? An quam adiudicas illi, obedientia, quanquam nec fidelis sit nec pura, debet ei sufficere, & vel hac forte sua sic abire contentus, tanquam congrua suâ portione? Certè si sic Cæsari sat esse putas obedientiam vllam, vtcunque infidelis ea fit, vtcunque non depurata, non eris hercisceundæ hæreditatis huic? Iudicem te iniquum ostendis, abdicamus te hoc munere.
units.tr: But where you speak of God, you join to him a Vicar; yet that one whom you join there is not alone. For the King also performs the place of Christ, and is himself called Christ: nor is he alone in sacred things. For Christ appointed several, not only one; as the Father sent me, so I send you. He who hears you hears me: as the ancient Eusebius rightly said of them, but the Priests are the Vicars of Christ. For the one you name here was neither any man at all, nor anywhere, when Christ uttered those words: for Christ did not admit a Vicar during his presence on earth at that time. Nothing could be rendered to one who did not exist anywhere. But there were also Kings on earth then who were Vicars of Christ, when there was no other vicar besides them. But neither is that quite equal. Since you want obedience owed to both, you offer Caesar bare obedience: to your man here you offer it clothed in a double garment, faithful and pure. Why not then the same to Caesar as well? Or is the obedience you assign to him, though it is neither faithful nor pure, enough for him, and perhaps is he to depart content with this portion of his as being his suitable share? Certainly if you think any obedience at all is enough for Caesar, however unfaithful it may be, however unrefined, you will not be fit to divide the inheritance with him? You show yourself an unjust judge; we remove you from this office.

units.la: Quintò autem iam regero tibi, nec corrumpi verba Breui opus esse, nec verba pro verbis substitui. Potest annotari locus; supra à nobis annotatus est, Pagina 15. lin. 19 (appono iam paginam & lineam.) Juramentum in Breui dici fidei & saluti adversari, Pagina 15. lin. 16. In Juramento verba hæc sunt, præstabo veram obedientiam. (Ea obedientia, eiusdem modo est, quippe quæ ad defensionem modò, Regis contra proditores tantùm se porrigat) pag. eadem, lin. 22. In sacris, de Rege præcipiente, subdito obediente, nihil ibi quicquam. Habes obedientiam illam ciuilem, fidei & saluti adversari. Habes locum annotatum. Quid quæris amplius?
units.tr: Fifthly, I now reply to you again, that there is no need either to corrupt the words of the Brief or to substitute words for words. The passage can be cited; it was cited by us above, page 15, line 19 (I now add the page and line). The oath in the Brief is said to be opposed to faith and salvation, page 15, line 16. In the oath the words are these: I will render true obedience. (That obedience extends only to the defence of the King against traitors, and is of this kind alone.) The same page, line 22. In sacred matters, concerning a King commanding and a subject obeying, there is nothing whatever there. You have that civil obedience, opposed to faith and salvation. You have the passage cited. What more do you seek?

units.la: TU vero nota nobis locum, ubi nugæ, ubi conuitia quæ sic omittis: vel fatere, quòd omittendo, nugator ipse sis. Optandum dixit Apologia, ut Pontifex priusquam hoc mandatum suum Pontificijs dedisset, definijsset illud, pro re credenda; Habet enim hanc potestatem Papa, nec vos negatis. Nec tu, ut puto, nugari dices aut conuitiari illum, qui de spiritus Papalis infallibilitate, vel de novis, si ille proponat, credendus verba fecerit. Nam hæc quidem olim erant feria, non nugæ; & encomia, non conuitia Pontificum vestrorum. {a}Tanquam Papa enim, multa potest declarando, nedum fidei articulum, tmò & novum inducendo. Vis altum? {b}Collige hic, Principem Ecclesiæ Christiani, Vicarium, posse super fide Catholicâ, declarationem facere, etiam articulum fidei facere, si sumatur articulus fidei, pro eo quod credere oporteat, cum prius ex præcepto Ecclesiæ, necessario non oporteret. Hæc si nugæ, si conuitia, cur illa non sustulit de Jure suo Canonico Gregorius 13. cùm Augiæ ibi stabulum repurgaret? si reliquit, si non omisit; omitte nos, dic tu illum nugatorem, dic vestros homines Conuitiatores: vestra enim hæc sunt, & à vobis. Imò tute ipse pòst, pag. 67. non omittis id agere, quod hic appellas nugas agere. Quin serio nobis narras, si per articulos fidei significentur quæcunque dogmata, quæ fide Catholicâ credi debent (nec nobis hîc alia significantur) tum verò non dubitare vos, quin à Pontifice vestro multi fidei articuli condi possint; nec tamen dum ista dicis, conuitiaris, credo, Pontifici. Quid ille verò, qui nuper in os dixit Paulo ipsi 5°. {c}Commissum ei munus à Deo excelso, non modò articulos indeterminatos determinandi, sed etiam fidei Symbolum condendi: atque hoc ipsum Orthodoxos. omnes, omnium facultorum agnouisse, & palam confessos esse? An-non ille insignis nugator, egregius conuiciator, si hæc nugæ sint & conuicia, quas hic te dicis omittere? Quare autem librum suum Pontifici inscripsit? Quare Pontifex suscepit inscriptum? Quare Academia approbauit? Quare nugas has & conuicia omittere illum non coëgit?
units.tr: But you, note for us the passage where there are trifles, where there are reproaches, which you thus leave out: or confess that, by leaving them out, you yourself are the trifler. The Apology said it was to be wished that the Pontiff, before he had given this mandate of his to the Papists, had defined it as a matter to be believed; for the Pope has this power, and you do not deny it. Nor, I think, will you say that he who spoke about the infallibility of the Papal spirit, or about new matters to be believed, if the Pope should propose them, was trifling or reproaching. For these things were once holy and not trifles, and eulogies, not reproaches, of your Pontiffs. For as Pope, he can, by declaring many things, not only an article of faith, but even by introducing a new one. Do you want something deep? Gather from this that the Prince of the Christian Church, the Vicar, can, concerning the Catholic faith, make a declaration, even make an article of faith, if an article of faith is taken to mean what must be believed, when before, by the precept of the Church, it was not necessary to believe it. If these are trifles, if they are reproaches, why did Gregory XIII not remove them from his own Canon Law, when he was there cleansing the stable of Augeas? If he left them there, if he did not omit them, then leave us alone, call him a trifler, call your men reproachers: for these are your things, and from you. Indeed, you yourself afterwards, on page 67, do not omit to do what here you call doing trifles. Indeed you tell us seriously that if by articles of faith are meant whatever doctrines must be believed by the Catholic faith (and nothing else is meant here by us), then you do not doubt that many articles of faith can be framed by your Pontiff; yet while you say these things, you do not, I believe, reproach the Pontiff. What of him who lately said to Paul himself, in his fifth chapter: a task entrusted to him by almighty God, not only to determine indeterminate articles, but also to frame a creed of faith; and this very thing all the Orthodox of all faculties have acknowledged, and have openly confessed? Is not he a notable trifler, an eminent reproacher, if these are trifles and reproaches, which you here say you leave out? Why did he dedicate his book to the Pontiff? Why did the Pontiff accept the dedicated work? Why did the Academy approve it? Why did he not compel him to leave out these trifles and reproaches?

units.la: Sed vbi tandem se iactat Author Apologiæ grauem Theologum? tute hic leuem pseudologum te potius ostendis, qui sic iactas mendacia. Ille vero contrà; nondum quatuor folia sunt, cùm ita ipse de Theologiâ suâ, quantulacunque ea est. Nec erunt etiam quatuor folia, cùm deprecatur inuidiam gloriæ aucupandæ, quòd concertationem instituit cum Cardinale viro tam docto. Poterat ne vel ille magis modestè de se, vel tu magis odiosè de illo dicere? At in te, Torte, quàm iure optimo retorqueri potest iactantia quàm torques, qui Typographos conducticios habes: vnum è Politâ[?], qui Libellum tuum elegantem sanè; Opus tuum eruditissimum; alterum ab extremo vsque Rheni littore, qui libellum tuum insignem, te autem excellentiùs ingenij Theologum, hic Germanus iactet, ille Italus, vt in ore sis omni populo? Da in totâ Apologiâ simile quid; & ille sit, tu ne sis strenuus ille iactator.
units.tr: But where at last does the author of the Apology boast himself a serious theologian? You yourself here show yourself a light pseudologue, who thus boast of lies. He, on the contrary, not yet four leaves in, speaks thus of his own theology, however small it is. Nor will there even be four leaves before he deprecates the envy of seeking glory, because he entered into a contest with a Cardinal so learned. Could he have spoken of himself more modestly, or you of him more odiously? But against you, Torte, with how much right can that boasting be turned back, you who twist it, who have hired printers: one from Polita[?], who calls your little book quite elegant, your very learned work; another from the far shore of the Rhine, who lauds your remarkable little book, and you as a theologian of more excellent talent, this German, that Italian, so that you are on every people's lips? Put in the whole Apology something similar; and let him be that vigorous boaster, and you not be he.

units.la: Quicquid autem ibi reliqui habes ad Dilemma, memoriter iam lector tenet, ita sæpe inculcasti, quàm sine veritate, tam sine verecundiâ omni, cogis Catholicos ad fidei abnegationem; muniris aditum ad Iuramentum Primatus; nam hæc tibi suprà, nec semel, demonstrata. Credo certè non semel; sed & suprà & hîc debere te Lectori ludibrium, & quoties tibi mentio fit demonstrationum tuarum, aliquid ibi monstri simile, nihil legitimæ demonstrationis. Transferunt scopum, petunt principium, concludunt à dicto secundum quid, ducuntur à disparatis, elenchi meri sunt, veræ [illegible, ~2 letters] nihil habent, nec quicquam demonstrant, nisi infœlicem fuisse te, qui in præceptorem non incideris, qui te Analytica posteriora melius doceret. Qui fidem Subditi affirmat, fidem Catholici non negat: fidei ergo Catholicæ negatio, pro medio hic esse non potest.
units.tr: But whatever else you have there concerning the Dilemma, the reader now holds in memory, so often have you repeated, with as little truth as shame of any kind, that you force Catholics to renounce their faith; you pave the way to the Oath of Primacy; for these things have been demonstrated to you above, and not once. I certainly believe not once; but both above and here you ought to be a laughing-stock to the Reader, and whenever mention is made of your demonstrations, something monstrous like them, nothing of legitimate demonstration. They shift the target, beg the principle, conclude from a statement made only in a certain respect, are led from things unlike, are mere sophistical refutations, have nothing of true [illegible, ~2 letters], and demonstrate nothing, except that you were unlucky in not having fallen in with a teacher who would have taught you the Posterior Analytics better. He who affirms the subject's faith does not deny the Catholic's faith: therefore the denial of the Catholic faith cannot be the means here.

units.la: Parenesis etiam ad Martyrium, malè fundata. Arenosum enim totum, quod dicis de præparatione ad Iuramentum Primatus, vt phrenesis potiùs quàm parenesis dici debet. Nam si præparatio, cur in illo solo sistitur? Non debuit; pergeret verò Rex, & praeparato iam, secundum illud, de Primatu, quasi formam induceret. At omnino in primo sistitur, secundum non inducitur; non vlli; (cedò enim, si potes exemplum.) Quare in hoc terminus motus est, nec vel principium noui, vel aditus ad aliud de Primatu. Libero ergo te metu Iuramenti alterius, quod, vt video, valde te torquet, nec sinit respirare, ita semper meticulosus es, ne tectè, ne obscurè (poteras autem dicere, ne torte) contineat nouam illam haeresin de Primatu Regio. Quae tamen si haeresis; certè non noua cùm & Reges sub Testamento veteri omnes Primatum illum tenuerint; & Prophetae tum omnes in eo, ac Sacerdotes acquieuerint. Vel potiùs si haeresis; noua, & ab incude vestrà; vetus enim non fuit. Omnes illum Prophetae ad apicem tenuerunt: nec enim apicem vllum nos nostris Regibus tribuimus, quem illi tum suis non tribuerunt. Sed vide ne contrà prorsus sit, quàm tu dicis; ne, quae ibi commemorantur in Iuramento, depositiones Regum, inuasiones, tumultus, praeparatio sint & dispositio, & per ea aditus fiat potiùs ad Primatum Pontificis. Tum quod vltimum, stultissimum; ideò detinceri in carcere Archipresbyterum, vt tædio victus iuret in Primatum. Nec enim custodia eiusmodi est, quâ detinetur, vt eius illum valde tædere debeat; nec in eâ delatum ei vnquam illud de Primatu; & iuret, ne iuret, nemo hîc vel metuit vel optat, súsque déque est; & Matthaeus haec omnia vidit in somnijs, & rectè rem hanc totam concludere potuit, [illegible, ~3 letters]
units.tr: A parenesis (exhortation) to martyrdom, badly grounded. For what you say about the preparation for the Oath of Supremacy is all sand; it ought to be called a phrenesis rather than a parenesis. For if it is a preparation, why does it stop at that alone? It should not have done so; the King would go on, and, the preparation already made, would introduce the form concerning the Primacy, as it were. But it stops entirely at the first step, and the second is not introduced; by no one (come now, give me an example if you can). So in this matter the motion has its end, and it is neither the beginning of anything new nor a route to anything else concerning the Primacy. I therefore free you from fear of the other oath, which, as I see, torments you greatly and does not let you breathe; you are always so fearful lest it contain, cunningly or obscurely (you could have said "tortuously"), that new heresy concerning the royal Primacy. Yet if it is a heresy, it is certainly not new, since all the kings under the Old Testament held that Primacy, and all the prophets and priests then acquiesced in it. Or rather, if it is a heresy, it is new, and forged in your own workshop; for it was not old. All the prophets held it to the top; for we do not attribute to our kings any summit which they did not likewise attribute to theirs. But take care lest the matter be quite the reverse of what you say; lest the things mentioned there in the Oath, the depositions of kings, invasions, tumults, the preparation, are rather dispositions, and through them an approach is made to the Primacy of the Pontiff. Then, the last point, most foolish: that the Archpriest was detained in prison so that, overcome by weariness, he would swear to the Primacy. For the custody in which he is held is not of such a kind that it ought greatly to weary him; nor has that matter concerning the Primacy ever been brought before him in it; and whether he swears or does not swear, no one here either fears or desires it, and it is all one to them; and Matthew saw all these things in dreams, and was able rightly to conclude this whole matter, [illegible].

units.la: Voluit Apologia, quod in Breui mittendo perperam fecerat Pontifex; id meliorem in partem interpretari; credulum paulò magis, quàm par erat Pontificem, quorundam sermonibus fuisse. In eam partem peccâsse etiam Clementem 8vm. etiam Pium 5um. simili errore errässe.
units.tr: The Apology wished to interpret favourably what the Pontiff had done wrongly in sending the Brief; that he had been somewhat more credulous than was fitting, through the words of certain men. That Clement VIII also erred in that direction, and that Pius V likewise went astray by a similar error.

units.la: Nam hisce in rebus, quae facti sunt, posse interdum Pontifici errorem obrepere (dicam cum Matthaeo) inter omnes conuenit, salua tamen eius, in ijs quae Cathedrae sunt, infallibilitate. Vides Lector, quod mitissimum æquissimumque fieri potuit, id hîc factum fuisse. Quid Matthaeus? clamat nefas ingens, Pontifices simul, tres, leuitatis & temeritatis accusari; Clementem verò etiam perfidiae. Ne verò; falluntur interdum Reges prudentes & boni, falluntur & Pontifices, dum ijs adhibent fidem, in quibus fidem esse oportuit, nec fuit tamen; Et Leues tamen non sunt, nec temerarij: cadunt enim, faciles hij motus in generosam indolem. Atque ita excusare voluit factum Pontificis, & crimen in rumores transferre sæpe non veros. Non finit. Humanum est errare. Non cadit autem in Vaticanos Deos infirmitas hæc tanta. Homines non sunt. Quicquid humanum est, ab ijs alienum putat.
units.tr: For that in these matters, which are matters of fact, error can sometimes creep upon the Pontiff (I will say with Matthew) is agreed by all, the infallibility of his teaching in those matters which pertain to the Chair remaining safe. The reader sees that what could be done most gently and fairly has been done here. What does Matthew do? He cries out an enormous impiety, that three Pontiffs are accused at once of levity and rashness; and Clement even of treachery. But no: wise and good kings are sometimes deceived, and Pontiffs too are deceived, while they give credence to those things in which credence ought to have been given, and was not. And yet they are not light-minded, nor rash; for these easy impulses fall upon a noble disposition. And so the Apology wished to excuse the Pontiff's deed, and to transfer the blame onto rumours that were often not true. He does not allow it. "To err is human." But such great weakness does not befall the Vatican gods. They are not men. Whatever is human, he thinks foreign to them.

units.la: De Pio primùm.vel verum hoc, vel non veri nostrates vestri, qui sermone, hoc, nec solùm sermone, etiam scriptus affirmârunt. Surrepsisse tum ei Mortonum & Webbum, transfugas nostros, & per suggestiones mendacij plenas, decepto, Bullum surripuisse. Quod cum hic constaret Lincolniensi pridem Episcopo Watsono (qui & tum & diu pòst in vivis) mirum illi in modum displicuisse, quòd ita se Pius passus sit induci in errorem, quem præviderat Watsonus, & prædixit, nec Sedi Romanæ utilem, & Pontificijs hic omnibus fore perniciosum, cùm ex eo necessitas quasi quædam impositæ Reginæ fuerit, seculiores in eos pòst leges sanciendi. De Paulo 5o. non minùs verum: qui, hic inter Pontificios moderati magis, sic omnes afsectos, sic sensisse omnes, nempe vel fictitium fuisse Breve illud, vel certè surreptum per fraudem quorundam, vel abreptum per importunitatem, nec ab Illo sponte purâ unquam emanare potuisse. Quid si autem & Pontifex ipse tantundem fassus sit, ubi Brevis sui per quorundam Principum Legatos iniecta mentio? Penes Authores fides sit. Quid si & purgavit se de Breui sic emisso, apud Principem aliquem exterum, nempe, quòd Breve primum per obreptionem, se quidem non intento ad rem, vel tale quid cogitante, procuratum fuerit? Ad secundum verò, quòd petractus quasi invitus, dum Collegij Inquisitorum rem importunius urgeret: addito, etiam promissio, & data fide, deinceps iam cautiorem fore se, si quid tentandum in rebus Britannicis: De quo viderint [?] ipse. Interim mitior haud ulla afferri potuit excusatio, quàm quæ in Apologiâ allata est, & allegatas fecisse, quod fecit, Pontificem, non plenè informatum, nec fuisse tam illi perspecta omnia, quin, quod tum nescirat, paulò pòst exploratum magis habere potuisset [?].
units.tr: First, concerning Pius: either this is true, or your countrymen are not truthful, who have affirmed it not only by speech but also in writing: that Morton and Webb, our renegades, stole upon him, and that, deceived by suggestions full of lies, he was tricked into issuing the Bull. When this became known here to the late Bishop of Lincoln, Watson (who was alive then and long afterwards), it displeased him in a remarkable way that Pius had allowed himself to be led into an error which Watson had foreseen and foretold, which would be useful neither to the Roman See nor to all the Papists here, since from it a certain necessity was as it were imposed on the Queen of enacting laws afterwards against them, with the secular arm. Concerning Paul V, it is no less true: who, more moderate here among the Papists, has felt thus, and all the adherents have thought thus, namely that that Brief was either fictitious, or certainly obtained surreptitiously by the fraud of certain men, or wrung out by importunity, and could never have emanated from him of his own pure will. What if the Pontiff himself also confessed as much, when mention was made of his Brief by the legates of certain foreign princes? Let the authors be trusted. What if he also cleared himself concerning the Brief thus issued, before some foreign prince, namely, that the first Brief was procured by obreption, he himself not having intended the matter, or thinking anything of the kind? As to the second, that he was drawn back as if unwillingly, while the College of Inquisitors urged the business more importunately: with the addition also of a promise, and a pledge given, that henceforth he would be more cautious, if anything were to be attempted in British affairs. Let them see to that themselves. Meanwhile no milder excuse could be offered than that which was brought forward in the Apology, and that they had alleged that the Pontiff, in doing what he did, was not fully informed, nor had all things been so clearly seen by him that he could not have gained a firmer knowledge of what he did not then know, a little later.

units.la: De septicolli vero ciuitate, de Babylone suâ, ludos non patitur Tortus; serio dat; quæ in Epistolâ est B. Petri, quæq. in Apocalypsi, Apocalypsi, Babylonem, non aliam vllam vrbem esse, quàm Romam ipsam. Nos, quod dat, accipimus non illibenter. Itaque auidè auent homines, hinc Petrum Roma, alicubi in scripturis reperire, potiùs vt Babylonem velint esse Romam, vbi Petrus fuit; quàm vt Petrus Roma non fuerit. Valdè enim illorum interest ad Caput fidei, vt Petrus Roma credatur fuisse, non fide piâ quae in historijs est, sed maiore, Sacrarum nempe literarum. Etsi & illud quidem totum, praeter Leges Theologiae, quae si Mysticae est, seu Symbolicae, non est argumentativa. Etiam praeter Leges Epistolae; quae etsi tota sit mysteriorum plena, locum tamen, vnde scripta, designare non solet mysticè, ne si locus non sit certus, nec ipsius Epistolae fides sit certa. Qui verò, si locus allegoricus Babylon sit, non & allegorica persona Marcus, qui mox sequitur? vel si hic literalis, quidni & illa? Quorsum autem Petrus, Roma scribens, Romam non ausus Romam nominare; quam Paulus, cùm inde scriberet, vrbem Romam, ciues Romanos, & ausus, & nominauit? Atque adeò Diuus Iohannes, cùm librum scriberet, cuius singuli versus singula mysteria sunt; vbi tamen ad Ecclesias scribendum fuit septem vrbium, proprijs nominibus singulas quasque designauit, easque voluit esse non mysticas, in libro alioquin per totum mystico. Etsi verò sint ista, vt dixi; non piget tamen Tortum habere confitentem, quòd non in Epistolâ modò Petri, sed & in Apocalypsi, Babylon Roma sit. De eo tantùm nobis hic erit iam, quaenam illa ibi Roma Babylon; aut Roma quo tempore Babylon esse caeperit. Cui rei tot ibi circumstantias adhibet B. Iohannes, vix vt in eâ errare cuiquam contingat. Quae enim Babylon ibi: eadem meretrix magna dicitur, quae sedet super aquas multas, cum quâ fornicati sunt Reges terrae; quae Bestia ibi insidet habenti capita septem & cornua decem. Septem autem illa capita, septem sunt montes, in quibus sita Roma. ——Et quae de septem totum circumspicit orbem Montibus, Imperij Romae Deúmq. locus: Edoctum autem ibi se dicit B. Iohannes à Spiritu, de rebus quae venturae essent. Quodsi iam, Romam ibi (quo tu sensu vis) designauit, nihil venturum edocuit Spiritus; Ethnica enim tum Roma in Auge erat vel maximè. Propheticus verò is liber totus haberi solet; nimis autem illa misella tum prophetis foret, si praediceret, fore, vt persequeretur Roma Christianos. Vidit verò hoc priufpriusquam in Patmon relegatus esset; fusum Iacobi fratris sui, multorum sanguinem sub Nerone fusum: sensit ipse, & pars magna fuit illius cum persecutionis. Prophetiam ergo totam evacuat, si Ethnica ibi Roma sit. Tum Reges illi decem, (qui numerus certus pro incerto) quomodo tum inebriati de vino prostitutionis meretricis, qui tum scilicet nulli erant? Stante enim & vigente Roma Ethnica, eclipsin passi sunt, qui usquam tum Reges erant, vestigiales omnes, Reguli potius dicendi quam Reges: Reges tum demum, cum illa retro sublapsa ferretur. Neque vero periculum tum ebrietatis vllum a meretrice, vel ab illius amoribus. Oderant enim illam, perijsse expectebant, & (quod tu ante dixisti de Gregorio) vellent nollent, illi tum per vim atque ingratias seruiebant: Etiam Bestia illa altera, quae cornua duo habebat similia agni, qui poterat suppetias ferre Roma Ethnica, in qua, quamdiu quidem Ethnica nec CHRISTVM professa, nullum prorsus CHRISTI vestigium, nihil penitus, quod ulla ex parte referret agnum?
units.tr: Concerning the seven-hilled city and its Babylon, Tortus does not suffer jests; he takes it seriously; what is in the Epistle of St Peter and what is in the Apocalypse, that Babylon is no other city than Rome itself. We accept, not unwillingly, what he gives. And so men eagerly desire to find somewhere in the Scriptures "Peter at Rome," and would rather have Babylon be Rome, where Peter was, than that Peter was not at Rome. For it is very much in their interest, for the head of the faith, that Peter be believed to have been at Rome, not on the pious faith that is in histories, but on a greater one, that of the Sacred Letters, namely. Although that whole matter, apart from the rules of theology, which if it is mystical, or symbolic, is not argumentative. Also apart from the rules of the Epistle; which, although it is wholly full of mysteries, nevertheless does not usually mystically designate the place from which it was written, lest, if the place is not certain, the credibility of the Epistle itself also be uncertain. But if Babylon is an allegorical place, is not Mark, who immediately follows, an allegorical person too? Or if he is literal, why not she too? Why, moreover, when Peter wrote from Rome, did he not dare to name Rome, when Paul, writing from there, both dared and named "the city of Rome" and "Roman citizens"? And so Saint John, when writing his book, every verse of which is a separate mystery, yet where he had to write to the seven churches of cities, designated each one by its proper name, and wished them not to be mystical, in a book otherwise mystical throughout. Although these things are as I have said, nevertheless Tortus does not grudge having it confessed that not only in Peter's Epistle but also in the Apocalypse, Babylon is Rome. Here we shall be concerned only with what that Rome-Babylon there is; or when Rome began to be Babylon. To this matter Saint John adds so many circumstances there that it is hardly possible for anyone to go wrong in it. For what Babylon is there: the same is called the great harlot, who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication; the beast that sits there has seven heads and ten horns. Now those seven heads are seven mountains, on which Rome is situated. ... And it is of the seven-hilled city, which looks out over the whole world, the seat of the Empire and of the gods of Rome: Moreover, Saint John says that he was taught there by the Spirit concerning the things that were to come. If now he designated Rome there (in the sense you wish), the Spirit taught nothing to come; for Pagan Rome was then at its very height. But that book as a whole is commonly held to be prophetic; yet that poor little city would have been too wretched for prophecy, if it had predicted that Rome would persecute the Christians. But John saw this before he was banished to Patmos; the blood of James his brother shed, the blood of many shed under Nero: he himself perceived it, and he was a great part of that persecution. He therefore empties the whole prophecy, if Pagan Rome is meant there. Then those ten kings (a certain number put for an uncertain one), how were they then drunk with the wine of the harlot's fornication, when there were then, of course, no such kings? For while Pagan Rome stood and flourished, those who were anywhere then kings were all eclipsed, rather to be called petty kings than kings: they became kings only when that city was carried backwards and fell. Nor indeed was there then any danger of drunkenness from the harlot, or from her loves. For they hated her, expected her ruin, and (as you said before of Gregory) whether they would or no, they then served her by force and against their will. Even that other beast, which had two horns like a lamb, who could bring aid to Pagan Rome, in which, as long as it was pagan and had not professed Christ, there was absolutely no trace of Christ, nothing at all that in any way resembled a lamb?

units.la: Luculentae quidem satis haec circumstantiae; mitto illas tamen: verbis ipsis stringo, quae satis diserta sunt, ad tempus, quo implenda fuit haec prophetia, perspicue designandum. Versu 8o dicitur dilucide: Bestia quam vidisti, fuit, & non est, & ascensura est de Abysso, & ibit in interitum. Fuit (inquit B. Iohannes) & non est. Erat autem tum Roma Ethnica erat, & erat tum florentissima, cum haec agerentur. Falso ergo tum diceretur, non est, sed ascensura est, si de Roma quae tum erat diceretur. Paulo autem infra vers 12o. Decem cornua, quae decem ibi Reges, regnum (inquit) nondum acceperunt, sed potestatem tanquam Reges una hora accipient cum Bestia. Negare vero non potes, scribente haec B. Iohanne, Babylonem, Romam esse tum quidem non potuisse. Reges enim tum nondum potestatem acceperant, ac neque diu post acceperunt, donec Roma iam Christiana. Nec ergo Romam Ethnicam, Babylonem fuisse. Quin etiam interitus ipse, quem interminatur ibi Babyloni, liquidiorem adhuc multo rem facit. Nec enim verbum ibi vllum de conflagratione eius, quae Roma olim Ethnicae contigit a Gothis ac Vandalis incensae: quin de interitu potius alius & generis & modi repentini (scilicet, & tanto impetu, quasi vi magna molaris lapis mitteretur in mare. Haud enim (inquit) pòst, unquam inuenietur. Non autem (quantacunque ei potentia est) mersum in mare molarem natare denuò, facturus est Pontifex.
units.tr: These circumstances are quite clear enough; I pass them over, however. I touch only on the words themselves, which are plain enough, to show clearly the time at which this prophecy was to be fulfilled. At verse 8 it is said plainly: "The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to ascend out of the Abyss, and will go to destruction." "It was," says St. John, "and is not." But Ethnic Rome was then in existence, and was then at the height of her power, while these things were being done. It would therefore have been false then to say "is not, but is about to ascend," if what was meant were the Rome that then existed. A little further on, at verse 12, the "ten horns," which are ten kings, "have not yet received a kingdom," says he, "but will receive authority as kings for one hour with the beast." Nor can you deny that, when St. John was writing these things, Babylon, that is Rome, could not then have been the one meant. For the kings had not yet received authority, nor did they receive it for a long time afterwards, by which time Rome was already Christian. So Babylon was not Ethnic Rome. Moreover, the destruction itself which is there threatened for Babylon makes the matter far clearer still. For there is no word there about the burning of that Rome which was once Ethnic and was set on fire by the Goths and Vandals; rather, the ruin described is of another kind and manner, sudden (namely, with such violence, as if a great millstone were cast into the sea): "It shall never be found again," he says. Nor will the Pontiff, however great his power, make a millstone sunk in the sea float again.

units.la: Porrò verò, ibi dicitur, quòd postea, vox in eâ Musicorum, vel Artificum non audietur, quod Artifex non inuenietur in eâ amplius, vox molae amplius non audietur, lux lucernae amplius non lucebit, vox sponsi & sponsae in posterum conticescet. Ibi accumulat denique quicquid usquam est artis vel verborum, quae id ponant ante oculos, deploratam & desolatam iri Babylonem sine entitatis spe omni, quasi non Ens in aeternum. Quódsi, praeterea nihil foret, satis esset tamen, ad institutum praesens, in ipsa descriptione illorum qui cum illa mercaturam facient. Mercatores eius (inquit) Principes terrae. Omnes Gentes erraverunt in Veneficijs eius. Nam neque haec Roma Ethnica quadrare possunt, quae vi solâ atque armis gentes sibi subegit, nec eas unquam ita Veneficijs incantauit, ut non primâ quâque vel leuissimâ occasione datâ (vires modo essent) vindicarent se in libertatem, & ad arma conclamarent; Verùm enim, quae illa tandem Roma sit (non enim certè Ethnica) quae merces instituit de animabus hominum, optime omnium nobis dixerit Cardinalis ipse. Et ipse quidem (quod in Apologiâ notatum est) fatetur rem totam: Decem enim Reges meretricem contremabunt, quod de Româ quae Ethnica fuit intelligi non posse, puto abundè iam mihi demonstratum est.
units.tr: Furthermore, there it is said that "afterwards the voice of musicians and artists shall not be heard in her, no artisan shall be found in her any more, the sound of the millstone shall be heard no more, the light of the lamp shall shine no more, the voice of bridegroom and bride shall be silent for ever." There he piles up, finally, everything of art or words anywhere that might set before the eyes that Babylon will be ruined and laid waste, with no hope of any existence left, as if she were "not being" for ever. And if there were nothing else, it would still be enough for the present purpose in the very description of those who trade with her: "Her merchants," he says, "are the princes of the earth. All nations have gone astray through her sorceries." For neither can this Ethnic Rome fit these words, which subdued nations to herself by force and arms alone, nor did she ever so enchant them with sorceries that they did not, on the first or slightest opportunity given (if only they had the strength), claim their liberty for themselves and cry out to arms. But what that Rome is (certainly not Ethnic), which has set up a traffic in the souls of men, the Cardinal himself could best tell us all. And he himself indeed (as was noted in the Apology) admits the whole matter: "For the ten kings will make the harlot desolate," which I think I have now sufficiently shown cannot be understood of the Rome that was Ethnic.

units.la: Ut verbo igitur expediam. Quae sunt apud B. Iohannem de ruinâ Romae praedictiones, de quâ Româ sunt? De eâ, cui opem feret Bestia; cui cornua agnino similia: quae in templo Dei sedet: Cui cum Regibus terrae foederata pactio: Quae vino prostitutionis suae inebriat eos: Quae veneficijs seduxit. De eâ (inquam) Româ, quae extollit se super omne quod dicitur Deus, non, quae ipsa, nescio quot minutulos & patellares Deos venereatur, quod illa fecit Ethnica: De eâ Româ quae agnum specie refert, scriptam tamen habet in fronte blasphemiam: De eâ Româ, cuius merces, hominum animae, dum licitari facit homines nummo salutem suam: De eâ, quae fuit olim sub Regibus septem, sed B. Iohannis aetate non fuit (etsi etiam tum mysterium illud occœpit operari) non fuit (inquam) sed ascensura fuit tum demum ad fastigium suum, cùm decem ibi Reges potestatem suam accepturi essent, postquam scilicet Romae Ethnicae iugum excussissent. De eâ Româ, quam decem Reges (non eluuies illa barbara Vandalorum vel Gothorum) postquam diu seducti essent ipsius veneficiis, tandem igne consumaturi sunt; non ad cladem aliquam, unde postconualesceat, sed ad perniciem eius sempiternam, vt reges sit[?], non minùs vbi Roma, quàm vbi Troia fuit. Dabit enim Deus in corda Regum, vt Romam hanc excindant penitus, sicut dedit Satanas olim in corda Barbarorum, vt illam succenderent. De eâ denique Româ, quæ per Pseudoprophetam suum, vim habet signa faciendi, quæ cum Pseudoprophetâ suo, atque ille cum eâ, vtrumque mittentur in stagnum ignis, ac sulphuris, in æternum. Verè autem à Torto[?] dicitur, Romam Christianam perditam non iri. Non certè, sed illam quæ inebriata est Sanctorum sanguine, & Martyrum Iesu Christi, Antichristianam scilicet. Ea enim perdenda est, cuius in fronte scriptum nomen blasphemiæ.
units.tr: To sum up in a word, then. What are the predictions in St. John concerning the ruin of Rome, and of what Rome are they? Of that Rome which the beast will aid; whose horns are like those of the lamb; which sits in the temple of God; with which the kings of the earth have made a covenant; which makes them drunk with the wine of her fornication; which has seduced by sorceries. Of that Rome (I say), which exalts itself above everything that is called God, not the Rome which itself worships I know not how many little gods and household gods, as Ethnic Rome did. Of that Rome which resembles the lamb in appearance, yet has blasphemy written on its forehead. Of that Rome, whose merchandise is the souls of men, while it makes men bid for their salvation with money. Of that Rome which was once under seven kings, but in the time of St. John was not (though even then that mystery had begun to work), was not (I say), but was about to ascend to its height when the ten kings were to receive their power there, namely after they had shaken off the yoke of Ethnic Rome. Of that Rome, which the ten kings (not that barbarian flood of Vandals or Goths) will at last burn with fire, after they have been long led astray by her sorceries; not to some disaster from which she might recover, but to her everlasting destruction, so that she shall be no less where Rome was than where Troy was. "For God will put it into the hearts of the kings to tear this Rome up utterly, just as Satan once put it into the hearts of the barbarians to set her on fire." Lastly, of that Rome which, through its false prophet, has the power of working signs, which with its false prophet, and he with her, "shall both be cast into the lake of fire and brimstone for ever." Indeed, it is rightly said by Torto that "Christian Rome shall not be destroyed." Certainly not; but that Rome which is "drunk with the blood of the saints and of the martyrs of Jesus Christ," that is to say, the Antichristian one. For it is that Rome, on whose forehead is written "the name of blasphemy," which is to be destroyed.

units.la: Minimè verò mirum, si ista quæ dixi, tam vel claram, vel certam in scriptis Patrum interpretationem non habeant. Operabatur enim modò mysterium tum iniquitatis. Signatus adhuc liber erat huius Prophetiæ. Verissimum autem verbum est; ænigma esse Prophetiam omnem, cum nondum completa est; vt, quamus Prisci illi omni genere charismatum, vitæ verò sanctimoniâ, longo nos interuallo superârint: mirari tamen non debeat quis, si non illis tum, adeo explicita omnia fuerint, quàm nobis, per Dei gratiam, iam sunt, qui consummatam iam Prophetiam illam quotidie oculis vsurpamus. Et tamen id quoque miretur quispiam, quòd & Illi etiam horum multa, quasi per transennam viderint, quòd nimirum ita a Tertullianus: Sic & Babylon apud Iohannem nostrum, Romanæ urbis figuram portat, proinde & magna, & regno superba, & Sanctorum debellatricis. {b} Hieronymus autem. Cum in Babylone versarer, & purpurata meretricis esset colonus, & iure Quiritum viuerem. Idem; cum Marcellam Româ Bethleem commigrare vellet, Hic, puto, locus sanctior est Tarpeia rupe, quæ de cælo saepius fulminata, ostendit quid Domino displiceret. Lege Apocalypsin Iohannis, & quid de muliere purpurata, & scripta in fronte blasphemiâ, septem montibus, aquis multis, & Babylonis tantetur[?] exitu, concutere. Exite (inquit Dominus) de illâ. At verò Augustinus, Condita est Roma velut altera in occidente Babylon, & velut prioris filia Babylonis. {e} Victorinus quoque: Scripta ibi in tubus, ruina magna Babylonis ciuitatis, id est, Roma. Etiam {f}O-rosius: Ecce similis Babylonia ortus & Roma, similis potentia, similis magnitudo, similia tempora.
units.tr: It is not at all surprising if the things I have said do not have a clear or certain interpretation in the writings of the Fathers. "For the mystery of iniquity was already at work. The book of this prophecy was still sealed." And the saying is most true: "every prophecy is an enigma until it is fulfilled." So, although those ancients surpassed us by a long interval in every kind of spiritual gift, and in holiness of life, yet no one ought to wonder that not everything was then as explicit to them as it is now to us, by the grace of God, who daily have before our eyes that prophecy already fulfilled. And yet someone may also wonder that they too saw many of these things, as it were through a crack; for Tertullian says: "So also Babylon in our John bears the figure of the city of Rome, and therefore both great and proud of her kingdom, and a destroyer of the saints." {b} Jerome also: "When I was living in Babylon, and was the tenant of the purple harlot, and lived by the right of the Quirites." The same: "When Marcella wished to migrate from Rome to Bethlehem: This place, I think, is holier than the Tarpeian rock, which is often struck by lightning from heaven, and shows what displeases the Lord. Read the Apocalypse of John, and what it says of the woman clothed in purple, with blasphemy written on her forehead, with seven hills and many waters, and of the destruction of Babylon. Come out of her" (says the Lord). But Augustine says: "Rome has been founded like a second Babylon in the West, and like the daughter of the former Babylon." {e} Victorinus too: "There, written in the tubes, the great ruin of the city of Babylon, that is, Rome." Also {f} Orosius: "Behold, Rome has risen like Babylon, with like power, like greatness, like times."

units.la: Sed quid ego haec, cùm vnanimis sit ista Patrum pene omnium sententia? Nam de Roma fronte Christi nomine signata, quod affers[?]; nulla est in Apocalypsi Babylon, cuius signata frons Christi nomine: Christi nomen deleri oportuit prius, & deletum est, quàm blasphemia ibi scriberetur. Postquam autem ibi scripta blasphemia, tum demum verè Babylon fuit, verè est. Sed necdùm Apocalypsis completa vo-bis[?], necdum cecidit Babylon illa vestra, quae si, ut dicis, scriptam iam habet in fronte Christi confessionem, cadere non poterit: atque ita non verus vates Iohannes. Ille verò & vates verus, & casura est Babylon illa vestra; ideo autem casura, quia Christi confessionem illam expunxit, & loco eius, blasphemiae multiplicis nomen ibi iam inusit, & quidem maiusculis literis, ut quivis vel qui transcurrit, legere possit sic inustam.
units.tr: But why do I say these things, when this opinion is held almost unanimously by the Fathers? For as to Rome having Christ's name signed on her forehead, which you bring forward: there is no Babylon in the Apocalypse whose forehead is signed with Christ's name. The name of Christ had to be erased first, and it was erased before blasphemy was written there. But after blasphemy was written there, then at last Babylon truly was, and truly is. But the Apocalypse is not yet fulfilled for you, and that Babylon of yours has not yet fallen; if, as you say, it already has the confession of Christ written on its forehead, it cannot fall, and so John would not be a true prophet. But John is a true prophet, and that Babylon of yours is going to fall; and it is going to fall because it has blotted out that confession of Christ, and in its place has already stamped there the name of manifold blasphemy, and indeed in capital letters, so that anyone who even passes by can read it stamped there.

units.la: Qua in re, ea veritatis vis est, ut etiam Iesuitas vestros adigat, qui in eum librum non ita pridem commentarios scripserunt, non solùm de Romà Ethnicà, verùm & de Christianà, Babylonis ibi nomen interpretari, ac delendam denùo confessionem Christi de fronte eius, post deletam autem, blasphemiae nomen ibi inscribendum. Sic Ribera{g} De Romà intelligendum, non solùm quales sub Ethnicis Imperatoribus olim fuit, sed etiam quales in fine saeculi futura est. Et post, {h}Babylonem dictam esse, non solùm quòd hoc illi nomen, tempore, quo Iohannes haec scribebat, maximè conveniret; sed etiam quòd tempore, quo haec explebuntur, (necdum enim expleta esse) non minùs quàm ante; conveniet. Sic Iesuita alter Viegas: {i}Omnia quae in hijs capitibus commemorantur, in Romanam urbem apertissimè quadrant. Caeterùm nomen Babylonis ad eam Romam transferendum, quae antequam reciperet fidem Christi, Idolis seruiebat: & ad eam etiam, quae erit tempore Antichristi. Erit ergo tempore Antichristi Roma Babylon, non solùm Ethnica, eáque tum in desertum & solitudinem cadet, vt ait Ribera vester. Sed haec omnia, vix quicquam ad institutum sermonem de rumoribus, qui vos Romae circumuolant; nisi quia tibi hic digredi libuit, vt Babylonem salutares. Nam cuam[?] Hieronymi aetate, cùm Christi nomen in fronte gereret Roma, etiam tum hoc morbo laborabat, vt, eò confluerent toto ex orbe rumores undique, quorum si nullis Roma tum credidit; quid, eo loco, opus Hieronymo ita rem referre? Profectò nec pauciores Roma iam famigerull[?], nec minus est aurium ad nouitates prurientium, quàm cùm Hieronymus ibi purpurata meretrici[?] colonus esset.
units.tr: In this matter the force of the truth is such that it compels even your Jesuits, who not long ago wrote commentaries on that book, to interpret the name of Babylon there not only of Rome Pagan but also of Rome Christian: that the confession of Christ must be erased again from her forehead, and that after it has been erased, the name of blasphemy must be written there in its place. Thus Ribera understands Rome to be meant not only as she once was under the pagan emperors but also as she will be at the end of the age. And afterwards he says that Babylon is so called not only because that name best suited her at the time when John was writing these things, but also because at the time when these things are fulfilled (for they have not yet been fulfilled) it will suit her no less than before. So another Jesuit, Viegas: "Everything that is recorded in these chapters fits the city of Rome most exactly. Moreover, the name of Babylon is to be transferred to that Rome which, before it received the faith of Christ, served idols, and also to that which will exist at the time of Antichrist. Therefore at the time of Antichrist Rome will be Babylon, not only pagan, and she will then fall into desolation and solitude, as your Ribera says." But all these things hardly bear on the subject of my discourse, namely the rumours which fly about you at Rome; unless you chose to digress here so that you might greet Babylon. For in the time of Jerome, when Rome bore the name of Christ on her forehead, she was still suffering from this disease, that rumours from every quarter flocked together there from the whole world; and if Rome then believed none of them, why, in that place, was there any need for Jerome to report the matter in such a way? Surely Rome now is no less full of gossipmongers, nor is there less itching of ears for novelties, than when Jerome was there, a colonist of a purple-clad harlot.

units.la: Dum verò in eo totus est, vt Pontifices suos Pium & Paulum tam anxiè excuset ab omni erroris labe, siue ex aliorum malâ fide, siue ex suâ; interserit nescio quomodo & Clementis 8[?]. defensionem, de Breuibus huc ab eo transmissis, vergente ad occasum tum Regno R. Elizabethae. Ex dialecto autem Papiensi, more suo aspergit primùm mendaciis Authorem Apologiae, quorum illi copiosa domi messis est. Breuibus enim illis, ait, non vt iste mentitur, IACOBUM, tum Scotiae Regem, à folio exclusit, sed consilium dedit, quale dare decebat Summum Pontificem. Post verò paulò, oblitus personae suae, non quasi Capellanus de Sacello, sed quasi Cardinalis ipse iam de Consistorio egressus. Habemus (inquit) exemplaria Breuium illorum in manibus, & ijs diligenter inspectis, nusquam inuenimus nomen IACOBI Regis, aut alterius particularis personae. Hic fere iam illi larua de vultu delapsa est; non hæ Capellanum ampullæ decent, Habemus in manibus, & nusquam inuenimus. Interest multùm, Dauusne loquatur, an Heros; sed recolligat se, larvam reponat, cautius rem gerat in posterum. Mentiri autem suum nusquam magis obtrudit, quàm vbi ipse est mendacissimus. Cur enim mentitur ipse de nominatim ibi exclusò in Breui Rege, quod nusquam in Apologia dictum est? Id modò dictum: exclusum ibi, ne à Pontificijs reciperetur in regem, qui vel nostræ religionis cultor esset ipse, vel cultores toleraret; ac per hoc, non minùs Regi obnunciatum esse, quàm alij cuicunque, qui alterius, quàm vos in fide, professionis esset. Verè ergo ibi dictum, nec vetius quid dici potuit; quantum in se erat, Clementem tum Breuibus illis egisse, vt Rex iam noster, vt quiuis alius, quocunque demum iure niteretur, si sic, vt Papa in religione non sentiret, à capessendis Regni huius gubernaculis esset exclusissimus. Ego verò id fidenter dixerim, perinde Breuibus illis exclusum folio hoc suo, ac si nomine ibi proprio & natiuo, IACOBI Regi, designatus esset. Quid enim interest, nominetur quis, an ita ad vivum describatur, ut cuivis in promptu sit, quem ibi velit Pontifex? Ius Regū hæreditarium, quis tum nesciebat? quis vero religionem ignorabat, quam ille, ex quo voces primo, & literas formare potuit, voce, scripto, praesentia sua semper professus est? Annon ille exclusus? Quid illa ergo sibi volunt verba, Quantumcunq; propinquitate sanguinis niteretur? Quis ille vero, qui nixus propinquitate sanguinis? Quis fuit? quis esse potuit? An est quisquam tam obtuso pectore, ut quo illa tendant, quem petant, non intelligat, nisi nomen nominetur?
units.tr: While he is wholly intent on excusing so anxiously his Pontiffs Pius and Paul from every stain of error, whether arising from the bad faith of others or from their own, he somehow also inserts a defence of Clement VIII concerning the Briefs sent from there by him, at a time when the reign of Queen Elizabeth was drawing toward its close. Then, in his Papist dialect, after his manner, he first sprinkles the author of the Apology with lies, of which he has an abundant harvest at home. For, he says, by those Briefs, not as this fellow falsely claims, did he exclude James, then King of Scotland, from the throne, but he gave counsel of the kind that became the Supreme Pontiff to give. Afterwards, a little later, forgetting his own character, speaking not as a chaplain of the chapel but as a cardinal who has himself just come out of the consistory, he says: "We have copies of those Briefs in our hands, and having examined them carefully, we have nowhere found the name of King James, or of any other particular person." Here the mask has almost slipped from his face; such bombast does not become a chaplain: "We have in our hands, and nowhere have we found." It makes a great difference whether Davus speaks or a hero; but he collects himself, replaces the mask, and will manage the matter more cautiously in future. Yet he never insists more on his lying than where he is himself most lying. For why does he lie himself about the King being expressly excluded in the Brief, which is nowhere said in the Apology? The point made was only this: he was excluded there so that he should not be received by the Papists as king, he who was either himself a worshipper of our religion or would tolerate its worshippers; and therefore he was declared to be no less barred from the Crown than any other person of a different profession of faith from yours. What was said there was therefore true, and nothing truer could have been said; in so far as it lay in him, Clement at that time had by those Briefs aimed at ensuring that our King, as any other, whatever right he might rest upon, if he did not think in religion as the Pope did, should be most thoroughly shut out from taking up the government of this realm. For my part I would confidently say that he was excluded by those Briefs in this his own folio just as if he had been designated by his own proper and native name, the King James. For what difference does it make whether a man is named, or is so drawn to the life that anyone may readily know whom the Pontiff means there? Who then did not know the hereditary right of kings at that time? Who indeed was ignorant of the religion which he, from the time he could first form words and letters, always professed by voice, by writing, by his presence? Was he not excluded? What, then, do those words mean, "However much he might rest upon nearness of blood"? Who was that man who rested upon nearness of blood? Who was he? Who could he be? Is there anyone with a heart so dull that he does not understand, unless the name is named, at what those words aim and whom they seek?

units.la: Quale autem consilium illud, quod dare decebat Pontificem? Nempe operam darent, ut eligeretur Rex. Eligeretur autem? Ain' vero, ut eligeretur? Quid opus hoc? Erat, qui Antiquo stemmate, Regio sanguine, Hæreditario iure, Stirpis proximitate, Optimo titulo, vendicare poterat. Quorsum hîc, eligeretur? Itáne, in Regnis, ubi successionis iure Reges nascuntur, conclamat Pontifex ad electionem, ad vota, ad suffragia? Quorum verborum, quæ mens, qui sensus sit, credo iam Reges omnes per Europam, qui hoc iure regnant, satis aduertisse. Idem ante tentárat Lutetia in Regno Gallicano. Idem hîc iam tentat in Nostro. En quale consilium dare deceat, dare soleat, quale etiam in Regum aliorum successione quâcunque, (cûm se derit occasio) dare paratum sit; Conclaue credo in regna omnia inducturus, si daretur. Verum dic porrò, quis tandem eligeretur? Qui ad religionem Catholicam bene affectus. Menaaciter [?] & hoc; utcunque enim affectus bene, nisi ciusmodi esset, qui religionem Catholicam non modò toleraret, sed omni ope & studio promoueret; exclusus tamen adhuc, quisquis fuit ille Regum, nisi & iureiurando se id praestiturum suscipieret. Quare, in tota hac narratione nihil sani; vanitate, falsitate referta omnia. Post vero etiam, illud suadere vult homo lepidus, Abfuisse tantum ut excluderetur IACOBUS Rex, ut includeretur vel maximè scilicet. Spes enim maxima, illum à Romanâ fide suscipiendâ non abhorrere. Verum ut res ibi, ita & spes, falsa utráq;: At ministri eius spem dederunt: sed fallaces; quibus tamen, cùm in rem suam est, cùm libet; credulus satis Clemens, Pius, Paulus, quis non?
units.tr: But what was that counsel which it became the Pontiff to give? Namely, that they should take pains that a King be elected. Elected, though? Do you really say, that he be elected? What need is there of this? There was one who could claim by ancient lineage, by royal blood, by hereditary right, by proximity of stock, by the best title. Why here "be elected"? Is it so that, in kingdoms where kings are born by right of succession, the Pontiff calls for "election, votes, suffrages"? I believe all the kings of Europe who reign by this right have sufficiently noticed the mind and meaning of these words. The same thing was attempted before at Paris in the Gallican kingdom. The same thing is now attempted here in ours. Behold what counsel it befits to give, what it is customary to give, what kind of counsel is ready to be given even in the succession of any other kings whatever (whenever the occasion arises); I believe he would bring in a conclave into all kingdoms, if it were allowed. But tell me further, who then would be elected? "One well disposed toward the Catholic religion." That is a deceitful phrase too; for however well disposed, unless he were such a one as would not merely tolerate the Catholic religion but promote it with all his power and zeal, still whoever of the kings he might be would be excluded, unless he undertook by oath to perform this. Therefore in this whole account there is nothing sound; all is full of vanity and falsehood. Afterwards, moreover, the witty man wishes to persuade us of this: "So far was King James from being excluded, that he was rather included, most certainly. For the greatest hope was that he would not shrink from receiving the Roman faith." But as the matter there is false, so the hope is false too on both counts: indeed his ministers gave hopes, but deceitful ones; and upon these, when it suits their purpose and whenever it pleases them, Clement, Pius, Paul, and who not, are credulous enough.

units.la: Quia Rex ipse ad Pontificem scripsit, etiam ad Cardinales Aldobrandinum & Bellarminum, literas plenas humanitatis, quibus, praeter caetera, petebat, ut aliquis è Gente Scotorum Cardinalis crearetur, ut haberet Romae, per quem facilius & tutius cum Pontifice negotia sua tractaret. Enimuero de hoc quod iam retulit Matthaeus, in negotio hoc Literarum, si quàm bono id eventu, tam etiam bono in Regem animo retulisset, merito illi à nobis gratia habenda esset, quasi de officio sanè perhumano. Certè enim successu non caruit, quò suus inde Regi honor iam saluus sit. Ex eo enim occasio illi data, atque ansa occulti cuiusdam maleficij eruendi, quo sic eruto, integritatem fidei atque honoris sui, sartam tectam habebit. Tecto autem sic atque latente, ut diu iam latuit, atque tectum fuit, alio post alio tempore recruduisset forte, cùm elapsa iam esset occasio omnis, eius eruedi. Simul, ut de eo ipso, certior redderetur, qui in eo Regis fidem de se efellit, suam in Rege fidem violavit. Nec enim potest Regi accidere quicquam optatius, quàm, unde ei detur in sensus eorum intimos (qui ei intimi sunt) penitiùs introspicere, & quorum ab eo fides multa committenda sunt, eorum certa sit an sublesta fides, explorare. Cùm enim obiecisset Matthaeus scriptas ad Pontificem à Rege literas, (rem ita crassam ut manu teneri posset) facere non potuit, quin acriùs in eam rem inquireret. Repetit autem, fouisse se in sinu serpentem, & verè tandem deprehendit, fraudem sibi ab eo factam, qui Maiestati suae à Secretis literarum. De quo, etsi incertos priùs aliquos rumusculos inaudisset, cùm paulò pòst, quàm Româ perlatæ essent, nonnulli, nescio quid ibi tale auditum sibi mutirent: at, ex eo iam tempore, nunquam certi quid, eâ de re, datum est cognoscere; ita, qui facti author fuerat, dum sibi malè metueret, texerat rem probè, & quasi tenebris obuelàrat. Sic ergo habet. Surrepsit Regi furtim, atque ad literas, quas narras, malis artibus elicuit manus Regiæ subscriptionem Secretarius tum Regius. Quo autem consilio hoc; siue quòd propenderet animo ad religionem Pontificiam; siue quòd, lucro illi atque commodo fortè ea res futura fuit; siue quòd, impensè faueret propinquo suo Episcopo Vasionensi Cardinalatum ambienti; (cuius in gratiam erant literæ illæ adornatæ) siue etiam quòd Edwardo Dromonio Equiti gratificari vellet, qui rem totam procurabat atque vrgebat; quo (inquam) consilio, aut, horum quid fuerit, illi ipsi notum; præterquam, illi ipsi, notum credo nemini. Rei autem totius modum, & cum substantiâ ipsâ circumstantiis omnes, quibus Regi imposuit, dum surriperet ei literas, nemo melius magisque ad vivum referat, quàm Author ipse criminis: Cuius est, quam subjicio hîc, non expressa per vim, vel per fraudem illecta, sed libera sanè confessio, atque omni modo spontanea, ad mentem ipsius, ipsiusque manu, signata.
units.tr: "Because the King himself wrote to the Pontiff, and also to the Cardinals Aldobrandini and Bellarmine, letters full of courtesy, in which, among other things, he asked that some Cardinal of the Scottish nation be created, so that he might have at Rome someone through whom he could more easily and safely transact his business with the Pontiff." Indeed, as to what Matthew has now reported in this business of the Letters, if he had reported it with as good a spirit toward the King as with a good outcome, he would rightly deserve thanks from us, as for a service most courteous indeed. For it certainly did not lack success, by which his own honour with the King is now secure. For from it an occasion was given him, and an opportunity of ferreting out a certain hidden wrong-doing, by which, once that was brought to light, he would keep the integrity of his faith and honour intact. But the wrong-doing, hidden and concealed as it had long been lying hid and covered, might perhaps have broken out again at some other time, when every opportunity of ferreting it out had passed. At the same time, so that he might be more certainly informed about that very man who, in this matter, deceived the King's trust regarding himself, and violated his own trust in the King. For nothing more welcome can befall a King than to be given a means of looking more deeply into the innermost feelings of those who are closest to him, and to ascertain whether the trust placed in them, in which many matters must be committed, is sure or unsound. For when Matthew had charged that letters had been written by the King to the Pontiff (a thing so gross that it could be held in the hand), he could not help inquiring more keenly into the matter. He, however, repeats that he had nursed a serpent in his bosom, and at last truly discovered the fraud that had been practised upon him by the one who, as Secretary of the King's Letters, was entrusted to his Majesty. Concerning him, although they had earlier heard some uncertain rumours, when a little after the letters had been carried from Rome, some men murmured that they had heard I know not what such thing there; but from that time onward it was never granted to know anything certain about the matter; so he who had been the author of the deed, while he feared badly for himself, had covered the thing well and veiled it as in darkness. So it stands. The then royal Secretary stealthily stole upon the King, and by wicked arts drew from his hand the signature to the letters you speak of. But with what purpose this was done; whether because he leaned in mind toward the Papist religion, or because perhaps that business would turn out to his gain and advantage, or because he earnestly favoured his kinsman, the Bishop of Vaison, who was seeking a Cardinal's hat (and for whose sake those letters had been drawn up), or even because he wished to oblige Sir Edward Drummond, who was managing and pressing the whole affair; by which purpose (I say), or which of these it was, is known to himself; beyond that, I believe, it is known to no one. But the whole manner of the affair, and every circumstance of the substance itself, by which he imposed upon the King while he was stealing the letters from him, no one can recount better or more to the life than the author of the crime himself. His is the confession which I append here, not extracted by force, nor enticed by fraud, but a free and altogether voluntary confession, signed with his own mind and hand.

units.la: DECLARATIO, atque Confessio D. de Balmerinoch, REGIÆ Maᵗⁱ facta, ac DOMINIS qui ei à Sanctiore CONSILIO sunt, de literis quibusdam, quas ille, per fraudem surrep- titiè scribendas REGIO nomine, atque ROMAM, ad Papam CLEMENTEM 8um. quasi suâ Maiestate essent, mittendas curavit. Anno 1598.
units.tr: Declaration and Confession of Lord Balmerinoch, made before the King's Majesty and before the Lords of the Privy Council, concerning certain letters which he took care to have written, by fraud and surreptitiously, in the King's name, and sent to Rome, to Pope Clement VIII, as if they were from His Majesty. Year 1598.

units.la: DOMINVS de Balmerinoch, habitâ de eo quæstione, cùm crimen hoc illi obiectum esset, quòd per malas artes, perque surreptionem literas illas procurâsset, (quibus è literis imputatio, maximè, ut falsa, ita scandalosa in Regem, quâ ad Regis nominis honorem, quâ ad Religionis catholicam professionem redundâssent) postquam variis modis, offensam negando, subticendo, transferendo, extenuando nihil profecisset, ingenuè tandem agnovit atque confessus est. Quòd scilicet Ann. 1598. adductus ad id precibus * Archiepiscopi Glascuensis, qui tum legatum agebat Respōnsalem Maiestatis suæ in Galliâ, præsertim verò Episcopi Vasionensis ac aliorum quorundam, procurante negotium hoc Edwardo Dromonio Equite, quem illi tum huc legârant eo nomine, ut interuentu suo, mutuæ quædam inchoari possent atque reciproca vices inter Regem Maiestatem & Pontificem.
units.tr: Lord Balmerinoch, when the question was put to him, since the charge was brought against him that by wicked arts and by surreption he had procured those letters (by which letters an imputation, most of all false and scandalous against the King, redounded both to the honour of the King's name and to the profession of the Catholic religion), after he had accomplished nothing by various means, denying the offence, keeping silent, shifting the blame and minimising it, at last frankly acknowledged and confessed. Namely that in the year 1598, persuaded by the entreaties of the Archbishop of Glasgow, who was then acting as the King's Majesty's envoy in France, and especially of the Bishop of Vaison and certain others, the business being managed by Sir Edward Dromonius, whom they had then sent here for that purpose, so that through his intervention some mutual dealings might be begun, and reciprocal exchanges between the King's Majesty and the Pontiff.

units.la: Idem Dominus de Balmerinoch, postquam ei rei assensum suum praebuisset, Regem ad id saepenumero incitare conatus est, eique, illiusmodi delineatas à se literas obtulit, quas manu Regia signatas vellet ad Papam. Ubi autem, Regis animum, à quacunque scriptione eius generis alienum reperisset; nec id modò, sed incœptum illud damnare penitus, de commercio ullo habendo cum Pontifice; qui titulis scilicet illis atque attributis à Rege compellari expectaret, quibus Maiestas eius, conscientiâ suâ teneretur, ne apud eum ratione ullâ uti posset, quâcunque de causâ.
units.tr: The same Lord Balmerinoch, after he had given his assent to this matter, often tried to urge the King to it, and offered him letters of this kind which he had drawn up himself, which he wished to be signed by the royal hand and sent to the Pope. But when he found the King's mind averse to any writing of that kind, and not only that, but utterly condemning the undertaking to have any dealings with the Pontiff, who (so he expected) would address him with those titles and attributes which His Majesty, in conscience, was bound not to use towards him for any reason whatever.

units.la: Idem Dominus de Balmerinoch, & Edwardus Dromonius, cùm in manum convenissent tamen, de incœpto suo ad exitum perducendo; egerunt de modo, quo imponere possent Regiæ Maiestati, & quales cupiebant literas, abeo elicere. Itaque se, Dromonij manu descriptas, adornâsse post literas, quasi à Rege nimirum, ad Pontificem: Quarum hic ferè tenor: nempe ut Pontifici gratias ageret de humanitate, atque gratiâ pristinâ: ut Episcopum ei Vasionensem commendaret, quem in Cardinalium Collegium cooptari cuperet, quòfic, negotia sua (cùm ita opus) melius ibi Romæ expedire posset.
units.tr: The same Lord Balmerinoch and Edward Dromonius, when they had nevertheless met together to bring their undertaking to an end, discussed the manner in which they could impose upon the King's Majesty, and what kind of letters they wished to draw from him. Accordingly he confesses that he, with Dromonius's hand copying them, had composed letters after the fashion of letters from the King, of course, to the Pontiff. Their substance was roughly this: namely, that he should thank the Pope for his kindness and former favour; that he should recommend to him the Bishop of Vaison, whom he wished to be co-opted into the College of Cardinals, so that he might be able to manage his affairs there at Rome the better, if the need arose.
