units.la: Quò verò, astu rem gerere, & Regiam ad eas literas subscriptionem lucrifacere possent, hanc inter se rationem initam, dictus Dominus de Balmerinoch confitetur: primùm, ut interserentur in medio multarum, cùm essent aliquando literæ multæ subscriptione Regiâ signandæ: tum, ut ne offerrentur ita signandæ, nisi eo demùm tempore quo Rex venatum ire properaret, quò, ita repentè tùm oblatas non vacaret excutere, aut quæ essent, aut ad quos, curiosiùs observare: tertiò, ut stilus, atque tituli, quibus de more compellari solet Pontifex, omitterentur prorsus, necubi comparerent in literis; ne, si dum inter scribendum esset, traiectu forte oculi in aliquem de titulis illis inciderent, fraus tota deprehendi posset, sed relicto ibi ad titulos quod satis esset, interuallo, y[?] post, commodè per otium addi possent atque inseri. Atque ex hoc eorum instituto fatetur idem dictus Dominus de Balmerinoch (fide quam ei Rex habuit, perfidè & se violatâ) aliquo post die, mane primo, venatum exeunte Rege, atque iter quantum potuit maturante, inter literas tum alias ad Duces Florentiæ atque Sabaudiæ, atque alias ad Cardinales {a}quosdam pro Episcopo Vasiorensi latinè scriptas, cùm ad Pontificem antè i.m[?] Rex abnegâsset, se ullo modo adduci posse, ut scriberet, nec tale quicquam proinde suspicari posset) inseruisse illas ad Pontificem, eíque tum, Regem (inscium, nec tale quid cogitantem) subscripsisse.
units.tr: As to how they might manage the matter cunningly and win the royal signature to those letters, the said Lord Balmerinoch confesses that they devised this plan between them: first, that the letters should be slipped in among many others, since sometimes many letters were to be signed with the royal signature; then, that they should not be offered for signing except at the very time when the King was hastening out to hunt, so that, being offered so suddenly, he would have no leisure to examine them carefully, either what they were or to whom they were addressed; thirdly, that the style and titles with which the Pope is customarily addressed should be omitted altogether, lest they appear anywhere in the letters; for if, while the letter was being written, the eye should by chance fall upon one of those titles, the whole fraud might be detected. Instead, a sufficient space being left there for the titles, they could be added and inserted later, conveniently and at leisure. And from this plan of theirs, the said Lord Balmerinoch confesses (in breach of the faith which the King had placed in him, and betraying it) that some days later, early in the morning, as the King was setting out to hunt and hastening his journey as far as he could, among other letters then written in Latin to the Dukes of Florence and Savoy, and others to certain Cardinals on behalf of the Bishop of Vaison, he inserted those letters addressed to the Pontiff, although the King had earlier refused to be brought to write to the Pope and could not have suspected any such thing; and the King, unaware and not thinking of any such matter, then subscribed them.

units.la: Id ubi factum: fatetur porrò dictus Dominus de Balmerinoch, se quidem auchore, Edwardum Dromonium titulos post apposuisse, atque stilum Pontificis, tum in capite ipso literarum, tum verò & in imâ chartâ, ubi interstitium inter contextum ipsum, & manus Regiæ appositionem, nempè vocem Sanctitatis, & vocem filius, & eiusdem generis reliqua, quæ Pontifici tum accommoda, & ad rem suum putabant opportuna. Post verò iussu suo, literas illas à famulo quodam suo obsignatas esse, impresso illis tum Regio signaculo. Quod ad literas autem, quæ ad Cardinales missæ, obsigillatas eas dicit idem D. de Balmerinoch, sed sine superscriptione ullâ appositâ, eidem Edwardo Dromonio traditas, pro arbitrio Archiepiscopi Glasguensis, eis, si & quando ei videretur, mittendas. Comperisse se autem post, duas ex eis, peruenisse ad manus Cardinalium Aldobrandini & Bellarmini; tertiam verò, quæ Cardinali Caietano inscripta & destinata (quòd is tum in Curia Romana Protectorem ageret Scoticæ nationis) frustrà inscriptâ, frustrà destinatam fuisse, cùm is, interea dum perferretur, certè priusquam ei traderetur, diem suum obijsset. Præterea etiam, fatetur idem D. de Balmerinoch, cum veniret post in quæstionem tota res ista, viuente adhuc nuper Regina ELIZABETHA, quòd Legatus eius peruenisse diceret ad aures Re-ginæ de eiusmodi literis ad Papam scriptis, deque ijs Regem insimularet; se quidem, dictum D. de Balmerinoch, cum de totâ tum re, an ita se haberet, Rex acriùs inquireret; quicquam eiusmodi vnquam à se factum, serìò pernegâsse. Fatetur prætera, egisse se etiam atque etiam cum Edwardo Dromonio (qui de transmarinis tum partibus in Scotiam venerat, accersitus eò literis D. de Balmerinoch, quò per eum quoque huiusce rei veritas elucere posset) vt & ipse à se negata, negaret. Quod & ab Edwardo Dromonio præstitum est, qui vllas à se literas illiusmodi, ad Papam delatas esse, strenuè etiam Regi inficiatus est. Cùm verò hæ-reret ei tamen suspicio adhuc aliqua, atque eâ de causâ dictus Dromonius in carcerem amandatus esset in Arce Edinburgensi, intercedente dicto Dno. de Balmerinoch apud Regem, dimissus post, atque libertati suæ redditus est. Qui ipse, cùm Romam reditum suum adornaret, fatetur idem Dominus de Balmerinoch, egisse se cum dicto Dromonio quàm poterat enixè, atque vehementer, vt quocunque modo posset, literas illas Regis ad Pontificem arte aliquâ recuperaret, recupe-ratas autem statim corrumperet. Id quod Dromonius facturum se sanctissimè suscepit: se verò ipsum, D. de Balmerinoch fatetur, quod penes eum tum erat exemplar literarum, quodque ad id vsque tempus secum retinuerat, tùm demum concidisse, atque penitus corrupisse.
units.tr: When this was done, the said Lord Balmerinoch further confesses that he, on his own authority, had Edward Dromonius afterwards add the titles and the style of the Pontiff, both at the head of the letters and at the very foot of the sheet, where the space between the text itself and the royal signature lay, namely the word "Holiness", the word "son", and other things of the same kind, which they then thought suitable for the Pope and useful for their purpose. Afterwards, by his order, the letters were sealed by a certain servant of his, the royal seal having been impressed upon them. As for the letters that were sent to the Cardinals, the same Lord Balmerinoch says they were sealed, but without any superscription added, and were handed over to the same Edward Dromonius, to be sent at the discretion of the Archbishop of Glasgow, whenever and if he thought fit. He later learned that two of them had come into the hands of Cardinals Aldobrandini and Bellarmine; but the third, which was addressed and destined for Cardinal Caietan (because he was then acting in the Roman Curia as protector of the Scottish nation), was addressed in vain and sent in vain, since he died, meanwhile, while it was being carried, certainly before it could be delivered to him. Moreover, the same Lord Balmerinoch confesses that when this whole affair later came into question, while Queen Elizabeth was still living, and it was said that her envoy had come to the ears of the Queen about letters of this kind written to the Pope, and accused the King of them, he (the said Lord Balmerinoch) had seriously and flatly denied that anything of this kind had ever been done by him, when the King inquired more keenly into the whole matter and whether it was so. He further confesses that he pressed Edward Dromonius again and again (who had come to Scotland from overseas, summoned there by letter from Lord Balmerinoch, so that the truth of this matter might also come to light through him) to deny, as he himself had denied, that anything of the kind had been sent by him. And this Edward Dromonius did, stoutly denying to the King that any letters of that kind had been carried to the Pope by him. But since some suspicion still clung to him, and for this reason the said Dromonius had been committed to prison in the castle of Edinburgh, the said Lord Balmerinoch intervening with the King, he was afterwards released and restored to his liberty. When the same Lord Balmerinoch was himself preparing his return to Rome, he confesses that he pressed the said Dromonius as earnestly and vehemently as he could, that by some art he should somehow recover those letters of the King to the Pontiff, and, once recovered, immediately destroy them. Dromonius most solemnly undertook to do this; but Lord Balmerinoch confesses that he himself, since the copy of the letters was in his possession and he had kept it with him up to that time, finally cut it up and utterly destroyed it.

units.la: Iam verò, vt hoc facto operæ pretium sanè fecisti, cùm ex verbis quis subst[?]uctio per te Regi data sit, Quæstionis huius, per quam parum sanctæ quorundam[?] in Regem fides patefacta est, quia nulla vna res magis exisitmationem eius ledere[?] lædere potuisset, (existimationem dico, vitâ suâ longè ei antiquiorem:) ita, coronares hoc opus tuum, si & illud quoque ingenuè expromeres, quid occulti lateat sub illa voce tuâ præter cætera, quò ita, ope tuâ atque operâ, non hoc modò, sed & cætera illa nôsse detur, quæ in fictitiis illis literis comprehensa sunt. Suspicioni enim magis obnoxia vox ista ex ore vestro, qui de Ecclesiâ Romanâ estis, quàm si alius quis diceret, præter cætera. Nôsti quæ seria, imò quanta vobis mysteria lateant, in verbis Apostoli, Cetera, cùm venero, disponam. Totum enim Officium Missæ, vt nunc quidem eam celebratis, proximo suo ad Corinthum appulsu edocuisse & disposuisse Apostolum, cùm cætera illa disponeret. Iniecta autem inde Regi, nec sine iustâ causâ, suspicio, ne prolixæ aliquæ promissiones in ijs literis factæ fuerint, cùm ex eis Clementi facta fides, Regem à Catholicâ vestrâ fide non abhorrere.
units.tr: Now then, since you have certainly done a worthwhile thing in this, when from your words it is clear what undertaking was given to the King by you, this inquiry, by which the untrustworthy faith of certain men towards the King was revealed, since no single matter could have injured his reputation more (I say reputation, far more precious to him than his life), so you would crown this work of yours if you also frankly disclosed what lies hidden under that phrase of yours, among other things, so that by your help and labour it might be granted to know not only this, but also those other things which are contained in those fictitious letters. For that phrase, coming from your mouths, who belong to the Roman Church, is more open to suspicion than if anyone else said among other things. You know what serious, indeed what great mysteries lie hidden in the words of the Apostle, The rest I will set in order when I come. For it is the whole Order of the Mass, as you now celebrate it, that the Apostle taught and arranged on his recent arrival at Corinth, when he was setting in order those other things. Moreover, a suspicion has been cast upon the King from this, and not without just cause: that some lengthy promises may have been made in those letters, since by them faith was given to Clement that the King was not averse to your Catholic faith.

units.la: Sed vt appositè dicam; Catera illa quæcunq; fuerint, quicquid ibi scriptum: nego tamen Clementē Papam ex ijs venisse in spem vllam, Regem in Religione mutaturum. Ratio autem cuiusvis obuia, siue ad Clementis actiones respicias, quæ literas demum illas subsecutæ sunt, siue etiam ad ipsius Regis. Ad Clementis, parum Illum eis literis fidei habuisse; Nam nisi parum habuisset, celâsset saltem in sinu: si enim eo ipso tempore, arcanum illud euulgaret, in magnum id Regis & dedecus & discrimen cederet. At ille (quod quidem iam compertum, postquam res exijt in vulgus) ille (inquam) tantum aberat, vt celârit, vt vix quisquam eò de Gente Scotorum venerit, cui non statim ostenderit, etiam percontatus sit, illâne ipsa Regis manus videretur, ipsiusne [illegible, ~2 letters], etiam, à quibusdam transferri passus sit. Tum, quod moratus quiuis ex humanitate ipsâ, [?]ælatus quiuis ex solertiâ politicâ facturus fuerat, respondisse saltem debuit comiter, si petitioni de Cardinali nollet annuere. Ille verò, nec verbo respondit, nec postulationi quicquam vnquam detulit. Hoc autem, diffidentiæ eius sanè tribuendum, quòd literis illis parum crederet, tanquam fucatis, non veris: Non enim certè arrogantiæ; cùm ipse Clemens aliquot post annis vltrò ad Regem literas dederit, perferente illas Iacobo Lindsejo Equite. Quæ etsi erant profectò plenæ humanitatis, vsitatis tamen ibi Clemens titulis abstinuit; nec se Patrem ibi, portuit, nec fuit tamen; Et Leues tamen non sunt, nec temerarij: cadunt enim, faciles hij motus in generosam indolem. Atque ita excusare volunt factum Pontificis, & crimen in rumores transferre sæpe non veros. Non finit. Humanum est errare. Non cadit autem in Vaticanos Deos infirmitas hæc tanta. Homines non sunt. Quicquid humanum est, ab ijs alienum putat.
units.tr: But to put it to the point: whatever those "other matters" were, whatever was written there, I deny that Pope Clement entertained any hope from them that the King would change his religion. The reason is obvious, whether you look at Clement's actions, which followed those letters, or at the King's own. As for Clement: he clearly did not put much trust in those letters. For if he had not put little trust in them, he would at least have kept them hidden in his bosom. If at that time he had published the secret, it would have brought great shame and danger upon the King. But the King (as is now well known, since the matter became public) was so far from concealing it that scarcely anyone came from Scotland to whom he did not immediately show the letters, and he even asked them whether it seemed to be the King's own hand, and, indeed, allowed some of them to be copied. Then, what anyone would have done out of simple courtesy, and anyone out of political shrewdness, he at least should have done: he should have answered courteously, if he were unwilling to grant the request concerning the Cardinal. But Clement neither replied in a word nor ever gave any ground on the request. This, however, must be attributed to his distrust, that he did not believe those letters, thinking them forged rather than genuine. It was certainly not arrogance, since Clement himself, some years later, of his own accord wrote a letter to the King, which was carried by Sir James Lindsay. Although that letter was indeed full of courtesy, Clement nevertheless refrained there from the usual titles; he did not call himself "Father" there, and yet he was not without it. And yet these are not trivial or rash matters, for such easy movements fall upon a noble nature. And so they wish to excuse the Pontiff's deed and often shift the blame onto rumours that are not true. That will not do. "To err is human." But such great weakness does not befall the gods of the Vatican. They are not men. Whatever is human, they think alien to themselves.

units.la: De Pio primùm. vel verum hoc, vel non veri nostrates vestri, qui sermone, hoc, nec solùm sermone, etiam scriptis affirmarunt. Surrepsisse tum ei Mortonum & Webbum, transfugas nostros, & per suggestiones mendacij plenas, decepto, Bullam surripuisse. Quod cum hic constaret Lincolniensi pridem Episcopo Watsono (qui & tum & diu post in vivis) mirum illi in modum displicuisse, quòd ita se Pius passus sit induci in errorem, quem præviderat Watsonus, & prædixit, nec Sedi Romanæ vtilem, & Pontificijs hic omnibus fore perniciosum, cùm ex eo necessitas quasi quædam imposita Reginæ fuerit, seuerioresin eos pòst leges sanciendi. De Paulo 5o. non minùs verum: qui, hic inter Pontificios moderati magis, sic omnes afsectos, sic sensisse omnes, nempe vel fictitium fuisse Breue illud, vel certè surreptum per fraudem quorundam, vel abreptum per importunitatem, nec ab illo sponte purâ vnquam emanare potuisse. Quid si autem & Pontifex ipse tantùmdem fassus sit, vbi Breuis sui per quorundam Principum Legatos intecta mentio? Penes Authores fides sit. Quid si & purgauit se de Breui sic emisso, apud Principem aliquem externum, nempe, quòd Breue primùm per obreptionem, se quidem non intento ad rem, vel tale quid cogitante, procuratum fuerit? Ad secundum verò, quòd pertractus quasi inuitus, dum Collegii Inquisitorum rem importunius vrgeret: addito, etiam promisso, & data fide, deinceps iam cautiorem fore se, si quid tentandum in rebus Britannicis: De quo viderit ipse. Interim mitior haud vlla afferri potuit excusatio, quàm quæ in Apologià allata est, & allegatas fecisse, quod fecit, Pontificem, non plenè informatum, nec fuisse tam illi perspecta omnia, quin, quod tum nesciret, paulò pòst exploratum magis habere potuisset.
units.tr: First, as to Pius: either this is true, or our people, your people, are not telling the truth, and they have affirmed it not only in speech but in writing too: that Morton and Webb, our renegades, then got at him and, by deceitful suggestions, deceived him into surrendering the Bull. When this came to light, the former Bishop of Lincoln, Watson (who was alive both then and long afterwards), was wonderfully displeased that Pius had allowed himself to be led into an error which Watson had foreseen and foretold: that it would be neither useful to the Roman See nor, here, a grave harm to all the Papists, since from it a certain necessity was, as it were, imposed upon the Queen of enacting harsher laws against them afterwards. As to Paul V, it is no less true: he, more moderate than the rest among the Papists, felt and thought all of them the same, namely that the brief in question was either fictitious, or at least obtained by the fraud of certain persons, or extorted by importunity, and could never have issued from him of his own pure will. What if the Pontiff himself confessed as much, when mention of his brief, sent through the envoys of certain princes, was made without concealment? Let the authors be trusted. What if he also cleared himself, before some foreign prince, concerning a brief sent out in this way: namely, that the brief was first procured by obreption, while he himself was not intent on the matter, nor thinking anything of the sort? As for the second point, that he was drawn in, as it were unwillingly, while the College of Inquisitors pressed the matter more insistently: adding also a promise and a pledge of faith that from then on he would be more cautious, should anything be attempted in British affairs. Let him see to that himself. Meanwhile no milder excuse could be offered than the one put forward in the Apology: that the Pontiff, not being fully informed, and not having all things so clearly perceived, could have ascertained more fully, a little later, what at that time he did not know, and so he acted as he did.

units.la: De septicolli vero ciuitate, de Babylone suâ, ludos non patitur Tortus; serió dat; quæ in Epistola est B. Petri, queq, in Apocalypsi, Apocalypsi, Babylonem, non aliam ullam urbem esse, quàm Romam ipsam. Nos, quod dat, accipimus non illibenter. Itaque avidè avent homines, hujus Petrum Romæ, alicubi in scripturis reperire, potiùs ut Babylonem velint esse Romam, ubi Petrus fuit; quàm ut Petrum Romæ non fuerit. Valdè enim illorum interest ad Caput fidei, ut Petrum Romæ credatur fuisse, non fide quæ in historijs est, sed maiore, Sacrarum nempe literarum. Etsi & illud quidem totum, præter Leges Theologiæ, quæ si Mystica est, seu Symbolica, non est argumentativa. Etiam præter Leges Epistolæ; quæ etsi tota sit mysteriorum plena, locum tamen, unde scripta, designare non solet mysticè, ne si locus non sit certus, nec ipsius Epistolæ fides sit certa. Qui verò, si locus allegoricus Babylon sit, non & allegorica persona Marcus, qui mox sequitur? vel si hic literalis, quidni & illa? Quorsum autem Petrus, Romæ scribens, Romam non ausus Romam nominare; quàm Paulus, cùm inde scriberet, urbem Romam, cives Romanos, & ausus, & nominauit? Atque adeò Divus Iohannes, cùm librum scriberet, cuius singuli versus singula mysteria sunt; ubi tamen ad Ecclesias scribendum fuit septem urbium, proprijs nominibus singulas quasque designauit, easque voluit esse non mysticas, in libro alioquin per totum mystico. Etsi verò sint ista, ut dixi; non piget tamen Tortum habere confitentem, quòd non in Epistolâ modò Petri, sed & in Apocalypsi, Babylon Roma sit. De eo tantùm nobis lis erit iam, quænam illa ibi Roma Babylon; aut Roma quo tempore Babylon esse cœperit. Cui rei totâ ibi circumstantias adhibet B. Iohannes, vix ut in eâ errare cuiquam contingat. Quæ enim Babylon ibi: eadem meretrix magna dicitur, quæ sedet super aquas multas, cum quâ fornicati sunt Reges terræ, quæ Bestia ibi insidet habenti capita septem & cornua decem. Septem autem illa capita, septem sunt montes, in quibus sita Roma. Et quæ de septem totum circumspicit orbem Montibus, Imperij Romæ Deumq. locus: Edoctum autem ibi se dicit B. Iohannes à Spiritu, de rebus quæ venturæ essent. Quodsi iam, Romam ibi (quòd tu sensu vis) designauit, nihil venturum edocuit Spiritus; Ethnica enim tum Roma in Auge erat vel maximè. Propheticus verò is liber totus haberi solet; nimis autem mille illa missella tum prophetiæ forent, si prædiceret, fore, ut persequeretur Roma Christianos. Vidit verò hoc priusquam in Patmon relegatus esset; fusum Iacobi fratris sui, multorum sanguinem sub Nerone fusum: sensit ipse, & pars magna fuit illius tum persecutionis. Prophetiam ergo totam evacuat, si Ethnica ibi Roma sit. Tum Reges illi decem, (qui numerus certus pro incerto) quomodo tum inebriati de vino prostitutionis meretricis, qui tum scilicet nulli erant? Stante enim & vigente Roma Ethnica, eclipsin passi sunt; qui uspiam tum Reges erant, vectigales omnes, Reguli potius dicendi quam Reges: Reges tum demum, cum illa retro sublapsa ferretur. Neque vero periculum tum ebrietatis ullum a meretrice, vel ab illius amoribus. Oderant enim illam, periisse expetebant, & (quod tu ante dixti de Gregorio) vellent nollent, illi tum per vim atque ingratias serviebant: Etiam Bestia illa altera, quae cornua duo habebat similia agni, qui poterat suppetias ferre Roma Ethnica, in qua, quamdiu quidem Ethnica nec CHRISTVM professa, nullum prorsus CHRISTI vestigium, nihil penitus, quod ulla ex parte referret agnum?
units.tr: As for the city of the seven hills and its Babylon, Tortus does not allow himself to be trifled with; he gives it in earnest: what is in the Epistle of St Peter, and what is in the Apocalypse, that Babylon is no other city than Rome itself. We, since he gives it, accept it not unwillingly. And so men eagerly desire to find somewhere in the Scriptures that Peter was at Rome, and rather that Babylon should be Rome, where Peter was, than that Peter was not at Rome. For it is greatly in their interest, for the foundation of their faith, that Peter should be believed to have been at Rome, not on the faith that rests on history, but on a greater one, namely that of the Sacred Letters. Yet even that whole argument, apart from the rules of theology, which, if it is mystical or symbolic, is not argumentative, is also apart from the rules of the Epistle; which, though it is wholly full of mysteries, does not usually designate mystically the place from which it was written, lest, if the place were not certain, the Epistle's own credibility should not be certain either. But if Babylon is an allegorical place, is not Mark, who immediately follows, an allegorical person too? Or if he is literal, why not she as well? Again, why did Peter, writing from Rome, not dare to name Rome, when Paul, writing from there, both dared and named the city of Rome and the Roman citizens? And so, too, the Divine John, when writing his book, each verse of which is a separate mystery, yet where he had to write to the churches of seven cities, designated each one by its proper name, and wished them to be non-mystical, in a book otherwise mystical throughout. Although these things are as I have said, it does not trouble us to have Tortus confess that Babylon is Rome not only in the Epistle of Peter but also in the Apocalypse. Our dispute will be only about what that Roman Babylon is there, or at what time Rome began to be Babylon. For this matter St John sets down all the circumstances there, so that it hardly could happen that anyone errs in it. For the Babylon there is the same one called the great harlot, "who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication, and upon whom the beast sits having seven heads and ten horns." "And those seven heads are seven mountains on which Rome is situated." And "the place which looks around the whole world from its seven mountains, the seat of the Empire and of the god of Rome." And St John says there that he was taught by the Spirit concerning things that were to come. If, then, he designated Rome there (as you wish to take it), the Spirit taught nothing about the future; for Pagan Rome was then at its very height. Yet that book is generally regarded as wholly prophetic; but those thousand trifles would be prophecy indeed, if it foretold that Rome would persecute the Christians. But John saw this before he was relegated to Patmos: the blood of his brother James, and the blood of many shed under Nero; he himself felt it, and was a large part of that persecution at the time. He therefore empties the whole prophecy, if Pagan Rome is meant there. Then those ten kings (a certain number put for an uncertain one): how were they then made drunk with the wine of the harlot's fornication, when, of course, there were none at that time? For while Pagan Rome stood and flourished, they suffered eclipse; whoever were kings anywhere at that time were all tributaries, to be called petty kings rather than kings; they became kings only when that city was swept down and carried away backwards. Nor was there any danger of drunkenness then from the harlot or from her loves. For they hated her, longed for her ruin, and (as you said before of Gregory) whether they wished it or not, they then served her by force and against their will. Also, that other beast, which had two horns like a lamb, who could bring help to Pagan Rome, in which, as long as it was pagan and had not professed Christ, there was absolutely no trace of Christ, nothing at all that in any part resembled a lamb?

units.la: Luculentae quidem satis haec circumstantiae; mitto illas tamen: verbis ipsis stringo, quae satis diserta sunt, ad tempus, quo implenda fuit haec prophetia, perspicue designandum. Versu 8° dicitur dilucide; Bestia quam vidisti, fuit, & non est, & ascensura est de Abysso, & ibit in interitum. Fuit (inquit B. Iohannes) & non est. Erat autem tum Roma Ethnica, & erat tum florentissima, cum haec agerentur. Falso ergo tum diceretur, non est, sed ascensura est, si de Roma quae tum erat diceretur. Paulo autem infra vers 12°. Decem cornua, quae decem ibi Reges, regnum (inquit) nondum acceperunt, sed potestatem tanquam Reges una hora accipient cum Bestia. Negare vero non potes, scribente haec B. Iohanne, Babylonem, Romam esse tum quidem non potuisse. Reges enim tum nondum potestatem acceperant, ac neque diu post acceperunt, donec Roma iam Christiana. Nec ergo Romam Ethnicam, Babylonem fuisse. Quin etiam interitus ipse, quem interminatur ibi Babyloni, liquidiorem adhuc multo rem facit. Nec enim verbum ibi ullum de conflagratione eius, quae Roma olim Ethnica contigit a Gothis ac Vandalis incensae: quin de interitu potius alius & generis & modi repentini scilicet, & tanto impetu, quasi vi magna molaris lapis mitteretur in mare. Haud enim (inquit) post pòst, unquam invenietur. Non autem ( quantacunque ei potentia est) mersum in mare molarem natare denùo, faćturus est Pontifex.
units.tr: These circumstances are clear enough; I pass over the rest. I will touch only on the words themselves, which are plain enough, to show clearly the time when this prophecy was to be fulfilled. In verse 8 it is said plainly: "The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to ascend from the abyss, and will go into destruction." "It was" (says St John), "and is not." But Rome was then pagan, and was at that time at the height of its flourishing when these things were happening. It would therefore be false to say "is not, but is about to ascend" if it were speaking of the Rome that then existed. Again, a little further on, in verse 12: "The ten horns, which are ten kings there, have not yet received a kingdom, but they receive authority as kings for one hour with the beast." You cannot deny that, when St John was writing this, Babylon could not have been Rome, for the kings had not then received this authority, nor did they receive it for a long time afterwards, until Rome was already Christian. Therefore Babylon was not pagan Rome. Indeed, the destruction itself which is threatened there against Babylon makes the matter far clearer still. For there is no word there about its burning, such as pagan Rome suffered when it was set on fire by the Goths and Vandals; rather, it is a destruction of another kind and manner altogether, namely sudden and with such force, as if a great millstone were cast into the sea. "For," it says, "it shall never be found again." But the Pontiff, however great his power, will not make a millstone that has been sunk in the sea float again.

units.la: Porrò verò, ibi dicitur, quòd postea, vox in eâ Musicorum, vel Artificum non audietur, quòd Artifex non invenietur in eâ amplius, vox mola amplius non audietur, lux lucernae amplius non lucebit, vox sponsi & sponsae in posterum conticescet. Ibi accumulat denique quicquid usquam est artis vel verborum, quae id ponant ante oculos, deploratam & desolatam iri Babylonem sine entitatis spe omni, quasi non Ens in aeternum. Quòdsi, praeterea nihil foret, satis esset tamen, ad institutum praesens, in ipsa descriptione illorum qui cum illa mercaturam facient. Mercatores eius (inquit) Principes terrae. Omnes Gentes erraverunt in Veneficiis eius. Nam neque haec Roma Ethnica quadrare possunt, quae vi solâ atque armis gentes sibi subegit, nec eas unquam ita Veneficiis incantauit, ut non primâ quâque vel leuissimâ occasione data (vires modò essent) vindicarent se in libertatem, & ad arma conclamarent; Verum enim, quae illa tandem Roma sit (non enim certè Ethnica) quae merces instituit de animabus hominum, optimè omnium nobis dixerit Cardinalis ipse. Et ipse quidem (quod in Apologiâ notatum est) fatetur rem totam: Decem enim Reges meretricem contremabunt; quod de Româ quae Ethnica fuit intelligi non posse, puto abundè iam mihi demonstratum est.
units.tr: Moreover, it is said there: "Afterwards, the voice of musicians and craftsmen shall not be heard in it, no craftsman shall be found in it any more, the sound of the millstone shall be heard no more, the light of the lamp shall shine no more, the voice of bridegroom and bride shall be silent for ever." There, in short, the author piles up everything that exists of art or of words to set before our eyes that Babylon will be laid waste and made desolate, without any hope of being, as if it were "not being" for ever. And if nothing else were there, it would still be enough for our present purpose in the very description of those who trade with her: "Her merchants," it says, "are the princes of the earth. All the nations have been led astray by her sorceries." For neither can this pagan Rome, which subdued nations to itself by force and arms alone, fit this description, nor did it ever so enchant them with sorceries that, at the first or slightest opportunity (if only they had the strength), they did not claim their liberty and cry out to arms. But as for what that Rome truly is (certainly not pagan), which "carries on a trade in the souls of men," the Cardinal himself has said it best of all. He indeed admits the whole matter (as was noted in the Apology): "For the ten kings will make the harlot tremble"; and I think I have already sufficiently shown that this cannot be understood of the Rome that was pagan.

units.la: Ut verbo igitur expediam. Quae sunt apud B. Johannem de ruina Romae praedictiones, de quâ Româ sunt? De eâ, cui opem feret Bestia; cui cornua agnino similia: quae in templo Dei sedet: Cui cum Regibus terrae foederata pactio: Quae vino prostitutionis suae inebriat eos: Quae veneficiis seduxit. De eâ (inquam) Roma, quae extollit se super omne quod dicitur Deus, non, quae ipsa, nescio quot minutulos & patellares Deos veneretur, quod illa fecit Ethnica: De eâ Româ quae agnum specie refert, scriptam tamen habet in fronte blasphemiam: De eâ Româ, cuius merces, hominum animae, dum licitari facit homines nummo salutem suam: De eâ, quae fuit olim sub Regibus septem, sed B. Johannis aetate non fuit (etsi etiam tum mysterium illud occoepit operari) non fuit (inquam) sed ascensura fuit tum demum ad fastigium suum, cùm decem ibi Reges potestatem suam accepturi essent, postquam scilicet Roma Ethnica iugum excusissent. De eâ Româ, quam decem Reges (non eluuies illa barbara Vandalorum vel Gothorum) postquam diu sedulli essent ipsius veneficiis, tandem igne concrematuri sunt; non ad cladem aliquam, unde postea conualesceat, sed ad perniciem eius sempiternam, vt leges sit, non minùs vbi Roma, quàm vbi Troia fuit. Dabit enim Deus in corda Regum, vt Romam hanc excindant penitus, sicut dedit Satanas olim in corda Barbarorum, vt illam succenderent. De eâ denique Româ, quae per Pseudoprophetam suum, viuo habet signa faciendi, quae cum Pseudopropheta suo, atque ille cum eâ, vtrique mittentur in stagnum ignis, ac sulphuris, in aeternum. Verè autem à Torto dicitur, Romam Christianam perditam non iri. Non certè, sed illam quae inebriata est Sanctorum sanguine, & Martyrum Iesu Christi, Antichristianam scilicet. Ea enim perdenda est, cuius in fronte scriptum nomen blasphemiae.
units.tr: To put it in a word, then. What are the predictions in St John about the ruin of Rome, and which Rome is meant? It is the Rome which the beast will aid; whose horns are like those of the lamb; which sits in the temple of God; with which the kings of the earth have a covenanted pact; which makes them drunk with the wine of her fornication; which has seduced by sorceries. Of that Rome (I say), which exalts itself above everything that is called God, not the Rome which worships I know not how many little and petty gods, as pagan Rome did. Of that Rome, which bears the likeness of the lamb yet has blasphemy written on its forehead. Of that Rome, whose merchandise is the souls of men, while it makes men bid for their salvation with money. Of that which was once "under seven kings," but in the age of St John was not (although even then that mystery had begun to work); it was not (I say), but was going to ascend to its height only when the ten kings were about to receive their power, namely after they had shaken off the yoke of pagan Rome. Of that Rome, which the ten kings (not that barbarian deluge of Vandals or Goths) will, after they have long been eager for her sorceries, at last burn with fire; not for some calamity from which she might afterwards recover, but for her everlasting destruction, so that it may be said that there is no more trace of Rome than there is of Troy. "For God will put it into the hearts of the kings to utterly overthrow this Rome, just as Satan once put it into the hearts of the barbarians to set her on fire." Lastly, of that Rome which, through her false prophet, has the power of working signs before the living; which, together with her false prophet, and he with her, both will be cast into the lake of fire and brimstone for ever. Truly, however, the Torturer says that Christian Rome will not be lost. Certainly not; but she who is drunk with the blood of the saints and the martyrs of Jesus Christ, that is, Antichristian Rome, will be. For that is the city which is to be lost, "on whose forehead is written the name of blasphemy."

units.la: Minimè verò mirum, si ista quae dixi, tam vel claram, vel certam in scriptis Patrum interpretationem non habeant. Operabatur enim modò mysterium tum iniquitatis. Signatus adhuc liber erat huius Prophetiae. Verissimum autem verbum est; aenigma esse Prophetiam omnem, cùm nondum completa est; vt, quamuis Prisci illi omni genere charismatum, vitae verò sanctimoniâ, longo nos intervallo superârint: mirari tamen non debeat quis, si non illis tum, adeo explicita omnia fuerint, quàm nobis, per Dei gratiam, iam sunt, qui consummatam iam Prophetiam illam quotidie oculis vsurpamus. Etiamen id quoque miretur quispiam, quòd & Illi etiam horum multa, quasi per transennam viderint, quòd nimirum ita {a}a Tertullianus: Sic & Babylon apud Iohannem nostrum, Romana urbis figuram portat, proinde & magnae, & regno superbae, & Sanctorum debellatricis. {b}Hieronymus autem. Cùm in Babylone versarer, & purpurata meretricis essem colonus, & iure Quiritum viuerem. {c}Idem; cùm Marcellam Româ Bethleem commigrare vellet, Hic, puto, locus sanctior est Tarpeiâ rupe, quae caelo saepius fulminata, offendit quod Domino displiceret. Lege Apocalypsin Iohannis, & quid de mulieris purpurata, & scriptâ in fronte blasphemiâ, septem montibus, aquis multis, & Babylonis tantetur exitu, contucre [?]. Exite (inquit Dominus) de illâ. At verò {d}Augustinus, Condita est Roma velut altera in occidente Babylon, & velut prioris filia Babylonis. {e}Victorinus quoque: Scripta ibi in tubis, ruina magna Babylonis ciuitatis, id est, Roma. Etiam {f}Orosius: Ecce similis Babylonia ortus & Roma, similis potentia, similis magnitudo, similia tempora. Sed quid ego haec, cum unanimis sit ista Patrum pene omnium sententia? Nam de Roma fronte Christi nomine signata quod affers; nulla est in Apocalypsi Babylon, cuius signatis frons Christi nomine. Christi nomen deleri oportuit prius, & deletum est, quam blasphemia ibi scriberetur. Postquam autem ibi scripta blasphemia, tum demum vere Babylon fuit, verèque est. Sed necdum Apocalypsis completa vobis, necdum recisit Babylon illa vestra, quae si, ut dicis, scriptam iam habet in fronte Christi confessionem, cadere non poterit: atque ita non verus vates Iohannes. Ille vero & vates verus, & casura est Babylon illa vestra; ideo autem casura, quia Christi confessionem illam expunxit, & loco eius, blasphemiae multiplicis nomen ibi jam invisit; & quidem maiusculis litteris, ut quivis vel qui transcurris, legere possit sic invisam. Qua in re, ea veritatis vis est, ut etiam Iesuitas vestros adigat, qui in eum librum non ita pridem commentarios scripserunt, non solum de Roma Ethnica, verum & de Christiana, Babylonis ibi nomen interpretari, ac delendam denuo confessionem Christi de fronte eius, post deletam autem, blasphemiae nomen ibi inscribendum.
units.tr: It is by no means surprising if these things which I have said do not have so clear or certain an interpretation in the writings of the Fathers. "For the mystery of iniquity was already at work. The book of this prophecy was still sealed." And this is most true: "every prophecy is an enigma until it has been fulfilled"; so that, although those ancient writers surpassed us by a long interval in every kind of spiritual gift, and in holiness of life, no one should wonder if all these things were not then as explicit to them as they are now to us, by the grace of God, who every day gaze upon that prophecy as already fulfilled. Yet someone might also wonder that they too saw many of these things, as it were through a crack in the door; for example, Tertullian: "So also Babylon in our John bears the figure of the city of Rome, and therefore of the great, the haughty in kingdom, and the destroyer of the saints." And Jerome: "While I was dwelling in Babylon, and was a farmer of the purple harlot, and lived under the right of the Quirites." The same: "When Marcella wished to migrate from Rome to Bethlehem." "This place, I think, is holier than the Tarpeian rock, which, though often struck by lightning from heaven, has offended the Lord." Read the Apocalypse of John, and what is said of the purple woman, and of blasphemy written on her forehead, of the seven hills, of the many waters, and of the destruction of Babylon; consider it. "Come out of her," says the Lord. But Augustine says: "Rome was founded like a second Babylon in the west, and like the daughter of the former Babylon." Victorinus also: "Written there in the trumpets, the great ruin of the city of Babylon, that is, Rome." Also Orosius: "Behold, Rome arose as a likeness of Babylon, with like power, like greatness, like times." But why do I say these things, when this opinion of almost all the Fathers is unanimous? As for what you bring forward about Rome bearing the name of Christ on her forehead, there is in the Apocalypse no Babylon whose forehead bears the name of Christ. The name of Christ had to be erased first, and it was erased, before "blasphemy" could be written there. But after blasphemy was written there, then at last Babylon truly was, and truly is. But the Apocalypse is not yet fulfilled for you, and that Babylon of yours has not yet fallen; if, as you say, it already has "the confession of Christ" written on its forehead, it cannot fall, and thus John would not be a true prophet. But he is a true prophet, and that Babylon of yours is going to fall; and it is going to fall because it has blotted out that confession of Christ, and in its place has now inscribed there the name of manifold blasphemy; and indeed in capital letters, so that anyone who even runs past may read it as hateful. In this matter, the force of truth is such that it compels even your Jesuits, who not long ago wrote commentaries on that book, to interpret the name of Babylon there not only of pagan Rome but also of Christian Rome, and to say that the confession of Christ must be erased again from her forehead, and after it is erased, the name of blasphemy is to be inscribed there.

units.la: Sic & {g}Ribera: De Roma intellegendum, non solum qualis sub Ethnicis Imperatoribus olim fuit, sed etiam qualis in fine saeculi futura est. Et post. Babylonem dictam esse, non solum quod hoc illi nomen, tempore{h} quo Iohannes haec scribebat; maximè conueniret; sed etiam quod tempore, quo haec explebuntur (necdum enim expleta esse) non minus quàm ante; conueniet. Sic Iesuita alter{i} Viegas[?]. Omnia quae in his capitibus commemorantur, in Romanam urbem apertissimè quadrant. Caeterum nomen Babylonis ad eam Romam transferendum, quae antequam reciperet fidem Christi, Idolis seruiebat: & ad eam etiam, quae erit tempore Antichristi. Erit ergo tempore Antichristi Roma Babylon, non solum Ethnica, eaque tum in desertum & solitudinem euadet, ut ait Ribera vester.
units.tr: Likewise Ribera: "It must be understood of Rome, not only as it once was under the Ethnic emperors, but also as it will be at the end of the age." And afterwards: "Babylon is so called not only because this name most fitted it at the time when John was writing these things, but also because at the time when these things will be fulfilled (for they have not yet been fulfilled) it will fit no less than before." Likewise another Jesuit, Viegas[?]: "Everything that is recorded in these chapters squarely fits the city of Rome. Moreover, the name Babylon is to be transferred to that Rome which, before it received the faith of Christ, served idols, and also to that which will be in the time of Antichrist. There will therefore be in the time of Antichrist a Rome that is Babylon, not only the Ethnic one, and that one will then be reduced to a desert and solitude, as your Ribera says."

units.la: Sed haec omnia, vix quicquam ad institutum sermonem de rumoribus, qui vos Romae circumvolant; nisi quia ibi hic digredi libuit, ut Babylonem salutares. Nam evam Hieronymi aetate, cùm Christi nomen in fronte gereret Roma, etiam tum hoc morbo laborabat, vt, eò confluerent toto ex orbe rumores vndique, quorum si nullis Roma tum credidit; quid, eo loco, opus Hieronymo ita rem referre? Profectò nec pauciores Roma iam famigeruli, nec minus est aurium ad nouitates [?] prurientium, quàm cùm Hieronymus ibi purpurata meretricu colonus esset.
units.tr: But all this has scarcely anything to do with the present discussion of the rumours that fly about you in Rome; unless it pleased me to digress here, so that I might greet Babylon. For in the time of Jerome, when Rome bore the name of Christ on her forehead, she was already suffering from this disease, so that rumours from every quarter flocked together to her. If Rome at that time believed none of them, why, in that place, was there any need for Jerome to report the matter in this way? Surely Rome now has no fewer rumour-mongers, and the ears of those itching for novelties are no fewer than when Jerome was living there, a farmer of purple-clad harlots.

units.la: Dum verò in eo totus est, vt Pontifices suos Pium & Paulum tam anxiè excusèt ab omni erroris labe, siue ex aliorum malâ fide, siue ex suâ; interserit nescio quomodo & Clementis 8ᵗ.defensionem, de Brevibus huc ab eo transmissis, vergente ad occasum tum Regno R. Elizabethae. Ex dialecto autem Papiensi, more suo aspergit primùm mendacijs Authorem Apologiæ, quorum illi copiosa domi mesis est. Brevibus enim illis, ait, non vt ille mentitur, Iacobum, tum Scotiæ Regem, à folio exclusit, sed consilium dedit, quale dare decebat Summum Pontificem. Post verò paulò, oblitus personæ suæ, non quasi Capellanus de Sacello, sed quasi Cardinalis ipse iam de Consistorio egressus. Habemus (inquit) exemplaria Brevium illorum in manibus, & iis diligenter inspectis, nusquam inuenimus nomen Iacobi Regis, aut alterius particularis personæ. Hic ferè iam illi larua de vultu delapsa est; non hæc Capellanum ampullæ decent, Habemus in manibus, & nusquam inuenimus. Interest multum, Davusne loquatur, an Heros; sed recolligat se, larvam reponat, cautiùs rem gerat in posterum. Mentiri autem suum nusquam magis obtrudit, quàm vbi ipse est mendacissimus. Cur enim mentitur ipse de nominatim ibi exclusio in Brevi Rege, quod nusquam in Apologiâ dictum est? Id modò dictum: exclusum ibi, ne à Pontificijs reciperetur in regem, qui vel nostræ religionis cultor esset ipse, vel cultores toleraret; ac per hoc, non minùs Regi obnunciatum esse, quàm alij cuicunque, qui alterius, quàm vos in fide, professionis esset. Verè ergo ibi dictum, nec verius quid dici potuit; quantum in se erat, Clementem tum Brevibus illis egisse, vt Rex iam noster, vt quiuis alius, quocunque demum iure niteretur, si sic, vt Papa in religione non sentiret, à capessendis Regni huius gubernaculis esset exclusissimus. Ego verò id fidenter dixerim, perinde Brevibus illis exclusum folio hoc suo, ac si nomine ibi proprio & natiuo, Iacobi Regis, designatus esset. Quid enim interest, nominetur quis, an ita ad vivum describatur, ut cuivis in promptu sit, quem ibi velit Pontifex? Ius Regù hæreditarium, quis tum nescibat? quis verò religionem ignorabat, quam ille, ex quo voces primò, & literas formare potuit, voce, scripto, præsentiâ suâ semper professus est? Annon ille exclusus? Quid ille ergo sibi volunt verba, Quantumcunq; propinquitate sanguinis niteretur? Quis ille verò, qui nixus propinquitate sanguinis? Quis fuit? quis esse potuit? An est quisquam tam obtuso pectore, ut quò illa tendant, quem petant, non intelligat, nisi nomen nominetur?
units.tr: Yet while he is entirely occupied in excusing so anxiously his Pontiffs Pius and Paul from every stain of error, whether arising from the bad faith of others or from their own, he somehow inserts also a defence of Clement VIII, concerning the Briefs sent hither by him, at a time when the reign of Queen Elizabeth was sinking towards its end. In his Pavian dialect, moreover, he sprinkles, in his usual way, first of all lies against the author of the Apology, of which he has a copious stock at home. For, he says, by those Briefs, not as he falsely claims did he exclude James, then King of Scotland, from the throne, but he gave counsel, such as it became the Supreme Pontiff to give. Afterwards, however, forgetting his own character, speaking not as a chaplain of the chapel, but as a Cardinal now come out of the Consistory himself, he says: "We have copies of those Briefs in our hands, and having inspected them carefully, we have nowhere found the name of King James, or of any other particular person." Here his mask has almost slipped from his face; such words do not become a chaplain of the flask: "We have them in our hands, and nowhere have we found." It makes a great difference whether Davus speaks or a hero; but he gathers himself, puts his mask back on, and will act more warily in future. Yet he never thrusts his lying more forcefully upon us than when he himself is most lying. For why does he himself lie about the exclusion, named in the Brief, of the King, which is nowhere said in the Apology? What was said was only this: that he was excluded there, lest he should be received by the Papists as king, who either was himself a follower of our religion or tolerated its followers; and by this, he was no less declared to the King than to any other person whose profession of faith was other than yours. Therefore it was rightly said there, and nothing truer could be said: as far as lay in him, Clement in those Briefs had acted so that our King, as any other, whatever right he might rest on, if he did not think in religion as the Pope, would be most thoroughly excluded from taking up the government of this realm. I, however, would confidently say that in those Briefs he was excluded from this throne just as if James the King had been designated there by his own proper and native name. For what difference does it make whether a man is named, or so described to the life that anyone may readily see whom the Pontiff means there? Who then did not know the hereditary right of kings? Who was ignorant of the religion which he (James), from the time he could first form voices and letters, has always professed by voice, by writing, and by his presence? Was he not excluded? What then do the words "however much he might rest on closeness of blood" mean for them? And who was he who "rested on closeness of blood"? Who was he? Who could he have been? Is there anyone with a mind so dull that he does not understand, unless the name is named, where those words tend and whom they aim at?

units.la: Qualè autem consilium illud, quod dare decebat Pontificem? Nempe operam darent, ut eligeretur Rex. Eligeretur autem? Ain' verò, ut eligeretur? Quid opus hoc? Erat, qui Antiquo stemmate, Regio sanguine, Hæreditario iure, Stirpis proximitate, Optimo titulo, vendicare poterat. Quorsum hîc, eligeretur? Itáne, in Regnis, ubi successionis iure Reges nascuntur, conclamat Pontifex ad electionem, ad vota, ad suffragia? Quorum verborum, quæ mens, qui sensus sit, credo iam Reges omnes per Europam, qui hoc iure regnant, satis aduertisse. Idem ante tentárat Lutetia in Regno Gallicano. Idem hîc iam tentat in Nostro. En quale consilium dare decet, dare soleat, quale etiam in Regum aliorum successione quâcunque, (cùm se dederit occasio) dare paratus sit; Conclave credo in regna omnia inducturus, si daretur. Verùm dic porrò, quis tandem eligeretur? Qui ad religionem Catholicam bene affectus. Mendaciter & hoc; utcunque enim affectus bene, nisi ciusmodi esset, qui religionem Catholicam non modò toleraret, sed omni ope & studio promoueret; exclusus tamen adhuc, quisquis fuit ille Regum, nisi & iureiurando se id præstitutum suscipéret. Quare, in totâ hac narratione nihil sani; vanitate, falsitate referta omnia. Pòst verò etiam, illud suadere vult homo lepidus, Abfuisse tantùm ut excluderetur IACOBVS Rex, ut includeretur vel maximè scilicet. Spes enim maxima, illum à Romanâ fide suscipiendâ non abhorrere. Verùm ut res ibi, ita & spes, falsa utráq;: At ministri eius spem dederunt: sed fallaces; quibus tamen, cùm in rem suam est, cùm libet; credulus satis Clemens, Pius, Paulus, quis non?
units.tr: But what kind of counsel was that which "it became the Pontiff to give"? Namely, that they should "take pains that a King be elected." But was he to be elected? Do you really say, that he should be elected? What need was there of this? There was one who could claim by ancient lineage, by royal blood, by hereditary right, by proximity of stock, by the best title. Why here, "be elected"? Is it so, that in kingdoms where kings are born by right of succession, the Pontiff calls out "to election, to votes, to suffrages"? I believe that all the kings of Europe who reign by this right have sufficiently noticed the meaning and sense of those words. The same thing was previously attempted at Paris in the Gallican kingdom. The same thing is now attempted here in ours. "Behold the kind of counsel it becomes him to give, which he is accustomed to give, and which he is ready to give also in the succession of any other kings whatever, whenever occasion offers"; I believe he would bring in a conclave into all kingdoms, if it were allowed. But tell me further, who then would be elected? "One well disposed towards the Catholic religion." This too is a lie; for however well disposed he might be, unless he were such a one as would not merely tolerate the Catholic religion but promote it with all his power and zeal, whoever that King was would still be excluded, unless he undertook to do this under oath. Wherefore, in this whole account there is nothing sound; everything is crammed with vanity and falsehood. Afterwards, moreover, the witty fellow wants to persuade us that "JAMES the King was so far from being excluded that he was rather, of course, most fully included. For the greatest hope is that he would not shrink from embracing the Roman faith." But as the matter there, so also the hope is false on both counts. "His ministers gave hope," but deceptive hope; yet to these, when it suits their purpose and when it pleases, Clement, Pius, Paul, who is not credulous enough?

units.la: Quin Rex ipse ad Pontificem scripsit, etiam ad Cardinales Aldobrandinum & Bellarminum, literas plenas humanitatis, quibus, praeter catera, petebat, ut aliquis è Gente Scotorum Cardinalis crearetur, ut haberet Romae, per quem facilius & tutius cum Pontifice negotia sua tractaret. Enimverò de hoc quod iam retulit Matthaeus, in negotio hoc Literarum, si quàm bono id euentu, tàm etiam bono in Regem animo retulisset, merito illi à nobis gratia habenda esset, quasi de officio sanè perhumano. Certè enim successu non caruit, quò suus inde Regi honor iam salvus sit.
units.tr: Indeed, the King himself wrote to the Pontiff, and also to the Cardinals Aldobrandini and Bellarmine, letters full of courtesy, in which, among other things, he asked that some Cardinal from the Scottish nation be created, so that he might have at Rome someone through whom he could more easily and safely transact his affairs with the Pontiff. Indeed, as to what Matthew has now reported about this letter-business, if he had reported it with as good an outcome as with a good disposition towards the King, he would deservedly be thanked by us, as for a truly most courteous service. For certainly it did not lack success, by which his own honour toward the King is now safe.

units.la: Ex eo enim occasio illi data, atq; ansa occulti cuiusdam maleficij eruendi, quo sic eruto, integritatem fidei atq; honoris sui, sartam tectam habebit. Tecto autè sic atq; latente, ut diu iam latuit, atq; tectum fuit, aliquo pòt alio tempore recruduisset forte, cùm elapsa iam esset occasio omnis, eius eruedi. Simul, ut de eo ipso, certior redderetur, qui in eo Regis fidem de se fefellit, suam in Regè fidem violauit. Nec enim potest Regi accidere quicquam optatius, quàm, unde ei detur in sensus eorum intimos (qui ei intimi sunt) penitiùs introspicere, & quorum ab eo fides multa committenda sunt, eorum certa sit an subiecta fides, explorare.
units.tr: For from this an occasion was given to him, and a handle for uncovering a certain hidden mischief, by which, once uncovered, he will keep the integrity of his faith and honour intact and unharmed. But concealed and lurking as it has long lain hidden and covered, it might perhaps have broken out again at some other time, when every opportunity of uncovering it had already slipped away. At the same time, so that he himself might be more certainly informed about that very person, who in this matter "broke faith with the King concerning himself, and violated his own faith toward the King." For nothing more desirable can befall a King than that, through what is given him, he should look more deeply into the innermost thoughts of those who are most intimate with him, and make certain whether the faith of those to whom he must commit many things is sound or false.

units.la: Cùm enim obiecisset Matthaeus scriptas ad Pontificem à Rege literas, (rem ita crassam ut manu teneri posset) facere non potuit, quin acriùs in eam rem inquireret. Reperit autem, fouisse se in sinu serpentem, & verè tandem deprehendit, fraudem sibi ab eo factam, qui Maiestatis suae à Secretis literarum. De quo, etsi incertos priùs aliquos rumusculos inaudisset, cùm paulò pòst, quàm Româ perlatae essent, nonnulli, nescio quid ibi tale auditum sibi mutinerent: at, ex eo iam tempore, nunquam certi quid, eâ de re, datum est cognoscere; ita, qui facti author fuerat, dum sibi malè metueret, texerat rem probè, & quasi tenebris obuelârat. Sic ergo habet.
units.tr: For when Matthew had charged that letters had been written to the Pope by the King (a thing so gross that it could be grasped by hand), he could not help inquiring more keenly into the matter. He found, however, that he had been nursing a serpent in his bosom, and at length truly discovered the deceit practised upon him by the man who was Secretary of His Majesty's letters. Concerning him, although at first they had heard some vague rumours, when, a little after the letters had been carried to Rome, some men there murmured to them that something of the kind had been heard, yet from that time onward they were never given to know anything certain on that matter. So the author of the deed, while he was anxiously fearful for himself, had covered the affair well and, as it were, veiled it in darkness. Thus, then, the matter stands.

units.la: Surrepsit Regi furtim, atque ad literas, quas narras, malis artibus elicuit manus Regiæ subscriptionem Secretarius tum Regius. Quo autem consilio hoc; siue quòd propenderet animo ad religionem Pontificiam; siue quòd, lucro illi atque commodo fortè ea res futura fuit; siue quòd, impensè fauceret propinquo suo Episcopo Vasionensi Cardinalatum ambienti; (cuius in gratiam erant literae illæ adornatæ) siue etiam quòd Edwardo Dromonio Equiti gratificari vellet, qui rem totam procurabat atque urgebat; quo (inquam) consilio, aut, horum quid fuerit, illi ipsi notum; præterquam, illi ipsi, notum credo nemini. Rei autem totius modum, & cum substantiâ ipsâ circumstantias omnes, quibus Regi imposuit, dum surriperet ei literas, nemo melius magisve ad viuum referat, quàm Author ipse criminis: Cuius est, quam subjicio hic, non expressa per vim, vel per fraudem illecta, sed libera sanè confessio, atque omni modo spontanea, ad mentem ipsius, ipsiusque manu, signata.
units.tr: The King was secretly crept upon, and by evil arts the then Secretary of the King drew from him the subscription of the King's hand to the letters you speak of. But with what purpose this was done, whether because he leaned in mind towards the Papist religion, or because the thing would perhaps be to his gain and advantage, or because he wished eagerly to do a favour to his kinsman, the Bishop of Vaison, who was seeking a cardinal's hat (for whose sake those letters had been drawn up), or even because he wished to oblige Sir Edward Drummond, who was procuring and urging the whole business: with what purpose (I say), or which of these it was, is known to himself alone; and, I believe, to no one else besides himself. But the manner of the whole affair, and all the circumstances with the matter itself, by which he imposed upon the King while he was stealing the letters from him, no one can relate more fully and more vividly than the author of the crime himself. Of his, which I subjoin here, is not a confession forced out by violence or drawn out by deceit, but a free, and in every way voluntary, confession, set down in his own mind and in his own hand.

units.la: DECLARATIO, atque Confessio D. de Balmerinoch, Regiæ Maiestati facta, ac Dominis qui ei à Sanctiore Consilio sunt, de literis quibusdam, quas ille, per fraudem surreptitiè scribendas Regio nomine, atque Romam, ad Papam Clementem 8um. quasi sibi à Maiestate sua essent, mittendas curauit. Anno 1598.
units.tr: Declaration and Confession of Mr. Balmerinoch, made to the King's Majesty and to the Lords of the Privy Council, concerning certain letters which he caused to be sent to Rome, to Pope Clement VIII, by fraud and stealth, written in the King's name, as if they were from His Majesty. Year 1598.

units.la: DOMINVS de Balmerinoch, habitâ de eo quæstione, cùm crimen hoc illi obiectum esset, quòd per malas artes, perque surreptionem literas illas procurâsset, (quibus è literis imputatio, maximè, vt falsa, ita scandalosa in Regem, quâ ad Regij nominis honorem, quâ ad Religionis castam professionem redundâsset) postquam variis modis, offensam negando, subticendo, transferendo, extenuando nihil profecisset, ingenuè tandem agnouit atque confessus est. Quòd scilicet Ann. 1598. adductus ad id precibus * Archiepiscopi Glascuensis, qui tum legatum agebat Responsalem Maiestatis suæ in Gallia, præsertim verò Episcopi Vasionensis ac aliorum quorundam, procurante negotium hoc Edwardo Dromonio Equite, quem illi tum huc legarant eo nomine, vt interuentu suo, mutuæ quædam inchoari possent atque reciprocæ vices inter Regem Maiestatem & Pontificem.
units.tr: Mr. Balmerinoch, when the matter was examined and this charge was laid against him, that by wicked arts and by stealth he had procured those letters (which letters contained an imputation, chiefly as false as it was scandalous against the King, reflecting both on the honour of the royal name and on the pure profession of religion), after he had achieved nothing by various means, denying the offence, keeping silent, shifting the blame and minimising it, at last frankly acknowledged and confessed. That is to say, in the year 1598, he was persuaded to this by the entreaties of the Archbishop of Glasgow, who was then serving as His Majesty's envoy in France, and especially of the Bishop of Vaison and certain others, the business being managed by Edward Dromonius, a knight whom they had then sent over here for this purpose, so that through his mediation some mutual dealings might be begun and reciprocal exchanges take place between the King's Majesty and the Pope.

units.la: Idem Dominus de Balmerinoch, postquam ei rei assensum suum praebuisset, Regem ad id saepenumero incitare conatus est, eique, illiusmodi delineatas à se literas obtulit, quas manu Regia signatas vellet ad Papam. Ubi autem, Regis animum, à quacunque scriptione eius generis alienum reperiisset; nec id modò, sed incœptum illud damnare penitus, de commercio ullo habendo cum Pontifice; qui titulis scilicet illis atque attributis à Rege compellari expectaret, quibus Maiestas eius, conscientiâ suâ teneretur, ne apud eum ratione ullâ uti posset, quâcunque de causâ.
units.tr: The same Mr. Balmerinoch, after he had given his assent to this matter, often tried to urge the King to it, and offered him letters of this kind which he had drafted himself, wishing them to be sent to the Pope under the King's hand and seal. But when he found the King's mind averse to any writing of that kind, and not only that, but utterly condemning the whole undertaking of having any dealings with the Pope, who, of course, would expect to be addressed by the King with those titles and attributes by which His Majesty held himself bound in conscience, so that he could not on any ground, for any reason whatever, make use of him.

units.la: Idem Dominus de Balmerinoch, & Edwardus Dromonius, cùm in manum convenissent tamen, de incœpto suo ad exitum perducendo; egerunt de modo, quo imponere possent Regiæ Maiestati, & quales cupiebant literas, abeo elicere. Itaque se, Dromonij manu descriptas, adornâsse post literas, quasi à Rege nimirum, ad Pontificem: Quarum hic ferè tenor: nempe ut Pontifici gratias ageret de humanitate, atque gratiâ pristinâ: ut Episcopum ei Vasionensem commendaret, quem in Cardinalium Collegium cooptari cuperet, quòfic, negotia sua (cùm ita opus) meliùs ibi Romæ expedire posset.
units.tr: The same Mr. Balmerinoch and Edward Dromonius, although they had come together to bring their enterprise to completion, discussed the manner in which they could impose upon the King's Majesty and extract from him the kind of letters they wanted. So they had, with Dromonius's hand, drawn up letters, supposedly from the King, to the Pope. The substance of these was, in short: that he should thank the Pope for his kindness and former favour; that he should commend to him the Bishop of Vaison, whom he wished to be admitted into the College of Cardinals, so that he might more easily transact his business there at Rome, as the situation required.

units.la: Quò verò, astu rem gerere, & Regiam ad eas literas subscriptionem lucrifacere possent, hanc inter se rationem initam, dictus Dominus de Balmerinoch confitetur: primùm, ut insererentur in medio multarum, cùm essent aliquando literæ multæ subscriptione Regiâ signandæ: tum, ut ne offerrentur ita signandæ, nisi eo demùm tempore quo Rex venatum ire properaret, quò, ita repentè tùm oblatas non vacaret excutere, aut quæ essent, aut ad quos, curiosiùs observare: tertiò, ut stilus, atque tituli, quibus de more compellari solet Pontifex, omitterentur prorsus, necubi comparerent in literis; ne, si dum inter scribendum esset, traiectu forte oculi in aliquem de titulis illis incideret, fraus tota deprehendi posset, sed reliEto[?] ibi ad titulos quod satis esset, interuallo, ỿ[?] post, commodè per otium addi possent atque inseri. Atque ex hoc eorum instituto fatetur idem dictus Dominus de Balmerinoch (fide quam ei Rex habuit, perfidè à se violatâ) aliquo post die, mane primo, venatum exeunte Rege, atque iter quantum potuit maturante, inter literas tum alias ad Duces Florentiæ atque Sabaudiæ, atque alias ad Cardinales {a} quosdam pro Episcopo Vasionensi latinè scriptas, cùm ad Pontificem ante i.m Rex abnegâsset, se nullo modo adduci posse, ut scriberet, nec tale quicquam proinde suspicari posset, inseriisse illas ad Pontificem, eisque tum, Regem (infscium, nec tale quid cogitantem) subscripsisse.
units.tr: As to how they might act cunningly and obtain the King's signature to those letters, the said Mr. Balmerinoch confesses that they devised this plan between themselves: first, that the letters be inserted in the middle of many others, since there were sometimes many letters to be signed with the royal signature; second, that they not be offered for signing except at the very time when the King was hurrying out to hunt, so that, being presented so suddenly, he would have no leisure to examine them closely, either what they were or to whom they were addressed; third, that the style and titles by which the Pope is customarily addressed should be omitted altogether, so that they should appear nowhere in the letters, lest, if by chance while he was reading his eye should fall upon any of those titles, the whole fraud might be detected; but that, once the rest was in place, the titles might be conveniently added and inserted afterwards, at leisure, in the blank space left for them. And in accordance with this plan of theirs, the said Mr. Balmerinoch confesses (abusing the trust the King had placed in him, which he had treacherously violated) that some days later, early in the morning, as the King was setting out to hunt and he hurried the journey as much as he could, among other letters then written in Latin to the Dukes of Florence and Savoy and to certain Cardinals on behalf of the Bishop of Vaison, he slipped in those letters to the Pope, since the King had earlier refused to be persuaded that he should write, and could not suspect anything of the kind; and then the King, unaware and not thinking any such thing, signed them.

units.la: Id vbi factum: fatetur porrò dictus Dominus de Balmerinoch, se quidem authore, Edwardum Dromonium titulos post apposuisse, atque stilum Pontificis, tum in capite ipso literarum, tum verò & in imâ chartâ, vbi interstitium inter contextum ipsum, & manus Regiæ appositionem, nempe vocem Sanctitatis, & vocem filius, & eiusdem generis reliqua, quæ Pontifici tum accommoda, & ad rem suam putabant opportuna. Post verò iussu suo, literas illas à famulo quodam suo obsignatas esse, impressoque illis tum Regio signaculo.
units.tr: When this was done, the said Mr. Balmerinoch further confesses that he himself, at the instigation of Edward Dromonius, afterwards added the titles and the style of the Pope, both at the head of the letters and at the foot of the page, where there was a gap between the text itself and the royal signature, namely the word "Holiness," and the word "son," and other things of the same kind, which they then thought suitable for the Pope and useful for their purpose. Afterwards, at his command, those letters were sealed by a certain servant of his, and the royal seal was impressed on them then.

units.la: Quod ad literas autem, quæ ad Cardinales missæ, obsigillatas eas dicit idem D. de Balmerinoch, sed sine superscriptione vllâ appositâ, eidem Edwardo Dromonio traditas, pro arbitrio Archiepiscopi Glascuensis, eis, si & quando ei videretur, mittendas. Comperisse se autem post, duas ex eis, peruenisse ad manus Cardinalium Aldobrandini & Bellarmini; tertiam verò, quæ Cardinali Caietano inscripta & destinata (quòd is tum in Curiâ Romanâ Protectorem ageret Scoticæ nationis) frustrà inscriptâ, frustrà destinatam fuisse, cùm is, interea dum perferretur, certè priusquam priufpriusquam ei traderetur, diem suum obyisset. Praeterea etiam, fatetur idem D. de Balmerinoch, cum venire post in quaestionem tota res ista, vivente adhuc nuper Reginâ ELIZABETHA, quòd Legatus eius pervenisse diceret ad aures Reginae de eiusmodi literis ad Papam scriptis, deque ijs Regem insimularet; se quidem, dictum D. de Balmerinoch, cum de totâ tum re, an ita se haberet, Rex acrius inquireret; quicquam eiusmodi unquam à se factum, serio pernegâsse. Fatetur praeterea, egisse se etiam atque etiam cum Edwardo Dromonio (qui de transmarinis tum partibus in Scotiam venerat, accersitus eò literis D. de Balmerinoch, quo per eum quoque huiusce rei veritas elucere posset) ut & ipse à se negata, negaret. Quod & ab Edwardo Dromonio praestitum est, qui vllas à se literas illiusmodi, ad Papam delatas esse, strenuè etiam Regi inficiatus est. Cum verò haereret ei tamen suspicio adhuc aliqua, atque eâ de causâ dictus Dromonius in carcerem amandatus esset in Arce Edinburgensi, intercedente dicto D^no. de Balmerinoch apud Regem, dimissus pòst, atque libertati suae redditus est. Qui ipse, cum Romam reditum suum adornaret, fatetur idem Dominus de Balmerinoch, egisse se cum dicto Dromonio quam poterat enixè, atque vehementer, ut quocunque modo posset, literas illas Regis ad Pontificem arte aliquâ recuperaret, recuperatas autem statim corrumperet. Id quod Dromonius facturum se sanctissimè suscepit: se verò ipsum, D. de Balmerinoch fatetur, quod penes eum tum erat exemplar literarum, quodque ad id usque tempus secum retinuerat, tum demum consumpsisse, atque penitus corrupisse.
units.tr: As for the letters which were sent to the Cardinals, the same Mr. Balmerinoch says that they were sealed, but with no address written on them, and were handed over to the same Edward Dromonius, to be sent, at the discretion of the Archbishop of Glasgow, whenever and if he thought fit. He afterwards learned that two of them had reached the hands of Cardinals Aldobrandini and Bellarmine; but the third, which was addressed and destined for Cardinal Cajetan (because he was then acting as Protector of the Scottish nation in the Roman Curia), had been addressed and sent in vain, since he, in the meantime, while it was being carried, certainly died before it could be delivered to him. Furthermore, the same Mr. Balmerinoch confesses that when this whole affair later came into question, while Queen Elizabeth was still alive, and it was said that her envoy had reached her ears concerning such letters written to the Pope and accused the King of them, he, Mr. Balmerinoch, when the King inquired more sharply into the whole matter and whether it was so, firmly denied in earnest that anything of the kind had ever been done by him. He further confesses that he pressed Edward Dromonius again and again (who had come to Scotland from overseas, summoned there by letters from Mr. Balmerinoch, so that through him also the truth of the matter might come to light) to deny it as well, as if it had not been done by himself. And this Edward Dromonius did, stoutly denying to the King also that any such letters had been carried to the Pope by himself. But since some suspicion still lingered, Dromonius was sent to prison in the castle of Edinburgh; afterwards, through the intercession of the said Mr. Balmerinoch with the King, he was released and restored to his liberty. When the same Mr. Balmerinoch was preparing his return to Rome, he confesses that he urged the said Dromonius as earnestly and vehemently as he could to recover, by some means, those letters of the King to the Pope, and to destroy them at once once they were recovered. Dromonius solemnly undertook to do this; but Mr. Balmerinoch confesses that he himself, since the copy of the letters was in his possession and he had kept it with him up to that time, finally used it up and utterly destroyed it.

units.la: Iam verò, ut hoc facto operae pretium sanè fecisti, cum ex verbis quis substructio per te Regi data sit. Quaestionis huius, per quam parum sanctâ quorundam in Regem fides patefacta est, quâ, nulla unquam res magis existimationem eius lædere potuisset, (exi-stimationem dico, vitâ suâ longè ei antiquiorem:) ita, coronares hoc opus tuum, si & illud quoque ingenuè expromeres, quid occulti lateat sub illa voce tuâ prater catera, quò ita, ope tuâ atque operâ, non hoc modò, sed & catera illa nôsse detur, quæ in fictitijs illis literis comprehensa sunt. Suspicioni enim magis obnoxia vox ista ex ore vestro, qui de Ecclesiâ Romanâ estis, quàm si alius quis diceret, prater catera. Nôsti quæ seria, imò quanta vobis mysteria lateant, in verbis Apostoli, Catera, cùm venero, disponam. Totum enim Officium Missæ, vt nunc quidem eam celebratis, proximo suo ad Corinthum appulsu edocuisse & disposuisse Apostolum, cùm catera illa disponeret. Iniecta autem inde Regi, nec sine iustâ causâ, suspicio, ne prolixæ aliquæ promissiones in ijs literis factæ fuerint, cùm ex eis Clementi facta fides, Regem à Catholicâ vestrâ fide non abhorrere.
units.tr: Now, you have certainly done a worthwhile thing in this act, since from your own words it can be seen what foundation you have laid for the King. By this inquiry, through which the faithlessness of certain men towards the King has been revealed, nothing could ever have damaged his reputation more (I say reputation, which is far dearer to him than his life), so you would crown this work of yours if you also frankly disclosed what lies hidden beneath your phrase "among other things," so that, with your help and effort, one could know not only this but also those "other things" which were contained in those fictitious letters. For that phrase, coming from your mouths, you who belong to the Roman Church, is more open to suspicion than if anyone else were to say "among other things." You know what serious, indeed what great, mysteries lie hidden in the words of the Apostle, "The rest I will set in order when I come." For the Apostle, on his next arrival at Corinth, is said to have taught and arranged the whole Office of the Mass, as you now celebrate it, when he set in order "those other things." Moreover, a suspicion has arisen in the King, and not without good cause, that some lavish promises may have been made in those letters, by which Clement might be assured that the King was not averse from your Catholic faith.

units.la: Sed vt appositè dicam; Catera illa quæcunq; fuerint, quicquid ibi scriptum: nego tamen Clementè Papam ex ijs venisse in spem vllam, Regem in Religione mutaturum. Ratio autem cuiusvis obuia, siue ad Clementis actiones respicias, quæ literas demum illas subsecutæ sunt, siue etiam ad ipsius Regis. Ad Clementis, parum Illum eis literis fidei habuisse; Nam nisi parum habuisset, celâsset saltem in sinu: si enim eo ipso tempore, arcanum illud eiulgaret, in magnum id Regis & dedecus & discrimen cederet. At ille (quod quidem iam compertum, postquam res exijt in vulgus) ille (inquam) tantùm aberat, vt celebrit[?], vt vix quisquam eò de Gente Scotorum venerit, cui non statim ostenderit, etiam percontatus sit, illâne ipsa Regis manus videretur, ipsiusne αὐτόγραφον[?], etiam, à quibusdam transferibi passus sit. Tum, quod moratus quiuis ex humanitate ipså, cordatus quiuis ex solertiâ politicâ factuurus fuerat, respondisse saltem debuit comiter, si petitioni de Cardinali nollet annuere. Ille verò, nec verbo respondit, nec postulationi quicquam vnquam detulit. Hoc autem, diffidentia eius sanè tribuendum, quòd literis illis parum crederet, tanquam fucatis, non veris: Non enim certè arrogantiæ; cùm ipse Clemens aliquot pòst annis vltrò ad Regem literas dederit, perferente illas Iacobo Lindsejo Equite. Quæ etsi erant profectò plenæ humanitatis, visitatis tamen ibi Clemens titulis abstinuit; nec se Patrem ibi, nec Regem filium suum, nec cum Apostolicâ vllâ benedictione impertijt: quod tamen solenne est ei, cum salutat per literas Principem vllum, qui ex ipsius Catechismo, Catholicus est. Quasi si Princeps Principi, ita Regi tum scripsit, quòd satis scilicet exploratū habaret, Regi cum eo in religione minimè convenire. At verò de literis ibi, quas aliquanto ante à Rege acceperat, altum silentium. Sanè, verbum ibi de illis additum oportuit, postquam quod per illas petijt non impetrauit. Ita quidem par fuit, quando id multo magis ex dignitate Principis, salutanti per literas comiter, comiter respondere; quàm si ipse, alteri occupet prior scribere; præsertim, si quas scribit litera petitoria sint, vt erant tum Pontificis, nec mentio in ijs tamen vlla literarum, quas ipse prior acceperat. Atque hæc, si Pontificem.
units.tr: But to speak to the point: whatever those other things were, and whatever was written there, I deny that Pope Clement drew from them any hope that the King would change his religion. The reasoning is obvious whether you look at Clement's actions, which followed those letters, or at the King's own. As for Clement: he evidently placed little faith in those letters. For had he placed much, he would at least have kept them hidden in his bosom; if at that time he had published the secret, it would have brought great disgrace and danger upon the King. But he (as is now known, since the matter has come out into the open) was so far from keeping it quiet that hardly anyone came from Scotland to whom he did not show them, and he even asked whether they seemed to be the King's own hand, whether they were in his own autograph, and allowed some to be copied. Then, any man of courtesy would have done, and any man of political shrewdness would have done, what he ought to have done: at least replied politely, if he did not wish to grant the request about the Cardinal. But he neither answered a word nor ever made any move on the request.
