This must be ascribed to his distrust, because he put little faith in those letters, as though they were forged and not genuine: certainly not to arrogance, since Clement himself some years later sent letters to the King of his own accord, carried by Sir James Lindsay. Although these were indeed full of courtesy, Clement nevertheless refrained from the usual titles there: he did not style himself Father, nor the King his son, nor bestowed any apostolic blessing, which yet is customary for him whenever he greets by letter any prince who, by his own catechism, is Catholic. It is as if he wrote to the King as one prince to another, evidently because he was sure the King did not agree with him in religion. But there was complete silence about the letters which he had received from the King some time before. Certainly a word about them ought to have been added, since what he had sought through them he had not obtained. It was right, when a prince courteously greets by letter, that he should be answered courteously, and all the more so from the dignity of a prince; rather than that he himself should take the initiative of writing to another; especially when the letters he writes are petitions, as those of the Pontiff then were, and yet there was no mention in them of the letters which he had himself received first. And these are the points, if you look at the Pope.

units.la: Sin Regem spectes, constans ille quidem, suíque semper similis, in toto vitæ curriculo, Religionis Professor. Sermo domesticus, forensis; quæ scripsit, quæ fecit, quàcunque demum occasione, testimonia sunt, imò præconia sunt, tam publica, tam sonora, vt credibile non sit, ita desipuisse vnquam Papam, vt secus de eo sentiret. Quòdsi, præterea nullus esset (quî tamen sunt plurimi) Testem vnum cito tibi emri exceptione maiorem, Βασιλεὺς δώρων[?], Librum, quem iam pridem scripsit, & inscripsit Primogenito suo Nobilissimo Principi Henrico; quem Librum & in lucem edidit, priusquam regnum hîc suum apud nos capesseret. Liber ille, per se solus sufficere debet sensato cuiquam, ad furtivas illas literas, aspectu ipso primo profligandas. Ludibrium ergo merum, & quod indignetur quispiam, esse quempiam, qui persuaderi sibi patiatur (cui nota sit Regis ab ineunte ætate educatio, iterata sæpe fidei suæ professio publica, assidua dicta, scripta, facta, concionum sacratum[?] nunquam intermissa confessatio, Eucharistiæ sacrosanctæ, bis térue quotannis participatio) qui persuaderi (inquam) sibi patiatur; omnibus tamen hÿs, hÿs (inquam) omnibus, vnas illas literulas apud Pontificem momento suo præponderâsse. Quò tamen hîc, mente, atque fide optimâ gererentur omnia, quò & Pontifici & Clero suo æternùm occluderetur os; ipso in Limine regni satis superque prospexit huic rei Rex; dum in mandatis daret D.Iacobo Lindsceio Equiti, ut referret ad Pontificem, quæ illum rationes, (quâ, conscientiâ; quâ, existimationis suæ) retinerent, quo minus ad literas illas responsum daret, quas Lindseius pertulerat; unaque certiorem redderet, si quas unquam literas accepisset quasi a Rege scriptas, eas, ut absque omni dubio pro fucatu vel furtivis haberet. Quod ipsum etiam Rex Legato Responsali suo apud Regem Galliae præcepit, ut & ille Nuncio Pontificis significandum curaret, qui tum erat Lutetiae. Quod superest perstringo breui: Luce clarius hinc consequi, haud unquam iustam Pontifici causam fuisse, ut in animum suum induceret, propendere Regem ad Catholicismum suum. Proinde cum per Breuia illa sua omni aditu excluderet, quibus præscriptio vllla iuris ad regnum, nisi qui simul procliues essent ad Romanam religionem; mentem illi atque animum fuisse, Iacobi Regis, à solio excludendi.
units.tr: But if you look at the King, he was indeed constant and always like himself, throughout the whole course of his life, a professor of religion. His domestic and public speech, what he wrote and what he did on whatever occasion, are testimonies, indeed proclamations, so public and so loud that it is not credible the Pope could have been so foolish as to think otherwise of him. And even if there were no other witness (though there are very many), you have a witness, quickly to be trusted beyond exception: the Book which he long ago wrote and dedicated to his firstborn, the most noble Prince Henry; which Book he also published before he took up his kingdom here among us. That book alone ought to be sufficient for any sensible person to refute at first sight those furtive letters. It is therefore sheer mockery, and something to provoke indignation, that anyone should allow himself to be persuaded (though he knows the King's upbringing from earliest youth, his repeated public profession of faith, his constant words, writings and deeds, the uninterrupted confession of his sermons, and his participation in the most holy Eucharist twice or three times a year) that all these things, all of them (I say), were outweighed with the Pope by those one little letters. But so that everything here might be done in the best mind and faith, and so that the mouth of the Pope and his clergy might be closed for ever, the King on the very threshold of his kingdom took sufficient and more than sufficient care of this matter; when he gave instructions to Sir James Lindsay to report to the Pope what reasons (whether of conscience or of his own esteem) kept him from giving an answer to those letters which Lindsay had carried; and at the same time to inform him that, if he ever received any letters supposedly written by the King, he should regard them without any doubt as forged or furtive. The King also ordered his agent at the court of the King of France to take care that the Pope's nuncio, who was then at Paris, should be informed of this too. As for what remains, I touch on it briefly: it follows from this, clearer than light, that the Pope never had a just cause to persuade himself that the King was inclined to Catholicism. Therefore, since by his Briefs he shut out every approach, by which no claim to the kingdom could be prescribed unless its holders were at the same time inclined to the Roman religion, it was his mind and purpose to exclude James the King from the throne.

units.la: Quodsi spem forte aliquam in sinu suo foueret Pontifex, Regem in religione mutaturum, siue id è literis, siue quòd ita narrarent Regis subditi, quorum fides suspecta: at hoc, de literis ad Papam Regis qui potuit, vniuersis, qui per Angliam tum erant constare? vel illud etiam, quid male feriati illi, Papæ auribus insusurrâssent? Verum enim, Bullæ illæ Clementinæ ad omnes erant: Ad dilectos filios eius Nobiles Catholicos omnes per Angliam. Ad Clerum totum, & Populum Anglicanum, quas, illi ad vnum omnes, qui scirent, quis Regi tum in Religione animus, non poterant non eo sensu interpretari, quasi contra Regem ex professo mugirent. Literæ autem illæ, susurrus ille clandestinus soli Pontifici notus, aut forte illi, qui intimi tum erant ei à Consiliis. Euincam autem hoc, exemplo vnico. Erat non ignobili familiâ quidam, in fidem Romanam propensus, (qui tamen æquus esset & faueret iuri Regio) is paulò ante Reginæ obitum, eò adduxit sacerdotem quendam familiarem suum, ut ad Garnettum literas daret, peteretque ab eo, uti operam suam in eo poneret apud Catholicos suos, quò in Regis ius, cùm tempus ferret, vellent esse æquiores. Ibi Garnettus, sic respondit; Nihil sibi negotij fore, cum iure Regis, vel eo promouendo: ineterasse[?] enim adeo Regem in religione sibi contrariâ, in eâque duxisse callum, ut spes nulla conuersionis iam de eo superesset. Audisse Garnettum, qui agmen hic ducebat Iesuitarum, ut Breuium Papalium(quæ tum illi in manibus erant) interpretem egerit; nec illi vnquam in mentem venerit, (quod vos iam facitis) in eum sensum trahere, vt includi potius intra illa Regem, quàm excludi per illa diceret, aut speciosa hac fraude mentem Pontificis infucaret? Imminò, ecce tibi ex transuerso penitus, cùm præconio publico denunciatus vbique Rex, Breuia illa, quasi quæ nulli iam rei essent, quasi prorsus iam irrita, quasi actum de ijs, abiecit in focum, atque exusit illico. Non faceres Garnettes, seruares apud te sedulò, postquam Regi fauebant, proferres in lucem, cùm maximè opus, ostenderes palam, fidem ex illis faceres, quàm in Regem propitius Clementis animus, qui non excluserit eum Solio, non; sed incluserit potius. Sed neque Garnetus hæc ipse credidit; & tu, à nobis postulas vt credamus? Verùm nec bonâ fide Matthæus euasionem hîc istam afferre potuit. Etsi enim acceptis hijs tum literis, subdubitare potuit Clemens, vel Clerus Romanus, & in obscuram spem venire conuersionis Regiæ: at quæ deinceps ab eo ipso die subsecutæ sunt Regis actiones omnes, ad eum ipsum diem quo scribebat hæc Tortus, ita in illustri rem ponunt, siue quæ exin scripserit, egeritue spectes; siue quæ Pontifici de sententia suâ totâ per internuncios suos hîs iam significârit, (quod & supra retuli:) vt ex solâ maleuolentia, nec aliâ ratione vllâ, latebram hanc iam modò quæsierit, & diuerticulum perfidiæ suæ. Quæ ipsa, iam tandem in scenam hic producit, postquam tam multis, tam liquidis indicijs innotuit orbi terrarum vniuerso, de Regis nostri, in pietate & officio, stabili & perpetuâ mansione. Nec ergo, (vt concludit Tortus) non perfidus Clemens, sed ipse sua frustratus: verùm & ipse sua frustratus, & tamen perfidus; atque ipse Clementem purgare cùm voluit, & illum non purgauit, & seipsum insuper inquinauit.
units.tr: But if perhaps the Pope nursed some hope in his bosom that the King would change his religion, whether from the letters or because the King's subjects so reported (whose good faith is suspect), what could be known to all who were then in England about the King's letters to the Pope, or even what those idle fellows whispered in the Pope's ears? For the Clementine Bulls were addressed to all: "To our beloved sons, all the Catholic nobles throughout England; to the whole clergy and the English people"; and all of them, everyone who knew what the King's disposition then was in religion, could not but interpret them in the sense that they were openly bellowing against the King. But those letters, that secret whisper known only to the Pope, or perhaps to those who were then his closest councillors. I will prove this by one example. A certain man of no ignoble family, inclined to the Roman faith (yet fair and favourable to the King's right), shortly before the Queen's death brought along a certain priest of his household, so that he might write a letter to Garnet and ask him to use his influence with his Catholics, so that when the time came they would be more favourable to the King's right. There Garnet replied as follows: that he would have no business with the King's right, nor with promoting it: for the King had become so hardened in a religion opposed to his own, and had grown so callous in it, that no hope of conversion now remained for him. Garnet, who led the Jesuit band here, had heard the Papal Brief (which were then in his hands) and had acted as its interpreter; and it never came into his mind (as you now do) to twist it in that sense, that it said the King was rather shut in by it than shut out, or to infuse the Pope's mind with this specious deceit? Indeed, look at you, quite perversely, when the King was proclaimed everywhere by public herald: those Briefs, as though they had no effect now, as though they were utterly void, as though the matter about them was finished, he threw into the fire and at once burned. You would not have done so: Garnet, you would have kept carefully by you, since they favoured the King; you would have brought them out into the light when it was most needed, you would have shown openly, and made it plain, how favourable Clement's mind was towards the King, who had not shut him out from the throne, no; but had rather shut him in. But Garnet himself did not believe this; and do you ask us to believe it? Indeed Matthew could not in good faith put forward this evasion here. For although, on receiving those letters at that time, Clement or the Roman clergy may have wavered and come to some faint hope of the King's conversion; yet all the King's actions that followed from that day onward, down to the very day on which Tortus wrote these things, put the matter in such clear light, whether you look at what he wrote and did afterwards, or at what he has already signified to the Pope through his intermediaries about his whole opinion (as I also reported above), that he has now sought this hiding-place and refuge for his treachery out of ill will alone and for no other reason. This very thing he now at last brings onto the stage here, after it has become known to the whole world, through so many and so clear indications, that the King of ours remains steadfast and constant in piety and in duty. Therefore (as Tortus concludes), Clement was not treacherous, but deceived by his own devices; yet he too was deceived by his own devices and was treacherous all the same; and when he wished to clear Clement, he did not clear him, and moreover he defiled himself.

units.la: FUisse in Anglia non negat Tortus, qui primum Breue confictum existimârunt. Quare autem existimârunt confictum? Quòd caperent hac fraude, Catholicis imponere, & ad iuramentum suscipiendum perducere. Quinam verò hij qui sic existimârunt? Catholici, scio, dicet. Ergo Catholici, Catholicis imponunt per fraudem? Ergo Catholici impostores sunt, & artem Dæmonis factitant? sic videtur; sic beare solet Tortus Catholicos suos. Sed dic dum obsecro hoc rursum; ideone hoc exi-stimabant, stimabant,quia cupiebant hæc fraude Catholicis imponere? Quàm vero hæc non cohærent? Imò ideo potius non existimabant. Certè enim si alijs in eo fucum facere voluerunt, ipsi id nunquam in animum induxerant. Nemo alij per fraudem imponit, qui quod ipse sentit, id alij author est ut sentiat. Error in eo esse potest, sed bonâ fide agit, fraus esse non potest; quæ tum demum interuenit, cùm quod ipse non credit, alios ut credant inducit. Illi verò (ut Tortus fatetur) confictum Breve crediderunt. Quare Torti causa non causa, & medicus indoctus Pontifex, qui erravit primùm in morbi causâ, pòst etiam in pharmaco suo spirituali adhibendo, quo fraudem curare voluit, quæ nulla ibi fuit. Inscitia hominis fortassè aliqua; Dæmonis ars, vel fraus, ibi nulla. Sed neque hominis inscitia etiam: Causa illa fuit vera, quæ in Apologiâ est; quòd sanè nihil in eo censerent Pontifice dignum, Theologicum in toto Breui nil, sed neque Logicum. Perspicuum debere esse ait, quod tamen Archipresbyter non perspicit, non alij præter illum, cætera satis perspicaces. Multa fidei aduersa continere dicit in Iuramento, sed tantùm dicit: ubi, quâ parte continentur, non indicat. Excusserunt verò omnes eius angulos Archipresbyter cum suis, nec, in quicquam ibi fidei aduersum, inciderunt. Pontificaliter tandem satis, ne suscipiatur prohibet, idq; sub pœnâ salutis animarum; at illi suscepe-runt, & benè tamen de salute suâ sperare non desinunt. Politicæ verò in eo prudentiæ non sanè multum. Regis enim animum læsit, iam ante illis infensum ex scelere tam infando, quem proin placare debuit, & mitiorem reddere. Potuit verò, si damnâsset facinus, si animaduertisset in participes criminis, &c, (vel eo nomine, quòd sceelus tam fœdum quidam è suis admisissent) edixisset reliquis omnibus, ut suscepto promptè Iuramento & præteritum illud nefas expiarent, & omnem similis pòst machinandi, suspicionem auerterent. Nec sanè, vel sensum communem sapuit, quin terebrosa magis hæc Pontificeis, quàm cordata prohibitio.
units.tr: It is not denied by Tortus that it was in England; those who first thought it a forgery did so. Why did they think it a forgery? Because they wished to deceive Catholics with this trick and bring them to take the oath. Who were those who thought so? "Catholics," he will say, I know. So Catholics deceive Catholics by fraud? So Catholics are impostors and practise the art of the Devil? That seems to be so; this is how Tortus is accustomed to flatter his Catholics. But I beg you, say it again: did they think this because they wanted to impose on Catholics by this trick? How do these things not cohere? Rather, they did not think it for that reason. For if they wished to deceive others by it, they had never brought it into their own minds. No one deceives others by fraud who makes others believe what he himself believes. There can be error in such a case, but he acts in good faith; it cannot be fraud, which arises only when someone induces others to believe what he himself does not believe. But those men (as Tortus admits) believed the Breve to be forged. Therefore the cause of Tortus is no cause, and the Pontiff is an unskilled physician, who first erred in diagnosing the disease and then in applying his spiritual remedy, by which he wished to cure a fraud that was not there. Perhaps there is some ignorance on the man's part; the art of the Devil or fraud is there none. But not even ignorance of the man: that cause was the true one set out in the Apology, namely that they judged nothing in it worthy of the Pontiff; the whole Breve contained nothing theological, but nothing logical either. It ought to be clear, he says, which the Archpriest does not see, though others, apart from him, are quite sharp-sighted. In the oath, he says, it contains many things adverse to the faith, but he only says so: where, in what part, they are contained, he does not indicate. But the Archpriest and his people have examined every corner of it, and found nothing in it adverse to the faith. Pontifically enough, at last, it forbids it to be taken, and that under pain of the salvation of souls; yet they took it, and still do not cease to hope well concerning their salvation. Indeed, there is not much political prudence in it. For it wounded the King's mind, already hostile to them because of so unspeakable a crime, whom it ought therefore to have appeased and made milder. But if he had condemned the deed, if he had punished the accomplices of the crime, etc., (even on the ground that some of his own had committed so foul a crime), he could have ordered all the rest to take the oath promptly and to expiate that past wickedness, and to turn away all suspicion of such plotting in future. Nor did he show even common sense, since this prohibition is more the work of a boring mind than of a wise one.

units.la: Cui enim bono? Nihil lucri, plurimum incommodi allatura: exin durior futura suorum conditio, & Breve hoc illos in noua vada & breuia detrusurum. Iam verò illud, in quo, Theologiæ, prudentiæ, sensati hominis vestigium vix vllum; quæ fraus amoliri à Pontifice, & vel confictum alicubi in angulo suspicari, vel si à Roma fuit, per male feriatos quosdam Pontifici excussum esse?
units.tr: For to whose good? It would bring no gain and very much harm: their condition would thereafter become harsher, and this Breve would drive them into new shallows and shoals. And what of this, in which there is scarcely any trace of theology, prudence, or a sensible man: what fraud was to be removed by the Pontiff, and whether he should suspect a forgery somewhere in a corner, or, if it came from Rome, whether it was extorted from the Pontiff by certain idle men?

units.la: Omninò autem in novo hoc pharmaco, secus se res habet quàm Tortus autumat. Primùm, eo sumpto, deterius agro quàm antè: tum, nulla id aegri culpa, sed medici ipsius, qui lenire debuit pharmaco, & (manifesto errore) quo lenire debuit, magis irritauit. Non geminauit culpam; Imò bis geminauit. Gemina culpa, dum quod temere primò fecerat, iterum iam facit, vt consulto fecisse videatur: Deinde gemina altera; prior, interdicti ante Iuramenti, ne iurent; posterior, indicti iam periurij, vt abiurent. Fraudem detexit: At nulla erat quam detegeret; (suprà docui) Tenebras dissipauit; Tenebrae verò etiam manent, nec lucem vllam appoluit Brcui fecundo [?]; quo periculum fieret, quod obscurum in primo: tantùm eàdem, quà priùs, caligine, rem involuit denuo. Veritati aditum patefecit; Imò posteriore hoc, quasi nouo repagulo, aditus ei magis etiam interclusus. Et hoc tu spirituale pharmacum appellas? Egregium verò pharmacum; egregius medicus, qui temperauit, quo hausto recurrit acrior paroxysmus: morbus aegro, medico moeror augetur. Quanquam de medico minùs curandum: illum credo non conficiet moeror. Interim aegri tinguntur, qui ipsi cùm vident, peiore loco quotidie res suas; demissâ voce (sic tamen vt audiantur interdum) mutare sic solent; Durus Pater Papa Paulus, si mitigare noluit mala nostra, at grauiora non redderet, nec semper de tolerando onere verba faceret; aliquando de tollendo cogitaret; vtinam verò manum saltem, à Brevibus scripitandis continueret.
units.tr: But in this new remedy the matter stands altogether otherwise than Tortus claims. First, having taken it, the patient is worse off than before; then, this is the fault not of the patient but of the physician himself, who ought to have soothed with the remedy, and (by a manifest error) irritated more by that very means by which he ought to have soothed. He did not double the fault; rather he doubled it twice. A double fault: first, what he had done rashly he now does again, so that he seems to have done it deliberately; then a second double: the first being the prohibition before the oath, that they should not swear; the second being the command, after the perjury, that they should abjure. "He has exposed the fraud": but there was none to expose (as I showed above). "He has dispelled the shadows": but the shadows remain, and he has brought no light to bear by a second Breve, by which the danger might be tested, which was obscure in the first; he has only wrapped the matter again in the same darkness as before. "He has opened a way to the truth": nay, by this second barrier, as it were, the way is still more closed off to it. And do you call this a spiritual remedy? An excellent remedy indeed; an excellent physician, who tempered it so that, once drunk, a sharper paroxysm returns: the disease grows for the patient, and for the physician grief. Yet there is less need to be concerned about the physician: I believe grief will not destroy him. Meanwhile the patients, who themselves see their affairs growing worse day by day, are accustomed to mutter thus in low voices (yet so that they are sometimes overheard): "Hard Father, Pope Paul, if he was unwilling to lessen our evils, at least he might not make them heavier, nor always speak of enduring the burden; sometimes he might think of removing it; would that at least he would restrain his hand from writing Breves."

units.la: IN breuiculo breuiore id agit Tortus; vt siqui iurârunt Iuramentum, abiurent denuo. Quid opus? faciat Pontifex ipse, qui iurati, vt iniurati sint. Tu hoc posse dixisti; nodos scilicet hos resoluere: iam ipsos qui nexi sunt, iubes abrumpere, & redire illis iuramenta per iugulum. Sed abrumpant sanè, si illicitum: An doces illicitum? Petis, imò sumis hoc, quod nemo tibi dederit, atque hæc ferè est Papiensis probatio. Nos licitum probamus, quia congenitum, quia nobiscum in ipso ortu coortum, quia de iure naturali: quando, cuius quisque patriæ, vt pars toti: patriæ patri, vt membrum capiti subijcitur, atque obligatur; naturæ nexu, qui omni sponsione fortior. Nec tu hoc negas (nec enim potes) sed duertus[?] alió vt dicas, neminem in ortu illo obligari ad Pontificis potestatem abnegandam. Non sanè ad abnegandam, nisi in casu, quo potestas eius, nexui primo illi atque naturali contraueniat. Vt patriæ in quâ; ita Principi sub quo nascitur quis, ex Iuramento congenito debetur ab eo fides. Affirmatiua hæc: ad affirmatiuam semper sequitur negatio oppositi. Siqua ergo me potestas adiget ad fidei oppositum, naturâ sic debitæ & datæ: illam mihi potestatem abnegare, religio non erit. Tenetur quis summo Principi contra hostes suos, quicunque tandem illi sunt, opem ferre? Eo ipso tenetur opem non ferre, imò opem negare hosti cuicunq;, summum illum Principem suum, oppugnanti. Nexus ergo, quem dixi naturalis, haud quenquam obligat ad potestatem Pontificis abnegandam, nisi in casu, quo potestatem suam exercet Ponufex, quo minùs subdito nexum illum suum naturalem retinere liceat. Vel (si ita malis) potestatem Pontificis non negabit, negabit impotentiam. Potestas enim quæ ad malum, potestas non est, impotentia est. Malum autem naturæ legem violare: contra quam siquid moliatur Pontifex, impotentia illa in illo est, potestas non est. Potestas enim non datur, nisi contra vitia, contra quæ si Pontifex potens esse nolit, sed contra bonum naturæ nexum, non potestatem ei vllam negabit quispiam, sed hanc quam negat, negabit esse potestatem.
units.tr: In a very short little work Tortus aims at this: that if any have sworn the oath, they should abjure it again. What need? Let the Pontiff himself make them, who have been sworn, unsworn. You said this could be done; namely, to loosen these knots: now you order those who are bound to break them, and you give back the oaths to them by the throat. But let them break them indeed, if it is unlawful: do you prove it unlawful? You seek, or rather you assume, what no one has granted you, and this is almost the Papist proof. We prove it lawful, because it is innate, because it arose with us at birth, because it is from natural law: when each man is subjected and bound to his country as a part to the whole, and to his father as a limb to the head, by the bond of nature, which is stronger than any promise. Nor do you deny this (for indeed you cannot), but by turning aside you say something else, that no one at that birth is bound to renounce the Pontiff's power. Certainly not to renounce it, except in the case in which his power conflicts with that first and natural bond. As a man owes faith to the country in which he is born, so he owes faith to the prince under whom he is born, by a congenital oath. This is an affirmative: to an affirmative there always follows the denial of the opposite. If, therefore, some power compels me to the opposite of faith, with the nature of the debt so given and granted, it will not be a matter of religion for me to renounce that power. Is anyone bound to bring aid to the supreme prince against his enemies, whoever they may be? By that very fact he is bound not to bring aid, nay, to deny aid to any enemy whatsoever who attacks that supreme prince of his. Therefore the bond which I called natural does not bind anyone to renounce the Pontiff's power, except in the case in which the Pontiff exercises his power so as to forbid the subject to retain that natural bond of his. Or (if you prefer it so), he will not deny the Pontiff's power, but will deny his impotence. For a power that is directed to evil is not power, it is impotence. But to violate the law of nature is evil: if the Pontiff attempts anything against it, that impotence is in him, and it is not power. For power is given only against vices; if the Pontiff is unwilling to be powerful against these, but against the good bond of nature, no one will deny him any power, but what he denies, he will deny to be power.

units.la: Quod pòst affers, sublime certè est, & de nouâ Kabalâ, forte à Torto primùm, vix enim credo priùs, à quoquam promulgatâ. Ortus cuique duplex; naturalis, [supernaturalis: Certè. Est vero cuique, naturali in ortu, iuramentum connaturale ad obediendum Principi Politico: De hoc etiam conuenit. At est etiam cuique in ortu supernaturali, seu [illegible, ~8 letters] su[?], congenitum aliud, & tacitum iuramentum, ad obediendum Principi spirituali, Christi vicario, Papæ. Malè, congenitum, primò; Subditi quidem gignuntur, & nascuntur, non fiunt: Christianus nemo vel gignitur, vel nascitur, sed fit. Non ergo congenitum ei, qui genitus non est. Bene tamen certè dixit, tacitum. Tacitum enim quidem, &, si voles, surdum iuramentum hoc, adde etiam, si libet, absurdum. Tacitum; tacuerunt enim de eo, ante te omnes. Surdum; nemo enim audijt. absurdum; quia extra modum, absonum, vt cuiquam in Baptismo nostro præstetur iusiurandum, præterquam Seruatori Christo; aut cuiusquam in nomine, præterquàm Sanctissimæ Trinitatis. Nam quò te propripis? An tu personam quartam, ascriptam iam vis Baptismo? Et cui tandem Baptismo? non Iohannis; nam nondum tum in rerum natura Pontifex; Non Enti autem, vix quispiam sponsionem facit. Sed neque Baptismo Christi. Qui potuit, cum post resurrectionem Christi demum, Petrus pascere iussus? priùs enim Dominus tuus non permittit. Quotquot ergo ante illum diem baptizati, cùm nullus præter Christum Princeps spiritualis esset; nulli præter eum Principi illud tum iusiurandum in se receperunt. Tum Petrus ipse, (nam & ipse Baptismo initiatus est) an iurauit iuramentum hoc? Cui verò iurauit? Aut an fuit illi Baptismus peculiaris per se? At nos hîc, qui scripturas solas sapimus, nec ad Kabalam vestram admisi sumus, mysterium illud credidimus à Christo institutum, abluendis peccatis nostris, nobisque in mysticum corpus suum, quod est Ecclesia cuius ipse caput, initiandis. Atque vt beneficium hoc totum nobis ab Illo vno: ita vni Illi proinde officium hoc totum deberi à nobis, vni Illi præstandum esse, nec præter eum, mortalium vlli. Credo autem Apostolorum sæculo inauditum, vt in quenquam illorum baptizatus tum quisquam fuerit, præterquam in Christum solum, & mortem eius, cui & consepultus est, quem & induit. Nec qui tum baptizabant, in nomine suo id faciebant; non Paulus Crispum in suo, nec Petrus Cornelium in suo; nec sæculo, nec à sæculo Apostolorum, tale quid auditum. Vnde ergo emerfit, nouum hoc & nuperum dogma? In Baptismo nostro vel expressam, vel tacitam nos sponsionem facere de vllo alio Capite, vel agnoscendo, vel ei obediendo, quàm CHRISTO solo capite, cuius membra sumus pro parte suâ quisq;: CHRISTO, qui est Saluator corporis sui: CHRISTO, qui est primogenitus ex mortuis vt sit in omnibus ipse Primatum tenens: Capite, ex quo totum corpus compactum est & connexum, recipitq; ab ea & veritatis sensum & Charitatis motum per influxum gratiæ? Tum, (quod ante memini monere me,) si Vicarius modo est, non is honor haberi Vicario solet, vt iuretur ei fides, cùm Principi ipsi tantùm proprius ille sit, & peculiaris. Deniq; si iuretur etiam; at illud Principi Politico interpositum in ortu naturali, prius est; vestrum hoc, posterius. Prius enim nascimur, quàm renascimur; prius quod naturale, deinde quod spirituale; illud natura; vestrum hoc, gratia. Naturam autem gratia non tollit, non labefactari, qu[?]in perfici potiùs, & quasi nouâ accessione firmari magis; [?]ut vero diu iam in Theologorum Scholis receptum est. Idem enim vtriusque Legis author, & natura, & gratia: quod posuit vnâ, non tollit altera; nec superinducit gratiam, vt soluat natura vinculum, sed vt astringat magis; vt, apud nullos tam sancta sint natura officia, quàm apud Christianos. Superueniente ergo pòst, Baptismo, natura nexui non derogatur, nec eo fit, quò minùs sua in quemque officia cõstent, filij in Patrem, Patriæ filij in Patriæ patrem. Quare, si à capite rem arcessas, obtinemus. Desponsam in ortu ipso fidem, posterius aliquod siue recentius Iuramentum (si modò est aliquod tale) exauthorare non potest. Hoc verò nostrum, de fide, obsequio, defensione Principi præstandâ, expressio tantùm est illius primi: quocirca nullo modo licebit eiurare. Et tu frustra ortum supernaturalem inuocas, vel opem exposcis à Baptismo, qui, ad datam natura dictante fidem, vel laxandam, vel minuendam, rogatu tuo manum suam nunquam vllo modo porriget. Nihil ergo affers, cur, quod bene iuratum est Iuramentum, eiurari debeat. Atque hæc ad Breue, breuius breue.
units.tr: What you say next is certainly lofty, and it is a new Kabbalah, perhaps first put forward by Torto, for I hardly believe anyone promulgated it before. "Every person's birth is twofold: natural and supernatural." Certainly. And indeed, in natural birth, each person has a connate oath of obedience to the political prince: on this too we agree. But in supernatural birth, too, each person has another congenital and tacit oath, of obedience to the spiritual prince, Christ's vicar, the Pope. Here you go wrong, first in calling it "congenital." Subjects are indeed begotten and born, not made; no Christian is begotten or born as a Christian, but becomes one. So it cannot be congenital to one who was not begotten. You certainly did well, however, to call it "tacit." For tacit it is, and if you like, deaf as well; add, if you please, "absurd" too. Tacit: indeed, all who went before you have been silent about it. Deaf: for no one has heard it. Absurd: because it is beyond all measure absurd that anyone should be made to swear an oath in our Baptism other than to the Saviour Christ, or that anyone should be baptized in any name other than that of the most holy Trinity. For where are you going with this? Do you now want to add a fourth person to Baptism? And to what Baptism, pray? Not John's, for the Pope did not yet exist in the nature of things at that time; and no one makes a pledge to a non-existent person. But neither is it the Baptism of Christ. How could Peter have been ordered to feed the flock, when that was only after Christ's resurrection? For before then your Lord did not permit it. So all who were baptized before that day, since no one but Christ was spiritual prince, took on no such oath to any prince other than him. Then Peter himself (for he too was initiated by Baptism), did he swear this oath? And to whom did he swear it? Or was there for him a peculiar Baptism of its own? But we here, who are wise in Scripture alone and have not been admitted to your Kabbalah, believe that rite was instituted by Christ to wash away our sins, and to initiate us into his mystical body, which is the Church, of which he is the head. And just as this whole benefit comes to us from that one alone, so this whole duty is owed by us to that one alone, to be rendered to him and to no other mortal. I believe, moreover, that in the age of the Apostles it was unheard of that anyone baptized at that time should be baptized into any name except Christ's alone, and his death, "with whom also he was buried, and whom he put on." Nor did those who then baptized do so in their own name: Paul did not baptize Crispus in his own name, nor Peter Cornelius in his; nothing of the kind was heard of in that age or in the age after the Apostles. Whence, then, has this new and recent dogma emerged? In our Baptism we make no pledge, either express or tacit, to acknowledge or obey any head other than Christ alone, "of whom we are each members in our own part": Christ, "who is the Saviour of his body": Christ, "who is the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he may have the pre-eminence": the head, "from whom the whole body, fitly joined and knit together, receives through the influence of grace both the sense of truth and the motion of charity." Then (as I recalled earlier that I should point out), even if he is a vicar, that honour is not usually paid to a vicar, that faith should be sworn to him, since that is peculiar to the prince himself alone. Finally, even if it is sworn, the oath sworn to the political prince at natural birth is prior; yours is posterior. For we are born before we are reborn; "first what is natural, then what is spiritual": the former is nature, yours is grace. But grace does not take away nature, nor does it weaken it, but rather perfects it and, as it were, strengthens it by a new addition, as has long been received in the schools of the theologians. For the author of both laws is the same, both of nature and of grace; what he has established by the one, the other does not take away; nor does he introduce grace in order to loosen the bond of nature, but to bind it more tightly, so that among none are the duties of nature so holy as among Christians. Therefore, when Baptism follows later, the bond of nature is not weakened, nor does it follow that the duties of each person toward nature cease to hold: children toward their father, and the children of the fatherland toward the father of the fatherland. Wherefore, if you fetch the matter from its source, we gain our point. The faith pledged at birth itself cannot be annulled by a later or more recent oath (if there is any such). Our oath, however, concerning faith, obedience and defence to be rendered to the prince, is only the expression of that first one; therefore on no account will it be lawful to renounce it. And you invoke a supernatural birth in vain, or you ask help from Baptism, which, to the faith given as nature dictates, will never in any way extend its hand to loosen or diminish it at your request. You therefore bring nothing to show why an oath that has been rightly sworn ought to be renounced. And so much for the Breve, "briefer brief."

units.la: (*) PRÆTERVECTI iam sumus Breuia & Vada Pontificis. Nihil ibi profundum; depressa omnia. Ventum iam, ad Cardinalis Epistolam, dicerem non tam vadosam: nisi, pariter ad laudem, pariter, ad conuitia moueri illum, Tortus monuisset. Nescias quid agendum: laudes, non laudes, par gratia est: Ad dogmata Catholica, ad sinceritatem fidei, sensus ei inest aliquis: ad reliqua, stupidum planè prædicat. Ergo ille, vt videtur, plusquam homo est, vt nec benedictione, nec maledictione moueatur: Tortus autem, minùs quàm homo, qui etsi laudes Domini sui, forte, at conuitia tamen, quæ dicit in cum torta, dissimulare non debuit. Sacellanus merito exsacellandus; qui, vtcunque minùs moueatur Dominus ipsius; tamen is irâ se tortum monstare, Papiam, Romam, Capuam, permiscere debuit. Cùm non fecerit, & ad contumelias (quas dicit) in Dominum, tam lentus sit, (quod Itali vix faciunt, præsertim Capellani) in suspicionem adducor, vt credam, non hîc personam Torti, sed personatum Tortum in scenam nobis prodijsse; vereor autem ne Cardinalis ipse sit. Potest enim Cardinalis contumelijs non moueri: sed quis, ingeri conuitia in Dominum suum, Sacellanus ferret, æquo animo? quis Sacellanum ferret, sic ferentem? Characterem vbique Cardinalis agnoscas, sed clarâ luce clarius, duxisse hîc calamum. Nec enim vox Sacellanum sonat; Dominus ipse certè.
units.tr: (*) We have now sailed past the shallows and shoals of the Pontiff. Nothing there is deep; everything is low-lying. We have now come to the Cardinal's letter, which I would not call so shallow, had not Torto warned that it moves him equally to praise and to abuse. One does not know what to make of it: "praises, not praises," the grace is the same. As to Catholic doctrines and sincerity of faith, he shows some feeling; on the rest he proclaims himself plainly stupid. So he, it seems, is more than a man, since he is moved neither by blessing nor by cursing; and Torto is less than a man, who, though he perhaps praises his lord, ought not to have overlooked the abuse which he hurls at him in his writing. The chaplain deserves to be unchaplained; who, however little his lord may be moved, should at least have shown himself twisted with anger, and stirred up Pavia, Rome, Capua. Since he has not done so, and is so slack toward the insults (which he says) against his lord (as Italians hardly ever are, especially chaplains), I am led to suspect, and to believe, that it was not the person of Torto who came forward on our stage here, but Torto in a mask; and I fear that it is the Cardinal himself. For the Cardinal may be unmoved by insults; but what chaplain would bear abuse hurled at his lord with an equable mind? Who would put up with such a chaplain, bearing it so? You may recognise the Cardinal's character everywhere, but more clearly than clear daylight, here he has drawn the pen. For the voice is not that of a chaplain; certainly it is the lord himself.

units.la: At, illud de benedictione & maledictione, simul ex uno ore prodeunte, magis Tortum sapit. Coniecit enim in equuleum, & fidiculis suis prauè dctorsit [?] & verba & mentem Apologiæ [?]; in quâ nusquam nisi blanda mentio (nusquam penè sine laude aliquâ) de personâ Cardinalis. Sed habet tamen recognitione digna quædam (& ipse iam quædam recognouit) habet & alia forte quæ nondum recognouit; de quibus cùm sermo est Apologia, non blanditur ei sanè, scapham, scapham dicit, & hoc, malè tu dicis, maledicere [?]. Verè enim & benè taxatur, quod malè ab eo dictum, seruatâ tamen personæ eius (quàm par fuit) ratione, nec vsquam vel verbo violatæ. At te, credo, malè habet, quòd in personam eius non inuolârit, quod tu facis vbique, ita petulanter, quasi satiram scribas, & quasi ex ore, quasi ex calamo, sola quidem ubi maledictio procedat.
units.tr: But that remark about "blessing and cursing proceeding at once from one mouth" savours more of Torto. For he has thrown into the rack, and with his strings has wrongly twisted both the words and the meaning of the Apology; in which there is nowhere anything but flattering mention (nowhere almost without some praise) of the Cardinal's person. Yet it contains certain things worthy of reconsideration (and he himself has already reconsidered some), and perhaps it contains others which he has not yet reconsidered; about which, when the Apology speaks, it does not flatter him at all, but calls a spade a spade, and says this: "you speak ill, to curse." For what is ill said by him is rightly and well censured, yet with due regard, as far as was fitting, for his person, and nowhere violated even by a word. But you, I believe, are vexed that he has not swooped down upon his person, as you do everywhere, so wantonly, as if you were writing a satire, and as if from the mouth, as if from the pen, only cursing were to come forth.

units.la: Duo sunt autem apud nos Iuramenta: alterum diu iam de Primatu Regio ad res Ecclesiae; alterum, quod nuper editum, de Rege incolumi seruando. Status causae hic iam est. An liceat Iuramentum hoc suscipere nuper Edicto propositum. Qui posteriore hoc iam omisso, totus fertur in prius illud, annon aberrat à statu causae? Fateris ipse rem, cum dicis Cardinalem ad detegendas nescio quas fraudes collineasse: Detexit ergo fraudem, sed reliquit causam. Sed quae tandem fraus illa? Omnino enim sine fraude hic res geritur. Si fidem cuiusquam & religionem explorare volumus, defertur illi Iuramentum illud prius de Primatu; perraro id, & perpaucis: Si non fidem, sed fidelitatem pertentare, proponitur secundum hoc pro incolumitate Regia. Vbi insidiae hic vllae? Vis scire, Lector, vbi? Vis & aliud hic à Torto mysterium discere? In eo; quòd non solum iurent, quid praestare debeant erga Regem, sed etiā quid possit vel non possit summus Pontifex. Nec prius illud tamen valde sollicitos habet, quid possit. Possit, quantum vis, quantum vult ipse; quanto plus possit, tanto melius, deponere, disponere, inuadendi, tumultuandi, vim afferendi authoritate dare; leges, vota, iuramenta soluere: sed, quid non possit, id demum grande nefas attingere. Quid enim non potest Pontifex? Quis potestati eius limitem ponat vel metam? Hoc illud erat scilicet tam fraudulentum, in modificato illo Iuramento, quòd modificata ibi potestas Pontificis, vt non possit in Regem nostrum (& quod non in illum, nec in alios) omnia, pro suo arbitratu, statuere, facere, fieri iubere. Hæc enim causa erat (ait Tertus) cur Cardinalis ibi dixerit Catholicam fidem peti. Illius enim fidei, articulus est, ne quis, quacunque de causa attingere audeat, quid possit vel non possit summus Pontifex. Oceanus enim limites suos habet, vltra quos progredi non potest: potestas Pontificia non habet. Atque hæc illa fraus est, quam vt detegeret Cardinalis, aberrauit à causâ, nec sine fraude tamen.
units.tr: There are two oaths among us: the one concerning the royal primacy in ecclesiastical affairs, which has long been in use, and the other, recently published, concerning the preservation of the King's person. Here is the state of the question: whether it is lawful to take the oath proposed in the recent edict. Having now set aside this latter oath, does he who is wholly carried off to the former one not stray from the state of the question? You yourself admit the matter when you say that the Cardinal aimed at detecting I know not what frauds: "He detected the fraud, but he left the cause." But what fraud was that, after all? For here indeed the business is carried on wholly without fraud. If we wish to test anyone's faith and religion, that former oath concerning the primacy is offered to him; this is very rarely done, and to very few. If we seek to test not faith but fidelity, the second oath, for the safety of the King, is proposed. Where is any snare here? Do you want to know, Reader, where? Do you also want to learn from Tortus some other mystery here? It lies in this: that they swear not only what they ought to render to the King, but also what the supreme Pontiff can or cannot do. Yet that former oath does not greatly trouble itself over what he can do. He can do as much as he likes, as much as he wishes; the more he can, the better: to depose, to dispose, to grant authority for invading, for stirring up tumults, for using force, to dissolve laws, vows and oaths. But what he cannot do, that alone is touched as a great impiety. For what can the Pontiff not do? Who sets a limit or boundary to his power? This, clearly, was that so fraudulent thing in the modified oath: the Pontiff's power was modified there so that he could not (and this not only against our King but against others too) decree, do, or order everything at his own pleasure. For this, says Tertus, was the reason why the Cardinal there said that the Catholic faith was being sought. For it is an article of that faith that no one, for whatever reason, dare touch what the supreme Pontiff can or cannot do. "For the ocean has its limits, beyond which it cannot advance: the Pontifical power has none." And this is that fraud which the Cardinal, in order to detect it, strayed from the cause, and yet not without fraud.

units.la: Dicit enim peti Catholicam fidem de Primatu; dicendum erat, peti Catholicam fidem de omnipotentiâ Sedis Apostolicæ. Potest Primatus (credo) consistere, etsi aliquid non possit: omnipotentia vero non potest, nisi possit omnia: Atqui de illâ hic agitur Pontificis omnipotentiâ, Symboli noui parte faciendâ; noui (inquam) Symboli, quod nunc Roma procudi dicitur, cuius præludia vidimus in Paulo 5°. depicto, cum hac inscriptione: Summo Monarchæ, Vicedeo, & Omnipotentiæ Pontificiæ propugnatori acerrimo. Nos vero ingenuè fatemur, contineri eâ Iuramenti formulâ, & quid subditi præstare debeant erga Regem, & quòd Pontifici potestas nulla prohibendi ne præstent, quod præstare debent; ne faciant, quod officij sui est, vt faciant; ne reddant Cæsari, quæ Cæsaris sunt. Quòd nisi hoc tentet Pontifex, nihil ibi contra, quem gerere amat, Primatum. Nec enim potentia eius in formulâ illâ attingitur absolutè, tantùm ex hypothesi, vt quæ, conditionalis sit tota; nec, nisi dissponat de regnis non suis; exteros ad invasionem, subditos ad rebellionem sollicitet. Quo casu, fas, & affirmare, & iurare, quòd hoc non possit Pontifex.
units.tr: For he says that the Catholic faith concerning the primacy is sought; he ought to have said that the Catholic faith concerning the omnipotence of the Apostolic See is sought. The primacy can, I suppose, stand even though it cannot do something; but omnipotence cannot be unless it can do all things. And yet what is at issue here is the omnipotence of the Pontiff, to be made a part of the new Creed; a new Creed (I say) which is now said to be forged at Rome, the preludes of which we have seen in the picture of Paul the Fifth, with this inscription: "To the Supreme Monarch, Vice-god, and most fierce champion of Pontifical omnipotence." We, however, frankly confess that this formula of oath contains both what subjects ought to render to the King, and that the Pontiff has no power to forbid them to render what they ought to render, to prevent them from doing what is their duty, or from rendering to Caesar what is Caesar's. Unless the Pontiff attempts this, there is nothing there against the primacy, which he loves to bear. For his power is not touched in that formula absolutely, but only under a hypothesis, so that the whole of it is conditional; nor unless he were to dispose of kingdoms not his own, and stir up foreigners to invasion and subjects to rebellion. In that case it is right both to affirm and to swear that the Pontiff cannot do this.

units.la: Aperit se etiam magis Sectione proximâ. Primò tamen philosophatur pauca, de Rono[?], ex causâ integrâ; Malo, ex singulis defectibus: vt ergo juramentum sit malum, vt respuendum, non id necessarium esse, vt singulæ eius partes malæ sint; satis enim si vel una sit mala. Sed huic (si vllam partem æqui dixisset Pontifex) Regis optimi clementiâ abundè iam antè satisfactum erat, cùm facta fides, delata conditio, si notâssets, quæ vna illa esset, quæ plures, vel delendi eas, vel benignâ interpretatione mollendi. Tum verò, non partem vllam, substantiam ipsam damnavit, & scopum: iam ad partes nos revocat; & si de illis vel una maculam habet, satis in eo putat ad totum reijciendum. Ita illic, vbi pars vlla corrigi potuit, totum displicet: hic, vbi totum damnare non potest, pars vlla sufficit, si ad eius stomachum non sit. Nam de quatuordecim illis propositionibus (quæ quasi artus sunt & membra Iuramenti) plurimas dicit attingere Sacrosanctam potestatem Vicarij Christi. Plurima illæ, quot sint, & id quoque mox narrat subsequente sectione, vndecim scilicet de quatuordecim. Tres tantùm excipit, putà primam & duas vltimas; quanquam penultimam arrosit iam antè, quæ est de plenâ authoritate Iuramenti deferendi; sed tres istas iam excipit, quæ tam fœlices fuerunt, vt nusquam in ijs vel nomen Papæ legeretur. Vbi enim Papæ nomen (quasi esset in nomine illo contagio quædam) malæ sunt omnes, eas omnes reijcit: reijcit autem, eo quòd imminutum eant[?] Pontificis potestatem; quòd dicant hoc vel illud, Papam non posse, cui nempe liceant, penes quem sint, qui possit omnia: Hæc est enim fides Catholica. Hic tamen si non tergiversari, sed bona fide rem gerere velles, undecim illus, quas sic vellicare videri vis, undecim alias opponere debuisti, pro more scholæ, contradictorias, ut sic collato pede, conserta manu, non cauponari bellum liceret, sed belligerare. Non est factum. Quare autem non, Lector facilè coniecerit. Deforme enim spectaculum, undecim illus in terminis suis, sic contradicentes, sub uno aspectu ponere; caput quatiat, contrahat frontem Lectoris, si videat; videat, detractâ larua, Ecclesiam vestram, quàm parum propitia sit Regibus. Quid ergo fit? Attingere dicis, undecim illus, primatum in spiritualibus. Quid si autem attingant, dum citra noxam? sed neque attingunt primatum in spiritualibus undecim, illæ; & tu, cum omnes debebas, duas tantùm delibas de undecim, nec illas tamen.
units.tr: He reveals himself even more in the following section. First, however, he philosophises a little: "on the good, from the whole cause; on the evil, from individual defects": so that the oath may be evil and to be rejected, it is not necessary that each of its parts be evil; for it is enough if even one is. But to this (if the Pontiff had said any part of what is right), the most excellent clemency of the King had already been fully satisfied, since it was made known and the condition offered, that if he had noted which one was the one and which the several, he might either delete them or soften them by a kindly interpretation. Then indeed he condemned not any part but the substance itself and the aim; now he recalls us to the parts, and if he finds a stain in even one of them, he thinks that is enough to reject the whole. Thus there, where some part could be corrected, the whole displeases him; here, where he cannot condemn the whole, any part suffices, if it is not to his taste. For concerning those fourteen propositions (which are as it were the limbs and members of the oath) he says that most of them touch the most sacred power of the Vicar of Christ. How many "most" they are, he also tells us soon after in the following section: namely eleven of the fourteen. He excepts only three, namely the first and the last two; although he had already gnawed at the penultimate, which concerns the full authority of administering the oath; but these three he now excepts, which were so fortunate that nowhere in them is even the name of the Pope to be read. For where the name of the Pope (as if there were some contagion in that name) is in all of them evil, he rejects all of them: he rejects them, moreover, because they diminish the Pontiff's power, because they say that this or that the Pope cannot do, to whom, forsooth, things are permitted, in whose hands they are, who can do all things: for this is the Catholic faith. Here, however, if you wished not to shuffle but to deal honestly, you ought to have set against those eleven, which you wish to seem to pluck at in this way, eleven others contradictory to them, according to the custom of the school; so that, foot to foot and hand to hand, the war would be waged not by hucksters but by fighters. This was not done. Why not, the Reader will easily guess. For it is an unsightly spectacle to place those eleven, contradicting one another in their terms, under a single view; the Reader would shake his head and knit his brow if he saw it; let him see, with the mask removed, how little your Church is favourable to Kings. What then is done? "You say that those eleven touch the primacy in spirituals." But what if they touch it without harm? Yet the eleven do not touch the primacy in spirituals at all; and you, when you ought to have touched all of them, merely nibbled at two of the eleven, and not even those.

units.la: Quæro enim, utrum Princeps hæreticus à Pontifice excommunicari possit, an ulli quæ ibi sit propositioni repugnet? an uspiam ibi mentio hæretici? an uspiam quem possit vel non possit Pontisex excommunicare? Lustra oculis, designa locum, appone numerum. Videbis tuam hanc causam {a}spiritualem nullam ibi esse. Hæc ibi nusquam est: Dic de illis quæ sunt. 1. Potest Pontifex deponere Reges. 2. Potest disponere de regnis. 3. Potest extraneo cuicunq; inuadendi licentiam dare. 4. Potest subditos contra Regem suum armare. 5. Potest vim personæ Regis asserendi, authoritatè concedere. 6. Potest interdicere, nè Regem defendant. 7. Potest, siquas sciant contra Regem initas proditiones, eas, ne retegant. 8. Potest instillare opinionem hanc: Principes à subditis deponi posse, aut occidi. An & hæ causæ spirituales sunt? An hæ Primatum eius in spiritualibus attingunt? In Juramento insunt omnes hæ. Cur tu igitur has, cur decem de hijs, quæ sic (ut ais) Pontificem attingunt, non excusisti? imò cur non attigisti? Piguit, credo; vidisti nihil in illis spirituale, nisi {a}spiritualia nequitiæ forte, quæ dicit Apostolus.
units.tr: For I ask whether a heretical Prince can be excommunicated by the Pontiff, or whether anything in that proposition opposes it; whether there is any mention of a heretic there; whether there is anything there about what the Pontiff can or cannot excommunicate. Scan with your eyes, mark the place, add the number. You will see that your cause is not spiritual there at all. It is nowhere there: say something about those that are. 1. The Pontiff can depose Kings. 2. He can dispose of kingdoms. 3. He can grant to any foreigner licence to invade. 4. He can arm subjects against their King. 5. He can grant authority to assert the force of the King's person. 6. He can forbid them to defend the King. 7. He can, if they know of any treasons begun against the King, forbid them to reveal them. 8. He can instil this opinion: that princes can be deposed or killed by their subjects. Are these causes also spiritual? Do these touch his primacy in spirituals? All these are contained in the Oath. Why then did you not excuse these, why did you not excuse the ten of these which, as you say, touch the Pontiff in this way; nay, why did you not touch them? You were ashamed, I suppose; you saw nothing spiritual in them, unless perhaps "spiritual wickednesses," as the Apostle says.

units.la: QVasi[?] de lubrico loco igitur elapsus, citò recipit inde sed ad excommunicandi potestatem in Juramento negatam Pontifici; nec tamen ibi negatam uspiam: quàmq; ille negatam & hîc & alibi, sæpe iam, sed frustrà, & falsò semper asserit. Non obstat Juramentû, quò minùs sententiam si volet proferat; id modò agit ut.
units.tr: As if, having slipped away from a slippery place, he quickly retreats from there to the power of excommunication, denied in the Oath to the Pontiff; yet it is nowhere denied there; and he asserts, here and elsewhere, often now, but in vain, and always falsely, that it is denied. The Oath does not stand in the way of his pronouncing a sentence if he wishes; he merely aims at this: that the sentence pronounced should not stand in the way of subjects remaining in the faith, etc., or of their performing their duty even against the wishes of the Pontiff; and that they should not wish for that freedom of a false name, by which the Pope is accustomed to free them from their due subjection.

units.la: {a} Eph.4.12. vt non obstet sententia illa prolata, quò minùs maneant in fide subditi, &c vel inuito Pontifice officiū faciant; ac illam falsi nominis libertatem nolint, quā solet liberare Papa à debitâ per eos subiectione. Et cur tu hic populū nominas, quasi gentem vel coetum per se, &c sui iuris, quos Iuramentum dicit vllos subditorum suorum: subditi autem sui dum sint, Catholici an Haeretici sint, nihil interest; reddere debent Regi, quā debent obedientiam; quo debito, non magis liberare eos potest Pontifex, quàm aere alieno? Quodsi authoritatē habet à fide liberandi, unde habet? Quo authore habet? vbi in sacris literis potestas haec illi data? Nos locum notamus, vbi {b}Christus reddi iubet, vbi {c}Apostolus [?]id est debita dicit: Tu fac, alium notes, si habeas modò, vbi ne reddantur, quae sic debita sunt, authoritatem cuiquam indulsit, vel Christus, vel Apostolus, quenquam liberandi.
units.tr: Eph. 4.12. So that the sentence pronounced does not prevent the subjects from remaining in the faith, or from performing their duty even against the will of the Pope; and so that they do not wish to have that freedom of a false name, by which the Pope is accustomed to free them from the subjection owed by them. And why do you here name the people, as if they were a nation or a community in its own right and self-governing, whom your Oath calls any of its subjects? But so long as they are his subjects, it makes no difference whether they are Catholics or heretics; they must render to the King the obedience they owe. From that debt, can the Pope free them no more than from a debt of money? If he has authority to release from faith, whence does he have it? By whose authority does he have it? Where in the sacred letters has this power been given to him? We note the place where Christ bids what is owed to be rendered, where the Apostle says what is owed. You do it: point out another, if you have one, where either Christ or an Apostle has granted anyone authority to release from paying what is so owed.

units.la: Nec enim Doctores tui Scholastici hic audiendi sunt, nec facultatem vllam habent, quo Christus, quo Apostoli nusquam liberarunt, eo, Pontifici, vt liberet, nouum ius faciendi. Scholastici enim Doctores tui, qui sunt, aut vnde? quàm verò antiqui? quo saeculo nati? Annon saeculo demum decimotertio emerserunt, post Henricum quartum, quintum, sextum; post Fredericum primum & secundum; post Philippum, Imperatores indignè habitos? Nonne postquàm Pontificibus illis vires adessent; virus hoc suum in Scholam effuderunt, & licere tum coepit hoc quod dicis, cùm quicquid libuit licuit, cùm quid posset vel non posset Papa nefas attingere? Aliùs verò repetenda vobis res est de iure magis adhuc antiquo, vltra scilicet saeculum Hildebrandi, qui, author libertatis huius, iuris conditor, doctrinae traditor fuit, qui primus grassari ausus in Henricum Caesarem. Vel vnum proferri vis à nobis Catholicum authorem cui, non probetur haec subditorum absolutio à debitâ Principi obedientiâ? Factum idiam antea, & plures vno prolati. Venericus, Conradus, Walthramus, Sigebertus, Eberhardus. Io. Parisiensis, Petrus de Vincis, Occam, Dantes, Marsil. Patauinus, Maior, Author Libri, cuius initium Rex pacificus. Nos vel vnum proferri volumus à vobis, qui ante Hildebrandum hoc fecerit, quiante Henricum quartum, passus fuerit. {a}Ante hunc non legimus aliquem, ait {a}Viterbiensis. Lego & relego (ait {b}Frisingensis) & nusquam inuenio quenquam ante hunc. {c}Gemblacensis verò; Cum pace omnium bonorum, hæc (inquit) novitas, non dicam hæresis, nec dum in mundo emerserat. Habes à tribus, qui circiter id tempus vixerunt, ex Italiâ, Germaniâ, Galliâ; ante Hildebrandum, quæ vobis Catholicæ iam fidei pars est, si non hæresin, novitatem tum quidem habitam fuisse. Hildebrandi de schola discipuli, Doctores tui omnes; ut, hîc iam inter nos controversia finis non sit, si inter illos nullæ sint controversiæ. Quis enim tum illorum ausus est hiscere? Quis aliter de Papâ, quàm cum stupore summo, cum interiectione (Papè) verbafacere? Alterius hæc fori sunt.
units.tr: Nor are your Scholastic teachers to be heard here, nor do they have any power by which Christ and the Apostles, who never released anyone, should give the Pope a new right to release. For what are your Scholastic teachers, and whence do they come? How ancient are they? In what century were they born? Did they not emerge only in the thirteenth century, after Henry IV, V and VI; after Frederick I and II; after Philip, emperors treated shamefully? Did they not, after those popes had gained strength, pour out their poison into the School, and did what you say begin to be lawful then, when whatever pleased was lawful, when it was a crime to touch on what the Pope could or could not do? But the matter must be taken up with you from an even older law, beyond the age of Hildebrand, who, author of this liberty, founder of the law, and transmitter of this doctrine, was the first to dare to rage against Henry the Emperor. Do you want us to produce a single Catholic author for you who does not approve this absolution of subjects from their due obedience to the Prince? That has been done before, and more than one. Ven[erius], Conrad, Walthram, Sigebert, Eberhard, John of Paris, Peter de Vinea, Ockham, Dante, Marsilius of Padua, the author of the book whose beginning is "Rex pacificus." We want you to produce one from yourselves who did this before Hildebrand, who suffered it under Henry IV. "Before him," says the Viterbiensis, "we do not read of anyone." "I read and re-read," says the Frisingensis, "and nowhere find anyone before him." But the Gembloux writer says: "With all good men's peace, this novelty, I will not say heresy, had not yet emerged in the world." You have it from three who lived about that time, from Italy, Germany and Gaul, that before Hildebrand what is now already a part of the Catholic faith for you was, if not heresy, then at least regarded as a novelty. The disciples of Hildebrand's school are all your teachers; so that there is no end to the controversy between us here, if there are no controversies among them. For who of them then dared to open his mouth? Who spoke of the Pope otherwise than with the greatest astonishment and the exclamation "Pape!"? These matters belong to another court.

units.la: Tum, quales ibi Doctores, talia Concilia; nec antiqua, quæ ab Innocentio 3o. modò sunt, post annos à Christo mille ducentos; neq; Generalia, quæ solùm, nec totius Europæ; nec libera, quæ, ut ais, erant, S V B Innocentio, Gregorio, Clemente, Leone, reliquis. Et verè quidem S V B iis erant, & illi S V P E R Concilia hæc, nec quicquam definitum ab istis, quæ S V B, nisi quod ab illo qui S V P E R præfinitum esset. Tum, neque sic, Concilia de ipsis, sed ipsi de se Pontifices verba faciunt, & insinuando dicuntur, quæ ibi dicuntur, potiùs quàm definiendo. Lateranense, nihil habet de Pontifice, tum neque si haberet, magnoperè id ad rem. Concilia enim non habent potestatem disponendi de rebus seculi; nec ulla constitutio Iuris Canonici potest Regno præiudicare, circa administrationem temporalem. Tria quæ succedunt, Lugduni duo, unum Vienna, nusquam in Conciliis locum habent: inter Decretalia Pontificum referuntur ex illis quædam, unde & tu citâsti. Sed quid dicit tamen Lugdunense prius? Cardinales eosdem obsecrantes, ut pensantes attentius quid iis immineat, cum agitur de creatione Vicarij Iesu Christi, &c. Quis hic loquitur? Pontifex ipse de seipso. Quid verò Lugdunense posterius? Unde & nos eiusdem Apostoli effecti successores, & ipsius Redemptoris in terris locum tenentes. Cuius verba? Pontificis; qui ipse se dicit locum Christi tenentem. In Viennensi autem; si ibi cum Summâ Trinitate & fide Catholicâ locum habeat Pontifex, mira narras; sed nusquam apparet locus ille, nisi de proœmio dicas, cui, nihil cum Concilio. Constantiense, {a}Dominus tuus reijcit ex numero Generalium, quæ probata sint, sed tamen illud quid refert? Inter articulos Iohanni Hus impositos (verè an secus non disputo,) damnatur unus, quòd diceret Papam non esse Vicarium Christi, vel Successorem Petri, si vitas moribus illi contrarius[?]. nempe Papam, qui nequam sit, Papam tamen esse. Quis negat? Quid hæc ad rem? Tum Lateranense sub Leone (etsi nec {a}vobis Concilium sit) tamen ex eo, quid affertur? Pastor æternus in soliditate Petræ, Petrum eiusque Successores instituit. Quis dicit? Leo decimus, qui, (si Leoni decimo credimus) Vicarius Christi est. Postulatum haud æquum sanè, ut credatur ipsis in causa ipsorum. Sed quò tamen evadent hæc: Ut sit Vicarius Christi Pontifex. Sit, si voles. Omnes Sacerdotes {b}Vicarij eius sunt. Vel si singularem malis, Imperator Vicarius est Dei, ita Anastasius Papa ad Anastasium Cæsarem: Rex quisque in Regno suo, ita Eleutherius ad Lucium nostrum: Etc {c}Carolus Magnus Rector Religionis & Ludovicus. Quare si in Vicario, si in Rectore vis vlla est; & ad illos spectat, ut Pontificem corrigant, & cogant in ordinem.
units.tr: Then, such as the teachers there, such are the Councils; nor the ancient ones, which are only from Innocent III, about twelve hundred years after Christ; nor are they General, which are only of part of Europe, not of the whole; nor free, which, as you say, were held under Innocent, Gregory, Clement, Leo and the rest. And indeed they were under them, and those men were above these Councils, and nothing was defined by those under them, except what had been settled beforehand by the one above. Then, the Councils do not speak about the popes, but the popes speak about themselves, and what is said there is said by way of hinting rather than defining. The Lateran [Council] says nothing about the Pope; and even if it did, that would matter little to the question. For Councils have no power to dispose of secular affairs, nor can any constitution of Canon Law prejudice a kingdom in the matter of temporal administration. The three that follow, two at Lyons and one at Vienne, have no place among the Councils: certain of them are reckoned among the Decretals of the Popes, and from these you also cited. But what does the earlier Lyons Council say? "The Cardinals, urging the same men to weigh more carefully what is threatened to them when the creation of the Vicar of Jesus Christ is concerned," etc. Who speaks here? The Pope himself, about himself. And what does the later Lyons Council say? "Since we too have been made successors of the same Apostle, and hold the place of the Redeemer himself on earth." Whose words are these? The Pope's, who himself says he holds the place of Christ. But in the Vienne Council, if the Pope has a place there together with the Holy Trinity and the Catholic faith, you tell wonderful things; yet that place appears nowhere, unless you mean the preface, which has nothing to do with the Council. As for Constance: your master rejects it from the number of the General Councils that have been approved; but what does that matter? Among the articles imposed on John Hus (whether truly or otherwise I do not dispute) one is condemned, namely that he said the Pope was not the Vicar of Christ or the successor of Peter, if his life were contrary to his morals; that is, that a Pope who is worthless is still Pope. Who denies it? What has this to do with the matter? Then the Lateran [Council] under Leo (though it is not a Council for you) yet from that, what is brought forward? "The eternal Shepherd, in the firmness of the rock, has established Peter and his successors." Who says this? Leo X, who (if we believe Leo X) is the Vicar of Christ. It is hardly a fair demand that he be believed in his own cause, in their own case. But where will all this end? Suppose that the Pope is the Vicar of Christ. Let it be so, if you wish. All priests are his vicars. Or if you prefer the singular, the Emperor is the Vicar of God; so Pope Anastasius to the Emperor Anastasius: "Each king in his own kingdom"; so Eleutherius to our Lucius; and so on. "Charles the Great, Rector of Religion," and Louis. Wherefore, if there is any force in a vicar or in a ruler, it belongs to them to correct the Pope and bring him into line.

units.la: Quòd si autem, causa hæc utique spiritualis sit, correptio etiam debet esse, qualis spiritualem causam & offensam decet, spiritualis & ipsa; nec vltra censuras spirituales, Rector spiritualis progredi. Nam fides & obseruantia, quâ Principi tenetur subditus, spirituale debitum non est, aut ecclesiasticum. Debetur enim & defertur Principi, qui extra Ecclesiam, vbi spirituale nihil est: solutio igitur ab illâ, spiritualis pœna non est, & cùm spiritualis pœna non sit, in causa spirituali, propter delictum spirituale infligi non debet. Congeneres enim æquum est esse culpam & pœnam; nec mucrone Episcopali feriri quæ in Rempublicam, nec gladio sæculari quæ in Ecclesiam: altera alterius opem, si videtur, exposcat, altera alterius fines non invadat. Eò vsque igitur recte procedit res. Hæresis causa spiritualis: excommunicatio pœna spiritualis. Plectere vult, cùm spiritualis Rector sit, crimen spirituale? plectat vero, sed pœna spiritualis: Sistat ibi modò. Sin & subditos fide soluendos, & terras, inuasioni subiiciendas porrò inferret[?], frustra inferret[?], egressus iam fines potestatis suæ; quæ vbi crimen spirituale, supplicio spirituali affecit, non habet vltra, quod agat. Suppleet eis censeo, quibus illius supplicij ius est: ipse non invadat, nec gladio rem gerat, quem Petrus antecessor eius in meliore multò causâ iussus est recondere: nec igne, quem Zebedei filios, Dominus de cœlo non est passus denocare. Manumittendi vel seruos, vel subditos: alienandi vel fundos: vel Imperia: ius illi nullum.
units.tr: But if this cause is indeed spiritual, the correction too ought to be of a kind that befits a spiritual cause and offence, itself spiritual; and the spiritual Ruler should proceed no further than spiritual censures. For the faith and obedience by which the subject is bound to the Prince is not a spiritual or ecclesiastical debt. For it is owed and rendered to the Prince, who is outside the Church, where there is nothing spiritual; therefore release from that is not a spiritual penalty, and since it is not a spiritual penalty, it ought not to be inflicted for a spiritual offence in a spiritual cause. For it is fair that the fault and the penalty be of the same kind; neither should what concerns the Commonwealth be struck with the episcopal crozier, nor what concerns the Church with the secular sword. Let each seek the other's help, if it seems good, but let neither invade the other's bounds. So far, then, the matter proceeds rightly. Heresy is a spiritual cause; excommunication is a spiritual penalty. If the spiritual Ruler wishes to punish a spiritual crime, let him punish it, but with a spiritual penalty: let him stop there. But if he were to go further and bring it about that subjects are released from their faith, and lands are made subject to invasion, he would bring it about in vain, having already passed the limits of his power; for where he has punished a spiritual crime with a spiritual penalty, he has no further power to act. I think those to whom the right of that punishment belongs should supply what is lacking; he himself should not invade, nor wage war with the sword, which his predecessor Peter was commanded to sheathe in a far better cause, nor with fire, which the Lord did not allow the sons of Zebedee to call down from heaven. As for manumitting either slaves or subjects, or alienating either lands or empires: he has no right to these.

units.la: Recurris dein ad Lateranense, quasi ad asylum: in eo triarij tui sunt. Quod, nescio cur maximum dicis, nisi propter 800. ibi Priores & Abbates; nam Episcoporum numero maiora multò fuerunt: nec cur celeberrimum; nec enim ibi celebre quicquam, nisi quod tam multi tum conuenerunt, ut nihil agerent. Quare autem ad Lateranense, seculo demum decimo tertio? An per mille annos & ducentos, quibus steterat tum Christiana res, satis cautum non erat, vel prouisum contra haereses, ut Lateranensi primùm hoc curæ fuerit? Nullúmne priùs ab haresi periculum? Et an, tûm demum coepit periculum, quod tum primùm necesse, ut subditi fide soluerentur? Qui fuit ab Abbate Ioachim, quem nemo; vel ab Almerico, quem non multi sectati sunt, timor tantus, (nam hi soli à Plaini nominantur) ut tam violentum hoc, & morbo penè peius remedium adhibendum esset, quod tamen in Manichaeos, Arrianis, Nestorianis, Pelagianis, Eutychianis, Monothelitis, tot alijs haeresibus multò & magis perniciosis, & latiùs proseminatis, Ecclesia non adhibuit. Quid autem ibi actum in Concilio? Nihil quidem de eo quod dicis, Conciliariter decretum, aut definitum: Significetur id summo Pontifici, qui subditos fidelitate soluet, & terras inuadendas concedet. Arrogatur hic quidem Pontifici ius, non datur; & præsumitur quod fuerat antè in praxi, non decernitur; quasi incidenter ibi modus præscribitur, res ipsa ex proposito non definitur; Concilium ci ut faciat potestatem non decrevit. Tum nec rectè rem refers; præcidis ibi, multa; excommunicetur ibi, dicitur, sed per quem? per Metropolitanum & comprouinciales Episcopos. Ante ergo nouitiones præuias, ante sententiam ab Episcopis dictam, nihil Pontifici quod agat: Expectanda ei saltem censura Episcoporum, etiam annus post censuram integer. Tum in Dominos principales ibi nihil statuitur, sed vel in eos, qui non habent, vel si habent, saluare Domini principalis: Omissus autem ibi casus, si Domini principales ipsi sint. Apud nos quidem non magis vnquam receptum celebre illud tuum Concilium Lateranense, quàm Tridentinum in Gallia. Nam & Principi hiç subsidia soluuntur, addo etiam soluta sunt iam inde ad Henrico tertio, qui mox fuit post Concilium, inconsulto Pontifice contra 46um. capitulum. Et tametsi sapè ex bonâ fide ortum non habeat, tamen hîc apud nos currit praescriptio, contra 41um. Et verò, contra ipsum hoc, quod in manibus iam habemus capitulum 3um. Clericorum bona, qui de haeresi convicti, Ecclesiis non applicantur, sed abeunt in fiscum; vt nihil quidem ad nos Concilium tuum Lateranense. Neque verò vim suam videtur habuisse Decretum hoc Innocentij tertij: vt eliciendâ proin paulò post fuerit à Frederico 2o. Constitutio eius triplex, Patauij, contra Haereticos. Quae ipsa Constitutio plus semper in se momenti habere visa est, quàm Decretum hoc. Agere enim & procedere voluerunt in Haereticos ex Constitutione illâ Iudices suos, Innocentius 4o. Alexander 4o. & Clemens 4o. Pontifices, non ex capitulo hoc Lateranensi: nunquam id facturi ex Caesaris lege, non suâ, nisi Caesaris, quàm suam, plus in se momenti, ac roboris habere statuissent.
units.tr: You then turn to the Lateran Council, as to a place of refuge: in it are your three champions. Why you call it the greatest, I do not know, unless it is because of the 800 priors and abbots present there; for the bishops were far more numerous. Nor why you call it the most celebrated: nothing celebrated was done there, except that so many gathered and then did nothing. But why the Lateran Council only in the thirteenth century? Over the course of the 1,200 years during which the Christian cause had stood, was there not enough caution, or provision made against heresies, that the Lateran was the first to take this up? Was there no danger from heresy before? And was the danger only beginning then, the danger that subjects had to be absolved from their oath of fidelity? What fear was so great, from Abbot Joachim, whom no one knows, or from Amalric, whom not many followed (for these alone are named by Platina), that such a violent remedy, almost worse than the disease, had to be applied? Yet the Church did not apply it against the Manichaeans, Arians, Nestorians, Pelagians, Eutychians, Monothelites and many other heresies far more pernicious and more widely spread. But what was done there at the Council? Certainly nothing decreed or defined in council in the way you say: "Let it be signified to the supreme Pontiff, who shall absolve the subjects from fidelity and grant the lands to be invaded." Here indeed a right is claimed for the Pontiff, not given; and what had previously been the practice is presupposed, not decreed. As if in passing a method is prescribed there, while the matter itself is not defined on purpose; the Council did not decree that he should have the power. Nor do you report the matter rightly: you cut out much there. It is said there that he should be excommunicated, but by whom? "By the metropolitan and the neighbouring bishops." Therefore, before the preliminary admonitions, before the sentence pronounced by the bishops, the Pontiff has nothing to do: at the very least, the judgement of the bishops must be awaited, and even a full year after that judgement. Then, as to the principal lords, nothing is laid down there, but either against those who do not have them, or, if they have them, "the rights of the principal lord are preserved." The case in which the principal lords themselves are concerned is left out. Among us, indeed, your famous Lateran Council was never received any more than the Council of Trent in France. For subsidies are paid to the Prince here, and I add, have been paid since the time of Henry III, who came shortly after the Council, without consulting the Pontiff, contrary to the 46th chapter. And although it often does not arise from good faith, nevertheless here among us prescription runs, against the 41st. And indeed, against this very chapter, which we already have in hand, the third chapter: "The goods of clerics convicted of heresy are not applied to the churches, but go to the treasury." So your Lateran Council has nothing to do with us. Nor does this decree of Innocent III seem to have had its own force, since it was afterwards drawn out by Frederick II in his threefold constitution at Padua against heretics. That constitution has always seemed to have more weight in itself than this decree. For Innocent IV, Alexander IV and Clement IV, Pontiffs, wished their judges to act and proceed against heretics under that constitution, not under this Lateran chapter; they would never have done so had they judged that the law of Caesar, not their own, but Caesar's, had more weight and strength in itself than their own.

units.la: Quanquam non malè id à me quaesitum, Quid ibi actum? Nihil enim actum, quod quidem constet. Et ille locus ad marginem, caput illud tertium, nec illud solum, sed & reliqua, & corpus ipsum Concilij iugulauit. Platina de toto hoc Concilio, tam magno, tam celebri, verba ficse habent. Venere multa, tum quidem in consultationem; nec decerni tamen quicquam apertè potuit.
