Venere multa, ait Platina; tu fidus interpres Platinae, non multa, sed unum modo de multis venisse ais, nempe de terrâ Sanctâ recuperandâ solùm. Nec potuit de multis quicquam, (aut ille) tu verò non de multis quicquam, sed de uno hoc articulo inter multa; nihil certi definiri potuit. Non dicit hoc Platina; dicit, multa quidem tum in consultationem venisse, (non vnum illud) neque tamen (non vnum de multis, sed) neque quicquam ibi tum decerni potuisse: Non quidem aperte, vt siquid ibi habeatur decretum, clanculum & malis artibus obtrusum sit. Sed neque tute tibi hic constas. Nam quod ibi definitum esse negas de terrâ Sanctâ, non minùs certè definitum est quàm caetera, nempe cap. 71, Ad liberandam terram Sanctam de manibus impiorum, &c. vt si non illud, nec alia decerni potuerint; vel enim nihil tum aliud, vel si alia, & illud inter alia, nec minùs quàm alia decretum fuerit. Sed vt fides Concilij huius suspecta sit; multa certè faciunt. Facit primò, quòd ante Cochlaeum nusquam extiterit: qui primus illud (quod sciam) mortalium edidit, idque non ante annum 1538. Nam qui triennio ante Concilia nobis dedit Iacobus Merlin, nullum, tum habebat quod ederet: Cochlæus autem (quis verò nescit Cochlæi mendacia?) descripta sibi dicit Decreta hæc, ex antiquo codice; sed neque unde sibi Codex ille, vel à quo, nec quâ fide fuerit, verbum vllum addit. Nec alius credo fuit Codex ille antiquus, quàm Codex Decretalium, in quo illa sparsim inserta, quæ ille inde collecta, sic in vnum corpus consarcinauit; sed stultè tamen consarcinauit, atque ita vt periret indicio suo. Quis enim credat? quis ferat celeberrimum tuum Lateranense Concilium, citare & Decreta sua referre ex Lateranensi Concilio, id est, ex seipso? Concilia quidem vbi de seipsis loquuntur, sic ferè loqui solent, Haec Sancta Synodus: Placuit huic Sancto Concilio. At hoc Concilium, de Lateranensi, id est, de seipso, sic loquitur, tanquam de Concilio alio peregrino: Fuit, & Noscitur fuisse, tanquam de praeterito; non iam sedente, idque Sex minimùm in locis cap.17. bis autem cap.29. cap.33. cap.45. cap.61. In Lateranensi Concilio piâ fuit institutione prouisum. De multâ prouidentiâ; fuit in Lateranensi Concilio prohibitum. Et Dispoluatur[?] collatio secundum statutum Lateranensis Concilij. In Lateranensi Concilio noscitur fuisse prohibitum. Haec, quisquam Concilij ipsius verba putet? Annon de alio quodam mentionem fieri? Quid ergo? Cochlæus somniat? Ab ipso Papâ Innocentio haec Decreta in formam hanc redacta fuisse, aliquanto post celebratum Concilium? Aliquanto post? Non placet illud, post Concilium celebratum Concilij Decreta scribi; Id quod, (inquit Cochlæus) cordatus Lector facilè deprehendet ex capitulis quibusdam; vbi tria notat de Sex illis quæ mihi ante indicata sunt. Sed non ita vappa fuit Innocentius, vt hac verborum formulâ Decreta conderet, vt Synodum sic loquentem induceret, In Lateranensi Concilio noscitur fuisse prohibitum, vel fiat hoc, secundum quod prouisum est in Lateranensi Concilio, cum Synodum ibi ipsam loquentem inducat. Quid ergo fuit? Platina credimus; Non est decretum ibi quicquam, non potuit ibi decerni quicquam. Improbauit Innocentius ipse Abbatis Ioachim libellum, damnauit ipse Almericum. Verba sunt Platina: Non enim Concilio ea ascribit, sed ipsi. Et vt haec, ita cæterà, de quibus decerni nihil potuit, relata post, per eum in Decretalia sua. Siqua in Concilio tractata, placuerunt, appositâ mentio de illis; quòd in Lateranensi provisa sint: vt de Sex illis quæ paulò ante mihi notata, inter quas tamen Caput illud Cochlæi tertium, non est vllum. Non enim Concilij, caput illud; verè autem Caput 13. Extrau: De Hæreticis, nempe Innocentij ipsius Decretum, non Concilij, vbi quicquam decerni non potuit.
units.tr: Yet my question, "What was done there?", was not badly asked. For nothing was done, at least as far as is certain. And that marginal passage, that third chapter, and not that alone but the rest too, and the very body of the Council, you have strangled. Platina has these words about this whole Council, so great and so celebrated: "Many matters came up then for consultation; yet nothing could openly be decreed." "Many matters came up," says Platina; you, the faithful interpreter of Platina, say not many matters but only one of many came up, namely the recovery of the Holy Land alone. Nor could anything of many matters (or he) be decreed; but you say not anything of many matters, but "of this one article among many, nothing certain could be defined." Platina does not say this; he says that indeed many matters came up then for consultation (not that one alone), and yet (not one of many, but) that nothing at all could be decreed there then: not openly, so that if any decree is found there, it was thrust in secretly and by evil arts. But you are not consistent with yourself here either. For what you deny was defined there about the Holy Land was defined no less certainly than the rest, namely in chapter 71, "For freeing the Holy Land from the hands of the impious," etc. So if that and no others could be decreed, then either nothing else was decreed at all, or if others were, that one was decreed among them no less than the others. But that the faith of this Council is open to suspicion, many things certainly make it so. First, it is that before Cochlaeus it never appeared anywhere. He was the first (as far as I know) of mortals to publish it, and not before the year 1538. For James Merlin, who three years before the Councils gave us them, then had nothing to publish. Cochlaeus, however (who does not know the lies of Cochlaeus?), says that these decrees were copied out for him from an ancient codex; yet he adds not a word as to where that codex came from, from whom, or with what faithfulness it was kept. Nor do I believe that codex was any other than the Codex of Decretals, in which those things were scattered and inserted, and which he gathered from there and so patched them together into one body; but he patched them together foolishly, and in such a way that they perished by their own evidence. For who would believe it? Who would bear that your most celebrated Lateran Council should cite and report its own decrees from the Lateran Council, that is, from itself? Indeed, when councils speak of themselves they commonly speak in this way: "This holy synod: it has pleased this holy council." But this Council, speaking of the Lateran, that is, of itself, speaks as if of some other foreign council: "It was," and "it is known to have been," as of the past, no longer sitting; and that in at least six places: in chapter 17, twice in chapter 29, chapter 33, chapter 45, chapter 61. "In the Lateran Council provision was made by pious institution." "Of much providence": "it was forbidden in the Lateran Council." And "let the collation be dissolved according to the statute of the Lateran Council." "It is known that it was forbidden in the Lateran Council." Would anyone think these are the very words of the Council itself? Is not mention being made of some other council? What then? Does Cochlaeus dream? "These decrees were drawn up in this form by Pope Innocent himself, some time after the Council was celebrated"? Some time after? That does not please: "the decrees of the Council were written after the Council had been celebrated." Which, says Cochlaeus, "a judicious reader will easily detect from certain chapters," where he notes three things from the six I have already pointed out. But Innocent was not so foolish as to frame decrees in this verbal form, to bring in the Synod speaking thus, "In the Lateran Council it is known to have been forbidden," or "let this be done according to what was provided in the Lateran Council," since he introduces the Synod itself speaking there. What then was it? We believe Platina: "There is no decree there, nothing could be decreed there." Innocent himself condemned the book of Abbot Joachim; he himself condemned Amalric. These are Platina's words. For he does not ascribe them to the Council but to himself. And, as these, so the other matters, about which nothing could be decreed, were related afterwards by him in his own Decretals. If any matters treated in the Council pleased him, a mention of them was added, that they were provided for in the Lateran; as with those six which I noted a little before, among which, however, there is not that third chapter of Cochlaeus. For that chapter is not of the Council; it is truly chapter 13 of the Extravagants, "On Heretics," namely a decree of Innocent himself, not of the Council, in which nothing could be decreed.

units.la: {b}Audit verò Matthæum Parisiensem qui ipse tum vixit, de maximo illo tuo & celeberrimo Concilio, rem vt erat, referentem. Concilium autem illud Generale, quod, more Papali, grandia primâ fronte præ se tulit, in risum & scommata desiit, quo Archiepiscopos, Episcopos, Abbates, Decanos, Archidiaconos, omnesque adid Concilium accedentes, indisfectum est. Postquam enim profectus Innocentius, vt litem inter Genuenses, & Pisanos componeret; quid factum fuerit, narrat Parisiensis. Cùm iam nihil geri in tanto negotio cernerent, redeundi ad sua cupidi, veniam sigillatim petierunt. Quibus Papa non concessit, antequam sibi grandem pecuniam promisissent, quam à Mercatoribus Romanis, prius accipere mutuò, Papæq. soluere coacti sunt: Papa, iam acceptâ pecuniâ quasi tuofum hoc Concilium dissoluit gratis, totusque Clerus abiit tristis. Erat, quod vnum tibi erat Lateranense, quæ cesserit; vnum erat, iam nullum est, vt iam, spes sibi Pontifex, nec vllum superstes refugium, nisi in Decretalibus sui; quibus, nisi inferat quod suo proposito satis futurum sit, dignus sanèque qui sacer fit.
units.tr: {b}He hears Matthew Paris, who lived at that time himself, relating that great and most celebrated Council of yours as it really was. That General Council, which at first sight showed great pretensions in the Papal manner, came to laughter and mockery, since it was deserted by Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, Deans, Archdeacons, and all who came to the Council, one by one. For after Innocent set out to settle the dispute between the Genoese and the Pisans, Paris recounts what happened. When they saw that nothing was being done in so great a matter, they, eager to return to their own affairs, asked for leave one by one. The Pope did not grant it until they had promised him a large sum of money, which they were forced to borrow first from Roman merchants and then pay to the Pope. Then the Pope, now that the money was received, dissolved this Council of yours, as if for nothing, and the whole clergy went away sad. There was one Lateran Council, which has passed away; there was one, and now there is none; so now the Pontiff has no hope left and no refuge remaining except in his Decretals, which, unless they bring something sufficient for his purpose, are worthy of being held sacred.

units.la: Vbi autem nominatus forte Platina, opportunum duxit Concilium suum Lateranense in medio rehinquere, ei valedicere; quasi an ibi quicquam decerni potuerit annon potuerit; aut quid Concilio fiat, non magnopere curaret; & delabitur ad Iohannem Angliæ Regem, ibi in Platina in vita Innocentij vestigalem factum in Othonem etiam inibi depositum; magis scilicet, de gloriâ Pontificis anxius, quàm de Concilij authoritate; post autem acclamat quasi ad facinus à se factum, magnum & memorabile: Non potuit adduci author, qui minus faceret ad rem nostram, vbi Imperator exactus, Rex ad vectigal redactus est: Pergat igitur Adversarius, & similes Authores ad nos convincendos frequenter adducat: Quid restat iam, nisi vt pœnitect, Platinam vnquam adduxisse, nec quisquam deinde aliquid de eo citare audeat? Non tamen hoc, Torte, subduxta satis ratione. Primùm enim, vbi nos de iure quæritmus, tu respondes de facto; Nullo iure factum, nec ipse negare potes, cùm prius factum fuerit crit, quàm ius fuerit faciendi; cum Othonem ipse Platina dicat depositum prius fuisse, quàm Concilium vllum aut statuerit, aut fuerit quod statuere posset, deponendum esse. An is Pontificum mos, primò, rem facere, post, faciendum decernere? Qui Concilium affers, vt doceas propter haeresin deponi posse, exemplum subijcis Imperatoris, ante Concilium vllum depositi; nec tamen propter haeresin vllam depositi. Nam nec illius haeresis vlla legitur, propter quam depon. debuit: Recuperata tantùm quaedam oppida, vnde iram Pontificis in se concitârat. Tempore enim quo vacabat Imperium, Papa Castilla[?] plurima occupaverat, quae ad Imperium pertinebant: unde Imperator, quia quod suum erat revocare studuit, ipsum Papam sine merito, ad iram provocavit: Sed & illud forte haeresin sapiebat, vt & alia saepe, quaecunque non ad stomachum Pontificis. Jurare[?] compulit, vt dispersa Imperij iura revocaret: Revocantem exiuramenti religione, anathemate percutit: Certè Innocentij ipsi, Otho magis innocens. Hoc Othoni factum, quem Innocentius elevans attollit: quem enim paulo ante confirmauerat, eundem post, nullâ suâ culpâ turpiter deseruit, cùm contra Philippum rivalem Imperij Caesarem ipsum verum, infoelicitèr rem gesisset. Huic quoque ipsi Othoni, titulis Imperij privato, qui substitutus est Fridericus 2[?], quàm lubrico loco sederit, quis nescit? Mirum modis tum Papa ludos faciebant Imperatoribus, & illa Tyrannidis in Pontifice indicia erant, non authoritatis iustae; & debitatis in Caesare, non causae iniustae.
units.tr: When Platina happened to be named, he thought it expedient to leave his Lateran Council in the middle and bid it farewell, as if it mattered not whether anything could be decreed there or not, or what became of the Council; and he slides over to John, King of England, who there, in Platina's life of Innocent, was made a tributary, and Otho was also deposed there. He was evidently more anxious about the glory of the Pontiff than about the authority of the Council. Afterwards he exclaims as if it were a great and memorable deed done by himself: "No author could be brought who would do less for our cause, where an emperor was expelled and a king reduced to paying tribute. Let the Adversary therefore continue, and often bring forward such authors to convince us." What remains now, except that he repent of ever having brought forward Platina, and that no one afterwards dare to cite anything from him? Yet, Torte, you have not reckoned this well enough. For first, when we ask about right, you answer about fact: "done without right"; nor can you yourself deny that the fact necessarily came before the right to do it, since Platina himself says that Otho was deposed before any Council either had decided, or was able to decide, that he should be deposed. Is this the custom of the Pontiffs, first to do a thing and afterwards to decree that it should be done? You who bring forward a Council to teach that someone may be deposed on account of heresy, you add as an example an Emperor deposed before any Council, and yet not deposed on account of any heresy. For no heresy of his is read of on account of which he ought to have been deposed; only certain towns were recovered, from which he had roused the Pontiff's anger. For during the time when the Empire was vacant, the Pope had seized very many lands which pertained to the Empire; whence the Emperor, because he strove to recall what was his own, provoked the Pope himself, without merit, to anger. But perhaps that also smacked of heresy, as often other things did, whatever was not to the Pontiff's liking. He compelled him to swear that he would recall the scattered rights of the Empire; and when he recalled them, he struck him with anathema on the pretext of the sanctity of the oath. Certainly Otho was more innocent than Innocent himself. This was done to Otho, whom Innocent raised up and exalted; for the one whom he had just confirmed, the same he afterwards shamefully deserted, through no fault of his own, when Otho, the true Emperor, had unsuccessfully conducted affairs against Philip, the rival of the Empire. Who does not know on what slippery ground Frederick the Second sat, who was substituted for this same Otho, now stripped of the titles of the Empire? In remarkable ways the Popes then made sport of the Emperors, and those were signs of tyranny in the Pontiff, not of just authority; and of debt in Caesar, not of unjust cause.

units.la: De Rege Iohanne quid mirum? Ii sic Caesares tum habuit Innocentius, quòd meruerit libi; cùm esset ei Othonis exemplum ante oculos Nepotis sui, cuique ipse fauisset contra Pontificem; praesertimcùm & Iohannem ipsum Innocentius (nullo etiam tum edito Lateranensi Decreto, nec sanè propter haeresin expositum) praedixit praedæ Gallorum? Nec id, quia Nepotem suum Arthurum, legitimum regni heredem, contra iuris fas, mandasset trucidari; lentus enim ad facinus tam leve Pontifex: sed quia grande sceleris admisit, dum quem ei Papa nolenti & nescienti obtrusit[?] Archiepiscopum, cùm non primò quoque tempore sisteret. Egregiam verò laudem Pontificis: Excideràt tum Iohannes suorum benevolentiâ, inciderat in defectionem vt[?]unum[?], factis à Papa facta, defectus à suis: Gallus quasi Hannibal ad portas; vndique angustiæ. Quo in discrimine suo, cùm Innocentij Papæ auxilio diuino (vt ait Platina) Iohannes vti vellet, parum in eo expertus est mentis diuinæ. Sensit enim clausum sibi diuinum eius auxilium omne, nisi grandi precio, vtriusque scilicet regni, pacisci cum eo vellet. Credo autem, si se conuertisset ad Deum, vel si Innocentius Deo plenus, minoris multò cum eo tràfigere potuisse. Illetum, nisi se regno Iohannes exuat, nihil audit: atque ita vt se exueret, planè per vim perpulit. O virum sanctum! ô speculum innocentiæ! Nam quòd tu voluisse refers Iohannem, haud alia in eo facto fuit voluntas eius, quàm qualem dixisti Gregorij fuisse erga Imperatorem, vellet nollet, cùm domi turbatæ res, cùm foris, hostis imminaret. Sed quid tum si voluit Rex? Regnum ipsum noluit, vniuersitas regni, quæ in causa hac contradicere potuit, per os Archiepiscopi contradixit, eaque contradictio eius de iure fuit admittenda. Noli ergo nimis blandiri tibi de re nihili: multis enim modis nulla fuit, ea tum subiectio. Concessa primùm non sine periurio, nam contra solenne iuramentum Deo à Rege præstitum, ante impositam illi de more coronam. Secundò, Reseruatain eo Iustitia, Libertates, Regalia, per verba, [Saluis nobis, & haredibus nostris, Iustitijs, Libertatibus & Regalibus nostris] atq; ita concessio de iure nulla. Tertiò, Reclamatum ei est à Regno, Semper clàm & palam reclamante, cum profundis suspiriis Stephano Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi. Quartò, Relaxatum pòst, quicquid in eo pactum: sic habet Eulogij Author. An. 1214. Conuocatum est Parlamentum Londonijs, præsidente Archiepiscopo, cum toto Clero, & sectâ Laicali; in quo, per Domini Papæ præceptum; illa obligatio prefata, quam Rex Domino Papæ fecerat, cum fidelitate & homagio relaxatur omnino, septimo die Iulij. Apud Tortum quidem b Thomas Morus ius testis habeat necesse, qui Cancellarius Regni, vt verum posset cognoscere, & Martyr sanctus, vt nollet fallere. Vis ab illo ipso audire, quæ eius sententia de vestro hoc vectigali? Verba eius sunt: Quodsi dicat quis, (quod verum est, dicere non nullos) vectigales factas à Rege Iohanne Angliam & Hiberniam Papa, & Sedi Apostolica, sub censu annuo mille marcarum; & nos verò vicissim audemus dicere, verè idab eò non dici; quodd, nec Roma tota, diploma vel concessionem talem proferre vel posset iam, vel vnquam potuerit. Quodsi autem posset, tamen id nihili prorsus esset: nam neque Regem Angliæ villum, Papæ vnquam Regnum suum dono dare potuisse, nec terram suam vectigalem facere, etiamsi id maximè vellet: nec iam soluitur ei pecunia, nec vnquam soluta est.
units.tr: What is surprising about King John? Innocent had such Caesars then, because he had deserved them; since the example of Otho was before the eyes of his own nephew, whom he had himself favoured against the Pontiff; especially since Innocent foretold the plunder of the French for John himself (even though the Lateran Decree had not yet been published, nor was he certainly exposed on account of heresy). Nor was it because he had ordered his nephew Arthur, the lawful heir of the kingdom, to be slain contrary to the law of right (for the Pontiff was slow to such a light crime), but because he committed a great crime, while the Pope forced upon him, against his will and without his knowledge, an Archbishop, since he did not at the first opportunity present him. An excellent praise indeed of the Pontiff! John had then fallen from the goodwill of his own people, he had fallen into defection, made by the Pope's deeds, abandoned by his own; the Frenchman was at the gates like Hannibal; on every side, straits. In this peril of his, when John wished to use the divine help of Pope Innocent (as Platina says), he showed little experience of the divine mind. For he perceived that all the divine help was closed to him, unless he wished to bargain with him at a great price, namely of both kingdoms. But I believe that if he had turned to God, or if Innocent, full of God, had been able to deal with him, he could have come to terms with far less. He hears nothing of the Lord, unless John strips himself of the kingdom; and so, that he might strip himself, he plainly drove him by force. O holy man! O mirror of innocence! For that you report John to have "willed" it, there was no other will in him in that deed than the kind you said Gregory had towards the Emperor, "whether he willed it or not," when affairs were troubled at home and an enemy threatened abroad. But what if the King willed it? The kingdom itself did not will it, the whole body of the realm, which could contradict in this cause, contradicted through the mouth of the Archbishop; and that contradiction of theirs ought by right to have been admitted. Do not, therefore, flatter yourself too much about a thing of no account; for in many ways that subjection then was null. First, it was granted not without perjury, for it was against the solemn oath sworn by the King to God before the crown was placed upon him, as is customary. Second, in it were reserved "Justice, Liberties, Royal Rights," in the words [Saving to us and our heirs our Justices, Liberties and Royal Rights]; and so the concession was null by right. Third, the kingdom protested against it, "always secretly and openly protesting, with deep sighs, to Stephen, Archbishop of Canterbury." Fourth, afterwards whatever was agreed in it was relaxed; so the author of Eulogius has it: "In the year 1214 Parliament was convoked at London, the Archbishop presiding, with the whole clergy and the lay party; in which, by command of the Lord Pope, that aforesaid obligation, which the King had made to the Lord Pope, together with fealty and homage, was wholly relaxed, on the seventh day of July." Among you Tortus indeed, Thomas More must be a necessary witness, who was Chancellor of the kingdom, so that he could know the truth, and a holy martyr, so that he would not wish to deceive. Do you wish to hear from him himself what his opinion is about this tribute of yours? His words are these: "But if someone should say (which is true, that some say it) that England and Ireland were made tributary by King John to the Pope and the Apostolic See, under an annual tax of a thousand marks; we, in turn, dare to say that this is truly not said by him; because neither the whole of Rome could now or ever could have produced such a charter or grant." But even if it could, that would be of no account at all: for neither could the King of England ever give his kingdom as a gift to the Pope, nor make his land tributary, even if he most wished it; nor is the money now paid to him, nor was it ever paid.

units.la: Quodsi, quæ tum fuerit hominum sententia de facto illo, scire vis; potes ex Stephano Cardinale ipso Romanæ Curiæ, ex Papali gratiâ speciali, inuito etiam Rege Iohanne, facto hîc Archiepiscopo. Is, vtcunque concessio Regis sui in rem Papæ erat, {a}ante altare S. Pauli in Ecclesiâ Cathedrali Londinensi, cùm redderet coronam Rex, conficiens scriptum toti mundo execrabile, contradixit, appellatione interposuit. Potes & ex ore Capitalis tum Hostis eius Philippi Galliarum Regis, cuius hæc verba referuntur à Matthæo Parif. {b}Regnum Angliæ patrimonium B. Petri nunquam erat, nec est, nec erit. Nullus Rex vel Princeps potest dare regnum suum, quod est Respublica, sine assensu Baronum suorum, qui Regnum illud tenentur defendere. Et si Papa hunc errorem defendere decreuerit, perniciosum Regnis omnibus exemplum perhibebit. Heu quantum deterior Regum omnium per eum conditio? Ita enim poterit, processu temporis, per aliquem desidem Hæredem meum, fieri de Franciâ: & tendens manus ad cœlum, addidit, Quod Deus, quod Deus, quod Deus auertat; & eruperunt lacrymæ ab oculis eius. Tunc quoque magnates omnes vno ore clamare cœperunt, quòd pro illo articulo starent vsque ad mortem: ne videlicet Rex aut Princeps per solam voluntatem suam posset Regnum dare, vel tributarium quomodo libet facere, unde nobiles Regni efficerentur serui.
units.tr: If you want to know what people at that time thought of that deed, you can learn it from Cardinal Stephen himself, of the Roman Curia, made Archbishop here by special papal grace, even though King John was unwilling. He, however much the concession of his king was in the Pope's favour, protested and lodged an appeal before the altar of St Paul in the cathedral church of London, when the king surrendered the crown, drawing up a writing hateful to the whole world. You can also learn it from the mouth of the then chief enemy of his, Philip, King of the French, whose words are reported by Matthew Paris: The kingdom of England was never, is not, and will never be the patrimony of St Peter. No king or prince can give his kingdom, which is a commonwealth, without the consent of his barons, who are bound to defend that kingdom. And if the Pope decides to defend this error, he will set a dangerous example for all kingdoms. Alas, how much worse will the condition of all kings be through him? For in this way, as time goes on, it could happen through some idle heir of mine that France would be subjected; and stretching his hands to heaven, he added: May God forbid it, may God forbid it, may God forbid it; and tears burst from his eyes. Then also all the magnates began to cry out with one voice that they would stand for that article unto death, lest a king or prince should be able, by his own will alone, to give away the kingdom or make it tributary in any way, whereby the nobles of the kingdom would become slaves.

units.la: Sed quorsum hæc de Rege Iohanne? An vt vras nos, dum commemoras Regnum hoc nostrum, Ecclesiæ Romanæ esse? Nihil agis. Nam antiquissimo tempore, etiam antequam sic oblatum esset à Rege Iohanne, Ecclesiæ Romanæ fuit. Ita rem refert Augustinus Steuchus, Bibliothecarius Pontificis, idque ex Registro Alexandri 3i. iam inde scilicet à Donatione Constantini, vt nulli rei concessio illa Iohannû[?] fuerit, tantùmque Papæ dederit, quod suum iam erat. Quid tu autem, Regnum nostrum commemoras vnum, quasi & alia omnia Regna eodem loco non sint? Faxo vero vt habeatur mihi à te gratia: augebo enim Petri patrimonium. Non enim Regnum hoc Angliæ solùm, sed & reliqua omnia, quæ per Europ̄am [?] sunt Regna (nec vel vnum excipio) omnis (inquam) sunt Pontificis. Constat hoc ex Regiftro Gregorij 7ⁱ. apud Steuchum (secundo libro contra Vallam pro Donatione Constantini.
units.tr: But why this about King John? Do you mean to show, by mentioning this our kingdom, that it belongs to the Roman Church? You achieve nothing. For in the most ancient time, even before it was so offered by King John, it belonged to the Roman Church. Augustinus Steuchus, librarian to the Pope, reports the matter thus, and from the register of Alexander III, going back to the Donation of Constantine, so that that concession was not of John's making, but merely gave to the Pope what was already his. But why do you mention our kingdom alone, as though all other kingdoms were not in the same position? I will indeed do you the favour of letting you have my thanks: for I will enlarge St Peter's patrimony. For not only this kingdom of England, but all the rest which are kingdoms throughout Europe (I except not even one), all (I say) belong to the Pope. This is established from the register of Gregory VII, cited by Steuchus in the second book against Valla in defence of the Donation of Constantine.

units.la: Petrus Rex ARRAGONIAE venit Romam quinto anno Innocentij tertij, obtulitq; sponte totum Regnum B. Petro & S. R. Ecclesiae, ibiq; accepit in feudum praedictum Regnum. Itemq; pro Regno SARDINIAE certam pecuniam (summam) constituit se daturū. Melior autem haec multò concesso,magis in honorem sedis Apostolicae, quia sponte oblata: quam Regis Iohannis, quę per vim extorta & metum, metum (inquam) qui vel in constantem virum cadere potuisset.
units.tr: Peter, King of Aragon, came to Rome in the fifth year of Innocent III and of his own accord offered the whole kingdom to St Peter and the holy Roman Church, and received the aforesaid kingdom back in fief. Likewise for the kingdom of Sardinia he agreed to give a certain sum of money. But this grant is much better, and made more to the honour of the Apostolic See, because it was offered of its own accord, than that of King John, which was extorted by force and fear, fear (I say) such as could have fallen even upon a steadfast man.

units.la: Regnum HISPANIAE ex antiquis constitutionibus B. Petro & S.R.Ecclesiae in ius & proprietatem traditum est, quod omnes Hispania Reges sciunt.
units.tr: The kingdom of Spain, by ancient constitutions, was handed over to St Peter and the holy Roman Church in right and ownership, as all the kings of Spain know.

units.la: Regnum HVNGARIAE etiam antequam à Saracenis occuparetur, S. R. Ecclesiae proprium est à Rege Stephano traditum
units.tr: The kingdom of Hungary, even before it was occupied by the Saracens, was handed over by King Stephen as the proper possession of the holy Roman Church.

units.la: Regnum DANORVM est peculium, & vectigal S. R. Ecclesiae, & vt subiectioni obnoxiij, Apostolicae sedi annuū vectigal p.r.soluit.
units.tr: The kingdom of Denmark is the peculium and tribute of the holy Roman Church, and as a subject and bound by subjection, it pays an annual tribute to the Apostolic See.

units.la: Regnum CROATIAE & DALMATIAE à Demetrio Rege tributarium factum ducentorum Byzantiorum tributo.
units.tr: The kingdom of Croatia and Dalmatia was made tributary by King Demetrius with a tribute of two hundred bezants.

units.la: Regnum RVSSIAE iuris est & disiunctionis R. Ecclesiae, donatum Regi Demetrio a Gregorio septimo.
units.tr: The kingdom of Russia is of the right and property of the holy Roman Church, given to King Demetrius by Gregory VII.

units.la: Regnum PORTVGALLIAE Ecclesiae Romanae est.
units.tr: The kingdom of Portugal belongs to the Roman Church.

units.la: Regnum BOHEMIAE vectigal pendit Apostolicae sedi centum librarum argenti.
units.tr: The kingdom of Bohemia pays a tribute of one hundred pounds of silver to the Apostolic See.

units.la: SVECIA quoq;, ac NORVEGIA vt subiectae, soluunt R. Ecclesiae vectigal. Nam de GALLIA notum, quid Bonifacius 8. scripserit Philippo tum Regi, & quomodo ei veteta monumenta explicuerit, quod Romana Ecclesiae, & in sacris, & in prophanis, spiritualibus & temporalibus, Gallia subesset;quo necesse esset, Pontificem, vt Dominum Regni sui, eum venerari & colere.
units.tr: Sweden too, and Norway, as subject, pay tribute to the holy Roman Church. For what Boniface VIII wrote to Philip, then King of France, is well known about France, and how he explained to him from old records that France was subject to the Roman Church, both in sacred and in profane matters, spiritual and temporal, so that it was necessary for the Pope, as lord of his kingdom, to revere and honour him.

units.la: De POLONIA sic {a}Krantzius: Lakoldus à Pontifice Rex nominatus, omne regnum fecit B. Petro tributarium.
units.tr: Concerning Poland, Kranzius writes thus: Lokietek, named king by the Pontiff, made the whole kingdom tributary to St Peter.

units.la: De SCOTIA sic {b}Polydorus Virgilius. Bonifacius Pontifex indixit Eduardo Regi, ne amplius posthac Scotos bello vexaret, quod, id Regnum antea in Romani Pontificis fidem & potestatem à Scotis ipsis permissum fuisset. Et ideo asseuerabat, sibi soli integrum esse, cuicunq; liberet dare, auferreue.
units.tr: Concerning Scotland, Polydore Vergil writes thus: Pope Boniface declared to King Edward that he should no longer harass the Scots with war, because that kingdom had formerly been committed by the Scots themselves to the faith and power of the Roman Pontiff. And therefore he asserted that it was for him alone to give or take it away to whomever he pleased.

units.la: De SICILIA, sic Clemens 5ᵃ. Non est silentio relinquendū, quod ipse Rex Siciliae, noster, & Ecclesiae Romanae, ratione Regni praedicti, notorie subditus, homoꝯ[?], ligeus, & vasallus in eodem regno continuum habet domicilium.
units.tr: Concerning Sicily, thus Clement V: It must not be passed over in silence that the King of Sicily himself, our vassal and vassal of the Roman Church, by reason of the aforesaid kingdom, is notoriously a subject, liege man and vassal, and has a continuous dwelling in the same kingdom.

units.la: Rex item Insularum de MAII accepit eas à S.R. Ecclesiâ in fundam, si Steucho credas. Quod nisi credas, videas iam apud Martam nuper recocta[?], ut si non Regnus ipsis Papa, at eorum [illegible, ~2 letters] seipsum oblectare posset, Satin' hoc Regnorum? Satin' vectigalium? Cur tu igitur nos solos recenses? Cur non & omnes hos, nobiscum unà? Dic uno verbo, Pontificis omnia Regna mundi sunt. Pontifex Princeps est mundi huius. Ita Pontificis honori consultum erit magis, ita & ærario. In quod tamen ærarium non admodum multa inferri credo de vectigalibus hijs, nec Paulum quintum multò ex illis ditiorem, quàm ex Nostris: Rationes quidem constant probè, argentum [illegible, ~2 letters].
units.tr: The king of the islands of May likewise received them in fief from the holy Roman Church, if you believe Steuchus. And if you do not believe him, you may see now in Marta, lately recooked, that if the Pope were not king of them, yet he could amuse himself with them. Is that enough of kingdoms? Is that enough of tributes? Why then do you enumerate us alone? Why not all these with us together? Say it in one word: all the kingdoms of the world are the Pope's. The Pope is the prince of this world. Thus the honour of the Pope will be better served, and so will the treasury. Into that treasury, however, I do not believe very much is brought from these tributes, nor is Paul V much richer from them than from ours: the accounts indeed stand well; the silver [illegible].

units.la: At etiam Platinam vis à nobis frequenter adduci? Quà vero de re? An de vitis Pontificum Romanorum, de quibus scripsit? An de 40. Capitulis & amplius contra Iohannem 24um probatis in Concilio Constantiensi, in quibus, crimina multa, & quidem gravissima, propter quæ depositus? An de Paulo secundo qui Hæreticos pronunciauit, qui nomen Academiæ, vel loco vel sero, nominâsse? An de Simoniacâ prauitate Bonifacij noni contra ius sâsqi omnia vendentis, &c, quæ ab eo palam habitæ sunt, nundinis indulgentiarum? An vero de rusticitate Vrbani sexti, an stupiditate Cælestini quinti, an stoliditate Iohannis 22di? Sive de fraude, ambitione, arrogantia Bonifacy octavi, & de præclaro, quod eius vitæ subnectit, epiphonemate, Discant igitur huius exemplo &c. An illud maius, quomodo illis conuenerit cum Senatu suo, Populóq; Romano per annos quinquaginta, quatuorq̃ nec per quadringentos pax inter eos constans fuerit, vel certa. Quoties ab illis, Sanctissimi Domini, Vicarij Christi, urbe pulsi, quoties, prius etiam accepti? Nisi velis potius, de Benedicto nono, Silvestro tertio, Gregorio sexto, qui sedem uno tempore occupárunt, quos tres Platina ille cuius a tria dicit monstra terribilia quibus Onuphrius 4ti addit, Iohannem quendam, quo sedes tum Apostolica vexabatur. Quanquam non tres modò istos, sed & alios plerosque in Benedicto 9o, portenta, in Christophoro primo, monstra, veritus non est appellare. Peperit nobis tanta licentia peccandi hæc portenta. Quos tanquam monstra quædam è medio, brevi Deus sustulit. Quot suris & latrones per posticum ingrediuntur. Quomodo Bonifacius octavus Cælestinum impostura deluserit: Christophorus Leonem vi detruserit: Damasus Clementem veneno sustulerit. Quàm bene de Formoso inter Stephanum sextum, & Sergium tertium, inter Theodorum secundum, & Iohannem decimum conuenerit: qui illum exhumârunt, digitos praciderunt, in Tiberim cadauer proiececerunt. De Siluestro secundo, Mago: Iohanne 13. incesto: Bonifacio septimo sacrilego: Iohanne 8. fœminâ. Pergere vis etiam & Platinam adducere, qui triginta S. R. Ecclesiæ Schismata recensét, in quibus biceps, triceps, S. R. Ecclesia per annos 50. Apud quem per annos 180. perque Pontifices 50 plus minus, seriatim sibi succedentes, vix quenquam Pontificis nomine dignum potes adducere; quos ita nominâsse quenquam, miratur ipse qui nominat. Qui in Romano, Benedicto quarto, Christophoro, Sergio tertio, Siluestro tertio, Bonifacio octauo, epiphonemata subiungit, per quas artes Papatus occupari, quibus studijs administrari, quo fere exitu concludi soleat. Da veniam Lector; iubet, vrget Matthaus, hæc adducere, ad se suos q; conuincendos. Pergat igitur Matthaus, & remittat nos ad Platinam, ei similes Authores iubeat nos frequenter adducere, & ansam ipse det sæpe, similes Authores adducendi.
units.tr: But do you also want Platina brought forward by us frequently? On what matter, though? About the lives of the Roman Pontiffs, about which he wrote? Or about the forty chapters and more against John XXIII, approved at the Council of Constance, in which many crimes, and indeed most grave ones, on account of which he was deposed? Or about Paul II, who declared heretics those who had named the Academy, either in place or in time? Or about the simoniacal depravity of Boniface IX, who against all law sold everything, etc., which were openly carried on by him, in the markets of indulgences? Or indeed about the rusticity of Urban VI, the stupidity of Celestine V, or the stolidity of John XXII? Or about the fraud, ambition, and arrogance of Boniface VIII, and about the famous epiphonema he appends to his life, Let them therefore learn from this example, etc.? Or the greater matter, how it agreed with them and their Senate and the Roman People: for fifty-four years, nor within four hundred, was there a peace that was constant or sure between them. How often were they, the most holy Lords, Vicars of Christ, expelled from the city; how often, even after being received? Unless you would rather speak of Benedict IX, Silvester III, and Gregory VI, who occupied the See at one time, whom that Platina calls three terrible monsters, to whom Onuphrius adds John, a certain man, by whom the Apostolic See was then troubled. Although he did not hesitate to call not only these three but also many others portents, and Benedict IX portents, and Christopher I monsters. Such great license in sinning produced these portents for us, whom God shortly removed from the midst as certain monsters. How many thieves and robbers enter by the back door! How Boniface VIII deceived Celestine by imposture; Christopher thrust out Leo by force; Damasus removed Clement by poison. How well it agreed concerning Formosus between Stephen VI and Sergius III, between Theodore II and John X, who dug him up, cut off his fingers, and threw the corpse into the Tiber. Concerning Silvester II, a magician; John XIII, incestuous; Boniface VII, sacrilegious; John VIII, a woman. Do you wish also to bring forward Platina, who recounts thirty schisms of the holy Roman Church, in which the holy Roman Church was two-headed, three-headed, for fifty years? With whom, through one hundred and eighty years, and through some fifty Pontiffs succeeding one another in order, you can scarcely bring forward anyone worthy of the name of Pontiff; that someone should be so named, he himself who names them wonders. He who appends epiphonemata to the lives of Romanus, Benedict IV, Christopher, Sergius III, Silvester III, and Boniface VIII, by what arts the papacy was seized, with what zeal it was administered, and by what end it is usually brought to a close. Pardon me, reader; Matthew bids and urges me to bring these things forward, to convict him and his own people. Let Matthew therefore go on, and send us back to Platina, and let him bid us frequently bring forward authors like him, and let him himself often give the occasion for bringing forward such authors.

units.la: Reperto in Concilijs Toletanis Iuramento fidei, reperto in Aquisgranensi Iuramento fidelitatis, de salute Regiâ, ne quisquam quolibet machinamento, tractet de nece, vel interitu Regis, de Rege potestate sua exuendo, Regni gubernaculum priuando, ne quis, quâlibet suasione à Rege deficiat, vel eius Contrarijs se copulet: vtroq; autem Iuramento in Conciliis illis approbato, seuerè etiam sancito, cùm eadem summa sit, idem scopus Iuramenti Regij: quò se vertat nescit; in omnes partes se versat, vt declinare possit, nec potest tamen. Primò enim causatur, quod illi tum Reges Catholici & Orthodoxi fuerint, nostèr autem Rex abEcclesiâ alienus. Quasi Regibus nisi Catholicus, nisi intra Ecclesiam sint, fides nulla debeatur; quasi Regibus Aegypti, Babylonis, Persiæ fidem non præstare; quasi Achabo, Iehoramo, Manasse, iusiurandum detrectare; quasi Constantio, Iuliano, Valenti, sacramento se non obligare liceret. Dic hoc ergo aperte, Regem qui ab Ecclesiâ alienus est, Regem iam non esse. Catholico deberi fidem, non Catholico non deberi; iusiurandum negare, fidem temerare ei fas esse; veteres in populo Dei sub lege, in Ecclesiâ primitiua sub Christo, peccâsse in eo omnes, quòd fidem seruauerint: Dic (inquam) hoc, & noue herefeos auauthor esto. Sed neque tamen sic effugies. Nam si Rex alie-nus est ab Ecclesiâ, quid Papæ cum alienis? Cur limites suos egreditur? Quid es de iis, qui foris sunt, iudicare? Cum iis Regibus agat qui intra Ecclesiam, aliena ne curet, & quæ ad eum nihil attinent: Nisi & dogma etiam fabricari vis de nouo, & proferre imperium Papæ, etiam in Reges qui extrà sunt; hoc argumento, quod Paulus ea verba dixerit, Quid mihi de iis qui foris sunt iudicare? Petrus non dixerit; vt satis insulsè {a}quidam è vobis Iesuita.
units.tr: Found in the Iuramentum fidei of the Councils of Toledo, found in the Iuramentum fidelitatis of Aachen, concerning the safety of the King: that no one, by any device whatsoever, should plot the murder or destruction of the King, strip him of his power, deprive him of the government of the realm, or, by any persuasion, turn away from the King or join himself to his enemies. Both oaths were approved in those Councils and sanctioned with severity; since the substance is the same, the aim of the royal oath is the same. Where it turns, it does not know; it turns in every direction so that it may evade, and yet it cannot. For first it pleads that those kings were Catholic and orthodox, whereas our king is alien to the Church. As if no faith were owed to kings unless they were Catholic, unless they were within the Church; as if one were not bound to keep faith with the kings of Egypt, Babylon and Persia; as if one might refuse an oath to Ahab, Jehoram and Manasseh; as if one were free not to bind oneself by oath to Constantius, Julian and Valens. Say this openly, then: a king who is alien to the Church is no longer a king. Faith is owed to a Catholic, not owed to a non-Catholic; it is lawful to refuse an oath and to violate faith with him; the ancients among the people of God under the law, and in the primitive Church under Christ, all sinned in this, that they kept faith. Say this (I say), and be the author of a new heresy. But even so you will not escape. For if the King is alien to the Church, what has the Pope to do with aliens? Why does he go beyond his own bounds? What have I to do with judging those who are outside? Let him deal with those kings who are within the Church, and not meddle with things alien that do not concern him. Unless you wish to fabricate a new doctrine as well, and extend the authority of the Pope even over kings who are outside, on the argument that Paul spoke those words, What have I to do with judging those who are outside?, but Peter did not say them; as one of you Jesuits has done, rather foolishly.

units.la: Diffisus huic, aliud mox arripit. Non enim quà Catholici, sed quà Reges, iuratur illis; In illis Concilijs non agi de nouo & illicito iuramento: Regium autem nouum & illicitum. Da hoc illi, nouum esse & illicitum, & obtinebit in causâ; Nega: & nullus est. Nos verò vtrumque negamus: nam neque nouum est, sed vetus renouatum: & si nouum, dum è re natum, nouitatis nulla culpa est. Nouum est à Pio 4°. instítutum, mox à Synodo Tridentinâ: cur Papæ nouum liceat condere; Regibus, si causa est, nouî condendi ius non sit? Quis hoc vnquam reprehendit? Licitum verò hoc, si illa duo licita. Nec enim in nostro quicquam, cuius in Toletano, & Aquisgranensi illo, vis omnis non continetur. Nam quod ibi positum de non copulando sefijs, qui Regû Contrarij sunt, facile ad Pontificem ipsum extendi potuit; & illi tum extendissent, si tum fuisset, vt nunc est, Regum Contrarius.
units.tr: Distrusting this, he next seizes on another point. For the oath is not sworn to them as Catholics, but as kings; those Councils did not treat of a new and unlawful oath, whereas the royal oath is new and unlawful. Grant him that it is new and unlawful, and he will win his case; deny it, and there is no case at all. We, however, deny both: for it is not new but an old thing renewed; and if it is new, since it arose from the circumstances, there is no fault in novelty. It is new that was instituted by Pius IV, and soon after by the Council of Trent: why may the Pope be allowed to frame something new, but kings, if there is cause, have no right to frame something new? Who has ever found fault with this? But it is lawful if those two things are lawful. For in our oath there is nothing of the whole force of that Toledan and that Aachen oath, which is not contained there. For what is laid down there concerning not joining oneself to those who are contrary to kings could easily have been extended to the Pontiff himself; and they would then have extended it, had he then been, as he now is, contrary to kings.

units.la: Cùm nec acquiescere posset in hoc responso suo, alium adhuc lapidem mouet. In illis Conciliorum Iuramentis nihil addi, quòd potestatem Christi Vicarij vllo modo attingat. Sanè nec in nostro hoc, nisi Regû Cõtrarius sit, nisi suadeat à Rege deficere: tum enim illi, & nos cum illis, copulam omnem cum illo abiuramus. Sed quid? Vlcusne forte habet potestas Pontificis, an vlcus ipsa est, vt nullo modo attingere liceat; vt Tortus hic Pontificalem vocem vsurpet, & quasi de Cathedrâ dicat, Nos decernimus? Nos Iuramentum illud, nullo modo à Catholicis viris suscipi posse decernimus. Nobis verò, libido nulla incessit Pontificis nominandi, libenter nomini eius parceremus; adigit ille nos, dum per Emissarios suos, per Brenia sua miscet se temporalibus, ingerit se Regum rebus, momentisque Rerumpublicarum, dum potestate sua vtitur, ad non sua; vt si maximè vellemus ab illo nominando, à potestate eius attrectanda, abstinere,non liceat. Is ipse necessitatem nobis iniecit, de potestate sua mentionem faciendi, dum potestate sua abutitur ad malum, ( si potestas illa dicenda sit, quæ ad malum est) nempe ad Reges potestate exuendos, gubernaculis priuandos, quorum utrumque ne fiat, expressè cauetur in Toletanis.
units.tr: Since he could not rest content with this answer, he moves yet another stone: nothing is added in those oaths of the Councils that touches in any way the power of Christ's Vicar. Certainly nor in our oath either, unless he is contrary to kings, unless he urges one to desert the King: for then they, and we with them, abjure every bond with him. But what? Is the power of the Pontiff perhaps a sore, or is it itself a sore, so that it is not lawful to touch it in any way; so that Tortus here assumes the voice of the Pontiff and speaks as from the Chair, saying, We decree? We decree that that oath can in no way be taken by Catholic men. As for us, no desire has seized us to name the Pontiff; we would gladly spare his name. But he compels us, since through his emissaries and his briefs he mingles himself in temporal affairs, thrusts himself into the affairs of kings and the moments of commonwealths, and while he uses his power for things not his own, it is not lawful for us, even if we most wished it, to abstain from naming him and from touching his power. He himself has laid upon us the necessity of mentioning his power, since he abuses his power to evil (if that is to be called power which is for evil), namely to strip kings of their power and deprive them of the government; and both of these are expressly guarded against in the Toledan councils.

units.la: Post suum illud Decernimus, & postquàm iam contra scelus illud inexpiabile detonuit, quod illi in se omnes admittunt, qui Pontificis potestatem vllo modo attingunt: pergit porrò Satis pro imperio, & rationem præscribit, quam Reges omnes tenere vult, si quando illis ex tetro aliquo facinore (quale fuit hic Catholicorum apud nos in Regem) aliquos de subditis suis suspectos habeant. Locus sanè, Lectoris attentione dignus. Si metuat sibi Rex à proditione aliquâ, non Iuramentum vllum condat, quo diffluentem subditorum fidem astringat sibi arctius; non; sed adeat sanè Pontificem, abeo petat, vt præcipiat omnibus, sub excommunicationis pœnâ ipso facto incurrenda, vt nemo iuramentum præstitum violare, aut aduersus Principem coniurare, aut hostes ipsius iuuare præsumat. Audiam Matthaei sententiam, de tam pulchrâ hac ratione suâ, quam Regibus præscripsit. Petitio (inquit) iustissima, & omnino admittenda. Primo ergo, sic Iuramentum condere oportet, vt sit absque vllâ omnino Papæ mentione. Post, Papæ supplicare, vt ille subditis præcipere dignetur, ne violent. Papa autem, petitionem tum benignus admittet; atque ita omnia recto ordine procedent.
units.tr: After his We decree, and after he has already thundered against that inexpiable crime which all those commit who in any way touch the power of the Pontiff, he goes on with Enough for authority, and prescribes the course which he wishes all kings to follow if at any time, from some foul crime (such as that of the Catholics among us against the King), they hold any of their subjects suspect. The passage is certainly worthy of the reader's attention. If the King fears some treason, let him not frame any oath whereby to bind the wavering faith of his subjects more tightly to himself; no; but let him certainly approach the Pontiff, and ask him to command all, under the penalty of excommunication to be incurred by the very deed, that no one presume to violate an oath taken, or conspire against the Prince, or aid his enemies. Let us hear Matthew's judgement on this so fine a plan of his, which he has prescribed for kings. The petition (he says) is most just and wholly to be admitted. First, therefore, the oath must be framed so as to have no mention whatever of the Pope. Afterwards, the king should petition the Pope that he deign to command his subjects not to violate it. And the Pope, being then kind, will admit the petition; and thus all things will proceed in right order.

units.la: Quid si autem non supplicet Rex, nec præcipiat Pontifex, de non violando iuramento? Tum verò, anne coniurare fas, & hostes iuuare Regis, sic (vt iubetur) non supplicantis? ita videtur sanè. Quid si autem petat Rex, Papa verò non admittat? Quid si iusta ei non videtur Regis petitio? Quo in loco tum res nostræ? Quid si denique admittat petitionem, & præcipiat sub excommunicationis pœnâ ipso facto incurrenda, ne fidem violent, ne hostes iuuent? Annon qui præcepit, quod præcepit, reuocare, cùm volet, poterit? Tum verò quid agimus? vbi sumus? quid tum fiet denique? Videtisne id agi, vt omnia ab illius beneplacito, arbitrio, nutu pendeant, vt violare fidem liceat, liceat coniurare, hostes iuuare liceat, nisi Ille ne velit, vt nisi Illi petitio porrigatur, nisi Ille petitionem admittat, nisi Ille sic semel admissam post non revocet, Reges in tuto ne sint? Manifeste hoc quaeritur. At quae (malum) petitio haec, vt quod officium cuiusque est, id ei non liceat facere, nisi Papa proprio, nisi impetrata ab eo venia? Officium enim certe, non violare iusiurandum, non aduersus Regem coniurare, non hostes eius vel rebelles iuuare: at, nisi Rex supplicandum censeat Pontifici, nisi supplicanti Pontifex annuat, nusquam tuta fides; ossicium iam officium non est.
units.tr: What if, however, the King does not petition, and the Pontiff does not command, regarding the non-violation of the oath? Then, is it lawful to conspire and aid the King's enemies, in this way (as is ordered) without a petition? So it seems indeed. What if, however, the King petitions, but the Pope does not admit it? What if the King's petition does not seem just to him? In that case, what becomes of our affairs? What if at last he admits the petition, and commands under the penalty of excommunication to be incurred by the very deed, that they not violate their faith, nor aid the enemies? Will he who has commanded what he commanded not be able to revoke it whenever he wishes? Then indeed what are we doing? Where are we? What will happen at last? Do you see that the aim is to make everything depend upon his good pleasure, judgement, nod, so that it is lawful to violate faith, lawful to conspire, lawful to aid the enemies only if he is unwilling; so that unless a petition is put to him, unless he admits the petition, unless he does not afterwards revoke what was once admitted, kings are not to be safe? This is plainly what is sought. But what sort of petition is this (curse it), that a thing which is each man's duty should not be lawful for him to do, unless the Pope gives leave, unless pardon is obtained from him? For it is surely a duty not to violate an oath, not to conspire against the King, not to aid his enemies or rebels: yet unless the King thinks that the Pontiff should be petitioned, and unless the Pontiff nods to the petitioner, faith is nowhere safe; the duty is no longer a duty.

units.la: At etiam haec hactenus omnia tum demum concedit Mathaeus, si sit, nisi sit, Princeps Catholicus. Quid si autem ab Ecclesia alienus? Ne sic quidem improbabit tamen sedes Apostolica, neque prohibebit, dum concludat iuramentum a se propositum intra hos limites, vt ne mentionem ibi faciat vllam de excommunicatione Pontificia, vt ne potestatem Pontificis vllo modo attingat, sed verba iuramenti contra proditores ipsos & innasores dirigat. En sceleus[?], quod omnino cauere oportet: non, ne comprimat aut contrectet, sed ne attingat; non, ne duro aliquo & inciuili, sed ne vllo modo. Ergo, quod ab Ecclesia alienus, ergo quod de noua iuramentum instituit, (quae prius obiecit) nihil iam ad rem: ergo illa tum allegata, nihil. Alienus sit; Iuramentum condat; dum ne illicitum: illicitum autem, non alia de causa, quam quod attingat aliquo modo Pontificis potestatem; petat proditores ipsos; taceat de Pontifice; nihil peccat Iuramentum; nec quia abnegat fidem: nec quia iuramentum perfidia est: nec quia coniunctum eum infidelitate.
units.tr: But Matthew concedes all these things so far only if the prince is, or is not, a Catholic prince. What if he is alien to the Church? Even so, the Apostolic See will not disapprove, nor will it forbid, provided that the oath proposed by him is confined within these limits: that it make no mention there at all of Papal excommunication, and in no way touch the power of the Pontiff, but direct the words of the oath against the traitors and invaders themselves. Here is the snare [?], which must be guarded against entirely: not that it should suppress or handle [the power], but that it should not touch it; not that it should do so with some harshness or incivility, but that it should not do so in any way. Therefore, that he is alien to the Church, and that he has instituted a new oath (which they objected before), is now nothing to the point; therefore those things then alleged are nothing. Let him be alien; let him frame an oath; provided it is not unlawful. And it is unlawful for no other reason than that it touches the power of the Pontiff in some way; if it seeks the traitors themselves and is silent about the Pontiff, the oath sins in nothing; nor because it renounces faith, nor because the oath is perfidy, nor because it is joined with infidelity.

units.la: Quid ergo? Delemusne[?] de iureiurando nomen Pontificis, vt nusquam ibi de eo mentio sit? Non illibenter id quidem, si integrum nobis esset, & nisi deleto eius nomine, iusiurandum quoque integrum esset delendum, quippe nulli rei tum futurum, si omissa Papae mentio. Dicam autem, quo argumento, & rem a fonte deducam: iam enim deduxit nos Cardinalis confessio, ad ipsum Causae totius Cardinem. Vnum hoc (vt vides) iam, illos male habet, quod Pontifex ibi nominatus, alioquin parsisset Breuibus, non improbasset Iuramentum, non prohibuisset. Statim patefacta prodicione pulucariá[?], quaesitum (vt moris est) qui authores, qui participes tam nefandi criminis: viginti (plus minus) eruti[?]; nemo inter eos alienum
units.tr: What then? Shall we delete the name of the Pontiff from the oath, so that there is no mention of him there at all? I would not be unwilling to do so, if it were entirely in our power, and if, with his name deleted, the oath itself were not also to be deleted entire, since it would then serve no purpose, the mention of the Pope being omitted. But I shall say by what argument I do so, and I shall trace the matter back to its source; for the Cardinal's confession has already led us to the very hinge of the whole cause. This one thing (as you see) already troubles them, that the Pontiff is named there; otherwise he would have spared the Briefs, would not have condemned the oath, would not have forbidden it. As soon as the treachery was revealed, the usual inquiry was made into who were the authors and who the accomplices of so abominable a crime: some twenty (more or less) were dragged out; none among them alien

units.la: Note: the text in the lower right is not a note; it is the catchword, placed in bottom_margin. ab Ecclesiâ, haereticus nemo: ad vnum omnes (quales Roma Catholicos facit) Catholici Catholicissimi. Quaesitum deinde, quâ re adducti, quidue dolentes, hoc tam atrox & immane facinus, in animum induxissent: respondent ad vnum omnes, non aliâ vllâ de causâ, quàm Catholicae hîc in regno religionis revocandae. Denique quaesitum, quare cum ijs, qui inter eos sacris praerant (vt sunt Sacerdotes, vt Patres societatis) priùs rem non communicâssent, quàm in tam vetitum nefas ruerent: Illi enim detestati essent sine dubio, & ab Illis discere potuissent, quàm se execrando sceleri in eo devouissent. Falsi autem sunt non modò conscios fuisse sceleris, (quos dixi Sacerdotes & Patres) sed, magnopere etiam authores sibi fuisse: se ab illis, per Sacramenta, tum Poenitentiae, tum Eucharistiae, ad illud obeundum, quasi ad opus Catholicum, saepe confirmatos. Nihil hîc nisi Catholicum, siue finem spectes, propter quem: siue actores, siue authores ipsos facinoris. Catholici omnes.
units.tr: Note: the text in the lower right is not a note; it is the catchword, placed in bottom_margin. from the Church, no heretic at all: all of them, one and all (such as Rome makes Catholics), most Catholic of Catholics. Then they were asked what had led them, or what grief had moved them, to take this so atrocious and monstrous deed into their minds; they all answer, one and all, for no other cause than the restoration of the Catholic religion in this kingdom. Finally, they were asked why they had not first communicated the matter with those who presided over sacred things among them (such as the priests and the Fathers of the Society), before rushing into so forbidden a wickedness. For those men would undoubtedly have detested it, and could have taught them how they might refrain from devoting themselves to that execrable crime. But they are false not only in saying that the priests and Fathers I have mentioned were accomplices in the crime, but in claiming that these men were greatly its authors for them: that they had often been strengthened by them, through the Sacraments, both of Penance and of the Eucharist, to undertake it, as if it were a Catholic work. Nothing here but Catholic, whether you look to the end for which it was done, or to the doers and authors of the deed itself. All Catholics.

units.la: Quid ergo? Omniúmne Catholicorum eadem mens, votum idem? Absit; De multis spes melior. An verò illi soli sic affecti, & cum illis mortua proditio? Optet hoc quis; sed quis speret? Forte ergo alij quidam malè affecti; videtur: alij quidam secus; ita spes est. Conuenit, vt inter hos sit discrimen aliquod: vt enim, periculosum malù tanquam bonù fidere; ita, iniquum bonos cum malis perdere. Quaesitum tum inter Regni Proceres, Quid agimus, vt detur hos ab illo internoscere? Conclusum ita tandem: Probentur sanè Iuramento◆ quo de Regis, de Regni securitate caueatur; Eo cauto, caetera quae illis scrupulo futura, quoad eius fieri potest, ne attingantur. Quorsum itaque tam multa ibi, quorsum vlla ibi Papae mentio? Poterat caueri illud, nec ille nominari. Imò non poterat; Non poterat, non attingi potestas eius: nam nisi interiecta ibi eius mentio, perinde erat, acsi nullum omnino iusiurandū foret. Ad homines, apposita haec Papae mentio. Habent enim hij homines, clausam in pectore[?], in omni sermone, pacto, promisso, iuramento, clausulam hanc tacitam [nisi Papa secus senserit, nisi aliud Papa iusserit, nisi aliter Papa visum fuerit] Tum etiam, qui laxiores, hanc [ᴗAge[?], iurabo, si ita necesse est, obligabo me: Romae est, qui me soluat denuò]. Duo haec mysteria, cum Catechismo statim docentur; prima haec cura est, initiantur ijs tanquam rudimentis; post eadem semper inculcantur sedulo.
units.tr: What then? Is the mind of all Catholics the same, and their wish identical? Far from it; our hope is better concerning many. But were those alone so disposed, and with them the treachery dead? Who would wish this, but who would hope it? Perhaps, then, certain others are ill-disposed; it seems so: certain others are otherwise; so there is hope. It is fitting that there be some distinction between these: for just as it is dangerous to trust the bad as if they were good, so it is unjust to destroy the good along with the bad. Then among the Peers of the kingdom the question was raised: what shall we do, so that these men may be distinguished from those? It was finally concluded thus: let them indeed be tested by an oath, by which the King's person and the safety of the kingdom may be secured; with that secured, let the other things which might cause them scruple be left untouched, as far as it can be done. Why, then, so much there, why any mention of the Pope there at all? That matter could have been secured without naming him. Indeed it could not; it could not be secured without touching his power: for unless his mention were inserted there, it would be just as if there were no oath at all. This mention of the Pope was added for the sake of these men. For these men have a hidden clause shut up in their breast, in every discourse, pact, promise and oath: "unless the Pope thinks otherwise, unless the Pope has ordered something else, unless it has seemed otherwise to the Pope." Then also, those who are more lax have this: "Go on, I will swear, if it is so necessary; I will bind myself; there is someone at Rome who will release me again." These two mysteries are taught at once along with the Catechism; this is the first care: they are initiated into them as the rudiments; afterwards the same things are diligently impressed again and again.

units.la: Quid juvat autem, aut cui bono est, jurare fidelem se fore, si sic mentem gerat, fidelis ero, quoad hoc me siuerit Pontifex; vbi non siuerit, vale fides? Nemo pius est, qui pietatem cauet, ait Ethnicus. Qui, cum cautione, cum conditione (nisi hoc, nisi illud) pius est, is certe, vel apud Ethnicos, pius non est. Absoluta res est Pietas, caueri non vult: at hijs, quantumcunque bona res, nisi Papa probet, non bona. Fecit ea res, vt pernecessaria additio illa, Papa non obstante, cum absque illa, quod reliquum est, inane prorsus.
units.tr: But what good does it do, or to whose advantage is it, to swear that one will be faithful, if one holds this mind: "I will be faithful, so far as the Pope allows me; when he does not allow it, farewell faithfulness"? "No one is pious who guards against piety," says the heathen. He who is pious with a caution, with a condition (unless this, unless that), is certainly not pious, even among the heathen. Piety is an absolute thing and does not wish to be guarded; but with these men, however good a thing it is, it is not good unless the Pope approves. That addition, "the Pope notwithstanding," has made the rest, without it, utterly empty; it is so very necessary.

units.la: Verum hoc Papa non faciet. Non faciet? Quis hoc praestabit? Qui in Henrico 8º. qui in Regina Elizabetha Anglis, fecit: Qui in Henrico 3º. & 4º. Gallis, fecit: Qui in Laurentio Donato Veneto, fecit; idem denuo cum volet, faciet. Pius 5º. Sixtus 5º. si fecerunt: Paulus 5º. vbi volet, faciet. Imo Paulus 5º. in Venetis, si iam fecit; idem Paulus, cum visum fuerit, annon idem in Anglis facturus est? Quis vetabit, cum iudicabit expedire? Iudicabit autem expedire, cum vires aderunt. Quare nulli rei iusiurandum vllum, absque hac clausula; quin ludibrium iuramenti merum, non iuramentum, si haec defuisset: Non deponam, non deponenti consentiam, non si Papa me iusserit; reus ero iuramenti, etsi Papa me soluerit. Sic oportuit, aut omnino non oportuit.
units.tr: But, you say, the Pope will not do this. He will not? Who will guarantee this? He who did it to Henry VIII of the English, who did it to Queen Elizabeth; who did it to Henry III and Henry IV of the French; who did it to Lorenzo Donato of Venice; the same man, whenever he wishes, will do it again. Pius V and Sixtus V did it, if you like; Paul V will do it wherever he wishes. Indeed, Paul V in Venice, if he has already done it; the same Paul, when it seems fit to him, will he not do the same among the English? Who will forbid it, when he judges it expedient? But he will judge it expedient when he has the power. Wherefore no oath whatever is valid without this clause; indeed, if this had been lacking, it would be a mere mockery of an oath, not an oath: "I will not depose, I will not consent to one who deposes," not even if the Pope has ordered me; "I shall be guilty of perjury," even if the Pope has released me. So it had to be, or it ought not to have been at all.

units.la: Habemus interim confitentem Mattheum, si intra hos limites constituisset Iuramentum, nec mentionem Censurae Pontificiae fecisset, nec attigisset vllo modo potestatem eius, non improbaret, non prohiberet. Attenditisne? Illud ergo est. Non iniustum est, quod iuratum est: Iuramentum non malum de se; deferri potest, praestari potest, sine euidentissima, granissimaque iniuria diuini honoris; salua etiam fide; neque praeter hoc vnum peccat quicquam, quod mentio ibi facta excommunicationis Pontificiae, quod potestatem Pontificis aliquo modo attigit: absque hijs foret, quiuis exigere, quiuis subire posset. Nefas enim vel mentionem facere Censurae; nefas potestatem eius vllo modo, vllo (inquam) modo attingere. Quae an causa satis iusta fit, ipsi viderint. Nam certe nisi mentio de ijs aliqua, nisi aliquo saltem modo attingas potestatem eius, incerta erunt hic omnia; omnia ex illius arbitrio pendebunt; omnia durante beneplacito eius manebunt, nec vlterius. Et hoc quidem à Pontifice quaeritur. Infere Papae mentionem, non iurabunt: exime, iurabunt. Quis haec interpretari nescit? Quis quò tendant non videt? Dandum ergo necessitati, quòd nominatu Pontifex, quòd tacita ibi eius potestas. Et illa, in veteribus Concilijs laudata iuramenta, etsi verbis non ijsdem, idem hoc volunt. Iurant ibi, quòd se Regum Contrarijs non copulabunt: Regum Contrarium tantundem valet. Eâ enim voce (vt seres habet) Papa continetur, Contrarium Regum, & Regnorum omnium, vbi ipse non regnat. Nec tu hoc videris abnuere. Causaris[?] enim quòd Iuramentum, adiunctam habeat mentionem Pontificum, & potestatis suae; dein, quòd adiunctam habeat perfidia notam: ita nota perfidia ubi Pontifex, cum potestate sua. Vnum enim hoc ibi appositum criminaris.
units.tr: Meanwhile we have Matthew confessing that, if he had confined the Oath within these limits, and had made no mention of the Pontifical Censure, and had in no way touched upon his power, he would not have condemned it, nor forbidden it. Do you take note? That is the point. What is sworn is not unjust: an oath is not evil in itself; it can be offered, it can be performed, without the most evident and grievous injury to the divine honour, and with faith also preserved; nor does it sin in anything beyond this one thing, that there is a mention there of Pontifical excommunication, that it in some way touches the power of the Pope: without these things, anyone could demand it, anyone could undertake it. For it is wicked even to make mention of the Censure; wicked to touch his power in any way at all, in any way (I say) whatever. Whether this is a cause just enough, they themselves will see. For certainly, unless there is some mention of these things, unless you touch his power at least in some way, everything here will be uncertain; everything will depend on his will, everything will remain only so long as his pleasure lasts, and no longer. And this indeed is what is asked of the Pope. If you insert a mention of the Pope, they will not swear; remove it, they will swear. Who does not know how to interpret this? Who does not see where these things tend? Therefore one must yield to necessity: that the Pontiff is named, that his power is tacitly there. And those oaths praised in the ancient Councils, although not in the same words, mean this same thing. They swear there that they will not join themselves to the enemies of kings: "the enemy of kings" is worth just as much. For by that word (as the Latin usage has it) the Pope is comprised: "the enemy of kings and of all kingdoms," where he himself does not reign. Nor do you seem to deny this. For you complain that the Oath has an added mention of the Pontiffs and of their power; then, that it has an added mark of perfidy: thus the mark of perfidy is where the Pontiff is, with his power. For this one thing you accuse as added there.

units.la: TUa vero est, non Apologiae, calumnia illa de Bellarmino proditionum in Reginam, vel authore, vel conf. 10. Non enim Authoreius[?] id voluit dicere, nec ei vnquam in mentem venit. Illud autem & voluit, & merito potuit: non satis auspicatam fuisse illam inter Cardinalem & transfugas nostros familiaritatem. Nam hy[?] Illum falsis rumoribus: Ille hos prauis opinionibus oppleuit. Dum enim audiùs illas (quas circumferri tum dicebas) lectiones illius imbiberent; de tantisper praestanda à subditis obedientia, dum vires adsint; cùm adsint autem, excutiendo Principe: egerunt id apud nos omni ope, & operâ, vt in atrum illum diem vires colligerent. Dum credunt illi, de indirecta Pontificis potestate in Principes, facti sunt ipsi subditi indirecti, & indirectè hic multa in Principem machinati sunt. Hoc illud erat quod dicebat Apologia, prodiisse illos è schola Bellarmini, cum suis hisce depravatis dogmatibus: illum enim Authorem citasse saepe, illius vocem pro oraculo habuisse. De Campiano familiari suo, si eum non pudeat, inde est, quia exaruit iam forte in eo color ille virtutis. Nam quod tu scire illum ais: nos hic scimus, infeitiam esse meram, Martyrem causa facit, non poena. Causa autem illi, quae religionem attingeret, haud vlla obiecta est; non vel illa, quae potuit de Primatu Pontificis. Causa, de quâ legitimo iudicio publicè convictus, quòd procurandi causâ, non salutem civium, sed ruinam ciuitatis, totúsque Reipublicæ, & ad res nouas animos addendi, vires colligendi, venisset in Angliam. Propter causam vero eius naturæ, non magni, credo, habenda, mors cuiusquam; nec enim id vsquam legitur, pretiosam in conspectu Domini, mortem proditorum. Vis autem pro certo scire, quantus ille, quàm capitalis proditor? Vbi ab illo, damnato iam capitis, quæreretur, Esséne Regina de iure, & legitima, an pretensa solùm & de facto Regina: respondere renuit. Tum, si immitteret huc Papa copias suas, contra Patriam, contra Principem, quid ageret: cuius à partibus staret; respondit, à Papæ; responsum manu consignauit. Poterat verò superstes esse, si ibi tum sensisset, vt ciuem bonum sentire par erat. Sensit Hartus, & sententiam in eo suam, sibi prodesse sensit: venia illi data, vt & Bosgrauio Iesuitæ, & Rishtono, & Hortono, qui cum Harto eadem senserunt (& contrà quàm Campianus) ne si Papa quidem ipse cum copijs suis veniret, defecturos se tamen, à Regina, vel ab officio discessuros. Sed bene habet, quòd excusa est illa post (quam dicis) Collatio: & in eâ nonnihil habetur, quod Hartus ibi, bonus vir (vt tu eum appellas) & bonus Catholicus, Pontificis potestatem, ad Principes deponendos (quam tu ita totus astruis) planè pernegat; idémque secum sentire Catholicos multos asserit; vt vel Hartus non bonus Confessor, vel malus certè Martyr Campianus. Nam quod hic extruxit, ille diruit: non vnius fidei vtrèque, in hoc grauissimo fidei dogmate.
units.tr: Yours, however, is not the Apology's calumny about Bellarmine, that he was the author or the confederate of treasons against the Queen. For the author of the Apology did not wish to say this, nor did it ever come into his mind. But this he did wish, and rightly could say: that the familiarity between the Cardinal and our deserters was not sufficiently auspicious. For these men filled him with false rumours, and he filled them with depraved opinions. For while they imbibed those lectures of his (which you said were then circulated) concerning the obedience to be rendered by subjects for so long as their strength allowed, and, when that strength was present, to cast out the Prince: they worked for this among us with every effort and every labour, so that they might gather their forces for that dreadful day. While they believe in the indirect power of the Pontiff over Princes, they themselves became indirect subjects, and indirectly they have plotted much against the Prince here. This is what the Apology meant when it said that they came forth from Bellarmine's school with these depraved dogmas of his: for they often cited that author, and held his voice as an oracle. As for Campian, his familiar friend, if he is not ashamed of it, the reason is this: that colour of virtue has perhaps already dried up in him. For what you say you know of him: we here know that it is sheer ignorance; a cause makes a martyr, not a punishment. But no cause touching religion was laid against him, not even that which could concern the Primacy of the Pontiff. The cause was one for which, convicted by a lawful public judgment, he had come into England for the purpose of procuring not the safety of citizens, but the ruin of the commonwealth, and the overthrow of the whole State, and of stirring up minds to revolution, of gathering forces. And on account of a cause of such a nature, which I believe is not to be held in great esteem, the death of anyone is not precious; for nowhere is it read, "precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of traitors." But do you wish to know for certain how great that man was, how capital a traitor? When he, already condemned to death, was asked whether the Queen was Queen by right and lawfully, or only pretended and Queen in fact, he refused to answer. Then, if the Pope were to send his troops here against the country and against the Prince, what would he do, and on whose side would he stand? He answered: on the Pope's side; and he signed the answer with his hand. Yet he could have survived, had he then felt as a good citizen ought to feel. Hart felt, and felt that his opinion in this matter served him: he was granted pardon; so too the Jesuit Bosgrave, and Rishton, and Horton, who held the same opinion as Hart (and contrary to Campian), that even if the Pope himself came with his troops, they would nevertheless not defect from the Queen or depart from their duty. But it is well that that Conference which you mention was published afterwards; and in it there is something to be found: that Hart there, a good man (as you call him), and a good Catholic, plainly denies the power of the Pontiff to depose Princes (which you so entirely maintain); and he asserts that many Catholics think with him. So either Hart was not a good confessor, or Campian, certainly, was a bad martyr. For what the one built up, the other tore down: both were not of one faith in this most grave dogma of the faith.

units.la: DE eo autem, quod post vellicas, conscientiæ causâ nihil in quenquam à Rege statutum; cùm multæ tamen soluendæ sint; cùm nisi soluantur, carceres adeundi sint: satis iam antè responsum, vbi de Legis Mulctatitiæ æquitate egimus; quæ tamen ipsa Lex, diu iam antè, nec à Rege primùm statuta est. Sacerdos haud vllus actus in exilium, nisi qui lege, capitis damnatus, cum mitiore exilij poenâ mortem commutare posse, beneficij loco numerauit. Blackwellus ipse, non multo, credo, habitor, cùm in carcerem veniret, quàm iam est: quem, quasi maceratum ibi, moeres. Nec tibi notum, quid illi posset obijci: id constat, non modò functionem Presbyteri, sed & iurisdictionem Archipresbyteri exercuisse; idque diu, idque authoritate peregrinâ, cuius apud nos multò quàm simplicis Presbyteri, vt causa grauior, ita poena seueritor: nihil in eum statutum est, nisi mitè. Nemo verò suspensus, nemo dissectus, propter Iuramentum non susceptum, nec factum id, nec fieri potest; Lex nulla patitur; calumnia haec mera est.
units.tr: As for what he adds afterwards, that the king has decreed nothing against anyone on grounds of conscience, while many fines must still be paid, and if they are not paid, prisons must be entered: I have already answered this sufficiently, where we treated of the fairness of the Fining Law; yet that very law was not first enacted by the king, but long before. No priest was ever sent into exile unless, condemned to death by law, he was granted the exchange of death for the milder penalty of exile, which was counted as a favour. Blackwell himself, I believe, has not been living for long in the prison he is now in, and you lament him as if he were being worn away there. Nor is it known to you what could be objected to him: it is established that he exercised not only the office of priest but also the jurisdiction of archpriest, and that for a long time, and by a foreign authority, which among us is a graver cause, and so a more severe penalty, than that of a simple priest: nothing has been decreed against him except mildly. But no one has been hanged, no one disembowelled, on account of an oath not taken; neither that has happened nor can it happen; no law permits it; this charge is pure calumny.

units.la: Carnettus autem plurimùm merito suo morte multatus, quem tu, nescio cur dicis, virum omni genere doctrinae, & vitae sanctitate incomparabilem.
