Doctrinâ si quam habuit, sibi habuit; Nemo illi eam eluere, nemo extundere potuit: deprecatus semperin re literariâ, collatione omnem. Profectò, in chartis eius, quae repertae sunt, in toto sermone nihil usquam reconditae eruditionis: Bacchum enim certè magis redolebat, quàm Apollinem. Siquid autem de Theologiâ incidisset, ablegabat ad alium, nescio quem, collegam suum: se enim per annos iam multos rebus gerendis fuisse, totum in praxim politicam incubuisse: eam praxim, doctrinam sibi omnem (siqua unquam fuit) expectorâsse: ut nostri, qui hominem adierunt, non alio sensu, doctrinam eius incomparabilem putârint, quàm quod eam sibi nunquam comparare potuerit. De Sanctitate verò eius, vellem mitteres; atque utinam de Sobrietate dicere posses, vix enim est, ut qui sobrie non bibat, sanctè vivat, vel sanctitatem sibi veram comparare possit. Ille verò, quàm saepe non sobrius, nimis multis notum: quod tu, nisi incomparabilem eius sanctitatem praedicâsses, à me nunquam audijsses. Tace verò deinceps de sanctitate, ne plus etiam adhuc, quod nolis, audias.
units.tr: Carnet, however, was punished with death, for very good reason, and you say, I know not why, that he was a man incomparable in every kind of learning and in holiness of life. If he had any learning, he kept it to himself; no one could wring it out of him or extract it: he always avoided discussion in literary matters. Indeed, in the papers of his that were found, there is nowhere in the whole discourse any recondite erudition: he smelt of Bacchus far more than of Apollo. If anything on theology came up, he sent the questioner away to another colleague of his, I know not whom: for he said that he had been for many years engaged in public affairs and had devoted himself entirely to political practice, and that practice had drained out of him all the learning he ever had (if he ever had any). So our men who approached the man thought his learning incomparable in no other sense than that he had never been able to acquire any. As for his holiness, I would like you to say nothing; and would that you could speak of his sobriety, for scarcely can one who does not drink soberly live holily, or acquire true holiness for himself. But how often he was not sober is too well known to many: and you would never have heard this from me, had you not proclaimed his holiness incomparable. Be silent henceforth about holiness, lest you hear, what you would not wish, even more.

units.la: Est & illa calumnia, affectu eum supplicio, quia reuelare noluit, quae falsâ conscientiâ reuelare non potuit. Non enim ab uno rem resciuit, sed pluribus; & ab uno illo, qui vobis forte notus, non unâ ratione, sed pluribus, nec semel, sed saepius resciuit, nec à solo, sed cum comite, ut si, unâ ratione reuelare non potuerit, potuerit aliis: Tum, si maximè in confessione resciuisset; at potuit tamen, personâ non reuelatâ, tantum reuelare, quantum sat erat, immani illi sceleri auertendo. Potuit, & debuit, idque ex doctrinâ vestrâ debuit, ut cui venia sit à confitente facta, ut reuelare posset. Tùm, reuelauit etiam, in pudorem tum vestrum, tum suum: nimirùm, rem totam illi à conscio criminis significatam, non ut peccatum, sed quam ipse prius intellexerat. Signata haec manu eius, prolata palàm, palàm probata sunt; Et vos tamen negatis, qui Romae estis, qui praeter auditum nihil habetis: auditum autem ab iis, qui vobis illudunt ipsi rem secus se habere sciunt. Admirabilis profectò impudentia est, ea mendacia literis mandare, ex mendacis aliculus transfuga pertusâ fide, quæ Garnetti hic autographo, quæ Actis publicis refutantur.
units.tr: There is also the calumny that he was put to death because he would not disclose what, with a false conscience, he could not disclose. For he did not learn the matter from one person but from several; and from that one man, who is perhaps known to you, he learned it not by one means but by several, and not once but more often, and not from one alone but with a companion; so that, if he could not disclose it by one means, he could by others. Moreover, even if he had learned it in confession, yet he could nevertheless disclose so much of it, without naming the person, as was enough to avert that monstrous crime. He could, and he ought to have done so, and by your own teaching he ought: since the one who made the confession had given him leave to disclose it. Then, he did disclose it, to the shame both of you and of himself: namely, the whole matter, which had been signified to him by the accomplice in the crime, not as a sin but as something he himself had already understood. This, written in his own hand, brought out openly, has been openly proved; and yet you deny it, you who are in Rome, who have nothing but hearsay, and hearsay from those who mock you while knowing that the matter stands otherwise. It is truly an astonishing impudence to commit to writing those lies, from the leaky faith of some deserter from the liar's camp, which are refuted by Garnet's own autograph and by the public records.

units.la: SI Juramentum, cùm rigidum est, displicet, cùm temperatum, ne sic quidem placet, annon iusta reprehensio? Annon Christus ipse reprehendat, quibus nec Johannes Baptista rigorem suum, nec ipse lenitatē suam probare potuit; præsertim, cùm, non minùs res ipsa, quàm verba moderata? Quî enim euadas hîc? Effer aliquid planè; ad irritandum tendit: tempera; ad decipiendum. Si rigidè quid dictum, furor est: si moderatè, fraus: & ibi fraus, vbi tamen fraus vel maximè cauetur. Quæ verò ibi fraus? Quòd non aperte introducit Primatum Regium in Spiritualibus, sed tectè tendit ad eundem finem, sub prætextu, & colore fidelitatis. Nec aperte verò, nec tectè etiam. Age enim; percurre mihi vndecim illa Juramenti capita, torquè quantum potes; pòst, frontem ter perfrica, ac dic, vbi in toto Juramento, Spirituale aliquid Regi tribuitur. Vult in eo Rex non deponi, non ditione spoliari, non inuadi, non sine subditis relinqui, arma contra se non geri, vim non afferri, vult fidem à suis, vult defensionem sibi praestari, vult mala consilia detegi, vult non occidi, vult Juramentum hoc non eludi, vult fraude vestrâ non decipi. Hæc (ni fallor) tua illa vndecim sunt. Vbi hic Spirituale quicquam? Vbi, vel tectè, primatus vllus in spiritualibus? Erue nobis si potes, si est tibi pudor aliquis, quâ clausulâ latet, negatio illa Apostolici, assertio Regij Primatus: ostende vestigia alicubi impressa, per quæ, ad fictitium illum finem tuum tendat Juramentum. Annon potest saluus Pontifici Primatus esse, nisi Rege non saluo? Tædet me calumniæ tam putidæ. Præstigiæ Satanæ (quas dicis) in oculis tuis sunt, in quodcunque speculum contueris, reflectunt in te; nec aliam calcas spinam, quàm eam, quam fers infixam: in Juramento enim nulla est, nec tendit ad fraudem; tu ubique pertendis, & pertingis ad stultitiam, denique & transcurris etiam; nec quicquam tibi pensi est quid dicas, dum dicas malè. Posset autem eludi artificium hoc vestrum, caueri posset illi de Primatu suo spirituali. Quidsi enim sic præfari detur? Regi fidem seruabo, etsi hoc nolit Pontifex; quantumuis primum haberi vult in spiritualibus. En Regi negatus; Pontifici assertus Primatus: Non minus tamen, scio, illud tum Pontifex, quàm hoc iam, iurare permitteret.
units.tr: If the oath, when it is harsh, displeases, and when it is moderate, does not please even so, is not the reproof just? Would not Christ himself rebuke those in whom neither John the Baptist could approve his severity nor he himself his gentleness; especially since the matter itself is no less moderate than the words? For how do you escape here? If you state something plainly, it tends to provoke: if you soften it, to deceive. If something is said harshly, it is madness; if moderately, it is fraud: and there is fraud where fraud is most carefully guarded against. And what fraud is there? That it does not openly introduce the royal Primacy in spiritual matters, but tends covertly to the same end, under the pretext and colour of fidelity. Neither openly, nor even covertly. Come now; run through for me those eleven heads of the oath, twist them as much as you can; then rub your forehead three times and tell me where in the whole oath anything spiritual is granted to the king. The king wishes in it not to be deposed, not to be stripped of his dominion, not to be attacked, not to be left without his subjects, that no arms be borne against him, that no violence be inflicted, he wishes fidelity from his own people, he wishes defence to be afforded him, he wishes evil counsels to be revealed, he wishes not to be killed, he wishes this oath not to be evaded, he wishes not to be deceived by your trickery. These (unless I am mistaken) are your eleven. Where is anything spiritual here? Where, even covertly, any primacy in spiritual matters? Draw out for us, if you can, if you have any shame, what clause hides that denial of the Apostolic and that assertion of the royal Primacy: show us footprints anywhere impressed, by which the oath tends to your fictitious end. Can the Pontiff's Primacy not remain safe unless the king is unsafe? I am weary of such putrid calumny. The illusions of Satan (as you call them) are in your eyes; in whatever mirror you look, they reflect back upon you; nor do you tread any other thorn than the one you carry stuck in you: for in the oath there is nothing, and it does not aim at fraud; you stretch everywhere, and reach into folly, and finally even run past; nor do you care what you say, provided you say it badly. Yet your trick could be evaded, and he could have been guarded against regarding his spiritual Primacy. For what if the oath were framed thus? "I will keep faith with the king, even if the Pontiff does not wish it; however much he wishes to be held first in spiritual matters." See: the Primacy denied to the king, asserted to the Pontiff: yet I know the Pontiff would no less have permitted that to be sworn then than this is now.

units.la: VBi dixit Apologia, Rex nouum fidei articulum non cõdit, nec se de articulo aliquo iudicem constituit; rapit ille statim ad Pontificem. Nihil autem opus hoc; nemo illum id facere, dixerat: sed tamen rapit, contradicendi studio solo. Ecce autem, vt se expediat. Negat, à Pontifice nouos fidei articulos condi posse: si tamen per articulos fidei significantur, quaecunque dogmata quae fide Catholicâ credi debent, tum concedit, posse; nec dubitat sic multos fidei articulos ab eo conditos. Nihil egit: nam nos neutros, nec hos, nec illos articulos à Rege condi posse dicimus. En ergo, vt aërem verberauit. Articulos autè hic nobis facit duûm generum. Qui immediata reuelationis sunt, eos autem non condi. Quidni vero? Quia à Prophetis & Apostolis, illi literis mandati sunt. Quid tum postea, nisi Papa illis authoritatem suam impertiat? Audi glossam vestram:Aduerte, quòd verba textus non sunt verba Papæ, sed Salomonis in Prou ca. 26: sed, quia textus hic, est Canonizatus, facit fidem, & inducit necessitatem, sicut si editus esset à Papâ: quia omnia nostra authoritatem, quibus authoritatem nostram impertitimus. Quodsi ergo authoritatem suam non impertiisset ei Papa; quodsi ergo canonizatus non fuisset, non fecisset fidem, sicut si editus esset à Papâ: proinde non valuisset. Tum{b}Stapletoni nota sententia. Pastorem Hermae, vel Clementis Constitutiones, etiam ad Canonem addi posse, si id ita videatur. Nec tu ergo plenè nobis hic edisseris authoritatem Pontificis. De altero genere dogmatum, quae fide Catholicâ credi debent, à Pontifice dicis eiusmodi multa condi: Sed coadiuuantibus Concilijs Episcoporum. Nec in eo satis consulis dignitati Pontificis; vel sine Concilijs ab eo conduntur, cur illis molestus sit? Errare sine illo possunt Concilia, quantumuis numerosa: Ille si solus sit, si sine illis, errare non potest, memor modò sit vt sedeat in Cathedrâ. Noli ergo abundare in superfluis: serua autem Pontifici illibatum honorem hunc potestatis suae, abeat quò volet onerosa haec multitudo coadiutorum. Sed, nec illud attificiose satis à te positum, vt articulus fidei dici debeat, quod ex articulo deduc[?]tum fit. Articuli enim principia sunt; quae verò deducta ex ijs, sunt conclusiones. Tum, quis ita loquitur, quis locutus est vnquam, condere immediatas reuelationes Dei? Quis ita cerritus, vt diceret, Pontifex condit reuelationes Dei ? Imò condit reuelationes suas, carnis & sanguinis, atque illas obtrudit Ecclesiæ, ac suscipi vult tanquam reuelationes Dei. Quis etiam tam infoelici genio natus, vt nesciat, explicare & deducere, non esse condere? Omnino conditam rem esse oportere, priusquàm ex eâ deduci possit quid, aut de eâ explicari. Sed hæc tua est dexteritas in distinguendo. Absit autem, vt quoties explicatur quid, aut deducitur ex articulis,condantur noui.
units.tr: WHERE the Apology said, "The king does not frame a new article of faith, nor does he constitute himself judge of any article; you immediately snatch at the Pontiff." Yet there was no need for this; no one had said that he did it: but still you snatch, from the sheer zeal of contradicting. See now how he extricates himself. He denies that new articles of faith can be framed by the Pontiff: yet if by articles of faith are meant whatever doctrines must be believed in the Catholic faith, then he concedes that they can be, nor does he doubt that many articles of faith have been framed by him in this way. He has accomplished nothing: for we say that neither these nor those articles can be framed by the king. So here, he has beaten the air. He makes for us articles of two kinds: those which are of immediate revelation, which he says are not framed. Why not indeed? Because they were committed to writing by the Prophets and Apostles. What then afterwards, unless the Pope bestows his authority on them? Hear your gloss: "Note that the words of the text are not the words of the Pope, but of Solomon in Proverbs 26: but because this text is canonised, it makes faith and induces necessity, just as if it had been published by the Pope: because all our authority, to which we have imparted our authority." Therefore, if the Pope had not imparted his authority to it; therefore, if it had not been canonised, it would not have made faith, as if it had been published by the Pope: and so it would not have been valid. Then there is the well-known opinion of Stapleton: that the Shepherd of Hermas, or the Constitutions of Clement, may also be added to the Canon, if it seems so. Nor, therefore, do you fully set out for us here the authority of the Pontiff. Of the other kind of doctrines, which must be believed in the Catholic faith, you say that many such are framed by the Pontiff: "But with the assistance of the Councils of Bishops." Nor in this do you sufficiently consult the dignity of the Pontiff: or if they are framed by him without the Councils, why is he troubled by them? Councils, however numerous, can err without him: if he is alone, if without them, he cannot err, provided only he remembers "to sit in the Chair." Do not therefore abound in superfluities: preserve for the Pontiff unimpaired this honour of his power, and let this burdensome multitude of helpers go wherever it likes. But nor is it cleverly enough put by you, that what is deduced from an article ought to be called an article of faith. "For articles are principles;" but what is deduced from them "are conclusions." Then, who speaks thus, who has ever spoken of framing immediate revelations of God? Who is so crazed as to say that the Pope frames the revelations of God? Indeed he frames his own revelations, of flesh and blood, and thrusts them upon the Church, and wishes them to be received as revelations of God. Who also is born with so unlucky a genius as not to know that to explain and to deduce is not to frame? Surely a matter must first be framed before anything can be deduced from it, or explained concerning it. But this is your dexterity in distinguishing. Far be it, however, that whenever something is explained, or deduced from the articles, new ones are framed.

units.la: Illud autem cecidit sanè incommodè,quòd in Conciliis quę nominas, Niceno, C P.[?] Ephesino, nullus Pontifex comparuit; Omnia ibi ab Episcopis deducta, explicata: Pontifex nihil vel explicuit, vel deduxit. Sed postea approbauit, inquies: suffragio quidem suo,sicut cæteri; at explicata, & deducta ab aliis. Verùm eòdem res recidit. Nec enim facerent fidem hæc, non magis quàm Proverbia Salomonis, nisi illis authoritatem suam Papa impertijset. Quare, nihil opus, vt sic, in duo genera dispescerees: par est enim eademque de vtrisque ratio. Sed est, & adhuc genus tertium, quale nimirum de stigmatibus Francisci; nec primarius articulus, nec primaryi explicatio: de quo tamen, sic decernit non nemo Pontifex, vt qui oppositum teneret, haereticus censeretur.
units.tr: It was certainly an awkward thing, though, that in the Councils you name, the Nicene, Constantinopolitan and Ephesine, no Pontiff appeared. Everything there was set out and explained by the bishops; the Pontiff explained and deduced nothing. But, you will say, he afterwards approved them: by his vote indeed, like the rest; but the matters had been explained and deduced by others. Yet the matter comes to the same thing. For these would not carry authority, any more than the Proverbs of Solomon, unless the Pope had lent them his authority. Therefore there is no need to divide them into two kinds in this way, for the reasoning is equal and the same for both. But there is also a third kind, such as the stigmata of Francis: neither a primary article nor a primary explanation. Yet concerning this, some Pope has so decreed that whoever held the opposite would be judged a heretic.

units.la: Atque hæc de Articulis Simile autem iudicium est, de Pontificis iudicio. Non constituit se iudicem,an articulus fidei recipiendus sit: constituit se iudicem, quando dubium est, an quid ad fidem pertineat, annon pertineat, & tum discernit à quâ parte sit veritas. Duplex est ergo iudicium de articulis fidei; prius, an articuli sint recipiendi: sic non iudicat Papa de articulo fidei, sed illis iudicium suum subijcit: posterius, an quid ad fidem pertineat: sic autem iudicat, & subijcit Articulos iudicio suo. Mira verò loquendi proprietas: vt sententia, de quâ dubium est, pertineatne ad fidem,annon pertineat,atque in quâ discerni non potest,à quâ parte sit veritas,dicatur articulus fidei, id est,principium Theologicum; sic enim sunt articuli. Mira autem distinctio: Non est Papa iudex de articulo, an recipiendus sit; est tamen iudex de sententiâ, an pertineat ad fidem: Quasi articulus ipse, ad fidem non pertineat, non sit de ijs, quæ ad fidem pertinent: Quasi etiam, quod ad fidem pertinet, ad articulum aliquem non pertinet: Quod autem pertinet ad articulum, articulus dici non potest; nihil enim pertinere potest, ad seipsum; nam duo sunt; id quod; id ad quod pertinet. Quasi denique alia sit, & non una apud vos fides, eademque tum de articulis, tum de sententijs ad fidem pertinentibus: Quasi pari fide non credatis purgatorium, & Passionem; Sanctorum invocationem, & Dei; Francisci stigmata, & Christi; articulos, & dogmata; cum ubique Medium proponens idem sit, nec in hijs magis quàm in illis infallibile. Mira verò subtilitas hæc tua, quamque alius nugas diceret. Tolli verò iubes aquinocationem; tollatur sanè, tolli enim digna est: Calumnia [?] verò nulla est ibi, nisi tua. Nemo enim Pontificem, tute ipse solus, huius eum criminis allegasti.
units.tr: So much for the articles. The judgement concerning the Pope's judgement is similar. He does not constitute himself judge whether an article of faith is to be received; he constitutes himself judge when it is doubtful whether something pertains to the faith or not, and then he distinguishes on which side the truth lies. The judgement concerning articles of faith is therefore twofold: first, whether the articles are to be received; in this sense the Pope does not judge an article of faith, but submits them to his own judgement. Second, whether something pertains to the faith; in this sense he does judge, and he submits the articles to his judgement. A remarkable use of words indeed: that a proposition, about which it is doubtful whether it pertains to the faith or not, and on which the truth cannot be discerned as lying on one side or the other, is called an article of faith, that is, a theological principle; for thus the articles are. A remarkable distinction too: the Pope is not judge of an article as to whether it is to be received, yet he is judge of a proposition as to whether it pertains to the faith. As if an article itself did not pertain to the faith, and were not among the things that pertain to the faith. As if what pertains to the faith did not pertain to some article! And what pertains to an article cannot be called an article, for nothing can pertain to itself; there are two things: that which is, and that to which it pertains. Finally, as if among you there were a different faith, and not one and the same faith, both concerning articles and concerning propositions pertaining to the faith! As if you did not believe with equal faith in purgatory and the Passion, in the invocation of saints and of God, in the stigmata of Francis and of Christ, in articles and dogmas; when the one who proposes the mean is everywhere the same, and in these no more than in those is he infallible. Remarkable indeed is this subtlety of yours, which another would call trifles. You bid us do away with equivocation; let it certainly be done away with, for it deserves to be. But there is no calumny there, except your own. For no one but you yourself has charged the Pontiff with this crime.

units.la: Ad odiosam illam Cardinalis collationem, Successoris Petri, & Successoris Henrici octaui, respondet Apologia, facilius probari posse, succedere Regem suis maioribus, tam persona quàm virtutibus; quàm succedere Papam Petro, siue quoad personam id, siue quoad doctrinam. Mittis doctrinam, laudo; est enim difficillimæ probationis: De persona assumis; Fide Catholicâ credi, ubi nullus haesitandi relinquitur locus, Romanum Pontificem, Sancto Petro, in Apostolicâ dignitate & potestate succedere. Crudè tamen nimis à te ponuntur ista, & indistinctè. Mittis enim, de persona: De Pontifice dicis ingenere. At Regi Iacobo Papam Paulum 5tum. debebas opponere, non Pontificem Romanum indefinitè. Tametsi enim de Pontifice (ut quidem confusè capitur) multa vobis implicitâ fide credantur: at (puto) quid actum in Conclavi de Paulo 5o. in Pontificem assumendo, non fide Catholicâ credi vobis, aut, præterquàm morali certitudine vllâ posse concludi. Noli tamen de Pontifice ipso, ne in genere quidem, fidem tuam ita valdè præcipitare: nam, & de eo, saltem aliquem relinqui locum haesitandi, faxo mox videas. De Rege nostro, quòd is Henrico 8o. succedat, est ita ut dicis, Catholicâ fide non tenemus; vestra sit illa impudentia, de Pontifice. Qui negat, haereticus non sit: certè, ut neque qui solem meridie lucere; sed stips, sed caudex, sed fungus. Moralis hîc certitudo sola; sic est; sed maior quàm Pontificis vestri. Naturâ enim constat & stirpe, non Comitijs, quibus, nullus Euripus incertus magis; atque, in quæ si liceat inquirere, quàm multa sunt, quæ aliquà admittunt Juris exceptionem? unde illa vobis tot Schismata exciterunt.
units.tr: To that hateful comparison of the Cardinal, between the successor of Peter and the successor of Henry VIII, the Apology answers that it can more easily be proved that a king succeeds his ancestors both in person and in virtues, than that the Pope succeeds Peter, whether in person or in doctrine. You set aside doctrine, and I commend you for it, for it is most difficult to prove. As to the person, you assume that by Catholic faith it is believed, where no room is left for doubt, that the Roman Pontiff succeeds Saint Peter in apostolic dignity and power. Yet these things are put too crudely by you, and without distinction. You set aside the person, and speak of the Pontiff in general. But you ought to have opposed Pope Paul V to King James, not the Roman Pontiff indefinitely. For although many things about the Pontiff (as he is commonly understood in a confused way) are believed by you with implicit faith, yet (I think) what was done in the Conclave when Paul V was chosen Pontiff cannot be believed by you with Catholic faith, nor concluded with anything beyond moral certainty. Yet do not stake your faith so rashly on the Pontiff himself, not even in general; for you will soon see that some room for doubt is left concerning him too. That our king succeeds Henry VIII is, as you say, not held by us with Catholic faith; that impudence is yours, concerning the Pontiff. Whoever denies it is not a heretic: certainly no more than one who denies that the sun shines at noon. But (you say) they are blockheads, dolts, mushrooms. Here there is only moral certainty; so it is; but it is greater than that of your Pontiff. For it rests on nature and descent, not on elections, than which no tide is more uncertain; and if it were permitted to inquire into those, how many things there are that admit some exception of law! Whence those many schisms of yours have arisen.

units.la: Interim verò, si forte lib.2.cap.12. voces illæ non sunt, pie credi, (nam de morali certitudine, verba ibi nulla citantur) nodus ille, vix dignus vindice; Res ipsa ibi est: nec te hoc latere potuit. Nam lib.4°.cap.6°. Synonyma sunt Cardinali, probabile est, & pie credi potest: Probabilia ergo quæ sunt, pie vobis creduntur. Reperies autem eo ipso in loco, nempe lib.2. cap.12. Non est improbabile, Petri Sedem Romæ locatam, Domino jubente, unde tota vobis pendet Successionis ratio. Non est hoc improbabile; tantùm ergo probabile hoc est: Quare pie tantùm credi potest. Res ergo ibi est, atque assatim.
units.tr: Meanwhile, if perhaps the words in book 2, chapter 12, are not "piously believed" (for no words about moral certainty are cited there), that knot, scarcely worthy of a champion, is in fact there, and you could not have failed to notice it. For in book 4, chapter 6, the Cardinal's words "it is probable" and "may be piously believed" are equivalent. Things that are probable, therefore, are piously believed by you. You will find, moreover, in that very place, namely book 2, chapter 12: "It is not improbable that the seat of Peter was established at Rome by the Lord's command," on which the whole reasoning of succession for you depends. "It is not improbable": therefore this is only probable. Hence it can only be piously believed. The matter is thus there, and in abundance.

units.la: Neq; verò unum modò hoc; permulta, ibi dicuntur à Cardinale, quæ si credi oportet à vobis, pie oportet; ex pietate, non debito; ex devotione, non necessitate vllâ; atque adeò, de quibus si detur Cardinali certitudo moralis, haud amplius, credo, postulet. Sunt enim non pauca illic, de quibus præclarè vobiscum agatur, si vel moraliter certa sint. Nam illud ibi, Tametsi forte non sit, tamen omninò asserendum esse quod sit, fatis[?] forte sit, nimis forte, si quis in animum inducat, ut pie velit credere.
units.tr: Nor is this the only instance. Very many things are said there by the Cardinal which, if you ought to believe them, you ought to believe piously: out of piety, not out of obligation; out of devotion, not out of any necessity. And so, if the Cardinal is granted moral certainty concerning them, he will not, I think, ask for more. For there are not a few there, on which you would be dealt with very handsomely, if they were even morally certain. For that passage reads: "Although perhaps it is not so, yet it must be asserted absolutely that it is so; it is perhaps too perhaps, if anyone brings himself to wish to believe piously."

units.la: Fide verò Catholicâ qui potest? cùm tot necesse est concurrant hypotheses, ut constet Successionis negotium illud; nec omnes possint esse de fide, ubi nullus relinquitur hæsitandi locus. Quis autem nescit, ubi præmissa moraliter tantùm certa sunt, non elici conclusionem nisi moralis certitudinis? Ita quidem, hîc apud nos Transalpinos, deteriorem semper atq; debiliorem partem sequitur conclusio. Vide mihi jam de tuâ hac Successionis fide.
units.tr: But who can hold it with Catholic faith? Since so many hypotheses must concur for that business of succession to be established, and not all of them can be "of faith, where no room is left for doubt." Who does not know that, where the premises are only morally certain, the conclusion cannot be drawn except with moral certainty? Thus indeed, here among us across the Alps, the conclusion always follows the worse and weaker part. See now, I beg you, to your faith in this succession.

units.la: Quod, totius structuræ fundamentum est illi, nempe, Monarchia est Regimen optimum, id aliâ ratione constat forte, de fide certè Catholicâ non est.
units.tr: What is the foundation of the whole structure for him, namely, that monarchy is the best form of government, may perhaps be established on some other ground, but it is certainly not a matter of Catholic faith.

units.la: Tum, si optimum sit an Ecclesia quoq; optimum, de eo etiam quæri porrò poterit. Non enim semper quod de se optimum, id ita, [illegible, ~8 letters] ait Philosophus, hîc, hîc, nunc. Non ita forsitan Ecclesia. Nec enim si Ecclesia cœtus sit optimus; sequitur, ut ei propterea optimum de se regimen conveniat. Non sanè. Color purpureus, color optimus; at quo nolletis colorari vultus vestros, vel Dominus tuus, vel tu, quæ est tamen corporis vestri pars optima.
units.tr: Then, if it is the best, the question can further be asked whether the Church is also the best. For what is best in itself is not always so [illegible, about 8 letters], as the Philosopher says: "here, here, now." Perhaps the Church is not so. For even if the Church is the best assembly, it does not follow that for that reason the best government in itself belongs to it. Certainly not. Purple is a good colour; yet you would not wish your faces to be coloured with it, or your lord, or yourself, though this is nevertheless the best part of your body.

units.la: Deinde verò, an dici possit Petrus Monarcha, aut liber ei ita inscribi, Petro Monarcha summo; hæsitet quis, propter Christi verbum, Reges Gentium sic: vos autem non sic: Reges Gentium Monarchæ; quare haud quenquam de Apostolis Monarcham dici voluit. Et tu bona fide dic; an credis, notam fuisse Petro Monarchiam hanc suam; & cùm Româ iam esset, ac Neronem ibi conspiceret, vnquamne illi venisse putas in mentem, cogitationem hanc; vt Iste nunc imperat: at ego tamen Monarcha summus sum, quando, Christus mihi dixit, Pasce, id est, Regio more impera.
units.tr: Next, can it be said that Peter was a monarch, or can a book be inscribed to him thus, "To Peter, the supreme monarch"? Someone may hesitate because of Christ's word: "The kings of the Gentiles do so, but you shall not do so: the kings of the Gentiles are monarchs." Therefore he did not wish any of the Apostles to be called monarch. And you, in good faith, tell me: do you believe that this monarchy of his was known to Peter? And when he was already at Rome and saw Nero reigning there, do you think it ever came into his mind to think this thought: "He now commands; yet I am nevertheless the supreme monarch, since Christ said to me, 'Feed,' that is, 'rule in royal fashion'"?

units.la: Etiam Primatus ipse, in petrâ fundatus non est. Niti enim inprimis loco Scripturæ, de quo liberum nobis vult esse {a}Augustinus, velimúsne de Petro intelligere, annon velimus. Harum duarum sententiarum, quæ sit probabilior, eligat Lector. Semel quidem aliquo in loco, de Petro: post autem sæpissimè, aliter interpretatum esse. Quare probabilior illi sententia, vt non sit de Petro. Vt ergò piè posset, necessariò non debeat, sic intelligi. Saltè in medio rem reliquit Augustinus: Non oportuit, si basis in eâ sit totius Monarchia. Sensus enim loci illius, nisi de fide Catholicâ sit, labascit vobis statim Monarchia vestra omnis.
units.tr: The Primacy itself is not founded on the rock. For it rests first of all on Scripture, which Augustine wants us to be free about: whether we will understand it of Peter, or whether we will not. Let the reader choose which of these two opinions is more probable. Once, certainly, in one place, it is understood of Peter; but very often elsewhere it has been interpreted otherwise. Therefore the opinion that it is not about Peter is the more probable. So it may be understood in this way, piously, but it need not be. Augustine leaves the matter in the middle: it was not necessary, if the foundation in that were the whole Monarchy. For unless the sense of that passage is about the Catholic faith, your whole Monarchy straightway totters.

units.la: Iam si de Petro fateamur; at in illo, dignitas hæc personalis tantum ex Christi institutione fuit, nec à Christo, vlli certo loco allegata, sed absolutè in personam Petri collata; Vt ergo, quod de Christi institutione est, in personâ Petri, Catholicâ fide credamus: at, quod non est de Christi institutione, in personâ Pontificis si piè credatur, satis est.
units.tr: Now if we grant that it is about Peter, yet in him this dignity was personal only, by the institution of Christ, and it was not assigned by Christ to any certain place, but was conferred absolutely upon the person of Peter. Therefore, what is of the institution of Christ we believe with the Catholic faith in the person of Peter; but what is not of the institution of Christ, it is enough to believe piously in the person of the Pontiff.

units.la: .Dein, de dignitate hac in Petro, hæsitatio noua; an in eâ Petro succedatur: cùm de Apostolis reliquis nemo successorem habeat. vbi piè credendum est (non enim, credo, de Catholicâ fide) summam in Ecclesiam potestatem in Petro fuisse ordinariam: in reliquis omnibus Apostolis, delegatam, & extraordinariam.
units.tr: Next, concerning this dignity in Peter, there is a new doubt: whether it is succeeded to in him, since no other of the Apostles has a successor. Here it must be believed piously (for it is not, I think, a matter of the Catholic faith) that supreme power in the Church was ordinary in Peter, but in all the other Apostles it was delegated and extraordinary.

units.la: Sed si ordinaria; quomodo localis sit, vt Pontifici Romano sit locus? Ex facto Petri (non institutione Christi) postea localis facta est. seu potius mixta, (nam de eo etiam hæsitat {a}Cardinalis, ac proin nobis etiam relinquit hæsitandi locum) & Successio haec tota, ex instituto Christi: Successionis ratio ex facto Petri. Vbi, pietate magnâ opus puto, quâ credat quis, vt factum Petri, id est humanum, sit rei ratio, quae ab instituto Christi est, id est, diuina; vt Successionis ratio, ab hominis facto fit, Successio ipsa, non sit humana, & humani iuris: Denique vt ex facto humano fides Catholica cuiquam pendeat.
units.tr: But if it was ordinary, how is it local, so that there is a place for the Roman Pontiff? From the deed of Peter (not from the institution of Christ) it was afterwards made local, or rather mixed (for Cardinal Bellarmine also hesitates about this, and so leaves us also room to hesitate). And this whole succession, from the institution of Christ: the manner of succession from the deed of Peter. Here, I think, great piety is needed, by which one believes that the deed of Peter, that is, something human, is the ground of a matter which comes from the institution of Christ, that is, something divine; so that the manner of succession, which comes from a human deed, is not itself human and of human right: and finally, so that the Catholic faith of anyone depends upon a human deed.

units.la: Magnus verò hîc hæsitandi relinquitur locus. Nam, qui hîc, in facto Petri rem ponit Cardinalis, idem tamen eodem ipso capite affirmat, quòd Romanum Pontificem, totius Ecclesiae Pontificem, siue Apostolicum Pontificem Christus ipse {a}creârit. Si Christus ipse, quid facto Petri opus? Foeda obliuio. Redit tamen postad Petri factum denuò; Ita totus hîc fluctuat.
units.tr: Here, however, a great place for hesitation is left. For the Cardinal, who here places the matter in the deed of Peter, yet in that same chapter affirms that Christ himself created the Roman Pontiff, the Pontiff of the whole Church, or the Apostolic Pontiff. If Christ himself, what need of the deed of Peter? A shameful forgetfulness. Yet he returns afterwards to the deed of Peter again; thus he wavers here entirely.

units.la: De facto Petri (in quo ratio tota illi Successionis est) hæsitatio noua, an à se fecerit, an verò à Christo. Interdum enim Christi nutu, interdum iussu, interdum inspiratione factum asserit. Non sine diuino nutu id factum ait: Nutus autem non satis certus: Locum remotum, vt erat tum Roma, non satis certò designat. Quare insistit in reliquis, ac primò dicit, {b}Non est improbabile Dominum etiam apertè iussisse, vt Sedem suam Petrus ita figeret Romae, vt Romanus Episcopus absolutè ei succederet. At puto, piam credulitatem, satis esse ad illud credendum, quod non est improbabile; Catholicam verò fidem non requiri.
units.tr: Concerning the deed of Peter (on which the whole ground of that succession rests) there is a new doubt: whether he did it of himself, or rather at the bidding of Christ. For at times he asserts that it was done by the nod of Christ, at times by command, at times by inspiration. He says it was done not without a divine nod; but the nod is not certain enough: it does not designate with sufficient certainty a remote place, such as Rome then was. Therefore he insists on the rest, and first says: It is not improbable that the Lord also openly commanded that Peter should so fix his seat at Rome that the Roman bishop should succeed him absolutely. But I think that a pious credulity is enough to believe what is not improbable; the Catholic faith is not required for it.

units.la: Sed in hoc non acquiescit, transit enim & dicit, {c}Sed quicquid de hoc fit, quasi de re momenti non magni, fit, ne fit. Et meritò. Nam si Dominus perspicuè Petro apparens, hoc illi imperâsset, tunc verè diuino praecepto diceretur, Sedes Petri Romae esse constituta. Non enim facto Petri, sed verbo Christi. Tum verò de fide esset; at, nec Ipse quidem vult esse de fide. Quare eò potiùs propendet, vt Christus quidem id aperte non iusserit, sed {d}dicatur iussisse, quia id Petrus fecit Deo inspirante, quomodo omnia Decreta & praecepta Ecclesiae, dici possunt diuina, quae tamen mutabilia sunt. Mutabilia autem quae sunt, annon sufficit, si piè credantur?
units.tr: But he does not rest in this, for he passes on and says: But whatever happens concerning this, as though it were a matter of no great moment, it happens or it does not happen. And rightly so. For if the Lord, appearing plainly to Peter, had commanded him this, then it would truly be said to be by a divine precept that the seat of Peter was established at Rome. For it would be by the word of Christ, not the deed of Peter. Then indeed it would be of faith; but he himself does not wish it to be of faith. Therefore he inclines rather to this: that Christ indeed did not openly command it, but it is said to have been commanded, because Peter did it with God inspiring him, just as all the decrees and precepts of the Church can be called divine, and yet they are changeable. But those things which are changeable, is it not enough if they are piously believed?

units.la: Etiamsi verò constaret, Christum imperâsse Petro, vt Romae Sedem collocaret; (quod tamen non liquet) at vt eam ibi immobiliter collocaret; non sequitur, non constat. Audi ergo sententiam Cardinalis. {e}Quoniam ergo non constat, quemodo Christus iusserit Petro vt Romae Sedem collocaret; ideo non est de fide, divino & immutabili praecepto Romae Sedem esse constitutam, sed tamen, ut diximus, est probabilissimum, & pie credendum. Ubi habes pie credendum in terminis terminantibus: & jam subito, probabilissimum id, in superlativo gradu, de quo paulo ante, sat illi erat, non est improbabile.
units.tr: Even if it were established that Christ commanded Peter to set his seat at Rome (which, however, is not clear), yet that he should set it there immovably does not follow; it is not established. Hear, then, the Cardinal's opinion: Since therefore it is not established how Christ commanded Peter to set his seat at Rome, therefore it is not of faith that a seat was established at Rome by a divine and immutable precept; but nevertheless, as we have said, it is most probable and to be piously believed. Here you have to be piously believed in set terms; and presently, most probable, in the superlative degree, whereas a little before it was enough for him that it is not improbable.

units.la: At illud, quem non perplexum relinquat, quod ab eo ibi positum est? {a}Tametsi forte non sit de iure divino, Romanum Pontificem, quis Romanus Pontifex est, Petro succedere in Praefecturam totius Ecclesiae: tamen si quis absolute petat, an iure divino Romanus Pontifex sit Caput totius Ecclesiae (non est autem, nisi sic Petro succedat) omnino id asserendum esse? Annon hic merito quis haesitet? Primum, num Catholica fides vestra, pro obiecto habet, quod forte non est? nam quod forte non est, forte etiam & est. Tum illud, Forte non est, tametsi autem forte non sit: tamen si quis petat an sit, omnino id asserendum esse: Cuius vero, haec, fides concoquat?
units.tr: But what does he leave unperplexed in what he says there? Although perhaps it is not by divine right that the Roman Pontiff, as Roman Pontiff, succeeds Peter in the headship of the whole Church: nevertheless, if anyone asks absolutely whether by divine right the Roman Pontiff is the head of the whole Church (and it is not, unless he so succeeds Peter) must it be asserted wholly? Ought not someone rightly hesitate here? First, does your Catholic faith have as its object what perhaps is not? For what perhaps is not, perhaps also is. Then that: It perhaps is not, although perhaps it is not: yet if anyone asks whether it is, it must wholly be asserted that it is. But whose faith digests this?

units.la: Nec minus in eo justa haesitandi ratio, quod dicit: {b}Licet forte non sit de iure divino, Romanum Pontificem, ut Romanum Pontificem, Petro succedere: tamen id ad fidem Catholicam pertinere. Pertinere dicit ad fidem, non esse de fide; ac lepide satis rem explicat, de Pauli penula, quam etsi iure divino non habuit Paulus, nec Troade reliquit; habuisse tamen, & reliquisse ibi, de fide est. Est certe; expresse enim hoc habetur in sacris literis de Pauli penula: at de Petri Pallio, vel Sede Apostolica, aut quod Pontifex Petro successurus esset, non habetur ibi quicquam. Fatetur vero hoc. Etsi autem non habeatur in Scripturis: illud tamen (quod perinde est) haberi ex Traditione Apostolica Petri. Apostolica vero Traditio illa Petri, unde habetur? Declaratur, inquit. At Pauli Epistola per se clara est; Petri traditio declaratione opus habet. Multum interest. Et qui tandem declarant? Duo Pontifices, Marcellus & Leo, qui Petrum dicunt Romam iisse Christi iussu. Duo testes domestici; alter vero suppositi[?]tius. At de hijs ipsis ita post Cardinalis: {c}Non definiunt hanc rem, tanquam de fide, sed narrant ut historiam. Non sunt autem de fide Pontificum narrationes, sed Decreta. Ita, nec post declarationem, de fide sunt ista, relinquitur etiam haesitandi locus.
units.tr: There is no less a just reason for hesitation in what he says: Although perhaps it is not by divine right that the Roman Pontiff, as Roman Pontiff, succeeds Peter: nevertheless that pertains to the Catholic faith. He says it pertains to the faith, not that it is of faith; and he explains the matter rather wittily, using the case of Paul's cloak: which, even if Paul did not have it by divine right, nor left it at Troas, yet that he had it and left it there is of faith. It is certainly so; for this is expressly stated in Holy Scripture about Paul's cloak; but about Peter's pallium, or the Apostolic See, or that a Pontiff was to succeed Peter, nothing is stated there. Yet he confesses this. And although it is not in the Scriptures, that (which is just the same) is said to be had from the Apostolic tradition of Peter. But that tradition of Peter, from where is it had? It is declared, he says. But Paul's epistle is clear in itself; Peter's tradition needs a declaration. There is a great difference. And who at last declare it? Two Pontiffs, Marcellus and Leo, who say that Peter went to Rome at Christ's bidding. Two domestic witnesses; and the second is rather dubious. But concerning these very men the Cardinal says afterwards: They do not define this matter as of faith, but relate it as history. Yet the narrations of the Pontiffs are not of faith, but decrees. So, not even after the declaration are those things of faith, and room for hesitation remains.

units.la: Sed videamus etiam factum Petri a quo localis ista, seu mixta iuxta[?] dignitas, habet vim omnem. Petrus primùm, Romam iverit, Romæ fuerit, necesse est. Quòd Babylone fuerit, esto sanè de fide. Quòd Roma Babylon, alius fortè non daret (non enim ducitur argumentum à Sensu mystico) verùm esto sanè. Sit Roma Babylon, potiùs quàm locus in Scripturis nullus sit, qui dicat Roma fuisse Petrum: at de Sensu mystico potest fortè pia, Catholica fides esse non potest.
units.tr: But let us also see the deed of Peter, from which that local, or mixed, dignity has all its force. It is necessary that Peter first went to Rome and was at Rome. That he was at Babylon, let it certainly be granted to be of faith. That Rome is Babylon, another would perhaps not grant (for an argument is not drawn from a mystical sense), but let it certainly be granted. Let Rome be Babylon, rather than that there be no place in the Scriptures which says that Peter was at Rome: but about a mystical sense piety may perhaps be, but the Catholic faith cannot be.

units.la: Ut verò Roma sederit Episcopus, ex historiâ id habetur: Historiæ autem historicæ, non Catholicâ fide habentur: Certitudo de illis omnis, moralis est, Catholica non est. Sulpitius dixit, vel Optatus; creditur ijs, sed morali, non Catholicâ fide.
units.tr: But that the bishop sat in Rome is known from history. Historical accounts, however, are held on historical grounds, not on the Catholic faith. All certainty about them is moral; it is not Catholic. Sulpicius said it, or Optatus; we believe them, but with moral faith, not Catholic faith.

units.la: Sederit Episcopus; transmisit ergo Episcopatum: sed quis nobis fidem faciet, cum Episcopatu Apostolicam quoque dignitatem, & potestatem, vel non totam, sed duas eius tertias, transmifisse, aut aliam quàm quæ illi, tanquam Episcopo competebat? An & hoc de fide Catholicâ? Unde verò habetur? quis scripsit?
units.tr: He sat as bishop; therefore he handed on the episcopate. But who will give us assurance that along with the episcopate he also handed on the apostolic dignity and power, or not all of it but two-thirds of it, or a power other than that which belonged to him as bishop? Is this also "of the Catholic faith"? Where is it found? Who wrote it?

units.la: Illud autem, quis nobis expediat? Petrum non adiunxisse Pontificatui Episcopatum urbis Romæ, sed euexisse Episcopatum Romanum in Pontificatum, ut iam Pontifici uno tantum Pallio opus sit. Non enim esse duo iam Episcopatum Urbis, & Pontificatum Orbis, nisi potentiâ. An requiris etiam ad hoc fidem Catholicam, in quâ nullus hæsitandi relinquitur locus? An parem fidem de Pallio Pontificis, & de Pauli penulâ? An ægrè ferres, si hæc piè tantum credamus?
units.tr: And what of this: who will explain it to us? That Peter did not join the bishopric of the city of Rome to the pontificate, but raised the Roman bishopric into the pontificate, so that the Pope now needs only one pallium. For there are not two things, the bishopric of the City and the pontificate of the world, except by power. Or do you require Catholic faith for this too, in which no room for doubt is left? Or do you require the same faith about the Pope's pallium as about Paul's cloak? Would you be annoyed if we believed these things only in a pious way?

units.la: Tum & alia adhuc difficultas: Electionis formam ipsam quæ nunc est, quæque Successores Petro facit, quis probabit nobis, quòd de fide Catholicâ sit? Fides Catholica de iis est, quæ semper eadem: hæc verò mutata sæpè. Olim per Clerum fuit, populumque Romanum; post, interveniente authoritatis Imperatoriæ. Hi diu iam ambo exclusi sunt. Qui iam successor Petri, per Cardinales eligitur in Conclavi: Petri verò ætate, diu post Petrum, neque Conclavis, neque Dominorum Cardinalium in Orbe nomen auditum est.
units.tr: Then there is another difficulty: who will prove to us that the form of election which now exists, and which makes the successors of Peter, is "of the Catholic faith"? Catholic faith concerns those things which are always the same; but this has often been changed. In former times it was by the clergy and the Roman people; afterwards, with the intervention of imperial authority. Both have long since been excluded. The one who is now successor of Peter is chosen by the Cardinals in conclave; but in Peter's time, and long after Peter, the name of conclave or of the lord Cardinals was not heard of in the world.

units.la: Alia etiam in Successione hæsitatio. Nam ipse hic Cardinalis hæsitat, qui Romanum Pontificem dicit {*}proprie succedere Petro, non ut Apostolo. Non ergo nisi improprie in Apostolicâ dignitate, & potestate succedere. De eo verò quod proprie non est, annon si piè credatur fas est?[?]
units.tr: There is also another doubt about the succession. For this very Cardinal hesitates, who says that the Roman Pontiff succeeds Peter *properly*, not as an apostle. Therefore he succeeds only improperly in the apostolic dignity and power. But is it not permissible to believe in piety about that which is not proper?

units.la: Nec minor in Successionis serie; Ibi, vel in limine ipso impingimus. Quasi enim niti nos nollet Successione vestrâ Deus: ita, de primâ omnium Successione, de primo omnium Petri Successore, rem voluit esse incertam. Scis ipse, post mille demum, ac ducentos amplius annos, versum illum editum de Clemente.——Nutat adhuc mundus, sit quartus, sit ne secundus. Ità nec ibi omnia explicata sunt.
units.tr: "Nor is there less difficulty in the series of succession"; there we stumble, or rather at the very threshold. For God, as if he did not wish us to rest on your succession, willed the matter of the first of all successions, of the first of all successors of Peter, to be uncertain. You yourself know that only after a thousand and more than two hundred years was that verse on Clement published: "The world still wavers: is he the fourth, or is he the second?" So not even there is everything explained.

units.la: Pòst verò, intercurrunt illinc, tot Haeretici, Liberius, Anastasius, Honorius, Iohannes 22°, tot monstra, & portenta teterrima: hinc tot schismata, quae vos ipsi ad triginta numeratis, in quibus, quis de tribus, vter de duobus, Petri Successor fuerit, tot scrupuli; ut si de morali certi esse possitis, maior vobis certitudo quaerenda non sit. Possem & alia accumulare; sed haec satis sunt. Concurrant omnia haec necesse est. Haec si tu postules, de fide Catholicâ facere, vnâ operam des (quod ille in Comoedià) ut cum ratione insanias; nisi certitudine enim morali non consistunt haec: bene etiam, si illâ. Et si credendi vobis vox allubescit, piè credenda sunt; aliter enim à vobis credi nequeunt.
units.tr: Afterwards, from that side, so many heretics intervene: Liberius, Anastasius, Honorius, John XXII, so many monsters and most foul portents; and from this side so many schisms, which you yourselves count at about thirty, in which, who of the three, which of the two, was the successor of Peter; so many scruples. So that if you can be certain only with moral certainty, you should not seek any greater certainty for yourselves. I could heap up other things as well, but these are enough. All these things must concur. If you demand that these be made matters of Catholic faith, you may as well do (as that character says in the comedy) the one thing: go mad with reason. For these things do not stand except on moral certainty; well, even on that, if so. And if the voice of belief pleases you, they are to be believed in piety; for otherwise they cannot be believed by you.

units.la: Redeo iam ad illud, quod initio posui; posui autem ex Alphonso, & Mirandulâ. Sic habet {a} Alphonsus: Quamuis credere teneamur ex fide verum Petri successorem, esse supremum totius Ecclesiae pastorem: non tamen tenemur eâdem fide credere Leonem aut Clementem esse verum Petri successorem: quoniam non tenemur ex fide Catholicâ credere, eorum quemlibet rectè, & canonicè fuisse electum. {b}Picus etiam Mirandula, qui scripsit nobis Theoremata de fide, non finit nos Catholicâ fide hoc credere, nisi & Catholicâ nobis fide constet Pontificem Canonicè electum esse. Iam verò, verum à duabus tertijs Cardinalium, vtrum Canonicè electus, id verò fide Catholicâ constare non potest. Aliquis ibi saltem haesitandi locus. Sedit Pontifex quidam, cuius electioni duae partes assensæ non sunt. Rem refert eo loco Mirandula. Annon ergo locus haesitandi? Sedit alter, qui dubius animi, an anima sua immortalis, referente eodem. De eo certè relinquitur haesitandi locus. Denique; sederunt simul tres Pontifices; Balthasar de Cossâ, Angelus de Corarys, Petrus de Lunâ. Ibi verò nutavit fides Catholica, nec vllus tum locus, nisi haesitationi; Successor Petri quis fuerit, nec dum constat: si vllus fuit, injuria illi facta; Omnes enim depositi: si nullus fuit, quid fide tum factū? Certè Henrici 5ti, qui fuit per id tempus Rex Angliæ, certa magis Successio, quàm Romani tum Pōtificis: & tu tamen, de fide vis esse, & de Catholicâ fide? Neq; vero semel hoc contigit; Benedictus 9°, Silvester 3°, Greg. 6°, tria teterrima monstra (sic enim Platina, quem nos ubi frequenter adducere) simul Petri Successores: Onuphrius verò addit & quartum, Iohannem. Quis istorum fuit Chiron? Difficile dictu, locus haesitandi. Abi ergo cum tuâ Catholicâ fide: morali certitudine contentus esto, quando an Canonicè intret, non potest esse certitudo vlla nisi moralis, nempe, si rectè rem referant, qui de Conclaui sunt. Quid opus ergo hîc tentare per nefas quicquam, cùm per fas liceat aut malâ fide rem gerere, cùm si optimâ fide gerat, propositi compos esse potuerit?
units.tr: I now return to what I put at the beginning; I put it forth from Alphonsus and Mirandula. Thus Alphonsus says: "Although we are bound to believe from faith that the true successor of Peter is the supreme pastor of the whole Church, we are nevertheless not bound by the same faith to believe that Leo or Clement is the true successor of Peter, since we are not bound from Catholic faith to believe that any one of them was rightly and canonically elected." Picus also of Mirandula, who wrote to us theses concerning faith, does not allow us to believe this by Catholic faith, unless it is established to us by Catholic faith that the Pope was canonically elected. Now, whether he was canonically elected by two-thirds of the Cardinals, that cannot be established by Catholic faith. There is at least some room there for doubt. One Pope sat, to whose election two parts did not assent. Mirandula relates the matter in that place. Is there not therefore room for doubt? Another sat, who was doubtful in mind whether his soul was immortal, according to the same author. About him certainly room for doubt is left. Finally, three Popes sat at the same time: Balthasar of Cossa, Angelo of Corario, Peter of Luna. There indeed Catholic faith wavered, and there was no place then except for doubt; who was the successor of Peter is not yet established: if there was one, a wrong was done to him, for all were deposed; if there was no one, what then was done in faith? Surely the succession of Henry the Fifth, who was king of England at that time, was more certain than that of the Roman Pontiff then; and yet you wish to be "of faith", and "of the Catholic faith"? Nor did this happen only once: Benedict IX, Sylvester III, Gregory VI, three most foul monsters (for so Platina, whom we often cite), at once successors of Peter; Onuphrius indeed adds a fourth, John. Which of these was the Chiron? Hard to say: room for doubt. Go away then with your Catholic faith; be content with moral certainty, since whether he enters canonically there cannot be any certainty except moral, namely, if those who are in the conclave report the matter correctly. Why then is there any need to attempt anything here "through wrong", when it is permitted to act "through right" or in bad faith, since if he acted in good faith he could have been master of his purpose?

units.la: Quæritur iam, an Principem vllum vnquam Pontifex cædi mandauerit. Quæritur, sed malè. Quæstionis is status non est: sed, an Princeps vllius iustam sibi vnquam à Papâ timendi causam habuerit. Hic importunè, de cæde mentio fit à Cardinale; quasi nullum Principi periculum, nisi vitæ; quasi extra cædem, nihil Principi metuendum. Vbi, semel hoc habeto. Generosa indoles pro pari habet, de vitâ, & de Regno deponi: cædi mandet Pontifex, si de Regno cedere: Perinde enim est. Verùm, Cædi non mandauit, ex mente Cardinalis iam, nihil aliud significare dicit Tortus, quàm quòd non submisit Sicario. Quid interest ad cædem; si immisit Exercitū, si concitauit Seditionem? Parui enim refert, per vim pereas, an fraudem, (quanquam in vtroque vis) per fraudem dico Sicarij, an per vim Militis. Mallet verò Rex quiuis, (si est illi animus vere Regius) perire solus, Sicarij manu, quàm cum Ciuium suorum strage ingenti, ingenti ditionum vastitate. Sed siue id per hostes, siue per rebelles, siue per Sicarios fiat, siue denique nihil horum fiat, nec vitâ, sed Regno tantum quærat excuere: stat quod initio positum, iusta Principibus causa metuendi.
units.tr: The question now is whether a Pope ever ordered a prince to be killed. It is asked, but badly. That is not the state of the question; the question is whether any prince ever had a just cause to fear from the Pope. Here, unseasonably, mention is made of killing by the Cardinal, as if there were no danger to a prince except to life, as if nothing were to be feared by a prince apart from slaughter. Know this once and for all: a noble disposition holds it equal to be deprived of life or of the kingdom. Let the Pope order him killed, if he is to give up the kingdom: for it is all one. But, "he did not order him killed", in the Cardinal's sense, now means, says Tortus, nothing other than that he did not send an assassin. What does it matter for the killing, if he sent an army, if he stirred up sedition? For it matters little whether one perishes by force or by fraud (though in both there is force): by fraud I mean by an assassin's hand, or by force of a soldier. Any king would prefer (if he truly has a royal spirit) to perish alone, by the hand of an assassin, rather than with a great slaughter of his own citizens and a great devastation of his lands. But whether this comes about through enemies, or through rebels, or through assassins, or finally whether none of these happens, and he seeks to shake off not his life but only his kingdom: the position laid down at the beginning stands, that princes have just cause to fear.

units.la: Verùm Pontifices aduersus Imperatores bella vix leguntur, nisi defensionis causâ: Leguntur ergo & ab ipsis gesta: sed quot putas ab aliis gesta, ab ipsis excitata? Ars enim illa Pontificum, domi sedere in otio, per alios bella gerere, subditis interdicere ne pareant, maledicere si pareant, edicere ut insurgant, maledicere nisi insurgant in Principem, Regna illorum prædæ exponere, sine labore, periculo, saepe & sine sumptu, hostes suos debellare. Non approbauit (ais) ; fortasse non diplomate, non consensu expresso; sed habet alterum, (quem vos dicere soletis) interpretatiuum. Quid si autem, quod ipsi facere non libet, Cardinalium alicui mandet? verbi gratia, Comensi; qui cum Reginam ELIZABETHAM caedi mandauit, & Parreio vt id faceret author fuit; an id quisquam, insscio atque inuito Pontifice, mandatum putet, aut, si executioni mandatum fuisset, ab Illo improbatum iri? Legantur tamen (inquis) Imperatorum Bella aduersus Pontifices. Sed quis Imperatori, Pontifici bellum indixit, non ab eo prius lacessitus, non vel tactus fulmine, vel tonitru exterritus, non vel Riuali, vel Rebelli aliquo prius in eum concitato?
units.tr: But popes are scarcely read of making war against emperors except in defence: so they are read of also doing deeds themselves; but how many, do you think, were done by others and stirred up by them? For that art of the popes is to sit at home in idleness, to wage wars through others: to forbid subjects to obey, to curse them if they obey, to order them to rise up, to curse them unless they rise against the prince, to expose their kingdoms as prey, to subdue their enemies without labour, danger, and often without expense. "He did not approve it," you say; perhaps not by a document, not by express consent; but he has another, which you are wont to call "interpretative." What if, however, he commands to some Cardinal what he himself does not want to do? For example, Como, who ordered Queen Elizabeth to be killed, and was the author of this for Parry to do it; would anyone think that this was commanded without the knowledge and against the will of the Pope, or, if it had been commanded for execution, that it would have been disapproved by him? "Yet", you say, "wars of emperors against popes are read of." But who declared war on a pope against an emperor, who had not first been provoked by him, or struck by a thunderbolt, or terrified by thunder, or first had someone, a rival or a rebel, stirred up against him?

units.la: De Henrico quarto Imperatore, Nihilne hoc ad rem facit, quòd Filio non licuit Patri parentare? quòd interdicta illi Patris sepultura? Nihilne hoc ad rem, quòd in Patrem & viuentem, & mortuum, Filius coactus sit esse impius: in viuentem, contra quem arma gesserit: in mortuum, quem exhumatu proiecerit? quòd non satis in viuo passus sit Papae liuor, sed neque post fata quieuerit? Neq; enim honorificam Papa Sepulturam (vt tu vis) reprehendit, sed sepulturam: quam non honorificam, sed omnino nullam esse voluit. Humari enim noluit, humatum exhumari iusit: nec potuit reconciliari Episcopus Leodiensis, nisi conditione hac, vt effoderetur denuò cadauer Henrici. Exhumatum est cadauer, Spiram pheretro delatum; ibi in Capella quadam S. Affrae deserta, siue in Cella quadam eius, stetit quinque annis inhumatum. Mandato (inquit {a}Viterbiensis) Romani Pontificis è coemeterio eiicitur, eique omnis Christiana sepultura denegatur. —Papa caput cleri iubet hinc corpus remoueri: Filius ossa Patris doluit fore cum sceleratis. Tantaseueritas Papae, vt mortuum humari non sineret, ait {b}Helmoldus. Factum verò hoc Pontifice cum sepeliri vetante, {c}Sigonius: hortatu Papae, ipse {d}Binnius. Nihilne hoc ad rem, quòd morientibus infiet Pontifex, Manes mordeat, saeuiat in morticina, nec vel ipsa morte satietur?
units.tr: Concerning Henry IV the Emperor: does it make no difference to the matter that a son was not permitted to hold funeral rites for his father? That his father was denied burial? Does it make no difference to the matter that the son was compelled to be impious towards his father both living and dead: towards the living one, against whom he waged war; towards the dead one, whom he had dug up and cast out? That the pope's malice was not satisfied with the living man, but did not rest even after death? For the pope did not object to an honourable burial (as you would have it), but to burial as such, which he wished to be not honourable but wholly absent. He refused to have him buried; having been buried, he ordered him dug up. The bishop of Liège could not be reconciled unless on this condition: that Henry's corpse be dug up again. The corpse was exhumed and carried to Speyer on a bier; there, in a certain deserted chapel of St Afra, or in a cell of hers, it stood uninterred for five years. By command (says the author of Viterbo) of the Roman pontiff it was thrown out of the cemetery, and all Christian burial was denied it. The pope, head of the clergy, ordered the body removed from there; the son grieved that his father's bones would lie among the wicked. Such was the pope's severity that he would not allow the dead man to be buried, says Helmold. Sigonius records that this was done by the pope forbidding burial; Binius records it as done at the pope's urging. Does it make no difference to the matter that the pontiff, when the dying man was in his power, bit at his shade, raged against the corpse, and was not satisfied even by death itself?

units.la: Nec id nouum iam, affigere ei, vel affingere haeresin aut Schisma, cui eum Pontifice lis vlla, quando Illi non parere, peccatum est ariolandi, sœcleus Idololatriae, haeresis denique haereticissima. Quae enim illa haeresis fuerit, docet {e}Sigonius; Filius, Paternâ terna haeresi repudiata Pontificiam obedientiam suscepit. Obedientiam Pontificis non suscepere ea demum haeresis fuit Patris. Filius autem Orthodoxus, vt Pontifici obsequium praestaret, impius fuit in Patrem; Nam quod sub Censurâ defunctus est: idem hoc Ignatio Patriarchae Constantinopolitano contigit, qui & ipse, cum sic obiret, in eius, quod ms[?] suum putauit defensione (quae & Imperatoris quoque Henrici causa fuit) non modò non sepultura caruisse, sed & miraculis claruisse dicitur. Quòd verò naturali morbo extinctum dicis: naturalis is morbus non erat; nec tu hoc nescis. Deiectus iam, & defectus à subditis suis, à propinquis, & (quod omnem immanitatem superat) à filio suo; filio suo, qui ex vtero suo egressus erat, quaerente iam animâ suam: ipso animi angore, ipso carceris foetore contabuit; eóq; praeter naturam morbo, non naturali vllo extinctus est.
units.tr: Nor is it a new thing to fasten upon him, or to fabricate against him, heresy or schism, when for any man the crime of not obeying the pontiff is the crime of divination, the sin of idolatry, and, in short, the most heretical heresy. What that heresy was, Sigonius teaches: the son, having rejected his father's heresy, took up Papal obedience. To have refused obedience to the pontiff was that father's heresy. The son, however, being orthodox, was impious towards his father in order to render obedience to the pontiff. For that he died under censure: the same happened to Ignatius, Patriarch of Constantinople, who, when he died in the same way, in defence of what he thought to be his own cause (which was also the cause of the Emperor Henry), is said not only to have lacked burial but to have been renowned for miracles. But as for your claim that he died of a natural illness: it was not a natural illness, and you do not fail to know this. Deposed and forsaken already by his subjects, by his kinsmen, and (which surpasses all savagery) by his own son, by his own son who had come forth from his own womb, while his soul was already seeking its way out, he wasted away from the very anguish of spirit, from the very stench of the prison; and so he died of a sickness beyond nature, not of any natural one.

units.la: Ad Sixti quinti orationem illam de caede Henrici tertij Francorum Regis, verecundatur paululùm Tortus; & hoc primum in responso, ingenuitatis signum dedit. Quin tu age, quod ingenuum agere par est. Potestis, rem tu à Domino; ille de Consistorio rescisceere, vcrâne an secus. Si vera, cur pudet fateri? si secus, cur piget negare? Quorsum illud tuum; esto tamen, si rem putas Pontifici probrosam fore? Aegrè ergo admisit, sed tamen admisit tandem. Vidit enim in Consistorio Secreto, non tam esse secreta omnia, vt non emanent in vulgus; & quâquam nullus excepit, at dum adhuc in memoriâ recens erat, statim à discessu poterat quis; capita eius & vim omnem referre in Commentarios. Sed quid coniecturis opus est? Tortus ipse, vt alibi saepe, ita sui hic parum memor, qui primò neminem dicit excepisse: idem, aliquos, post dicit, alta Consistorij breviter annotasse. Admittit ergo. Et quid in eâ reperies, inquit, nisi laudes & admirationem sapientiæ & prudentiæ Dei? Et quodnam illud sapientiæ opus, quod ita vnicè admiratur? Quod simplex Monachus, non mutato habitu, non gladio clypéoque armatus, ad Regem libere penetrauit. At hoc sanè non ita valdè mirandum: illud potiùs, si penetrâssęt ad Regem Monachus, gladio, clypéoque armatus. Nam quòd inermis, suspicio de eo nulla; sin armatus, non ita credo per medios Satellites, viam expeditam habuisse. Nihil ergo in admiratione illâ Sixti, admiratione dignum.
units.tr: Regarding the speech of Sixtus V on the slaying of Henry III, King of the French, Tortus is somewhat abashed, and in his reply he gives, for the first time, a sign of candour. Come, do what is fitting for a candid man. You can learn the matter from your master; let him find out from the Consistory whether it is true or not. If it is true, why are you ashamed to admit it? If it is not, why are you reluctant to deny it? What is that of yours: "Granted, nonetheless, if you think the matter would be disgraceful to the pontiff"? So he admitted it, reluctantly, but he did admit it at last. For he saw that in a Secret Consistory not everything is so secret that it fails to leak out to the common people; and although no one took notes, while the matter was still fresh in memory anyone could, immediately after the meeting, set down its main points and force in commentaries. But why do we need conjectures? Tortus himself, as often elsewhere, is here little mindful of himself: he first says that no one took notes, then afterwards says that "some" briefly noted the main points of the Consistory's proceedings. So he admits it. "And what will you find in it," he says, "except praises and admiration of the wisdom and prudence of God?" And what is that work of wisdom which he so uniquely admires? "That a simple monk, without changing his habit, not armed with sword and shield, freely penetrated to the King." But this is surely not so very wonderful; it would be more so if the monk had penetrated to the King armed with sword and shield. For that he was unarmed, there is no suspicion of that; but if he was armed, I do not believe he had a clear path through the midst of the royal guards. Nothing, therefore, in that admiration of Sixtus is worthy of admiration.

units.la: Monitio verò magis adhuc insana. Eum, qui dixit, Nolite tangere Christos meos, velle, à quoquam occidi Christos suos: quo, nullus erat in Scriptura locus, (si vniuersam euoluisset) Sixti propositò magis ex toto diametro contrarius, nec qui, quod ille probare voluit, magis aperte refutaret. Locus, qui à Rege scriptus, & de Regibus, nominatim verò de Regibus non tangendis, eum aliquis tam insulsus fit, vt adduceat ad eadem Regi probandam, tanquam opus diuinæ voluntati consentaneum? Certè, {a}Toletano Concilio id monstri simile visum: Cùm Dominus dicat, Nolite tangere Christos meos, & Dauid, Quis (inquit) extendet manum suam in Christum Domini, & innocens erit? Esse tamen quosdam, quibus nec vitare metus fit periurium, nec Regibus inferre exitium. Sic Patres illi, secus longè quàm Sixtus, locum illum accommodant: monitionem inde longè aliam, quàm Sixtus elicuint, vt hinc Lector intelligat, quàm aptè cuneos suos ad nodos applicent Pontifices, quàm benè illis & Concilijs suis, inter se conueniat. Concilia ad Reges, imò Propheta ad Reges; Pontifex ad Cardinales, quos & ipsos iam Christos Domini appellat, non Pontificem solum. At hos Christos nostros, vitos Cardinalitiâ dignitate fulgentes, Dauid, nec vnctos Domini agnouit, nec (quamuis propheta esset) praeuidit vngendos. Hunc iam Sixti Christum (nempe Cardinalem) tangere non oportuit: at illum Dauidis Christum, (Regem scilicet) vnico cultelli ictu necari! Et hoc dignum, illius prudentiâ, opus, qui dixit, Nolite tangere Christos meos! Melius certè insisteres in Oratione hac negandâ (nimirum Sixti illam fuisse) quàm vt haec tam male cohaerentia illius sic nomine effutires.
units.tr: The admonition, however, is even more insane. That the one who said "Touch not my Christs" wished his own Christs to be slain by anyone: no passage of Scripture (if one were to go through the whole of it) is more utterly contrary to the purpose of Sixtus, nor could any refute more plainly what he wished to prove. A passage written by a King, and about Kings, and specifically about not touching Kings: could anyone be so foolish as to adduce it to prove the very same thing for a King, as a work consonant with the divine will? Surely the Council of Toledo regarded this as a monstrous thing: when the Lord says, "Touch not my Christs," and David says, "Who shall stretch forth his hand against the Lord's Christ, and be guiltless?" There are, however, some for whom neither fear of perjury avails to restrain them, nor do they shrink from bringing destruction upon Kings. Thus those Fathers apply that passage quite differently from Sixtus, and draw from it an admonition far different from the one Sixtus extracted, so that the reader may understand how aptly the pontiffs fit their wedges to the knots, and how well they agree with themselves and with their councils. Councils address Kings; indeed the Prophet addresses Kings; the pontiff addresses Cardinals, whom he now calls "Christs of the Lord," not only the pontiff. But these "our Christs," shining with the dignity of the cardinalate, David did not recognise as anointed of the Lord, nor (though he was a prophet) did he foresee that they would be anointed. This "Christ of Sixtus" (namely a Cardinal) was not to be touched; but that "Christ of David" (namely a King) is to be slain with a single stroke of a knife! And is this work worthy of the wisdom of him who said, "Touch not my Christs"? You would certainly do better to insist on denying that this speech was Sixtus's than to blurt out, in his name, these things that cohere so badly.

units.la: At Cardinalis ille Regi nostro affinis; Etiam Dux frater eius. Quodsi, morte tum periit ius fasque mulctatus Cardinalis, (de quo instituti iam nostri non est quicquam decernere) quid attinebat de Cardinale verba facere, silere de Duce? Vterque enim ex aequo Regi propinquus sanguine. Sic praeter ius fasque ca caedes facta est, pariter in Duce peccatum est. Quorsum ergo (Fratre omisso, & quidem natu maiore) Cardinalem Regi occinit, quasi propinquum suum? Non enim qua Cardinalis, vel Sacerdos, Regi propinquus: sed qua Princeps de stirpe & stemmate Guiforum, vt haec de affinitate res tota silentio potuerit praeterir.
units.tr: "But that Cardinal was related to our King": even the Duke, his brother, was. Yet if the Cardinal, having been punished, perished by a deed contrary to right and law (concerning which it is not part of our present purpose to pronounce anything), what was the point of speaking about the Cardinal and keeping silent about the Duke? For both were equally near to the King by blood. Thus that slaughter was done beyond right and law, and the sin was equal in the Duke. Why then does he sing of the Cardinal to the King, as though he were his kinsman, while omitting the Brother (and indeed the elder one)? For the Cardinal was related to the King not as a cardinal or priest, but as a prince of the stock and lineage of the Guises; so that this whole matter of kinship could have been passed over in silence.

units.la: Iam verò, vir Sacratus Fraterculus dicitur, (nec tamen laudatur) tur) mirum autem quòd & illum Christum Domini non scripserit. Vir autem iste Sacratus, vltus est virum Sacratum alium, & Christum Domini, nempe Cardinalem, nec Regis Henrici; quasi ille, neque Sacratus esset, neque Christus Domini. Vbi tu, si Scripturam sapores, si Concilia spirares, Regem Sacratum diceres, & Christum Domini: illum, execrabilem parricidam, & Christicidam. Iam, quod adhuc magis execrandum, Deum ipsum in scelcris societatem vocat, nec satis illi dicere, fuit, permisit; sed, vltus est (inquit) Deus Christum suum. Regem Deus per alium sacratum virum, id est, Monachum, interfecit. Ita Deus Regem interfecit, per Monachi manum: manum commodauit Monachus; interfector, & author caedis Deus ipse, etiam mors Christi eius opus manus Dei. Et haec Consistorij secreti Theologia est: haec ibi Pontificis Theologica praelectiones.
units.tr: Now, indeed, the "holy friar" is spoken of (and yet is not praised) ... It is remarkable, however, that he did not also write him down as a "Christ of the Lord." But that holy man avenged another holy man, and a "Christ of the Lord," namely the Cardinal, and not King Henry; as though he were neither holy nor a Christ of the Lord. Here you, if you had a taste for Scripture, if you breathed the Councils, would call the King holy and a Christ of the Lord, and that other an execrable parricide and killer of Christ. Now, what is even more execrable: he calls God himself into the fellowship of this crime, and it is not enough for him to say that God "permitted" it; rather, "God avenged his Christ," he says. "God slew the King through another holy man," that is, a monk. Thus God slew the King, by the hand of a monk: the monk lent his hand; the killer and author of the slaying was God himself; even the death of Christ was the work of God's hand. And this is the theology of the secret Consistory: these are the theological lectures of the pontiff there.

units.la: Quòdsi Deus tam aegrè ferat, tangi à quoquam Christos vestros Cardinales: Cùm {a}Pius 4. Cardinalem Carafam, virum Sacratum, Christi Domini, & Paulo 4° arctissimo sanguinis vinculo coniunctum, in carcere strangulari iusit; vbi tum vltio diuina substitit? Cur id sine manifesto diuinae prouidentiae miraculo tulit inultum Pius 4°? Cur & {b}Vrbanus 6°, qui septem sacratos viros, & Christos Domini; Cardinales, durius quidem habuit? Quinò enim immissos atque obstrictos in saccis, demersit in mari: duorum autem reliquorum corpora (postquàm morte multâssēt[?],) in furno exiccata, iussit asseruari in sarcinis, & mulis impositâ, (cùm iter vsquam[?] haberet) ante se cum Petasis suis Purpureis, pompam ducere: nec tamen vllum Sacratum virum Fraterculum excitauit Dei prouidentia, qui Christos illos vestros Domini, tam indignè habitos vlcisceretur.
units.tr: But if God is so grievously displeased that anyone should touch your Christs, the Cardinals: when Pius IV ordered Cardinal Carafa, a holy man and a servant of Christ the Lord, bound by the closest bond of blood to Paul IV, to be strangled in prison, where then did divine vengeance stand still? Why did Pius IV let that pass unavenged without a plain miracle of divine providence? Why too did Urban VIII, who treated seven holy men, Christs of the Lord, the Cardinals, more harshly still? For he had them sealed in sacks and sunk in the sea; and the bodies of the two remaining men, after they had died, he ordered dried in an oven, packed on mules in baggage, and carried before him in procession (since he had a journey somewhere) with their purple hats; yet the providence of God did not raise up any holy friar to avenge those Christs of yours, the Lord's, treated so shamefully.

units.la: Illud verò ibi multos malè habet: quòd qui definire omnia tam facilè potuit Pontifex, tamen Monachus ille, rectè an secus egerit, non definiuit; quódque, cùm opus Dei praedicandum suscepisset, non & opus hominis damnandum quoque suscepit; sed pendère fuit orbem Christianum animi dubium, fueritne Regis mors, quasi Seruatoris nostri, an verò quasi Holophernis & Madianitae: Monachus autem ipse, Herodi & Pilato; an verò Iudithae & Phineae annumerandus.
