Secretum hoc seruare sibi voluit & suis, inter arcana Consistorij, ne forte, si virum tam tam sacratum execratus esset, ne, si in Clementem illum fuisset inclementior, si Pilatum aliquem definiisset vel Herodem: decesset post Pontifici materia, divinae providentiae laudibus euehende, quam ille ex simili eventu, saepiùs cupit decantare. Enimuero, ibi de Pilato, de Herode, in totâ oratione mentio nulla; tantùm Eleazari & Iudithae exempla ibi sunt; Monachum cum illis confert, praefert, ut quid de illo senserit, facilis sit coniectura.
units.tr: Yet what troubles many there is this: the Pontiff, who could so easily decide everything, did not decide whether that monk acted rightly or otherwise; and that, though he had undertaken to proclaim the work of God, he did not also undertake to condemn the work of man. Instead the Christian world was left in doubt of mind, whether the king's death was like that of our Saviour, or rather like that of Holofernes and the Midianite; and the monk himself is to be counted with Herod and Pilate, or rather with Judith and Phinehas. He wished to keep this secret for himself and his own, among the secrets of the Consistory, lest perhaps, if he had cursed so holy a man, or if he had been harsher toward that Clement, or had decided that some Pilate or Herod, the Pontiff would have lost the matter for extolling the praises of divine providence, which from a similar event he desires to sing again and again. Indeed, there is no mention at all of Pilate or Herod in the whole speech; only the examples of Eleazar and Judith are there, and he compares and prefers the monk to them, so that it is an easy guess what he thought of him.

units.la: Multos (inquam) hoc habet male: illud verò omnes pessimè, quòd vbi mactatus Rex aliquis; tum Consistorium habet Pontifex, Cardinales convocat, orationem meditatur, meditatam profert, Dei providentiam, iustitiam, laudibus in coelum extollit: Vbi diram proditionem eius fit [?] Rex aliquis, nihil horum; vacuum Consistorium, orationes nullae, mutus Pontisex, non manifestum ibi miraculum vllum, non encomium vllum, aut oratio panegyrica, de laudibus divinae providentiae. Perditio Regis, laudes habet sitas [?], & admirationem; ex salute Regum, nec admiratio Dei, nec laus. Ad mortem Cardinalis venit illi in mentem statim: ad necem Regis; excidit illi prorsus quis dixerit, Nolite tangere Christos meos. Quin statuatur in vitros fabratos [?], Carnetum & Oldcornum, illum criminis conscium; hunc laudatorem: si lex aliqua feratur, ad reliquos participes eruendos; magno statuum [?] animi moerore consternatur Pontifex, & afflictio illi mirum in modum angetur.
units.tr: It troubles many (I say) in this way; but it troubles everyone most badly that when some king is slain, the Pontiff then holds a Consistory, summons the Cardinals, composes an oration, and delivers the composed oration, raising the providence and justice of God to heaven with praises. When some king suffers a dire betrayal, none of this happens: the Consistory is empty, there are no orations, the Pontiff is mute, there is no manifest miracle, no eulogy, no panegyric oration on the praises of divine providence. The destruction of a king has its praises placed [?], and admiration; but at the salvation of kings there is neither admiration of God nor praise. At the death of a Cardinal he thinks at once of it; at the murder of a king it slips entirely from his mind who said, "Touch not my Christs." Indeed let it be set up in fashioned glass [?], Garnet and Oldcorne, the one a partner in the crime, the other a praiser; if some law is passed to root out the remaining accomplices, the Pontiff is dismayed with a great [?] sorrow of spirit, and his affliction is wonderfully increased.

units.la: Quòd fuit autem dictum de referendo in Sanctos fraterculo illo; sine authore non dicitur, etsi author non dicitur; puta, aliquem ex iis, qui acta Consistorij breuiter annotare solent. Nec dissimile verò, quoniam qui ita Deum tum laudare gestiebat; eum verisimile est, & in Sanctum Deum laudare voluisse. Poterat autem pleno ore, atque in concreto, sive illud, opus Dei fuit, ita ille, Sanctus Dei qui perpetrauit. Quidni autem Sanctus, cui apparuit Angelus, & facti author fuit? Cui pater spiritualis (conspirans [?] in eo cum Pontifice prorsus, atque eodem spiritu afflatus) idem ipsum Iudithae exemplum; imitandum proposuit; in quo Sixtus ipse laudando, post tam diligenter insistit; cui denique; de operis merito praemióque prolixè pollicitus est.
units.tr: But as for what was said about that friar being referred to the saints, "nothing is said without an author," though no author is named; suppose it is one of those who are accustomed to note briefly the acts of the Consistory. Nor is it unlike, since he who was so eager then to praise God, it is likely he wished to praise him also as a holy God. He could, however, with full voice and in the concrete, say that it was the work of God, and so that man was a holy man of God who perpetrated it. And why should he not be a saint, to whom an angel appeared and who was the author of the deed? To him his spiritual father (agreeing in this entirely with the Pontiff, and inspired by the same spirit) proposed the very example of Judith to be imitated; in which Sixtus himself, in praising, so diligently insists after such fashion; to whom finally he promised at length the reward and merit of the work.

units.la: Proditio quidem multo etiam magis tetra erat, in quâ comprehensi Garnetum cum Oldcorno suo, quàm fuit illa fraterculi[?]: qui tamen ambo relati jam inter Martyres, & (quâ a Jesuitis) Sancti sunt, ut non careat omni verisimilitudine consilium illud: proin eximendum albù, inferendum inter nigra Torti mendacia; utpote de iis, qui non in album sanctorum, sed in nigrum Daemoniorum referri merentur.
units.tr: The betrayal indeed was far more foul even than that friar's, in which Garnet with his Oldcorne were caught; yet both of these, now already counted among the martyrs, are (by the Jesuits' reckoning) saints, so that that counsel is not without all verisimilitude: therefore it should be removed from the white list and inserted among the black lies of Tortus; since they deserve to be recorded not in the white roll of saints, but in the black roll of demons.

units.la: Dicendum jam, ecquam vim habeant, quæ in Bellarmino contradictiones notatæ sunt: an nusquam secum pugnet, sed constans ubique sit, & sui similis. Certè recognoit sua nuper, in quibus discedit sæpe à seipso; Quid ergo desperet quis, fieri posse, ut & in aliis uniformis non fuerit, eandem semper sententiam non dixerit?
units.tr: Now it must be said what force those contradictions have which have been noted in Bellarmine: whether he nowhere contradicts himself, but is consistent everywhere and like himself. Certainly he has recently revised his own works, in which he often departs from himself. Why then should anyone despair that, in other matters too, he was not uniform, and did not always state the same opinion?

units.la: Neque verò contemni potuit à te, nisi immeritò, contradictio ibi prima. Maior enim certè est, ac proin minus contemnenda contradictio, quæ tractatum integrum, quàm quæ sententiolam unicam euertit. Quodsi totum illud pentabiblon eius de Justificatione, eò tendat, ut inhærentem in nobis justitiæ habitum, & emanantem ex eo operum justitiam statuat; quò ita, non solà Christi justitiâ nobis reputatà niti, sed & in nostrâ etiam pariter liceat fiduciam ponere; annon uno quasi impetu funditus euertit disputationem illam omnem, qui tandem sic concludit, Tutissimum non esse nobis nisi hoc, ut fiduciam nostram totam in misericordiâ Dei solâ; totam inquam in solâ reponamus? Eludis illud; Non quasi nulla (inquis) possit fiducia in bonis operibus collocari. Potest ergo fiducia aliqua in bonis operibus collocari; at nisi tutius hoc sit, ne potest quidem. Nec tu illud, credo, volebas: potest, sed hoc tutius non est; id est, potest, sed temerè. Potest ergò aliqua: at contradicit, Non potest fiduciæ pars aliqua, sed oportet totam in solâ misericordiâ collocare: Tutissimum enim hoc est. Quod namque tutius, quod tutissimum est, id in rebus animæ semper cuique faciendum.
units.tr: Nor indeed could that first contradiction be despised by you, except undeservedly. For a contradiction is certainly greater, and therefore less to be despised, when it overturns an entire treatise, than when it overturns a single little opinion. If that whole five-book work of his on Justification tends to establish an inherent habit of righteousness in us, and works of righteousness flowing from it; so that we may not only rest on the righteousness of Christ imputed to us, but also equally place our confidence in our own; does it not, in one rush, utterly overturn that whole disputation, which at last concludes thus: that nothing is safest for us except this, that we place our whole confidence in the mercy of God alone; whole, I say, in God alone? You evade this, saying: "not as though no confidence could be placed in good works." Therefore some confidence can be placed in good works; but unless this is safer, it cannot even be placed. Nor, I think, did you wish that: it can be placed, but this is not safer; that is, it can be placed, but rashly. Therefore some confidence can be placed; but he contradicts, that no part of confidence can be placed, but it is fitting to place the whole in mercy alone: for this is safest. For whatever is safer, whatever is safest, that must always be done by each man in matters of the soul.

units.la: Quod verò è Bernardo affers de præsumptione, alienum plane à proposito. Obsecro te, an fiducia jam tibi præsumptio est? Præsumptio in vitio semper; fiducia virtus, quippe confirmata Spes. Aliud longè præsumere, aliud fiduciam ponere. Præsumit, qui merita nulla habet, vel falsa; fiduciam ponit, qui & aliqua habet, & vera. Tu dicis aliqua, dicis & vera merita nostra esse, fiduciam ergo in illis collocabimus; ad fidendum merita habebimus, non præsumendum, quod iure, merito possumus: præsumptionem longùm valere iubebimus, quæ fallax est, quia falsis innixa; nos verù fidimus, in quibus potest (dicis ipse) fiducia aliqua, dicit Dominus tuus, fiducia nulla, collocari. Nulla enim in meritis, si tota nobis in solâ misericordiâ Dei collocanda est: collocanda autem, si id tutius.
units.tr: What you bring from Bernard about presumption is plainly foreign to the point. I beg you, is confidence now presumption to you? Presumption is always a vice; confidence is a virtue, being indeed a strengthened hope. To presume is one thing, to place confidence is quite another. He presumes who has no merits, or false ones; he places confidence who has some, and true ones. You say that we have some merits, and that they are true, so we shall place confidence in them; we shall have merits to trust in, not to presume upon, which we can rightly and deservedly have: presumption we shall bid farewell for good, since it is deceptive, being propped on falsehoods; but we trust in those in which (you yourself say) "some confidence" can be placed; your Lord says "no confidence." For no confidence is to be placed in merits, if the whole must be placed in God's mercy alone; but it is to be placed if that is safer.

units.la: Utile tamen est, inquis: Merito contemni posset responsio hæc tua. Quæstio primùm, nobis de utili non est. Sit tamen; si inutile factu, ne faciendum quidem. Si non potest in bonis operibus fiducia collocari, nisi inutiliter; non potest in illis collocari. Non est utile (inquis) respicere propria merita. Si non respicere, certè nec fidere; si non utile, nunquam faciendum quod utile non est. An id dicis licere nobis, quod nisi inutiliter non licet? An id possumus, quod tutò non possumus? Ad superbiam evitandam, non est utile. At hîc etiam aliud fiducia, aliud superbia; fidere licet, ipse dicis, superbire haud unquam licet. Sed neque vel si non superbias, sed fidas tantum, tutissimum, ut fiduciæ partem ullam in meritis, sed ut totam in solâ Dei misericordiâ repones, in eamq; solam respicias.
units.tr: "Yet it is useful," you say: this your response could rightly be despised. The question is not first of all about usefulness for us. Grant it nonetheless: if it is useless to do, then it must not be done either. If confidence cannot be placed in good works except uselessly, it cannot be placed in them. "It is not useful," you say, "to look to one's own merits." If one must not look to them, certainly one must not trust in them either; if it is not useful, what is not useful must never be done. Do you say that we are permitted what we are permitted only uselessly? Or can we do what we cannot do safely? It is not useful for avoiding pride. But here too confidence is one thing, pride another: to trust is permitted, as you yourself say; to be proud is never permitted. But even if you are not proud, but only trust, it is safest not to place any part of confidence in merits, but to place the whole in God's mercy alone, and to look to that alone.

units.la: Æque ridiculum; Non est utile, quia incerti sumus an habeamus merita. At non potest ulla in meritis fiducia poni, si an habeamus incerti simus. Incertis enim non est fidendum.
units.tr: Equally ridiculous: it is not useful, because we are uncertain whether we have merits. But no trust at all can be placed in merits if we are uncertain whether we have them. For one cannot trust in things that are uncertain.

units.la: Et quæ est ista Lectoris ludificatio, licet, non licet; licet, quia vera salutis causa sunt; non licet, quia an tales tibi sint, incertum es? Ecclesia docet, præcipuam spem & fiduciam in Deo ponendam esse; aliquam tamen etiam in meritis poni posse: Bellarminus docet, totam in solâ misericordiâ Dei ponendam esse; id est, nullam in meritis poni posse. Tutissimum ergo non facere, quod Ecclesia docet. Illa docet in meritis aliquam: Ille docet, tutissimum, non aliquam, id est, nullam in meritis, sed totam in solâ Dei misericordiâ. Nulla, & Aliqua, notæ contradictionis sunt. Annon hoc est misere fluctuare?
units.tr: And what is this trickery of the reader's, "it is permitted, it is not permitted"? It is permitted, because merits are the true cause of salvation; it is not permitted, because you are uncertain whether they are such for you? The Church teaches that the chief hope and trust must be placed in God, yet that some trust may also be placed in merits. Bellarmine teaches that the whole trust must be placed in God's mercy alone; that is, that no trust at all can be placed in merits. So it is safest not to do what the Church teaches. She teaches that some trust is to be placed in merits; he teaches that the safest course is not some trust, that is, no trust in merits, but the whole trust in God's mercy alone. "No" and "some" are marks of contradiction. Is this not to waver wretchedly?

units.la: Secundam, ut potes, expedi. Nunquam Charybdin sic vitabis, quin in Scyllam incidas. Non movet Deus, vel inclinat, ad malum moraliter: Movet Deus vel inclinat ad malum moraliter. Charybdis est; vitas sic; Non movet moraliter (id est) imperando: movet moraliter (id est) occasionem immittendo. Esto. Moraliter moveri[?], id est, morali modo: Morali ergo modo Genus est: per modum imperij, per modum occasionis, Species duae. Posterior recte dicitur, Deum moraliter monere, id est, per modum occasionis: affirmatur enim ibi Genus de Specie. Prior vero, non recte, Moraliter enim monere Genus est; Per modum imperij, Species. Non debet negari Genus, ubi de sola Specie agitur. En tibi Scyllam. Falsum enim hoc, Non monet Deus moraliter; nec explicatio iuvat, id est imperando non monet, quia insistit statim Adversarius, Imo id solum, non est moraliter monere; est & modus alter apud Thomam: occasionem scilicet immittendo, atque ita monet Deus. Debuit vero, primo loco Speciem nominasse, non Genus totum; non monere scilicet Deum imperando, dicere debuit; non monere moraliter, dicere non debuit: quia & occasione monere, moraliter etiam monere est. Vis in exemplo rem videre? Non monet Deus ad malum moraliter, id est, imperando: Asinus non est animal, id est, ratione praeditum. Ita, vero si loqui liceat, quis sibi unquam contradicet?
units.tr: Steer through the second difficulty as best you can. You will never avoid Charybdis without falling into Scylla. God does not move, or incline, to evil morally; God moves, or inclines, to evil morally. That is Charybdis; you avoid it thus: he does not move morally (that is, by commanding); he moves morally (that is, by offering an occasion). Granted. To be moved morally, that is, in a moral manner: so "morally" is the genus, and "by way of command" and "by way of occasion" are the two species. The latter is rightly said: "God admonishes morally," that is, by way of occasion; for there the genus is affirmed of the species. The former, however, is not rightly said: "to admonish morally" is the genus; "by way of command" is the species. A genus must not be denied where only the species is in question. There is your Scylla. For this statement, "God does not admonish morally," is false; nor does the explanation help, namely "he does not admonish by commanding," because the opponent immediately insists: "Indeed that alone is not to admonish morally; there is also another mode, according to Thomas: namely by offering an occasion, and so God admonishes." You ought, in the first place, to have named the species, not the whole genus: you ought to have said "God does not admonish by commanding," and not said "God does not admonish morally," because to admonish by occasion is also to admonish morally. Do you want to see the matter in an example? "God does not admonish to evil morally, that is, by commanding: an ass is not an animal, that is, endowed with reason." So, if one may speak truly, who would ever contradict himself?

units.la: IN tertiâ, tibi id usu venit, quod Cardinali post dicit Apologia, dum praesentem iam impetum declines, quid causâ ipsâ fiat, nihil moraris. Adhibes enim hic (cum melior ad manum non esset) mucidam illam distinctionem, quâ cuiusque telo occurritur apud te, Succedunt, & proprie non Succedunt, quam tamen hic adhibes satis improprie; Episcopos Apostolis succedere improprie: Non succedere autem proprie. Atque inter duo illa cum distinctio nulla sit, omnes te Logicae peritissimum esse, & communi sensu abundare praedicent, necesse est. Priore loco affirmat Cardinalis, succedere, sed non proprie: posteriore autem, non succedere proprie: Et haec tu putas Cardinale digna! Nec vides Cardinalem ex eo probare, quod Episcopi iure divino, maiores sunt Presbyteris, quia succedunt Apostolis: quibus si non succedant nisi improprie, argumenti Eius vis omnis corruit; nec enim, maiores erunt tum Episcopi presbyteris, nisi improprie. Ita dum hic cuadat[?] modo; quid alibi patiatur Dominus tuus, an ignoret Logicam, an careat communi sensu, an probet proprie, quod probare ibi instituit, an improprie: tua nihil refert. Oportet enim certe, ut Apostolis loco illo priore succedant, & proprie succedant: Nam nisi Apostoli proprie maiores fuerint septuaginta Discipulis, nisi Episcopi Apostolis succedant item proprie, non concludit ibi prepositum[?]. Ita dum hic cuadat[?] modo; quid alibi patiatur Dominus tuus, an ignoret Logicam, an careat communi sensu, an probet proprie, quod probare ibi instituit, an improprie: tuâ nihil refert. tum. Proprie ergo, eo loco succedunt Apostolis, vbi tu vis, non proprie.
units.tr: In the third, what happened to you is what your author says of the Cardinal after: "while you are now warding off the attack that is already upon you, you do nothing to advance the cause itself." For here you bring in (since a better one was not at hand) that mouldy distinction by which you meet every weapon among yourselves, "they succeed, and properly they do not succeed"; and yet here you use it quite improperly: "bishops succeed the Apostles improperly; they do not succeed properly." And since there is no distinction between those two statements, everyone must declare you most skilled in logic and abounding in common sense. "In the former place the Cardinal affirms that they succeed, but not properly; in the latter, that they do not succeed properly." And you think these things worthy of the Cardinal! Nor do you see that the Cardinal proves from this that "bishops by divine right are greater than presbyters, because they succeed the Apostles": if they succeed the Apostles only improperly, the whole force of his argument collapses; for bishops would then be greater than presbyters only improperly. So, while here he manages it in this way, what your lord suffers elsewhere, whether he is ignorant of logic, lacks common sense, or proves properly what he there set out to prove, or improperly, is of no concern to your cause. For it is certainly necessary that they succeed the Apostles in that earlier place, and succeed properly: for unless the Apostles were properly greater than the seventy disciples, and unless bishops succeed the Apostles likewise properly, the proposition does not follow there. So, while here he manages it in this way, what your lord suffers elsewhere, whether he is ignorant of logic, lacks common sense, or proves properly what he there set out to prove, or improperly, is of no concern to you. Therefore they succeed the Apostles properly in that place where you want them to succeed "improperly".

units.la: Tum quod addis, de Apostolis, quatenus Episcopi particularium Ecclesiarum affirmare hæc Cardinalem, de tuo addis. Nihil ibi de particularibus Ecclesijs Ephesi, vel Hierosolyma; sed neque de Iacobo vel Iohanne. Nam si esset Ephesi Episcopus Iohannes, Timotheo succederet, quem Paulus ibi Episcopum constituerat; non Timotheus Iohanni. Deinde verò etiam, enervaret argumentum eius penitus. Nec enim plures Episcopi, succederent Apostolis, quàm duodecim illi qui particularibus illis Ecclesiis præerant, quarum Apostoli fuerant Episcopi primi. Quid reliquis iam fieret? Illi Presbyteri maiores non essent; non certè. Non enim Successores nisi duodecim illi soli: reliqui verò non maiores Presbyteris, nimirum, qui Apostolis non succederent. En vt agas causam Domini tui! En quàm futilia facis vt dicat, ne sibi contradicat! Nam in loco altero, tam magna Cardinali causa præ manibus fuit, ita totus ei intentus (quò scilicet omnes Episcopi non aliunde accipiant iurisdictionem suam, quàm à Papâ) vt oblitus plane Clericorum suorum, ac totus defixus in Pontifice, nolit succedere Episcopos Apostolis iurisdictione vllâ, sed solo ordine: Magnum enim incommodum, si ex æquo omnes succederent Apostolis, ex æquo omnes iurisdictionem suam ab Apostolis haberent, nec pendèrent omnes à Papâ; cùm tamen in {a} libro de Clericis, quatuor argumentis probet, non ordine solùm, sed etiam iurisdictione Episcopos Apostolis successisse. Quin eum ipsum locum, quem adducit, libro de Clericis, quod Spiritus Sanctus eos posuit Episcopos, vt probet, ipso Domino instituente, Episcoporum propriam esse curam, & gubernationem Ecclesiæ: Eum ipsum (inquam) {b} libro de Pontifice, soluit; nec à Spiritu Sancto positos vult, nisi mediante Pontifice. Quòd enim ibi dicit, Episcopos non proprie succedere Apostolis, quatenus Apostoli erant, id est, missis in omnem terram: non minùs militat contra Pontificem, qui non prædicat in toto Orbe: nec missus est in omnem terram: nec scribit libros Canonicos: nec habet donum linguarum aut miraculorum magis, quàm reliqui Episcopi. Tum, & eo ipso in loco, ita Cardinalis: Romanus Pontifex proprie succedit Petro, non vt Apostolo. Vtiam, per vos, Apostoli successores nullos habeant, habebant, nec vel Petrus ipse, Pontificem ipsum. Tàm tu dextre concilias hic nobis contradictionem hanc tertiam.
units.tr: Then, what you add, "concerning the Apostles, insofar as they are bishops of particular churches, the Cardinal affirms these things": you add this from your own. There is nothing there about the particular churches of Ephesus or Jerusalem; nor indeed about James or John. For if John were bishop of Ephesus, he would succeed Timothy, whom Paul had there appointed bishop, not Timothy succeed John. Moreover, it would wholly weaken his argument. For the bishops who succeeded the Apostles would not be more than those twelve who presided over those particular churches, of which the Apostles were the first bishops. What would then become of the rest? They would not be greater presbyters; certainly not. For there would be successors only of those twelve alone, and the rest would not be greater than presbyters, namely because they would not succeed the Apostles. See how you plead your lord's cause! See how trivial are the things you do, so that he may not contradict himself! For in the other passage, so great a cause lay before the Cardinal, and he was so intent on it (namely, that all bishops receive their jurisdiction from no source other than the Pope) that, quite forgetting his clergy, and wholly fixed on the Pontiff, he is unwilling that bishops succeed the Apostles in any jurisdiction, but only in order. For it would be a great inconvenience if all alike succeeded the Apostles, all alike had their jurisdiction from the Apostles, and all did not depend on the Pope; although in his book On the Clergy he proves by four arguments that bishops succeeded the Apostles not only in order but also in jurisdiction. Indeed, the very passage he cites in that book, "that the Holy Spirit set them as bishops," in order to prove that, by the Lord's own institution, the proper care and government of the Church belong to bishops, that same passage (I say) he dissolves in his book On the Pope, and does not want them set by the Holy Spirit except through the mediation of the Pope. For what he says there, that bishops do not succeed the Apostles properly insofar as the Apostles were, that is, sent into all the world, fights no less against the Pontiff, who does not preach throughout the whole world, is not sent into all the world, does not write canonical books, and does not have the gift of tongues or of miracles more than the other bishops. Then, in that same place, the Cardinal says: "The Roman Pontiff succeeds Peter properly, not as an Apostle." Would that, through you, the Apostles had no successors, or rather that Peter himself had no successor, the Pontiff himself. So dexterously do you here reconcile for us this third contradiction.

units.la: AT in Quartâ, verbo rem conficis. Distingue (inquis) tempora. Verùm hic nihil opus est, tempora distinguas, si nullo tempore Iudas credidit. Nullo autem tempore credidisse euincit locus ille Chrysostomi (è loco enim Chrysostomi affert {a}Cardinalis) nos enim (aiebat ibi Petrus) credidimus & cognoui-mus, quia tu es CHRISTVS filius Dei viuentis. Cùm dixisset Petrus, Et nos credidimus; eximit CHRISTVS è numero Iudam, Iudam excipit Dominus de Collegio credentium. CHRISTVS ergo monuit, non esse verum de omnibus. Quid tandem? credidisse illos omnes: non enim credidit Iudas. Non tum, dices. Imò verò credidimus, de praeterito dicitur, quasi diu iam ante credidissent. Eximit ergo, ex eorum numero Iudam, qui ante crediderant. Tum paulò ante, verf. 64. ita loquitur; Sciebat enim ab initio, quinam erant non credentes. Ab initio dicit, non tum demum; sed ab initio conuersationis suae cum Discipulis: Et quinam essent credentes ab initio, non, quinam post essent à fide defecturi. Non enim, ideo quia scandalizati sunt, dici potuerunt non credentes: sed non in fide permanentes. At ille, simpliciter dicit, quinam essent non credentes. Nec modò infideles fuisse ostendit, sed causam etiam assignat infidelitatis; quae est, ex remotione gratiae attrahentis. Subjicit enim, quod multò adhuc magis rem ponit in aperto: propterea dixi vobis, nemo potest venire ad me, nisi datum sit ei à patre. Cuius vocis, propterea, is sensus est; Scilicet ideo Christum, qui essent non credentes, quòd sciret nisi eis à Patre datum esset, vt credendo venirent, venire non posse. Non venisse ergo Iudam, quòd ei à Patre datum non esset, vt veniret: A Patre, (inquam) Iude datum non esse: non igitur venisse. Qui autem non venerat discedere non poterat. Denique {b}Alcuinus noster diserte rem exprimit. Vnus ex duodecim erat Iudas, non fide, sed numero: non veritate, sed simulatione.
units.tr: But in the fourth you settle the matter with a word. "Distinguish the times," you say. Yet here there is no need to distinguish times, if Judas never believed at any time. That he never believed at any time is proved by that passage of Chrysostom (for the Cardinal quotes it from Chrysostom): "For we," said Peter there, "have believed and have known that you are Christ, the Son of the living God." When Peter had said, "And we have believed," Christ excludes Judas from the number, Christ excepts Judas from the college of believers. Christ therefore warned that it is not true of all. What then? That all of them believed? For Judas did not believe. Not then, you will say. But indeed, "we have believed" is said in the past tense, as if they had believed long before. He therefore excludes from their number Judas, who had believed before. And a little before, at verse 64, he speaks thus: "For Jesus knew from the beginning who were the unbelievers." He says "from the beginning," not only then; but from the beginning of his conversation with the disciples. And "who were believers from the beginning," not who would afterwards fall away from the faith. For they could not be called "unbelievers" merely because they were scandalized, but "not remaining in the faith." Yet he simply says "who were unbelievers." And he shows not only that they had been unfaithful, but also assigns the cause of their unbelief, which is the withdrawal of the drawing grace. For he adds, what places the matter even more openly: "For this reason I have said to you, no one can come to me unless it has been given to him by the Father." The sense of that word "for this reason" is this: that Christ knew that those who were unbelievers could not come, by believing, unless it had been given to them by the Father. Judas therefore did not come, because it had not been given to him by the Father that he should come: it had not been given to him, I say, by the Father, so he did not come. But he who had not come could not depart. Finally, our Alcuin expresses the matter plainly: Judas was one of the twelve, not in faith but in number; not in truth but in pretence.

units.la: IN Quintâ; Praecepto morali de substantiâ operis iubetur quis, non solùm obseruare, vel implere praeceptum; sed ita obseruare, vt peccatum non committat; id est, (Cardinale ipso interprete) praeceptum cum omnibus circumstantiis obseruare. Nam quid? Operis substantiam, intelligis nudam, nec debitus ve[?] itam circumstantijs : id est utcunq; factam , nec modo, nec loco , nec tempore, quo oportet? Imo lateris ipse de tempore[?]dum dicis ; Qui facit eleemosynam quando tenetur ex praecepto; Qui facit quando, ita tu : Quidni autem, qui facis ubi? &c, qui cui? &c, qui unde etiam tenetur? Ex praecepto enim tenetur, non modo ut faciat quando, quae temporis circumstantia est; sed ut faciat ubi, quae loci. Tu, temporis circumstantiam apponis: nos, eodem iure cateras.
units.tr: In the Fifth point: a moral precept concerning the substance of a work requires that a person not only observe or fulfil the precept, but observe it in such a way that he commits no sin; that is, (as the Cardinal himself explains) to observe the precept with all its circumstances. For what then? Do you understand the substance of the work as bare, not clothed with its due circumstances, that is, done in whatever way, not in the manner, place or time in which it ought to be done? Indeed you say of the time in the very words: "He who gives alms when he is bound by precept..." and so you go on: "Why not also he who gives where...? etc., who to whom? etc., whence" is he also bound? For he is bound by precept not only to give at a certain time, which is a circumstance of time, but to give in a certain place, which is a circumstance of place. You add the circumstance of time; we, by the same right, the others.

units.la: Sed mitto &c illam, &c cateras. Quaero quae sit operis substantia? Ea scilicet, quae speciem operi dant, ad substantiam operis concurrere, ne tu quidem negabis. In Eleemosyna, quae tandem illa? Tria scilicet haec insunt in substantia Eleemosynae: ut demus nostrum; ut indigenti; ut ex misericordia demus. Horum trium siquid deest, perit de operis substantia. De pecunia furtiua si faciat quis Eleemosynam, peccatum admittit: non enim de suo. Pariter, si diuiti: non enim indiget. Pariter si non ex misericordia: non autem ex misericordia, si ex inani gloria, si ut laudetur, si sine deprauato faciat. Finis enim hic speciem dat in moralibus. Praeceptum autem morale est de Eleemosyna; ut quod tu de vitioso fine suggeris, plane fit extra oleas. Cum enim Cardinalis ipse nobis explicat, quid sit secundum substantiam operis, requirit, ut fiat bonum opus, secundum moralem quandam honestatem: Moralis autem honestas, sine fine debito, nulla est. Quin si Cardinalem ipsum audimus; Opera infidelium, ob finem prauum, ad quem referuntur, peccata simpliciter sunt. Quare excludat alios fines, alia peccata, bonum morale: finem in praecepti morali opere, excludit praeceptum ipsum; sine quo, nec substantia est, nec species operis, secundum moralem honestatem. Nec ergo hic verba sola sonant contrarium, sensus ipse contrarius est. Praeceptum seruare, ut peccatum non committatur: Seruare etiam cum peccato, id est, etiamsi peccatum committatur.
units.tr: But I pass over that and the others. I ask: what is the substance of the work? Surely those things which give the work its species, which you will not deny concur to the substance of the work. In almsgiving, what, finally, is that? Clearly these three things are present in the substance of almsgiving: that we give what is ours; that we give to the needy; that we give out of mercy. If any one of these three is lacking, the substance of the work perishes. If someone gives alms from stolen money, he commits a sin, for it is not his own. Likewise, if to a rich man, for he is not needy. Likewise if he does not give out of mercy; but he does not give out of mercy if he gives out of vainglory, in order to be praised, or if he gives with a corrupt intention. For this end in moral matters gives the species. But the moral precept concerns almsgiving; so that what you suggest about a vicious end plainly falls outside the olive grove. For when the Cardinal himself explains to us what is according to the substance of the work, he requires that the work be done according to a certain moral honesty. But moral honesty without the due end is nothing. Indeed, if we hear the Cardinal himself: the works of unbelievers, on account of the wicked end to which they are referred, are simply sins. Therefore, whoever excludes other ends excludes other sins; he who excludes the moral good, that is, the end, in a work of moral precept, excludes the precept itself, without which there is neither substance nor species of the work according to moral honesty. Nor, then, do the words alone sound contrary here; the sense itself is contrary. "To observe the precept, so that sin is not committed": to observe it even with sin, that is, even if sin be committed.

units.la: QVale[?] & illud in Sexta: Contradictiones ab Apologia proponi ad Lutheranos, quasi Cardinalis sit Lutheranus. Apud Lutheranos (inquis) contradictio hac. Apud vos vero quae? Retinere fidem, quae per dilectionem operatur; & lethaliter peccare. Petrus autem fidem illam ex dilectione operantem non retinuit, sed aliam mortuam, & sine operibus. Vide hoc pri-mum, mùm, quàm obtusè. Id enim agit, eo loco Cardinalis, vt miris modis efferat B. Petri priuilegium, quod ei concessum, vi orationis Christi, Ego rogaui pro te, ne deficeret fides tua. Fides tua ( interprete iam Torto) mortua scilicet fine operibus, sine ailectione, quę Sto Iacobo, fides Dæmonum, & pro hac fide rogauit Christ[?], ne in Petro deficeret. Illustrem verò (vt narras) Petri prærogatiuam, & Christi orationem magni faciendam, quæ Petro impetrauit, vt permaneret in eo fides nescio quæ cadauerosa, informis, æquiuoca, falsi nominis, quæ & in Dæmone posit permanere. Ita tu, dum aliquid chartæ illinas, non valde referre putas, quam Christo oranti, quam Petro, pro quo oratum est, quam Cardinali ipsi iniuriam asseras, quam etiam Pontifici cuius ibi res agitur, ne posit in eo deficere fides Dæmonum, à quâ, vestra omnium fides pendet. Aliam, credo, Cardinalis Petro prærogatiuam vindicare voluit quàm vt perseueraret in fide Dæmonum; aliam Pontifici.
units.tr: Quale? Also that in the Sixth: that contradictions are put forward by the Apology against the Lutherans, as if the Cardinal were a Lutheran. "Among the Lutherans (you say) there is this contradiction. But among you what? To hold faith which works through love, and to sin mortally." Peter, however, did not hold that faith working through love, but another faith, dead, and without works. See first of all this, how obtusely. For the Cardinal, in that place, aims to extol in marvellous ways the privilege of Blessed Peter, which was granted him by the power of Christ's prayer: "I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail." Your faith (by Torto's own interpretation) is dead, that is, without works, without love, which for St James is the faith of demons; and for this faith Christ prayed, that it might not fail in Peter. But the illustrious prerogative of Peter (as you tell it), and the prayer of Christ to be held in high regard, which obtained for Peter that there should remain in him some faith, I know not what, carcass-like, shapeless, equivocal, of false name, which can also remain in a demon. Thus you, while smearing some paper, think it does not greatly matter how much injury you do to Christ who prayed, to Peter for whom the prayer was made, to the Cardinal himself, and also to the Pontiff, in whose case the matter is at issue, lest in him there fail the faith of demons, on which the faith of you all depends. I believe the Cardinal wished to vindicate for Peter a different prerogative than that he should persevere in the faith of demons; and a different one for the Pontiff.

units.la: Tum, quæ fuit in Petro fides, cum Christus hoc promitteret, mortua non fuit; pro mortuâ ergo Christus non orauit. Nam si mortua, defecerat iam: si iam autem defecerat, quomodo, ne deficeret orare potuit Christus? Addo etiam, quòdsi mortua, potiùs vt in eo talis fides deficeret orare debuit; quàm vt ne deficeret. Tum, fidem illam Paulinam, quâ creditur ad iustitiam, fidem mortuam esse, quis te docuit? Non certè Apostolus, qui proximo statim versu subiungit; idque rationem reddendo, Dicit enim scriptura, omnis, qui in eum credit, non confundetur. Nec Petrus ergo confusus ita fuisset, coram ancillulâ, si non amisisset eam; sed retinuisset, & vel sic falrem in Christum credere potuisset. Non {a}Theophylactus (vnde citauit hæc Cardinalis) qui, fidem radicem dicit, & radicem eam vixisse, id est, fidem in eo viuam adhuc fuisse.
units.tr: Moreover, the faith which was in Peter when Christ promised this was not dead; therefore Christ did not pray for a dead faith. For if it was dead, it had already failed; and if it had already failed, how could Christ pray that it might not fail? I add also that, if it were dead, Christ ought rather to have prayed that such a faith should fail in him, than that it should not fail. Further, who taught you that the Pauline faith, "by which one believes unto righteousness," is dead faith? Certainly not the Apostle, who in the very next verse adds this, giving the reason: "For the Scripture says, whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." Nor, then, would Peter have been so put to shame before the little maidservant, if he had not lost that faith; but had retained it, and even so he could have believed in Christ fully. Nor does Theophylact (from whom the Cardinal cites these things) say otherwise, who calls faith the root, and says that the root lived, that is, that faith was still alive in him.

units.la: Pòst verò etiam ais, amisisse Petrum confessionem oris, non fuisse tamen hereticum, vel infidelem. Nulla ergo in oratione Christi vis, nullum ex eâ P. tro priuilegium. Non sibi ipsi; læthaliter enim peccauit. Non Ecclesiæ: nam si confessionem oris amittere posset, (Christi oratione non obstante,) quicquid intus in corde sentiat, non confirmabit, sed peruertet Ecclesiam, quæ ab ore illius pendet, in corde quid lateat scire non potest. Sed hoc, credo, à te positum, in gratiam Liberij, Honorij, Iohannu22b[?] qui, etsi oru confessionem, addo, & manus subscriptionem amiserunt; non tamen (vt pie credendum est) fuerunt haeretici. Quid tum? confessione suâ[?] interim, Ecclesiae nocuerunt: quae magis in tuto foret, si salua illis sit confessio oris, pereat autem de corde fides, id est, hætesin[?] corde credant, ore ne confiteantur.
units.tr: Afterwards, moreover, you say that "Peter lost the confession of the mouth, yet was not a heretic or unbeliever." Therefore there is no force in Christ's prayer, and no privilege for Peter from it. Not for himself; for he sinned mortally. Not for the Church: for if he could lose the confession of the mouth (notwithstanding Christ's prayer), whatever he inwardly feels in his heart he will not confirm, but will pervert the Church, which hangs upon his mouth; what lies hidden in the heart it cannot know. But this, I believe, you have put forward for the sake of Liberius, Honorius, and John XXII, who, although they lost their confession, I add, and the subscription of their hand, were nevertheless (as it is piously to be believed) not heretics. What then? By their confession meanwhile, they harmed the Church; which would be safer if the confession of the mouth remained safe for them, while faith of the heart perished; that is, let them believe in the heart, and not confess with the mouth.

units.la: Tertiò lethaliter peccare vis, & fidem [?]nuisse, quæ effet ad iustitiam dispositio; id est, dispositionem ad vitam habuisse, & tamen mortuam fuisse. Quod tibi (credo) accidit, ex nimiâ logicæ peritiâ, vbi nisi dispositio omnis ad habitum sublata fit, priuatio (qualis lethi) non solet introduci. Tu verò vnâ operâ, & disponere potes ad vitam, & tamen lethe homines dare.
units.tr: Thirdly, you wish that "one may sin mortally, and yet have had faith which was a disposition to righteousness"; that is, to have had a disposition to life, and yet to have been dead. This, I believe, happens to you from excessive skill in logic, where unless every disposition to a habit is removed, a privation (such as death) is not usually introduced. But you, in one and the same work, can both dispose to life and yet give men death.

units.la: Quemadmodum & illud, acutè sanè vidisti, si Apostolus existimaret fidem, quâ creditur ad iustitiam, sufficere ad perfectam iustitiam sine charitate, non adderet, Ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Certè si ad salutem sufficere crederet, vt corde quis credat; non adderet, ore fit confessio ad salutem. Ad iustitiam autem credidit sufficere, alioqui non diceret, Credi corde ad iustitiam. Ad iustitiam enim non creditur, si non satis illud ad iustitiam, corde credere, si plus ad iustitiam quæratur, quàm vt corde ad eam credatur. Nec diceret tum, ore autem, sed, ore etiam, non ad salutem, sed ad iustitiam confessio facienda est.
units.tr: Likewise also that you have seen very keenly: "If the Apostle thought that faith, by which one believes unto righteousness, sufficed for perfect righteousness without charity, he would not add, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. For certainly, if he believed it sufficed for salvation that one believe with the heart, he would not add that confession with the mouth is made unto salvation. But he believed it sufficed for righteousness; otherwise he would not say, with the heart one believes unto righteousness. For one does not believe unto righteousness if it is not enough for righteousness to believe with the heart; if more is sought for righteousness than that one believe unto it with the heart. Nor would he then say, but with the mouth, but with the mouth also, confession must be made not unto salvation but unto righteousness."

units.la: Tum, quale illud, ex defectu Charitatis, caruit confessione oris. Quasi, confessio oris, charitatis, & non fidei actus proprius, & primarius; Quasi non disertá sit, tam Prophetae vox, quàm Apostoli, Credidi, propter quod locutus sum. Quasi Theophylactus hoc ibi non dicat, confessionem solam, fidem radicem, & radicem viuam non, (vt tu ais) emortuam fuisse. Quasi Glossa ipsa hoc, quasi Thomas & Schola tota non tenant; vt si proprie, ex confessionis defectu quis arguat; dicendum sit ei, ex defectu fidei caruit confessione oris, potiùs quàm ex defectu charitatis. Denique, vt modis omnibus miserè iacere videas responsionem hic tuam; Nec defectus in B. Petro tum charitatis. Ita {a}Bernardus. Petrus cùm peccauit, charitatem non amisit, quia peccauit in veritatem, potiùs quàm charitatem. Ita {b}Leo: Vidit in te Dominus, non fidem fictam, non dilectionem auersam, sed constantiam fuisse turbatam: abundauit fletus, vbi defecit affectus, & fons charitatis lauit verba formidinis. Ecce, non auersam tum in Petro charitatem: Ecce etiam, vel tum in eo fontem charita-tis. tis. Ita, qui sibi nunquam contradicit Cardinalis ipse, in Petro, (cum Christum negauit,) non fuisse extinctam charitatem sed mansisse dicit, Leo non auersam, Bernardus non amissam. Manet ergo adhuc contradictio. Non amisit fidem, adde iam, nec charitatem, Et, Peccauit tamen Petrus peccatum lethale.
units.tr: Then, what is that about: "from lack of charity he lacked confession of the mouth." As if confession of the mouth were an act of charity and not a proper and primary act of faith; as if it were not plainly expressed by the voice of the prophet and of the Apostle, "I believed, therefore I spoke." As if Theophylact did not say here that confession alone, faith the root, and the living root, was not (as you say) dead. As if the Gloss itself did not hold this, as if all of Thomas and the Schools did not hold it; so that if one were properly to argue from a lack of confession, it would have to be said to him that he lacked confession of the mouth from lack of faith, rather than from lack of charity. Finally, so that you may see your response here lying miserably in every way: there was no lack of charity in Blessed Peter at that time. Thus Bernard: "When Peter sinned, he did not lose charity, because he sinned against the truth rather than against charity." Thus Leo: "The Lord saw in you not feigned faith, not averted love, but constancy disturbed: weeping abounded where affection failed, and the fountain of charity washed away the words of fear." Behold, not averted charity in Peter at that time: behold also, even then, in him the fountain of charity. Thus the Cardinal himself, who never contradicts himself, says that in Peter, when he denied Christ, charity was not extinguished but remained; Leo says not averted, Bernard not lost. Therefore the contradiction remains. "He did not lose faith," add now, "nor charity." And: "Yet Peter sinned a mortal sin."

units.la: IN Septimâ verò, ostendis ipse te terris, dein occultas; occultas, dein ostendis, sub nouâ illâ distinctione tuâ, clam & palam, occultè & aperte: frustra tamen, nec secus quàm Cumanus vester aures suas. Nam etsi oppugnare facto, & execrari verbo idola potest Antichristus; at abhorrere (quod animi & cordis est) non potest idola, si illa clam habeat. Nimis aperte Cyrillus, idola odio habebit. Potestne autem odio habere quis, non quod in aperto, sed quod in occulto veneratur? Quare, ludendum erat tibi hîc, terminis æquiuocis, & adhibenda Glossa vestra nova: Abhorrebit, odio habebit, id est, non abhorrebit, non odio habebit: odio tantùm habere, abhorrere se tantùm simulabit; alioqui locum hunc nunquam conciliâsses: Patres fortè Societatis, sic loquuntur, Odi Diabolum, id est, odisse me simulo: Patres Antiqui sic loquuti non sunt: quem oderant, ex animo oderant, tecte non oderant; teque odisse, qui affingis illorum sententijs, parum ex illorum sententiâ, sensum hunc odiosum, & compingis eos in numerum vestrorum Æquiuocantium. Dic autem, sodes, quæ erit vsquam, vnquam, contradictio, si sic liceat conciliare? Est, id est, non est; sed videtur esse: Abhorret, id est, non abhorret, sed simulat se abhorrere. Abhorret credo, lector, te ista sic conciliantem.
units.tr: In the Seventh chapter you show yourself to the world, then hide yourself; you hide, then show yourself, under your new distinction: secretly and openly, covertly and overtly. But in vain, and no differently from your Cumaean, you stop up your ears. For although Antichrist can oppose idols by deed and curse them by word, he cannot abhor idols (which belongs to the mind and heart) if he keeps them in secret. Cyril says plainly, he will hate idols. But can anyone hate what he worships not openly but in secret? Therefore you had to play here with ambiguous terms, and bring in your new gloss: he will abhor, he will hate, that is, he will not abhor, he will not hate; he will only pretend to hate and only pretend to abhor. Otherwise you would never have reconciled this passage. Perhaps the Fathers of the Society speak thus: I hate the Devil, that is, I pretend to hate. The ancient Fathers did not speak thus: those whom they hated, they hated from the heart; they did not hate covertly. And you, who attach to their opinions a hateful sense that is scarcely theirs, and enlist them among your equivocators, are the one who hates. Tell me, please, what contradiction will there ever be anywhere, at any time, if things may be reconciled in this way? It is, that is, it is not; but it seems to be. He abhors, that is, he does not abhor, but pretends to abhor. Reader, I believe you abhor this manner of reconciling.

units.la: IN Octauâ, postquam verecundiæ limites semel transfilij, facit, quod ibi sequitur, apud Oratorem. De oblatione seu (quod idem est) Sacrificio quæritur. De oblatione autem, id est, actione ipsâ offerendi: non de re oblatâ. De Sacrificio, id est, actione sacrificandi; non re, quæ sacrificatur. In Missâ enim iam sumus, quæ quidem, res oblata non est, sed tantùm offerendi actio: Vera ergo offerendi actio, celebratur verbis consecrationis. Locus hic primus est. Locus verò secundus. Positio super altare, non est actio offerendi. At consecratio verborum, & positio super altare, re, ratione, naturâ, tempore, ordine, diuersa sunt; nec positio, super altare incipit, nisi consecratione peractâ, id est, (si Cardinali credimus) nisi verâ oblatione celebratâ atqy peractâ, vera oblatio non inchoatur. Hæc quis non videt, quàm pugnantia? Hic conciliator Tortus officium suum facit, id est, torquet voces duas, Oblatio: Celebratur. Oblatio, id est, res oblata. Celebratur, id est, in altari esse incipit. Locus certè male conciliatus. Prior male, de oblatione. Octo in capite illo propositiones Cardinalis facit: postquam tribus primis expediuit de sacrificio, (accipiendo sacrificium, pro re, quæ sacrificatur, sive oblationem, pro re quæ offertur;) quinque reliquis, explicat, quid sit proprie sacrificium sive oblatio, accipiendo sacrificium pro actione sacrificandi, sive oblationem, pro actione offerendi) nempe, è quinque iisdem partibus, quâ parte, sit ipsa oblatio, id est, actio offerendi. Propositione quartâ, docet, non esse in oblatione præcedente consecrationem: quintâ, non esse in oblatione consecrationem subsequente: sextâ, non esse in fractione: septimâ, non esse in consumptione, nisi ex parte: octavâ demum, in Consecratione consistere Sacrificij essentiam. Bis autem hoc. Per consecrationem veram & realem immolationem fieri: Verbis consecrationis, veram & solennem oblationem celebrari: Denique hoc ipsum ita esse, quinque argumentis confirmat; & nisi sit: non Christum, non Apostolos obtulisse unquam, aut sacrificasse. Bene ergo, & gnauiter officium suum facit, qui negat verba consecrationis ad oblationem concurrere formaliter: cùm toties ibi Cardinalis ingeminet, in consecratione consistere Sacrificij essentiam: & maiusculis literis appositum, ut si luscus sit Tortus, legere tamen possit, consecrationem ad essentiam sacrificij pertinere. Ad materiam certè non pertinet: ad formam igitur. At ille tamen, non formaliter ait. Atque hæc prior eius tortura, oblationis, id est, actionis offerendi pro re oblatâ.
units.tr: In the Eighth chapter, after he has once leapt over the limits of modesty, he does what follows there, before the Orator. The question concerns the oblation, or (which is the same thing) the Sacrifice. But the oblation, that is, the very act of offering, not the thing offered; the Sacrifice, that is, the act of sacrificing, not the thing which is sacrificed. For we are now in the Mass, where the thing offered is not the matter, but only the act of offering. The true act of offering is therefore performed by the words of consecration. This is the first point. The second point is this: placing upon the altar is not the act of offering. But the consecration of the words and the placing upon the altar differ in thing, reason, nature, time and order; nor does the placing upon the altar begin unless the consecration has been completed, that is (if we believe the Cardinal) unless the true oblation has been celebrated and completed; the true oblation is not begun. Who does not see how contradictory these things are? Here the conciliator Tortus does his duty, that is, he twists the two words, oblation and celebrated. Oblation, that is, the thing offered. Celebrated, that is, begins to be upon the altar. Certainly the passage is badly reconciled. The first is wrongly taken as of the oblation. In that chapter the Cardinal sets out eight propositions. After he has dealt with the first three concerning sacrifice (taking sacrifice for the thing sacrificed, or oblation for the thing offered), he explains with the remaining five what the sacrifice or oblation properly is, taking sacrifice for the act of sacrificing, or oblation for the act of offering. Namely, from those same five parts, by the part in which the oblation itself, that is, the act of offering, consists. In the fourth proposition he teaches that consecration does not precede in the oblation; in the fifth, that consecration does not follow in the oblation; in the sixth, that it is not in the breaking; in the seventh, that it is not in the consumption, except in part; in the eighth finally, that the essence of the Sacrifice consists in the Consecration. He says this twice: that through the consecration the true and real immolation is made; by the words of consecration the true and solemn oblation is celebrated. Finally he confirms by five arguments that this is so, and that unless it were so, Christ and the Apostles never offered or sacrificed. Well and diligently, then, does he do his duty who denies that the words of consecration concur formally in the oblation, since the Cardinal repeats so often there, the essence of the Sacrifice consists in the consecration; and it is set in capital letters, so that Tortus, even if he is one-eyed, could still read that the consecration pertains to the essence of the sacrifice. It certainly does not pertain to the matter; therefore it pertains to the form. Yet he says not formally. And this is his first twisting, of oblation, that is, of the act of offering, into the thing offered.

units.la: Posterior; quod Cardinalis celebrari dicit; id Tortus in altari esse incipere. Sed manifestâ fraude. In altari enim esse incipere, dicit Cardinalis, mediante manu Sacerdotis; atque hæc ipsius ibi verba sunt, Manu, non ore, & digitis, non verbis. Hanc Sacerdotis manum bis præcidit Tortus duobus in locis; & sperauit impositurum selectori, victimam per verba consecrationis effici, & in ará Domini collocari. Effici quidem, per verba, verum est: sed per manum Sacerdotis, non per verba, in ará collocari, quis non videt? Verbis & consecratione, oblatio illa fit, priore loco [?]manibus autem & positione fit, posteriore. Atque ita haec per Tortum contradictio, nisi mala fide, conciliari non potest.
units.tr: The second: where the Cardinal says celebrated, Tortus says begins to be upon the altar. But this is a manifest fraud. For the Cardinal says that it begins to be upon the altar through the hand of the priest; and these are his very words there, by the hand, not the mouth, and by the fingers, not the words. Tortus cuts off this hand of the priest in two places, and hoped to impose on the reader that the victim is made by the words of consecration and placed on the altar of the Lord. That it is made by the words is indeed true; but that it is placed on the altar by the hand of the priest, and not by the words, who does not see? That oblation is made by the consecration and the words in the former place, but by the hands and the placing in the latter. And so this contradiction, as Tortus has it, cannot be reconciled except by bad faith.

units.la: DE Nonâ. Mundi finem ignotum, diem novissimum incertum esse, nec esse solum incertum, sed & forte, subito prorsus & inopinato superventurum in omnes, qui sunt super faciem terrae; sicut diem Diluvij, Sodomae; quasi laqueum in volucres, furem nocturnum, partum mulieris, instar fulguris repentini, multis in locis monet Salvator. Tu hoc arripis; incertum esse iam, sed non, si iam est, ita semper fore; Non enim cum Antichristus regnare coeperit. Nam sciunt cum omnes (Cardinale Calculatore) diebus quadraginta quinque post annos tres & dimidium; sive menses quadraginta duos; sive dies 1260. Christum certò venturum, mundi finem, diem novissimum certò futurum. Non ergo illis improviso veniet filius hominis. Illorum erit tum scire tempora & momenta, per vos tam, posita extra potestatem Patris: Illis notum erit, quod Angelis ignotum: Nec repentinus, ut Diluvij; ita Iudicij dies Veniet enim Antichristus (ut vos asseritis) sic, ut latere non possit. Is ubi venerit, in digitis statim supputabunt, annos & menses exactè (nec in eo ambigui erunt, solares sint, an lunares: Lunares enim erunt, sponsore {a}Domino tuo imò, & dies ipsos praecisè; nec falli poterunt: certo enim certius, dies abesse non poterit, quadraginta quinque diebus ab Antichristo mortuo, Christum sine dubio venturum, Mundi finem fore. Constat enim quòd non erunt nisi quadraginta quinque dies ad finem mundi post mortem Antichristi. Habebunt ergo in numerato, & expectabunt diem novissimum, diem nempe quadragesimum quintum, nec dicent, pax & tuta omnia. Et illa de adventu secundo in Euangelio, quasi furis, laquei, partus, fulguris, fabulae merae sunt, falsa omnia. Videsne tam concinnâ hac conciliatione tuâ everti Scripturae vim omnem, Euangelium, Epistolas, Christum ipsum denique, falsi teneri?
units.tr: On the Ninth point. The end of the world is unknown, the last day uncertain; and not only uncertain, but that it will come suddenly and quite unexpectedly upon all who are on the face of the earth, like the day of the Flood and of Sodom, like a snare upon birds, a thief in the night, the pangs of a woman in labour, like a sudden lightning: the Saviour warns of this in many places. You seize on this: it is now uncertain, but not if it is now, and it will not always be so. For not when Antichrist has begun to reign. For all know (with the Cardinal as calculator) that forty-five days after three years and a half, that is forty-two months, or 1260 days, Christ will certainly come, and the end of the world, the last day, will certainly be. Therefore the Son of Man will not come upon them unawares. Then it will be theirs to know the times and seasons, which through you are placed outside the power of the Father. It will be known to them, which is unknown to the angels. Nor will the day of judgment be sudden, as the Flood was. For Antichrist (as you assert) will come in such a way that he cannot be hidden. When he has come, they will at once count up on their fingers the years and months exactly; nor will they be in doubt about it, whether they are solar or lunar. For they will be lunar, by the guarantee of your Lord, indeed the very days precisely; and they cannot be deceived. For, more certain than certain, the day cannot fail to be forty-five days after the death of Antichrist, when Christ without doubt will come and the end of the world will be. For it is agreed that there will be only forty-five days to the end of the world after the death of Antichrist. They will therefore have it in hand and will await the last day, namely the forty-fifth day, and they will not say peace and all is safe. And those sayings in the Gospel about the second coming, like the thief, the snare, the labour pains and the lightning, are mere fables, all false. Do you see, by this neat reconciliation of yours, how all the force of Scripture is overturned, the Gospel, the Epistles, Christ himself finally held to be false?

units.la: Et tamen Scripturam ipsam perstrahere audet in societatem sceleris, & dicere; Si hac contradictio est, in ipsâ Scripturâ divinâ est: utrumque enim in Scripturâ divinâ habetur. Verba forte in Apocalypsi sunt: sensus in Apocrypsi cerebri tui. Non enim servo revelavit, quod non Filio, nec Iohannes Christo con-
units.tr: And yet he dares to drag Scripture itself into the company of his crime, and to say: If this is a contradiction, it is in Scripture itself; for both are found in divine Scripture. The words are perhaps in the Apocalypse; the sense is in the Apocrypse of your brain. For it was not revealed to the servant what was not revealed to the Son, nor does John contradict Christ.

units.la: {a} De Pontif. lib.3.cap.8. contradicit: contradiceret, si certum daret tempus, quod Christus incertum; si diem praevisum, quem Christus improvisum. Sed nemo scit quando Antichristus veniet. Quid tum? Cùm venerit, ecquis tum sciet? Ecquis tum exploratum habebit, mundi terminum definitum? Ergo frustra vigilare tum iussit Christus, vigilare quidem semper omnes, sed illos qui tum futuri, peculiari quadam ratione; frustrà (inquam:) quae enim aliàs incerta, tum fore certissima. Sed neque quisquam scit, quando in toto mundo Evangelij praedicatio sit complenda. Quàm vero dissimile? Ibi, quando complenda, nemo scit: Hic vero scit quisque, quando complendum sit regnum Antichristi, tali anno, mense, die. Sine vero, ut Cardinalem hic alloquar verbis suis. Sequitur ex hoc errore, nosse Cardinalem, quando finietur mundus, quod tamen est contra verba Domini. Sic vero (ut tu facis) Scripturas inter se conciliare, quid aliud est, quàm Paulum cum Christo conculcare? In fine mundi, de fine, homines incertissimos fore, dicunt illi: tum vero, tum certissimos fore.
units.tr: {a} In De Pontificio, book 3, chapter 8. He would contradict, if he gave a certain time, when Christ gives an uncertain one; if he foresaw the day, when Christ gave it unforeseen. But no one knows when Antichrist will come. What then? When he has come, who will know then? Who will then have it established, the limit of the world defined? Therefore Christ bade them watch in vain then, all indeed watching always, but those who are to be then in a peculiar way; in vain, I say; for things which are otherwise uncertain will then be most certain. But neither does anyone know when the preaching of the Gospel in the whole world is to be completed. And how very unlike is this! There, no one knows when it will be completed; but here everyone knows when the kingdom of Antichrist is to be completed, in such and such a year, month, day. But let me address the Cardinal here in his own words. It follows from this error that the Cardinal knows when the world will end, which is nonetheless against the words of the Lord. Thus to reconcile the Scriptures with one another in your way is nothing else than trampling Paul underfoot with Christ. Those men say that concerning the end of the world men will be most uncertain about the end; then indeed they will be most certain.

units.la: Atque, ut tua haec quàm male conciliata sint; & vobis inter vos, quàm non bene conveniat, Lectori constet; appono hic {a}Blasij de Viegas Iesuitæ, sententiam hâc totâ de re. Sic ille, longè secus, quàm vos. Verùm, utrùm plures quàm quadraginta quinque dies à morte Antichristi, vsque ad diem iudicij excurrere debeant, incertum est, & illud etiam minimè exploratum, ut ait Lyranus in Cap. 39. Ezek. utrùm illi dies futuri sint usuales ut nostri, an pro annis computari debeant, quemadmodum & Ezek. cap. 4. dicitur diem pro anno dedi tibi. Iuxta quam sententiam, incognitus adhuc manet dies iudicij. Sanè admodum probabile est, incertas futuras eius temporis inducias. Etenim Dominus, Matth°. 24. agens de suo aduentu ad iudicium, sic ait, Sicut erant in diebus ante diluuium, comedentes, & bibentes, & nubentes, & nuptui tradentes, vsque ad eum diem quo intrauit Noe in arcam, & non cognouerunt, donec venit diluuium, & tulit omnes: ita erit aduentus filij hominis. Quàm Christi sententiam, Doctores referunt, ad illud tempus quod effluet, à morte Antichristi, vsque ad diem iudicij, & 1.Thess 5. Dies Domini sicut fur in nocte, ita veniet: cùm enim dixerint, Pax & securitas, tunc repentinus superueniet interitus. Non est autem verisimile tam breui, quadraginta quinque dierum spacio, post mortem Anti-christi, christi, homines vsque adeo depositos tanta persecutionis memoriam, vt, in eâ viuant securitate, otio, & deliciis, quæ ante diluuium præcessisse memorantur. Accedit, quod Christus Dominus docet, diem iudicij incognitum omnibus mortalibus futurum. Si autem quadraginta quinque tantum dies à morte Antichristi vsque ad diem iudicij deberent excurrere, certè possent eius temporis homines, eum diem certò designare. Pater itaque Blasius conciliare hæc nunquam posset, Tortus viderit.
units.tr: And so that the reader may see how badly your statements fit together, and how poorly you agree among yourselves, I set down here the opinion on this whole matter of Blasius de Viegas, the Jesuit. He speaks quite differently from you. Whether more than forty-five days must elapse from the death of Antichrist until the day of judgment is uncertain, and it is also by no means established, as Lyranus says on Ezekiel chapter 39, whether those days will be ordinary days like ours, or whether they ought to be counted as years, just as Ezekiel 4 says: "I have given you a day for a year." According to this opinion, the day of judgment remains unknown. It is certainly very probable that the interval of that time will be uncertain. For the Lord, Matthew 24, speaking of his coming to judgment, says: "As in the days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark, and they did not know until the flood came and swept them all away: so will the coming of the Son of Man be." The Doctors refer this saying of Christ to the time that will flow on from the death of Antichrist until the day of judgment; and 1 Thessalonians 5: "The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. For when they say, 'Peace and security,' then sudden destruction will come upon them." Now it is not likely that within so short a space as forty-five days after the death of Antichrist, men will have so far laid aside the memory of so great a persecution that they will live in that security, idleness and pleasures which are recorded to have gone before the flood. Add to this that Christ the Lord teaches that the day of judgment will be unknown to all mortals. But if only forty-five days were to elapse from the death of Antichrist until the day of judgment, then surely men of that time could fix that day with certainty. Therefore Father Blasius could never reconcile these things; let Tortus see to it.

units.la: DE Decimâ. Sedes Antichristi vbi futura, Romæne, an Hierosolymis, nihil hîc ad contradictionem, neque controuersia de eo nobis vlla. Nec tamen opus tibi eâ de re tantoper[?]umultuari. Non enim Lutherani soli Romæ fore censent Sedem Antichristi: censent & Iesuitæ; atque Illi inter eos qui debent rem optimè cognoscere, vtpote qui in Apocalypsin, lucubrationes suas ediderunt, Ribera & Viegas; nec leuiter perstrinxerunt, vt Dominus tuus, sed incubuerunt penitus, vt fides ex eo maior illis habenda sit. Esto verò tu, vel propter Patres illos, Luthero æquior; neque rem adeo indignè feras, si dicatur dixisse Dominus tuus, quod duos Compatres eius dixisse non pœnitet. Lis tota est de incendio. Neque ibi venatione opus vllum; prosilit enim ipsa per se, & procurrit contradictio, absque cane vllo venatico. In eodem enim capite Romæ ardet; semel à decem Regibus: iterum ab Antichristo incensa. In cineres semel versa, qui potest iterum conflagrare? Hæc contradictio est: Hanc expedi.
units.tr: On the Tenth: "Where will the seat of Antichrist be, at Rome or at Jerusalem?" There is nothing here bearing on the contradiction, nor is there any controversy with us about it. Nor is there need for you to make such a fuss about it. For it is not only the Lutherans who think the seat of Antichrist will be at Rome; the Jesuits think so too, and those among them who ought to know the matter very well, since they have published their studies on the Apocalypse, Ribera and Viegas, and they did not touch on it lightly, as your Lord did, but went into it thoroughly, so that their opinion ought to carry more weight. Indeed, you yourself, perhaps out of regard for those Fathers, are kinder to Luther; nor do you take it so badly if it is said that your Lord has said what his two co-fathers do not regret saying. The whole dispute is about the burning. Nor is there any hunting needed there; the contradiction leaps out of itself and runs forward, without any hunting dog at all. For in the same chapter Rome is burned: once by the ten kings, and again burned by Antichrist. If Rome has once been turned into ashes, how can it burn again? This is the contradiction: untie it.

units.la: Si decem Reges (inquis) comburent purpureã Meretricem, id est Romam, & si Antichristus illam odio habebit, & per illos decem Reges comburet, quomodo Sedes illius erit? Decem Reges comburent, & Antichristus per decem illos Reges comburet; vnicâne hæc, an gemina combustio? Videtur gemina. Vltrò enim Reges, & sponte suâ eam comburent: pœ[?] verò, iussu Antichristi. An verò sedens Hierosolymis Antichristus, mittet inde Romam, Reges decem, combustum eam? Nequaquam; non mittet; non missione vllâ, vel iussione Antichristi comburent eam: Deus dabit in corda eorum, vt id faciant. Si enim Reges mittat, cur Decem? Vnus sat erat ei negotio, vnus Alaricus, vnus Totila. Et cur Reges? Calones multò meliores sunt incendiarij. Sed mittet ne combustum? Qui potest, quæ iam ante combusta est? Sic respondebunt enim Reges, factum hoc iam ante, Iam cinis est, vbi Roma fuit. Tuum vero commentum, quòd Antichristus per Reges comburet, atque ita vna modò sit, Antichristi & decem Regum combustio, commentum merum est. Antichristi enim illa concrematio, non nisi sero fiet, in fine mundi. Non autem veniet Antichristus ante defolatonem [?] Imperij Romani. Decem vero Reges, vno simul tempore regnabunt, qui diuident inter se Romanum Imperium, vt ita penitus desolatum faciant. Ita primò per decem Reges comburetur Roma, vt ita diuidatur, & desoletur Imperium. Desolato Imperio, venit Antichristus; Antichristus tandem in fine mundi Romam comburet. Bis ergo arsura Roma: atque hoc [?], in quo se exercere facultas illa tua conciliatiua, quomodo conflagrare secundò possit, quæ semel deflagrauit: quomodo, vel exurat eam post Antichristum, quæ à decem Regibus ante exusta est; vel decem Reges, ante exurere possunt, ab Antichristo post exurendam. Quam tu, haud vnquam, credo, conciliabis, nisi Romam dicas, quasi Phœnicem, ex suis cineribus renasci, atque ita demum renatam, quasi Titij iecur, nouam esse Antichristo materiam, & syluam denuò comburendi. Venare vero tu nobis hîc aliquam, si potes, cohærentiam.
units.tr: "If the ten kings (you say) burn the purple harlot, that is Rome, and if Antichrist will hate her and burn her through those ten kings, how will she be his seat?" The ten kings will burn her, and Antichrist will burn her through those ten kings: is this one burning or two? It seems to be two. For the kings will burn her of their own accord and on their own initiative, but Antichrist will do so by command. But will Antichrist, sitting at Jerusalem, send the ten kings from there to Rome to burn it? By no means; he will not send them; they will not burn it by any sending or command of Antichrist: God will put it into their hearts to do so. For if he sent the kings, why ten? One was enough for his business: one Alaric, one Totila. And why kings? Camp-followers are much better incendiaries. But will he send them to burn what is already burned? For the kings will answer thus: "This has been done already; now it is ashes where Rome once was." Your invention, that Antichrist will burn her through the kings, so that there is only one burning, of Antichrist and of the ten kings, is sheer invention. For that burning by Antichrist will not happen until late, at the end of the world. But Antichrist will not come before the desolation of the Roman Empire. Yet the ten kings will reign at one and the same time, and they will divide the Roman Empire among themselves, so as to make it utterly desolate. So first Rome will be burned by the ten kings, so that it is divided and the Empire is laid waste. With the Empire laid waste, Antichrist comes; Antichrist at last, at the end of the world, will burn Rome. So Rome is to burn twice; and how this can be made to agree, in which your power of reconciling is to be exercised: how can she who has once been burned up burn a second time; how can Antichrist burn her afterwards, when she was already burned by the ten kings before; or how can the ten kings burn her before, when she is to be burned by Antichrist afterwards? You will never, I think, reconcile this, unless you say that Rome, like the Phoenix, is reborn from her own ashes, and that, once reborn, like the liver of Tityus, she becomes new matter for Antichrist and a forest to be burned again. Now, if you can, hunt out for us here some coherence.

units.la: DE vndecimâ, faxo intelligas, vbi contradictio fit. Si in Papâ solo omnis iurisdictio, nec in alijs vlla nisi ab ipso deriuata; solus ille atque vnus veri nominis Episcopus, reliquì titulo tenus; & (vtcunque nomenclaturam illam declinas) verè Vicarij. Quid enim Vicario faciat quisquam, quod illis Papa non facit, quoties libet, dat, aufert, sublimat, deprimit, committit, referat, concedit, reuocat, creat, auget, minuit, penitus ad nihil redigit? Quid amplius Præsidi Princeps, aut Prætori suo? Quare necesse habent, non Dei solùm, sed etiam Apostolicæ Sedis gratiâ, Episcopos se esse confiteri. Vis etiam quod maius, adhuc? Optarent verò esse Vicarij eius Episcopi; (nisi minorum Gentium Vicarios libeat dicere) minus enim sæpe sunt quàm Vicarij. Nam si Presbyterum aliquem, cum Vicariâ potestate ablegarit ad eos Pontifex in remotas regiones; omnes isti Principes Episcopi, Vicario illi Presbytero fasces submittunt, pro superiore suo agnoscunt, mandata ab Illo accipiunt, vt qui, maiorem à Papâ iurisdictionem acceperit, maior Vicarius[?] sit, quàm Episcopi. Sed tu, qui Apologiæ Authorem somniare putas contradictiones, abi ad Augustinum Triumphum, magni apud vos nominis Authorem; vide, an ibi vigilans apud eum legere possis, Episcopum Romanum, immediatè esse Episcopum cuiusque Ecclesiæ; quare, reliquos mediste; quare, illius tantùm Vicarios, nec iam Cocpiscopos (vt Romanus olim reliquos, reliqui Romanum scripserunt) sed planè Chorepiscopos suos.
units.tr: On the Eleventh, I will make you understand where the contradiction lies. If all jurisdiction is in the Pope alone, and in the others there is none except what is derived from him; then he alone is the one true Bishop in the proper sense, while the rest have the title only; and (however you may shift that terminology) they are truly vicars. For what can anyone do as vicar that the Pope does not do for them, whenever he pleases: give, take away, raise up, cast down, commit, refer, grant, revoke, create, enlarge, diminish, reduce entirely to nothing? What more could a prince be to his prefect, or a praetor to his deputy? Therefore they must confess that they are bishops not only by the grace of God but also by the grace of the Apostolic See. Do you want something greater still? They would prefer to be vicars of his bishops (unless you choose to call them vicars of the lesser nations), for they are often less than vicars. For if the Pontiff sends some priest with vicarial power into remote regions, all those princely bishops submit their fasces to that vicar-priest, acknowledge him as their superior, receive commands from him, so that he who has received greater jurisdiction from the Pope is a greater vicar than the bishops. But you, who think the author of the Apology is dreaming up contradictions, go off to Augustinus Triumphus, the author of great name among you; see whether, reading him carefully, you can find there that the Roman bishop is immediately bishop of each church; hence the rest are mediate; hence they are only his vicars, and no longer co-bishops (as the Romans once wrote of the rest, and the rest of the Roman), but plainly his chorbishops.

units.la: Quem verò dicis contradictionis spiritum, in vobis est; ni esset, Gregorio saltem parceretis. Is, Vniuersalis titulum, velut sacrilegum & profanum, non in Iohanne solùm Constantinopolitano, sed etiam in ipso Romano damnat, explodit, execratur; idque non hoc, aut illo sensu, sed simpliciter & absolutè. Ita Gregorium sibi ipsi facitis contrarium. Illud verò conciliat Cardinalis (scilicet vt tu hic omnia) Simpliciter & absolutè, admi[?]-nauit, nimirum, quatenus tribuitur Episc. Constantinopolitano, Absolutè, quatenus. Et hoc vobis conciliare est, sed unde non magna vobis opinio conciliatur apud bonos, cum bonis bene agendi.
units.tr: As for the spirit of contradiction which you speak of, it is in you; if it were not, you would at least spare Gregory. He condemns, explodes and execrates the title "Universal" as sacrilegious and profane, not only in John of Constantinople but also in the Roman himself; and he does this not in this or that sense, but simply and absolutely. So you make Gregory contrary to himself. But the Cardinal reconciles this (namely, as you do everything here) by saying: "He condemned it simply and absolutely," that is, insofar as it is attributed to the Bishop of Constantinople, "absolutely," insofar as... And this is what it is to reconcile for you, but it is not from this that you gain much good opinion among good men, who act well with good men.

units.la: AGedum verò, videamus an iusta Christianis Principibus causa iam sit, vt metuant sibi à Pontifice. Fuit quidem olim. Vbi id queritur Tortus, quod de vllo metu, præterquam mortis nobis sermo fit, & interiecta dicit verba, de attentatis per Pontificem contra Reges, quæ apud Cardinalem nulla sunt. Id vnii de cade per sicarios affirmâsse; de hoc vno timore dixisse. Vbi, quanam Torti fortunâ, seu potiùs quonam infortunio id accidat nescio; vbi ficti meminit vel falsi, semper ficti falsiq; tenetur ipse, vt hic iam, de cæde per Sicarios videlicet; videlicet hoc in Bellarmino nusquam est. Assumentum hoc Torti est, qui verba hæc fingit, & affingit Domino suo. Potest verò mandari cædes, nec conduci Sicarius. Tam enim cadi mandauit Reginam Pius quintus, cùm Rebelles hîc excitauit; quàm Sixtus quintus, cùm Parreium huc parricidam immisit. Vide ergo hîc, quàm sis iniquus.
