Attentare in Reges dixit Apologia: cadem imperare dixit Cardinalis; annon eôdem ambo recidunt? Vix intelligas sanè, quid interfit. Non attentat in Reges, nisi qui hostili in cos animo; quo animo qui fit, annon cadem fieri iubebit, factam approbabit? Abesse quidem non potest, quin eiusdem hominis fit, qui in animum inducat in Reges attentare, Clasicum etiam canere, & de medio sublatos velle.
units.tr: At last let us see whether Christian princes now have a just cause to fear the Pope. There once was. Here Tortus complains that I speak of no fear except that of death, and he adds the words about attempts made by the Pope against kings, which in Cardinal Bellarmine are nowhere to be found. He says I asserted this only about murder by assassins, and I spoke of this one fear alone. Where, by Tortus's luck, or rather by what misfortune, this happens I do not know. Where does he recall anything fictitious or false? He himself is always held to what is fictitious and false, as he is now, namely with regard to murder by assassins; and this is nowhere to be found in Bellarmine. This assumption is Tortus's own: he invents these words and attributes them to his master. But murder can be commanded without an assassin being hired. Pius V certainly commanded the murder of the Queen when he stirred up rebels here, and Sixtus V likewise when he sent the parricide Parry hither. See then here how unjust you are. The Apology said "attempt against kings"; the Cardinal said "command murder." Do not both come to the same thing? You can scarcely understand what difference there is. No one attempts against kings except with hostile intent toward them; and whoever has such intent, will he not order the murder and approve it once done? It certainly cannot be that the one who resolves to attempt against kings, and even to sound the trumpet and wish them removed from the midst, is not the same man.

units.la: Quanquam, usurpara illi vox attentandi, quòd de Coronâ etiam Reges, non de vitâ solâ solliciti sint. Tace verò tu, nisi vis esse insulsus: quasi de vitâ solâ solliciti sint Principes, de imperio non sint: quasi dum eos Pontifex de vitâ securos reddat, nihil vltrà quaerant, aequo animo sinant de regno suis statuere pro arbitratu: quasi denique apud generosas indoles (quales aut in Regibus sunt, aut nusquam; idem planè non fit, in Coronam, & in vitam attentare. Apud ingenuum quemque; ita res est: Honor & vita pari passu ambulant, imò Honor vitam contrà non carus: Honoris interesse maius est omni interesse, etiam vel vitae ipsius; & generosa indoli, emori sic satius est per honorem, quàm per dedecus viuere. Recte ergo illud subiecit Apologia, diu laudatos à Pontifice Imperatores, idem verò penitus submersos etiam, periisse. Idem haec illis sunt, eodem redeunt, non esse, &, non imperare. De Regibus certè verum, si vsquam verum, vbi non sint qui fuerint, non est cur velint viuere. Et est eorum Principum apud viuentes existimatio melior, in historijs memoria multò gloriosior, qui cùm imperare non possent, fortiter occubuerunt; quàm eorum, qui cum imperio priuati, priuatâ vitâ contenti, dum viuere modò possent, turpiter succubuerunt. Quanquam nec qui sic succubuerunt, diu fuerunt superstites, pudor illis & dedecus exedermunt cor: Scribetur & illis Pontifex mortis causa. Parum enim interest, maerore quis, an plaga corpore quis, an Spiritu vulnerato intereat. Vel ergo hoc dixit Cardinalis, vel nihil dixit. Sed tu nunquam Dominum tuum fingesi tam ineptum, vt Reges ita miserè solari velit: Bono animo estote: nolite verò timere; nihil attentabit Papa ad cedem vestram, tantummodò depositionem minatur; nec vt itam vobis, sed sceptra ereptum venit; nec per Sicarios hoc, sed per Legiones exteras, vel per Rebelles de subditis vestris effectum dabit. Viden haec quàm putidè, vt vel isthuc dicere debeat, vel de totâ causâ penitus silere? Nam & hoc ante illi obiectum, quòd cùm inessent in Iuramento multae, praeter hanc vnam de caede; depositio scilicet, expositio in praedam, invasio, incitatio ad Rebellionem, Rebellio denique ipsa; vnam illam de caede arripuit, cetera, quasi non vidisset, sciens prudens dissimulauit. Nec id, quia parum idonea ab illis causa metuendi, sed quòd illa omnia, & facta saepe fuisse à Pontifice, & verò etiam fieri potuisse, varijs per Controversias suas locis, non dixisset modò, sed ferió etiam triumphâsset. Vt ergò ne sit Regibus terrori Pontifex; non modò nihil moliri debet in personas, sed neque in status eorum. Nec specimen hoc argumenti fictum est; sed sine hoc nec specimen argumenti fingi potest; nec finxit ibi quicquam, sed monuit Cardinalem, quid ab eo nequiter praetermissum; quid porrò probatum oportuit, nisi causâ cadere vellet. Sed quare tandem non transijt haec Tortus, si ficta, si levia, si non à Cardinale prolata? Non ausus est. Sunt enim & haec, non vanae timoris causae, nec minùs insite, quàm Illius illa Vidit hoc Tortus, & cum timorem inde suffum[?] Regibus incuti videret, timuit ipse transfire; Cuique exemplo responsum suum, quale quale, commentus est.
units.tr: Yet the word "attempt" is used of him, because kings are anxious not only about their life but also about their crown. But hold your tongue, unless you wish to be insipid: as if princes were anxious about their life alone and not about their rule; as if, while the Pontiff renders them secure of their life, they would seek nothing further, and calmly allow their kingdom to be disposed of at another's pleasure; as if, finally, among noble natures (such as are found in kings, or nowhere) it were not plainly the same to attempt against the crown and against the life. In every free man it is so: honour and life walk side by side, indeed honour is not dear if life is opposed to it. "The interest in honour is greater than every interest, even of life itself"; and for a noble nature it is better to die with honour than to live in disgrace. Therefore the Apology rightly added that emperors praised for a long time by the Pontiff, and then utterly sunk, have perished. For these are the same things and return to the same: not to be, and not to rule. Of kings it is certainly true, if ever true of anything, that where they are not what they were, there is no reason they should wish to live. And among the living, the esteem of those princes is better, and in histories their memory is far more glorious, who, when they could not rule, fell bravely, than of those who, deprived of rule and content with a private life, provided only they could live, sank down shamefully. Yet even those who sank down thus did not long survive; shame and disgrace consume their heart. The Pontiff will be written as the cause of their death for them too. For it matters little whether a man perishes by grief, by a wound to the body, or by a wounded spirit. Either the Cardinal said this, or he said nothing. But you never portray your master as so foolish as to wish to console kings in such a miserable way: "Be of good courage, and do not fear: the Pope will attempt nothing against your lives; he threatens only deposition; he comes not to take your lives but your sceptres; he will bring this about not by assassins but by foreign legions, or through rebels from among your subjects." Do you see how foolishly these things are said, so that he must either say this or keep silent about the whole matter altogether? For this too was objected to him before: that although many things were contained in the oath, besides this one about murder (namely deposition, exposure to plunder, invasion, incitement to rebellion, rebellion itself), he seized upon that one about murder alone, and knowingly and deliberately passed over the rest as if he had not seen them. Nor was this because they were unsuitable causes of fear, but because all these things had often been done by the Pontiff, and indeed could have been done, and he would not merely have said so in various places of his Controversies but would even have triumphed over them. So then, that the Pontiff may not be a terror to kings, he ought not only to attempt nothing against their persons, but not against their states either. Nor is this example of an argument invented; but without it not even an example of an argument can be devised. He invented nothing there, but reminded the Cardinal what he had wickedly omitted, and what ought to have been proved further, unless he wished to fall by his own cause. But why, in the end, did Tortus not pass over these points, if they are fictitious, if they are trivial, if they were not put forward by the Cardinal? He did not dare. For these too are not empty causes of fear, and are no less inherent than that one: "Tortus saw this," and when he saw that fear was thereby instilled into kings, he himself feared to pass over it. For each example he has invented some answer of his own, of whatever quality.

units.la: Atque primò extimuisse Henricum quartum, sed filialem eius timorem fuisse, Censuræ Papalis, non crudelem, mortis, vel (quæ morte pejor) depositionis; nec impulsum terrore amittendi Imperij, sed sponte (ôos!) & conscientia merâ ad illam sese humiliatem deiecisse. Credo huic (Lector) inposterum. Verè enim hic mihi fas verba ipsius vsurpare de ipso, ut semper sui similis perseveret, cum non habeat, quod verè respondeat, ipse fingit. Explico enim tibi eos Authores tantum, qui ibi in Apologiâ annotati in margine. Hâc commotione coactus Rex, Romam humiliter, ut potè veniam ab Apostolico postulaturus, inimicu non sperantibus, petendit. Audin' Vrspergensem? Commotione coactus Principum & Populi quasi Regno exui vereretur, non sponte autem, ut absolui mereretur. Platina. Decernunt Principes Alemanniae, ut à Gregorio, Henricus supplex veniam errati petat: Quod se fallurum, Rex ipse interposito iuramento, pollicitus est. Ex decreto Principum igitur, non dictamine conscientiae. c Schafnaburgensis verò qui tum vixit: Cum bis terque, missis Legatis, à Principibus suis pacem petijsset, neque ullam supplicationis genus praetermisisset, & reiectus esset, & nunciam accepisset ab eis, siante dies m anniuersarium Excommunicationis suae non absolueretur, regnum deinceps repetere non posse: Romani contendit. Nec ecclesiae ergo id factum, ut regnum repetere posset: non sponte; ut Censurâ absolutus. Etiam & illis adjicio alios. 4 Authorem vitæ Henrici 4ti. Plerique Episcopi se ab eius auxilio retrahebant, quod & maior pars Procerum facilitabat. Tum vero (non conscientiâ ullâ adductus, sed) videns rem suam in arctò sitam, inito tam occulto, quàm afflicto consilio, subitum & inopinatum iter, in occursum Apostolici arripuit. {e}Brunonem, Henricus autem vagans per Italiam, loco, sed magis animo, quid ageret nesciebat, quia quicquid ageret; Regnum perdere timebat. Nisi enim supplex ad Apostolicum venirét, & per eum solutus à Banno fuisset, regnum se non recepturum pro certo sciebat. {f}Cuspinianum: Omnes Regnicolæ Pontifex ab obedientiâ absolvit; quod magnum peperit in imperio dissidium, adeo ut Rex Henricus, compelleretur etiam inuitus Romam petere, & summo Pontifici adhærere, ut secum gratiam iniret. Tu, sponte, dicis: Ille, adeo ut compelleretur etiam inuitus. Quid quod {g}Sigonius, in summum discrimen Regni admittendi adductum, fecisse id dicit?
units.tr: And first, that Henry IV was indeed afraid, but that his fear was filial, of the papal censure, not a cruel fear of death, or (worse than death) of deposition; and that he was moved not by fear of losing his empire but of his own accord (oh!) and by sheer conscience he humbled himself and cast himself down to it. I believe this, dear reader, for the future. For here it is right for me to use his own words about himself, so that he may keep consistent with himself, since he has no true answer and so invents one. For I explain to you only those authors who are noted in the margin there in the Apology. Under this disturbance the king was compelled to go humbly to Rome, intending to seek pardon from the Apostolic See, not expecting an enemy. Do you hear Ursperg? Compelled by the disturbance of princes and of the people, as he feared being stripped of his kingdom, not of his own accord, so that he might deserve to be absolved. Platina: The princes of Germany decree that Henry should humbly seek pardon of error from Gregory; the king himself promised, with an oath interposed, that he would do this. Therefore it was by the decree of the princes, not by the dictate of conscience. But the Schafnaburgensis who lived at that time says: When he had twice or thrice, by sending envoys, sought peace from his princes, and had omitted no kind of supplication, and had been rejected, and had at last received word from them that unless on the day of the anniversary of his excommunication he were absolved, he could not afterward recover the kingdom, he hastened to Rome. Nor was it done by the Church, therefore, that he might be able to recover the kingdom; not of his own accord, but in order to be absolved from the censure. I add others besides these too. The author of the life of Henry IV: Most of the bishops withdrew from his help, which the greater part of the nobles also made easier. Then indeed, not led by any conscience, but seeing his affairs placed in a narrow strait, having taken a plan as secret as it was troubled, he seized a sudden and unexpected journey to meet the Apostolic See. Bruno: Henry, wandering through Italy, did not know what to do, in place, but still more in mind, because whatever he did, he feared to lose the kingdom; for unless he came as a suppliant to the Apostolic See and were released from the ban through him, he knew for certain that he would not recover the kingdom. Cuspinianus: The Pontiff absolved all the inhabitants of the kingdom from obedience, which produced a great discord in the empire, so that King Henry was compelled, even against his will, to seek Rome and cling to the supreme Pontiff, so as to win grace with him. You say "of his own accord"; he says "so that he was compelled, even against his will." What of Sigonius, who says that it was done by one brought to the greatest peril of losing the kingdom?

units.la: {h}Tum Laziardus, Partem regni ab eo defecisse, Saxones adversus eum bella parâsse, quâ te motum, ac sibi timentem, Pontificem adiisse. Vbi hîc meritum absolutionis? vbi metus Excommunicationis? vbi vel huius, vel illius mentio? Cùm Regnum timeret perdere, ait Bruno; Cùm Regnum alioqui repetere non posset, Schafnaburgensis; In summum discrimen adductus Regni amittendi, Sigonius. Audis, non Censuram, sed ne Regnum perderet, timuisse? Vbi sponte an ea tua deiectio? Imò, Coactus, ait Vrspergensis, commotione; Decreto Principum, Platina; Videns res suas in arctò sitas, Author vitæ; adeo ut compelleretur etiam inuitus, Cuspinianus. Et hoccine tu vocas, sponte se deiecere?
units.tr: Then Laziardus says that part of the kingdom had fallen away from him, that the Saxons had prepared wars against him, and that, moved by this and fearing for himself, he approached the Pontiff. Where here is the merit of absolution? Where is the fear of excommunication? Where is any mention of this or that? "When he feared to lose the kingdom," says Bruno; "when he could not otherwise recover the kingdom," says the Schafnaburgensis; "brought to the utmost peril of losing the kingdom," says Sigonius. Do you hear? He feared not the censure, but lest he lose the kingdom. Where is your "of his own accord" in that deposition? Indeed, "forced," says Urspergensis, "by the disturbance"; "by decree of the princes," says Platina; "seeing his affairs in a tight spot," says the Author of the Life; "so that he was compelled even against his will," says Cuspinianus. And do you call this "they deposed themselves of their own accord"?

units.la: Denique qui Henricum bene nouerit, & quomodo post, bis ab eodem Gregorio, etiam ab Vrbano secundo, & Paschali secundo, ter minimùm excommunicatus, nihil id fecerit, perstiterit, innodatus etiam Censuræ diem extremum obierit, non multùm ei à Censurâ Pontificiâ; sed (qui erat) timorem omnem, à Regni amissione fuisse, necesse est fateatur.
units.tr: Finally, anyone who knows Henry well, and how afterwards he was twice excommunicated by the same Gregory, and also by Urban the Second and Paschal the Second, at least three times, and how he did nothing about it, persisted, and died bound by the censure, must concede that he had no great concern for the Pontifical censure, but (as was the case) that he had every fear of losing the kingdom.

units.la: DE Friderico primo scrupulum primò injicit, de Historia dubiâ fide. Dubiâ? Quare? Quòd eam non referant quatuor saltem Historici, Genebrardus, Platina, Sigonius, Sabellicus. Poterat ex Sabellico ipse sibi respondum dare. Non tradunt hoc illi, fateor; sed num propterea negant? At tradunt alij. Non Genebrardus [?]; at Maffonius popularis eius, in vitâ Alexandri refert. Non Platina, qui vitas Pontificum scripsit; at Ciacconius, qui & ipse scripsit, nec minùs accuratè. Non Sigonius, at Bergomensis: non Sabellicus; at Petrus Iustinianus. Addo, & de Germaniâ Nauclerus, & Mutius, & de Graeciâ ipsâ Gennadius, & Bessarion Cardinalis. Nec dubitanter hoc. Inter eos, qui res Venetas scripsit Iustinianus, & quid Venetijs fa{a}ctum optimè nosse poterat. Deposuit purpuram Fridericus, & humi procumbens Pontificis pedes exosculatus est. Alexander autem Friderici collo planta superposita, Davidicum illud protulisse dicitur, Super aspidem, &c. Cum autem diceret Imperator, Non tibi, sed Petro; Pontifex impressâ fortiùs planta, Et mihi, ait, & Petro.
units.tr: Concerning Frederick the First, you first cast doubt on the story, as being of doubtful faith. Doubtful? Why? Because at least four historians do not record it: Genebrardus, Platina, Sigonius, Sabellicus. You could have given yourself an answer from Sabellicus. "They do not hand this down to him," I grant; but do they therefore deny it? Yet others do hand it down. "Does not Genebrardus?" But Maffonius, his fellow countryman, in the Life of Alexander, reports it. Not Platina, who wrote the lives of the Popes; but Ciacconius, who also wrote, and no less accurately. Not Sigonius, but Bergomensis; not Sabellicus, but Petrus Justinianus. I add, from Germany, Nauclerus and Mutius, and from Greece itself, Gennadius and Cardinal Bessarion. Nor do they say this doubtfully. Among those who wrote the affairs of Venice is Justinianus, and he could know very well what was done at Venice. "Frederick laid aside the purple, and, lying prostrate on the ground, kissed the Pontiff's feet." But Alexander, having placed his foot on Frederick's neck, is said to have uttered that verse of David, "Upon the asp, etc." And when the Emperor said, "Not to you, but to Peter," the Pontiff, pressing down his foot more firmly, said, "To me, and to Peter."

units.la: {b}Bergomensis itidem. Alexander vniuerso astante populo Imperatori iussit, vt se humi proßernerent, & veniâ denuò postularet. Quo facto, Alexander Pontifex Imperatoris collum pede comprimens, ait, scriptum est, Super aspidem &c. Ac hÿ quidem ambo de ditione Venetâ, quibus Sabellicus tuus plurimùm tribuit, cæterisque, in Patriæ suæ rebus præferendos censet. Denique (quia fieri hic cupio compendium) qui huic ipsi historiæ totus incubuit Hieronymus Bardus excusus Venetijs 1584: Viginti minimùm Authores commemorat, omnes Catholicos, Antiquos omnes; etiam verba apponit eorum, qui calcatas à Papâ Caesaris cervices, disertis verbis testantur omnes; Fac legas, si otiùm est, nec eris iam dubius fidei; Historia enim dubiæ fidei non est. Genebrardus quidem procubuisse dicit; piguit, credo, plura. Sed nec hoc, exemplo Petri. Petrus, non vel hoc tulit in Centurione, tulit in Caesare ipso, qui Petri Successor tenuit.
units.tr: Bergomensis likewise: Alexander, with all the people standing by, ordered the Emperor to prostrate himself on the ground and ask pardon again. When this was done, Pope Alexander, pressing the Emperor's neck with his foot, said, "It is written, 'Upon the asp, etc.'" These two indeed are from the Venetian territory, and your Sabellicus attributes very much to them, and others think they should be preferred in matters of their own country. Finally (since I wish to make a short cut here), Hieronymus Bardus, who devoted himself wholly to this very history, published at Venice in 1584, mentions at least twenty authors, all Catholics, all ancient; he also sets down the words of those who all expressly testify that the Pope trampled on the Emperor's necks. Do read them, if you have leisure, and you will no longer be doubtful of the faith; for a history of doubtful faith it is not. Genebrardus indeed says he fell prostrate; he was ashamed, I believe, to say more. But not even this, by the example of Peter. Peter did not bear it even in the Centurion; he bore it in the Emperor himself, who held the place of Peter's successor.

units.la: Regem verò Petrus Praecellentem diceret, & Honorandum, non aspidem & conculcandum. Etsi verò Genebrardum, plura piguit; at {c}Maffonium non piguit de calcata ceruice meminisse, Cum Caesar inclinatâ ceruice collum pedi Alexandri submisisset, dixissetque Pontifex, Super aspidem, &c. Vel ergo, reclamante Baronio, constat Historiæ fides sua, à Graecis, Italis, Gallis, Germanis. Timuit, inquis, nihil Fridericus, nisi excommunicationem. Timuit verò. {d}Platina ipse tuus, aliud timuisse narrat. Quid Proceres palam illi minati essent, rediturosé in Germaniam, ni properè cum Pontifice in gratiam rediret. {e}Laziardus & {f}Polonus, Timens ne à Dominio suo caderet. Vt cum Pontifice Romano pacis foedera libenter inire coactus sit; Et maximè, quod eius filius à Venetiarum
units.tr: Yet Peter would have called the king "most excellent" and "to be honoured," not "an asp" to be trampled underfoot. And although Genebrardus was ashamed to say more, Maffonius was not ashamed to mention the trampled neck, when the Emperor, with bowed neck, had submitted his neck to the foot of Alexander, and the Pontiff had said, "Upon the asp, etc." Therefore, either, with Baronius objecting, the trustworthiness of the history stands firm, attested by Greeks, Italians, Frenchmen, and Germans. Frederick, you say, feared nothing but excommunication. But he did fear: your own Platina relates that he feared something else: namely, that the nobles had openly threatened him that they would return to Germany unless he quickly came to terms with the Pontiff. Laziardus and the Pole (fearing lest he fall from his dominion), so that he was compelled to enter willingly into treaties of peace with the Roman Pontiff; and especially because his son was held captive by the Doge of Venice.

units.la: {a} Lib. 2. rerum venet. Principe captivus tenebatur : {a}Bergomensis. {b}Nauclerus, Protestati sunt se cum derelicturos, & Successorem ab Electoribus postulaturos, quibus deterritus minu,&c. Timuit ergo, Ne Proceres deficerent; Ne domino excideret; Ne in filium captum durius quid statueret Pontifex; Deterritus est minu; Quare abrogationem Imperij timuit, excommunicationem non timuit.
units.tr: Book 2 of the Venetian affairs; Bergomensis. Nauclerus: they protested that they would desert him and ask the electors for a successor, and he was deterred from this by the threat... Therefore he feared that the nobles would revolt, that he would fall from his lordship, that the Pontiff might decide something harsher regarding his captive son; he was deterred by these. Therefore he feared the abrogation of the empire, not excommunication.

units.la: DE Henrico sexto, Historiam parum verisimilem esse dicis; Et est certè; idque vitio vertimus Pontifici, quòd vera sit de falsu illius narratio, quæ vix verisimilis est. Quam tamen ipse hic dicis parum verisimilem, nec ullam rationem pati, ut credamus, fateris post veram, & à Baronio admissam, & credu[?] ipse homo constans, & nos sinis[?] credere. Quid verò, si annosus senex Cœlestinus? An nescis ambitionem non senescere? Quid porrò si summâ antea comitate? Papatus superbum, aut invenit, aut facit. At Simultates illi cum Henrico nullæ. Quid opus, quem tam placidum habebat ut ouem? At fuissent forte, nisi passus hanc ab eo contumeliam. Ranulphus autem noster eâ diligentiâ, eruditione, fide Author est, ut à multis præclaris viris, etiam Polydoro Virgilio vestro, egregius Historicus habeatur, nec Sigonij aut Sabellici vestris cedit, quique, si in rem vestram, quicquam vel solùm retulisset, quantùis[?] preuij foret.
units.tr: Concerning Henry the Sixth, you say the history is hardly credible; and indeed it is not; and we have censured the Pontiff for this, that the account of his falsehood is true, which is scarcely credible. Yet you yourself here say it is hardly credible, and that it bears no reason that we should believe it, after admitting the true account, which Baronius also accepts, and that he himself was a steadfast man, and that you allow us to believe it. But what if Celestine was an aged old man? Do you not know that ambition does not grow old? What if he had previously been of the greatest courtesy? The papacy either finds or makes a man proud. But he had no quarrels with Henry. What need was there, since he had him as gentle as a sheep? But perhaps they would have had them, had he not suffered this insult from him. Our Ranulphus, however, is an author of such diligence, learning, and faithfulness that he is held by many distinguished men, even by your Polydore Vergil, to be an outstanding historian, and he is not inferior to your Sigonius or Sabellicus; and if he had reported anything, even only one thing, in your favour, how much would he have been prized!

units.la: Verùm, non ille solùm hoc; Rogerius etiam {a}Houedenus, Ranulpho prior, quoque ipse tum vixit, & Historiam suam scripsit, cùm hæc Henrico sexto fierent, ita rem gestam narrat: Sedebat Dominus Papa in Cathedrâ Pontificali, tenens Coronam auream Imperialem inter pedes suos, & Imperator inclinato capite, recepit Coronam, & Imperatrix similiter de pedibus Domini Papæ. Dominus autem Papa statim percussit cum pede suo Coronam Imperatoris, & deiecit eam in terrâ. Nec tamen, si tibi credimus, timuit Imperator. Non valdè quidem speravit hoc omine. Non enim bonæ spei signum Coronæ excussio, aut læti auspicij: præsertim ab hoc Pontifice, cui Bubonis verum cognomen erat; aut male auspicatâ. Nec iratus fuit, inquis. Qui scis? An exta eius tum, & cor inspexisti (novus aruspex) quòd bilem omnem à præcordijs abfuisse affirmas? Imò non potuit irasci facto, quoniam intellexit, latère in eo mysterium (nec enim sine mysterio calcari Coronas à Papâ) nempe, posse malis meritis amitti Coronam. Tria verò hic insunt; 1. quod decussa ei Corona fuit; 2. quòd 2. quod à Pontifice decussa ; 3. quod pede Pontificis. Quicunque demum Coronam ei decussisset ; decussio illa à quocunque demum facta, satis monere potuit, Coronam amitti posse, etsi alius id fecisset, quàm Papa. Quid Papa opus fuit ? Houedenus, mysterium illud explicat, significans, quòd ipse Papa potestatem eiiciendi eum, ab Imperio habet, si ille demeruerit. Non in eo ergo mysterium quòd amitti Corona, sed quòd tollente eam Pontifice amitti posset. Melius adhuc {a}Cèstrensis. Designans per hoc, quòd ipse Papa habet potestatem creandi Imperatorem, si mererit, & deijciendi, si demererit. Plenius hoc quidem multò, & magis ad rem : non quid Imperator pati, sed quid Papa facere ; creare, si mereri iudicet ; deijcere, si demereri.
units.tr: But it is not only he who says this; Roger of Hoveden also, earlier than Ranulphus, lived at that time too and wrote his history, when these things were done under Henry the Sixth, and he narrates the event thus: "The lord Pope was sitting in the pontifical chair, holding the imperial golden crown between his feet, and the Emperor, with bowed head, received the crown, and the Empress likewise from the feet of the lord Pope. But the lord Pope immediately struck the Emperor's crown with his foot, and cast it down on the earth." Nor, if we believe you, did the Emperor fear. He did not hope very much from this omen. For the shaking off of a crown is not a sign of good hope or a happy augury, especially from this Pontiff, whose true surname was Bubo, or from one ill-begun. Nor was he angry, you say. How do you know? Did you inspect his entrails and heart then (a new soothsayer), that you affirm all bile was absent from his heart? Indeed he could not be angry at the deed, since he understood that a mystery lay in it (for crowns are not trodden on by the Pope without a mystery), namely, that a crown can be lost through bad deserts. Moreover, three things are contained here: first, that the crown was struck from him; second, that it was struck by the Pontiff; third, that it was by the Pontiff's foot. Whoever at last had struck the crown from him, that striking, by whomever it was done, could well have warned that a crown can be lost, even if someone other than the Pope had done it. What need was there for the Pope? Houedenus explains that mystery, signifying that the Pope himself has the power of casting him out of the empire, if he has deserved it. Therefore the mystery lies not in the crown being lost, but in its being lost when the Pontiff took it away. Cestrensis is better still, designating by this that the Pope himself has the power of creating the Emperor, if he deserves it, and of casting him down, if he has ill deserved. This is much fuller and more to the point: not what the Emperor was to suffer, but what the Pope was to do: to create, if he judges him to deserve it; to cast down, if he judges him to deserve otherwise.

units.la: Hactenus verò edocti fumus, cur decussa corona, cur à Pontifice : Sed si, vel manu deiecisset Pontifex Coronam, satis per illud, priuatiua illa potestas Pontificis significari potuit ; quorimpede[?] factum ; nam neque illud mysterio suo carere potuit : Forte ut admoneret, Pontificis pedem, partem infimam, Imperatoris vertice summo sublimiorem, & vel (applosione pedis, efficere, cùm libet, ut decidas ei de capite diadema. Mira verò (ut video) mysteria latent, in calcibus Pontificis. Unus ibi Patrem, calcibus suis docuit, quomodò psalmi versum illum intelligeret, Super aspidem, &c. Alter hic filium calcibus docet, quâ ratione possit Coronam amittere. Quis non desculpetur[?] pedes tam mysticos ? Ridicula hæc sunt, sed Tortus magis, qui Pontifices scribit, circumferre in calcibus, monitiones tam sanctas, & salubres.
units.tr: Thus far we have learned why the crown was struck off, and why by the Pontiff. But if the Pontiff had thrown the crown off with his hand, that alone could have signified the privative power of the Pontiff; whether that was done [quorimpede?]; for that act could not lack its mystery either. Perhaps it was to warn that the Pontiff's foot, the lowest part, is raised higher than the Emperor's crown-top, and that by a blow of the foot he can, whenever he pleases, knock the diadem from his head. Truly, as I see it, marvellous mysteries lie hidden in the Pontiff's heels. Here one taught his father with his heels how to understand that verse of the psalm, "Upon the asp," etc. Here another teaches his son with his heels by what reasoning he can lose the crown. Who would not be excused for such mystical feet? These things are ridiculous, but Tortus is more so, who writes that the Popes carry about in their heels such holy and wholesome warnings.

units.la: DE Philippo dixisse fatetur Apologiam quod ad rem facit, nisi quòd admissa ibi manifesta falsitas. Illa verò quæ ? Philippum ab Othone interemptum. Id verum fuerit, an falsum, quid ad timorem Philippi ? Timuit Innocentij, verba minantia &c metuenda, magis apta Sicario, quàm Vicario Christi : Aut Ego Illum, aut Ille Me. Erupisse verò illum in verba hæc, qui eâ ætate suit, & plerisque eorum quæ scribit ipse interfuit, narrat {b}Urspergensis. Audita sibi dicit. Non enim adfuit loquenti forte ; sed à fide dignis audita ; alioqui haud unquam retulisset in Historiam. Relatu verò difficilia & vix credenda, tam erant indigna Pontifice : quò fuit Innocentij minor innocentia. Sed quæ vix credenda, credenda tamen. Non enim primus in exemplo hoc Innocentium : Eadem ipsa dixerat Henrico quarto Gregorius septimus, vel eadem, vel certè grauiora. Sic Greg. obijcit per Epistolam Imperatori; {a}Scilicet vt tuus verbis vtar, Quod aut Tu moreris, aut Mihi animsi Regnúmq; tolleres. Eadé verò verba (præter Cuspiniánū) grauissimus Author tuus {b}Nauclerus repetit. Timor verò, è verbis illis; quod instituto satis erat, præsertim si non dixit modò Pontifex, sed & sanctè deierauit (vt {c}Cuspiniánus Author est) nec Pontifici fas vnquâ peierare: Excitasse dein, atqs incitâsse Bertholdi primò, pòst etiâ Othonem illi æmulû constat; abrogâsse ei imperiû; Othonem contra ius fásq; omne coronâ(se;(quem igitur ne nunc quidé Germani habent pro Imperatore legitimo ;) multa in Philippi perniciem machinati esse. Hæc illi timorem auxerint necesse est. Respondit tandem verbis exitus. Cæsus autem est, siue ab Othone Palatino, siue ab Othone Landgrauio, siue à Vitelspachio tuo, nec tamen, vt tu vis; priuato; sed Comite, non id, credo, magnopere refert quis Otho cæsor fuit: Philippus cæsus est. Ita, non peierauit Innocentius; Ademptum illi diadema, vita quoque adempta est. Neq; verò, quòd Historicis inter se non conuenit, quis ille percussor fuerit, valdè hoc ad rem. Illud ad rem: Pontificem minù terruisse, nec frustra terruisse ; ademisse enim ei diadema. Timuisse verò Philippum, nec frustra timuisse ; amisisse enim diadema. Timor autem ibi probandus erat, sedes non erat.
units.tr: The Apology confesses that it has said something about Philip which bears on the matter, except that a manifest falsehood was admitted there. But what was it? That Philip was slain by Otto. Whether that is true or false, what does it have to do with Philip's fear? He feared Innocent's words, threatening and terrible, more fitting to an assassin than to the Vicar of Christ: "Either I shall have him, or he shall have me." That these words burst forth from him, Urspergensis, who lived in that age and was present at most of the things he writes, relates. He says they were heard by him; he was not perhaps present at the speaking, but heard them from trustworthy men; otherwise he would never have recorded them in his History. Hard to tell and scarcely credible, they were so unworthy of a Pontiff, by which Innocent's innocence was the less. But though scarcely credible, they are nevertheless to be believed. For Innocent was not the first in this example: Gregory VII had said the very same to Henry IV, or things the same or more grievous. Thus Gregory objects by letter to the Emperor: "Namely, to use your own words, that either you die, or I am to be..." and "you would take away the kingdom." The same words, apart from Cuspinianus, your very grave author Naucler repeats. Fear, indeed, arose from those words; which was enough for the purpose, especially if the Pontiff not only said them but swore solemnly (as Cuspinianus is the authority), and it is not right for a Pontiff ever to forswear himself. Then it is established that he stirred up and incited first Berthold, and afterwards Otto, his rival; that he took away the empire from him; that Otto, against all right and law, was crowned (whom the Germans now do not even regard as the lawful Emperor); that they plotted much to Philip's ruin. These things must have increased his fear. At last the outcome answered the words. He was struck down, whether by Otto the Palatine, or by Otto the Landgrave, or by your Wittelsbacher, and not, as you wish, by a private man but by a Count. Whichever Otto was the slayer, I believe it matters little: Philip was struck down. So Innocent did not forswear himself; the diadem was taken from him, and his life too was taken. Nor does it matter much that the historians do not agree as to who that killer was. What matters is this: the Pontiff frightened him less, and not in vain; for he took away his diadem. And Philip feared, and not in vain; for he lost his diadem. The fear, however, was there to be proved, not the seat.

units.la: Qui vero Philippum primò, dein Othonem, imperio viderat excussos ab Innocentio, Fridericus secundus: annon verisimile abatur illi ante oculos, iusta metus occasio? Cùm & tertiò, fulmine afflatus & deiectus Imperio, & Principum suorum fide nudatus: Et nonne vita eius etiàm petita est? {d}Qui in expugnato Scala castro capti, annon hoc morientes fassi sunt; authore se Pontifice, negotium illud in se suscepisse? Post verò etiam, Theobaldus cum alijs quinque, nonne idem agresi sunt; & annon Imperatori in animo fuisse illos, postquam in potestatem iam eius venissent, {e}per diuersa mundi climata, ad omnes Reges & Principes, cum Bulla Papali imprecatio in fronte, ibidem inuentâ, in publicam proditionis notitiam destinare? Sat erant haec timori probando. Praeteris omnia haec, vt um vellicas, in quo tamen multa peccas. De venene negas. At qui {f}aetate illa vixit {f}Matthaeum Parisiensis, affirmat; Redijt, inquit, in Apuliam, vt dicitur, potionatus. Affirmat & {a}Chronicon Augustense. In Apuliam rediit, & veneno extinctus, sepultus est in Fungi. Etiam {b}Chronologica Compilatio apud Pistorium. Fridericus anathematizatus, & imperiali honore priuatus, veneno interijt. Etiam {c}Sigonius vester. In Apulia, idibus Decembris veneno est mortuus, cuius mortis Manfredus suspicionem tulit. Tu rem totam reijcis in Manfredam, Manfredus autem, maturauit modò illi exitu puluillo, potius quàm exitui causam fuit. Nam si, vt narrat Parisiensis, venenum lathiferum & efficax valde potioni immiscet est, praeuertit modò horam Manfredus; si concessisset ei exigui temporis vsuram, si paululum modò sustinuisset, veneni vi expirâsset: vt ille, mori modò fecerit; iâmiâ morituurum.
units.tr: As for Frederick II, who had seen Philip first, then Otto, thrown from the empire by Innocent: was it not likely that a just occasion for fear was before his eyes? Since also a third time, struck by a thunderbolt and deposed from the empire, and stripped of the loyalty of his princes; and was not his life also sought? Those captured at the storming of the castle of Scala, did they not confess as they died that the Pontiff was the author of that undertaking? Afterwards also, did not Theobald with five others do the same; and was it not in the Emperor's mind, once they had come into his power, to send them through the different climes of the world, to all kings and princes, with a papal curse-bull found in them, to make public the knowledge of the treason? These things were enough to prove fear. You pass over all these things, as if you were plucking at a fly, though in this you go wrong in many ways. You deny the poison. But Matthew Paris, who lived in that age, affirms it: "He returned," he says, "to Apulia, as it is said, poisoned." The Augsburg Chronicle also affirms it: "He returned to Apulia, and having been killed by poison, was buried at Fungi." Also the Chronological Compilation in Pistorius: "Frederick, excommunicated and deprived of imperial honour, died by poison." Also your Sigonius: "In Apulia, on the Ides of December, he died by poison, whose death Manfred was suspected of." You throw the whole matter onto Manfred; but Manfred merely hastened his end by a pillow, rather than being the cause of the end. For if, as Paris relates, he mixed a deadly and very effective poison into the drink, Manfred merely anticipated the hour; if he had granted him a short space of time, if he had only held out a little, he would have expired from the power of the poison: so that Manfred merely made him die sooner, who was going to die anyway.

units.la: Manfredum verò, quem terrae filium fateris ipse, potuit & Apologia Manfredum quendam appellare. Nullâ enim re, nisi scelere magnum, viperam potiùs quandam, & foedum parricidam, qui ei; à quo spiritum acceperat, spiritum interelusit. Ab eo {d}Cuspinianus factum, id nullus dubitat; siue ab hostibus, {d}aut Pontifice corruptus id fecerit, (omnes autem illi hostes à Pontifice tum erant) siue quis ad Siciliae regnum aspiraret. Non autem posterius hoc, quòd Siciliae regnum ambiret, cum testamento scriptus esset haeres Siciliae, ait Sigonius. Quare, prius il{e}lud: quòd à Pontifice corruptus fuerat. Sed Cuspinianus rem refert, ex Petro de Vineis. Quo potest? cum & Petrus de Vineis in suspicionem ipse venerit, quasi criminis particeps? Eius enim (apud {f}Parisiensem) Dominus Papa cor, eneruando muneribus & pollicitis maximis inclinarat; vt, de Manfredo per Pontificem corrupto, magis adhuc verisimile sit. Verum Cuspinianus, in Pontifices affectus vix bene. At erat tamen bonus Catholicus, nec de haeresi suspectus vnquam, nec à Pontifice laesus. Male tamen affectus. Quis verò posset in illos bene affici, qui tot illorum scelera, fraudes, caedes, legerit, sciuerit, scripserit, quot Cuspinianus? Veneno ergo mortuus Fridericus, vt Parisiensis: Cuius motus Manfredus suspicionem tulit, vt Sigonius: Is autem à Pontifice corruptus, vt Cuspinianus.
units.tr: Manfred, whom you yourself call "son of the earth," the Apology could also call "a certain Manfred." For by nothing but crime, a great viper rather, and a foul parricide, who extinguished the breath of him from whom he had received breath. That Cuspinianus did this from him, no one doubts; whether he did it, corrupted by enemies, or by the Pontiff (and all those enemies were then with the Pontiff), or whether someone aspired to the kingdom of Sicily. But the latter is not the case, that he was seeking the kingdom of Sicily, since he had been named heir to Sicily in the will, says Sigonius. Therefore the former: that he had been corrupted by the Pontiff. But Cuspinianus relates the matter from Peter de Vineis. How can that be? Since Peter de Vineis himself came under suspicion, as if he were a partner in the crime? For the Lord Pope had won over his heart (according to Paris) with gifts and very great promises; so that, with Manfred corrupted by the Pontiff, it is even more likely. Yet Cuspinianus is scarcely well disposed toward the Popes. But he was nevertheless a good Catholic, never suspected of heresy, never injured by the Pope. Yet he was ill disposed. But who could be well disposed toward those whom he had read of, known of, and written about, with as many of their crimes, frauds, and murders as Cuspinianus? So Frederick died by poison, according to Paris; the movement of which made Manfred suspected, according to Sigonius; and he was corrupted by the Pontiff, according to Cuspinianus.

units.la: Quem verò ibi proximo in loco Alexandrum Apologia innuat, non est quòd te valdè de eo torqueas. Alexander is tertius est. Nihil autem in Iouio de Alexandro tertio satis illi negotium facessit qui tertius ab hoc. Quàre erat ibi in
units.tr: As for the Apology hinting at Alexander in the next place there, you need not torture yourself greatly about him. Alexander is the third. Nothing in Jovius concerning Alexander the Third troubles him very much, who is third from this one. Therefore there was in there...

units.la: {a} Ad ann.1230 margine allegatio Iouij, ea sequens Sexti exemplum spectabat, Typographi errore factum, vt poneretur summa in pagina, loco non suo. At, quam ibi recitat ab Alexandro tertio datam timendi causam, ea Friderico primo data fuit. Illius expressam ad vinum imaginem misit Sultano Pontifex, tum cum Fridericus pugnaret in Asia, viaq; per literas egit, curaret illum de medio tollendum, si securus regnare vellet. Atque haec e Germanica Historia, de Friderico Barbarossa, & apud Barnum de vitis Pontificum, in vita Alexandri tertij, qui illi vltimus est de Pontificum numero. Apud Baleum idem, qui Iohannem Marium authorem citat: idem apud Scardium reperies, qui Cremonensem. Admodum autem infensus erat Alexandro Friderico: vestra hoc Papia sensit: multatus Episcopus vestem Pallio & Cruce, quod à partibus Friderici steterat. Quo tempore, Papia in Synodo, maiores tui Papienses omnes Theologi & Iurisconsulti longè aliter sentiebant, quam tu modò. Siquidem inter omnes tum conuenit, posse Pontificem ab Imperatore iure depoui, vt & reipsa ibi depositus est Pontifex.
units.tr: In the margin at the year 1230, the citation of Jovius, following the example of Sixtus, was intended, made by a printer's error, so that the sum was placed at the top of the page, not in its own place. But what he recites there as the cause of fear given by Alexander the Third was given to Frederick I. The Pontiff sent to the Sultan an expressed image of him in wine, when Frederick was fighting in Asia, and by letter urged that he be removed from the midst, if he wished to reign in safety. This is from the German History, concerning Frederick Barbarossa, and in Barnes's lives of the Popes, in the life of Alexander the Third, who is the last of the number of the Popes. In Bale the same, who cites John Marius as author; the same you will find in Scardius, who cites Cremonensis. Frederick was extremely hostile to Alexander: your Pavia felt this; the bishop who had stood on Frederick's side was fined the pallium and the cross. At that time, at Pavia, in the Synod, your ancestors the Pavians, all theologians and jurists, thought quite differently from you now. For at that time all agreed that the Pontiff could be deposed by the Emperor by right, as indeed the Pontiff was deposed there in fact.

units.la: QUI vero in Pauli Iouij secundo Historiarum Libro, vidisti Alexandri tertij Epistolam nullam ad Sultanum, (nulla enim ibi erat, quam videres) at poteras verba haec; saltem iam poteris, postquàm ubi delineata sunt. Nec multo post, ipse Gemes, ad Caietam moritur, eratq; constans fama Alexandrum, (ut Barbarus Princeps inimici Regis gloria atq; spectaculo subtraheretur, & ipse obiter propositá à Bajazethe praemia promereretur) lethiferum pulverem Saccharõ, quibus Turca poculis omnibus vtebatur, miscuisse. Is erat pulvis ad fallendum candore mirabilis, nec iniucundo admodum sapore, qui non acriore vi protinus, sicuti praesentanea venena, spiritus vitales opprimeret, sed sensim illabendo, exitiali tarditate grassaretur.{a} Guicciardinus etiam. Non defuere, qui crederent Bajazethem, cognito Regu Gallia in Italiam apparatu, per Iacobum Bucciardum, apud Bajazethem Pontificis Legatum, Pontificem pecunià corrupisse, vt Gemen vitâ privaret. Eius mors, à Pontifice, lento veneno procurata fuisse, constanti hominum opinione credita est. Pariter {b}Sabellicus. Zizimum vt veneno tolleret, ab initio Gallici tumultus, per literas, cum Alexandro egerat Barbarus Rex, magnû auri pondus, si eam sibi operam nauasset, pollicitus. Quae & ipsae {c}Cuspiniani quoque verba sunt. Quod vero Cuspinianus dicit, mortuum est veneno Zizimus Alexandro Pontifice haud ignorante, id ipsum quoque Sabellicus: Fuerunt qui crederent, eum veneno sublatum, fuisseq; Alexandrum Pontificem eius consilij non ignarum. Ut si iniquior sis in Cuspinianum, quòd Catholicus cum sit, male tamen fuerit affectus in Pontificem; habeas jam vestros homines, Iovium, Guicciardinum, Sabellicum, quibus tutò credas, nec fides in hoc tua vacillet amplius.
units.tr: But you who in the second book of Paulus Jovius's Histories saw a letter of Alexander the Third to the Sultan (there was none there for you to see), could have said these words; at any rate you can now, since they have been sketched out there. Not long after, Gem died at Caieta, and it was a firm rumour that Alexander, so that the barbarian prince might be removed from the glory and spectacle of his enemy the King, and so that he himself might in passing earn the rewards offered by Bajazet, had mixed deadly powder into the sugar with which the Turk used to drink all his cups. It was a powder wonderfully white to deceive the eye, with no unpleasant taste at all, which did not at once overwhelm the vital spirits with a fiercer force, like immediate poisons, but, slipping in gradually, worked on with a deadly slowness.{a} Guicciardini too. There were not lacking those who believed that Bajazet, having learned of the King of France's preparations for an expedition into Italy, had bribed the Pontiff with money through Jacopo Buccardo, the Pontifical Legate at Bajazet's court, so that he might deprive Gem of life. His death, it has been commonly believed, was brought about by the Pontiff with a slow poison. Likewise Sabellicus: the barbarian King had written to Alexander, at the beginning of the French disturbance, promising a great weight of gold if he would take the trouble to remove Zizim with poison. These are also the very words of Cuspinian. And what Cuspinian says, that Zizim died by poison with Pope Alexander not ignorant of it, Sabellicus also says: there were those who believed he had been removed by poison, and that Alexander the Pontiff was not unaware of this plan. So if you are unfairly disposed towards Cuspinian, because, although he is a Catholic, he was nonetheless ill-disposed towards the Pontiff, you now have your own men, Jovius, Guicciardini, Sabellicus, whom you may safely believe, and your faith in this matter need waver no more.

units.la: Ut tu autem hic delitias facis, ut minutias quaeris; Scribit factum haud ignorante Pontifice, sed iussu Pontificis id factum, non scribit. Quasi nescias quid valeat, Non ignorante. Disce ex Conradini nece. Non negavit ibi Pontifex, Iurisconsulti vestri exponunt, id est, concessit. Ita hic, Non ignarus, id est, conscius criminis fuit, atque adeo Author. Ubi enim Pontifex pars, prima pars est, caput est; Nunquam Accessorij naturam sequitur, semper Principalis. Alios ad illum accedere æquum, non illum ad alios. Tum de summâ haesitas. Propositâ à Baiazethe praemia sunt, ait Iovius. Pontifex pecuniâ corruptus, ait Guicciardinus. Pecunia illa, magnum auri pondus, ait Sabellicus. (Atque ita quidem par, ut Magnus Pontifex, Magni Turcæ fratrem, non nisi Magno pretio tolleret.) Summa ipsa denique, notata atque nominata à {d}Iovio. Ducenta millia aurerum nummûm: pacta scilicet, nec tu scio, dubitas, quin numerata. Non ita solet oscitanter pacisci Pontifex, ut illudi sibi patiatur; nec æquum erat, à Turcâ præcipuè: sic enim summo vestro cum dedecore, Turca Sanctissimo impositum fuisse diceretur. En ergo, ut potestatem nullam hic habeat Apologiæ Author ad historias addendi: tu fac potestatem habeas de calumniis detrahendi.
units.tr: But as for you, here you make trifles and hunt for trivia: "He writes that the deed was done not without the Pontiff's knowledge, but he does not write that it was done by the Pontiff's command." As if you did not know what "not without the knowledge" means! Learn from the execution of Conradin. "The Pontiff did not deny it there," your jurists explain, that is, he granted it. So here, "not without knowledge" means that he was party to the crime, and therefore its author. For where the Pontiff is a party, he is the first party, he is the head; "the nature of an accessory never follows the principal, the principal always follows the accessory. It is right for others to come to him, not for him to come to others." Then you hesitate over the main point. The rewards offered by Bajazet, says Jovius. The Pontiff bribed with money, says Guicciardini. That money, a great weight of gold, says Sabellicus. (And thus it is indeed fitting that a Great Pontiff would not remove the brother of a Great Turk except for a great price.) Lastly, the sum itself, noted and named by Jovius: two hundred thousand gold coins. Agreed upon, of course, and, I know, you do not doubt it was paid. The Pontiff does not bargain so carelessly as to allow himself to be cheated; nor was it fitting that this happen, especially by a Turk, for then, to your supreme shame, it would be said that the Most Holy One had been imposed upon by the Turk. Here, then, the author of the Apology has no authority to add to the histories; you, for your part, have the authority to remove calumnies.

units.la: AT de Henrico secundo nostro, nimis in aperto res est, vapulasse eum. {c}Carnem suam nudam disciplinæ virgarum supponens, à singulis viris Religiosis, quorum multitudo magna convenerat, Ætius[?] ternos vel quinos excepit. Ita Matthaeus Parisien-sis, Honedenus, Neubrigensis, Walsinghamus, Capgrauius, Author vitæ & processus Thomæ. Atq; hoc ex mandato Pontificis. Sic enim Honedenus, {a}Promisit & alia quaedam, quae non oportet scripturæ serie denotare. Et {b}Author vitæ. Iniunxerunt[?] Legati Papæ actiam[?] ei secretius alia quaedam, quae ad communem audientiam non pervenerunt, quæ nostri homines de virgæ disciplinâ fere intelligunt. Hæc ille cum passus esset, timuisse illum concedis, sed iudicium Dei, & Censuras Ecclesiæ. Censuras Ecclesiæ forte, erant enim timendæ, quæ tam erant rigidæ; nam de Iudicio Dei bene sperare potuit. {c}Quia audita Thomæ nece, per quadraginta dies, sedit mœrens, & acerbiorè multò plus quàm mortuorum fecit luctum, lugentium cibos comedit, equum non ascendit, nulla causa, nulla consultatio, nulla querela ingrediebatur ad eum, sedebat solitarius, ingemiscens, & dolens, sæpius hoc iterans, Heu, heu accidisse sic. {d}Qui accepto primùm nuncio de morte Thomæ, Omnipotentem Deum testem innocauit, quòd opus illud nefarium, nec suâ voluntate vel conscientiâ commissum est, nec suo artificio perquisitum. Qui, {e}coram Legatis Papæ iurauit, quòd neque mandauit, neque voluit, quòd Archiepiscopus interficeretur, & quando audiuit, vehementer mortem eius doluit. {f}Addidit etiam ex propriâ voluntate, quòd propter mortem Patris sui, vel Matris suæ, nunquam tantùm doluit. Qui denique & {g}vltro ad tumulum eius protestatus est publicè, quòd mortem eius nec mandauit, nec voluit, nec suo artificio perquisiuit.
units.tr: But as for our Henry the Second, the matter is too plainly open that he was flogged. "Offering his bare flesh to the discipline of rods, he received three or five strokes from each of the many religious men who had gathered." Thus Matthew of Paris, Hoveden, Neubrigensis, Walsingham, Capgrave, the author of the Life and Process of Thomas. And this was done by the Pontiff's command. For thus Hoveden: "He promised also certain other things which it is not fitting to set down in the course of the narrative." And the author of the Life: "The Legates of the Pope also enjoined upon him, more secretly, certain other things, which did not come to public hearing, and which our people largely understand as pertaining to the discipline of the rod." When he had suffered these things, you concede that he feared, but the judgment of God and the censures of the Church. The censures of the Church, perhaps, for they were to be feared, being so severe; but of the judgment of God he could well hope the best. "Because, on hearing of Thomas's death, he sat for forty days in grief, and made a mourning far more bitter than that of the dead, he ate the food of those who mourn, did not mount his horse, no business, no consultation, no complaint came to him; he sat alone, groaning and grieving, often repeating this, 'Alas, alas, that it should have happened so.'" He who, on first receiving the news of Thomas's death, called upon Almighty God as witness that that wicked deed was committed neither by his will nor with his knowledge, nor was it devised by his contrivance. He who swore before the Legates of the Pope that he had neither ordered nor wished that the Archbishop should be killed, and when he heard of it, he grieved his death exceedingly. He added also of his own accord that he had never grieved so much even at the death of his own father or mother. He who finally, of his own accord, at the tomb of Thomas, publicly protested that he neither ordered nor wished his death, nor devised it by his contrivance.

units.la: At prætèr Deum, Pontifex placandus fuit, cui nulla tum Imperatori pœna congrua, nisi curuata ceruicus visa est: nulla Regi præterquam puerilis illa virgarum pœnitentia. Misit primò Rex ad Pontificem, qui eum de crimine purgaret, Richardum Barre. Is receptus non est. Post illum, alios quatuor; Nec eos videre voluit. Tum, ab admissis, Regem nec nominari sustinuit, tanquam Papæ abominabile esset nomen Regis. Ac etiam, de Regis Regnique grauamine diutissimè tractauit, & immutabiliter disposuit Dominus Papa in Regem nominatim, & totam terram eius, cismarinam & transmarinam, interdicti ferè sententiam. Denique & hoc ipsum per Senonensem Archiepiscopum, in cismarinas eius ditiones executioni mandatum est. Et miserant tum à Pontifice duo Legati, Gratianus & Viuianus, qui magnis, & diuersis vexationibus Regem angariauerunt, volentes eum & terrâ suâ interdicto supponere. Sed Rex Angliæ, inde præmonitus, ante illorum ingressum, ad præsentiâ summi Pontificis appellauit, & sic se & terram suam à grauamine illorum custodiuit. At tum, Apostolicam timens severitatem, admare properauit, & de Normanniâ in Angliâ transfretauit, præcipiens quòd nullus Breuis lator, cuiuscunque fuerit conditionis vel ordinis, permitteretur transfretare neque de Normanniâ in Angliam, neque de Angliâ in Normanniam, nisi priùs datâ securitate, quòd nullum malum vel grauamen quæreret Regi, nec Regno suo. Hæc Honedenus. A quo habes, Regem Henricum: Papæ seueritatem, Cardinalium vexationes, & angarias, latores Breuium, malum & grauamen, & regni sui, & suum extimuisse.
units.tr: But beyond God, the Pontiff had to be appeased, for no punishment seemed to the Emperor fitting for him except a bowed neck; for the King there was nothing but that childish penance with rods. First the King sent to the Pontiff Richard Barre, to purge him of the crime. He was not received. After him four others; nor would he see them. Then, from the things admitted, he could not even bear to hear the King named, as if the name of King were hateful to the Pope. Also, the Lord Pope dealt at great length with the King's and the kingdom's grievance, and resolved unalterably that an interdict should be pronounced against the King by name and all his land, on this side of the sea and beyond it. Finally this too was carried into effect through the Archbishop of Sens in his territories on this side of the sea. At that time, too, two Legates had been sent by the Pontiff, Gratian and Vivian, who harassed the King with great and various vexations, wishing to place him and his land under an interdict. But the King of England, forewarned of this, before their arrival appealed to the presence of the Supreme Pontiff, and so guarded himself and his land from their oppression. Then, fearing the apostolic severity, he hastened to the sea, and crossed from Normandy into England, commanding that no bearer of briefs, of whatever condition or order, should be permitted to cross either from Normandy into England or from England into Normandy, unless security had first been given that he would seek no harm or grievance against the King or his kingdom. These are the words of Hoveden. From him you have that King Henry feared the severity of the Pope, the vexations and harassments of the Cardinals, the bearers of briefs, the harm and grievance both to his kingdom and to himself.

units.la: DE Nauarræ regno abalienato, non temerè est quòd omittis dicere, iubes consulere Historicos. Quid opus? Fatere tu quod res est. Quodcunque præterea Hispanus Regibus ius est; scis tamen Historicos, si consulantur, respondituros statim, mulctatum Regno Nauarrenum à Iulio secundo; multatitio regno donatum ab eo Hispanum: Ita scilicet voluit, iussit Summus tum Pontifex. De Regum titulis nemo te differere vult. Quid ad nos de illis? Alio forte titulo nititur Hispanus: De eo non quæritur: De Pontificis tui, de Iulij donatione quæritur. De Pontificis facto dicendum tibi erat; & dixisses scio, iubens, nisi vidisses, nodum hunc, te vindice, expediri non posse. Quanquam autem ibi, de re ipsâ nihil attingas; at ex indole tuâ visum est, vocu-lam saltem vellicare. Dixerat enim Apologia Regem Nauarræ, qui sic Regno spoliatus, Regùm patrem, qui iam regnat: Auus is erat, vel proauus. At vel apud Iurisconsultos, qui loquuntur ad libram, Patrus nomine Auus Filij Nepos demonstrari intelligitur, atque ita leges ipsæ loquuntur. Consule, si placet, & te hic fatere canem Æsopicum, qui captâsti umbram, dimissâ substantiâ; neutiam tamen tenuisti. Res verò ita se habuit de Regno Nauarreno apud {a}Nebrif. Papæ Iulio, bellum tum erat cum Ludouico Galliæ Rege, cuius à parte erat Iohannes Rex Nauarrenus, qui & Gallus ipse esset, & partem maximam patrimonij in Galliâ haberet. A Pontifice tum stabat Hispaniæ Rex. Is exercitum ducebat in Aquitaniam, contra Regem Galliarum. Per Nauarram verò mediam transire voluit, nec transitre modò, sed dum iret, rediret, tres, (quas nominare ei visum) arces munitas sibi tradi à Nauarreno, quæ in Hispanorum suorum interea manibus essent: Nisi è vestigio petitas arces in quos vsus dictum est, traderet; se omnia rapturum. Iniquum sanè postulatum. Ab Hispano tamen res relata ad Pontificem. Ab eo Rex Nauarræ (quòd Ludouico Galliæ Regi, hosti suo faueret) declaratur Schismaticus, atq; proinde Hæreticus. Quia verò identidem admonitus pertinaciùs agebat, & se tam non obscurè Gallum profitebatur; multatur regno, & omnibus fortunis, non modò ipse, sed & Vxor & Filij, cum omni Posteritate suâ: In Hispanum omne ius regnandi transfertur. Ita mirum Albanus belli Dux pro Hispano, Regis sui ius explicat apud Pampilonæ ciues, in regno Nauarræ vrbis primariæ, quam Albanus tum obsidebat. {a}De titulo dubitatis? Vniuersali Ecclesiæ atque Apostolico senatui credite, qui Regem vestrum Schismaticum, Hereticum, Apostolicæ sedis hostem publicum, atque reum læsæ Maiestatis declararunt, bona publicarunt, primo occupanti, & nominatim Principi nostro concesserunt. Aut igitur totum hoc Orthodoxæ[?] fidei nomen inane est, aut Rex vester, Dijs & hominibus inuisus, infamis, intestabilis, & à Christianorum communione segregandus est. Pergit dein, atque sibi ipsi obijcit: At dices quispiam, Quis unquam audiuit Regem, & eum quidem Regem, qui superiorem non habet, vocari in ius, inauditum, causæque indictâ, condemnari, regnoque spoliari? Respondet autem: Quasi nouum sit, & nunc primum adaures vestrū[?] peruenerit, à summo Pontifice Reges multari regno, imperio Imperatores. {b}Guicciardinus verò confert in pauca rem totam. Rex Arragonia, cum se Regnum Nauarra legitimè possidere alio nomine affirmare non posset, occupationem iure Pontificij Imperij factam esse Sacrosanctæ Sedū[?] authoritate afferebat. Habes quo titulo; Pontificis anathemate: Quâ de causâ; quia fidem seruabat Regi suo. Et annon propter fidem seruatam Regno exui, metus causâ satis iusta, constanti viro?
units.tr: As for the kingdom of Navarre being alienated, it is not without reason that you leave it out, saying "consult the historians." What need? Confess what the thing is. Whatever right the Spaniard may have to the kings' titles, you know nonetheless that the historians, if consulted, would at once reply that the kingdom of Navarre was punished and mulcted by Julius the Second, and that the Spaniard was given the kingdom so mulcted: so the Supreme Pontiff of that time willed and ordered. No one wishes to dispute with you about the kings' titles. What have we to do with those? The Spaniard may rest on some other title: that is not in question. What is in question is the donation of your Pontiff, of Julius. You ought to have spoken of the Pontiff's deed; and you would have done so, I know, had you not seen that this knot could not be untied with you as its champion. Although you touch nothing there of the matter itself, yet by your nature you thought fit at least to pluck at a little word. For the Apology had said that the King of Navarre, who was thus despoiled of his kingdom, was "the father of kings," who now reigns: he was his grandfather, or great-grandfather. But even among the jurists, who "speak by the balance," the word "grandfather" is understood to denote the grandfather of a son's son, and so the laws themselves speak. Consult them, if you please, and here confess yourself the Aesopian dog, who, having seized the shadow, let go the substance; yet you did not hold the shadow either. The matter, however, stood thus with regard to the kingdom of Navarre, according to Nebrissensis. Pope Julius was then at war with Louis, King of France, on whose side was John, King of Navarre, who was himself also a Frenchman and held the greatest part of his patrimony in France. The King of Spain then stood on the Pontiff's side. He led an army into Aquitaine against the King of the French. But he wished to pass through the middle of Navarre, and not merely to pass through, but, while going and returning, to have three fortresses (which he thought fit to name) handed over to him, fortified, which were meanwhile to be in the hands of his Spaniards: unless he received the requested fortresses forthwith, to be used for the purposes stated, he would plunder everything. A plainly unjust demand. Nevertheless the matter was referred by the Spaniard to the Pontiff. By him the King of Navarre, because he favoured Louis, King of France, his enemy, was declared a schismatic and therefore a heretic. Since, however, he was repeatedly admonished and persisted obstinately, and openly professed himself a Frenchman, he was mulcted of his kingdom and of all his fortunes, not only he himself, but his wife and sons, with all their posterity: all right to reign was transferred to the Spaniard. Thus the Duke of Alba, the remarkable leader of war, on behalf of the Spaniard, set out the right of his King before the citizens of Pamplona, the chief city in the kingdom of Navarre, which Alba was then besieging. "Do you doubt the title? Believe the universal Church and the apostolic senate, who declared your King a schismatic, a heretic, a public enemy of the apostolic see, and guilty of treason; they confiscated his goods and granted them, to the first occupant, and by name to our Prince. Either this whole name of the orthodox faith is empty, or your King, hateful to gods and men, infamous, detestable, is to be cut off from the communion of Christians." He then goes on and objects to himself: "But someone will say, who ever heard of a King, and indeed a King who has no superior, being summoned to judgment, condemned unheard, his cause not even put forward, and despoiled of his kingdom?" He answers, however: "As if it were something new, and had now for the first time reached your ears, that Kings are mulcted of their kingdoms, and Emperors of their empire, by the Supreme Pontiff." Guicciardini, moreover, sums up the whole matter in a few words: "The King of Aragon, since he could not affirm by any other title that he legitimately possessed the kingdom of Navarre, asserted that the occupation had been made by the right of the Pontifical Empire, by the authority of the Holy See." You have the title; the Pontiff's anathema. For what cause? Because he kept faith with his King. And is not being stripped of his kingdom on account of faith kept a sufficiently just cause of fear for a steadfast man?

units.la: SEquitur Proauum, Pronepos. Et in eo animus tibi vagatur: Apologia rem premit. Non enim vno Gladio diu iam pugnauit Pontifex: Gladius Gladium sequitur, materialis spiritualem: id quod de Proauo eius Iohanne dixit Iulius secundus (apud {c}Nebrissensem) vterque in Nauarrenum stringendus est Gladius, ac interim dum acuitur seculari, spiritualem in ceruices eius intentemus. Nec dixit modò, sed & reipsa ostendit, proiectis in Tiberim clauibus, Gladio suo spirituali: Deinceps verò plus sibi præsidij futurum in Pauli Gladio quàm Petri Clauè, palam professus est. In Nepote itidem ecce duo Gladij. Non ille modò Sixti 5ti. & Gregorij 14ti. de milliâ spirituali: sed & Gladius Liga Sanctæ. Ille verò non vnicus: aliquot Gladiorum millia in ceruices eius intentata; & illa, propter quotidianas strages quas edebant, Regi (quem suorum cura tangeret) certè metuenda. Tu spiritualem magis timuisse vis: Exislet
units.tr: Follows the "Grandfather, Great-grandson." And "in this your mind wanders": the Apology presses the point. For the Pope has not for long fought with one sword only: "Sword follows sword, the material the spiritual." That is what Julius the Second said of his grandfather John (quoted by Nebrissensis), that both swords must be drawn against the Navarrese, and meanwhile, while the secular one is being sharpened, we should aim the spiritual one at his neck. He not only said this but also showed it in fact, when he threw the keys into the Tiber, and openly professed that thenceforth more protection would be found in the sword of Paul than in the key of Peter. In the grandson likewise: "Behold, two swords." Not only that of Sixtus the Fifth and Gregory the Fourteenth concerning the spiritual weapon, but also the sword of the Holy League. Nor was that one alone: several thousand swords were aimed at his neck; and those, on account of the daily slaughters they caused, were certainly to be feared by the King, who would be concerned for his own people. You wish to show that you feared the spiritual sword more: perhaps someone else will come forward who fears the material one more. That each of them was feared, and not so much the former as the latter, no sensible person will deny. Therefore let the Apology keep to the matter at hand.

units.la: forte alius, qui materialem, magis. Vtrumque forte timuisse, nec tam illum tamen, quàm hunc, cordatus nemo negauerit. Quare intra rem consistat Apologia. Sed ea semper est charitas vestra in hoc negotio, Qui cedit vobis, ex sola conscientia id facit, nec nisi Censurae metu, vt nuper Dux Mutinensis cùm Ferrarâ cederet, non dubium, quin ex causâ, & motu merè Spirituali ex mero in Clementem officio: Nec cessionem eius fas, aliam in partem interpretari.
units.tr: But your charity in this business has always been such that whoever yields to you does so from conscience alone, and only from fear of censure, as recently the Duke of Modena did when he yielded Ferrara. There is no doubt that it came from a cause and a motion purely spiritual, from a pure sense of duty toward Clement; nor is it right to interpret his yielding in any other way.

units.la: Caeremonias verò vbi risit? Doluit potiùs collapsam ita iam apud vos Disciplinam, vt res tota ad frigidam Caeremoniam redierit. Olim, per Legatos caedi non solebant Reges, (paulò antè id in Henrico nostro vidimus) Ipsi flagellari solebant cum hominibus, & ab hominibus, idq; grauiter, ad verû dolorem, non leuiter modò ad significationem nescio quam. At iam, quia equum non potestis, ephippium caeditis: & cùm significatum ipsum vobis perijt, vmbratilem, & inanem modò ritum retinetis. Quodsi cui ridere libeat, rideat illud licet (ridiculum enim profectò) quod tu ita seriò quaeris, an magnum illi videatur, quod Legatus Regius leuiter percussus sit virgâ Sacerdotali, non ad dolorem vllum, sed sensum aliquem mysticum. Ne metuas; vobis forte hoc (quicquid id est) quantumuis leue, magnum videtur: nobis non magnum, quin perpusillum hoc quidem, atque adeo instar nihili, pro tam longâ ᵓApostasiâ[?], tam leuiter corripi; nisi quia, propeccato magno paululum supplicij satis est Patri.
units.tr: But where did he laugh at the ceremonies? He rather grieved that discipline among you had so collapsed that the whole matter had dwindled into a cold ceremony. In former times kings were not struck through envoys (as we recently saw in the case of our Henry); they themselves used to be whipped, along with men and by men, and that severely, to genuine pain, not merely lightly as some sort of signification. But now, since you cannot strike the horse, you beat the saddle; and when the thing signified itself has perished for you, you keep only a shadowy and empty rite. If anyone is inclined to laugh, let him laugh at it (for it is indeed ridiculous) when you so seriously ask whether it seems to him a great thing that the royal envoy was lightly struck with a priestly rod, not to any pain, but to some mystical meaning. Do not fear; perhaps to you this (whatever it is) seems great, however slight it may be: to us it does not seem great, but indeed very small, and almost as nothing, to be so lightly chastised for so long an apostasy; unless because "for a great sin, a little punishment is enough for the Father."

units.la: Quanquam Apologiam ibi nolo sic intelligas, quasi ex illâ virgâ percussione dolor magnus, vel liuor, vel vibex exiterint; aut quasi supra modum in poenâ illâ crudelis Pontifex. Non ille quidem crudelis in eâ; superbus magis & insolens, qui Principem tantum in Legati sui persona tàm indignis modis tractauerunt. Dolor forte minor: indignitas verò in virgâ non minor, si eâ vel leuiter attingas modò, ingenuum quemuis, quàm si caedas vel ad sanguinem. Ingenuum dico quemuis: Quanto autem maior, si tantum Regem in Legato suo; siue Pontificem re[?]spicias, insolentia fuit, qui fecit; siue Regem, indignitas, qui passus hanc contumeliam. Nisi quòd Regem excusent turbe domesticae, quae tum illi ita grauiter incubuerunt, vt necesse ei fuerit (cum Carolo Magno, de quo ante) ferte vix ferenda. Insolens enim profecto hoc; non aliam Regi poenitentiam comminisci posse, quàm virgarum; atque adeo audeo dicere, insolitum Apostolis quidem, quos virgâ aliquando caesos: virgâ autem vel Reges vel Regum Legatos cadere, vix unquam legas. Quos, qui Apostolis (scilicet succedunt), ferio caedunt, cùm datur; cùm non datur, Ceremonià contenti sunt: quâ tamen sciant, quid meriti, addo etiam, quid & passuri ferio, nec alieno humero, sed suo tergo, si adessent Clementi iam vires, quae Alexandro tum adfuerunt. Non aderant; venia ergo data est; & iam in Legatis abscentes vapulant.
units.tr: Yet I do not want you to understand the Apology there as if from that blow with the rod great pain, or a bruise, or a weal had come forth; or as if the Pope were excessively cruel in that punishment. He was not cruel in it indeed; rather proud and insolent, who treated a prince so unworthily in the person of his envoy. The pain was perhaps less: but the indignity with the rod is not less, if you merely touch even lightly any freeborn man with it, than if you beat him even to blood. I say any freeborn man: but how much greater, if you consider a king so great in his envoy; it was insolence on the part of him who did it, or indignity on the part of the King, who suffered this insult. Unless the domestic troubles excuse the King, which then weighed on him so heavily that he was obliged (as with Charlemagne, of whom above) to bear what could scarcely be borne. For this is indeed unusual: that one cannot devise any other punishment for a king than rods; and therefore I dare say that it was unusual for the Apostles, who were at times beaten with rods, but that you would scarcely ever read of kings or royal envoys being struck with a rod. Those who succeed the Apostles (as they claim) strike with the rod when they are given the chance; when they are not given it, they are content with the ceremony; yet let them know what they deserve, and I add, what they would also suffer if they were struck, not on another's shoulder but on their own back, if Clement had at that time the strength that Alexander then had. They were not present; therefore pardon was given; and now they are whipped in absentees, in envoys.

units.la: Quid si autem (inquis) vidisset Theodosium? Quidsi? Non vidisset in eo ludibrium, vidisset vim veram poenitentia. Neque vero Liga illi tum vlla imminebat; non urbes occupatae, non acies in procinctu; quicquid ab eo factum, vltro factum, vltro & sponte pura. Non contra illum Ambrosius legiones conscripserat, non Cardinales aut Iesuitas immiserat in urbem Regni caput, ne illa Imperatorem suum reciperet; non amittendi Imperij metus vllus Theodosio. Vidisset vero, non Legatum aliquem, sed ipsum Theodosium, in causa suâ, nec caeremonijs ludentem, sed serio iem agentem, nec alterius humerum pro eo leuiter, sed ipsius frontem à seipso graviter percussam; vidisset Significatum ipsum, doloris vim veram, non theatricam quandam & iocularem umbram Significationis sine Significato: vidisset hæc, & cum Theodosij lacrymis, suas, credo, miscuisset. At Significationem illam vestram (si vera narrant qui interfuerunt) omnes ibi tum siccis oculis inspectabant. Ludicra enim erat, & ad pompam: ut mirari subeat, quid tibi in mentem venerit, quòd ausus conferre cum illâ Theodosij. Quid habet illi simile Scena vestra, in quâ nullus capillus euulsus, non vel vlla lacrymula madidum Pauimentum. Profecto, si secutus in eo Theodosium, longo id intervallo; si imitatus illum, Archetypum suum, non satis ad viuum expressit.
units.tr: But what if (you say) he had seen Theodosius? What if? He would not have seen mockery in him, he would have seen the real force of repentance. Nor indeed was any league then hanging over him; no cities had been occupied, no armies were drawn up for battle; whatever he did, he did of his own accord, freely and sincerely. Ambrose had not raised legions against him, nor had he sent Cardinals or Jesuits into the capital of the realm, so that it would receive its emperor; there was no fear of losing the empire for Theodosius. But he would have seen, not some envoy, but Theodosius himself, in his own cause, not playing with ceremonies but acting in earnest, and not his shoulder lightly struck for him by another, but his own forehead struck severely by himself; he would have seen the thing signified itself, the real force of grief, not a certain theatrical and playful shadow of a signification without the signified; he would have seen these things, and, I believe, would have mingled his own tears with the tears of Theodosius. But that signification of yours (if those who were present report truly) everyone there at that time watched with dry eyes. For it was a sport and a show: so that one is moved to wonder what came into your mind, that you dared to compare it with that of Theodosius. Your scene has nothing like it, in which no hair is plucked out, nor is the pavement wet with even a single tear. Indeed, if in this he followed Theodosius, he followed him at a long distance; if he imitated him, his archetype, he did not express him sufficiently to the life.

units.la: Cùm verò aflisisse Regi Deum, ut pericula non pauca, nec leuia feliciter euaderet, & conatus nescio quos commemoras nefariorum hominum, quos iam non timeat; atque hoc ex eo, quod Legati sui humeros Pontificiæ virgulæ sic supposuit: omnino infeliciter huiusce rei mentio à te facta est. Namque hoc verbo expedisti ipse virgam, eâque Pontificem ipsum, eiisque Emiffarios[?] Iesuitas non leuiter percusisti. Respondè verò mihi; Rex ille, quâ fuerit tum in Deum religione, cùm sic astitit illi Deus, vt in tot prœliis tam fortiter pugnaret, tam fœliciter triumpharet. Ecquid non præsens Illi tum fuerit Deus? Ecquid non lateri Illius hœserit? An aut pauca tum aut leuia pericula euaserit? & an illa potiùs, non & pauca & leuia, iam fuerint (si tamen vlla fuerint) quæ exin euasit; præut illa fuerunt, quibus tum, missa[?] de cœlo manu liberauit Eum Deus? Respondè etiam de nefariis istis hominibus & conatibus eorū, qui pericula tum Illi, nec pauca, nec leuia creabant, quinam illi nefarij tandem? Annon de Ligâ vestrâ sanctâ? Annon vel Iesuita, vel Iesuitâ aliquo pleni, qui tum, nec prœlijs, nec prœlis Regi pepercerunt? Quorum Ille tamen conatus, & in acie apertos, & extra aciem clandestinos euasit; etiam tum, cùm virgas vestras contempsit. Respondè & hoc; Nefarius ille homo, quis fuit vel vnde, qui nondum percusso Legati humero, cultello tum Ei in fauces inuolauit? Nefarij illi qui genus, vnde homo, quorum Pyramidi olim incisa præconia? Cuius etsi iam lapides amoliti estis, at memoriam non estis, non poteritis, non magis quàm cicatricem de vultu Regio.
