Manet hœc in vultu, manebit illa in Historiâ, monumenta ambo nefariorum hominum, vestrâ de sectâ, quorum ab vno hoc exemplo, conatus Regibus metuendi sunt: Nam de nostra professionis hominibus, nemo vnquam extitit, qui contra Illum vel manum leuârit; qui non Ei semper fidus astiterit; tantum abest, vt vel in Caput eius, vel in Coronam, eorum quisquam quicquam vnquam tentauerit. Ego verò, quâ sum in Christos Domini Reges Christianos omnes obseruantiâ & fide, supplex Deum veneror, vt pergat porrò Regem illum ter Maximum, à conatibus nefariorum hominum liberare, etiam vel qui de Sacerrimâ Sectâ sunt, quos ille semper Authores habuit calamitatis suæ: vtque Regi etiam magis illustret oculos, quo in penitissimos eorum conatus, acie suâ penetret, vbique gentium iam, (quàm latè patet Europa) suspectos; saltem, vt inter eos, quos fidos sibi semper sensit; eosque, quos sanguinem suum hausisse aliquem, sitisse reliquum non semel expertus est, prudentiæ suæ putet esse, si prudenter sciat & maturè distinguere.
units.tr: Now as for your remark that God stood by the King, so that he escaped many dangers, and not slight ones, and that you mention certain attempts of wicked men, which he no longer fears, and this because he placed his shoulders under the Papal rod: the mention of this matter by you was altogether unfortunate. For by this word you yourself have disposed of the rod, and you have not lightly struck the Pope himself and his emissaries, the Jesuits. Now answer me: what was that King's religion at that time, when God so stood by him that in so many battles he fought so bravely and triumphed so happily? Was not God then present with him? Did He not cling to his side? Or did he escape few or slight dangers then? And were not those dangers, not both few and slight, which he escaped afterwards (if indeed there were any), just like those from which God freed him at that time by a hand sent from heaven? Answer also concerning those wicked men and their attempts, who then created dangers for him, not few and not slight: who, then, were those wicked men at last? Were they not of your Holy League? Were they not Jesuits, or full of some Jesuit, who at that time spared the King neither in battles nor in ambushes? Yet he escaped their attempts, both open ones in the field and secret ones outside the field; even then, when he despised your rods. Answer this too: that wicked man, who was he, or whence, who, before the envoy's shoulder had been struck, flew at him with a knife at his throat? Those wicked men of what kind, and whence the man, whose praises were once cut on a pyramid? Although you have now removed the stones, you are not and cannot be rid of the memory of it, no more than of the scar on the royal face. This remains on the face, and that will remain in history; both are monuments of wicked men of your sect, from whose single example kings must fear the attempts of such men. For among the men of our profession, no one has ever arisen who raised a hand against him; who has not always stood faithful to him; so far is it from the case that any of them has ever attempted anything against his head or his crown. As for me, with all the observance and faithfulness I bear toward the Christian kings, the Lord's anointed, I humbly worship God that He may continue to free that most great King from the attempts of wicked men, even those of the most accursed sect, whom he always had as the authors of his calamity; and that He may give the King clearer eyes, so that with his sight he may penetrate their most hidden attempts, now suspected everywhere among the nations (as far as Europe extends); at least, that among those whom he has always felt to be faithful to him, and those whom he has more than once experienced drinking some of his blood and thirsting for the rest, he may think it a mark of his prudence if he knows wisely and distinguishes in good time.

units.la: Fas verò mihi, non sine tortura Torti, locum hunc concludere, atque illud dicere : Astuisse[?] Regi Deum magis antè, quàm post virgidemiam[?]. Pericula quoque tum & plura, & grauiora euasisse; quanquam quid plura dico, vel grauiora? quae euasit omnia, tum euasit. Ab illis enim fuerunt omnia. Exin non pauca, non levia, nulla enim euasit; nam praeter illos suos nefarios infectum sensit neminem. Nefarios illos homines & hostes suos de Sectâ fuisse ad quam transijt: nefarios illorum conatus omnes tum cùm Noster esset feliciter euasisse: Plures quidem illi tum dentes, nec cultellum tam iugulo propinquum fuisse: nec enim modò ante in bello à Catholicis, sed & in pace post, inter Catholicos suos periclitatum esse.
units.tr: It is right for me, not without the torture of Tortus, to conclude this place and say this: God had been kinder to the King before than after the [...]. He also escaped more and graver dangers then; though why do I say more, or graver? He escaped all of them, and at that time he escaped them. For they all came from those men. Hence not a few, not slight ones, for he escaped none; apart from those wicked men of his he felt no one as an enemy. Those wicked men and his enemies were of the sect to which he went over: all their wicked attempts against our man were successfully escaped at that time. There were indeed then more teeth, and the knife was not so near the throat: for he was endangered not only before in war by the Catholics, but also afterwards in peace, among his own Catholics.

units.la: AT in Regina tu quidem totus euagaris, qui vbi de timore agitur capitis, Fortunarum, Imperij: stationem semper deseris, nec de eo unquam dicere vis, sed ad alium semper delaberis, timorem Iudicij Divini, de quo hic non quaeritur. Dic de illo cùm erit dicendi locus: dic de tribus capellis hic: An scilicet causa Reginae ulla fuerit, ut vitae luxe[?], ut Coronae, à Pontifice metueret. A Pontifice, qui illa Diris omnibus devouit; qui Regna eius praedae exposuit, qui subditis facem praetulit ad seditionem; qui Calices Sacros, qui vestes ipsas suas oppignorare; qui ipsis in castris (filiciternium[?] iam) militare voluit, potiùs quàm ut illum Regno non deturbaret; qui Signis suis, & Legionibus Hiberniam invasit, ipsum Hibernia Regnum, iusque eius transcripsit in Hispanum. A Pontifice, quo conscio, Percussor huc immissus à Cardinale Comensi: Dic an inter tot illas, nulla Ei causa fuerit, cur ab illo metueret. Mitte verò animam; Dies nondum est: noli ante Diem iudicare: noli te in Abyssum demergere Iudiciorum Dei. Nam, quam tu fidem Deo datam dicis, de fide Catholicâ seruandâ, nulla violauit; seruauit fidem, à facibus vestris puram seruauit: vtque Deo Illa, ita Deus Illi, & fidem seruauit; & fecit, vt data Ei fides à subditis suis in finem vsque inuiolata seruaretur; quantumuis saepe tentata à Iesuitis vestris, an posset labefactari. Nec vllus Christiani orbis Princeps magis, (absit verbo inuidiâ,) nullus æquè propitium sibi Numen sensit in Regno suo, vt Illa, si Regni felicitatem spectes, beata certè Regina.
units.tr: But you, indeed, wander about entirely in the matter of the Queen, who, whenever the question is of fear for life, fortunes or empire, always leave your post, and never want to say anything about it, but always slide off to another matter, the fear of divine judgment, which is not in question here. Speak about that when there is a place for speaking; speak here about the three goats: whether there was any cause for the Queen to fear, as the luxury of her life [?] or her crown, from the Pontiff. From the Pontiff, who devoted her to all the curses; who exposed her kingdoms to plunder, who held a torch to her subjects for sedition; who wanted to pawn the sacred chalices and her very garments; who wanted to serve as a soldier in the camps themselves (now [?]), rather than not drive him from the kingdom; who with his standards and legions invaded Ireland, and transferred the kingdom of Ireland and its right to the Spaniard. From the Pontiff, with whose knowledge a killer was sent here by Cardinal Como: tell me whether, among all those things, there was no cause for her to fear him. But let go of the soul; the day is not yet: do not judge before the day; do not plunge yourself into the abyss of God's judgments. For the faith which you say was given to God, of keeping the Catholic faith, he did not violate in any way; he kept faith, kept it pure from your torches: and as she kept faith with God, so God kept faith with her; and he brought it about that the faith given to her by her subjects was kept inviolate to the end, however often it was tried by your Jesuits, whether it could be shaken. Nor has any prince of the Christian world, (let the word be free of envy,) felt a divinity so favourable to himself in his kingdom as she did; if you look at the happiness of the kingdom, she is surely a blessed queen.

units.la: Diceres verò de Seditioso[?] illo Alani libello, quo tuetur bonus subditus, bonus Catholicus, Regina, vt omnia Acta Iudicialia seu Processus omnes Iuridicos, (ex quo publicata eius Excommunicatio) Diuino atque Humano iure prorsus irritos fuisse, atq; nullos: itanec Bellum per Eam licitè, quamuis iustissimâ de causâ, vel indici potuisse, velgeri. Primam enim illam conditionem esse in Bello legitimo, vt indici debeat ab ijs, quibus Suprema est, atque iusta authoritas indicendi: quam Illa iam Excommunicata non habet; praesertim cùm praeter Excommunicationem, Depositaquoq; sit de Dignitate Regiâ, à Vicario CHRISTI, cuius est in terris potestas Summa: subdititiq; eius non solùm soluti à fidelitate omni, iuramento, observantiâ, obedientiâ; sed eis expresse etiam interdictum, ne vel seruiant vel obsequantur, Personae cuiquam, ita Canonicè damnatae. Absque culpâ omni potuisse Davidem à Saule deficere; potuisse Duces Saulis, quae Regi erant omnia, Davidi tradere. Nec modò licitam fuisse rebellionem Idumeae, quam prius sibi subiecerat Rex Iehoram: sed & Libnam urbe propriam & suam iustè defecisse ab eo, & in hostiles manus sese in perpetuum tradere potuisse. Quorsum verò haec, nisi vt doceat fas cuiquam esse (quid dixi fas?) id cuique incumbere iam, posse & debere, & ad illud, tum officij, tum conscientiae nexu quemque obligatum esse, vt diripiant Eius omnia, & hostibus tradant: Rapere, Clepere, quae Eius flagitium nullum esse. Haec illius ibi consilia: & mendacia tua, si negas consilia illius fuisse.. Alani theoremata haec non potuisti, maluisti pessimum illud, & turpissimum Stanlei facinus tueri; sed vt decet proditionem, mendacio.
units.tr: But you would speak of that seditious little book of Allen, in which a good subject, a good Catholic, defends that the Queen, as all judicial acts or all legal processes (since her excommunication was published), were utterly void and null by divine and human right: and so war could not be lawfully declared or waged by her, even for a most just cause. For the first condition in a lawful war is that it must be declared by those who hold the supreme and just authority to declare it; which she, now excommunicated, does not have; especially since, besides excommunication, she has also been deposed from royal dignity by the Vicar of Christ, whose is the supreme power on earth; and her subjects are not only freed from all fidelity, oath, observance and obedience, but are expressly forbidden to serve or obey any person so canonically condemned. Without any fault, David could have revolted from Saul; Saul's commanders, who were everything to the king, could have handed them over to David. Nor was it only lawful for the Edomite rebellion, which King Jehoram had previously subjected to himself, but also the city of Libnah, its own and its own, could justly have revolted from him and could have handed itself over to hostile hands for ever. To what end are these things said, unless to teach that it is right for anyone (what did I say, right?) that it is now incumbent on each person, that he can and must, and that each is bound by the bond both of duty and of conscience, to plunder all her possessions and hand them to enemies: to seize, to steal, which is no crime against her. These are his counsels there: and your lies, if you deny that these were his counsels. You could not defend the theorems of Allen; you preferred to defend that most wicked and most shameful deed of Stanley; but, as befits treachery, with a lie.

units.la: Non enim abstulerunt Angli ab Hispano Dauentriam; sed inter vrbes alias, quas tum Regina Cautionis loco habuit, ab Ordinibus Belgicis acceperunt. Ea boni custodis Stanlei fidei concredita est. Is, si Catholicus prodire repente voluit, redderet depositum suum, Ei reddetet à quâ acceperat, quae illam fide optimâ acceperat, quò per eam caueret indemnitati suae. Quid ad illum quis verus vrbis Dominus?
units.tr: For the English did not take Deventer from the Spaniard; but among other towns, which the Queen then held as security, they received it from the Belgian Estates. It was entrusted to the faith of the good guardian Stanley. If he wished to go over suddenly as a Catholic, he should have returned his deposit, returned it to her from whom he had received it, who had received it in the best faith, so that by this she might guard her own safety. What to him is who the true lord of the town is?

units.la: Alia Depositi lex est, quàm vt sedeat quis iudex, de alieno Deposito: fidem Depositario liberaret, nec à facto tam foedo, auspicia sumeret religionis nouae; nec hijs primitijs perfidiae & proditionis Catholicissimum suum consecraret. De cuius Catholicâ fide quid senserint, haud sanè scio; de eâ fide, quam Principi suae datam violauit, videntur non admodum sensisse honorificè ad quos desciuit. Ecquid enim ex eo fidei illius concreditum est, ab illis, quorū causa fidem sic fefellit? Non sane; meritò autem illud. Perfidia placuit, perfidus diffidicuit, nec dignus ex eo vnquam est habitus, cuius fidei (quantumuis iam Catholicæ) vlla apud eos Dauentria crederetur. Sed ab hoc Stanlei facto, iactura aliqua, timor nullus; quare ad illud Matthæum diuertit: timor potiùs à libro illo virulento, quem Matthæus propterea planè prætermisit.
units.tr: There is another law of deposit than that someone should sit as judge over another's deposit: he should free the depositary from faith, nor take the auspices of a new religion from so foul a deed; nor consecrate his most Catholic self with these first fruits of perfidy and treachery. Of his Catholic faith, what they thought I certainly do not know; of that faith which he violated, given to his prince, those to whom he deserted seem not to have thought very honourably. For what of that faith was entrusted to them, for whose cause he thus broke faith? Certainly not; and justly so. Perfidy pleased, the perfidious man was distrusted, and from this he was never held worthy, whose faith (however Catholic now) would be believed by them in any Deventer. But from this deed of Stanley there is no loss, no fear; therefore he turns to that Matthew: the fear rather from that virulent book, which Matthew on that account plainly passed over.

units.la: QVt Regi causa fuit, vt sibi prospiceret, à Bullis prima fuit, quibus inclementer obnūtiatum est ei, à Clemente Papâ. Huic tu Nedo, Caneum male applicas; primò, non infuisse illis vllum certæ Personæ aut Nominis designationem. Non certè Nomen eius, connexis syllabis, sed designatio certa Personæ. Verba enim illa [Quantumcunq; niteretur Propinquitate Sanguinis] quis nescit quem designarent? Quis alius tum Propinquitate Sanguinis nitebatur? Eàdem operâ, Nomen inferre potuisset Iacobi Scotorum Regis, atque eo verborum circuitu describere, quem nôrant omnes, præter, supraque Mortales omnes niti Proximâ, Maximâ Sanguinis Propinquitate. Vacaturo propediem Regno, Catholicum potiri voluit Clemens, atq; vt ad populus curet [scilicet?]. Scribit Catholicis Anglis, vt curent, Catholicum regno potiatur. Quidsi autem non maximè Propinquus Sanguine? Quidsi Hæreditarium illi Regnandi Ius nullum? Curent tamen Catholici dum Catholicus sit) vt Regno potiatur. Quo ergo Sanguis, vel Semè Regium? Quò Vis & Iura Successionis? Quid iuuat Hæredem esse? Videtis quænam Romæ consilia coquat Pontifex, quàm infesta Regibus, quàm turbulenta. Laudat tamen consilium hoc Tortus dicitque, nullum eo magis salutare, magis Christianum, magis pium vel utile dari potuisse. Nimirum, vt vbi Regnum vacat, curent subditi, ne proximus tum Hæres Regnum adeat; nisi cum parte vnâ populi sui, de Religione transfigat: Curent, vt alius nullâ Propinquitate nixus, potiatur Regno, nullo iure Suo, dummodò Papam veneretur. Ilicet ergo, actum est: Regnorum Successio, cura iam populi: & ad hoc conclamat Pontifex, & Tortus laudat, & Salutare dicit consilium hoc tam perditum; Christianum, quale nec inter Gentes nominatum. Quas verò per Europam turbas dabit, si quæ ab antiquo Stemmate pendet Successio, ea iam ad popularem curam transferatur? Quid proximum huic, curent ne potiantur; nisi illud, curent, si potiti, ne diu potiantur. Catubeij [?] consequentia.
units.tr: AS the cause for the King was to provide for himself, the first came from the Bulls, by which he was pronounced against unmercifully by Clement, the Pope. To this you wrongly apply Nedo, Caneum; first, that there was in them no designation of a certain person or name. Certainly not his name, with the syllables joined, but the certain designation of a person. For those words [However much he relied on nearness of blood], who does not know whom they designated? Who else then relied on nearness of blood? By the same work he could have set down the name of James, King of the Scots, and by that circumlocution of words describe him, whom all know, beyond and above all mortals to rely on the nearest, greatest nearness of blood. With the kingdom about to be vacant soon, Clement wished a Catholic to possess it, and that the people should take care [namely?]. He writes to the English Catholics, that they should take care that a Catholic possess the kingdom. But what if he were not most nearly related by blood? What if he had no hereditary right to reign? Yet let the Catholics take care (provided he be Catholic) that he possess the kingdom. Then what of blood, or the seed of the royal line? What of the force and rights of succession? What good is it to be heir? You see what counsels the Pontiff brews at Rome, how hostile to kings, how turbulent. Yet Tortus praises this counsel and says that no counsel more salutary, more Christian, more pious or useful could be given. Surely, that where the kingdom is vacant, the subjects should take care that the next heir then does not take the kingdom, unless he transfers with one part of his people in religion: let them take care that another, relying on no kinship, should possess the kingdom, with no right of his own, provided he venerate the Pope. Straightway, then, it is done: the succession of kingdoms is now a care of the people; and to this the Pontiff cries out, and Tortus praises, and calls this so ruinous counsel salutary; Christian, such as was not named even among the Gentiles. But what troubles will it bring through Europe, if the succession, which depends on the ancient stem, is now transferred to the care of the people? What follows next to let them take care that they do not possess; except that: let them take care, if they have possessed, that they do not possess for long. Catubeij [?] consequence.

units.la: Quodsi populo cura nulla, vt constet Regi ius suum, excidere Iure omni? Quid ni? Neque miseret quicquam? Cur miseream [?]? Ipse in causa erat: penes Ipsum culpa omnis, iacturam Suam Sibi acceptam ferat: Nemo laditur nisi a seipso. En iam vt cohaereant haec. Non nominauit: Nec opus erat; ita designauit, cuius vt in procliui sit, celato nomine, de quo fabula narretur. Populo dein mandat quod curatum vult ne potiatur regno. Postremo inclementer dicit, totius mali causam a nullo praeterquam a seipso; si exclusus, ipse in causa erat. Quomodo in causa? Quid tandem peccauit? Spem fecit Pontifici & sefellit. Non fecit Ipse: vel Ipse vel ministri Eius. Ministri vero; Et an ea Papalis iustitia visitandi iniquitatem seruorum in Dominos, plectendi Reges, si Ministri delirarunt? An cuiquam incumbet praestare culpam non suam? Nec id quidem dicit, sed, vel Rex in causa, vel certe eius administri reprehendi debent. Debent forte reprehendi, reprehendantur ergo, si quid tale promiserint, Rex in causa ne fit; Quam nunquam meritus, reprehensione careat. Sed huc res redit. Propter malos ministros obnunciauit Regi Pontifex. Atque ita qui animum gerit, qui Sanguinis Ius nihili facit, qui populo ius facit Haeredes iustos excludendi, qui vbi minister in culpa, cudit in Regem, annon Hic Niger, annon Regi timendus & cauendus, ac bonis omnibus?
units.tr: Yet if the people have no care of it, so that the king's right is plainly forfeited, with all its legal force? Why not? Does he feel no pity at all? Why should I pity him? He was himself the cause: all the fault lies with him; let him bear the loss that he has brought upon himself: no one is harmed except by himself. See now how these things hang together. He did not name anyone; nor was there need to; he so pointed out, that it was easy to see whom he meant, the name concealed, about whom the story is told. Then he commands the people to take care that he does not gain the kingdom. Finally he says harshly that the cause of all the evil lies with no one but himself; if he was excluded, he was himself the cause. How the cause? What, after all, did he do wrong? He gave the Pontiff hope and deceived him. He did not do it himself: either himself or his ministers. His ministers, indeed; and is that papal justice of visiting the iniquity of servants upon their lords, of punishing kings, if the ministers have gone mad? Or does it fall to anyone to answer for a fault not his own? He does not even say this, but says: either the king is at fault, or certainly his officers ought to be blamed. If they ought perhaps to be blamed, let them be blamed then, if they promised any such thing; let the king not be at fault, who never deserved to be free from blame. But to this the matter comes back. Because of wicked ministers the Pontiff announced it to the king. And so he who bears a mind that makes nothing of the right of blood, who makes it a right for the people to exclude lawful heirs, who, when the minister is at fault, strikes at the king: is not this man black, is he not to be feared and guarded against by the king and by all good men?

units.la: DEfcedit post, in pulucrem Pulucraria Proditionis, sed in Nomine Mendacij, Calumnia, & Impudentia: ita enim sua fere auspicari solet. Pontifice negat macula vllius suspicione aspersum. Non suspicione? Atqui, crimen cuius tot Iesuitae participes, biennio toto non eclatum a Patre Claudio Generali, & per eum suboliiisse Pontifici, iure fufpiectur quispiam. Atqui, non alio fundamento nixa est tota haec proditio, quam Breuibus Pontificijs, a quibus aeterna ei macula, ab illa nempe clausula, Curarent Catholici ne Regno potiretur. Cum Coniurati e Breuibus illis, mentem Pontificis interpretati, non obscure affirmarent, Pontificem, cum curare vellet Catholicos, ne regno potiretur, eadem opera voluisse curare illos, ne diu potiretur: Si exclusum cupiebat, extrusum etiam cupere. Sed & in eo suspicio non leuis, quòd neque reformidabant in eo conscientiam Papæ: Missus enim Romam, qui totam Ei rem enarraret; sed ita missus, ne priùs eò, rei conficiendæ, quàm confecta iam notitia peruenirent.
units.tr: He goes on next, into the dust of the treachery's pit, but under the names of Lying, Calumny and Impudence: for this is how he usually begins his affairs. He denies that the Pontiff was stained by any suspicion of the crime. Not by suspicion? And yet a crime in which so many Jesuits took part, and which for two whole years was not disclosed by Father Claudius, the General, and through him was not reported to the Pontiff, rightly casts suspicion on someone. And yet this whole treachery rests on no other foundation than the Papal Briefs, by which his name is eternally stained, by that clause, Let the Catholics take care that he does not gain the kingdom. When the conspirators, interpreting the Pontiff's mind from those Briefs, openly affirmed that the Pontiff, when he wished the Catholics to take care that he did not gain the kingdom, had by the same act wished them to take care that he did not hold it long: if he desired him excluded, he desired him also thrown out. But in this too there is no slight suspicion, that they did not fear the Pope's conscience: for someone was sent to Rome to relate the whole affair to him; but he was sent in such a way that he would not arrive there before the business was done, and the news had already come after it was accomplished.

units.la: Ad Iesuitas venio. Carnettus (vt ais) constanter affirmauit, in eo scelere, non se, non vllum Iesuitam, vel consultorem, vel consentientem vllo modo fuisse. De Carnetto mox. Non vllum Iesuitam? Non vllo modo? vide, quà fide. Quid ergo sibi volebat, vox illa illius, ad primum nuncium detectì iam facinoris: At at! actum ergo de Societate totâ? Quid illa, quâ sæpe vsus apud DD. Delegatos Regios, qui quæstioni præerant? Ne, quicquid se fieret, vnius ob noxam, Societas tota petore apud eos existimatione foret? Quid illa, cùm excusaret se illis, quòd ita piger esset ad ea confitenda, quæ illum conscium arguebant, & quæ Delegatus tamen nota satis: Eòse inuitum magis ad confitendum accessisse, ne Societas ex facto suo male audiret, aut incurreret in reprehensiones hominum? Extant Reorum apud Acta publica spontaneæ confessiones; nec ipsi Rei post, vel in iudicio, vel in vltimo supplicio negabant, Iesuitas, & Consultores, & Consentientes fuisse.
units.tr: I come to the Jesuits. Garnet (as you say) firmly affirmed that in that crime neither he, nor any Jesuit, whether adviser or consenting party, had in any way been involved. About Garnet presently. Not any Jesuit? Not in any way? See with what good faith. What, then, did that cry of his mean, at the first news of the crime already discovered: Ah, ah! Is the whole Society therefore undone? What of that phrase, which he often used before the royal Commissioners who presided over the examination: Lest, whatever happened, through the guilt of one man the whole Society should be in ill repute with them? What of that, when he excused himself to them, because he was so slow to confess those things which convicted him of being privy to it, and which the Commissioner nevertheless knew well enough: that he had come to confession more unwillingly, lest the Society be ill spoken of for his deed, or incur the reproaches of men? The voluntary confessions of the accused are still extant among the public records; nor did the accused themselves afterwards, either at trial or at the final punishment, deny that the Jesuits, and the advisers, and the consenting parties had been involved.

units.la: Iesuita vnus Tesmundus quidam, ad quem remissus Batesius, postquam accitus est in numerum proditorum; cui ille in confessione suâ rem totam aperuit. Is Batesio persuasit, nec periculum ibi, nec peccatum subesse, rem licitam esse, & magno bono futuram; animúmque eius ad facinus firmauit, firmando Eucharistiam dedit. Hæc ille, Batesio rem confitente; nec consultor tamen fuit, nec vllo modo consensit in scelus?
units.tr: One Jesuit, a certain Tesmond, to whom Bates was sent back, after he was numbered among the traitors; to him he disclosed the whole affair in his confession. He persuaded Bates that there was neither danger nor sin there, that the thing was lawful and would be of great good; and he strengthened his mind for the deed, and gave him the Eucharist to confirm him. These things he did, while Bates confessed the matter; and yet was he not an adviser, and did he not in any way consent to the crime?

units.la: Iesuita alter Gerardus, confessus fuit, consentiens & consultor, qui uno eodemque tempore quinque simul viris, de conspiratorum numero, iuramentum taciturnitatis detulit, quòd per Sacram Trinitatem, perque quod tum sumpturi erant Sacramentum; nec reuelarent rem illam eorum tum fidei commendandam, nec nisi venia à reliquis data, vnquam ab executione desisterent; Iuramentum pòst, data illis Eucharistiâ obsignauit. Ille quidem, credo, consensit saltem.
units.tr: Another Jesuit, Gerard, confessed that he was a consenting party and an adviser, who at one and the same time bound five men of the number of the conspirators by an oath of secrecy, that by the Holy Trinity, and by the Sacrament they were then about to receive, they would not reveal that matter, which was then to be entrusted to their faith, and would never withdraw from its execution unless pardon was granted by the rest. Afterwards, having given them the Eucharist, he sealed the oath. He at least, I believe, consented.

units.la: Iesuita tertius Oldcornus, detectâ demum Coniuratione, quasi bonum factum defendit; nec quia successu caruit, ideo non laudandum; cùm & undecim Tribus iussu Dei ipsius contra Beniamin [?] pugnantes, bis profligatæ sint: cùm & Ludouici Galliæ Regis in Terrâ Sanctâ recuperandâ; & Christianorum in Rhodo retinendâ sanctum fuerit institutum, nec euentus tamen responderit [?]. Puto consentire in scelus, qui defendit, & laudat.
units.tr: A third Jesuit, Oldcorne, when the Conspiracy was at last discovered, defended it as a good deed; nor is it not to be praised because it lacked success, since also eleven tribes, fighting by God's own command against Benjamin, were twice routed; since also the holy undertaking of King Louis of France for the recovery of the Holy Land, and of the Christians for holding Rhodes, was holy, and yet the outcome did not answer. I think he who defends and praises it consents to the crime.

units.la: Quanquam quid istis immorer? Vno enim hoc, Tertius manifesto opprimitur. Is ipse, à quo rem totam, reliquæque partes singulas rescitult [?] Garnettus, à quo omnia speciatim audiuit, is ipse annon Iesuita? Et tamen negas, aut negat ille, vllum Iesuitam vllo modo, illius conspirationis, complicem vel conscium fuisse? O vos verecundos, ô veraces homines!
units.tr: But why should I linger over these? For by this one fact the third is plainly overwhelmed. He himself, from whom Garnet learned the whole matter and each of the single parts, from whom he heard everything in detail, is he not himself a Jesuit? And yet do you deny, or does he deny, that any Jesuit in any way was an accomplice or privy to that conspiracy? O you shameless men, O you truthful men!

units.la: Æquè verum isti nec Garnettum vllo modo Authorem fuisse. Ille vero Authori ipsi Catesbeio Author fuit; Bis Author; Primò cùm Breuia illa Clementis cum eo communicauit: pessimo consilio id; nam conspectis illis semel, fundauit se statim Cates-beius [?], atque super illis, omnes intentiones suas exedificauit: Verba Garnetti sunt, Audi enim, quale Dux inde Sceleris argumentum duxerit. Quàm reiicere tam licuit, eicere iam licet. Æquè licet curare iam, ne pergat potiri, atque tum ne patiretur Rex. Curare nos Catholicos hoc voluit Clemens. Age, ea mihi res cura iam erit! Ita omne malum à Breuibus, Breuia à Pontifice; Verè vt ouum ipsum à Basilisco hoc exclusum fuerit! Cùm incubaret pòst huic Basilisci ouo Catesbeius, ac multa secum versaret animo, de modo curandi ne diu potiretur Rex: venit illi in mentem inter alia, de Pulueré. Hæsit aliquantisper animi anceps; cùm videret, id sine suorum etiam magnâ strage, perfici non posse. Etiam vel illi bipedum nequissimo, tam horrendum, informe id sceleris visum est, vt principio nec tentandum existimaret. Substitit ergo paulisper; at cùm collegisset se, placuit eâ de re Patris Garnetti oraculum consulere. Hic iam Secundo, & Author, & Consultor est.
units.tr: It is equally true that Garnet was in no way the author of that same Catesby. Yet he was the author to Catesby himself; author twice over. First, when he shared those Briefs of Clement with him: a most evil counsel, for once Catesby had seen them he at once founded himself upon them and built all his designs upon them. These are Garnet's words; hear, for indeed, from this, what argument of crime the leader drew. As it was lawful to reject him then, it is lawful now to expel him. It is equally lawful now to take care that he does not go on gaining power, as it was then that the king should not suffer it. Clement wished us Catholics to take care of this. Come, this matter will now be my care! So all the evil comes from the Briefs, and the Briefs from the Pontiff; truly the very egg was hatched from this Basilisk! When afterwards Catesby sat brooding over this Basilisk's egg, and turned many things over in his mind, about the way of taking care that the king should not hold power long: among other things there came into his mind the Powder. He hung in doubt for some little while, seeing that it could not be done without a great slaughter of his own people too. Even that most wicked of two-footed creatures thought such a crime so horrible and monstrous that at first he judged it not even to be attempted. He therefore paused for a little; but when he had collected himself, he decided to consult Father Garnet's oracle on this matter. Here, now, for the second time he is both author and adviser.

units.la: Adit ergo Garnettum rectâ; quem de consilio suo bis conuenit, semel in ædibus vbi latitabat. Adit autem non solùm, sed vnà cum eo Grenwellus (Is Tesmundus est Iesuita, sed æquiuoco hoc Grenwelli nomine magis hic notus, quàm vero, atque eo dehinc nobis nominandus,) & ipse Conscius & Consultor, Ambo, vt in suscepto scelere confirmarentur. Quærunt: Cāsine [?] aliquo f.is esset [?], insontes vnà cum sontibus interneciui dare? Ibi Garnettus fassus, perculsum se quæstione illi, & in suspicionem statim venisse (id quod res erat) magnum aliquod maleficium meditati. Catisbeium Sed, respondit tamen; homo pius, & qui nullius in morte se miscere voluit, Quidni? Si tantum ex eo re bonum proventurum esset, quantum, aliquot insontium necem compensare posset. Nec semel hoc: alio etiam id tempore factum est, in Campis Suburbanis, quibus à Paludes nomen est, ubi, cum eâdem de re plenius cum adhuc consuluisset, plenius ei Garnettus per omnia satisfecit: Posse & licere cum noxiis innoxios suffla[?]ri, & magni meriti rem fore, si id magno alicui bono Catholicis futurum esset.
units.tr: So he goes straight to Garnet; whom he met twice about his plan, once in the house where he was hiding. He went not alone, but together with Greenwell (this is the Jesuit Tesmond, but better known here by the ambiguous name of Greenwell, and hereafter to be named by us so), himself also a privy party and adviser; both, so that they might be confirmed in the crime they had undertaken. They asked: whether by any means it could be arranged to destroy the innocent along with the guilty? Garnet, confessing that he was disturbed by the question, and at once came under suspicion (which was indeed the case) that some great wickedness was being plotted. Yet he answered Catesby, a pious man who wished to have no part in anyone's death, Why not? If so great a good would come from it, that it could make up for the slaughter of some innocent people. Nor was this said only once: at another time too it was done, in the Suburban Fields, which are called the Marshes, where, when he had consulted him again on the same matter more fully, Garnet satisfied him fully in every point: that it was possible and lawful to blow up the innocent with the guilty, and that it would be a thing of great merit if it were to bring some great good to the Catholics.

units.la: Atque eo responso sub, eos animos Catisbeio addidit, ut nihil amplius deliberaret unquam, sed ferretur pòstrotus ad Facinus. Quòd si quis, postea inhorruerunt ad Scelus tantum, (& quisque fere primo auditu inhorruit) statim il li in promptu responsio. Constare vero sibi Authoritate optimâ rem licitam esse, constare autem Authore Patre Garnetto, cuius sibi vox esset pro Oraculo. Nec quisquam post in societatem Sceleris ascitus, nisi illo quasi authoramento. Eo enim responso adducti Winterus, Rookwodus, reliqui, Incendiarius ipse denique Fauxius, alioquin haesitantes, animos sumpserunt ad Scelus. Pater enim Garnettus Consultor filius.
units.tr: Thanks to that answer he added such courage to Catesby that he never deliberated again but was carried headlong to the deed. And if anyone afterward shrank from the crime alone (and nearly everyone shrank at first hearing), they immediately had the ready reply: that it was certainly lawful, certainly by the best authority, namely from Father Garnet, whose voice was for them an oracle. Nor was anyone afterward admitted into the fellowship of the crime except under that, as it were, guarantee. For it was by that answer that Winter, Rookwood, the others, and finally Fawkes the incendiary himself, who had been hesitating otherwise, took heart for the deed. For Father Garnet was the adviser of the son.

units.la: Vide verò an credibile sit, Garnettum, qui cum ijsdem ipsis hominibus Catisbeio, Wintero, Grenvillo, non ita multò ante in unâ, atque alterâ Conjuratione fuerat, (vnâ, paulò ante obiqum Regitæ Regem Regnum incunta, alterâ) de Regis Hispani Copiis ad invasionem huc adducendis, cum tertia hac iam exclusum penitus fuisse. Vide an & illud credibile, cùm dixi unquam à latere eius Catisbeius defenderet, semper autem remotis arbitris rem suam agerent; quòd, (ut scriptum habetur illius) haud unquam libenter ferret rem sibi ullam esse cum Catisbeio nisi soli cum solo; cum, quaestione hac nunquam nisi in thesi pertentatum fuisse. Esto tamen; una haec quaestio, fuerit; Ex eâ quaestione nihilne subodorâtus est Garnettus, adeone obtusum pectus gestabat? Imò vel, ex ipsâ illâ quaestione, subolere sibi tum aiebat, moliri nescio quid Catisbeium, unde multorum neces; nocentium, innocentium consequi oporteret. Venit ergo vel inde in cognitionem generalem, & quanta sat erat Reo constituendo. Verba ipsius in ultimo supplicio, haec. A Catisbcio se, rem in genere intellexisse, & in hoc peccasse, quod celasset & praevertere neglexisset. Tum etiam, Quod, quae sibi comperta, Regina Mariae aperiuit non aperuisset, mortis sententiam iusti- simè in se pronunciatam. Extra confessionem ergo Sacramentalem, Generatim rem cognovit. Negat Tortus; Paterat Garnettus, Cui credimus?
units.tr: But see whether it is credible that Garnet, who had been in one or two conspiracies not long before with these same men, Catesby, Winter and Grenville (one a little before, to set the King of Scotland on fire, the other...), had been entirely excluded from this third one, concerning the bringing in of the King of Spain's forces for an invasion here. See also whether this is credible: that Catesby always defended his cause at Garnet's side, but that they always transacted their business with the witnesses removed; because (as it is written of him) he never willingly had any dealings with Catesby except alone with alone, although this question was never raised except in theory. Granted, however, that this was one question only; from that question did Garnet suspect nothing? Had he such a dull breast? Rather, he himself said that from that very question he then sensed that Catesby was plotting something or other, whence the deaths of many, both guilty and innocent, would have to follow. He therefore came to general knowledge from this, and as much as was enough to make the accused. His own words at the final punishment were these: that he had understood the matter in general from Catesby, and had sinned in this, that he concealed it and neglected to prevent it. Then also: that he had not disclosed what had been made known to him, which Queen Mary disclosed, a sentence of death most justly pronounced against himself. Outside sacramental confession, therefore, he knew the matter in general. Tortus denies it; Garnet admits it. Whom do we believe?

units.la: Debebat vero, utilius sic in Genere cognitionem habuit, eius, sicut in Specie cognitionem haberet, operam omnem date; si (vt ais) operam omnem dedit ut a Conspiratione desisti posset. Poterat autem id, non dico, si operam dedisset, sed si vel sine opera ullâ suâ audire rem modò voluisset. Per seipsum enim studuisse, quo minus Speciem cognovisset, & id quoque recognovit. Cum enim, aliquanto post cum Catisbeio ageret, ne in suo illo (quicquid id erat) incepto progredi vellet, nisi Pontificis assensus prius explorato: Mitte vero de Pontifice, (ait Catisbeius) de illius animo mihi dubium non est, atque adeo tute ipse et audire vis, rem ipsam fame scias, et eo dicto occepit ei rem totam pandere. Ibi vero, instare Garnettus ne faceret: non enim adduci posse se, ut audiat. Cur vero, rem cum posset tum, rescire noluit? Quae potest reddi ratio, nisi quòd Noluit intelligere ut bene ageret. Voluit nescire, quia noluit impedire? Frustrà ergo à te dictum & falsò: dedit omnem operam, ut à tali conspiratione desisteretur. Si dedisset, audisset, damnâsset, auerruncasset. Iam res ipsa loquitur: Ignorare maluit, quàm avertere.
units.tr: But indeed, he ought to have taken pains to have the knowledge in general, which he had, become knowledge in particular, just as he would have had it; if (as you say) he took every pains that the conspiracy might be stopped. He could have done this, I do not say if he had taken pains, but if he had merely been willing to hear the matter without any effort of his own. For he himself had tried to keep from knowing the particulars, and this too he admitted. For when, some time later, he was dealing with Catesby, that he should not wish to proceed in that undertaking of his (whatever it was) unless the Pontiff's assent had first been ascertained: "Let go of the Pontiff," said Catesby, "I have no doubt about his mind, and therefore you yourself wish to hear it and to know the thing itself by report," and with that word he began to lay the whole matter open to him. Then indeed Garnet urged him not to do so: for he could not be brought to hear it. But why, when he could then, did he refuse to learn the matter? What reason can be given, except that he was unwilling to understand, so that he might act well? Did he wish not to know because he was unwilling to hinder? Therefore what you have said is in vain and false: he gave every effort that he be turned away from such a conspiracy. If he had given it, he would have heard, condemned, and averted it. The thing itself speaks now: he chose to be ignorant rather than to turn it aside.

units.la: Sed dic, etiam: dedit ne omnem operam ut desisteretur? Quam vero? Romam scripsit ad Patrem Generalem quò is curaret scilicet Coniurationem Pontificii Breui aliquo praeveniri. Ridiculum; Romam scribere, ut inde hùc Româ rescriberetur, quo se hîc Catholici continerent; quorsum ambages hae? cur compendium non fecit itineris huius, hinc Romam, Româ huc denuò? cur idem hoc vnà operâ, cùm Superior ipse esset, domi hic cum suis conficere non potuit? Quando autem Romam sic scripsit? Non primi hoc quàm id illi compertum, confessum iam ini rem, antequam eum quem misit, nuncius Romam pervenire posset. Verùm egit cùm Grenwello, ut cum Catisbeio ageret, quò vellet desistere. Cur vero rem reiecit in Grenwellum? Cur ipse cum Catisbeio non egit? Actuurus erat scilicet. Quando autem? Nimirùm sexto demum Nouembris, poftridiè eius dieì qui Scelery designatus: Cùm peraƈta iam res, omnem operam daturus, nè petagi posset. Qui per sex menses o- peram nullam dederat, qui nullam; decimo ante die cùm ab Vrbe discederet, postridiè Dicì fatalis omnem operam daturus erat. Sed non ante. Sed Grenwello monente Catesbeius an de- stitit? Imò Grenwellus ipse an destitit? Imò, perstitit homo nequam, ac revelassi tandem prodìtione, huc illuc circumcurrauit, vt concitaret Papistas quoscunque poterat; ad arma contra Regem palam capienda. Et hoccine erat homynis, alios ex Superioris sui iussu, ab incepto revocantis? Quis credat Grenwellum Superiori suo tam immorigerum fuisse? Grenwellum, qui Conscius erat; qui Confessus de Scelere, qui ac Absolutus à Garnetto, nec alia lege, quàm vt desisteret: non tamen destitisse? perstitisse in scelere, alios vt persisterent animasse, Incendiarium animorum præstitisse se, Incendia- rio Pulueris tum comprehenso? Verum Garnettus, si desistit, vt dicis, voluit, atque vt posset, omnem operam dedit; quorsum Vota Precésque assiduè fecit; assiduè Missificauit, pro felicis fortunatoque illius Actionis successu? Ecquis pro eo Orat, pro eo Offert, quod factum nolle, à quo vellet desistere? Cùmq; illud Iesuitis in more positum: vt Misse quandam subinde, atque Orationcule speciales fiant, pro impetrandâ re aliquâ, quæ soli Patri Generali cognita: cur eo ipso tempore à Patre ipso Generali, exiit Edictum vt Misse illæ omnes, & Orationes iam, ex voto & sententiâ Patris Garnetti fierent; & pro successu eius rei, quæ tum illi præ manibus, quæque magno bono futura erat totis hic rei Catholicæ?
units.tr: But tell me, too: did he give every effort that it be stopped? But how? He wrote to Rome to the Father General, so that he would see to it, no doubt, that the Papists' conspiracy be forestalled by some swift measure. Ridiculous: to write to Rome so that from there it might be written back here, so that Catholics here might restrain themselves; why these circuits? Why did he not shorten this journey, from here to Rome, from Rome here again? Why could he not complete this same business in one stroke, when he was himself the superior, at home here with his own people? And when did he write to Rome thus? Not first, indeed, once it had been discovered to him, the matter already confessed, before the messenger he sent could reach Rome. Truly he dealt with Grenville, so that he might deal with Catesby that he should desist as he wished. But why did he throw the matter back on Grenville? Why did he not deal with Catesby himself? He was going to, no doubt. When, then? Namely on the sixth of November at last, the day after that day which had been designated for the crime: when the thing was already done, about to give every effort, lest it could be brought about. He who for six months had given no effort at all, who had given none; ten days before, when he was leaving the City, he was about to give every effort on the day after the fatal day. But not before. But at Grenville's warning did Catesby desist? Indeed, did Grenville himself desist? Indeed, that worthless fellow persisted, and at length revealed it by betrayal, ran hither and thither, so that he might stir up whatever Papists he could to take up arms openly against the King. And was this the conduct of a man who, by his superior's order, called others back from the undertaking? Who would believe that Grenville was so disobedient to his superior? Grenville, who was privy to it; who had confessed the crime, who had been absolved by Garnet, on no other condition than that he should desist: did he not desist? Did he persist in the crime, encourage others to persist, and show himself a fire-raiser of minds, when the gunpowder fire-raiser was then seized? But Garnet, if he desisted, as you say, wished it and so that he might be able, gave every effort; why did he constantly make vows and prayers, constantly celebrated Masses for the happy and fortunate success of that action? Who prays for, who offers for, that which he was unwilling to be done, from which he wished to desist? And since it is the custom among the Jesuits that from time to time certain special Masses and little prayers are made, to obtain some matter known only to the Father General: why at that very time did an edict go out from the Father General himself that all those Masses and Orations should now be made according to the wish and opinion of Father Garnet; and for the success of that matter, which was then in hand for him, and which was to be of great good to the whole Catholic cause here?

units.la: Quodsi ita, vt ais, detestatus est facinus, quid Coughtona egit inter facinorosos eo ipso tempore, quo ignem pulueris admotum oportuit? Cur alio, se non recepit? Cur eò? Coughtonam, inquam, qui locus conditus erat, quò Coniuratos omnes (si successu Scelus non catmisset) oportuit ad Eum conuolare? Cur ibi vix quatriduum ante designatum Sceleri diem, concionem habuit, in quâ hortatus auditores suos, sedulò orarent singulì, pro fausto eius actionis euentu, quæ tum erat in foribus? Quare, vbi detecta demum Coniuratio, literæ eò ad Garnettū cùm omni festinatione transmissæ à Coniuratis, qui tum in Vrbe, perfetente eas Batefio? Cur acceptis statim literis ijs erupit ei vox illa, Scelus hoc detectum, Societati toti, exitio fore? Cur communicato tum inter se consilio Grenwellus mox in Walliam festinauit, vt, quod occultâ proditione non poterant, aperta Seditione effectum darent? ad eamque rem Henlipa in ædibus Abingtoni, se à Patre Provinciali Garnetto missum, idque ab eo in mandatis habere, palam contestatus est? Hæccine erant hominis vt desisteretur ab incepto, satagentis? Nam de Sacramentali Confessione, quod ita Tortus vrget, vide quàm vacillet, nec vera fuit ibi Confessio: nec si vera, quicquam ad rem. Nihil autem hîc referam, quod manu ipsius consignatum non sit. An Confessio illa fuerit, Garnettus ipse mirificè trepidauit. Nam primò, non aliter innotuisse sibi quàm in ipsâ Confessione. Pòst, extra Confessionem quidem, sed relatione aliquâ ad Confessionem futuram habitâ. Tum, ne id quidem: sed per viam Consultationis, non quasi culpam aliquam delatam ad se, sed quasi rem aliunde cognitam. Tandem, seriò iussus respondere, id quod res erat, an reuerà in Confessione rem primò accepisset? Respondeo (inquit) Inambulasse nos, & Grenwellum enunciasse mihi rem totam sub Sigillo maximo; quod ego, de Sigillo Confessionis accepi, quanquam ille fortasse de minore aliquo intellexit. Bidùo pòst. Quod ad ea quæ à Grenwello audiui, non possum pro certo affirmare, animum illi fuisse ea narrandi tantum quàm sub Confessione. Potest vero & audet affirmare hæc Tortus, quæ Garnettus ipse non audet, non potest pro certo affirmare.
units.tr: But if, as you say, he detested the crime, what did Coughton do among the criminals at that very time, when the fire of the powder had to be applied? Why did he not withdraw elsewhere? Why there? Coughton, I say, in whose appointed place all the conspirators (if the crime had not succeeded) were to flock together? Why did he there, scarcely four days before the day designated for the crime, preach a sermon, in which he urged his hearers that each should earnestly pray for a favourable outcome of that action which was then at the doors? Why, when the conspiracy was at length discovered, were letters sent to Garnet there with all haste by the conspirators, who were then in the City, the letters being carried by Bates? Why, immediately on receiving those letters, did that exclamation burst from him: "This crime, detected, will be the ruin of the whole Society"? Why, when Grenville had then taken counsel with them, did he quickly hasten into Wales, so that what they could not accomplish by hidden betrayal they might bring about by open sedition? And to that end did he openly declare that he had been sent by Father Provincial Garnet to Henlip, in the house of Abington, and that he had this in his instructions from him? Were these the actions of a man who was busy that the undertaking be stopped? For as to sacramental confession, which Tortus presses so hard, see how it wavers, and that there was no true confession there; nor, even if it were true, does it count for anything in the matter. I will, however, say nothing here that is not signed with his own hand. Whether that was a confession, Garnet himself has been wonderfully alarmed. For first, he says he had learned of it in no other way than in the confession itself. Afterwards, outside the confession indeed, but with some reference to a confession to come. Then, not even that: but by way of consultation, not as though some fault had been reported to him, but as though the matter had been known from elsewhere. Finally, when he was seriously ordered to answer, whether in fact he had first received the matter in confession, as the thing was: "I answer," he said, "that we walked about, and that Grenville told me the whole matter under the greatest seal; which I understood as the seal of confession, although perhaps he understood it of some lesser one." Twice afterwards: "As to what I heard from Grenville, I cannot affirm for certain that his intention was to tell it merely as under confession." Tortus both can and dares to affirm these things, which Garnet himself does not dare, cannot affirm for certain.

units.la: Dicam autem vnde tanta hæc illius trepidatio. Initio confidentior erat; sciebat perisse Catisbeium, superesse quidem Grenwellum, sed elapsum fugâ putabat; ita, nisi vnum illum, neminem iam esse in vinculis cognitionis suæ conscium. Pòst verò, Grenwellum (per errorem) putabat comprehensum; metuebat autem, ne exiret per Grenwellum res, neue fateretur ille in Quæstione, de totâ re sermonem sibi fuisse cum Garnetto, idque extra Confessionem. Hinc ita fluctuabatur miser. Res tota, in hac ponitur per Garnetti literas, ipsius manu scriptas ad dilectissimos Patres suos & Fratres, datas, Dominicâ in ramis palmarum. Literis verò illis purgabat ipse se de duplici crimine, quo (vt viderur) scandalo magno fuerat, Patribus illis Fratribusque suis: vno, quòd omnino fassus esset, innotuisse sibi Proditionis negotium: altero, quòd Grenwellum insuper de eo accusâsset. acculaesset. Ad primum respondet: Nam quid facerem? Primò ex-cusabant me reliqui omnes Coniurati. Secundò, Catesbeius visus sem-per apud eos fuerat Authoritate mea, quâ adduxi pene omnes, ut bene sentirent de Negotio quod factum, ut ed vnum omnes me habe-rent pro Reo. Tertiò, Duo quidam Corycat[?] laudiderant me, cum Oldcorne colloquentem, atque tota de re apud eum differentem, quid ad obiecta singula responsurum esse. Quarto, Litera etiam ad me Au-rantiarum sueto scripta ad D. Annam, nescio quomodo in illorum manus peruenerant, quibus scientiam meam non obscure confessus sum. Vides ergo reclusisse rem; tum in reprehensiones suorum incurrisse, quòd hoc ipsum praefe tulisset; Litteris vero huius, Patribus suis, & Fratribus rationes idoneas reddens, cur de scientia sua (quod Patres illi valdè optabant) fergiuerfari non posset.
units.tr: I shall say, however, where this great agitation of his came from. At first he was more confident: he knew that Catesby had perished and that Grenwell survived, but he thought Grenwell had escaped by flight; so, unless that one man, no one was any longer in custody who knew of his dealings. Afterwards, however, he believed (by mistake) that Grenwell had been caught, and he feared that the matter would come out through Grenwell, and that under examination he would confess that he had spoken of the whole affair with Garnet, and that this had been outside confession. Hence the wretched man wavered this way and that. The whole matter rests on Garnet's letter, written in his own hand to his most beloved Fathers and Brothers, dated on Palm Sunday. In that letter he cleared himself of a double charge, by which (as it seems) he had caused great scandal to those Fathers and Brothers of his: first, that he had at all confessed that he had come to know of the plot against the state; second, that he had further accused Grenwell of it. To the first he replies: "For what was I to do?" First, all the other conspirators excused me. Second, Catesby had always seemed to them to be under my authority, by which I had brought almost all of them to think well of the business that had been done, so that they all held me to blame for it. Third, two men of Corycat had praised me when I was talking with Oldcorne and discussing the whole matter with him at length, as to how I would answer each objection. Fourth, a letter written to me in the usual manner of Orange, addressed to Mistress Anne, had somehow come into the hands of those men, to whom I openly admitted my knowledge. You see, therefore, that he had disclosed the matter, and then fell into the reproaches of his own people for having made this very thing public; but in this letter to his Fathers and Brothers he gives suitable reasons why he could not, as those Fathers very much wished, deny his knowledge.

units.la: Ad crimen alterum de accusato Grenvello, ita ibi respon-det: Sibi quidem, si fuga sibi consuluisset Grenvellum (putabat enim tum captiu & in Custodia) aliam aliquam rationem iniunxum su-isse, atq; (vt verbis ipsius ipsius vtar) fabulam aliam formalem sibi fuisse fingendam. Iam vero Ille cum comprehensus fit, ita facta opus exiliimasse, vt offensae partem aliquam in Grenvelli regiceret, quod Fratrem suum pro charitate sua fraternâ non agre laturum sperabat. Cùm enim rem scire me iam scirent omnes; alicunde petenda mihi fuit origo cognitionis meae. A Conspiratoribus Laicis non poterà, quod saepe illis dicto, scripto saneè protestatus essem, me illos non proditurum unquam. Secundò, Multorum mihi Confessiones visa erant. Omnes autem illa perag: Grenvellum accusabant atque me. Tertiò, Consultum ergo putavi, vt fatererem de Illo, quo & me simul atque illum excusare possem; neutri (scilicet) nostrum, consilium illud placuisse. Vides vt gesta fuerint haec ex compositio; vides, vnde fabula haec noua de Grenvello, & ipsius Confessione. At haec iam nulla fuisset, sed formalis alia fabula fingenda ei fuerat, nisi, per errorem, Grenvellum putasset in vinculis esse, & valdè sibi metuisset, ne Grenvellus confiteri prior occuparet, confessione aliquâ suâ rem (vt erat) in aperto poneret, atque ita durius secum ageretur. Hinc illae eius fluctuationes; Consessu est: Non est forte confessus: Illi forte animus non erat confitendi: Ego non audim affirmare confessionem illam fuisse.
units.tr: On the second charge, concerning the accused Grenwell, he answers there as follows: that for himself, if he had advised Grenwell to flee (for he thought him then captive and in custody), he would have imposed some other plan and, as I shall use his own words, that another invented story would have had to be devised for him. But now, when Grenwell had been caught, he judged that the matter had to be done in such a way that he might shift some part of the blame onto Grenwell, which he hoped his brother would not take badly, out of his fraternal charity. For since everyone now knew that I knew the matter, my knowledge had to be traced to some source. It could not be from the lay conspirators, since I had often and openly protested, both by word and in writing, that I would never betray them. Second, the confessions of many had come into his hands, and all of them, having been examined, accused Grenwell and me. Third, I therefore thought it advisable to confess about him, so that I might excuse both myself and him at once; neither of us (namely) liked that plan. You see how these things were arranged by agreement; you see whence this new story about Grenwell and his confession arose. But this would have been nothing, and another invented story would have had to be devised for him, had he not, by mistake, thought Grenwell was in chains, and greatly feared that Grenwell would take the initiative in confessing first and, by some confession of his own, put the matter (as it was) in the open, and so they would deal more harshly with him. Hence those wavering moves of his: "He confessed," "Perhaps he did not confess," "Perhaps he had no intention of confessing," "I do not dare to affirm that that confession took place."

units.la: Verùm, si vel maximè detur (quod tu maximè vis) Confessionem nem fuisse illam, at non alia lege admisit eam Garnettus vel audire voluit, quàm vt ei integrum esset eam reuelare, si quæstio de conuincendo haberetur; atque hoc præ se tulisse, tenerí nolle se ad retinenda ea, quæ tum Grenwellus narrabat, apud Superiores suos, siquando eâ de re in quæstionem venirent. Cautum enim hoc à se, scripto eius habetur ad Grenwellum ipsum: atque ita, eâ cautione, Sigilli vim omnem enervauit. Nam libertatem illi enunciare rem omnem, qui ius sibi fecerat ac libertatem eius enunciandæ.
units.tr: But even if it is granted (as you especially wish) that there was such a confession, Garnet did not admit it, nor did he wish to hear it, except on this condition: that it should be entirely open to him to reveal it, if a question about convicting him should arise; and he made it plain that he did not wish to be bound to keep those things secret, which Grenwell was then telling, from his superiors, should the matter ever come into question with them. For this caution on his part is found in his writing to Grenwell himself; and so, by this caution, he drained all the force of the seal. For he had granted himself the freedom to declare the whole matter, and that freedom of declaring it he had secured for himself.

units.la: At bona illa exhortatio quam dicis ab Vrbe tum transmissam, vt continerent se ab omni tumultu, vetus ea techna est, sæpe quidem detecta, ac proin semper suspecta: vt non alio magis tempore scribant inde Pontifices in eum finem, quàm cum maleficium maximè meditantur. Mulcere sic volunt Argos nostros, vt sibi ipsis dicant, pax & tuta omnia, quo sic repentina clades irruat in vos, nil tale suspicantes. Non erat certè, cur Monitionem illam nominares, quæ nobis pranuncia est procellæ certò tum semper imminentis. Quin & alia tum erat Monitionis huius ratio: Tam enim placuit, tam certæ spei erat Negotium hoc de Pulvere, vt nollent interturbari illud tumultu vllo, iuberent verò quiescere alios omnes, vt huic vni locus esset, in quo reposita illis spes omnis.
units.tr: As for that good exhortation which you say was then sent from the City, that they should restrain themselves from all tumult, this is an old trick, often detected, and therefore always suspected: Popes write thus to that end at no other time more than when they are most intent on some wickedness. They wish to soothe our people so that they may say to themselves, "All is peace and safety," so that a sudden disaster may fall upon you, suspecting nothing of the kind. There was certainly no reason for you to call that admonition a warning, since it was then always the sure forerunner of a storm about to come. Moreover, there was another reason for that admonition at the time: so certain and so well-pleasing was this business of the gunpowder, and so firm was their hope in it, that they did not want it disturbed by any tumult, but they ordered all the others to be quiet, so that there might be room for this one thing alone, in which all their hope was placed.

units.la: Videamus iam paucis de Garnetto, quidque illo in Publico Iudicio in rem vestram suamue dixerit. Fassus ibi primò, quod negare non potuit, responsione suâ, de tollendis simul innoxijs noxijs, Catisbeio consilium suum confirmasse, prolicito, atque ita animos addixisse, authoremque fuisse sceleris adeundi. Ex eoque responso eius, fontem post extitisse malorum omnium. Quicquid inde extructum, hac basi nixum: quisquis post pertractus in Coniurationem, hac Authoritate pertractus est. Fassus etiam, se ex illa Catisbeij quæstione suspicatum esse, monstri quid alteri Catisbeium, ac, in Generalem de factionis toto notitiam, extra confessionem venisse. Prætereà cùm idem post Catisbeium monstri vnum illud suum monstrare ei, atque rem totam speciatim enarrare vellet, deprecatum esse se. Potuit autem, quod suspicatus erat, certò scire tum: hisi & ipse monstrum illud alij etiam, quàm tellì maluisset. Fassus, egisse cum Catisbeio, ne Pontifice inconsulto procedere vellet: Ad quid verò procedere, nisi aliquid ei tum innotuisset? Actum etiam cum Catesbeio de Pontifice consensu impetrando. Consensu autem quam ad rem? Admodum se cautum fuisse semper, ne intentionem Conjuratorum probari sibi quisquam eorum existimare posset. Quam vero intentionem? Misisse pro rei successu prospero iam tum initio Parlamenti peragenda. Atque haec quidem omnia extra Confessionem. Scriptae etiam ab eo tum Garnetto suo Literae, in quibus spem bonam sibi dixit superesse, depulsurum se satis commodè accusationem de Pulveraria proditione, atque evasurum, eo quod defecturi essent in probatione: In probatione, dixit non enim dicere potuit, in rei veritate. Agnosce autem has eius pro Tribunali voces, in Publico Iudicio. Confessionem: Se plura admisisse, quam quibus diluendis iustam aliquam posset excusationem affingere. Petitionem alio loco, qua laesae Conscientiae perfossus stimulo, Deum & Regem supplex orat, ne cum Catholicorum reliquis suam unius ob noxam asperius ageretur. Votum etiam, ex abrupto, cum commotus esset, (ut videtur) vehementius: Vtinam vero Conjurationis huius subminimis negotium, mihi haud unquam innotuisset. Credo vel voces hae, vocis quamvis anari hominis satis esse posse, ut docebant Garnetti ad facinus illud, notitiam atque consensum interveniisse.
units.tr: Let us now see, in a few words, about Garnet, and what he said in that public trial concerning your affair or his own. There he first confessed what he could not deny: that by his answer, concerning the removal of the innocent together with the guilty, he had confirmed Catesby's plan, by approving it, and so had won over their minds, and had been the author of the crime to be undertaken. From that answer of his, a source of all the evils arose afterwards: whatever was built upon it, rested on this foundation; whoever was afterwards drawn into the conspiracy, was drawn in by this authority. He also confessed that, from that examination of Catesby, he had suspected that Catesby had revealed some monstrous thing to another, and had come, outside confession, to a general knowledge of the whole plot. Furthermore, when afterwards Catesby wished to show him that one monstrous thing of his own and to relate the whole matter in detail, he begged to be spared. He could, however, know for certain what he then suspected, unless he himself had preferred that monstrous thing to be concealed from others too. He confessed that he had dealt with Catesby, so that he should not proceed without the Pope's knowledge: but to proceed to what, unless something had then been made known to him? He also dealt with Catesby about obtaining the Pope's consent. But consent to what? He had always been very careful that no one of them could think his intention had been approved by him. But what intention? That he had sent for the successful outcome of the thing to be carried out already at the very beginning of Parliament. And all these things were outside confession. Also written by him at that time to his Garnet were letters in which he said that a good hope remained for him, that he would fend off with sufficient ease the accusation of the gunpowder treason, and would escape, because they would fail in the proof: in the proof, he said, for he could not say in the truth of the matter. Note, moreover, these words of his before the tribunal, in the public trial. The confession: that he had admitted more than he could meet with any just excuse. In another place, his petition, in which, pierced by the goad of a wounded conscience, he begs God and the King, as a suppliant, that his offence alone should not be treated more harshly than the rest of the Catholics. Also a vow, spoken suddenly, when he was moved (as it seems) more vehemently: "Would that the least part of this conspiracy had never come to my knowledge." I believe that these utterances, even though they are the words of a man of the most ordinary sort, may be enough to show, as the writings of Garnet also taught, that knowledge and consent intervened in that crime.

units.la: Instante autem post mortem, narrat Tortus quid fecerit; Longam orationem habuit. Nec id verè: non enim sanè longam. In eâ fidem Catholicam professus: & haereses Anglicanas liberrimè detestatus est. Neutrum verum. Eâdem libertate negavit, se Authorem, Complicem, Consultorem, aut ullo modo Consentientem Sceleris fuisse: Imò verò apertè fassus est, peccasse se, bis peccasse, Rem enim in genere se à Catesbeio intellexisse, & in hoc peccasse, quòd tum celaverit, tum prevertere neglexerit.
units.tr: Then, as the execution drew near, Tortus relates what he did. "He made a long speech." That is not really true; it was not long at all. "In it he professed the Catholic faith and freely renounced the Anglican heresies." Neither is true. With the same frankness he denied that he had been the author, accomplice, adviser, or in any way a consenting party to the crime. Indeed he openly confessed that he had sinned, had sinned twice: "For I understood the matter in general from Catesby, and I sinned in this, that I both concealed it and neglected to forestall it."

units.la: Cùm verò etiam tum subjicere vellet Garnettus, reliqua illa proditionis particularia, in confessione se à Grenwello habuisse, nevocabatur illi in mentem Henricus Montague, Eques illustris, qui Civitati Londinensi à Memoriâ est, qui qui autographum eius tum penes se habebat in promptu, Quatuor ista. Primò, Grenwellum illi rem significasse, non ut peccatum, sed quam ipse prius intellexerat, idq; consulendi gratiâ. Secundò, Catesbeium & Grenwellum, ipsum simul accessisse, ut in scelere suscepto confirmarentur. Tertiò, Grenwellum atq; Ipsum, Colloquium de particularibus in Proditione illâ per Pulverem Fulminalem, satis longo post tempore in Essexiâ habuisse. Quartò, Grenwellum percontatum esse à Garnetto, quis Regni Protector futurus esset; Garnettumque ei respondisse, id differendum esse, donec res esset acta & transacta. Ex quatuor hijs euinci, scelera illa aliunde quàm ex confessione, illi comperta fuisse: Hacque ipsa manu ipsius haberi consignata. Ad ea Garnettus: Quicquid sub manu suâ consignatum esset, verum esse. Secundò autem, Quòd, quæ sibi comperta, Regia Maiestati non aperuisset, mortis sententiam iustissimè in se pronunciatam, veniámque à Regiâ Maiestate precatus est. Tertiò verò ad populum conuersus, iterum se in Regem peccâsse confitetur, idque sibi dolori esse, quòd malè conscius fuisset, scilicet reticendo; & eo nomine veniam à Regiâ Maiestate iterum supplex petiit. Aduerte lector animum ad hæc; Ter confessum videbis Peccâsse se, quòd celâsset; Peccâsse etiam quòd præuertere neglexisset; Iustissimè se Capitis damnatum quod non aperuisset; Peccâse[?] quòd malè conscius fuisset, idque reticendo; Ter peccati veniam petijse. Quin & apud Annam suam, (apud quam æquiuocè nunquam, candidè semper animum eloqui solebat, & in cuius sinu omnia deponere) per literas, quæ etiamnum extant, vicem suam doluit, quòd non propter Religionem iam, sed Proditionem sibi tanquam Latroni moriendum esset. Et tamen audet Tortus contra conscientiam propriam, & contra testimonium multorum millium hominum, qui spectaculo interfuerunt, dicere, eum mortuum esse in abnegatione facinoris. Quod ille Spectaculum cur crudelissimum dicat, ne ipse quidem, credo, dixerit. Nec enim in eo factum quod ex legis sententiâ fieri debuit: Nihil enim semiuiuus pertulit. Emortui cadauer dissectum modò: Hoc námque iure utimur in eos qui proditionis damnati. Quæ verò hîc crudelitas fuit, cùm multò mitior fuerit pœna, quam Lex ipsa postulabat? Multò autem adhuc minùs crudelis spectaculum, quàm quæ Roma apud vos subinde conspiciuntur.
units.tr: When Garnet was about to add the remaining particulars of the treason which he had heard in confession from Greenwell, there came to mind Henry Montague, an illustrious knight, who is Recorder of the City of London, and who had Garnet's autograph statement ready at hand at that time. "These four things": First, Greenwell signified the matter to him, not as a sin, but as something he had himself previously understood, and this for the purpose of seeking counsel. Second, Catesby and Greenwell came to him together, so that they might be confirmed in the crime they had undertaken. Third, "Greenwell and he himself held a conversation about the particulars of that treason by gunpowder, a fairly long time afterwards, in Essex." Fourth, Greenwell asked Garnet who would be the Protector of the kingdom, and Garnet replied that this was to be deferred until the matter was done and finished. "From these four points it is proved that those crimes were known to him from some source other than the confession, and that this is recorded under his own hand." To these things Garnet replied: "Whatever was recorded under his hand is true." Second, however, that what had been known to him he had not disclosed to His Royal Majesty, he begged for the sentence of death, which had been most justly pronounced against him, and pardon from His Royal Majesty. Third, turning to the people, he again confesses that he has sinned against the King, and that it grieves him that he was privy to the matter and kept silent; and on that account he again humbly sought pardon from His Royal Majesty. Note, reader, his mind on these matters: you will see that he confessed three times that he had sinned in concealing; that he had sinned also in neglecting to forestall; that he was most justly condemned to death because he had not disclosed; that he had sinned in being privy to the matter and keeping silent about it; and three times he sought pardon for his sin. Moreover, in letters, which still survive, he lamented his lot to his Anne (to whom he was never equivocal, but always spoke his mind candidly, and in whose bosom he laid down everything), "that he now had to die not for religion, but as a thief for treason." And yet Tortus dares, against his own conscience and against the testimony of many thousands of men who were present at the spectacle, to say that he died in denial of the crime. Why he calls that spectacle "most cruel," I think not even he himself could say. For nothing was done there except what ought to be done by the sentence of the law: he suffered nothing while half-alive; only the body of the dead man was dissected, for this is the law we use against those condemned for treason. And what cruelty was there here, when the punishment was far milder than the law itself demanded? Indeed, a spectacle far less cruel than those which are from time to time displayed among you at Rome.

units.la: Dedetestatione quod dicis, verè quidem, Dixit enim, bis dixit: Semel, Consilium sceleratum, & susceptum scelus fuisse immane, atque huiusmodi, ut si peractum fuisset, non potuisset ipse[?]: non ex intimis sensibus totoque animo detestari. Iterum, dolere se maximè & peracerbè ferre, Catholicos tam atrox & immane facinus unquam suscepisse. Verè ego dixti, mortuus est in detestatione facinoris. At etiam cùm mutire vellet de Confessione nonnihil, admonitus de autographo suo, statim subticuit, nec abnegavit pòst quicquam. Professio autem fidei, quam dixti, haereseos detestatio haud vlla. Quicquid enim à Detestatione Facinoris reliquum erat temporis, id totum consumptum est, in purgatione suâ, & foeminae cuiusdam, de quâ male audiebat. Atque haec veraeorum Summa, quae instante morte ab illius ore excepta sunt, eáque pòst Edita, dein Versa in Latinum, Excusa Typis extant. Alia si tu, si quisquam orbi venditet, scito non in Authorem Apologiae, sed in vos quadrare tuum illud, Tam stolida à vobis mendacia, sine vllo testimonio, vel probatione congerit, vt necesse sit, vos omnem omnino pudorem & conscientiam exuisse.
units.tr: As to the detestation which you speak of, it is true indeed: for he did say, and said twice: "Once, that the plot was wicked and the crime undertaken was so monstrous, and of such a kind that, had it been carried out, he could not...; not from his innermost feelings and with his whole soul to detest it. Again, that he grieved most bitterly and bore it hard that Catholics had ever undertaken so atrocious and monstrous a crime." Truly, I said that he died in detestation of the crime. But also, when he wished to say something more about the confession, having been reminded of his autograph, he at once fell silent, and afterwards denied nothing. But a profession of faith, which you mention, and a detestation of heresy, there was none at all. For whatever time remained after his detestation of the crime was all spent in his vindication and in that of a certain woman, about whom he was being ill spoken of. And these are the true contents of what was taken down from his lips at the approach of death, and which, after being published, then translated into Latin, exist in print. If you, or anyone, should sell to the world other things, know that your saying, "Such lies are heaped up by you, without any testimony or proof, that you must necessarily have cast off all shame and conscience," applies not to the author of the Apology, but to you.

units.la: Ex ijs, quae iam dicta mihi, si nihil etiam quis addat, constat opinor, serò nimis te Sigilli vestri meminisse. Qui Terna vice confessus, Peccasse se quod Facinus celasset: Morte iustissimâ mulctatum, quod non aperuisset: Peccasse quod male conscius suisset: Qui Ter huius admissi veniam supplicitèr rogavit; aliter rem certè rescierat quàm ex Confessione. Nullum enim, quae sic inaudiuit celare, peccatum, imò peccatum non celare, & peccatum apud vos graue. Non debuit peccatum confiteri, non veniam petere eius, in quo non peccâsset. Non peccauit Sigillum non violando, propter quod tu (ob non violatum Sacramentum diuinum) capiti eius Martyrij Coronam induis. Verùm erras, Matthae, erras. Durum est contra stimulum calcare & laesa illi conscientia. Non de nihilo erat, quòd Semel, Iterum, Tertiò peccasse se testatus, & veniam orare. Dictamen id erat conscientiae: Illa accusante, frustra defensionem paras, Illa veniam petente, frustra Martyrem acclamas.
units.tr: From what has already been said to me, even if no one adds anything, it is clear, I think, that you remembered your seal far too late. He who confessed three times, that he had sinned in concealing a crime, that he had been punished with a most just death for not disclosing it, that he had sinned in being privy to it, and who three times humbly asked pardon for this offence, had certainly come to know the matter by some means other than the confession. For there is no sin in concealing what one has heard in such a way; nay, there is a sin in not concealing it, and a grave sin among you. He ought not to have confessed a sin, nor to seek pardon for that in which he had not sinned. The seal was not sinned against by not violating it; for which reason you, on account of the divine sacrament not being violated, place upon his head the crown of martyrdom. But you are wrong, Matthew, you are wrong. It is hard to kick against the goad, and his wounded conscience. It was not for nothing that he testified, "Once, a second time, a third time," that he had sinned, and begged pardon. That was the dictate of conscience: while it accuses, you prepare a defence in vain; while it begs pardon, you cry out in vain that he is a martyr.

units.la: Conuictus ergo est in Publico Iudicio, Confessus in vltimo Supplicio, nec tu dehinc iam negabis: vt nec Bibliopola Bernardus, qui cùm perpotâsset alicubi ad vesperam, ausus in Praefatione suâ conscribellare, Garnettum nescio qui, falso proditionis Anglicanae rumore asperserant; sumptâ, vt par erat, de liquidis similitudine. Scias verò tu, sciat & ille, vbi villum edormijt siccus iam & sobrius, non falso aliquo rumore Garnettum, sed veritatis voce & vi, Tabularum, Testium, Probationum luce, soliditate, pondere conuictum, ore proprio, manu propriâ confessum. Conuiciùm autem & confessum coram Consessu Honorario, summâ hominum Frequentiâ, Loco non minùs Celebri, quàm Camera vestra Imperialis: vbi rumori locus non est.
