units.tr: He was therefore convicted in public judgment, and confessed at the last punishment, and you will not deny it from now on: nor will the bookseller Bernard, who, having drunk deeply somewhere towards evening, dared to scribble in his Preface that "Garnet had been besmirched by I know not whom, by a false rumour of an English treason"; taking, as was fitting, a likeness from liquids. But you ought to know, and he too should know, that when he has slept off his drink, now sober and clear-headed, Garnet was convicted not by some false rumour, but by the voice and force of truth, by the light, solidity and weight of records, witnesses and proofs, and confessed with his own mouth and by his own hand. And the conviction and confession took place before an honourable assembly, with a great crowd of people, in a place no less celebrated than your Imperial Chamber, where there is no room for rumour.

units.la: Ibi [?]Aelio tum in eo instituta, in quâ, prolixè & diù, quamdiu quidem voluit ipse, causam dixit, si potuisset excutere aspergines illas. At ille,miser, non potuit. Non enim leuiter aspersus (natabant tum oculi Bernardo) sed penitus immersus Puteo ipsi Proditionis, Etiam Putei Profundo.
units.tr: There, at that time, in the trial instituted against him, in which he pleaded his cause at length and for as long as he himself wished, he could have shaken off those splashes, if he had been able. But that poor man could not. For he was not lightly splashed (Bernard's eyes were then swimming), but was utterly immersed in the very pit of treason, even in its deepest depth.

units.la: At de quibus sic dicit Nescio qui, homo stolidus sciat si volet, Qui & Quanti fuerint. Quinque enim Comites Illustrisimi, omnes Nobilitatis, Iustitiæ, Prudentiæ laude præstantes, Actioni præfuerunt: Qui & Assessores habebant, præter Vrbanum Prætorem, Primarios tres Regni Iudices, Iuris hic nostri prudentisimos, coram quibus Duodecimvirali inquisitione renunciatus est Reus. Tam verò enucleata in eo fuit Eorum sententia, vt in Comitijs post Regni,&Senatu,quo Sol Illustriorem non aspicit, vim Legis acceperit.
units.tr: But as for those of whom this I know not who speaks, let the foolish man know, if he will, who and how great they were. For five most illustrious counts, all surpassing in the praise of nobility, justice and prudence, presided over the proceedings; and they had assessors, besides the City Praetor, three chief judges of the kingdom, most learned here in our law, before whom the accused was declared guilty by a twelve-man inquiry. And their sentence was so clearly set out that, in the parliament after the kingdom and the Senate, upon which the sun does not look more illustrious, it received the force of law.

units.la: Et iste tamen nescio quis, Coloniensis homo nihili, audet sic Iustitiam Regni.Publicam traducere: Et aspersum modò dicere rumore, à nescio quibus: aspersus ipsè,credo,tum,imò perfusus humore aliquo, vt verè tum quidem nesciret qui, etiam, audeo dicere, nesciret quid scriberet.
units.tr: And yet this I know not who, a Cologne man of no account, dares thus to slander the public justice of the kingdom: and to say that Garnet was besmirched just now by rumour, from I know not whom; he himself, I believe, was then not merely splashed but drenched with some liquid, so that, truly, at that time he did not know who, and, I dare say, did not even know what he was writing.

units.la: Quod si neque conuiciùs neque confessus, quare capitis damnatus? Tantum inquis, quia Sigillum illæsum feruare voluit consitentis. Respondè sodes. Duo tantùm erant conscij, Titius & Titij Sodalis: Is qui, Is cui confessus est. Is qui confessus, comprehensus non est, proripuit se in pedes, abijt, euasit. Ille ergo nullus reuelauit. Quis iam reuelare alius potuit, quod sub Sigillo erat, nisi Is cui confessus erat: Is autem erat Garnettus,Titius ipse[?]. Solue verò nodum hunc. Qui potuit mortem oppetere pro eo, quod reuelatum non est? Non est enim reuelatum nisi si ab ipso fuit. Nam ab altero non fuit: tertius autem præter duos hos, nemo resciuit rem. Sic ergo se veritas habet: Mortuus est, quia Sigillum fregit, quia reuelauit,&vel te Iudice, optimo iure mortuus, qui tantum in se scelus, & vix morte piandum admisit, vt Sigillum violaret. Dic verò miram illam versutiam. Mira enim profecto erat, quâ quis cognoscere potuit de Confessione, quam solus Garnettus audierat, Garnetto ipso non revelante. Vides, quàm hæc à te posita, parum cautè. Verè enim omnino dictum ab Illustrissimo Comite, qui tum erat unus in Consessu Judicum; Confessionis secretum, quod prius detegere noluit Garnettus in alienam perniciem, post detexisse in suam: in eóque responsionem friuolam & futilem tum ab Illo, iam à vobis adhiberi. Friuolum enim & futile, si quis dicat, quod tu tamen ut dicas, necesse iam habes, Garnettum, qui ipse revelauit, ideo capitis damnatum, quia revelare noluit. Revelauit enim ipse, nec alius præter eum quisquam, quod præter ipsum nemo si maximè vellet, potuit revelare. Credo equidem subridere Nostrates, qui apud vos sunt, quod rem hanc ita sedulo agamus, ut constet conscium fuisse Garnettum: quibus ea res iamdudum notissima. Quin Mulierculæ ipsæ rem rescibant; &, Quò tandem nos duos recipiemus interim, dum pertransierit procella hæc, aiebat Garnetto suo, Anna sua? Ita Garnettus manu propria scripsit, ita videas licet in Ipsius autographo. An & Domina Anna confessionem Jesuitæ alicuius exceperat subSigillo, cui res ita perspecta? aut tu cuiquam ut persuadeas, quæ nec Mulierculis ipsis ignota erant; ea Garnetto ipsi nota non fuisse?
units.tr: But if he was neither convicted nor confessed, why was he condemned to death? You say only that it was because he wished to keep inviolate the seal of the one confessing. Pray answer. There were only two who knew the matter, Titius and the comrade of Titius: he who confessed and he to whom the confession was made. He who confessed was not seized; he took to his heels, went away, and escaped. He, therefore, revealed nothing. Who else could have revealed what was under the seal, except he to whom the confession was made? And he was Garnet, Titius himself [?]. Now untie this knot for me. How could he have suffered death for what was not revealed? For it was not revealed unless it was revealed by himself. For it was not revealed by another; and no third person apart from these two came to know the matter. So then the truth stands thus: he died because he broke the seal, because he revealed it; and, even by your judgment, he rightly died, who committed so great a crime, scarcely expiable by death, as to violate the seal. But tell us that wonderful cunning! For it would indeed be wonderful, by which anyone could come to know of a confession which only Garnet had heard, without Garnet himself revealing it. You see how carelessly these things were put forward by you. For it was truly said by the most illustrious count, who was then one of the judges in the court: "The secret of the confession, which Garnet was unwilling first to disclose to another's destruction, he afterwards disclosed to his own." And in that respect the reply, frivolous and trifling, was then employed by that man, and now by you. For it would be frivolous and trifling if someone were to say, which you nevertheless now of necessity have to say, that Garnet, who himself revealed it, was therefore condemned to death because he was unwilling to reveal it. For he did reveal it himself, and no one else but him could reveal what, apart from himself, no one, even if he wished most of all, could have revealed. I believe indeed that our countrymen who are among you smile that we pursue this matter so diligently, so as to establish that Garnet was privy to it: a thing well known to them for a long time. Indeed, the little women themselves knew the matter; and what did his Anne say to Garnet, "Where at last shall we two take refuge meanwhile, until this storm has passed?" So Garnet wrote with his own hand, and so you may see it in his autograph. Or did Mistress Anne too receive the confession of some Jesuit under the seal, she to whom the matter was so thoroughly known? Or can you persuade anyone that things which were not unknown even to the little women themselves were unknown to Garnet himself?

units.la: Sed & minuendus error est de Sigillo: Catholica doctrina (inquis) non permittit ad ullum malum vitandum Secretum Consessionis detegi. Non permittit? Quare non? Ne si id permissum fit, odiosa fiat confessio. Odiosa ne? Caue verò ne contrà odiosa magis fiat, si tegat, si foveat in sinu scelera talia, tam & odiosa, & perniciosa. Odiosa facta est olim & sublata sub Nesario, dum leuius multò scelus occultaret. Idem ipsum denuò ne contingat cauendum vobis: si non permittat Catholica vestra doctrina, tam infandum Scelus, (ut auerti possit maturè) in cognitionem venire. Non enim semel eâ de re Garnetto & Grenwello, quin nescio quàm sæpe, sermo illis fuerat. Nec hoc Garnettus negabat, sed quantumuis id sæpe factum, factum semper, sub virtuali nescio quâ ad primam illam relationem; eaque relatio, si vel centies de eâ egissent inter se, effecit, ut semper scilicet esset Sacramenti Secretum. Quodsi sic liceat inter se Scelera versare Confessario & Confitenti, ut, etsi vera tum Confessio nulla sit, tamen id satis sit, si relatio habeatur ad aliquam vel ante factam confessionem, vel post faciendam; quæ melior vsquam Sceleri Latebra? Cui enim id dicere non licebit; Extra confessionem rem audiui, & sæpe quidem: verùm aliqua tamen fuit inter nos relatio ad confessionem, vel aliquam quæ tum antegressa, vel saltem aliquam quæ post aliquando, subsecutura esset.
units.tr: But the error about the seal should also be lessened. "Catholic doctrine" (you say) "does not permit the secret of confession to be disclosed to avoid any evil." Does it not permit? Why not? Lest, if this were permitted, confession would become hateful. Hateful? Take care rather that it not become more hateful if it covers and fosters in its bosom such crimes, as hateful and as pernicious. Confession once became hateful and was abolished under Nectarius, when it was concealing a much lighter crime. You must take care that the same thing does not happen again: if your Catholic doctrine does not permit such an unspeakable crime to come to light, it cannot be averted in time. For Garnet and Greenwell had talked about this matter together, I do not know how often. Garnet did not deny it, but however often it was done, it was always done under some "virtual" reference to that first relation; and that relation, even if they had discussed it a hundred times between themselves, produced the effect that it was always the secret of a sacrament. If it is thus permitted for a confessor and a penitent to turn crimes over between themselves, so that, even though no true confession has taken place, it is enough if there is a reference to some confession either made before or to be made afterwards, what better hiding place could there be for a crime? For who would not be allowed to say: "I heard the matter outside confession, and often indeed; but there was nevertheless some reference between us to confession, either to one that had gone before, or at least to one that would sometime follow afterwards."

units.la: Sed instas tamen, Nec permittit (ais) hoc Catholica doctrina. Nusquámne gentium? In Gallia permittit certè. Námque ibi cum è Neustriâ Vir Nobilis Fratri Minori confessus esset, aliquando in animo sibi fuisse, vt Regem Franciscum occideret, pœnituisse autem se illius consilij: cumque data illi pœnitentiâ à Fratre, absolutus esset; Frater rem reticere noluit, Regi indicauit. Re ipsâ à Rege ad Senatum Parisiensem delatâ, quæstio de re tota habita est. Reus comprehensus supplicio vltimo affectus est: Fratri autem intentata nec Censura, nec Lis vlla. Nec est quòd dicas, timuisse sibi Senatum, à Rege; proinde voluntati eius licet minùs iustæ, parùisse. Notum enim non cadere in Senatum illum suspicionem eam, vt cui non infrequens sit, missa ad se, vel Edicta ipsa Regia, nisi sibi probentur, sæpe non exequi.
units.tr: But you press on: "Catholic doctrine does not permit this," you say. Nowhere in the world? It certainly permits it in France. For there, when a nobleman had confessed to a Franciscan friar that at some time he had intended to kill King Francis, but that he had repented of that plan; and when, having been given penance by the friar, he had been absolved, the friar did not wish to keep the matter silent and reported it to the King. The matter having been referred by the King to the Parliament of Paris, a full inquiry was held into the whole affair. The accused was arrested and put to the death penalty; but no censure or lawsuit was brought against the friar. Nor can you say that the Parliament feared the King and therefore obeyed his will, however unjust. For it is well known that that court does not fall under such suspicion, since royal edicts sent to it, often enough, are not carried out unless they are approved by the court itself.

units.la: Nec id solùm, sed & è Curia etiam Parisiensis Archiuis constat, capite multatum etiam {a}Dominum de Haulteuille, cùm denuò conualuisset, postquam moribundus, in Sacramento, reuelâsset Confessario suo intentionem sibi aliquando fuisse Regis de medio tollendi. Eam tamen rem constat post à Confessario patefactam, fuisse Domino illi capitalem.
units.tr: Not only this, but it is also established from the archives of the Parisian Court that Lord de Haulteville, too, was put to death, when, after he had recovered from a serious illness, he had revealed to his confessor, in the sacrament, while on his deathbed, that at one time he had intended to remove the King. It is nonetheless established that this matter, afterwards disclosed by the confessor, was a capital offence for that lord.

units.la: Tum quod recenti adhuc memoriâ est, {b}Petri Barierij supplicium vltimum, qui Meluni fractus in Rotâ, sententiam in Eum ferente Hospitij Regij Præposito. Is Lugduni, Fratri cuidam Iacobino (cui nomen Seraphino Banchi) propositum suum de nece Regiâ procurandâ, Sacramentaliter confessus est; nec vt mentem mutaret, à Fratre illo adduci potuit. Regis ergo Secretario, Seraphinus rem refert: Barierius in ludicio Publico damnatus, ad Supplicium tractus est. Permittit ergo, quæ in Gallia est, Catholica doctrina, vt ad Regis internecionem deuitandam, Sigillum resignare liceat. Quidni idem hoc liceat in Britanniâ nostra? Saltem Catholica hæc doctrina, vbique non valer, valet, ac proinde neq; Catholica est. Verùm res tota in opinione est. Quidam tetrici magis sunt: nonnulli sunt aquatores, quibus totum hoc reuelare, incasu non displicet: aut vt fidem quis Principi & Patria maiorem debeat, quàm Confitenti. Vera quidem omninò fuit illa Garnetti vox, Vltrò fateor, Leges quae celare haec prohibent apprimè esse iustas & salutares. Neque enim aequum est vt Principis salus ab alterius conscientia pendere debeat.
units.tr: Then there is the recent case of the execution of Pierre Barrière, who was broken on the wheel at Melun, the sentence being pronounced against him by the Provost of the Royal Household. At Lyons he had sincerely confessed to a certain Jacobin friar, named Seraphino Banchi, his purpose of procuring the king's death; nor could he be brought by that friar to change his mind. The Seraphinus reported the matter to the king's secretary; Barrière was condemned in public judgment and dragged to execution. Therefore the Catholic doctrine that prevails in France permits, in order to avert the destruction of the King, that the seal may be given up. Why should the same not be permitted in our Britain? At least this Catholic doctrine, which does not hold everywhere, holds in some places, and therefore is not Catholic. But the whole matter is a matter of opinion. Some are more severe; some are laxer, to whom it is not displeasing to reveal all this in case of need; or [they hold] that a man ought to owe more faith to the Prince and the country than to the penitent. Truly, Garnet's words were entirely correct: "I freely confess that the laws which forbid these things to be concealed are most just and salutary. For it is not fair that the safety of the Prince should depend on another's conscience."

units.la: Recte verò tu: Non permittit dicis Catholica doctrina, crimen vllum in Confessione reuelatum detegi. Non iam forte permittit, at permisit olim. Olim, quis nescit carmen—Haeresis est crimen, quod nec confessio celat.— Nec maior ratio certè est, cur non deberet celari Haeresis, quàm cur non Proditio tam Immanis. Sed olim permisit Catholica doctrina, in crimine quidem nondum Commissio, sed Committendo: praesertim (vt cum Scholâ loquar) Si Inconueniens inde Graue sequeretur. Sequebatur autem in vestro Gravissimum, & fuit illud inter Committenda Sic olim {a}Halensis noster, ex quo sciasquid hic Catholica doctrina permiserit apud Nos. Potest quis confiteri peccatum, non tamen vt praesens, sed potiùs vt est in proposito, de futuro, vt cùm dicit se velle fornicari, & nolle desistere. Dico ergo quòd non tenetur celare simpliciter, nec si Sacerdos talem Confessionem reuelaret, posset condemnari tanquam violator Sigilli confessionis: tamen quia hoc species esset mali, & infamia sequeretur, propter hoc credo, etsi non tenetur de iure talem confessionem occultare, debet tamen celare ratione publicae honestatis, nisi Inconueniens aliquod Graue sequeretur. Tunc enim credo, quod non esset confessio talis penitus tacenda, nec tamen publicè reuelanda propter periculum infamiae, sed cautè & secretò alicui qui posset & vellet prodesse innotescenda. Nec ea vnius Halensis mens, eadem & apud Italos vestros. Sic {b}Angelus. Quando quis confitetur, se velle facere aliquod malum, istud non est dictum in Poenitentiali Foro, & ideo propter rationem istius Sacramenti, non tenetur celare; sed quando peccatum committendum vergeret in periculum Communitatis, credo sine praeiudicio, quòd non solum potest, imò tenetur reuelare, ei qui potest prodesse, & vult non obesse, vt malo obuiatur. Eadem {c}Siluestri, qui Magister fuit Palatij Papalis. Licet reuelare Secretum Confessionis, si quis confitetur se velle facere aliquod malum, puta homicidium, quia istud non est dictum in Poenitentiali Foro.
units.tr: You rightly say, however: "Catholic doctrine, you say, does not permit any crime revealed in confession to be disclosed." Perhaps it does not permit it now, but it did permit it once. Once, who does not know the verse: "It is a crime, which even confession does not conceal, to be a heretic." Nor is there surely any greater reason why heresy should not be concealed than why treason so monstrous should not be. But Catholic doctrine once permitted it, in the case of a crime not yet committed but about to be committed: especially (to speak with the Schoolmen) "if some serious inconvenience would follow from it." Now in your case the most serious inconvenience would follow, and this was among the things about to be committed. So once our Alexander of Hales [said], from which you may know what Catholic doctrine has permitted among us here. Someone may confess a sin not as present, but rather as intended, of the future, as when he says that he wishes to commit fornication and is unwilling to desist. "I say, therefore, that he is not bound to conceal it absolutely, nor could a priest who revealed such a confession be condemned as a violator of the seal of confession; yet because this would be the appearance of evil and infamy would follow, for this reason I believe that, although by law he is not bound to hide such a confession, he ought nevertheless to conceal it for the sake of public decency, unless some serious inconvenience would follow." For then I believe that such a confession should not be entirely concealed, nor yet publicly revealed on account of the danger of infamy, but should be made known carefully and secretly to someone who could and would be of help. Nor is this the opinion of Alexander of Hales alone; it is the same among your Italians. Thus [says] Angelus: "When someone confesses that he wishes to do some evil, this is not said in the penitential forum, and therefore, on account of the nature of this sacrament, he is not bound to conceal it; but when a sin about to be committed tends to the danger of the community, I believe, without prejudice, that he not only may, but is bound to reveal it to one who can help and is willing not to harm, so that the evil may be prevented." The same [says] Silvester, who was Master of the Papal Palace: "The secret of confession may be revealed if someone confesses that he wishes to do some evil, for instance a homicide, because this is not said in the penitential forum."

units.la: Quando autem peccatum committendum vergeret in damnum vel periculum Communitatis, vel etiam privatæ personæ tertiæ, non solum non tenetur celare, sed tenetur manifestare, si id potest commodè sine damno suo, & cum proximi utilitate & peccantis. Ex Panormitano autem acerrimi iudicij viro, unà scias, & quæ apud illum Catholica doctrina tum fuerit hàc de re, & verò etiam quæ apud Innocentium quartum Pontificem maximum, cuius Authoritati quis Tortus opponet suam? Ita enim a Panormitanus. Sed circa ultimam partem quæro. Quidam fuit confessus Sacerdoti, quòd intendebat interficere Sempronium, vel aliud maleficium committere, & non poterat abstinere; numquid Sacerdos peccet revelando? Innocentius inflat, & tandem concludit, Quod hoc peccatum non dicitur detectum in Poenitentiâ, tum quia non habet Contritionem, tum quia est peccatum Comittendum. Unde Sacerdos debet, quantum cautius potest, revelare, ut peccatum impeditur. Plures referre non libet, unum modò adijciam b Dominicum Sotum, qui rigidior est in Custodiâ Sigilli, at ille tamen sic. Veruntamen sunt qui fingunt se accedere ad Confessionem, & tamen non veniunt, quò se accusent & remedium postulent animæ suæ, sed ut Confessorem forte perverant, aut favorem aut auxilium petant in perpetrandis flagitijs, ut temporibus nostris usu venisse fertur quibusdam qui in Pontificem conspiraverunt, & huiusmodi peccata celanda non sunt, sed statim potiùs denuncianda, quod plurimum timendum est in crimine hæresis. Quod ante illum docuit Innocentius, Non creamus istos confiteri ut Ministris Dei, qui non ut pœniteant, sed ut consilium vel auxilium ab aliquo recipiant, dicunt eis peccatum suum: licèt dicant, Hoc dico tibi in Confessione vel Pœnitentiâ. Quia non est verum quod dicit, in Pœnitentiâ nec ut Dei Ministro, cum consilium animæ non requirat: Et tales bene sunt cogenâi [?] super præmissis ferre testimonium.
units.tr: "But when a sin about to be committed tends to the loss or danger of the community, or even of some private third person, he is not only not bound to conceal it, but is bound to disclose it, if he can do so conveniently without loss to himself, and with the advantage of the neighbour and of the sinner himself." From Panormitanus, a man of most acute judgment, you may also learn both what Catholic doctrine then was on this matter with him, and indeed also what it was with Innocent IV, the greatest Pontiff, against whose authority what Tortus would set his own? For thus Panormitanus [writes]: "But I ask about the last part. Someone confessed to a priest that he intended to kill Sempronius, or to commit some other misdeed, and could not refrain; may the priest sin by revealing it?" Innocent swells up, and finally concludes: "That this sin is not said to be disclosed in penance, both because he does not have contrition, and because it is a sin about to be committed. Hence the priest must, as cautiously as he can, reveal it, so that the sin may be prevented." I do not care to cite more; I will add only one, Dominicus Soto, who is stricter in guarding the seal, yet he too says thus: "Yet there are some who pretend to come to confession, and yet do not come in order to accuse themselves and seek a remedy for their soul, but so that they may perhaps pervert the confessor, or seek favour or help in perpetrating crimes, as is reported to have happened in our times with certain men who conspired against the Pontiff; and such sins are not to be concealed, but rather to be announced at once, which is most to be feared in the crime of heresy." Which Innocent taught before him: "We do not allow those to confess as ministers of God who do not come to repent, but to receive counsel or help from someone; they tell him their sin, saying: 'I tell you this in confession or penance.' For it is not true, what they say, that it is in penance, nor [is it said] as to a minister of God, since he does not seek counsel for the soul. And such people are rightly compelled to bear witness concerning the aforesaid matters."

units.la: Colligeam jam ista. Peccatum quod quis confitetur ut Perpetrandum, non spectat ad Pœnitentiale Forum; non cadit sub Sigillo: Hoc verò Perpetrandum tum fuit. Peccatum quod vergis in periculum Communitatis, celandum non est, sed revelandum: vergebat hoc in Periculum Maximum Communitatis Maximæ. Peccatum de quo non accusat sed Confitens, nec animæ remedium quærit, detegi potest. In hoc, accusatio nulla. Non ergò in Pænitentiâ dictum, vel vt Dei Ministro. Potuit ergo cogi ad ferendum de re totâ testimonium. Postremò, vna eadémque videtur ratio eorum, qui in Pontificem conspirauerant, atque Horum, nisi quòd interest multùm, & Grauior multo Horum, qui non in Regem solum, sed vnà cum Rege Sobolem Regiam, Sacrum Senatum, Cætum tam immensum, insontes tam multos, perniciem tam tetram machinati sunt. Præcipuè, si (vt Sotus) non eò venit, quòd se accusat Confessor, sed vt consilium petat vel auxilium. Id quod in hoc factum.
units.tr: I will now gather these points together. A sin that someone confesses as one still to be carried out does not belong to the penitential forum and does not fall under the seal. This sin, however, was still to be carried out. A sin that tends toward danger to the community must not be concealed but revealed; this one was tending toward the very greatest danger to the greatest community. A sin that the penitent confesses without accusing anyone, and without seeking a remedy for his soul, may be disclosed. In this case there is no accusation. Therefore it was not said in penance, nor to him as a minister of God. He could therefore be compelled to give testimony about the whole matter. Lastly, the reason of those who conspired against the Pope seems one and the same as that of these men, except that there is a great difference, and the guilt of these men is much graver, since they plotted not only against the King but, together with the King, against the royal offspring, the holy Senate, so immense an assembly, so many innocent people, and so foul a destruction. This is especially so if (as Soto holds) the confession was not made because the penitent accuses himself, but in order to seek counsel or aid. And that is what happened in this case.

units.la: Non enim eò venit Grenwellus quò se accusaret (ait hoc Garnettus) aut remedium postularet animæ suæ; sed consultandi (id est) consilij petendi gratiâ: Non vt crimen, quod reprehenderet, sed vt de exequendi ratione Garnettus ei, consilium adhiberet. Quid enim illæ sibi quæstiones volebant, cùm sæpè pòst, alter alteri obuius esset? Quomodo succedit? quos progressus habet Res Pulueraria? Quid illa autem? Sublato Rege, atque Ordinibus, quis Regni demum Protector futurus esset? Vel vnica verò hæc Grenwelli quæstio, satis superque est, ad Laruam huic Consessioni detrahendam; satis superque vt ex eâ constet, quo animo Grenwellus ad Confessionem accesserit. Aduertit enim, scio, Lector, quæsiuisse hoc Grenwellum à Garnetto; Grenwellum, qui ipse Garnetto rem omnem reuelauit; à Garnetto, qui tamen nisi reuelante Grenwello, rem planè nesciebat.
units.tr: For Grenwell did not come in order to accuse himself (Garnet says so) or to ask for a remedy for his soul; he came for the sake of consultation, that is, to seek counsel, so that Garnet might advise him on the manner of carrying out the deed, not to rebuke a crime. For what did those questions mean to them, when afterwards they often met one another? How does it proceed? What progress has the gunpowder business made? And what of the other matter? Once the King and the estates were removed, who would in the end be the Protector of the realm? This single question of Grenwell's is enough and more than enough to strip the mask from this confession; it is enough and more than enough to show from it with what intention Grenwell came to confession. For you will notice, I know, reader, that Grenwell asked this of Garnet; Grenwell, who himself revealed the whole affair to Garnet; Garnet, who nevertheless knew nothing of the matter at all except through Grenwell's revelation.

units.la: Cui verò hinc non liquet, Garnettum, ad quem non aliter peruênit res, quàm ex confessione Grenwelli, plus hîc scisse Grenwello ipso de Protectore, atq; multò, quàm is qui ei rem retulit, in Negotio toto peritiorem fuisse? Sed vos, an bonâ fide soletis quæstiones huiusmodi, Succeditne? Progressus ne facit proditio? Quis futurus Regni Protector? pœnitentes atque inter confitendum percontari idque sub Sigillo? Malum vero Sigillum, & merito comminuendum, quo hæc tam turpia obsignantur.
units.tr: But who does not see from this that Garnet, to whom the matter came by no other route than through Grenwell's confession, knew more than Grenwell himself about the Protector, and was far more skilled in the whole business than the man who reported it to him? But do you, in good faith, customarily ask penitents such questions during confession, as "Does it succeed? Does betrayal make progress? Who is to be Protector of the realm?", and do so under the seal? A bad seal indeed, and one deservedly to be broken, by which such shameful things are sealed up.

units.la: Sed &c,qui in materiâ Sigilli Stoici sunt vel maximè, requiruntt tamen, vt Confessio ipsa Sacramentalis sit. At fuerítne ista Confessio: aut per viâ: aut nec per viam Confessionis: Garnettus ipse ad mortem vsque incertus. Tum & illud requirunt, vt verè fit Accusatio: Ita Sotus: Hæc vero Accusatio planè non fuit, quasi peccatum esset: sed Consultatio (teste vel ipso) putà, de Nouo Protectore, & alijs eiusdem generis. Postremò, vt maximè fuerit Confessio, tamen eo vno excepto, vt ne prodat Confitentem, {a}debet confessarius, cum maximâ diligentiâ præcauere pro Posse ne peccatum perpetrandum sibi in confessione detectum opere perpetretur. {b}Potest Superiori dicere, Vigila, quia Lupus est in Grege. {c}Debet monere eum, cui a re sescurafuit, vt inuigilet, & debet facere omnia quibus obuietur delicto commit-tendo. {d}Debet admonere Rempublicam, aut illum cui periculum imminet, vt caveant tali horâ, aut tali loco. {e}Debet occurrere quantum potest; Ciues ad custodiam ciuitatis incitare, atque omnia alia, quæ ad obuiandum Proditioni facere conuenit. Non enim alia Canonis cautio quàm hæc, {f}Caueat ne reuelet Peccatorem. Cap. Omnis utriusq.: non autem Peccata, si potest illa sine Peccatore.
units.tr: But those who are most strict about the matter of the seal, nevertheless require that the confession itself be sacramental. Yet whether this was a confession at all, or was made in the way of confession, or not in the way of confession, Garnet himself remained uncertain even to his death. Then they also require that it be a true accusation: so Soto. But this was plainly not an accusation, as if it were a sin; it was a consultation (as he himself testifies), about, for example, a new Protector and other matters of the same kind. Lastly, even if it had been fully a confession, yet, with one exception, namely that he must not betray the penitent, the confessor is obliged to take the greatest care, as far as he can, to prevent a sin disclosed to him in confession from being carried out in deed. He may say to a superior, "Watch, for there is a wolf in the flock." He ought to warn the one whose business it concerns to keep watch, and he ought to do everything by which the crime about to be committed may be opposed. He ought to warn the commonwealth, or the one threatened by the danger, that they should beware at such an hour or in such a place. He ought to come to meet it as far as he can; he ought to rouse the citizens to guard the city, and to do all the other things that are fitting for resisting such a betrayal. For the canon's only caution is this: let him beware of revealing the sinner (chapter "Omnis utriusque"), and not sins, if they can be dealt with without the sinner.

units.la: Iam verò vester hic Confessarius, esto, vt detur ei, reticere de persona Confitentis; præcauitne rem, pro posse suo cum maximâ diligentiâ? Fecitne omnia, ne perpetrari posset hoc Flagitium tam Atrox? Dixitne Superiori, Vigila? Admonuitne, vt caveret, tali Horâ, tali Loco? Excitauitne Ciues, ac alia omnia fecit, quæ ad obuiandum Proditioni tali, facere conueniebat? Nihil horum. Imò ad horam mortis in hoc peccasse se fassus est, quòd præuertere neglexisset. Quid ergo hijs vlterius immoramur? Quocunq; se vertat Matthæus, Martyrem suum Scelere plus magis inuoluit. Mortem pati debuit, potiùs quàm vt Sigillum violaret: violauit, eóque facto, factus est author mortis suæ. Poterat seuerè interdicere Confitenti, vt desisteret ipse, alios à Scelere reuocaret, sub pœnâ reuelandi, ni intra certum tempus id efficeret. Poterat credere Papæ Innocentio, & illæso Sigillo Sacramenti sui, Scelus adhuc perpetrandum, vergens in Periculum Summum totius Reipublicæ, detegere. Poterat vel Soto credere, & cùm non esset Accusatio ibi vlla, tutò reuelare, atq; ita perniciem à Patriâ, pœnam à seipso Capitalem auertere. Poterat subtricere Confitentem, & de Horâ & Loco commonefacere illorum aliquem, quibus periculum imminebat. Nihil horum fecit; iusta ergo illius percusio. Pie autem prosecto credere non potestis coronandum illum à Deo propter Sacramentum diuinum non violatum: Violauit enim illud turpiter. Nec propter fidei Catholicæ confessionem: Flagitiosè enim eius oblitus est. Sed neque detestationem hæresèon Protestantium: Ita enim erat intentus Charitati, & purgandæ Sororimu-licri, lieri, quam ubique secum circumduxit, ut Fidei, ut Haeresis mentio omnis ei penitus tum excidernt; Ut iam alia vobis merita quaerenda sint ex thesauro Ecclesiae & Societatis, quae Martyri vestro applicetis, alioqui Coronâ suâ (ut piè credi potest) carituro.
units.tr: Now then, let us grant that your confessor is allowed to keep silent about the person of the penitent: did he take care of the matter, as far as lay in his power, with the greatest diligence? Did he do everything to prevent so atrocious a crime from being carried out? Did he tell a superior, "Watch"? Did he warn them to beware at such an hour, in such a place? Did he rouse the citizens, and do all the other things that were fitting for resisting such a betrayal? None of these. Indeed, at the hour of his death he confessed that in this he had sinned, because he had neglected to prevent it. Why then do we linger over these things any longer? Wherever Matthew turns, he entangles his martyr more and more in his crime. He ought to have suffered death rather than violate the seal; he violated it, and by that deed he became the author of his own death. He could have sternly forbidden the penitent to proceed, and to call others back from the crime, under penalty of disclosure, unless he accomplished this within a certain time. He could have trusted Pope Innocent, and, with the seal of his sacrament left unharmed, disclosed the crime still to be carried out, which tended towards the greatest danger to the whole commonwealth. He could even have trusted Soto, and, since there was no accusation there, have revealed it safely, and so turned away destruction from the fatherland and capital punishment from himself. He could have dissuaded the penitent, and warned some of those who were threatened by danger about the hour and the place. He did none of these things; his punishment is therefore just. Surely you cannot piously believe that he is to be crowned by God on account of the divine sacrament not having been violated: for he shamefully violated it. Nor on account of the confession of the Catholic faith: for he forgot it in a disgraceful way. Nor on account of his detestation of the heresies of the Protestants: for he was so intent on charity and on cleansing his sister-woman, whom he carried about with him everywhere, that every mention of faith and of heresy had wholly slipped from his mind at that time. So you must seek other merits for your martyr from the treasury of the Church and of the Society, to attribute to him, otherwise he will be deprived of his crown (as one may piously believe).

units.la: Postquam autem Martyrium Garnetti confummâssent: proximum erat, ut, qui se tum in pedes coniecerunt Jesuitae, etiam ex Congruo, pro Confessoribus haberentur. Persecutione enim, illis propter iustitiam ingruente, ex consilio Christi fugerunt de vnâ ciuitate in aliam. Quis haec sine stomacho legat? Ergo, cui non par fuit vnquam Nefaria Proditio, Iustitia iam est? Animaduersio in Proditores, Persecutio? Proditores iam Nqui Confessores? Christus ipse fugae Illis consilium dat? Christi Vicarius fugientes excipit? Imo Conscientia illis Facinoris illius nulla, non Testium indicia vlla: Mansissent ergo si nulla; cur fugerunt? Redirent vero iam cum Muro suo Ahaneo[?]; subirent examen legitimum; sentirent nec Indicia, nec Testes deesse probandae de illis proditionis. Testes erunt, & Indicia, Grenwellum rem totam Garnetto partesque eius singulas reuelasse: Gerardum, Proditoribus iuramentum detulisse de non desistendo; Missa etiam & Sacramento obstrinxisse ad scelus: Hamondum Proditores omnes absoluisse à scelere, & Reatu eius omni etiam tum, cum patefactâ proditione, in Seditionem apertam ruerent. Conscientia illis cauterizata forte est, atque ita, ut tu dicis, sine Conscientia sunt; sed Testium satis erit, Indiciorum plusquam satis, si legitimâ Actione experiri volunt. Neq; vero fugerunt, nisi priùs omnia experti, an possent tubas, & faces esse, Seditionis nouae. An & id consilium Christi? Cum frustra id tentâssent, bis iam Rei, receperunt se ad bonum illum Hospitem suum & (quales illi sunt) Confessorum omnium.
units.tr: After they had completed the martyrdom of Garnet, the next step was that those Jesuits who then fled should also be regarded, by a kind of congruence, as confessors. For when persecution fell upon them on account of justice, they fled "by the counsel of Christ" from one city to another. Who can read this without indignation? So then, is that unspeakable treachery, for which there was never an equal, now justice? Is the punishment of traitors now persecution? Are traitors now made confessors? Does Christ himself give them counsel for flight? Does the Vicar of Christ receive the fugitives? Indeed, if they have no awareness of that crime, and no evidence of witnesses, then they would have remained if there were none; why did they flee? But let them now return to their own wall, and undergo a lawful examination; they will feel that neither indications nor witnesses are lacking to prove their treachery. There will be witnesses and indications: that Grenwell revealed the whole matter to Garnet and its individual parts; that Gerard required of the traitors an oath not to desist, and bound them to the crime even by the Mass and the sacrament; that Hammond absolved all the traitors from their crime, and from its guilt, even when, the treachery having been disclosed, they were rushing into open sedition. Perhaps their conscience has been cauterized, and so, as you say, they are without conscience; but there will be enough witnesses, and more than enough indications, if they wish to be tried by lawful action. Nor did they flee until they had first tried everything, to see whether they could be trumpets and torches of a new sedition. Was this also the counsel of Christ? When they had attempted this in vain, now twice accused, they withdrew to that good host of theirs, and (such as they are) of all confessors.

units.la: Quodsi Papae consuetudo non sit, vocandi in ius vbi accusator abest, vel testes; ne faciat sanè: Tantum expellat à se, faciat reuerti ad suos, vbi extant Indicia clara, vbi Testes omni exceptione maiores. Ne afficiat sanè Supplicio, sed ne excipiat Hospitio. Nam de Serenissimo Archi-duce quod subiungis, suauis homo es; scis Baldwino exceptionem esse fori. E Venetâ iam causâ, sat illi constat, Sacerdotes, praesertim verò Iesuitas, non conueniendos, nisi coram vel Pontifice, vel eius Delegato: Subditos Illos Ducum, Archi-ducum, Regum non esse, quin Papæ solius; absque eius voluntate, nihil de illis statui posse: voluntatem vero illius esse, vt de Confessoribus suis nemo pereat. Fallor autem, si non eadem hæc Regi responderit Legatus hic Serenissimi Archi-ducis, cùm adiustitiam postularetur Baldwinus: Iesuitam esse Baldwinum, apud Superiores suos conueniendum: apud Archi-ducem enim conueniri non posse. Sed tu tamen multum hallucinaris; non inspexisti sane, quæ nobis apud Acta sunt. Nominárunt vero, qui suppleio sic affecti, Baldwinum (atque fœdâ notâ notarunt) aliosque nonnullos, conscios, complices, consultores suos. Probari hæc contra absentes, scio, non probares; fac veniant modo; Abundè probatum erit, nec tu negabis: hic Testes, hic Tabulæ obsignatæ. Interim autem, dum probent innocentiam suam: exulent à vobis, à bonis omnibus: Tortus ne sit Patronus: Pontifex ne Fautor, Roma ne latebra sit tam perditorum eiuium. Hoc si faciat sapientissimus ille tuus Princeps, rem faciet se dignam; eluet maculam hanc omnem. Ni faciat, adhærebit illi, suspicionis nota non leuis: quod factum tam nolle dicit, fieri voluisse. Nec leuitas in suspicando vlla; ratio enim subest suspicandi, fauere illis, quos fouet; quos nec iubet, nec finit causam dicere; nec vocat ipse, nec remittit in ius; quos secum retinet, in conspectum suum venire finit, nec vel abigit saltem à se, qui famâ laborant, quòd in societate fuerint tam Nefandi Criminis. Tu, quantum voles excusa factum; quantum potes deprecare: Interest Pontificeis, si Famæ suæ consultum vult, si Existimationi; Scandalum istud à se quàm primùm amoliri.
units.tr: But if it is not the custom of the Pope to summon to court when the accuser is absent, or the witnesses; then by all means let him not do so. Let him only drive them from himself, and make them return to their own people, where clear indications exist, where witnesses are above all exception. Let him certainly not inflict punishment, but let him not receive them as guests. For as to what you add about the most serene Archduke, you are a charming fellow; you know that for Baldwin the exception is the forum. In the Venetian case it is already well established that priests, and especially Jesuits, are not to be summoned except before the Pope or his delegate; that those subjects of dukes, archdukes and kings belong to the Pope alone, and that nothing can be decided about them without his will; and that his will is that none of his confessors should perish. But I am mistaken if this same answer was not given to the King by the envoy of the most serene Archduke here, when Baldwin was demanded for justice: that Baldwin is a Jesuit and must be summoned before his superiors, for he cannot be summoned before the Archduke. But you are nevertheless greatly mistaken; you have certainly not looked into what has been done before us in the records. Those who were thus affected by the torture named Baldwin (and marked him with a foul note), and some others, accomplices, partners, and advisers of theirs. I know that these things could not be proved against absent men; let them only come, and it will be abundantly proved, and you will not deny it: here are the witnesses, here are the sealed documents. Meanwhile, while they are proving their innocence, let them be exiled from you and from all good men: let not Torture be their patron, let not the Pope be their supporter, let not Rome be a hiding place for such lost citizens. If your most wise Prince does this, he will do what is worthy of himself; he will wash away all this stain. If he does not, a mark of suspicion, and no slight one, will cling to him: since he says he was unwilling to do what he wished to have been done. Nor is there any levity in this suspicion; for there is a reason for suspecting that he favours those whom he cherishes; whom he neither orders nor allows to plead their cause, nor summons himself, nor sends back to court; whom he keeps with him, allowing them to come into his sight, and does not even drive away from himself those who labour under reputation because they were in the company of so nefarious a crime. You may excuse the deed as much as you like, and plead for it as much as you can: it is in the Pope's interest, if he wishes to care for his good name and reputation, to remove this scandal from himself as soon as possible.

units.la: Ad illud Cardinalis, Cur solus Rex Angliæ timet; Quis vnquam alius, ex omni Christianorum Principum numero, aut timuit, aut timet præter eum: respondit & alios aliquando, & sæpe multos, sibi à Pontifice timendi causam habuisse, etiam timuisse; nec ita esse affirmauit modò (quod tuferè facis,) sed probauit affatim. Falsum ergò quod non alius vnquam: Falsum etiam quòd Ille solus timeat. Non temere quidem Noster, sic vt Illi; non enim facere quæ Illi fecerunt, quæq; facere solent, qui timent: Confugere aliquò, supplices esse, aliorum operam implorare, mittere qui intercedant. Potuitne magis appositè? Quis vnquam alius timuit? Alij multi,& sæpe; Cur solus Rex timet? Noster ne timet quidem. Ubi ergo hic paradoxum? Timuerunt illi, Rex non timet. Illi enim vexati bellis, ad extrema redacti, ab hoste fusi, à vicinis deserti, denique, ne suis quidem satis fidere, sed & ab illis sibi timere: timuerunt ergo, & iure quidem. Regis ea causa non est. Nihil horum. A bellis, pax; non hostis ulus ad portas; vicini omnes foederati; Sui vero illum in oculis ferunt, in corde: simul, ut viuant, simul ut moriantur. Illi timent, Illum sibi plus timere vellent. Quàm dispar hic causa? Quàm vero disparata haec inter se? ut Illi tum quidem debuerint: Rex tam noster non debeat timere? Temerarij illi quidem fuissent, nisi timuissent, ut illorum res erant: Rex parum constans, si timeat. Sed neque, debet iam timere Rex ulus, (ut quod res est dicam.) Prælonga tum erant, prœut nunc sunt Pontificis cornua: exectà sunt, ex eo; quanquam etiam nunc mutilà fronte minitetur. Verùm vix ulla iam Illi vis, à se. Quae est à Principibus est; si potest clasicum canere, atque committere illos inter se: aut etiam à Plebe, si commoueure potest ut discessionem faciat, vel per Emissarios suos, ad atrox aliquod facinus praecipitem dare. Et annon magna Pontifici laus, quòd ita Regibus, & Regni terrori sit, quasi Demogorgon aliquis, ut cui, potestas iam omnis ad Destructionem sit?
units.tr: To the Cardinal's question, "Why does the King of England alone fear? Who has ever, from the whole number of Christian princes, either feared or fears besides him?", he replied that others at times, and often many, have had cause to fear the Pope, and indeed have feared; and he asserted that this is not so only now (as you usually do), but proved it abundantly. So the claim that no one else ever did is false; the claim that he alone fears is also false. Our king does not act rashly as they did, for he does not do what they did and what those who fear are accustomed to do: flee somewhere, become suppliants, implore the help of others, send envoys to intercede. Could it have been put more aptly? Who has ever feared besides? Many others, and often; why does the King alone fear? Our king does not even fear. Where then is the paradox? They feared, the King does not fear. For they were harassed by wars, reduced to extremity, routed by the enemy, deserted by their neighbours, and finally did not even trust their own people, but feared them too; so they feared, and rightly so. The King has no such cause. None of these things. Peace prevails over war; no enemy is at the gates; all the neighbours are allied; and his own people bear him in their eyes and in their hearts, both to live and to die together. Those others fear; he would have them fear him more. How different is this case? And how far apart are these matters? If those men ought to have feared then, why should our king, so unlike them, not be obliged to fear? They would have been rash had they not feared, as their situation was; the King would be inconsistent if he feared. But the King ought not to fear at all now (to tell the truth as it is). The Pope's horns were then very long, as they are now; they have been cut off since then, though even now he threatens with a maimed brow. But there is hardly any force left to him from himself. What he has is from the princes, if he can sound the trumpet and set them against one another; or even from the common people, if he can stir them to rebellion, or through his emissaries drive them headlong into some atrocious crime. And is it not great praise for the Pope that he should be such a terror to kings and to the kingdom, like some Demogorgon, since all his power is now for destruction?

units.la: Quodsi autem locum illum meliore oculo inspexeris, contendes ipse, falsum esse, quod ibi posuisti; nimirum omnem ibi à Rege timorem prorsus removeri. Panicum ibi timorem negat emunci posse, non omnem: Est enim Panicus, qui fine causa est ulli, attonitos tamen homines reddit, atque, ut ibi est, stupidos: est alter, qui cautos modò & solertes, vbi causa tamen subsit. Prior ille est, qui (apud te) degeneres animos arguit: Hic verò etiam in Generosos atque constantes cadit. Ac ut Leporinum illum à Rege abesse scimus, quàm longissimè: ita hunc, plus magis augeri, summis in votis nobis est. Minor enim multo est, quàm aut vellemus, aut fortasse etiam expedit. Ex eo autem timore erat, quòd Regni Ordines, magis Illi timentes, quàm Ipse sibi, voluerint Hircos vestros & Capras noxias ab Ouibus separare; separare autem quasi Vocali Signo Iniramenti illius, quo Illis, cauerent omnes post occursare. Nec trepidatum tamen in eo est, sed & ad tempus interrupta atque dilata Comitia sunt: & cùm conuenifsent denuo, lentè res acta, diu, multumque deliberata, serò tandem post Semestre, conclusa. Maturâssent magis, si magno illo, quem tu fingis, timore correptus Rex. Non fuit Illorum, qui exterriti essent, tam Elephantinis passibus incedere; Ceruinis pedibus prosilijssent, si timidi. Nihil autem ibi festinatum: cura maior, ut caute, quàm ut propere res ageretur. Quo in Iuramento, nisi oculus tibi malus fuisset, vidisses non timorem nostrum, qui non alius erat, quàm debuit; sed dedecus vestrum vidisses, & æternum opprobrium Pontificis vestri, contra quem, causa tam magna fuit, & tam iusta muni-endi Reges, Subditos iuramentis constringendi, ne violentiam inferrent in Personam Regis, neue Coniurationes inirent, in Salutem Reipublicæ. Vidisses hoc, & merito correptus pudore, de timore tacuisses.
units.tr: But if you look at that passage with a better eye, you will yourself contend that what you there asserted is false, namely that all fear is completely removed from the King there. The passage denies that panic fear can be removed, not all fear: for there is a panic fear that comes without any cause, and yet makes men astonished, and, as it is there, stupid; there is another which makes men merely cautious and careful, where there is nevertheless a cause. That first kind is what (in your view) indicates degenerate spirits; but this second kind falls even upon the noble and steadfast. And just as we know that the hare-like fear is as far as possible from the King, so we most earnestly wish that this other kind may increase more. For it is much smaller than we would wish, or perhaps even than is expedient. Now the fear was this: that the orders of the kingdom, being more afraid for themselves than he was for himself, wished to separate your goats and harmful he-goats from the sheep; and to separate them, as it were by the vocal sign of that oath, by which all were to be on guard against them afterwards. Nor was there any panic in this, but the assembly was also interrupted and postponed for a time; and when they had come together again, the matter was carried out slowly, long and much deliberated, and at last concluded late, after six months. They would have acted more quickly if the King had been seized by that great fear which you invent. It was not characteristic of men who had been terrified to advance with such elephantine steps; if they had been timid, they would have leapt with the feet of stags. Nothing was hurried there: the concern was greater that the business be done cautiously rather than quickly. In that oath, had your eye not been evil, you would have seen not our fear, which was no other than it ought to be; but you would have seen your disgrace and the eternal reproach of your Pope, against whom there was so great and so just a cause to fortify kings, and to bind subjects by oaths, so that they would not commit violence against the person of the King, nor enter into conspiracies, for the safety of the commonwealth. You would have seen this, and, rightly seized by shame, you would have kept quiet about fear.

units.la: Quanquam videris & tu, qui sic paradoxa venaris, ut hic te expedias, ne incurras Seruus in Dominum; cùm ille nolit, tu iubeas timere Regem; ille si timeat, temerarium dicat; tu temerarium, nisi timeat; ille causam nullam esse dicat, cur timeat; tu causas magnas, & graues; ille, nullum unquam è numero Principum; tu, tot magnos Imperatores, & Reges extimuisse; ille, Ne time; temerè enim facias, Constans non eris, si quem nemo Princeps timuit, tu timeas: Tu, Time verò; Multi enim timuerunt, & Magni; vide, ne dum Constantem te videre vult Dominus meus, Temerarium faciat. Ita, ait hic, negat ille; iubet alter, alter vetat. Quis hos homines spiritus agitat, nisi Contradictionis? Quis hæc illorum conciliet? Et tu tamen paradoxa crepas? Paradoxum hoc quidem tuum est, à te positum, nisi sit plus etiam quàm paradoxum, id est, paralogum: Contra enim rationem omnem, & vel sensum communem, simul quem reprehendis, quòd omninò timeat; eundem quòd plus magis non timeat, reprehendere.
units.tr: Yet you too have seen, you who so hunt for paradoxes that you extricate yourself here, lest the servant run into the master: since he does not want it, you order the King to fear; if he feared, he would call it rash; you call it rash unless he fears; he says there is no cause why he should fear; you say there are great and grave causes; he says no one ever did, from the number of princes; you say that so many great emperors and kings have feared; he says, "Do not fear"; for you would act rashly, and would not be steadfast, if you feared whom no prince has feared: you say, "But do fear"; for many and great men have feared; take care, lest my Lord, while he wishes you to appear steadfast, make you appear rash. So, says this man, he denies it; that man orders it; one orders, the other forbids. What spirit drives these men, if not that of contradiction? Who reconciles these things? And yet do you still boast of paradoxes? This paradox is indeed yours, set down by you, unless it is more than a paradox, that is, a paralogism. For against all reason, and even common sense, you rebuke him at the same time, because he altogether fears, for not fearing more.

units.la: Transit pòst, ad odiosam illam, & odiosè positam à Cardinali, Iuliani similitudinem. Primò verò, in Rebus dicit similitudinis summam positam, non in Personis. Cur ergo ita crudè rem reliquit Cardinalis? Cur non præfatus deferre se Personæ Regis, nec ad eam trahi velle, quæ de Iuliano sic diceret? Cur neque pòst restrinxit ad rem? & duritiem exempli honestâ aliquâ deprecatione mollivit, sed sic, quasi dimissolaculeo, statim anolauit? Denique cur non submisit Alium, cui plus cordis, minus oris, quàm Torto, qui nec Personae parcit iam; qui quasi non satis iam esset per se, magis etiam adhuc odiosam reddidit? Ab uno hoc discat quivis, quo animo sit in Reges Pontifex, cum suis Cardinalibus, qui sic immittunt Scurras suos, in Reges ipsos, & ore spurco libere grassari sinunt, in eorum nomina; quibus, tempus erat, cùm Pontifices quoque ipsi assurgebant. Quid autem affert bonus iste Christianus? Primò Juliani rem agit; patronum illi se praestat, & attollit Apostatam, ut Regem tantum deprimat. Non est (inquit) verum, Julianum Atheum fuisse. Atque idem, credo, diceret Apostolo {a}Paulo, qui Ephesios idola multa colentes, dixit ἄθεοι[?] fuisse. Non est verum, Paule, Atheos esse Ephesios, Polytheos dicere debuisti. Atque haec illius Auspicia sunt, ut mendacium impingat Apostolo, & Spiritum Sanctum loqui doceat.
units.tr: Next he passes on to that hateful comparison with Julian, which the Cardinal put in an odious manner. And first, he says the chief point of the comparison lies in the things, not in the persons. Why then did the Cardinal leave the matter so crudely? Why did he not first say that he meant nothing against the person of the King, nor wished to drag him into what was said of Julian in this way? Why did he not afterwards restrict it to the thing itself, and soften the harshness of the example with some honourable apology, but instead, as though he had let fly a sling-stone, immediately moved on? Finally, why did he not send in another man, one with more heart and less mouth than Torto, who now spares not even the person; who, as though it were not already odious enough in itself, made it still more so? Let anyone learn from this one instance what the Pope's mind is towards kings, together with his cardinals, who thus let loose their buffoons against the kings themselves, and allow them to rage freely with a filthy mouth against their names; names before which, when the time was, the Popes themselves used to rise. But what does this good Christian bring forward? First, he deals with the matter of Julian; he presents himself as his patron, and raises up the apostate, in order to depress only the King. "It is not true," he says, "that Julian was an atheist." And I believe he would say the same to the Apostle Paul, who said that the Ephesians, worshipping many idols, were atheists. It is not true, Paul, that the Ephesians are atheists; you ought to have called them polytheists. And these are his auspices, that he should impugn the Apostle with a lie and teach the Holy Spirit how to speak.

units.la: At neque Polytheus erat Julianus, sed plane Atheus, quamuis esset tum Pontifex Maximus, Nempe Irrisor Religionis suae, & Deorum, ad quos desciuerat. Quis hoc neget, qui vel legerit Caesares eius, ut, ibi de Jove, de reliquis Diis suis ludos faciat? Perinde bonus Ethnicus Pontifex iste Julianus, atque bonus Christianus Pontifex vester, Leo decimus, qui fabulam illam de Christo, sibi vobisque lucrosam valde fuisse, Bembo ridens asserebat; nec Christianus hic, nec Polytheus ille, sed utrque Atheus. Verissimum ergo verbum hoc, Atheum dici debere Clientem tuum (bone Patrone Juliani) nec tamen minus verum, Atheum quoque pari iure dici debere Leonem; atque illum etiam Atheum, qui apud {b}Mirandulam affirmabat quibusdam domesticis suis, nullum se Deum, etiam dum Pontificis sedem teneret credidisse. Illum quoque Atheum apud eundem, qui vivens familiari cuidam aperuit, apud se animarum immortalitatem minime credidam[?]. Omnes Catholicos, omnes Pontifices, nec tamen Christianos. Nihil ergo dicis cùm id asseris, Cùm Catholicus non sit, neq; Christianus est. Plus hic multò dicitur. Cùm Catholicus sit, tamen, non est Christianus; imò cùm Catholicae Ecclesiae Caput sit, Christianus tamen non est. En tibi, quò Julianus tuus te perduxit. Potest quis, Missas audire, potest facere, potest Caput Catholicae Ecclesiae Papam credere, potest Ecclesiae Cathol ex Caput & Papa esse; nec tamen Christianus.
units.tr: But Julian was neither a polytheist, but plainly an atheist, although he was then Pontifex Maximus; indeed a mocker of his own religion and of the gods to whom he had deserted. Who would deny this, who has even read his Caesars, where he makes sport of Jupiter and his other gods? Just as good an pagan Pontifex as that Julian was, so is your good Christian Pontiff, Leo the Tenth, who, laughing, used to assert to Bembo that that fable about Christ had been very profitable to himself and to you; neither this one a Christian nor that one a polytheist, but both atheists. Therefore this word is most true, that your client (good patron of Julian) ought to be called an atheist; and yet it is no less true that Leo ought equally to be called an atheist; and also that other atheist who, at Mirandola, used to assert to some of his household that he had believed in no God even while he held the Pontiff's seat. Also that other atheist, in the same place, who while living disclosed to a certain intimate friend that he by no means believed in the immortality of the soul. All Catholics, all Popes, yet not Christians. Therefore you say nothing when you assert that, since he is not a Catholic, he is not a Christian. Much more is said here. Though he is a Catholic, yet he is not a Christian; indeed, though he is the Head of the Catholic Church, he is nevertheless not a Christian. There you have where your Julian has led you. Someone may hear Masses, may do so, may believe the Pope to be the Head of the Catholic Church, may himself be the Head and Pope of the Catholic Church; and yet not be a Christian.

units.la: Quàm vero inepte philosophatur de secundo? Cùm Catholicus non sit, neque Christianus est. Vbi primò, Catholicum intelligit Romano more (vt ipse paulò pòst explicat) qui Romani Pontificis religionem sequitur. At hic talis, nisi falsi nominis, Catholicus non est. Vbi vide quam rem agam. Etsi Catholicus sit dixi modò, Christianum tamen non esse: Ne Catholicum quidem iam esse dico. Tu de Iacobo Rege quaeris, ego de Paulo Papa quinto, vter Catholicus verior, vter Catholicam, id est, diffusam Ecclesiam magis credat (ea enim vocis, Catholici, vis est) vter Nulli loco alligatam? Ac Rex quidem Catholicam planè agnoscit, perque omnes terras vbique disseminatam, nec vlli loco astrictam vult, nec vllo circumscriptam. Paulus Papa vester non sic audet, non vel Catholicam nominare, nisi Romanam addat. Romanam autem sic addendo, euertit Catholicam, quasi si credat, nulli loco ascriptam, vni tamen loco certo ascriptam; Catholicam Romanam, quasi dicat vniuersalem particularem, vel totum partem, quasi si Orbem compingat in Vrbem. Atque hoc qui credat, Catholicus non est, proin nec Christianus. En Vicarius iam Christi, cùm Catholicus non sit, Christianus non est. Sed nolo delirantem sequi. Hoc qui credit, Catholicus non est, Donatista est; sic enim illi olim credebant Ecclesiam Catholicam Africanam: sic vos nunc, illis per omnia similes, Catholicam Romanam. Atq; vt illorum, quia Africana erat, Catholica non erat, sed pars Donati: ita & vestra, quia Romana est, Catholica non est, sed pars Papae Romani; Atq; hoc qui neget, ad exemplum Torti [Catholicam Romanam] [Animal Asinum] appellandum censeo. Postremò, quid ita malè vobis conscij Catholicam non audetis vsurpare solam? Quorsum additis Romanam? Quid illa opus est, si praeter Romanam, Catholica nulla est? Neq; enim eà voce opus vllum, nisi vt distinguat vestram ab aliâ Catholicâ quae Romana non est. Ea quia merè Catholica, verè Catholica: vestra non verè, quia additione illà detrahitis; & priori illi [Catholicam] per posteriorem hanc [Romanam] derogatis.
units.tr: How very foolishly he philosophises about the second point! "Since he is not a Catholic, he is not a Christian." Here, first, he understands "Catholic" in the Roman manner (as he himself explains shortly afterwards): "one who follows the religion of the Roman Pontiff." But such a person, unless he is Catholic in name only, is not a Catholic at all. See how I am dealing with the matter. Although I have just said that he is a Catholic, I say that he is not a Christian; I now say that he is not even a Catholic. You ask about King James, I ask about Pope Paul the Fifth: which of them is the truer Catholic, that is, which believes more in the Catholic, or universal, Church (for that is the force of the word "Catholic"), and which believes in a Church bound to no place? The King plainly acknowledges the Catholic Church, spread abroad everywhere throughout all lands, and wishes it bound to no place and confined to no location. Your Pope Paul does not dare to call it Catholic without adding "Roman." But by adding "Roman" in this way, he overturns the Catholic Church: as if he believed it was assigned to no place, and yet assigned to one definite place; a "Roman Catholic Church," as if he meant a "universal particular" or a "whole part," as if he were squeezing the world into the city. Whoever believes this is not Catholic, and so not Christian either. Behold, the Vicar of Christ, since he is not Catholic, is not Christian! But I do not wish to follow a madman. Whoever believes this is not Catholic but a Donatist; for so the Donatists once believed the Church to be "the Catholic African Church." So you now, in every respect like them, (believe in) the "Catholic Roman Church." And just as theirs, because it was African, was not Catholic but a part of Donatus, so yours, because it is Roman, is not Catholic but a part of the Roman Pope. And if anyone denies this, I think he should be called, after the example of Tortus, an "[Roman Catholic] [Animal Ass]." Finally, why, being so conscious of your own bad case, do you not dare to claim "Catholic" alone? Why do you add "Roman"? What need is there of that word, if apart from the Roman there is no Catholic Church? For there is no need of that word at all, except to distinguish your church from another Catholic church which is not Roman. Because that other is simply Catholic, it is truly Catholic; yours is not truly Catholic, because by that addition you take away from it, and by this latter word [Roman] you detract from that former word [Catholic].

units.la: Sed vt Sycophantam hunc paulisper insanire patiamur, atq; vt Horatianus ille, Navem omnem quam conspexit in portu, suam putare, blandiri sibi de nomine Catholici, vbi & quando occurrit, quasi proprium sit suù & peculiare; ex ore proprio iudicemus ipsum. Pòst enim ex Paciano citat, Christianus, mihi nomen; Catholicus, cognomen. At non omnes, quibuis nomen idem
units.tr: But let us allow this sycophant to rave for a little while, and, as that Horatian fellow says, "every ship he sees in port he thinks is his own," so let him flatter himself about the name "Catholic" wherever and whenever it turns up, as if it were his own and peculiar to him. Let us judge him from his own mouth. For he cites from Pacian: "Christian is my name; Catholic, my surname." But not all men who have the same name

units.la: {p} ... (marginal mark at right margin, beside "cognomen") idem, idem & cognomen? Quàm ridicule? Omnes ne Matthaei, Torti, nulli recti? Euangelista ipse cùm Tortus non sit, nec erit Matthaeus? aut Typographus noster, cùm Bellarminus non sit, nec Robertus erit? Annon ea Lex, vti Nomen cognomine: a Christianus Catholico, latiùs vt patère debeat? Et quid ergo Paciano opus, Christiano Catholicorum addere? Sed dic etiam, qui Romani pontificis religionem non sequitur, id est, qui eo sensu Catholicus non est, non est Christianus? Non Christianus? Quid ergo est, si Christianus non est? vel cuius Sectae dicendus? Turcane? At nemo contra illos nostros hominibus, acriùs fortiùsque dimicat. An Iudaeus? At illos Romae Papa impunè finit habitare. Ergo Paganus? At illi Polythei, Papistis in eo, quàm nostris, similiores. Quarta verò iam Secta nulla est. Et illud quoque respondet, an iam nulli sub Turcâ gemant Christiani, nullaeque ibi sint Ecclesiae Christianorum? Vnde tamen, eo nomine commendati etiam à vobis, & vestrum hominibus commendati, crebrò huc ad nos Captivi multi commeant. Nullíne in Graecia, Russia, Armenia, Aethiopia, Christiani? Tortus deleuit omnes. Atque vt modò Ecclesiam Catholicam Romanam fabricatus est: itaiam Religionem Christianam Romanam meditatur; vt de Ecclesiâ non sit, Religionis expers sit, nec Catholicus iam, nec Christianus, qui Romanus non sit. At Christiana Romana Religio hactenus inaudita. Olim autem qui Haeretici, non inter Turcas, vel Iudaeos, vel Ethnicos centebantur; neque nisi qui de Christianis essent, Haeretici audiebant: nuper exortus Tortus, qui Christianos negat.
units.tr: {p} ... (marginal mark at right margin, beside "cognomen") have the same name and surname too? How ridiculous! Are all those named Matthew Tortus, and none of them right? Since the Evangelist himself was not Tortus, will he not be Matthew? Or our printer, since he is not Bellarmine, will he not be Robert? Should not that rule, that "name is to surname as Christian is to Catholic," be extended more widely? And what need then was there for Pacian to add "Catholic" to "Christian"? But tell me, too: whoever does not follow the religion of the Roman Pontiff, that is, who in that sense is not Catholic, is he not a Christian? Not a Christian? What, then, is he, if he is not Christian? Or to what sect is he to be assigned? A Turk? But no one fights more fiercely and bravely against those Turks than our people. A Jew? But Pope Rome allows those Jews to live there with impunity. Then a Pagan? But the polytheists are more similar to Papists in this than to ours. And there is no fourth sect. And here is another answer: are there no Christians still groaning under the Turk, and no Churches of Christians there? Yet from there, commended by that very name even by you, and commended by your own men, many captives often come hither to us. Are there no Christians in Greece, Russia, Armenia, Ethiopia? Tortus has wiped them all out. And just as he has now fabricated the "Roman Catholic Church," so he is also devising a "Roman Christian Religion," so that anyone who is not Roman is outside the Church, devoid of religion, neither Catholic now nor Christian. Yet a "Roman Christian Religion" has been unheard of until now. Formerly, heretics were not counted among the Turks, Jews or heathens; nor did anyone hear of heretics except those who were of the Christians. Only lately has Tortus arisen, who denies that they are Christians.

units.la: Quin vos ergo diruitis Consistorium, feriari iubetis Inquisitores vestros: Forù enim sunt Haeretici, Christiani iam non sunt. Deijs qui foris sunt quid ad illos iudicare? Quid ad Christi Vicarium eos, qui Christiani non sunt? Cur Ecclesiae vocem audiant, qui nihil habent commune cum Ecclesiâ? Quàm verò hìc sese Tortus memorem non praestat, quod tamen (cùm mendax sit) maximè praestare oportuit? Ante, Pontifici vindicat Haereticos excommunicandi potestatem: hinc materiam tollit potestatis. Qui enim poterit iam excommunicare qui intra communionem non sunt? Ita excutit iam fulmen de manu Iouis sui; abnegat Catholicam fidem de potestate Pontificis, atque ita Tortus ipse iam, cùm Catholicus non sit, neque Christianus est. Sed haec illius vecordia est. Vecordia certè, qui tot Regna & Gentes, quæ Romani Pontificis religionem non sequuntur, semel & simul proscribit omnes; Paganas asserit, Christianas negat. Ita Europa pars longè maxima, in Paganismo est. Quod nisi hunc tam procacem Scurram compescat Pontifex, videat ne assertio hæc erumpat in neruum denique. Quare autem non Christianos? Quid, tanti vel in fidem, vel Legem CHRISTI peccârunt, ut multandi sint hoc Christiani nomine? Quia ne mente Deo seruire volunt, non minùs quàm Spiritu, nec ignorata Linguâ Sacra sua murmurare? An quia bibunt ex calice omnes, nec sumunt ex Semisse Sacramentum? Seu quia similitudinem sibi nullam faciunt, quam adorent vel colant? vel id etiam, quia Sanctam Ecclesiam Catholicam, de Veteri Symbolo credunt, Romanam de Novo non credunt? An denique, quia CHRISTO nimio plus tribuunt, nec ei Sanctorum Suffragia in munere intercedendi adiungunt, operum merita in iustificandi, indulgentias Papales in satisfaciendi? Videtur ergo, quòd per excessum peccent, & nimis Christiani sint.
units.tr: Why then do you not dissolve the Consistory, and order your Inquisitors to take a holiday? For "those outside are heretics, and are no longer Christians." "What have I to do with judging those who are outside?" What business has the Vicar of Christ with those who are not Christians? Why should those who have nothing in common with the Church hear the voice of the Church? How little does Tortus show himself mindful of this, which, though he is a liar, he ought most of all to have shown! Earlier he claims for the Pope the power of excommunicating heretics; now he removes the very matter of that power. For how will he be able to excommunicate those who are not within the communion? So he now shakes the thunderbolt out of the hand of his Jupiter; he denies the Catholic faith concerning the power of the Pontiff, and thus Tortus himself, since he is not Catholic, is not Christian either. But this is his madness. Madness indeed, which at one stroke and all together condemns as pagan so many kingdoms and nations that do not follow the religion of the Roman Pontiff; it declares them pagan and denies they are Christian. Thus the far greater part of Europe is in paganism. Unless the Pontiff restrains this shameless buffoon, let him see that this assertion does not finally break out into an open sinew. But why not Christians? What have they sinned so greatly against the faith or the law of Christ that they must be punished with this name of Christian? Is it because they want to serve God in mind no less than in spirit, and do not murmur in a language unknown to them? Or because they all drink from the cup, and do not receive the sacrament in one half? Or because they make no image of Him to adore or worship? Or even because they believe in the holy Catholic Church from the Ancient Creed, and do not believe in a Roman one from a New Creed? Or finally, because they attribute too much to Christ, and do not add to Him the intercession of the saints in the office of interceding, the merits of works in justifying, or Papal indulgences in satisfying? It seems, then, that they sin by excess and are too Christian.

units.la: At etiam Patres per vim torquet, ut cum eo unà insaniant. Augustinum, qui Pelagium debere dicit, gratiam confiteri, si velit non solùm vocari, sed esse Christianus. Quid tum? Et pari operâ dicat Torto quis, debere & illum de Scurrili hac suâ in Regem petulantiâ poenitere, si velit non solùm vocari, verùm etiam esse Christianus. Esse Christianus, id est, verè & re ipsâ esse, quod titulo tenus erat: Esse Christianus, id est, intus & apud Deum esse, quod extra videri voluit & haberi apud homines. Multi enim & apud vos, tum Christiani, tum Catholici, credo, vocantur: quibus non magna cura, ut sint quod vocantur, non magis quàm Pelagio. Nec qui hæreses ergo sectantur solùm: quis enim nescit Augustinû locis multis negare Christianos, qui verbo confitentur Christum, factis negent? Scit hoc ita esse, qui legerit Homiliam eius secundâ in illa Apostoli verba, Omnis Spiritus qui confitetur Iesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo est. Quid agimus iam? Negamus Christianos, qui Christum vitâ negant, ore confitentur? Vide, ne ita ad miram paucitatem res Christiana redeat: Vide ne sic, Ecclesia vera, quæcunque tandem aut ubicunque sit, non vel ipsa multos habitura sit Christianos. Semper autem pessimè succedunt Torto exempla quæ adducit, vt Iuliani ante cum polytheismo suo: Vtri enim Polytheo similiores, ac proin Iuliano? Quosne Catholicos dicit, qui nescio quot, minorum Gentium Deos habent Medioxumos intercessores suos, non pauciores Iuliano ipso, atque in eâ similitudinis parte strenuè Iulianizant: An quos negat Christianos, Paganos esse vult, quos tamen Deo vno, vnoque Mediatore tum Redemptionis tum Intercessionis contentos esse, nec ipse negare potest? Ac Iuliani quidem ibi similitudo: hic verò etiam Pelagij, redit illi in verti-cem. Vtri enim meliùs, vtri magis honorificè sentiunt de gratiâ illâ; qui Pontificis religionem sequuntur, an qui Reformatam? Quis nescit, si ij Christiani non sunt, qui ingratiam ingrati sunt, qui Pelagum sapiunt: quàm cuiuis in proclivi sit dicere, vestros Catholicos hîc potiùs Christianos non esse, vtpote Pelagij pelago (qui sic vocari voluit, non esse Christianus) gradibus aliquammultis propinquiores? Quo in pelago cauendum vobis ne naufragium faciatis. Nos enim longè longiùs ab eo absumus.
units.tr: But he also twists the Fathers by force, so that he may go mad along with him. "Augustine, who says that Pelagius ought to confess grace, if he wishes not only to be called but to be a Christian." What of it? And with equal labour someone might say that Tortus too ought to repent of his buffoonish petulance against the King, "if he wishes not only to be called, but truly to be a Christian." "To be a Christian," that is, to be so truly and in fact, what in name only he was; "to be a Christian," that is, to be inwardly and before God, what he wished to appear outwardly and be held to be among men. For many, I believe, are called both Christians and Catholics among you too: for whom there is no great concern that they should be what they are called, no more than for Pelagius. Nor do those who merely follow heresies (deserve the name)—for who does not know that Augustine in many places denies that those are Christians who confess Christ in word and deny Him in deeds? He knows that this is so who has read his second Homily on those words of the Apostle, "Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ to have come in the flesh is of God." What are we now doing? Do we deny that those are Christians who deny Christ by their life, though they confess Him with their mouths? Take care lest the Christian cause falls back to such a wondrous paucity: take care lest, in this way, the true Church, wherever or whatever it may finally be, will not even itself have many Christians. But the examples Tortus brings always turn out badly for him, as that of Julian formerly with his polytheism: for which are more similar to the polytheist, and therefore to Julian? Those whom he calls Catholics, who have, I know not how many, gods of lesser nations as their middle-ranking intercessors, no fewer than Julian himself, and in that point of similarity vigorously play the Julianist? Or those whom he denies to be Christians, does he wish them to be pagans, though he himself cannot deny that they are content with the one God and the one Mediator, both for redemption and for intercession? There is a resemblance to Julian there; but here even that of Pelagius recoils upon him at the top. For which party thinks better and more honourably about that grace: those who follow the religion of the Pontiff, or those who follow the Reformed? Who does not know that if those are not Christians who are ungrateful for grace, who savour Pelagius, it is easy for anyone to say that your Catholics here are rather not Christians, since they are closer by several degrees to the Pelagian sea (which he wished to be called, and so was not a Christian)? In that sea you must take care lest you make a shipwreck. For we are far, far removed from it.

units.la: Athanasio autem & Cypriano, eadem ipsa responsio satisfaciet. Christiani vocem ibi ab illis premi strictiùs multò, quàm communi loquendi more vsurpari solet; nec de rigore dicendum Christianum, qui vt Arius in Deitatem Christi, vt Novatus in pænitentiam iniuriosus sit. Etiam, cùm de moribus indignis nomine Christiano, sermo illis est in Homiliis, siquis vt Tortus hîc, mendax, vel maledicus; & cum Christianum verè vel esse, vel dici, Patres ijdem negabunt.
