Alioqui, cùm discedunt à stricto hoc dicendi genere, nec rem ad viuum referant; quis nescit, passim apud omnes, qui locuti sunt, omnes qui scripserunt, etiam Ethnicos ipsos; Christiani nomine censeri, qui Christi nomen seruabant, cuicunque demum Sectæ addicti fuerant? Quis nescit etiam Hæreticos multa passos, vt Christianos, cùm sufficeret hoc nomen, vt reos tum constituerent? Nec vlla ratio patitur, vt Christiani nomenclaturâ excludantur magis, qui errant, quàm qui operantur malum. Neutri enim Spiritu Christi aguntur: Qui autem Spiritu Christi non aguntur, hi non sunt eius, nec nisi illius nomine dealbati. Non enim doctrina tantùm, vita etiam bona requiritur, vt nomini respondeant; vtrumque qui non adhibet, frustra Christianus appellatur. Patiatur ergo Tortus, qui idiomate suo Catholici non sunt, Christianos esse, ne exurgat forte aliquis, qui pariter contendat, eum quoque, utpote Obtrectatorem, Christianum non esse.
units.tr: Athanasius and Cyprian will be answered by the same reply. There the word "Christian" is taken far more strictly than common usage allows: one should not call someone a Christian in the strict sense who, like Arius with regard to the divinity of Christ or Novatian with regard to repentance, does him wrong. Likewise, when those Fathers in their Homilies speak of a Christian by name in connection with unworthy conduct, as when someone is a liar or a slanderer like Tortus here, the same Fathers will deny that such a person truly is, or can be called, a Christian. Otherwise, when they depart from this strict way of speaking and do not refer the matter to the living reality, who does not know that everywhere, in all who have spoken and all who have written, even among the heathens themselves, anyone who kept the name of Christ is counted as a Christian, whatever sect he had joined? Who does not know that many heretics also suffered as Christians, since the name alone was enough to make them liable to punishment? And no reason allows that those who err should be excluded from the name Christian more than those who do evil. For neither group is driven by the Spirit of Christ, and those who are not driven by the Spirit of Christ are not his, and are only whitewashed with his name. For the name Christian is not answered by doctrine alone; good life is required as well, and whoever lacks either of the two is called a Christian in vain. Let Tortus therefore allow that those who are not Catholics in his own language are Christians, lest someone arise who with equal force contends that he too, being a detractor, is not a Christian.

units.la: Dixit autem Pontificios Apologiae Author, alicubi Catholicos; quare ij iam soli Catholici, ipse non Catholicus. Nec id tamen sic feret. Dixit Orator Sextum Nævium virum optimum; Senex in Comoedia Duo: Heus bone vir! Uterque tamen, & Nævius, & Dauus, haud multo quam Tortus meliores. Dixit quidem, sed serio non dixit: auribus dedit. Dicet quis Turcam (si eum alloqui contingat) Muffulmanum; amant enim Turcae sic appellari, libenter audiunt, facilius capiuntur: nec, ex eo tamen concludes, qui sic appellet, sentire de Turcis quasi ij soli homines Consummati sint & Perfecti; quae tamen illius vocis vis est. Vos quoque gaudetis Catholici non minus appellari; nempe ut titulis Maiorum gaudent, qui Maiorum tamen rem omnem decoxerunt: Demulsit eo vos, ut aequioribus uteretur. Postquam argumentum inde ducitis, Turcae, ut se solos Consummatos; vos, ut solos vos recte in religione sapere putetis: quid restat iam, quam ut dehinc, vos Papistae sitis, illi Turcae; nec vel Catholici, vel Muffulmani amplius audiatis? Ita minime expedit, delinire malas indoles. Salomonis vera vox fuit; Quod curuum, tortumue est, tractes ut voles, rectum fieri non potest.
units.tr: The author of the Apology has called the Papists "Catholics" in some places; therefore they alone are now Catholics, and he himself is not. Yet he will not put up with this. The orator called Sextus Naevius "an excellent man"; in the comedy an old man says "Hey, good sir!" Yet both Naevius and Davus were hardly any better than Tortus. He did indeed say it, but not seriously: he was giving his ears a treat. Suppose someone, if he happens to address a Turk, calls him a "Muslim"; Turks like to be so called, they gladly listen and are more easily won over. Yet from this you will not conclude that the one who so addresses him thinks that Turks alone are "consummate" and "perfect," though that is the force of the word. You too are glad to be called "Catholics" no less, just as men glad of their ancestors' titles who have nonetheless squandered all their inheritance. He soothed you with this so that you would take his milder views. Since you draw this argument from it, that the Turks should regard themselves alone as "consummate," and you should think yourselves alone to be wise in religion, what remains now but that from here on you should be Papists and they Turks, and you should hear neither "Catholics" nor "Muslims" any more? So it is by no means expedient to soothe bad dispositions. The true word of Solomon was: "What is crooked or twisted you may straighten as you will, it cannot be made straight."

units.la: Æquè insulsum quod mox subijcit: Qui Catholicus non est, hoc ipso Hæreticus est. At si Hæreticus, hoc ipso Christianus. Nam id certum: Qui Christianus non est, eo ipso Hæreticus non est. Nisi enim qui Christianus sit, Hæreticus nemo est. Qui Catholicus non est, hoc ipso Hæreticus est? Turcæ ergo omnes Iudei, Pagani, Athei, hæreticæ prauitatis accusantur; Et de nouo iam feruet opus Inquisitoribus, ampla illis materia iam, plena Curia, qui intus sunt, qui foris, totum iam Orbem conuenturi sunt. Inquirunt enim in Hæreticos: at quisquis Catholicus non est, eo ipso Hæreticus scilicet. Nec illud sanè minus. Catholicum, atque Hæreticum contraria esse, ut diem & noctem, ut lumen & tenebras. Dies autem & nox, lumen & tenebrae, contraria non sunt, priuantia sunt, quorum ea natura est, vt nisi vni inesse, nisi de vno dici nequeant. Habitus praecesserit necesse, vbi privatio iam inest; vt iam Haereticus nemo esse possit, nisi qui Catholicus prius fuerit, vt euertat iam Periodo hac, quod praecedente posuit. Turca enim, Iudaei, Pagani, Catholici nunquam fuerunt. Dies illis aut lumen haud vnquam luxit, vt iam nocte, vel tenebris comprehendi queant. Tum, vt singula verba singula absurda scias; nec illa quidem Priuantium Lex est. Nam nec ibi id sequitur, vt qui non videat, caecus statim fit: Non enim Lapis, qui nec vidit vnquam; nec tamen caecus est, cùm nunquam viderit, vt visu posit priuari posse, & caecus fieri; Vt si priuantia maximè sint Catholicus & Haereticus; non tamen negato Catholico, vt haereticus sit, ex eo statim consequatur. Quanquam, quid ego haec confector, tam leuicula? nisi vt videat Lector, duo haec, Tor-tum, & Dialecticum, disparata esse, cumque è paruis suis Logicalibus, praepropere nimis se ad Theologia Scholas contulisse.
units.tr: What he adds next is equally foolish: "Whoever is not a Catholic is by that very fact a heretic." But if he is a heretic, by that very fact he is a Christian. For this is certain: whoever is not a Christian is not, for that very reason, a heretic. Indeed, no one is a heretic unless he is a Christian. "Whoever is not a Catholic is by that very fact a heretic"? So all Jews, pagans and atheists are then accused of heretical depravity. And now the work of the Inquisitors is already seething afresh; their material is already ample, the court is already full, and those inside and outside are about to gather together the whole world. For they inquire into heretics; yet whoever is not a Catholic is, of course, by that very fact a heretic. Nor is the following any less absurd: "Catholic and heretic are contraries, like day and night, like light and darkness." But day and night, light and darkness, are not contraries; they are privatives, of which the nature is such that they cannot be present in or said of anything except one thing. A state must necessarily have preceded wherever a privation is already present; so that no one could now be a heretic unless he had previously been a Catholic, which means that by this very statement he overturns what he had laid down before. For Turks, Jews and pagans have never been Catholics. Day or light has never dawned upon them, so that they can now be seized by night or darkness. Then, so that you may know that each word is absurd in its own way: even that is not a rule of privatives. For it does not follow there that someone who does not see at once becomes blind: a stone, which has never seen, is not blind, since although it has never seen, it cannot be deprived of sight and made blind. So even if Catholic and heretic were most certainly privatives, nevertheless, from the fact that a Catholic is denied, it does not follow at once that he is a heretic. Yet why do I labour over these trifles? Only so that the reader may see that these two, Tortus and the dialectician, are ill-matched, and that, having brought their little logical arts, they have rashly gone too far into the schools of theology.

units.la: Nec multò tamen melior Theologia. Non enim contraria ibi Catholicus & Haereticus: Orthodoxus potiùs, & Haereticus, qui scilicet vel rectè vel secus de Religionis rebus sentiat. Nam vox Catholica quid valeat, vel è Symbolo petendum: vbi posita, vt Ecclesiam, quae post Christum, ab eâ quae fuerat ante, distinguat; Christianam à Iudaicâ. Illa tum, intra vnam Gentem conclusa: Haec iam, quàm latè patet Orbis, tam latè diffusa est. Neque verò legitima vlla Catholici oppositio, ad haeresin vllam, praeterquam Donatistarum olim, qui ad suam solam Africanam: Papistarum hodiè, qui ad suam solam Romanam arctant quasi Ecclesiam, & de Catholicâ faciunt non Catholicam: ad Papistarum (inquam) aut siqua alia est, quae ad locum vnum praealijs Ecclesiae vniuersitatem reuocat. Benè inter se haec contrariantur; Vniuersalis, & pars Africae: Vniuersalis, & quae à Româ pendet: Locum enim spectant haec, qui vel vbique vel alicubi tantùm est. Vniuersalis autem, respectu Loci (quod sonat Catholicus) & Haereticus, ratione Peruersi Dogmatis, quid habent contrarium? Dic ergo siquid habes de Orthodoxo: id enim proprie Haretico aduersatur. Quanquâ etiam si Catholicum vrgeas, ne sic quidè res tibi rectè ecciderit, Nulli enim quàm vos minùs Catholici, minùs vniuersitati fauentes, proinde (si tu quidem rectè ratiocinaris) nec magis Haretici, nec minùs Christiani. Toti simul Fidei Christiana renunciauit Iulianus; Nunquam deseruit Religionem Rex, quam semel professus est; à Vestra, cui nunquam fuit, nunquam desciuit. Ecquid magis ex Diametro? Imò, non omnino verum est, nunquam deseruisse. Imò omnino verum est, te hic Sycophantam omnino agere. Quâ parte verum non est? Parentes Catholici erant. Non erant; vel Pater, vel Avus. Quid tum si erant? Parentes omnium, qui olim Christiani de Ethnicis, Ethnici fuerunt. Parentes omnium, qui iam apud Indos baptizantur, Ethnici & ipsi. Religio haereditaria non est. At Ritu vestro suscepit Baptismū; Quid Ritus ad Baptismum? Vtrobique Baptismus unus est; nec qui Ritu nostro Baptizati, vos de nouo tingitis, nec nos qui vestro; vtrobique Catholicae fidei professio: quâ ipsâ in professione, non mutamus, in quibus nobiscum estis; in multis enim nobiscum estis. Vbi mutatum quid, id eò factum, quòd in Ritu vestro discessum est, à casto integróque Dei cultu: & quòd, Ab initio non fuit sic. Vt in Cultu similitudinum contra Mandatum secundum, cuius vos vobis conscij, etiam olim Mandatum ipsum de Libris vestris expunxistis: Vt in Sacramento Eucharistia dimidiato, contra mentem Christi expressam: vt in Liturgia non intellecta, contra mentem Apostoli. Denique (quod & {a}Tridentina Synodus vestra fatetur) quae, sine temporum vitio, sine hominum incuria, & improbitate irrepserunt in Missam ipsam, in melius mutata, Reformata haec apud nos: apud vos etiam cùm fuerint, protestati nostri sunt, nobiscum vos in gratiam facilè reditituros, nec nisi sub ista protestatione secessum à vobis, quàm tantisper dum ista in melius mutaretur. Quicquid autem apud vos, pristinae Fidei aut Religionis: intactum apud nos manet. Nam Calvinista conuitium, protritum iam est. Nemo hic, addictus iurare in verba illius. Tanti est, quanti rationes quas affert pro se, nec pluris. Et vos si non magis addicti Papa & Pontifici, non essetis qui iam estis, quodque (merito vestro plurimum) auditis, Pontificij, & Papistae.
units.tr: Yet theology is not much better. For Catholic and heretic are not contraries there. Rather, the orthodox and the heretic are, namely one who thinks rightly or wrongly about the matters of religion. For what the word "Catholic" means must be sought from the Creed, where it is placed to distinguish the Church which came after Christ from that which had existed before, Christian from Jewish. The latter was confined within a single nation; the former is spread as widely as the world extends. Nor is any legitimate opposition of "Catholic" to any heresy, except that of the Donatists long ago, who restricted it to their own African church alone, and that of the Papists today, who narrow the Church to their own Roman church alone, and make the Catholic church into a non-Catholic one; or to the Papists (I say), or to any other that calls the universality of the Church back to one place apart from the others. These are well opposed to one another: the universal and a part of Africa; the universal and that which depends on Rome. For these terms look to a place, which is either everywhere or only somewhere. But what do "universal," in respect of place (which is what "Catholic" means), and "heretic," in respect of a perverse doctrine, have that is contrary? Tell me then, if you have anything, about the "orthodox," for that is what is properly opposed to the heretic. Yet even if you press "Catholic," things will not turn out well for you even so: for none of you are less Catholic, less favouring the universality, and therefore (if you reason rightly) neither more heretical nor less Christian. Julian "renounced the Christian faith as a whole all at once"; the king "never abandoned the religion" which he had once professed; from yours, to which he never belonged, he never departed. Could anything be more directly opposed? Indeed, "it is not altogether true that he never abandoned it." Indeed, "it is altogether true" that you here are acting the complete sycophant. In what part is it not true? "Their parents were Catholics." They were not; either the father or the grandfather was. What if they were? The parents of all who were once Christians from the Gentiles were Gentiles. The parents of all who are now baptized among the Indians are Gentiles too. Religion is not hereditary. But he received baptism by your rite. What has a rite to do with baptism? Baptism is one on both sides; neither do you rebaptize those who were baptized by our rite, nor do we those baptized by yours; on both sides there is a profession of the Catholic faith. In this very profession, we do not change "in those things in which you are with us"; for "in many things you are with us." Where something has been changed, it has come about because there has been a departure in your rite from the chaste and whole worship of God, and because "from the beginning it was not so." As in the worship of images, against the second commandment, of which you yourselves are conscious, and which you long ago struck the very commandment out of your books; as in the Eucharist, with its half-communion, against the express mind of Christ; as in a liturgy not understood, against the mind of the Apostle. Finally (as your own Council of Trent admits), those things which crept into the Mass itself, without fault of the times, without neglect or wickedness of men, and which have been changed for the better here among us and reformed, were such that, even where they were among you, we have protested that you would readily return to fellowship with us, and that our separation from you was made only under this protest, and only for so long as those things were being changed for the better. Whatever remains among you of the former faith or religion remains untouched among us. For the reproach "Calvinist" is now worn threadbare. No one here is bound to swear by the words of that man. He is worth exactly as much as the reasons he brings forward for himself, and no more. And if you were not more devoted to the Pope and the Pontiff, you would not be what you now are, and what you hear (and rightly so, given your deserts) "Pontiffs and Papists."

units.la: At vero, Quae haec tempora sunt? Quod seculum, vt sic audeat Sophista impudens, ore sacrilego bacchari in Reges, idque non alio fundamento, quàm, si vera sunt quae narrantur? Fabulae sunt, quae tibi narrantur, & à te. Idem iam, Rex qui semper fuit, & ex quo per aetatē sapere potuit, una illi semper, eadem[?] mens, mens, nec mutata vnquam sententia, vel de Ecclesiæ Regimine. Intimè semper sensit, extimè præ se tulit illam exterioris Regiminis formam, ferendam fortè ad tempus: hanc verò magis placere sibi, vti meliorem, vt magis ex mente Sacræ Scripturæ, vt cui Antiquitas magis faueat, vt quæ Monarchiæ magis conueniat. Enimuerò, quod tu hic de Popularí Formâ vellicas; qui de vobis cordati sunt, idem hoc facturos autumant Iesuitas, vbi sat illis virium, & tale quid, altâ mente illis repositum esse. Deinde, si postquam vidisset iam, nostram Regiminis Formam, illâ magis probâsset, quàm alteram cui assueuerat; an vel sic Religionem deserere? Quàm hoc verò absonum? Quando & apud vos dictio iuris exterior, Clauis proprie non sit; eamque vos multis sæpe mandatis, qui Laicorum in sorte sunt, exortes plane Sacri Ordinis vniuersi. Nec Religio est vobis sentire, & facere; quod si quis hic, vel faciat, vel sentiat, mutet in Religione. Sed tu pudori omni semel renunciâsti, qui hoc esse dicis fidei renunciare.
units.tr: But what times are these? What age is it, that an impudent sophist should dare, with a sacrilegious mouth, to rave against kings, and on no other foundation than this: "if the things that are told are true"? They are fables that are told to you, and by you. The same king, who has always been the same, and from the time he could reason with age, has always had one mind, and never changed his opinion, even about the government of the Church. He always inwardly felt, and outwardly showed, that that form of external government was to be endured perhaps for a time, but that another was more pleasing to him, as the better one, as more in accordance with the mind of Holy Scripture, as the one that antiquity favours more, and as the one that suits a monarchy more. Indeed, as for what you here carp at concerning a popular form, those of you who are sensible think the Jesuits will do the same, where they have strength enough, and that something of the kind lies hidden deep in their minds. Next, if, after he had now seen our form of government, he had approved it more than the other to which he had been accustomed, would he therefore desert his religion? How absurd is this! When among you the external power of judgement is not properly the key, and you often entrust it to many laymen, who are wholly excluded from the whole sacred order. Nor is it your religion to feel and act; but if anyone here either acts or feels, he changes his religion. But you have once for all renounced all shame, you who say that this is to renounce the faith.

units.la: Sequitur verò, vexata iam illi calumnia de Multis: sed ea iam sæpius mihi obtrita, quam hic tamen, quia nouì nihil habet quod afferat, obtrudit iterum; ego vicissim extrudo: quod, & longè impar pœna, (id quod scit ipse, si quicquam scit in Historiâ) & causa longissimè. Causa enim sub Iuliano, Christi nomen confiteri; dic tu hanc vestram esse apud nos —Clamabo perlse[?] — Frontem[?] de rebus: Néque verò de vllâ vestrâ quam dicis Religione deferendâ agitur, nisi illa Religio vestra est, in Regem machinari atque adeo insurgere, vbi Pontifex digito concrepuerit. Hæc illa est fides Catholica de Pontificis potestate, quæ vna vobis abneganda est: quam, ni abnegetis, fides Catholica vos, etiam Pontificem vestrum, pro suis abnegabit.
units.tr: Next comes the calumny about the many, already much assailed by him; but it has been thrust back by me so often that he thrusts it forward again here, because he has nothing new to bring; I in turn thrust it back: a punishment far from equal (as he himself knows, if he knows anything of history), and a cause very far removed. For under Julian the cause was to confess the name of Christ; tell me that this is your cause among us—"I will cry out…"—"the brow…" concerning matters. Nor is there any question of any religion of yours that you say must be abandoned, unless that religion of yours is to plot against the king and even to rise up against him, whenever the Pontiff snaps his finger. This is that Catholic faith concerning the power of the Pontiff, which alone you must renounce: which, if you do not renounce it, the Catholic faith will disown you, even your Pontiff, for its own sake.

units.la: Fines pòst, conferuntur inter se. Finis Iuliani vnus, Christianitatis euersio. Mutus ad hunc Tortus; vellicat tantùm Regis finem, is est Regni, & Religionis in Regno tranquillitas. Quàm verò ridiculè; fieri id à Rege, vt Catholici primùm, pòst etiam Puritani opprimantur? Vt hic homo solicitus est, non tantùm de Catholicis suis, sed de Puritanis etiam; quasi Cordi sint illi atque Curæ; quasi eis ex animo bene vellet, nollet opprimi: Putasne, de Illis laborat Tortus? Non sanè; id tantùm fatagit, vt & Illos quoque ad tempus fœderatos habeat, vt & illos quoque tumultuari faciat in pacem publicam; ni faciant, mox opprimendo à Rege: vt inuidiâ verbi hâc, illis quoque calcar admoucat, contra Principem & patriam attentandi. Et notum tamen satis, animum illi esse, si essent vires, & illos simul, & nos opprimendi. Finis alter Iuliani, vt Idololatriam reduceret. De hoc tacet etiam. Regis finem carpit, qui est, vt naturalis fidei sua, ac ciuilis obedientiæ professionem obsignent ita subditi. Quid hic carpit autem? scilicet, quòd in toto iuramento, naturalis fides, aut ciuilis obedientia ne semel quidem nominentur. Et ô rem carpendam! Atqui fidelitas & obedientia nominantur ibi, quod nisi vappa sit, fidem, (seu malis dicere fidelitatem) quæ ibi nominatur, non nisi naturalem; & obedientiam non nisi ciuilem potest intelligere. Nec enim Catholica illa fides (quanquam cum illâ amicè conspiret & hæc) nec obedientia, quam Creatura Deo, sed quam ciues Principi præstant, (etsi nec hæc quidem ab illa Dei, aliena est.) Quâ fide, quâque obedientiâ Iuliano etiam parerent Christiani; irent contra Gentem, contra quam illos ire iuberet, memores, fidem, obedientiam in Deum: fidei, obedientia in Cæsarem non officere.
units.tr: Afterwards, the ends are compared with one another. The one end of Julian was the overthrow of Christianity. Torturing Tortus turns to this; he merely carps at the king's end, which is the peace of the kingdom and of religion in the kingdom. How truly ridiculous: that the king should bring it about that Catholics first, and afterwards even Puritans, are oppressed! How anxious this man is, not only about his own Catholics, but about the Puritans too; as if they were dear to him and a care to him; as if he sincerely wished them well and would not have them oppressed. Do you suppose Tortus is labouring on their behalf? Certainly not; he is only busy to have those men too bound to him for the time being, so that they too may be made to stir up trouble against the public peace; and if they do not, then soon they will be oppressed by the king; so that, by the odium of this word, he may also spur them on to attempt something against the Prince and the country. And it is quite well known that his intention, if he had the strength, would be to oppress both them and us at the same time. The other end of Julian was to bring back idolatry. Of this he is silent too. He carps at the king's end, which is that subjects should thereby seal a profession of their natural faith and civil obedience. What does he carp at here, then? Namely, that in the whole oath natural faith or civil obedience are not named even once. And oh, what a thing to carp at! And yet faith and obedience are named there, for unless he is a fool, he can understand the "faith" named there (or you may prefer to say "fidelity") as nothing but natural faith, and the obedience as nothing but civil obedience. For that Catholic faith (although this too harmonises amicably with it) is not what I mean, nor is the obedience which the creature owes to God, but that which citizens owe to the Prince (though not even this is alien from that owed to God). With such faith and such obedience Christians would even obey Julian; they would go against the nation against which he ordered them to go, mindful that faith and obedience toward God do not hinder faith and obedience toward Caesar.

units.la: Negatur verò perpetuò potestas Pontificû. Negatur verò potestas ad malum; potestas ad Rebelliones, Proditiones, Seditiones excitandas; negatur, & ad campos Elysios negabitur à nobis. Dixi Phormio. Sed vbi interim similitudo vlla cum Iuliano; Tres capellæ nobis vbi sunt? Quid? an Iuliano in hoc Rex noster similis? Fauetne[illegible, ~4 letters]Idololatriæ? Audet pene quiduis Tortus, hoc tamen non audet dicere. At de hoc nobis sermo, in hoc collatio omnis est. Ille verò se, relictâ re, confert ad modum, quo Iulianus perduxit ad Idololatriam. Quid hoc ad rem? Perducit ne eòdem Rex? non perducit, imò abducit, quàm potest longissimè. Dissimile ergo totum. De re verò iam, non de modo quæritur. Non potest de re mutire quicquam, audiamus de modo. Sub colore Ciuilis obedientiæ id agit Rex, vt sibi obedientia Sacra tanquam Primati inSpiritualibus, præstetur. Vbi id agit? Quâ parte Iuramenti? Quoto articulo de quatuordecim illis? Designa locum, adhibe verba; torrorem age; exprime si potes inde sensum hunc, vt vsquam ibi agatur vel de Spiritualibus, vel de Primatu in Spiritualibus, vel de Rege in Spiritualibus Primate, vel de Sacrâ vllâ obedientiâ ei deferendâ: Sub colore, imò substantiâ ipsâ mendacij affirmat hoc Tortus: affirmat etiam supra sibi demonstratum esse, quod neque supra neque subter; neque factum est, neq; fiet unquam. Nec est enim ibi, ut monstrari possit, nec verbum ibi pertrahi potest ad Sacram obedientiam, aut Primatum Spiritualium: nec cui candor insit ullus, si legat, relegatque lusiurandum vel millies, tale quid ex eo unquam eruat: Tortum autem, quasi monstrum habeat, qui id ibi monstrari posse autumat.
units.tr: But the power of the Pontiffs is said to be denied for ever. Power to do evil is indeed denied; power to stir up rebellions, betrayals, seditions is denied; it is denied, and will be denied by us even to the Elysian Fields. "I have spoken, Phormio." But where in the meantime is any likeness with Julian? Where are our "three goats"? What? Is our king like Julian in this? Does he favour idolatry? Tortus dares almost anything, yet he does not dare to say this. But this is what the whole discussion and comparison is about. He, however, having left the matter aside, turns to the manner in which Julian led men to idolatry. What has this to do with the matter? Does the king lead men to the same thing? No, indeed he leads them away, as far as he can. The whole thing is therefore dissimilar. Now the question is about the matter, not the manner. He cannot mutter anything about the matter, so let us hear about the manner. Under the colour of civil obedience the king aims at this: that sacred obedience should be rendered to him as "Supreme in Spirituals." Where does he aim at this? In which part of the oath? In which of those fourteen articles? Point out the place, adduce the words; torture them; if you can, extract from there this sense: that anywhere there is any question of "Spirituals," or of "Supremacy in Spirituals," or of "the King as Supreme in Spirituals," or of any sacred obedience to be rendered to him. Under the colour—nay, in the very substance—of a lie, Tortus affirms this: he also affirms that it has been shown above that neither above nor below is it so, nor has it been done, nor will it ever be done. For there is nothing there from which it can be shown, nor can any word there be drawn to sacred obedience or to Supremacy in Spirituals; nor is there any man of candour who, if he reads and rereads the oath a thousand times, would ever extract anything of the kind from it. But Tortus, as if he had a monster, is the one who claims that this can be shown there.

units.la: Dicendum illi iam erat, de suâ illâ maximâ similitudine Regû & Iuliani, quoad Idololatriam. Non potuit miser; vidit Regem, ut initio à Iuliani Polytheismo, ita hic ab Idololatriâ abesse quàm longissimè. Utriusque quidem maculam foedam, sed Idololatriæ hanc imprimis, sibi & Catholicis suis adhærere; Defensionem sibi potiùs pro se, quàm Accusationem ullam in nos instituendam hic esse. Ubi, quâ parte sit Idololatria, facilè videt, non nostrâ scilicet, sed suâ. Unus enim hic articulus inter multos, quorum causâ, Papistæ, Hæretici à nobis (hâc quidem in re) verè Catholicis, censeantur. Hinc autem ut se explicet, inducit se in nouâ Hæresin, nescio dicam an vesaniam, an utrânque; utráque enim est. Se quidem Idololatras non esse, idola non colere, quòd scilicet colant imagines rerum existentium: Eas autem Idola non esse, quòd Idolum, non nisi imago sit rei nusquam existentis. O iecur Theologiæ! Nec aduertit homo acutus, dum hoc dicit, aperte se & Mosi, & verò etiam Deo ipsi contradicere, qui Legè suâ, quâ vetat Idola, vetat fieri omnem similitudinem eorum, quæ in cœlis sunt, vel in terrâ vel in aquis subter terram, quæ sunt Omnes puto Res alicubi existentes. Tam Torto cum Deo praeclarè conuenit; ut absterreat Deus, à cultu similitudinis omnis Rerum quæ usquam existant: Tortus autem contrà iubeat, Faciant verò, colant etiam similitudines Rerum ullas, si modò existant usquam. Idola enim (quicquid dixerit Deus) non esse nisi imagines solas Rerum nusquam existentium. Quare ex nouâ Theologiâ Torti dum Res modò exissat, in cœlo, terrâ, aquis, subter aquas, sit vel malus Dæmon, coram eo incuruare se, & in eo Deum adorare posse. Ad hanc enim insaniam nuper iam deuentum est, eámque libris editis docent, & defendunt boni Theologi, ineóque rem agunt Apostatæ Iuliani, qui si viueret iam, hoc idem ipse pro se diceret: non se Iovem lapidem, sed in lapide Iovem adorare; atque id multò minùs absurdè quàm {a}Vasquius in Diabolo Dei-um: vt si quaerat iam quisquam vbi illa similitudo maxima; reperiet inter duos Pontifices Maximos, Iulianum & Papam, in hac quidem maximam: atque similitudine hac sensim discessionem fieri à Christianismo ad Paganismum, à nouo iam isto Iuliano:
units.tr: He ought now to have said something about his own "greatest likeness of the King and Julian," as regards idolatry. The wretch could not; he saw that the King, as at the beginning he was far from the polytheism of Julian, so here he is as far as possible from idolatry. Of each the foul stain, but of idolatry especially, clings to himself and his Catholics; he should rather be defending himself than instituting any accusation against us here. Where the idolatry is, he easily sees: not in our part, of course, but in his own. For this one article is among many, on account of which Papists are considered by us (in this matter indeed) to be truly Catholics, and heretics. Hence, in order to explain himself, he introduces himself into a new heresy, I know not whether to call it madness or both; for it is both. He says that they are not idolaters, that they do not worship idols, because, of course, they worship images of things that exist; and that those images are not idols, because an idol is nothing but an image of a thing that exists nowhere. "O liver of theology!" Nor does this keen man notice that, in saying this, he openly contradicts both Moses and even God himself, who in his Law, by which he forbids idols, forbids the making of "every likeness of those things which are in heaven, or in the earth, or in the waters under the earth," which are, I suppose, all things existing somewhere. This agrees very well with Tortus, but with God it does not: God frightens people away from the worship of every likeness of things that exist anywhere; whereas Tortus, on the contrary, bids them make, and even worship, any likenesses of things, provided they exist somewhere. For idols (whatever God may say) are nothing but mere images of things that exist nowhere. Therefore, according to the new theology of Tortus, provided the thing exists, whether in heaven, on earth, in the waters, or under the waters, or is even an evil demon, one can bow oneself before it and adore God in it. For they have now come down to this madness, and good theologians teach and defend it in published books, and in this the Apostates of Julian act; and if he were alive now, he would say the same thing for himself: that he did not worship a stone as Jupiter, but worshipped Jupiter in a stone; and that he would do so much less absurdly than Vasquez, who in his book on the Devil says that God is the Devil… So if anyone now asks where that greatest likeness is, he will find it between the two Supreme Pontiffs, Julian and the Pope, in this indeed greatest; and by this likeness a gradual departure from Christianity to Paganism is being made, from this new Julian…

units.la: Proxima huic, de modo collatio. Iulianus subrepsit incautis: Rex nec ab incautis suscipi vult, nec incaute, sed sumpto ad cogitandum spacio. Nec surrepsit: nihil enim proponit ibi nisi explicatum & planum. Hic verò Tortus, crassum se singit, & simplicem, vt qui vias planas, ab asperis nequeat discernere; sed in planitie ipsa impingat in montes, nec vbi sint indicat tamen, nec de modo dissimili vel verbum facit, aut totâ de re. Tantum scias vbi aegrè illi sit, vbi dolor; iterum iam, & iam & semper ad negatam Pontificii potestatem manum habet; ibi dolor est, is mons est, quem in planitie, non sentit, sed somniat. Sed annon modus dissimilis? Nam quicquid hic negatur, apertè negatur, nemini subrepitur incauto. Non posse Pontificem ab obedientiâ Regis subditos absolvere, dicitur ibi dilucidè, diserte, non tectè, non tortuosè. Nec enim, quà Ille Rex est, quà illi subditi, potestas vlla in illos Pontifici; tantum quà Christiani. Reliqua ne dicuntur quidem, quae tu ibi fingis. Non dicitur, Iuro non esse parendum excommunicationi Pontificis: quin parebit, quousque locum habet Censura Ecclesiastica, in Sacris, in rebus Ecclesiae: in Politicis enim Censura locum non habet. Sed neque illud dicitur, Iuro Pontificem ab hoc iuramento me liberare non posse, quia legitimâ plenâque authoritate mihi ministratum est. Disiuncta sunt ibi haec, nec posterior prioris causa, nec quia legitimâ authoritate ministratum, sed quia legitimum, ideo liberare non potest. Potest enim & legitima authoritas esse, quae ministrat, & Iuramentum interdum minùs legitimum, quod ministratur. Hic verò, & quod defertur Iusiurandum, & à quâ defertur authoritas, legitima utraque, vt neutro nomine detrectari debeat.
units.tr: Next to this is the comparison of manner. Julian "creeps upon the unwary": the King wishes to be approached neither by the unwary nor carelessly, but with time given for thought. Nor does he "creep upon": he proposes nothing there but what is explained and plain. Here, however, Tortus pretends to be thick-witted and simple, as one who cannot tell the plain ways from the rough; yet in the very plain he stumbles upon mountains, and he does not indicate where they are, nor does he say a word about a dissimilar manner, or about the matter as a whole. You may only know where it pains him, where his hurt is: again and again, and always, he keeps his hand on the denied power of the Papists; there is his pain, there is the mountain he dreams of rather than feels in the plain. But is the manner not dissimilar? For whatever is denied here is denied openly; no one is crept upon while unwary. That "the Pope cannot absolve the subjects from obedience to the King" is stated there clearly, plainly, not covertly, not tortuously. For the Pope has no power over them as the King is King, or as they are subjects, but only as they are Christians. The other things you invent there are not even said. It is not said, "I swear that I am not to obey the Pope's excommunication": rather he will obey, so far as ecclesiastical censure has its place, in sacred matters, in the affairs of the Church; for in political matters censure has no place. But neither is this said: "I swear that the Pope cannot release me from this oath, because it was administered by a lawful and full authority." These things are set apart there: the latter is not the cause of the former, nor is it because of "administered by lawful authority," but because it is lawful, therefore he cannot release. For the authority which administers may be lawful, and the oath which is administered may sometimes be less lawful. Here, however, both the oath that is offered and the authority from which it is offered are lawful, so that neither can be rejected on either ground.

units.la: Benè autem habet, quòd omnes naturaliter horrent, quae ibi de Proditionibus, Conspirationibus, Regiae personae violentiâ & caede. Benè quòd hoc Tortus fatetur tandem; si tamen fatetur, nec reseruatam habere in mente euasionem Quid ergo? non vel illa iurent, se nullius Proditionis, Conspirationis in Regem, vt vel eius personæ eius inferendæ conscios fore, vel participes, ne fiat ita iubeat Pontifex? Nec tamen nescius est, quò tendant illa, absoluere ab obedientia, interdicere ne pareant? Vbi eo ventum est, Proditiones, Conspirationes, Cædes, quas ita naturaliter horret, non longè abesse? Ecquando enim visum, qui parere semel Regi noluit, vt ei religio fieret coniurandi, aut cui coniurandi religio non fuit, fuerit vlla, vim afferendi? Consequuntur ista se mutuò, & fere ita semper factum est, si semel interdixit ne pareant, edixit non itâ multò post, vt arma teneant. Quæro enim, cum absoluti, vt Regi ne pareant, cui parere eos velit Pontifex? Non enim nulli; non fauet Anarchiae. Ergo aly; cui Regnum in præsidium addixit. Quid ille vero? annon emulum suum primo quoque tempore casum vult? Reliquum est, vt qui naturaliter horrent hæc facientem, naturaliter etiam horrere debent, ad hæc subditos sollicitantem, & ab ea iuramento, quo cauentur hæc, Breuibus suis arcentem, atque abflerrentem.
units.tr: It is well that all men naturally shudder at the things there described: treasons, conspiracies, violence and murder against the royal person. It is well that Tortus at last admits this; yet if he admits it, let him not have an escape reserved in his mind. What then? Will they not swear, even these things, that they will be neither accomplices nor participants in any treason or conspiracy against the King, nor in the violence to his person, lest the Pope command that it be done? Nor is he unaware where those things tend: to absolve from obedience, to forbid them to obey. When it has come to this, are treasons, conspiracies and murders, which he so naturally shudders at, not far off? For when has any man who once refused to obey the King, and to whom conspiring was no matter of conscience, ever been found to have a conscience about bringing force? These things follow one another, and it has nearly always happened so: if the Pope once forbade them to obey, he soon after ordered them to take up arms. For I ask: when he has released them, so that they should not obey the King, whom does the Pope wish them to obey? For not to anyone; he does not favour anarchy. Therefore to another, to whom he has given over the kingdom for protection. And what of him? Does he not wish his rival's downfall at the first opportunity? It remains that he who naturally shudders at those who do these things ought also naturally to shudder at the Pope who, to these ends, solicits the subjects and, by his briefs, keeps them back from and drives them away from the oath by which these things are guarded.

units.la: Vltimum autem est: Iuliani omnia eò facta, vt Idololatriam perpetrarent subditi. Rex & ipse, & subditi ab Idololatria remotissimi; atque adeò non boni Catholici (stilo nouo) quòd adeo remoti. Hæc, vel primo intuenti dissimilitudo summa: Tortus verò sic torquebit, vt similitudo summa fit. Neque tamen, nuper natâ hac sua Idoli definitione, excutiet à se Iulianum sanum. Dicet enim, extitisse initio Ioluem suum paulò ante tempora Heroica, Saturni atque Opis filium: reliquos autem, quos coluit Deos, Iouis Sobolem fuisse. Ita, ne se quidem Idola colere, magis quàm Tortum: non enim Chimæram, vel Tragelaphum, non corpus humanum cum capite equino, nec imaginem vllam, nisi rei quæ aliquando extitit. Tum, quòd Tortum Idolum esse dicit imaginem falsi Dei; agnoscet etiam & hoc Iulianus; & de Torti Sanctis illis haud vllam, verum Deum fuisse, Tortum collegam suum statim admonebit. Quid restat igitur, quàm vt ruant alter in alterius complexus, atque de summâ hâc inter se similitudine mutuò gratulentur?
units.tr: The last point is this: all of Julian's doings were aimed at making the subjects commit idolatry. The King himself and the subjects are most remote from idolatry, and so are not "good Catholics" (in the new style), because they are so remote. At first glance this is the greatest dissimilarity; but Tortus will twist it until it becomes the greatest similarity. Nor, by this newly born definition of his idol, will he shake off the sane Julian from himself. For he will say that his Joluus, a son of Saturn and Ops, existed a little before the heroic times; and that the other gods whom he worshipped were the offspring of Jupiter. Thus he does not even worship idols any more than Tortus does: for he worships neither a Chimera, nor a goat-stag, nor a human body with a horse's head, nor any image except of something that once existed. Then, since Tortus says that an idol is an image of a false god, Julian too will acknowledge this; and he will at once remind his colleague Tortus that those saints of his were no true god. What remains, then, but that the two should fall into each other's embrace and congratulate one another on this supreme similarity?

units.la: Nam quod Apostolum perturbare cupit ad se, quòd is Idolum nihil esse dicat: nihil dicit. Non enim adeo ita falsò Idolum nihil nihil esse dixit Apostolus, nisi quantum ad id, quod esse putatur, rem scilicet, quam refert non habere, nec vim vllam, vt vel iuuet quicquam vel noceat, & (quod erat tibi instituti Apostolici) vt cibum vel sanctificet, vel polluat. Haec vna Patrum, vna omnium interpretum mens, déque eo expresse cauent, ne cum Terto tam plumbei simus, vt venisse vnquam putemus Apostolo in mentem, vt plane nihil putarit esse: cum & materia Idolo aliquid sit, vt lapis, lignum, metallum; & forma ab artifice in materiam inducta, aliquid etiam; nimirum qualitas: sed quoad id quod refert; ibi, pro quo fit vel colitur; id, quod illi de Idolo sentiunt; ea quidem ratione nihil esse: proinde, nihil in mundo, dixisse. In mundo quidem, non in vtramundana, non in Metaphysica Vsquq[?] vel Terti[?] phantasia, in qua aliquid est, quod nihil est; & alicubi, quod nusquam. Phantasmata haec mera sunt, & cerebri vestri Idola. Illa vero etiam dementia tua, vt quenquam existimes tam dementem, qui eo sensu Imagines, vel Christi, vel Sanctorum Idola putet, quod Christus, vel Sancti nusquam sint, vel nihil.
units.tr: As for his wish to disturb the Apostle with his claim that an idol is nothing, he says nothing. For the Apostle did not speak so falsely when he said that an idol is nothing at all, except as to that which is thought to be, namely the thing which he says has no existence, and no power to help anything or to harm, and (which was your concern in the Apostolic passage) to sanctify or to defile food. This is the one mind of the Fathers, the one mind of all interpreters, and they take care expressly on this point not to be so leaden-witted as Tertus, as to think that it ever came into the Apostle's mind that he judged it to be utterly nothing: since the material of an idol is something, such as stone, wood, metal; and the form introduced into the material by the craftsman is also something, namely a quality. But as to that which it signifies, that for which it is made or worshipped, what they feel about the idol, in that sense it is nothing; therefore he said "nothing in the world." "In the world," indeed, not in the other-worldly, not in the metaphysical fancy of Vsquq or Tertus, in which something is what is nothing, and somewhere is what is nowhere. These phantasms are pure, and idols of your brain. Yet your madness is such that you think anyone so mad as to suppose that images of Christ or of the Saints are idols in this sense, that Christ or the Saints are nowhere or nothing.

units.la: Scis ipse (nisi non vis scire) eas[?] alio longe sensu Idola a nobis haberi; quod scilicet sensu, Idolum erat Serpens ænëus, qui imago Serpentis fuit, Serpentis dico, proin rei existentis; & tamen Idolum, quod cultus iam abusum pateretur. Qua ratione, etsi Dei iussu conflatus fuerat Serpens ille, etsi miraculis insignis, etsi Christi ipsius Symbolum; tamen cum abusus illos pateretur (neque tamen tantos, quantos quotidie patiuntur Imagines apud vos) ab Ezechia sine scrupulo comminutus est: vt & si Ezechiam vos haberetis vllum, vestrae quoque illae essent comminuendae.
units.tr: You yourself know (unless you do not want to know) that in a quite different sense we hold them as idols. In that sense, the bronze serpent was an idol, which was an image of a serpent (I say of a serpent, therefore of a thing existing), and yet an idol, since it was already suffering abuse of worship. For this reason, although that serpent was cast by God's command, although it was remarkable for miracles, although it was even a symbol of Christ himself; yet, since it suffered those abuses (though not so great as those your images suffer daily), it was broken in pieces by Hezekiah without scruple. So that, if you had any Hezekiah, those images of yours would have to be broken in pieces as well.

units.la: Neque vero Anathema illud Septimae Synodi quicquam ad nos. Non enim Imagines, seu Christi, seu Sanctorum, Idola nominamus. Non sunt; quà à se certè; sed tamen Idola fieri posse dicimus, quà à vobis; non minus quam Serpens aeneus a Iudaeis, tum demum scilicet, si adorentur. Sunt enim similitudines eorum, qui in coelis, coram quibus prociditis, quaeque colitis; quod discernis verbis vetitum, lege Diuina. Imagines ergo in se, Idola autem Terto, vbi colere occepit: quo facto, & ille, & qui idem cum illo faciunt omnes, Idololatrae sunt.
units.tr: Nor does that anathema of the Seventh Synod concern us in any way. For we do not call images, whether of Christ or of the Saints, idols. They are not so in themselves, certainly; but we do say that they can become idols, as far as you are concerned, no less than the bronze serpent did among the Jews, namely when they are worshipped. For they are likenesses of those who are in heaven, before whom you fall prostrate, and whom you worship; which the divine law forbids, as you distinguish in words. Images, then, are images in themselves; but they are idols to Tertus, when he begins to worship them: by which act he, and all who do the same as he, are idolaters.

units.la: Accedit iam Tertus ad exemplum Eleazari: impeditus in via nonnihil conuitiis, & pugnę, quae tamen omittit semper, dimittit nunquam. Ibi verò, audet dicere (audet certè dicere) multa, utinam etiam vacaret probare) Eleazarum, non tam iustam causam fuisse carnis porcinæ non gustandæ, quam Papistæ iuramenti recusandi. Vbi, sumit primò eandem vbique esse, imperantis authoritatem. Nos non damus. Multum enim interesse, Breui Pauli quinti, Iuramentum; Verbo Dei, esum carnis porcinæ interdictum: multum autem interesse inter Verbum Dei, & Breue Pontificis. Tum, seriò nobis narrat, & extra iocum, mysterium magnum; potestatem Pontificis sui, rem esse longè superiorem carne porcinâ. Ridet, credo, Lector, ad sublimitatem carnis porcinæ, & collationem eius cum potestate Papæ, vtra sublimior. At si à macello petere voluit, si de carne instituere comparationem; de sapore vel precio debuit, non de sublimitate disputare, præsertim autem non de carne porcinâ, quæ certè sublimis non est, fere semper in cœno volutatur, vt non multum accedat ad potestatem Papalem, si longè sit quàm illa sublimior. Ridet hæc Lector: Pontifex non ridet, quòd cum porco se, potestatem suam cum suillis carnibus in comparationem adduxerit. Certè res erant non eiusdem generis, nec instituí debebat inter eas, vlla comparatio: Iodia autem est alea: Etiam sublime, in fumo pendente carne porcinâ, sublimior tamen est potestas Pontificia. Hæret verò adhuc nobis scrupulus. Nam si (quod opinor Aduersarius non negabit) impar sit, longéque sublimior authoritas verbi Diuini, quàm Breuis Pontificis; magis peccabit Eleazarus, qui porcinam gustabit, quod verbo Diuino; quàm qui Iuramentum suscipiet, quod Breui utroque prohibetur. Nec abnegabit tamen quis, potestatem Pontificis, aut sublimitatem eius præ carne porcinâ; sed authoritatem Dei dicentis, Ne gusta; sublimiorem putabit Pontificis authoritate, dicentis, Ne iure; & quidem tanto sublimiorem Diuinam hanc illâ Pontificiâ, adeóque plus tantò, quàm est potestas Pap.e sublimior carne porcinâ. Quare Eleazari in hac quidem re causa potior. Sed in hoc decipitur Tortus, vel decipere alios nixitur, quòd cùm de eo agitur, vtri parendum, Deo legem ferenti, an Papæ Breue scribenti; ille aliam rem agi affirmat, cum porco Papam, & potestatem Papæ cum porcinâ carne comparari.
units.tr: Tortus now comes to the example of Eleazar: hindered on the way somewhat by insults and fighting, which he always omits yet never dismisses. There, indeed, he dares to say (he certainly dares to say) many things (would that he had leisure to prove them as well) that Eleazar did not have so just a cause for not eating the flesh of swine as the Papists have for refusing the oath. Here he first assumes that the authority of the commander is everywhere the same. We do not grant it. For there is a great difference between an oath under a Brief of Pope Paul V and the prohibition of eating pig's flesh by the Word of God; and a great difference between the Word of God and a Brief of the Pope. Then he tells us seriously, and not in jest, a great mystery: that the power of his Pope is a thing far superior to pig's flesh. The reader, I suppose, laughs at the loftiness of pig's flesh, and at the comparison of it with the power of the Pope, as to which is the loftier. But if he wished to draw his comparison from the butcher's stall, if he was to institute a comparison about meat, he ought to have argued about flavour or price, not about loftiness; and above all not about pig's flesh, which is certainly not lofty, but almost always wallows in the mud, so that it does not much approach the Papal power, even if the latter is far loftier. The reader laughs at this; the Pope does not laugh, that he has brought his power into comparison with pig's flesh. Certainly the things were not of the same kind, and no comparison ought to have been instituted between them: "but the die is cast." Even "lofty," while the pig's flesh hangs in smoke, the Papal power is nevertheless loftier. But a scruple still troubles us. For if (as I think the adversary will not deny) the authority of the Divine Word is unequal to, and far loftier than, the Brief of the Pope, then Eleazar, who would taste the pig, would sin more against the Divine Word than he who takes the oath, which both Briefs forbid. Nor would anyone deny that the power of the Pope, or its loftiness, surpasses pig's flesh; but the authority of God saying "Do not taste" is loftier than the authority of the Pope saying "Do not swear," and indeed the divine command is loftier than the Papal one by so much, and therefore by just so much more than the power of the Pope is loftier than pig's flesh. Wherefore Eleazar's cause is the stronger in this matter. But Tortus is deceived in this, or strives to deceive others: when the question is whom one must obey, God giving the law or the Pope writing a Brief, he affirms that a different matter is being treated, namely that the Pope is compared with pig, and the power of the Pope with pig's flesh.

units.la: Pòst autem quæri dicit ab Apologiæ Authore, exemplum è Scri- ptura pturā[?] Diuinā, quo detractio obedientiæ stabiliatur. Et quærit quidem, sed nullum Torto ad manum erat, nullum profert; & dum nullum profert, nullum fatetur esse: Sed si velis pro stabiliendâ Pontificis potestate, tum vero habere se in promptu. At hoc nemo quærit. Quorsum enim? Quia labefactatur Iuramento potestas illa. Ne id quidem; intra limites suos tantum concludi-tur, vt decurrat aluceo suo, ne exundet in negotia quæ Ecclesiæ non sunt, sed Seculi; quæ inter Principem sunt & Subditos efficia, iis ne se immisceat; reliquis in rebus stabilis Pontifici potestas & immota manet. Verùm omninò audiendæ nobis sunt, quæ annotatæ illi sunt sententiæ pro Pontifice suo stabiliendo. Credo equidem vix venales, ita obtrudit. Agedum, inspiciamus. In Deuteronomio præceptum est; Satis aperte ibi legitur, Qui superbierit nolens obedire Sacerdotis imperio; &c. Satis ibi aliquid aperte legitur, sed non satis integrè citatur. Quid enim? an imperio Sacerdotis vtcunq;, qualicunque? An Aaronis imperio, vitulum adorare iubentis? An Abiathar imperio, contra Salomonem cum Adoniâ conspirantis? An Caiphæ imperio Christum morte dignum pronunciantis? Non opinor. Est ibi, præter ea, quæ Torto citare visum, vel supra paulò vel infrà, quod doceat nos quali Sacerdotis imperio; id Tortus non bonâ fide celauit. Ita præcedentia verba habent, Imperio Sacerdotu iuxta Legem Dei docentis, tum, sequeris sententiam eius; tum si superbierit nolens obedire, currit Lex ista contra te.
units.tr: Afterwards he says the Author of the Apology ought to be asked for an example from Divine Scripture by which the withdrawal of obedience is established. And he does ask, but he has no example at hand for Torto, and he produces none; and since he produces none, he admits there is none. But if you want an example for establishing the power of the Pontiff, then indeed he says he has one ready. Yet nobody asks this. For what purpose? Because that power is weakened by an oath. Not even that: it is confined within its own limits only, so that it runs in its own channel and does not overflow into matters which are not of the Church but of the world, which arise between prince and subjects; he should not meddle with these. In the remaining matters the power of the Pontiff is stable and remains unshaken. But truly we ought to hear in full the opinions which have been noted for him, to establish his Pontiff. I believe they are hardly for sale; this is how he pushes them forward. Come, let us look. In Deuteronomy a precept is given: "It is read quite plainly there, He that shall presume not to obey the sentence of the priest, etc." Something is indeed read quite plainly there, but it is not quoted completely enough. For what? Is it the command of the priest in any way whatever, of any kind? The command of Aaron, who ordered the calf to be worshipped? The command of Abiathar, who conspired with Adonijah against Solomon? The command of Caiaphas, who pronounced Christ worthy of death? I do not think so. There is, besides those things which Torto thought fit to cite, a little above or below, something which teaches us what kind of priest's command it is; Torto has concealed this without good faith. For the preceding words read: "by the command of the priest teaching according to the law of God"; then, "you shall follow his sentence"; then, "if he presume not to obey", that law runs against you.

units.la: Iam verò noua lis; An docuerit nos Paulus quintus Breui suo iuxta Legem Dei; imo lis nulla: Non enim docet ibi iuxta Legem Dei, nec docet quidem, loquitur sine lege, iubet, terret, ex mero imperio agit in Breuibus suis, non est Sacerdos iuxta Legem Dei docens. Non ergo præcepto hoc vlla eius potestas stabilitur.
units.tr: Now truly there is a new question: whether Paul the Fifth has taught us by his Brief "according to the law of God"; indeed there is no question at all. For he does not teach there according to the law of God, nor does he even teach; he speaks without law, he commands, he terrifies, he acts by mere authority in his Briefs; he is not a priest teaching according to the law of God. Therefore no power of his is established by this precept.

units.la: Placetne etiam exemplum eius inspicere? dices non magis appositum. Horrendum Dei iudicium in Core, Dathan, & Abiron, propter schisma & defectionem à Mose & Aaron, qui tum summi Sacerdotes. Hic, ne exemplum eius periret, necesse habuit Duos simul eodem tempore Summos Sacerdotes creare. Duos autem Summos? Phoca nobis opus est, vt vter hic summus, Romanus an Constantinopolitanus: Concilio Pisano opus, vt, Gregorius an Benedictus vter Summus, expediat. Quod si duo Summi, quid Phocâ opns, quidue Pisano Concilio[?] Sint Cyriacus & Bonifacius, sint Gregorius & Benedictus, vt Moses & Aaron, Summi ambo; Credo autem non æquis oculis aspecturum Paulum quintum doctrinam hanc de duobus Summis; & Censori Vosmero malam gratiam habiturum, quòd ita officitanter hunc locum prætererit. Mallet enim omissum inter nuga Torti & conuitia, horrendum hoc exemplum, quàm ita adhibitum, vnde suboleat cuiquam plures uno Pontifices Summos vnquam extitisse; ad illud exemplum, plures uno iam posse existere. Puto etiam ad illorum hæresin accessuru Pontificem non inuitum, qui postquam à Deo vocatus Aaron, Mosen exauthoratum sentiunt; nihil Mosi post, cum Pontificatu fuisse. Magis ad rem Pontificis, magis ad gustum opinio illa; qui mallet fratrem nullum habere (ne Mosen quidem) quàm non solus pontificari sine fratre.
units.tr: Is it also agreeable to look at his example? You will say it is no more apposite. "The dreadful judgment of God upon Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, on account of the schism and defection from Moses and Aaron, who were then high priests." Here, so that his example should not perish, he was obliged to create two high priests at the same time. But two high priests? We need Phocas, so that it may be seen which of them is the high priest, the Roman or the Constantinopolitan: we need the Council of Pisa, so that it may be settled whether Gregory or Benedict is the high priest. But if there are two high priests, what need is there of Phocas, or what need of the Council of Pisa? Let there be Cyriacus and Boniface, let there be Gregory and Benedict, like Moses and Aaron, both high priests; yet I believe Paul the Fifth will not look with an equal eye upon this doctrine of "two high priests", and he will be ill pleased with the Censor Vosmer, because he has so awkwardly passed over this passage. For he would rather have this dreadful example omitted among the trifles and abuse of Torto than adduced in such a way that it suggests to anyone that more than one Pontiff as high priest has ever existed, since by that example more than one can now exist. I think the Pontiff too will not be unwilling to come to the heresy of those who, after Aaron was called by God, feel that Moses was deposed, and that nothing was left to Moses after the priesthood. That opinion is more to the point of the Pontiff, more to his taste; he would rather have no brother at all (not even Moses) than to be priest alone without a brother.

units.la: Ne labascat authoritas Papalis, vides quæ fulcra supposuerit è Veteri, vult etiam & de Nouo; exorari non potest: sed non noua, vel de nouo edolata, imò vetera illa, quæ iam tempus erat vt respirarent paululùm, ita vexata diu, ita sæpe angarias passa; Quodcunque ligaueris; & Pasce oues. Prius illud, dictum à Christo, non Imperatori vel Regi; debebat autem addere, cùm multi tum Imperatores essent & Reges Christiani; atque ita aliquid diceret. Nam cùm nullus tum esset cui diceret, qui potuit ulli dicere? Quanquam etiam, si tum Reges suissent, non dedisset illis ligandi, soluendique potestatem: nec Imperator illam, nec Rex vllus vendicat: quare frustra adiectum, Non Imperatori vel Regi. Petro autem dictum illud, Petro, quem vicarium constituit super familiam suam. Sitonomum, credo, dicere voluit, quem dixit Vicarium, cui de tritici mensura distribuendâ munus incumbit. Verùm esto. Quis ille ergo ibi, quem constituit super omnia quæ possidet? Ei enim, qui super familiam constitutus οπμβων[?] cuique dando, & munere suo probè perfunctus fuerat, mereces hæc est, super omnia quæ possidet Dominus constituit. Mallet posterius hoc Papa; vna enim illi tritici cura nimis angusta est. Locus male adductus, non satis in eo rem egisti, vel Petri, vel Pauli quinti.
units.tr: So that the Papal authority may not totter, you see what props he has supplied from the Old Testament; he wants also to use the New. It cannot be wheedled out of him; but not new things, or things newly beaten out, but those old texts, which had long been time for them to breathe a little, so long harassed, so often made to suffer forced services: "Whatsoever you shall bind"; and "Feed my sheep." The former saying, spoken by Christ, is "not to the Emperor or the King"; but he ought to have added, since there were then many Emperors and Christian Kings, and so he would have said something. For when there was then no one to whom he might speak, how could he speak to anyone? Although also, if there had been Kings then, he would not have given them the power of binding and loosing: neither the Emperor nor any King claims it; therefore the words "not to the Emperor or the King" are added in vain. But to Peter that saying: "to Peter, whom he set as steward over his household." He wished, I believe, to call him a steward, whom he called the steward, whose office it is to distribute the measure of wheat. But grant it. Who then is that one there, "whom he set over all that he possesses"? For to one who was set over the household, and had faithfully discharged his duty of giving to each, the reward is this: "The Lord set him over all that he possesses." The Pope would prefer this latter; for care of a single measure of wheat is too narrow for him. The passage is badly adduced; you have not dealt sufficiently with it, either with Peter or with Paul the Fifth.

units.la: Sed ligat, & soluit Petrus. Liget verò, & soluat, sed iniusta vincula; Vinculum, quo Principi subditus ligatur, iustum (etsi Principi dyscolo) & secundum voluntatem Dei, ait Petrus ipse; quare Petrus haud solueret: Debitum, idque ex debito conscientiae maximo, ait Paulus; quare nec Paulus. Siquis ergo Pontificum soluere praesumpserit; iram Omnipotentis Dei, & Apostolorum eius Petri & Pauli se nouerit incursurum. Verum & mandauit vt omnes suas pascerent; sanè, mandauit; & in eo, Ouibus etiam, vt se pasci regique permitterent. Stabiliuit ergo potestatem eius, potestatem pascendi, quis negat? Sed duo haec Deus ipse nos docuit: opposita esse, Pascere, & cum authoritate imperare, ac potentiâ. Auferum autem imperium hoc, amarum pabulum; Regi ne iurate; Quod iurâstis iuramentum eierate; Regem deserite; Regi alij adhaerete, cui ego Regnum concessero. Suffocat, non pascit doctrina haec. Eleazarus, aut cuicunque bona mens, non magis eam gustaret, quàm carnes porcinas.
units.tr: "But Peter binds and looses." Indeed he binds and looses, but unjust bonds; the bond by which a subject is bound to a prince is just (though the prince be perverse) and according to the will of God, says Peter himself; therefore Peter would not loosen it. A debt, and that from the greatest debt of conscience, says Paul; therefore neither would Paul. If anyone therefore of the Pontiffs has presumed to loosen it, let him know that he will incur the wrath of Almighty God and of his Apostles Peter and Paul. But indeed he also commanded that all his sheep be fed; certainly he commanded it; and in that, that the sheep also should allow themselves to be fed and ruled. He established, therefore, his power, the power of feeding; who denies it? But God himself has taught us these two things to be opposed: to feed, and to command with authority and power. But this authority is a bitter fodder: "Do not swear to the king"; "Break the oath you have sworn"; "Desert the king"; "Adhere to another king, to whom I shall have granted the kingdom." This doctrine suffocates; it does not feed. Eleazar, or anyone of good mind, would no more taste it than pork.

units.la: Ad rem verò vel maximè Iuramentum Saulis, sed non vestram. Ad arma clamatum est; ingruebât hostis, defuit tempus; deferri non potuit singulis; simul omnes adiurauit. Etsi autem Rex solus suscepit, nec vir quisquam de populo; tamen quasi singuli suscepissent, ita religio fuit omni populo illud violare; etsi fatiscerent iam, etsi deliquium paterentur; mori illis satius fuit, quàm Regis iusiurandum transgredi. Fuerit verò temerè emissum; fuerit per illud, non satis consultum victoriae suae; qualecunque fuerit; at Populus tamen interim, quàm sollicitus de eo seruando? Vides, vt exhorruit ille, qui Ionathanem vidit de melle gustantem. Quantatum cura Prophetis edocendi populum, vt [?]os Regis observarent, & praecepta iuramenti Dei? Quanta autem Legum securitas, vt morte luendum esset illi, qui Regem adiurantem audisset, nec quasi ipse iuratus esset, ita se, & non minùs, iuramento Regio constrictum putaret? Quid quaerimus? Datae sunt fortes; Deus ipse de sinu [?]sulostensionem dedit, & quasi protraxit ad poenam Ionathanem, de spreto iureiurando Paterno. Haec ergo adducta vt doceant, quanti olim fuerit iusiurandum, quo Rex suos constrinxit, quanta eius religio, quam nemo detrectârit. Tu aliorsum trahis; & temeritatem eius inculcas; sed frustrà. Esto enim, temeritas in Saule fuit, quam luit poenâ periculo Primogeniti. At argumenti maior ex eo vis est, magis vos stringit. Si enim populus Dei iuramento tum tantum detulit, tam parum con-sulto: diu multumq; consulto, Comitijs Curiatis legitimè rogato, quale hoc nostrum est, plus adhuc multò magisque de-tulisset; vester quoque populus si Dei esset, non minus deferret.
units.tr: Indeed, the oath of Saul is most pertinent to the matter, but not yours. The cry to arms was raised; the enemy was pressing, there was no time; it could not be carried to each individually; he bound them all together by oath at once. Although the King alone undertook it, and not any man of the people, yet it was held as a matter of religion by the whole people, as if each had undertaken it, to violate it; even though they were already fainting, even though they were suffering failure; it was better for them to die than to transgress the King's oath. But let it be that it was rashly uttered; let it be that by it he had not sufficiently consulted the success of his own cause; whatever it was, yet how anxious was the people meanwhile to keep it! You see how he shrank back, who saw Jonathan tasting honey. How great was the care of the Prophets in teaching the people to observe the Lord's words and the precepts of God's oath! And how great was the security of the laws, that he who heard the King swearing should be put to death, unless he thought himself bound by the King's oath no less than if he had sworn himself! What more do we ask? Brave men were given; God himself gave a sign from the bosom of the lot, and as it were drew Jonathan to punishment for having despised his father's oath. These things, therefore, are brought forward to teach how highly the oath was esteemed of old, by which the King bound his people, how great its sanctity, which no one would have dared to disregard. You draw it in another direction, and you press its rashness; but in vain. For grant that there was rashness in Saul, which he paid for with the peril of his firstborn. But the argument from it has greater force, and binds you more. For if the people of God then bore the oath so little considered, but so much and so carefully considered, duly proposed to the Curiate Assembly, what is this of ours? It would have borne much more, and more strongly; your people too, if it belonged to God, would bear it no less.

units.la: AD Basilij exemplum, agnoscas Tortum statim ex responso suo. Par sanè fuit, nec iniquum ibi postulabat Apologia, quæ inibi erant verba planè proxima, à Cardinale apponi, nec ita sententiam decurtari: Esse enim verba illa nonnihil ad rem. Hic Tortus more suo, proterue primum. Noluit Bellarminus librum Theodoreti describere. Lineæ sunt vix duæ, quas adiectas cupiebat; lineas vix duas addere, hoc est Torto Theodoreti Librum totum exscribere. Quàm importunè! Verùm antiquum hîc obtinet. Vbi priùs, rationem aliquam allatam voluit Apologia in Breui; hoc ipso dicebat, perträhere nos Pontificem ad disputandum in Scholis Theologicis, vel ad librum integrum in Theologiâ conscribendum. Quod sex aut octo Lineis absolui poterat, id erat tum illi Librum conscribere: quod Lineâ unâ, atque alterâ poterat, id est illi iam Theodoreti Librum describere. Auferre autem istam proteruiam. Post verò effert (homo garrulus) consilium Domini sui, & fatetur id quod res est, quod ad rem suam facit, hoc Bellarminum adducere voluisse. Cur autem adducat, quod ad rem suam non facit? Atqui hoc iam ingenui non est: Locum integrum adducat, faciat ad rem suam, non faciat; id bonæ fidei est, de quâ non valdè se torquet Tortus, agat cà, an non agat Dominus, nisi faciat ad rem suam. Nescias, proterue magis hic ab eo responsum fit, an inepte.
units.tr: After the example of Basil, you will recognise Tortus at once from his reply. It was certainly fair, and the Apology did not ask for anything unreasonable, that the words which were there, being exactly the nearest ones, should be set down by the Cardinal, and that the sense should not be cut short in this way: for those words bear something on the matter. Here Tortus, as is his custom, first acts shamelessly. "Bellarmine was unwilling to copy out Theodoret's book." There are scarcely two lines which he wanted added; to add scarcely two lines, that is, to Tortus, is to copy out the whole of Theodoret's book. How unreasonable! But the old trick holds good here. Where the Apology earlier wished some reasoning to be brought forward in brief, it was saying by this very thing that it was drawing the Pontiff "to dispute in the theological schools," or "to write a whole book in theology." What could be finished in six or eight lines, that was then to write a book; what could be done with one line or another, that is, to copy out Theodoret's book already. But Tortus should put aside that shamelessness. Afterwards, however, this chatterer brings out his master's purpose and admits what is the case, that it served his own cause, that Bellarmine was wished to be brought in by this. But why does he bring in what does not serve his cause? Yet this is no longer the part of an honest man: let him bring in the whole passage, let him make it serve his cause or not serve it; that is a matter of good faith, about which Tortus does not greatly trouble himself, whether his master acts in this or not, unless it "serves his own cause." You would not know whether his reply here is more shameless or more foolish.

units.la: Tandem etiam, magni pendere Regis amicitiam dicit Cardinalem. Quod si faceret, næ ille rationes longè alias iniret, eius conciliandæ; nec si eam quæreret, factum Eius satis à se legitimum, quodque nemo est, qui meliorem in partem non possit interpretari, ita totus operam poneret, scriptiunculis suis odiosum reddere. Exempla sibi eligeret longè alia, & personarum, quibuscum Regem; & rerum, quibuscum Regis in eo consilium exæquaret: terminos etiam qui magis deceant (quæque ei non desunt, si ita animatus foret) adhibe-tet. Cum pietate verò dicis; Quidni? Et est hîc pietatis satis, eiusque summa in patriam, prolem, Principem, addo, & Deum ipsum, in summâ contra hos omnes impietate reprimendâ. Sed pietatem canet Cardinalis, ex Pontificis arbitrio pius, pietas illi tota ex eo pendet: quod illi placet pium est; quod secus, piandum. Fruatur sanè hâc pietate suâ.
units.tr: Finally, he also says that the Cardinal values the friendship of the King highly. But if he did, he would certainly take quite different steps to win it, and if he were seeking it, he would not devote all his effort to making his own deed, which he himself considers lawful enough, and which no one could fail to interpret in a better light, odious through his little writings. He would choose for himself examples quite different, both of persons, with whom he might compare the King, and of matters, with which he might compare the King's counsel in this affair; he would also use terms more becoming (which he would not lack, if he were so minded). "You say it with piety"? Why not? And there is enough piety here, and its sum lies in the country, the offspring, the Prince, I add, and God himself, in the overall suppression of impiety against all these. But the Cardinal sings the praises of piety; by the Pontiff's judgment, what is pious is pious, and piety depends entirely on that for him: what pleases him is "pious"; what does not, "to be expiated." Let him by all means enjoy this piety of his.

units.la: At etiam Tortum male habet, longa narratio de Valente, adhibita solum, ut liber grandior redderetur. Non adeo vero grandescit liber paginá vix unâ; factum narrare opus erat, non ut Liber grandior, sed ut fraus ibi vestra apertior redderetur. Nec illud prius à vobis positum: at Breue utrumq;[?] & non breuis Epistola, prius in Apologiâ posita, integra iterum à vobis reposita sunt. Et ea quidem constant non unica, sedecim ad minus paginis; non hoc credo, ut liber tuus multò gracilior redderetur. Poterat quidem, has verè nugas omittere emissor[?] iste nugarum. Illa verò non rectè à te instituta comparatio; quî potuit rectè à Torto? Non debuit cum Ariano componi osor Arij, atque Arianorum omnium; etiam Liberij Pontificis, quâ in Arianam hæresin subscripsit. Tum causa longè disparibus. Valentis persecutio Catholicorum fuit, quòd Catholici essent, quòd Christum Deum dicerent: vestra si qua est vexatio, ex causâ multum dissimili, quòd proditores estis; quidam certè fuistis, reliqui ciuitare[?] non vultis proditionem, non obstante Pontifice quem Christi Vicarium dicitis; atque in eo Christum infamatis, quasi ille obstare vellet Vicarium ullum suum, ne Reges tui, Subditi fideles sint. Quæ, si Catholicorum olim causa fuisset apud Valentem, non ille tum Ecclesias presbyteris nudâsset, sed Ecclesias ipsas cum presbyteris simul, adeoque nomen ipsum Catholicum eradicâsset. Quodsi Basilij hæc tum causa fuisset, qui diuinè innutritus erat sermonibus, salutâ pietate, non renuisset Imperatoris gratiam: sed quam Iuliano Apostatâ, vix ante annum; eandem iam Valenti Ariano fidem, atque obedientiam ciuilem lætus lubens detulisset: nec à Liberio sententiâ expectâsset, an Imperatori fidelis esse posset, quamquam obstaret ipse Pontifex; quin, si Ille Brevi aliquo suo obstitisset, Illum cum Breuibus suis valerelongum iussisset.
units.tr: But it also galls Tortus that "the long narrative about Valens was added only so that the book might be made larger." Yet the book is scarcely made larger by one page; it was necessary to relate the deed, not so that the book should be larger, but so that your fraud might be made more evident there. Nor was that point put forward by you first: but "the brief one of both, and the not brief letter," set out earlier in the Apology, were again restored entire by you. And these indeed amount to not a few, at least sixteen pages; I do not believe this was done so that your book might be made much slimmer. He could, to be sure, have omitted these truly trifles, this emitter of trifles. But that comparison, not rightly instituted by you, how could it be rightly instituted by Tortus? He ought not to have set beside the Arian the hater of Arius and of all Arians, even of the Pontiff Liberius, who subscribed to the Arian heresy. Then the causes are far unlike. The persecution of Valens was of Catholics, because they were Catholics, because they called Christ God; your vexation, if it is any, arises from a very dissimilar cause, because you are traitors. Some of you indeed certainly are, the rest of you do not wish to be traitors, though the Pontiff whom you call Christ's Vicar does not prevent it; and in this you defame Christ, as if he wished to hinder any Vicar of his from making your Kings and their faithful subjects. If the cause of Catholics had once been the cause before Valens, he would not then have stripped the churches of their presbyters, but would have uprooted the churches themselves together with the presbyters, and so the very name Catholic. But if this had been Basil's cause at that time, who had been nourished divinely in the words of salutary piety, he would not have refused the Emperor's favour; but the same loyalty and civil obedience which, scarcely a year before, he had gladly and willingly rendered to Julian the Apostate, he would now have rendered to Valens the Arian; nor would he have waited for a sentence from Liberius, whether he could be faithful to the Emperor, even though the Pontiff himself stood in the way; indeed, if he had stood in the way with some brief of his own, he would have bidden him farewell with all his briefs.

units.la: Atqui illa Dogmatis subtilitas quam dicis, ad vestras æquivocationes non malè quadrare posset: tenues enim certè sunt, nec aranearum telæ, magis eis subtiles: Ad Iuramentum nullo modo possunt; cauetur ibi contra illas apertè, lumen ibi apponitur, contra colores vestros. De negato autem ibi Primatus, vide an persuadere possis nuper-Archipresbytero. Ille vero & Jusiurandum jurauit, & zelator tamen est Primatus, quàm iniuratus, tàm juratus; nec occulte in eo uspiam latère deprehendit, quam vos fingitis abnegationem; & vos si colorem ullum ibi cernitis nisi candidum, strabos & tortu oculorum radijs esse iurabit. Quare vero ex Illo (si credis Illi) qui optimè tibi potest, & libentissimè vult confirmare, nec interrogatum se de causa fidei vel religionis. Comprehensus est, etiam detinetur ex alia causa. Plures enim sunt causæ ei, qui Archipresbyter hic tam diu fuerit, quàm una, fidei: satis illi quod vixit ex fide sua, fide (inquam) sua Juramento suo datâ. Deca etero, quòd in custodiâ est, custodia illa fortasse facit, non tam ne liber sit, quàm ut in vivis sit: ut quæ illum ab insidiis custodiat, quæ, si ut antea aberraret, non difficile illi intentari possent. Sed illud à te factum malè, quod omittis loco hoc, quo minimè omnium oportet, sententias illas labefactatrices potestatis Pontificiæ. Si noluisti id in gratiam nostram facere, at dedisses hoc Archipresbytero, qui labasceret forte, si labefactatam ibi cerneret Papæ authoritatem, authoritatem dico quam à Deo habet, non quam sibi nuper in Reges per fas, nefasque, arrogavit. Quare, & sententiam illam quam tu, quasi Delphica esset, ad omnes usus accommodas, retorqueret in te; obedire enim se Deo, qui dat salutem Regibus, dum Regem saluum vult, magis quàm hominibus malè conciliatis, (quorum te, in numero forte habet) qui Pontifici obtruditis: magis quàm Pontifici ipsi, qui cupidè arripit potestatem in salutem Regum quam Petrus, nec exercuit unquam, nec habuit, ut exerceret.
units.tr: Yet that "subtlety of doctrine" which you speak of might well suit your equivocations: for they are certainly thin, not even spiders' webs are more fine. They cannot be applied to the Oath in any way; there it is openly guarded against, a light is set there against your pretences.
