As for the denial of the Primacy mentioned there, see whether you can persuade the recent Archpresbyter. He swore the oath, and yet he is a zealot for the Primacy, as much sworn as unsworn; nor does he detect anywhere in it any hidden thing which you feign to be a denial, and if you see any colour there except white, you will swear that you are squint-eyed and have the rays of your eyes twisted. But why from him (if you believe him), who can very well and most willingly confirm it for you, that he was not questioned about the cause of faith or religion. He has been seized, and he is also detained on another cause. For there are more causes for him, who has been Archpresbyter here for so long, than the one, of faith: it is enough for him that he has lived by his faith, his faith (I say) given by his oath. Moreover, that he is in custody, that custody perhaps does not so much serve to keep him from being free as to keep him alive: so that it may guard him from ambushes, which, if he should stray as before, could not easily be threatened against him. But what you have done badly is that you omit in this place, where it is least of all fitting, "those sentences which undermine the power of the Pontiff." If you were unwilling to do this for our sake, you should at least have given it to the Archpresbyter, who might perhaps waver if he saw the authority of the Pope undermined there, the authority, I say, which he has from God, not what he has lately arrogated to himself over Kings by right and wrong. Therefore he would also turn back upon you that sentence which you apply to all uses as if it were Delphic: for he is obeying God, who gives salvation to Kings, while he wills the King to be safe, rather than men ill-disposed (among whom perhaps he counts you) who press the Pontiff upon you; rather than the Pontiff himself, who eagerly seizes a power for the salvation of Kings which Peter neither exercised nor had, to exercise.

units.la: Tum etiam amicè te admoneret, etsi familiaris eius olim, Cardinalis non dixit in Epistolâ totidem verbis: de reiciendâ Regis gratiâ: tamen cùm suadeat de Juramento facilè abiurando, quod ille, diu antè deliberatâ re, suscepit (salvâ autem, tum conscientiâ, tum pietate, quas nullâ in re, ex eo sibi læsas sentit) cùm hoc (inquam) suadeat; id ex eo consequi, ut gratiam, quam ei fecit Rex benignam atque verem, ingratus reiciat. Contineri verò in Epistolâ, non ea solùm, de quibus verba ibi fiunt, sed & ea, quæ inde consequuntur. Quod nisi te præceptor hoc olim tuus, Papiæ docuerit, eum te magno precio nihil sapere, docuisse. Interim vero aliam Basilij causam fuisse, quàm sua est; Valentis hoc exemplum non valere quicquam; sibi in animo non esse, reducere calculum; facti enim non poenitere.
units.tr: Then also he would kindly admonish you, although the Cardinal, once his intimate, did not say in the Letter in so many words: "that the King's favour is to be rejected." Yet since he urges the easy abjuring of the Oath, which he undertook after deliberating the matter long beforehand (his conscience and piety remaining safe, which in no respect he feels to have been harmed by it), since he urges this (I say), it follows from it that he, ungrateful, rejects the favour which the King kindly and truly granted him. But the Letter contains not only those things of which words are spoken there, but also those things which follow from them. Unless your teacher once taught you this at Pavia, he taught you at great cost that you know nothing. Meanwhile, that Basil's cause was other than his own; that this example of Valens is worth nothing; that it is not in his mind to reckon the account again, for he does not repent of the deed.

units.la: Quò pergit autem vlterius, vergit semper in deterius Cardinalis. Quale verò peccatum peccauit Archipresbyter? Peccatum Iuliani, Valentis, Marcellini, Petri: Apostatæ, hæretici, idolis sacrificantis, Christum cum anathemate abiurantis. Quò verò hæc? nisi vt præcipitem agat veterem olim amicum Cardinalis, in barathrum ipsum desperationis. Accedit ergo iam Cōsolator Tertus, & melius sperare iubet: non enim ex toto illos imitatum esse, nec plane in Apostasiam, hæresin, Idololatriam, blasphemiam demersum esse. Aliquà ergo ex parte mitigat, aliquà verò ex parte relinquit; vt, non omni ex parte sit; sit tamen hæc omnia: non tam quàm illi reus, sed reus tamen eorundem criminum: vt minor quantitas sit, eadem substantia. At ille, pueris vos ista narrare iubet; se omni ex parte illis dissimilem: inspexit in omnes Iuramenti partes, excussit singulas, nusquam ibi Iouis Linteum, non Multi Dij, nihil quò minus Christus sit Deus, non Ara, vel Victima. Quare nec illud quidem vestrum agnoscit [aliquà ex parte] nec Lapsum suum minorem, sed omnino nullum fuisse.
units.tr: Yet as the Cardinal goes on, he always slides into something worse. And what sort of sin did the Archpriest commit? The sin of Julian, Valens, Marcellinus and Peter: of apostates, heretics, those who sacrifice to idols, who renounce Christ under anathema. And to what end? Unless he means to drive his old friend of the Cardinal headlong into the very pit of despair. Then the "Consoler Tertus" comes in and bids him hope for better: he did not imitate them entirely, nor was he plunged wholly into apostasy, heresy, idolatry and blasphemy. So he softens it in part and leaves it in part, so that it is not in every respect the case, yet it is all the same: not as guilty as they were, but guilty of the same crimes, so that the quantity is smaller while the substance is the same. But he bids you tell these things to children: he is in every respect unlike them. He has looked into all the parts of the oath, examined each one, and nowhere is there a "linen of Jove", nor "many gods", nothing that stops "Christ being God", nor an "altar" or a "victim". Therefore he does not acknowledge your charge even [in part], nor does he admit that his fall was smaller, but that there was no fall at all.

units.la: Neque ipse tibi tamen constas. Postquam enim similitudinem sic, aliquà ex parte posfuisses, statim eodem spiritu, negas plane similitudinem in lapsu positam, sed in causâ. Nec id tamen verum est. Non enim aliud ibi agit Cardinalis, quàm quia in Lapsu similis fuit, in eo quoque similis sit, vt de prolapsione resurgat. Quorsum autem de causâ curaret? Neque enim si cecidit quis, id valdè ad rem, quomodo aut quâ tandem ex causâ ita cecidit; sed vt de casu suo, se quàm primùm erigat. Tu verò omnium hominum ineptissimus, qui causam tam accuratè enarras casus sui, ei homini, cui stare se etiam, virtute Dei, nec omnino cecidisse persuasum est. Rectè ergo vobis regerat, quod olim Iob amicis suis, Onerosi consolatores estis{a} ambo. Atillud certè non malè, quod ad lapsum suum corrigendum, qui certæ fidei non erat: hortati estis eum, ex Historia fidei non certa, Marcellini Historia, vt similia inter se essent, à quo hortatio sumpta, & ad quid, incerta vtráq. Multũ colore, imò substantiâ ipsâ mendacij affirmat hoc Tortus: affirmat etiam supra sibi demonstratum esse, quod neque supra neque subter, neque factum est, neque fiet vnquam. Nec est enim ibi, vt monstrari possit, nec verbum ibi pertrahi potest ad Sacram obedientiam, aut Primatum Spiritualium: nec cui candor insit vllus, si legat, relegatque iusiurandum[?] vel millies, tale quid ex eo vnquam eruat: Tortum autem, quasi monstrum habeat, qui id ibi monstrari posse autumat.
units.tr: Yet you are not consistent with yourself. For after you have so admitted the likeness, in part, you straightaway, with the same breath, deny outright that the likeness lies in the fall, but in the cause. Nor is this true. For the Cardinal is doing nothing else than this: since in the fall he was like them, he is to be like them also in this, that he rises again from the fall. Why, moreover, should he take care about the cause? For if someone has fallen, it matters little how or by what cause he fell, but only that he raise himself from his fall as soon as possible. But you, the most inept of all men, who so carefully recount the cause of his fall, are speaking to a man who is persuaded that he stands, by the power of God, and has not fallen at all. Rightly, then, may he answer you as Job once answered his friends: "You are all miserable comforters." But certainly this was not ill said: that to correct his fall, which was not of certain faith, you urged him by the history of Marcellinus, which is not a certain history, so that they might be alike; from whom the exhortation was taken, and to what end, both being uncertain. Tortus asserts this with much colour, indeed with the very substance of a lie: he also asserts that it was demonstrated to him above that what is neither above nor below neither has been done nor ever will be. For there is nothing there that can be shown, nor can a word there be drawn to sacred obedience or to the primacy of spiritual matters; nor is there any candour in anyone who, though he read and re-read the oath a thousand times, would ever extract such a thing from it. Tortus, however, as if he had a monster, asserts that it can be shown there.

units.la: Dicendum illi iam erat, de suâ illâ maximâ similitudine Regis & Iuliani, quoad Idololatriam. Non potuit miser; vidit Regem, vt initio à Iuliani Polytheismo, ita hic ab Idololatriâ abesse quàm longissimè. Vtriusque quidem maculam fœdam, sed Idololatriæ hanc imprimis, sibi & Catholicis suis adhærere; Defensionem sibi potiùs pro se, quàm Accusationem vllam in nos instituendam hic esse. Vbi, quâ parte sit Idololatria, facilè videt, non nostrâ scilicet, sed suâ. Vnus enim hic articulus inter multos, quorum causâ, Papistæ, Hæretici à nobis (hâc quidem in re) verè Catholicis, censeantur. Hinc autem vt se explicet, inducit se in novâ Hæresin, nescio dicam an vesaniam, an vtrâque; vtraque enim est. Se quidem Idololatras non esse, idola non colere, quòd scilicet colant imagines rerum existentium: Eas autem Idola non esse, quòd Idolum, non nisi imago sit rei nusquam existentis. O iecur Theologiæ! Nec aduertit homo acutus, dum hoc dicit, aperte se & Mosi, & verò etiam Deo ipsi contradicere, qui Lege suâ, quâ vetat Idola, vetat fieri omnem similitudinem eorum, quæ in cœlis sunt, vel in terrâ vel in aquis subter terram, quæ sunt Omnes puto Res alicubi existētes. Tam Torto cum Deo præclarè conuenit; vt absterreat Deus, à cultu similitudinis omnis Rerum quæ vsquam existant: Tortus autem contrà iubeat, Faciant vero, colant etiam similitudines Rerum vllas, si modò existant vsquam. Idola enim (quicquid dixerit Deus) non esse nisi imagines solas Rerum nusquam existentium. Quare ex nouâ Theologiâ Torti dum Res modò existat, in cœlo, terrâ, aquis, subter aquas, sit vel malus Demon, coram eo incurvare se, & in eo Deum adorare posse. Ad hanc enim insaniam nuper iam deuentum est, eámque libris editis docent, & defendunt boni Theologi, in eóque rem aguat Apostatæ Iuliani, qui si viueret iam, hoc idem ipse pro se diceret: non se Iouem lapidem, sed in lapide Iouem adorare; atque id multò minùs absurdè quàm Vasquius in Diabolo De-um: ut si quaerat iam quisquam ubi illa similitudo maxima; reperiet inter duos Pontifices Maximos, Iulianum & Papam, in hac quidem maximam: atque similitudine hac sensim discessionem fieri à Christianismo ad Paganismum, à novo iam isto Iuliano.
units.tr: He ought now to have spoken of his "greatest likeness of the King and Julian" as regards idolatry. The wretch could not; he saw that the King, as at the start from Julian's polytheism, so here is as far as possible from idolatry. The foul stain of both, but of idolatry above all, clings to himself and his Catholics; that here he should set up a defence for himself rather than any accusation against us. Where the idolatry lies he easily sees, not in our camp, of course, but in his own. For this is one article among many, on account of which Papists are deemed by us (in this matter at least) to be true Catholics. Then, in order to explain himself, he brings himself into a new heresy, I know not whether to call it madness or both; for it is both. He says that he indeed is not an idolater, that he does not worship idols, because he worships images of existing things; and that these are not idols, because an idol is only an image of a thing that exists nowhere. O liver of theology! Nor does this shrewd man notice, while he says this, that he openly contradicts both Moses and God himself, who by his Law, in which he forbids idols, forbids every likeness of those things which are in heaven, or on the earth, or in the waters under the earth, which are, I suppose, all things existing somewhere. How splendidly Tortus agrees with God: that God should frighten off from worship every likeness of things that exist anywhere; while Tortus, on the contrary, bids men to make and worship any likenesses of things at all, provided only they exist somewhere. For idols (whatever God may say) are nothing but images of things that exist nowhere. Hence, by the new theology of Tortus, so long as a thing merely exists, whether in heaven, on earth, in the waters, or under the waters, be it even an evil demon, one can bow oneself before it and adore God in it. For to this madness they have lately come, and the good theologians teach and defend it in published books, and in this the apostate Julian is busy, who, if he were alive now, would say this same thing for himself: that he did not worship Jupiter the stone, but Jupiter in the stone; and this with much less absurdity than Vasquez with his "God in the Devil"; so that if anyone now asks where that "greatest" likeness is, he will find it between the two Pontifices Maximi, Julian and the Pope, in this indeed the greatest; and by this likeness there is gradually made a departure from Christianity to paganism, from this now new Julian.

units.la: Proxima huic, de modo collatio. Iulianus subrepsit incautis: Rex nec ab incautis suscipi vult, nec incaute, sed sumpto ad cogitandum spacio. Nec surrepsit: nihil enim proponit ibi nisi explicatum & planum. Hic verò Tortus, crassum se singit, & simplicem, ut qui vias planas, ab asperis nequeat discernere; sed in planitie ipsa impingat in montes, nec ubi sint indicat tamen, nec de modo dissimili vel verbum facit, aut totâ de re. Tantum scias ubi aegrè illi sit, ubi dolor; iterum iam, & iam & semper ad negatam Pontificii potestatem manum habet, ibi dolor est, is mons est, quem in planitie, non sentit, sed somniat. Sed annon modus dissimilis? Nam quicquid hic negatur, aperte negatur, nemini subrepitur incauto. Non posse Pontificem ab obedi-entiâ Regis subditos absolvere, dicitur ibi dilucidè, diserte, non tectè, non tortuosè. Nec enim, quâ Ille Rex est, quâ illi subditi; potestas vlla in illos Pontifici; tantum quâ Christiani. Reliqua ne dicuntur quidem, quae tu ibi fingis. Non dicitur, Iuro non esse parendum excommunicationi Pontificis: quin parebit, quousque locum habet Censura Ecclesiastica, in Sacris, in rebus Ecclesiae: in Politicis enim Censura locum non habet. Sed neque illud dicitur, Iuro Pontificem ab hoc Iuramento me liberare non posse, quia legitimâ plenâq; authoritate mihi ministratum est. Disiuncta sunt ibi haec, nec posterior priorus[?] causa, nec quia legitimâ authoritate ministratum, sed quia legitimum, ideo liberare non potest. Potest enim & legitima authoritas esse, quae ministrat, & Iuramentum interdum minùs legitimum, quod ministratur. Hic verò, & quod defertur Iusiurandum, & à quâ defertur authoritas, legitima utraque, ut neutro nomine detrectari debeat.
units.tr: Next to this is the comparison regarding the manner. Julian "crept upon the unwary"; the King wishes to be received neither by the unwary, nor unwarily, but with time taken for thought. Nor did he "creep in": for he proposes nothing there but what is explained and plain. Here, however, Tortus pretends to be dull and simple, as one who cannot tell plain ways from rough; but he stumbles, even on the plain itself, into mountains, and yet does not show where they are, nor does he say a word about a different manner, or about the whole matter. Only know where he is in pain, where his grief lies: again and again, and again and always, he comes back to the "denied power of the Pontiff"; there is the grief, that is the mountain which he does not feel on the plain but dreams of. But is the manner not different? For whatever is here denied, is denied openly; no one is crept upon unwarily. "That the Pontiff cannot absolve subjects from obedience to the King" is said there clearly, expressly, not covertly, not tortuously. For there is no power of the Pontiff over them, neither as he is King, nor as they are subjects, but only as they are Christians. The rest is not even said, which you there feign. It is not said, "I swear that the excommunication of the Pontiff is not to be obeyed": rather it will be obeyed, so far as ecclesiastical censure has place, in sacred matters, in matters of the Church; for in political matters censure has no place. But neither is this said: "I swear that the Pontiff cannot free me from this oath, because it was administered with lawful and full authority." These things are disjoined there; neither is the latter the cause of the former, nor because it was administered with lawful authority, but because it is not lawful, therefore he cannot release from it. For the authority which administers may indeed be lawful, while the oath which is administered may sometimes be less lawful. Here, however, both the oath which is tendered and the authority from which it is tendered are lawful, so that on neither count ought it to be refused.

units.la: Benè autem habet, quòd omnes naturaliter horrent, quae ibi de Proditionibus, Conspirationibus, Regiae personae violentiâ & caede. Benè quòd hoc Tortus fatetur tandem; si tamen fatetur; nec referreseruatam habetin mente cuasionem †nisi Pontifex illa præceperit Quid ergo? non vel illa iurent, se nullius Proditionis, Conspirationis in Regem, vt vel cuduperfone eius inferendæ consci os fore, vel participes, ne sibi ita iubeat Pontifex? Nec tamen nescius est, quò tendant illa, absolucre ab obedientia, interdicere ne pareant? Vbi eò ventum? Proditiones, Conspirationes, Cades, quas ita naturaliter horret, non longè abesse? Ecquando enim visum, qui parere semel Regi noluit, vt ei teligio fiierit conspirandi, aut cui conspirandi religio non fuit, fuerit vlla, vim afferendi? Consequuntur ista se mutuò, & fere ita semper factum est, si semel interdixit ne pareant, edixit non ita multò post, vt arma teneant. Quæro enim, cùm absoluti, vt Regi ne pareant, cuiparere eos velit Pontifex? Non enim nullus, non fauet Anarchiæ. Ergo aly, cui Regnum in prædam addixit. Quid ille vero? annòn simulum suum primo quoque tempore cæsum vult? Reliquum est, vt qui naturaliter horrent hæc facientem, naturaliter etiam herrere debeant, ad hæc subditos sollicitantem, & absens Iuramento, quo cauentur hæc, Brevibus suis arcentem, atque absterrentem.
units.tr: It is well, however, that "all men naturally shudder" at what is said there about treasons, conspiracies, and violence and slaughter against the royal person. Well that Tortus at last confesses this; if indeed he does confess it, and does not keep in mind a reservation, "unless the Pontiff should command those things." What then? Might they not swear that they will be no party to any treason or conspiracy against the King, nor to any violence against his person, lest the Pontiff command them otherwise? Yet is he unaware where those things tend, namely "to absolve from obedience", to forbid them to obey? Where has it come to? Are treasons, conspiracies and slaughters, which he so naturally shudders at, not far off? For when has anyone who once refused to obey the King, been moved by religion to conspire, or for whom there was no religion of conspiring, been moved to inflict violence? These things follow one another, and it has nearly always been so: if once he forbids them to obey, he soon after commands them to take up arms. For I ask: when they are absolved so that they may not obey the King, to whom does the Pontiff wish them to obey? For not no one; he does not favour anarchy. Therefore it is another, to whom he has delivered the kingdom as prey. What, then, of that man? Does he not wish his rival to be slain at the first opportunity? It remains that those who naturally shudder at doing these things should naturally shudder also at those who solicit subjects to them, and who, though absent, by their Briefs hold back and terrify men from the oath by which these things are guarded against.

units.la: Vltimum autem est: Iuliani omnia eò facta, vt Idololatrium perpetrarent subditi: Rex & ipse, & subditi ab Idololatriâ remotissimi; atque adeò non boni Catholici (stilo nouo) quòd adeo remoti. Hæc, vel primò intuenti dissimilitudo summa: Tortura vero sic torquebit, vt similitudo summa fiat. Neque tamen, nuper natâ hac suâ Idoli definitione, excutiet à se Iulianum suum: Dicet enim, extitisse initio loquem suum paulò ante tempora Heroica, Saturni atque Opis filium: reliquos autem, quos colit Deos, Iouis Sibolem fuisse. Ita, ne se quidem Idola colere, magis quàm Tortum: non enim Chimæram, vel Tragelaphum, non corpus humanum cum capite equino, nec imaginem vllam, nisi rei quæ aliquando extitit. Tum, quòd Tortus Idolum esse dicit imaginem falsi Dei; agnoscet etiam & hoc Iulianus; & de Torti Sanctis illis haud vllum, verum Deum fuisse, Tortum collegam suum statim admonebit. Quid restat igitur, quàm vt ruant alter in alterius complexus, atque de summâ hâc inter se similitudine mutuò gratulentur?
units.tr: Last of all: "Julian did everything so that the subjects might commit idolatry; the King himself, and the subjects, are most remote from idolatry"; and therefore they are not good Catholics (new style) because they are so remote. At first glance this unlikeness is very great; but Torture will so twist it that it becomes a very great likeness. Nor, however, will he, having newly invented this definition of "idol", shake off his Julian: for he will say that at the start there existed a man of his, shortly before the Heroic times, a son of Saturn and Ops; and that the other gods whom he worships were sons of Jove. Thus he does not even worship idols any more than Torture does: for not a Chimaera or a goat-stag, not a human body with a horse's head, nor any image at all, except of a thing that once existed. Then, because Torture says that an idol is an image of a false god, Julian too will acknowledge this; and he will at once remind his colleague Torture that none of those saints of his was a true God. What remains, then, but that they should fall into each other's embrace and congratulate one another on this great likeness?

units.la: Nam quod Apostolum perturbare cupit ad se, quòd is Idolum nihil esse dicat, nihil dicit. Non enim tali [?]sensu Idolum nihil esse dixit Apostolus, nisi quantum ad id, quod esse putatur, rem scilicet, quam refert non habere, nec vim ullam, vt vel iuuet quicquam vel noceat, & (quod erat tibi instituti Apostolici) vt cibum vel sanctificet, vel polluat. Haec vna Patrum, vna omnium interpretum mens, déque eo expresse cauent, ne cum Terto tam plumbei simus, vt venise vnquam putemus Apostolo in mentem, vt plane nihil putarit esse: cùm & materia Idoli aliquid sit, vt lapis, lignum, metallum; & forma ab artifice in materiam inducta, aliquid etiam; nimirum qualitas: sed quoad id quod refert; illi, pro quo fit vel colitur; id, quod illi de Idolo sentiunt; eâ quidem ratione nihil esse: proinde, nihil in mundo, dixisse. In mundo quidem; non in vltramundana, non in Metaphysica Platonis vel Torti phantasia[?], in quâ aliquid est, quod nihil est; & alicubi, quod nusquam. Phantasmata haec mea sunt, & cerebri vestri Idola. Illa vero etiam dementia tua, vt quenquam existimes tam dementem, qui eo sensu Imagines vel Christi, vel Sanctorum Idola putet, quòd Christus, vel Sancti nusquam sint, vel nihil. Scis ipse (nisi non vis scire) eas alio longè sensu Idola à nobis haberi; quod scilicet sensu, Idolum erat Serpens aeneus, qui imago Serpentis fuit, Serpentis dico, proin rei existentis; & tamen Idolum, quòd cultus iam abusum pateretur. Quâ ratione, etsi Dei iussu conflatus fuerat Serpens ille, etsi miraculis insignis, etsi Christi ipsius Symbolum; tamen cùm abusus illos pateretur (neque tamen tantos, quantos quotidie patiuntur Imagines apud vos) ab Ezekiel sine scrupulo comminutus est: vt & si Ezechiam[?] vos haberetis vllum, vestrae quoque illae essent comminuendae.
units.tr: For as to his wish to draw the Apostle to his side, because he says that an idol is nothing, he says nothing. For the Apostle did not say that an idol is nothing in such a sense, but only as far as concerns what it is thought to be, namely the thing which he says it does not have, nor any power to either help anything or harm, and (which was your Apostolic purpose) to either sanctify or pollute food. This is the one mind of the Fathers, the one mind of all the interpreters, and they take express care on this point, lest we be so leaden with Tertullian as to think the Apostle ever came to the notion that it was plainly nothing: since the material of an idol is something, such as stone, wood, metal; and the form induced into the material by the craftsman is also something, namely its quality. But as to what it signifies, that for which it is made or worshipped, and what they think of the idol, in that sense it is nothing; and therefore he said "nothing in the world". "In the world", indeed; not in the otherworldly, not in the metaphysical fancy of Plato or Torture, in which something is what is nothing, and somewhere is what is nowhere. These fancies are mine, and idols of your brain. But that madness of yours, to think anyone so mad as to suppose that images of Christ or of the Saints are idols in the sense that Christ or the Saints are nowhere or nothing. You yourself know (unless you do not want to know) that we hold them to be idols in a quite different sense; in which sense the bronze serpent was an idol, which was an image of a serpent, I say of a serpent, therefore of a thing existing; and yet an idol, because it was already subject to abuse in worship. For this reason, although that serpent was cast by God's command, although remarkable for miracles, although a symbol of Christ himself; nevertheless, since it suffered those abuses (not, however, as great as those which your images suffer daily), it was without hesitation crushed to pieces by Ezekiel: so that, if you had any Hezekiah, your images too would have to be crushed.

units.la: Neque vero Anathema illud Septimae Synodi quicquam ad nos: Non enim Imagines, seu Christi, seu Sanctorum, Idola nominamus. Non sunt, quâ à se certè; sed tamen Idola fieri posse dicimus, quâ à vobis; non minus quàm Serpens aeneus à Iudaeis, tum demum scilicet, si adorentur. Sunt enim similitudines eorum, qui in coelis, coram quibus prociditis, quasque colitis; quod discertis verbis vetitum, lege Diuina. Imagines ergo in se, Idola autem Torto, vbi colere coepit: quo facto, & ille, & qui idem cum illo faciunt omnes, Idololatrae sunt.
units.tr: Nor indeed does that anathema of the Seventh Synod have anything to do with us: for we do not call images, whether of Christ or of the Saints, idols. They are not so in themselves, certainly; but we do say that they can become idols by your doing, no less than the bronze serpent did among the Jews, namely then, of course, if they are worshipped. For they are "likenesses of those who are in heaven", before which you fall prostrate and which you worship; which is forbidden in express words by the Divine law. So images are images in themselves, but idols to Torture, when he begins to worship them: by which act both he and all who do the same with him are idolaters.

units.la: Accedit iam Tertus ad exemplum Eleazari: impeditus in via nonnihil comitatus, & nugas, quas tamen timuit[?] semper, ptura Diuinâ, quo detractio obedientia stabilitatur. Et quærit quidem, sed nullum Torto ad manum erat, nullum profert; & dum nullum profert, nullum fatetur esse: Sed si velis pro stabilienda Pontificis potestate, tum verò habere se in promptu. At hoc nemo quærit. Quorsum enim? Quia labefactatur Iuramento potestas illa. Ne id quidem; intra limites suos tantum conclauditur, vt decurrat aluco suo, ne exundet in negotia quæ Ecclesiæ non sunt, sed Sæculi; quæ inter Principem sunt & Subditos officia, ijs ne se immisceat; reliquis in rebus stabilis Pontifici potestas & immota manet. Verùm omninò audiendæ nobis sunt, quæ annotatæ illi sunt sententiæ pro Pontifice suo stabiliendo. Credo equidem vix venales, ita obtrudit. Agedum, inspiciamus.
units.tr: Now Tertus comes to the example of Eleazar: somewhat hindered on the way by his retinue, and trifles, which nevertheless he always feared, ... by the Divine Word, by which the removal of obedience is made firm. And he does ask, but there was no one at hand for Torture, he produces no one; and while he produces no one, he admits there is none: but if you wish, in order to establish the power of the Pontiff, then indeed he has one ready. But no one asks this. For what purpose? Because that power is weakened by the oath. Not even that; it is confined within its own limits only, so that it runs in its own channel, lest it overflow into matters which are not of the Church but of the world, which are the duties between Prince and subjects; he should not meddle with these; in other matters the power of the Pontiff remains firm and unmoved. But truly we must hear what opinions have been noted down for him in support of his Pontiff. I believe indeed they are hardly saleable, so he forces them on us. Come, let us look.

units.la: In Deuteronomio præceptum est; Satis aperte ibi legitur, Qui superbierit nolens obedire Sacerdotis imperio, &c. Satis ibi aliquid aperte legitur, sed non satis integrè citatur. Quid enim? an imperio Sacerdotis vtcunq;, qualicunque? An Aaronis imperio, vitulum adorare iubentis? An Abiathari imperio, contra Salomonem cum Adoniâ conspirantis? An Caiphæ imperio Christum morte dignum pronunciantis? Non opinor. Est ibi, præter ea, quæ Torto citare visum, vel supra paulò vel infrà, quod doceat nos quali Sacerdotis imperio; id Tortus non bonâ fide celauit. Ita præcedentia verba habent, Imperio Sacerdotis iuxta Legem Dei docentis, tum, sequeris sententiam eius; tum si superbierit nolens obedire, currit Lex ista contra te. Iam verò noua lis; An docuerit nos Paulus quintus Breui suo iuxta Legem Dei; imo lis nulla: Non enim docet ibi iuxta Legem Dei, nec docet quidem, loquitur sine lege, iubet, terret, ex mero imperio agit in Breuibus suis, non est Sacerdos iuxta Legem Dei docens. Non ergo præcepto hoc vlla eius potestas stabilitur.
units.tr: "In Deuteronomy it is commanded; it is read there quite plainly: 'He who acts proudly, refusing to obey the command of the priest, etc.'" Something is indeed read there plainly, but it is not quoted fully enough. For what? Is it the command of a priest in any way whatever, of any kind? The command of Aaron, bidding them worship the calf? The command of Abiathar, conspiring with Adonijah against Solomon? The command of Caiaphas, pronouncing Christ worthy of death? I do not think so. There is, besides those things which Torture thought fit to quote, something a little above or below, which teaches us what kind of priest's command is meant; this Torture has concealed without good faith. For the preceding words read: "by the command of the priest teaching according to the Law of God"; then, "you shall follow his sentence"; then, "if he acts proudly, refusing to obey", that law runs against you. Now indeed a new question: Did Paul V teach us by his Brief according to the Law of God? Nay, there is no question at all: for he does not teach there according to the Law of God, nor does he even teach, he speaks without law, commands, terrifies, acts by sheer command in his Briefs; he is not a priest teaching according to the Law of God. Therefore no power of his is established by this precept.

units.la: Placètne etiam exemplum eius inspicere? dices non magis appositum. Horrendum Dei iudicium in Core, Dathan, & Abiron, propter schisma & defectionem à Mose & Aaron, qui tum summi Sacerdotes. Hîc, ne exemplum eius periret, necesse habuit Duos simul eodem tempore Summos Sacerdotes creare. Duos autem Summos? Phocâ nobis opus est, vt vter hîc summus, Romanus an Constantinopolitanus: Concilio Pisano opus, vt, Gregorius an Benedictus vter Summus, expediat. Quodsi duo Summi, Summi, quid Phocæ opus, quidue Pisano Concilio? Sint Cyriacus & Bonifacius, sint Gregorius & Benedictus, vt Mosès & Aaron, Summi ambo; Credo autem non æquis oculis aspecturum Paulum quintum doctrinam hanc de duobus Summis; & Censori Vosmero malam gratiam habiturum, quòd ita oscitanter hunc locum prætermierit. Mallet enim omissum inter nugas Torti & conuitia, horrendum hoc exemplum, quàm ita adhibitum, vnde suboleat cuiquam plures uno Pontifices Summos vnquam extitisse; ad illud exemplum, plures uno iam posse existere. Puto etiam ad illorum hæresin accessurum Pontificem non inuitum, qui postquam à Deo vocatus Aaron, Mosen exauthoratum sentiunt: nihil Mosi post, cum Pontificatu fuisse. Magis ad rem Pontificis, magis ad gustum opinio illa; qui mallet fratrem nullum habere (ne Mosen quidem) quàm non solus pontificari sine fratre.
units.tr: Shall we also look at his example? You will say it is no more apposite. "The dreadful judgement of God on Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, on account of the schism and defection from Moses and Aaron, who were then the chief priests." Here, so that his example should not perish, he was obliged to create two chief priests at the same time. But two chief priests? We need Phocas to tell us which is the chief here, the Roman or the Constantinopolitan: we need the Council of Pisa, so that it may be settled whether Gregory or Benedict is the chief. But if there are two chief, two chiefs, what need is there of Phocas, or of the Council of Pisa? Let Cyriacus and Boniface be, let Gregory and Benedict be, like Moses and Aaron, both chief; but I believe Paul V will not look with an equal eye on this doctrine of "two chiefs", and he will be ill-disposed towards the censor Vosmer, because he so carelessly passed over this passage. For he would rather have that dreadful example omitted among "the trifles and abuse of Torture" than adduced in such a way that it suggests to anyone that more than one chief Pontiff ever existed; by that example, that more than one can now exist. I think too that the Pontiff, not unwilling, will come close to their heresy, who, after Aaron was called by God, feel that Moses was deposed: that nothing was left to Moses afterwards, in the priesthood. That opinion is more suited to the Pontiff's cause, more to his taste; he would rather have no brother at all (not even Moses) than be the sole pontiff without a brother.

units.la: Ne labascat authoritas Papalis, vides quæ fulcra suppositi fuerit è Veteri, vult etiam & de Nouo; exorari non potest: sed non noua, vel de nouo edolata, imò vetera illa, quæ iam tempus erat vt respirarent paululum, ita vexata diu, ita sæpe angarias passa; Quodcunque ligaueris; & Pasce oues. Prius illud, dictum à Christo, non Imperatori vel Regi; debebat autem addere, cùm multi tum Imperatores essent & Reges Christiani; atque ita aliquid diceret. Nam cùm nullus tum esset cui diceret, qui potuit vlli dicere? Quanquam etiam, si tum Reges fuissent, non dedisset illis ligandi, soluendique potestatem: nec Imperator illam, nec Rex vllus vendicat: quare frustra adiectum, Non Imperatori vel Regi. Petro autem dictum illud, Petro, quem vicarium constituit super familiam suam. Sitonomum, credo, dicere voluit, quem dixit Vicarium, cui de tritici mensura distribuendâ munus incumbit. Verum esto. Quis ille ergo ibi, quem constituit super omnia quæ possidet? Ei enim, qui super familiam constitutus οἰκονόμος[?] cuique dando, & munere suo probè perfunctus fuerat, merces hæc est, super omnia quæ possidet Dominus constitui. Mallet posterius hoc Papa; vna enim illi tritici cura nimis angusta est. Locus male adductus, non satis in eo rem egisti, vel Petri, vel Pauli quinti.
units.tr: Lest the authority of the Papacy totter, you see what props he has put under it from the Old Testament, and he wants them from the New too. He cannot be persuaded otherwise. But these are not new props, nor newly fashioned ones; rather they are those old ones, which by now have been harassed so long and suffered so many hardships that it was high time they took a breath: "Whatsoever you shall bind" and "Feed my sheep." The first was spoken by Christ, not to an Emperor or a King. He ought to have added that there were then many Emperors and Christian Kings, and so would have said something. For since there was then no one to whom he could say it, to whom could he say it? Even if there had been Kings then, he would not have given them the power of binding and loosing: no Emperor claims it, and no King does either. Therefore "Not to an Emperor or a King" is added in vain. But to Peter was said that saying, "to Peter, whom he appointed over his household." You want the steward, I suppose, to be meant by the word "Vicar," to whom the task of distributing the measure of wheat falls. Granted. Who, then, is that one there, "whom he appointed over all that he possesses"? For to him who was appointed "over the household" as steward, and who had discharged his duty well, this is the reward, to be appointed "over all that the Lord possesses." The Pope would rather have this latter, for the care of wheat alone is too narrow for him. The passage is badly adduced, and you have not done enough in it, either for Peter or for Paul V.

units.la: Sed ligat, & soluit Petrus. Liget verò, & soluat, sed iniusta vincula; Vinculum, quo Principi subditus ligatur, iustum (etsi Principi dyscolo) & secundum voluntatem Dei,{a} ait Petrus ipse; quare Petrus haud soluerat: Debitum, idque ex debito conscientiae maximo, ait Paulus; quare nec Paulus. {b}Siquis ergo Pontificum soluere praesumpserit; iram Omnipotentis Dei, & Apostolorum eius Petri & Pauli se noverit incursurum. Ve-rum & mandanit ut omnes suas pascerent; sane, mandamit; & in eo, Ouibus etiam; ut se pasci regique permitterent. Stabiliuit ergo potestatem eius, potestatem pascendi, quis negat? Sed duo haec Deus ipse nos docuit: opposita esse: Pascere, & cum austeritate imperare; ac potentia. Austerum autem imperium hoc, amarum pabulum; Regi ne iurate; Quod iurasti iuramentum eierate; Regem deserite; Regi alij adhaerete, cuius ego Regnum concessero. Suffocat, non pascit doctrina haec. Eleazarus, aut cuicunque bona mens, non magis eam gustaret, quam carnes porcinas.
units.tr: "But Peter binds and looses." Yes, he binds and looses, but unjust chains. "The bond by which a subject is bound to a Prince is just (even if the Prince is perverse) and according to the will of God," says Peter himself; therefore Peter did not loose it. It is a "debt," and one owed "from the greatest debt of conscience," says Paul; therefore neither did Paul. If any of the Popes therefore presumes to loose it, let him know that he will incur "the wrath of Almighty God and of his Apostles Peter and Paul." But indeed they also commanded that all should feed his sheep; yes, they commanded it, and in that, "even the sheep"; that they should allow themselves to be fed and ruled by him. He has established, therefore, his power, the "power of feeding." Who denies it? But God himself has taught us that these two things are opposed: to feed, and to rule with austerity and by power. This austere rule, however, is a bitter food: "Do not swear to the King; abjure the oath you have sworn; desert the King; cleave to another King, whose kingdom I shall grant." This doctrine suffocates; it does not feed. Eleazar, or anyone of good mind, would no more taste it than swine's flesh.

units.la: Ad rem vero vel maximè Iuramentum Saulis, sed non vestram. Ad arma clamatum est; ingruebat hostis, defuit tempus; deserti non potuit singulis; simul omnes adiuravit. Etsi autem Rex solus suscepit, nec vir quisquam de populo: tamen quasi singuli suscepissent, ita religio fuit omni populo illud violare; etsi faciscerent iam, etsi deliquium paterentur; mori illis satius fuit, quàm Regis iusiurandum transgredi. Fuerit vero temerè emissum; fuerit per illud, non satis consultum victoriae suae; qualecunque fuerit; at Populus tamen interim, quàm sollicitus de eo seruando? Vides, ut exhorruit ille, qui Ionathanem vidit de melle gustantem. Quantatum cura Prophetis edocendi populum, ut os Regis observarent, & praecepta iuramenti Dei?{c} Quanta autem Legum seueritas, ut morte [?]luendum esset illi, qui Regem adiurantem audisset, nec quasi ipse iuratus esset, ita se, & non minus, iuramento Regio constrictum putaret? Quid quaerimus? Datae sunt fortes. Deus ipse de sinu [?]filio [?]ostentionem dedit, & quasi protraxit ad poenam Ionathanem, de spreto iureiurando Paterno. Haec eo addùcta ut doceant, quanti olim fuerit iusiurandum, quo Rex suos constrinxit, quanta eius religio, quam nemo detrectarit. Tu aliorsum trahis, & terroritatem eius inculcas; sed frustrà. Esto enim temeritas in Saule fuit, quam fuit penè periculo Primogenit. At argumenti maior ex eo vis est, magis vos stringit: Si enim populus
units.tr: But especially to the point is the oath of Saul, though not yours. The cry to arms was raised; the enemy was pressing; there was no time; it could not be deserted by individuals; he swore them all together. Although the King alone undertook it, and no man of the people did, yet it was held so sacred by the whole people, as if each had undertaken it, to violate it; even though they were now perishing, even though they were suffering a failure; it was better for them to die than to transgress the King's oath. Be it that it was rashly uttered; be it that through it he had not sufficiently considered his own victory; whatever it was, yet how anxious the people meanwhile were to keep it! You see how he shuddered, who saw Jonathan tasting honey. "How great was the care of the Prophets to teach the people to observe the mouth of the King and the precepts of God's oath?" And how great was the severity of the laws, that "he who heard the King swearing should be punished by death," and that he should not think himself bound by the King's oath any less, as if he himself had sworn it? What more do we seek? The lots were cast. God himself "gave a sign from the bosom of the son," and as it were drew Jonathan forth to punishment "for despising the paternal oath." These things are adduced so that they may teach how great once was the oath by which the King bound his people, and how great its sanctity, which no one would have dared to disregard. You drag it elsewhere, and you inculcate its terror; but in vain. For granted that there was rashness in Saul, which nearly cost the firstborn his life; yet from this the force of the argument is greater, and it binds you more: for if the people

units.la: {a} 1.Pet.2.19. populus Dei iuramento tum tantum detulit, tam parum confulto: diu multumq; confulto, Comitijs Curiatis legitimè rogato, quale hoc nostrum est, plus adhuc multò magisque de-tulisset; vester quoque populus si Dei esset, non minus deferret.
units.tr: {a} 1 Pet. 2.19. If the people of God had so readily borne the oath then, so rashly (though after long and careful deliberation), when the Curiate assembly had been lawfully convened, what this is of yours would have borne far more and more greatly; your people too, if they were God's, would bear it no less.

units.la: AD Basilij exemplum, agnoscas Tortum statim ex responso suo. Par sanè fuit, nec iniquum ibi postulabat Apologia, quæ inibi erant verba planè proxima, à Cardinale apponi, nec ita sententiam decurtari: Esse enim verba illa nonnihil ad rem. Hic Tortus more suo, proterue primum. Noluit Bellarminus librum Theodoreti describere. Lineæ sunt vix duæ, quas adiectas cupiebat; lineas vix duas addere, hoc est Torto Theodoreti Librum totum exscribere. Quàm importunè! Verùm antiquum hic obtinet. Ubi priùs, rationem aliquam allatam voluit Apologia in Breui; hoc ipso dicebat, perstrahere nos Pontificem ad disputandum in Scholis Theologicis, vel ad librum integrum in Theologiâ conscribendum. Quod sex aut octo Lineis absolui poterat, id erat tum illi Librum conscribere: quod Lineâ unâ, atque alterâ potest, id est illi iam Theodoreti Librum describere. Auferte autem istam proteruiam. Post verò effert (homo garrulus) consilium Domini sui, & fatetur id quod res est, quod ad rem suam facit, hoc Bellarminum adducere voluisse. Cur autem adducat, quod ad rem suam non facit? At hoc iam ingenni non est; Locum integrum adducat, faciat ad rem suam, non faciat; id bonæ fidei est, de quâ non valdè se torquet Tortus, agat eâ, an non agat Dominus, nisi faciat ad rem suam. Nescias, proteruè magis hic ab eo responsum sit, an inepté.
units.tr: As to the example of Basil, you will recognise Tortus immediately from his reply. It was certainly fair, and the Apology did not unjustly demand there that the words which were plainly next should be added by the Cardinal, nor that the sense should be cut short in this way: for those words are somewhat to the point. Here Tortus, in his usual manner, first acts shamelessly. "Bellarmine was unwilling to copy out Theodoret's book. There are scarcely two lines which he wished to be added; to add scarcely two lines is, for Tortus, to copy out Theodoret's whole book." How impudently! But the old trick holds here. Where previously the Apology wished some reason to be brought forward briefly, it said by this very thing that it was drawing the Pontiff "into disputing in the theological schools, or into writing a whole book in theology." What could be finished in six or eight lines, that was then for him "writing a book"; what can be done with one or two lines, that is now for him "copying out Theodoret's book." But remove that shamelessness. Afterwards, however, this chatterer brings forth his master's counsel, and confesses what is the case, that which serves his own purpose: that Bellarmine wished to bring this forward. But why should he adduce what does not serve his purpose? Yet this is no longer ingenuous: "Let him adduce the whole passage, let it serve his purpose or not"; this belongs to good faith, about which Tortus does not greatly trouble himself. Let him act on it or not, as his Lord does, unless it serves his purpose. You would not know whether his answer here is more shameless or more foolish. [5 continued note: none]

units.la: Tandem etiam, magni pendere Regis[?] amicitiam dicit Cardinalem. Quod si faceret, nam ille rationes longè alias iniret, eius conciliandæ; nec si eam quæreret, factum Eius satis à se legitimum, quodque nemo est, qui meliorem in partem non possit interpretari; ita totus operam poneret, scriptiunculis suis odiosum reddere. Exempla sibi eligeret longè alia, & personarum, quibuscum Regem; & rerum, quibuscum Regis in eo consilium exquireret: terminos etiam qui magis decent (quosque ei non desunt, si ita animatus foret) adhiberet. Cum pietate verò dicis; Quidni? Et est hic pietatis satis, eiusque summæ in patriam, prolem, Principem, addo, & Deum ipsum, in summâ contra hos omnes impietate reprimendâ. Sed pietatem cauet Cardinalis, ex Pontificis arbitrio pius, pietas illi tota ex eo pendet: quod illi placet pium est; quod secus, piandum. Fruatur sanè hâc pietate suâ.
units.tr: Finally, he also says that the Cardinal values the friendship of the King highly. Even if he did so, for he would take quite different measures to win it, nor, if he sought it, would his action be thought by himself sufficiently lawful, and there is no one who could not interpret it in a better light; thus he would expend all his effort in making himself hateful by his little writings. He would choose for himself quite different examples, both of persons with whom the King is connected and of matters on which he would seek the King's counsel in that way; he would also use terms which are more becoming (and these would not fail him, if he were so minded). "But you say this with piety"? Why not? And here there is enough piety, and of the highest kind, towards country, offspring, Prince, and I add God himself, in suppressing with the greatest force all impiety against these. But the Cardinal beware of piety: according to the Pontiff's judgement, "pious" and "piety" depend entirely on that for him; what pleases him is "pious," and what does not, is "to be expiated." Let him certainly enjoy this piety of his.

units.la: At etiam Tortum male habet, longa narratio de Valente, adhibita solum, vt liber grandior redderetur. Non adeo vero grandescit liber paginá vix vnâ; factum narrare opus erat, non vt Liber grandior, sed vt fraus ibi vestra apertior redderetur. Nec illud prius à vobis positum: at Breuevtrumq; & non breuis Epistola, prius in Apologiâ posita, integra iterum à vobis reposita sunt. Et ea quidem constant non vnicâ, sedecim ad minus paginis; non hoc credo, vt liber tuus multò gracilior redderetur. Poterat quidem, has verè nugas omittere emissor iste nugarum. Illa verò non rectè à te instituta comparatio; qui potuit rectè à Torto? Non debuit cum Ariano componi osor Arij[?], atque Arianorum omnium; etiam Liberij Pontificis, quâ in Arianam hærefin subscripsit. Tum causa longè dispar. Valentis persecutio Catholicorum fuit, quòd Catholici essent, quòd CHRISTVM Deum dicerent: vestra si qua est vexatio, ex causâ multùm dissimili, quòd proditores estis; quidam certè fuistis, reliqui ciuitare[?] non vultis proditionem, non obstante Pontifice quem CHRISTI Vicarium dicitis; atque in eo CHRISTVM infamatis, quasi ille obstare vellet Vicarium vllum suum, ne Reges tui, Subditi fideles sint. Quæ, si Catholicorum olim causa fuisset apud Valentem, non ille tum Ecclesias presbyteris nudâsset, sed Ecclesias ipsas cum presbyteris simul, adeoque nomen ipsum Catholicum eradicâsset. Quodsi Basilij hæc tum causa fuisset, qui diuinis innutritus erat sermonibus, salua pietate, non renuisset Imperatoris gratiam: sed quam Iuliano Apostatæ, vix ante annum; eandem iam Valenti Ariano fidem, atque obedientiam ciuilem lætus lubens detulisset: nec à Liberio sententiâ expectâsset, an Imperatori fidelis esse posset, quapquam obstaret ipse Pontifex; quin, si Ille Breui aliquo suo obstitisset, Illum cum Breuibus suis valerelongùm iussisset.
units.tr: But Tortus is also troubled by this: "a long narrative about Valens, introduced only to make the book bulkier." Yet the book is not made bulkier by a page scarcely one; it was necessary to narrate the fact, not to make the book bulkier, but so that your fraud might be made more evident there. Nor was that point first put forward by you: but "Breve utrumque" and "not a short letter," first put in the Apology, were again inserted by you entire. And these indeed amount to no fewer than sixteen pages at least; I do not think this was done so that your book might be rendered much slimmer. He could certainly have omitted these trifles, that emitter of trifles. But that comparison which you instituted was not rightly made; how could it be rightly made in Tortus's case? One should not have set the hater of Arius alongside the Arian, and of all the Arians, not even the Pontiff Liberius, by whom he subscribed to the Arian heresy. Moreover the cause is far different. The persecution of Valens was of Catholics, because they were Catholics, because they called Christ God; if there is any vexation of yours, it is from a very dissimilar cause, because you are traitors; certainly some of you are, and the rest of you will not renounce treason, notwithstanding the Pontiff whom you call Christ's Vicar; and in this you defame Christ, as if he wished to hinder any vicar of his, that your Kings and your faithful subjects might not be loyal. If the cause of Catholics had once been the cause before Valens, he would not then have stripped the Churches of their presbyters, but would have uprooted the Churches themselves along with their presbyters, and so the very name Catholic. And if Basil's cause had then been this, he, who was nourished on divine discourses, would not, with his piety preserved, have refused the Emperor's favour; but he would have gladly and willingly transferred to Valens the Arian the same faith and civil obedience which he had given barely a year before to Julian the Apostate; nor would he have awaited from Liberius a verdict on whether he could be faithful to the Emperor, even though the Pontiff himself stood in the way; indeed, if that Pontiff had stood in the way with some brief of his own, he would have bidden him farewell with his briefs.

units.la: Atqui illa Dogmatis subtilitas quam dicis, ad vestras aequiuocationes non male quadrare posset: tenues enim certè sunt, nec aranearum telæ, magis eis subtiles: Ad Iuramentum nullo modo possunt; cauetur ibi contra illas aperte, lumen ibi apponitur, contra colores vestros. De negato autem ibi Primatus, vide an persuadere possis nuper-Archiepresbytero. Ille vero & Iusiurandum iurauit, & zelator tamen est Primatus, quàm iniuratus, tàm iuratus; nec occulte in eo uspiam latère deprehendit, quàm vos fingitis abnegationem; & vos si colorem ullum ibi cernitis nisi candidum, strabos & tortu oculorum radijs esse iurabit. Quaere vero ex Illo (si credis Illi) qui optimè tibi potest, & libentissimè vult confirmare, nec interrogatum se de causâ fidei vel religionis. Comprehensus est, etiam detinetur ex aliâ causâ. Plures enim sunt causæ ei, qui Archiepresbyter hîc tam diu fuerit, quàm una, fidei: sat illi quod vivit ex fide suâ, fide (inquam) suâ Iuramento suo datâ. De cæterò, quòd in custodiâ est, custodiâ illâ fortasse facit, non tam ne liber sit, quàm ut in viis sit: ut quæ, illum ab insidijs custodiat, quæ, si ut antea aberraret, non difficilè illi intentari possent. Sed illud à te factum malè, quod omittis loco hoc, quo minimè omnium oportet, sententias illas labefactatrices potestatis Pontificiæ. Si noluisti id in gratiam nostram facere, at dedisses hoc Archipresbytero, qui labascéret fortè, si labefactatam ibi cerneret Papæ authoritatem, authoritatem dico quam à Deo habet, non quam sibi nuper in Reges per fas, nefasq; arrogauit. Quare, & sententiam illam quam tu, quasi Delphica esset, ad omnes usus accommodas, retorqueret in te; obedire enim se Deo, qui dat salutem Regibus, dum Regem saluum vult, magis quàm hominibus male conciliatis, (quorum te, in numero fortè habet) qui Pontifici obtrudutis: magis quàm Pontifici ipsi, qui cupidè arripit potestatem in salutem Regum quam Petrus, nec exercuit unquam, nec habuit, ut exerceret.
units.tr: Yet that subtlety you speak of could fit your equivocations well enough: they are indeed thin, not much finer than spiders' webs. As for the oath, they cannot be applied to it at all; the oath guards against them openly, it sets a light there against your colours. As for the denied "Primacy" there, let us see whether you can persuade the former Archpresbyter. He swore the oath, and he is as much a zealot for the Primacy, sworn as he is, as he was unsworn; nor is it detected that he hides anywhere in it the denial you pretend. And if you see any colour there but white, you will swear that you are squint-eyed and that your eyes are twisted in their rays. But ask him yourself (if you believe him), he who can best and most willingly confirm it for you, that he was not questioned about a matter of faith or religion. He has been seized, and is held on another charge. For there are many causes why the Archpresbyter has been here so long, rather than the one of faith: it is enough for him that he lives by his faith, by his faith (I say) given by his oath. As for the rest, that he is in custody, he perhaps makes that custody not so much to prevent his being free as to keep him on the roads, since it would guard him against ambushes, and if he were to wander as before, no small threats could be levelled at him. But it was badly done by you that you omit in this passage, where least of all it should be omitted, those sentences that weaken the power of the Pope. If you did not wish to do this for our sake, you should at least have given it to the Archpresbyter, who might perhaps waver if he saw there the authority of the Pope weakened, the authority I say which he has from God, not that which he has lately arrogated to himself over kings, rightly and wrongly alike. Wherefore that sentence of yours, which you apply to every use as if it were Delphic, would turn back upon you: for "to obey God, who gives salvation to kings", while he wishes the king to be safe, rather than "to men ill-disposed" (of whom perhaps he counts you among the number), who thrust themselves upon the Pontiff, rather than upon the Pontiff himself, who greedily seizes a power for the salvation of kings which Peter neither exercised nor had, that he might exercise it.

units.la: Tum etiam amicè te admoneret, etsi familiaris eius olim, Cardinalis non dixit in Epistolâ totidem verbis de reijciendâ Regis gratiâ: tamen cùm suadeat de Iuramento facilè abiurando, quod ille, diu ante deliberatâ re, suscepit (salvâ autem, tum conscientiâ, tum pietate, quas nullâ in re, ex eo sibi læsas sentit) cùm hoc (inquam) suadeat; id ex eo consequi, ut gratiam, quam ei fecit Rex benignam atque uberem, ingratus reijciat. Contineri verò in Epistolâ, non ea solùm, de quibus verbis ibi fiunt, sed & ea, quæ inde consequuntur. Quod nisi te præceptor hoc olim tuus, Papiæ docuerit, cum te magno precio nihil sapere, docuisse. Interim verò alium Basilij causam fuisse, quàm sua est; Valentis hoc exemplum non valere quicquam; sibi in animo non esse, reducere calculum; facti enim non poenitere.
units.tr: Then, too, he would kindly admonish you, although once your intimate, the Cardinal did not say in his Letter in so many words "to reject the king's favour"; yet since he advises an easy abjuration of the oath, which the Archpresbyter took after long deliberation (his conscience and piety, in neither of which he feels himself wronged by it, remaining safe), since he advises this (I say), it follows from it that he rejects the favour the king has shown him, kindly and bountifully, as an ungrateful man. Indeed, what is contained in the Letter is not only those things about which words are spoken there, but also those things which follow from them. Unless your teacher of old, at Pavia, taught you this, he taught you in vain that you are nothing wise at great cost. Meanwhile, the case of Basil was other than his own; the example of Valens does not avail in the least; it is not in his mind to reckon the account again, for he does not repent of the deed.

units.la: QUò pergit autem ulterius, vergit semper in deterius Cardinalis. Quale verò peccatum peccauit Archipresbyter? Peccatum Iuliani, Valentis, Marcellini, Petri: Apostatae, haeretici, idolis sacrificantis, Christum cum anathemate abiurantis. Quò verò haec? nisi vt praecipitem agat veterem olim amicum Cardinalis, in barathrum ipsum desperationis. Accedit ergo iam Cosolator Tortus, & melius sperare iubet: non enim ex toto illos imitatum esse, nec plane in Apostasiam, haeresin, Idololatriam, blasphemiam demersum esse. Aliquâ ergo ex parte mitigat, aliquâ verò ex parte relinquit; vt, non omni ex parte sit; sit tamen haec omnia: non tam quàm illi reus, sed reus tamen eorundem criminum: vt minor quantitas sit, eadem substantia. At ille, pueris vos ista narrare iubet; se omni ex parte illis dissimilem: inspexit in omnes Iuramenti partes, excusit singulas, nusquam ibi Iouis Linteum, non Multi Dij, nihil quo minus Christus sit Deus, non Ara, vel Victima. Quare nec illud quidem vestrum agnoscit [aliquâ ex parte] nec Lapsum suum minorem, sed omnino nullum fuisse.
units.tr: But where the Cardinal goes on further, he always tends for the worse. But what sort of sin has the Archpresbyter committed? "The sin of Julian, Valens, Marcellinus, Peter: of apostates, heretics, of those who sacrifice to idols, who abjure Christ with anathema." But to what end are these things, unless to drive headlong his former friend, the Cardinal, into the very pit of despair? Now Tortus comes forward as a comforter, and bids him hope better: for he did not imitate them "in every respect", nor was he plainly plunged into "apostasy, heresy, idolatry, blasphemy". He therefore softens in one respect, and in another leaves it; so that he is not guilty "in every respect"; yet all these things are so: not guilty of them as they were, but guilty nonetheless of the same crimes, so that the quantity is less, the substance the same. But he bids you tell these things to children: that he is in every respect unlike them; he has examined every part of the oath, excused each one, and nowhere is there a "linen of Jove", not "many gods", nothing by which "Christ is not God", not an "altar" or a "victim". Wherefore he acknowledges neither that your comparison holds "in some respect", nor that his fall was smaller, but that it was altogether none.

units.la: Neque ipse tibi tamen constas. Postquam enim similitudinem sic, aliquâ ex parte posuisses, statim eodem spiritu, negas planè similitudinem in lapsu positam, sed in causâ. Nec id tamen verum est. Non enim aliud ibi agit Cardinalis, quàm quia in Lapsu similis fuit, in eo quoque similis sit, vt de prolapsione resurgat. Quorsum autem de causâ curaret? Neque enim si cecidit quis, id valdè ad rem, quomodo aut quâ tandem ex causâ ita cecidit; sed vt de casu suo, se quàm primùm erigat. Tu verò omnium hominum ineptissimus, qui causam tam accuratè enarras casus sui, ei homini, cui stare se etiam, virtute Dei, nec omnino cecidisse persuasum est. Rectè ergo vobis regerat, quod olim Iob amicis suis; {a}Onerosi consolatores estis ambo. Atillud certè non malè, quod ad lapsum suum corrigendum, qui certa fidei non erat: hortati estis eum, ex Historiâ fidei non certâ, Marcellini Historiâ; vt similia inter se essent, à quo hortatio sumpta, & ad quid, incerta vtráq;. Multũ autem rem vestram iuuat, quod subiungis: Satis id esse instituto vestro, etsi dubia historia illa, quod communi tamen consensu recepta sit. Sic est certè. Multa quæ dubia fidei, recepta apud vos communi consensu; atque dum ita recepta sint, vobis id satis: certa an dubia, historia an fabula, parum refert; æquè procedit res vestra. Hæc Tortus ipse nobis, ex ore proprio.
units.tr: Nor do you yourself agree with yourself. For after you had put the likeness so, "in some respect", immediately in the same breath you flatly deny that the likeness lies in the fall, but in the cause. Nor is that true either. For the Cardinal is doing nothing else than this: since he was alike in the fall, so in this also he may be alike, that he may rise again from the prostration. But why should he concern himself with the cause? For if a man has fallen, it matters little how or by what cause he fell; rather, that he should raise himself as soon as possible from his fall. But you, most foolish of all men, who narrate the cause of his fall so carefully, to a man who is persuaded that he stands, even by the power of God, and has not fallen at all. Rightly, then, may he answer you what Job once said to his friends: "Miserable comforters are you both." But that certainly was not ill done, that to correct his fall you exhorted him, who was not certain of the faith, from the uncertain history of the faith, the history of Marcellinus; so that they should be alike, the source from which the exhortation is drawn and the end to which it tends, both uncertain. But your cause is greatly helped by what you add: "That is enough for your purpose, even if that history is doubtful, since it is nonetheless received by common consent." So it is indeed. Many things are doubtful as to faith, received among you by common consent; and while they are so received, that is enough for you: whether certain or doubtful, history or fable, matters little; your cause proceeds equally well. This Tortus himself says to us, from his own mouth.

units.la: Sed vana Torti consolatio, & mendax; recrudescit vulnus. Quò enim non causâ, sed lapsu similem, & non multo minorem, (vt Tortus fabulatur) sed grauem inprimis Archipresbytero lapsum suum fuisse constet, adduci dicit Cardinalis in discrimen Iuramento Regio, vnum ex præcipuis fidei nostræ capitibus, ex præcipuis religionis Catholicæ fundamentis. Quasi scilicet Archipresbyter Iuramentum iurando, præcipuum illud fundamentum & caput eiurâsset. Quid grauius vel Petrus commisit, vel Marcellinus? in caput tantùm fidei præcipuum, in fundamentum modò religionis vtrque commisit. Idem, & non minor lapsus Archipresbyteri, Cardinale censente. Et Tortus ipse magni momenti fatetur esse, dum Gregorium adduci fatetur à Domino suo, vt doceat quanti momenti sit, Primatum Apostolicum denegare; quod scilicet Iuramento fit; quod, eo suscepto, fecit Archipresbyter. Verùm Primatus ibi Apostolicus non negatur; abest verò: Papala[?] modò, qui longè distat ab Apostolico, superatque illum multis gradibus. Neque verò Papalis Primatus pars vlla natiua; struma tantùm adnata, quæ neque caput est, neque cauda[?] fidei Catholicæ. Ad Papalem autem Primatum confirmandum adduci Gregorium, (quo, vix quenquam magis ab eo constat abhorruisse) id verò fidem omnem superat. Verùm quò magis superat, eò magis Cardinale dignum; cuius non est probare, nisi quæ paradoxa mera sunt.
units.tr: But Tortus's consolation is vain and false; the wound breaks out again. For while it is established that the Archpresbyter's fall was not a matter of cause but of a fall similar to his, and not much less (as Tortus idly tells), but above all a grave fall, the Cardinal says he is brought into peril of the royal oath, "one of the chief heads of our faith, one of the chief foundations of the Catholic religion." As if, forsooth, the Archpresbyter by swearing the oath had abjured that chief foundation and head. What graver offence did Peter or Marcellinus commit? Both committed an offence against the chief head of the faith alone, and against the foundation of religion alone. The same, and no less a fall of the Archpresbyter, in the Cardinal's judgment. And Tortus himself confesses it to be of great moment, while he admits that Gregory is brought forward by his master, to teach how great a matter it is to deny the Apostolic Primacy; which of course is done by the oath, which the Archpresbyter did when he took it. But the "Apostolic" Primacy is not denied there; rather, it is absent: only the Papal, which is far removed from the Apostolic and surpasses it by many degrees. Nor is the Papal Primacy any natural part; it is only a scar grown on, which is neither the head nor the tail of the Catholic faith. But that Gregory should be brought forward to confirm the Papal Primacy (from whom it is established that scarcely anyone shrank more from it) this surpasses all faith. But the more it surpasses, the more worthy it is of the Cardinal, whose office it is to prove nothing but mere paradoxes.

units.la: DE Gregorio ipso, pauca primùm; post autem de sententiâ ipsius. Torto, hæc iam mora debetur, qui ex ingenio suo quod in Apologia rectè positum, perverte[?] per calumniam. Dixit ibi Author, nescire se, cur Apostolus noster vocetur Gregorius, nisi quod legârit huo[?] Augustinum cum sociis, qui Saxones ad fidem traduceret. Id Tortus sic detorquet, quasi dixisset nescire se omnino, cur Gregorius Apostolus noster dicendus sit, neque addidisset causam, veram causam, nec aliam, quam addetet[?] Cardinalis ipse fi[?], cur vocet Apostolum nostrum, causam redderet. Hæc, docta est & solida Torti responsio: Reponam illi vicem. Cur Tortum sycophantam vocet quis nescio, nisi quòd vbi causa nulla est, ibi per summam nequitiam, aliquid semper calumniatur. Non hic dico nescire me: sed & scire quòd sit, & causam scire cur calumniator dicendus sit. Sed illud scilicet erat; Salsum illud dictetum suum de Bucero & Martyre, quo grauidum illi ingenium, lucem aspicere non poterat, nisi quòd se scire dixit Apologia, cuiusque causam scire, id Tortus nescire eum, finxisset saltem. Perisset alioqui nobis tam lepida hæc facetia: Verùm, diu antequam huc intrulissent pedem vel Bucerus vel Martyr, præcipuum hoc caput fidei de Primatu Papæ, expunctum è Symbolo nobis. Nihil ergo illi contulerunt ad sectam de Primatus capite exectio; quæ vos pessimè habet, præ quâ, reliquæ omnes veniales sunt. Quanquam si ad duos istos, quos dicis, duo illos conferas, Hildebrandum atque Turbanum sectæ vestræ authores: minus in illis reperies literarum, virtutis, humilitatis, denique spiritus Apostolici.
units.tr: Concerning Gregory himself, a few things first; afterwards concerning his opinion. Tortus, this delay is owed to him now, who by his own cleverness twists by calumny what was rightly stated in the Apology. The Author there said that he did not know why our "Apostle" is called Gregory, except that he had sent Augustine with companions to bring the Saxons to the faith. Tortus so twists this as if he had said he did not know at all why Gregory should be called our Apostle, and had not added the cause, the true cause, nor any other, which the Cardinal himself added, to give the reason why he calls him our Apostle. This is Tortus's "learned and solid" answer: I will repay him in kind. Why anyone should call Tortus a sycophant I do not know, unless that where there is no cause, there he always calumniates something with the greatest wickedness. I do not say here that I "do not know": but I know that it is so, and I know the cause why he ought to be called a calumniator. But that, of course, was his witty saying about Bucer and Martyr, by which his pregnant wit could not look upon the light, unless he had at least pretended that he did not know the cause of that which he said in the Apology "he knew". Otherwise this pleasant jest of his would have perished for us. But long before Bucer or Martyr set foot here, this principal head of the faith, the Primacy of the Pope, was struck out of the Creed for us. Therefore they contributed nothing to the sect by the excision of the head of the Primacy, which holds you in the worst state, beside which all the rest are venial. Yet if you compare those two whom you name, the two founders of your sect, Hildebrand and Turbanus, you will find in them less of learning, virtue, humility, and in short of apostolic spirit.

units.la: Esto igitur; vocetur Apostolus Gregorius, quando ita Beda placuit (quanquam siquis seuerior existat, litem ei mouere possit de hoc nomine) Non enim, si vere Apostolus dicendus sit, alios mittere; ire ipse debebat: Nam non dicit Christus; Sedete, & mittite; sed, Ite, prædicate, Apostolis suis. Sed neque omnium Primus in Insulam hanc misit: tute hoc fateris, Quadringenta plùs annis ante illum, Eleutherium hunc misisse. Ne-que etiam (quod Apostoli faciebant) fundamenta hic iacere fidei, quin super alieno fundamento extruxit: Nam præterquam quòd Britones hic sub Septem Episcopis fidem Christianam, (quam initio statim susceperant) saluam semper retinuerunt: etiam eo ipso loco, quò missi à Gregorio appulerunt, ante eorum appulsum, Ecclesia erat, quæ hodie Cantuaria superest, in quâ, Regina, cùm Ethelredo presbytero suo, ritu Christiano Rem Divinam, palam, quotidie procurabat. Multum ergo abest, ut proprie loquendo Apostolus ille fuerit, si ouî animus sit vobiscum funem ducere. Verùm cessit de eo vobis Apologia; ego etiam cedo; placet dilatare vocem Apostoli, ut vocetur eo nomine, quia misit, qui operam hic suam collocarint. Optauit ergo Apología, ut siquos hodie huc Pontifex inmitteret, Maiores suos imitari vellet, Gregorium, qui non nisi permissu Regis: Eleutherium, qui non nisi rogatu Regis, suos huc legârunt. Rectè autem optauit. Nam neque tu hoc ipsum pôst optandum negas, si impetrari posset. Sed redis ad ingenium; abberras à proposito; votum aliud nuncupas, vt tam vellet retinere Gregorij & Eleutherij doctrinam Rex cum suâ, quàm suorum Praedecessorum vestigijs per omnia diligenter insistit Pontisex. Eleutherij verò doctrinam, ausim dicere, per omnia retinet: nec à Gregorio discedit, nisi quantum ipse ab Eleutherio. Habes ergo votum prius. De posteriore videris; an se Catholicae totius Ecclesiae Episcopum scripsisset Gregorius, quod vester hodie facit: an Regem Dei Vicarium in regno suo diceret, quod dixit Eleutherius, vester hodie negat.
units.tr: Very well, let Gregory be called an Apostle, since Bede was pleased to call him so (though if anyone is stricter, he could bring a quarrel against him over this name). For if he were truly to be called an Apostle, he ought to have gone himself rather than sending others: Christ does not say to his Apostles, "Sit and send," but "Go, preach." Nor was he the first to send anyone to this island: you yourself admit that Eleutherius sent men here more than four hundred years before him. Nor did he, as the Apostles did, lay the foundations of faith here, but built upon another's foundation: for besides the fact that the Britons under their Seven Bishops always kept the Christian faith (which they had received at the very beginning), even in the very place where the men sent by Gregory landed, before their arrival there was a Church, which survives today at Canterbury, in which the Queen, together with her priest Ethelred, openly and daily performed divine service according to the Christian rite. It is therefore far from the truth, speaking properly, that he was an Apostle, if you wish to draw a rope with that man. But the Apology has yielded this point to you, and I too yield; let us be content to stretch the word "Apostle" so that he may be called by that name because he sent men who have since laboured here. The Apology therefore wished that if the Pontiff were now to send anyone here, he would be willing to imitate his predecessors, Gregory, who sent his men only with the King's permission, and Eleutherius, who sent his only at the King's request. And it wished rightly; for you yourself do not deny this very thing is to be wished, if it could be obtained. But you return to your character, wander from the point, and name another wish: that the King, with his own people, would be willing to keep the teaching of Gregory and Eleutherius, just as the Pontiff diligently follows the footsteps of his predecessors in all things. As for the teaching of Eleutherius, I would venture to say, he keeps it in all things, and departs from Gregory only as far as Gregory departed from Eleutherius. So you have your first wish. As for the second, you must see to it; whether Gregory wrote himself Bishop of the whole Catholic Church, as your man does today, or whether he said the King was God's Vicar in his kingdom, as Eleutherius said, which your man today denies.

units.la: Pertexit pòst Catalogum eorum, qui sub Principibus Paganis, atque Arianis Christianam fidem, etiam absque Principum venia propagârunt. Quid opus hoc? Hoc idem praedicent vestri, nec aliud praeterea quid, quàm illi, & bonâ cum venia praedicent. Verùm, haec illis conditio non placet: non satis est praedicare CHRISTVM: est illis, non vnum ex praecipuis, sed praecipuum fidei caput. Papalis potestas; atque eius proinde praecipua illis cura est; idque ita, vt neminem recipiant, nisi stipulantibus sibi ante omnia spondeat, se ad omnia Papae iussa paratum fore, nec Regi diutiùs pariturum, quàm id ita Papae visum fuerit. Hoc Cardinalis dixit Caput praecipuum esse; hocilli, quasi praecipuum sit, inculcant sedulò. Atqui, quos memoras sub Diocletiano & Constantio, tum Eusebius ille, qui mutato habitu peragrabat provincias; alius generis, alia longè ab hijs diuersa praedicabant: si clam Regnum vspiam ingressi sunt, ita sunt ingressi, vt fidem in Christum plantarent, non vt fidem in Principem supplantarent; Subditos ita animatos redderent, ita suspensos à nutu Pontificis, vt si ille propitius, tum cives: sin infensus, tum hostes haberent. Vestri hoc faciunt, ex praecipuo illo fidei capite hoc faciunt. Interest Pontificis, vt sit illud non vnum modò, sed primum de Capitibus fidei, atque illud ergo Cardinalis ita, non temere nuncupavit. Vides hic quantum interfit. Neque verò vestri sic inuitos habent Principes, neque mutato habitu opus esset, nisi iamdudum hic satis compertum esset, vos cum doctrinâ vestrâ Seditionis tionis semina permiscere, ac in religione Latebram proditi- oni quaerere. Euangelium vestrum, Euangelium pacis non est; & Gentium, non conuersio sed perversio; nec tam Ecclesiæ edificatio, quam ruina Reipublicæ. Tot vestris insidijs, tot machinis toties petiti, nupero hoc tam tetro scelere admonui (etsi Cardinalis nullus monuisset) sciunt satis; quòd sit vnum illud de praecipuis Capitibus fidei vestræ; ac proinde fidem illam suspe- ctam habent, cuius est illud Caput praecipuum. Neque quicquam tibi honestæ frontis reliquum est, qui haec ad calumniam pertinere calumniaris. Tam sunt enim multa, tam multis vicibus repetita, tam non leniter impressa, sed notis ignéis inusta, tam denique manifesto deprehensa, vt calumniae locum non relinquant.
units.tr: After this he goes on to give a catalogue of those who, under pagan and Arian princes, spread the Christian faith even without the princes' permission. What need is there of this? Your men preach the same thing, and nothing more than those did, and they preach it with the princes' goodwill. But this condition does not please them: it is not enough to preach Christ; for them it is not one of the chief things, but the chief head of faith. Papal power, and therefore its primacy, is their chief concern; and this so much that they receive no one unless he first promises them, by a binding stipulation, that he will be ready for all the Pope's commands, and will obey the King no longer than the Pope sees fit. The Cardinal said this was the chief head; they insist on this diligently, as though it were chief. Yet those whom you mention under Diocletian and Constantius, and that Eusebius who wandered through the provinces in changed dress, preached quite different things, of another kind, far removed from these: if they entered a kingdom secretly anywhere, they entered so as to plant faith in Christ, not to undermine faith in the Prince; they made their subjects so disposed and so dependent on the nod of the Pontiff that, if he were favourable, they would have them as citizens, but if hostile, as enemies. Your men do this, and they do it from that chief head of faith. It is in the Pontiff's interest that it should be not merely one among many, but the first of the heads of faith; and so the Cardinal named it thus, not carelessly. You see here how much it matters. Nor do your men keep princes so unwilling, nor would there be any need to change dress, unless it had long since been sufficiently established here that you mix the seeds of sedition with your teaching, and seek a hiding place for treason in religion. Your gospel is not the gospel of peace; and its conversion of the nations is not a conversion but a perversion; nor is it so much the building up of the Church as the ruin of the commonwealth. Attacked so often by your snares and machines, they know well enough, from this recent and so foul crime, which I warned of (even if no Cardinal had warned), that this is one of the chief heads of your faith; and therefore they hold that faith under suspicion whose chief head this is. Nor is any shred of honest face left to you, who slander these things as calumny. For there are so many of them, repeated so many times, impressed not lightly but branded with fiery marks, and at last so plainly caught, that they leave no room for calumny.
