units.la: Quàm verò miserum est, negare non posse, quod turpe est confiteri: Fuisse dicis: addé fuisse multos, fuisse saepe, fuisse non de vulgo, sed primarios viros, qui in actu ipso proditionis perierint; fuisse Sacerdotes, etiam Patres Iesuitas, qui consilijs istis praeierint; nec semel iniérint, sed saepe redierint ad consilia ista proditoria. Ex desperatione hoc dicis: imò desperatæ sunt res vestræ, cùm ad desperationem confugitis. Tu quidem supra dixisti: ego plus etiam quàm dixi, probaui nullum eis tum desperandi causam fuisse, quin sperandi potius & si poterat illos spes vlla mitiores reddere. Non tamen ex Catholica doctrinâ (inquis) neq; ex rectâ ratione. Non sanè ex Catholicâ verâ, sed Catholicâ vestrâ tamen, quam rectè hîc distinguis à varior rectâ, quæ homines non perducit ad ea, quæ tu ipse paulò ante dixeras, horrere omnes naturaliter. Regia enim doctrina est, ut Princeps vobis ex animo sit, quantumuis legitimus haeres sit, Regno excludi, alium eligi posse: posse dixi? imò oportere. Haec Clementina vestra fuit, quâ ex doctrinâ, tota illa nuperâ proditio profeminata est. Vestra haec ratio est: quem excludi oportuit, certè illum oportebit, quàm primùm exturbari. Vestra haec doctrina ex Garnetti tripode, Fiat ut lupus, sicut lupi pereant simul. Parum autem hoc visum in oculis vestris; non Regem perire vnum, sed Patrem vnà cum stirpe & familiâ suâ, Regem vnà cum Senatu, fuq. Papa loquire [illegible, ~6 letters] voluistis. Vestra haec ratio. Potest etiam & locus Consiliis habendis ex antiquo sacer, subjecto pulvere fulminis instar, diffari[?] Vestra stra hæc doctrina{4}. Posse homines ad Consilia hæc, Catholica Confessionis sigillo, Catholici Iuramenti vinculo, Catholici Sacramenti voto, atque nexu, Catholicarum precum solenni indictione, Catholici Sacrificij oblatione firmiter obligari. Vestra hæc doctrina rebellionem spirans, Ex radice colubri egrediatur regulus: Detestanda proditione subsequatur, aperta rebellio; palam edocta à Patre Societatis, in quâ, quinque è primarijs extincti sunt. Vestra hæc ratio: De proposito tam Catholico, tam ex doctrinâ Catholicâ poenitendum non est. Quare, fuerunt, qui cum laqueo collum inserrent, ad extremum usque spiritum; spirârunt doctrinam hanc, nec huius doctrinæ praxin ut damnarent adduci potuerunt; imò, qui animos alijs addiderunt, ut facerent, imò qui mirati sunt, à nullo vestrûm Apologia scribi sui huius tam præclari facinoris. Quod & vos iam strenuè præstitistis, postquam Garnettum & Oldcornum in Martyrologium vestrum retulistis: Quorum ille, Garnettus, (post Clementem 8um, qui quidem admissum noluit, nec permissum voluit) unus fuit è præcipuis Capitibus Catholicæ huius Conspirationis, cùm contra Iesum bonus Iesuita iusssit audacter eos, vnà eradicare tritissimum cum Zizaniis: Hic, Oldcornus, alterum Caput præcipuum, qui laudavit pro concione factum iam infectum: & cùm expediationem Israelis contra Gibeam, Ludovici in terram sanctam, non sine rectâ ratione exæquarunt. Atque ita Illi, ex Catholicâ quidem doctrinâ vestrâ rem aggressi sunt, & ratione ex doctrinâ vestrâ capitibus recte petitâ; nec tamen vel[illegible, ~3 letters] vôsque ipsi partim ex sympathiâ vestrâ Catholicâ, partim ex mirabili quodam[?] sed stramineo signo, quantum quidem in vobis, rem totam comprobastis.
units.tr: How wretched it is to be unable to deny what is shameful to confess! You say, "It happened." Add: it happened many times, it happened often, and those were not common men but the foremost men, who perished in the very act of treason; there were priests, even Jesuit Fathers, who led the way in these plots, and they did not enter upon them once, but often returned to these treacherous plans. You say this arises from despair: indeed, your affairs are desperate when you flee to despair. You indeed said so above; I have shown more than that, that they then had no cause for despair at all, but rather for hope, and that if any hope could make them more gentle, it could. "Yet not from Catholic doctrine," you say, "nor from right reason." Certainly not from true Catholic doctrine, but from your Catholic doctrine, which you rightly distinguish here from right reason, which does not lead men to those things which you yourself had said a little before, that all men naturally shudder at. For it is the royal doctrine that the Prince, however lawful his heir, may be excluded from the kingdom by you, and another chosen. May be? Nay, that it ought to be so. This was your Clementine doctrine, and from this doctrine that whole recent treason was sprung. "This is our reasoning," you say: whoever ought to be excluded, certainly he will ought to be thrown out as soon as possible. "This is our doctrine, from Garnet's tripod: Let him become a wolf, that the wolves may perish together." It seemed little in your eyes that one King alone should perish, but that the Father together with his line and family, the King together with the Senate, and so on, were to be ruined, as you wished the Pope to speak. "This is our reasoning." The place for holding councils, sacred from of old, may also be laid under powder like a thunderbolt; "Your doctrine." That men may be firmly bound to these councils by the seal of Catholic confession, the bond of the Catholic oath, the vow and tie of the Catholic sacrament, by the solemn proclamation of Catholic prayers, by the offering of the Catholic Sacrifice. Your doctrine, breathing rebellion: "From the root of the serpent let the basilisk come forth; let open rebellion follow the detestable treason"; this was openly taught by a Father of the Society, in which five of the foremost were put to death. This is your reasoning: one must not repent of a purpose so Catholic, so grounded in Catholic doctrine. Hence there were those who put a noose round their necks, to the last breath; they breathed out this doctrine, and could not be brought to condemn the practice of this doctrine; nay, they who encouraged others to do it, nay, they who admired it, not one of you has written an Apology for this so splendid deed of theirs. Which you too have now vigorously done, after you put Garnet and Oldcorn into your Martyrology: of whom Garnet (after Clement VIII, who indeed would not have it done, nor wished it allowed) was one of the chief heads of this Catholic conspiracy, since, against Jesus, that good Jesuit ordered them to root out the wheat together with the tares; and Oldcorn, another chief head, who praised from the pulpit what had been done and was now undone, and who likened the expedition of Israel against Gibeah to the expedition of Louis into the Holy Land, not without right reason. And so they undertook the matter from your Catholic doctrine, and sought the chief heads by reasoning rightly from your doctrine; and yet you yourselves, partly from your Catholic sympathy, partly from some wonderful but straw-like sign, have, as far as in you lies, approved the whole affair.

units.la: Alteram verò illam, ne tu quidem differiteris, doctrinam vestram esse, de defectione subditorum à Principe ad sibilum Musfox; quæ est in Babylone, id est, Romæ. Te enim dicis hoc supra docuisse, dixisse memini; non docuisse, hilsubere tutum docere sit. Verùm quando Doctorem Brenuum te præstitieris defectionis illius, intrabit statim proditio, per fenestram illam. Fiat de Principe non Princeps, de Subdito non Subdito: non Subditos, contra non Principem, quid non tentabit? Non parcet hostilam Ecclesiæ, non abstinebit ab ijs, quæ naturaliter omnes horrent, Cæde, & Violentia. Non tamen hoc fiet (inquies) nisi in schisma prius incidat, vel haeresin. Quasi hoc schisma non sit & haeresis, Pontifici per omn a obsequentem non esse: Quasi haeresis ulla fuerit Iohannis Regis Nauarrae, praeterquàm quòd in bello à Pontificis parte non steterit: Haeresis ulla Philippi Pulchri, praeterquàm quòd se totum non permiserit arbitrio Papae. In omni enim re, si non primas deferant Primatui eius, statim Rei sunt haeresis; & merito: negant enim unum ex praecipuis capitibus fidei Christianae. Non est tamen doctrina haec noua. Imò noua, si ad veterem conferatur. Agnoscis ipse hoc, dum non ante Lateranense Concilium, id est, non ante seculum decimumtertium dicis approbatam. Per annos mille ducentos ubi latuit? Tum, neque usu Christiani populi per multa secula receptam, sed abusu Pontificum in Christianum populum per aliquot secula usurpatam; receptam autem nisi per vim, haud ullo seculo, reclamante semper Principe, cui facta vis est, etiam, qui potuit, resistente: Populo autem Christiano, cui vix ullo inde seculo tranquillitate frui licuit, Papalem in eo factum, atque violentiam detestante.
units.tr: Yet the other point, which you cannot deny either, is that your teaching is that subjects defect from their prince at the hissing of Musfox, who is in Babylon, that is, in Rome. For you say that you taught this above; I remember you said it, not that you taught it. It is safe to teach, not to be taught. But since you have made yourself a doctor of that defection, treachery will at once enter through that window. Let there be no prince who is a prince, and no subject who is a subject: what will he not attempt against subjects who are not subjects, and against a prince who is not a prince? He will not spare the enemies of the Church, nor abstain from those things which all men naturally shudder at: slaughter and violence. Yet this will not happen (you will say) unless he first falls into schism or heresy. As if this schism and heresy were not the refusal to obey the Pope in everything! As if there had been any heresy in John, King of Navarre, except that he did not stand on the Pope's side in the war! As if there had been any heresy in Philip the Fair, except that he did not surrender himself wholly to the will of the Pope! For in every matter, if they do not give first place to his primacy, they are at once guilty of heresy; and rightly so: for they deny one of the chief articles of the Christian faith. Yet this doctrine is not new. Rather, it is new if it is compared with the old. You yourself acknowledge this, when you say that it was not approved before the Lateran Council, that is, before the thirteenth century. Where was it hidden for twelve hundred years? Moreover, it was not received by the use of the Christian people through many ages, but was usurped by the abuse of the Popes against the Christian people over several ages; and it was received, in no age, except by force, with the prince, to whom violence was done, always protesting, and resisting too as far as he was able; and the Christian people, who hardly in any age was allowed to enjoy tranquillity, detested the papal act in this and the violence of it.

units.la: AT quò Pontificis Primatus unum iam fiat de praecipuis capitibus fidei nostrae; Pontifex ipse Caput fidei faciendus est, atque ad hanc rem Gregorius testis quaeritur. Largitur Gregorius Iohanni Panormitano Pallium, monet Palliatum, ne reuerentiâ Sedis Apostolicae turbari ab ullo sinat; rationem reddit: mansurum enim integrum membrorum statum, si Caput fidei iniuriâ non pulsetur, & Canonum authoritas maneat incolumis. Hic ergo Gregorius, ac proin Papa, fidei Caput. Quid agimus iam? Credimusne in Papam? Quidni? Papa in fide, ut Caput in corpore, Summitas ipsa totius fidei. Fides autem cuius, quo sensu acceptae? an inhaerenus virtutis Theologicae, quae cuique in corde est? Nemo sanus dixerit. Obiecti igitur fidei, id est, rerum credendarum. Rerum ergo credendarum Caput Papa; Credenda, membra sunt; inter Credenda, Caput principalem locum habet, Papa scilicet. In quid vero fidei credimus, si in Caput non credimus? Non habet fides ipsa, altius, illustrius, eminentius quicquam quàm Caput suum, in quod tendat, in quod recumbat, in quo spem omnem ponat ac fiduciam.
units.tr: But so that the primacy of the Pope may now be made one of the chief articles of our faith, the Pope himself must be made the head of the faith, and Gregory is called as a witness for this matter. Gregory bestows the pallium on John of Palermo, and advises the one wearing the pallium not to allow the reverence due to the Apostolic See to be disturbed by anyone; he gives the reason: the integrity of the state of the members will remain, if the head of the faith is not struck with injury, and the authority of the canons remains unharmed. Here, then, Gregory, and therefore the Pope, is the head of the faith. What are we doing now? Do we believe in the Pope? Why not? The Pope is in the faith as the head is in the body, the very summit of the whole faith. But faith of what kind, and in what sense taken? Is it the inherent theological virtue which each person has in his heart? No sane person would say so. Therefore it is the object of faith, that is, the things to be believed. The Pope, then, is the head of the things to be believed; the things to be believed are the members; among the things to be believed, the Pope, namely, holds the principal place as head. But in what do we believe as faith, if we do not believe in the head? Faith itself has nothing higher, more illustrious, more eminent than its head, towards which it strives, on which it rests, in which it places all its hope and trust.

units.la: Occurrit tamen Papa primus (ut volunt) qui non aliam ob causam Christum[?] glorificatum dicit, {*}quam ut fides nostra sit in Deum. Ergóne Papa Deus, vt fides nostra in eum, in Deum sit? Petrus verò {a}& ipse homo erat. Occurrit & alius qui tam de Petro, quàm de se affirmat, {b}Non dominamur fidei vestræ. At certè æquum, vt dominetur Caput corpori suo; si Papa fidei Caput, fides Papæ corpus, vt & dominetur Papa fidei. Hæc Paulus de se negat, de reliquis Apostolis: non debet verò licere Sedi Apostolicæ, quod Apostolis non licuit. Occurrunt & alia multa. Duo enim sæpe, tres, quatuor interdum Papæ; ita tria fidei Capita, non unum: fides triceps, tricephala. Interdum biennio, septennio, Papa nullus; toto ergo tempore hoc fides carebat Capite: fides acephala. Papa sæpe, contra Papam, vt Sabinianus contra Gregorium, Stephanus contra Formosum, Sergius contra Stephanum; ita fidei Caput, contra Caput fidei, quasi Amphisbæna: fides anticephala. Papa interdum Arianus, Eutychianus, Monothelita, (quod adhuc peius) Atheus est: ita Caput fidei fidem destruet. Papa interdum unum pecus (vt scribit de Calestino Baldus) qui quod de manè faciebat, de [?]sero revocabat: ita Caput fidei iam cerebrum non habet. Denique quod hic metuit Gregorius, venit superillum; Non solùm enim turbatum, atque pulsatum iniuriâ Caput hoc fidei, sed aliquando etiam (quæ summa iniuria est, summa pulsatio) detypbatum est, atque amputatum. Quid dixi Caput? Tria simul Capita præcisa sunt in Concilio Constantiensi, & iacuit Ecclesia tum (vt Poëta) ingens litore truncus. Atque hoc ipsum iam metuere videtur Cardinalis. Agi enim dicit de ipso fidei Capite amputando. Pulsant hæc quidem nec leuiter Gregorianum hoc Caput vestrum. Consultum itaque sibi hoc fore putant Ecclesiæ membra; si relinquant Cardinali atque tibi Caput hoc fidei vestræ; adhæreant autem Authori fidei suæ & Capiti vero Christo, qui consedit iam, non in Apostolicâ Sede, sed in Throno Patris Cælestis, vbi turbari, vbi iniuriâ pulsari non potest, de quo vel tollendo, vel amputando secura sint.
units.tr: Yet there occurs the Pope first (as they will have it), who says that Christ was glorified for no other reason than that our faith might be in God. Is the Pope then God, so that our faith is in him, in God? But Peter was himself also a man. Another occurs too, who affirms of himself as of Peter: "We do not lord it over your faith." But surely it is fitting that the head should rule over its own body; if the Pope is the head of the faith, the faith is the body of the Pope, so that the Pope may also rule over the faith. Paul denies this of himself, and of the other Apostles: yet what was not permitted to the Apostles ought not to be permitted to the Apostolic See. Many other things also occur. For there are sometimes two, sometimes three, sometimes four Popes; so there are three heads of the faith, not one: a three-headed faith, a tricephalous one. Sometimes for two or seven years there is no Pope; so for all that time the faith lacked a head: a headless faith. The Pope often acts against the Pope, as Sabinian against Gregory, Stephen against Formosus, Sergius against Stephen; so the head of the faith acts against the head of the faith, like an amphisbaena: a faith with heads at both ends. Sometimes the Pope is an Arian, a Eutychian, a Monothelite (which is still worse), or an atheist: so the head of the faith will destroy the faith. Sometimes the Pope is a foolish beast (as Baldus writes of Celestine), who undid in the evening what he had done in the morning: so the head of the faith now has no brain. Finally, what Gregory fears here comes to pass beyond it: this head of the faith has not only been disturbed and struck with injury, but sometimes (which is the greatest injury, the greatest striking) it has even been mutilated and cut off. What have I said, "head"? Three heads were cut off at once at the Council of Constance, and the Church then lay (as the poet says) a huge trunk on the shore. And the Cardinal seems to fear this very thing. For he says that the matter concerns the cutting off of the very head of the faith. These things indeed strike, and not lightly, at this head of yours, Gregory's. They therefore think it will be to the advantage of the members of the Church if they leave this head of your faith to the Cardinal and to you; but let them cling to the Author of their faith and to the true Head, Christ, who now sits not in the Apostolic See, but on the throne of the heavenly Father, where he cannot be disturbed or struck with injury, and concerning whose removal or cutting off they may be secure.

units.la: Huic Capitis languori, dum Tortus mederi vult, Caput fidei dicit esse Papam suum, tropicè, non secundum literam; atque ad [Hoc est Caput] adhibet Metonymiam, quam si quis adhiberet, ad [Hoc est corpus] cœlum terræ, scio, permisceret. Caput fidei, id est, Caput fidelium siue Ecclesia. Sed nihil agit. Ex eo enim probat Cardinalis, Primatum vestrum unum esse de praecipuis capitibus fidei vestrae & Catholicae religionis fundamentis, quòd Gregorius seipsum dicat Caput fidei. Utrobique ergo fides eadem, non alio sensu in praemissis, nempe res credenda, obiectum fidei; in conclusione, alio, nempe fideles, subiectum fidei. Non si te rotes, si te torqueas, quasi lumbricus, hic te expedias. Quicquid enim de fidelibus sit, non est Caput praecipuum fidei vestrae, non est Fundamentum religionis Pontifex. Verùm neque sic sensu tuo Caput est. {a}Caput enim Ecclesiae, {b}Caput corporis Ecclesiae, CHRISTI tituli sunt. Eodem autem modo Caput, quo Fundamentum: vester hic argumentandi modus, à Fundamento ad Caput. {c}Fundamentum autem aliud nemo potest ponere; quare Caput aliud nemo potest imponere; ut si nec aliud Fundamentum, nec aliud Caput. Quanquam Fundamenti facilior multiplicatio, quàm Capitis: Plura enim & in Sacris literis {d}Fundamenta; at Capita plura nec ibi reperias, nec Corporis analogia patitur. At Ecclesia Corpus unum. Monstrosum verò Corpus, cui plus uno sit Capite; (atque ut vobis occurram) cui duo Capita, quanquam alterum principale, ministeriale alterum. Ubi Corpora multa sunt, ut familiae, Capita multa dicuntur: ubi varia doctrinae genera, Capita multa: ubi Corpus unum Ecclesiae, Caput non nisi unum. Fides hic nobis suadet, extra Scripturam non sapere; Ratio, à naturâ corporis non discedere.
units.tr: To cure the weakness of this head, Torturus wishes to heal it, saying that the Pope is the head of the faith, his own, figuratively and not according to the letter; and he applies to [This is the Head] a metonymy, which if anyone applied to [This is the body] would, I know, confuse heaven with earth. The head of the faith, that is, the head of the faithful or the Church. But he accomplishes nothing. For from this the Cardinal proves that your primacy is one of the chief articles of your faith and the foundations of your Catholic religion, because Gregory calls himself the head of the faith. In both places, then, the faith is the same, but not in the same sense: in the premises, namely the thing to be believed, the object of faith; in the conclusion, in another sense, namely the faithful, the subject of faith. You may turn and twist yourself, you may wriggle like a worm, you will not thereby extricate yourself here. For whatever the faithful may be, the Pope is not the chief head of your faith, nor is the Pope the foundation of religion. Nor is he the head in your sense either. For "head of the Church" and "head of the body of the Church" are titles of CHRIST. Moreover, he is head in the same way as foundation: this is your method of argument, from foundation to head. But no one can lay another foundation; therefore no one can impose another head, as if there were neither another foundation nor another head. Yet the multiplication of the foundation is easier than that of the head: for there are several foundations in Sacred Letters; but you will find no several heads there, nor does the analogy of the body allow it. But the Church is one body. A monstrous body, however, is one which has more than one head; (and to meet you) which has two heads, even though one is principal and the other ministerial. Where there are many bodies, as families, many heads are spoken of; where there are various kinds of teaching, many heads: where the Church is one body, there is only one head. Faith here persuades us not to savour anything beyond Scripture; reason, not to depart from the nature of the body.

units.la: Verùm, ut Mus uni non fidit antro: alterum habet Caput fidei, (id est) Caput per quod Ecclesia fidem discit & docet. Quid audio? Caput discentium, Caput docentis; at haec, duo iam Capita sunt. Qui docet, discentem docet; qui discit, à docente discit: ibi intellectus agens, hîs patiens; ibi dat, hic accipit. Idemne Caput, praeceptoris & discipuli? Idemne agit Caput in se, & eodem simul tempore patitur à se? Idem sibi dat, à se accipit? Torques nos, Torte. Ecclesia haec, unane quae discit simul & docet? Non opinor. Certè alij docent, alij discunt in Ecclesiâ. An hij qui docent, omnes Pontificis caput sumunt mutuum, nec sine eo docere possunt? Illi etiam qui discunt, caput idem, nec sine eo discere? Iam si Ecclesia Fidem discit, per Caput Pontificis, eademque per Caput Pontificis Fidem docet, mirum narras Caput Pontificis, super docentis humeros, superque discentis, uno eodemque tempore. Mēiltrolum ante Corpus, iam Caput. Sed neque id proprie, vt Caput seu Fidei, seu doctrinæ, de docente (qui iam habet) & de discente, qui nondum habet, capax nondò est ex æquo prædicetur. Minùs autem adhuc proprie: Primatum vtrique Capiti, docenti, atque discenti ex æquo conuenire. Primus enim qui docet; qui discit, in secundis consistit. Atque hoc iam ex præcipuis fidei capitibus vnum esse dicitur, vt credamus Pontificem Ecclesiæ Caput esse, per quod & discit, & docet fidem suam; sine eo neminem in Ecclesia quicquam vel docere vel discere, à summo præceptore ad discipulum infimum: vt anima potiùs, quam Caput dici mereatur, qui ita sit totus in toto, & totus in qualibet parte. Atque hic sanè titulus, longè supra titulum est Vniuersalis Episcopi, etiamsi tuo sensu sumatur. Solus enim est, qui docet in Episcopis, nec id modò, sed solus etiam, qui discit in populis; solus, lingua docentium, solus etiam auris audientium: Verè vniuersalis.
units.tr: But, as the mouse does not trust one hole, you have another head of the faith (that is, a head through which the Church learns and teaches the faith). What do I hear? A head of those who learn, a head of the one who teaches; but these are now two heads. He who teaches, teaches the learner; he who learns, learns from the teacher: there the intellect is active, here passive; there he gives, here he receives. Is it the same head of the teacher and of the disciple? Does the same head act upon itself and at the same time suffer from itself? Does it give to itself, receive from itself? You torment us, Torturus. Is this Church one which both learns and teaches at once? I do not think so. Certainly in the Church some teach and others learn. Do those who teach all take the borrowed head of the Pope, and can they not teach without it? And those too who learn, the same head, and can they not learn without it? Now, if the Church learns the faith through the head of the Pope, and the same Church teaches the faith through the head of the Pope, you tell a marvellous tale: a head of the Pope, upon the shoulders of the teacher, and upon those of the learner, at one and the same time. A head before the body, now a head. But it cannot properly be said of a head, whether of faith or of teaching, that it can be predicated equally of the teacher (who already has it) and of the learner, who does not yet have it. Still less properly: that primacy belongs equally to both the head that teaches and the head that learns. For the one who teaches is first; the one who learns stands in the second place. And this is now said to be one of the chief articles of faith, so that we believe the Pope to be the Head of the Church, through whom it both learns and teaches its faith; without him no one in the Church can teach or learn anything, from the highest teacher to the lowest disciple: so that he deserves to be called a soul rather than a head, who is thus wholly in the whole and wholly in every part. And this title, indeed, is far above the title of Universal Bishop, even if it is taken in your sense. For he alone is the one who teaches among the bishops, and not only that, but he alone also is the one who learns among the peoples; the only tongue of the teachers, the only ear of the hearers too: truly universal.

units.la: Quæro autem, quid Panormitani Pallio cum Fide? aut, (si ita malis) quid Sedi cum Fide? Quòd enim Sedes ibi sit, ex facto Petri initium habuit: Facta autem Petri (quæ quidem in Sacris literis non habentur) de Fide non sunt. Quodsi autem Fides de Sede fuerat, quid opus ei, Canones adiungere? Quorsum ibi de illo mentio, aut illorum authoritate incolumi seruandâ? An de Gregorio etiam prædicantur Canones, aut eorum Authoritas, vt dicere liceat, sicut Gregorius est Caput, ita Gregorius est Authoritas Canonum? Inaudita prædicatio, & cui similis vix legenda, credo, in libro . Sed enim si Caput est, est & Authoritas: copulantur enim illa, nec licet disiungere. Atque in hæc se absurda præcipites dare coguntur, dum Gregorio vim faciunt, cuius ea mens est: Statum membrorum pacatum tum fore, si non modò Fidei Caput seruetur illæsum, sed & Canonum quoque authoritas maneat intemerata: à quibus scilicet Canonibus habeat respectum suum Sedes Apostoli, & à quibus ius habeat Pallij conferendi: vt nihil ad fidem aut Fidei caput, vel Pallium vel Sedes; verùm ad Canones à quibus est illis, sua omnis, quam habent authoritas: quos ipsos, non fidem solùm; incolumes Gregorius vult esse. Ab vtrisque enim, & fide illæ sâ, & illis intemeratis, pendere incolumitatem & pacem membrorum Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: I ask, however, what the Pall of Panormitanus has to do with the faith; or (if you prefer) what the See has to do with the faith? For that the See is there had its beginning from a deed of Peter; but the deeds of Peter (which are indeed not contained in the Sacred Scriptures) do not belong to the faith. But if the faith were concerned with the See, what need would it have to add the Canons? Why is there any mention of them there, or of the need to keep their authority intact? Or is it preached of Gregory too that the Canons, or their authority, are such that one may say: just as Gregory is the Head, so Gregory is the authority of the Canons? This is an unheard-of assertion, and I believe one hardly to be read in any book. But if he is the Head, he is also the authority, for these things are joined together and cannot be separated. And they are forced to rush headlong into these absurdities while they do violence to Gregory, whose mind it is that the state of the members would be peaceful then, if not only the Head of the faith were preserved unharmed, but also the authority of the Canons remained inviolate: from which Canons, namely, the See of the Apostle has its regard and from which it has the right of conferring the Pall; so that nothing pertains to the faith or the Head of the faith, or the Pall or the See, but to the Canons from which all their authority comes to them; and Gregory wants these very Canons, not the faith alone, to be kept unharmed. For the soundness and peace of the members of the Church depend on both: on the faith, which is pure, and on those Canons, which are inviolate.

units.la: Ad libram Terti, jam venio. Sic enim dixerat Apologia. Noluit Gregorius Oecumenicus Episcopus dici: noluit ergo Caput fidei, qui titulus multò plus habet ponderis; 7 orto autem leuiùs pendit. Atque hîc obtrudit nobis primò commentitium sensum Oecumenici, quasi siquis sit Oecumenicus, solus is sit atque ita solus, ut præter eum Episcopus non sit in Orbe universo. Commentitius hic sensus est: res ipsa loquitur. Utriusque Romæ Episcopi, tum veteris tum nouæ, jam sunt, jamdudum fuerunt Oecumenici; & sunt tamen (per Dei gratiam) Episcopi ex eo, nihilo pauciores. At hoc Gregorius dicit. Non dicit. Dicit enim a Mauritio Augusto, utinam vel fine alicuius (non sublatione sed) imminutione unus fit, qui vocari appetit universalis. Dicit b Constantiæ Augustæ: illud appetere Iohannem (non ut alij ne sint, sed) ut omnibus dignior esse videatur. Dicit c Eulogio Alexandrino: Per elationem pompatici sermonis, Christi filij fludet membra subiugare Subiugare dixit, non amputare ulla. Dixit d Iohanni ipsi; appetere eum vocabulum hoc (non ut solus esse, sed) ut nulli subesse, & solus omnibus praesse videretur. Dicit id conari (non ut ullum tollat, sed) ut cuncta Christi membra sibimet, Vniuersalis appellatione supponat. Dicit ei, e Quid dicturus es, qui non solum Pater, sed Generalis Pater in mundo vocari appetis? Generalis Pater dixit, solus non dixit. Et, quod omnem hic scrupulum tollit, dicit, f cupere Iohannem Episcopis semetipsum vocabulo elationis praeponere, eoque sub se premere. At praeponere se, premere sub se non potest nisi sunt quos premat, quibus se praeponat. Voluit ergo praeesse Iohannes, praeponere se, dignior illis esse, Pater Generalis vocari: reliquos autem Episcopos, non abdicare; sed premere sub se, subponere, subiugare, imminuere illos, non ad nihilum redigere.
units.tr: I now come to the book of the Third. For thus the Apology had said: Gregory, the ecumenical bishop, did not wish to be called so; he therefore did not wish to be the Head of the faith, which title carries much more weight; but the lesser title weighs less. Here he first thrusts upon us a made-up sense of "ecumenical," as if whoever is ecumenical must be so alone, and so alone that there is no other bishop in the whole world apart from him. This sense is invented: the thing itself speaks. Both bishops of Rome, of the old and of the new, are now, and have long been, ecumenical; and yet (by the grace of God) they are bishops, no fewer for that. But Gregory does not say this. He does not say it. For he says, to Maurice Augustus: "would that one of them, by the diminishing (not the removal) of some other, may become the one who desires to be called universal." He says to the Empress Constantia: that John desired this (not so that others should cease to be, but) "so that he might seem more worthy than all." He says to Eulogius of Alexandria: "Through the elation of a pompous title he strives to subject the members of the Son of Christ." He said "subject," not "cut off" any. He said to John himself that he desired this title (not so that he alone should be, but) "so that he might seem subject to none and alone to preside over all." He says that he attempts this (not so that he might remove any, but) "so that he might subject all the members of Christ to himself by the appellation of universal." He says to him: "What will you say, who desire to be called not only Father but General Father in the world?" He said General Father; he did not say sole. And, which removes every doubt here, he says that John desired to set himself above the bishops by the word of elation, and so to press them down beneath himself. But one cannot set oneself above, or press beneath oneself, unless there are those whom one presses down and over whom one sets oneself. John therefore wished to preside, to set himself above them, to be more worthy than they, to be called General Father; but he did not abdicate the other bishops: he wished to press them beneath himself, to subordinate, subjugate, and diminish them, not reduce them to nothing.

units.la: At dicit hoc, locu citatis. Imò cuincam è locis ipsis quos citat Tortus. Gregorium hoc non dicere. Non in primo; proximis enim plane verbis subiungit: g Quia illum (Iohannes videlicet) imitatur, qui spretis in sociali gaudio Angelorum Legionibus, ad culmen conatus est singularitatis erumpere: dicens, Super astra cæli exaltabo Solium meum. Luciferi imitatorem dicit hic Iohannem: at is conatus non est solus Angelus appellari; illo verò cæteros passus est Angelorum, & locum & titulum reuncre: tantùm eminere inter illos voluit, exaltare solium suum, & esse quasi dicas, Papa ᴗAngelorum. Ad illius ergo exemplum id egit Iohannes, vt esset inter Episcopos, quasi Lucifer inter Angelos; vt essent quidem Episcopi, sed ipse Lucifer esset Episcoporum. Non in secundo. Nihil in eo quod moretur nos; derogari dicit cæteris, non abrogari Patriarcharum nomen; id quod subsequente statim periodo magis explicat, dum dicit, fratrum suorum honorem imminuere. Imminuere dixit, non in totum tollere. Non in tertio. Tota enim ibi res in aperto ponitur, quàm sit hic, quem Tortus affert, sensus insensatus. Mortuus enim tum Iohannes; Cyriacus Successor eius sedebat Constantinopoli; Decennio toto sederat Iohannes, vsurpárat Oecumenici titulum ad mortem vsque; neglexerat Gregorij monita. Quanquam autem gesisse se per totos decem annos pro Oecumenico; nullum tamen, ne vnum quidem, per tempus illud Episcopum exauthorauit. Quare commentum hoc metum, de nullo tum futuro vel Episcopo vel Patriarchâ, si Episcopus sit vllus Oecumenicus. Cyriacus ipse, vt in Sede, sic in titulo, successit Iohanni; Episcopos non abrogauit: Synodum Episcoporum indixit, cui cum Eusebius interesse vellet, petit ab eo Gregorius Epistolâ hac suâ, ne ei titulo subscribat, ne quid circa locum aliquem vel personam (putà suam) præiudicialiter ibi censeatur. Atqui nec in Synodo illâ, nec vndecim post annis, quibus præfuit illi Sedi Cyriacus (idque cum titulo Oecumenici) aut loco motus Episcopus quisquam, aut metus iniectus vlli, vt moueretur. Quare, somnia hæc vestra sunt. De Cyriaco certum, non cessisse illum priùs titulo hoc Oecumenici, quàm abiudicâsseт illum Phocas Constantinopolitano, atq; eundem in Romanum transtulisset. Factum verò hoc in odium Cyriaci à Phocâ illi infenso, & in Bonifacij hoc rogantis fauorem, qui se cum Apocrisiarius esset, in gratiam Phoca infinuâsseт, filiúmque tum eius è Baptismo suscepisset. Phocae autem decretum hoc ita refert ² Baronius, Solum Romanum Pontificem esse dicendum Oecumenicum, nempe Vniuersalem. Constantinopolitanum vero nequaquam.
units.tr: But "he says this in the places cited." Indeed, I will show from the very places which Tortus cites that Gregory does not say this. Not in the first; for in the very next words he adds: "Because he (John, that is) imitates him who, scorning the legions of Angels in the social joy, strove to break out to the height of singularity, saying: I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven." Here he calls John an imitator of Lucifer; but that attempt was not to be called the only Angel; rather he wished to surpass the rest of the Angels in place and title: he wished to tower above them, to exalt his throne, and to be, as it were, "Pope of the Angels." Following his example, then, John did this, so that he would be among the bishops as Lucifer among the Angels; so that there would indeed be bishops, but he himself would be the Lucifer of the bishops. Not in the second. There is nothing in it that should detain us; he says the others are derogated, not that the name of the Patriarchs is abrogated; which the following period, immediately after, explains more clearly, when he says "to diminish the honour of his brothers." He said diminish, not remove altogether. Not in the third. For the whole matter there is set out openly, how senseless is the sense which Tortus brings forward here. For John was then dead; his successor Cyriacus sat at Constantinople. John had sat for the whole decade, had usurped the title of Ecumenical until death, and had disregarded Gregory's warnings. Although he had, indeed, behaved for the whole ten years as ecumenical, yet during that time he deposed no bishop, not even one. Therefore this invention is a fear of no bishop or patriarch then to come, if any bishop is ecumenical. Cyriacus himself, both in the See and in the title, succeeded John; he did not abrogate the bishops: he summoned a Synod of bishops, and when Eusebius wished to attend it, Gregory asks him in this letter of his not to subscribe to that title, lest anything be judged there prejudicially concerning some place or person (namely his own). Yet neither in that Synod, nor in the eleven years afterward during which Cyriacus presided over that See (and that with the title of Ecumenical), was any bishop moved from his place, nor was fear instilled into anyone so that he would be moved. Therefore these are your dreams. Concerning Cyriacus it is certain that he did not give up this title of Ecumenical before Phocas deprived the Constantinopolitan of it and transferred the same to the Roman. This was done, however, out of hatred of Cyriacus by Phocas, who was hostile to him, and in favour of Boniface, who, being apocrisiarius, had insinuated himself into the good graces of Phocas, and had then stood as godfather to his son at Baptism. Baronius reports this decree of Phocas thus: "Only the Roman Pontiff is to be called Ecumenical," that is, Universal. The Constantinopolitan, by no means.

units.la: Nihil ergo vsurpârunt Iohannes atque Cyriacus, quàm quod statuente Phocâ, ex eo iam Romanus sibi vendicat; sub quo manent loco suo, atque Episcopi sunt, atque ita sub Iohanne manfissent, fuissent, nec iis, titulus Oecumenici quicquam obstitisset. Interim, perpauxillo temporis interuallo, magna in nomine hoc mutatio facta est. In Constantinopolitano cum fuit, stultum[?], superbum, scelestum, perversum[?], prophanum, blasphemum fuit: idem autem intra biennii unius spacium in Romano, nihil horum est.
units.tr: John and Cyriacus therefore usurped nothing beyond what, by the decree of Phocas, the Roman now claims for himself; under whom they remain in their place, and are bishops, and so would have remained under John, and the title of Ecumenical would not have hindered them in any way. Meanwhile, within a very short interval of time, a great change was made in this name. When it was in the Constantinopolitan, it was "foolish," "proud," "wicked," "perverse," "profane," "blasphemous"; but within the space of barely one biennium it is none of these in the Roman.

units.la: Mira autem Phocæ sententia, qui statuerit nomen (si Gregorio credimus) scelestum & blasphemum Constantinopolitano non convenire; esse enim Romano proprium. Mira etiam Bonifacij mens qui acceptauerit; nec præferri, vel præesse omnibus voluit Constantinopolitanum; sibi enim & Romanis Pontificibus, deberi hoc, quanquam qui hoc faceret (Gregorio teste) Luciferi imitator in eo esset, præcursor Antichristi. Verus autem Propheta Gregorius, quò se tandem daret vox ista. Dixit enim Imperatori de vocabulo illo,{a} qui eo gauderet, honori se per illud Imperij superponere, & annon id ita factum est? Dixit Aniano, {b}in isto scelesto vocabulo consentire, nihil est aliud, quam fidem perdere; & fides nihilne detrimenti passa est, ex quo consensit in titulum illum Phocas? Verum quidem utrumque Gregorij vaticinium; & Imperio & Ecclesiæ perniciosa vox ista: & Successor eius Bonifacius; quoad imperium Lucifer, quoad Ecclesiam Antichristus.
units.tr: Wondrous indeed is the judgment of Phocas, who decided (if we believe Gregory) that the name, wicked and blasphemous, does not belong to the Constantinopolitan, since it is proper to the Roman. Wondrous too is the mind of Boniface, who accepted it; and he did not wish the Constantinopolitan to be preferred to all or to preside over all; for this, he held, was owed to himself and the Roman Pontiffs, although whoever did this (by Gregory's testimony) would be an imitator of Lucifer in it, a forerunner of Antichrist. Gregory was a true prophet: where that word would finally lead. For he said to the Emperor about that title, that "whoever rejoices in it, through it sets himself above the Empire"; and has this not come to pass just so? He said to Anianus that "to consent to that wicked title is nothing other than to lose the faith"; and has the faith suffered no harm since Phocas consented to that title? Truly both of Gregory's prophecies are true: this word is destructive both to the Empire and to the Church; and his successor Boniface is, as to the Empire, Lucifer, and as to the Church, Antichrist.

units.la: Sed diserta verba sunt, Restat vt vos Episcopi non sitis: Solum conetur Episcopus appellari. Explicet ergo Gregorius ipse se. Sic autem ipse ad Iohannem, {c}Cupis Episcoporum nomen, tui comparatione calcare. Tui comparatione, dicit. Quæ dicit ergo, comparatè dicit, non absolutè. Sitis quidem Episcopi, sed illius comparatione ne sitis, & ille non absolutè solus, comparatione tamen vestri solus appellandus. Admisso enim Oecumenico, qui vnus imminet reliquis, reliquos sub se premat, excidere illos iure pristino Episcoporum, quo omnes eiusdem meriti, eiusdem erant & Sacerdotij; nec potentia Romæ sublimiorem Episcopum, nec paupertas Euganbij[?] inferiorem faciebat; {d}Priuari omnes honore hoc debito, si priuatum aliquod vni detur (vt ad Mauritium Gregorius) ac proinde eius quidem (quod ante fuerant) comparatione, ne Episcopos quidem dicendos esse: loquendi more vetusto, quo, vbi quis non sit qui fuerat, ne esse quidem dicitur: atque vt solus esse dicatur, qui aliquà in re singularis est. Qui enim Patres erant, fieri Filios, Patrum huius Generalis; qui Pastores erant, transire in Gregem illius, atque eius comparatione Gregem iam dicendos esse. Atque hanc vim habent verba Gregorij; huc spectant: Aliò non possunt, nisi contra historiarum fidem, quâ id constat, etsi per annos Viginti, titulum Oecumenici mordicus retinerent Iohannes primùm, & post eum Cyriacus: toto tamen tempore illo, haud unquam conatos Episcopatum vllî abrogare, aut, quasi soli Episcopi essent, se gerere, vel sibi solum [?] Episcopi nomen vsurpare. Nihil ergo erat quòd exhorresceret hoc vocabulum Oecumenici Gregorius, nihil cur non æquè libenter acciperet: æquè libenter (inquam) atque vix biennio post mortem eius, accepit id Bonifacium, quippe qui non minorem in eo vim sciret ad Hierarchiam constituendam, quàm in Capitis fidei vocabulo, imò maiorem; quid enim fides ad Hierarchiam? qui hoc (inquam) sciret, & id vnum in eo quæreret, vt quasi Caput, vnus omnibus præsideret. Quærat ab Authoribus suis {a} Paulo Diacono, & {b}Anastasio: dicent illi Constantinopolim primam esse voluisse, non solam; atque eum primatum Romæ post à Phocâ attributum. Quæret tu à {c}Platinâ, & {d}Sabellico: dicent tibi, Bonifacium tertium à Phocâ obtinuisse, vt Romana Ecclesia esset omnium aliarum Caput; atque ægrè, necfine multâ magnâque contentione Romano datum esse: Vocabula Oecumenici, & Capitis (quæ vos iam fere distinguitis) eandem apud illos rem (primatum vtraque) denotâsse: nec magis Capitis hoc, quàm illud Oecumenici, ne si oblatum quidem ei fuisset, Gregorium libenter vel accepturum, vel vsurum fuisse.
units.tr: But the words are explicit: "It remains that you should not be bishops; let the bishop alone try to be called bishop." Let Gregory himself explain himself. For he writes to John thus: "You desire to trample on the name of bishops in comparison with yourself. In comparison with yourself," he says. So what he says, he says comparatively, not absolutely. You may indeed be bishops, but in comparison with him you must not be; and he is to be called the only one, not absolutely the only bishop, but the only one in comparison with you. For once the Ecumenical, who looms over the rest and presses them down beneath him, is admitted, they lose their former right as bishops, by which all were of the same merit and the same priesthood; neither did the power of Rome make the higher bishop, nor the poverty of Euganbius make the lower. "All would be deprived of this due honour if some private person were given to one" (as Gregory writes to Maurice), "and accordingly, in comparison with him, they should not even be called bishops (what they had been before), by the old manner of speaking, by which, where someone is no longer what he was, he is not even said to be; and so that someone is said to be the only one who is singular in some respect." For those who were fathers would become sons of this General Father; those who were shepherds would pass into his flock, and in comparison with him they would already be called a flock. These are the force and meaning of Gregory's words; to this they look. They cannot be taken otherwise without going against the testimony of history, by which it is established that, although for twenty years John first, and after him Cyriacus, clung tenaciously to the title of Ecumenical, yet throughout that whole time they never attempted to abrogate the episcopate of anyone, or to conduct themselves as if they alone were bishops, or to usurp for themselves the name of bishop alone. There was therefore nothing for Gregory to shudder at in this word "Ecumenical," nothing why he should not accept it equally willingly: equally willingly, I say, as he who, scarcely two years after Gregory's death, accepted it, Boniface; who knew it had no less force for establishing the hierarchy than the word "head of the faith" had, indeed greater; for what has faith to do with hierarchy? He who knew this, I say, and sought in it this one thing, that as a kind of head he might preside alone over all. Let him ask his own authors, Paul the Deacon and Anastasius: they will tell him that Constantinople wished to be first, not only; and that this primacy was afterwards granted to Rome by Phocas. Let him ask you, Platina and Sabellicus: they will tell you that Boniface III obtained from Phocas that the Roman Church should be the head of all the others; and that it was given to the Roman with difficulty, and not without much and great contention. The words "Ecumenical" and "head" (which you now almost distinguish) denoted the same thing for them (both primacy): and this "head" was no more than that "Ecumenical"; nor, even if it had been offered to him, would Gregory have accepted it willingly or used it.

units.la: Atque vt semel dicam de voce Capitis. Gregorius illam non obscurè docet, perinde exhorruisse se, atque alteram Oecumenici. Lege quæ scribit ad {e}Eulogium. Fa, inquit, quam prætendebat humilitate, iactantiam sumpsit Iohannes, ita vt vniuersa sibi tentet ascribere, & omnia, quæ soli vni Capiti cohærent, videlicet Christo, per elationem pompatici Sermonis, eiusdem Christi sibi audet membra subiugare. En vt hoc reprehendit Gregorius in Iohanne, quòd sibi tanquam Capiti omnia conatus sit subiugare Christi membra, quæ soli vni Capiti cohærent Christo. Qui, si solus Caput est, Gregorius ne Capitis quidem nomen libenter acceptur erat, quo, ad Iohannis exemplum omnia sibi Christi membra subiugaret. Nec
units.tr: And, to say once for all about the word "head": Gregory teaches clearly enough that he shuddered at it just as much as at the other, "Ecumenical." Read what he writes to Eulogius. "John," he says, "under the pretext of humility, took up arrogance, so that he attempts to ascribe everything to himself, and dares, by the elation of a pompous speech, to subjugate to himself all the members of Christ himself, which cohere to the one Head alone, namely Christ." See how Gregory reprehends this in John: that he attempted to subjugate to himself, as if he were the head, all the members of Christ, which cohere to Christ alone as the one Head. If he is the only Head, Gregory would not have willingly accepted even the name of head, by which, on John's example, he would subjugate to himself all the members of Christ.

units.la: aliter {f}Iohannem ipsum alloquitur. Si Paulus Apostolus, membra Dominici corporis, certis extra Christum quasi Capitibus, & ipsis quidem Apostolis, subjici particulariter cuitabat: tu, quid Christo uniuersalis scilicet Ecclesia Capiti, in extremi iudicij es dicturus examine, qui cuncta eius membra tibimet conaris universalis appellatione supponere? Vides, nec Apostolis quidem ipsis concedere Gregorium, ut illis quasi Capitibus membra Christi subjiciantur vel particularia: tantùm abest, ut vel Iohannem, vel se, Caput fidei, id est, (te interprete) Caput fidelium, vel Ecclesiae universalis, vel haberi, vel appellari, æquo animo unquam pateretur. Rectè ergo Apologia, & ad rem. Noluit Hierarchiae Caput dici Gregorius, noluit ergo Fidei; plus enim multo Fides, quàm Hierarchia, plus multò illius, quàm huius Caput denominari.
units.tr: Nor does he address John himself otherwise. "If the Apostle Paul forbade the members of the Lord's body to be subjected in particular to certain heads outside Christ, and indeed to the Apostles themselves, what will you, who try to subject all his members to yourself under the name of universal, say to Christ, the universal Church's Head, in the examination of the last judgment?" You see that Gregory does not concede even to the Apostles themselves that the members of Christ should be subjected to them as heads, whether particularly or universally: so far is it from the case that he would ever willingly suffer himself, or John, to be held or called the head of faith, that is (by your interpretation) the head of the faithful, or of the universal Church. The Apology is therefore right and to the point. Gregory was unwilling to be called head of the hierarchy, therefore he was unwilling to be called head of the faith; for faith is far more than hierarchy, and it is far more the head of the one than of the other that is to be named.

units.la: Nec sensit Author argumentum suum debile: Tu potiùs videris non sentire, quando firmum sit argumentum, quando debile. Sic enim ille Non dixit hoc Gregorius: si dixit, minùs id caute dixit: id est, non dixit, quod si diceret, parum certè caute loqueretur. Parum enim caute sanè, (idque Cardinale téque ipso suffragante) si unus hoc affirmaret, tanquam proprij aliquid, cæteris repugnantibus. Cæteri enim certè repugnarent, ut Caput fidei præter Christum quis diceretur; nec cæteri solùm repugnarent illi, sed & ipse sibi, si, quod nulli Apostolo, sed soli uni Christo convenire dixisset, ut Caput esset, id sibi assumeret. Sibi autem ipsi repugnare, hominis est, ad se parum attenti, & de quo rectè dici potest, minùs caute locutus est. Quid ergo est, quod hîc causaris dictum esse in Apologiâ, dixisse interdum de Patribus Cardinalem, minùs eos caute locutos esse? Tute hoc agnoscis ipse. Nam si in eâdem omnes sententiâ non convenient aliquando, is qui aliquid proprij unus affirmat, cuique cæteri refragantur, non id satis caute affirmauit, vel consultò; ac per hoc inter eos censendus, qui minùs caute locuti sunt: fatetur autem (fatente te) Cardinalis illud interdum Patribus euenire; fatetur ergo Patres non semper caute loqui. Convenient, credo, inter nos facilè, Patres, cum in eâdem sententiâ non convenient, non omnes fatù[?], aliquos saltem minùs caute locutos; illos dico, quorum doctrina sequenda non est, quibus (tanquam minùs cautis) minùs credimus. Quare vel in eo loco inuenitur, secundùm vim quidem sententiæ, etsi non totidem verbis: minus caute locutus est. Adeone verò hoc tibi videtur indignum Cardinale, vt Patres dicat, minus interdum caute locutos esse? At non vbique tamen sic Patres habet, quasi loquantur semper ad libram. Dicit {a}per excessum interdum loqui; dicit, {b}minus proprie; dicit, {c}si sic accipiatur in ijs sententia, vt verba sonant, ferendam non videri. Atqui ita per excessum loqui: minus proprie: vt alius sit sensus, quàm verba sonant: caute loqui non est. Dicit, {d}benignâ expositione opus habere. Non haberent, si sermo illis minus cautus nunquam exciderat. Tum vbi {e}Ambrosium opponit Chrysostomo, alter eorum vix locutus est caute. Tum vbi ex {f}Augustino loca duo, duo ex {g}Hieronymo adducit, sibi inuicem contraria; vtroque certe loco, non satis: altero saltem, minus caute videntur locuti. Cùm {h}exi-stimauit à Cypriano verba quædam referri, vbi Cypriani verba nil tale sonant, parum in eo cautus Augustinus. Cùm {i}exceptionem dicit admittere testimonium eius, non satis cautum eius testimonium: si cautum enim, exceptione careret. Cùm {k}in errore fuisse videtur Hieronymus, atque idem eâdem de re, in errore non fuisse, vbi fuisse videtur in errore, videtur certè, non satis caute sententiam suam eloquutus. Denique qui Patres, qui {l}è Patribus præcipuos, in quibusdam non leuiter lapsos affirmat, plus dicit, quàm minus caute locutos. Plus enim est minus rectè sentire, quàm minus caute loqui; nec debet cui plus licet, minus non licere. Noli ergo phrasin illam ita refugere. Hæc enim qui dicat de Patribus, quæ dixisse illum constat, si religio haud vlla erit dicere, minus aliquando vel accuratè, vel caute, animi sui sensa eloquutos esse.
units.tr: Nor did the author perceive that his argument was weak. You rather seem not to perceive when an argument is firm and when it is weak. For he did not say that Gregory said this: if he said it, he said it less cautiously; that is, he did not say what, had he said it, he would certainly have spoken rather incautiously. For he would certainly have spoken incautiously if one man affirmed this as something of his own, with the others opposing it, and with the Cardinal and yourself supporting this. For the others would certainly oppose that anyone be called head of the faith except Christ; and not only would the others oppose him, but he himself would oppose himself, if he had said that what belongs to no Apostle, but to Christ alone, namely to be head, he assumed for himself. But to contradict oneself is the mark of a man who is not sufficiently attentive to himself, and of whom it can rightly be said that he spoke less cautiously. What, then, is the reason why you here accuse the Apology of saying that the Cardinal at times spoke of the Fathers as having spoken less cautiously? You yourself acknowledge this. For if on some occasions they do not all agree in the same opinion, the one who alone affirms something of his own, which the others oppose, has not affirmed it cautiously or deliberately enough; and by this he is to be counted among those who spoke less cautiously. But you confess (you being witness) that the Cardinal sometimes says this of the Fathers; you therefore confess that the Fathers do not always speak cautiously. We shall agree easily enough, I believe, that when the Fathers do not agree in the same opinion, not all of them are wrong, but at least some spoke less cautiously; those, I mean, whose teaching is not to be followed, and whom (as less cautious) we believe less. Therefore even in that passage the sense, though not in so many words, is found: "he spoke less cautiously." Does this seem to you so unworthy of a Cardinal, that he should say the Fathers at times spoke less cautiously? But the Fathers do not everywhere speak as if always weighing every word. They say that they speak "at times by excess"; they say "less properly"; they say "if taken in that sense, as the words sound, it does not seem to be tolerable." But to speak "by excess," "less properly," so that the meaning is other than the words sound, is not to speak cautiously. They say that they need "a kindly interpretation." They would not need it if their speech had never slipped "less cautiously." Then, where he sets Ambrose against Chrysostom, one of them "scarcely spoke cautiously." Then, where from Augustine he adduces two passages, and two from Jerome, mutually contrary to one another; in either passage certainly "not sufficiently"; in at least one of them, "they seem to have spoken less cautiously." When he thought that certain words were quoted from Cyprian, where Cyprian's words sound nothing of the kind, Augustine was rather incautious in this. When he says that his testimony admits an exception, his testimony is "not sufficiently cautious": for if it were cautious, it would be free of exception. When Jerome "seems to have been in error," and the same man, on the same matter, says he "was not in error," where he seems to have been in error, he certainly seems to have expressed his opinion "not sufficiently cautiously." Finally, whoever affirms that the Fathers, and among the Fathers the principal ones, "in some things slipped not lightly," says more than that they "spoke less cautiously." For to "think less rightly" is more than to "speak less cautiously"; and he to whom more is permitted ought not to be forbidden less. Do not, therefore, so shun that phrase. For if anyone says of the Fathers what it is certain he said, there will be no scruple in saying that they at times expressed the feelings of their mind "less accurately, or less cautiously."

units.la: Iam verò, vt nomen Capitis ad Regem reuocetur, vel à Gregorio, vel alio quoquam, arte mirabili opus non est. Præstituit nobis voce, Spiritus sanctus; Sic Regi suo Propheta Samuel. {m}Nonne cum parvulus esses in oculis tuis, Caput in tribus Israel factus es? Inter tribus verò Israel, tribus Leui: Caput ergo Rex, vel tribus Leviticæ; quâ in tribu tum, Pontifex Ahimelech sub Rege Capite suo. Mirabilis inertiæ, negare hoc, non artis, hoc probare. Tum Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Præsul (nec Gregorio minus vel sanctus vel doctus) Chrysostomus, eandem hanc vocem Capitis, reuocaut ad Theodosium, eumque [illegible, ~8 letters] dixit,non solùm Caput, sed quod in Capite ipso maximè sublime est, Capitis Verticem , idque omnium in terris hominum. Puto autem fuisse tum in terris hominem , qui Romanus Episcopus diceretur, ut possit expositio hæc in hominem cadere, qui sanae[?] mentis sit. Tu vide, satin' sanus sis, qui in Samuelem, & Chrysostomum quasi audaces & impudentes, ita debaccharis.
units.tr: Now, as for calling the king the "Head," there is no need for any wonderful skill, whether borrowed from Gregory or anyone else. The Holy Spirit has set the word before us: so the prophet Samuel to his king: "When you were little in your own eyes, were you not made head over the tribes of Israel?" Among the tribes of Israel, however, was the tribe of Levi; so the king is head, or of the Levitical tribe, in which tribe the priest Ahimelech served under his head, the king. It is a strange sort of idleness to deny this, not a skill to prove it. Then the bishop of the Catholic Church, Chrysostom (no less holy or learned than Gregory), calls back this same word "head" to Theodosius, and [illegible, ~8 letters] said that he was not only the head but the very summit of the head itself, and this of all men on earth. I suppose, however, that there was then a man on earth who was called the Roman bishop, so that this explanation could apply to a man of sound mind. See for yourself whether you are sane, who rave in this way against Samuel and Chrysostom as if they were bold and shameless.

units.la: Sed Gregorius tamen, ad nos reuocari non vult, nec Regem Caput agnoscere. Ille verò vult. Agnouit enim, atque in hac ipsa cum Iohanne de Primatu controuersia sua agnouit; petijtque Pontifex ipse (per Sabinianum Pontificem & ipsum, et proximum) ut piissimus[?] Dominus Mauritius ipsum illud negotium iudicare dignaretur. Credo, pro Capite agnouit, cuius iudicio, capitalem hanc de Capite litem volens vltrò submisit, ad cuius arbitrium Primatus, vel staret, vel caderet. Verùm Gregorius ibi de Sede Apostolicâ non turbandâ loquitur. Loquitur; sed, non eò referenda verba illa, quæ ponis de Capite fidei illæso; sed illa quæ supprimis, De Canonum authoritate intemeratâ conseruandâ, à quibus suus, quem habet, honor Sedi Romanæ. Nullû enim fidei Caput est, Apostolum ibi sedisse; Canones forte fauent. Ad integrum ergo membrorū statum vtrumque requirit, vt & Fidei ne fiat iniuria, & vt Canones ne temerentur. Vtcunque enim Caput Fidei non pulsetur, turbidum tamen fore statum membrorum, nisi & Canonibus sua constet authoritas, à quibus in ordine continentur. Nec Tortus negat. Epistolam enim dicit esse de vsu Pallij; & est certè integra. Quid verò fidei cum Pallio? Ecquid, fidei caput vllum pulsabitur iniurià, siue Panormitanus Episcopus incedat Palliatus, siue Pallio careat? In Canonem forte aliquem peccetur venialiter, si Iohannes Pallio vtatur parum concinnè; si loci minùs opportunis, si Festis non duplicibus: Fidei quidem nihil interest. Quare ad hoc propositum verba illa non ponit de fidei capite; quæ si poneret, extra propositum essent, cûm vsus Pallij, Fidei nullus sit, quæ tantò melior, quanto minùs palliata.
units.tr: But Gregory, nevertheless, does not want the title recalled to us, nor the king acknowledged as head. He, however, does want it. For he acknowledged it, and acknowledged it in this very controversy with John over the primacy; and the pontiff himself asked (through Sabinianus, a pontiff also and his successor) that the most pious [?] lord Maurice would deign to judge that very matter. I believe he acknowledged him as head, since he willingly submitted to his judgment this capital dispute about the head, by whose decision the primacy would either stand or fall. Yet Gregory there speaks of not disturbing the Apostolic See. He speaks; but those words you set down about the head of the faith left unharmed are not to be referred there; rather, those you suppress are: about preserving the authority of the canons inviolate, from which the honour he holds for the Roman See comes. For it is no head of the faith that the Apostle sat there; the canons perhaps favour it. He therefore requires both for the whole state of the members: that no injury be done to the faith, and that the canons not be violated. For however the head of the faith is not struck, the state of the members would nonetheless be troubled unless the authority of the canons, by which they are held in order, also stood firm. Nor does Torto deny it. For he says the letter concerns the use of the pallium; and it is certainly genuine. But what has the faith to do with the pallium? Will any head of the faith be injured by this, whether the bishop of Palermo walks about palliated or lacks the pallium? Perhaps some canon is violated venially, if John uses the pallium rather untidily; if at less suitable places; if on feasts that are not double: the faith certainly has no stake in it. Therefore, for this purpose, he does not set down those words about the head of the faith; and if he did, they would be beside the point, since the use of the pallium has nothing to do with the faith, which is all the better the less it is palliated.

units.la: Quærit autem hic, subiratus: Quid in hoc negotio habent Reges? Habent verò in negotio fidei: sed in fidei negotio, Pallio nihil negotij est. Sed & nonnihil habuerunt negotij Imperatores circa inuestituram Pontificum: nec Panormitani modò, sed Romani etiam ipsius. Nam si nihil, quî factum, vt tam multum Illis negotij Pontifices olim circa id facesserent? Quid Regibus cum Pallio, quod est infigne Archiepiscoporum? Certè cum Baculo & Annulo aliquid, absque quibus frigeret Pallium, & Gerenti, & verò etiam Mittenti; nec tam modica lana tam immodico precio venderetur. Etiam Tortus, cui tam sæpe in ore impudentiæ, nisi ei & in fronte foret, non tam hæc superbè interrogaret: qui vel imperitiâ summâ est, si nesciat, vel non summâ verecundiâ, si neget, etiam in Gregorio ipso Pontifice faciendo, Imperatorem negotium habuisse, nec sine eo Pallium vel ipsum gerere, vel alijs mittere potuisse. Quare si est aliquis Pallio cum Fide, etiam in illâ Fidei procuratione Caput, Impetratorem fuisse.
units.tr: But he asks here, in anger: "What have kings to do with this matter?" They do have something to do with it, in matters of faith: but in the matter of faith there is nothing to do with the pallium. Yet the emperors did have some business concerning the investiture of pontiffs, and not only those of Palermo but of Rome itself. For if they had nothing to do with it, how did it come about that pontiffs once took such great trouble over it? "What have kings to do with the pallium, which is the badge of archbishops?" Certainly with the staff and the ring something, without which the pallium would be cold, both for the wearer and, indeed, for the sender; nor would such a small piece of wool be sold at so excessive a price. Even Torto, who so often has "impudence" on his lips, if he did not have it on his forehead too, would not ask so arrogantly: he shows either the greatest ignorance, if he does not know, or no small lack of shame, if he denies that even in the making of Gregory himself, the pontiff, the emperor had business, and that without him the pallium could not be worn by the pontiff himself or sent to others. Therefore, if there is anyone "with the faith" in the pallium, the head was also the one who obtained it, even in that very handling of the faith.

units.la: Quàm verò impotenter fert, subnexam ibi in Apologiâ Gregorij suggestionem Putes, Gregorium iam fidei suæ Caput non credere. Nam si crederet, paulò magis patienter monentem sustineret, ut Caput fidei Pontifex Deum timeret, nec in mortem cuiuslibet (nedum Principum) se misceret. Non fuit Sabinianus Præfectus: certè, nec Cardinalis: successit in Pontificatu Gregorio; sed inter duo hæc fidei Capita vix bene conveniebat. uterq; tamen fuit Pontifex. Tanto æquius Pontificem audire, quod & à Pontifice uno suggeritur, & per Pontificem alterum. Sed nihil ad rem suggestio hæc. Nihilne ad rem, Ne in mortem se misceat? Pôst salutem animæ, quid magis ad rem quàm vita corporis? At Pontifex non occultè per Sicarios, sed publicè per Censuras agit cum Principibus, si inobedientes sint. Agit. Quid hoc verò ad rem? Id dicere debebas, non occultè per Sicarios, sed publicè per Censuras, miscet se in morte Regum: Deo enim suggestio erat. Quodsi agendi verbum, tam illi placuit, etiam cum quibusdam, ita per Censuras egit, ut animas egerint. Etsi enim Censuræ eius, aciem nullam habeant, agunt tamen, & quasi Tubæ sunt & Classica, quasi Prætextus & Latebræ seditionum: ut postquam emissa semel sunt, cum Principe non secus agere liceat, quàm cum hoste, & sine scrupulo, cuique se in illius morte miscere. Ubi, male à te oppositæ Censuræ Sicarijs. Sicarij mortem inferunt vel Regibus. At Rex jam uspiam est, qui post nescio quot Pontificum, nescio quoties iteratas Censuras, superstes tamen est. Illud dictum oportuit: non occultè per Sicarios, sed publicè per armatas cohortes, miscere se in morte cuiuslibet hominis. Ita enim praeter illa, quae Patres narrauerunt nobis, vidimus ipsi, miscentem se Pontificem in morte multorum millium, fame, peste, gladio, quotidie pereuntium, potius quam Regi suo legitimo, urbis portas aperirent. Per Sicarios tamen, non facit. Quasi referat Sicarij manu quis cadat, an militis; cadat modo. Quasi valde interfit, submittatne Sicarium, an Cardinalem qui authoritate, Iesuitam qui disputando, Concionatorem, qui declamando animos addant subditis, ad Regem quoque modo trucidandum: Dolus an virtus quis in hoste requirat? Forte autem Sicarius ad manum non est, qui operam deferat. Nam si sit Parreius[?], non deerit Cemensis[?], qui operam illam, pergratam Pontifici spondeat, & (si effectam dederit) amplâ mercede transfigat.
units.tr: How impotently, however, he bears the insinuation placed there in Gregory's Apology, you would think, that Gregory did not believe that the head of his faith was already... For if he believed it, he would bear more patiently one who warns him a little more mildly, so that the pontiff, as the head of the faith, would fear God, and would not mix himself into the death of anyone whatever (let alone princes). Sabinianus was not a prefect: certainly not a cardinal either: he succeeded Gregory in the pontificate; but between these two heads of the faith hardly any agreement was possible. Yet both were pontiffs. All the more fair to hear a pontiff, since it is suggested both by one pontiff and through another pontiff. But this suggestion is nothing to the point. Is it nothing to the point, "that he should not mix himself in death"? After the salvation of the soul, what is more to the point than the life of the body? But the pontiff does not act secretly through assassins, but openly through censures, against princes if they are disobedient. He acts. But what is this to the point? You ought to have said this: "not secretly through assassins, but openly through censures," he mixes himself in the death of kings: for it was a suggestion to God. But if the word "act" so pleased him, even with some, "he acted through censures so that they acted upon souls." For although his censures have no edge, they nonetheless act, and are like trumpets and bugles, like a pretext and hiding place for sedition: so that once they have been sent forth, one may deal with a prince no differently than with an enemy, and without scruple, anyone may mix himself into his death. Here, the censures you set against assassins are badly opposed. Assassins bring death even to kings. But is there any king anywhere who, after I know not how many pontiffs and I know not how often repeated censures, is nonetheless still alive? That statement should have been made: "not secretly through assassins, but openly through armed cohorts," to mix oneself in the death of any man whatever. For so, besides those things the Fathers have told us, we ourselves have seen the pontiff mixing himself in the death of many thousands, perishing daily by famine, plague and sword, rather than opening the gates of the city to his lawful king. Yet he does not do so "through assassins." As if it mattered whether someone falls by the hand of an assassin or of a soldier; so long as he falls. As if it mattered greatly whether he sends an assassin, or a cardinal who by his authority, a Jesuit who by disputation, a preacher who by declamation, add spirit to the subjects, to slaughter the king also in whatever way: "Does one look for trickery or valour in an enemy?" Perhaps, however, no assassin is at hand to lend his service. For if there is a Parreius [?], there will be no lack of a Cemensis [?], who will promise that service, most pleasing to the pontiff, and (if he has carried it out) will run the king through for a generous reward.

units.la: Sed quorsum nobis, aut unde mentio de Sicarijs? Quis Sicarios hic nobis submisit? Tortus. Nam de Sicarijs apud Cardinalem, ne syllaba. Sicille: Pontifex nunquam Principem vllum caedi mandauit. Vi, an fraude; Marte, an arte mandârit, si mandârit, Cardinalis non verax. Occultene se in morte misceat an aperte, clam, an palam miscebat se in morte, Tortus mendax est. Palam id & publicè factum à Pontifice non ibit inficias: Gregorius id non faceret, ne sic quidem in morte se miscereret[?]. Satis id instituto nostro. Novae Fidei iam Caput Pontifex, per quam plus ei licet, quam licuit Gregorio. Remittimus ergo Torto Sicarios suos, ac quamuis ei doleat, iterum Pontifici breviter suggestionem illam Gregorij, ne se in morte cuiuslibet hominis miscet, si vult Gregorij Praedecessoris sui vestigijs diligenter insistere.
units.tr: But why do we have mention of assassins, or whence does it come? Who has put assassins before us here? Torto. For about assassins, not a syllable in the cardinal's words. Thus: "The pontiff has never ordered any prince to be killed. Whether he ordered it by force or by fraud, by war or by art, if he ordered it, the cardinal is not truthful. Whether he mixes himself in death secretly or openly, privately or publicly, Torto is a liar. The pontiff will not deny that he did this openly and publicly: Gregory would not have done this, not even in this way would he have mixed himself in death [?]." That is enough for our purpose. The pontiff is now the head of the new faith, through which he is permitted more than Gregory was permitted. We therefore return to Torto his assassins, and although it grieves him, we again briefly set before the pontiff that suggestion of Gregory's, that he should not mix himself into the death of any man whatever, if he wishes to follow diligently in the footsteps of Gregory, his predecessor.

units.la: Etsi autem iniquum est, ut in causa sua quis testimonium dicat (vel si ipse Papa sit) tamen cum Cardinali vix alij ad manum essent, quos proferret, post Gregorium iam, Leonem audire cogimur. Maximos viros (ut erant maximè) sed tamen in hac Sedis suae causa, parcius adhibendos. Vix enim erat, ut Spartam suam ornare nollent, quâ & ipsi vicissim ornarentur. Verum alij non suppetunt, nisi qui tepidè hanc causam agunt. Nec enim facile reperias qui tam velint zelatores esse Sedis aliena quam sua. Leonis verò verba perverti nihil opus; concedi vobis possunt. Prima quidem spectare, ad Petri persona ipsam, Papam nihil attinere: Etiam nec Vltima, [Cui quisquis] ibi dicitur, non, [Quisquis] habet Sedi:] Huic Sedi, Cardinalis addidit de suo. Cui autem, de Petro dicitur, non de Sede. Media verò, quis non concedat? Abiit ut quisquam recedat à soliditate Petri; sed soliditas eius, non in Sede eius, putri ligno, sed in Fide, quouis saxo solidiore, in quo & ipsam, Leo ipse constituit.
units.tr: Although it is unjust for anyone to give testimony in his own cause (even if he is the Pope himself), yet, since there were scarcely any others at hand whom he could produce besides the Cardinal, we are now forced to hear Leo after Gregory. "Men most great (as they were most great)," but nevertheless in this cause of his See they are to be called in more sparingly. For it would hardly be that they would not wish to adorn their Sparta, by which they in turn would be adorned. But others are not available, except those who handle this cause half-heartedly. For you will not easily find men who are as eager to be zealots for another's See as for their own. The words of Leo need not be perverted; they can be granted to you. The first clauses indeed concern the person of Peter himself, and have nothing to do with the Pope: nor does the last, "to whom whoever," which is said there, [say] "whoever has to the See," but the Cardinal added "to this See" of his own accord. "To whom," however, is said of Peter, not of the See. And the middle clauses, who would not grant them? It is impossible that anyone should "depart from the firmness of Peter"; but his firmness is not in his See, a rotten timber, but in the Faith, a rock more solid than any, on which Leo himself also established the See.

units.la: Sed neque nos Sedi dignitatem ullam invidemus: quam ab ultimâ usque antiquitate habuit eam retineat, dum à soliditate tamen Petri non recedat. Quorsum autem ad hæc verba, Tortum quis agat?
units.tr: But neither do we grudge the See any dignity whatever: let it keep whatever honour it has had "from the most ancient antiquity," provided that it does not "depart from the firmness" of Peter. But why does anyone drag Tortus into these words?

units.la: Quàm verò in eo importunus, quòd traducit Authorem Apologiæ, quasi Leoni ibi conuitium dixerit. Quàm tu à modestiâ omni, tam ille abest à conuitio; nec qui vir fuerit Leo, quàm gloriæ appetens, quàm dominandi cupidus, attingit ibi vel verbo. Alius fecit: si ratione facti reddidit, quid culpas? Si non reddidit, quis laudat? Male quod fecit, sibi fecit. Quid hæc ad Nostrum? Vbi candor? Sed à re quis candorem requirat, qui, eo quòd Leonem ambitiosum ad laudes Petri dixerit (quod & potest & solet dici in bonam partem) notâsse dicis ambitionis bonum Patrem. Vbi vix dicat lector quid magis miretur, insciitiam [?], an nequitiam, an vtramq., an vtraque deteriorem malitiam. Quis enim nisi iniquæ mentis, ambitionem dicat, si quis in laudes non suas, verùm alienas (Sancti scilicet alicuius) non studiosus modò, sed etiam ambitiosus existat? Ambitionem, de alieno honore quis audiuit vnquam? Quid quod neque Leonem distinguit ab Hortensio; immodicè laudasse Hortensium ibi dicitur, Leo non dicitur. Excellat verò Leo Sanctitatis gloriâ; excelluit & Petrus; alicubi tamen, non recto pede ambulauit. Nec piaculum sit, si quis idem Leoni accidisse dicat, quod Petro Domino suo: dum tamen verbo non violet, dum (quod facit Apologia) arbitrium ponat in aduersarij sui Cardinalis ipsius consciëntiâ. Quî si id expromat nobis ingenuè, quod dictat ei consciëntia, fateatur scio, in illis {a}de assumpto Petro in consortium Individuæ Trinitatis: de non solum Deo, sed Petro etiam inspirante: Et illis, {b}nihil à bonorum fonte Deo, in quenquam sine Petri participatione transfire: à medio discessum esse, eaq; condonari potiùs iam posse eloquentiæ, quàm sanctè ab eo tum affirmari potuisse.
units.tr: How importunate he is in this, in that he accuses the author of the Apology as though he had spoken there an "insult" to Leo! As far as you are free of all modesty, so far is he from "insult"; nor does he touch on, even by a word, what sort of man Leo was, how eager for glory, how desirous of domination. Another has done so: if he has given an account of the deed, why do you blame him? If he has not given one, who praises it? What he did badly, he did to himself. What has this to do with our man? Where is his candour? But who would ask candour of the matter, when he, because he called Leo ambitious for the praises of Peter (which can be and commonly is said in a good sense), says that the good Father "noted" an "ambition"? Here a reader can hardly say what he marvels at more: ignorance, or wickedness, or both, or whether both are a worse malice. For who, unless of an unfair mind, would call it "ambition" if someone should not only be eager but even ambitious for praises not his own, but another's (that is, of some saint)? Has anyone ever heard of "ambition" for another's honour? Moreover, he does not distinguish Leo from Hortensius; there it is said that he "praised Hortensius immoderately," Leo is not mentioned. But indeed Leo excels in the glory of holiness; Peter too excelled; yet somewhere "he did not walk with a straight foot." Nor would it be a sin if someone should say the same happened to Leo as to Peter his Lord, provided he does not offend in his words, provided he (as the Apology does) puts the judgment in the conscience of his opponent, the Cardinal himself. But if he should frankly disclose to us what his conscience dictates, let him confess, I know, those things about Peter being taken into fellowship of the undivided Trinity, and that God inspires not only God but Peter as well; and those things, that nothing passes from God, the fountain of goods, to anyone without the participation of Peter; that there has been a departure from the middle, and that these things can now be pardoned rather to eloquence than to what was then asserted by him as sound.

units.la: Falsa ergo quæ de ambitione. Æquè falsa quæ de Historiâ non verè relatâ. Vbi, non negat paria ibi Priuilegia vtrique tributa. Negat Contentionem, sed quâ fronte? Annon à Leonis Legatus ibi contentio est manifestè mota?
