Pridiè enim cùm de aequalitate istâ Priuilegiorum utriusque Romæ referretur ad Concilium: vltrò statim discesserunt, Leonis tum Legati; {a}Rogati vt subsisterent, & de istis communicarent, penitus recusárunt; causam etiam addiderunt: aliter se habere in mandatis. Post discessum eorum, relatum ad Iudices, qui iusserunt, vt Patres negotium hoc Priuilegiorum inspicerent. Postridiè verò Legati rursus interceßerunt; {b}circumuentos se dixerunt; Patres ei Canoni subscribere coactos. Reclamárunt ibi omnes; Neminem coactum. Tum Legati negare Canones Constantinopolitani primi in Synodicis Canonibus haberi. Pòst, iusíque mandatum suum proferre, protulerunt; quo (ne quis putet Leonem contentionis huius immunem) mandauit{c}: Leo, vt seruarent omnimodo Personæ suæ dignitatem, & si qui forte Ciuitatum suarum splendore confisi, aliquid sibi tentarent vsurpare, hoc (quâ dignum erat Constantiâ) retunderent. Praeuidit ergo Contentionem ibi tum glisceré, & Constantinopolitanum Ciuitatis suæ splendore confisum, aliquid moliri, quo par fieret Romano: Non obstante tamen hoc Leonis mandato, de integro relatum ad Patres; singuli ibi, praesentibus Legatis suffragati sunt. Iudices sententiam tulerunt, {d}oportere Episcopum vrbis Regiæ, nouæ Romæ, ijsdem primatibus Honoris, & Ipsum dignum esse. Patres omnes acclamárunt, Sententiam iustam; Omnes se eadem sentire, Omnes in sententia permanere, Hoc omnibus placere, Omnia ordinatè decreta esse: Quid tum Lucentius vicarius Leonis? {e}Sedes Apostolica praesentibus humiliari non debet; (humiliata ergo tum Romana Sedes, vel Legato Romano iudice) petit circumduci Canonem; queritur de iniuriâ Sedis Romanæ; repulsam tulit à Iudicibus, à Synodo tota. Paucis rem totam retuli, cuiuis vt perspicuum fiat quàm bonus vir Tortus, quàm veridicus, qui Contentionem inter eos vllam negat tum extitisse.
units.tr: False, therefore, is what is said about ambition. Equally false is what is said about a history not truly related. Here he does not deny that equal privileges were granted to both there. He denies the "contention," but with what face? Is not a contention plainly stirred up there by Leo's legate? For the day before, when this "equality" of the privileges of both Romes was referred to the Council, the legates of Leo at that time immediately withdrew of their own accord; asked to stay and take part in these matters, they utterly refused, and they even added a reason: "they had other instructions." After their departure, the matter was reported to the judges, who ordered that the Fathers should examine this business of privileges. But on the following day the legates again interposed; they said they had been "circumvented"; that the Fathers had been "forced" to subscribe to that canon. All there cried out: "No one has been forced." Then the legates denied that the canons of the First Council of Constantinople were held among the Synodical Canons. Afterwards, when they were asked, they brought forward their mandate; in it (lest anyone think Leo free from this contention) he had commanded: "that they should by all means preserve the dignity of his person, and if any, trusting in the splendour of their cities, should attempt to usurp anything for themselves, they should repel this in a manner worthy of Constantinople." He therefore foresaw that the contention was then kindling there, and that the Constantinopolitan, trusting in the splendour of his city, was contriving something by which he might become equal to the Roman. Nevertheless, notwithstanding this mandate of Leo, the matter was referred afresh to the Fathers; individually, in the presence of the legates, they gave their votes. The judges pronounced sentence: "that the bishop of the royal city, New Rome, ought to have the same primacies of honour, and himself be worthy of them." All the Fathers acclaimed: "A just sentence"; "All think the same, all remain in the sentence, this pleases all, all things have been decreed in order." What then did Lucentius, Leo's vicar, say? "The Apostolic See ought not to be humbled in the presence of [others]" (so the Roman See was then humbled, the Roman legate being judge); he asks that the canon be set aside; he complains of the injury done to the Roman See; he was rebuffed by the judges, by the whole Synod. I have related the whole matter briefly, so that it may be made clear to anyone how good a man Tortus is, how truthful, who denies that any contention arose between them at that time.

units.la: De paribus verò vtrique concessis Priuilegijs, quomodo se expediet Tortus? Paria (inquit) Priuilegia intelligebant, respectu inferiorum. Sed quis Tortum hic Concilij interpretem constituit? aut vnde hunc habuit intellectum suum? Lucentius, credo, rem melius intellexit Torto. Is de iniuriâ Sedis Romanæ, &c
units.tr: But as to the "equal" privileges granted to both, how will Tortus extricate himself? "They understood equal privileges," he says, "with respect to inferiors." But who has appointed Tortus here as interpreter of the Council? Or whence has he got his understanding? Lucentius, I believe, understood the matter better than Tortus. He, about the "injury of the Roman See," etc.

units.la: {a} Concil.Edit. Venet.Tom.2. pag.334.
units.tr: {a} Council, Venice edition, vol. 2, p. 334.

units.la: {c} Ibidem.
units.tr: {c} Ibid.

units.la: {d} Ibidem 339.

{e} Ibidem. &c Leonis, ibi queritur; non de 'Antiochena, aut Alexandrina; & Sedem ibi Apostolicam humilitatem dicit. Tum ratio quam ibi reddunt Patres Decreti sui, non inferiorum modò respectu redditur, sed ad pares quoque se porrigit. Quæ enim habuerat tum Sedes Senioris Romæ honoris Priuilegia,{a} à Patribus habuisse, quòd penes eam tum Imperium fuisset: cùm Imperium iam, & Senatus, sint penes Constantinopolim, eadem quæ Romæ olim tributa sunt, ratione eadem Constantinopoli iam esse tribuenda. Ratio hæc omnes respicit; non inferiores solùm. Omnium ergo respectu intelligendus Canon. Satis hæc clara per se: & Torto negotium exhibebant. Sudat ergo hic & in omnem partem se torquet. Arx enim ista causæ; quare, ruenti quatuor rationum fulcimenta subijcit, sed caduca. Primò, Renouari tantùm à Chalcedonensi Canonem Constantinopolitanum, quo honor habetur Constantinopolitano, sed post Romanum. Falsum hoc primò. Agnoscere se quidem dicunt Canonem illum Patres Chalcedonenses; quæ verò ipsi ibi statuunt,{b} [illegible, ~14 letters] definire se dicunt & decernere; renouare non dicunt: agnoscere autem aliis terminis, quàm qui ponuntur à te; æqualia nempe ibi utrisque (etiam in Constantinopolitano) Priuilegia esse decreta.
units.tr: {e} Ibid., etc. Leo there complains; not about Antioch or Alexandria; and he calls the Apostolic See humble there. Then the reason which the Fathers give there for their decree is rendered not only with respect to inferiors, but extends also to equals. For the privileges of the honour of Senior Rome which the See then had, it had from the Fathers because the empire was then seated there; since the empire and the Senate are now seated at Constantinople, the same privileges which were once granted to Rome must now be granted to Constantinople by the same reasoning. This reason regards all; not inferiors only. The canon is therefore to be understood with respect to all. These things are clear enough in themselves, and presented the matter to Tortus. He therefore sweats here and twists himself in every direction. For this is the citadel of his cause; wherefore, to prop up the collapsing [cause], he brings four supports of argument, but they are feeble. First, that the Constantinopolitan canon, by which honour is given to the Constantinopolitan but after the Roman, was only renewed by the Council of Chalcedon. This is false, first of all. The Chalcedonian Fathers indeed acknowledge that canon; but what they themselves establish there, [illegible], they say they define and decree; they do not say they renew: and to acknowledge it on other terms than those which are laid down by you; namely, that equal privileges were decreed there for both (even in the Constantinopolitan canon).

units.la: Idem quoque haberi dicit in Epistolâ Concilij ad Leonem; salsò & id etiā. Ac primò quidem ludit voce Cōfirmationis. Non enim aliter, quàm suffragio suo confirmari à Leone petit Decreta sua Synodus, nec Leo ipse aliter respondet, quàm ea se toto corde complexum esse. Martiani Sacrā (quod suprà docui) Synodus confirmata est, Leonis suffragio approbata. Sed in eâ epistolâ (ait Tortus) nullam mentionem faciunt parium Priuilegiorum. Nam quid opus hoc vt facerent, cùm Canones ipsos integros, ad Leonem tum transmitterent; Dicunt autem ibi, se renouâsse Canonem secundæ Synodi. Ne id quidem; confirmâsse se dicunt, renouâsse non dicunt. Sed & præterea{c} opportunum credidisse se, propter Imperatores ipsos, qui super eo delectabantur, propter Senatum, propter Vrbem ipsam, honoris eius confirmationem ab Vniuersali Concilio celebrari. Quæ verba quid sibi velint, exinde scias, quod scribant ibi Patres, Leonis locum tenentes in Concilio vehementer illis resistere tentâsse. Non autem sine dubio resisterent, si confirmatus ibi modò fuisset canon Synodi secundæ; secunda; qui ipse prius à Damaso fuerat approbatus. Tum, neque Leo ipse tot postea Epistolis suis apud Imperatorem, Imperatricem, Anatolium, alios nescio quot, tam in Canonem illum acriter inuecheretur, si nihil ibi aliud actum, quam prius in Concilio Generali, cui & praedecessor suus assensum praebuisset. Non cohaerens hūc[?] Torti, Illa verba Leonem pupugerunt, {c}[illegible, ~3 words] Constantinopolitanum, [illegible, ~4 words] quae verba reperias in hoc; in Concilio secundo Generali nusquam reperias. Nec ex eo quicquam efficitur, quòd in Epistolis suis Leo non meminit parium Priuilegiorum. Sed de Alexandrino atque Antiocheno meminit modò, qui paulò depresi erant, antepositò illis tum Constantinopolitano. Quis enim non videt liberiorem multò Leonem esse potuisse, addo & acriorem, si illorum; (id est) si alienam causam ageret, non suam? Sibi factam iniuriam, negligeret, alijs acerbè persequeretur? Sed humiliatam eo Canone Sedem Romanam: iniuriam Leoni factam, credimus Leonis Legatis in Synodo clamantibus; Torto frustra reclamante, si ad rauim usque clamet.
units.tr: He says the same is held in the Council's letter to Leo; this too is falsely said. And first he plays on the word "confirmation." For the Synod asks Leo to confirm its decrees in no other way than by his suffrage, nor does Leo himself respond in any other way than by embracing them with his whole heart. The Sacred [council] of Marcian (as I showed above) was confirmed, approved by the suffrage of Leo. But in that letter (says Tortus) they make no mention of equal privileges. For why would they need to do this, since they were then sending the canons themselves, entire, to Leo? They say there, however, that they have renewed the canon of the second Synod. Not even that; they say they confirmed it, they do not say they renewed it. But moreover they believed it fitting, on account of the emperors themselves, who took delight in it, on account of the Senate, on account of the City itself, that the confirmation of its honour be celebrated by the Universal Council. What these words mean you may know from this, that the Fathers write that Leo's legates in the Council tried to resist them vehemently. They would not doubtless have resisted if only the canon of the second Synod, the second, had been confirmed there; which itself had earlier been approved by Damasus. Then, neither would Leo himself, in so many subsequent letters of his to the Emperor, the Empress, Anatolius, and I know not how many others, have inveighed so bitterly against that canon, if nothing else had been done there than had been done earlier in the General Council, to which his predecessor too had given assent. Tortus's [argument] does not cohere: those words stung Leo, [illegible] Constantinopolitan, [illegible], which words you may find in this; in the second General Council you will nowhere find them. Nor does anything follow from this, because "in his letters Leo makes no mention of equal privileges." But he mentions only the Alexandrian and the Antiochene, who were somewhat lower, placing the Constantinopolitan before them. For who does not see that Leo could have been much freer, I add also more vehement, if he were pleading their cause, not his own? That he would neglect the injury done to himself, and pursue with bitterness that done to others? But that the Roman See was humbled by that canon: that the injury was done to Leo, we believe the legates of Leo shouting in the Synod, though Tortus protests in vain, even if he shouts himself hoarse.

units.la: De Gregorij autem Epistolâ illâ ad Eusebium viderit Tortus, atque amplius etiam deliberet censeo. Dominus enim pijssimus Imperator, siue is Mauritius fuit, nunquam Gregorio professus est Constantinopolitanum subijci, nec Constantinopolitano titulum Oecumenici negauit: siue Phocas; nec is, nisi post mortem Gregorij demum, hoc agnouit. Viderit etiam, quis ille fuerit Gregorij Frater, Eusebius Episcopus ciuitatis Constantinopolitanae, cùm certum sit, nullum Constantinopoli Eusebium, vel ætate Gregorij, vel centum, siue ante siue post eum annis Episcopum fuisse. Viderit annon Epistola illa meritò in dubium vocari debeat, tanquà adulterina. Viderit annon plures apud Gregorium ciusdem furfuris (non enim farinae,) si sit otium excutere. Sed annon mira Torti arrogantia, qui putet persuadere se posse cuiquam, etiam conetur probare, è Leone, è Gregorio (quae bis ibi in Canone Chalcedonensi leguntur) aequalia seu paria. Priuilegia non significare?; Videmus, nec semel; Paria ibi Priuilegia. Ille ibi non videre nos probat, quae videmus; quòd Leonis Epistolae parium Priuilegiorum mentionem non faciunt. Quae verò est, si hæc non est impudentia? Verè ergo scriptum in Apologia, Concilij Chalcedonensis Patres aequales Authoritatem Constantinopolitano Patriarchæ ascripsisse, nec vllo modo passos esse Romanæ sedis super illam Priuilegium, non [vnum] illud à Torto est; sed non authoritatis [?]. Nam de primâ sede non contendimus. Verè & illud, contendisse cum Romano Constantinopolitanum de Primatu, non quòd prior illo esse voluerit, vt Iohannes pòst: sed quòd aequalis illi, quod tum Anatolius satagebat.
units.tr: As for that letter of Gregory to Eusebius, let Tortus see to it, and I advise him to think it over further. For the most pious Emperor, whether it was Maurice, never professed to Gregory that Constantinople should be made subject to him, nor did he deny the title of Ecumenical to the Constantinopolitan; or if it was Phocas, he acknowledged this only after Gregory's death. Let Tortus also see who that brother of Gregory, Eusebius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, was, since it is certain that no Eusebius was bishop of Constantinople either in Gregory's time, or a hundred years before or after him. Let him see whether that letter ought not rightly to be called into doubt as spurious. Let him see whether, if he has the leisure to sift them, there are not many more of the same chaff (not wheat) in Gregory. But is it not a remarkable arrogance in Tortus, who thinks he can persuade anyone, that he even tries to prove from Leo and from Gregory (which are read there in the Chalcedonian canon) "equal" or "like" privileges? Do the words "privileges" not signify? We see, and more than once: "like privileges" are there. He proves that he does not see what we see, because Leo's letters do not mention the privilege of equal rights. But what is this, if it is not impudence? So it was rightly written in the Apology that the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon ascribed equal authority to the Constantinopolitan patriarch, and in no way allowed the privilege of the Roman see over it; that "not one" is Tortus's; but not of authority [?]. For we do not contend about the first see. It is also true that the Constantinopolitan contended with the Roman about primacy, not because he wished to be prior to him, as John later did, but because he wished to be equal to him, which Anatolius at that time was striving for.

units.la: Etsi autem (dicit ibi Apologia,) tantum Petro detulit (tantum, non nimis multa, vt Tortus, qui in his nimis multus est) tamen nihil Caesari ademit, sed & honoris vocabula, & Authoritatis Priuilegia ei cunctis attribuit, potestatemque eius agnouit Concilia conuocandi, arbitratu suo. Hic Tortus ad tria illa priora mutos [?] vel quae negare non posset, vellicat potestatem conuocandi Concilia. Relabimur ergo quo prius, ad vim atque iura Concilia indicendi. Torti ea culpa est; qui experiri iterum vult in hac causa, quotiescunque tamen fecerit, inauspicato id facturus. Nec enim vt quam laborat magis Causa Pontificia, quàm hac vnâ in re; nec vllius Pontificis, magis quàm Leonis; cuius tot extant Epistolæ, non mandantes Concilium fieri; non, sed demisse petentes, nec tamen impetrantes; non impetrantes vel de loco vel de tempore, & tamen obtemperantes: vt penè referre pigeat. Quid autem hîc iam refert? Negari non posse, quin in Conciliis Generalibus indicendis aliqua esset Imperatoris Authoritas. Supra, interdum congregata dixit ab Imperatore: at nos ibi semper, nec nisi ab Illo. Hîc iam aliqua (inquit) fuit Authoritas Imperatoris: nos verò non aliqua, sed summa, & sola, quoadusque quidem res Imperij inclinatæ non sunt.
units.tr: Yet although (the Apology says there) "it gave so much to Peter" ("so much," not "too much," as Tortus, who is too much in these matters), "it nonetheless took nothing from Caesar, but also attributed to him all the titles of honour and the privileges of authority, and acknowledged his power of convoking councils at his own discretion." Here Tortus, against those first three points, which he could not deny, carps at the power of convoking councils. We slip back therefore to where we were before, to the force and rights of calling a council. That is Tortus's fault, who wants to try again in this matter; yet however often he does so, he will do it without good omens. For nowhere is the Papal cause more labouring than in this one point, nor is there any pope to whom this applies more than Leo, of whom so many letters survive, not commanding that a council be held, but humbly asking, and yet not obtaining, "not obtaining either the place or the time," and nonetheless complying: so that it nearly shames one to recount it. But what does it matter here now? "It cannot be denied that in calling general councils there was some authority of the Emperor." Above, he said "sometimes they were gathered by the Emperor's order"; but we there say "always," and never except by him. Here now he says there was "some" authority of the Emperor; we say not "some," but supreme and sole, so long as the affairs of the Empire are not in decline.

units.la: Docui de primis quatuor Conciliis Generalibus iam antè: addo iam de quatuor posterioribus. Concilium Constantinopolitanum (secundum, ac Generale Quintum, iuxta pium iussum à Deo euffeditii Imperatoris Iustiniani convenisse, habetur pluribus locis Concilij. Dico autem illud hîc: Si Pontifi-cius sit, vt mandet Concilia fieri, cur Concilio huic Quinto (si ipse illud fieri mandauerat) suo, à se conuocato, interesse recusauit?, cùm tamen per id tempus esset Constantinopoli Pontifex ipse Romanus, legatus eò ex mandato Theodahati Gotthorum Regis?
units.tr: I have already taught about the first four general councils; I now add the four later ones. The Council of Constantinople (the second, and the fifth general council), which, according to the pious command of God and of the most pious Emperor Justinian, assembled, is recorded in many places in the proceedings of the council. I say this here: if the Pontiff ordered councils to be held, why did he refuse to attend this fifth council (if he himself had ordered it to be held), which was convened by himself, since at that time the Roman Pontiff himself was at Constantinople, having gone there as a legate by the command of Theodahad, king of the Goths?

units.la: Concilium Constantinopolitanum tertium, ac Generale Sextum, (ut & de se testatur ipsum) {b}secundum Imperialem sanctionem congregatum est: Praesidente in singulis eius Actionibus Imperatore Constantino. Extat ibi Divali Sacra ab Imperatore ad Domum Pontificem.
units.tr: The third Council of Constantinople, and the sixth general council, (as it itself also attests) was gathered by imperial sanction, the Emperor Constantine presiding at each of its sessions. There is there a sacred edict from the Emperor to the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Quo interea de de vivis sublato Agatho, qui ei in Sede Romanâ successit, {c}respondet Divali.
units.tr: Meanwhile, with Agatho, who succeeded him in the Roman See, having died in the interval, he replies by edict.

units.la: Audi vero quo stilo, quàm sine mandato vllo. Hÿs Mansuetissimis rerum Domini Divali Apicibus animatus, melioris sum refectus confidentiâ paulatim, ÿs [?], quaper [?] Mansuetissima Fortitudinis vestrae Sacram dudum praecepta sunt efficaciter promptam obedientiâm exhibere, ut personas, quales secundùm temporis huius defectum, ac servilis Provincia qualitatem poterant inveniri, pro obedientiae satisfactione inquirerem, & ut ad Pijssimae Tranquillitatis vestrae vestigia properarent, hortarer. Et paulò post. Ideoque secundum Pijssimam lufsionem à Deo Protegenda Mansuetudinis vestrae pro obedientiâ quam debuimus, non pro confidentiâ eorum scientia, quos dirigimus: praesentes confamulos, cum omni cordis devotione, curauimus demandare. Pòst etiam. Pro quibus flexo mentis poplite supplicíter Vestram ad mansuetudinem semper intentam Clementiam deprecamur, ut iuxta Benignissimam atq; Augustissimam Imperialis Sacra promissionem acceptione eos dignos efficiat, atque placabiles aditus, eorum, humillimis suggestionibus accommodare dignetur. Denique Non enim nobis eorum scientia confidentiam dedit, ut de hâc Servuli Vestri Serenissimi Principatus Romanâ urbe ad Pijs [?] vestra vestigia auderemus eos dirigere, sed hoc Imperialis vestra Benignitas, clementer iubens hortata est, & nostra pusillitas quod iustum est obsequenter implevit. Audis hic Pontificem, Imperialis iussioni in Concilij negotio efficaciter promptam obedientiam exhibentem: Urbem Romanam & Provinciam, Imperialis Principatus Servilem urbem & Provinciam esse, profitentem: Pro obedientiae (quam debere se fatetur Imperatori) satisfactione, Legatos ad Sacra eius Vestigia demandantem: Flexo mentis poplite, supplicíter deprecantem: Pusillitatem Pontificalem, quae Benignitas Imperialis iubet, obsequenter implentem. Quàm haec verò verba, mandantis non sunt?
units.tr: Hear in what style, and how without any command: "Animated by these most gentle edicts of the Lord of all things, I have gradually been restored to better confidence, [...] since your most gentle Fortitude long ago commanded that a prompt and effective obedience be shown, that I should seek out persons such as, given the present lack of time and the servile quality of the province, could be found, for the satisfaction of obedience, and should exhort them to hasten to the footsteps of your most pious Tranquillity." And a little after: "Therefore, according to the most pious command of your Mansuetude, which is protected by God, we have taken care, out of the obedience we owed, and not out of confidence in the knowledge of those whom we direct, to entrust the present fellow-servants to you with all devotion of heart." Afterwards also: "For whom, with bended knee of mind, we humbly beseech your Clemency, always intent on mildness, that according to the most kindly and most august promise of the imperial sacred word, it may make them worthy of acceptance, and deign to accommodate placable approaches to their most humble suggestions." Finally: "For their knowledge did not give us confidence to dare to direct them from this city of Rome to the footsteps of your Most Serene Principate, but your imperial Kindness, commanding and exhorting clemently, and our littleness has dutifully fulfilled what is just." Here you hear the Pontiff, showing prompt and effective obedience to the imperial command in the matter of the council; professing that the city of Rome and the province are servile to the imperial principate; for the satisfaction of the obedience (which he confesses he owes to the Emperor) sending legates to his sacred footsteps; humbly beseeching with bended knee; dutifully fulfilling the Pontifical littleness what the imperial Kindness commands. Are these words not those of one who commands?

units.la: Concilium Nicenum secundum, ac Generale Septimum, {a}per pium Imperatorum Decretum, congregatum se, ipsâ in fronte lo-
units.tr: The second Council of Nicaea, the seventh general council, gathered by the pious decree of the Emperors, as the very heading of it says,

units.la: {a} Tom.3.pag. 453 quitur. Legitur ibi Diploma Imperatoris, in quo, Synodum se congregâsse bus assetit.{b} Hunc (inquit) petitioni {Tharasij scilicet Constantinopolitani Episcopi} annuere tum visum est, mecoque nutu iussu convenire, imo, ut verius loquar, Deo sic volente, Nobis vero Praeuntibus congregari vos. Legitur ibi in Epistolà
units.tr: (a) Vol. 3, p. 453 ... It is read there that the imperial edict, in which it says that it had convened the synod, sits. "This," it says, "it then seemed fit to grant to the petition (namely of Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople), and to assemble by our nod and command; or rather, to speak more truly, God so willing, and we leading, you were gathered." It is read there in the letter

units.la: {c}Adriani Papae ad Imperatores: Nuper vero per piam vestram iussionem, de voluntate vestra instructi, Omnipotentem Deum pro vestro Imperio precibus sollicitauimus. {d}Hac Serenitati vestrae Potentiae cum omni humilitate, & sincero corde disquitienda offerimus; obsecrantes interim, ex animi fauore vestram Manuetudinem obtestando, & veluti praesentes Genibus aduoluti & coram Vestigia Pedum volutando ego cum fratribus meis, coram Deo supplico, ut Sacras Imagines restitui, & firmari iubeatis. Legitur in Epistolà Concilij ad Imperatores: {e}Vos Sacrum hunc nostrum copiosum in hac Nicaensium Metropoli conuenire iussistis cae- tum. Etiam in Synodicâ ad omnes vbique Episcopos: Deo placuit, Pios & fideles Imperatores excitare, qui nos in splendidam Metropolim Nicaeam conuocarent.
units.tr: (c) of Pope Adrian to the Emperors: "Lately, indeed, instructed by your pious command, and by your will, we have implored Almighty God with prayers for your Empire." (d) "We offer this to your Serenity and Power with all humility and sincere heart to be examined; beseeching meanwhile, from the favour of our mind, and calling upon your Mildness, and as though kneeling before you in person and rolling at the feet before your face: I with my brethren, before God, beg that you order the sacred images to be restored and confirmed." It is read in the letter of the council to the Emperors: "You commanded that this our sacred and numerous assembly should meet in this metropolis of Nicaea." Also in the synodal letter to all bishops everywhere: "It pleased God to raise up pious and faithful Emperors, who should summon us to the splendid metropolis of Nicaea."

units.la: De Constantinopolitano quarto, ac Generali Octauo (vt vos quidem vultis) dicendum iam. Graeci vero octauum nullum agnoscunt, Septem tantum. Hoc Patriarchicum potius fuisse quam Generale, quòd in eo tractatum non sit de Fidei negotio vllo; quòd particularis tantum causa inter Ignatium & Photium acta, quae totam Ecclesiam nihil attinebat. Permulta autem fidem illi detrahunt. Nam Iulianus Cardinalis de Octauo isto, nihil sibi vobisque curae esse {f}aperte dixit in Concilio Florentino. Et Canonum numerus non concordat. Vos enim viginti septem edidistis, at Codices Graeci, quatuordecim tantum habent. Tum vestrum hoc Octauum, quod sub Adriano fuisse vultis, ab altero subsequente, quod sub eius Successore Iohanne fuit, antiquatum est. Photius enim, qui in vestro hoc depositus, in illo altero Iohannis, restitutus, praesentibus tum Legatis, Iohannis locum tenentibus Paulo & Eugenio, Iohanne ipso etiam Romano restitutionem eius approbante. Praeterea, facies ipsa Concilij posterioris, Generali similior, in quo trecenti & octoginta Episcopi fuerint, cum in vestro centum modò essent. Denique, Imperator ipse Basilius, quantum fuerit mutatus in Photium, quo animo in vestrum illud prius Concilium, in Martinum Pontificem, ib Ecclesiam ipsam Romanam; legas ex Epistola Ste{a}phani, ibi ad Basilium.
units.tr: Now to speak of the fourth Constantinopolitan council, and the eighth general council (as you indeed wish). The Greeks, however, acknowledge no eighth, only seven. This was more a patriarchal than a general council, because no matter of faith at all was treated in it; only a particular cause, acted between Ignatius and Photius, which did not concern the whole Church at all. Very many things, moreover, detract from its authority. For Cardinal Julian plainly said at the Council of Florence that this eighth council was of no concern to himself or to you. And the number of canons does not agree: for you have published twenty-seven, but Greek codices have only fourteen. Then this your eighth council, which you wish to have been under Adrian, has been superseded by the other following one, which was under his successor John. For Photius, who was deposed in your council, was restored in that other one of John, with the legates then present, Paul and Eugenius, deputizing for John, and John himself, the Roman, approving his restoration. Moreover, the very face of the later council, more like a general one, in which there were three hundred and eighty bishops, whereas in yours there were only a hundred. Finally, the Emperor Basil himself, how much he had changed towards Photius, and with what attitude towards that former council of yours, against Pope Martin, and against the Roman Church itself, you may read from the letter of Stephen there to Basil.

units.la: Sed non contendam; fuerit Generale. Sic initio loquitur Basilius apud Surium, {b}Cùm diuina & benignissima prouidentia nobis, Gubernacula Vniuersalis Nauis commisisset, omne studium an-ripuimus, ante publicas curas, Ecclesiasticas dissoluere procellas Surio, opus fuit marginali Nota; quæ hæc est, De eiusdem administratione hæc accipienda sunt. Frustrà. {c}Binnius enim iam post Naui, apposuit, Ecclesiastica, vt Basillus iam Gubernator sit Vniuersalis Nauis Ecclesiastica. Scio Binnium pro, nobis, legere, vobis, sed perperam. Itaque enim sensus esset ibi nullus. Sic enim dicturus Imperator. Cùm illis (puta Episcopis) non sibi, gubernacula commissa sint, se tamen operam dedisse, vt Ecclesiae controuersiae componerentur. Sed ita sunt Editiones vestrae: vtinam exemplaria ipsa Græca aspicere liceat; facilè sic vestra fraus omnis eluceret.
units.tr: But I will not argue the point; let it be a General Council. Basil begins in this way, as quoted by Surius: "Since by a divine and most gracious providence the helm of the universal ship has been committed to us, we have undertaken every effort, before public affairs, to dissolve the storms of the Church." Surius needed a marginal note, which reads: "These things are to be understood of his administration alone." In vain. For Binnius, after the word "ship," has added "ecclesiastical," so that Basil is now the governor of the ecclesiastical universal ship. I know that Binnius reads "vobis" instead of "nobis," but this is an error, since on that reading the sense would be nothing at all. For the Emperor would be saying: "Since the helm has not been committed to them (namely the bishops), but I have nonetheless taken care that the controversies of the Church be settled." But your editions read thus; I wish I could see the Greek manuscripts themselves, for your whole fraud would then easily come to light.

units.la: Sed & in vestro hoc, vestigia sunt veritatis. Actione sexta, {d}Persuasum est nobis, Sanctæ huic & Oecumenicæ Synodo, quam à Deo coronatus Imperator noster, de componendâ, & restituendâ Ecclesiâ Constantinopolitanâ coegit. Actione septimâ: {e}Imperator omnem operam dedit, vt ex aliis Patriarchis Legatos cuocaret, Conciliumque Generale cogeret, eamque rem perfecit. Postremò, sic {f}Stephanus Papa, in Epistolâ suâ ad Basilium, Quid præcauit Romana Ecclesia? Nonne pro veteri Synodorum Constantinopolitanarum more, te imperante, Legatos misit? Quid quærimus? Mandauit atque imperauit Imperator: Eo imperante Pontifex Legatos mittit. Reliqua verò post Concilia nihil motamur, quippe solius Occidentalis, non totius Oecumenica dici non merentur.
units.tr: But in your own texts too there are traces of the truth. In the sixth action: "It has been persuaded to us that this holy and ecumenical Synod, which our Emperor, crowned by God, compelled to be convened for the settling and restoring of the Church of Constantinople..." In the seventh action: "The Emperor gave every effort that he might summon legates from the other patriarchs and convene a General Council, and he accomplished this matter." Finally, Pope Stephen, in his letter to Basil, says thus: "What did the Roman Church take care of? Did she not, in accordance with the old custom of the Synods of Constantinople, send legates during your reign? What more do we seek? The Emperor commanded and ordered; under the Emperor's command the Pontiff sends legates. As for the councils that came after, we make no complaint, since they deserve to be called not ecumenical but merely Western."

units.la: Rationem verò reddit Tortus, cur aliquam saltem Imperatoribus relinquat in Conciliis habendis authoritatem: Quòd non deceret conuenire (ut Episcopos, absque eius consensu. Non deceret autem? Quidni? Si Pontificem conuocare decebat, cur illis turpe sit conuocanti parere, adeóque etiam conuenire? Forte & indecorum Pontifici conuocare: Nihil enim illum decet, nisi mandata Cæsari dare. Cæsar tamen, si consensum Episcopis negare poterat, [illegible, ~12 letters] conuenicndi po-test
units.tr: But Tortus gives the reason why he leaves to the Emperors at least some authority in calling Councils: "Because it would not be fitting to convene (the bishops) without his consent." Would it not be fitting? Why not? If it was fitting for the Pontiff to convene them, why would it be shameful for them to obey one who convenes them, and so even to assemble? Perhaps it is also unbecoming for the Pontiff to convene them: for nothing becomes him except to give orders to Caesar. Yet Caesar, if he could deny the bishops his consent, [illegible, ~12 letters] could convene them.

units.la: {a} Apud Binn, Tom.3.part.2. pag.900. est & Pontifici (credo) connocandi. Verum alia res erat.
units.tr: In Binnius, vol. 3, part 2, p. 900, it is (I believe) also for the Pontiff to convene. But that is another matter.

units.la: Nec enim illud non decuit, sed non licuit; cum lege de Conventiculis cautum esset, ne vel Religionis causa haberi possent Conventus, nisi consensu Casaris prius intervenien te.
units.tr: For it was not that this was unfitting, but that it was not lawful; since the law concerning conventicles provided that assemblies could not be held even for religious reasons unless Caesar's consent had first intervened.

units.la: Addit vero, quod niteris. Pios Imperatores saepe de Ecclesia bono & pace sollicitos Concilia indixisse, sed postquam a Pontifice mandatum acceperint. Imperatores vero sollicitos de Ecclesia? Non oportuit. Nihil ad illos pertinet de rebus Ecclesiasticis, praeter reverentiam. Ad illos sollicitudo illa non pertinet. Quid Pontifex interim? Haec enim illius provincia; Sinetne Imperatorem sic limites transilire? Sint utique, ut videtur, mandato dato. Eo dato licet; non dato, non licet. Defeigitur [?] non illicitum. Posset & haec etiam Reges cura decere, & pertinere ad omnes. Tota res in Pontifice vel annuente, vel abnuente. Petant ab eo, ab eo sumant mandatum, & fruantur sane. Quodsi ita fiat, vtinam vnico mandato rem transigat; exoneret se qui tam longe abest; in illos transfundat, qui quid Ecclesiae necessitates postulent, propius intuentur: Alius hoc iam diceret. Quin si non licet hoc illis, qui in plebis fortefunt [?]; nec Pontificis mandatum facere potest, ut possit licere. Sin lic potest, sitne a se honesta [?]; quidni idem liceat, Pontifices nutu non expectato? Debet vero negari (falsum enim est) praecipuam fuisse Romani Pontificis authoritatem in Conciliis indicendis. Probat autem: Quam vero id apte? Non enim rata fuisse sine eius consensu. At neque verum illud: Rata enim Concilia, in quibus Pontifices depositi, sine eorum autem, qui depositi, consensu, quis non videt? At vero absque Principis consensu rata forte ut Canones, apud conscientias fidelium; rata ut leges nunquam erant ut constituerent, quibusque Censura, verbalis est, non realis gladius. Ita & rata sine Pontifice, & sine Imperatore non rata.
units.tr: But he adds what you lean upon: that pious Emperors, anxious for the good and peace of the Church, often indicted Councils, but only after they had received a command from the Pontiff. Emperors anxious about the Church? It was not proper. Nothing pertains to them concerning ecclesiastical affairs, except reverence. That anxiety does not belong to them. And the Pontiff meanwhile? For this is his province. Does he allow the Emperor to overstep the boundaries in this way? They may indeed, as it seems, provided a command has been given. If it has been given, it is permitted; if not given, it is not permitted. [Something] is not unlawful. This care might also befit kings and pertain to all. The whole matter rests with the Pontiff, either consenting or refusing. Let them ask of him, let them receive the command from him, and by all means enjoy it. But if it is so done, I wish he would settle the matter with a single command; let him unburden himself, he who is so far away, and transfer it to those who look more closely at what the needs of the Church require. Another would say this already. Indeed, if this is not permitted to them, who are among the people [?], neither can he make it a command of the Pontiff so that it might be permitted. But if it can be permitted, is it honourable in itself? Why should the same not be permitted to the Pontiffs without waiting for a nod? But it must be denied (for it is false) that the Roman Pontiff had a pre-eminent authority in convening Councils. He proves it thus: "How aptly, indeed?" For they were not valid without his consent. But neither is that true: for who does not see that Councils in which Pontiffs were deposed were valid without the consent of those who were deposed? But indeed, without the consent of the prince, they were perhaps valid as canons before the consciences of the faithful; valid as laws they never were, to establish anything, since their censure is verbal, not a real sword. Thus they were valid without the Pontiff, and without the Emperor they were not valid.

units.la: Verum in Chalcedonensi Synodo iubetur Dioscorus surgere, nec sedere inter Episcopos, quod Synodum ausus facere, absque Pontificis authoritate, quod, inquiunt, nunquam licuit, nunquam factum est. Iubetur? a quibus? A Legatis Leonis. Inquiunt qui? ipsi Leonis Legati. Verum, non ex eo quod iubetur quid, sed ex eo quod iubenti pareretur, concludi solet. At Dioscorus non paruit. Legati surgere illum: Iudices sedere etiam iusserunt, nisi & Legati ipsi vnà surgerent. Damnatus tum quidem Dioscorus, non quòd absque Pontificis authoritate Synodum fecisset, quin ex causâ longè alia, {a}contumacis absentia, quòd sistere se nollet vocatus à Concilio; cùm sibi malè conscius esset, propter iniustè, & per vim à se depositos Flauianum & Eusebium. Quam tu verò affers, nulla damnationis causa; ac ne audita quidem est à Iudicibus, neque verò audiri debuit. Legitimè enim indicta Synodus illa Ephesina, non minùs legitimè, nec alia authoritate, quàm haec Chalcedonensis ipsa. Legitur ibi Sacra Imperatorum Theodosij & Valentiniani, {b}quâ iubent Ephesi Concilium fieri: cui & Leoni ipse paruit, coque misit Legatos suos Iulianum Episcopum, ac Hilarium Diaconum; qui & ipsi ibi cum interfuerunt, & sanctiti fortassè audierunt; sed audierunt tamen, primatum, & primum authoritatem in Synodo illâ, Dioscoro ab Imperatoribus delegatam. Non ergo de Synodo illegitimè factâ reus ibi Dioscorus, non magis quàm Leo. Licuit fieri, si factum est, ut Ephesinum illud, ita Chalcedonense hoc Concilium, sine Leonis authoritate{c} verumque: In utroque mandatum illi erat ab Imperatore, in utroque paruit, in neutro mandavit. Sed ideo reus Dioscorus, quia contra ius & fas suffragia extorsit per vim, & Flauianum, nullo seruato Iuris ordine, condemnauit immeritò. Illud[?]
units.tr: But in the Council of Chalcedon Dioscorus is ordered to rise and not to sit among the bishops, because he dared to hold a Synod without the authority of the Pontiff, which, they say, was never permitted and never done. Ordered? By whom? By the legates of Leo. Who say so? The legates of Leo themselves. But a conclusion is usually drawn not from the fact that something is commanded, but from the fact that the one commanding is obeyed. Yet Dioscorus did not obey. The legates ordered him to rise; the judges also ordered him to sit, unless the legates themselves rose together with him. Dioscorus was then condemned, not because he had held the Synod without the authority of the Pontiff, but for a quite different cause, "the contumacious absence," because he would not present himself when summoned by the Council, since he was conscious of wrongdoing, on account of Flavian and Eusebius whom he had unjustly and by force deposed. But what you bring forward was no cause of condemnation; nor was it even heard by the judges, nor ought it to have been heard. For that Synod of Ephesus was lawfully indicted, no less lawfully and by no other authority than this very Council of Chalcedon. There is read there the sacred edict of the Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian by which they order a Council to be held at Ephesus; to which edict Leo himself also submitted, and he sent his legates, Julian the bishop and Hilarius the deacon, who were themselves present there, and perhaps heard the holy men; yet they heard them, but the primacy and the first authority in that Synod had been delegated to Dioscorus by the Emperors. Therefore Dioscorus was not a defendant there for an illegitimately held Synod, no more than Leo was. It was permitted to be done, if it was done, both that Ephesine Council and this Council of Chalcedon, without the authority of Leo; and in both cases the command was given to him by the Emperor; in both he obeyed, in neither did he command. But Dioscorus was indeed the defendant, because he extorted votes against law and right by force, and condemned Flavian undeservedly, without observing any order of law. That...

units.la: Falsum & illud nihilominùs, quod affers è Synodo septimâ, irritum ibi iudicatum fuisse Constantinopolitanum quoddam, quod ab Imperatore congregatum fuisset, sine consensu Apostolicae Sedis. Nulla ibi mentio de Imperatoris potestate; nulla de eo, quod sine consensu Papae Romani congregatum ab eo fuisset: Quid ibi dicitur, hoc est: Non potuisse Synodum illam Vniuersalem dici, {d}quòd cineque Papa Romanus, neque Alexandrinus, neque Antiochenus, vel Hierosolymitanus, vel per se, vel per Legatos, aut literas interfuisset, quemadmodum fieri in Synodis amat. Neque certè cùm hijs omnes abessent, Vniuersalis ea Synodus dici potuit. Verùm, tam ex reliquorum absentiâ, hoc quàm ex Romani, qui cooperarius in eâ negatur fuisse, tam reliquis fellicet ibi cooperarijs suis. Verbum autem vel de indictâ Synodo; vel de indicendi authoritate, ibi nullum. Nec authoritas ibi defuit, eâdem enim etiam illa authoritate congregata est, qui Nicena secunda: Illa antea De-
units.tr: That also is false nonetheless, what you adduce from the seventh Synod: that a certain Constantinopolitan Synod, which had been gathered by the Emperor without the consent of the Apostolic See, was judged there to be null and void. There is no mention there of the Emperor's power; none of the fact that it was gathered by him without the consent of the Roman Pontiff. What is said there is this: that that Synod could not be called universal, because neither the Roman Pontiff, nor the Alexandrian, nor the Antiochene, nor the Jerusalemite, either in person, or through legates, or by letters, had taken part in it, as is customary in Synods. Nor indeed, since all these were absent, could that Synod be called universal. But from the absence of the rest, as much as from the fact that the Roman was said not to have cooperated in it, and of course the rest of his co-workers there. But there is nothing there either about the indicting of the Synod, or about the authority of indicting it. Nor was authority lacking there, for it was gathered by the same authority as the Second Nicene: ...

units.la: {d} Cf. Tom.3.pag.146. cretum Constantini & Leonis in Nicena iuxta Decretum Constantini & Irenæ. Sed præsentia defuit Patriarcharum; ea vna res in causa fuit, ne Generalis haberi posset. Satis autem esset de Concilio Romano in causa Symmachi re- spondere; Generale id non fuisse, de quo nobis iam quæritur. Nihil ergo ad propositum nostrum: Etsi in eo etiam, non tam de potestate Congregandi, quàm de causa Congregationis quæsitum est. Non de potestate. Præcepto enim Gloriosissimi Regis Theodorici è Regionibus diuersis conuenerunt; in eo- que, potestatem in eo agnoverunt Congregandi, vel sine Pontifice. Alioquin enim ne conuenissent quidem; substitissent domi; præter Regis præceptum, Pontificis Authoritatem expectassent, nec vel domo aliter pedem mouissent. Quare cùm ex præcepto Regio conuenerint, non vocati à Pontifice; potestatem ad hoc in Rege sciuerunt, eique detulerunt. Postquam verò conuocati iam de causa quærerent, eamque audirent esse, vt de Pontifice suo sererent sententiam; scirent autem, minoribus in maiorem potestatem nullam esse, nisi qui Maior est, minorum se iudicio spontè submittat; in eâ quidem causâ responderunt, quod res erat, absque Pontificis consensu, ne vocandos quidem fuisse, nec iam cùm adessent, posse de causâ cognoscere: nec enim Antistitem suum, minorum iudicio, id est, suo, subiacere posse, nisi ipse se subijciat. In hac itaque causa opus erat, vt Rex ijs testatum faceret, præter Pontificis conscientiam, nihil ab illis, nec in aduentu factum, nec in iudicio faciendum esse. Actum ergo ibi de causa, & Episcoporum ad causæ cognitionem potestate, non autem Regia ad Synodum conuocandam: Satis tamen vel in eo Concilio elucet Regia potestas: iussu enim Regijs præceptionibus Symmachus ipse Papa, ante patrimonij vel Ecclesiarum receptionem in disceptationem venire. Tum, vbi dicerent accusatores Symmachi, crimina apud Regiam notitiam constare; responsum, si constituissent illa Regi, non illorum audientia rem commissurum, sed ipsum de re tota cognituru fuisse. Post, conferunt se ad iuditiam Principalem; eique omnia per relationis seriem ingerunt, fatentur Dominum Regem facultatem habere quod vellet faciendi. Sine Regis notitia aliquid decernere non præsumunt. Quod decernunt, id iuxta mandatum Principis, secundum Principalia praecepta se facere testantur, quae illorum hoc potestati tribuebant. Postremò, quae Theodorici Regis in {a}Regis Sym-machum potestas, ex eo scias, quòd cum in electione eius Schisma exitisset, inter Laurentium & Symmachum; Ravennam ambo evocati coram Rege, ubi potestati Regiae delatû ut de electione pronunciaret: nec, nisi ex sententiâ Regis Symmachum tum Papa factus est. Papam qui facere potuit, potuit Sciudicare[?]. {b}Johannem qui paulò pòst in sede successit, scis ipse judicio Theodorici in carcere diem obijsse. Ad Constantinopolitani primi Epistolam, responsum à me suprà, Non esse Epistolam illam Concilij: Non esse in Epistolâ verba illa ex mandato: Germanam Concilij Epistolam, illud ab Imperatore indictum profiteri.
units.tr: Cf. vol. 3, p. 146. The decree of Constantine and Leo, at Nicaea, according to the decree of Constantine and Irene. But the presence of the Patriarchs was lacking; that alone was the cause why it could not be held to be General. It would be enough, however, to answer concerning the Roman Council in the case of Symmachus; that was not a General one, which is what we are now inquiring about. Nothing therefore to our purpose: although in that case too the question was not so much about the power of convening as about the cause of the gathering. "Not about the power." For by the command of the most glorious King Theodoric they assembled from different regions; and in that they acknowledged the power of convening, even without the Pontiff. Otherwise they would not even have assembled; they would have stayed at home, and, apart from the King's command, would have awaited the Pontiff's authority, nor would they have moved a foot from home otherwise. Wherefore, since they assembled by the royal command, not being summoned by the Pontiff, they knew the power for this lay in the King, and they referred it to him. But after they were summoned and were now asking about the cause, and heard that it was to pass sentence on their own Pontiff; and they knew that the lesser cannot have power over the greater unless the greater himself voluntarily submits to the judgment of the lesser, they answered in that matter that, as the thing was, it was without the Pontiff's consent that they should not even have been summoned, nor, now that they were present, could they take cognizance of the cause: for their own prelate could not be subject to the judgment of his inferiors, that is, of themselves, unless he himself submitted. In this case therefore it was necessary for the King to make it known to them that, apart from the Pontiff's conscience, nothing was to be done by them, either in coming or in judging. The cause was therefore acted upon there, and the bishops' power to take cognizance of the cause, but not the royal power to convene the Synod: yet even in that Council the royal power is clearly evident; for by the royal decrees Symmachus himself, the Pope, was ordered to come into dispute before the receiving of the patrimony or of the churches. Then, when the accusers of Symmachus said that the crimes were established before the King's knowledge, it was answered that, if they had established them before the King, he would not commit the matter to their hearing, but would himself take cognizance of the whole affair. Afterwards they betake themselves to the principal judgment, and lay everything before him in an orderly report, and they confess that the lord King has the power to do what he wishes. They do not presume to decide anything without the King's knowledge. What they decide, they declare that they do according to the command of the prince, in accordance with the princely precepts, which granted this power to them. Lastly, as to the power of King Theodoric over Symmachus the King, you may know this from the fact that, when a schism had arisen at his election between Laurence and Symmachus, both were summoned before the King at Ravenna, where the matter was referred to the royal power, so that he might pronounce concerning the election; and Symmachus was made Pope only by the sentence of the King. He who was able to make a Pope was able to judge him. As for John, who succeeded in the see a little later, you know that he died in prison by the judgment of Theodoric. As to the first letter of the Constantinopolitan Synod, I have answered above: that it is not a letter of the Council; that the words are not in the letter "by command"; that the letter claims to be the genuine letter of the Council, which declares that it was indicted by the Emperor.

units.la: Ad literas Hadriani secundi in Synodo vestrâ Octavâ, in quibus verba illa; Volumus per Tuae Pietatis industriam Constantinopoli numerosum convocare Concilium. Primùm, ibi per Torti industriam, verbum aliud pro alio positum. Convocare dicit Tottus, {c}celebrari dicit Hadrianus. Interest autem nonnihil, inter volumus convocare, & celebrari volumus; celebrari potest ab Imperatore; volumus convocare, nisi ad Pontificem, referri non potest. Tùm, volumus ibi dicit, sed sine jubemus; quae vox per se posita, mandandi vim non habet; docet potiùs quid cupiat, quàm quid mandet fieri. Sumere licet exemplum ex ipsâ illâ Synodo. Sic ibi Legati Patriarchales. Imperatorem alloquuntur, Actione sextâ. {d}Volumus omnino ut legatur libellus Sanctae Romanae Ecclesiae: sine imperio tamen. Nimium id quidem foret, mandare Imperatori, non Papam modò, sed Legatos etiam Patriarcharum. Quare, quid cupiant eâ voce, non quid jubeant exprimere voluerunt, ut ibi Legati, sic in Epistolâ suâ Hadrianus. Quanquam post nongentos jamannos, excusso tum penè, obnoxio certè valdè illis Imperatore Orientis, (Basilio hoc praesertim, qui per eadem Domini sui, invasor Imperij) elato magis stilo usus Pontifex, quàm quo compellare solebant Imperatores priscos, Pontifices qui praedecessores eius. Cui rei, praeviit illi viam Nicolaus cui successit, qui in {*}Michaelem fuerat immodestior. Eo enim jam tempore, coeperunt Genebrardi Pontifices Apostatici.
units.tr: On Hadrian the Second's letters in your Eighth Synod, in which these words occur: "We wish, through the diligence of Your Piety, to convene a numerous Council at Constantinople." First, here Torthus, through his diligence, has put one word for another. Torthus says "convene"; Hadrian says "celebrate." There is some difference between "we wish to convene" and "we wish to celebrate": a council may be celebrated by the emperor; "we wish to convene" cannot be referred to anyone but the Pontiff. Then, he says "we wish" there, but not "we command." That word, placed by itself, does not have the force of commanding; it shows what he desires rather than what he orders to be done. One may take an example from that very Synod. So the Patriarchal legates address the emperor in the sixth action: "We wish by all means that the libel of the Holy Roman Church be read; yet without command." That indeed would be too much: to order the emperor, not only the Pope but also the legates of the Patriarchs. Therefore, as the legates there, so Hadrian in his letter, wished to express by that word what they desire, not what they command. Although, after nine hundred years, when the emperor of the East, almost shaken off then and certainly very much subject to them (Basil especially, who was the usurper of his own lord through the same means), the Pontiff used a more elevated style than the emperors of old were accustomed to be addressed by, their predecessors the Pontiffs. For this matter, Nicholas, whom he succeeded, who had been more immoderate toward Michael, had prepared the way. For already at that time the Apostate Pontiffs of Genebrard began.

units.la: In Sixto fui similis Tortus. Quod in Epistolâ est, {a}nostrâ authoritate Synodum congregari iussit; id ille sic posuit, nostrâ authoritate Synodum conuocauit. Nec enim Imperator conuocauit Synodum illam ex Pontificis authoritate, sed iussit eam congregari à Pontifice, authoritate non Pontificis, sed suâ; propterq; causam superiùs à me redditam in Symmacho. Purgabat in eâ Synodo Sixtus sese, atque subijciebat se Episcoporum iudicio; quorum in illum iurisdictio nulla, nisi Sixtus eam ipse volens illis detulisset. Ad eam rem, Sixti interventu opus. Nec ergo hoc quicquam ad rem. Taceo quod nec Concilium illud Generale; & Epistolæ datæ ibi sub Consulibus, qui nulli vnquam fuerunt, & vel {b}Baronio ipsi, Concilij illius Acta corruptissima, nec vllo modo confisunt. Pars etiam huius Epistolæ posterior, assumentum integrum alterius (Fa-biani) Epistolæ, ante annos centum scriptæ. Successit Fabiano Cornelius, cuius qui Epistolas legerit apud Cyprianum, & cum vestris Fabiani contulerit; nisi illi natus sit nullus, totam hanc fraudem statim odoretur.
units.tr: In Sixtus I was similar to Tortus. What is in the letter, "by our authority he ordered a Synod to be gathered," he put thus: "by our authority he convened a Synod." For the emperor did not convene that Synod by the authority of the Pontiff, but ordered it to be gathered by the Pontiff, not by the authority of the Pontiff, but by his own; and for this reason I explained the cause above in Symmachus. In that Synod Sixtus cleared himself and submitted himself to the judgment of the bishops, over whom he had no jurisdiction unless Sixtus himself, willing it, had granted it to them. For that matter, the intervention of Sixtus was needed. Therefore this is nothing to the point. I pass over that neither that General Council, nor the letters given there "under the Consuls," who never existed, and even Baronius himself, judge the Acts of that Council to be most corrupt, nor do they trust them in any way. Also the latter part of this letter, "an entire assumption of another (Fabian) letter," was written a hundred years before. Cornelius succeeded Fabian; whoever has read his letters in Cyprian, and compared them with your Fabian, unless he was born without a nose, will at once smell out this whole fraud.

units.la: Ad vltimum denique & in vltimo, quasi totus ex fraude compositus, dolosè rem gerit Tortus: Putes Synodum ibi Generalem indici. Celauit enim coepiscopos ibi {c}Leonis Tarraconenses, Asturicenses, Carthaginenses, Lusitanos Episcopos, quos omnes in Prouinciali Galæcia Synodo conuenire voluit, procurante rem Turbio Asturicensi. Generalis ea quidem, si ad Prouinciæ illius Dicœceses referatur, vt siquis Italiæ Generalem diceret; Sin absolutè Generalem quæras, nihil minùs quàm Generalis, de quâ tamen probandum suscepit Tortus. Mirum autem citari de Leone locum; cuius tot sint in tam multis Epistolis, petitiones pro Synodis ab Imperatore indicendis, singulæ autem, singula testimonia, nihil Leoni iuris in Synodos Generales. Citat tamen vel ex eo. Collige iam: Septem protulit: tres particulares, Leoni, Sixti, Symmachi; vnam suspectam, nempe Octauam. De reliquis, Secundâ, Tertiâ, Septimâ, testimonia manifestò falsa.
units.tr: Lastly, and at the end, as if wholly composed from fraud, Tortus deals deceitfully with the matter: you would think a General Synod was being announced there. For he concealed the co-bishops there of Leo: the bishops of Tarragona, Astorga, Cartagena, and Lusitania, whom he wished all to meet in the Provincial Synod of Galicia, the matter being managed by Turibius of Astorga. That synod is indeed General, if it is referred to the dioceses of that province, as if anyone should call a synod of Italy a General one; but if you ask for a General one absolutely, it is nothing less than General, which Tortus nevertheless undertook to prove. It is, however, strange that a passage from Leo is cited; of whom there are so many petitions in so many letters for synods to be convened by the emperor, each one giving a single testimony, none giving Leo any right over General Synods. Yet he cites him even from that. Now gather: he has brought forward seven: three particular ones, of Leo, Sixtus, and Symmachus; one suspect, namely the Eighth. Of the rest, the Second, Third, and Seventh, the testimonies are manifestly false.

units.la: Digressio autem est Torto, siquis de lege diuinâ verba faciat, ad eámque optet, & hanc & reliquas omnes quæstiones nostras reuocari. Quid ergo cius mentio fuit Cardinali? Quid Pontifici, qui obedientiam non postulat, nisi quę fit secun-dùm. dum Scripturas Sanctas: si sua nolunt ad hanc amusim exigi? Si eius memoriam sepultam cupiant, cur ipsi tam importune sermonem iniiciunt de praestanda se erga Scripturas Sanctas obedientia, de morte vel pro syllaba una divinae legis oppetenda? Video autem iam, quid rei sit. Vbi de Capite fidei, Pontifice agitur, recta via est; vbi de lege Dei, digressio statim. Vtinam vero ne fit; vtinam frequentior vobis illius memoria; sed tam rara eius apud vos mentio, ut si quis de Lege Dei loqui velit, necessario illi digrediendum sit.
units.tr: Moreover, it is a digression for Tortus, if someone speaks about the divine law, and wishes that this and all our other questions be recalled to it. Why then was mention of it made to the Cardinal? Why to the Pontiff, who does not demand obedience except that which is according to the Holy Scriptures, if they are unwilling for their own things to be measured by this rule? If they desire his memory buried, why do they themselves so importunately introduce the discourse about rendering obedience to the Holy Scriptures, about facing death for even one syllable of the divine law? I now see, however, what the matter is. Where the discussion is about the Head of the faith, the Pontiff, the way is straight; where it is about the law of God, there is at once a digression. Would that it were not so; would that his memory were more frequent among you; but his mention among you is so rare that if anyone wishes to speak about the Law of God, he must necessarily digress.

units.la: Tria vero notauit Apologia, quibuscum Legi Dei male conuenit: Eucharistiam mutilatam; Missam priuatam; verba Canonis non integra. Vbi nouam rationem init Tortus, ex uno de tribus (quod falsum autumat) reliqua duo docere vult non vera. Vere noua docendi ratio; quamquam ratio vix patitur, cum in tribus tam inter se disiunctis, possit unum forte vix scopum ferire, ut duo tamen reliqua non aberrent. Sed aberrat ibi in nullo; ne in tertio quidem. Nam de duobus primis, Eucharistia mutila, Priuata Missa, habemus, ut video, Tortum rerum & confitentem. Sic enim Synodus ipsa Tridentina: Etsi Christus Dominus in ultima Cena venerabile hoc Sacramentum in utraque specie instituit, & Apostolis tradidit; licet ab initio Christianae religionis, non infrequens utriusque speciei usus fuerit: tamen, b segranibus & iniustis causis adductam, hanc consuetudinem sub altera specie approbare, & pro lege habendam decernere? id est, digredi a lege Dei, quae est de utraque specie, & legem alteram, quae est de una tantum, ei superinducere. Sed & ex summo honore, quo Patres Sanctos & antiquos, Tridentini ibi Patres prosequuntur, Ex sexto Iohannis non recte colligi dicunt, utriusque speciei communionem a Domino praeceptam esse, utcunque iuxta varias Sanctorum Patrum & Doctorum interpretationes ita intelligatur. De Missa priuata optat Sancta Synodus, d ut in singulis Missis fideles Eucharistia participatione communicent, id est, ut nulla sit Missa priuata; contrarium tamen statuit eius quod optat. Dicit continere Missam, magnam populi fidelis eruditionem: non tamen videtur ei expedire, ut vulgari lingua celebretur; qua una ratione perciperet populus eruditionem illam, quae in Missa continetur. Vt ille, qui contra Apologiam Ecclesiae nostrae scripsit, optare dicit vos, ut intelligat populus totam Litur[?]giam publicam: Nec {b}negare se, bonum esse, si intelligerent. Non negare id bonum esse, optare vt fiat; ne tamen fiat, decernere.
units.tr: Three things, however, the Apology noted, with which the Law of God does not agree well: the Eucharist mutilated; the private Mass; the words of the Canon not complete. Here Torthus takes up a new method: from one of the three (which he claims is false) he wishes the other two to teach untruths. Truly a new method of teaching; although the method hardly allows it, since among three so disjoined from one another, one might perhaps barely hit the mark, so that the other two would not go astray. But he goes astray in none of them; not even in the third. For concerning the first two, the mutilated Eucharist and the private Mass, we have, as I see, Torthus both admitting and confessing the facts. For the Tridentine Synod itself says: "Although Christ the Lord in the last Supper instituted this venerable Sacrament in both kinds and delivered it to the Apostles; although from the beginning of the Christian religion the use of both kinds was not infrequent: nevertheless, to approve this custom of the one kind, induced by grievous and unjust causes, and to decree that it be held as law?" That is, to depart from the law of God, which concerns both kinds, and to superinduce upon it another law, which concerns one kind only. But also, from the highest honor with which the holy and ancient Fathers are honored by the Tridentine Fathers there, they say it is not rightly gathered from the sixth of John that communion in both kinds was commanded by the Lord, however that may be understood according to the various interpretations of the holy Fathers and Doctors. Concerning the private Mass the holy Synod wishes "that in each Mass the faithful may communicate by sacramental participation," that is, that there be no private Mass; yet it decrees the contrary of what it wishes. It says the Mass contains great instruction for the faithful people; yet it does not seem expedient to it that it be celebrated in the vernacular tongue, by which single means the people would perceive that instruction which is contained in the Mass. As he who wrote against the Apology of our Church says, he wishes that the people understand the whole public Liturgy; nor does he deny that it would be good if they understood. To deny that this is good is not to wish it done; yet to decree that it not be done.

units.la: In Canone Missæ vestro, desunt verba [Quod pro vobis traditur, vel frangitur] quæ apud Paulum & Lucam habentur. Ea Canonis natura iam, nihil vt ei deesse, nihil superesse debeat. Paulus vero, ea se à Domino accepisse asserit, à Domino accepta Corinthijs tradere. Quandoquidem ergo Paulus ea sic à Domino dicit sibi tradita; Canoni verba illa deesse, minimè consentaneum. Aliud autem est rem referre, quod Euangelistæ faciunt; aliud ex spatio per omnes relationem, Canonem solenni modo contexere, quod incumbit Ecclesiæ. Vel ergo, non accepit à Domino illa Paulus, vel si accepit, vobis detrahenda non erant. Tametsi vero Iustinus, Cyrillus, Emesenus cùm aliud agerent, verba forte non referrant; tametsi verba omittant, quid hij omnes ad Paulum? Verùm Iustinus apud Ethnicos Canonem vulgare non debuit; perstrinxisse sat erat vtcunque. Cyrillus autem sumpsit sibi pro themate ipsa illa Pauli verba, ad Catechesin illam. Quæ autem sic sumpsit (puto) omissa noluit. At verò Emesenus delibat tantùm pauca carpitim per totam Homiliam, nec in rem serio incumbit. Nec nos illos reprehendimus; leuiter, & in transcursu rem attigerunt: Canonem ex professo recenset nemo. Vos autem reprehensione digni, qui pro Canone obtruditis, qui Canon non est: forma enim verborum, quam Christus tradidit, per omnia debuit à vobis illibata seruari.
units.tr: In your Canon of the Mass, the words [which is given for you, or broken] are lacking, which are found in Paul and Luke. The nature of the Canon ought now to be that nothing be lacking in it and nothing superfluous. But Paul asserts that he received those things from the Lord, and delivered to the Corinthians what he had received from the Lord. Since therefore Paul says those things were delivered to him thus from the Lord, it is by no means consistent to say that those words are lacking from the Canon. It is one thing to relate a matter, as the Evangelists do; it is another, from a space of relation through all, to compose the Canon in a solemn manner, which belongs to the Church. Either Paul did not receive those words from the Lord, or, if he did receive them, they were not to be withdrawn by you. Although, indeed, Justin, Cyril, and Emesenus, when they were doing something else, perhaps did not relate the words; even if they omit the words, what do all these have to do with Paul? Justin, however, among the heathen, ought not to have made the Canon common; it was enough to have touched on it in some way. But Cyril took for his theme those very words of Paul, for that catechesis. What he took up thus, he (I think) did not want to omit. Emesenus, however, merely touches on a few things here and there throughout the whole Homily, and does not seriously apply himself to the matter. Nor do we reprehend them; they touched the matter lightly and in passing: no one professedly recounts the Canon. You, however, are worthy of reprehension, who thrust upon us as the Canon what is not the Canon: for the form of words which Christ delivered ought to have been preserved by you entire in all respects.

units.la: Sed quæ Torto mens, cùm de Canone ageretur, vt nullum nobis Canonem citàrit; cùm tam multi exstant, pro diuersis Ecclesijs diuersi; omnes tamen in verbis hijs consentientes? Videas enim in Canone Missarum {a}Iacobi, {b}Clementis, {c}Basilij, {d}Chrysostomi, {e}Ambrosij, in {f}Anaphorâ Syrorum, in {g}Canone Vniuersali Æthiopum religiosissimè recitata verba hæc, quæ desunt in vestro. Oppositio verò satis hic clara, non integri, ad integrum: nec conciliabitis vnquam, neque Cardinalis, neque tu, vt Christus & dixerit, Quod pro vobis tradetur, & non dixerit. Et fatetur reus hic Tortus addidisse Paulum & Lucam verba hæc, quod pro vobis frangitur. Addidisse autem cui? Cui, nisi Petri Canoni antiquiori, iam ante pleno atque integro, vt ista iam superflua fuerint: Quod enim pleno additur, superfluum sit necesse. Quæ vox, parum abest à blasphemia; addidisse Paulum & Lucam ad Christi verba: Supplevisse (credo) dicere voluit, debuit quidem, omissa scilicet priùs à Matthæo & Marco, quæ proinde supplenda in Canone vestro. Alioqui Canonem habetis, in quo aliquid omissum, atque ita imperfectum. Sic enim Papa vester: Innocentius: Inter Euangelistas, quæ omittuntur ab vno, supplentur ab alio. Optimè ergo non habet se Canon vester, eò quòd desint ei verba vlla, vtcunque pauca, Christi tamen, & à Christo, Paulo tradita, vt nobis traderetur.
units.tr: But what was Tortus's thinking, when he was discussing the Canon, that he cited no Canon to us, though there are so many, different for different churches, yet all agreeing in these words? For you will find these words, which are missing from yours, recited most scrupulously in the Canon of the Masses of James, Clement, Basil, Chrysostom, Ambrose, in the Anaphora of the Syrians, and in the Universal Canon of the Ethiopians. The opposition here is clear enough: it is an incomplete against a complete. Neither the Cardinal nor you will ever reconcile it, so that Christ both said "which is given for you" and did not say it. And this defendant Tortus admits that Paul and Luke added the words "which is broken for you." But added to what? To the older Petrine Canon, surely, which was already full and complete, so that these additions were superfluous: for what is added to a full thing must be superfluous. This expression comes close to blasphemy: "Paul and Luke added to the words of Christ." He meant, I suppose, to say "supplied": they ought, indeed, to have supplied what Matthew and Mark had omitted, and so those things are to be supplied in your Canon. Otherwise you have a Canon in which something is omitted and so is imperfect. For thus your Pope Innocent says: "Among the Evangelists, what is omitted by one is supplied by another." Therefore your Canon is not in good shape, since it lacks any words at all, however few, of Christ and handed down by Christ through Paul, so that they might be handed down to us.

units.la: Nec argumentis euincit quicquam. Referunt quidem Matthæus & Marcus cœnam Domini, omissis verbis illis; quod est argumentum certissimum ex Matthæo & Marco Canonem conficiendum non esse. Ex Paulo potiùs & Luca, qui verba illa supplent. Ex pleno enim texendus nobis Canon, non inde vbi aliquid prætermissum est. Nam, quod subijcit de ijs, qui cùm solius Matthæi vel Marci Euangelium haberent, non rectè consecrarent, si apud eos verba integra non essent; quis perdat operam respondendo? cùm certum sit, si fuissent integra, Paulum illis vel Lucam nihil addituros: cùmque apud eos Canon non pendeat ab Euangelio vllo, vt quibus dubium non sit, per annos aliquot Canonem extitisse consecrandi, priusquam vllum adhuc de quatuor Euangelijs conscriptum esset.
units.tr: Nor does he prove anything by argument. Matthew and Mark indeed relate the Lord's Supper with those words left out; which is the most certain argument that a Canon should not be drawn from Matthew and Mark. It should rather be drawn from Paul and Luke, who supply those words. For the Canon must be woven for us from the full account, not from the place where something has been passed over. As for what he adds about those who, having only the Gospel of Matthew or Mark, did not consecrate rightly if the words were not complete among them: who would waste effort in answering that? Since it is certain that, if the words had been complete, Paul or Luke would have added nothing to them; and since among those people the Canon does not depend on any Gospel, so that there is no doubt they had a Canon of consecration for some years before any of the four Gospels had been written.

units.la: 2°. Non fauent Canoni vestro tres illi, Iustinus, Cyrillus, Emesenus: Canonem enim non referunt aut edunt vllum. Qui verò edunt, adhibent verba hæc: Iacobus, Clemens, Basilius, Chrysostomus, Ambrosius, in eoque damnant Canonem vestrum imperfecti. 3°. Si fuit à Petro Canon Romanus, antiquior est: Pauli Epistolæ, Lucæ Euangelio; hæc tum serò nimis illa supplentur à Paulo. Si fuit; primùm, de tempore totum illud incertum, an fuerit antiquior; tum, an à Petro fuerit. Imò à Petro fuit; ita narrant Leo nonus, & Aquinas. Qui homines Duo; quorum hic plus mille ducentis; ille plus mille quinquaginta annis Petro posterior. Quâ fide narrant? Suâ. Quid verò narrant? Leo nonus, Aliquid contulisse Ecclesiæ Romanæ Petri præsentium in memoriâ passionis recolendâ. Quid ad rem? Aquinas, In [hoc est enim] enim, de feranâ rem esse sed dicen-dum, dum; appositum in verbis formæ, secundum consuetudinem Romanæ Ecclesiæ, à B. Petro deriuatum. Dicendum hoc quidem non est ab homine tám recenti. Dicendum potius vobis cum Clemente vestro Pontifice Romano Petri ipsius Discipulo. Epistolâ fecundâ ad fratrem Domini. Sic ille, Sicut (inquit) à Beato Petro accepimus & omnium Apostolorum Patre, qui claves Regni cœlestis accepit, qualiter tenere debemus de Sacramentis, quæ geruntur in Sanctâ, ita ex ordine nos decet instruere. Habes, obiiuno[?] eius libro, ubi impleuit, ex Petri ipsius ore descriptum Canonem, in quo habentur verba quæ desunt in vestro, Quod pro vobis fran-gitur[?]; Eadem & in Iacobi Missâ sunt; Eadem sunt apud Paulum, vt iam tribus Apostolis nixi; Leonem vestrum nonum & Aquinatem, nihil faciamus.
units.tr: Second, those three, Justin, Cyril and Emesenus, do not favour your Canon: for they neither relate nor publish any Canon. But those who do publish one use these words: James, Clement, Basil, Chrysostom, Ambrose, and in so doing they condemn your Canon as imperfect. Third, if there was a Roman Canon from Peter, it is older than the Epistles of Paul and the Gospel of Luke; these then supplied those things far too late. If there was one: first, the whole matter is uncertain as to time, whether it was older at all; then, whether it was from Peter. "Indeed it was from Peter," say Leo the Ninth and Aquinas. Two men: the one more than twelve hundred years, the other more than one thousand and fifty years after Peter. On what authority do they relate it? Their own. But what do they relate? Leo the Ninth: "Peter contributed something to the Roman Church, to be recalled in the remembrance of the Passion, as he was present." What has this to do with the matter? Aquinas: "In [this is indeed] ... that the matter is to be said, but to be said..." (the text here is corrupt), "adapted in the words of the form, according to the custom of the Roman Church, derived from Blessed Peter." That is not a thing to be said by a man so recent. Rather, the thing to be said is what your Roman Pontiff Clement, a disciple of Peter himself, says to you, in his second letter to the brother of the Lord. Thus he: "As" (he says) "we have received from Blessed Peter and the Father of all the Apostles, who received the keys of the heavenly kingdom, how we ought to hold concerning the Sacraments that are performed in the Holy..., so it is fitting that we instruct in order." You have ... in his book, where he fulfilled it, the Canon written from Peter's own mouth, in which are contained the words which are missing from yours, "which is broken for you." The same words are also in the Mass of James; the same are in Paul; so, leaning now on three Apostles, let us make nothing of your Leo the Ninth and Aquinas.

units.la: Postremò, prudenter monés[?] verba inter se contraria non esse, quæ in Canone vestro, quæq; apud Paulum & Lucam. Non sanè verba; sed habere verba illa & carere illa, contraria inter se sunt. Est ergo contrarietas aliqua. Sed neque Matthæus & Marcus breuius, Paulus & Lucas fusius rem eandem scribunt: sed illi nec fusius nec breuius, nec omnino rem scribunt, pro nobis traditum: hi verò, penitus omissum ab illis (præsertim cum à Domino id accepissent) scribere voluerunt. Vos, quasi à Domino non esset, vel quasi quæ à Domino sunt, vobis curæ non essent, neglexistis; atque ita Canonem Missæ habetis, à Canone Scripturæ alienum.
units.tr: Finally, you wisely point out that the words in your Canon are not contrary to those in Paul and Luke. Words in themselves are not contrary; but to have those words and to lack them are contrary to each other. There is therefore some contrariety. Yet neither do Matthew and Mark write the same thing more briefly, nor Paul and Luke more fully: rather, the former do not write the matter either more fully or more briefly, nor do they write it at all as handed down to us; while the latter wished to write what had been wholly omitted by the former (especially since they had received it from the Lord). You, as if it were not from the Lord, or as if what is from the Lord were of no concern to you, have neglected it; and so you have a Canon of the Mass alien to the Canon of Scripture.

units.la: SAnderus vero, qui laudauit perduelles Anglos, fax fuit ad perduellionem Hyberniam, ipse in eâ perduellis, visus est Authoris dignus inprimis, quem laudatus vir Bellarminus, veteri amico suo commendaret. Sic sunt hodie Cardinales: si quis operam locet, vt in dubiâ hac luce, Visibilitatem adiuuet Monarchiæ Pontificiæ (quæ iam subit crepusculâ) quò infirmis oculis eâ paulò magis conspicua reddatur: sit maledicus, maleficus, sit fœdus proditor; tangens eum statim virgulâ suâ, exibit subitò Scriptor Aureus; Sententia eius verè aurea; quæ, si cor requiras, plumbea; si frontem, ferrea potiùs dicendæ erant. Sed dic serio; verène aureæ? Etiamne primis, quâ dicitur Regina; {a}Exercuisse officium docendi, & Euangelizandi hic in Angliâ, idque non minore authoritate, quàm Christus, aut Moses unquam fecerunt? quod omnes norunt ærugi-nosum esse men-dacium. dacium, Etiamne illa, quâ Subditi non tolerare Principem suum {b} iubentur, sed alium illi surrogare? At hoc prius, omnes diccbas naturaliter horrere: iam aurum est purum, postquam Midas ei digitum admouit. Et illa, quâ {c}Episcopos potestas asseritur, sententia sua Regem deponendi, & renouandi à Regno? Illa quoque, quâ Rex Sacerdote minor, nec vllam potestatem, nisi ab hominibus {d}habere dicitur? Quale verò lutum habetis Romae, si hoc vobis aurum videtur? Bene tamen, quòd videri dixit. Videtur enim aurum quibusdam, quicquid splendet; & sunt mendacia ibi quidem valdè splendida. Bene etiam, quòd omittit hæc aurea, qui tamen omittere solet, non nisi nugas & mendacia. Verè autem hæc quidem talia, & hîc iam Torti omisit locum habet. Perinde enim verum, Papam Rhinocerotis nasum habere, ac Reginam hic docendi officium exercuisse; perinde serum, Papam Ostiensi minorem, ac Regem Episcopo, exao[?] quòd Regem immunget. Quæ cur quis refellat, ita putida, vt sua ipsorum dilluitatis[?]?
