Satis est Lectori enarrasse, quales sibi sententiæ verè aureæ esse videantur, vt tu illi verè Aurum animal videaris, qualo[?] olim fuit Madaurensis, aut quale nuper nobis edidit vester {*}Atrebatensis, & Asinus si velis, sin malis Vitulus aureus.
units.tr: Sanderus, who praised the English rebels, was a torch to rebellion in Ireland, himself a rebel in it, and he seemed especially worthy of the author whom the praised man Bellarmine would commend to his old friend. So it is today with the Cardinals: if anyone takes the trouble, in this doubtful light, to help the Visibility of the Papal Monarchy (which is now entering twilight), so that it may be made a little more conspicuous to weak eyes, let him be a slanderer, a malefactor, a foul traitor: as soon as they touch him with their little rod, an Aureus Scriptor will come forth at once. His sentence is truly golden; yet if you look at its heart it is leaden, and if at its brow it should rather be called iron. But tell me seriously: are they truly golden? Even that first one, by which it is said that the Queen (who exercised the office of teaching and evangelising here in England, and that with no less authority than Christ or Moses ever did) ... which everyone knows is a verdigris-covered lie? Even that one by which subjects are ordered not to tolerate their Prince but to set another over him? But that first one, all of you would say, you naturally shudder at; now it is pure gold, since Midas has touched it with his finger. And that one by which power is asserted for bishops to depose the King by their sentence and to remove him from the kingdom? That one too, by which the King is said to be less than a priest, and to have no power except what he has from men? What sort of mud do you have in Rome, if this seems gold to you? Yet it is well that he said "seems." For whatever shines seems gold to some; and there are indeed lies there that are very splendid. It is also well that he omits these golden things, though he is wont to omit nothing but trifles and lies. Truly, these indeed are such, and here Tortus has now omitted his place. It is as true that the Pope has a rhinoceros's nose as that the Queen exercised the office of teaching here; equally late, that the Pope is less than the Bishop of Ostia, and that the King is subject to the Bishop, since he ... the King. Why should anyone refute things so foul that they wash away their own dirt? It is enough to have shown the Reader what kinds of opinions seem to be truly golden to them, so that you may appear to him as a true golden ass, like the one of old from Madaura, or like the one your Atrebatensis lately published for us; and an ass if you like, or if you prefer, a golden calf.

units.la: PRO uno illo fidei vestræ grauissimo dogmate, & offensem & Morum, supplicio affectos, cùm diceret Cardinalis idem erat, ac si diceret, pro solo Primatus, si pro hoc altera nuptiarum, & prolis Regiæ. At neque Duces dicendi erant duo illi, quos nemo sequeretur. Non sanè, sub Regina Elizabetha, sub quâ non vnum vllum reperias, pro causa Primatus, Capitis damnatum. Nuntiatorem verò agit Tortus[?]. Nec enim pro illa negat Apologiæ Author morte multatos, sed pro vno illo; idque non alio Teste euincit, quàm Moro ipso, qui, quod res erat, ingenuè fassus est, quodque omnes sciunt rerum nostrarum non imperitus. Credisne Cardinalis & Legeleergo[?] totidem verbis apud Cardinalem Capisanum? Confessionem hanc Mori ipsius {e}etiam pro Tribunali. Quòd nisi in negotio Successionis proterue se gessissent, non habitatum quidem fuisset de illis quæstio Capitalis. Illa ergo causa, nec sola fuit, nec primu;[?] Prima enim de prole Regis; accessit ad primam illam hanc tanquam ad cumulum; per quam tamen non stetit, quin superfutes[?] esse possent, absque primâ illâ fuisset. Malè ergo à vobis pro vnâ illâ causâ palsi dicuntur, quae non vna, quaeque si vlla fuit, in postremâ fuit cur paterentur.
units.tr: As for that one most grave dogma of your faith, with which offence and morals are punished: when the Cardinal said this, it was the same as if he said "for the sole primacy," and if for this the other of royal marriage and offspring. But those two men should not be called leaders, whom no one would follow. Certainly not under Queen Elizabeth, under whom you will find not one single man condemned to death for the cause of the Primacy. Tortus is acting as a messenger of falsehoods here. For the author of the Apology does not deny that men were punished with death for it, but for that one (the Oath of Supremacy?) ... and he proves this by no other witness than More himself, who, as the matter was, frankly confessed it, and who is not unversed in our affairs, as all know. Do you believe the Cardinal and ... in the very words, before Cardinal Capisanus? This confession of More's was made even before the tribunal. And if they had not behaved shamelessly in the matter of the Succession, the question of capital punishment would not have arisen concerning them. That cause, therefore, was neither the only one nor the first: for the first was about the king's offspring; this was added to the first as a kind of heaping-up; yet it did not stand in the way that they could be ... without the first. Therefore it is wrongly said by you that they suffered "for that one cause," which was not one, and which, if it was any, was the last cause for which they suffered.

units.la: Pergit autem etiam nugas agere, & revocari posse dicit causam principalem pro quâ palsi ad Primatum Pontificu. Et quid tandem eò revocari non potest? Audi verò Soritem. Successio in Regno, ad prolem; proles legitima, ad nuptias legitimas; nuptiae illae ad alias illegitimas; illae, ad irritam dispensationem; dispensatio ad potestatem soluendi; potestas soluendi ad Primatum. Vtinam ne in memore: Propius quidem absunt abiegna illae trabes in memore Pelio, à Bello Troiano, quàm Successionis negotium à Primatu. Eâdem operâ revoces ad Primatus causam, quam voles rebellionem; vel Sanderi in Hybernia; Nec enim tantum distat, vt non possit etiam ad Primatus causam revocari. Rebellio eius à Reginae depositione; depositio à Bullâ Papali; Bulla Papalis à potestate deponendi Principes; potestas à Primatu. Ex quo sequitur, vt Sanderus, qui mori maluit; quàm in Hybernia perduellem non agere, pro legitimâ potestate Summi Pontificis in Regnis disponendis, mortem oppetierit. Denique revoces eò, vel si libet, atomos Democriti, & earum concursum; est enim (vt Glossatores asserunt) causa causarum.
units.tr: He goes on to play the fool as well, and says that the principal cause for which they were charged with treason, the Primacy of the Pope, can be traced back. And what indeed cannot be traced back to that? Listen to the sorites: succession in the kingdom depends on offspring; legitimate offspring on lawful marriage; those marriages on other unlawful ones; those on an invalid dispensation; the dispensation on the power of loosing; the power of loosing on the Primacy. Would that it were not so in the case of the memorable... Those fir beams on Pelion are indeed nearer to the Trojan War than the matter of the succession is to the Primacy. By the same labour you may trace back to the cause of the Primacy whatever you like: the rebellion; or Sander's business in Ireland. For the distance is not so great that it cannot also be traced back to the cause of the Primacy. His rebellion depends on the deposition of the Queen; the deposition on the Papal bull; the Papal bull on the power of deposing princes; that power on the Primacy. From which it follows that Sander, who preferred to die rather than not act as a traitor in Ireland, died for the lawful power of the Supreme Pontiff in disposing of kingdoms. Finally, you may trace it back there, or if you like, to the atoms of Democritus and their concourse; for it is (as the glossators assert) the cause of causes.

units.la: Illud autem non optimè succedit Torto, quod de causâ carnali subijcit, vt ferè infœlix est semper in parallelis suis. Dixerat Apologiae Author potiùs copulam carnalem quàm Primatum Spiritualem Roffensi atque Moro, Martyrij causam fuisse. Non malè id dixerat. Hic Tortus; Carnalem ergo etiam Sanctissimo Domini Praecursoris fuisse Martyrij causam, cùm illata illi mors fuerit ab Herode, propter improbatum à Baptistâ liberè matrimonium eius illegitimum. Quo verbo ipse se miser cruentat. Quod enim illud (Torte) matrimonium? Annon cum fratris vxore? Annon hæc Baptistæ, vox, vitâ suâ constitit; Non licet tibi habere vxorem fratris tui? Quæ verò Mori causa atque Roffensis? Annon ex toto diametro contraria? Non licet tibi non habere vxorem fratris tui; Licet verò habere, Non licet dimittere. Vt, si iniusta fuerit Praecursoris mors, illorum sit iustissima; si ille Martyr; hoc, aliud quid, quod dicere nolo. Ille enim, ne fratris vxorem retineret, mortuus est: hoc, ne dimitteret. Ille, non licere hoc Herodi dixit: hij Henrico & licere; & vero etiam vt se-cus faceret, non licere. Poteratne Martyrum suorum causæ magis incommodare? Sed fatale hoc Torto malum, nihil vt ab eo torqueri contingat, quod multò in illum magis non possit retorqueri. Pergat igitur, & exempla talia nobis frequenter adducat. Valdè enim hæc Primatus causam agunt, grauissimum hoc fidei dogma mirum in modum roborant.
units.tr: But Tortus does not succeed well in what he adds about a carnal cause, as he is almost always unlucky in his parallels. The author of the Apology had said that it was the carnal union rather than the spiritual Primacy that was the cause of martyrdom for Rochester and More. He had not said this badly. Here Tortus: "Then the carnal union was also the cause of martyrdom for the most holy Forerunner of the Lord, since death was inflicted on him by Herod, on account of that unlawful marriage which John had freely condemned." In this word he wounds himself, poor man. For what is that "marriage", Tortus? Is it not with a brother's wife? Did not this word of John cost him his life: "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife"? But what is the cause of More and Rochester? Is it not wholly the opposite? "It is not lawful for you not to have your brother's wife; but it is lawful to have her, it is not lawful to dismiss her." So that, if the death of the Forerunner was unjust, theirs would be most just; if he was a martyr, so is this other, and something else which I do not wish to say. For the one died so that he would not keep his brother's wife; the other, so that he would not put her away. The one said to Herod that it was not lawful; these say to Henry that it is lawful; and indeed, even that he should act otherwise is not lawful. Could he have harmed the causes of his own martyrs more? But it is a fated evil for Tortus that nothing he twists should happen to be turned back on himself even more heavily. Let him therefore go on, and frequently bring us such examples. For these very things greatly advance the cause of the Primacy and wonderfully strengthen that most serious dogma of the faith.

units.la: Opponit Apologia in dogmate illo, Vni Roffensi, Anglicanæ tum Ecclesiæ consensum vniuersalem: Vniuersali magis, quàm vni credendum. Vniuersalis autem non solet esse nomen ingratum. Nota est Ecclesiæ; Titulus est Pontificis novo sensu, quem Gregorius hebetior non vidit, qui absolutè damnauit; Bonifacius tertius Gregorio acutior errorem statim deprehendit. Tertus tamen Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ assensum vniuersalem non probat; Quasi (inquit) Christiana Ecclesia vniuersitas ad vnius Insulæ angustias redigi debeat. Obtusè verò. Quis hoc postulat? Quis agit? Cum vno Roffensi, Anglicana Ecclesia vniuersa confertur. Æquum autem, vt vniuersi hic, vno plus sapiant. Quid hic homo importunus Christianam vniuersitatem ingerit? Nulla vniuersalis ibi memoria, nisi vt argumentum eâ commendatius redderetur, cùm inter notas vobis sit Ecclesia. Potè verò etiam, consensum hic Angliæ vniuersalem, nihil aliud fuisse calumniatur, quàm consensum, partim adulatorum, partim timidorum. Seuerus homo. Romæ enim adulatores exulant iampridem; nemo ibi blanditur Pontifici; Exosum à sæculo iam Pontificibus id genus hominum: quare diu est, ex quo vox ibi vlla assentatoris audita, inscriptio vlla assentatoris visa est. Non ibi legas inscriptum ita Pontifici librum, PAVLO V. VICE Dei; Quo ipso in titulo nescio an id aduertat Papa, fac tu ergo illum admoneas, impleuisse eum iam mensuram suam. Computari enim ibi posse ab eo numerum Bestiæ. Est enim (vix fausto id quidem omine) sed est tamen in noua illa illius inscriptione, nota ipsa, & numerus Antichristi.
units.tr: The Apology, against the single voice of Rochester, sets against that dogma the universal consent of the English Church at that time: that one should believe the universal rather than the single. Now "universal" is not usually an unwelcome name. It is a mark of the Church; it is a title of the Pope in a new sense, which the duller Gregory did not see, who condemned it outright; Boniface III, sharper than Gregory, at once detected the error. Tortus, however, does not accept the universal consent of the English Church, saying: "As if the universality of the Christian Church ought to be reduced to the narrow limits of one island." Clumsily indeed! Who demands this? Who argues it? The universal English Church is compared with the single voice of Rochester. It is fair that here the many should be wiser than the one. Why does this troublesome man thrust in the universality of the Christian Church? There is no mention of "universal" there, except to make the argument more commendable by it, since the Church is among the marks for you. Indeed he may also slander this universal consent of England as nothing other than the consent partly of flatterers, partly of the timid. A severe man! For at Rome flatterers have long been exiled; no one there fawns on the Pontiff; that kind of men has been hated by the Pontiffs for ages; so that for a long time no voice of a flatterer has been heard there, and no inscription of a flatterer has been seen. Let no one read there a book so addressed to the Pontiff: "PAUL V, IN THE PLACE OF GOD"; in this very title I do not know whether the Pope notices it. You, then, must warn him that he has now filled up his measure. For there it can be counted by him as "the number of the Beast." Indeed (a sign hardly fortunate, to be sure) there is in that new inscription the mark itself, and the number of Antichrist.

units.la: Abest etiam inde à Româ vis omnis atque metus. Timidus ibi nemo. Collegium Inquisitorum, nemini vel vim facit vel metum incutit. Liberum ibi cuiq; sententiam dicere, & quod in pectore habet securè promere. Credo autem, si sic liceret, qui nobiscum in religione sentirent, ne Romæ quidem desituros. turos: Dixisti verò, solito infortunio tuo, nostros adulatores. Nulli mortalium minùs. Qui Historias legerit nostrorum hominum, Parisiensis, Houedeni, Florilegi, Walsinghamij; non inuitus hoc de illis feret testimonium: etiam cum quidem cùm adularetur Pontifici Orbis Christianus penè totus, nostros, ac penè solos nostros, stetisse rectos; non valdè Illi incuriuâsse se: neque extare vsquam plus ingenuæ libertatis, quàm in libris & literis nostrorum hominum. Nisi illud forte fit; adulationu Pontifex capax non est, Rex est. Officium facit, imò minus officio, qui in gratiam Pontificis, strenuè agit Benedictium: Vbi quid pro Rege, contra Illum, dicitur, ibi statim interuenire solet adulatio: Verùm, qui vel Tonstallum cùm sciffet; vel Hetham (vt binos binis regerem, reliquos mittam) non credo dixisse homines ad assentationem compositos, nec minùs vel scientes officij, vel in officio constantes, quàm vel Morum vel Roffensem: & tamen secus quàm illi de Primata Regio sentientes. Sed illi post mutarunt in sententiâ; sed alij tamen perstiterunt. Binos itidem de illis nominabo, Latimerum & Ridleium; qui duo tam vel adulari spreuerunt, vel timere, vt viui potius flammis exuri mallent, quàm in Pontificis post Primatum consentire; Quod tamen Parasiti fere non faciunt.
units.tr: Moreover, from Rome all force and fear are far away. No one there is timid. The college of Inquisitors neither uses force against anyone nor instils fear. Everyone there is free to give his opinion and to speak out boldly what he has in his heart. I believe, however, that if it were permitted in this way, those who think with us in religion would not cease even at Rome. But you have said, with your usual ill luck, that our men are flatterers. Of all mortals, none less so. Whoever reads the histories of our men, Paris, Hoveden, Florence of Worcester, Walsingham, will bear this testimony about them not unwillingly: that when almost the whole Christian world was flattering the Pontiff, ours, and almost ours alone, stood upright; that they were not very careless of him; and that nowhere is there more of noble freedom than in the books and letters of our men. Unless perhaps it be this: that the Pontiff is incapable of flattery, the King is capable of it. He does a service, or rather less than a service, who, to win the Pontiff's favour, vigorously champions Bellarmine; whenever something is said for the King and against him, flattery is wont to step in at once. But whoever knew Tunstall, or Heath (to match two with two, I will pass over the rest), I do not believe spoke as men composed for flattery, nor less knowing their duty or constant in it, than More or Rochester, and yet holding views different from theirs about the Royal Primacy. But those later changed their opinion; yet others persisted. Likewise I will name two of them, Latimer and Ridley, who so scorned either to flatter or to fear that they preferred to be burned alive in the flames rather than consent, after the Primacy, to the Pontiff; which, however, parasites almost never do.

units.la: Verùm consensui nostro contra Roffensem, opponis pro illo consensum Ecclesiarum, idq; toto terrarum orbe diffusarum Toto terrarum orbe? vt nihil pudet? Quicquid vel in Asia est, vel Africa Ecclesiarum, quis nescit diu iam à Primatu vestro, non stetisse, non stare; sed neque eius quæ in Europa, partem maximam? De eâ verò, quæ reliquæ per Europam est, sufficit hoc nobis: qui primò iniquiores erant, cessisse post in sententiam nostram, & doctos exemplo nostro, multò iam & illos, maximâ ex parte vestrum Pontificis iugum excusisse. In vtràque quidem causâ Roffensis iacet. Siue enim Matrimonium Regis spectes, Diplomata habemus Academiarum (quæ tum erant per Europam maximè illustres) quatuor consensu vniuersali constat, Roffensem (secus multò quàm Baptistam) illegitimum cum fratris vxore matrimonium approbâsse: siue Primatus negotiû, post libros illos quin in Apologiâ nominantur, post libros alios à nostris editos, non diu cõtinuit se opinio illa intra vnius Insulæ angustias; diffudit se statim, magis magisque inualuit; vt passimiam & ubique, nec dogma fidei, nec vel extra fidem vullius vel gravitatis dogma, vel etiam ponderis habeatur.
units.tr: But against our consent against Rochester you set up in opposition the consent of the Churches, and that spread over the whole orb of the earth. Over the whole orb of the earth? Are you not ashamed of anything? Whatever Churches there are in Asia or Africa, who does not know that they have long not stood, and do not stand, under your Primacy; and that the greatest part of those in Europe do not either? As for the rest of those throughout Europe, this is enough for us: that they, who at first were more unfavourable, afterwards came over to our opinion, and that, instructed by our example, they, and by now very many of them, have for the most part thrown off the yoke of your Pontiff. In both matters Rochester stands. For if you look at the King's marriage, we have the judgments of the Academies (which at that time were the most illustrious throughout Europe); it is established by universal consent of four that Rochester (far less than John the Baptist) approved an unlawful marriage with a brother's wife. Or if you look at the business of the Primacy: after those books which are named in the Apology, and after other books published by our men, that opinion did not long remain within the narrow limits of one island; it spread at once, and gained strength more and more; so that everywhere and in all places it is held neither as a dogma of faith, nor as a matter of any weight or importance even outside the faith.

units.la: At de hijs, qui Duces hos secuti sunt ad simile supplicium, reducas calculum si sapis, longè absunt ab innumeris; numerus sunt; nec magnus. Illi verò ex Monachis pendè & plebejis, ad viginti quinque credo, vel circiter, idque Henrico regnante. Nam de Reginæ Regno, silere te iubeo. Alia illis mortis causa, qui passi sub eâ: ex eo quòd Primatum Papalem affirmaret, nemo in Capitis iudicium vocatus est. Quare qui de ullis sunt (hâc de re) sub Reginâ cæsis, libros vel Surij, vel Sanderi; præstat ad thus, & scombros ablegare: nihil enim in illis spectates, nisi sterquilinium horribile mendaciorum. Sin autem delectetur quis Carnificinæ spectaculo: adeat censeo, & spectet libros, qui de vestrâ Inquisitione extant, passim omni immanitate pleni: dolebunt illi oculi, dolebit & cor. Investrú verò, quæ de nobis subinde cuditis, figmenta vestra eximat quis, exempla nostra nec multa superunt si numerum annorum spectes; nec magna si pœnarum qualitatem; & de ijs, qui Roffensis vel Mori ducatum, subsecuti sunt, per annos plus sexaginta iam planè nulla.
units.tr: But as for those who followed these leaders to a similar punishment, if you are wise, you will reckon the tally: they are far from innumerable; they are a number, and not a large one. Those among them who were monks and common people, I believe about twenty-five, or thereabouts, and that under King Henry. For concerning the Queen's reign I order you to be silent. Those who suffered under her had other causes of death: no one was summoned to a capital trial merely for affirming the Papal Primacy. Therefore, whoever are slain on this account under the Queen, the books of Sanders or of Surius may be sent off to the incense and the mackerel; for you will find in them nothing but a horrible dunghill of lies. But if anyone delights in the spectacle of butchery, I advise him to go and look at the books that exist about your Inquisition, everywhere full of every savagery: those eyes will grieve, and the heart will grieve too. As for the fictions that you keep minting about us, let anyone take them away; our examples are not many if you look at the number of years, nor great if you look at the kind of punishments; and as for those who followed the lead of Rochester or More, over more than sixty years there is now plainly none at all.

units.la: QUod prima Regum cura religio sit, quòd eorum prima authoritas, ad res Religionis tum stabiliendas tum reformandas, subnotare voluit Author Apologiæ, loca aliquot Sacræ paginæ: ea sic refutat Tortus, ut quid calcibus valeat, potiùs quàm quid capite, sciat Lector; cursim scilicet. At stare debuit, & pedem figere, Arx ista causæ totius: vel si currendi illum libido incessebat, conijcere se penitus in fugam. Nam ne mouisse quidè pedem præstabat, quàm sic præter-propter causam cursum adornâsse. A more institutóque Israelis orditur Apologia; inde enim vim habet, atque nervos suos quæstio hæc omnis. In Israele enim populo suo, regnum instituit Deus, & Ecclesiam in Regno, ex mente suâ. Exemplum inde nobis sumendum est, cùm in Testamento Novo nullum habeamus. Nusquam ibi in unum coaluerunt Ecclesia & Imperium; procul se habuit Imperium ab Ecclesiâ. Quare quæ penes Regem in religione partes sint, inde nobis petendæ; ubi gemellæ quasi sunt, & amicè conspirant, Politia & Ecclesia; non ubi secedunt à se invicem. Ab illo igitur fonte Israelis arcesimus hanc causam, & ab eo exemplo, (vbi simul sunt, vbi Ecclesia in Regno) Ecclesiæ, Regnique nostri regimen informamus. In Israele autem, nondum os reperi tam durum, quod negare etiam auderet, præcipuas in re religionis partes, penes Regem extitisse: vel vno hoc argumento, quòd per sacræ Historiæ seriem totam, mutato novi Regis animo, mutata semper est facies Religionis. Eáque in Religione mutatio Regi semper ascribitur, quasi factum eius. Nec Pontifices vnquam vel præstare poterant, vt fieret mutatio in melius; vel ne fieret in peius, impedire. Penes eos autem, si Religionis tum Summa fuisset, aliquis aliquando Pontifex, etiam Rege secus affecto, præstitisset hoc tamen; vt cultum Dei illibatum, pars aliqua populi saltem, retineret.
units.tr: That the first care of kings is religion, and that their first authority extends to establishing and reforming matters of religion, the author of the Apology wished to point out by citing several passages of Holy Scripture. Tortus refutes these in such a way that the reader learns what they are worth in the heel rather than in the head: that is, he runs through them hurriedly. But that stronghold of the whole cause ought to have stood firm and planted its foot; or, if the urge to run was upon him, he should have fled entirely. For it was better not even to have moved a foot than to have launched a race that barely touches the cause. The Apology begins from the custom and institution of Israel, for this whole question derives its force and sinews from there. For God established a kingdom and a Church within the kingdom among his own people Israel, according to his own purpose. From this we must take an example, since in the New Testament we have none. Nowhere there did Church and empire grow together into one; the empire kept far away from the Church. Therefore the parts the king has in religion must be sought from there, where polity and Church are, as it were, twins and agree in friendship, not where they separate from one another. So from that fountain of Israel we draw this cause, and from that example (where they are together, where the Church is in the kingdom) we shape the government of our Church and kingdom. Now in Israel I have not yet found a face so hard as to dare to deny that the principal parts in matters of religion belonged to the king; and this argument alone is enough: throughout the whole series of sacred history, as the mind of each new king changed, the face of religion always changed with it. And this change in religion is always ascribed to the king, as his deed. Nor could the high priests ever either bring about a change for the better or prevent one for the worse. Yet if the supreme authority in religion had lain with them, some high priest at some time, even with a king ill-disposed, would have achieved this at least: that some part of the people would keep God's worship unimpaired.

units.la: Exemplum primum Regis Iosaphat, cuius impressa in eo capite non leuia vestigia, quam fecerunt præcipuæ partes in religione renovanda. Hic ita properè transcurrit noster nomen, vt nec nomen eo loco legere posset Ecclesia. Subsistat paululùm; & legat, non totidem syllabis; sed Ecclesiam tamen. Quid est enim Ecclesia, quàm populus ad Deum verum reuocatus? Legitur verò versu illo, Egressus Rex ad populum de Berseabe usque ad montem Ephraim, reuocauit eos ad Dominum Deum Patrum suorum. Reuocauit ad Deum, id est, fecit, vt essent Ecclesia; fecit autem id authoritate suâ Regiâ, quâ & constituit ipse post ad versum ectianum Iudices in Ierusalem de Leuitis, Sacerdotibus, & Principibus familiarum ex Israel, ad causam Domini iudicandam, vbi quæstio de Lege, & Cæremoniis. Quæ verò maior Authoritas, quàm dandi, delegandi Iudices ad res Sacras? Vide verò, vt cursim legerit Tortus. Non enim, distinguitur ibi (vt ait officium Regis ab officio Pontificis. Nimis festinauit. Pro regis quidem distinguitur. Non enim Zabadias filius Ismael, Rex, sed Dux in domo Iuda: quare Præfectus modò Regis ad res Regni. Idem ille Rex ad res Domini, (illis quos ostauo versu constituerat Iudicibus) Pontificem præsidere iusit: vtrique prouinciam suam discriminauit; Duci, quæ ad Rempublicam: Pontifici, quæ ad Religionem. Quo facto, non minùs hæc quàm illa docuit, ad Regis inprimis curam pertinere, cùm & reducere populum ad Dei cultum, & reuocato Iudices dare, authoritate suâ posset, & inter Iudices, causas dispertiri, & quû præsideat, & ad quas, iure Regio præscribere. Verba enim illa lectionis vulgatæ, quæ ad Regis officium pertinent, quæ tibi currenti aciem perstrinxerunt, nusquam in fonte[?] sunt. Res Regū ibi dicuntur, quæ scilicet spectabant ad terrenam politiam: ut Dei, quæ ad Cœlestem. Coniungi autem debent Regnum & Ecclesia; confundi non debent: distinctas ut causas habent, ita & fora habere, sed sub Rege habere, nec minus Ecclesiam, quàm Regnum; cuius authoritate atque imperio sedent Iudices, præsident Amarias hys, Zabadias illis; cognoscit de causis utraque ad forum suum pertinentibus, sed Rege tamen iubente; ut utrobique locum habeat illud: Si Iudex es, cognosce; si Rex es, iube.
units.tr: The first example is King Jehoshaphat, whose deeds in that chapter left no slight traces, the principal parts he played in renewing religion. Here our author hurries past so quickly that the Church could not even read the name in that place. Let him pause a little, and read, not by so many syllables, but the Church nonetheless. For what is the Church but the people called back to the true God? It is read in that verse: "The king went out to the people from Beersheba to the hill of Ephraim, and called them back to the Lord God of their fathers" (2 Chron. 19). He called them back to God, that is, he made them to be the Church; and he did this by his royal authority, by which he also afterwards appointed judges in Jerusalem, from the Levites, the priests and the heads of families of Israel, to judge the cause of the Lord, where the question concerns the Law and the ceremonies. What greater authority is there than to give and delegate judges for sacred matters? But see how hurriedly Tortus read. For there he does not distinguish, as he says, "the office of the king from the office of the priest." He was too hasty. There is indeed a distinction, but for the king's part. Zebadiah the son of Ishmael was not king but ruler in the house of Judah: therefore he was the king's prefect for the affairs of the kingdom. That same king, for the things of the Lord (for those judges whom he had appointed in the eighth verse), ordered the high priest to preside: he divided their provinces between them, the one for the commonwealth, the other for religion. By doing this he taught no less the one than the other, that the care of the king in the first place pertains to bringing the people back to the worship of God, and that he could, by his own authority, both recall the people and appoint judges, and divide the causes among the judges, and prescribe by royal right who should preside and over what. For those words of the common reading which concern the king's office, which struck your eye as you ran through them, are nowhere in the source. "The affairs of the king" are said there, meaning those which pertained to the earthly polity, as "the affairs of God" pertain to the heavenly. Kingdom and Church ought indeed to be joined; they ought not to be confused. As they have distinct causes, so they have distinct courts, but both are under the king, and the Church no less than the kingdom; by whose authority and command the judges sit, Amariah presides over those matters and Zebadiah over those; each court takes cognisance of the causes pertaining to its own jurisdiction, but at the king's command; so that in both places that saying holds: "If you are a judge, examine; if you are a king, command."

units.la: Repurgâsse corruptelas, sustulisse[?] abusus non negat Dauidem; de loco cæcato[?] paululum hæsitat. Ubi mysticè id forte intellexit, quod alibi sæpe dicitur ad literam. Locus est de cæco & claudo tollendo per Dauidem; nimirum si ad Dauidem spectet, de templo cæcum, & claudum tollere; spectare & illud ut omnes abusus tollat. Nec enim alunde abusus existere, quàm vel de inscitiâ, quòd cæci sint homines; vel de incuriâ, quòd in officio claudicent. Enimuerò, & de aliis sæpe, & præcipuè de eâ (quòd Populus adoleuit[?] in Excelsis) corruptelâ per Reges non sublatâ, totiès, tam clarâ voce de Regibus queruntur Sacræ literæ, ut locus nullus negationi relictus sit. Non negat ergo, Regi Tortus id ex officio incumbere, ut etiam quæ in doctrinâ sunt abusus, & corruptelas tollat, sed post Ecclesiæ declarationem. Nos verò, citra declarationem omnem, ubi repurgatæ sunt corruptelæ per Reges, docemus: Tortus verò loca aliquot apponere debuit, ubi illa Ecclesiæ declaratio præcesserit: quæ nisi præcesserit, Regis nullum tum erat (ut videtur) officium.
units.tr: He does not deny that David purged corruptions and removed abuses; he hesitates a little over the "blinded place." Perhaps he understood this mystically, which is often said elsewhere "according to the letter." The passage concerns the removal by David of "the blind and the lame" (2 Sam. 5): namely, if it looks to David to remove from the temple "the blind and the lame," it looks also to his removing every abuse. For abuses arise from no other source than either from ignorance, because men are blind, or from carelessness, because they limp in their duty. Indeed, Holy Scripture complains so often and so clearly of kings, both about this and often about that corruption (that "the people grew up on the high places") which was not removed by the kings, that no place is left for denial. Tortus therefore does not deny that it falls to the king's office to remove abuses and corruptions even in matters of doctrine, but only after the Church's declaration. We, however, without any declaration at all, teach that where corruptions have been purged by kings; but Tortus ought to have set down some passages where that declaration of the Church went before: and unless it had gone before, the king then had (so it seems) no office.

units.la: Sed Regi erat in promptu excusatio: Non iussulis; Ecclesia enim non declarauit. Ecclesia proinde culpanda, non Rex, qui nihil mouere debet, nec excelsa diruere[?], nisi postquam id ita faciendum declarauit Ecclesia. Atqui Regi id semper, Ecclesia nunquâ vitio datum legimus quòd Excelsa fleterint[?]. Regi ergo, siue declaret hoc, siue non declaret, etiam ante Ecclesiæ declarationem, id ex officio munus incumbit, déque eo neglecto Deo rationem redditurus est. Tota igitur mentio declarationis Ecclesiæ, præterquam quòd fictitia est, hîc etiam est intempestiua.
units.tr: But the king had an excuse ready: "I did not command it; the Church did not declare it." So the Church, not the king, is to be blamed, since the king ought to move nothing, nor overthrow the high places, until the Church has declared that this must be done. But we read that the king was always blamed for it, and that the Church was never blamed for having overthrown the high places. Therefore for the king, whether he declares this or does not declare it, even before the Church's declaration, the duty of his office lies upon him, and he will have to give account to God for neglecting it. The whole mention of "the Church's declaration," therefore, apart from being fictitious, is here also out of place.

units.la: Reportasse Arcam agnoscit, sed Sacerdotes vna idem hoc fecisse cum Rege. Quid si autem vna? Regis in eo partes praecipuae. Quis interfuit non quaeritur, sed quis praefuit: De Primatu enim agitur. Praeeunte hoc Illius imperio factum, nec vel ante vel omnino factum, nisi postquam Regis ad illud authoritas interuenit. Dein Ludendi veniam Regi facit, idque dicit humilitatis fuisse. At Ludere, humilitatis non est, gaudij potius. Tum, si humilitatem prae se ferre voluit, post Arcam ei, non ante, saltandum erat; a fronte habenda erat Arca, non a tergo. Nam, quod ante saltauit, id eo potius videtur fecisse, ut se illis praeire viam doceret, & Primatum tenere in negotio Arcae reportandae; gaudere autem & exaltare, quod sic teneat. Nam quod caute admodum Tortus subnectit, Non licuisse tamen Davidi Arcam contingere: quis id affirmauit? Nec Regi quidem Nostro licet, nec vlli, aut Sacra administrare, aut attrectare quicquam, quod potestatis sit mere Sacerdotalis, ut sunt Liturgia, Conciones, Claues, Sacramenta. Arcam figant loco suo Reges. Attingant post illi, quos ea cura tangit, ex suscepto munere Ministerij sui.
units.tr: He acknowledges that the king "brought back the Ark," but says that the priests did the same thing together with the king. What if they did it together? The king's part in it was the principal one. The question is not who took part, but who presided: for the matter concerns primacy. It was done at his command, going before them, and not before or at all unless the king's authority had intervened in it. Then he grants the king the pardon of "dancing," and says that this was a sign of humility. But dancing is not humility, but rather joy. Moreover, if he wished to display humility, he ought to have danced after the Ark, not before it; the Ark ought to have been carried in front, not behind. For what he danced before it seems rather to have done in order to show that he was leading them along the way and held the primacy in the business of bringing back the Ark, and rejoiced and exulted because he held it so. As for what Tortus, very cautiously, adds, "Yet it was not lawful for David to touch the Ark": who affirmed this? Neither is it lawful for our king, nor for anyone, either to administer sacred things or to handle anything that belongs purely to priestly power, such as the liturgy, sermons, keys, sacraments. Let kings fix the Ark in its place. Afterwards let those touch it whom that care concerns, by virtue of the office of ministry they have undertaken.

units.la: Ad Reges etiam spectare fatetur, edificare Templa, Dedicare, sed ad Regum Magnificentiam. Esto autem ut Magnificentia fuerit in edificando: at in Deo dicando aliud quiddam fuit, quam Magnificentia Dedicare enim Deo Templa, actus est primarius, neque cuiusquam, nisi cuius partes in Religione prima. Dedicatum autem a Salomone Templum, non magis negari potest, quam edificatum. Nec (quod Tortus concedit) interfuit modo solennitati illi cum reliquo populo, ex pietate, sed & praefuit ex authoritate. Nec enim sine summa authoritate praestari poterant illa, quae in persona sua praestitit Salomon in illis Solennijs. Negare non poterat haec, ita in luce posita. Negat ergo post attigisse in Templo munus Sacerdotale, quod & nos pariter cum eo negamus. Tum, ex eo sequi dicit, ut Primatus Regi nulla ratione conueniat. Sed perperam. Quae enim in Templis fiunt a Sacerdotibus virtute officij sui, fere sunt Ordines, in quibus quid facit Pontifex, quod non idem facit Sacerdos quilibet? Missam decantat, Creatorem creat, aspergillum tractat, denique, in quo insistit Tortus, thuribulum quoq; & thus adolet non minus simplex Sacerdos, quam Papa Paulus ipse. Primatus Papalis extra Templum fere est: In Templo parificantur ei multi. Sed neque in ijs quæ Pontificalis sunt muneris Regi ius facimus, nec incensum adolere sinimus, nec id facere, cuius typus tum erat incensum. Bone Deus! quàm hæc sæpe à vobis iactata, quàm extra rem semper: pudeat ita coccyzare sine fine. Semel autem habe hac de re sententiam nostram. Non nos Regi potestatem tribuimus, quam habere voluit Osiæ; solam illam quam Iosiæ habuit; Iosiæ, non Osiæ Primatum vindicatum imus.
units.tr: The author concedes that building temples and dedicating them belong to kings, but to the king's magnificence. Granted that magnificence was involved in the building; yet dedicating a temple to God was something else than magnificence. To dedicate temples to God is a primary act, and belongs to no one except those whose role in religion is first. That Solomon dedicated the temple cannot be denied any more than that he built it. Nor (as Tortus grants) was he present at that solemnity merely with the rest of the people, out of piety; he also presided by authority. For those things which Solomon performed in person at those solemn rites could not have been done without the highest authority. Tortus could not deny this, since it is so plainly before us. He therefore denies that Solomon then touched a priestly office in the temple, and we too deny this along with him. Then he says that it follows from this that primacy is in no way fitting for the king. But this is wrong. For the things done in temples by priests by virtue of their office are mostly orders of service; and what does the high priest do that any ordinary priest does not do too? He sings the Mass, creates the Creator, handles the aspergillum; finally, the thing Tortus insists on, he also swings the censer and burns incense, no less than any simple priest, or Pope Paul himself. Papal primacy lies mostly outside the temple; within the temple many are made equal to him. But we do not grant the king a right in those things which belong to the pontifical office, nor do we allow him to burn incense, nor to do that which incense then signified as a type. Good God! How often these things have been boasted of by you, and how always beside the point; shame on such endless cuckoo-calling. But once and for all, hear our opinion on this matter. We do not ascribe to the king the power which he wished Osee to have, but only that which Josiah had; we claim for Josiah, not for Osee, the primacy.

units.la: De Libro legis, nouum Torto videtur, quòd de nouo repertus dicitur. At si in manibus tum Liber ille fuisset, non dicam omni populo, sed vel ipsis Sacerdotibus; si non nouus planè; quid attinebat referri in Historiam Sacram; quòd dum aliam rem ageret Helkias Sacerdos, reperisset Librum Legis? Quorsum etiam ita obstupescit Rex, si ab antiquo illi notus, aut cur ita de illo loquitur, Liber ille qui repertus est? Denique quorsum ad Prophetisam ablegat Sacerdotem Helkiam, consulturum eam de verbis Libri, nisi quia etiam Sacerdoti ipsi ignotus & planè nouus? Quâ de re non inuitus credo audiet Tortus Caietanum suum. Non nouum illi, quod Torto. Sic enim ille. Tanto tempore neglecta erant diuina tempore Manassis, vt Liber legis tanquam res nouiter inuenta scribatur. Libro sic reperto, à Rege lecto, consulta de eius sensu Prophetisâ, non Pontifice, non expectata declaratione Ecclesiæ, indixit Rex Conuentum, in eo iubet recitari Librum, recitato fœdus nouum init cum Domino; populum quoque ad fœdus adiurauit. Tum præcipit ipsi Pontifici Rex, reliquisque Secundi ordinis Sacerdotibus, vt eijciant è Templo, atque exurant vasa omnia quæ Baali Sacra fuerant, vt Excelsa demoliantur. Mandauit post de Pascha nouo faciendo, denique de Religione totâ in integrum reformandâ. Et quid hîc est (ait Tortus noster) pro Primatu Regis in rebus Ecclesiasticis & Spiritualibus? Puto res Spirituales & Ecclesiasticas esse Cætum indicere, fœdus de Religione sancire, peregrinum cultum abolere, verum, mandato suo instaurare; & in his omnibus cùm præcipit Pontifici Rex, paret Regi Pontifex, nihilne hoc apud Tortum pro Regis Primatu? Tortum nihil moror; apud alios non tortos, sed rectos, rectì amantes, non dubito, quin plurimum sit in exemplo Iofia pro Primatu Regio, nec alium quærimus quàm Iofiæ, nec alius vindiciæ sunt, in totâ Apologiâ.
units.tr: The Book of the Law seems new to Tortus, because it is said to have been found anew. But if that book had been in the hands of all the people then, I will not say of the people only, but even of the priests themselves; and if it was not altogether new, what was the point of recording in sacred history that while Helkiah the priest was doing something else, he had found the Book of the Law? Why also is the king so astonished, if it was known to him from of old, or why does he speak of it thus: "that book which has been found"? Finally, why does he send the priest Helkiah to the prophetess to consult her about the words of the Book, unless because the book was unknown even to the priest himself and entirely new? On this point, I believe, Tortus will not be unwilling to hear his Cajetan. It was not new to him, as it is to Tortus. For he says: "The divine things had been so neglected in the time of Manasseh that the Book of the Law is written as a thing newly discovered." With the book thus found and read by the king, and the prophetess, not the high priest, consulted about its meaning, and without waiting for a declaration from the Church, the king called an assembly; at it he orders the book to be read; after it had been read he made a new covenant with the Lord; he also bound the people to the covenant by oath. Then the king commands the high priest himself and the other priests of the second order to cast out of the temple and burn all the vessels which had been made for Baal, and to pull down the high places. He afterwards commanded the making of a new Passover, and finally the complete reformation of the whole religion. "And what is this here" (says our Tortus) "for the king's primacy in ecclesiastical and spiritual matters?" I think that to call a sacred assembly, to ratify a covenant concerning religion, to abolish foreign worship, and to restore the true worship by his own command, are spiritual and ecclesiastical matters; and in all these things, when the king commands the high priest, the high priest obeys the king. Is this nothing to Tortus concerning the king's primacy? I will not trouble myself with Tortus; but I do not doubt that among others who are not twisted but upright, who love uprightness, there is very much in the example of Josiah for royal primacy, and we seek no other than Josiah, and there is no other defence in the whole Apology.

units.la: Redintegrati cum Deo fœderis, partes præcipuas penes Regem fuisse, Rex Iofias testis omni exceptione maior. Ezekias hoc idem fecit, authorque fuit Sacerdotibus ut facerent. Idem etiam Asa[?], idque interposito Iuramento. De Nehemiâ, quòd illius tempore Reges non fuerint, puerilis is fere Catullus est. Nam si Nehemias id potuit, qui Dux tantùm, cuique delegata tantùm potestas; annon Rex multò magis? Nehemias verò Author fœderis illius, & primo loco signavit. Admittit ergo pertinere ad Reges, non tamen ex aliâ ratione, quàm quod Reges in causâ sint, cur populus à Deo recedat per Idololatriam. Etiamne id locum habet in Regibus, quos nominaui, Asâ, Ezekiâ, Iosiâ? An vel recesserunt ipsi à Domino, vel populo unquam causâ fuerunt recedendi? Quæ hæc vesania est? Pontifices verò, quos penes summa potestas est Terto, cur non opposuerunt se murum pro domo Israel? cur non populo fuerunt in causâ, ne recederent? An est illorum potestas in Religione maximâ, nec vim habent tamen, vel retinendi in officio populi, vel ad officium revocandi? Reges sinunt abducere à Deo populum, ipsi nisi mandauerit Rex nunquam reducunt? Passim enim per Fastos Sacros quod in Religione fit, à Rege fieri dicitur, Regis factum esse; Pontifices haud unquam, nisi ex Regis mandato. Nam de isto per Iehoiadam Pontificem fœdere, quis non videt quàm ineptum? non enim ab illo ictum, nisi ut Regis tum Protectore. Rex Ioas puer septennis, Iehoiada autem Custos Regis, optimo iure Custos, ut cui vitam cum Regno deberet Rex. Quod verò factum ibi, Regiâ Authoritate factum, quæ tum penes Pontificem; eo, (cum per ætatem Rex nondum posset) Regni res procurante.
units.tr: That the principal parts in renewing the covenant with God belonged to the king, King Josiah is a witness beyond all exception. Hezekiah did the same, and was the author for the priests to do likewise. Asa did the same too, and that with an oath interposed. As for Nehemiah, the claim that there were no kings in his time is a childish piece of trifling, almost a Catullus-like absurdity. For if Nehemiah could do it, who was only a governor, to whom power had only been delegated; would not the king much more? Nehemiah, indeed, was the author of that covenant, and signed first. He therefore admits that it pertains to kings, yet not for any other reason than that kings are the cause why the people fall away from God through idolatry. Does this hold also for the kings I have named, Asa, Hezekiah, Josiah? Did they either fall away from the Lord themselves, or ever become the cause of the people's falling away? What madness is this? But the priests, in whom Tortus places the supreme power, why did they not set themselves as a wall for the house of Israel? Why were they not a cause to the people that they should not fall away? Or is their power in the greatest matter of religion such that they have no force either to keep the people in their duty or to recall them to duty? Do the kings allow the people to be led away from God, and do they themselves never bring them back unless the king has commanded it? For throughout the sacred annals whatever is done in religion is said to be done by the king, to be the king's deed; the priests never do anything except by the king's command. For as for that covenant made through the priest Jehoiada, who does not see how absurd it is? For it was not struck by him except as the king's protector. King Joash was seven years old, and Jehoiada was the guardian of the king, rightly so, as the king owed him his life along with his kingdom. But what was done there was done by royal authority, which at that time rested with the priest, since the king, being still too young, was managing the affairs of the kingdom.

units.la: Ad Regem pertinet, intrare Templum ipsum, Serpentem ibi aeneum confringere, quem fecerat Moses, cùm abijsset in superstitionem serpens ille; cùm (quod vos imaginibus vestris quotidiè facitis) thurificaret ei populus. Rectè factum hoc (ait Tortus;) Causam addit, & addit causæ, Quoniam (inquit) populus ad Idololatriam propensus, Serpenti illi, ut Numini cuidam, Sacrificia offerre cœperat. Non cœperat; Non offerre Sacrificia: Non ut Numini. Omnia hæc additamenta Torti (non minùs quàm Serpens ille) tortuosi, & in omnem se partem rotantis ut euadat. Non cœperat. Verba enim Scripturæ sunt, Quin usq; ad illum diem; de quibus, ita Cardinalis Caietanus. Perseuerantia describitur huius abusionis usque ad tempus Ezekiæ, ad manifestandam magnanimitatem Ezekiæ, ad exterminandum toleratas superstitiones tanto tempore. Non Sacrificia offerre. Suffitus enim non est Sacrificium, nedum Sacrificia. Non ut Numini. Plus multo candoris in {b}Caietano. Venerabantur Serpentem illum, thurificantes illi, ratione accepti beneficij, non adorando illum ut Deum, sed honorando ut beneficium signum datum à Deo. Quæ veneratio superstitiosa erat, utpote præter legem divinam, & propterea Ezekias abstulit. Falsa ergo causa hæc Torti. Verùm dicendum illi erat, de authoritate, quâ fecit Rex, non de causâ propter quam fecit. Nam si authoritate Rex propriâ atque suâ resecare potest superstitiones, quas & Sacerdotes ipsi tolerant, & à longo tempore tolerârant; si Serpentes æneos à Mose factos, Dei ipsius iussu factos, miraculis insignes, Christi denique typos comminuere, postquam abierunt jam in abusum; parum aberit à Primatu authoritas illa Regia, si sic pertingat in Templum, atq; ista ibi tractet tam Ecclesiastica. Subest autem hic & alia fraus Torti.
units.tr: It pertains to the king to enter the temple itself and break in pieces the bronze serpent which Moses had made, when that serpent had turned into superstition, when the people burned incense to it, as you do daily with your images. Tortus says this was rightly done; he adds a cause, and adds to the cause: "since," he says, "the people, prone to idolatry, had begun to offer sacrifices to that serpent as to some divinity." It had not begun; it did not offer sacrifices; "not as to a divinity." All these additions of Tortus are (no less than that serpent) twisting and turning on every side so as to escape. "It had not begun": for these are the words of Scripture, "Quin usque ad illum diem" (for up to that day); concerning which Cardinal Cajetan says thus: "The persistence of this abuse is described up to the time of Hezekiah, to show Hezekiah's greatness of mind, and to root out the superstitions tolerated for so long a time." "Not to offer sacrifices": for burning incense is not a sacrifice, much less sacrifices. "Not as to a divinity": there is much more candour in Cajetan. "They venerated that serpent, burning incense to it, on account of the benefit received, not worshipping it as God, but honouring it as a sign of a benefit given by God. This veneration was superstitious, as being beyond the divine law, and for that reason Hezekiah removed it." This cause, then, of Tortus is false. But he ought to have spoken about the authority by which the king acted, not about the cause on account of which he acted. For if by his own proper authority the king can cut away superstitions which even the priests themselves tolerate, and had tolerated for a long time; if he can crush bronze serpents made by Moses, made by God's own command, distinguished by miracles, and finally types of Christ, once they have passed into abuse; that royal authority would be not far from primacy, if it so extended into the temple and handled there such matters as ecclesiastical. But another deceit of Tortus lies here as well.

units.la: A Serpente enim confracto, ad Idololatras delabitur pœnis afficiendos, id est à rebus, ad personas. Quasi Serpens Idololatra esset, non Idolum. Personas ita demum subjicit gladio Regis, si priùs ab Ecclesiâ damnatæ sint. Sed reuocamus ad Res. Plus enim multò in Res ipsas ius habere, quàm agere cum personis. Nec tamen damnauit, vel declarauit Ecclesia Serpentem æneum confringendum. Ezekias ipse idem damnauit, & declarauit, idem confregit. Semper infereit nobis Ecclesiæ sententiam, de suo, nunquam locum ei rei adducit ulum. Hàc ergo etiam ratione seruiunt Reges Deo, ut Res ipsæ corrigant, & si ita opus, redigant in pulverem, atque ita non in personis modò, sed & in rebus Primatum tenent.
units.tr: For by breaking the serpent he slides on to punish the idolaters, that is, from things to persons, as if the serpent were an idolater and not an idol. He subjects persons to the sword of the king only if they have first been condemned by the Church. But let us return to the things. For the right over the things themselves is far greater than the right to act against persons. Yet the Church neither condemned nor declared that the bronze serpent must be broken. Hezekiah himself condemned and declared it, and himself broke it. Tortus always brings in the sentence of the Church from his own resources and never adduces any place of Scripture for it. Kings therefore also serve God in this way, that they correct the things themselves and, if need be, reduce them to dust; and so they hold the primacy not only over persons but also over things.

units.la: Ad Regem pertinet missio Sacerdotum, ut erudiant populum, & unà cum Sacerdotibus Principum, ut quod illi scientiâ docent, hij authoritate sauciant; quos illi scientiâ docere non possunt, hij authoritate coercent. Quid hoc verò aliud est quàm reformareformationem publicam instituere? Quorsum enim apparatu hoc tanto opus erat, nisi posteriora Asæ tempora, nescio quid deformitatis contraxissent, quam Filius eius Iosaphat, missione hac tam solenni reformare instituit? Studium hic Tortus vidit & Zelum in Rege, Primatum non vidit. At, Mittere, solebat authoritatis esse, non Zeli: Et Mittens eo ipso maior Misso, quòd Mittat eum, qua ratione Pater Filio maior est. Zelus autem in utroque par, Misso & Mittente. Non ultima quidem Primatus pars in Pontifice, Missiones eius. Verùm in Pontifice sic quidem: postquam transijt in Regem, Authoritas statim omnis euanescit, Zelus succedit. Iam verò, ut Missiones eleuet, calido nimis Consilio docendi munus ad Primatum proprie pertinere autumat. Vereor etiam ne tristi successu. Nam si ex quo, docendi munere defungi desierunt Pontifices, Primatus ad eos proprie non pertinuit, Primatum qui potest capere capiat. Vix enim credo Torti atanus, Pontificem vllum docentem audiuit. Credo autem, Tortum poenitebit dicti, sic enim Propheta Pontifice maior; sic Sanctissimo Domino multi Dominicani, quibus à docendo, cognomen Praedicatorum; sic denique maiores erunt, quos vt docerent misit Iosaphat, quàm Rex ipse qui misit. Nam nos quidem hic in Gubernando Primatum ponimus, non docendo; & Regem non Doctorem summum, sed Gubernatorem dicimus, vt iam dirimi posit lis, & hercisci inter Regem & Pontificem: Pontifex vt Summus sit in docendi munere quod proprie pertinet ad Primatum suum: in Gubernandi Rex, quod ille solum sibi vendicat vt suum; nec illum alterum Pontificalem docendi inuadet vnquam. Sed vereor vt stet Pontifex huic Torti Primatus proprio; & aegrè ferat praereptum sibi alterum illum improprium Gubernandi. Quod autem adijcit auctarij loco, de vltimo eius supplicio, qui Pontifici non paret (addere tamen debuit, iuxta Dei legem respondentis) id verò, pro eo non facit, contrà potiùs. Dicat enim: qui ita Pontifici non paret, in eum vbi aget Pontifex? apud Quem Reus sistetur? Quis sententiam feret? Quis capite plectet immorigerum? Est, qui spreto Pontifici ius dicet; Is ipse, quisquis est, per me, Primatum ferat.
units.tr: It belongs to the king to send priests to instruct the people, and, together with the priests, to send princes, so that what the former teach by knowledge, the latter wound by authority; what the former cannot teach by knowledge, the latter restrain by authority. But what else is this than to set up a public reformation? For why was such a great preparation needed, unless the later times of Asa had contracted some deformity, which his son Jehoshaphat undertook to reform by this so solemn sending? Here Tortus saw the zeal in the king, but did not see the primacy. But to send was wont to be a matter of authority, not of zeal; and the one who sends is greater than the one sent by that very fact that he sends him, in the way that a father is greater than a son. Zeal, however, is equal in both, in the one sent and in the one sending. Certainly the primacy in the Pontiff is not the least part, namely his sendings. But in the Pontiff it is so: once it has passed over to the king, all authority at once vanishes and zeal succeeds. Now indeed, to lift up these sendings, he rashly claims in his heated counsel that the office of teaching properly belongs to the primacy. I fear also that it will end badly for him. For if, since the Pontiffs ceased to discharge the office of teaching, the primacy has not properly belonged to them, let him who can take the primacy take it. For I hardly believe that Tortus has ever heard any Pontiff teaching. I believe, however, that Tortus will regret his saying, for thus the prophet is greater than the Pontiff; thus many Dominicans, who from teaching have the name of Preachers, are greater than the Most Holy Lord; thus finally those whom Jehoshaphat sent that they might teach will be greater than the king himself who sent them. For we indeed here place the primacy in governing, not in teaching; and we call the king not the supreme Teacher but the Governor, so that the dispute between the king and the Pontiff may now be settled and divided: let the Pontiff be supreme in the office of teaching, which properly pertains to his primacy; in governing, let the king be supreme, which he alone claims as his own; nor will he ever invade that other, pontifical, office of teaching. But I fear the Pontiff will not stand by this proper primacy of Tortus, and will bear badly that other, improper, power of governing is snatched from him. As for what he adds by way of an appendix, about the last punishment of him who does not obey the Pontiff (though he ought to have added, according to the law of God, as he answers), this does not favour him at all, but rather the contrary. For let him say: where will the Pontiff act against one who thus does not obey him? Before whom will the accused be brought? Who will pronounce sentence? Who will put the disobedient to death by the head? There is someone who will pronounce judgment, scorning the Pontiff; he himself, whoever he is, bears the primacy through me.

units.la: Ad Regem etiam pertinet, alio adhuc modo Pontificius dicere, eumque (ita exigentibus eius demeritis) exauthorare; & in locum ᴗAbiathari Sadocum surrogare. Facit hoc credo, ad Primatum Regis. Versat hic se in omnem partem Tortus; ter cuncum hunc conatur reuellere; ter perdit operam, nec repellit tamen. Litem primò resoluit lite, sed iniquâ & falsâ. Si Rex Pontificem hunc; alius Pontifex Reginam Athaliam & regno priuauit & vitâ. Non Reginam (Torte) quæ contra ius fasque omne, solium, non sine tot Nepotum suorum cæde & sanguine, per summum scelus occupârat. Sospes tum & superstes Regni verus hæres, verus Rex Ioas, quo in viuis existente, Athalia Regina esse non potuit. Quo lubet ergo nomine appelles, vel si voles Tygridem, ferinæ enim crudelitatis: Nos Reginam negamus, nec id vnquam dabimus, vt cum legitimo Pontifice illegitimam non Reginam, sed Regni Vsurpatricem componens, litem hanc hâc lite resoluas. Nec sibi in Athaliâ suâ satisfacit Tortus, alterâ vice tentatis; sic pote. Aliud est facta Regum referre, aliud Authoritatem probare. Quid audio? Illud dicere vult, sed eloqui non audet, factum hoc contra ius à Salomone, quod Pontificem abdicârit. Ita, vt Pontificis Primatum erigat, incurrit in Salomonem. Nam si authoritatem hoc Regis non probat, factum ergo sine authoritate legitimâ; sin legitimè factum, authoritati probandæ satis est. Peccauit ergo Salomon, & Sadoc intrusor, & Abiathar Sanctus Confessor potiùs; quàm vt Regi constet Primatus suus. Videtisne os hominis?
units.tr: It belongs also to the king, in yet another way, to depose a Pontiff, and (as his demerits require) to deprive him of his office, and to substitute Zadok in the place of Abiathar. I believe this serves the king's primacy. Here Tortus turns himself in every direction; three times he tries to tear up this whole thing; three times he loses his labour, and yet he does not drive it away. First he resolves the dispute by a dispute, but an unjust and false one: "If the king deprived this Pontiff, another Pontiff deprived Queen Athaliah both of her kingdom and of her life." Not a queen, Tortus, who against all right and law seized the throne by the greatest crime, not without the slaughter and blood of so many of her own grandchildren. The rightful heir and true king Joash, safe and surviving at that time, while he was alive Athaliah could not be queen. Call her by whatever name you please, or if you wish a tigress, for she was of savage cruelty: we deny that she was a queen, and we will never grant it, so that by setting an illegitimate usurper of the kingdom, not a queen, beside a legitimate Pontiff you may settle this dispute by this dispute. Nor is Tortus satisfied with his Athaliah, having tried it a second time; thus he speaks: "It is one thing to relate the deeds of kings, another to prove authority." What do I hear? He wants to say that, but dares not utter it: that this deed was against law by Solomon, who removed the Pontiff. So, in order to raise the primacy of the Pontiff, he runs into Solomon. For if this deed of the king does not prove authority, then the deed was without lawful authority; but if it was lawfully done, it is enough to prove authority. So Solomon sinned, and Zadok the intruder, and Abiathar rather was the holy confessor; rather than that the primacy should stand firm for the king. Do you see the man's face?

units.la: Sed ne sic quidem etiam satisfacit sibi. Nouam ergo formam assumit Proteus, priori plane contrariam. Omittit enim quod tribui solet factum hoc Salomoni, vt Propheta, non Regi; non Regiam, sed extraordinariam potestatem diuinitùs obtinenti. Dixit omittere se hoc, nec omisit; potuit tamen, ita prorsus omissione dignum. Non vt Regi tribui solet factum hoc Salomoni, sed vt Propheta: Factum, vt Propheta? Imò Dictum, vt Propheta. Per Prophetam res prædicitur, per alios opere completur sæpe non Prophetas, sæpe & Reprobos. Qui prædicit, is Propheta est: Qui, quod prædixit ille, post implet, obsignat prophetiam, Propheta ipse non est. Alioqui & Herodes Propheta, per quem factum est, {a}vt impleretur sermo Domini per Prophetam de Infantum nece; Et Milites Prophetæ, per quos {b}Vt Sermo alius Propheta impleretur, Cùm iecerunt fortes super tunicam Christi, Cùm adceto cum potárunt. Et Pharisæi; per quos alius, {a}Cùm oderunt Christum gratis; Et filius denique perditionis Iudas ipse Propheta, per quem alius, {b}Cùm leuaret contra Christum calcaneum suum; Nunquid omnes hi inter Prophetas? Omnes, si id satis ad suscitandum Prophetam, vt fiat per eum quid, unde impletur Sermo Domini. Per hos enim omnes, factum est aliquid unde impletus Sermo Domini. Apage vero hos Torti Prophetas. A quo vero solet hoc tribuit? A Domino eius: Qui satis improprie fecisse hac dicit Salomonem, {c}Vt Prophetam, & Diuinae Iustitiae executorem: quae duo tamen disparata sunt. Propheta enim Diuinae Iustitiae Nuntius est, Interpres est; Executor non est. Interpres Prophetiae suae, non Executor alienae Satis & illud improprie, Non vt Regem, sed vt Diuinae Iustitiae Executorem. Quasi Rex ipse, Diuinae Iustitiae Executor proprie non sit. Sed neque eiecit Rex Abiathar ad illum finem, vt impleretur Sermo Domini, sed ex lasse Maiestatis crimine; fuit modo consequens ad eiectionem Abiathar impletio Prophetia; atque eo loco, [Vt] consecutionem denotat, non causam finalem, quod te {d}Tostatus docere potuit. Quodsi Spiritui Sancto quid soleta[?] tribuere, non vno loco ille factum hoc Regi tribuit: Verf.26. Abiatharo quoque dixit Rex; Rex, qui proxime praecedente versu Adonijm caedi iusserat, idem versu hoc iusit quoque Abiathar loco cedere. Verf.35. Posuit Rex Sacerdotem Sadoc pro Aliathar; Rex: utrobique, quasi contra vos, expresso Regis nomine. Ita huic Regi factum tribuit Spiritus Sanctus, quod Spiritus Torti non Regi, sed Prophetae. Potestate Regiâ, negas. At haec voces, Abi ad Agrum tuum, ibi te contine: Et, Vir mortuus es, sed non interficiam te, Regis sunt, non Prophetae. Relegare homines: vbi mortis rei sunt vitam illis indulgere: Poenam Capitalem in mitiorem, Depositionis, commutare: Potestatis Regiae sunt, Prophetae non competunt. Denique, quā potestate, Banaiam pro Ioabo constituit super Exercitum, (quamtu, spero, Propheticam non dices, sed Regiam) eâdem, nec aliâ Sadocum pro Abiatharo constituit super Sacerdotum; Regiâ utrumque, utrumque vno eodemque versu; non vnâ in priore incisō potestate, nimirum Regiâ: aliâ in posteriore, nempe Propheticâ. Postremò, vt miserè laborare illi causam scias, ad miserrimum illud effugium se recipit Extraordinariae potestatis, ad quam confugere non solet quis, nisi cui deplorata res est, nisi cui Ordinarij nihil est quod respondeat. Ut enim qui vitâ priuari dignus, non vitâ priuetur, sed Munere, Ordinaria Regis potestas est; Extraordinariam Prophetæ, non requirit. Bonum factu erit semper, utcunq; factu fit, cùm Ordinariâ non potest, Extraordinariâ quadam nescio quâ facultate medicari.
units.tr: But not even so does he satisfy himself. So Proteus takes on a new shape, plainly contrary to the former. For he leaves out what is usually attributed to Solomon for this deed, that he acted as a prophet and not as a king; not by royal but by extraordinary power obtained from God. He said he left this out, and yet he did not leave it out; he could have done so, and it is entirely worthy of being left out. "Not as this deed is usually attributed to Solomon as king, but as a prophet: a deed done as a prophet?" Nay, a saying done as a prophet. Through a prophet a thing is foretold; through others, often not prophets, often even reprobates, it is accomplished by deed. He who foretells is a prophet; he who afterwards fulfils and seals what that man foretold is not himself a prophet. Otherwise Herod was a prophet, through whom it was done that the word of the Lord spoken by the prophet about the slaughter of the infants might be fulfilled; and the soldiers were prophets, by whom another prophet's word was fulfilled, when they cast lots upon Christ's garment, when they gave him vinegar to drink. And the Pharisees, by whom another word was fulfilled, when they hated Christ without cause; and finally Judas himself, the son of perdition, a prophet, by whom another word was fulfilled, when he lifted his heel against Christ. Are not all these among the prophets? All of them, if that were enough to raise up a prophet, so that through him something is done by which the word of the Lord is fulfilled. For through all of these something was done by which the word of the Lord was fulfilled. Away with these prophets of Tortus! But from whom is this usually attributed? From his Lord: who says, rather improperly, that Solomon did this as a prophet and an executor of divine justice; yet these two are different things. For a prophet is a messenger and an interpreter of divine justice; he is not its executor. He is the interpreter of his own prophecy, not the executor of another's. Also this is improper: "not as a king, but as an executor of divine justice." As if the king himself were not properly an executor of divine justice. But the king did not cast out Abiathar for that end, that the word of the Lord might be fulfilled, but for the crime of high treason; the fulfilment of the prophecy followed upon the expulsion of Abiathar, and in that place [ut] denotes sequence, not final cause, as Tostatus could have taught you. But if the Holy Spirit is wont to attribute anything to someone, in more than one place he attributes this deed to the king: verse 26. The king also said to Abiathar; the king, who in the immediately preceding verse had ordered Adonijah to be killed, in this verse likewise ordered Abiathar to give way. Verse 35. The king put the priest Zadok in place of Abiathar; the king: in both places, as if against you, the name of the king is expressly given. Thus the Holy Spirit attributes this deed to this king, which is not the spirit of Tortus, but of the king, not of a prophet. You deny it is royal power. But these words, "Go to your field, and stay there," and "You are a dead man, but I will not slay you," belong to the king, not to a prophet. To banish men, where they are liable to death, to grant them life, to change capital punishment into a milder one, deposition: these belong to royal power and do not befit a prophet. Finally, by what power he appointed Benaiah over the army in place of Joab (which you will not, I hope, call prophetic but royal), by the same power, and no other, he appointed Zadok over the priests in place of Abiathar; both by royal power, both in one and the same verse; not in the former clause one power, namely royal, and in the latter another, namely prophetic. Lastly, so that you may know how wretchedly his cause labours, he retreats to that most wretched refuge of extraordinary power, to which no one is wont to flee unless his case is desperate, unless he has nothing that the ordinary powers can answer. For that the one who is worthy to be deprived of life should be deprived not of life but of office is the ordinary power of the king; it does not require an extraordinary power of a prophet. It will always be good to act, however it is done, when it cannot be remedied by the ordinary power, by some extraordinary faculty, I know not what.

units.la: Post enumeratas iam Ecclesiastici regiminis partes penè singulas, ad quas allegatæ ex verbo Dei sententiæ ad minus singulæ: prodit nobis Tortus in aciem, & iubet pro toto iam Regimine verbum Dei aliquod allegare. De toto enim, inquit, nobu[?] quæstio est. Annon de partibus simul[sumptis ?] Et quid totum, nisi partes non singulæ, sed sic in unum coaceruatæ? Quid verò actum nobis toto hoc tempore? Quorsum illa tot spectant iam allegata? Id quaeritur, inquit, An Regi conuenit Regimen Ecclesiasticum. Profecto autem si conueniant illa Regi, dare Iudices in causis Ecclesiæ; dare Iudicum Præsidentes, abusus in Religione & corruptelas tollere; Arcam reportare, & præire[?] reportandæ; Templa dedicare, & adeam rem Cœtus indicere; Libro legis recitato pracipere Pontifici de repurgando Dei cultu; Si fœdus renouare de Religione reformandâ; Si Templum ingredi, & aneum Serpentem confringere; Si Missiones Sacerdotum facere; Si Pontificem ipsum ejicere, atq; exauthorare, ne sit Pontifex: Hæc si Regi omnia sic conueniant, conuenit & Regimen Ecclesiasticum. Quantillum enim hæc absunt à toto Regimine, cùm vix ulla defit pars? Non ergo deseruit Authorem Apologiæ, vbi maximè oportuit Verbum Diuinum: deseruit Tortum, ubi minimè oportuit, ad tot loca respon-sum commodum. Faciat hæc quæ dixi Rex, nec ad Primatum suum præterea quicquam requiret. De docendi munere; de dubijs in lege locis, explicandis, nulla fuit illis tum, nulla nobis iam erit cum Pontifice pro Rege controuersia.
units.tr: After listing almost all the parts of ecclesiastical government, for each of which at least one saying from the Word of God has been cited, Torture now comes forward into battle and orders that a word of God be cited for the whole government at once. "The question," he says, "is about the whole, not about the parts taken together." But what is the whole, if not the parts, not taken singly but gathered into one? What, then, has been done by us all this while? To what end do all those things already cited bear upon the matter? "The question," he says, "is whether ecclesiastical government befits a king." Certainly, if these things befit a king, that is: to appoint judges in causes of the Church; to appoint presiding judges, and to remove abuses and corruptions in religion; to bring back the ark and to lead the way in bringing it back; to dedicate temples and to call an assembly for that business; to command the high priest, when the book of the law has been read, to purge the worship of God; to renew the covenant concerning the reformation of religion; to enter the temple and break the bronze serpent in pieces; to send out priests on missions; to remove the high priest himself and deprive him of office, so that he is no longer high priest. If all these things befit a king, then ecclesiastical government befits him too. For how far do these things fall short of the whole government, when hardly any part is missing? Therefore the author of the Apology has not "abandoned the Word of God where it was most needed"; rather, he has abandoned Torture where it was least needed, by offering a convenient answer to so many passages. Let the king do what I have said, and he will ask for nothing further as regards his supremacy. "On the office of teaching, and on explaining the obscure places of the law," there was no controversy then between the Pontiff and the king, and there will be none now between us and the king.

units.la: Etiam, ut quàm laboret inuidiâ in Regum nomen prodat, titulos ipsos arrodit, nec vel illis gaudere sinit homo malleolus. Ita re, nomine, spoliatos vult; ita omni ex parte imminutum it Regiam Dignitatem. Quàm 'id autem inscitè? In primo-tituló[?], quo Filius Altissimi Rex dicitur, restrictus est & tenax, soli Salomoni peculiarem vult; non generatim Regibus conuenire. Statim autem verbis proximis, quasi Lethargiâ correptus, profusus est, toti Israeli communicat, cuius in Deuteronomio Deus, Pater dicitur. Tandem etiam ad omnes extendit, qui dicere possunt Pater noster qui es in coelis, id est, omnino omnes. Ita negat Regibus primo, soli Salomoni seruatum vult; eodemque spiritu, solius Salomonis titulum impertit etiam infimis de plebe. Nec aduertit, quod etsi Petrus Regem honorari, idemque omnes honorari iubeat, nemo tamen dubitet, quin alio honore Regem, quam omnes: ita etsi Deus, idem Regi idemque nobis Pater; alia tamen, longe alia ratione Regi quam nobis; Communiore aliqua nobis, Regibus autem propiore quadam, atque illis singulari.
units.tr: Also, so that you may reveal how hard he labours under odium against the name of kings, he gnaws at the titles themselves, and this little hammer-man does not let him rejoice even in these. He thus wants them stripped of both substance and name; in this way the royal dignity is diminished in every respect. But how unskilfully he does this! In the first title, by which the king is called "Son of the Most High," he is narrow and tenacious: he wants it reserved for Solomon alone and not to belong to kings in general. Yet straightway, in the words that follow, as if seized with lethargy, he becomes lavish: he shares it with all Israel, of whom God is called Father in Deuteronomy. Finally he extends it to all who can say "Our Father, who art in heaven," that is, absolutely everyone. Thus he denies it first to kings, wanting it kept for Solomon alone; and with the same spirit he grants the title of Solomon alone even to the lowest of the common people. Nor does he notice that although Peter bids us honour the king, and likewise bids us all honour, no one doubts that the king is honoured with a different honour from all others. So too, although God is the Father of the king and likewise of us, it is yet in a different and far different manner for the king than for us: for us in a more general way, for kings in a certain closer way, and for them in a singular way.

units.la: Quod ipsum, & de loco Psalmi dici potest, qui etsi non incommodè quadrare potest omnibus qui ius dicunt: tamen quis non videt, aliter competere Iudicibus, quibus potestas à Rege delegata, aliter Regi ipsi, cui à Deo immediate; cuius ita Iudices in Prouincia personam sustinent, vt Rex ipse Dei? Quare ab illo per gradus intermedios itur ad Deum; Rex ipse Deo proximus; cui proin Dei nomen, peculiari quadam, atq; insigni magis adhuc ratione conuenit. Multo quidem magis Moses, & meliore iure nomen Dei vendicet, qui id tum populo, quod Reges pòst, praestitit, (tum cùm solus sederet, & Israeli ius diceret) quàm aliy[?] illi, quos Dei iussu, in partem pòst sollicitudinis vocauit; qui etsi & ipsi Dij vocantur in lege, erant tamen vt Re, ita Titulo, Mosi multis gradibus inferiores.
units.tr: The same can also be said of the passage of the Psalm, which, although it can not inappropriately apply to all who administer justice, yet who does not see that it belongs in one way to judges, to whom power has been delegated by the king, and in another way to the king himself, to whom it belongs immediately from God? In the province the judges so sustain the king's person that the king himself is God's. Therefore one goes from him through intermediate degrees to God; the king himself is nearest to God; to him, accordingly, the name of God belongs by a certain peculiar and still more distinguished reason. Much more indeed does Moses, and with better right, claim the name of God, who gave to the people, as the kings later did, that office which he performed when he alone sat and declared law to Israel, than those others whom by God's command he called to share his cares afterwards; who, although they too are called gods in the law, were nevertheless, as in office so in title, many degrees inferior to Moses.

units.la: Nec multus iam nobis sermo de Christo seu Vnctio Domini: sat supra de eo dictum. Ibi Tortus, quod & hic, molitur, vt nomen sit Pontifici commune cum Rege. Nec hic nec ibi locum vllum apponit, nec dictis fidem facit. Nos Christum Domini de Pontifice dictum, non damus. Nec moramur vnctiones Torti. Nam & citra oleum Cyrus Christus Domini dicitur, & ante Chrisma, Christi, Psal.105. A Deo titulus, qui latenter vngit, & in occulto, quos Regno destinat.
units.tr: Nor have we now much more to say about Christ or the Anointing of the Lord; enough has been said above about that. There Torture, as here, labours to make the name common to the Pontiff and the king. Neither here nor there does he set forth any place, nor does he make his assertions credible. We do not grant that "the Christ of the Lord" was said of the Pontiff. Nor do we dwell on Torture's anointings.
