For even without oil Cyrus is called "the Christ of the Lord," and before the chrism, "Christ" (Ps. 105). It is a title given by God, who anoints secretly and in hiding those whom he destines for the kingdom.

units.la: Titulum quartum nescit, aut vnde irrepserit. Siquid ego adiuto, ecquid cedet de sententia? Lege ergo totidem verbis 2.Chr.9.8. Dilexit te Deus, vt poneret te super Solium suum. Ibi Solium Dauid, Solium Dei. Deinc iam fac titulum agnoscas, saltem ne dicas irreptitium, ne nos te arreptitium dicamus.
units.tr: He does not know the fourth title, or whence it has crept in. If I help you, will anything come of the matter? Read therefore, in so many words, 2 Chronicles 9:8: "God loved you so as to set you upon his throne." There the throne is David's, and the throne is God's. Then at last learn to acknowledge the title, or at least do not call it a usurped title, lest we call you a usurper.

units.la: Titulum Serui Dei, exufflat, vt vulgarem, vt Creaturis omnibus communem, quo tamen Moses & Dauid, tanquam admodum honorifico indigetarunt se, atque supra res reliquas creatas paululum extulerunt: En Spiritum hominis, qui quod Reges sibi honori ducunt, tam superbe abijcit, atque conculcat. Nec enim Serui Dei dicendi omnes, nedum omnia quæ Deo seruiunt. Nec Seruum esse Regem quocunque modo dicimus, sed sic, ut Deus ipse Seruum suum agnoscat. Ex officio enim seruiunt omnia, etiam quæ neque possunt velle seruire. Non tamen multos puto agnoscet pro Seruis, & ex ijs, quos agnoscit, qui illustri maximè loco seruiunt, per eminentiam quandam Serui sunt, nec cæteris similes, vel simili loco habendi. Serui enim non æquales.{*} Seruum se Dei dixit Saul; Serui huius Dei Saulis, Achimelech Summus Sacerdos{a} bis Seruum se profitetur. Seruus Dei Salomon: Hic tamen Seruus, {b}Abiathar (ut tu eum dici vis) Conseruum suum deposuit. Videat autem Tortus si tam numerosos nobis faciat Dei Seruos, nec pauciores quàm sunt Creaturæ; nec ita, is, qui Serui Seruorum Dei dici vult, Seruus cogatur esse Bipedum atque Quadrupedum omnium, &c; quod adhuc maius est, Dæmonum. Seruiunt enim Deo & illi, Gregoriano more, velint nolint, quorum tamen non feret (scio saltem) ut Seruus sit Pontifex.
units.tr: He blows away the title "Servant of God," as a common title shared by all creatures; yet Moses and David, as if it were a very honourable title, claimed it for themselves and raised themselves a little above the other created things. Behold the spirit of man, who so proudly casts away and tramples underfoot what kings count to their honour. For not all are to be called "servants of God," much less all things that serve God. Nor do we say that a king is a servant in any way whatever, but in such a way that God himself acknowledges him as his servant. For all things serve by duty, even those which cannot will to serve. Yet I do not think he will acknowledge many as his servants, and among those he does acknowledge, those who serve in the most illustrious place are servants in a certain eminent sense, and are not to be treated as like the rest, or as having a similar place. For servants are not equals. Saul called himself "the servant of God"; the servant of this God Saul, the high priest Ahimelech, twice professes himself "servant." Solomon was "God's servant"; yet this servant Abiathar (as you wish him to be called) set aside his fellow-servant. Let Torture see whether he makes God's servants so numerous for us, and not fewer than there are creatures; and so that he who wishes to be called "servant of the servants of God" is not compelled to be the servant of all bipeds and quadrupeds, and so on; and what is still greater, of demons. For those also serve God, in the Gregorian manner, "whether they will or no"; yet he will not endure (I know at least) that the Pontiff be a servant.

units.la: Titulum Angeli obliquis oculis aspicit: Soli Dauidi vindicat, & illi, qua Sapiens, non qua Rex. At in Sacerdotes depluit generatim. Ita unus Rex Angelus; Sacerdotes Angeli ad unum omnes. Quàm ubique malignus in Reges? Nec tamen solus Dauid Angelus; Etiam Rex Tyri {c}Cherub dicitur, qui puto vobis in Choris Angelorum: Rex (inquam) Tyri, homo Ethnicus; ut iam spero, per Tortum liceat, quod Paganis datum est nomen, Regibus Christianis non negare.
units.tr: He looks askance at the title "Angel": he claims it for David alone, and for him "as wise, not as king." But he rains it down on priests generally. So the one king is an "angel"; the priests are all "angels" alike. How everywhere malignant he is against kings! Yet David is not the only "angel": the king of Tyre too is called a "cherub," which I think you have among the choirs of angels. The king of Tyre, I say, a heathen man; so that, as I hope, through Torture it may be permitted not to deny Christian kings a name which was given to pagans.

units.la: Esse secundum cor Dei, etsi eo loco de Dauide dicitur; potest tamen, & ad alios commeare, qui Dauidi similes; Ezekiam puta vel Iosiam, ut sic proprius esse desinat. Nec sequitur quod de Saulo addis & Achabo. Potest enim esse, & est ex corde Dei Rex, (Magistratus ipse scilicet) ut ille tamen non sit, qui Magistratum gerit. Recte enim id animaduersum, non Tiberio vel Neroni reddi iuberi officia hæc, sed Cæsari.
units.tr: "To be according to the heart of God," although it is said of David in that place, may nevertheless also pass to others who are like David, say Hezekiah or Josiah, so that it may no longer be peculiar to him. Nor does what you add about Saul and Ahab follow. For a king may be, and is, according to the heart of God (namely the magistrate himself), yet he who bears the magistracy may not be. For it has been rightly observed that these duties are required to be rendered not to Tiberius or Nero, but to "Caesar."

units.la: In titulo Luminaris, cùm negare non posset, tamen moreretur iam, si non aliquâ noceret. Non ergo satis illi Sacerdotes vocare in societatem nominis, vt ita, sicut Rex, sic Sacerdos; nisi Regem deprimendo, dicat, magis Sacerdoti convenire quàm Regi, nomen Luminis: non veteri argumento Bonifacij, & analogiâ Solis ad Lunam, sed certè quod nihilo plus sapiat. Illi dicebantur Lucerna Israel, nempe Reges: Hij autem, nimirum Sacerdotes, Lux Mundi. Maior autem Mundus quàm Israel: Maior ergo, (fortasse, & tanto maior) Sacerdos Rege. At cùm hoc Seruator diceret, Vos estis Lux mundi, duodecim illos affatus, quierant tum Omnes, nec praeter eos vllj, Apostoli. Itidem, si Omnes per Orbem Reges daretur alloqui, illis quoque idem illud suum diceret Christus, Vos estis Lux mundi. Cùm vnum tantùm alloquitur, Vnius Gentis Regem, Lucernam Israel dicit, cuius Rex erat; Atque simili modo, si vnius Gentis Episcopum affari contingeret. Vt septem illos Apocal.
units.tr: In the title "Light," since he could not deny it, yet he would already be dead, if he did not harm it in some way. It was therefore not enough for him to call priests into fellowship of the name, so that, as the king, so the priest; unless by depressing the king he says that "the name of Light befits the priest more than the king": not by the old argument of Boniface and the analogy of the sun to the moon, but certainly because he knows no more than nothing. Those were called "the lamp of Israel," namely the kings; these, that is the priests, "the light of the world." But the world is greater than Israel; therefore the priest is greater than the king (perhaps, and by so much greater). But when the Saviour said, "You are the light of the world," addressing those twelve, the all were then the apostles, and no others besides them. Likewise, if it were granted to address all the kings of the world, Christ would say that same thing of them too, "You are the light of the world." When he addresses only one, the king of one nation, he calls him "the lamp of Israel," of which he was king; and in a similar way, if it happened to address the bishop of one nation. As the seven angels of the Apocalypse...

units.la: 1. Septem Stellas diceret Septem Ecclesiarum; Singularis scilicet Singulas; non autem vel Stellas, vel Lucernas, Orbis Vniuersi.
units.tr: 1. "Seven stars" would mean "seven churches"; the singular would mean "each one," not "stars" or "lamps" of the whole world.

units.la: In vltimo, vt agnoscas Tortum à principio in finem vsque Regibus inimicum, vbi Apologia Regem, Nutritium nominauit; ille Pontificem Patrem, quo, Nutritius inferior multò est, vt potiores semper sint partes Pontificis; quod Reges mordeat. Citat autem huic rei nescio quid ex Augustini Epistolâ quadam, (non enim illâ, quam numeri notant.) At aequior hîc fit censeo. Absque hijs enim foret Nutricijs noster, Pater Vester Pontifex esuriret strenuè, atque algeret, nec ita inflatus, obsericatus incederet, aut pompaticè ingrederetur Dominum Dei. Quodsi autem, momenti quid sit in Patris nomine, nihil opus adeamus Augustinum, atque alicunde apud eum ex Epistolae angulo aliquo, Patris nomen eruamus. Sacrae literae, non Nutritij modò nomen, vel Nutricis; etiam Patris, atque Matris ad Principes accommodant non inuitae. Debora, {a}Mater dicitur in Israel. Ezekias Pater, atque, audi etiam, Sacerdotum. Sic enim Sacerdotes affatur ipsos. 2. Chron. 29. 11. Filij mei, nolite vero negligere. Vt Rex, iam Pater sit, & Sacerdotum Pater; ne quid eo titulo insolescant, aut supra Reges se efferant. Quem enim honorem habent Principes, non alia Lege habent, quàm Quinta, quae est de Patre honorando, propter paternam de Patriâ curam, nec minùs paternam de Ecclesiâ. Quicquid ergo praeterea habet, hoc habet ex verbo Dei Apologia, & Rex Nutritius Ecclesiæ sit, & Pontificis ipsius, etiam, vt Pater sit. Diu autem hoc, & per aliquot secula, non modò ante Henricum octauum, sed etiam ante Pontificem vel Paulum primum.
units.tr: In the last part, so that you may recognise that Tortus is hostile to kings from beginning to end, where the Apology calls the king a "nursing father" (Nutritius), he calls the Pope "Father," although a nursing father is far inferior to that, so that the Pope's parts are always the stronger, which galls kings. He cites, however, I know not what from a certain Epistle of Augustine (not that one which the numbers mark). But I think this point is fairer here. For without these, our nursing father would be your Father the Pope, who would starve and freeze vigorously, and he would not walk about so puffed up and sealed, or "enter in pomp into the Lord's house." But if the name of Father carries any weight, there is no need to go to Augustine and dig up the name of Father from some corner of an Epistle of his. The Holy Scriptures apply not only the name of nursing father, or nurse, but also of father and mother, to princes, and not unwillingly. Deborah is called "a mother in Israel." Hezekiah was a father, and, hear this too, of the priests. For he so addresses the priests: "My sons, be not now negligent" (2 Chron. 29. 11). So the king is already a father, and a father of the priests; lest they should grow proud on account of that title or raise themselves above kings. For the honour which princes have they hold by no other law than the Fifth, which is concerning honouring the father, on account of the paternal care for the country, and no less the paternal care for the Church. Whatever else he has, therefore, he has from the Word of God. The Apology: the king is the nursing father of the Church, and of the Pope himself too, so that he may be a father. This has been so for a long time, and for several centuries, not only before Henry VIII, but even before Pope Paul I.

units.la: ET sunt ista quidem ex Testamento Veteri satis solida Fundamenta, & quæ tu haud facilè conquelles. Nam de Nouo ibi quæ adijciuntur, eò spectant, ne quis ex eo, quod alienitum à Christo Reges terræ, imminutam putet, vel eorum in subditos potestatem, vel subditorum in eos fidem; neue pristino suo iure excidisse videantur. Non quòd ad Reges infideles Primatum pertinere probent, non sanè magis ad hos in Nouo, quàm ad Ahasuerum vel Nabuchodonozor in Veteri (delirat hæc Tortus) sed quòd Cæsari, si Christianus fiat, vt Constantino; idem iuris sit in Ecclesiam, quod in Veteri, Iosiæ fuit; reditus statim fiat ad iura Regum Israel, quam primùm facti sunt Reges Israel Dei, & eorum quisque CHRISTO nomen dederit. Interim autem, sit vel infidelis, sit vel Hæreticus, oretur pro eo, non minùs quàm pro Nabuchodonozor; nemo vitæ eius insidietur, non magis quàm Ahasueri. Fidem penes semet ipsos habeant Christiani subditi coram Deo; cæteris in rebus pietatem colant: ad eamque se Conscientiæ nexu teneri discant à Paulo; voluntatem hanc Dei esse, discant à Petro. Non ergo id agitur, vt Ecclesiæ Persecutores, Tiberij, Caij, Ecclesiæ Gubernatores habeantur; quem si quis eis titulum deferret, ne susciperent quidem; vt qui Ecclesiam ipsam totis viribus extirpatum iuerint: tantùm vt tuti sint à Sicâ, Veneno, Puluere Catholicorum suorum. Tum demum verò Ecclesiæ gubernacula capessant, cùm conuersi ad fidem fuerint. Reddenda enim Cæsari quæ Cæsaris sunt; Cæsaris sunt, quæ Cæsari debentur: Debentur autem Cæsari Christiano, quæcunque olim à Populo Dei sub veteri Lege Regibus suis officia, vel debita, vel persoluta fuìnt: quibus & debita tum erant & persoluta, subiectio & obedientia, non in Regni rebus solùm, sed etiam Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: And these things are indeed sufficiently solid foundations from the Old Testament, and such as you would hardly complain of. For what is added there concerning the New aims at this: that no one should think, because kings of the earth are alienated from Christ, either their power over subjects or the faith of subjects toward them is diminished, or that they seem to have fallen from their former right. Not that they prove the primacy belongs to unbelieving kings, any more than it belongs to such in the New Testament, or to Ahasuerus or Nebuchadnezzar in the Old (Tortus rambles on this), but that if Caesar becomes a Christian, as Constantine did, the same right over the Church shall be his as Josiah had in the Old; a return shall at once be made "to the rights of the kings of Israel," as soon as the kings of Israel become God's kings, and each of them gives his name to Christ. Meanwhile, whether he be unbelieving or heretical, let prayer be made for him, no less than for Nebuchadnezzar; let no one lay plots against his life, any more than against Ahasuerus. Let Christian subjects keep their faith to themselves before God; in other matters let them cultivate piety: and let them learn from Paul that they are bound to it by the bond of conscience; let them learn from Peter that "this is the will of God." Therefore the aim is not that persecutors of the Church, such as Tiberius and Caius, should be regarded as governors of the Church; if anyone were to give them that title, they would not even accept it, since they have striven with all their might to root out the Church itself: only that they may be safe from the dagger, poison and gunpowder of their own Catholics. Then at last they may take up the reins of the Church, when they have been converted to the faith. For "render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's" (Matt. 22); the things due to Caesar are Caesar's: and whatever was once owed or paid to the kings of God's people under the old Law, that is owed to the Christian Caesar; for in those former times subjection and obedience were both owed and paid to them, not only in matters of the kingdom but also of the Church.

units.la: Nemo autem est, qui non videat quàm sit absurdum hæc aliò detorquere; sed cùm hoc facit Tortus, cùm nequam facit, officium facit: quale illud, quòd aliquas tantùm sententias, de citatis, Regibus etiam Christianis ait, posse conuenire. Aliquas verò? Et quæ tandem!non conueniunt? Paganis autem conuenire omnes, neminem (pòst dicit) inficiari posse. Hoc ergò videri vult dicere; plus iuris esse Paganis Regibus, plus illis fauere Scripturas, quàm Regibus Christianis; & mox tamen,vt quo nodo teneas, planè nescias, doctrinam Principibus omnibus communem illisce contineri asserit, siue Pagani, siue Christiani sint. Non aliquæ ergo è citatis; omnes Principum Christianorum sunt. Quale etiam illud ,quòd sententias aliquas ex citatis detorquet, ad Principes Ecclesiasticos, vel potiùs aliquam, nempe eam Apostoli, quà omnem animam iubet subditam esse Potestatibus sublimioribus. Hanc sententiam ad Ecclesiasticos Principes pertinere ait, cùm nec vlli tum essent Ecclesiastici qui Principes dicerentur; & si essent, tamen ad eos applicari non posset locus Apostoli, qui de ijs est Potestatibus, quæ gladium gestant,&c quibus tributum penditur. Ecclesiastici verò tum, mucronem gladij sæpe gestabant in ceruicibus, capulum in manibus non gestabant: nec Publicanos adhuc habebant vlos, qui tributa sua, ac vectigalia exigerent ab ijs, qui subditi, in Principatu suo. Tum Apostoli,in eas Potestates includi non poterant, quibus (si quid vidit Chrysostomus) etiam Apostoli ipsi subditi iubentur esse.
units.tr: But there is no one who does not see how absurd it is to twist these things elsewhere; yet when Tortus does this, even when he does it wickedly, he performs his office: as with his remark that only "some sentences" of the cited passages could apply to Christian kings. "Some," indeed? And which ones, pray, do not apply? He says afterwards that it cannot be denied that all of them apply to pagans. So he wishes to say this: that pagan kings have more right, and the Scriptures favour them more, than Christian kings; and yet soon after, so that you may not know clearly what knot he is holding, he asserts that the doctrine contained there is common to all princes, whether they be pagan or Christian. Therefore it is not "some" of the cited passages; all of them belong to Christian princes. The same holds for his twisting of "some sentences" from the cited passages so as to apply them to ecclesiastical princes, or rather to one of them, namely that of the Apostle by which he bids "every soul be subject to the higher powers." He says this sentence pertains to ecclesiastical princes, although at that time there were no ecclesiastics who were called princes; and even if there were, the Apostle's passage could not be applied to them, since it concerns those "powers" which "bear the sword," etc., to whom "tribute is paid." Ecclesiastics at that time often carried the point of the sword at their necks, but did not carry the hilt in their hands; nor did they yet have any tax-collectors who would exact their tributes and duties from those who were subjects in their principality. Nor could the Apostles then be included among those "powers," to whom (if Chrysostom saw anything) the Apostles themselves are also bidden to be subject.

units.la: Quæ verò post ibi format, per sanè similia sunt formanti argumenta; iures à Torto formata; formá enim hominem ad viuum referunt. Alioqui, si quid in eo recti, si curuam in terris animam non gerat, sciat loca primùm à se, posita locis non suis; de tribus vltimum, primo loco in Apologiâ stare: duo priora, quæ ille loco suo mouit, postremo. Vt autem locata ab eo male, ita & luxata esse. Vltimum eius pro Cæsare esse, ille luxauit, quasi contra Papam esset. Duo priora contra Papam, luxauit, quasi essent pro Cæsare. Sinat stare locis suis, sinat ad quem destinata sunt, scopum petere; tum verò legat vel leuiter Analytica sua Priora, nec ita valdè diligenter euoluat, reperiet non magno labore, medium terminum. Hoc autem modo. Qui se Vicarium facit eius, cuius regnum non est huius Mundi, in Regna huius Mundi ius non habet. Vicarium se facere eius cuius Regnum non est huius Mundi, Medius terminus. Qui Gentium non dominatur vt Rex, non dominatur in Reges Gentium. Dominari Gentium vt Rex, Medius terminus. Atque duo hæc contra Papam, qui sub Primatus specie vsurpat sibi ius Dominij in Regna mundi, in Reges Gentium. Vltimum non contra Papæ ius, vt tu oppidò quàm inepte, sed pro Cæsaris iure est. Ad hunc modum. Quod Cæsaris est scilicet tum, cùm iam Christianus factus est, id Cæsari reddendum. Obedientia etiam in rebus Religionis Cæsaris est Christiani iam facti. Medius terminus. Quod Cæsaris est iam Christiani: Iam Christiani dico; quo ita analogia seruetur Regum Israëlis sub Veteri Lege: Christianorum sub Nouâ. Tum demum enim Rex istius debiti capax est, cùm est in Ecclesiâ, vt Iosias: non cùm extrà, vt Ieroboam.
units.tr: But the arguments which he then forms are very like forming arguments; you may sense they are formed by Tortus; for they represent the man to the life. Otherwise, if there were anything right in him, if he did not bear a crooked soul on earth, let him know that he first placed things in places not their own: of the three, the last stands first in the Apology; the two earlier ones, which he has moved from their place, stand last. And as he placed them badly, so he has also dislocated them. Its last point, which is for Caesar, he has dislocated as if it were against the Pope. The two earlier points, against the Pope, he has dislocated as if they were for Caesar. Let them stand in their own places, let them aim at the target for which they were intended; then let him read lightly at least his own Prior Analytics, and not unroll it too carefully, and he will find without great labour the middle term. And in this way. "He who makes himself the vicar of him whose kingdom is not of this world has no right in the kingdoms of this world." To make oneself the vicar of him whose kingdom is not of this world: the middle term. "He who does not rule over the Gentiles as a king does not rule over the kings of the Gentiles." To rule over the Gentiles as a king: the middle term. And these two are against the Pope, who under the appearance of primacy usurps for himself a right of lordship over the kingdoms of the world, over the kings of the Gentiles. The last point is not against the Pope's right, as you, Tortus, rather foolishly say, but is for Caesar's right. In this way: what is Caesar's, namely when he has already become a Christian, is to be rendered to Caesar. Obedience in matters of religion is also Caesar's, once he is a Christian. The middle term: "What is Caesar's is of the Christian already." I say "already Christian," so that the analogy with the kings of Israel under the Old Law is preserved, and that of Christians under the New. For then only is the king capable of that duty when he is in the Church, as Josiah was, not when he is outside it, as Jeroboam was.

units.la: Nos verò Testamentum Nouum à Vetere non diuellimus; ex vtroque ius Regum astruimus. Habuerunt Reges in Vetere Primatum suum, atque inde nerui sunt & lacerti causæ nostræ. In Nouo autem, deteriore iure non sunt. Sub eâdem ergo conditione, idem illis Primatus debetur, idem reddendus est. Tu verò Torte ne sic ludas Scripturæ locis; quæ (vtcunque ludas illis) non potes eludere; & vtcunque abuti potes patientiâ, at iudicio Lectoris non potes. Sentit enim hæc ludicra non esse, seriò rem agi; adeo stabiliri illis Primatum, vt tu succutiendo non sis. Ecclesia verò Catholica, tantum abest vt eum Primatum detestata fit; vt Carolum, vt Ludouicum {a}Rectores Religionis, Actis publicis Cöciliaribus, dixerit, scripserit; Inter Rectorem verò & Gubernatorem quid interest? Aut sinulla ei vox satis est, nisi Gubernatoris, legat in Synodo suâ Oecumenicâ Basilium Gubernatorem Vniuersalis Nauis Ecclesiastica. Caluinus autem vt Papam Regem: ita Regem Papam non probauit; neque nos quod in Papâ detestamur, in Rege approbamus. At & ille nobiscum, & nos cum illo sentimus, easdem esse in Ecclesiâ Christianâ Regis Iacobi partes; quæ Iosiæ fuerunt in Iudaïcâ, nec nos vltrà quicquam fieri ambimus, & Tortus si scopum ferire voluit, non aërem verberare, Septem illa petere debuit & configere, quæ hoc ipso in loco ponuntur Regis in Religionis munera, & ad quem solum scopum collimare Iuramentum Primatus Regij; Rex ipse (qui quid ipse petat, optimè omnium nouit) non dissimulanter asserit. Quos verò Puritanos appellat, si Regium Primatum detestentur, detestandi ipsi. Profitentur enim, subscribunt, iurant indies. Sed & illi quod faciunt, ingenuè faciunt, & societatem in hoc Torti, ipsúmque adeo Tortum, tanquam mendacem hominem, & alibi de alijs, & hic de se; ac Sycophantam egregium detestantur.
units.tr: But we do not tear the New Testament from the Old; from both we establish the rights of kings. The kings had their primacy in the Old, and thence are the sinews and muscles of our cause. In the New, however, they are not in a worse position in right. Under the same condition, therefore, the same primacy is due to them, the same must be rendered. But you, Tortus, must not thus play with the passages of Scripture; for however you may play with them, you cannot make them vanish; and however you may abuse the patience of the reader, you cannot abuse his judgement. For the reader perceives that these are not jests, but that the matter is treated in earnest, so firmly is the primacy established for them by these passages that you cannot shake it. The Catholic Church, however, so far from detesting that primacy, has called Charles and Louis "rulers of religion" in its public Councils' acts and writings; and what is the difference between "ruler" and "governor"? Or if no word is enough for him except "governor," let him read in its Ecumenical Synod that Basil is called "governor of the universal ecclesiastical ship." Calvin, however, did not approve of "the king as Pope," just as he did not approve of "the Pope as king"; nor do we approve in the king what we detest in the Pope. But both he with us and we with him agree that in the Christian Church the parts of King James are the same as those of Josiah in the Jewish Church; nor do we strive for anything further to be done. And if Tortus wished to strike the target and not beat the air, he ought to have aimed at and hit those seven things which are set down in this very place as the king's duties in religion, and which the oath of royal primacy aims at as its sole target; the king himself (who knows best of all what he himself seeks) openly asserts this. As for those whom he calls Puritans, if they detest the royal primacy, they themselves are to be detested. For they profess, they subscribe, they swear every day. But they too do what they do openly, and they detest any fellowship with Tortus in this, and Tortus himself, as a liar in other matters and here about himself, and as a notable sycophant.

units.la: Atque vt semel defungar totâ hac de Primatu Regio Quæstione, semel vt constet Primatus apud nos quæ iura sint, quid illius nomine intelligendum veniat; atque ita cesset vestra dehinc, cesset aliorum calumnia de vestro, & à vobis conficto, non nostro, & à nobis agnito Primatu: paucis sic accipe sententiam nostram.
units.tr: And so that I may finish once and for all with this whole question of the Royal Primacy, so that it becomes clear what rights the Primacy has among us and what is meant by that name, and so that from now on your calumny ceases, and the calumny of others, concerning a Primacy invented by you and not ours, and not acknowledged by us, take my opinion in a few words.

units.la: Primò, Sub Primatus nomine Papatum nouum Rex non inuehit in Ecclesiam; sic enim statuit, vt non {a}Aaroni Pontifici, ita nec {b}Ieroboamo Regi ius vllum esse, conflatum à se Vitulum populo proponendi vt adoret (id est) non vel fidei nouos articulos, vel cultus Diuini nouas formulas procudendi.
units.tr: First, under the name of Primacy the King does not introduce a new Papacy into the Church. For he holds that just as Aaron the High Priest had no right, so neither did Jeroboam the King have any right to set before the people the calf he had cast, for them to worship; that is, to forge new articles of faith or new forms of divine worship.

units.la: Neque verò id agit Rex, ne patitur quidem, vt sibi potestas fit, vel incensum adolendi cum {c}Oziá, vel Arcam attrectandi cum {d}Ozá, quod vos toties tam odiosè inculcatis.
units.tr: Nor indeed does the King aim at this, nor does he even permit that power be given to him to burn incense with Uzziah, or to handle the Ark with Uzzah, which you so often and so hatefully press upon us.

units.la: Vestrum illud (quod ad Primatum Pontificium proprie pertinere dicitis) docendi munus, vel dubia Legis explicandi, non assumit, non vel Conciones habendi, vel Rei Sacræ præeundi, vel Sacramenta celebrandi; non vel Personas sacrandi, vel Res; non vel Clauium ius, vel Censuræ. Verbo dicam; nihil Ille sibi, nihil nos Illi fas putamus attingere, quæ ad Sacerdotale munus spectant, seu potestatem Ordinis consequuntur. Omnino vestra hæc calumnia est, in odium conficta, & Regis, & nostrûm: Regis, quòd Ille sibi hæc arrogaret; Nostrûm, quòd nos Illi ista tribuamus. Procul hæc habet Rex; procul à se abdicat.
units.tr: That office of yours (which you say properly belongs to the Papal Primacy), namely the teaching office, or the explaining of doubtful points of the Law, he does not assume; nor does he hold sermons, or preside over sacred rites, or celebrate the sacraments; nor does he consecrate persons or things; nor does he claim the right of the keys, or of censures. In a word: he does not think it lawful for himself, nor do we think it lawful for him, to touch those matters which belong to the sacerdotal office or follow from the power of Orders. This calumny of yours is altogether invented out of hatred, both of the King and of us: of the King, because you say he arrogates these things to himself; of us, because you say we ascribe them to him. The King keeps far away from these things; he renounces them far from himself.

units.la: Atqui in hijs quæ Exterioris Politiæ sunt, vt præcipiat, suo sibi iure vendicat; nosque adeo Illi lubentes merito deferimus. Religionis enim curam, rem Regiam esse, non modò Pontificiam, & in Regijs primam; quámquè Ille non solùm foris ab externâ vi, sed & domi ab incuriâ hominum adferre teneatur. Vos quidem ipsi, si vis instet vlla, rem Regiam clamatis: Ille verò, si collapsa sit Disciplina, non minùs Regiam.
units.tr: Yet in those matters which belong to external polity, he claims for himself by his own right the power to command, and we therefore gladly and rightly defer to him in this. For the care of religion is a royal concern, not only a Papal one, and it is the first of royal concerns; and he is bound to bring this care not only abroad, against external force, but also at home, against the carelessness of men. You yourselves, indeed, if any violence threatens, cry out that it is a royal matter; but he, if discipline has collapsed, says it is no less a royal matter.

units.la: Nam cùm Lege ipsâ Dei {e}Custos sit & Vindex; non secundæ modò Tabulæ, sed & primæ: primæ quoque ad se curam pertinere putat, & primam primæ. Et cùm {a}Omnis ani-ma Ei subjici iubetur: animæ etiam consultum vult; magis autem id atque prius, quàm corpori.
units.tr: For since he is, by the Law of God itself, its guardian and avenger, not only of the second table but also of the first, he thinks the care of the first table pertains to him too, and the first of the first table most of all. And since it is commanded that every soul be subject to Him, he also wishes to provide for the soul; and this more, and before, than for the body.

units.la: Vis illa dicam Sigillatim quæ sint? Quodcunque in rebus Religionis Reges Israel fecerunt, nec sine laude fecerunt, id vt Ei faciendi ius sit ac potestas. Leges authoritate Regiâ ferendi, ne blasphemetur Deus (non negabitis; fecit {b}Rex Babel) vt ieiunio placeatur Deus, fecit {c}Rex Ninive: vt Festo honoretur, fecit {d}Esther cùm Purim, {c}Machabæus, cùm Encœnia promulgaret. Denique iis omnibus de rebus, de quibus in Codice, in Authenticis, in Capitularibus à Constantino, Theodosio, Iustiniano, Carolo Magno Leges latæ leguntur.
units.tr: Shall I say separately what those powers are? Whatever the kings of Israel did in matters of religion, and did not without praise, that he has the right and power to do. To enact laws by royal authority, so that God is not blasphemed (you will not deny it; the King of Babylon did so); so that God is honored by fasting, the King of Nineveh did so; so that a feast is honored, Esther did so when she proclaimed Purim, and Maccabeus when he proclaimed the Feast of Dedication. Finally, in all those matters concerning which laws are read as having been enacted in the Code, in the Authentics, in the Capitularies, by Constantine, Theodosius, Justinian and Charlemagne.

units.la: Tum, delegandi qui de Lege sic Latâ iudicent, quod {f}Iosaphat. Tum subditos, ne sic legem violent, iuramento obstringendi, quod & {g}Asa & {h}Iosias.
units.tr: Then, to appoint those who judge according to the law so enacted, as Jehoshaphat did; then to bind subjects by oath not to violate the law in this way, as both Asa and Josiah did.

units.la: Quòd siqui in Leges ita latas committant, etsi Religionis ea causa sit, sive {i}Pseudoprophetæ crimen est, sive {k}Idololatræ, sive {l}Blasphemi, sive {m}Sacrapolluentes, in eos authoritate Regiâ animadvertendi.
units.tr: And if anyone should commit offenses against laws so enacted, whether in this matter of religion it is the crime of false prophets, or of idolaters, or of blasphemers, or of those who pollute sacred things, he has authority by royal power to punish them.

units.la: Conuentus authoritate suâ indicendi; Etiam de Arcâ reducendâ, & figendâ loco suo, quod fecit {n}Dauid: Etiam de Populo ad Dei cultum reuocando, quod {o}Iosaphat: Etiam de Templo dedicando, quod {p}Salomon: collapso instaurando, quod {q}Ioas: polluto purificando, quod {r}Ezekias.
units.tr: To summon assemblies by his own authority; also concerning the bringing back of the Ark and its fixing in its place, as David did; also concerning the recall of the people to the worship of God, as Jehoshaphat did; also concerning the dedication of the Temple, as Solomon did; concerning the restoration of what had fallen, as Joash did; concerning the purification of what was polluted, as Hezekiah did.

units.la: Quanquam verò, non frustra sibi præceptum putet à Deo, {s}vt describat sibi Legis exemplar, secum habeat semper, legat sedulo, & {t}dies noctésque meditetur, condiscat inde cultum Dei vel ad ipsas vsque Ceremonias; nec hoc Illi dictum, vt totus ab alieno ore pendeat, Ipse quâ à se nihil planè dijudicet: In hijs tamen {u}Os Eleazari, non inuitus consulet, & requiret legem ab eis, quorum labia scientiam custodiunt: adhibebit in sacris Legibus ferendis, quos adhibere par est, quoque ratio suadet, rerum illarum consultissimos, déque iis optimè respondere posse. Et in hijs, quæ ad Deum pertinent {x}Amariam Sacerdotem, non Zabadiam Ducem iubebit præsidere.
units.tr: Although indeed he does not think it in vain that he has been commanded by God to write out for himself a copy of the Law, to keep it always with him, to read it diligently, and to meditate on it day and night, so as to learn from it the worship of God even down to the very ceremonies; nor is this said to him so that he should hang wholly on another's mouth, and himself judge nothing at all: nevertheless, in these matters, he will consult, not unwillingly, the mouth of Eleazar, and will seek the law from those whose lips keep knowledge; in enacting sacred laws he will employ those whom it is fitting to employ, and whom reason also suggests, the most learned in those matters and those who can answer well concerning them. And in those matters which pertain to God he will order Amariah the Priest, not Zebadiah the Leader, to preside.

units.la: Quoad Personas; Omnibus omnium Ordinum ius dicendi: qui fit (dicam stilo Scripturæ) {y}Caput Tribus Leni, non mi-nūs nùs quàm cæterarum, nec minùs Clericorùm quàm Laicorum Rex: Contra Abiathar siquis superbierit, {a}Decreto suo compescendi; etiam Abiathar ipsum, si ita meritus, Pontifi-catu {b}abdicandi.
units.tr: As to persons: the right of judging belongs to all men of every order; that is (to speak in the language of Scripture), the King is the head of the tribe of Levi, as gently as of the others, and no less of the clergy than of the laity. Against Abiathar, should anyone grow proud, he may restrain him by his decree; and even Abiathar himself, if he so deserved, he may depose from the Priesthood.

units.la: Quoad Res. Excelsa diruendi; id est, peregrinum cultum abolendi; necmodò Vitulum aureum ab Aarone conflatum, quod {c}Moses, sed & Serpentem aneum à Mose erectum confringendi, quod {d}Ezechias; Et sive in Idololatriam abeat Vitulus aureus, sive in superstitionem Serpens aneus, utrumque comminuendi.
units.tr: As to things: to pull down high places, that is, to abolish foreign worship; not only to break the golden calf cast by Aaron, as Moses did, but also the bronze serpent set up by Moses, as Hezekiah did; and whether the golden calf turns to idolatry, or the bronze serpent to superstition, to crush both.

units.la: Nam de rebus, quæ ad decorem Domus Dei spectant, quædici solent Adiaphora, statuendi, quod {e}Jous[?]; Et quæ materia schismatis esse assolent, futiles & inutiles Quæstiones, authoritate suâ compescendi, quod {f}Constantinus; ne vos quidem ipsi negatis ius esse.
units.tr: For he may also decide those matters which pertain to the adornment of the House of God, which are commonly called adiaphora (indifferent things); and he may suppress by his own authority futile and useless questions which are wont to be the matter of schism, as Constantine did; you yourselves do not deny that this is his right.

units.la: Postremò; si de Christianis exemplum malitiis, id postulat, ut Episcopus sit [illegible, ~3 letters] quod Constantinus: ut Rector Religionù, quod non modò Carolus Magnus, sed & Ludovicus Pius.
units.tr: Lastly: if the example of Christians' malice requires it, that the Bishop be [illegible], as Constantine was; that he be ruler of religion, as not only Charlemagne but also Louis the Pious was.

units.la: Hæc Primatus apud nos iura sunt, ex iure Diuino. Reliqua Chimæra vestra sunt, quibuscum quasi cum umbrâ vestrâ [illegible, ~5 letters] si libet, quantum libet, instituite. Nos illa non feriunt; Lectori, perinde ut affectus erit, vel stomachum, vel risum mouent.
units.tr: These are the rights of the Primacy among us, from divine right. The rest are your chimeras, with which you may, as with your own shadow, [illegible] contend as much as you please and for as long as you please. We are not struck by them; they move the reader, according to his disposition, either to disgust or to laughter.

units.la: DIctum iam de officijs deque Titulis, quibus dignantur Reges Spiritus Sanctus: quibuscum quàm bellè conueniat Cardinali, notauit Apologia. Quodsi in Cardinalem redundet ex eo fonte inuidia, vnde Regibus illam conflare voluit, quis non par pari relatum dicat? Quàm bellè verò iam inter se conciliet Tortus, age videamus. Verba Cardinalis, Magis proprie Seruus dici debet, qui præest, quàm qui subditus est. Falsò posita primò. Non enim magu proprie dici debet, qui nec proprie debet. Proprie autem dici non debere, docet idem ipse Cardinalis eodemipso in loco; dubitat enim, an vlla seruitus in Principatu Politico; Deinde, Despoticam subiectionem veram & propriam seruitutem dicit. At subditi, proprie loquendo Principum [illegible, ~4 letters] non sunt. Docet & Tortus, qui ideo Seruos dici vult, non quasi subiecti sint (at proprie seruitutis ratio in subiectione est) sed quia laborant regendo propter bonum publicum. Labor autem proprie seruitus non est; nec qui laborant, eo ipso quòd laborant, proprie seruire dicuntur. Laborant etiam, qui liberi sunt; neque Seruus proprie in virgâ venit, ipse potius virgæ & correctioni subiacet. Quodsi autem ex eo Seruus quis proprie dicatur, quod propter bonum publicum, & populi utilitatem operetur, liber qui propter suum: mali omnes proprie liberi, boni proprie Serui, nec nisi boni. Nisi bonos enim vix reperies, qui quærant quæ sua non sunt; aut laborent propter bonum aliud quàm suum.
units.tr: I have now spoken of the offices and the titles by which the Kings are honored by the Holy Spirit; the Apology has noted how neatly these agree with a Cardinal. But if envy falls on a Cardinal from the same source from which he wished to stir it up against Kings, who would not say that it is returned in kind? But let us see how neatly Torti now reconciles these things with one another. The Cardinal's words: "He ought to be called a servant more properly who presides than he who is subject." This is falsely put, first. For he ought not to be called "more properly" a servant who ought not to be called one "properly" at all. That he ought not to be called one properly, the same Cardinal teaches in the same place; for he doubts "whether there is any servitude in political principality." Then he says that "despotic subjection is true and proper servitude." But "subjects," properly speaking, are not [illegible] of Princes. Torti also teaches, who wishes them to be called servants for this reason, "not because they are subject" (but the reason for proper servitude "lies in subjection"), but because they labor in ruling for the public good. Yet labor is not properly servitude; nor are those who labor, by the very fact that they labor, properly said to serve. Free men too labor; nor does the servant "properly" come into the rod, but rather he is himself subject to the rod and to correction. But if, moreover, someone is called a servant "properly" for this reason, that he works for the public good and the advantage of the people, then the free man who works for his own is free; all wicked men are "properly" free, and all good men "properly" servants, and none but good men. For you will scarcely find any who seek what is not their own, or who labor for any good other than their own.

units.la: Atque ut falsò posita, ita nihilo verius, ex Paulo, Gregorio, Augustino confirmata. Paulus enim & Gregorius de Politico Principatu non loquuntur: Cardinalis de Politico. Quid Augustinus? Etiam qui imperant seruiunt iis, quibus videntur imperare. Sic est.. At hoc multum abest à dicto Cardinalis. Nusquam enim hic magis proprie, ac ne proprie quidem. Quin (ut ibi Augustinus) officio consulendi & prouidendi misericordiâ seruiunt; ut Tortus ipse respondet, labore, non subiectione seruiunt. Magis ergo proprie quod dixit, minùs cautè dixit, vel potius nimis inuidiosè dixit. Quod te autem malè habet de voce Mancipij Anglicè positâ, non Serui; ideo habet, quia vim vocis ignoras. Serui enim hic apud nos, quorum cùm sui Mancipij esse nequeant, ne vindictâ quidem Prætoris, & vox & conditio longè durior. Utinam verò tam de voculâ non laborares. Principes enim Mancipia sua facit Papa, si ad rem attendas; Stratores suos, stapedam tenere, Ceruices conculcandas dare: Mancipia quos facit, Mancipia dici cur non permittat? Durius multò facere hæc, quàm dicere.
units.tr: And as it is falsely put, so it is no truer, confirmed from Paul, Gregory and Augustine. For Paul and Gregory do not speak of political principality; the Cardinal speaks of political. What of Augustine? "Even those who rule serve those over whom they seem to rule." That is so. But this is far from the Cardinal's saying. For here nowhere is "more properly" said, nor even "properly." Rather (as Augustine there says) they serve "by the duty of caring for and providing with mercy"; as Torti himself replies, they serve by labor, not by subjection. So what he said, "more properly," he said too carelessly, or rather he said it too odiously. As for what troubles you about the English word "mancipium" (bondsman) rather than "servant": it troubles you because you do not know the force of the word. For the servants here among us, who cannot be the property of their masters, are not even subject to the punishment of the Praetor, and their condition and name are far harsher. Would that you were not troubled by such a small word! For the Pope, if you look at the matter, makes his Princes his mancipia: his grooms, to hold the stirrup and to offer their necks to be trampled on; why should he not allow those whom he makes mancipia to be called mancipia? To do these things is much harsher than to say them.

units.la: Verba Chrysostomi; Sensus Bellarmini. Cohibeat Regem Diaconus, si cùm indignus sit, idque palàm constet, accedat tamen ad Sacramentum. Cohibeat & Medicum[?], si ad noxium quid, vel insalubre manum admoueat. Cohibeat[?] & Equiso, si inter equitandum, adigat equum per locum præruptum, vel salebrosum, cui subsit periculum. Etiamne Medico, etiamne Equisoni suo subiectus Rex? Sed de maiori potestate loquitur, sed eâ, ad rem noxiam procul arcendam: quâ in re charitatis semper potestas est maxima. Verùm dic, nunquámne Cardinalis dixit in loco, Chrysostomum multa per excessum loqui? Ego non dico; id dico, non tam curandum, quæ Chrysostomi mi verba, quàm quis animus Cardinalis in citando. Caput illud Cardinalis euoluat Lectorintegrum; videat annon toto illo Capite, animus illi Reges deprimendi.
units.tr: Words of Chrysostom; sense of Bellarmine. Let the deacon restrain the king, if, though unworthy, and this is plainly established, he approaches the sacrament. Let him restrain the physician too, if he lays his hand on something harmful or unwholesome. Let the horseman restrain him also, if while riding he drives the horse over a precipitous or rough place where there is danger. Is the king then subject even to his physician, even to his horseman? But Chrysostom speaks of a greater power, namely the power to keep off harm, and in such a matter the power of charity is always greatest. Come now, has the Cardinal never said in some place, that Chrysostom says many things in excess? I do not say so; I say that we should not so much be concerned with what Chrysostom's words are as with what spirit the Cardinal has in citing them. Let the reader unroll that chapter of the Cardinal in full and see whether, throughout that whole chapter, his spirit is not bent on crushing kings.

units.la: Quod ipsum responsum ferat, ad Presbyterum ante Imperatorem de poculo bibentem. Illustre exemplum: praesertim si & addas facti rationem, {a}quòd digniorem existimauit Imperatore Presbyterum; tum, quòd integrum ei non esset (puta admisisset in se scelus graue) nisi Presbyterum Imperatori praetulisset. At Presbyter iste Cardinalis non erat; Cardinales autem Regibus non praeferuntur, Socij tantum sunt. Quare peccauit iudicio hoc suo, vel iudicio vestro. Tum, neque Maximus, cui factum hoc, Imperator erat, sed Rebellis in Imperatorem, & tanquam Rebellis caesus paulò post à Theodosio. Tortus autem satis se dixisse putat, cùm Cardinalem ait, ex se hoc non affirmare. Quorsum autem affert ex alio, nisi vt affirmet ex se? Non enim perstringit, quod fecerit. Quae illius intentio cum afferret? Sine dubio, vt Reges moratos redderet. Aberrat enim omnis inuidia procul, procul & omnis maleuolentia; prae amore, Regem infra Presbyteros atque Diaconos ablegauit. Lector autem qui sapit, putabit in Martini exemplo illo, magis Maximi patientiam, quàm Martini modestiam elucere.
units.tr: He brings forward the answer to the presbyter who drank from the cup before the emperor. A notable example, especially if you add the reason for the act: that he thought the presbyter more worthy than the emperor; and then that it would not have been right for him (suppose he had committed a grave sin) unless he had preferred the presbyter to the emperor. But that presbyter was not a Cardinal, and Cardinals are not preferred to kings; they are only their companions. Therefore he erred in this judgment of his, or in your judgment. Further, Maximus, to whom this happened, was not the emperor but a rebel against the emperor, and, as a rebel, he was slain shortly afterwards by Theodosius. Tortus, however, thinks he has said enough when he says the Cardinal does not affirm this on his own account. But why does he bring it forward from another source, unless it is in order to affirm it on his own account? For he does not censure what he did. What purpose could his intention have had in bringing it forward? Undoubtedly, to make kings more modest. For every envy is far, far away, and every ill will too; out of love, he has dismissed the king beneath the presbyters and deacons. A reader with sense, however, will think that in that example of Martin, the patience of Maximus shines forth more than the modesty of Martin.

units.la: De Regum authoritate, quòd ex iure diuino non fit, quòd immediatè à Deo non descendat, Cardinalis ait; Tortus probat; Afferri enim Scriptorum sententia communi. At nec omnium, nec optimorum. Deriuatam enim in Mosen authoritatem à Deo ipso summam, nullo mediante corpore collectiuo, in quo locata primùm à Deo authoritas illa fit, post inde in Mosen collata. Idem post factum in Regibus, sine lege vlla tum Regia: Populus[?] nihil contulit: CHRISTI Domini, non CHRI[illegible, ~2 letters] populi sunt. Oleo Sancto infuso signare id Deus voluit, & consignare: ex Sion Sanctuario suo, non ex Millo Conuentus Popularis loco, authoritatem illis esse. Quo ipso Oleo testatus est, quàm vel Propheticam, vel Sacerdotalem, tàm Regiam etiam Diuini iuris esse. Tam (inquam,) nisi hic Regibus praerogatiua sua fit; aliqua certè; vel ex eo, quòd per eminentiam nomen habeant Christorum Domini; vel ex eo, quòd Solium Regis, Solium Dei: Cathedra Pontificis Cathedra Petri modò est. Quod enim apponit Tortus de Regno in Rempublicam interdum mutato, nimis crassum est. Acutus homo non distinguit inter formam, atq; authoritatem Regiminis; forma de hominibus esse potest; de cœlo semper est authoritas. Qui rem quidem hic paulò magis expenderit, hinc, semel à Deo collatam Regi potestatem, propagari in stirpe perpetim lineâ non interruptâ; illinc, in Pontifice interrumpi subinde, novo semper Pontifici de novo potestatem applicari, putet certè Pontificis authoritatem mediatè ab Ecclesiâ esse; à Deo immediatè non esse; & inanem planè Chimæram vestram esse Potestatis Pontificiæ, à demortuo præcedente vsque ad nouum renunciatum, in aere pendulæ; tum autem [illegible, ~6 letters] in succedentem demissæ. Vos ergo expedite de Pontifice. Nos de Rege videbimus, præsertim cùm de Romano vestro Cardinalis ipse trepidet, cùm ita vobis suadet. a Tametsi forte non sit de iure diuino, Romanum Pontificem Petro succedere in Præfecturam totius Ecclesiæ: tamen si quis absolutè petat, an iure Diuino Romanus Pontifex sit Caput totius Ecclesiæ, omnino id esse asserendum. Nobis non licet esse tam disertis, Omninò id asserere de Iure Diuino esse, quod tamen forte de Iure Diuino non est.
units.tr: Concerning the authority of kings, that it does not come by divine right, that it does not descend immediately from God, the Cardinal says; Tortus proves it, for the opinion of the writers in common is cited. But it is not the opinion of all, nor of the best. For the supreme authority, derived from God himself into Moses, was without any intervening collective body, in which that authority was first placed by God and afterwards conferred upon Moses. The same happened afterwards in the kings, with no law of kingship then in place: the people contributed nothing; they are the Lord's Anointed, not the anointed of the people. God willed to mark and seal them by the pouring of holy oil; from his sanctuary in Zion, not from Millo, the place of the popular assembly, they have their authority. By that very oil he testified that kingship is of divine right just as much as prophecy or priesthood. So (I say), unless kings have some prerogative here, certainly some prerogative, if only from this, that they bear by eminence the name Christs of the Lord; or from this, that the throne of the king is the throne of God, while the chair of the Pontiff is only the chair of Peter. For what Tortus adds, that the kingdom is sometimes changed into a commonwealth, is far too crude. A clever man does not distinguish between the form and the authority of government; the form can be from men, but the authority is always from heaven. Whoever weighs this matter a little more carefully will surely think this: on the one hand, power once conferred by God upon the king is handed down in the line of his stock perpetually and without interruption; on the other, in the Pontiff it is interrupted from time to time, the power being applied anew to each new Pontiff; and the authority of the Pontiff is certainly mediately from the Church, not immediately from God; and your power of the Pontiff is plainly an empty chimera, hanging in the air from the predecessor who has died until the new one is proclaimed; and then it is let down into the successor. So you, go and sort out the Pontiff. We shall see about the king, especially since the Cardinal himself trembles about your Roman one, when he so advises you. Although perhaps it is not of divine right that the Roman Pontiff succeeds Peter in the headship of the whole Church, yet if anyone asks absolutely whether by divine right the Roman Pontiff is the head of the whole Church, this must be affirmed without qualification. We are not allowed to be so eloquent: to affirm without qualification that it is of divine right, which perhaps is not of divine right.

units.la: Depositos ab Imperatore Pontifices fatetur; sed negat potuisse iure deponi. Ergòne iniuriâ depositi (quos ibi nominat) Johannes 12. Gregorius 6, duo, non homines sed monstra hominum,& propudia generis humani? Non audet iniuriâ dicere. Quid dicit? Non propriè depositos ab Imperatoribus, sed à Concilijs Episcoporum. Etiamne de poni potest Papa à Concilio non Generali, à Concilio Episcoporum aliquot? Caue Torte; Etiamne ab illegitimo Concilio? Quæro enim an fuerit legitimum? Nam si legitimum, quo depositus Johannes 12, legitimus & Canon In Synodo. Caue & hic. b Baronius enim iam & Vestri homines, potiùs quàm admittant Canonem illum pro legitimo, Concilium illud mutarunt in Conciliabulum; atque ita iam Johannes 12, vir optimus, in Concilio illegitimo, per iniuriam depositus. Quare Confessor ad minimum; Martyr etiam sine dubio futurus, nisi post confessus fuisset in adulterio. Sed hæ technæ vestræ sunt. Nobis, qui nescimus illas, satis est, quòd legitimus Pontifex potuit iure deponi à Rege; nempè Abiathar à Salomone, idque proprie, sine Concilio omni, vel legitimo, vel illegitimo. Et in illâ Historiâ neminem extitisse in totâ Pontificum serie, qui Regem vllum deposuerit.
units.tr: He admits that Pontiffs were deposed by the emperor; but he denies that they could be deposed by right. Then were those (whom he names there) John 12, Gregory 6, two men, not men but monsters of men and the disgrace of the human race, deposed wrongfully? He does not dare to say wrongfully. What does he say? Not properly deposed by the emperors, but by councils of bishops. Can a Pope also be deposed by a council that is not general, by a council of some few bishops? Beware, Tortus! Also by an illegitimate council? For I ask whether it was legitimate. For if it was legitimate, by which John 12 was deposed, then the canon In Synodo is legitimate too. Beware here as well. For Baronius and your men already, rather than admit that canon as legitimate, have changed that council into a conventicle; and so John 12, a most excellent man, was deposed wrongfully in an illegitimate council. Therefore he was at least a confessor, and without doubt would have been a martyr too, had he not afterwards confessed to adultery. But these are your tricks. For us, who do not know them, it is enough that a legitimate Pontiff could be deposed by right by a king; namely Abiathar by Solomon, and that properly, without any council at all, whether legitimate or illegitimate. And in that history, no one arose in the whole series of Pontiffs who deposed any king.

units.la: Nusquámne apud Cardinalem extat locus eiusmodi, quo Episcopis liceat Reges deponere? At tu modò locum huiusmodi apud Sanderum, verè aureum dixisti. Quòd si verè aureus, Cardinalem dedecere non potest. Afferre ibi vos dicit, atque merito afferre, Quoscunque Reges Christianos, ita Episcopis & Presbyteris subesse, ut per sententiam eorum deponi possint. Credo autem tibi, Episcopos, cùm in bonâ gratiâ Pontificis sunt, dici ab eo Venerabiles fratres; sed si bilem moverint, an vllus fuerit Papa tam iracundus nescio, qui illos mancipia dixerit: certè aliqui (si vera narrant Historiæ) vt Mancipia habuerunt; etiam (si bene memini) Cardinales. Cur enim non habeant, qui socios eorum Reges sæpè sic habuerunt?
units.tr: Is there nowhere in the Cardinal's work a passage of this kind, by which it is lawful for bishops to depose kings? But you have just now called a passage of this kind in Sanders truly golden. If it is truly golden, it cannot disgrace the Cardinal. There you say they bring forward, and rightly bring forward, whatever Christian kings are so subject to bishops and presbyters that they can be deposed by their sentence. I grant, however, that bishops, when they are in the good graces of the Pontiff, are called by him "venerable brothers"; but if they stir his bile, I do not know whether there has ever been a Pope so irascible as to call them slaves. Certainly some (if the histories tell the truth) have held them as slaves; even (if I remember rightly) Cardinals. For why should they not hold as slaves those who have so often treated kings, their fellows, in that way?

units.la: De interuallo quod est inter Ecclesiasticos & Principes, hijs illi quid præstent, mollire iam nititur: non dici de quibuslibet Ecclesiasticis (putà de Curatis) sed de Principibus Ecclesiarum. At quibuslibet Ecclesiasticis animarum cura est; etiam fortè Minoritùs maior animarum cura, quàm Maioritùs. Denique rem reijcit in Nazianzenum; totidem verbis ibi haberi. Quid verò? Tam longè Episcopos supra Principes esse, quàm est anima supra corpus. At nec longè supra ibi est, nec tam longè su-pra. Liberè loquentem se ferre vult Præsidem Prouinciæ, (non Imperatorem; is vos error diu exercuit, iam deposuistis) esse enim sibi dicit Principatum, eumq; maiorem, aut Spiritum Carni cedere oportere. Modestè satis hoc. Vestri enim hic homines animaduerterunt, totum hominem vtrique potestati subiectum, tam Ecclesiasticæ quàm Politicæ. Nam & religio in corpus ius exercet; & ad animas quoque pertingit ciuilis obedientia, nec inanimis res est. Quare totum hominem, quâ terrenæ fœlicitatis capax, subiectum Politicæ; eundem totum, quâ capax est æternæ, subiectum Ecclesiasticæ. Non rectè igitur instituit à vobis quasi partis cum parte comparationem, cùm si proprie loqui detur, vtrobique, in totum, æquale ius fit. Præsidi etiam, cui prouincia in ciuilibus modò, curæ est, recté comparati Episcopum, Regi non recté: cui in vtrisque cura incumbit, cui vtriúsque & ∪Amariæ[?] & Zabadiæ designatio. Qui verò Nazianzenum bene nôrit, ad illius animum non putet esse, sic dilatari atque extendi verba eius ad sensum ab indole eius alienum, & à totâ vitæ ratione; qui longè aberrat, vt præ Ecclesiasticis sic Principes eleuaret. Non erat hoc illorum, vel morum vel temporum.
units.tr: Concerning the gap that lies between churchmen and princes, he now strives to soften what they bring: it is not said of any churchmen whatever (for example parish priests) but of the princes of the churches. But every churchman has the care of souls; perhaps even the lesser has a greater care of souls than the greater. Finally, he throws the matter back upon Nazianzen, saying that the same words are found there. But what then? Bishops are as far above princes as the soul is above the body. But they are not far above there, nor so far above. He wishes the one who speaks freely to be a governor of a province (not an emperor; that error has long troubled you, and now you have abandoned it), for he says that the principate is his, and that the greater must yield to the spirit rather than to the flesh. This is modest enough. For your men here have noticed that the whole man is subject to both powers, the ecclesiastical as much as the political. For religion exercises right over the body, and civil obedience also reaches to the souls, and it is no lifeless matter. Therefore the whole man, as far as he is capable of earthly happiness, is subject to the political power; and the same whole man, as far as he is capable of eternal life, is subject to the ecclesiastical. It is not right, therefore, for you to set up a comparison as if of part with part, since, if we are to speak properly, there is in each case an equal right over the whole. The comparison with a bishop is rightly made with a governor of a province, who is concerned only with civil matters; it is not rightly made with a king, on whom the care of both falls, and the designation of both Amaria and Zabadia. But whoever knows Nazianzen well will not think that his mind was such that his words were stretched and extended in this way to a sense alien to his character and to his whole manner of life, which strays far from the purpose of raising princes above churchmen. That was not in keeping with their morals or with their times.

units.la: Bonæ fidei iam actionem instituit, de loco non recté citato. Non ibi dicit Regem per Subditos suos deponi posse. Non ibi? Sed annon dicit omnino? Si non ibi, annon alicubi? Quid iuuat autem, si ad præsens intermittat paroxysmus, pòst autem tanto recurrat acrior? Tamen ex loco citato quæro. Deposuit Reges Pontifex, solâne id sententiâ suâ? Legisti quenquam, qui latâ statim sententiâ deposuerit cum Sceptro Coronam? quenquam qui non, quâ potuit, restiterit? Quid tum Pontifex? Quod vitii[?] faciunt; ad Populum provocat; per subditos rem agit, interdicit ne pareant, edicit vt insurgant; facit primò non subditos, pòst hostes etiam. Desertus, profligatus à suis Rex, ita demum cessit, quicunque cessit. Res eò redit; deponit Populus, non Pontifex, etiam vbi Pontifex deponit. Absque illo, fulmen eius contemnant, sententiæ obnuncient: vt & contempserunt & obnunciârunt nonnulli, quibus Populi sui fides sublesta non fuit. Quanquam de Cardinalis mente quid quærimus? Remittit nos ad Sanderum suum, inter aurea cuius dicta iam antè in Apologiâ numeratur & illud: Rex, qui Pontificis authoritati se subjicere recusabit, nullo modo tolerandus est, sed omnem operam Subditi dare debent, vt alium in eius locum quamprimum surrogetur. Audis, Subditi operam dare debent: debent quamprimum. Subditorum operam quæritur, quæ si desit, frustra tonet fulgurétque Pontifex. Nec alia vel Philopatri mens, vel Didymi, vel Rossei. Denique cur delicias faciat hîc Tortus? Turbatis non ita pridem in Gallia rebus, non alia tum doctrina Parisiùs regnauit; nisi gessisset ibi rem cædendo Populus, Pontifex sedendo haud quicquam effecisset.
units.tr: He has begun a fair-minded discussion of a passage not cited correctly. There he does not say that a king can be deposed by his own subjects. Not there? But does he not say it outright? If not there, does he not say it somewhere else? What good is it, moreover, if the attack subsides for the moment, only to return later more violently? Still, I ask about the passage cited. Did a pope depose kings by his sentence alone? Have you read of anyone who, once the sentence was pronounced, at once gave up the sceptre along with the crown, or who did not resist with all the means he had? What then does the pope do? What they do when they are unable to do more: he appeals to the people, works through the subjects, forbids them to obey, orders them to rise up. He makes them first not subjects, and afterwards even enemies. A king deserted and overthrown by his own people gives way at last, whoever it is that gives way. The matter comes back to this: the people deposes, not the pope, even when the pope pronounces the deposition. Without the people, they may despise his thunderbolt and disregard his sentences, as some did despise and disregard it, men whose trust in their own people was not shaken. Yet why do we ask about the cardinal's intention? He refers us to his Sanders, among whose golden sayings the following is already counted earlier in the Apology: A king who refuses to submit himself to the authority of the pope must in no way be tolerated, but all subjects ought to take pains that another be substituted in his place as soon as possible. You hear it: subjects ought to take pains; ought to do so as soon as possible. It is the effort of the subjects that is sought, and if that is lacking, the pope thunders and flashes in vain. Nor is the intention of Philopater, or of Didymus, or of Rossaeus any different. Finally, why does Torts here make a fuss? When affairs were not long ago in turmoil in France, no other doctrine held sway in Paris; and unless the people had acted by striking, the pope by sitting idle would have accomplished nothing whatever.

units.la: Qui paulò suprà, depositos agnouit Pontifices duos Iohannem[?] i 2um. & Gregorium 6um. idque propriè à Concilijs Episcoporum: mutavit jam mentem Tortus, & negat, ullo modo deponi[?] posse. Nemini enim mortalium permissum esse, de iis judicare. At mortales credo erant, qui in Concilio Constantiensi tres simul Pontifices judicârunt, etiam deposuerunt, idque legitimè; alioqui Sedis invasor Martinum Quintum, qui tribus illis furrogatus est; nec illorum melior conditio, qui ei post successerunt, omnes malæ fidei possessores. At hæc noua tum fuisset Theologia, & explosa ab eis: Non posse à Generali Concilio judicare Papam; de quâ inter omnes Theologos & Juris consultos hodie non puto convenire.
units.tr: A little earlier he acknowledged that two popes, John XXIII and Gregory XII, were deposed, and that this was done properly by councils of bishops. Torts has now changed his mind and denies that they can be deposed in any way. For it is not permitted to any mortal to judge them. But I believe that they were mortals who at the Council of Constance judged three popes at once and also deposed them, and did so lawfully; otherwise the usurper of the see, Martin V, who was substituted in place of those three, would be in an illegitimate position, and the condition of those who afterwards succeeded him, all possessors in bad faith, would be no better. But that doctrine, that a general council cannot judge a pope, would then have been a novelty, and rejected by them; and I do not think that today all theologians and jurists agree on it.

units.la: Verùm scriptum id in Generalibus Concilijs ante multa secula; Nemini mortalium permissum esse judicari de Pontifice. Quinque ibi Romana Concilia citat Cardinalis; Sinuessanum, Siluestri, Sixti tertij, Symmachi, Adriani secundi, in quibus si domi ipse sibi Pontifex ius dicens, seipsum absoluerit, non referret admodum. Sed nec in illis hoc dicitur, præter forte Sinuessano, aut Siluestrino, quorum iam pudere incipit vel Cardinales ipsos. Reliqua non negant à Concilio Generali, totam Ecclesiam repræsentante, loco moueri posse. Omnia hæc in Constantiensi excussa satis, nec obstabant tum eis quò minus de Pontifice sententiam ferrent. Generalia ibi plura non sunt; duo sunt tantùm, nec valdè ad rem.
units.tr: But that was written in the general councils many centuries ago: that it is permitted to no mortal to be judged concerning a pope. The cardinal cites five Roman councils there: Sinuessa, Silvester, Sixtus III, Symmachus, Hadrian II, in which, if the pope himself, pronouncing law at home, had absolved himself, it would not greatly matter. But this is not said in those councils, except perhaps in the Sinuessan or Silvestrine, which even the cardinals themselves are beginning to be ashamed of. The rest do not deny that a pope can be removed from his place by a general council representing the whole Church. All of this was thoroughly examined at Constance, and it did not then prevent them from pronouncing sentence against a pope. There are no more general councils there; there are only two, and these do not bear much on the matter.

units.la: Quorum in priore, Chalcedonensi, inter alias causas satis permultas (duodecim enim propter quas depositus ibi tum Dioscorus) & illa est, quòd in Leonem petulantior fuisset. At nec sola fuit, nec præcipua depositionis causa; sed quia procax in Concilium, & quia ter vocatus non comparuit. Neque verò ita exhorruit rem illam Concilium ut narrat Cardinalis; & de Nemine mortalium, syllaba ibi nulla. Non magis quàm in posteriore illo (nuperiam Octavo Generali facto) cuius nondum satis limati Canones, partim enim integri, partim in compendium redacti, quòd commodè & emendata exemplaria vobis deessent. Quodsi autem id permissum dicerent nemini; nemini vni sentirent: licere tamen Concilio quod vni non licet. Certum illud; ventilatâ hæc omnia à Cusano, Cameracensi, Gersone, quique eandem post sententiam tutari sunt, Panormitano, Maiore, Almaino. Certum autem, Purifijs hæresin esse, hoc quod tu affirmas, defendere; vbi si dicere audetis Parisienses Concilijs pluribus Generalibus lucem mouere, quæ non vultis, audietis. Se enim, Conciliorum Generalium Defensores, vos oppugnatores esse.
units.tr: Of these, the first, Chalcedon, lists among its many other causes (for there were twelve reasons for which Dioscorus was deposed there) also this one: that he had been too insolent toward Leo. But this was neither the only nor the chief cause of the deposition; it was because he was defiant toward the council, and because, though summoned three times, he did not appear. Nor did that council so shrink from the matter as the cardinal relates; and there is no syllable there about no mortal. No more is there in that later one (the Eighth General Council, held recently), whose canons are not yet sufficiently polished, for some were given in full, others reduced to a summary, since correct and corrected copies were lacking to you. But if they said that this is permitted to no one, they would be saying that it is not permitted to any single person: yet the council may do what one person may not. That is certain. All these points were debated by Cusanus, Cameracensis, Gerson, and those who defended the same opinion afterwards: Panormitanus, Major, Almain. It is certain, however, that to defend what you affirm is heresy among the Puritans; and if you dare to say that the Parisians bring light to bear on several general councils in a way you do not wish, you will hear it. For they, the defenders of the general councils, are the opponents of you.

units.la: Quem verò post, Tortus distraxit articulum in duos, is in Apologia vnus est, duabus ex clausulis constans, oppositis inter se. Papa obedientiam deberi propter conscientiam; Regi deberi propter ordinem politicum. Vbi vix bona fide Tortus: diuulsit enim, qui vnus erat, procudens nobis ex vno duos. Nec enim negare voluit Author legitimis Ecclesiæ Rectoribus subijci Christianos, etiam propter conscientiam, non minùs sanè quàm Reipublicæ. Id notauit, in Papæ obedientia vrgeri conscientiam; in Principis, politicum ordinem satis esse. Atque, vt in priore vos reprehendimus, non Patres, qui si in viuis essent, nollent in sensum vestrum verba sua pertrahi, nec ad tam odiosam Principum abiectionem applicari: atque, vt Concilia vos accusatis, quòd Pontifices deposuerint, nos sacram hanc in illis & necessariam authoritatem defendimus: atque, vt verbum Dei, quique est in verbo Dei locum & planum, & plenum maximè, de obedientia in Principem propter conscientiam, Principi vindicamus; vt hæc omnia priore loco: ita in posteriore de calumnia quam obijcit, Tortum conuenimus; conuenimus autem ex ore proprio. Si enim Clerici eius vere Regum Subditi non sint; nec verè tenentur eorum Legibus, quippe eâ authoritate latis, à quâ illi immunes. Quod faciunt ergo (dum Leges obseruant,) conscientiæ nexu nullo[?] faciunt; tantùm ex rationis dictamine, quasi si bene monenti auscultarent, non autem parerent imperanti; nulla Legis vis est, ad eos obligandos; vbi vis nulla ad obligandos, ibi Conscientia libera. Conscientiæ ergo vi, Clerici nihil debent: ratione tantùm, & respectu ad politicum ordinem ipsi se continent in officio; Lege autem, vel conscientiâ Legis non continentur. Nec id culpam minuit, quòd non ibi disputet Cardinalis de eâ, quæ Regibus debetur obedientiâ. Disputet, non disputet; obiter, ex proposito rem tractet: ita disputare debet & tractare, vt de subiectione propter conscientiam nulli vel Laici vel Clerici eximantur. Vis legis, vtrobique eadem, eadem utrobique ad Leges, ad Legum obedientiam obligatio.
units.tr: As for what Torts afterwards did: he divided the article into two, though in the Apology it is one, consisting of two clauses opposed to each other. Obedience is owed to the pope on account of conscience; obedience is owed to the king on account of political order. Here Torts is scarcely acting in good faith: he has split what was one, forging two out of one. For the author did not wish to deny that Christians are subject to the lawful rulers of the Church, even on account of conscience, no less surely than to the commonwealth. He noted this: that in the obedience to the pope conscience is pressed, while for the prince political order is enough. And just as in the former case we rebuke you, who do not quote the Fathers (who, if they were alive, would not want their words drawn into your sense, nor applied to such a hateful casting down of princes); and just as, when you accuse the councils of deposing popes, we defend this sacred and necessary authority in them; and just as we claim for the prince the word of God, which has its place and plain, and especially full, meaning in the word of God concerning obedience to the prince on account of conscience: so in the latter case, concerning the calumny he brings against Torts, we have caught him out, and caught him out from his own mouth. For if his clergy are not truly subjects of kings, then they are not truly bound by their laws, since those laws are enacted by an authority from which they are exempt. What they therefore do (while they observe the laws) they do without any bond of conscience; only from the dictate of reason, as if they were listening to one giving good advice, not obeying one who commands. There is no force of law to oblige them; where there is no force to oblige, there conscience is free. By the force of conscience, then, the clergy owe nothing: they confine themselves to their duty only by reason, and with regard to political order; but they are not bound by law, or by the conscience of law. Nor does this lessen the fault, that the cardinal does not discuss there the obedience due to kings. Whether he discusses it or does not; whether he treats the matter incidentally or on purpose: he ought to discuss and treat it in such a way that no one, whether layman or cleric, is exempt from subjection on account of conscience. The force of law is the same on both sides; the obligation to the laws, to obedience to the laws, is the same on both sides.

units.la: Lex in Clericos vim nullam habet, vi Legu[?] nihil faciunt. Cives ergo sunt, & legibus civilibus vivere non tenentur. Quid proximum jam, nisi ut Reges Clericorum Superiores non sint amplius, neque Clerici Regum subditi; Rex Laicorum Rex sit, non Clericorum? Fatetur verum hoc Tortus, ta-men rixatur de lanâ caprinâ. Clerici, dici voluit: noluit apponi verba, qui & nati sunt & degunt in Regnis Principum. Non quod vera non sint, sed quod non opus erat ad ea descendere: id est, quia Torto & Torti Domino veritate nihil opus erat: potest taceri, nec dici veritas, nisi quando Tortus opus iam ea esse significaret. Imo ut vera, ita opus adea descendere. Putet enim aliqui[?] quis Clericos alienos, natos Papae peregrè huc forte venientes, subditos dici Regis nostri. Nequa fraus fit, opus erat adijcere, etiam qui nati, etiam qui aetatem hic agunt, ipsos illos Clericos vestros, Regem tamen pro Superiore non agnoscere. Consequi vero ex eo, quod Garnettus, Oldecornus, reliqui Proditores, proditionis rei esse nequeant, actio in illos nulla instituti: non est enim crimen illud nisi Subditi in Regem. Ille verò jam non vere Rex, illi etiam neque vere jam subditi. Effutiit[?] ista temere Emanuel Sa, puto illi disciplinam propterea datam, deleta post sunt de Aphorismis eius, non quod vera non sint, sed quod non erat opus ad ea descendere. Tempus erit cùm opus erit. Tum vero descendent ad illa, vel ruent potius. Ruere enim ad haec oportet ex abrupto, non per gradus descendere. At haec invidiam conflant; quid opus ad illa descendere? At haec solertiam excitant; opus ad illa descendere. Si non opus, vobis forte non opus; opus Regibus.
units.tr: Law has no force over the clergy; by the force of law they do nothing. They are therefore citizens, and are not bound to live by civil laws. What follows next, then, except that kings are no longer superiors of the clergy, nor are the clergy subjects of kings; that the king is king of the laymen, not of the clergy? Torts admits this to be true, yet he quarrels over goat's wool. He wished the words to be stated as clergy: he did not wish the words who both are born and dwell in the realms of princes to be added. "Not that they are not true, but that there was no need to descend to them": that is, because for Torts and his lord there was no need of truth; truth can be passed over and not spoken, unless Torts should signify that it is now needed. Indeed, as they are true, so there was need to descend to them. For someone might think that foreign clergy, born in the pope's lands, coming here perhaps from abroad, are called subjects of our king. So that no fraud is practised, it was needful to add: even those who are born, even those who spend their lives here, your very clergy, nevertheless do not acknowledge the king as superior. And the consequence of this, that Garnet, Oldcorne, and the other traitors cannot be guilty of treason, so that no action is brought against them, is that the crime is not a crime unless it is committed by subjects against the king. But he is no longer truly king, and they too are no longer truly subjects. Emanuel Sa rashly blurted out these things; I think the teaching was given him for this reason, and afterwards, in the deletion of his Aphorisms, it was blotted out: not that they are not true, but that there was no need to descend to them. There will be a time when there will be need. Then indeed they will descend to them, or rather fall upon them. For one must rush to these things abruptly, not descend to them by steps. But these things stir up hatred; why is there need to descend to them? These things rouse cleverness; there is need to descend to them. If there is no need for you, perhaps there is no need for you; there is need for kings.

units.la: De altero autem membro, Ipsis fas sit Principes suos iudicare, debuit negare Tortus illud, suos. Sui enim non sunt Principes, ijs qui verè non sunt Subditi. Sed ne concitaret odium, conflaret invidiam, maluit in voce Ipsis nodum quaerere. At vox illa scirpus est, Ipsis (id est) Ecclesiastici. Ecclesiasticis fas est Principem suum iudicare. Quibusdam concedit, Quibuslibet negat. At Ecclesiasticus licet si quibusdam licet; atque ea propositionis vis est ubi signo caret, nec vi vocis ulla, Ecclesiasticis, significat cuicunque Ecclesiastico. Dixisset aliquid si vni id Pontifici licere dixisset: peccatum enim tum esset numero. Iam non illi soli, præter illum pluribus, permittit hoc. Tantùm; hanc Regibus gratiam facit, ne privatum quemq; Sacrificum pro Iudice suo agnoscant, neve ullum, nisi in Ecclesiastica aliquâ dignitate positum. Manet tamen illud. Etiam qui maximè privatus est, exemptus est à subiectione Principis. Ita Subditus non est, ita Carnifex esse potest, etsi Iudex forte non potest. Magnas verò agere gratias Principes Cardinali, qui hæc de illis tam benigna, tam se digna vel dicat, vel credat, vel somniet.
units.tr: Concerning the other clause, "It shall be lawful for them to judge their own princes," Tortus ought to have denied the word "their."
