For those who are not truly subjects are not their princes. But so as not to stir up hatred or kindle envy, he preferred to seek a knot in the word "them." That word, however, is a stumbling-block: "them" (that is, "ecclesiastics"). It is lawful for ecclesiastics to judge their prince. He grants this to some, denies it to any. But if it is lawful for "some," then it is lawful for "ecclesiastics"; and that is the force of the proposition where there is no sign, and the word "ecclesiastics" by its own force signifies "any ecclesiastic whatsoever." He would have said something if he had said that this is lawful for one pope, for then it would be a sin only in number. As it is, he does not grant this to that one alone, but to several besides him. He only grants this favour to kings, that they should not recognise any private priest as their judge, nor any unless he holds some ecclesiastical dignity. Yet that remains: even the most private person is exempt from subjection to the prince. So he is not a subject, and so he can be an executioner, even if perhaps he cannot be a judge. Truly, the princes owe great thanks to the Cardinal, who says, believes or dreams these things about them so kindly, and so worthy of himself.

units.la: Saltem, si nec sub lege conscientiæ, nec sub Rege personas habeant: at in rebus quæ merè civiles sunt, vel in minimis earum subijciantur saltem Clerici. Ne id quidem, nisi ex discretione tantùm. Laudatur enim erga Regem obedientia si discreta sit & oculata, vel in minimis; quæ tamen erga Patrem Societatis non laudatur, nisi cæca sit & indiscreta, etiam in maximis. Non ergò nisi ex discretione tantùm, vel in minimis; idque (si Torto fas credere) consentiente in hoc, atque approbante Schola totâ Theologiæ, atque Iuris utriusque: ut nec Theologus fit, nec Iurisconsultus, qui id in dubium vocet. De eo verò (si placet) videamus. Convenire dicis nec in dubium verti. Audio, non credo. Video enim {a}Sotum de Quæstione hac [An Clerici à potestate civili exempti] ita scribentem, De hac quæstione partim cum Hæreticis nobis lis est, partim inter Catholicos non satis convenit. Aliqui ergo vestri in dubium vertunt. Video & asserentem, Personas Ecclesiasticas, neque iure diuino neque humano esse omnino à Legibus civilibus exemptas. Addit autem & rationem. Quia Clerici non obstante Clericatu suo, Cives tamen sunt Reipublicæ, & membra eius. Civilis autem Respublica non gubernatur, nisi Legibus Principum. Quatenus ergo ad pacem spectat Respublica, tenentur Clerici eü obedire. Quòd nisi res ita se haberet, addit absurdum: Alioquin, Clerici Hispani, non magis tenerentur Legibus Hispanis obtemperare, quàm Gallicis: quod est falsum. Ne verò ex discretione solâ hoc facere videantur, pergit porrò. Enimvero si Rex precia frumenti, vel quarumcunq; rerum moderetur: Clerici carius vendentes mortaliter delinquunt, & ad restitutionem sicut Laici tenentur; & idem est de multiù aliys Legibus. Quod ipsum probatur &c b Victoria: Cùm præterquam quod Ministri sunt Ecclesiæ, Cives etiam sint Clerici, Ciuium lege viuere tenentur. Tùm & ratione hàc vtitur. Rex Clericorum etiam Rex est, non Laicorum. Nec administrant temporalia, nisi potestate Principum temporali: Potestati ergo eius temporali sunt subditi. c Medina vero argumentum inde ducit, Quòd Lex Euangelica non dissoluit obligationem naturalem quæ præerat, nec debita prius contracta vel carnis, Coniugi: vel æris, Creditori: vel seruitutis, Domino: vel obedientiæ, Principi. Ne Baptismo quidem solui posse hæc. Quod si non Baptismo, certè nec Sacerdotio: si non ex eo quòd Christiani, nec ex eo quòd Clerici.
units.tr: At least, if they have no persons under the law of conscience nor under the king, yet in matters that are purely civil, or in the smallest of them, the clergy at least should be subject. Not even that, except from discretion alone. For obedience towards the king is praised if it is discreet and clear-sighted, even in the smallest matters; yet obedience towards the Father of the Society is not praised unless it is blind and indiscreet, even in the greatest matters. Therefore not "except from discretion alone, or in the smallest matters"; and this (if it is right for Tortus to believe it) with the whole school of theology and of both laws agreeing and approving in this, so that no one becomes a theologian or a jurist who would call it into doubt. But let us look at this (if you please). You say they agree and it is not doubted. I hear, I do not believe. For I see Soto writing thus on this question [Whether clergy are exempt from civil power]: "On this question we have a dispute partly with heretics, partly among Catholics there is not sufficient agreement." Some of yours, then, do call it into doubt. I also see him asserting that ecclesiastical persons are not at all exempt from civil laws, either by divine or by human right. He also adds a reason: "Because clergy, notwithstanding their clerical state, are nonetheless citizens of the commonwealth and its members. But the civil commonwealth is not governed except by the laws of princes. Insofar, therefore, as the commonwealth looks to peace, the clergy are bound to obey it. But if matters were not so, he adds an absurdity: otherwise Spanish clergy would be no more bound to obey Spanish laws than French ones, which is false." And so that they may not seem to do this from discretion alone, he goes on further: "Indeed, if the king regulates the price of corn or of whatever goods: clergy who sell dearer sin mortally and are bound to restitution just as laymen are; and the same holds for many other laws." This very thing is proved, etc., by Victoria: since, apart from the fact that they are ministers of the Church, clergy are also citizens, they are bound to live under the law of citizens. He also uses this reason: the king is king of the clergy as well, not only of the laity. Nor do they administer temporal affairs except by the temporal power of princes: therefore they are subject to his temporal power. But Medina draws an argument from this: that the Gospel law does not dissolve the natural obligation that preceded it, nor debts previously contracted: of the flesh, to a spouse; of money, to a creditor; of servitude, to a master; of obedience, to a prince. Nor can these be dissolved even by baptism. And if not by baptism, certainly not by priesthood: if not because they are Christians, then not because they are clergy.

units.la: Quo etiam iure, in dubium vertitur. Qui quiduis probare se posse putant, diuino contendunt{c}; Qui modestè magis sapiunt, humano: Non enim diuino. d Si iure diuino res examinanda, nec Clerici nec eorum res à iurisdictione Seculari immunes. e De Iure diuino, nihil dici debet, quod ex ipso iure diuino ostendi non potest. f In Iure diuino nulla lex apparet, quæ verè diuina sit. Ius diuinum duplex: Veteris Testamenti,& Euangelij. g In Veteri Testamento dubio procul Sacerdotes à Principibus Secularibus iudicatur. h Nullus est in Euangelio apertus locus, quo eximantur. Potest per Pontificem, potest per consuetudinê restringi vel limitari immunitas hæc tota. Quare positiui & humani iuris est. Nam si diuini esset, non Pontifex illam, non consueto vllà ex parte imminueret. Nihil illis iuris in Ius Diuinum. Quæ currit in eam præscriptio, non curreret, si diuini iuris esset. Etiam manente immunitate, est tamen in personas Clericorum Principi ius suum, Si crimen atrox; Si Clericus in profundum venit malitiæ; Si ter monitus. Non esset autem vel in hijs: si, vt ne esset, Lege Diuinâ cautum foret.
units.tr: By what right, too, is this called into doubt? Those who think they can prove anything at all contend it is by divine right; those who are more modestly wise, by human right: for not by divine right. "If the matter is to be examined by divine right, neither the clergy nor their goods are immune from secular jurisdiction." "Nothing should be said about divine right that cannot be shown from divine right itself." "No law appears in divine right that is truly divine. Divine right is twofold: of the Old Testament and of the Gospel." "In the Old Testament, without doubt, priests were judged by secular princes." "There is no clear place in the Gospel by which they are exempted." This whole immunity can be restricted or limited by the Pope, can be restricted by custom. Therefore it belongs to positive and human right. For if it were of divine right, the Pope would not diminish it in any way, nor would custom. Nothing of right is given to them in divine right. The prescription which runs against it would not run if it were of divine right. Even while the immunity remains, the prince nonetheless has his right over the persons of clergy: if the crime is grave; if the cleric has gone down into the depths of malice; if he has been admonished three times. Yet there would not be such a right even in these cases if it had been provided for by divine law that it should not be so.

units.la: Tum, vario iure hac in re vtuntur Gentes variæ. In Gallia subijciuntur Clerici in realibus tantùm: At ab antiquo hic apud Nos, & in realibus, & in personalibus. Idem verò vbique ius esset, si Diuinum esset: Varietas humanum reuincit. Deniq; si à Cardinale quæritimus, quo iure totum hoc; respondet, {*}iure partim diuino, partim humano, partim neutro.
units.tr: Then, various peoples use various rights in this matter. In France clergy are subject only in real matters; but from of old here among us, in both real and personal matters. Yet the law would be the same everywhere if it were divine: variety refutes that it is human. Finally, if we ask the Cardinal by what right all this is, he answers: "by right partly divine, partly human, partly neither."

units.la: * De Cleric.lib. 1.cap.28. Quàm hæc verò dissoluta, partim hoc, partim illo, partim neutro? Quis in istis acquiescat?
units.tr: "On the Clergy, book 1, chapter 28." How loose is this: "partly this, partly that, partly neither"? Who can rest in such things?

units.la: De antiquissimis temporibus, in dubium vertitur. Primùm, ab initio non fuit sic. Non enim sub Lege natura. Potestates enim sub eâ non erant distinctæ. Antequam autem distinctæ potestates, ijsdem omnes, Clerici, Laici Legibus viuebant. Non sub Lege Veteri, audisti paulò ante Couarruuiam; non sub Nouâ, audisti Sotum. Christus de Pilato Præside fassus, habuisse in se potestatem, eamque desuper datam. Paulus stare se ad Tribunal Cæsaris, vbi ipsum vbi oportuit (non liberum ei erat) iudicari. Idem ipse Paulus legem fert. Omnis anima Potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit: Potestatibus scilicet, gladium gerentibus; Potestatibus, Tributa & Censum recipientibus. Omnis anima, etiam Apostoli, etiam Euangelistæ, Chrysostomo ita asserente. Canon Generalis est (aut Victoria,) Exceptio autem in Scripturis non ponitur. Petrus verò, quibus scripsit Pascite qui in vobis est Gregem, Compresbyteris suis: ijsdem ipsis scripsit; Subditi estote Regi; quia hæc est voluntas Dei. In Primitiuâ autem Ecclesiâ Subiectos fuisse docet, ad Canonem Sicut, Cauf. 11. Quæst.1., Gratianus ipse. Ex hys datur intelligi, quòd in Ciuili Causa Clericus ante Ciuilem Iudicem conueniendus est. Est verò Deo gratia: designatas habemus iam vt res, ita tempora rerum; quoto seculo demùm, à quo Principe, immunitas quæque concessa est. Atque hoc, debemus Causæ Venetæ, quæ fecit, vt penitiùs nuper diu totam Quæstionem hanc inquireretur.
units.tr: Concerning the most ancient times, it is called into doubt. First, from the beginning it was not so. For it was not under the law of nature. For powers under it were not distinct. But before the powers were distinct, all, clergy and laity alike, lived under the same laws. Not under the Old Law, as you heard a little earlier from Covarruvias; not under the New, as you heard from Soto. Christ, speaking of Pilate the governor, confessed that he had power over him, and that it had been given from above. Paul stood before the tribunal of Caesar, where he ought to be judged (it was not free for him). The same Paul also lays down a law: "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers": to the powers, that is, which bear the sword; to the powers which receive tribute and tax. "Every soul," even of apostles, even of evangelists, as Chrysostom asserts. "It is a general canon (or Victoria's), and no exception is laid down in the Scriptures." Peter, however, to whom he wrote "Feed the flock which is among you," to his fellow elders: to those same men he wrote, "Be subject to the king, because this is the will of God." Moreover, that in the primitive Church they were subject, Gratian himself teaches, in the canon "Sicut," Causa 11, question 1. "From these things it can be understood that in a civil cause a cleric must be called before the civil judge." Thanks be to God, we now have the times of these things marked out, as well as the things; in what century at last, and from which prince, each immunity was granted. And this we owe to the Venetian case, which caused this whole question to be investigated far more thoroughly lately.

units.la: Cùm verò ad duo Capita reuocetur tota hæc Clericorum Exemptio; Quoad bona, Quoad personas: Quoad bona Cardinalis humani iuris asserit; Quoad personas non audet dicere, diuini; id tantùm dicit, Iuris esse Diuino valdè conformè. Quod, quid aliud est quàm hæsitare? Diuini non potuit, humani noluit; commentus est tertium, quod illi neutrum est, conforme Diuino. Verùm ne de personis quidem satisfacit sibi: In loco Apostoli, Omnis anima Potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit: illud, omnis anima (inquit) includit Clericos; (id est) personas Clericorum: Illud, ideo tributa præstatis, alicitur etiam de Clericorum bonis. Bona Clericorum nisi eximantur priuilegio Principum, tributa præstant. Animæ ergo Clericorum nisi eximantur eodem Priuilegio, Potestati Seculari subditæ sunt ei, cui de bonis tributa præstant. Fauent è Patrum numero Chrysostomus; è Scholasticorum Aquinas. Tum, quod de bonis adducit non eximendis Bellarminus, idem ipsum pro persona adduci potest, Clericorum scilicet. Nullum proferri potest Dei Verbum, quo ista exemptio confirmetur. In verbis enim Christi, Mat. 17. non habetur, vt Augustinus: saltem, non iubetur, vt Bellarminus: colligitur tantum per consequentiam; nec necessariam, sed probabilem; totaque rei origo exemplo nititur, cui Iuris Diuini nomen indere, nec Cardinali tutum videtur, vel consultum satis. Humano itaque iure data sunt, à Regibus data. Non enim immunitates has dederunt vel Pontifices vel Concilia; receperunt enim eas Pontifices atque ij, ex quibus Concilia constant: quas receperunt, ipsi sibi dare, à se recipere non potuerunt. Agnouit autem in Bona, potestatem Cæsaris Seruator: reddi iussit Cæsari: reddi, non dari: debitum ergo, non gratuitum. Tributum solui iussit; quod iussit solui tributum, ne scandalo esset, & ipse soluit. Agnouit in seipsum potestatem Præsidis: agnouerunt Apostoli exemplo illius. Vsus beneficio ciuium Paulus, & lora euasit & iniquum forum declinauit. Imperando Petrus [illegible, ~5 letters] legem ferendo Paulus [illegible, ~5 letters], subiectionem vtrumque sanciuit. Tu verò, si habes quo haurias, hauri nobis (quæso) ex Nathan Propheta prono in terram Regem adorante, & dicente {a}Nunquid à Domino meo Rege exiit verbum hoc, & mihi non indicasti Seruo tuo? Hauri nobis (inquam) Reges magis proprie Seruos esse, quàm Dominos: Vel ex illis Dauidis, Sadocum Pontificem, & Nathan Prophetam alloquentis, {b}Tollite vobiscum Seruos Domini vestri. Si Funem habes & Situlam, hauri nobis ex Rege Salomone, {c}Abiathar, Pontificem deponente: nunquam depositum à Rege Pontificem. Hauri ex loco Apostoli, Omnis anima subdita sit: Non omnem animam, non enim Clerici vllius animam. Hauri de Chrysostomo qui vel Prophetas vel Apostolos subditos air, id, de facto fuisse, non iure; neutros nec Apostolos, nec Prophetas subditos fuisse.
units.tr: Since, however, this whole exemption of clergy is referred to two heads, "as to goods" and "as to persons": as to goods, the Cardinal asserts that it is of human right; as to persons he does not dare to say divine; he says only that it is "very much in conformity with divine right." What is this but hesitation? "He could not say divine, he would not say human"; he has invented a third thing, which is neither, yet in conformity with divine. But he does not even satisfy himself about persons: in the apostle's place, "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers": "every soul," he says, includes clergy (that is, the persons of clergy). "Pay tribute," from that also is inferred concerning the goods of clergy. Clergy goods, unless they are exempted by the privilege of princes, pay tribute. The souls of clergy, therefore, unless they are exempted by the same privilege, are subject to the secular power, to him to whom they pay tribute from their goods. Chrysostom favours this among the Fathers; Aquinas among the Schoolmen. Then, what Bellarmine adduces concerning "goods" not to be exempted can equally be adduced "for persons," namely of clergy. "No word of God can be produced by which this exemption is confirmed." For in the words of Christ, Matt. 17, it is not found, as Augustine says; or at least it is not commanded, as Bellarmine says: it is gathered only by inference, and not a necessary but a probable one; and the whole origin of the matter rests on example, to which the name of divine right is given, and it does not seem safe or sufficiently advisable to the Cardinal. Therefore they were given by human right, given by kings. For neither popes nor councils granted these immunities; the popes and those of whom councils consist received them: what they received, they could not give to themselves, nor receive from themselves. But the Saviour acknowledged Caesar's power over goods: "Render to Caesar," he ordered; "render," not "give": a debt, therefore, not a gift. He ordered tribute to be paid; and because he ordered tribute to be paid, lest there be offence, he himself paid it. He acknowledged the power of the governor over himself; the apostles acknowledged it by his example. Paul, using the benefit of citizenship, both escaped the lash and avoided the unjust court. Peter, commanding, and Paul, laying down the law, both sanctioned subjection. But you, if you have something to draw with, draw for us (I ask you) from Nathan the prophet, when the king fell prone on the ground and worshipped, and said: "Has this word not come out from my lord the king, and have you not told it to your servant?" Draw for us (I say) that kings are more properly servants than lords. Or from those words of David, addressing Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet: "Take with you the servants of your lord." If you have a rope and bucket, draw for us from King Solomon, deposing Abiathar the priest: "never was a priest deposed by the king." Draw from the apostle's place, "Let every soul be subject": not every soul, for not the soul of any cleric. Draw from Chrysostom, who says that even prophets or apostles were subject: this was so in fact, not by right; neither the apostles nor the prophets were subject.

units.la: Magis ad animum vobis, Pontifex nomen à Numâ haurire. Origine ergo vox illa Romana, & prophana est. In Scriptura non legitur: quî potest, cùm Romana vox sit? Scripturæ autem natiuæ, Hebraicè vel Græcè tantùm; Latinè nisi per Interpretem non loquantur. Sed diu perscrutatus, tandem in Libri Iudith capite quodam reperit verba hæc, Ioachim Summus Pontifex. De Libro autem suo vbi reperit, non securus, præfari cogitat, Sacrum esse: Etsi Caluiniani non recipiant, at receptum esse tamen in Nicenâ Synodo. Itane, receptum? Quo Canone? Imò, Hieronymus hoc asserit. Quid tandem? Synodus Nicena cum in numero Sanctarum Scripturarum legitur computasse. Legit ergo alicubi hoc Hieronymus. Sed cùm legisset, num credidit ipse, ut nos cum eo credamus? Non credidit. Lectione enim illa non obstante ter reiecit ipse Librum Iudith de Canone; 1. Prologo Galeato in Pentateuch. 2. in Libros Regum. 3 in Proverbia. Non ergo affirmat ita receptum fuisse; legisse se affirmat, sed apud incertum Authorem suspectâ fide, de quo & ipse dubitavit. Verba enim ipsa, Legitur computasse, vel Lindano vestro, dubitantis suspicionem indicare videntur. Alioqui, quem recepisset Nicena Synodus, reciperet & ipse, nec ita ad eos qui extra Canonem sunt, toties ablegaret. Tum, qui Concilio Nicæno interfuerunt b Athanasius & c Eusebius, neuter recipit; facerent, si pro Canonico à Concilio approbatus fuisset. Etiam, quæ octoginta post annis (Lindano suputante) Nicenam sequuta est Laodicena Synodus, non accensuit. Dein, ætate illà floruerunt Hilarius, f Nazianzenus, g Epiphanius summi viri, Nicenam Synodum venerati omnes, quorum nemo tamen recipit; Et qui post illos non diu, Hieronymus & h Ruffinus in hoc concordes, etsi in multis non ita. Postremò omni ætate viri doctissimi, etiam qui post Carthaginensem Synodum vixerunt i Isidorus, k Damascenus, l Hugo à Sancto Victore, m Lyranus: Vestri quoque & de vestris non infimi: n Antoninus, o Dionysius Carthusianus, p Tostatus, q Caietanus.
units.tr: It is more fitting for you to draw the name Pontifex from Numa. So that word is Roman and profane in origin. It is not read in Scripture: how could it be, since it is a Roman word? The native Scriptures are in Hebrew or Greek only; they do not speak Latin except through an interpreter. But after searching for a long time, he at last found in a certain chapter of the Book of Judith these words, Joachim the high priest. As for where he found that book, he is not without care in prefacing it with the claim that it is holy. Although the Calvinists do not receive it, yet it was received at the Nicene Synod. Received indeed? By what canon? Rather, Jerome asserts this. And what then? The Nicene Synod, when it is read to have counted it among the number of the holy Scriptures. So he read this somewhere, Jerome. But when he had read it, did he himself believe it, as we believe with him? He did not. For, notwithstanding that reading, he himself thrice rejected the Book of Judith from the canon: (1) in the Galeatus prologue to the Pentateuch; (2) on the Books of Kings; (3) on the Proverbs. He therefore does not affirm that it was so received. He affirms that he read it, but in an uncertain author of doubtful trustworthiness, about whom he himself was doubtful. For the words themselves, It is read to have counted it, to your Lindanus seem to indicate the suspicion of one who doubts. Otherwise, whatever the Nicene Synod had received, he too would have received, nor would he so often have sent back those who are outside the canon. Then, Athanasius (b) and Eusebius (c), who were present at the Council of Nicaea, receive it neither; they would have done so had it been approved by the Council as canonical. Also, the Laodicean Synod, which followed the Nicene by eighty years (by Lindanus's reckoning), did not count it among them. Next, in that age flourished Hilary (f), Nazianzen (g), and Epiphanius (g), great men, all of whom revered the Nicene Synod, yet none of them receives it. And those who came not long after them, Jerome and Rufinus (h), agree on this, though not on many other things. Finally, in every age the most learned men, even those who lived after the Synod of Carthage: Isidore (i), Damascene (k), Hugh of St Victor (l), Lyra (m); and yours too, and from your own ranks no lowly ones: Antoninus (n), Dionysius the Carthusian (o), Tostatus (p), Cajetan (q).

units.la: q Instit. Com. in lib. Histor. Libro Iudith? Ioachim Pontifex Summus. Liber Iudith an Latinè scriptus? Non, sed Graecè; Graecè quomodo habetur? ἀρχιερεὺς[?] id est, Sacerdos Magnus. Sacerdos magnus Pontisex non est. Aut si demus tibi, vt analogiâ quâdam Pontisex sit; at Summus maximúsue non erit. Vnus enim in Veteri Testamento Pontifex siue Sacerdos Magnus: Maximus autem, vel Summus dici non potuit, nisi plures essent Pontifices, Maximo illo minores, Summo inferiores. Nisi ergo tibi condonetur Liber ipse; nisi & vitiosa translatio; iacet Pontifex tuus Maximus. Nec enim Sacerdos Pontifex, & Magnus toto gradu distat, & minor est Maximo. Quo vero Interpretis vitio legitur ibi in Vulgatâ Pontificis nomen; eodem ipso, vbicunque per vetus Testamentum legitur, eodem, vbicunque per Nouum. Non in Scripturis legitur Pontifex, nisi translatis, interpolatis per vos; nec Spiritus Sanctus, sed vester Interpres ibi posuit. Nec est enim vox vlla in Nouo, quae Pontificem designet, nisi ἀρχιερεὺς, id est, Summus vel praecipuus Sacerdos. At tibi alius credo Pontificum gradus est; alius Sacerdotum; nec relatione ad Sacerdotes vestros (sic enim quiuis Sacerdos Magnus Pontifex, etiam Archipresbyter) sed ad Pontifices suos, Pontifex Maximus est.
units.tr: q Institutes, commentary on the historical books. Does "Libro Iudith?" mean the Book of Judith? "Joachim the high priest." Is the Book of Judith written in Latin? No, but in Greek. How is it given in Greek? ἀρχιερεύς [?], that is, Great Priest. A great priest is not a high priest. Or, granting you that by some analogy he might be a high priest, he will not be the highest or greatest. For in the Old Testament there is only one high priest, or Great Priest. But greatest or highest could not be said unless there were several high priests, lesser than that greatest one and inferior to the highest. Unless, therefore, your book itself is pardoned, and also its faulty translation, your Pontifex Maximus lies in the dust. For a priest is not a pontiff, and great is not a whole grade apart, and is less than greatest. But whatever the interpreter's fault by which the name Pontifex is read there in the Vulgate, the same fault appears wherever it is read in the Old Testament, and the same wherever it is read in the New. Pontifex is not read in the Scriptures except in translated, interpolated form by you; it was not the Holy Spirit but your interpreter who put it there. For there is no word in the New Testament which designates a pontiff, except ἀρχιερεύς [archiereus], that is, the highest or chief priest. But I believe that for you there is one grade of Pontiffs, another of priests; and not in relation to your priests (for thus any priest who is great is a pontiff, even an archpriest), but in relation to their pontiffs, he is the Pontifex Maximus.

units.la: Verùm esto; voculam de Scripturâ Ethnicâ nullam nobis fas attingere, ne Parentandi quidem: vobis liceat transumptâ de Numae Sacris voce, vestrum Pontificem nuncupare. At, cui stomachum non faciat quod ibi sequitur, vt quia Christus Magnus Pontifex, Papa sit Maximus[?] vt ita meliore iure, maiore titulo sit Papa vester, quàm Christus. Quâ fronte hoc? nisi forte, nihil interesse putes inter Magnum & Maximum, Summum scilicet gradum & infinitum. Vt, Magnus Christo satis ampla vox sit, Pontifici non sit, cui, nisi Maximi, nulla satis idonea sit dicenda. Quasi posset Pontifex piè dici Maximus, cùm Christus dicatur non nisi Magnus. Potuit quidem Apostolus, qui Christum Magnum scripsit, scripsisse Maximum: Quodsi illum Maximum scripsisset, subsistere potuit Papa vnico infra Christum gradu. Iam nec aequali contentus est; Magni titulus sordet illi; Alexandri, Pompeij, Caroli: positivum nihil Papam decet. Christus si volet consistat in tertijs, Magnus sit: Vicarius eius plus vltra duos gradus consecendit, Maximus salutari vult. Nec alia Patris hic sors quàm Filij. Nec minùs extolli vult Pontifex, & supra Patrem. Sat erat Christo, si Papa diceret, Pater Sancte: Pontifex, si Eum Patrem Sanctum modò dicas, obliquis te oculis aspicient. Pater Sanctus salutari non sustinet; nec vel scribi vel dici, nisi Pater Sanctissimus. Et quid hoc aliud est, quàm non dicó sinitlem esse velle Altissimo: sed extolli super omne quod dicitur Deus?
units.tr: But granted; I grant that we must not touch that little word from heathen Scripture at all, not even as used of the funeral rites; let it be lawful for you to call your Pontifex by a word taken over from the sacred rites of Numa. But who would not be offended by what follows there: that because Christ is the Great Priest, the Pope is the Greatest, so that he may have better right and higher title as Pope than Christ? With what face do you say this? Unless perhaps you think there is no difference between Great and Greatest, that is, between the highest degree and the infinite. So that Great applied to Christ is a word broad enough, but not for a Pontiff, for whom nothing is fit to be said except the Greatest. As if a Pontiff could rightly be called the Greatest, when Christ is called only Great. The Apostle, who wrote Christ the Great, could indeed have written the Greatest; but had he written that Greatest of Christ, the Pope could have stood one single grade below Christ. Now he is not content with an equal place; the title Great is distasteful to him: of Alexander, Pompey, Charles; the positive degree suits the Pope not at all. If Christ wishes to remain among the tertiary ones, let him be Great; his Vicar ascends beyond two degrees and wishes to be saluted as the Greatest. Nor is the Father's lot here different from the Son's. Nor does the Pontiff wish to be raised less, and above the Father. It was enough for Christ, if the Pope said, Holy Father; the Pontiff, if you merely say Holy Father of him, will look at you with sidelong eyes. Holy Father he does not tolerate even to be saluted; he will not be written or spoken of except as Most Holy Father. And what is this other than not saying that he wishes to be like the Most High, but to be exalted above everything that is called God?

units.la: Ecce autem alterum. Patum ei visum, vt quantum Maximus Magno, tantum Papa Christo praestet, (sic enim gradibus distant tantum) nisi ex toto genere distent: Papa fidei Caput sit, pro quo ante pugnauit strenuè; Rex ne sit, imò Christus ne sit quod iam agit. Optâssem enim magnopere, vt nomen hoc Capitis fidei, Christo cum Papa communé esset, cupissem admodum, vt Papa Christo illud communicare, Christus illud de Papa participare posset; sed quaesiuit loca diligenter, nec vsquam vllum reperit, qui tribuat. Caput fidei Papa, legitur apud Gregorium: Caput fidei Christus non legitur. Fidei Author, sed non Caput, & Caput Ecclesiae, sed non Fidei, legitur apud Apostolos; Caput fidei nusquam legitur. Dolens ergo votum emittit. Optâssem (inquit) vt Aduersarius vel vnum locum netâssel in toto volumine Bibliorum, vbi Apostoli hoc nomen soli Christo tribuerint. Quorsum autem soli? Quid opus? cùm nec omnino, nec cum alio quidem tributum ibi, satis scias ipse. Sed tamen obsecro te Turre[?], si vlla apud te fidei pars sit, quae fidei pars Christus, si Caput fidei non est? Quo in membro locas? Quid erit ad fidem? An humerus, cervix, vertebra prima, sub Capite Papa? Sine vero te exorem, vt vel Occiput sit saltem, & vel aliqua in parte Capitis haereat.
units.tr: But here is another point. He thought it fitting that, just as the Greatest surpasses the Great, so the Pope surpasses Christ (for they differ by such degrees), unless they differ in kind altogether: the Pope is the head of faith, for which he has fought valiantly before; let him not be King, nay, let Christ not be what he now is. For I had greatly wished that this title, head of faith, were common to Christ and the Pope; I would very much have wished that the Pope could share it with Christ and Christ could share it from the Pope. But he searched the passages diligently, and nowhere found one which gives it. The head of faith, the Pope, is read in Gregory; the head of faith, Christ, is not read. The author of faith, but not the head, and head of the Church, but not of faith, are read in the Apostles; head of faith is nowhere read. Grieving, then, he utters a wish: I would have wished (he says) that my opponent had sought out, in the whole volume of the Bible, even one passage where the Apostles ascribe this name to Christ alone. But why alone? What is the need? When you yourself know well that it is not ascribed there at all, nor even to anyone else. But still, I beg you, Turre [?], if you have any part of faith at all, what part of faith is Christ, if he is not the head of faith? In what member do you place him? What will he be to faith? Is he a shoulder, a neck, the first vertebra, with the Pope under the head? Allow me, I beg, to plead that he at least be the back of the head, and remain in some part of the head.

units.la: Imò vero ait; sit si volet Caput Ecclesiae, legitur illud; Caput fidei, nec sit, non legitur. At hoc iam aliquid est: tandem[?], si vt saepe mendax, ita aliquando memor Tortus. Quid est enim Caput fidei, vel Totto? Caput fidelium; Caput Ecclesiae, Caput per quod Ecclesia fidem & disciplinam docet: Caput Ecclesiae? Quare & fidei Caput iam; salua res est. Ter enim hoc de Christo legitur totidem verbis: at de Papa credo vix vel vno loco, in toto volumine Bibliorum. Secundo, Qui Caput Ecclesiae, idem & fidelium Caput; fideles enim Ecclesia; Quanquam & Caput anguli cùm dicitur, fidelium dicitur; fidelium de Iudaeis, fidelium de Gentibus, qui quasi paries geminus consurgit, connexus in Christo lapide angulari. Tertiò, Caput [illegible, ~2 letters]em per quod Ecclesia fidem & discit & docet, ita Christo conuenit, vt praeter Christum nemini, qui solus eruditam linguam donat loquenti (etiam si vel Papa sit) vt doceat; solus aurem intelligentem Auditoris vt discat. Ita, vel Torto etiam interprete Caput fidei Christus. Legitur verò hoc in Volumine Bibliorum; & Inimici sint Iudices.
units.tr: Nay, indeed he says: let it be, if he wishes, head of the Church; that is read; head of faith, let it not be, it is not read. But this is already something: at last, if Tortus, as often a liar, is at some time mindful. For what is head of faith, or for Tortus? Head of the faithful; head of the Church, head through whom the Church teaches and learns faith and discipline: head of the Church? Why then head of faith too; the matter is safe. For this is read three times of Christ in the same words; but of the Pope, I believe, scarcely in one place in the whole volume of the Bible. Second, he who is head of the Church is also head of the faithful; for the faithful are the Church. Indeed, when head of the corner is spoken of, it is said of the faithful; of the faithful from the Jews, of the faithful from the Gentiles, who rise like a twofold wall, joined in Christ the corner stone. Third, head [illegible, about two letters] through which the Church learns and teaches faith, so belongs to Christ that, apart from Christ, it belongs to no one, who alone gives an educated tongue to the speaker (even if he be the Pope) so that he may teach, and alone gives an understanding ear to the hearer so that he may learn. Thus, even with Tortus as interpreter, Christ is head of faith. But this is read in the volume of the Bible; and let his enemies be the judges.

units.la: At non solus Christus Caput. Quàm ridiculè? Quasi deillorum numero Caput non sit, quæ si sint, sola sint: nisi sola, esse non possint. Vnicum enim est Caput, vni corpori: Ecclesia vnum corpus: nisi bicipitem Aquilam fingas, aut tricipitem Geryonem, cui tot capita sint, quot in Mitrâ Pontificiâ Coronæ. Christus autem solus Ecclesiæ Caput, non Papa. Ecclesia enim corpus Christi solius, non Papæ; nec vos, qui audetis valdè, sic tamen audetis loqui, vt Papæ corpus dicatis Ecclesiam. Solus (inquam) Christus Caput (vt Apostolus Capitis vim explicat) ex quo totum corpus compactum & connexum per omnem iuncturam submini-strationis, secundum operationem in mensuram vniuscuiusque membri, augmentum corporis facit. Iunctura submini-strationis; operatio in mensuram membrorum, corpori incrementum, ab Illo solo. Quodsi iunctura, quâ fidelis quisque Christo connectitur, fides sit: Caput fidei solus Christus; cuius Capitis minister (putà Atlas[?], vel Brachium) Paulus, (quidni autem & Petrus?) non autem vel hic, vel ille, Caput. Nec tu vnquam effugies vim vocis quam attulisti, Authoris fidei. Fidei enim Caput est, qui Author; cùm Caput author sit & origo sensus omnis, & motus, qui inde in reliqua membra deriuantur; vt si syllaba non sint, mens sit; vsque adeo autem sit, vt qui negét esse, non longè absit ab Hæresi; Hæresi autem Blasphemâ, vt cui, Fidei præter Christum, Caput sit, vel Author.
units.tr: But "not Christ alone is Head." How ridiculous! As if those who are heads were not among their number, and if they were, they would be alone; unless they could not be alone. For there is one Head, for one body: the Church is one body. Unless you feign a two-headed eagle, or a three-headed Geryon, which has as many heads as the crowns on a Papal mitre. Christ, however, is the sole Head of the Church, not the Pope. For the Church is the body of Christ alone, not of the Pope; nor do you, who dare very much, speak so as to call the Church the body of the Pope. Christ alone (I say) is Head (as the Apostle explains the force of the word "head"), "from whom the whole body, fitted and joined together through every joint of supply, according to the working in due measure of each individual part, makes the increase of the body." The joint of supply, the working in due measure of the members, the increase of the body: all these come from Him alone. But if the joint by which each believer is connected to Christ is faith, then Christ alone is the Head of faith; and Paul (why not Peter too?) is a minister of this Head, a bearer of its weight (the Atlas or the arm), but neither this man nor that one is the Head. Nor will you ever escape the force of the word you have brought forward, "author of faith." For the author is the head of faith, since the head is the author and origin of all sense and motion, which flow from it into the remaining members, as if they were not syllables but the mind itself. Indeed, it is so true that whoever denies it is not far from heresy; and heresy is blasphemy, since to whom faith has a head or author other than Christ, that person is guilty of this.

units.la: Vtcunq; verò duæ illæ voculæ Caput fidei, apud Gregorium sint; excogitauit tamen sensum eis Cardinalis, quem Gregorius nunquá cogitauit. Maior autem eius audacia, qui sensum illū excogitat, quàm eius, qui accusat ita excogitantem. Sed neq; Gregorius is fuit, qui peccare non posset; nec si peccauit (& vel Petrus fuit) peccante accusare, nefas. Qui secus ausit dicere, reperiet qui ausit accusare. Excusamus autem libenter Gregorium, nec id illi in mentem vnquam venisse dicimus. Scis vero ipse in ore esse omni Populo, Gregorium e Romanû Episcopû bonû, vltimum; è malis[?] primum fuisse. Quâ de bonû vltimû, quis velit accusare? Quâ de malû primû, quis ausit defendere? Multa sunt illius sanè praeclara. Etiamne omnia? Vestrorum non nemo accusauit illum, quòd ad fabellas nimis credulus; Alius, quòd Imagines, vt, confringi noluit à Sereno, ita, vetuit adorari; Alius, quòd ita temerè excanduit in nomen Vniuersalis, nec adhibuit lepidam aliquam distinctiunculam, quod vos iam studiosè facitis. Vos hæc audetis accusare audaculi: non omnibus id datum est. Egit verò id Author Apologiæ, vt commodâ interpretatione leniret, siquid in Titulo illo durius, quem siquis formulâ loquendi propriâ vrgeat, error sanè fit in Theologiâ, si alius eum, quàm Pontifex vsurparet: qui tamen homo est & ipse circundatus infirmitate, non ita confirmatus in actu gratiæ, quin possit errare: vt, cui cor sit, causa non defuit, illius interdum accusandi.
units.tr: However, whatever those two little words, "head of faith," may mean in Gregory, the Cardinal has devised a sense for them which Gregory never thought of. Yet the audacity of the one who devises such a sense is greater than that of the one who accuses him of so devising. But Gregory was not one who could not sin; nor, if he did sin (and Peter too was a sinner), is it wrong to accuse a sinner. Whoever dares to say otherwise will find someone who dares to accuse. We gladly excuse Gregory, and we say that this never came into his mind. You yourself know that it is on everyone's lips that Gregory was the best of the Roman bishops, the last, and the first of the bad. Who would wish to accuse the best and the last? Who would dare to defend the first of the bad? He indeed has many outstanding qualities. Are all of them? Some of your own men have accused him of being too credulous about fables; another, because he would not allow images to be broken by Serenus, but forbade them to be worshipped; another, because he flared up so rashly at the name "Universal," and did not use some neat little distinction, as you now diligently do. You dare to accuse him of these things, you bold little men: not everyone is given this gift. The author of the Apology, however, aimed, by a fair interpretation, to soften whatever is harsher in that title; for if anyone were to press it in its proper sense, it would surely be an error in theology for anyone other than the Pope to use it. Yet he too is "a man, surrounded by weakness, not so confirmed in the act of grace," that he cannot err; so that, since he has a heart, there was not lacking a reason at times for accusing him.

units.la: CLaudit verò iam Responsionem vt par est; quasi si dicat, Iudicet Lector si ausit. Nihil enim rogatum vult Lectorem; nihil deprecatur; imò iudicium ferre non sinit: tantùm (pro fastu suo) iubet aperiat oculos, admittat radios Torti, quibus quasi lumine amictus incedit; affulgebit ei statim iubar, quo omnia intuitiuè videat, vt discursu nihil opus. O superciliûm! Non rogo lectorem vt iudicium ferat quasi de re dubiâ. Feret verò non rogatus iudicium de hoc tam superbo postulato, quasi de Re non dubiâ, quasi de Re, de Homine non dubiâ arrogantiâ. Ad extremum valedicere simul voluit, & maledicere: & quod pessimum genus maledicendi, ei, qui bene dixerat. Perstrinxi suprà. Lacinias verò quasdam hic Tortus habuit, è Paciano, Cyrillo, Augustino, tam detritas, vt sine illis iam Papistis non fiat Liber. Quid illæ narrant? Nomen Catholici honorificum. Quis negat? Quis non omnia bona de eo dicat? Nam potest non de eo Magnificè sentire, qui de Symbolo rectè sentiat. Sed hoc nomen tribuit Rex Pontificijs in Apologiâ. Quid tum si tribuit? Bono animo es; Seriò non dixit; seriò dictum id nemo intellexit; seriò nec ipse tu: non potuisti, qui aliquammultis in locis Pontificios vos, & Papistas, & Papicolas dici itidem legisti, tam multis verò, totics, tam sæpe, etiam sæpiùs, quàm Catholicos. Noluit tamen semper sic, ne bilem totam moueret, abstinuit interdum: nec Ironia tamen fuit, Charientismus potius.
units.tr: Tortus now closes his Reply as is fitting, as if he were saying, "Let the reader judge if he dares." For he asks the reader for nothing; he begs for nothing; indeed he does not allow him to pass judgement. He merely (in keeping with his arrogance) bids him open his eyes and admit the rays of Tortus, with which he walks clothed as in light; at once a brightness will shine on him, by which he may see everything intuitively, so that there is no need for reasoning. O the haughtiness! I do not ask the reader to pass judgement as if on a doubtful matter. Yet he will pass judgement, unasked, on this so arrogant demand, as on a matter that is not doubtful, as on a man's arrogance that is not doubtful. Finally, he wished to bid farewell and curse at once, and that the worst kind of cursing, against the one who had spoken well. I have touched on this above. But Tortus has some rags here, taken from Pacian, Cyril and Augustine, so worn out that without them the Papists' book would not exist. What do they say? The name "Catholic" is an honourable one. Who denies it? Who would not say all good things about it? For one may not think highly of it, if he rightly thinks about the Creed. But "the King in his Apology has given this name to the Papists." What if he has given it? Be of good cheer! He did not say it seriously; no one understood it seriously; nor did you yourself: you could not, since you have read in many places that you, and "Papists," and "Papist-worshippers," are called in the same way, yet far more often, many times, so often, even more often than "Catholics." Nevertheless he did not always speak so, lest he stir up all your bile; he sometimes refrained. Yet it was not irony, but rather a kindly pleasantry.

units.la: Ita enim fieri amat, qui decoxit paternam rem, de stemmate tamen patrio blanditur sibi & titulo generis; Generosus audire vult; nisi audiat, non libenter auscultat. Dicam ergo Generosum hunc, etsi degenerem, vt aures arrigat: dicam & Saracenum, (vt ipse se diu iam nuncupauit) qui verò Agarenus, quo vtar æquiore: & cum B. Paulo, Festum Optimum, qui tamen vix bonum; & vos Catholicos, qui tamen nihil minùs. Etiam, si Matthæus cognomen suum illibenter audiat, Tortum se dici ægrè ferat, faciam illi hanc gratiam, vt Atatthæum, non Tortum sed Deflexum, illum nominem. Ad hoc exemplum delinire vos eo verbo voluit, nec quomodo appellandi estis, sed quomodo appellari gaudetis, Catholici vocabulo, paululum permulcere.
units.tr: For this is how one who has squandered his paternal estate likes to be treated: he flatters himself with his father's lineage and his family title; he wants to be called "well-born," and unless he hears it, he does not willingly listen. So I shall call this man "well-born," though a degenerate one, so as to prick up his ears; I shall also call him a "Saracen" (as he himself has long since styled himself), though I would rather use "Hagarene"; and with blessed Paul, "Festus the Most Excellent," though he is scarcely good; and you "Catholics," though you are nothing less. Even if Matthew unwillingly hears his own surname and is vexed to be called "Tortus," I shall do him this favour, and name him not "Tortus" but "Atatthaeus," that is, "the Crooked." By this example he wished to soothe you with that word, and to coax you a little with the name Catholic: not how you ought to be called, but how you delight to be called.

units.la: Quodsi incidisset in alium quenquam ⌣Matthæum præterquam qui Tortus esset, aliam credo gratiam retulisset. Prima enim eius gratia, mendacium prodigiosum. Sedet enim hic in Telonio suo mendaciorum Matthæus; verba numerat; tertio quoque verbo Catholicos se dici legit. ⌣Admone verò oculos Lector, quod te paulò ante Matthæus voluit; Ter mille ibi verba, per Sexaginta penè paginas reperies, nec vel semel in illis Catholici nomen. Paginæ sunt in toto centum octodecim; de illis centum sunt, nec vsquam in eis vox illa Catholici. Multo verò sæpiùs Tortum hic mentientem legas, nec tertio quoque verbo, mentientem tamen. Vide ergo quàm Catholicè mendax. Dignum verò hoc, quo claudat extremum mendaciorum agmen: Extremum enim est vtroque sensu, vtraque vocis vi. Secunda autem gratia, maledictum plus quàm barbarum. Nam neque Barbari hanc vicem referunt, vt qui cómiter appellet, maledico dente mordeant. Non est Catholicus, aduersum quos scribit, à quorum communione se alienum profitetur. Ille verò nec aduersum vos scribit, quâ Catholicam vilam veritatem[?]
units.tr: But if he had lit upon any other Matthew than one who was Tortus, I believe he would have got a different favour. For his first favour is a prodigious lie. For here Matthew sits at his toll-booth of lies; he counts words; he reads that you are called Catholics "every third word." But, reader, direct your eyes, as Matthew himself just now wished you to do: you will find there about three thousand words, across nearly sixty pages, and not once in them the name "Catholic." The pages in all are one hundred and eighteen; of these, one hundred are concerned with the matter, and nowhere in them does the word "Catholic" appear. You will read, however, much more often that Tortus here is lying, and not "every third word," yet lying nonetheless. See therefore how Catholically he lies! It is worthy of this, that he should close the final column of his lies: "final" indeed in both senses, by the full force of the word. His second favour is a curse more than barbarous. For not even Barbarians return such a turn, that when they are courteously addressed they bite with a venomous tooth. "He is not Catholic," against whom he writes, from whose communion he professes himself estranged. But he does not write against you in that he professes or declares himself estranged from your communion, unless for as long as you return to that primitive Catholic [Church]...

units.la: rem tem tenetis ; nec alienum se à communione vestrâ, vel profitetur, vel protestatur, nisi tantisper dum ad Catholicam illam Primitivam redeatis. Nobiscum verò, de Orthodoxi nomine, litem movere si vultis ; de Catholici non potestis ; de cuius & re & voce credimus ut vos, etiam melius quàm vos. Vos enim cesisistis ipsi de Catholica nomine, cùm nuper Romanam ei infoeliciter adieciistis: & Catholicam, (id est, totius Orbis) ad Romanam, (id est, Unius urbis) redegistis: Catholicam, id est, Orbe toto diffusam, & Romanam, quae tamen Orbis totius una tantùm urbs est. Catholica Romana, noua vox: tantùndem autem valet, ac Catholica non Catholica, Romana non Romana, Catholica non est; ut vos iam (si ita loqui fas, & id vocis natura ferat) Catapolici potiùs quàm Catholici dicendi sitis.
units.tr: ...the thing you hold; nor does he profess or protest himself estranged from your communion, except for the time being, until you return to that Catholic and primitive one. But if you wish to start a quarrel with us over the name "Orthodox," you cannot over the name "Catholic"; for we believe concerning both its reality and its word that we have it as you do, and even better than you. For you yourselves have yielded the name "Catholic," since you have lately unhappily added "Roman" to it: and you have reduced "Catholic" (that is, of the whole world) to "Roman" (that is, of one city only): "Catholic," that is, spread through the whole world, and "Roman," which is nevertheless only one city of the whole world. "Catholic Roman" is a new phrase: and it amounts to the same as "Catholic not Catholic," "Roman not Roman," "Catholic is not." So that you should now (if it is lawful to speak so, and the nature of the word allows it) be called Catapolics rather than Catholics.

units.la: Enimuerò quòd ita Catholicae Romanam addidistis (dixi iam) perinde est, ac si Catholicam aliam agnoscerêtis, non Romanam. Distinctionis id gratiâ factum est: distinguitis eâ voce vestrâ, ab eâ quae Catholica est, Romana non est. Alioqui quid opus, quid attinebat, si unâ modò Catholica sit, commissuram hanc rudem & nouam, ei assuere? Vos ergo sitis de Catholicâ Romanâ vestrâ, quae extra Symbolum est: Nos de illâ quam credimus, quae merè Catholica est nec ad Romam restricta, qualis in Symbolo. Etiam quae Orthodoxa quoque est; quae non adorat, vel colit omnem similitudinem: quae non adorat quod nescit: quae ex Christi Calice bibere iubet omnes: quae orat spiritu, orat & mente non minùs: quae, in quos non credit non invocat: in quâ, Caput fidei Christus, Vicarius eius Spiritus Sanctus: De hac nos & sumus, & esse profitemur. Vos verò, cùm multa apud vos reliqua sint adhuc de Catholicâ fidei dogmatibus, quanquam nonnihil fermentata, membra quidem Catholicae, etsi non sana membra, dicere sustinemus. Quando verò regulam illam nondum didicistis [Inter bonos bene agier:] quando, dicat vobis bene quis, dicat male, par gratia est; quando, quae humanitate solâ, necessitate nullâ indulsit vobis Rex, aliorsum accipitis, atq; in prauum sensum detorquetis: quid restat, nisi ut dehinc iam Catholicos vos nemo dicat, nisi ipsi, vos? Quod quidem sedulò facturum se deinceps, sanctissimè in se suscepit Rex Serenissimus. Liberam enim ex eo vocem emisit palàm & publicè, multis, méque ipso cum multis audiente, honorem se hunc nemini dehinc Torto, vel Torti similis habiturum, vt Catholici nomine dignetur; postquam morem hunc vestrum tam Barbarum cognouit, qui clementer vobis dicunt, in eos inclementer conuitiis regerendi; nec perdet vlteriùs iam vocem tam bonam apud homines non bonos: malè eam locauit apud malos; cùm tam inurbani estis, pœnitet locâsse; parciùs pòst adhibebit, imò ne adhibebit quidem. Eritis per Eum quod estis, & quæ non vultis, (sed quæ debetis tamen) in posterum à Rege semper audietis.
units.tr: Indeed, when you added "Romana" to "Catholica" in this way (as I have already said), it is just as if you acknowledged a different Catholic Church, not the Roman one. You did it for the sake of distinction: by your word you distinguish what is Roman from what is Catholic, and what is Roman is not Catholic. Otherwise, why would you need to stitch this crude and new patch onto the one word "Catholic", if there were only one Catholic Church? So let you have your "Roman Catholic" church, which lies outside the Creed. We speak of the church we believe in, which is simply Catholic and not restricted to Rome, such as the one in the Creed. It is also Orthodox: it does not worship or honour any image; it does not worship what it does not know; it bids all to drink from the cup of Christ; it prays in spirit and prays with the mind no less; it does not invoke those in whom it does not believe; in it Christ is the head of the faith and the Holy Spirit is his Vicar. Of this church we are and profess ourselves to be members. As for you, since many remnants of the Catholic doctrines of faith still remain among you, though somewhat leavened, we are willing to call you members of the Catholic Church, though not sound members. But since you have not yet learned that rule, "Good men should do well among good men," and since, whether someone speaks well of you or ill, it makes no difference to you; and since you take in a wrong sense, and twist to a bad meaning, what the King has granted you out of mere kindness and no necessity, what remains but that from now on no one should call you Catholics, except yourselves? This the most serene King has solemnly undertaken to do diligently from now on. For he has openly and publicly declared, with many people and myself among them listening, that he will never again grant this honour, to be called Catholic, to anyone who is a Torto or like Torto, since he has come to know your custom, so barbarous that you return abuse for courtesy, and insults for kindness. He will no longer waste that good word on people who are not good; he has spent it badly on the bad, and since you are so uncivil, he regrets having spent it; from now on he will use it more sparingly, or rather, he will not use it at all. You will be by him what you are, and you will always hear from the King what you do not wish to hear, but what you nevertheless ought to hear.
